0.title: Luke: The Gospel of the Saviour of the World
0.overview:
Luke is the longest book in the New Testament. It is also, in the judgment of many, the most beautiful — a Gospel written by a physician who was also a literary artist, a historian who was also a theologian, a Gentile who understood the Jewish roots of everything he was describing better than most of his contemporaries. When Luke sets out to write an orderly account of the things that have been accomplished among us, he produces something that is at once a careful historical document, a theological masterpiece, and a pastoral letter addressed to a world hungry for good news.

The author never names himself, but the ancient tradition is unanimous: this is Luke, the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14), the companion of Paul (2 Timothy 4:11; Philemon 24), the man who stayed with Paul when everyone else had left. He was almost certainly a Gentile — the only Gentile author in the New Testament — and this shapes everything he writes. He sees in Jesus the fulfilment not just of Israel's hopes but of the deepest longings of the whole human race. His Gospel is addressed to Theophilus, probably a Roman official of some standing, and through him to the entire Gentile world. Luke wants the world to know that what happened in Judea was not a local religious event. It was the turning point of all of history.

Luke writes in two volumes: the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles. Together they tell the story of what Jesus began to do (the Gospel) and what he continued to do through his Spirit in the church (Acts). The Gospel ends where Acts begins — with the ascension and the promise of the Spirit. This two-volume structure matters for reading Luke: his Gospel is not a self-contained biography but the first act of a larger drama, the story of how the good news of the kingdom moved from a manger in Bethlehem to the centre of the Roman world. The Gospel is movement toward Jerusalem; Acts is movement from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.

Luke's great themes are the themes of the kingdom come in unexpected ways. He gives more space than any other evangelist to women, to the poor, to Samaritans, to Gentiles, to tax collectors and sinners — the people whom polite religious society had written off as beyond the reach of God's grace. He is the Gospel of the outsider welcomed in. He shows Jesus praying at every major turning point of his ministry. He is the Gospel of the Holy Spirit, who appears from the first chapter to the last. And above all, he is the Gospel of joy, because at the centre of everything is the announcement that the Saviour has come, and his name is Jesus.

1.title: The Announcement of the King
1.overview:
Chapter 1 of Luke is one of the most carefully constructed passages in all of Scripture. Before a single miracle is performed, before a single sermon is preached, before Jesus has spoken a word in public — Luke gives us seven scenes of annunciation, visitation, and praise that set the theological coordinates for everything that follows. He is telling us, from the very first verse, what kind of Gospel this is going to be: historically grounded, theologically rich, and written to produce the certainty of faith in a world that desperately needs it.

The chapter opens with a prologue that is unlike anything else in the New Testament — a formal literary preface, modelled on the prefaces of great Hellenistic historians like Thucydides and Polybius, establishing Luke's credentials as a careful historian and his purpose as a pastoral one. He has investigated everything carefully; he writes in orderly sequence; his goal is that Theophilus may have certainty about the things he has been taught. This is not mythology. This is history — specific, datable, verifiable history — and Luke wants his reader to know it.

From the prologue, the chapter moves into a world saturated with Old Testament atmosphere. Zechariah and Elizabeth are introduced in language that echoes Abraham and Sarah; the angel Gabriel appears as he did to Daniel; Mary's Magnificat is the New Testament's Psalter. Luke is making the claim that the long story of Israel — the story of promise and longing and waiting — has reached its culmination. The God who made promises in Eden, who called Abraham, who spoke through the prophets, is now fulfilling everything he said. The silence of four hundred years is over. The angel's voice breaks into a world that thought God had gone quiet, and nothing will ever be the same.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The prologue of Luke is the one place in the Gospels where the author steps out before the story begins and speaks in his own voice about how he wrote it. What he says in four verses establishes the whole intellectual and pastoral framework of what follows. He is writing history — but history in the service of faith. He has predecessors; he has done his own research; he has a named recipient; and he has a stated goal.

The word in v. 1 for what the many compiled is diēgēsis, a narrative that leads a reader through events from end to end. The “orderly” of v. 3 is a different word, kathexēs, meaning in sequence, each thing in its proper place. That need not mean a rigid diary order; Luke sometimes gathers material by theme rather than by date. What he promises is an account with a shape you can follow and trust.

The “many” who had already attempted this were not writing fraudulently, and Luke names their work without a sneer. But he has something to add: his own careful investigation, traced back to the source, from the eyewitnesses themselves. The word in v. 2 is autoptes — those who saw with their own eyes. Luke's history is not rumour at several removes. It is testimony from the people who were there.

Theophilus is greeted as “most excellent,” a formal Roman honorific used of senior officials (cf. Acts 23:26; 24:3; 26:25). He may be a patron who funded the research, an official investigating the Christian movement, or a recent convert who needs the foundations confirmed. The goal Luke states in v. 4 is asphaleia — the firm ground that comes of knowing that what you believe is true. For Luke, faith is grounded in history or it is not Christian faith at all.

Which raises the question a thoughtful reader feels at once: if Luke sifted sources like any careful historian, in what sense is this God's word rather than Luke's book? Scripture's answer is that it is both. The same Spirit who fills Elizabeth and Zechariah in this chapter was at work in the physician who went looking for people who had been there — guiding the questions, the witnesses, the material kept and the order set (cf. 2 Tim. 3:16; 2 Pet. 1:21). God did not bypass Luke's mind; he used it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The prologue's insistence on eyewitness testimony and careful investigation is the New Testament's answer to every form of Christianity that treats the historical details of the gospel as negotiable. Luke does not begin with timeless spiritual principles. He begins with what happened. The things accomplished among us are events — specific, dateable, observable events — and his first act as a historian is to establish their factual grounding.

This rules out from the start any reading of the Gospel as mythology, allegory or spiritual symbol. The incarnation, the miracles, the death, the resurrection: these are things that took place, in a named reign, in a known country, in front of people who could be questioned about them.

The goal of certainty (asphaleia) is the pastoral heart of the prologue. Luke is not writing to entertain, nor primarily to persuade the uncommitted. He is writing to confirm the faith of someone already taught the Christian story who needs to know that what he has been taught is true. That is the function of historically grounded preaching in every generation — not to introduce people to a religious experience but to settle them in a historical faith.
verseByVerse.examples:
The prologue models what responsible handling of the gospel looks like for any teacher or preacher: go back to the sources, investigate carefully, present the findings in order, and do it all in the service of the hearer's certainty. The person in the pew wrestling with doubt does not need vague spiritual reassurance. He needs the kind of careful, ordered account Luke is about to provide.

The best pastoral response to doubt is rarely “just trust.” It is nearer to “let me show you why trust is reasonable” — which is precisely what the next twenty-three chapters do.

And asphaleia is a gift the gospel gives to those who receive it on its own terms: not the brittle certainty of someone who has never been challenged, but the settled certainty of someone who has looked at the evidence and found it solid. Theophilus is meant to close this Gospel knowing not only that Jesus is Lord but why that claim can be trusted — and equipped to give the reason to anybody who asks.

verseByVerse.quote: Inasmuch as many have undertaken to compile a narrative of the things that have been accomplished among us, just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word have delivered them to us,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many have undertaken to compile an account of the things that have been fulfilled among us, just as they were handed down to us by those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word.

Meaning first. Luke opens with one long, balanced sentence (vv. 1–4) in polished literary Greek, like the prefaces of the Greek historians: what follows is researched, reliable history. From verse 5 his style turns to the flavour of the Greek Old Testament, because this story belongs to the Bible’s story. The chapter is the morning of the gospel: God breaks four hundred years of silence, an old priest and a young virgin receive impossible promises, two mothers meet, and two songs are sung that the church has never stopped singing. Its theme is Zechariah’s own name, the LORD remembers, and at its centre is the Son of the Most High, conceived by the Holy Spirit.

Who was Luke? The early church unanimously named Luke, the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14), as the author of this Gospel and of Acts, which is its second volume (Acts 1:1). He was a companion of Paul; in Acts, he slips into “we” when he was present (Acts 16:10–17; 20:5–28:16). He was probably a Gentile (Colossians 4:10–14 lists him apart from the men of the circumcision), and if so he is the only Gentile author in the New Testament. His two books make up over a quarter of the New Testament.

He opens with paperwork. Luke does not open with a vision, a genealogy or a voice from heaven. Picture the desk: several accounts of Jesus stacked in front of him, a list of people who were there, and a Gentile physician checking one against the other. That is where the third Gospel begins: not in a trance, but in an inquiry. Luke is about to tell a story with an angel in it. He begins by saying where he got it.

Inasmuch as many have undertaken to compile a narrative. Others had already written accounts of Jesus. What the many produced is a narrative: not a scrapbook of sayings but an account that carries a reader from one end of the events to the other. Luke does not attack the others; he mentions their work without a sneer. A man forging a religion suppresses the rival accounts. A man reporting an event welcomes them, because more witnesses make a case stronger, not weaker.

Who were the many who had written before Luke? Most likely they included Mark, probably the earliest Gospel, and other written and oral accounts from the eyewitnesses. Luke shares much material with Mark and Matthew, and has much that is found only in his Gospel, such as the birth of John, the shepherds, the Good Samaritan and the prodigal son. He was not an eyewitness himself, but he says he investigated everything carefully from those who were (v. 2).

Of the things that have been accomplished among us. “Accomplished” (peplērophorēmenōn): fulfilled, brought to completion. Luke is not describing incidents that merely happened. He is describing promises that landed. This is a key theme of the whole book: what God promised, he has done, and the risen Christ will say it in the last chapter, that everything written about him in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled (24:44).

Just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses. The apostles and others who had been with Jesus from the start (Acts 1:21–22). The word is autoptai, from autos (self) and a root meaning to see: those who saw it with their own eyes. It belonged to the vocabulary of Greek historical writing. The Gospel rests on eyewitness testimony, not legend.

And ministers of the word. “Ministers” (hypēretai): servants, attendants, the under-rowers of a ship. They did not invent the message; they served it, and spent their lives handing it on. “The word” here is the gospel message, spoken of almost as a person, as though the message itself had a household of servants.

The word they served had a face. Luke names one group with two roles, eyewitnesses and servants of the word, because what they handed on was what they had seen. The message had servants because at its heart stood a person. Luke does not call Jesus the Word, as John does, but his witnesses could have said what John says: that which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we looked upon and have touched with our hands, concerning the word of life (1 John 1:1). The gospel is not an idea about God illustrated by a life. It is a life: a birth, a ministry, a death and an empty tomb. Every promise Luke calls accomplished was accomplished in him, and the servants of the word had watched it happen.

Have delivered them to us. “Delivered” (paredosan): handed down, the technical word for passing on a tradition carefully, the word Paul uses when he says he delivered as of first importance what he also received (1 Corinthians 15:3). Luke places himself in the second generation: he received it from the eyewitnesses. What does that actually mean for us? It means the chain between Jesus and your Bible is short and can be named: the men and women who saw him, then a careful writer who questioned them, then the book in your hands. Paul could tell the Corinthians that most of the five hundred who saw the risen Lord were still alive to be asked (1 Corinthians 15:6).

If Luke did research, how is this God’s word? It is both Luke’s careful work and God’s word, and the one does not crowd out the other. The same Spirit who fills Elizabeth and Zechariah later in this chapter was at work in the physician who went looking for people who had been there, guiding the questions he asked, the witnesses he found, the material he kept and the order he set it in (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21). God did not bypass Luke’s mind. He used it. The research is not a crack in the doctrine of inspiration; it is how, in this case, inspiration went about its work. So you can read Luke with both a historian’s confidence and a worshipper’s reverence.

In a sentence. Luke begins by noting that many had already written accounts of what God had fulfilled, based on what the original eyewitnesses and servants of the word had handed down.

On a Tuesday. Your faith rests on the testimony of eyewitnesses, carefully passed on. It is not a myth or a feeling, and it does not depend on how you feel this morning. When someone at work says the Gospels are legends written long afterwards, you do not need to panic or to bluff. You can say, honestly, that the author tells us he checked his material against the people who were there, and invite them to read him and judge.

For worship. God did not leave his saving acts to rumour. He accomplished them in history, in front of witnesses, and then raised up servants to carry the word and a physician to write it down, so that a reader two thousand years away could hold it in his hands. The Lord of glory submitted his life to the scrutiny of eyewitnesses. He has nothing to hide, and everything to give.
verseByVerse.note: Luke did not claim to be an eyewitness himself; he gathered the testimony of those who were.

verseByVerse.quote: it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
It seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus.

It seemed good to me also. A modest statement of purpose. Luke adds his work to the others. And now he steps forward in the first person, and every phrase is a claim he means to be held to.

Having followed all things closely for some time past. “Followed” (parēkolouthēkoti) is one word in Greek: to follow alongside, to trace a matter back along its course. Luke did research. And “for some time past” is stronger than it sounds: anōthen, from the top, from the source. He has walked up the stream to the spring. He had opportunity: he was in Judea for the two years of Paul’s imprisonment at Caesarea (Acts 24:27), and could have met Mary, James the brother of Jesus (Acts 21:18), and others. The birth narratives may come from Mary herself, who treasured these things and pondered them in her heart (2:19, 51). And he goes back to the very start: not, as Mark does, to a grown man at the Jordan, but to an old couple in the hill country and a girl in Nazareth.

An order that leads to a cross. Luke’s order has a shape, and the shape is Christ’s. The Gospel opens in the temple with a priest who cannot bless the waiting people (1:22), and it closes in the temple with disciples praising God after Jesus has lifted his hands and blessed them (24:50–53). Its long middle is one journey: when the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51). An orderly account of this life cannot help but lead where he himself was going, to a city, a cross and an empty tomb.

To write an orderly account. “Orderly” (kathexēs): in sequence, one thing after another in its proper place, arranged logically. Readers sometimes trip over it when they lay Luke beside Matthew and Mark and find the same episodes in a different order. Luke is not promising a diary timed to the day. He is promising an account with a shape that can be followed: material grouped so that the sense of it comes through, as when he sets the rejection at Nazareth at the head of the ministry because it is the doorway into everything after it (4:16–30). Orderly does not mean chronological to the hour. It means nothing has been thrown in at random.

Most excellent Theophilus. “Theophilus” means friend of God or loved by God. “Most excellent” (kratiste) was a title for Roman officials and people of rank; Luke uses it of Governor Felix and Governor Festus in his second volume (Acts 23:26; 24:3; 26:25). Theophilus was probably a real person of high social standing, perhaps Luke’s patron who paid for the copying and circulation of the book. He was already instructed in the faith (v. 4). Luke could have addressed the longest book in the New Testament to the church at large. He addressed it to one man who needed it, by name.

Does it matter that the Gospels differ in order? No, and seeing why helps you read them well. Ancient writers, like good modern biographers, often arranged material by theme as well as by date, and no one thought that dishonest. Each Gospel writer tells the same Jesus from his own angle, with his own emphases, for his own first readers. Where they differ in order or detail, they are like four honest witnesses describing one event: their differences show they did not copy each other mechanically, and their agreement on everything that matters is all the stronger for it. When you meet a difference, ask what each writer is emphasising. It is usually illuminating.

But was Luke not biased, writing as a believer? Every historian writes from somewhere, and a writer who cares about his subject is not for that reason unreliable. The question is whether he tells you his sources and lets you check him. Luke does: he names rulers, places and dates that could be tested (3:1–2), and archaeology has repeatedly confirmed the titles and details of his second volume. And notice what he does not hide: the doubt of a priest (v. 20), the slowness of the disciples, the denial of Peter (22:54–62). A man inventing heroes does not write like that. Bias would have made him tidy. Luke was simply faithful.

In a sentence. Having researched everything carefully from the beginning, Luke decided to write an ordered account for Theophilus, a man of rank.

On a Tuesday. Christian faith welcomes investigation. Don’t be afraid to study the evidence for what you believe. Read a Gospel straight through in a sitting, as Theophilus would have heard it, and notice how it hangs together. And if you have a friend who needs it, remember that God’s largest works often come with one person’s name at the top: the letter, the book, the conversation you give to one particular person may be the thing God uses.

For worship. The God who could have written the gospel across the sky chose to have it gathered by a careful doctor, interview by interview. The Son who was before all things consented to have a beginning that could be traced: a mother who could be asked, a village that could be visited, a road whose stages could be set in order. He is not a timeless idea hovering over history. He walked through it, step by step, toward Jerusalem, and he knows each friend of God by name.
verseByVerse.note: Theophilus means “friend of God.” “Most excellent” was a title used for Roman officials, which suggests a man of rank.

verseByVerse.quote: that you may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That you may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught.

That you may have certainty. The word is asphaleia: firmness, security, reliability. It is built from a (not) and sphallō (to trip, to make to stumble): literally, un-trippability. Greek writers used it of a bolted door or ground that will not give way underfoot, and it comes last in the Greek sentence, for emphasis. Luke did not write so that Theophilus would feel warmer about Jesus. He wrote so that when Theophilus put his weight down, the floor would hold. Faith is not a leap in the dark; it rests on reliable facts.

Concerning the things you have been taught. “Taught” (katēchēthēs), from which comes catechism: instructed by word of mouth. Theophilus had been instructed in the Christian faith, perhaps as a new believer or an enquirer. Theophilus has already been instructed, and Luke thinks he needs a book anyway. That cuts across a habit common in the church, which treats evidence as entry-level material a believer graduates from. The longest book in the New Testament was written for a Christian’s certainty.

Know for certain who he is. Luke uses the matching adverb, asphalōs, at the climax of the first Christian sermon: let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified (Acts 2:36). That is the certainty Luke’s two volumes exist to give, and it is first the risen Lord’s own gift. When the disciples met him, frightened and doubting, he did not tell them to believe harder. He said: see my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see (24:39). He ate fish in front of them (24:42–43) and opened the Scriptures to them. Luke says he presented himself alive by many proofs (Acts 1:3). Christ himself handed over the evidence, and Luke is only carrying it on.

A test worth running. Take the thing you believe most firmly about Christ, and ask: how do I know that? If the honest answer is “because I have always been told so”, that is precisely where Theophilus was, and God thought it worth a whole Gospel to move him past it. A faith never examined is not necessarily a false faith. It is an untested one, and everything gets tested eventually.

Afraid to look. Some readers fear examining what they believe in case it does not survive. Luke is not nervous. A man who had assembled a beautiful legend would not begin by telling you he checked it against the people who were there (John 20:31; 1 Peter 3:15). Certainty, in this book, is not a temperament or the confidence of someone who has never doubted. It is the settledness of a man who went and looked.

Is certainty the same as assurance of salvation? They are related but not identical. Luke’s certainty is first about the facts: that these things really happened and mean what the apostles said they mean. Assurance of salvation is a believer’s confidence that he himself is in Christ. The first feeds the second. The Westminster Confession says assurance rests on the truth of God’s promises, on the inward evidence of grace, and on the witness of the Spirit (Westminster 18.2). The promises come first, and they are only as solid as the history behind them. So when your assurance wavers, do not begin by examining your feelings. Begin where Luke begins: with what God has done in Christ.

What if I still have doubts after reading? Doubt is not the same as unbelief, and a doubting believer is still a believer. Bring the doubt into the open: name it, ask a pastor or a mature friend, read what thoughtful Christians have written on the question. Keep reading the Gospels themselves, because Christ is his own best evidence. And keep using the means of grace, the word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, while the question is being answered. Many believers find that a doubt honestly faced leaves their faith firmer than it was before.

In a sentence. Luke wrote so that Theophilus could be sure of the truth of what he had been taught.

On a Tuesday. If your faith feels uncertain, read the Gospels. God gave them to make you sure. Pick one question you have never actually answered for yourself, perhaps how you know Jesus rose, and spend this week looking into it. Floors are tested by putting your weight on them.

For worship. God is not content that his children should merely hope. He wants them to stand on ground that will not give way, and so he gave us not a mood but a record, written by a man who checked his sources, about a Saviour who really lived, really died and really rose. Our certainty rests on him, and he does not trip.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–25 — Birth of John the Baptist Foretold
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
With v. 5 Luke moves from the historian's prologue to the historian's narrative, and the contrast could hardly be sharper. From a formal Hellenistic preface he plunges into a world saturated with the Old Testament. Zechariah is a priest; Elizabeth is a daughter of Aaron; and they are described in language almost identical to the description of Abraham and Sarah — both righteous, both blameless, and she barren.

A reader steeped in the Hebrew Scriptures recognises the pattern at once. God is about to do something only God can do. He did it with Sarah, with Rebekah, with Rachel, with Hannah. Now he does it a last time, because the child born of this barren womb will prepare the way for the one who needs no human preparation to be born.

The setting of the announcement is itself a sermon. Zechariah is at work, in his division's week of service, chosen by lot for the incense offering — the one duty most priests never received and no priest received twice (vv. 8-10). The whole multitude is praying outside at the hour of incense. God breaks four hundred years of silence not at a moment of revival but in the middle of an ordinary rota.

Gabriel has not appeared in Scripture since the book of Daniel, and the detail is deliberate. Daniel received angelic revelation about the end of the exile and the coming of an Anointed One; Gabriel's reappearance signals that what Daniel waited for is arriving.

The announcement about John is a mosaic of Old Testament promise: the prohibition on wine and strong drink (echoing the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6 and the birth of Samson), the filling with the Spirit from the womb (echoing Jer. 1:5 and Isa. 49:1), and the ministry in the spirit and power of Elijah (fulfilling Mal. 4:5-6). Every detail is a fulfilment of something Israel had been promised and had been waiting for.

Zechariah's response is entirely understandable and entirely insufficient. He asks how he can know — and then supplies his evidence, which is his age. He is asking for proof while the proof stands in front of him. The muteness that follows is as much mercy as discipline: nine months in which he can speak nothing except what God has spoken, and a limit written into the sentence (“until the day that these things take place”).

The chapter does not hurry past what that cost him publicly. The crowd waiting outside expected the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26 and did not receive it; a man came out of the Holy Place making signs, and there was no benediction that day (vv. 21-23). And he stayed to the end of his rota, serving out his days in silence.

Elizabeth's response, by contrast, is hidden joy. Her first recorded words are not about the child but about God: the Lord has done this for me, and he has looked on me to take away my reproach among people. She understands what Zechariah will need months to grasp — that this is grace, and grace needs no explanation.
verseByVerse.theology:
The barrenness of Elizabeth, like that of Sarah and Hannah before her, is the Old Testament's persistent symbol of human inability and divine sufficiency. The child of promise is always the child who could not have been born by human power alone. That is not incidental; it is the pattern of grace. God works precisely where human capacity has run out.

The child born to a barren womb, the nation born out of an enslaved people, the Messiah born of a virgin — the pattern holds in every case, and the point is the same in every case: salvation is of the LORD, and not of man.

Gabriel's description of John's ministry — that he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, and go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah — identifies John as the fulfilment of Malachi 4:5-6, the last prophecy of the Old Testament. Israel's canonical story ends with the promise of Elijah. It begins again here, with his arrival.

And the four hundred years of silence end not with a king or an army but with a priest's speechless vision in the temple. God's timing is consistently unexpected, and his entry points are consistently the last places power would have chosen.
verseByVerse.examples:
Zechariah's request for a sign is the response of a man whose theology was correct and whose faith, in the moment, was smaller than his knowledge. He knew the God who opens barren wombs. He had read the stories and offered the prayers. But when the answer stood in front of him he asked for evidence.

The gap between what we confess and what we trust in the moment is one of the most honest things the Bible shows about the life of faith. And Gabriel's response is not contempt but the gift of silence: a season of enforced dependence on what God has said rather than on what Zechariah can say.

Elizabeth's instinct to remain in seclusion for five months (v. 24) is the instinct of someone who knows that a gift this size needs to be received before it is announced. A soul that has received extraordinary grace sometimes needs to be quiet with it before it can speak of it.

The rush to publicise every experience of God's goodness can short-circuit the deeper work the grace was given to do. Elizabeth sits with the miracle, lets it form her, and waits.

verseByVerse.quote: In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. And he had a wife from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. And they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and statutes of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. He had a wife from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. They were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and statutes of the Lord.

The style changes. The polished Greek of the prologue stops, and the next sentence could have come out of the book of Judges: in the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest. From here to the end of chapter 2 Luke writes a Greek full of Hebrew idiom, because the story is walking back into the world of the Old Testament: a temple, a priest, a barren wife and an angel. The story of Jesus continues the story of Israel. The Old Testament ended with a promise of Elijah coming (Malachi 4:5–6); this Gospel begins with the birth of the one who comes in Elijah’s spirit (v. 17).

In the days of Herod, king of Judea. Herod the Great ruled the Jewish land as Rome’s client king from 37 to 4 BC. He was an Idumean (Edomite), not a son of David, a builder of vast ambition (the temple included), and a paranoid tyrant who murdered his wife and three of his sons. Luke names that throne in his first narrative sentence so that nobody mistakes what kind of night it was when the light came. Since Herod died in 4 BC, Jesus was born before then, probably around 6–5 BC (our calendar, calculated in the sixth century, is a few years out).

Two kings in one chapter. Luke’s first sentence names a king, and before the chapter is out an angel names another. Herod held the throne of Judea by Rome’s favour, without a drop of David’s blood. To Mary, Gabriel will say of her son: the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David, and of his kingdom there will be no end (vv. 32–33). Luke sets them side by side on purpose. One is the king Israel had, the other the King God had promised. Herod built a temple of white stone to make his name great; the true King will be carried into that temple as a baby in his mother’s arms (2:22–38), and will grow up to call it his Father’s house (2:49). Herod’s kingdom was divided among his sons as soon as he died. The kingdom of David’s son has no end.

A priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. “Zechariah” means the LORD remembers, which is what this chapter is about (vv. 54, 72). There were several thousand priests in Jesus’ day (one careful estimate puts it at about 7,000, with nearly 10,000 Levites besides), organised since David’s time into twenty-four divisions; Abijah’s was the eighth (1 Chronicles 24:1–19). Each division served in the temple for a week, twice a year, and all served at the great feasts.

And he had a wife from the daughters of Aaron. Elizabeth was also of priestly descent, priestly on both sides, which was considered a special blessing. “Elizabeth” (Elisheba) means my God is an oath, or my God is fullness. Aaron’s wife had the same name (Exodus 6:23). Put the two names together and you have the chapter in miniature: the LORD remembers, and my God has sworn an oath. Zechariah will sing exactly that, the oath that he swore to our father Abraham (v. 73).

Righteous before God, walking blamelessly. “Before God”: not just in the eyes of men. Blameless? Luke has read the same Scriptures that say none is righteous, no, not one (Psalm 14:3; Romans 3:10–12). He is not contradicting them. This is covenant language, the verdict given of Noah (Genesis 6:9) and of Job (Job 1:1). Not sinless; Zechariah will doubt (v. 20). It means that when they sinned they brought the sacrifice God had appointed, and that there was nothing in their lives a neighbour could point at and say: there is where they let God down. It is the description of a life with nothing hidden in it, and it is one of the kindest words in the Bible, because it is a standard an ordinary believer can actually be held to.

Were they saved by their blamelessness? No. Their righteousness before God was the righteousness of faith, the same by which Abraham believed the LORD and it was counted to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6). They looked forward to the promised redemption, offered the sacrifices that pointed to it, and lived out their trust in obedience. Their blameless walk was the fruit of grace, not the price of it. That is why the word is a comfort and not a threat: God does not require you to be sinless to be called righteous. He counts you righteous in Christ, and then works in you a life that can, by his grace, be honestly called blameless.

In a sentence. In the time of Herod the Great, a godly, faithful priest named Zechariah and his wife Elizabeth, both of priestly descent, lived blamelessly before God.

On a Tuesday. Faithful, ordinary obedience over many years, unnoticed by the world, is precious to God. He is about to act through people like this. Ask whether there is anything in your life a neighbour could point at and say: there is where he lets God down. Not whether you are sinless, but whether there is something hidden that you are refusing to bring to the cross. Bring it, and walk on in the open.

For worship. While Herod built his palaces in blood, God was watching an old couple in the hill country, and he wrote their names in his book as righteous. The LORD remembers. He has always kept a people for himself in the darkest reign, and he was about to keep the oath he had sworn to Abraham, through these two, in this generation, under this king. No tyrant’s throne can hide his faithful ones from his eyes.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great ruled Judea for Rome until 4 BC. The priests were organised in twenty-four divisions, each serving in the temple for a week at a time; Abijah’s was the eighth.

verseByVerse.quote: But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were advanced in years.

But they had no child. One word, and the whole picture inverts. In Israel, children were seen as God’s blessing (Psalm 127:3–5), and childlessness was often a cause of grief and social shame (v. 25), sometimes thought to be a sign of God’s displeasure. For this godly couple, it was a painful mystery.

Stage it properly. They are old now. There is a room in that house that was going to be for a child. There were the early years of quiet confidence, then the years of remedies and of prayers with a shape to them, then the year, and every couple who has walked this road can name it, when they stopped saying when and started saying if, and then stopped saying anything at all. Elizabeth has held other people’s babies for forty years and handed them back. And in first-century Judea childlessness was a public verdict as well as a private grief: a barren woman walked through the market under a rumour that God had looked at her and turned away. Elizabeth’s own word for it, when it is lifted, is oneidos: disgrace, the thing people say about you (v. 25).

Because Elizabeth was barren. The Bible’s great births often begin with barrenness: Sarah (Genesis 18), Rebekah (Genesis 25:21), Rachel (Genesis 30:1, 22), Samson’s mother, the unnamed wife of Manoah (Judges 13), and Hannah (1 Samuel 1). The Old Testament keeps returning to the same closed door, and it is never an accident of the plot. In each case, God opened the womb to give a child who would play a key part in his purposes, making sure that when the child arrived nobody could mistake where he came from. And both were advanced in years, literally advanced in their days, beyond the age of having children (v. 18), as Abraham and Sarah were (Genesis 18:11). Humanly, it was impossible.

From a barren womb to a virgin’s. The line of closed wombs is not a string of separate miracles. It is a road, and this verse stands near its end. Six months later the same angel will go to a girl in Nazareth with a greater impossibility, and he will point her to this very house: your relative Elizabeth in her old age has also conceived a son (v. 36). Every barren womb God opened prepared the way for the day when a child would come who had no human father at all, because he was not merely a gift to the line of Adam but God’s own Son entering it. Sarah’s son carried the promise. Mary’s Son is the promise. Elizabeth stands at the hinge between them, the last of the barren mothers and the sign given to the virgin.

Said carefully. This has to be said carefully, because a childless reader is holding this page. Elizabeth conceived, and so did Hannah and Sarah. Thousands of women just as righteous, who prayed just as long, did not. It would be a cruelty to read this verse as a pattern with your name in it: hold on faithfully and the answer will come. Some of the most God-fearing people who ever lived went to their graves without the thing they had asked for every day.

The circumstance is not the verdict. What the verse does say is this. The silence of God is not the absence of God. Luke has just recorded that these two were righteous before God, which means that whatever the barrenness was, it was not a verdict, and it was not a punishment. The village had read the evidence and got the sentence exactly backwards. And the reason for their waiting was not in them at all: the forerunner of the Messiah could not be born until the Messiah was six months away. They could not have known it. For forty years the reason for their sorrow was a reason that had not happened yet.

So what may a childless couple take from this? Not a promise that you will conceive; God has not made that promise, and anyone who makes it for him is unkind. Take this instead: your childlessness is not God’s verdict on you, and it is not a punishment. He sees the grief, the empty room, the conversations that change direction when you come in. Your life is not second-class in his kingdom; some of the most fruitful servants in Scripture had no children, and our Lord himself had none. You may pray honestly for a child, use wise medical help, consider adoption, and weep. And you may know that the God who held Elizabeth’s sorrow for forty years is holding yours, with purposes that may be stored far ahead of you.

And for those around them? Be careful with your words. Do not ask young couples when they are going to have children. Do not offer formulas or stories of friends who conceived after they relaxed. Remember the childless on Mother’s Day and Father’s Day, and at the dedication of babies. Include them in the life of families in the church, not as spare helpers but as brothers and sisters. And never, by look or word, become the village that passed a sentence on Elizabeth.

In a sentence. Despite their godliness, Zechariah and Elizabeth had no child, because she was barren and they were both old.

On a Tuesday. Faithful people suffer disappointments that make no sense. That does not mean God has forgotten them. Keep trusting. Name the long sorrow you carry, and say aloud to God: this is not your verdict on me, because Christ has borne the verdict. Then bring it to him again today, as Zechariah once did.

For worship. A God who can hold a plan steady through four hundred years of prophetic silence can be trusted with the twenty years you have been waiting. He was not absent from that house in the hill country; he was preparing, in the very place of their grief, the birth of the one who would prepare the way of the Lord. He does not promise every sufferer a Gabriel. He has given something greater: a Son who entered our sorrows himself, and who makes even the barren places bloom in the end.
verseByVerse.note: Barrenness was a deep sorrow and often a social shame. Scripture’s great births often begin with a barren woman.

verseByVerse.quote: Now while he was serving as priest before God when his division was on duty, according to the custom of the priesthood, he was chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense. And the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was serving as priest before God when his division was on duty, according to the custom of the priesthood, he was chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense. And the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense.

He was chosen by lot. There were thousands of priests and exactly one incense altar, and the duties of each day were assigned by lot. The highest honour was to pass alone into the Holy Place and burn incense at the golden altar in front of the veil. The custom was that a man once chosen was taken out of the draw, so that as many as possible might have the day: once in a lifetime, and many never did. This was Zechariah’s once. An old man, at the end of a lifetime of faithful and unremarkable service, drew the lot for the greatest moment his office could ever give him. The lot is not chance: the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD (Proverbs 16:33). God chose this day, this man.

To enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense. The temple here is the sanctuary building itself (naos), which only priests could enter. Incense was offered every morning and evening on the golden altar inside the Holy Place (Exodus 30:7–8). The priest would put fresh incense on the coals, so that the fragrant smoke rose before the curtain that hid the Most Holy Place. Incense was a picture of prayer rising to God: let my prayer be counted as incense before you (Psalm 141:2; Revelation 5:8; 8:3–4).

And the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense. Probably the evening sacrifice, around 3 p.m. Prayer outside, incense inside: the people’s prayers going up to God together. So here is the scene at the moment God breaks four hundred years of silence: a crowd in a courtyard praying, and one old man alone in the smoke, doing what his fathers had done, on the settled understanding that this is what you do and God does not answer out loud any more.

Where God chose to interrupt. Not at a revival meeting, but at the appointed duty, taken in its turn, by a man whose name had come out of a container. Zechariah went to work that morning knowing it was the biggest day of his career and having no idea it was the biggest day in four centuries. The routine is not the opposite of the encounter. In this chapter it is the address.

The curtain he stood before. Zechariah stood alone at the golden altar with one curtain between him and the Most Holy Place, a curtain he would never pass and only the high priest could, once a year, with blood (Hebrews 9:7). Luke will bring us back to that curtain at the end. When Jesus hung on the cross, from the sixth hour to the ninth hour there was darkness, and the curtain of the temple was torn in two (23:44–45). The ninth hour was the afternoon hour of prayer (Acts 3:1), the hour, if this was the evening offering, when the crowd here stood praying outside. Generations of priests had burned incense before that veil, and the people had prayed outside it. What they were waiting for was the death that would tear it.

Does God still direct things through chance? Yes, in the sense that nothing is chance to him. The Westminster Confession says God orders all things, including what seem to us accidents, by his providence (Westminster 5.2). That does not mean we should make decisions by drawing lots or opening the Bible at random; after Pentecost the apostles are never again recorded casting lots, because the Spirit and the Scriptures guide the church. It does mean that the shuffle of your week, the job allocation, the seat on the train, the person next to you at the hospital, is not random. You may walk into it expecting God to be there.

In a sentence. On the once-in-a-lifetime day when Zechariah was chosen by lot to offer incense in the Holy Place, the people were praying outside.

On a Tuesday. Treat your ordinary duties as the place God is most likely to meet you. Go to the shift, the school run, the weekly meeting, the Sunday service, expecting nothing dramatic and everything from God. And pray with God’s people: the crowd in the courtyard was part of the answer.

For worship. Your prayers, offered through Christ our high priest, rise to God like incense. Zechariah stood once in a lifetime before the curtain; our great High Priest has passed through it for ever, and lives always to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25; 10:19–22). The God who guided a lot into an old priest’s hand now draws near to every believer, every day, through his Son. There is no draw to win and no once in a lifetime. The way into the holy place is open.
verseByVerse.note: With so many priests, the honour of offering incense in the holy place came to few, perhaps once in a lifetime. It was offered morning and evening while the people prayed outside.

parallels.desc: let my prayer be counted as incense

verseByVerse.quote: And there appeared to him an angel of the Lord standing on the right side of the altar of incense. And Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There appeared to him an angel of the Lord, standing on the right side of the altar of incense. Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him.

An angel of the Lord. The silence is broken. There had been no prophet in Israel for about four hundred years, since Malachi. Now God speaks again, through an angel. Zechariah was in the middle of a fixed liturgy, in a room he had never stood in before, and when he raised his eyes somebody was there.

Standing on the right side of the altar of incense. The altar of incense stood in the Holy Place, just before the curtain of the Most Holy Place. The right side was the side of favour, and the detail says the visitor was not passing through. He was waiting. Zechariah had been chosen by lot that morning. The messenger had been at that altar by appointment.

And Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him. Fear before divine visitation is a recurring note in Luke (1:29–30, 65; 2:9; 5:8–10; 8:37). It is the right response of sinful creatures to the holy. The angels of popular imagination are decorative and harmless. Again and again an angel who appears to a human being has to begin by saying do not be afraid, and he says it because it is necessary. Isaiah came apart at the seams (Isaiah 6:5). Daniel’s strength drained out of him and he fell on his face (Daniel 10:8–9). John, who had leaned on Jesus’ chest at supper, fell at the feet of the glorified Christ as though dead (Revelation 1:17). These are not nervous men. The reason is not that angels are hostile. It is that a creature made of dust and carrying a conscience cannot meet the unfallen without discovering what he is. Put plainly: in the presence of someone who has never sinned, a sinner suddenly sees his own sin with nothing to hide behind, as Isaiah did when he cried, woe is me, for I am a man of unclean lips (Isaiah 6:5). Fear here is not a failure of faith. It is accurate perception arriving all at once.

The thing the equipment was for. Zechariah has spent his life inside the machinery of holiness: the courses, the lots, the incense, the washings, the curtain, every part of it designed to manage the distance between a holy God and a people who could not survive him unmediated, that is, without a go-between to stand for them and a sacrifice to cover them. Now a messenger from God’s presence stands in the room, and he has come to say that what the machinery was for is on its way. Within the year the forerunner will be born, and behind him the Lord himself, come in a body of flesh (vv. 17, 35). The fear that fell on Zechariah is answered in Luke by Christ. When Peter fell at his knees and said, depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord, Jesus said to him: do not be afraid (5:8–10). The holy one came near so that sinners could stand in his presence and live.

Do angels still appear today? Scripture does not slam the door: some have entertained angels unawares (Hebrews 13:2), and they are sent out to serve those who will inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14). But notice the shape of every appearance in the Bible. Nobody summons one. Nobody has a method. They arrive on God’s errand, say what they were sent to say, and go. And notice what they are for. Not to be looked at, but to carry a message. Since the message of the gospel is now complete and written down, we should not expect angels to bring new revelation, and we should test anyone who claims one has (Galatians 1:8). Angels serve us still, mostly unseen. From the moment Gabriel opens his mouth, he is no longer the interesting thing in the room.

In a sentence. An angel of the Lord appeared beside the altar of incense, and Zechariah was terrified.

On a Tuesday. God often comes when we are faithfully doing our ordinary duties. Be faithful where you are. And let the fear of God back into your worship: not terror of a hostile God, but the awe of a creature before the holy. If church has become comfortable to the point of casual, read Isaiah 6 before Sunday.

For worship. The holiness that undid Zechariah at the incense altar has not grown smaller in two thousand years. The fire is the same fire. What has changed is who stands between it and us. The radiance of God’s glory took the flesh of dust-made men, carried our guilt into the holiest place of all, and came out alive. Now the God before whom Isaiah came apart and John fell as though dead receives sinners and eats with them (15:2). The creature who could not survive his presence is brought into it as a son.
verseByVerse.note: The altar of incense stood just before the curtain of the Most Holy Place.

verseByVerse.quote: But the angel said to him, 'Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the angel said to him: do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John.

Do not be afraid. The first words of God’s messengers to frightened people throughout Luke (1:30; 2:10; 5:10; 8:50; 12:7, 32). The news is good. God does not appear in order to destroy.

For your prayer has been heard. Which prayer? The text never says. Zechariah is an old man. His wife is long past childbearing. Whatever he had once prayed about a son, he had very likely stopped praying it years ago.

Two answers, both true. The first is that the prayers of twenty and thirty and forty years ago were heard when they were prayed. The file was never closed. The answer was scheduled for a date that had nothing to do with Zechariah’s biology and everything to do with a second child six months behind this one. The second is probably nearer. The priest at the incense altar prayed for Israel: for the redemption of Jerusalem, for the coming of the Lord to his temple, for the end of the silence. That is the prayer on his lips when Gabriel arrives. And the answer he is handed is a son, because the son is how the nation gets its answer. He prayed for the redemption of Israel and was told to go home to his wife. Both readings say the same thing about God: he does not lose requests, and when he answers, he often answers on a scale that makes the request look like a rough draft.

The answer behind the answer. John is not the end of the answer. He is its first word. The prayer at the incense altar was for the Lord to come to his people, and Gabriel’s reply is a herald whose whole life will say: he is coming, and he is right behind me. The redemption Zechariah asked for will lie in a manger, and before the year is out the old priest will sing that God has visited and redeemed his people and raised up a horn of salvation in the house of David (vv. 68–69). He asked for the redemption of Israel. God answered with his own Son.

Heard is not the same as granted. Now the harder half, because somebody reading this has a prayer that has gone twenty years without a word. Notice exactly what Gabriel says and does not say. He does not say your prayer has been granted. He says it has been heard. Paul asked three times and was told no, and the no was itself the answer (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). What this verse forbids is the conclusion the silence keeps pressing: that the request fell into a room with nobody in it. It was heard, every time. God has never once not been listening. He has often not yet been speaking.

The setting for the jewel. Had Elizabeth conceived at thirty, the child would have been a comfort to his parents. Because she conceived in old age, barren, the child was a sign to a nation. Those decades of grief were the setting the jewel had to be cut for. That does not explain anybody else’s waiting; most waiting gets no explanation this side of the grave. It is evidence that the category exists.

And you shall call his name John. God names him, not the father. “John” (Yôḥānān) means the LORD has been gracious, or the LORD has shown favour. The name is the message: God is being gracious to his people. The child’s name will be God’s choice, and so will everything else about him.

Should I keep praying for something I have prayed about for years? Yes, unless God has plainly closed the door, as he did for Paul, or the thing itself has become impossible or wrong. Jesus told a parable precisely so that his people would always pray and not lose heart (18:1). Keep praying, but let the prayer grow: bring the request, and also the grief, the questions and your submission to his will, as Jesus did in Gethsemane. Many long prayers end not with the thing asked for but with a heart reshaped to want God more than the thing. Either way, the prayer was heard.

In a sentence. The angel told Zechariah not to fear, for his prayer had been heard: Elizabeth would bear a son, and he was to be called John.

On a Tuesday. God hears prayers you have stopped praying. Never think a prayer offered in faith has been lost. Find the request you quietly gave up on, and bring it back to him today, not demanding an answer but trusting that it has been heard, and that he answers on a scale larger than your asking.

For worship. The LORD is gracious: that is the name of the child, and the name of the God who gave him. He keeps no unopened letters. And beneath every heard prayer lies a deeper hearing. In the days of his flesh the Son offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, and he was heard because of his reverence (Hebrews 5:7). For his sake the Father bends down to the faintest sigh of the least of his people, and the old man’s forgotten prayer and our own half-hearted ones go up to him as incense, perfumed by his Son.
verseByVerse.note: John means “the LORD has been gracious.”

parallels.desc: Sarah will bear you a son

verseByVerse.quote: And you will have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, for he will be great before the Lord. And he must not drink wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother's womb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will have joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, for he will be great before the Lord. He must not drink wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother’s womb.

And you will have joy and gladness. Joy is a theme of Luke’s Gospel from beginning (2:10) to end, when the disciples return to Jerusalem with great joy (24:52). Gladness here is exultation, a joy that cannot keep still.

And many will rejoice at his birth. His birth will matter to the whole people. The joy is not private. Elizabeth’s neighbours will rejoice at the birth (v. 58), but Gabriel says many will, and he is looking well past the village. A childless couple’s sorrow was a household matter. This child’s arrival is a public event.

For he will be great before the Lord. Not great in the world’s eyes: John will be beheaded in Herod’s prison (9:9), and Mark tells us it was at the request of a girl who had danced at a birthday party (Mark 6:21–28). The sentence still stands. Greatness before the Lord is not measured by anything visible. Jesus said no one born of women is greater than John (7:28). But note: of Jesus, the angel will say simply “he will be great” (v. 32), with no qualification. John is great before the Lord; Jesus is the Lord before whom John is great.

And he must not drink wine or strong drink. The rule for a Nazirite, a person set apart to God by a vow (Numbers 6:1–4). Samson and Samuel were Nazirites from birth (Judges 13:4–5; 1 Samuel 1:11). But a Nazirite took the vow himself, or a parent dedicated a child, as Hannah did. John neither takes it nor is given it by Zechariah. God imposes it before the boy exists. The consecration is not the family’s offering to God. It is God’s claim staked on a child not yet conceived.

Does this make total abstinence the higher path? No, and Luke himself blocks that road. A few chapters on, Jesus says that John came eating no bread and drinking no wine and they said he had a demon, and the Son of Man came eating and drinking and they called him a glutton and a drunkard (7:33–34). The same Bible that gives John’s austerity gives Christ at a wedding in Cana where the wine ran out (John 2:1–11). John’s abstinence is a uniform, not a law. It marks him as the wilderness prophet, the man standing outside the system and calling the system to repent. A believer who abstains is free to, and many do for good reasons: their own weakness, a family history, a brother who struggles. A believer who drinks in moderation is not a lesser Christian. Drunkenness is always sin. And anyone using this verse to grade another man’s holiness should notice who the abstainer’s Master turned out to be.

And he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother’s womb. Instead of being filled with wine, he will be filled with the Spirit (compare Ephesians 5:18). From before birth, set apart by God, as Jeremiah was known and consecrated before he was formed (Jeremiah 1:5), and as the Servant was called from the womb (Isaiah 49:1). Luke means John’s equipping for his office rather than a doctrine of infant conversion, and it becomes visible later in this chapter when he leaps in the womb as Mary arrives with the unborn Jesus (v. 41). The Holy Spirit is a major theme of Luke and Acts. What does filled with the Spirit actually mean here? It means that God himself was at work in John from the first, shaping and empowering him for his task, so that the boldness the crowds would later meet at the Jordan was not a strong temperament but God’s gift (compare v. 80).

What does this say about the unborn? An unborn child can be filled with the Spirit. The child in the womb is a person, known and called by God. John was filled with the Spirit before he was born, and in v. 41 he leaps in Elizabeth’s womb at the coming of the Lord. Scripture speaks of the unborn as persons whom God knows and forms (Psalm 139:13–16; Jeremiah 1:5). These verses are not a full argument on their own, but they fit the whole biblical witness that life in the womb is human life, made in God’s image, and so is to be protected. And notice the direction of grace: before John could believe, refuse or want anything at all, God had already begun.

And for parents who have lost a child before birth? God knew that child, formed that child and loved that child, and the child’s life was real and is not lost to him. Grieve it as the death of a person, because it was. Scripture gives good hope for those who die in infancy: David said of his dead baby, I shall go to him (2 Samuel 12:23), and the Reformed confessions teach that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases (Westminster 10.3). Believing parents may rest that child in the hands of a merciful God.

In a sentence. John would bring great joy, be great before the Lord, be set apart like a Nazirite, and be filled with the Holy Spirit even before birth.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the unborn children you know. God knows them and can work in them even now. And measure greatness the way Gabriel did: ask not how visible your life is, but whether it is great before the Lord. A faithful, unseen life is measured in heaven, not on the feed.

For worship. The joy at John’s birth was borrowed light. John himself would say so: the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore this joy of mine is now complete (John 3:29). God filled him, named him and claimed him before he drew breath, and all of it was to make him glad in another. That is the glory of the Son: the greatest man born of women was made for the joy of pointing at him, and he counted it complete.
verseByVerse.note: No wine or strong drink was the rule for a Nazirite, someone set apart to God.

parallels.desc: before you were born I consecrated you

verseByVerse.quote: And he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, and he will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, and he will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared.

And he will turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God. John’s work: repentance, turning back to God (3:3). Notice the direction of the turning. Not to a programme, a party or a temple. To God himself. That is what repentance is, and it is why John’s preaching will sound so much ruder than religion usually does.

And he will go before him. Before whom? Grammatically, before the Lord their God of the previous line. John goes before the Lord God himself, and the one who comes after John is Jesus. Gabriel never says it outright, but the sentence leaves no room for anything less. Malachi had promised a messenger to prepare the way, and then: the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple (Malachi 3:1). Isaiah’s voice in the wilderness prepares the way of the LORD, and makes straight a highway for our God (Isaiah 40:3), and Luke will apply it to John and Jesus (3:4–6). The forerunner’s greatness lies wholly in the one behind him. When John finally stood aside, it was not for a greater prophet. It was for God come in the flesh.

In the spirit and power of Elijah. Not Elijah reincarnated, but with the same Spirit-given power and prophetic boldness. Elijah confronted a wicked king and queen (1 Kings 18–21); John will confront Herod and Herodias (3:19–20).

Was John Elijah or not? Keep Gabriel’s exact wording in mind, because a reader with an open Bible will hit a puzzle here. When the priests came out and asked John point-blank, Are you Elijah?, he answered flatly, I am not (John 1:21). Yet Jesus said of that same man, he is Elijah who is to come (Matthew 11:14). They are not contradicting each other; they are answering two different questions. John denies what his questioners meant: that he was the Tishbite himself, returned in person from heaven. Jesus affirms what Malachi meant: that the promised forerunner had come at last, in the spirit and power of Elijah, exactly as Gabriel says here. The prophecy was never that a man would come back. It was that a ministry would come again: the same blunt voice, the same rough clothing, the same summons to a nation to turn round before the LORD arrives. And it gives no support to reincarnation, which Scripture rules out (Hebrews 9:27).

To turn the hearts of the fathers to the children. Israel had not heard a prophetic word for four hundred years, and the last words in the last book of their Scriptures were from Malachi 4:5–6: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes. And he will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers. The Old Testament closes there, waiting, and Gabriel picks the sentence up.

The kitchen table. Do not hurry past the domestic clause. God announces the greatest turning point in the history of the world, and among the first effects named is that fathers will turn towards their children. True repentance restores broken relationships, especially in families. Where a nation goes cold towards God, the cold shows first at the kitchen table, and where God returns, so does the thaw. A man who has not spoken properly to his son in eleven years and has a hundred good reasons why: Malachi says the coming of the LORD reaches into that, and Gabriel says it has started. Revival that leaves a family exactly as it was is not the revival Malachi promised.

And the disobedient to the wisdom of the just. Turning rebels to the understanding and way of life of the righteous. Repentance is not only feeling sorry; it is a change of mind that becomes a change of path.

To make ready for the Lord a people prepared. The purpose of John’s ministry: a people ready for the Lord when he comes, as Isaiah 40:3 foretold (3:4–6). This has been the job description of every servant of God since. Everything about John, the desert, the voice, the diet, the crowds, exists to get a people ready for somebody else. He is the road, not the city.

What if the relationship cannot be mended? Sometimes the other person refuses, or is dead, or is dangerous. Repentance asks you to do what lies with you (Romans 12:18): drop the grudge before God, confess your own part, make the approach if it is safe and wise, and keep the door open. It does not ask you to put yourself or your children back under abuse, and reconciliation with an abuser needs genuine repentance on his side, proven over time, with wise help. Where the other person will not come, you can still forgive in your heart and leave the matter with God. The turning of hearts begins with yours.

In a sentence. John would turn many in Israel back to God, going before the Lord in Elijah’s spirit and power, as Malachi promised, to prepare a people for him.

On a Tuesday. True repentance shows itself in restored relationships, especially in families. Is there a relationship your repentance needs to mend? Write the name down. Then do one concrete thing this week: a phone call, a letter, an apology without excuses, a meal.

For worship. The God who closed the Old Testament with a promise reopened history by keeping it, word for word. He does not forget his last sentence. And the deepest turning of a father’s heart was never Zechariah’s or ours. It was his own. Jesus would tell of a father who saw his son a long way off, felt compassion, and ran (15:20). That is the Father the forerunner went before: a God whose heart is turned toward rebellious children, who sent his Son to bring them home.

parallels.desc: Elijah will turn the hearts of fathers to their children
he is Elijah who is to come

verseByVerse.quote: And Zechariah said to the angel, 'How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zechariah said to the angel: how shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years.

How shall I know this? Zechariah asks for a sign, a proof. Every reader stops here, and the question is always the same. Why is Zechariah struck dumb for asking, when Mary asks what looks like the same question sixteen verses later and is answered kindly? Gideon laid out a fleece twice (Judges 6:36–40); Abraham asked how he could know, in almost these words, and was given a covenant ceremony instead of a rebuke (Genesis 15:8). But Zechariah had an angel of God standing in front of him, in the temple, telling him what God would do, and still asked for proof.

For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in years. He looks at the circumstances, not at God. He knows about Abraham and Sarah, but he cannot believe it for himself. That little for is the whole difference. He is not asking Gabriel to explain; he is explaining to Gabriel. He has weighed the announcement against what he knows about ageing bodies, and the announcement has lost. Gabriel’s own diagnosis two verses later says precisely this and nothing else: because you did not believe my words.

The contrast with Mary. Mary will also ask a question (v. 34). But hers is a question of how, not whether. She asks how this will be, since she is a virgin: a question about mechanism, asked by somebody who has already accepted that it is going to happen. Zechariah doubts and asks for proof. The angel’s different responses show the difference (vv. 20, 35, 45).

Every condition for faith. He is standing in the Holy Place. An angel is in front of him. The incense is still rising. Every external condition for faith a human being could ask for is in place, and the man’s mind goes to his age.

The sign God was already giving. Zechariah wanted a sign to prove the promise, and he could not see that the promise was the beginning of the sign. In Luke, God’s answer to how shall I know is always his Son. The shepherds will be told: this will be a sign for you: you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger (2:12). Simeon will hold that baby and call him a sign that is opposed (2:34). And when a later crowd demands proof, Jesus will refuse them every sign but one, the sign of Jonah (11:29–30), his own rising from the dead. Zechariah asked for something he could hold. Within the year God would put the answer in human arms.

Does God strike down those who doubt? No. Read what the Bible actually contains. The psalmists shout at God for whole psalms, and the shouting is in the Scriptures. Job argues for thirty chapters and is vindicated over his tidier friends. A father cries I believe; help my unbelief, and gets his son back the same hour (Mark 9:24). Thomas demands to put his hand in the wound and is offered the wound (John 20:27). God is not brittle. He has never once been rattled by an honest question. What happened to Zechariah is not the punishment of doubt. It is the granting of a request. He asked for a sign, and he got one, and it was himself. He wanted evidence he could hold. God gave him nine months of it, attached to his own face. It is one of the oldest mercies in Scripture that God so often gives us exactly what we asked for, in the form we would never have chosen.

So what is the difference between honest doubt and unbelief? Honest doubt brings its struggle to God and wants to believe; it says help my unbelief. Unbelief has already weighed God’s word against something else and decided the something else is more reliable. The first is a weak faith asking for help; the second is a verdict against God. You can tell which you are in by what you do with the question: whether you take it to God and his word, or use it as a reason to stay away. If you are worried that your doubts mean you have no faith, the very worry is often a sign that you want to trust him.

In a sentence. Zechariah, looking at his and Elizabeth’s age, asked the angel how he could be sure of this.

On a Tuesday. When God’s promise seems impossible, look at the God who promises, not at your circumstances. Notice your own little for: I cannot be forgiven for that, for I have done it too often; God cannot use me, for I am too old. Each one weighs his word against your record. Turn the sentence round, and put his faithfulness after the for.

For worship. Zechariah weighed God’s word against an old man’s body, and the word did not notice. It simply came true. God’s faithfulness does not wait on ours. John was conceived in a house where the father could not speak a word of faith, and the Son came into a world that had not believed him either. The LORD keeps his oath because of who he is, not because of who we are, and that is why a doubting heart can still lean its whole weight on him.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel answered him, 'I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news. And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day that these things take place, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel answered him: I am Gabriel. I stand in the presence of God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news. And behold, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day that these things take place, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time.

I am Gabriel. He does not argue biology with the old priest. He gives his name and his post, and that is the whole of the rebuttal. Gabriel (God is my strength, or man of God) appears in the Old Testament only in Daniel (8:16; 9:21), where he came to a man in exile with a message about how long the waiting would be: the seventy weeks decreed for Daniel’s people, and at the end of them an Anointed One (Daniel 9:24–27). Gabriel is the angel of the countdown. That he should come now signals that the time Daniel spoke of has arrived. A priest steeped in Daniel is being told by the very messenger who announced the clock that the clock has run out, and he asks him for a sign. Gabriel is one of only two holy angels named in the canonical Scriptures (with Michael).

I stand in the presence of God. One of the highest angels, who serve in God’s immediate presence. It is a courtier’s phrase: the words he brings have just come out of the throne room. The answer to how shall I know is: because the one who tells you stands before God. To weigh his words against a doctor’s estimate is not caution. It is a category error.

And to bring you this good news. “Bring good news” (euangelisasthai), the verb from which gospel and evangelise come. The gospel begins here, in an old man’s ear, beside an altar, and Luke makes plain what it is about. The next time an angel uses the word, it is to say: I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord (2:10–11). And when Jesus opens his ministry, he reads that the Spirit has anointed him to proclaim good news to the poor (4:18). Daniel’s countdown ended in an Anointed One, and here the messenger of the countdown brings the first news of him. The good news is never only that God has done something. It is that God has sent someone.

You will be silent and unable to speak. The sign he asked for, and a discipline. He could not believe the word, so he will not be able to speak a word. Verse 62 suggests he could not hear either. It is easy to read that as punishment and stop there, but look at what it does to him. Zechariah is a priest, and a priest’s work runs on words: the blessing, the recitation, the teaching, the pronouncing. He is stripped of the one faculty his whole office depends on, and left with nothing to do but turn over what Gabriel said. It was also a mercy: nine months is exactly the time it takes to watch a promise you refused to believe come true in front of you, day by day, in your own house, unable to say a word about it to anybody.

Until the day that these things take place. There is a limit written into the sentence. The discipline has an end date, and the end date is the fulfilment. God does not put him in the dark and leave him there. He puts him in the dark until the light he refused to believe in comes into the room.
