This is the faith that sees the invisible reality and speaks it before it is seen.

The theology of the Magnificat is the theology of the great reversal — the consistent pattern in which God works through what the world considers weak, low, foolish and despised, to accomplish what power and wisdom cannot. The proud are scattered; the mighty brought down; the humble exalted; the hungry filled; the rich sent away empty.

This is not a manifesto for violent revolution — every verb has God as its subject — but the testimony of a God whose ways are not our ways, who chooses the foolish things of the world to shame the wise (1 Cor. 1:27). Mary has understood it because she has lived it: she is herself the lowly servant God has honoured beyond imagining.

And the song ends where the story began, with Abraham (vv. 54-55) — the reversals are not God changing his policy but God keeping an old appointment. Then, with no transition at all, Luke notes that Mary stayed three months and went home (v. 56). She walked back to Nazareth visibly pregnant, to a fiancé who would decide to divorce her. The extraordinary is set down in the middle of the ordinary, and the ordinary is where it has to be carried.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Magnificat's use of the past tense for events that have not yet occurred — he has scattered the proud, he has brought down the mighty — is the linguistic form of prophetic certainty. The prophets of Israel consistently spoke of future events in the past tense when the certainty of God's word made the outcome as sure as if it had already happened.

Isaiah 53 does exactly this, narrating the Servant's suffering and vindication in the past tense centuries before either occurred. Mary's song places her in that prophetic line — not as one who has received a vision of the future but as one who has received the seed of the future in her own body and understands what it means.

The “humble estate” of Mary is a condition of insignificance and social unimportance. God has looked upon it — deliberately noticed — not despite it but through it. This is the theology of election that runs from Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, and David the youngest over his brothers, to Galilee over Jerusalem and Mary over every princess in Israel.

God's choices consistently invert the world's criteria. The reason is not that the lowly are inherently virtuous. It is that the glory of a grace which chooses them cannot possibly be confused with a favour granted on the basis of merit.
verseByVerse.examples:
The Magnificat has been sung in Christian worship since the earliest centuries — in the evening prayer of the church, in the liturgies of East and West, in the hymns of the Reformation — and set to music by composers from Monteverdi to Bach. It is not merely a beautiful poem. It is the church joining Mary's song, declaring that the God who did great things for her is doing great things still.

Every Christian who sings it stands in the line of Mary's witness: scattering the proud, filling the hungry, keeping covenant with his people, is what he is still doing.

It is also among the most politically subversive texts in the New Testament — not because it calls for revolution but because it announces a King whose reign will outlast every human empire, whose justice will overturn every human injustice, and whose mercy will outlive every human cruelty.

The church that sings this song is the community that knows how the story ends, and that knowledge shapes how it lives now: not grasping for power, not trusting in the mighty, not filling itself with the world's goods, but living in the pattern of the God who scatters the proud and exalts the humble.

verseByVerse.quote: And Mary said, 'My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary said: my soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Saviour.

The Magnificat. Mary’s song is called the Magnificat, from its first word in Latin (magnifies). Mary answers Elizabeth’s shout with a song, and it is not the song of a startled teenager. It is woven from Old Testament phrases, especially Hannah’s prayer at the birth of Samuel (1 Samuel 2:1–10), and from the Psalms, Isaiah, Genesis, Micah and Job: something like fifteen allusions in ten verses. When a girl who has hidden Scripture in her heart is put under sudden pressure, what comes out is what was already in. The song has four movements: what God has done for Mary (vv. 46–49), his character (v. 50), what he does in the world (vv. 51–53), and what he has done for Israel (vv. 54–55).

Textual note: Mary or Elizabeth? Nearly all manuscripts say that Mary spoke these words; a few early Latin witnesses name Elizabeth. The song fits Mary: the lowly servant (v. 48) and the God who has done great things for her (v. 49).

My soul magnifies the Lord. “Magnifies” (megalynei): makes great, declares the greatness of, enlarges. God cannot be made greater than he is, so think of two lenses. A microscope makes something small appear larger than it is. A telescope lets something unimaginably vast appear nearer its true size. Worship is never the first. Mary is not inflating God. She is bringing him close enough to be seen as he actually is, and everything else in the picture, including her own alarming circumstances, takes its proper proportions the moment he does. “Soul” and “spirit” are parallel: her whole inner being. Hannah began: My heart exults in the LORD (1 Samuel 2:1).

And my spirit rejoices in God my Savior. “Savior” (sōtēr). Mary needed a Saviour. There is the sentence that settles the question raised by Gabriel’s greeting (v. 28): whether Mary was full of grace to give, or a sinner who had been graced. A great deal of devotion has been built on Mary: that she was conceived without sin, that she remained sinless all her life, that she may be asked to carry our requests to her Son. And here, in the second line of her own song, with the Holy Spirit upon her, Mary calls God my Saviour. Not the Saviour, in general. Mine. A person who needs no rescue does not use that word, and never has. She was not sinless; she rejoiced in the God who saves sinners (Habakkuk 3:18). Mary is not standing above the redeemed and looking down. She is standing inside them, singing, the first of a very long line of people who had nothing to bring and were given everything.

The Saviour she carried. And notice where the Saviour she rejoices in is at that moment. A few months later an angel will tell shepherds: unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord (2:11). The God Mary calls her Saviour is about to be born of her as a Saviour. She sings to the God who saves while the salvation is growing inside her, and the child she carries is the only way her own sins will ever be dealt with. The mother needed her Son to rescue her. That is the strangest and most glorious relationship in the chapter: Mary gave him his human life, and he would give his life for hers.

How do I magnify the Lord when I do not feel like it? Mary’s song did not come from nowhere; it came from Scripture she had already stored up. So fill yourself with God’s words, especially the Psalms, so that they are there when you need them. Then begin with what you know, not what you feel: tell God who he is and what he has done in Christ, aloud if you can. Feelings often follow truth spoken in faith. And sing with the church. On days when you cannot sing, let the congregation sing for you. Praise is not pretending that things are fine; it is seeing God as he really is, which is always the truest thing in the room.

In a sentence. Mary began her song by declaring the greatness of the Lord and rejoicing in God her Saviour.

On a Tuesday. Look at his greatness until you can sing about it, and rejoice in him as your Saviour. Notice what you magnify by habit: the problem, the person who wronged you, your own worries. Turn the telescope round today and point it at God.

For worship. The Lord whom Mary magnified is greater than every telescope ever pointed at him. He has been at the work of rescue since Eden, he has never yet abandoned a promise, and the heavens are too small to hold him. Yet he is not far off. He is God my Saviour, a rescuer with a name, close enough to be sung to by a village girl and by the least of his people since. There is no danger of magnifying him too far. The whole of eternity will not be long enough to get him into proportion.
verseByVerse.note: Mary’s song, known as the Magnificat, is woven from Old Testament phrases, especially Hannah’s prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: for he has looked on the humble estate of his servant. For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed; for he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he has looked on the humble estate of his servant. For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed; for he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name.

For he has looked on the humble estate of his servant. “Humble estate” (tapeinōsin): lowliness, low social position, the state of counting for nothing. Mary is not describing her humility as a virtue. She is describing her social altitude, which was ground level. And looked on is a deliberate turning of the head: the choosing to notice. Hannah prayed: if you will indeed look on the affliction of your servant (1 Samuel 1:11). God chose her because of her lowliness, not despite it.

God’s settled method. That is the logic of God’s choosing right through the Bible. Not the eldest son but the youngest. Not the impressive brothers but the boy left out in the field with the sheep. Not the capital but a village. Not the priest but the girl. God looks in the direction nobody else is looking, and that is not a consolation prize for people who did not make the first team. It is his settled method, and Paul states it in so many words: God chose what is low and despised in the world, so that no human being might boast in his presence (1 Corinthians 1:26–29).

The lowliness he took. The God who looked on Mary’s humble estate did more than look. Her Son would take that estate as his own. Paul says he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death (Philippians 2:7–8). And Luke himself, in his second volume, quotes Isaiah’s words over the suffering Servant with the very noun Mary uses here: in his humiliation justice was denied him (Acts 8:33). The lowliness Mary sang about from below, her Son entered from above. He went lower than Nazareth, lower than the manger, down to a criminal’s death, so that the lowest of the low could be lifted with him.

From now on all generations will call me blessed. A prophecy that has come true: not that she will be worshipped, but honoured as the one God blessed. Leah said something similar at the birth of Asher (Genesis 30:13). Protestants have often been so anxious about what has been built on Mary that they have quietly declined to obey a plain sentence of Scripture. Elizabeth has just called her blessed. Mary says it here with the Holy Spirit on her. A church that never calls Mary blessed is not being careful; it is disagreeing with the text. So call her blessed. She is the most favoured woman who ever lived.

For he who is mighty has done great things for me. She gives the reason in the very next breath, and the reason is not herself. She is blessed because of what was done to her, not because of anything she can do for anybody else. That is the difference between honouring Mary and praying to her, and it is the difference between a mirror and a lamp. A mirror is not honoured by being stared at. It is honoured by being looked along, to the light it is turned towards.

Should Christians pray to Mary or ask her to intercede? No. Generations call her blessed because God chose her; she herself calls God my Saviour (v. 47). Scripture gives one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), through whom every believer may come boldly to the throne of grace (Hebrews 4:14–16). Prayers addressed to Mary, as in the Hail Mary, give her a role Scripture never gives. We honour her best by sharing her faith: let it be to me according to your word (v. 38).

And holy is his name. God’s name is God himself, as he has revealed himself. He is holy: set apart, utterly pure, majestic. Holy and awesome is his name (Psalm 111:9). Mary’s blessedness leads her to worship God’s holiness. She has just said that the greatest thing which ever happened to a human being happened to her, and her sentence ends by getting out of the way.

In a sentence. Mary praised God for looking on her lowliness, foretold that all generations would call her blessed, and gave the glory to the Mighty One, whose name is holy.

On a Tuesday. God looks on the lowly. If you feel insignificant, remember that he chose a poor girl from Nazareth for the greatest privilege a human being has ever had. And when someone praises you this week, do what Mary did: in the very next breath, give the reason, and the reason is him.

For worship. Holy is his name, the Mighty One whose greatness no generation has measured. And the holiness that could have consumed us has bent down and looked on us with favour. Every generation that calls Mary blessed is, in the end, calling him glorious, because the great things done for her were done in her Son, and in him great things are done for every lowly sinner who comes: a name written in heaven, a robe put on, a place at the feast.

parallels.desc: look on the affliction of your servant
holy and awesome is his name

verseByVerse.quote: And his mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And his mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation.

And his mercy. This verse is the hinge of the song. Everything before it is about Mary; everything after it is about the world. And the joint between them is mercy. Mary moves from what God has done for her to who God is. “Mercy” (eleos) translates the Hebrew ḥesed, God’s steadfast, covenant love: not pity felt at a distance but committed, covenanted loyalty, the love that has bound itself and will not walk away. It is the love of a God who keeps steadfast love for thousands (Exodus 34:6–7). Mary is saying that what has happened to her is not an exception. It is a sample.

Is for those who fear him. Few phrases do more damage when misheard. To fear God is not to be terrified of him, but to revere him, take him seriously, trust and obey him. Every reader who has ever lain awake wondering whether God is waiting to catch him out should hear that clearly: that is not what the Bible means. The fear of God is what a man feels standing at the foot of something vast: the awe that reorders him, that makes him careful, that puts everything else in the room into proportion. It is entirely compatible with running to him. In fact it is the only thing that makes running to him make sense, since a God small enough not to be feared would be too small to be worth reaching. Mary, who feared him, ran to him singing; and Solomon had said long before that wisdom starts in that same awe (Proverbs 9:10).

From generation to generation. Psalm 103:17: But the steadfast love of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him. His mercy does not run out. What he did for Abraham, he does for Mary, and for everyone who fears him, in every generation, including ours. A teenager is singing about grandchildren she will never meet. The covenant God does not deal with people in isolation; his mercy has a long reach, and the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself (Acts 2:39).

Mercy with a face. Mary sings of mercy in general terms, but her own song is the first sign of how it will arrive. Within months her relative’s husband will sing of the same mercy and name its coming: because of the tender mercy of our God, whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high (v. 78). The covenant love that bound itself to Abraham was never only an attitude in heaven. It was on its way to earth in a person. In Christ the mercy of God has hands that touch lepers, a voice that tells a sinful woman her sins are forgiven (7:48), and a body given for us. From generation to generation, everyone who receives the mercy Mary praised receives it from him.

What about my child or grandchild who has walked away? Take hold of this verse in prayer. The mercy that reached Mary in Nazareth had been travelling towards her since Abraham. It does not lose speed with distance, and it does not require the previous generation to have finished the job. Nothing in this verse guarantees a particular grandchild; it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise, because every person must come to Christ by his own faith, and God’s mercy is his to give. What it does say is what kind of God is being prayed to: one whose stated habit is to keep turning up in a family long after the people who first prayed for it are dead. So keep praying, keep loving, keep the door open, and live the gospel in front of them.

In a sentence. God’s steadfast mercy rests on those who revere him, in every generation.

On a Tuesday. If you are afraid of God in the wrong way, as a judge waiting to catch you out, bring that fear to the cross, where his anger against your sin was spent on Christ. Then learn the right fear: the awe that makes you careful with his name, honest in your work and quick to run to him.

For worship. The mercy of God does not wear thin with use. Every generation draws on it as though no one had drawn before, and it is as full for the last as for the first. It held Abraham, it held a girl in Nazareth, and it holds the weakest believer reading this today, because it was secured once for all at a cross and is kept by a living Saviour. From everlasting to everlasting his steadfast love is on those who fear him, and the generations rise up, one after another, to tell of it.

parallels.desc: the steadfast love of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him

verseByVerse.quote: He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts; he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts; he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty.

The past tense. The song turns outward, and the tense turns strange. He has scattered, he has brought down, he has exalted, he has filled, he has sent away. All the verbs are in the past tense (the Greek aorist), and none of it has visibly happened. Rome is at the height of its power; Herod is still in his palace. This is the prophetic past: when God has spoken, the outcome is so certain that it can be reported as history, as Isaiah described the Servant’s suffering and vindication seven centuries before a nail was driven (Isaiah 53). Mary also describes what God has always done, and is now doing again. And she can do it for one reason: the thing that guarantees the reversal is already inside her. From where she is standing the war is over. What remains is the clearing up.

He has shown strength with his arm. God’s arm is a picture of his power in action, especially at the exodus: with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm (Deuteronomy 26:8; Isaiah 51:9; 52:10). And Isaiah asks, to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed? (Isaiah 53:1), and answers with the suffering Servant. The arm of the LORD, in the end, is a crucified man.

He has scattered the proud in the thoughts of their hearts. The proud plan in their hearts, and God scatters their plans, as at Babel (Genesis 11). Notice where Mary locates the pride: not first in palaces but in the thoughts of the heart. It is the quiet conviction that I am the author of my own life and need nothing from God, and it can wear religious clothes as easily as royal ones. Luke will show a Pharisee standing in the temple thanking God that he is not like other men, and going home unjustified (18:11–14). Pride is not only the sin of tyrants. It is the sin of anyone who comes to God with something to show.

He has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate. The great reversal. Hannah sang: The LORD makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and he exalts (1 Samuel 2:7–8). This is a major theme of Luke’s Gospel: the last will be first and the first last (13:30), the humble exalted and the exalted humbled (14:11; 18:14), blessings on the poor and woes on the rich (6:20–26). Herod sits on his throne; Mary’s son will lie in a manger. But God will reverse it.

He has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty. Psalm 107:9. Hunger here is both physical and spiritual: those who know their need, and hunger for God (6:21; Matthew 5:6). The rich are those who are self-satisfied and need nothing from God (12:16–21; 16:19–31; 18:24–25).

The line most readers would rather skip. The rich he has sent away empty is uncomfortable, because most people reading this are, by any measure the world has ever used, the rich. And Luke of all the evangelists refuses to let us spiritualise it away: this is the Gospel of the rich fool, the rich man and Lazarus, and the ruler who went away sad. But the mechanism is exact. The hungry are filled and the rich are sent away empty, and both go home with what they arrived with room for. Nobody is turned away at the door for owning things. They are sent away empty because they came full, and a full man cannot be filled. Money is dangerous not because God objects to it, but because it is the most efficient device ever invented for producing the sensation of not needing anything.

What it does not mean. Not a political manifesto, or a call for revolution, as some liberation theologians have read it. Read the verbs. Every one of them has God as its subject. Mary is not summoning anybody to storm anything. She is describing what God does, and the way he is doing it at this moment is by placing himself inside a poor girl in an occupied province. The overthrow is real, and it is total, and there is no army in it. Nor does it mean that all poor people are saved and all rich people lost. But it does show that God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble (James 4:6), that he cares about the poor and the oppressed, and that his kingdom overturns the world’s values. These are real social realities as well as spiritual ones, and the church should reflect them.

So what should a comfortable Christian do with this? Not feel vaguely guilty and carry on. First, come to God hungry: confess that nothing you own can save you, and ask him to fill you with Christ. Second, hold your money with an open hand: give generously, regularly and sacrificially, especially to the poor and to the work of the gospel (1 Timothy 6:17–19). Third, notice the lowly around you, the poor, the elderly, the overlooked, and treat them as God does. Wealth is not a sin, but it is a test, and the question is whether it has become the thing you trust.

In a sentence. Mary sang of the God who by his mighty arm scatters the proud, topples the powerful, lifts up the lowly, fills the hungry, and sends the self-satisfied rich away empty.

On a Tuesday. On which side of the great reversal are you: the proud and self-sufficient, or the humble and hungry? Think of the last time something went badly wrong: a diagnosis, a bill, a phone call at an odd hour. What was the first thing reached for? For most of us the honest answer is a resource: savings, a contact, a plan. There is nothing wicked in any of that. But whatever gets reached for first is, in practice, the thing being trusted. The reversal Mary is singing about is not chiefly about who owns what. It is about who, when the ground moves, still has anything left to stand on. Come to God empty, and be filled.

For worship. The God of the Magnificat is the God of the great reversal, and he has done it supremely in his Son: the one who was rich became poor, the mighty one was brought low to a cross, and God exalted him to the highest place. Through that reversal he fills the hungry with himself. No throne is safe from him, and no beggar is beyond him. The song a girl sang in the hill country is the song the whole creation will sing at the end.

parallels.desc: he brings low and he exalts

verseByVerse.quote: He has helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring forever.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring for ever.

He has helped his servant Israel. Mary’s song ends where the story of salvation began: her last lines reach back past David and Moses to Abraham. Isaiah 41:8–9: But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen, the offspring of Abraham. God has come to the aid of his people. The word for help is the hand under the elbow of a man who is going down.

In remembrance of his mercy. God has not forgotten. Through centuries of silence, oppression and exile, he remembered. When God remembers, it never means that something had slipped his mind. God remembered Noah, and the waters went down (Genesis 8:1). God remembered his covenant, and heard the groaning in Egypt (Exodus 2:24). Remembering, in the Bible, is a promise coming due. The name Zechariah means the LORD remembers (v. 5), and Zechariah will sing the same (v. 72).

As he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring forever. God’s promise to Abraham: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed (Genesis 12:3; 22:18). That promise was made to a childless man called out of Ur, roughly two thousand years before this girl opened her mouth in a hill-country kitchen. This is the root of the whole story.

The offspring the oath was about. The help God sends Israel is not a policy. It is a child. Paul notices that the promise was made to Abraham and to his offspring, singular, and says: who is Christ (Galatians 3:16). Mary sings of Abraham’s offspring with Abraham’s offspring under her heart. Luke will show the two halves of the promise meeting in one pair of arms, when old Simeon takes the baby in the temple and calls him a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel (2:32). Help for Israel and blessing for all the families of the earth were never two promises. They were one Son.

An old appointment. Notice what this does to the reversals she has just sung. They are not God changing his policy, or finally losing patience with the powerful. They are God keeping an old appointment. They are covenant faithfulness arriving in a world arranged the wrong way up.

Does God still have promises for the Jewish people? Christians who love the Scriptures disagree on the details, especially in reading Romans 11. All agree on what Mary sings here: that God has kept his promise to Abraham in Christ, Abraham’s offspring, and that the gospel is to the Jew first (Romans 1:16). Many in the Reformed tradition, from the Puritans onward, have also expected a great turning of Jewish people to Christ before the end (Romans 11:25–26). What no Christian may say is that God has forgotten Israel, or that the Jewish people can be saved apart from their Messiah. The mercy Mary praised is offered to them in her Son, and we should pray and work for it.

In a sentence. Mary ended her song by praising God for helping his people Israel, remembering the mercy he promised to Abraham and his descendants for ever.

On a Tuesday. God keeps his promises, however long it takes. Pick the promise you are tired of waiting for, and set it beside the two thousand years between Abraham and Mary. Then thank him, today, for the promises he has already kept to you in Christ.

For worship. Two thousand years is a long time to hold a sentence steady. Kingdoms rose and were levelled. The family that carried the promise sold one of its own sons into slavery, and worshipped a calf, and split in two, and went into exile, and came back smaller. The line thinned until it ran through a village carpenter and a girl nobody had heard of. And not one syllable of what God said to Abraham was ever withdrawn, renegotiated, or quietly allowed to lapse. He had bound himself by an oath, to a man long dead, about descendants not yet born, and he kept it, because that is what he is like. There has never been a moment in the history of the world when it was safe to bet against his word, and every promise that now includes us is sealed in the blood of Abraham’s Son.

parallels.desc: Israel, my servant, offspring of Abraham

verseByVerse.quote: And Mary remained with her about three months and returned to her home.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary remained with her about three months and returned to her home.

About three months. Until near the time of John’s birth, since Elizabeth was in her sixth month when Mary arrived (v. 36). Whether Mary stayed for the birth Luke does not say, and it is better not to guess; he rounds off Mary’s part of the story first, as he often does, and then turns to John’s birth.

And returned to her home. To Nazareth, along the same four or five days of road, around three months pregnant, which is to say beginning to show. She returns to a village where everyone knows her and Joseph, and every one of them can count. She has no evidence of any kind. Her only account of herself is that an angel came into the room, and the one other person on earth who would believe it is now eighty miles behind her.

What happened next. Matthew tells us that Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly (Matthew 1:19), and it took an angel in a dream to stop him. Matthew does not say whether Joseph learned of the pregnancy before her journey or after it. Either way, Mary walked home to a fiancé who had every reason to conclude she had betrayed him, and to a village that would agree with him.

Nobody warned her. Gabriel told her about the child, the kingdom, the Spirit and her relative. He said nothing about the whispering, or the look on Joseph’s face. She found out the way everybody finds out: by arriving.

The shame he shared from the womb. Mary did not walk that road alone. The child under her heart was walking it with her, already sharing the suspicion that fell on her. Before he could speak, the Son of God was already the reason his mother was suspected; years later his enemies would still sneer that they, at least, were not born of sexual immorality (John 8:41). He began his human life under a cloud he had not earned, and he ended it under a sentence he had not earned, numbered with the transgressors (22:37). From the first months of his life the Lord of glory was content to be misjudged, so that those who are rightly judged might be cleared.

Why does God not tell us what obedience will cost? Because he wants us to trust him, not the plan. If we knew every hard thing in advance, we would lean on our own preparations; instead he gives us enough light for the next step and promises to be with us on the road. Jesus did tell his disciples to count the cost (14:28), so we are not to follow blindly. But the details usually come as we go. What God does tell us in advance is the end: that he will never leave us, and that he will bring us home.

In a sentence. Mary stayed with Elizabeth about three months and then went home.

On a Tuesday. Time spent with mature believers strengthens you for what lies ahead. Mary had three months with Elizabeth before she faced Nazareth. If you are about to walk back into something hard, a workplace, a family, a diagnosis, find your Elizabeth first. And if you are the mature believer, make room in your house and your week for the younger one who needs you.

For worship. Luke reports the whole thing in one sentence and moves on, and that restraint is itself a kind of testimony. The mother of the Lord did not get an easier road on account of who she was carrying. She got the ordinary road, walked in the ordinary way, with heaven inside her and nobody able to tell. And the One she carried would one day set his face to go to Jerusalem, and walk every mile of it with his eyes open, so that none of his people would ever walk a hard road alone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 57–66 — The Birth of John the Baptist
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The birth of John is narrated with characteristic Lukan brevity — one verse for the birth itself, and then immediate attention to what matters most, which is the naming. In Jewish custom the name was given at circumcision on the eighth day, and was normally taken from the father's family. The community assumes the child will be called Zechariah.

Elizabeth insists that he will be called John. The community is astonished — there is nobody in the family by that name — and they turn to Zechariah himself. He calls for a writing tablet and writes: his name is John. And immediately his mouth is opened, his tongue is loosed, and he speaks.

The sequence is telling. Zechariah does not begin to speak until he has first obeyed. The muteness that fell at his unbelief is lifted not when he privately makes up his mind but when he publicly and irrevocably acts on the word Gabriel gave him. The name John was not Zechariah's choice; it was God's command (v. 13).

By writing it without qualification he is doing what Mary did in a different register: surrendering his own preference and his family's expectation to the word of God. And the moment he does, the word God gave him is restored to his own mouth.

A small detail in v. 62 fills out the whole nine months. The family made signs to him, which suggests he could not hear either. He had been sealed inside his own head since the day at the altar, with nothing in there but Gabriel's sentence.

The neighbours and relatives are filled with fear, and they laid up all these things in their hearts — a phrase that will appear again of Mary after the shepherds' visit (2:19) and after the temple episode (2:51). Luke's Gospel is full of people who receive these events and hold them, turning them over, not fully understanding but refusing to let go.

That is the posture the gospel consistently produces: not an immediate confident grasp of everything, but the faithful keeping of what has been received, waiting for the understanding that comes in its own time.
verseByVerse.theology:
The crowd's question — what then will this child be, for the hand of the Lord was with him — is the question the rest of Luke-Acts will answer. John will be the voice crying in the wilderness, the preparer of the way, the greatest among those born of women (7:28).

He will baptise Jesus, proclaim the coming kingdom, confront Herod, and die in prison before Jesus's ministry reaches its climax. He is the last and greatest of the prophets, the hinge between the old covenant and the new. The hand of the LORD that the community perceives is the hand that has been shaping him for this purpose since before his birth.

The motif of a whole community sharing in the response to God's action — neighbours and relatives rejoicing, all who heard wondering, everyone laying these things up in their hearts — reflects Luke's consistent understanding that the gospel is not a private transaction between an individual and God. It is a public event that transforms communities.

The birth of John affects not only Zechariah and Elizabeth but the entire social network of their neighbourhood. The ripple of grace always extends further than the point of impact.
verseByVerse.examples:
Zechariah's obedience at the naming — writing “his name is John” without qualification, against the family's expectation — is the delayed obedience of a man whom nine months of silence have changed. He came into the temple a man of correct theology and insufficient trust. He emerges from the silence a man who writes the word of God on a tablet before he says a word of his own.

The discipline has done its work. The man who needed a sign is now content to be one — the father who names his child what God chose, regardless of what the neighbours think.

The fear that falls on the community is the biblical response to the nearness of the holy. This is not terror but the awe that the presence of God in human history always produces. They sense that something larger than ordinary life is moving through the birth of this child, and they are right.

The instinct to hold that sense carefully — to lay it up in the heart — is exactly the right response to grace that exceeds our comprehension. Not analysis, not immediate explanation, but faithful keeping: holding what has been received until it is better understood.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. Her neighbours and relatives heard that the Lord had shown great mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her.

Now the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son. Exactly as the angel said. Nine months earlier a mute priest came home from the temple with an announcement he could not make. The house has been silent ever since. Now there is a baby crying in it.

And her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown great mercy to her. Literally that the Lord had magnified his mercy with her, the same verb as Mary’s my soul magnifies (v. 46). Luke records their theology rather than their congratulations: mercy, covenant kindness, the word Mary has just sung twice and Zechariah will use twice more. They do not call it luck. They name the one who did it.

And they rejoiced with her. The angel had promised: many will rejoice at his birth (v. 14). Here is the first instalment: a house full of neighbours. Rejoice with those who rejoice (Romans 12:15). And hold that against verse 25. The reproach she named, the thing people said, has become the thing people celebrate. The same social circle that had carried a verdict about Elizabeth for forty years is now in her house, delighted. Nothing about her has changed except that God acted.

A village’s joy, then the world’s. This is the herald’s birth, and the joy it brings is the size of a hill-country village. Six months later another birth will be announced, not by neighbours passing the word but by an angel in the night sky: I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people (2:10). John’s birth fills a house; Jesus’ birth fills the heavens with a multitude praising God. The scale is the point. The joy at John is real, and Gabriel promised it (v. 14), but it is a lamp lit before the dawn. The neighbours rejoice that the Lord showed mercy to Elizabeth. The angels rejoice that the Lord has come to show mercy to the world.

No human verdict is final. The village’s opinion of Elizabeth was the best guess of people who could only see the outside; it was wrong for forty years, and it was overturned in an afternoon. Not every unjust verdict is overturned in this life, and it would be dishonest to promise otherwise. But no human assessment is final. The verdict still standing at the end will be God’s, and his had called her righteous (v. 6) the entire time the village was talking.

What if people have misjudged me and never changed their minds? Then you are in good company: the prophets, the apostles and our Lord himself were misjudged to the end of their lives on earth. Do what you can to put things right, honestly and humbly, especially if there is some truth in what is said. Then leave your reputation with God, who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). Paul said it is a very small thing to be judged by any human court; it is the Lord who judges me (1 Corinthians 4:3–4). On the last day every hidden thing will be brought to light, and if you are in Christ, the verdict will be the one already given: no condemnation.

In a sentence. Elizabeth gave birth to a son, and her neighbours and relatives rejoiced with her at the Lord’s great mercy.

On a Tuesday. When God blesses someone you know, rejoice with them wholeheartedly, without envy. Go round, send the message, bring the meal. And when you describe their blessing to others, do what Elizabeth’s neighbours did: name the Lord who gave it.

For worship. The Lord magnified his mercy, and the house that had been silent filled with a crying baby and rejoicing neighbours. He turns reproach into celebration, and he does it in front of the very people who passed the verdict. His mercy is never small and never private: it spills over, and those who stand near it are made glad.

parallels.desc: everyone who hears will laugh over me

verseByVerse.quote: And on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child. And they would have called him Zechariah after his father, but his mother answered, 'No; he shall be called John.' And they said to her, 'None of your relatives is called by this name.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the eighth day they came to circumcise the child. They would have called him Zechariah after his father, but his mother answered: no; he shall be called John. They said to her: none of your relatives is called by this name.

And on the eighth day they came to circumcise the child. Circumcision on the eighth day was the covenant sign God gave to Abraham (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3). John is born into the covenant people and receives its sign, on the day God set. The forerunner of the new covenant begins his life marked with the sign of the old one.

The Lord under his own law. Eight days after his own birth, Jesus will lie where John lies here, and receive the same sign and his name (2:21). The one who gave the covenant to Abraham submitted to its mark. Paul gives the reason: God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5). From his eighth day the Son was keeping, for his people, the law they had broken, and he kept it all the way to the cross, where it was fulfilled. John is circumcised because he is a son of Abraham. Jesus is circumcised because he came to be the obedient son of Abraham that none of Abraham’s other sons had been.

Does circumcision here support infant baptism? Paedobaptist brothers, whose godliness and learning we honour, argue that baptism has replaced circumcision as the covenant sign and should likewise be given to the infants of believers. This commentary holds, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession (29.2), that baptism belongs to those who profess repentance and faith. Circumcision marked physical descent within the old covenant people, which included believers and unbelievers alike. The new covenant people are those who know the Lord, from the least to the greatest (Jeremiah 31:34; Hebrews 8:11), born not of blood but of God (John 1:13), and the New Testament shows baptism following faith (Acts 2:41; 8:12). The true counterpart of circumcision is the circumcision of the heart by the Spirit (Colossians 2:11–12). Both sides agree that children of believers are to be brought up in the faith and prayed for from birth.

And they would have called him Zechariah after his father. Naming at circumcision was customary, and naming a son after his father or grandfather was common. It was a proud thing to do: a first son, born to an old priest by a miracle, carrying his father’s name and his father’s office. Everyone in the room assumed it.

No; he shall be called John. His mother answers as flatly as a sentence can be put. And Zechariah has been unable to speak for nine months, so how does Elizabeth know the name? Either he wrote it out for her at some point during the silence, or she was told it by the Spirit. Luke does not say, and it is better not to invent. What Luke does record is that when the moment came, the woman with no standing at all in that discussion contradicted her entire family, in public, on the strength of a word from God, and did not soften it.

None of your relatives is called by this name. The room’s response is not theological. It is social: not the name is wrong but the name is not ours. It is the oldest objection in religion and the least examined: we have never done it that way. The name breaks with family tradition. Something new is beginning. John belongs not to his family’s line, but to God’s purpose. His name says: the Lord has been gracious.

The pressure of people who mean well. It is not persecution. Nobody is threatening her. It is a room full of people she loves and will still be living among next week, all of whom think she is making a mistake, and all of whom mean well. That is far harder to withstand than hostility, and it is the form most believers actually meet. She had nothing to appeal to except what God had said. It was enough, and she held it for the whole length of the argument, alone, until somebody put a writing tablet into her husband’s hands.

Is tradition always wrong then? No. Elizabeth was keeping the tradition of circumcision on the eighth day, gladly, because God had commanded it. Family customs and church traditions are often good gifts, carrying the wisdom of those who went before. The question is what has authority. Where a custom simply expresses love and order, honour it. Where it contradicts what God has said, God’s word wins, however much you love the people who hold the custom. Scripture alone binds the conscience (Westminster 20.2). And when you have to break with a custom, do it with the same firmness and the same love Elizabeth showed: no sneering, no lecture, just a clear no and a reason.

In a sentence. At the child’s circumcision, the relatives wanted to name him after his father, but Elizabeth insisted he be called John, a name no one in the family had.

On a Tuesday. Obeying God sometimes means breaking with family expectations. Do it graciously, but do it. Think of the area where the room full of people who love you is quietly pulling you away from what God has said: how you spend Sunday, how you handle money, whom you marry, how you raise your children. Hold to the word, and keep loving the room.

For worship. God names his servants, and his name for this child was grace. He breaks into family lines and old expectations to do something new, and he gives an old woman the courage to stand alone on his word. Nothing in our customs binds him. He has always been the God who does a new thing, and the new thing is always mercy.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision on the eighth day was the covenant sign given to Abraham; the name was often given then.

verseByVerse.quote: And they made signs to his father, inquiring what he wanted him to be called. And he asked for a writing tablet and wrote, 'His name is John.' And they all wondered. And immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed, and he spoke, blessing God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They made signs to his father, asking what he wanted him to be called. He asked for a writing tablet and wrote: his name is John. And they all wondered. Immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed, and he spoke, blessing God.

And they made signs to his father. Signs, not questions: a small detail that changes the picture of the whole nine months. Zechariah’s condition in verse 22 is described with the word kōphos, which in Greek covers both an inability to speak and an inability to hear; it is the word used of the deaf man in Mark 7:32. And the room’s behaviour suggests it, since people do not usually gesture at a man who can hear them. So Zechariah may have spent nine months not merely unable to speak but unable to hear. He could not hear his wife’s voice, or the child cry. He had asked for evidence, and God had sealed him inside his own head with nothing in there but the sentence Gabriel had spoken.

And he asked for a writing tablet. A wooden board coated with wax, written on with a stylus. His name is John. Not his name shall be, which is what Elizabeth said, but his name is. He is not casting a vote. He is reporting a fact settled nine months earlier in a room with an angel in it, by a word he had not believed and now obeys exactly.

And immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed. And they all wondered: husband and wife, who could not have consulted each other in words in front of them, agreed. At the moment he obeyed, the discipline was lifted, as Gabriel had said (v. 20). Notice when his voice comes back. Not when he privately came round. Not in the sixth month, when the pregnancy became undeniable. Not at the birth. Immediately after he wrote the name. The silence lifted at the point of public, irreversible obedience: when he put in writing, in front of the whole family, at the cost of every expectation in the room, the word he had refused to believe.

And he spoke, blessing God. His first words after nine months of silence were praise: not an explanation, not an account of the altar, not a complaint about the discipline. The doubter has become a worshipper; his song follows (vv. 68–79). Something had been done in that silence which could not have been done any other way, and the God who did it had shut his mouth in the first place for exactly this.

The first loosened tongue. This loosened tongue is a sign of what is coming. Isaiah had said that when God came to save, the ears of the deaf would be unstopped and the tongue of the mute would sing for joy (Isaiah 35:4–6). When John, in prison, sends to ask Jesus whether he is the one who is to come, Jesus answers with that list: the blind receive their sight, the deaf hear (7:22). The first deaf ears and mute tongue opened in this story belong to John’s own father, on the day John is named. The age of the Messiah begins in that house with a loosened tongue blessing God, and the one who will loosen tongues across Galilee is already growing in his mother’s womb in Nazareth.

Does God always lift discipline when we obey? God’s discipline always has a purpose and a limit, and he delights to restore. Very often, as here, the turning point comes when we stop arguing and obey. But do not make it a formula, as though obedience were a coin that buys an end to hardship. Some consequences of sin remain in this life even after repentance: David was forgiven, and his child still died. What is always lifted at once is the barrier between you and God: when you confess, he is faithful and just to forgive (1 John 1:9). The relationship is restored immediately, and the rest is in a Father’s wise hands.

In a sentence. When asked, Zechariah wrote that the child’s name was John, and at once he could speak again, and his first words were praise to God.

On a Tuesday. Is there a step of obedience you have agreed with privately but never taken publicly: a confession to make, a decision to announce, a baptism to ask for? Write the name on the tablet. And when God brings you through a hard season, let your first words afterwards be praise, before the explanations.

For worship. Zechariah was silent for his own unbelief. Another would be silent for ours. Luke tells us how the Ethiopian read it: like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth (Acts 8:32). The Lamb of God stood before Herod and made no answer (23:9), and because he held his peace under judgement, mouths like Zechariah’s are opened in blessing, and the dumb are taught to sing. He does not waste our hardest months. He bought our songs with his silence.
verseByVerse.note: A writing tablet was a wooden board coated with wax.

verseByVerse.quote: And fear came on all their neighbors. And all these things were talked about through all the hill country of Judea, and all who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying, 'What then will this child be?' For the hand of the Lord was with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fear came on all their neighbours, and all these things were talked about through all the hill country of Judea. All who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying: what then will this child be? For the hand of the Lord was with him.

And fear came on all their neighbors. Awe at the evident work of God: the same reaction that fell on Zechariah in the temple, now spread across a district. This is the proper human response to discovering that God is actually operating in the neighbourhood: not excitement, not curiosity, but fear. It is a reaction Luke will record again and again across his two volumes: at the catch of fish (5:8–9), at the stilling of the storm (8:25), at the raising of the widow’s son (7:16), and after Ananias and Sapphira, when great fear came upon the whole church (Acts 5:11). A God who can be discussed comfortably has usually not turned up yet.

And all who heard them laid them up in their hearts. The news spread through all the hill country of Judea, and some would remember it thirty years later, when John appeared preaching in the wilderness. They kept thinking about it, as Mary did (2:19, 51). This is one of Luke’s signature motifs. It describes people who do not understand what they have seen, cannot explain it, and will not put it down. They store it.

Keeping what you cannot yet explain. Something happens with God’s fingerprints on it and no available explanation: a providence that cannot be coincidence; a prayer answered in a way that raises more questions than it settles; a suffering that will not resolve into a lesson. The usual responses are to force a meaning onto it, or to shrug it off. Luke’s neighbours do neither. They carry it, unexplained, and wait. Some of what God does is only legible years later, and the people who can read it then are the ones who kept it.

What then will this child be? The question everyone asked. It hangs over the hill country, unanswered, for thirty years. Luke will answer it, but not yet: the greatest of the prophets, and the forerunner of the Lord.

The question behind the question. Luke’s Gospel is full of people asking who someone is, and this is only the first. The answer to it lies wholly in another. When John is grown, crowds will wonder whether he might be the Christ, and he will say: he who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie (3:15–16). Then the question moves to Jesus. Who is this, that he commands even winds and water? (8:25). Who do you say that I am? (9:20). What John will be can only be answered by who Jesus is. The hill country was right to wonder at the child. It would take the cross and the empty tomb to show how much greater was the one he went before.

For the hand of the Lord was with him. Luke’s comment, and it says the answer is not in doubt. God’s power and favour were on him from the beginning (Acts 11:21). All through the Old Testament that phrase means one thing: God has taken hold of a life for a purpose of his own. Whatever the child turns out to be, it has already been decided.

How do I lay things up in my heart in practice? Write them down. Keep a simple record of answered prayers, providences you could not explain, verses that came alive at a particular time. Tell them to your family. Return to them when you are discouraged, as Israel was told to remember the wilderness (Deuteronomy 8:2). And resist the urge to tie every event to a neat lesson. It is enough to say: God was in this, and I do not yet see why. The meaning often arrives years later, and the record lets you see it when it does.

In a sentence. Awe spread through the hill country, and everyone who heard wondered what this child would become, for the Lord’s hand was clearly on him.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the children you know: that the hand of the Lord would be with them. Name them before God, one by one. You do not know what they will be, but you know who can take hold of a life.

For worship. The hand of the Lord is not short. It took hold of an old couple’s baby in the hill country and shaped him for thirty years in secret, and it has taken hold of every one of his people. What then will this child be? Whatever God has decided, and God decides well.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Zechariah's song — called the Benedictus from its first word in Latin, “Blessed” — is the longest prophecy in Luke's first chapter and in many ways its theological climax. Where Mary's Magnificat looked back at what God has done throughout Israel's history, the Benedictus looks forward to what God is now doing through the two children, and across the whole sweep of the covenant from Abraham to this moment.

It is the song of an old priest who has spent nine months in silence, and who opens his mouth for the first time not with relief or apology or explanation but with praise and prophecy.

The song falls into two movements. The first (vv. 68-75) is about Jesus: the God of Israel has visited and redeemed his people, has raised up a horn of salvation in the house of David, and has fulfilled the oath he swore to Abraham, so that his people might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness all their days.

The second (vv. 76-79) is about John: the child will be called the prophet of the Most High, will go before the Lord to prepare his ways, and will give knowledge of salvation through the forgiveness of sins, because of the tender mercy of God by which the sunrise will visit them from on high. The two movements map exactly onto the two births — the greater to Jesus, the preparatory to John.

Verse 77 is the interpretive key to the whole song, and it answers the objection a modern reader raises at v. 71. Rome was never overthrown; Jerusalem fell within a lifetime. But the salvation Zechariah means is defined by Zechariah himself: knowledge of salvation in the forgiveness of their sins. The enemies in view are deeper than any empire.

The image of the sunrise from on high is among the most beautiful in Luke's Gospel. Zechariah the priest knows his prophets — the great light dawning on a people in darkness (Isa. 9:2), the sun of righteousness rising with healing (Mal. 4:2) — and the image he chooses reaches back through centuries of longing.

The Sunrise — the one who gives light to those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death, and who guides their feet into the way of peace. Nine months of silence have filled this man's mouth with something far better than anything he said before it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Benedictus is covenant theology at its most compact. Zechariah identifies the coming of Jesus as the fulfilment of three overlapping promises: the Davidic covenant (the horn of salvation in the house of David, vv. 69-70), the Abrahamic covenant (the oath sworn to Abraham, vv. 73-75), and the prophetic promise (the forerunner going before the Lord, vv. 76-77).

All three lines of God's covenant faithfulness converge in the two children born in this chapter. The God who made promises to Abraham two thousand years earlier is fulfilling them — not approximately, not symbolically, but specifically, in the births of two real children at a datable moment in history.

The purpose of that salvation is stated with remarkable precision in vv. 74-75: that we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him all our days. Salvation is not merely rescue. It is freedom for a particular kind of life.

The one delivered from the enemy's hand is freed not for autonomous self-determination but for worship — for service before the face of God, in holiness and righteousness, without the crippling fear that guilt and condemnation produce. This is the goal of redemption: a people who serve God freely because they have been freely saved.
verseByVerse.examples:
Zechariah's first words after nine months of silence are praise and prophecy — not self-vindication, not explanation, not a word of reproach for the community that doubted him. The discipline of the long silence has produced a man who, when he opens his mouth, speaks entirely about God and about what God is doing.

That is the fruit of involuntary silence used well: what comes out at the end is not our own words. Preachers, teachers and parents forced into seasons of silence — made to listen rather than speak, to receive rather than give — often find that what finally emerges is purer and truer than anything they said before it.

The Benedictus ends with John: the child grew and became strong in spirit, and was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel. The wilderness is both his geographical home and his spiritual formation. He is being shaped in hiddenness for the public ministry that will announce the Coming One.

Every major figure in redemptive history has had a wilderness — Abraham, Moses, David, Elijah, Paul, and the Lord himself. The wilderness is not the failure of the plan. It is the formation of the messenger, and it cannot be hurried.

verseByVerse.quote: And his father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying, 'Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people
verseByVerse.commentary:
His father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying: blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people.

The Benedictus. Zechariah’s song is called the Benedictus, from its first word in Latin (blessed). Like Mary’s, it is woven from the Old Testament. It has two halves: praise for what God has done through the Messiah of David’s line (vv. 68–75), and a prophecy about John’s role (vv. 76–79). Zechariah, a priest, praises God first for the Messiah, not for his own son: John is secondary; Jesus is the centre.

Filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied. The priest who doubted now speaks as a prophet. The Spirit of prophecy, silent in Israel for centuries, is speaking again, and the first thing the man does is not explain or describe what he saw. He preaches.

Blessed be the Lord God of Israel. A traditional Jewish blessing; it is how the Psalms bless God (Psalm 41:13; 72:18; 106:48), and Zechariah the priest has said the words thousands of times. He has never once said them about this.

For he has visited. “Visited” (epeskepsato): come to look after, care for. It does not mean a social call. It is the word for God coming to see about his people with the intention of acting, as when he had seen the affliction in Egypt (Exodus 3:16; 4:31), or a shepherd looking over a flock. God himself has come to his people, in the person of Jesus (7:16; 19:44).

And redeemed his people. Literally made redemption for his people (lytrōsis). Redemption is release by payment of a price, the buying back of a slave or a prisoner. The exodus was God’s great act of redemption in the Old Testament (Exodus 6:6), and the same idea lay underneath the redemption of every firstborn son, bought back with a payment to the priests (Numbers 18:15–16). Now God has acted to bring a greater redemption, which Jesus will accomplish by giving his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). Again the past tense: it is as good as done, though the Messiah is not yet born. Zechariah does not yet know what the price is going to be. He knows the transaction has begun.

Four hundred years of quiet. From Malachi to Gabriel is roughly four centuries without a prophet. Empires came and went; the Maccabees fought and won and were corrupted; the temple was defiled, cleansed, and rebuilt in marble by a murderer, and heaven said nothing. Generations of faithful Israelites prayed and died without hearing a word. And then, in the ordinary rotation of a village priest’s week of service, he came. He had not gone anywhere. He had not lost interest. He had not been waiting for Israel to improve, because Israel had not improved. The silence was never abandonment; it was an appointment being kept from the other end of it, on a date fixed before the world was made.

Redeemed from what, and at what price? From slavery to sin and from the condemnation it deserves. We were not merely lost; we were held, under the curse of the law and the sentence of death. The price was not silver or gold but the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish (1 Peter 1:18–19). He took our place and bore the penalty we owed, so that we might go free. That is why a Christian is not his own: he was bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Redemption is both a release and a change of owner.

In a sentence. Filled with the Spirit, Zechariah blessed the God of Israel for coming to his people and bringing them redemption.

On a Tuesday. If God feels silent in your life, remember the four hundred years, and remember how they ended. Keep praying and keep serving in the ordinary rotation of your week. And when you notice his visiting, a providence, an answered prayer, a word that lands, say aloud what Zechariah said: blessed be the Lord.

For worship. Blessed be the Lord God of Israel. He did not send a deputy to look in on us. He came himself, in his Son, and the visit cost him everything. The God who saw the affliction in Egypt and came down saw ours, came down further, and paid the redemption price with his own blood, so that the visited are bought, owned and loved for ever. He has never yet been late for anything, and his visit has not ended: he will come again for those he has redeemed.
verseByVerse.note: Zechariah’s song, known as the Benedictus, celebrates God’s faithfulness in terms of the Old Testament promises.

parallels.desc: blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel
he sent redemption to his people

verseByVerse.quote: and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David, as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old, that we should be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us;
verseByVerse.commentary:
And has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David, as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old, that we should be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us.

And has raised up a horn of salvation for us. A horn was a symbol of strength, like the horns of a wild ox or bull (Deuteronomy 33:17; Psalm 92:10), and specifically of strength that acts. A horn of salvation is a mighty Saviour. David called the LORD my rock and the horn of my salvation (Psalm 18:2). And there is one text Zechariah is almost certainly echoing: There I will make a horn to sprout for David; I have prepared a lamp for my anointed (Psalm 132:17). The rescue God has raised up is not an idea or a message. It is a power, and it is in David’s house.

In the house of his servant David. The Messiah comes from David’s line, as promised (v. 32). Zechariah was from Aaron’s line, but he praises God for the king from David’s line, not the priest from his own. Mary’s child, not yet born, is the horn.

As he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old. Everything happens according to Scripture. The prophets spoke God’s word (Acts 3:21). Zechariah’s point is that none of this is new. The salvation arriving in his own household is the one the prophets described for centuries, and he wants it on record that God has not improvised.

That we should be saved from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us. Psalm 106:10. Zechariah would have thought first of Israel’s political enemies, the Romans. But the deeper enemies are sin, death and Satan (Hebrews 2:14–15; Colossians 2:15). Jesus came to deliver from these.

Was Zechariah wrong about the enemies? Rome was not overthrown. Israel was not liberated. About seventy-five years after this song Jerusalem was burned and the temple pulled down stone from stone. Zechariah is speaking, Luke says, filled with the Holy Spirit, so the question deserves a straight answer. Two things answer it, and the second is much the stronger. The first is that Zechariah is repeating the language of the covenant promises, and covenant language about enemies runs deeper than any particular empire. The enemies Scripture finally names are not Roman. They are sin, death and the devil, and a Gospel that ends at an empty tomb has something to say about all three. But the better answer comes from Zechariah himself, six verses later. He defines the salvation he is singing about in so many words: to give knowledge of salvation to his people in the forgiveness of their sins (v. 77). That is his own gloss on his own prophecy. The rescue he means is not from an occupying army. It is from guilt. The old priest who had spent his life killing animals for other people’s sins is announcing that the sins themselves are about to be dealt with.

The deeper deliverance. Rome could take a man’s property, his freedom and his life. It could not touch the thing that would still have been wrong with Israel on the morning after Rome fell.

Does Christ also save me from people who hate me? Not always from their hostility in this life; he told his disciples they would be hated for his name (21:17). But he saves you from their power to harm you finally. They can take your job, your reputation, even your life, and they cannot touch your soul or separate you from God’s love (12:4–7; Romans 8:35–39). Meanwhile he commands you to love them and pray for them (6:27–28), because the same horn of salvation that rescued you can rescue them. Your real enemies, sin, death and the devil, he has already defeated.

In a sentence. God has raised up a mighty Saviour from David’s line, as the prophets foretold, to rescue his people from their enemies.

On a Tuesday. Christ is your horn of salvation, stronger than every enemy you face. Trust his strength. Name the enemy that feels strongest this week, the temptation, the fear, the accusation, and set it beside the empty tomb.

For worship. The horn has sprouted for David, and it is the strength of God in human flesh. He did not rescue his people by breaking Rome but by breaking death, and every enemy that could have destroyed us lies under his feet. As he spoke by his prophets, so he has done, and the God who promised is the God who saves.
verseByVerse.note: A horn was a symbol of strength, like a bull’s horns.

parallels.desc: I will make a horn to sprout for David

verseByVerse.quote: to show the mercy promised to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant, the oath that he swore to our father Abraham, to grant us that we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him all our days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To show the mercy promised to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant, the oath that he swore to our father Abraham, to grant us that we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him all our days.

To show the mercy promised to our fathers. God’s covenant love, promised long ago: you will show faithfulness to Jacob and steadfast love to Abraham, as you have sworn to our fathers from the days of old (Micah 7:20). Zechariah now reaches back past David to Abraham, and names the guarantee.

And to remember his holy covenant. God remembers his covenant: not that he had forgotten, but that he now acts on it (Exodus 2:24; Psalm 105:8–9). Zechariah’s name, the LORD remembers, is fulfilled; and Elizabeth’s name contains the word oath.

The oath that he swore to our father Abraham. Genesis records one occasion on which God, in so many words, swore an oath to Abraham, and it comes in the most terrible chapter of the book. It came on a mountain, after a knife had been raised over a bound boy and a hand had stopped it: By myself I have sworn, declares the LORD, I will surely bless you, and in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed (Genesis 22:16–18). God swore by himself, because there was no one greater (Hebrews 6:13–18). The promise Zechariah is standing on is underwritten by God’s own existence. It cannot fail without God failing.

The mountain and the hill. And it is worth seeing what happened on that mountain and what did not. Abraham was spared his son. The ram was in the thicket, and the father walked down the hill with the boy beside him. When the promise sworn there finally came due, the Father who swore it climbed a hill outside Jerusalem with his own Son, and there was no ram, and he did not spare him (Romans 8:32).

That we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear. The purpose of redemption is not simply freedom, but service. Salvation is not merely being got out of something. It is being got out in order to be free for something, and the something is worship. Freed from slavery to sin and fear, we are free to serve God, as Israel was freed from Egypt to worship God (Exodus 4:23). “Serve” (latreuein) means worship as well as serve; it is the word for priestly service, the temple word, and Zechariah, a priest, applies it to the whole people. “Without fear”: without fear of enemies, and without fear of God’s judgement, because we are forgiven (Romans 8:15; 1 John 4:18).

Without fear. A great many believers serve God with a low, constant dread running underneath everything: of not having done enough, of a God who is quietly disappointed, of the sin that keeps coming back. Such a person prays like an employee filing a report to a supervisor who is already unimpressed. That is not the arrangement. Zechariah puts deliverance first and service second, and the order is not decorative. The fear has to be dealt with before the serving can begin, and God deals with it himself. Perfect love casts out fear, for fear has to do with punishment (1 John 4:18). The reverent awe of verse 50 stays, and deepens for ever. The cringe goes. A servant still trying to secure his position is not yet doing the work; he is auditioning for it.

In holiness and righteousness before him all our days. The life of the redeemed: holiness toward God and righteousness toward others, every day of our lives (Ephesians 4:24; Titus 2:11–14). Salvation produces a changed life, and all our days means all of them, not only the good ones.

How do I get rid of the dread? Not by trying harder to deserve God’s approval, which only feeds it. Go back to the order of the verse: delivered first, then serving. Look at the cross, where the punishment you fear was borne in full by Christ; there is nothing left for you to pay. Remind yourself that you are a son, not a hired hand: you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but the Spirit of adoption (Romans 8:15). Confess sin quickly and specifically, and take God at his word when he forgives. Then serve because you are accepted, not in order to be. The dread may linger as a habit of mind; answer it each time with the gospel.

In a sentence. God has kept the covenant oath he swore to Abraham, rescuing his people so that they can worship and serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness, all their days.

On a Tuesday. You were redeemed in order to serve. Serve God today, not in fear, but as one set free, in holiness and righteousness. Take the task you are dreading because you might not do it well enough for God, and do it as a forgiven child doing something for his Father.

For worship. Zechariah served at the altar for a lifetime and stood in the Holy Place once, trembling. Now the whole redeemed people are priests, serving in the presence of God without fear, because the oath sworn on Moriah was kept on Calvary and nothing is left to be afraid of. We stand on a promise underwritten by God’s own being. We serve him not as slaves cringing before a master but as sons rejoicing before a Father, all our days, and all our days will open at last onto a day that has no end.

parallels.desc: the covenant he made with Abraham

verseByVerse.quote: And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways, to give knowledge of salvation to his people in the forgiveness of their sins,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways, to give knowledge of salvation to his people in the forgiveness of their sins.

And you, child. For eight verses Zechariah has sung about somebody else’s son. Now he turns to his own, eight days old, perhaps holding him in his arms, and speaks to him directly. These are the only recorded words Zechariah ever addressed to John.

Will be called the prophet of the Most High. Jesus will be called Son of the Most High (v. 32); John is the prophet of the Most High. A great title, the first true prophet in Israel for four centuries, but not the greatest, and a father is making the ranking. Zechariah, holding his miracle baby on the day of his circumcision, tells him plainly that he is the servant of another. There is not a trace of ambition in the sentence.

For you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways. Malachi 3:1 and Isaiah 40:3 laid together: prepare the way of the LORD. John goes before the Lord, and the one he goes before is Jesus. And notice the pronoun, because it is quietly enormous. In both prophets, the one whose way is being prepared is the LORD himself, the God of Israel, named by his covenant name. Zechariah applies it to the child in Mary’s womb. Again, Jesus is identified as the Lord God.

To give knowledge of salvation to his people. Not to save them himself, but to tell them what salvation is and where it is found: Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! (John 1:29). John’s work is not to procure the forgiveness, he cannot, but to make it known, so that people understand what is on offer and who is offering it. Preaching does not create the salvation. It carries the news of it, and news is useless in a locked drawer.

In the forgiveness of their sins. Here is what the Benedictus has meant all along: not first freedom from Rome, but forgiveness of sins. Zechariah, and Luke, make clear that the enemies of verse 71 are, above all, our sins and their consequences. John will preach a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins (3:3). Jesus will send his disciples to proclaim repentance and forgiveness of sins in his name to all nations (24:47). That is the standard by which every claim to be preaching the gospel can be measured, and it has not shifted in two thousand years.

The truth about ourselves. John’s method of giving that knowledge, when he came to preach, was not what most people expect of a herald of good news. He told people the truth about themselves. You cannot hand a man the knowledge of forgiveness while he is convinced there is nothing to forgive. That is why the road to Bethlehem runs through repentance, and why a preacher who never troubles anybody has not prepared a way for anything.

How do I know my sins are forgiven? Not by a feeling, though feelings of peace often come, but by God’s promise to everyone who turns from sin and trusts in Christ. If you have come to him confessing your sin and relying on his death for you, he has forgiven you, completely, because he is faithful to his word and just to the blood of his Son (1 John 1:9).
