Your story matters as a witness to what he has done, but the heart of it is the message: who Jesus is, that he died for sinners and rose again, and that he calls everyone to turn and trust him. Say it simply, as the shepherds did. You do not need answers to every objection; you can say, I do not know, but I know this. And do not be discouraged if people only wonder. Your task is to tell; it is the Spirit’s work to turn wonder into faith.

In a sentence. Having seen the child, the shepherds told everyone what had been said about him, and all who heard were amazed.

On a Tuesday. You don’t need credentials to tell others about Jesus. Tell what you have heard and seen. And examine your own wonder: has it ever gone through the doorway? If you love the Christmas story but have never bowed to the child in it, do it today.

For worship. The first sermon about Jesus Christ was preached by shepherds in a village at night, and its whole content was a baby and what God had said about him. From that night to this, the Lord has never needed impressive heralds, because the news carries its own glory: the Son of God has been born for sinners. The empire that despised those men has gone. The news they carried has gone out into the languages of the earth, and the child they spoke of is still the Saviour, Christ the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: But Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart.

But Mary treasured up all these things. The but is doing real work: everybody else in the room wondered; Mary went deeper. “Treasured up” (synetērei): kept carefully, held on to, the way a person stores something valuable rather than leaving it out. “Things” is rhēmata, words and events. This is probably one of Luke’s hints at his source: who else could have told him these things, but Mary herself (1:2–3)? If she is the source behind these chapters, this verse is her own account of what she was doing while everybody else was exclaiming.

Pondering them in her heart. “Pondering” (symballousa): literally throwing together, putting together, comparing, thinking through, seeking the meaning. It is the word a person would use for comparing two accounts, or matching a piece to the pattern. So this is not vague reverie. Mary is doing something specific and strenuous. She now has in her possession an angel’s announcement, a relative’s prophecy, her own song, a birth in a stranger’s animal quarters, and a group of shepherds at midnight with a story about an army in the sky. She cannot make one picture of it yet. She lays the pieces alongside each other and keeps turning them. She did not understand everything (v. 50), but she reflected on it.

A believer’s inner method. Something happens that has God’s fingerprints on it and no available explanation. The two usual responses are to force a meaning onto it at once, or to let it go as nothing. Mary does neither. She holds it, unexplained, and works at it. That means keeping a record of what God has actually done and said, so that it is still there in five years when a piece arrives that makes sense of it; resisting the urge to tidy providence into a lesson while it is still happening; and carrying an unresolved thing for a long time without either abandoning it or pretending it is resolved.

The child at the centre of the pieces. Every piece Mary was turning over concerned one person. The angel had called him the Son of the Most High, whose kingdom would have no end (1:32–33). The shepherds had heard him called Saviour and Lord. And she had just wrapped him in cloths and laid him where the animals ate. Mary was among the first on earth to hold together, in one heart, the pieces of what the church would spend centuries learning to confess: that the baby she nursed was her Lord, truly man and truly God, one person. She could not yet see how. She did not let go of either half.

What does Christian meditation look like? It is not emptying the mind, as in Eastern practices, but filling it with God’s word and turning it over. Take a short passage, read it slowly several times, and ask: what does this say about God? About Christ? About me? What does it command, promise or warn? Connect it to other things you know of Scripture, as Mary connected the angel’s words with the shepherds’ story. Then turn it into prayer and praise. Ten unhurried minutes on a few verses will often do more than an hour of skimming. Psalm 1 calls the man blessed who meditates on God’s law day and night.

In a sentence. Mary carefully kept all these things and kept thinking them over in her heart.

On a Tuesday. Don’t just be amazed by Christ. Treasure and ponder what God has said and done. Take time today to reflect on a passage of Scripture. And keep the record: write down the thing God did this year that you still do not understand, and come back to it.

For worship. Twelve years later Luke says the same of her again (2:51), and there is no sign she had it all worked out even then. The God who gave her the pieces did not leave her holding them for ever. After the cross and the empty tomb Luke shows her among the disciples in the upper room, praying with those who now knew who her son was (Acts 1:14). The child she had pondered in the straw was the risen Lord she worshipped. He is patient with his ponderers, and he gives them, in his time, the whole picture, which is himself.

parallels.desc: his father kept the saying in mind

verseByVerse.quote: And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, as it had been told them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, as it had been told them.

And the shepherds returned. To their flocks, to their ordinary work. Their circumstances were the same; they were not. These men had seen the glory of God break over a hillside, heard the armies of heaven, found the Messiah of Israel lying in a feeding trough, and told everybody in the village. And when the night was over there was nothing for them to do except go back out to the flock and take the next watch. Luke does not record that any of them left their trade, or that they were ever heard of again.

Glorifying and praising God. They join the angels’ song (v. 14). The night did not deliver them from the ordinary; it went with them into it. Everybody who has come down from a mountaintop knows the temptation: the conference ends, the retreat closes, Tuesday arrives, and we conclude that the real thing was up there and this down here is the interval between. The shepherds’ testimony is the opposite. The glory came to them at work, in the middle of a shift, and sent them back to the same sheep praising.

The angels left, and the child stayed. Why could they go back praising? Because what they had seen was not a vision that faded with the light. The angels went back into heaven (v. 15); the child stayed. The glory had not visited a hillside and withdrawn, as it once withdrew from the temple in Ezekiel’s day. It had taken flesh in a village down the road, and would grow up in Nazareth, walk the roads of Judea and Galilee, and die for the sins of men like them. Their ordinary work was now done in a world where God was with them in a man. That is still the Christian’s footing on a Monday: not the memory of a high moment, but a living Lord who is present in the ordinary because he once entered it.

For all they had heard and seen, as it had been told them. Heard (from the angel) and seen (the child): everything matched. The word of God and the facts agreed. Luke closes the section by underlining that last clause once more. The word came; they acted on it; they found it exactly as promised; and their praise is specifically for the correspondence between the two. That is what the whole chapter has been about since its first verse.

Should a new believer leave his job to serve God? Usually not. Paul told the Corinthians that each should remain in the condition in which he was called, and serve God there (1 Corinthians 7:17–24). God calls some to leave their nets and preach, and the church should test such a call. But most believers glorify God by going back to the sheep: doing their ordinary work honestly, well and joyfully, for the Lord and not for men (Colossians 3:23). The question is not whether your job is spiritual enough, but whether you do it with praise.

In a sentence. The shepherds went back to their work praising God for all they had heard and seen, exactly as they had been told.

On a Tuesday. Go back to your ordinary work today glorifying and praising God. Christ is born, and everything is as he said. Take one moment in the shift, the commute or the washing-up to say aloud what you have heard and seen of him.

For worship. Everything was as it had been told them: the decree, the town, the trough, the song. The God of Bethlehem is the God whose word and works never come apart, and on that night they met most perfectly, because the Word himself, as John calls him, lay in a manger. Shepherds went home in the dark, singing, to a job nobody respected, and heaven had sung first, because the Lord of glory had become their neighbour.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–40 — Jesus Presented at the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The presentation is the scene where the old covenant meets the new — where the long story of Israel's worship, sacrifice and waiting encounters the one the whole system had been pointing at.

Joseph and Mary come to Jerusalem for two duties, both required by the law: the purification of the mother forty days after the birth of a son (Lev. 12:1-8), and the presentation of the firstborn to the LORD (Exod. 13:2, 12-15; Num. 18:15-16). They bring the offering of the poor — two birds rather than a lamb and a pigeon — which tells us plainly what the family's circumstances were. The King of heaven and earth was raised in poverty.

Simeon is described in the language of the faithful remnant: righteous, devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, with the Holy Spirit upon him. That phrase, the consolation of Israel, comes from Isaiah 40 — “Comfort, comfort my people” — the promised end of exile and return of God to his people. Simeon has been waiting inside that chapter his whole life, and the Spirit has promised him he will not die before he sees the Lord's Christ.

Now, as a young couple with the offering of the poor come into the courts, the Spirit moves him. He takes the child into his arms, and everything he has spent his life waiting for is a warm weight in his hands.

His song — the Nunc Dimittis — is among the most moving passages in Luke. The verbs are those of a sentry being stood down after a long watch. He can go now: his eyes have seen God's salvation, and the salvation he is holding is not for Israel only but “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” — the fulfilment of Isaiah's Servant Songs (42:6; 49:6) and the universal scope of the gospel announced before it has begun.

And then the shadow falls. The child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, a sign to be opposed; and a sword will pierce Mary's own soul. Joy and sorrow are not opposites in Luke's Gospel. They are twins, born of the same truth. The one who is the light of the world will be rejected, and the one whose birth the angels celebrated will die on a cross. Simeon holds the baby and sees all of it.

Anna is the second witness the law required (Deut. 19:15) — a daughter of Asher, one of the tribes long written off as lost, who has given decades of widowhood to fasting and prayer in that building and who arrives at exactly the right hour. And the section closes with the family's return to Nazareth and a single sentence covering the boy's whole childhood: he grew, became strong, was filled with wisdom, and the favour of God was upon him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Simeon's announcement that the child is “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (v. 32) is the fulfilment of Isaiah's Servant Songs and the theological seed of the entire Gentile mission of Acts. From the moment of the presentation, Luke's Gospel contains within it the global church. The child in Simeon's arms is not merely the king of the Jews; he is the light of the world.

This is why Luke, writing for a Gentile reader, is the Gospel that most fully develops the universal reach of the good news. The trajectory is established here, in the temple courts, by an old man who has waited his whole life to say what he now says and who is ready to die.

Simeon's warning to Mary — that a sword will pierce her own soul — has been understood in the tradition as pointing to her presence at the crucifixion (John 19:25-27). The word is rhomphaia, the great broad sword, and Simeon does not soften it. The sword is the sword of grief, of the suffering that participation in the Son's mission inevitably involves.

But the clause “that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed” shows a wider purpose. The coming of Jesus forces a crisis of decision in every heart; he does not leave people neutral. He is “appointed for the fall and rising of many” — the stone of Isaiah 8:14 laid in the middle of the road. His presence divides, and in dividing it discloses what was already there.
verseByVerse.examples:
Simeon's “now you are letting your servant depart in peace” is the model of a death well prepared for — not the resignation of a man who has given up, but the discharge of a sentry who has received what he was waiting for. And notice what his peace does not rest on: not on achievement (we are told nothing of what he accomplished), not on longevity, but on what his eyes have seen.

The Christian who has seen that same salvation — not with physical eyes but with the eyes of faith, and has taken hold of it — has precisely what Simeon had, and may face death on precisely the same terms. Not because death is nothing, but because what lies beyond it is the same Christ known in life.

Anna is Luke's portrait of long faithfulness. She had been waiting most of her adult life — decades of widowhood — for the redemption of Jerusalem. She did not give up, did not grow cynical, and did not stop praying because the answer had not come. When it came, she was exactly where she had always been.

Her years were not the waiting room for her ministry; they were the making of it. Sixty years of fasting and prayer produced a woman who could recognise God in a poor family's arms when everyone around her saw a queue — and who knew, by name, everyone in Jerusalem who was waiting to be told. The reward of patient faithfulness is rarely glamorous. It is being in the right place when God acts.

verseByVerse.quote: And at the end of eight days, when he was circumcised, he was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the end of eight days, when he was circumcised, he was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.

When he was circumcised. On the eighth day, as the law required (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3), like John (1:59). Eight days old, and the first blood he ever shed was shed in obedience to the law he had written. Circumcision was the sign of the covenant given to Abraham. It marked a boy as belonging to the covenant people, under its promises and under its obligations.

In the flow. Verse 21 closes the birth story and opens the temple scenes. Luke has told the beginnings of John and Jesus side by side: two announcements, two births, two circumcisions and namings (1:59–63). But John’s naming set the whole hill country talking, and Jesus’ naming passes in half a verse, because the greater child came more quietly. The verse also starts a thread Luke will pull all through the chapter: everything is done as the law required (vv. 22–24, 27, 39). The child who is circumcised under the law is carried into the temple, where the law’s own faithful servants, Simeon and Anna, will recognise him as the one it was all pointing to.

Under the law, all the way down. Luke gives it half a verse, and it is worth more. The Son of God enters his own creation and, before he is nine days old, is cut with a knife in submission to a requirement he himself laid down. He does not stand outside the law and gesture at it from a distance. He steps under it, all the way down: born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5). There was no way to redeem people who were under something except by getting under it with them. From the beginning he fulfilled it perfectly, on our behalf (Matthew 5:17).

He was called Jesus. The LORD saves (1:31). It was a common enough name; there are several men of that name in Josephus, and that is part of the point. The name over the cross would be an ordinary name from an unremarkable town.

The name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb. Mary and Joseph obeyed exactly. The naming was not a family decision made in the weeks after the birth; it was settled by Gabriel before there was anything to name.

The knife and the name. Hold the two halves of the verse together, because Luke has put them in one sentence for a reason. On the same day the child is cut into the covenant, he is given the name that says how the covenant will finally be kept. The knife and the name arrive together, and they will arrive together again at the end: the blood and the saving, the wound and the rescue, in the same event.

Why did Jesus need to keep the law for us? Because we have not kept it, and God’s law still stands. Christ did two things for his people. He bore the penalty for our disobedience on the cross, and he lived the perfect obedience we owed, from the eighth day to the last. Both are counted to everyone who trusts him: our sins to him, his righteousness to us (2 Corinthians 5:21). That is why a believer can stand before God not merely pardoned but accepted as righteous. This is what the Bible calls justification: God declaring a sinner righteous in his sight, not because of anything the sinner has done, but because Christ’s obedience and death are credited to him (Romans 4:5). Your record before God is not your week; it is his life.

In a sentence. On the eighth day Jesus was circumcised and named Jesus, as the angel had commanded before he was conceived.

On a Tuesday. Jesus kept God’s law from his first week of life, for you. His obedience is counted as yours. When you fail today, do not try to cover it with extra effort. Confess it, and rest on the obedience that began in Bethlehem and was finished on the cross.

For worship. Jesus does nothing in this verse; it is done to him. He is carried, held, named and cut, entirely passive, at eight days old. The first thing the Saviour ever did about our salvation, he did by being handed over to somebody else’s hands, and the last thing he did about it, he did the same way. The Lord of the law became its subject, so that its subjects might become sons.

parallels.desc: the name given by the angel

verseByVerse.quote: And when the time came for their purification according to the Law of Moses, they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord (as it is written in the Law of the Lord, 'Every male who first opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord') and to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the Law of the Lord, 'a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the time came for their purification according to the Law of Moses, they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord (as it is written in the Law of the Lord, every male who first opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord) and to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the Law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.

The time came for their purification. Forty days after the birth the family goes up to Jerusalem, and Luke combines two separate requirements of the law into one visit. After giving birth to a son, a mother was ceremonially unclean for forty days, and then brought an offering to the priest: a lamb for a burnt offering and a pigeon or dove for a sin offering. If she could not afford a lamb, she could bring two doves or pigeons instead (Leviticus 12:1–8). This was never a statement that childbirth was sinful; it belonged to a whole system of laws about blood and life and the boundary between the holy and the ordinary, teaching Israel by repetition that God is not to be approached casually. Unclean did not mean dirty or guilty. It meant she could not, for that time, touch anything holy or come into the sanctuary (Leviticus 12:4). The holy God lived among his people, and his nearness was so serious that even life’s most natural events had to be marked before his presence.

Why their purification? A reader with Leviticus open will trip over the pronoun. The law prescribes purification for the mother alone. The child needs none; Joseph needs none. Luke is probably describing the family’s observance as a whole, the household going up together to discharge what the law laid on them, so that the pronoun covers the journey rather than the rite. It may include Joseph, or the family, or simply be loose phrasing. Some later copies smoothed it to her, which is where the older English reading comes from; but their is the harder and better-attested wording, and a copyist is far likelier to have tidied a difficulty than to have created one.

To present him to the Lord. Every firstborn son belonged to God, because God had spared Israel’s firstborn at the Passover, when the firstborn of Egypt were not (Exodus 13:2, 12–15). The firstborn had to be redeemed, bought back, by a payment of five shekels to a priest (Numbers 18:15–16). Luke does not mention the payment, but speaks of presenting him, as Hannah presented Samuel to the Lord for his service (1 Samuel 1:22–28). Jesus is truly holy to the Lord, given wholly to God. What Luke shows is the firstborn handed over to the Lord, who will himself pay a much larger price, not have it paid for him.

Nothing to be purified from. The oddity is worth sitting with, because the whole scene is saying it. Of every person in the temple courts that day, this forty-day-old child is the one with nothing whatever to be purified from. He is holiness itself, carried in a girl’s arms, and he is brought in anyway, counted in with the rest, circumcised on the eighth day and presented on the fortieth like any other son of Israel.

A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons. The offering of the poor (Leviticus 12:8). Mary brings the birds: Mary and Joseph could not afford a lamb. That single detail tells us what the family’s finances were, and it should be allowed to land. Jesus was born into a poor family. The King of heaven and earth was raised by people who could not afford the standard offering. He grew up in a house where the cheaper option was chosen because it had to be. Anyone who has ever stood at a counter and taken the smaller thing because the larger one was out of reach has stood where Mary stood that morning, and the child she was carrying grew up in that house on purpose.

Was Mary a sinner? The law required a mother to bring a sin offering after childbirth (Leviticus 12:6–8), and Mary brought it, as every mother did. Roman Catholic teaching holds that Mary was preserved from all sin. But Mary herself calls God my Saviour (1:47), and Scripture says all have sinned (Romans 3:23) with the single exception of her Son. She shared the common need of all people for a Saviour, and obeyed the law that provided for it. She too was a sinner needing atonement, and her atonement was in her arms.

Does Jesus understand money worries? Yes, from the inside. He grew up in a house that counted coins, worked with his hands for a living, later had nowhere to lay his head, and depended on the gifts of others (8:3; 9:58). He is not a distant Lord who cannot sympathise. Bring your bills, your fears about the rent and your shame about being poor to him in prayer; he knows the counter where you take the cheaper thing. And if you are not poor, remember that the Lord himself was raised by people who chose the two birds. Look out for those in your church who are choosing them now.

In a sentence. Forty days after his birth, Mary and Joseph brought Jesus to the temple to present their firstborn to the Lord and to offer the poor family’s sacrifice for Mary’s purification.

On a Tuesday. Everything you have, including your children, belongs to God. Present them to him in prayer today, by name, as Mary and Joseph did.

For worship. She could not afford a lamb, and she was carrying the Lamb of God (John 1:29). The God who asked a lamb of every mother in Israel provided the one Lamb for every sinner, and laid him first in the arms of a poor girl holding two birds. The birds were offered that day and forgotten. The Lamb grew up, walked back into the same courts, and offered himself once for all, so that no mother and no sinner need ever bring another.
verseByVerse.note: Forty days after the birth of a son the mother brought a purification offering. Firstborn sons belonged to the LORD and were redeemed. Two birds instead of a lamb was the offering of the poor.

parallels.desc: every firstborn is holy to the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon, and this man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. And it had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon, and this man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him. It had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ.

A man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon. Luke turns the camera away from the family to a man crossing the temple courts, and tells us four things about him in a single verse. He is not said to be a priest; he is an ordinary godly man, and his words in verse 29 imply he was old. He was righteous toward God’s law and devout (eulabēs), careful and reverent, the same covenant vocabulary used of Zechariah and Elizabeth in chapter 1.

Waiting for the consolation of Israel. “Consolation” (paraklēsin): comfort, encouragement. The phrase has an address. It comes from the great turn in Isaiah: Comfort, comfort my people, says your God (Isaiah 40:1), the announcement that the exile is over, that the warfare is ended, that God is coming back to his people along a road made straight in the desert. Simeon has been living inside that chapter. He is not waiting for a general improvement in the national mood. He is waiting for God to keep a specific promise in a specific book. He was one of the faithful remnant, the believing few within Israel whom God always kept for himself (Romans 11:5), who were waiting, like Anna (v. 38) and Joseph of Arimathea (23:51).

The comfort was coming as a child. Isaiah’s comfort was never going to be a better political season. Its heart was that God himself would come: Behold your God (Isaiah 40:9). Luke will quote that same chapter when John the Baptist appears, as the voice crying in the wilderness to prepare the way of the Lord (3:4–6), and the one whose way John prepares is Jesus. So the consolation Simeon waited for was not an event but a person, the Lord’s own Christ, and when he came, he was small enough to hold. Every promise of comfort in the prophets had been travelling toward this child, and every comfort the church has known since has flowed from him.

And the Holy Spirit was upon him. The Spirit, who had been silent in Israel, is now active: on Elizabeth, Zechariah, Mary, John and Simeon. Three times in three verses Luke mentions the Spirit in connection with Simeon (vv. 25, 26, 27): upon him, revealing to him, moving him into the temple. Israel had had no prophet for four centuries, and now the Spirit is everywhere in this Gospel’s opening. The silence is not merely being broken. It is being flooded.

That he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Christ. A personal promise. “The Lord’s Christ”: the Messiah who belongs to God, God’s anointed one (Psalm 2:2). We are not told when that promise was given, or how long ago. It had been revealed, and it stood. Which means Simeon had been carrying a private word from God for years, possibly for decades, with no way of proving it to anybody, no date attached, and a body that was visibly running out of time. Every year that passed made the promise harder to hold and closer to fulfilment, and he had no means of telling which.

The promise not yet kept. That is a position a good many older believers know from the inside: the thing God once made you sure of, which has still not happened, and which you have long since stopped mentioning to people because of the way they look at you. Simeon’s promise was kept. It was kept at the last possible end of a long life, in a place he had walked through a thousand times, on a morning that began like every other.

Should I expect personal promises from God like Simeon’s? Simeon lived at a unique moment, when the Spirit was announcing the Messiah’s arrival, and his revelation was part of that. Today God speaks to us through his completed word, and its promises are ours in Christ: they are more sure than any private impression (2 Peter 1:19). Be careful about treating a strong feeling as a promise from God; many have been badly hurt by doing so. But the shape of Simeon’s life is ours: we too are waiting, for Christ’s return, on the strength of God’s word, and that promise will be kept as surely as his was.

In a sentence. Simeon, a righteous and devout man in Jerusalem waiting for God’s promised comfort, had been told by the Holy Spirit that he would see the Messiah before he died.

On a Tuesday. Waiting on God is not wasted time. Wait faithfully, as Simeon did, for what God has promised. Fill the waiting with what filled his: the Scriptures, the house of God, prayer, and an eye open for Christ.

For worship. For years a man walked the temple courts carrying a promise nobody else could see, and God never once forgot it. The comfort of Israel was on its way to him the whole time, down the road Isaiah had seen made straight, and it came at last through the gate in the arms of a poor couple. The God of all comfort does not keep his promises late. He keeps them at the hour he set, and in keeping his word to one old man he kept it to the world.
verseByVerse.note: “The consolation of Israel” means the comfort God had promised his people.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came in the Spirit into the temple, and when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the Law, he took him up in his arms and blessed God and said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came in the Spirit into the temple, and when the parents brought in the child Jesus to do for him according to the custom of the Law, he took him up in his arms, blessed God and said:

And he came in the Spirit into the temple. Luke does not say Simeon decided to go to the temple that morning; he says he came in the Spirit, led at exactly the right moment, on a day when the courts were full of people.

When the parents brought in the child Jesus. Into the temple courts, perhaps the Court of the Women: one poor couple among many, with a baby. Consider the arithmetic of that morning. The temple complex covered something like thirty-five acres. Mary and Joseph had come to do a small, ordinary thing that dozens of families did every week. They were not expecting to be met. Simeon did not know who he was looking for; he had a promise, not a description. And out of all that crowd the old man walks straight to the right child.

Most appointments look like this. Neither party is aware of what is about to happen, and most of the appointments God keeps are like that from the inside. There is no sense in the room of a scene being staged. There is an old man following an impulse, a young couple doing their duty, a queue for the offerings, and a providence that has been arranging this meeting for longer than anyone present has been alive.

He took him up in his arms. The old man takes the baby in his arms. The long wait ends in an embrace. It is one of the great pictures of Scripture, and it is easy to hurry past because it is so quiet. Here is the old covenant, in the person of a man near the end of his life, standing in the temple that had been the centre of Israel’s worship for a thousand years, and it reaches out and takes the new covenant into its arms, in the form of a six-week-old baby. Everything the temple existed to do, everything the sacrifices had been pointing at, everything the prophets had been promising, is now a warm weight in an old man’s hands. The whole system is holding the thing it was built to announce, and the thing it was built to announce is going to make the system unnecessary.

And blessed God. Not a speech to the crowd, nor an announcement to the priests. The first response of a man who has just received what he waited a lifetime for is to turn away from the gift and speak to the Giver.

How can I know the Spirit is leading me? The Spirit leads above all through the Scriptures he inspired, and he never leads contrary to them. He also guides through godly counsel, through providence, and through desires he shapes in a heart soaked in his word, as Simeon’s was. Most of his leading is not felt as a dramatic impulse at the time; it is seen afterwards, when you notice that you were in the right place. So do not wait for a sensation before you act. Walk in obedience to what is written, pray for guidance, and trust that he is ordering your steps even when you cannot feel it.

In a sentence. Led by the Spirit into the temple just as Jesus’ parents brought him in, Simeon took the child in his arms and praised God.

On a Tuesday. When God gives you a good gift today, do what Simeon did: before you speak about it to anyone, speak about it to him.

For worship. The God who fills heaven let himself be lifted by an old man’s arms, and the hands that had waited a lifetime closed round the one who holds all things together. Simeon held the Christ and turned at once to bless the Father, which is exactly what the Son came to bring us to do. Blessed be the God who put his Son into an old man’s arms, and puts him, by faith, into ours.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation that you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation that you have prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel.

The Nunc Dimittis. Simeon’s song is called the Nunc Dimittis, from its first words in Latin (now you dismiss). It has been sung at evening services for something like fifteen hundred years, and it is the shortest of the three songs in Luke’s opening. It is also the only one sung by somebody who is about to die.

Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace. Two words carry the picture. “Lord” here is not the usual kyrios but despotēs, Master, the word for the master of a household with absolute authority over his slaves, the word a slave used of his owner; and servant is doulos, the slave himself. “Depart” (apolyeis): release, dismiss, discharge, stand a man down, as a master releases a slave from duty, or as a watchman is relieved at the end of his shift. Simeon had been on watch for the Messiah. Now he has seen him, and he can be released: he can die in peace. He is not saying he wants to die. He is saying his watch is over and he may go off duty. A man who has seen Christ is ready to die.

According to your word, for my eyes have seen your salvation. The promise that he would see the Lord’s Christ before he died has been kept. Simeon looks at a forty-day-old baby and says: I have seen your salvation. He does not say I have seen the one who will bring salvation. He says he has seen salvation itself. In his arms. Salvation is not a thing, an idea or a system. It is a person. To see Jesus is to see God’s salvation. All the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God (Isaiah 52:10).

Prepared in the presence of all peoples, a light for revelation to the Gentiles. Not only for Israel. This is where the song opens out. Isaiah 42:6 and 49:6, where the LORD says it is too small a thing for the Servant merely to restore Israel: I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth. In the temple of Israel, at the presentation of a Jewish baby, under the law of Moses, a devout old Jewish man announces that this child is salvation for the Gentiles. Before Jesus has spoken a word, before a single disciple is called, the global reach of the gospel is announced in the temple courts by a man who is ready to die. This is the theme of Luke and Acts: the gospel goes from Jerusalem to the nations (24:47; Acts 1:8; 13:47, where Paul quotes the same verse). Every Gentile who has ever come to Christ came in through a door that Simeon saw standing open.

And for glory to your people Israel. The Messiah is Israel’s greatest glory, the one in whom all her history and hope are fulfilled: from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all (Romans 9:5).

A death well prepared for. This passage is read at more funerals than almost any other in Luke. Simeon is the picture of a death well prepared for, and notice what it does not depend on. Not on achievement: we are told nothing whatever about what he accomplished. Not on longevity, or on being ready in some general sense. He can go because my eyes have seen your salvation. His peace rests entirely on something outside himself which he has laid hold of. That is available. Nobody now will hold the infant Christ in the temple. But the salvation Simeon saw with his eyes is the same salvation offered to faith, and the man or woman who has taken hold of it has exactly what Simeon had, and may be discharged on exactly the same terms.

What happens to a believer at death? Depart in peace is exactly right. The believer’s soul goes at once to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). There is no purgatory to pass through, because Christ has already made full purification for sins (Hebrews 1:3), and no sleep of the soul in between: the dying thief was promised, today you will be with me in paradise (23:43). The body rests in the grave until Christ returns and raises it in glory (Westminster 32.1). So a Christian may face death as Simeon did, not with bravado but with peace, because his watch is over and his Master is calling him home.

In a sentence. Simeon praised God that he could now die in peace, for he had seen God’s salvation, a light to reveal God to the Gentiles and the glory of Israel.

On a Tuesday. If you have seen Christ by faith, you can face death in peace. Pray Simeon’s prayer at the end of the day, as the church has done for centuries at evening prayer. Every night’s sleep is a small rehearsal of the last one; go to it in the same peace.

For worship. The Master who posted Simeon on watch is the Master who relieved him, and he did it by putting his salvation into the old man’s hands. The light that rose that morning in a corner of the temple was prepared for all peoples, and it has crossed every sea to reach us. Because the child Simeon held would go down into death and come up out of it, the servants of this Master are not dismissed into the dark. They are dismissed in peace, into the presence of the one they waited for.
verseByVerse.note: Simeon’s song is known as the Nunc Dimittis, from its first words in Latin.

parallels.desc: my salvation to the end of the earth
all the ends of the earth shall see

verseByVerse.quote: And his father and his mother marveled at what was said about him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His father and his mother marvelled at what was said about him.

His father. Luke calls Joseph Jesus’ father, as Mary does (v. 48). He has spent a chapter and a half establishing that Joseph is not this child’s father. Now he calls him one, without comment. There is no contradiction and no carelessness. He was his legal father, who raised him, though not his biological father (3:23: as was supposed). Joseph is the father of this boy in every way that a life is lived: he named him, presented him, taught him a trade, protected him, and raised him, and Luke is content to use the ordinary word for it.

Marveled at what was said about him. Even after angels and shepherds, they were amazed, perhaps especially by the words about the Gentiles. Mary has had an angel in her room, a prophecy from Elizabeth, and a song of her own; Joseph, Matthew tells us, an angel in a dream; and shepherds have come to the manger with an account of an army in the sky. And now, six weeks later, a total stranger in the temple takes their baby in his arms and says things about him that leave them astonished. They marvelled. Which means they had not exhausted this. There was more in the child than they had grasped, and they knew it.

Never exhausted. That is a curiously encouraging verse for anyone who has been a Christian for a long time and quietly suspects everyone else understands more than they do. If the mother of Jesus, forty days in, with Gabriel’s words still ringing, could be astonished by something a stranger said about her own son, then the ordinary experience of finding that Christ keeps exceeding your account of him is not a sign of immaturity. It is a sign of accuracy.

A word for stepfathers and adoptive fathers. Any man raising a child who is not his by blood may take heart here. The Son of God was brought up by one, and Scripture calls that man his father without a footnote. The work you do in naming, providing, teaching and protecting is real fatherhood in God’s eyes. And it is a picture of the gospel itself: God adopts sons who were not his by nature, and is not ashamed to be called their Father.

In a sentence. Joseph and Mary were amazed at what Simeon said about Jesus.

On a Tuesday. The more you learn about Christ, the more there is to marvel at. Never lose your wonder. This week, read one passage about him you think you know well, and ask what you have never noticed in it.

For worship. The eternal Son, whose Father is in heaven, let a carpenter be called his father on earth, and let himself be carried, named and taught in a Galilean workshop. Those who stood nearest him were the first to be astonished at what was said about him, and they were not the last. On the day he comes he will be marvelled at among all who have believed (2 Thessalonians 1:10), and that wonder will never wear thin, because there is no bottom to his riches and no edge to his glory.

verseByVerse.quote: And Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother, 'Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that is opposed (and a sword will pierce through your own soul also), so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother: behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that is opposed (and a sword will pierce through your own soul also), so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed.

And Simeon blessed them. Simeon has blessed God; now he blesses the parents. He does not bless Jesus; the child is the source of blessing. Then he turns to Mary alone, perhaps because Joseph would not live to see what follows, and says something that must have taken the warmth out of the morning.

This child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel. Now a darker note. The word is appointed: set, placed there on purpose. And note the order: fall first, then rising. Jesus will divide Israel. Some will fall because of him, stumbling over him; others will rise, be raised up, through faith in him. Simeon is echoing Isaiah, where the LORD of hosts says he will become a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling, and many shall stumble on it, and fall and be broken (Isaiah 8:14–15). He is the stone that some stumble over and others build on (Isaiah 28:16; 1 Peter 2:6–8; Luke 20:17–18). The child is a stone laid in the middle of Israel’s road, and it is not possible to walk past him without either tripping over him or standing on him. No one can be neutral toward him.

And for a sign that is opposed. A sign spoken against. Jesus will be rejected, opposed, contradicted, and finally killed. Simeon does not say the child will meet some opposition; he says that being contradicted is part of what the sign is. Anyone who has hoped that a sufficiently winsome presentation of Christ would stop people objecting to him has hoped for something Simeon ruled out in the temple courts before Jesus could speak.

And a sword will pierce through your own soul also. A personal prophecy for Mary alone, set in brackets in many Bibles. The word for sword is not the small blade a soldier carried at his belt. It is rhomphaia, the great broad sword, the word used in the Greek Old Testament for Goliath’s weapon. Simeon does not soften it. She will suffer deep grief. Her son will be rejected and misunderstood, even by his own family (8:19–21). And John tells us she stood by the cross and watched him die (John 19:25), and there was nothing whatever she could do. The joy of the angels’ song is not the whole story. The salvation of the world will cost her the agony of seeing her son crucified.

So that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed. That is the purpose clause, and it explains the rest. Jesus reveals what is in people’s hearts. How people respond to him exposes what they really are (5:22; 6:8; John 3:19–21). He does not merely divide people; he shows what was already there. Everybody who meets him ends up disclosing something about themselves that they might otherwise never have had to face. He is the great revealer. The reaction to Jesus is a reading of the person reacting.

In the flow. Until now every voice in Luke 1 and 2 has spoken of joy: Gabriel, Elizabeth, Mary, Zechariah, the angels, the shepherds, Simeon’s own song. This verse is the first shadow. From here Luke’s Gospel shows both halves of Simeon’s word coming true: tax collectors and sinners rising, while his own town tries to throw him off a cliff (4:28–29) and the leaders plot his death. At the cross the two halves meet in two men crucified beside him, one mocking and one asking to be remembered (23:39–43). The hearts were revealed by how they met him. This is a word spoken to a mother about her son, and it is worth handling as one. There are parents reading this who have watched a child suffer and could do nothing: an illness, an addiction, a court, a coffin. It is a particular kind of pain and it does not answer to the usual comforts, because the wound is not in you, and the helplessness is the whole of it. Two things stand in this verse for such a reader. The first is that Mary was told in advance, some thirty years in advance, and it did not make it easier; God does not seem to think forewarning is the same as sparing. The second is heavier and better. The sword went through her because the nails went through him, and he was there by appointment, and what looked from the foot of that cross like the end of everything was the hour the whole world had been waiting for since Eden. The grief was real. It was not the last word about the grief.

Why do people react so strongly to Jesus? Because he does not allow neutrality. He claims to be Lord and Saviour, and that claim either draws a person to him or offends him. People can be polite about religion in general, but Jesus puts his finger on the heart: our pride, our self-righteousness, our love of sin. So do not be surprised when friends are hostile, and do not water down the gospel to avoid offence. Pray for them, love them, and remember that some who stumble over him today may rise through him tomorrow. Paul himself first opposed the sign.

In a sentence. Simeon prophesied that Jesus would cause many in Israel to fall and rise, would be opposed, would reveal people’s hearts, and that Mary’s own soul would be pierced as by a sword.

On a Tuesday. How you respond to Jesus reveals your heart. And following him may bring grief as well as joy. That is not a sign that God has failed. Ask yourself honestly where you have been stumbling over him rather than building on him, and come back to the stone.

For worship. The child in Simeon’s arms was appointed for a cross, and the sword that pierced his mother’s soul was the shadow of the spear that, as John records, pierced his side. God did not spare his Son, nor the mother who loved him, because he was determined to spare us. The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone, and all who rest their weight on him will never be put to shame.
