verseByVerse.quote: And there was a prophetess, Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in years, having lived with her husband seven years from when she was a virgin, and then as a widow until she was eighty-four. She did not depart from the temple, worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day. And coming up at that very hour she began to give thanks to God and to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a prophetess, Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was advanced in years, having lived with her husband seven years from when she was a virgin, and then as a widow until she was eighty-four. She did not depart from the temple, worshipping with fasting and prayer night and day. Coming up at that very hour, she began to give thanks to God and to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.

A man and a woman. The law required two witnesses for a matter to be established (Deuteronomy 19:15). God provides them: an old man, and now an old woman. Luke often pairs a man and a woman: Zechariah and Mary, Simeon and Anna, and many others in the Gospel.

A prophetess. Like Miriam, Deborah and Huldah in the Old Testament (Exodus 15:20; Judges 4:4; 2 Kings 22:14), and the daughters of Philip (Acts 21:9). God spoke through her. God gave prophecy to men and women at the dawn of the gospel, as Joel had promised (Acts 2:17).

Does Anna show that women should prophesy or preach today? Anna’s gift belongs to the time when God was making his new work known, before the Scriptures were complete; it is not a pattern for new revelation today, since the canon is closed and the foundational gifts have ceased. And her ministry was in the temple courts, speaking to those who came, not in leading the worship of Israel, which belonged to the priests. The New Testament reserves the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), while honouring women’s gifts in countless ways. What Anna does show is that a godly woman’s prayer and witness are precious to God, and that she may and should speak of Christ to everyone who will listen.

Anna, the daughter of Phanuel. Luke gives Anna a genealogy, which is unusual for a woman in an ancient text and is not decoration. Anna is the Greek form of Hannah, grace, the name of Samuel’s mother, whose prayer Mary echoed (1:46–55). Phanuel is the same name as Peniel, face of God, where Jacob wrestled with God (Genesis 32:30).

Of the tribe of Asher. One of the northern tribes of Israel, carried off by Assyria in 722 BC and popularly written off as lost. Some families had kept their genealogies. Here is a daughter of Asher, in the temple, at the presentation of the Messiah. The lost tribes were not lost to God. Whatever else the exile did, it did not lose anybody God intended to keep. The Messiah comes for all Israel.

Having lived with her husband seven years, and then as a widow until she was eighty-four. Married young, widowed young. Or, as the ESV footnote has it, a widow for eighty-four years, which with seven years of marriage from girlhood would make her over a hundred. Either way, a very long widowhood, and it is the picture that matters: a woman married in her teens, widowed after seven years, and never remarried, who then gave the whole remaining length of her life to God in that building. Widows were among the most vulnerable people in Israel. Anna did not remarry, but devoted herself to God: she who is truly a widow has set her hope on God and continues in prayers night and day (1 Timothy 5:5).

She did not depart from the temple, worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day. Perhaps she lived in one of the rooms in the temple courts, or was there at every service. Decades of turning up: fasting and prayer, night and day, in a temple that had grown corrupt and would be a den of robbers by the time her Messiah cleared it. Nothing to show for any of it. No congregation, no title, no record, and, so far as anyone watching could tell, no answers. She kept praying anyway. That is the whole of Anna’s biography until this morning.

And coming up at that very hour she began to give thanks to God. Not that day; that hour. She walks into the right court at the right moment after roughly sixty years of showing up, and begins to give thanks, literally to confess, acknowledge, praise.

And to speak of him to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem. “Redemption” (1:68): the liberation God had promised: the LORD has comforted his people; he has redeemed Jerusalem (Isaiah 52:9). There was a circle of faithful people waiting, and Anna told them all: he has come. She was one of the first to preach Christ. Which tells us something else about her. She knew who those people were. Sixty years in that temple had shown her exactly which of the crowd were praying for the same thing she was, and when the answer came she knew where to take it.

The redemption of Jerusalem was a child. Anna spoke of him to people waiting for Jerusalem to be redeemed, and that is a staggering thing to say about a baby six weeks old. Luke lets the phrase echo to the end of his Gospel. On the road to Emmaus two disciples say, with the light gone out of them, we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel (24:21). Anna was right, and so were they; they had not yet understood how it would be done. Jerusalem would be redeemed not by a sword but by this child’s own blood, shed outside its walls, and sealed by his rising on the third day. The risen Lord himself would open the Scriptures to them and show that this was the way it had to be (24:26–27).

For the one whose life looks like the sixty years. Something needs saying here for the reader whose life looks more like Anna’s sixty years than like Anna’s one hour. There are believers who have prayed for a marriage, a child, a church, a country, for decades, and have watched nothing move. It is very easy to conclude that the years were the waste and the answer would have been the point. Anna’s years were not the waiting room for her ministry. They were the making of it. Sixty years of fasting and prayer are what produced a woman who could recognise God in a poor family’s arms when the priests around her saw a queue, and who had, ready to hand, the names of everyone in Jerusalem who needed to be told. The single hour was the harvest. The decades were the field.

Should Christians fast today? Jesus assumed that his disciples would fast after he was taken from them (5:35; Matthew 6:16–18), and the early church fasted when seeking God’s guidance (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). It is not commanded on fixed days, and it earns nothing. But it is a good discipline: going without food, or something else, for a time, in order to give that time and hunger to prayer and to say to God that you want him more than his gifts. Start small, a meal rather than days, and talk to your doctor if you have health concerns. Keep it between you and God.

In a sentence. Anna, an aged widow and prophetess who spent her life in the temple in prayer and fasting, arrived at that moment, thanked God, and told everyone waiting for redemption about the child.

On a Tuesday. A life of prayer is never wasted, however long and unseen. And older believers can be among the most effective witnesses of all. If you are older, alone or widowed, your prayers are not the leftovers of a life; they may be its centre. And if you are younger, find the Annas of your church and ask them to pray for you.

For worship. God remembered a widow from a lost tribe and brought her into the right court at the right hour, after sixty years of prayer. He wastes no tear and no petition. He gathers the scattered of Israel and the lonely of every nation, and gives them a reason to give thanks: the redemption of Jerusalem has come, and his name is Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: Asher was one of the northern tribes. The ESV notes that verse 37 can also mean she had been a widow for eighty-four years.

parallels.desc: the widow who continues in prayers night and day

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had performed everything according to the Law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth. And the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom. And the favor of God was upon him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had performed everything according to the Law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth. The child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom, and the favour of God was upon him.

And when they had performed everything according to the Law of the Lord. Luke closes the infancy narrative with obedience to the law, which he has stressed again and again (vv. 22, 23, 24, 27, 39): the Saviour came from an obedient, devout Jewish home. Luke does not record the visit of the wise men, the flight to Egypt and the massacre at Bethlehem (Matthew 2), which happened between the presentation and the return to Nazareth. Each Gospel writer selects.

Do Luke and Matthew contradict each other? This is the sharpest question in the two birth narratives, and it is better faced than stepped over. Matthew has the magi arriving, the flight into Egypt, Herod’s killing of the boys of Bethlehem, and only after Herod’s death the settling in Nazareth. Luke moves from the temple courts to Nazareth in a single sentence, as though nothing came between. But look at what Luke’s sentence actually claims. He says they had performed everything according to the Law of the Lord: he is closing the temple business, not publishing the next morning’s itinerary. And Matthew leaves exactly the room Luke needs. The magi come to a house (Matthew 2:11), not to a stable; and Herod kills the boys two years old or under, reckoning by what the magi had told him (Matthew 2:16), which places their visit months and possibly more than a year after the night of the manger. So a sequence holds both accounts without strain: the birth, circumcision on the eighth day, presentation on the fortieth, a settled stay in Bethlehem, the magi, Egypt, Herod’s death, and the return north. And it is Matthew who supplies the reason for the very move Luke reports here without explaining it: they went to Nazareth rather than back to Bethlehem because Archelaus was now reigning in Judea and Joseph was afraid to go there (Matthew 2:22).

Two witnesses, not competitors. The two Gospels are two witnesses telling what each was given to tell. Matthew writes from Joseph’s side, with Judea’s danger in view; Luke writes from Mary’s side, with the temple’s faithfulness in view. Luke is not concealing Egypt. He told us at the outset that he had sifted his material and arranged it (1:3), and no witness who selects is thereby lying about what he leaves out.

And the child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom. Jesus grew as a normal child. His humanity was real: he learned to walk, to talk, to read, and in his human mind he was not born knowing everything, but was filled with wisdom as he grew (v. 52). Luke uses very nearly the same words of John at 1:80. A real boy, developing in a real body, in an ordinary Galilean village.

And the favor of God was upon him. “Favor” (charis): grace. God’s delight rested on him, not as a reward earned, but as the settled delight of a Father in his Son. What Luke gives instead of drama is a dozen silent years in a hill town, and one sentence to cover them. The Son of God spent the greater part of his earthly life doing nothing that anybody thought worth writing down, and the Father’s favour rested on every day of it.

Did Jesus do miracles as a child? No. The Gospels say nothing of it, and John tells us that the water made wine at Cana was the first of his signs (John 2:11). The stories of a wonder-working boy come from later legends, not from Scripture. That silence is itself a teaching: the eternal Son lived for thirty years as an ordinary village boy and working man, without display, pleasing his Father in hidden obedience. His ordinary years were not a delay before the real work; they were part of the perfect life he lived for us.

In a sentence. After fulfilling the law, the family returned to Nazareth, where Jesus grew strong and full of wisdom, with God’s favour on him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus spent nearly thirty years in an ordinary town, growing up. Faithfulness in ordinary life is God’s will for most of us, most of the time. If your days are made of school runs, spreadsheets and meals, you are walking a road the Son of God walked for longer than any other.

For worship. The favour of God rested on a boy in Nazareth whom nobody noticed, and the Father’s delight was full. Every hidden day of those years was holy, obedient and pleasing to God, and every one of them was lived for his people. He sanctified ordinary life by living it, and he is not ashamed to call us brothers.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–52 — The Boy Jesus in the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The only story from Jesus's childhood in any of the four Gospels is this one: Jesus at twelve, in the temple, sitting among the teachers, leaving the learned astonished. Luke includes it not as a charming anecdote but as a theological statement. Before the public ministry begins, Jesus is already defined by a relationship with his Father that supersedes every other claim on him — including the entirely legitimate claim of his parents.

It is worth noticing what the story is not. The apocryphal gospels of later centuries are full of tales of the boy Jesus working wonders and settling scores. In the one childhood story Scripture preserves, he performs no miracle at all. He asks questions, and then goes home and does as he is told.

The setting is Passover — the feast of Israel's redemption, commemorating the night the LORD passed over the houses marked with blood. Jesus is twelve, the year before a Jewish boy took on personal responsibility for the commandments, and this is the last Passover of his childhood. The irony Luke intends is deep: the Passover Lamb has come up to keep the Passover.

When Mary and Joseph discover him missing from the caravan and search three days, her question is entirely natural and entirely human: “Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress.” Scripture lets her say it, and does not correct her tone.

Jesus's answer contains the first recorded words of his life, and they are a claim of identity: “Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?” The word must (dei) is one of Luke's great theological words, marking the divine necessity that drives the whole redemptive plan. And the Father he names is not Joseph. He distinguishes — gently, but unmistakably — between the father who has been searching for him and the Father whose house he is in.

He had not run away, and he had broken no commandment; his surprise is genuine that after twelve years they had to be told where he would be. And then, having said it, he goes down with them to Nazareth and is subject to them for another eighteen years.
verseByVerse.theology:
The word dei — “it is necessary,” “I must” — runs through Luke and Acts and marks the divine necessity driving the story forward: the Son of Man must suffer (9:22); he must rise on the third day (24:7); the Scripture must be fulfilled (22:37). Here, at twelve years old, Jesus uses it for the first time.

This is not a child defying his parents. It is the Son of God expressing the first law of his existence: he must be about his Father's business. The whole of Luke's two-volume work is the outworking of that single must, from the temple courts in Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.

Jesus's submission after the episode — “he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them” (v. 51) — is the answer to anyone who reads his words in the temple as a claim to be exempt from ordinary human obligations. He is subject to his parents: not one act of compliance but a settled condition sustained for eighteen years.

And he genuinely grows (v. 52). The one who knows all things grows in knowledge; the one who is all-powerful grows in stature; the one in whom all wisdom is hidden grows in wisdom. This is the mystery of two natures in one person, and it means the incarnation was never a costume. It was real human life, lived fully from the inside.
verseByVerse.examples:
Mary and Joseph “did not understand the saying that he spoke to them” (v. 50) — and Mary “treasured up all these things in her heart” (v. 51). For the second time in the chapter Luke shows her holding what she does not yet understand, refusing to let go of it, waiting for the understanding to arrive.

This is one of the most honest and most encouraging pictures of faith in the Gospel. The mother of the Son of God did not always understand what he was doing. But she did not discard what she could not explain. She kept it, turned it over, and waited — and she was still carrying this one twenty years later when she stood at the foot of a cross and it began to make sense.

The closing verse is the New Testament's summary of the hidden years: Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favour with God and man. Eighteen years of silence before the public ministry begins — of growing, learning, working, and being formed in a village nobody wrote about.

The God who could have compressed everything into three years of public ministry chose instead to spend thirty in ordinariness. That is the pattern of divine formation: the long preparation, the hidden years, the slow work of wisdom and character before the public work begins. Anyone impatient to skip the hidden years has not yet understood how God shapes the people he uses.

verseByVerse.quote: Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the Feast of the Passover. And when he was twelve years old, they went up according to custom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His parents went to Jerusalem every year at the Feast of the Passover. And when he was twelve years old, they went up according to custom.

The only story of Jesus’ boyhood. The four Gospels tell us nothing of Jesus between infancy and about thirty, except this one episode. Later legends, the so-called infancy gospels of the following centuries, are full of tales of the boy Jesus: making clay birds fly, striking a playmate dead and raising him again. The canonical Gospels record one incident, and in it the boy does nothing miraculous at all. He asks questions in a temple and goes home and does as he is told. This story, probably from Mary, gives a single window into his growing self-awareness.

In the flow. This story is framed by two short summaries of the boy’s growth (vv. 40, 52), and it is the hinge between Luke’s infancy chapters and the ministry. Until now others have spoken about Jesus: angels, shepherds, Simeon, Anna. Here, for the first time, he speaks for himself, and his first words are about his Father (v. 49). The next time we meet him he is about thirty, at the Jordan, and the Father’s voice from heaven calls him my beloved Son (3:22). Here the Son says my Father; there the Father says my Son.

Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the Feast of the Passover. The law required every Jewish man to go to the sanctuary for three feasts each year: Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles (Deuteronomy 16:16). Those who lived far away often went only once, at Passover. Women were not required to go, but Mary did. A devout family, and a poor one: the journey is eighty miles each way, on foot, and it costs a working man the better part of two weeks every spring. The boy learned the Scriptures in a village synagogue, worked in a builder’s shop, and walked to Jerusalem with his family every Passover for twelve years.

The Lamb at the Passover. And it is Passover, which Luke has not chosen at random. This is the feast of the lamb whose blood on the doorposts meant the destroyer passed over the house; the feast of Israel’s redemption out of Egypt; the meal that every year told a nation how it had been bought. The Lamb of God is twelve years old and has come up to keep it. He will come up to keep it again, and the last time he does, he will take the bread in his hands at that meal and say something no one had ever said about it before.

And when he was twelve years old. In Jewish practice, as later written down in the Mishnah, a boy of thirteen became a son of the commandment, responsible to keep the law himself; the formal bar mitzvah ceremony came later still, and how fixed the age was in Jesus’ day we cannot be sure. The year before, he would begin to be prepared, and perhaps taken to the feast to learn. So this is the last Passover of his childhood and the threshold of his responsible life, which is exactly the moment Luke chooses to show him, once, before drawing the curtain again for eighteen more years.

They went up according to custom. Families travelled together in large caravans, with relatives and neighbours from their towns, for safety and company; from Nazareth the journey took about four days.

How can a family make worship a habit today? Begin with the Lord’s Day: be in church with your children every week, not when it suits, so that gathering with God’s people is simply what your family does. Add something simple at home: a short Bible reading and prayer at a meal, a psalm or hymn, praying for one another by name. Let children see you read Scripture and pray on your own. Talk about the sermon on the way home. Jesus grew up in a household where the rhythm of worship was fixed and costly, and he learned it there. Children notice what their parents treat as non-negotiable.

In a sentence. Jesus’ parents went to Jerusalem every year for Passover, and when he was twelve, they took him as usual.

On a Tuesday. Regular worship with God’s people shaped Jesus’ childhood. Make worship a habit of your family’s life. Look at next month’s calendar and see what is competing with the Lord’s Day, and decide now which wins.

For worship. Every spring a boy from Nazareth walked eighty miles to stand in the courts where lambs were killed for Israel’s redemption, and his Father knew whose death they had been rehearsing for fifteen hundred years. The Son did not avoid that road. He walked it with his family, year after year, until the year he set his face to walk it to the end. Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7), and the feast he kept as a boy he now spreads for us, with bread he calls his body, given for us.
verseByVerse.note: Every Jewish man was to go up to Jerusalem for the great feasts; families travelled together in large groups.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the feast was ended, as they were returning, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem. His parents did not know it, but supposing him to be in the group they went a day's journey, but then they began to search for him among their relatives and acquaintances, and when they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, searching for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the feast was ended, as they were returning, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem. His parents did not know it, but supposing him to be in the group, they went a day’s journey. Then they began to search for him among their relatives and acquaintances, and when they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, searching for him.

When the feast was ended. Passover and Unleavened Bread lasted eight days. Some pilgrims left after the first two days; Jesus’ parents stayed for the whole feast. Now the part every parent reads with a tightening in the chest.

The boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem. Deliberately, as his answer shows (v. 49). Not disobedience: his parents had not told him to stay with them, and assumed he was with the group. A twelve-year-old in that culture had considerable independence.

Supposing him to be in the group. In a large caravan, children ran among relatives and friends. Pilgrim caravans travelled in extended family groups, perhaps, as some have suggested, with the women and younger children setting out earlier and the men catching up, and a twelve-year-old on the threshold of adulthood could plausibly have been with either party. Each parent may have thought he was with the other. It was not neglect.

They went a day’s journey. About 20 miles (30 km). Then, at the evening camp, they discovered he was missing. They search among their relatives and acquaintances: the horrible widening circle, the same question asked of one face after another. And when they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem: a day’s walk back, in the dark of the mind, to a city of tens of thousands full of Passover crowds.

When God seems lost. This passage has comforted believers for centuries, because it is exactly the shape of an ordinary Christian trouble. There are seasons when a person who has known God for years cannot find him. Prayer goes flat. The Bible reads like a manual. Nothing has been consciously renounced, and nothing is there. Notice what Mary and Joseph did. They did not press on to Nazareth hoping he would turn up. They went back to the last place they had him, and they kept looking until they found him. And notice where he turned out to be: not lost at all, not hiding, not withdrawn in displeasure. He was in his Father’s house, exactly where he had always been, doing exactly what he had come to do, and it was they who had walked a day’s journey in the wrong direction while assuming he was somewhere in the group.

Going back, not going further on. The sense of absence is real and the distress is real. But the searching is a going back, not a going further on: back to the word, back to the place he said he would be, back to the last thing he actually said.

Can a Christian lose Christ? Not in the sense of losing salvation. Those whom the Father has given him, no one will snatch out of his hand (John 10:28–29), and the Westminster Confession teaches that true believers can neither totally nor finally fall from grace (Westminster 17.1). But a believer can lose the sense of his presence, through sin, neglect or a trial God sends, and it can last a long time (Westminster 18.4). The remedy is the one in this passage: do not assume, go back. Return to his word, confess what you know is wrong, come to the Lord’s Table, keep company with his people, and keep seeking. He has not moved.

In a sentence. After the feast, Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem without his parents knowing; after a day’s travel they discovered he was missing and went back to search for him.

On a Tuesday. Even Jesus’ godly parents assumed too much. Don’t assume Christ is with you; seek him: you will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart (Jeremiah 29:13). Ask yourself honestly when you last had real communion with him, and go back there today.

For worship. The Son who was missing for three days was never lost at all; he was in his Father’s house. And when his friends lost him again, to a tomb near this same city, he was not lost then either; he was finishing his Father’s work, and on the third day he was found alive. Our fears walk a day’s journey in the wrong direction, and his faithfulness stays exactly where his word said it would be, until we come back and find him there.

verseByVerse.quote: After three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. And all who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. And all who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers.

After three days. One day out, one day back, and a day searching: three days in which the two people responsible for the safety of the Son of God did not know where he was. Many readers have heard an echo here, and it is a fair one. The next time Mary’s son is lost to her, it will be in the same city, at the same feast, and after the third day he will be found again, alive, and still about his Father’s business, and the grief of those days will be immeasurably worse.

They found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers. Probably in the colonnades of the temple courts, where the teachers of the law sat with their pupils, especially during and after the feasts. The picture is not a boy lecturing the professors, which is how the story is often told and is not what Luke says. He is sitting among them, the posture of a student, listening and asking questions. That was exactly how rabbinic instruction worked: the teacher put a question, the pupils answered, the pupils asked in return, and understanding was reached by exchange. And yet his questions showed remarkable insight.

And all who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers. “Understanding” (synesei): insight, intelligence. He was asked questions too, and his answers astonished the experts. He is holding his own with the finest theological minds in Israel, in the temple, at twelve. Twenty years later, the teachers in this same temple would be astonished, and then furious, at his answers (20:26, 40).

Remarkable, and learning. Two things about this scene pull in opposite directions until they are held together. The first is that his understanding is genuinely remarkable: the wisdom Luke announced in verse 40 is now visible, and it is not a normal twelve-year-old’s grasp of Scripture. Something is here that the teachers cannot account for. The second is that he is learning. He listens; he asks. The eternal Son, who as God knows everything, is a boy in a real human mind that has to be taught, and he is being taught, by ordinary Jewish teachers, in the ordinary way, out of the Scriptures. The wisdom Luke reports is not information downloaded past his humanity. It is the wisdom of a boy who has been listening carefully to the word of God since he could speak, and has never once let any of it go.

No shortcut. There is no shortcut here that we are not offered. The way the boy Jesus came to know the Scriptures is the way anybody comes to know them: by sitting where they are taught, listening to them, asking about them, and turning them over. He did it perfectly, and he did it by the ordinary means.

Is it all right to ask questions in church? Yes, and Jesus did. Ask your pastor about the sermon, join a Bible study where questions are welcome, ask older believers how they understand a hard passage. Good questions come from humility, a desire to understand and obey, not from a wish to catch someone out or to show off. And when you are the one being asked, do not be afraid of saying, I do not know; let us look it up together. A church where nobody asks questions is usually a church where nobody is listening.

In a sentence. After three days of searching, they found Jesus in the temple among the teachers, listening and asking questions, and everyone was amazed at his understanding.

On a Tuesday. Jesus listened and asked questions. Learn God’s word humbly, by listening and asking. Take one question from your reading this week to someone who can help you with it.

For worship. The Wisdom of God sat among the teachers as a learner. He who gave the law to Moses listened to men explain it, and asked them questions about his own word. There is no humility like his. And in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3), opened to everyone who comes to learn from him.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers of the law sat with their pupils in the temple courts, teaching by question and answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And when his parents saw him, they were astonished. And his mother said to him, 'Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress.' And he said to them, 'Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father's house?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When his parents saw him, they were astonished. His mother said to him: son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in great distress. He said to them: why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?

Son, why have you treated us so? His parents were astonished to find him there, calmly among the teachers. Then comes the natural reproach of a frightened, relieved mother. Mary speaks; mothers often do. That is not a serene woman. That is a mother at the end of three days, and Luke does not clean it up. She is not asking for information; she is asking the question every frightened parent asks the moment the fear turns to relief, which is how could you do this to us.

Honest before God. Scripture lets her say it. The mother of the Lord speaks sharply to the Son of God, in the temple, in front of the teachers, and the Bible reports it without embarrassment and without correcting her tone. There is a whole permission in that for people who have been taught that honesty with God must first be made polite.

Your father and I have been searching for you in great distress. She calls Joseph your father. “Distress” (odynōmenoi): anguish, pain, a foretaste of the sword Simeon said would pierce her soul (v. 35).

Why were you looking for me? Then the first recorded words of Jesus in this Gospel, the first words of his that anybody wrote down, and they are a question answering a question. Not rudeness, but surprise. Why search everywhere? You should have known where I would be.

Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house? These are Jesus’ first recorded words, and they are full of meaning. “My Father”: Mary said your father, meaning Joseph; Jesus says my Father, meaning God. At twelve, he is aware of his unique relationship to God as his Father. “Must” (dei): divine necessity, the word Jesus will use of his destiny of suffering. Luke will use it again and again across his two volumes for the compulsion of God’s plan: the Son of Man must suffer (9:22), must rise on the third day (24:7), the Scripture must be fulfilled in him (22:37; 24:26). Here it appears for the first time, on the lips of a twelve-year-old, and everything that follows in Luke and Acts is the working out of it. Even as a boy, he knows he is under his Father’s purpose. That does not mean he was pushed along against his will. It means the Father’s plan made his road certain, and the Son gladly made it his own: no one takes my life from me, he would say, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18).

In my Father’s house, or about my Father’s business? Literally in the things of my Father, which can mean his Father’s house, the temple, or his Father’s affairs, his Father’s business, as the King James has it. If your Bible reads about my Father’s business, nothing is wrong. The Greek will carry either sense, and both meanings fit; the two are not rivals, since the house is where the business is done.

Did Jesus sin by worrying his parents? A careful reader is entitled to ask. He is under the fifth commandment like every other Jewish boy, and he has just caused his parents three days of anguish. If he broke that commandment, the whole gospel comes apart, because a Saviour who needs saving cannot save anybody. He did not, and the answer is in his own reply. He had not run away, and he had not been forbidden to stay. He had done nothing his parents told him not to do; he had assumed, and his words say he expected them to assume it too, that when the caravan left, everyone would know where the son of this family would be. His did you not know is not insolence. It is genuine surprise that after twelve years they had to be told. Causing someone distress is not always a sin; the sin would have been disobedience or disregard, and there was neither.

A prior claim. And there is the gentlest possible correction inside it. Mary said your father and I. He answers by naming a different Father, and by locating himself in that Father’s house. He is not disowning Joseph, whom he will go home and obey for another eighteen years. He is telling his mother, once, and then not again for a very long time, that there is a prior claim on him, and that she of all people had the means to know it.

In a sentence. When his distressed mother reproached him, Jesus answered, in his first recorded words, that they should have known he must be in his Father’s house.

On a Tuesday. Be honest with God about your distress; Mary was. And then listen for his answer, which may be a gentle question back: did you not know where I would be? Go to his house and his word this week expecting to find him there.

For worship. Jesus called God my Father from his youth, in a way no one had ever done before, because he was the eternal Son. And through him, we too may call God Father: God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, Abba! Father! (Galatians 4:6). The boy who knew he belonged in his Father’s house now brings many sons to glory (Hebrews 2:10), and, as John records his promise, has gone to prepare a place for them in that house (John 14:2).
verseByVerse.note: These are Jesus’ first recorded words.

verseByVerse.quote: And they did not understand the saying that he spoke to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they did not understand the saying that he spoke to them.

They did not understand. Even Mary and Joseph, after the angels and the prophecies, did not understand. Luke could have left that out. A writer building a legend would have had the parents nod wisely; instead he records that the two people closest to Jesus on earth heard him explain himself and did not follow it. Mary is not portrayed as all-knowing; she too had to learn.

Take the measure of what they knew. Mary had been visited by Gabriel and told this child would be called the Son of the Most High, and she had sung a song about it. Joseph, Matthew tells us, had been told in a dream who the boy was, and had taken his family to Egypt to keep him alive. They had heard shepherds, and Simeon, and Anna. If anyone on earth had the material to understand a sentence about the boy’s Father, it was these two. They did not understand it. The mystery of who Jesus was, and what his relationship to his Father meant, was too great to take in at once.

Understanding comes in instalments. This is a liberating verse for the reader who suspects that a real Christian ought to find all this clear by now. The mother of Jesus did not always know what her son meant. She had more evidence than any of us will ever have, and there were things he said that went straight past her. Understanding, in Scripture, is not the entry fee for faith. It is one of the things faith is given, in instalments, over a long time, and usually later than we would like.

Two ways with what we do not understand. Mary’s response is not to demand that he explain himself again, and it is not to decide that the saying cannot have meant much. She kept it in her heart (v. 51), as she had kept the shepherds’ words (v. 19). There is a way of handling what we do not understand that quietly disposes of it, filing it under things that are probably not important, or that scholars disagree about, or that will make sense one day, and then never returning to it. And there is Mary’s way, which is to put it somewhere safe and go on carrying it.

Not understood until he opened it. Luke uses almost the same words again of the Twelve. When Jesus tells them that he must be delivered up and suffer, they did not understand this saying (9:45; 18:34). The sayings of Jesus about his Father and his road were too large for the people who loved him best, until the evening of the resurrection, when the risen Lord opened their minds to understand the Scriptures and showed them that the Christ should suffer and rise on the third day (24:45–46). The things about Jesus are not grasped by being cleverer than Mary. They are opened by Jesus himself, and they open from the cross and the empty tomb.

What should I do with a passage I cannot understand? Do not throw it away and do not force it. Read it in its context, compare it with clearer passages on the same subject, since Scripture interprets Scripture (Westminster 1.9), and ask for help from a good commentary or a pastor. If it still will not open, put it on the shelf with a note and keep reading. The things necessary for salvation are plain in Scripture (Westminster 1.7); harder things can wait. Many believers find that a passage that baffled them for years suddenly opens in a hard season, because they kept it.

In a sentence. Jesus’ parents did not understand what he meant.

On a Tuesday. It is all right not to understand everything about God at once. Keep treasuring and pondering, as Mary did. Write down the saying of Jesus that puzzles you most, and carry it with you this month.

For worship. The Son of God spoke plainly to his own mother, and she could not take it in, and he did not love her less for it. He went home and lived under her roof for eighteen years, bearing with her slowness as he would later bear with the Twelve. He is the Teacher who does not despise slow pupils, and the Lord who does not leave his people holding riddles for ever: the words he once spoke over their heads he now speaks into their hearts, and they find that every one of them was about his love.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them. And his mother treasured up all these things in her heart. And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went down with them, came to Nazareth, and was submissive to them. His mother treasured up all these things in her heart. And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favour with God and man.

And he went down with them and came to Nazareth and was submissive to them. The Son of God, conscious of his unique relationship with his Father, went home and obeyed his parents. The boy who has just spoken of a Father greater than Joseph gets up, walks eighty miles home, and puts himself under the authority of a village builder and a poor woman for the next eighteen years. “Submissive” (hypotassomenos): continually subject, obedient. Not a single act of compliance but a settled condition, sustained through his teens and into his manhood, working as a carpenter (Mark 6:3). He kept the fifth commandment perfectly, for us. His awareness of his heavenly Father did not lead him to despise his earthly parents.

Higher calling, nearer duty. There is no contradiction between verse 49 and verse 51, and the pairing is the whole point. Being about his Father’s business, for a twelve-year-old in Nazareth, meant obeying his mother. Anyone who has ever used a sense of higher calling as a reason for neglecting a plain nearer duty has the shape of this passage exactly backwards.

And his mother treasured up all these things in her heart. The second time in this chapter, with the same verb as at verse 19. She still does not understand it, and she still will not let it go; very probably she is the one who later told Luke.

And Jesus increased in wisdom. Growth in understanding. In his human nature, Jesus really learned and developed: although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered (Hebrews 5:8). This does not deny his deity, but affirms the reality of his humanity. He was not a divine being pretending to be a child, but a real child, growing up.

How can God increase in wisdom? Sit with that phrase, because it is one of the sharpest windows in the New Testament onto who Jesus is, and a thoughtful reader is right to stop at it. How can the eternal Son, the one through whom all things were made and in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3), increase in wisdom? Did he not already know everything? The answer is the mystery the church has confessed from the beginning: in the one person of the Son there are two whole natures, divine and human, and they are not blurred into a third thing (Westminster 8.2). According to his divine nature he knew all things and never learned anything. According to his human nature he really was a boy in Nazareth who had to learn his letters, memorise the Scriptures, listen to the rabbis, and grow, mind and body together, as every child grows. The verse is not loose language. It is the exact truth about him. He did not merely appear to be a developing child; he was one. This is the same reality met from the other side in his own confession that he did not know the day of his return (Mark 13:32): all-knowing as God, genuinely limited as man, in the one undivided person.

And in stature, and in favor with God and man. Stature may also mean years, or maturity. The words were used of the boy Samuel (1 Samuel 2:26): loved by God and by people. A balanced, whole development: intellectual, physical, spiritual and social. This is the model of godly growth. And it covers silently the hidden years in Nazareth, ordinary years of work, family, synagogue and prayer.

Why it matters. It matters for more than doctrine. It means the Lord his people follow was once twelve, and once seven, and once an infant who could not lift his own head; that he knows growing up from the inside, and what it is to learn slowly and not yet understand. Bring your child’s struggles, and your own memories of growing up, to one who has been there.

What if my parents are not godly or ask me to do wrong? Honour them still: speak respectfully, help them, care for them in age. But obedience to parents is always in the Lord (Ephesians 6:1), and God’s command comes first. If a parent tells you to sin, you must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), and say so as gently as you can. If a parent is abusive, you are not required to submit to harm; tell a trusted adult, a pastor or the authorities, and get safe. Jesus obeyed Mary and Joseph because they were godly and asked nothing against his Father’s will. Your obedience, like his, is first to the Father.

In a sentence. Jesus returned to Nazareth and obeyed his parents, while Mary treasured these things, and he grew in wisdom, in stature, and in favour with God and people.

On a Tuesday. If you are a child or a teenager, Jesus obeyed his parents; you can too. And at any age, aim to grow as he did: in wisdom, in body, and in favour with God and others. Ask which of the four is being neglected in your life this year, and take one step in it.

For worship. He did not play at being human. He became it, and grew into it, and lived it out through eighteen unrecorded years in a hill town, so that at last a fully human life could be offered to the Father, from beginning to end, with nothing missing. The humanity he took up in order to save ours was the real thing, all the way down. Every year of it was obedience, and every year of it was for us.

parallels.desc: the boy Samuel grew in favour with the LORD and with man

3.title: The Voice and the Son
3.overview:
Chapter 3 marks the formal beginning of the story Luke has been preparing for since chapter 1. Thirty years have passed in a single verse (2:52). Now the word of God comes to John in the wilderness, and the ministry of preparation begins. Luke anchors the moment in history with a precision unmatched anywhere in the Gospels: the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, the governorship of Pontius Pilate, the tetrarchies of Herod and Philip and Lysanias, the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas. Seven named officials, layered like the rings of a tree, establishing exactly when the word of God broke in. Luke the historian is insisting: this happened. You can date it. You can place it. It is not legend.

John's ministry is introduced through Isaiah 40 — “the voice of one crying in the wilderness” — establishing that his role is not to be the destination but the signpost. He is the voice; another is the Word. His message is the message of the prophet: repent, be baptised, bear fruits worthy of repentance. The crowds who come to him receive not comfort but confrontation: “You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?” John is the great deflater of religious presumption — the man who tells Israel that Abrahamic descent is not a sufficient credential before the coming Judge. The axe is at the root of the trees. The one who comes after him will separate the wheat from the chaff with an unquenchable fire.

The chapter ends with two moments of quiet immensity: the baptism of Jesus, where the Trinity is revealed in a form no theologian could have anticipated — the Son in the water, the Spirit as a dove, the Father's voice from heaven — and the genealogy, which traces Jesus's lineage back through David, through Abraham, through Adam, to God himself. Luke's genealogy runs in the opposite direction from Matthew's and reaches further back: not just to Abraham (the Father of Israel) but to Adam (the father of the human race). Jesus is not merely the King of the Jews; he is the son of Adam come to undo what Adam did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — John the Baptist Prepares the Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke opens the public ministry with a synchronism — a dating device borrowed from the great historians of the ancient world, who anchored their narratives in the reigns of known rulers. Seven officials are named: Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate, Herod Antipas, Philip, Lysanias, and the high priests Annas and Caiaphas.

This is the world into which the word of God intrudes: Roman imperial power, Jewish client kings, and a compromised religious leadership. And the word comes to none of them. It comes to John, in the wilderness, the son of a village priest. The contrast is pointed. All the power of the world is irrelevant to God's timing; the word comes when God is ready, to whom God chooses, in the place power does not trouble to look.

The names are also checkable, and they have been checked. Lysanias of Abilene was long cited as proof of Luke's carelessness until an inscription from the reign of Tiberius turned up near Damascus honouring exactly that man in exactly that office.

John's message has three parts. First, a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins — a rite John did not invent, but radically reapplied. Jewish practice may already have had a baptism for Gentile converts entering the covenant people; John baptised Jews, which said out loud that being born inside the covenant was not enough and that Israel itself needed converting. It was scandalous, and it was meant to be.

Second, a demolition of presumption: “Do not begin to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father.' For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.” Ethnic heritage is no substitute for personal repentance, and the axe is already at the root.

Third, practical instruction to three specific groups who ask the same question — what shall we do? The crowds are told to share a spare tunic and their food. Tax collectors are told to collect no more than the authorised figure. Soldiers are told not to extort, not to lay false charges, and to be content with their pay. Notably, neither the tax collectors nor the soldiers are told to leave their work. Repentance in John's mouth has hands and feet, and all three answers land on money.

The climax is not John's own proclamation but his announcement of another: “He who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.” The one who follows is not an improved John; he is of a different order altogether. And Luke calls the whole of this preaching — vipers, axe, unquenchable fire and all — good news (v. 18).

The section closes with Herod shutting John in prison for confronting him over his marriage to his brother's wife. The voice is silenced immediately before the Word begins to speak. The herald makes way for the King.
verseByVerse.theology:
John's declaration that God can raise up children to Abraham from stones is the most radical possible challenge to the theology of ethnic privilege. It disconnects the promise from the bloodline and reconnects it to faith and repentance.

This is not the abolition of the covenant with Abraham; it is the clarification of what that covenant always meant. Paul will develop the same argument in Galatians 3 and Romans 4: the true children of Abraham are those who share Abraham's faith, not merely his biology. John stands at the hinge of the covenants and announces what the new covenant will make explicit — the community of God is defined by repentance and faith, not by descent.

The baptism of the Holy Spirit and fire announces two aspects of the Coming One's work that belong together. The Spirit is the agent of new birth and renewal, the fulfilment of Ezekiel's new heart and Joel's outpouring. Fire is the agent of purification — the refiner's fire that burns away dross, and the thresher's fire that consumes chaff.

John does not separate these two; they are two sides of one coming. For those who receive him the fire purifies; for those who reject him it consumes. Everyone who meets Christ is touched by fire. The only question is which kind.
verseByVerse.examples:
John's instruction to the crowds, the tax collectors and the soldiers is one of the clearest demonstrations in the Gospels that repentance is not a feeling but a change of direction that shows. The crowd asks “what shall we do?” and the answer is not “attend synagogue more faithfully” or “pray more earnestly.” It is “share your tunic and your food.”

The tax collector's repentance looks like honest accounting; the soldier's looks like honest soldiering. Genuine repentance always takes the shape of the specific sin it is turning from — and in both those cases it meant staying in a compromised trade and doing it straight, at real financial cost, alongside colleagues who would not.

John's willingness to confront Herod Antipas over his adulterous marriage (v. 19) — knowing what it would cost him — is the model of prophetic courage before political power. He did not reserve his hard message for crowds who could do him no harm; he took it to the palace, where it was entirely unnecessary and entirely dangerous.

The man who tells the crowd hard truths and comfortable things to the powerful has not yet learned from John. And John's own end is worth facing honestly: he did everything he was sent to do, and finished in a cell. Faithfulness is not always repaid in this life.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, and Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea, Herod tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness.

Meaning first. Luke 3 brings us from the hidden years to the public stage. After years hidden in the wilderness (1:80), John the son of Zechariah receives the word of God and begins to preach a baptism of repentance, preparing the way of the Lord as Isaiah foretold. He warns the crowds of the wrath to come, strips away their trust in descent from Abraham, tells ordinary people exactly what repentance looks like at the wardrobe, the tax table and the barracks, and points away from himself to one mightier, who will baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire. Herod silences him. Then Jesus steps into the river among sinners, the heavens open, the Spirit descends and the Father speaks: You are my beloved Son. Luke closes with a genealogy that runs backwards past David and Abraham to Adam, the son of God, to show that this is the Saviour of the whole human race, the second Adam come to undo what the first Adam did.

Luke the historian. Luke dates John’s ministry the way ancient historians dated great events, with a list of rulers: seven names, in strict order of precedence, one emperor, one governor, three tetrarchs, two high priests. Then the sentence turns and the word of God goes past every one of them, and lands on a man in a desert. The structure is the argument. In other words, the sentence itself preaches: Luke lists the power of the world in full, and then shows God passing every name on it to speak to a man nobody had put on any list.

In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea. Tiberius succeeded Augustus in AD 14. His fifteenth year was about AD 28–29 (depending on how the years were counted, and whether from his co-regency with Augustus, which began in AD 11–12). Jesus’ ministry began shortly after. Pilate was prefect from AD 26 to 36.

Herod being tetrarch of Galilee. Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruled Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39. “Tetrarch” originally meant ruler of a quarter of a kingdom, then any minor ruler under Rome. He would imprison and behead John (v. 20; 9:9). His brother Philip, another son of Herod the Great, ruled the territory north-east of Galilee from 4 BC to AD 34, and rebuilt Caesarea Philippi.

And Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene. A region north-west of Damascus. For a long time this name was used to convict Luke of carelessness. The only Lysanias the history books knew of was a king of Chalcis executed in 36 BC, some sixty years too early to be reigning here. Then the ground gave up its witness. An inscription found near Damascus, from the reign of Tiberius, names a Lysanias as tetrarch: a later Lysanias, holding exactly the office Luke assigns him, in exactly the period Luke places him. Luke was right, and his critics had been working from an incomplete list.

Luke can be checked. This is not an isolated rescue. Again and again, a detail in Luke once called a blunder has turned out to be precise: the city officials of Thessalonica, whom he calls politarchs (Acts 17:6), the proconsul of Cyprus (Acts 13:7), the chief man of Malta (Acts 28:7). So when he says the word of God came in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, with these men in these offices, he has earned the right to be believed. He is reporting something that happened, at a time that could have been marked on a Roman calendar.

During the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas. There was officially one high priest. Annas held the office from AD 6 to 15, when the Romans deposed him. But he remained the power behind the office; five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas (AD 18–36) held it after him. Jews may have regarded Annas as still the true high priest, since the office was meant to be for life.

The court that would try the King. Read the list again and notice how many of these names will meet Jesus at the end. Pilate will sentence him (23:24). Herod Antipas will mock him and send him back in a splendid robe (23:11). The high priest’s house will hold him on the night of his arrest (22:54); John tells us he was taken first to Annas (John 18:13), and Matthew that Caiaphas presided (Matthew 26:57). And the charge laid before Pilate will be that he forbade tribute to Caesar (23:2). Luke names, at the opening of the ministry, the very men before whom it will close. They thought they held the power. The word that passed them by was preparing the way of the one they would crucify, and whom God would raise and seat above every ruler on that list.

The word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness. The language of the Old Testament prophets, the standard formula for the call of a prophet: the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:2), to Hosea, to Joel, to Jonah. Israel had not heard it in four hundred years, and Luke’s readers would have felt the shock: the line of the prophets, which everybody assumed had closed, has just been reopened. Not in Rome, not in Jerusalem, not in the palace or the temple, but in the wilderness, to the son of a country priest.

Where God speaks. All the power in that list is irrelevant to God’s timing. The word comes when God is ready, to whom God chooses, in the place power does not bother to look. It was always so: Moses at the back of the wilderness, Elijah at a brook, Amos among the sycamore figs. God had a temple, a priesthood and a high priest in that list, and did not use them.

Does God still speak like this today? Not by calling new prophets with new words to add to Scripture. John was the last prophet of the old order, and the word of God came to its fullness in Christ, who is God’s final word (Hebrews 1:1–2). That word is now written, complete and sufficient (Westminster 1.6). But God still speaks it, through the Scriptures read and preached, and he still bypasses the powerful to do it. The word that came to John in the wilderness comes to you when you open your Bible, and it has the same authority.

In a sentence. In about AD 28, under Tiberius, Pilate, the Herods and the high priests Annas and Caiaphas, God’s word came to John in the wilderness.

On a Tuesday. The gospel is rooted in real history, and God still bypasses the powerful to speak through the humble. Do not wait for the important people in your church, your town or your country to take notice before you take God’s word seriously. It has always come first to the wilderness.

For worship. The word of God passed by the palace and the temple and came to a man in the desert, and that is how our God has always loved to work. He lets emperors give their names to the years, and then fills the year with his own deed. Men called it the fifteenth year of Tiberius; heaven knew it as the year the voice began to cry, Prepare the way, and the Lord himself came walking down from Nazareth to the river. The names of the powerful are remembered now chiefly because they lived when he spoke.
verseByVerse.note: Luke dates John’s ministry like a historian: Tiberius’s fifteenth year was about AD 28–29. Philip ruled lands north-east of the lake; Abilene lay north-west of Damascus. Annas had been deposed as high priest but still held great influence; his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went into all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet, 'The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John went into all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet: The voice of one crying in the wilderness, prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.

Into all the region around the Jordan. The Jordan valley, north of the Dead Sea, a hot, low-lying region. A place of crossing: Israel had entered the promised land by crossing the Jordan under Joshua, out of forty years in the wilderness (Joshua 3). Elijah was taken up near there (2 Kings 2:6–11). And the geography preaches. John stands at that same river calling the nation to come out and start again, as if the whole history since had to be wound back and begun once more from the crossing.

Proclaiming a baptism of repentance. A baptism that expressed repentance. “Repentance” (metanoia) means a change of mind leading to a change of life: turning from sin to God. It is not primarily an emotion. A man can weep over his sin all night and repent of nothing; a man can turn round with a dry face and have repented completely. The test is not how sorry you felt but which way you are now facing.

Whom he baptised. Jews were used to ritual washings for purification, and Gentiles who converted to Judaism were probably baptised, the washing by which a pagan entered the covenant people. The startling thing was not that John baptised, but whom he baptised: Jews, God’s own people, called to be baptised like Gentiles. To ask a son of Abraham to be immersed like a Gentile convert was to say something scandalous out loud: that being born inside the covenant was not enough, that Israel itself needed converting. That is why, when the crowd reaches for the credential it assumes will settle the matter, we have Abraham as our father, John knocks it away so hard. He had already answered it by the water he was standing in.

For the forgiveness of sins. John promised forgiveness to those who truly repented. Not that the water itself forgave, but that it was the sign of a repentance God would honour. And John’s baptism pointed forward to the one who would actually win forgiveness, by his death (1:77; 24:47).

Did John’s baptism itself forgive sins? No. Forgiveness came from God to those who repented; the washing was the sign of their turning. John’s baptism prepared for the Christ, and those who had received it were later baptised in the name of Jesus (Acts 19:4–5). Christian baptism, too, does not forgive by the water; it is the sign of a forgiveness received by faith, which is why it belongs to those who have repented and believed (Acts 2:38, 41). The water is precious as a sign, and nothing in it saves.

As it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet. Isaiah 40:3–5. Isaiah 40 begins the second half of Isaiah, the great prophecies of comfort and return from exile: Comfort, comfort my people (Isaiah 40:1). John is the voice crying in the wilderness: not the King, but the voice that announces him.

Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. The image behind it is a road gang. When a king was to visit a region, men went ahead to make the road passable: filling holes, cutting through ridges, straightening the route so the royal party could come through. In Isaiah, it is the LORD God himself who is coming, to lead his people home. John prepares for Jesus, so Jesus is the Lord God who is coming. That is what John is: not the king, but the road crew. And what he is levelling is not a highway in the desert but the ground in front of a nation’s heart, so that when the King comes there is a way in. The preparation is moral and spiritual: repentance.

In the flow. These verses are the promise of chapter 1 coming true. At John’s birth his father sang that the child would go before the Lord to prepare his ways and give his people knowledge of salvation in the forgiveness of their sins (1:76–77). Here is the grown man doing exactly that, in those very terms. Luke will end his Gospel with the same two words, repentance and forgiveness of sins, proclaimed in Jesus’ name to all nations (24:47). John’s message is not set aside by the gospel; it is the first form of it, and it opens the road on which the Lord himself is about to walk.

How do I know if I have really repented? Look at the direction, not the feelings. Have you come to see your sin as an offence against God, not merely as a mistake or an embarrassment? Have you turned to him for mercy in Christ, rather than trying to make up for it yourself? And are you, by his grace, setting yourself against that sin, even if you still stumble? Real repentance is not perfection; it is a changed direction that keeps turning back to God each time you fall. If you find you still love the sin and have no wish to leave it, ask God to grant you repentance (2 Timothy 2:25). He gives what he commands.

In a sentence. John preached throughout the Jordan valley a baptism expressing repentance for the forgiveness of sins, fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy of a voice preparing the way of the Lord.

On a Tuesday. What in your life needs straightening to make way for the Lord? Repentance is the road on which he comes. Name one specific thing, not your character in general but a particular habit, attitude or relationship, and turn it round this week.

For worship. Isaiah said the LORD himself was coming down the road, and the one who came was Jesus of Nazareth. God did not send a deputy to bring his people home. He came himself, on foot, to the river where John was crying out, and went on from there to Jerusalem and the cross, where the way into his presence was opened for good. He does not wait for sinners to level their own hearts. He sends his word ahead to do it, and then he comes, and every one who turns finds the road open.

verseByVerse.quote: Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low, and the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low, and the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.

Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be made low. Road-building language. The picture is of a landscape being made passable, and it works in both directions at once: valleys come up, mountains come down, and the result is a road on which everybody is walking at the same height. It is also a picture of the reversal Mary sang of (1:52): the lowly lifted up, the proud brought down.

Nobody arrives on the level he was standing on. That is what the coming of Christ does to people. The person crushed flat by failure, by shame, by years of being nobody, is lifted; the person built up high on competence and reputation and being right is brought down. Both are uncomfortable and both are necessary, and the ones who find it hardest are not usually the ones in the valley.

And the crooked shall become straight, and the rough places shall become level ways. Crooked means twisted, bent out of true: crooked lives made straight, like the tax collectors and soldiers who come to John. Every honest person knows something in themselves answering to it: the habit of self-protection, the small dishonesty that has been there so long it feels structural. Isaiah says the road crew has been sent for that too.

And all flesh shall see the salvation of God. Here is why Luke kept quoting. Matthew and Mark quote only the first verse of Isaiah’s passage; Luke, writing with the whole world in view, goes on two more verses to reach this line, because it is his great theme. “All flesh” means all humanity, Gentiles as well as Jews. It is the universal note that has already sounded in this Gospel, in the angel’s all the people (2:10) and in Simeon, who saw God’s salvation in the baby in his arms (2:30–32). Luke’s Gospel ends with repentance and forgiveness of sins proclaimed to all nations (24:47), and Acts ends with Paul in Rome declaring that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles (Acts 28:28).

What it does not mean. The sentence is sometimes stretched further than it goes. It does not say all flesh shall be saved. It says all flesh shall see the salvation of God. The salvation will be public, visible, put where nobody can claim it was hidden from them. That is a promise about the reach of the announcement, not about the response to it, and John goes straight on to make brutally clear that seeing and receiving are not the same thing. It gives no ground for the idea that everyone will be saved in the end, or that people may be saved without hearing of Christ. Salvation is through conscious faith in him, and that is why the announcement must go to all flesh.

What about people who have never heard? They are not saved by their ignorance, and they are not condemned for rejecting a Christ they never heard of; they are condemned for their sin against the light they had (Romans 1:18–20; 2:12). That is exactly why this verse matters. God has determined that all flesh shall see his salvation, and he has given his church the task of showing it to them (Romans 10:13–15). The right response to the question is not speculation but prayer, giving and going. And we may trust that the Judge of all the earth will do right.

In a sentence. Isaiah’s prophecy promised the levelling of every obstacle, the straightening of the crooked, and the revelation of God’s salvation to all humanity.

On a Tuesday. Ask honestly whether you are in the valley or on the mountain: crushed by shame, or propped up by pride. Either way, bring it to Christ. And pray this week by name for one people group or country that has not yet seen the salvation of God.

For worship. Isaiah’s highway runs through every landscape there is, valley and mountain, Jew and Gentile, and at the end of it stands not a principle but the Son of God. The salvation all flesh was promised to see is a man: born where shepherds could find him, lifted up on a cross outside Jerusalem where the whole city could look, and now proclaimed to the ends of the earth. No corner of the world lies too far off his road, and ours did not.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke continues the quotation to “all flesh shall see the salvation of God.”

parallels.desc: my eyes have seen your salvation

verseByVerse.quote: He said therefore to the crowds that came out to be baptized by him, 'You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said therefore to the crowds that came out to be baptised by him: you brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?

He said therefore to the crowds. These are not his enemies. They are not the delegation from Jerusalem or the men who will later arrest him. They are the crowds that came out to be baptised by him, people who walked into the desert to repent, and this is how he greets them. Matthew says he addressed this to the Pharisees and Sadducees (Matthew 3:7); Luke applies it to the crowds in general, many of whom, it seems, had come out of curiosity or because it was the thing to do.

You brood of vipers. A shocking way to greet people who came to be baptised. The picture behind it is one every farmer in that country knew. When a fire swept through the dry scrub of the wilderness, or stubble was burned off a field, the snakes would come racing out ahead of the flames. John looks at a crowd streaming down to the river and says: I know what you look like. You look like the wildlife leaving a fire. These people were fleeing the coming judgement like snakes running from a fire, without any change of nature. Many readers also hear in the phrase an echo of the serpent of Genesis 3, as Jesus would say to his opponents in John’s Gospel that their father was the devil, not Abraham (John 8:39–44).

Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? The question is not a compliment on their foresight. It is sarcastic: who told you that running for the water would be enough? Do you think a dip in the river is enough to escape? “The wrath to come”: God’s judgement, the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:1; Zephaniah 1:14–18; 1 Thessalonians 1:10). John was not ashamed to preach the wrath of God. Without it, the good news makes no sense.

Why so hard on people doing the right thing? Because he can see what they have come for. There is a way of pursuing religion which is entirely about damage limitation: getting into the water, getting the ritual done, getting the insurance in place, and changing nothing whatever. A man may be perfectly sincere in wanting to escape the consequences of his sin and have no interest at all in leaving it. John will not baptise that. His terms follow at once: fruit that matches repentance.

What is the wrath of God? A modern reader may find it harder than the snakes, and it needs saying plainly, because it is regularly caricatured. The wrath of God is not divine temper. It is not God losing control, or taking offence, or reacting badly. It is the settled, holy, entirely just opposition of God to everything that ruins what he has made. And it is worth asking honestly what the alternative would be. A God who looked at cruelty and abuse and betrayal and felt nothing would not be a kinder God; he would be a moral vacancy. We do not admire that in people. We do not call a man good because he can watch a child harmed and remain unmoved. The wrath of God is the shadow cast by the love of God: it exists because he cares, infinitely, about what is being done to his world and to the people in it.

Should a Christian fear God’s wrath? Not as one still under it. If you are in Christ, the wrath your sins deserved fell on him; he propitiated it, turned it away by bearing it himself (Romans 3:25; 1 John 2:2). Jesus delivers us from the wrath to come (1 Thessalonians 1:10), and there is now no condemnation (Romans 8:1). So a believer fears God with reverence and awe, but not with the terror of a condemned man. If you are not in Christ, the fear is a mercy: it is God’s warning while there is still time to flee to the only shelter.

In a sentence. John confronted the crowds as snakes fleeing a fire, asking who had warned them to escape God’s coming wrath.

On a Tuesday. Don’t treat religious ritual as fire insurance; flee to Christ with a changed heart. Ask yourself whether your church-going, your baptism, your prayers are a way of keeping God at a safe distance, or of coming to him.

For worship. John announces the wrath as coming, which means it is not here yet, which means there is time. That is the only reason a man stands by a river shouting at people instead of standing back and letting it arrive. And the God whose wrath is coming is the God who sent his own Son to stand under it in our place. The fire that should have fallen on us fell on him, and those who flee to him are safe for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: Bear fruits in keeping with repentance. And do not begin to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bear fruits in keeping with repentance. And do not begin to say to yourselves, we have Abraham as our father. For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.

Bear fruits in keeping with repentance. John has two terms: bear the fruit, and drop the credential. The phrase is precise: fruits that match. He is not asking for a general improvement. Repentance is not only an inner feeling, or a ritual. True repentance shows itself in a changed life, as a healthy tree shows itself by its fruit (6:43–45). It produces something visible and appropriate to the thing repented of, and John goes on to give three worked examples, to the crowd, the tax collectors and the soldiers, so that nobody can pretend the demand was vague. Paul preached the same: that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance (Acts 26:20).

Fruit is evidence, not payment. This is where an anxious believer can get badly hurt. Fruit is evidence of repentance; it is not the cause of it, and it is not what earns anything. A tree does not become an apple tree by producing apples. But the fruit is how you can tell.

What if I look at my life and see so little fruit? There is a kind of self-examination that is faithful and a kind that is corrosive, and the difference is where it looks for the answer.
