The corrosive kind stands under the tree counting, gets a number it does not like, and concludes it is not really a Christian. The faithful kind notices the shortage and goes back to the root. John’s whole ministry was about turning people to God, and a man frightened by his own lack of fruit is a man in the exact condition John was preaching for. So do not despair; go back to Christ, abide in him, and ask for his Spirit. Fruit grows from the vine, not from anxiety (John 15:5). And ask a trusted believer what they see; others often see fruit that we cannot.

And do not begin to say to yourselves, We have Abraham as our father. John can see the words forming. This was the answer everybody had ready: descent from Abraham, circumcision, membership of the covenant people. Many Jews believed that being physical descendants of Abraham guaranteed God’s favour; some later rabbis taught that Abraham sat at the gate of hell to turn back any Israelite. John says: your ancestry will not save you.

For I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. He is probably pointing; the Jordan valley is full of stones. There may be a pun in Aramaic between children (banayya) and stones (abnayya). God does not need you. The God who made Isaac out of a dead womb can make a son of Abraham out of a rock, which means the family tree that seemed to guarantee everything guarantees nothing at all. And he will: Gentiles, as dead to God as stones, will become Abraham’s children by faith (Galatians 3:7, 29). The true children of Abraham are those who share his faith (Romans 4:11–12).

Abraham’s one true offspring. Who, then, are Abraham’s children? Paul answers by pointing to one man. The promises were made to Abraham and to his offspring, and that offspring is Christ (Galatians 3:16); and if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise (Galatians 3:29). Nobody becomes a child of Abraham by being born from him. People become his children by being joined to his Son. And the man John is preparing for is the one tree in all Israel that would bear every fruit God looked for: the Son in whom the Father is well pleased. The axe John describes is aimed at every root but his, and those who are grafted into him by faith are safe from it.

The modern credentials. They are not hard to name. Christian parents. Baptism, whether as an infant or as a believer. Membership of a good church. Thirty years in the same pew. Every one of these is a genuine mercy, and not one of them is the thing itself. A man may be inside all of it and still have never once turned round.

Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Not the branches: the root. This is not pruning. And even now means the blade is already resting against the wood: not a threat about the distant future but a description of the present moment, with the axeman standing there. Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire, the fire of God’s judgement. The fig tree has had its time (13:6–9).

Then is a Christian upbringing worthless? Far from it. It is one of the greatest privileges a person can have: hearing the gospel from childhood, seeing faith lived, being prayed for daily (2 Timothy 3:15). But privilege is not the same as possession. Every child of believing parents must personally repent and trust Christ, and every one may. If you grew up in the church, thank God for it, and make sure you have done more than inherit the vocabulary. If you are a parent, do not assume your children are saved because they are yours; pray for them, teach them, and call them to Christ.

In a sentence. John demanded that repentance be shown in changed lives, warned that descent from Abraham would not save them, and declared that God’s judgement was ready to fall on every fruitless tree.

On a Tuesday. What fruit of repentance can be seen in your life? Don’t rely on your background; rely on Christ, and bear fruit. Pick the area where your repentance has stayed in words, and find the fruit that matches it: the apology, the repayment, the changed habit.

For worship. God does not need any of us, and he chooses us anyway. He who can raise children for Abraham from the stones of the Jordan raised us, dead as stones, and made us his children. The axe was laid at the root of every tree, and on the way to the cross Jesus called himself the green wood (23:31): the one living tree that deserved no fire took the blow, so that dead wood might be joined to him and live.

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds asked him, 'What then shall we do?' And he answered them, 'Whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none, and whoever has food is to do likewise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowds asked him: what then shall we do? He answered them: whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none, and whoever has food is to do likewise.

What then shall we do? It is the right question, the one the preaching was for (Acts 2:37; 16:30). They do not argue with him; nobody points out that he has just called them snakes. The crowd hears that the axe is at the root and asks the only sensible thing a man can ask in that position. Three groups ask the same question (vv. 10, 12, 14), and only Luke records this section.

The most surprising answer. Here is the last of the prophets, with the crowds of Israel in front of him and the whole weight of the old covenant behind him, asked point-blank what repentance requires. He does not say: come to the temple. He does not say: fast, pray, keep the feasts, tithe, study. He says: share.

Whoever has two tunics is to share with him who has none. The tunic was the basic garment worn next to the skin. Most people had one; a second was a luxury for the poor. So the instruction is not sell everything and it is not give until you are destitute. It is startlingly modest and startlingly concrete: if you have two and somebody near you has none, that is what the second one is for. And whoever has food is to do likewise. Love your neighbour as yourself: if anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him, how does God’s love abide in him? (1 John 3:17–18; James 2:15–16).

Whose is the second coat? Which lands somewhere very specific for a modern reader, because the honest arithmetic is uncomfortable. Almost nobody reading this owns two tunics. We own thirty, in a wardrobe, several of which have not been worn in two years. And John’s test is not what percentage we give away; it is whether the surplus is understood to be ours or understood to be for somebody. That is the shift he is asking for, and it is a shift of ownership before it is a shift of behaviour. The person who thinks of the second coat as their property, from which generosity is an occasional deduction, will always give a little and feel good about it. The person who thinks of the second coat as already belonging to whoever has none will simply hand it over, and will not think of it as generosity at all.

What it does not mean. Not that salvation is earned by giving things away. Nor a political programme of enforced equality. Nor that it is wrong to own more than one of anything, or to save for the future (Proverbs 6:6–8; 1 Timothy 5:8). But a heart that has truly turned to God will turn toward the needy.

The one who was stripped of everything. John asks for the second tunic. The one whose way he prepares would give far more. Paul grounds all Christian giving in exactly this: you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, for your sake he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:8–9). At the end of Luke’s Gospel the soldiers cast lots to divide his garments as he hangs on the cross (23:34): the Lord of all was stripped of the last thing he had, and he gave his life with it. John’s demand is the first step of repentance; the cross is what makes it glad. People who have seen what Christ gave do not need to be argued into handing over a coat.

So how much should I give? Scripture gives no fixed percentage for the new covenant, but it gives principles. Give first to the Lord’s work through your local church, regularly and in proportion to what you have been given (1 Corinthians 16:2). Give generously and cheerfully, not reluctantly (2 Corinthians 9:6–7). Many believers find the Old Testament tithe a helpful starting point, not a ceiling. And keep your eyes open, as John says, for the person near you who has none: the brother out of work, the neighbour with an empty fridge. Generosity starts with what is in front of you.

In a sentence. When the crowds asked what to do, John told them to share their spare clothing and food with those who had none.

On a Tuesday. Look at what is in the wardrobe, the fridge, the account, and ask, of the part beyond what is actually needed: whose is that? Then find one thing you have two of that someone near you needs, and give it this week.

For worship. Behind John’s small demand stands the immeasurable generosity of God, who did not hold back his own Son as too precious to give, but gave him up for us all, and with him graciously gives us all things (Romans 8:32). He clothes the naked in the robe of his Son’s righteousness. The God who asks us for a second coat has already given us his best, and he has never asked his people for anything he had not first poured out on them.
verseByVerse.note: The tunic was the inner garment; a second one was a spare.

verseByVerse.quote: Tax collectors also came to be baptized and said to him, 'Teacher, what shall we do?' And he said to them, 'Collect no more than you are authorized to do.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tax collectors also came to be baptised and said to him: Teacher, what shall we do? He said to them: collect no more than you are authorised to do.

Tax collectors also came to be baptized. Tax collectors were among the most despised people in Jewish society: Jews working the Roman revenue system. Rome sold the right to collect taxes to the highest bidder, who paid in advance and collected what he could, keeping the surplus; the system ran on extortion. So a tax collector was, to his neighbours, both a traitor working for the occupying power and a thief with legal protection. Later rabbinic writings treat their testimony as worthless, and the Gospels lump them in with prostitutes. Yet they came to John, and later to Jesus (5:27–32; 15:1; 19:1–10), and they call John Teacher, a courtesy the crowds did not bother with. The despised were often more ready to repent than the respectable.

Collect no more than you are authorized to do. Now watch what John does not say. He does not tell them to quit. Here is a profession soaked in injustice, tied to a pagan empire, despised by every godly person in Israel, and the prophet’s instruction is: do the job honestly. Take the legal figure and not a penny more. The state has the right to taxes (20:25; Romans 13:6–7). Repentance does not usually mean leaving your calling, but living differently in it.

What it cost. For a tax collector, honesty would mean a dramatic loss of income; the profit was in the margin. John is telling these men to accept a permanent drop in income in exchange for a clear conscience, and to go on working alongside colleagues who will not do the same and will do better out of it. That is far harder than resigning. Resigning is over in a day. This is every day.

Friend of tax collectors. John sends these men back to the tax table honest. The one he was preparing for would go further: he would sit down at their tables and be called a friend of tax collectors and sinners (7:34). Luke shows what that friendship did. Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector, is not told by Jesus to repay anyone. He is found, welcomed, and visited, and the repayment pours out of him unasked: half his goods to the poor, and fourfold to anyone he had defrauded (19:8). John could describe the fruit. Jesus is the one who makes the tree new, because the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (19:10).

Should I leave a job in a compromised industry? There is a persistent instinct that real repentance ought to mean leaving: leaving the industry, the firm, the compromised environment, and that staying is a failure of nerve. Sometimes leaving is right, and Scripture knows of work that cannot be done honestly at all: if your job requires you to lie, cheat, or take part in what God forbids, you must obey God rather than men. But John’s answer to a room full of men in a corrupt trade was to send them back into it clean. Ask whether you can do this work without sinning. If you can, stay and be the honest one, at whatever cost. If you cannot, seek counsel, pray, and plan your way out.

In a sentence. When tax collectors asked what they should do, John told them to collect only what was required, nothing extra.

On a Tuesday. Repentance shows itself at work. Be scrupulously honest even when it costs you: the expenses claim, the timesheet, the invoice, the tax return. That is the shape of most Christian obedience: not a dramatic exit, but the same desk, done straight, with less money and no applause, for years.

For worship. The God of John the Baptist did not wait for tax collectors to become respectable before he called them. He let them come down to the water with the rest of Israel, he sent his Son to call one of them from the tax booth to follow him (5:27–28), and he wrote the names of such men in heaven. There is no profession so despised that his grace cannot walk into it, and no ledger so crooked that the blood of his Son cannot cover it and his Spirit set it straight.
verseByVerse.note: Tax collectors typically profited from whatever they could collect above the amount owed.

verseByVerse.quote: Soldiers also asked him, 'And we, what shall we do?' And he said to them, 'Do not extort money from anyone by threats or by false accusation, and be content with your wages.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Soldiers also asked him: and we, what shall we do? He said to them: do not extort money from anyone by threats or by false accusation, and be content with your wages.

Soldiers also asked him. Their question has a small word in it that changes the tone: and we, what shall we do? They have heard him answer the crowd and the tax collectors, and they want to know whether there is anything for men like them. These are probably not Roman legionaries but Jewish soldiers in the service of Herod Antipas, or police who protected the tax collectors, the muscle standing behind the table; possibly some Gentiles. They had power, weapons and poor pay, and the temptations that go with them, which explains the instructions John gives.

Do not extort money from anyone by threats or by false accusation. “Extort by threats” (diaseisēte): literally shake down, intimidate, use violence to get money; it is what happens when a man with a weapon stands near a man with a purse. “False accusation” is sykophantēsēte, from which comes sycophant: to accuse falsely, to blackmail. A soldier could report a man, the report would be believed, and the man would pay to make it go away.

And be content with your wages. The root of their sins was discontent and greed. Contentment is the cure (Philippians 4:11–12; 1 Timothy 6:6–10; Hebrews 13:5). Again, John does not tell them to leave the army. He sends them back to the barracks with two things to stop doing and one thing to start being.

Contentment turns rules into freedom. That third instruction turns the other two into something more than rules. John has diagnosed the root. Why does a soldier lean on people? Because his pay is poor and there is money to be had. Deal with the extortion by prohibition alone and you have a man permanently resentful, obeying with clenched teeth. Deal with it by contentment and the temptation loses its handle. Contentment is not the same as having enough, nor a temperament some people are born with. Paul learned it in prison (Philippians 4:11–13). It is something acquired, slowly, by people who have found something they cannot lose and have begun to reckon everything else against it.

May a Christian serve as a soldier or police officer? Yes. John does not tell the soldiers to leave the army, but to be honest and content in it. Jesus commended a centurion’s faith without telling him to resign (7:9), and the first Gentile household to receive the Spirit was a centurion’s (Acts 10). The state bears the sword as God’s servant to restrain evil (Romans 13:4). Some Christians are pacifists and read Jesus’ teaching as forbidding all violence; they are brothers to be respected, and their consciences honoured. But this verse, and the state’s God-given sword, point the other way. The soldier, like everyone else, is held to justice: no abuse of power, no cruelty, no unjust orders obeyed.

Three answers, all at the wallet. And notice that all three of John’s answers, to the crowd, to the tax men, to the soldiers, are about money. The last prophet of the old covenant had one question in the desert about what repentance looks like, and three times he answered it at the wallet. Not because money is the worst of sins, but because it is the place where a man’s actual convictions are recorded, in figures, whether or not he agrees with them.

A centurion at the cross. Luke keeps soldiers in view to the end of his Gospel. Soldiers mock Jesus on the cross and offer him sour wine, saying, if you are the King of the Jews, save yourself (23:36–37). The one man who had all power refused to use it for himself, and when he died, the centurion in charge praised God and said, Certainly this man was innocent (23:47). John told soldiers to stop taking by force. Jesus showed a soldier what power is for: laid down, to save others. That is where a soldier’s repentance finds its root, and a centurion was the first to say so at the foot of the cross.

How do I learn contentment? Paul calls it a secret he learned (Philippians 4:12), so it can be learned. Start by giving thanks, specifically and daily, for what you have; gratitude starves discontent. Notice the comparisons that feed it, the adverts, the feeds, the friend’s new house, and starve them. Remember what you cannot lose: Christ has said, I will never leave you nor forsake you, and that is the reason Hebrews gives for being content (Hebrews 13:5). And give some away; generosity loosens money’s grip. Contentment does not mean you may never seek a better wage, but that your peace does not depend on getting it.

In a sentence. John told soldiers not to use their power to extort money by violence or blackmail, and to be content with their pay.

On a Tuesday. Whatever power you have, at work or at home, never use it to take from others. And be content with what God has given you. Think of the small powers you hold, over a child, an employee, a customer, a spouse, and ask whether any of them is being used to get what you want at someone else’s cost.

For worship. The soldiers of Herod came to the river asking whether there was anything for men like them, and there was. The Lord they did not yet know is a portion no one can extort and no one can confiscate. In him the anxious find rest and the grasping find enough, because the God who owns the cattle on a thousand hills (Psalm 50:10) has given himself to his people, and a man who has God has nothing left to shake out of anyone.
verseByVerse.note: These were probably Jewish soldiers serving Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: As the people were in expectation, and all were questioning in their hearts concerning John, whether he might be the Christ, John answered them all, saying, 'I baptize you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the people were in expectation, and all were questioning in their hearts concerning John whether he might be the Christ, John answered them all: I baptise you with water, but he who is mightier than I is coming, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptise you with the Holy Spirit and fire.

As the people were in expectation. Messianic hope was intense. Many were waiting for the promised Messiah, and here was a prophet like Elijah. The crowds have reached the point of asking the question out loud, or nearly out loud: all were questioning in their hearts concerning John.

Whether he might be the Christ. It is not an unreasonable guess. He is the first prophetic voice in four hundred years; the whole country is going out to him; and Israel had been waiting a very long time. John could have had it, not by seizing anything, merely by not correcting them, letting the question hang. Instead John answered them all, and did not let it hang for a sentence.

I baptize you with water. John’s baptism was only water, an outward sign. Water can wash a man’s skin and leave his heart untouched, and John knows it.

But he who is mightier than I is coming. John points away from himself. Throughout his ministry, he made himself small, to make Christ great: He must increase, but I must decrease (John 3:30).

The strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. Untying a master’s sandals and washing his feet was the job of the lowest slave. Later rabbis said a disciple should do anything for his teacher that a slave would do, except untie his sandals; that was too degrading, left to Gentile servants. John says: I am not even worthy to do the lowest slave’s task for him. The greatest of the prophets (7:28) considers himself unworthy to be the Messiah’s slave. That is not modesty, nor a poor self-image; it is arithmetic, from a man who has seen accurately the difference between himself and the one coming. And it set him free. A man who needs the crowd’s admiration will always be tempted to keep a little of it for himself. John could give all of it away, because his joy was somewhere else: in the voice of the bridegroom, as he would put it (John 3:29).

In the flow. The crowds have just asked three times, What then shall we do? (vv. 10–14), and John has answered. Now the question underneath comes to the surface: who is John, and is he the answer? His reply moves the whole chapter on. What people must do is repent; what they need is someone who can change them from the inside, and John cannot. So the passage turns from the river to the one who is coming, and the next scene shows him: the Spirit whom John says he will give comes down on Jesus himself at the Jordan (v. 22).

He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. The great promise. The contrast is not between two grades of the same thing. John’s baptism was outward; the Messiah’s will be inward. What is coming is a drenching in God himself. The prophets had promised that God would pour out his Spirit in the last days: the promise of Ezekiel, a new heart and a new spirit put inside a man (Ezekiel 36:25–27), and of Joel, the Spirit poured out on all flesh (Joel 2:28–29). John can put a man under the water. Only one person can put the Spirit inside him. Jesus will do this, as God does. Fulfilled at Pentecost, when tongues of fire rested on the disciples (Acts 2:1–4; 1:5). What does that actually mean? To be baptised with the Spirit is to have God himself come to live inside you, so that the change reaches the place water cannot: a new heart that begins to love God, trust Christ and turn from sin (Romans 5:5; 8:9).

What does and fire mean? Some take it as the tongues of fire at Pentecost (Acts 2:3), others as a refining of believers. “Fire” has a double meaning: purifying fire for those who repent (Malachi 3:2–3), and the fire of judgement for those who do not (v. 17). The more likely reading is that it is one baptism with two outcomes, as John’s picture of the winnowing fork goes on to show: the Spirit for those who repent, and fire, the fire of judgement, for the chaff. One baptism of Spirit and fire: purifying the wheat, burning the chaff. John announces a Messiah who will both save and judge.

Where Christians differ: the baptism of the Spirit. Pentecostal teaching holds that baptism in the Spirit is a second experience after conversion, usually evidenced by speaking in tongues. They point to Acts, where the Samaritans and the Ephesian disciples received the Spirit after believing (Acts 8:14–17; 19:1–7), and to the disciples themselves at Pentecost. Sincere Christians differ here, and many who hold that view love Christ better than most of us. Verdict: in the New Testament, all believers are baptised by the Spirit into Christ at conversion (1 Corinthians 12:13; Romans 8:9). Those moments in Acts were the special occasions on which the gospel crossed new frontiers, and Pentecost was the unique, once-for-all outpouring at the beginning of the new age. Peter, explaining to the Jerusalem church what happened at Cornelius’s house, applies John’s words to that household the moment they believed, saying God gave them the same gift as he gave to us when we believed (Acts 11:16–17). Paul says plainly that in one Spirit we were all baptised into one body, and that anyone without the Spirit does not belong to Christ. Every Christian has it. Believers are commanded to be continually filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), but not to seek a second baptism. That is not a reason to want less of the Spirit’s work; it is the ground for asking for more of it, out of security rather than out of fear.

I have been told I lack the baptism of the Spirit. What now? If you trust in Christ, you have the Spirit; you could not call Jesus Lord without him (1 Corinthians 12:3). You are not a second-class Christian waiting for a missing experience. Many believers have spent years anxious about this, and the anxiety itself is not from God. Thank him that you are already joined to Christ by his Spirit. Then ask, as Jesus told us to ask (11:13), for more of the Spirit’s work: more love, more holiness, more boldness, more joy. Seek him through the means he has given, the word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and fellowship, rather than through a particular sensation.

In a sentence. When people wondered if John was the Messiah, he said the coming one was far greater than he, and would baptise not with water but with the Holy Spirit and fire.

On a Tuesday. Like John, point away from yourself to Christ. When someone praises you this week, or gives you more credit than you deserve, correct it gladly and send the praise where it belongs. And thank God that if you belong to Christ, you have his Spirit.

For worship. The greatest man born of women was not worthy to untie his sandals, and this Lord, as John’s Gospel records (John 13:4–5), knelt and washed his disciples’ feet. He who is mightier than all pours out the Spirit of God on dust, and makes sinners into temples. John could only wet the skin. Christ gives himself.
verseByVerse.note: Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s job.

verseByVerse.quote: His winnowing fork is in his hand, to clear his threshing floor and to gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
His winnowing fork is in his hand, to clear his threshing floor and to gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.

His winnowing fork is in his hand. John’s last recorded image is a farmyard, and it is not a gentle one. After harvest, grain was threshed, beaten or trodden to loosen the husks, on a hard, flat threshing floor of packed earth or rock, often on a hilltop to catch the wind. Then it was tossed into the air with a winnowing fork, a broad wooden shovel. The heavy grain fell back onto the floor; the light chaff blew away, and was swept up and burned. The tool does not create the difference between wheat and chaff. It reveals it. And the fork is already in his hand: not fetched when needed, held. He will clear his threshing floor completely, and the separating is about to begin.

And to gather the wheat into his barn. The repentant, the true people of God, will be gathered safely. The Messiah will save. This is the first thing named, and it should not be hurried past on the way to the fire. The purpose of a harvest is the grain. The whole operation exists for the barn.

But the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire. There is no way to soften that and no honest reason to try. Chaff was burned; it was worth nothing and it was got rid of. The unrepentant will be judged, with fire that cannot be put out (Mark 9:43, 48). This is the doctrine of hell in a single image, and it comes from the mouth of the man Jesus called the greatest of the prophets, as it comes, more often and more plainly, from the mouth of Jesus himself. The Messiah is not only Saviour but Judge (John 5:22; Acts 17:31). Notice: it is his threshing floor, his wheat, his barn. Everything belongs to him.

Where Christians differ: is hell conscious and eternal? Some evangelicals hold that the wicked will finally be destroyed and cease to exist, pointing to the picture of chaff burned up and to words like destroy (Matthew 10:28). Verdict: the mainstream of the church has not read it that way, and the words of Christ are hard to bend in that direction. The fire here is unquenchable, and Jesus sets eternal punishment beside eternal life in the same sentence (Matthew 25:46); the smoke of their torment goes up for ever and ever (Revelation 14:11). The punishment is conscious and unending (Westminster 33.2). What is not in dispute among any who take the text seriously is the reality of the judgement and the finality of it.

How can this be good news? Luke goes straight on to call all of this preaching good news (v. 18). How can it be? Because the alternative to a God who separates is a God who does not care what happens to his world, who lets the cruelty and the abuse and the lies go into the barn along with everything else, for ever. A universe with no final sorting is a universe where nothing is ever put right. The fire is terrible; a harvest with no fire in it would be a harvest with no justice in it.

How can a loving God send anyone to hell? Because he is holy and just, and sin against an infinitely holy God is infinitely serious. Hell is not God losing his temper; it is God giving people, justly, what their sin deserves and what they have chosen: a life without him, for ever. But the same God has done everything needed to save: he sent his Son to bear that very judgement in the place of all who trust him. No one goes to hell who wanted Christ and was refused. If the doctrine troubles you, let it drive you to Christ, and to pray and speak for those who do not know him. It troubled the apostles too, and it made them preachers.

In a sentence. The coming one will separate humanity like a farmer winnowing, gathering the wheat into his barn and burning the chaff in unquenchable fire.

On a Tuesday. Everyone will be either wheat or chaff. There is no third category. Make sure you belong to Christ. And think of one person you love who is not yet his. Pray for them today by name, and look for the opening to speak.

For worship. The winnower is announced before he arrives, by a man sent out ahead of him for that purpose, standing in a river, with the water still running. Nobody has to be chaff. That is why he is shouting. The Judge with the fork in his hand is the Saviour who went into the fire for his wheat, and he will not lose one grain of it. Gathered into his barn, his people will be safe for ever.
verseByVerse.note: A winnowing fork tossed threshed grain into the wind; the heavy grain fell back and the chaff blew away.

verseByVerse.quote: So with many other exhortations he preached good news to the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So with many other exhortations he preached good news to the people.

With many other exhortations. Luke gives us only a sample of John’s preaching: there were months of it, and Luke has given us the shape rather than the transcript.

He preached good news to the people. “Preached good news” (euēngelizeto): evangelised. Go back over what has just been recorded. He called the congregation a nest of snakes. He told them the wrath of God was coming and asked who had tipped them off. He demolished the one credential they were all relying on. He said the axe was already against the root. He finished with a fire that cannot be put out. After all the warnings of wrath, the axe and the fire, Luke calls it good news. He was evangelising them.

One thing, not two. There is a persistent assumption that the hard parts of Christian preaching are the price of admission for the good parts: the unpleasant preliminaries a preacher gets through in order to arrive at the comfort. Luke does not see two things there. He sees one, and he calls all of it gospel, because the bad news makes the good news necessary and precious. A gospel without warning of judgement is not the gospel. If the axe really is at the root, then a man who tells you so is not being harsh; he is being kind at some personal cost, and the man who assures you the tree is fine is not being kind at all. Nobody thanks a doctor for a cheerful manner about a tumour he has decided not to mention. The news is only good if it is true, and if it is true, then the warning is part of the goodness.

Good news because of who was coming. What made John’s warnings good news was the one they announced. The axe was at the root, but the mightier one was at the door, and he was coming to baptise with the Spirit, to gather his wheat, and to save. Jesus himself would draw the line through John: the Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached (16:16). John evangelised by pointing; Jesus would evangelise by arriving, reading in the synagogue at Nazareth that the Spirit had anointed him to proclaim good news to the poor (4:18). The gospel John preached to the ordinary people of Judea was, in the end, a name.

How do I warn someone without driving them away? Let them see that you are warning them because you love them, not because you enjoy it or want to win. Speak about sin and judgement as one who stands under the same need, never from above. Be honest and plain, but gentle and patient (2 Timothy 2:24–26). Do not stop at the warning: always point to Christ, the way of escape, in the same breath. Choose your moment and listen first. And remember that it is the Spirit who convicts; your part is to be faithful and kind.

In a sentence. With many other appeals, John proclaimed the good news to the people.

On a Tuesday. Don’t be afraid to warn people of judgement. It is part of the good news, because it makes Christ’s salvation precious. And when the sermon on Sunday is hard, receive it as good news too: someone cares enough about your soul to tell you the truth.

For worship. The God who sent John is the God of the warning and the welcome. He tells the truth about the axe because he has already provided the shelter, and the shelter is his own Son, who took the blow in our place. Every hard word in his mouth is the sound of a door being held open. The whole of his word is good news, because the whole of it leads to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: But Herod the tetrarch, who had been reproved by him for Herodias, his brother's wife, and for all the evil things that Herod had done, added this to them all, that he locked up John in prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Herod the tetrarch, who had been reproved by John for Herodias, his brother’s wife, and for all the evil things that Herod had done, added this to them all: he locked up John in prison.

But Herod the tetrarch, who had been reproved by him for Herodias, his brother’s wife. Herod Antipas. Luke closes John’s story before Jesus’ begins, in two verses with a great deal held back. Herodias had been married to Herod’s half-brother (called Philip in Mark 6:17; not the tetrarch Philip of v. 1). She was also Herod’s own niece. On a journey to Rome, Herod had stayed with his half-brother and fallen for his brother’s wife, and the two agreed to marry. To marry her he divorced his own wife, the daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas, an insult that would eventually cost him a war; and Herodias divorced her husband. The marriage broke God’s law: you shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). John told Herod to his face that it was unlawful (Mark 6:18). A prophet confronting a king, like Nathan with David (2 Samuel 12) and Elijah with Ahab (1 Kings 21).

He did not have to. John’s ministry was at the Jordan, among crowds who came to him. Nobody required him to address the tetrarch’s marriage. He could have preached repentance to Judea for years without ever mentioning the palace, and he would have died an old man. He went to the one man in the country who could have him killed, and told him the truth about his private life.

And for all the evil things that Herod had done. His sins were many, so it was not one sermon about one marriage. John kept at it, across the whole range of the man’s conduct, and Mark tells us something Luke leaves out, that Herod was greatly perplexed by him and yet heard him gladly (Mark 6:20). There was a strange, doomed relationship there: a king who liked hearing the preacher who condemned him, and killed him anyway. It is possible to enjoy sermons for years and keep the one thing they keep naming. Herod could bear to hear about his sin; what he could not bear was to give up Herodias. A man who will not let go of his idol will in the end silence whoever names it.

Added this to them all, that he locked up John in prison. Instead of repenting, he silenced the preacher. Not a martyrdom scene, not a speech: a door shut, a summary clause, and the voice is gone from the story. Josephus tells us John was imprisoned in the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea. Herod later had him beheaded (9:9; Mark 6:17–29).

Faithfulness is not always repaid here. John did exactly what he was sent to do, without flinching, without ambition, without ever diverting the crowd’s admiration onto himself. And he finished in a cell in a desert fortress, and, as Mark tells us, was executed at a birthday feast because a girl danced well and her mother held a grudge. His reward was not in this life, and Jesus would say of him that among those born of women none is greater (7:28).

Luke’s order. Luke tells of John’s imprisonment here, before Jesus’ baptism (v. 21), though it happened later. He rounds off John’s story before turning to Jesus, so that the stage is clear for him. John decreases; Jesus increases. Luke’s placing is deliberate. The forerunner ends in prison on the page immediately before the one he announced steps into the river.

The forerunner goes first into the dark. John goes before Jesus even here. The same Herod who shut John’s mouth will hear of Jesus and say, John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things? (9:9). When at last they meet, Herod will question him at length, and Jesus will give him no answer at all (23:9). Matthew records Jesus saying that as they did to John whatever they pleased, so the Son of Man would suffer at their hands (Matthew 17:12). The prison at Machaerus is the first shadow of the cross. The one whose sandals John was not worthy to untie would follow his herald into the hands of wicked men, not because he could not escape them, but because he had come to die for sinners, Herod’s kind and John’s.

Should Christians speak out about the sins of public figures? Sometimes, yes. John did, and so did Nathan and Elijah. Church leaders have a duty to declare God’s law plainly, including to the powerful, and Christians may rightly say that what a ruler does is wrong. But notice John’s manner: he spoke to Herod, not merely about him; he was moved by the law of God, not by party politics; and he paid for it himself. Speak truth about public sin without gossip, without glee, and without forgetting the sins nearer home. And pray for rulers, including the ones you must oppose (1 Timothy 2:1–2).

In a sentence. When John rebuked Herod for marrying his brother’s wife and for his other sins, Herod added to his evil by imprisoning him.

On a Tuesday. Faithful preaching may cost you dearly. And beware of silencing those who confront your sin; it only adds to the sin. Think of the person who last told you a hard truth about yourself. Did you thank them, or shut the door?

For worship. Herod could shut a door on John, and the word of God was not bound. As the herald’s voice fell silent, the one he announced was beginning his work with heaven open over him. Kings lock up preachers, and the Lord of those preachers rises from the dead and reigns over every throne. John’s voice went quiet in a fortress by the Dead Sea; the Word he served is speaking still, in the languages of the earth, and no tetrarch has ever been able to answer him.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the tetrarch is Herod Antipas. Herodias had been married to his half-brother. Luke tells of John’s imprisonment here, ahead of the story, to close his account of John.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The baptism of Jesus is narrated with remarkable brevity in Luke — briefer even than in Mark. Luke does not linger on the event; the baptism itself is a participle, almost an aside. What he focuses on is what happens while Jesus is praying afterwards.

This is characteristic. Luke consistently shows Jesus at prayer at the great turning points of his ministry (3:21; 6:12; 9:18; 9:28; 11:1; 22:41). The baptism is not the centre of the scene; the prayer is. And what happens during it is the most explicit Trinitarian moment in the Synoptic Gospels: the Son in the water; the Spirit descending in bodily form like a dove; the Father's voice from heaven.

Why is Jesus baptised at all? John's baptism was for repentance and forgiveness, and Jesus has nothing to repent of. Matthew records John's protest and Jesus's answer: “Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness” (Matt. 3:15).

He is baptised not because he needs what the water signifies but because he is identifying himself with the people he came to save. He enters the water of repentance as the representative of those who need to repent; he will enter the waters of death as the representative of those who deserve to die. The Jordan is the first public act of the substitution that ends at Golgotha.

The Father's voice weaves two Old Testament texts together. “You are my Son” is Psalm 2:7, the royal psalm of the Davidic king. “With you I am well pleased” is Isaiah 42:1, the opening of the first Servant Song. Jesus is simultaneously the royal Son of David and the suffering Servant of Isaiah — the King who will reign and the Servant who will be crushed. Both identities are laid on him at the outset, and the whole ministry is the working out of what it costs to be both at once.
verseByVerse.theology:
The descent of the Spirit “in bodily form, like a dove” is Luke's careful insistence that this was a visible, physical event — not a vision or an inward impression but something anyone standing on the bank could have seen.

The dove carries a layered background: the dove of Noah signalling that the judgment was over (Gen. 8:8-12); the dove of the poor person's offering (Lev. 5:7; and 2:24 in this Gospel); and, most significantly, the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Gen. 1:2). The Spirit is over the water again. A new creation is beginning.

The Father's declaration comes before Jesus has performed a single public miracle, preached a single sermon, or won a single crowd. The pleasure of the Father in the Son is not contingent on performance; it is the expression of the love that existed between them before the foundation of the world (John 17:24).

That is the theological foundation of grace: the beloved Son is beloved before he does anything. And the Christian who is in Christ shares the status — not earned but given, not provisional but settled.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus praying at his baptism is the first instance of a pattern that runs through the whole Gospel. The implication is not that prayer is a mechanism that causes the Spirit to descend. It is that prayer is the posture of one who depends entirely on the Father rather than on his own resources.

The Son of God prays before every major act of his ministry — not because he lacks information or power, but because prayer is the expression of the relationship that defines him. The disciple who prays before decisions and transitions is not following a technique. He is following his Lord.

The Trinity is present at the Jordan in a way impossible to mistake and impossible to fully systematise. The three are distinct: the Son is in the water, the Spirit descends, the Father speaks. The three are simultaneously present, simultaneously active, simultaneously directed towards one redemptive event.

The doctrine of the Trinity is not a philosophical puzzle invented by later councils. It is the description of what happened at the Jordan. The church was simply trying to find words adequate to what the evangelists reported.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when all the people were baptized, and when Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, the heavens were opened,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When all the people were baptised, and when Jesus also had been baptised and was praying, the heavens were opened.

Now when all the people were baptized. Two details in that sentence are Luke’s alone. The first is when all the people were baptised: Luke puts Jesus in among the crowd, one of the people. He tells it briefly, without naming John, and does not describe the baptism itself at all; the verb is a participle, almost an aside. What interests him is not the ceremony but where Jesus was standing while it happened: in the same river, on the same day, with the same crowd, receiving the same sign. The second, that he was praying, comes a few words later.

And when Jesus also had been baptized. Which raises the question the chapter has been building towards. John was preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins (v. 3). What is the one man in history with nothing to repent of doing in that water? Why was the sinless Son of God baptised with a baptism of repentance? Matthew records John’s objection, and Jesus’ answer: let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness (Matthew 3:14–15). He is not there because he needs what the water means. He identified himself completely with the sinners he came to save, taking his place among them: standing in the sinners’ queue, at the sinners’ river, receiving the sinners’ sign, on the first day of his public life.

The opening move of the great exchange. What begins in the Jordan will be finished on a hill where he takes the sinners’ death. Everything he did between those two points he did in that position: numbered with the transgressors, from the Jordan to the cross (Isaiah 53:12; Luke 22:37). He began his ministry as he would end it: standing in the place of sinners. That is what is meant by the great exchange. He takes the place of sinners, with their guilt and their punishment, and they are given his place: his righteousness, which means his perfect record of doing right, and his welcome with the Father. God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21).

And was praying. Only Luke notes this, and it is the first appearance of something he will do all the way through. Prayer marks every turning point of Jesus’ life in Luke: here; before choosing the Twelve, when he prays all night (6:12); before Peter’s confession, praying alone (9:18); at the transfiguration, when he goes up to pray (9:28–29); in Gethsemane (22:41–44); on the cross (23:34, 46). The Son of God depended on his Father in prayer. The prayer does not cause the heavens to open, as though it were a technique. It is the posture of a Son who does nothing out of his own resources.

The heavens were opened. As Isaiah prayed: Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down (Isaiah 64:1). The barrier between heaven and earth is opened. God is about to speak.

Does Jesus’ baptism mean I should be baptised? Yes, though for a different reason. He was baptised to identify with sinners; we are baptised as sinners who have been joined to him, to show that we have died and risen with Christ (Romans 6:3–4). He commanded his disciples to baptise those who become disciples (Matthew 28:19), and the New Testament pattern is that those who believe are baptised (Acts 2:41; 8:12, 36–38). If you trust Christ and have never been baptised as a believer, speak to your pastor. It is not what saves you, but it is the obedience of the saved, and the Lord who stepped into the Jordan for you asks it of you.

In a sentence. After Jesus was baptised along with the people, while he was praying, heaven opened.

On a Tuesday. If the Son of God would not begin his ministry without praying, the question of whether prayer is a good use of time before a decision has been settled by somebody with far better reasons than ours to skip it. Before the big decision this week, the conversation, the interview, the purchase, stop and pray first.

For worship. The heavens Isaiah begged God to tear open were opened over a man standing in a river with sinners. The holy one waded into the water of repentance for a people who had everything to repent of, and he never left that place until he had carried their sins to the cross, where the curtain of the temple was torn in two (23:45). Heaven opened over him at the Jordan, and because of what he did at Calvary it stands open still for all who are found in him.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke notes that Jesus was praying.

verseByVerse.quote: and the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove; and a voice came from heaven, 'You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form, like a dove; and a voice came from heaven: You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.

The Trinity. The heavens open, and all three persons of the Godhead are present in one sentence. The Father speaks from heaven, the Son is baptised, the Spirit descends. One of the clearest revelations of the Trinity in Scripture: one God, three persons, each distinct and each active.

And the Holy Spirit descended on him. Anointing him for his ministry. He has been the Christ, the Anointed One, from his birth (2:11); now he is publicly anointed with the Spirit (4:18; Acts 10:38). To anoint is to set someone apart and equip him for a task: oil was poured on Israel’s kings and priests as the sign, and on Jesus God poured out the Spirit himself. It does not mean he became divine at the Jordan. It means that, as a man, he was publicly commissioned and filled with power for his work as Prophet, Priest and King. Isaiah had foretold it: the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him (Isaiah 11:2; 42:1; 61:1).

In bodily form, like a dove. Only Luke says in bodily form, and he adds it on purpose: a visible appearance, not just a feeling or an inward impression or a private vision. Something happened in the air over the Jordan that could have been seen by anyone standing there. Why a dove? The image has several roots and they run together. A dove came back to Noah over a drowned world with a leaf in its beak, and the judgement was over (Genesis 8:8–12): a new beginning after judgement. And at the very beginning, the Spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters (Genesis 1:2). The Spirit is over the water again. Something is being made new: a new creation begins.

You are my beloved Son. Then the voice, and it is two Scriptures woven together, and the combination is the whole programme of the ministry that is about to start. You are my Son is Psalm 2:7, where God says it to his anointed king: the coronation psalm of the Davidic king, the one who is given the nations for his inheritance. Jesus is the messianic King and the eternal Son. “Beloved” may also echo Genesis 22:2, Isaac, Abraham’s beloved only son, who was to be sacrificed.

With you I am well pleased. Isaiah 42:1: Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him. The opening of the first Servant Song, about the one who will not break a bruised reed (Isaiah 42:3); the later songs show the same Servant despised and crushed for the sins of others. Jesus is the Servant of the Lord, who will suffer and die for the sins of many (Isaiah 53). In one sentence the Father declares Jesus to be both the Son-King and the suffering Servant: the throne and the cross, laid on him together.

Before he had done anything. The Father is pleased with him before he has done any public ministry: before the first sermon, before the first healing, before a single disciple has been called. There is no ministry yet to be pleased with. The thirty years of hidden obedience in Nazareth pleased the Father. The delight is not a wage paid for work completed; it is the settled love of the Father for the Son, older than the world (John 17:24).

In the flow. The word Son is the thread that ties the next chapter and a half together. The Father says, You are my beloved Son (v. 22). The genealogy that follows ends with Adam, the son of God (v. 38). The devil’s first and last temptations begin, If you are the Son of God (4:3, 9). And at Nazareth the congregation asks, Is not this Joseph’s son? (4:22). Luke wants the reader to carry the Father’s verdict through every one of those scenes: whatever Satan suggests and whatever the neighbours assume, heaven has already said who he is.

Did Jesus become the Son of God at his baptism? No. He was the Son from eternity, and Luke has already said that the child to be born would be called the Son of God (1:35). Some ancient manuscripts here read today I have begotten you, which some took to mean he was adopted as Son at the Jordan; the better text reads with you I am well pleased. The baptism was the public anointing of the Son for his work, not his becoming Son.

For believers. Because we are in Christ, the Father’s words to him are true of us: in him, we are God’s beloved children, and God is pleased with us, not because of our performance, but because of his (Ephesians 1:6). That is the ground under the feet of everybody who is in Christ. The verdict spoken over him at the Jordan is the verdict spoken over all who are joined to him: not earned, not provisional, not reviewed annually. You do not work in order to be loved. You are loved, and then you work.

How can God be pleased with me when I keep failing? Because his pleasure in you rests on Christ, not on your record. When God looks at a believer, he sees him clothed in the righteousness of his Son, and he delights in him as he delights in his Son. Your failures grieve him, as a father is grieved, and he will discipline you for your good. But they do not change his verdict, because it was never based on you. So when you fail, do not hide from him; run to him, confess, and hear again over your head what he said over his Son’s: beloved. That is not licence to sin; it is the only soil in which real obedience grows.

In a sentence. The Spirit descended visibly on Jesus like a dove, and the Father declared from heaven that Jesus is his beloved Son, in whom he delights.

On a Tuesday. Begin today by hearing the Father’s verdict before you do anything at all. Work, serve and obey this week as one already loved, not as one trying to earn it.

For worship. Here is the Son, standing in the water where sinners stand, having taken their place before he has taken a step. Here is the Spirit, coming down on him as gently as a bird, to rest and not to depart. And here is the Father, speaking from the opened heavens to say what he thinks of him. Everything the world was made for, and everything it was ruined for, is standing in one river on one morning, and heaven is entirely delighted with him.

parallels.desc: the servant in whom God delights

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–38 — The Genealogy of Jesus Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke's genealogy is unlike Matthew's in three decisive ways: it runs backward, from Jesus to Adam rather than from Abraham to Jesus; it is placed after the baptism rather than before the birth narrative; and it extends past Abraham to Adam, and past Adam to God.

These are not inconsistencies but theological choices. Matthew writes for a Jewish readership and presents Jesus as the fulfilment of Israel's covenant story, beginning with Abraham. Luke writes with the world in view and presents Jesus as the answer to the human story, beginning at the Jordan — where his identity has just been declared by the Father — and tracing his lineage to the first man.

The genealogy also differs from Matthew's in many of the names between David and Joseph. Some hold that Luke traces the line through Mary; others that one evangelist follows legal succession and the other physical descent; others appeal to the complexities of levirate marriage. No solution is free of difficulty, and the church has lived with the two lists for two thousand years without resolving every detail.

What is clear is that the difference does work. Matthew's line runs through Solomon and the kings — the line that carries the legal right to the throne, and also the line under the curse pronounced on Jeconiah, that none of his offspring would prosper sitting on David's seat (Jer. 22:30). Luke's runs through Nathan, a son of David who never reigned and whose descendants never came under that word. On one common reading, the crown descends by one branch and the blood by another, and they meet in one child.

Most of the names between David and Joseph are otherwise unknown — dozens of men of whom Scripture records nothing except that the line ran through their houses. Further back the list passes through Ruth the Moabite, through Perez the son of Tamar, through Abraham who twice lied about his wife. God ran the promise straight through a family history containing foreignness, deception and disgrace, and did not clean it up first.

The placement after the baptism gives the list its frame. The Father has just said “You are my Son”; the genealogy answers the question whose son, exactly? He is the son of Joseph as registered; the son of David, which is his royal credential; the son of Abraham, which is his covenantal one; the son of Adam, which is his human solidarity. And at the end of the list — the son of God.

He is the Son of God who has become the son of Adam, so that the sons of Adam might become the sons of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The genealogy ending in “son of Adam, son of God” is Luke's most compact statement of the theology of the incarnation. Jesus traces his human lineage to the first human, establishing the full solidarity of his humanity with every person who has ever lived.

He did not merely appear in human form. He entered the long human story at its most specific and particular point, with real ancestors and a real history — which is what Paul means by “born of woman, born under the law” (Gal. 4:4). Fully embedded in the situation he came to redeem.

The contrast between Adam and Jesus implicit here becomes explicit in Romans 5:12-21 and 1 Corinthians 15:21-22, 45-49. Adam brought death; the second Adam brings life. Adam's disobedience constituted many sinners; the second Adam's obedience constitutes many righteous.

Luke's genealogy does not spell out that typology — that is Paul's work — but it establishes the premise on which the typology stands: Jesus is the son of Adam, which means Adam's story is part of his story, and his story is the answer to Adam's.
verseByVerse.examples:
The genealogy is one of the portions of Scripture readers habitually skip — a long list of unfamiliar names that looks like a necessary but uninspiring prelude. But it is the gospel in miniature. It announces that the salvation of the world came not through power or privilege but through the long, winding, sometimes scandalous history of real families making real choices.

Every name in the list is a person whose life contributed to the moment when the Son of God stood in the Jordan, and almost none of them had any idea of it. Providence is not abstract. It is as specific as a name — including the many names in this list about whom history has kept nothing else at all.

The final phrase, “the son of Adam, the son of God,” is the summary of everything the Gospel will demonstrate. Jesus is fully human and fully divine, and the two cannot be separated without destroying the gospel.

A Jesus who is only divine cannot save us, because he cannot represent us. A Jesus who is only human cannot save us, because he has no righteousness to give. The Jesus of Luke's genealogy — rooted in human history all the way back to Eden, and named by the Father as his Son — is the only Jesus who can do what needs doing.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age, being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph, the son of Heli, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Melchi, the son of Jannai, the son of Joseph,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age, being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph, the son of Heli, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Melchi, the son of Jannai, the son of Joseph.

Jesus, when he began his ministry, was about thirty years of age. Luke says about thirty, which is exactly what a careful historian writes when he does not have the precise date. But thirty is not a random figure; it was the age of maturity for public service. Levites and priests entered the service of the sanctuary at thirty (Numbers 4:3); Joseph stood before Pharaoh at thirty (Genesis 41:46); David began to reign at thirty (2 Samuel 5:4). Whatever else it signalled, it was the age at which a man in Israel was considered fit to be given a life’s work. Eighteen years of that life had gone by since the last thing Luke recorded, and not one line of them survives.

Being the son (as was supposed) of Joseph. Luke guards the virgin birth. He has spent two chapters establishing that Joseph is not this child’s father, and he will not now quietly contradict himself. Jesus was Joseph’s son by law, by household, by trade and by every register in Galilee; not by blood.

Why the genealogy is here. Matthew puts his genealogy at the very beginning, tracing Jesus forward from Abraham, to show that he is the son of Abraham and of David, the Jewish Messiah (Matthew 1:1–17). Luke places his after the baptism, just before the temptation, and traces it backward all the way to Adam, the son of God (v. 38). The voice from heaven has just called Jesus my Son. The genealogy shows him as the true Son, the new Adam, who will succeed where Adam failed, as the temptation (4:1–13) immediately shows.

The son of Heli. Now the difficulty any reader with two Gospels open will run straight into. Set Luke’s list beside Matthew’s, and from David onwards they do not match. Matthew says Joseph’s father was Jacob (Matthew 1:16). Matthew comes down through Solomon and the kings of Judah; Luke comes down through Nathan, another of David’s sons (2 Samuel 5:14), through names that appear nowhere in the royal chronicles. Matthew has roughly twenty-seven generations between David and Jesus; Luke has about forty-two.

Why do the two genealogies differ? Christians have answered this in three main ways. One: Luke gives Mary’s line, and Heli was Mary’s father, Joseph being reckoned son of Heli as his son-in-law. That fits Luke’s careful as was supposed and his close interest in Mary through chapters 1 and 2, though it must be granted that Luke writes son of Heli and not father of Mary. Two: Matthew gives the royal, legal line of succession through Solomon, and Luke the physical descent of Joseph through Nathan. Three: levirate marriage, the law by which a man who died childless had offspring raised up to his name by his brother (Deuteronomy 25:5–6), so that one man could have a legal father and a biological father under two names. The ancient historian Julius Africanus (about AD 220) gave this explanation, saying it came from Jesus’ own family relatives. Each answer carries a difficulty. Genealogies in that world were kept to make a point, not to satisfy a modern registrar, and these two evangelists are making different points. The more likely answer is that Matthew traces Joseph’s legal line through Solomon, the royal line, while Luke traces the physical line through Nathan, probably Mary’s, with Heli as Joseph’s father-in-law. Any of these is possible, and both Gospels trace Jesus to David: legally through Joseph, and by blood through his mother. The difference does real work rather than real damage: the crown comes down one branch of David’s family, and the blood, most likely, down another, and they meet in him.

In a sentence. Jesus began his ministry at about thirty, supposed to be Joseph’s son, and Luke traces his ancestry back from Joseph.

On a Tuesday. Jesus spent thirty years in preparation for three years of ministry. God’s timing in your life may be slower than you would like. Trust it. The years that seem to count for nothing are not wasted in his hands.

For worship. The Son of God waited thirty years before he spoke in public, content to be thought the carpenter’s son. He did not hurry his Father’s timetable or grasp at recognition. He who is the eternal Son allowed himself to be supposed something less, and the God who knows every name in the line knew exactly who he was. The Father’s timing was perfect, and his Son kept it.
verseByVerse.note: Thirty was the age of maturity for public service. Luke’s genealogy runs backward and differs from Matthew’s after David; many think Luke traces Mary’s line or Joseph’s legal line.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Mattathias, the son of Amos, the son of Nahum, the son of Esli, the son of Naggai, the son of Maath, the son of Mattathias, the son of Semein, the son of Josech, the son of Joda, the son of Joanan, the son of Rhesa, the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, the son of Neri, the son of Melchi, the son of Addi, the son of Cosam, the son of Elmadam, the son of Er, the son of Joshua, the son of Eliezer, the son of Jorim, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Simeon, the son of Judah, the son of Joseph, the son of Jonam, the son of Eliakim, the son of Melea, the son of Menna, the son of Mattatha, the son of Nathan, the son of David,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The son of Mattathias, the son of Amos, the son of Nahum … the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel … the son of Nathan, the son of David.

Names we do not know. Seven verses, thirty-five names, and almost none of them is known. From Joseph back to David, Luke names men who appear nowhere else in Scripture. Maath, Naggai, Esli, Josech, Joda, Elmadam, Cosam, Jorim, Melea, Menna: no stories, no deeds, no record of anything they said or did. Ordinary people, faithful or unfaithful, in whose line, generation after generation, God was working toward the birth of his Son. Whoever they were, they lived and died and left nothing behind them except that the line ran through their houses.

The son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel. Apart from Nathan and David at the end, only two names in the whole stretch surface elsewhere. Zerubbabel led the first return of the Jews from exile in Babylon, and laid the foundation of the second temple (Ezra 3; Haggai 1–2). Haggai prophesied that God would make him like a signet ring (Haggai 2:23). Both genealogies include him and his father Shealtiel, perhaps because the two lines crossed there. Everything either side of them is silence.

The son of Nathan, the son of David. Then, at verse 31, the list arrives at Nathan, and here is where the two genealogies do their different work. Luke’s line runs through Nathan, a son of David by Bathsheba (2 Samuel 5:14; 1 Chronicles 3:5), not through Solomon, as Matthew’s does. Matthew’s line runs from David through Solomon and the kings. That is the line that carries the legal right to the throne, and it is also the line that runs through King Jeconiah (Jehoiachin), Solomon’s descendant, of whom the LORD said that none of his offspring would succeed in sitting on the throne of David (Jeremiah 22:30). A curse lies across the royal succession.

The crown and the blood. Luke’s line runs from David through a son who never reigned, whose descendants never sat on the throne, and who therefore never came under that word. Put the two lists together and, on one common reading, something remarkable appears: the crown descends by one branch and the blood by another, and they meet in one child. Jesus, physically descended through Nathan (if Luke gives the physical line), escapes the curse, while inheriting the legal right to the throne through Joseph. However the details are explained, both lines meet in David, and the two lists agree on everything that matters.

God kept their names. There is a quieter thing in these verses for anybody who feels that their life has not amounted to much. History has kept nothing about these men except that they existed, married, and had a son. God kept their names. They had no idea what they were part of. Not one of them lived to see the point of his own place in the list. They simply took their turn, and every one of them was necessary, and every one of them is written down in the book that will outlast every other book, because the Son of God came through their houses.

Does an ordinary, unremembered life matter to God? Yes, more than we can see. Most believers will leave no mark on history: no book, no building, no name on a plaque. But God records what the world forgets. He numbers the hairs of your head (12:7), writes the names of his people in the book of life (Philippians 4:3), and remembers a cup of cold water given in his name (Matthew 10:42). A faithful marriage, children raised in the faith, honest work, prayers for a grandchild: these are the links through which he has always carried his purposes. You may never see what your place in the line was for. He does.

In a sentence. The genealogy continues back through the exile’s leader Zerubbabel to David’s son Nathan and to David himself.

On a Tuesday. You may never be remembered in the history books. But God is working through ordinary faithful generations. Your faithfulness matters. Take your turn today, in your home, your work and your church, as one of the links God is using.

For worship. Between David and Joseph lie some forty names of men who never saw what they were carrying, and the God who swore an oath to David carried it for them: through the exile, through the word spoken against Jeconiah’s line, through centuries when the royal house had come down to a builder’s yard in Galilee. Not one link broke, because the promise rested on his faithfulness, not theirs. And at the end of the line he set his own Son, the King who will reign over the house of Jacob for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s line runs through Nathan, David’s son, not Solomon.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz, the son of Sala, the son of Nahshon, the son of Amminadab, the son of Admin, the son of Arni, the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah, the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, the son of Terah, the son of Nahor,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz, the son of Sala, the son of Nahshon, the son of Amminadab, the son of Admin, the son of Arni, the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah, the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, the son of Terah, the son of Nahor.

The son of Jesse, the son of Obed, the son of Boaz. Now the names begin to be recognisable, and the whole familiar story comes back up through the list. This is the line of the book of Ruth, its last page (Ruth 4:18–22), and it is worth remembering what stands behind it. Boaz married Ruth, a Moabite widow, a foreigner, from a people the law had barred from the assembly of the LORD to the tenth generation (Deuteronomy 23:3). Their son was Obed, Obed’s son was Jesse, and Jesse’s son was David. The line of the Messiah runs directly through a woman who by birth had no right to be anywhere near it. Matthew names her (Matthew 1:5); Luke does not, but she is there. God’s plan included Gentiles from the beginning. Nahshon, a few names further back, was the leader of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness, at the head of the column when Israel marched (Numbers 1:7; 10:14).

The son of Perez, the son of Judah. Here the list goes somewhere most family trees would rather not. Perez was born to Judah by Tamar, his widowed daughter-in-law, whom Judah failed to provide for and then took for a prostitute at a roadside without recognising her (Genesis 38). It is one of the ugliest chapters in Genesis, a shameful story. And that is where the line runs. God worked even through human sin. Jacob had prophesied that the sceptre would not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10). Jesus is the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5:5).

The son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham. The patriarchs, to whom God made the promises (Genesis 12:1–3; 22:18), and the whole of the patriarchal history in three names. Jacob the deceiver; Isaac, born when his parents were long past hope of a child; Abraham, who twice passed his wife off as his sister to save his own skin, and who was given the promise anyway. Matthew begins here; Luke goes further back, to Terah and Nahor, Abraham’s father and grandfather, who lived beyond the Euphrates and served other gods (Joshua 24:2). God called Abraham out of a pagan family.

He did not clean it up first. What that stretch of the genealogy says, and says without a single word of commentary, is that God brought his Son into the world through a family history containing deception, prostitution, foreignness, cowardice, idolatry and long stretches of nothing at all. He did not clean it up first. He did not route around the shameful parts. He ran the line of the promise straight through Judah’s roadside and Ruth’s Moab, and then had it written down and read aloud in public for two thousand years. The family did not have to be made clean first, because the child at the end of it would make it clean. The Son of God took a family tree full of sin so that he could carry the sin itself: him who knew no sin God made to be sin for us (2 Corinthians 5:21). The one born of Judah and Tamar’s line is the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5:5), and the Lamb who was slain to ransom people from every tribe.

What about my family history? There is a mercy in that which is easy to miss. A family history is one of the things people are least able to change and most often ashamed of: the divorce, the addiction, the prison sentence, the abuse, the generations who never knew God. Luke is quietly reporting that the Saviour of the world has one too, and that God is not embarrassed by it, and did not require it to be respectable before he would work through it. Your family’s past does not decide your future in Christ. Patterns can be broken by grace (Ezekiel 18:14–17). Grieve what was wrong, forgive what you can, seek help where you need it, and begin a new line of faithfulness. God has done it before.

In a sentence. The genealogy goes back through David’s family, including Boaz and Ruth, to Judah and the patriarchs, and to Abraham’s pagan ancestors.

On a Tuesday. God’s grace runs through families with foreigners, scandals and idolaters. No family history is beyond his redemption. Pray today for the hardest member of your family, and for the generations after you.

For worship. The promise given to Abraham, that in his offspring all the families of the earth would be blessed, travelled down this line for two thousand years and never once depended on the people carrying it. God carried it himself, past Terah’s idols, Judah’s roadside and Ruth’s Moab, and brought it safely to a manger in Bethlehem. Now the blessing flows back out into every family on earth, Moabite and Gentile and ours, because the Offspring has come.

verseByVerse.quote: the son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah, the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech, the son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch, the son of Jared, the son of Mahalaleel, the son of Cainan, the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah, the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech, the son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch, the son of Jared, the son of Mahalaleel, the son of Cainan, the son of Enos, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.

Beyond Abraham. The last four verses take the line back past Abraham, past the flood, past the whole history of Israel, to the first man, following Genesis 11 and Genesis 5, and then one step further. Matthew’s genealogy stops at Abraham, because Matthew is establishing that Jesus is Israel’s Messiah. Luke keeps going, and the difference is the whole shape of his Gospel. He is writing for the world. Jesus is not only the Jewish Messiah, but the Saviour of the whole human race. This fits Luke’s great theme: all flesh shall see the salvation of God (v. 6).

The son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad. A note for the reader with a Bible open at Genesis, because there is a real puzzle here. This Cainan (v. 36) is not in the Hebrew text of Genesis 11:12, which runs Arphaxad, then Shelah, but appears in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), which Luke and his readers used. Some hold that the Greek preserves a name the Hebrew line dropped; others that a copyist’s eye slipped, since a Cainan appears a few names later in the list. It cannot be settled from where we stand. What is worth knowing is that ancient genealogies were not always complete; they could skip generations, since son of can mean descendant of. Matthew does so openly, and genealogies were never intended to function as a complete census of everyone who lived.

The son of Noah, the son of Enoch, the son of Seth. Noah, through whom the human race was preserved through the flood, narrowed to one boat. Enoch, who walked with God, and he was not, for God took him (Genesis 5:24). Seth, born after Abel was murdered and Cain went out from God’s presence; in his days people began to call upon the name of the LORD (Genesis 4:26).

The son of Adam, the son of God. The climax. Adam had no human father; he was created directly by God, and so called God’s son. Jesus also had no human father; he is the eternal Son of God made man. Luke has put the genealogy immediately after the baptism, and now the reason is plain. At verse 22 a voice from heaven said You are my beloved Son. At verse 38 the list arrives at the same title from the other end. The Son declared at the Jordan is traced back, through more than seventy generations of ordinary and disgraceful and forgotten people, to the son of Adam, and past Adam, who had no father, to God.

One of us. He is the son of Adam. That is the point of every name in the list. He did not appear in human form as a visitor wearing the costume of our race; he entered the human story at its most specific and particular point, with real ancestors and a real history, all the way back to the beginning.
