What Adam ruined, he is now inside, as one of us, from the same stock, subject to the same conditions, related by blood to every person who has ever lived.

The last Adam. And he is the Son of God. Adam, the first son of God, failed the test in a garden and plunged humanity into sin and death. Jesus, the true Son of God, is about to be tested in the wilderness (4:1–13), and will succeed. Where the first Adam was made and failed, the second Adam has come and will not. He is the last Adam, the head of a new humanity (Romans 5:12–21; 1 Corinthians 15:22, 45–49). As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive. To be the head of a humanity means that what he does counts for all who belong to him. Adam’s one disobedience brought condemnation on everyone in him; Christ’s obedience, shown first in the wilderness and finished on the cross, brings a right standing with God and life to everyone joined to him by faith (Romans 5:18–19).

Does it matter whether Adam was a real man? Yes. Luke places Adam in the same list as David and Abraham, as a real ancestor, and Paul’s whole argument in Romans 5 depends on one man’s sin bringing death and one man’s obedience bringing life. If there was no first Adam, the parallel with the last Adam loses its footing. Christians discuss many questions about Genesis and science, and should do so humbly. But the Bible’s teaching that all humanity descends from one man created by God, who fell, and that Christ came as the second head of a redeemed humanity, is part of the gospel itself.

In a sentence. Luke traces Jesus’ ancestry back through Noah and Seth to Adam, the son of God, presenting Jesus as the new Adam and Saviour of all humanity.

On a Tuesday. In Adam you were born into sin and death. In Christ, the last Adam, you can be born into new life. When you meet someone today, of any nation or background, remember that he is your relative through Adam, and that Christ came as his kinsman too.

For worship. Two men stand at the head of the human race, and the list that runs between them is a catalogue of what the first one’s failure cost. Every name is a man who was born and died. Every name is a link in a chain of dust returning to dust, stretching unbroken from a garden to a river in Judea, and at the end of it, standing in the water with the Spirit resting on him and his Father’s voice still in the air, is the one who came to break it: the last Adam, who would go down into the dust himself, and come up out of it on the third day with a new humanity in him.
verseByVerse.note: Luke traces the line back to Adam — Jesus belongs to all humanity. The Cainan of verse 36 appears in the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 11, not the Hebrew.

4.title: The Testing and the Anointing
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the chapter of beginnings and confrontations. It opens with the Spirit leading Jesus into the wilderness for forty days of testing — the place where Israel repeatedly failed, now entered by Israel's true representative who will not fail. It continues with the dramatic scene in the Nazareth synagogue where Jesus reads from Isaiah 61 and announces that the Scripture has been fulfilled in their hearing — only to be driven out of the town by the same people who had initially marvelled at him. And it concludes with a succession of healings and exorcisms in Capernaum that demonstrate in action what the Isaiah text announced in words: the kingdom of God has come.

The temptation narrative (vv. 1–13) is the interpretive key to the whole of Jesus's ministry. The devil offers Jesus three things — bread, power, and supernatural protection — and each offer is a shortcut around the path of obedience and suffering that leads to the cross. Jesus refuses each offer with the word of Scripture, demonstrating that the weapons of his warfare are not the weapons of power but the word of God and trust in the Father. The one who overcomes the devil in the wilderness will face him again, in various guises, throughout the ministry — and will face him definitively in the garden of Gethsemane and on the cross. The wilderness is not the final battle; it is the first.

The Nazareth sermon (vv. 14–30) is Luke's programmatic statement of Jesus's mission — the equivalent of the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew. Luke places it at the beginning of the public ministry as the manifesto of the kingdom: good news to the poor, liberty to the captives, sight to the blind, freedom for the oppressed, the year of the Lord's favour. The question the sermon raises — who is included in the “year of the Lord's favour”? — is answered by two Old Testament examples that the congregation finds intolerable: Elijah went not to an Israelite widow but to a Sidonian one; Elisha healed not an Israelite leper but a Syrian one. The good news of the kingdom is for the excluded, the foreigner, the unexpected. This is the gospel Luke has been writing toward since chapter 1 — and the congregation's response is homicidal rage.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The temptation follows immediately on the baptism: the Spirit who descended at the Jordan now leads Jesus into the wilderness for forty days. The sequence is deliberate. The Father's declaration of sonship — “You are my beloved Son” — is at once followed by the devil's challenge to it: “If you are the Son of God…”

The wilderness is where the identity given at the baptism is tested, and where the question of what kind of Son Jesus will be is answered. Will he use divine power for his own relief? Will he take the world's kingdoms by the world's methods? Will he force the Father to prove his care? The answer each time is no — and the no is spoken not by supernatural force but with the word of Scripture.

The three assaults correspond to Israel's three great wilderness failures. Israel hungered and grumbled (Exod. 16); Jesus is tempted to turn stone into bread. Israel worshipped the golden calf (Exod. 32); Jesus is offered the kingdoms for an act of worship. Israel tested God at Massah (Exod. 17:1-7); Jesus is urged to throw himself from the temple. At every point where Israel failed, Jesus stands — and he does it by the means available to every Israelite: the word of God, believed and obeyed. All three of his answers come from Deuteronomy, the book Moses gave Israel before they entered the land.

The final offer is the subtlest, because it comes with chapter and verse. The devil quotes Psalm 91 — accurately, so far as it goes. But he stops the quotation at “to guard you” and omits the psalm's own qualifier, “in all your ways.” The promise covers the paths of obedience; it does not cover a stunt. The temptation is not to misread a promise but to use one as leverage — to demand that the Father demonstrate his care by preventing the consequences of a chosen folly.

Jesus answers from Deuteronomy 6:16 and the memory of Massah. The difference between trust and testing is the difference between resting in God's faithfulness and requiring him to prove it on our terms. The person who says “I will believe God loves me if he does this specific thing” is not trusting God. He is testing him.

The section ends with a phrase Luke intends to be remembered: the devil departed “until an opportune time.” The wilderness was the opening exchange, not the war.
verseByVerse.theology:
The temptation establishes Jesus as the second Adam as well as the true Israel. Adam was tempted in a garden of abundance and failed; Jesus is tempted in a wilderness of deprivation and stands. Adam's failure brought sin and death into the human story; Jesus's obedience begins the reversal.

This is the logic Paul unpacks in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15: what the first Adam lost, the second Adam wins back. And the victory is not won by raw divine force but by the very means God made available to Adam — the word of God, and the decision to trust it rather than the alternative on offer.

The devil's departure “until an opportune time” (v. 13) signals that the conflict continues through the ministry — in the demons, in the religious leaders, in the crowd's wish for a political king. The appointed opportunity is the passion: “Then Satan entered into Judas” (22:3); “this is your hour, and the power of darkness” (22:53).

And at the cross the wilderness temptations return almost verbatim — save yourself; if you are the Christ; if you are the King of the Jews. What looks there like Satan's victory is the moment of his defeat, because the Son who refused every shortcut in the desert walked the full cost of obedience to its end.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus's weapon against every temptation is Scripture — received, remembered, and spoken with precision. He does not argue philosophically, does not marshal feelings, and does not reach for resources unavailable to ordinary disciples. He quotes the word of God.

That is not a pastoral cliché but a pattern with hard practical consequences. The Christian who has stored up Scripture has the weapon Jesus used. The Christian who has neglected it is left to improvise arguments in the moment, which is not a fair fight.

The devil quotes Psalm 91 accurately, and with a clause removed. The most dangerous misuse of Scripture is never the obviously wrong use; it is the superficially plausible one — a true promise lifted out of its context and used to license what the context forbids. Every cult and every proof-texted disaster has this shape.

Which is the argument for knowing not merely verses but the shape of the whole book. A man who knows a hundred verses can be beaten by a hundred and one. A man who knows what God is doing across the whole of Scripture can recognise a true verse being turned against its own purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness for forty days, being tempted by the devil. And he ate nothing during those days. And when they were ended, he was hungry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness for forty days, being tempted by the devil. He ate nothing during those days, and when they were ended, he was hungry.

Meaning first. Luke 4 shows the Son of God beginning his work, and the whole chapter is about the power of his word. In the wilderness he answers every temptation with Scripture, standing where Adam and Israel fell. At Nazareth he reads Isaiah’s promise of the Spirit-anointed one who brings good news to the poor and release to the captives, and says it is fulfilled today, in him; his own town then tries to throw him off a cliff for reminding them of God’s grace to a Gentile widow and a Syrian general. In Capernaum his word silences a demon, rebukes a fever and heals a whole street at sunset, and then he moves on to preach the kingdom everywhere. Who is he? The obedient Son and the anointed King, come to set captives free.

The setting. The genealogy has just ended with Adam, the son of God (3:38), and now the new Son of God faces the test the first Adam failed. Adam was tested in a garden, with every tree but one to eat from, and fell; Jesus is tested in a wilderness, starving, and stands. He is also the true Israel: God called Israel his firstborn son (Exodus 4:22), and that son failed its forty years of testing. All three of Jesus’ answers come from Deuteronomy 6–8, Moses’ words about that wilderness. The story of the human race and of Israel is being lived again, by one man, and this time to the end.

Full of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit who came down at the Jordan (3:22) now leads him into a desert, not away from God but deeper into the Father’s purpose. And Luke is precise about the direction of travel: he goes in full of the Holy Spirit, and he is led by the Spirit. Being full of the Spirit does not mean being spared temptation; it means being equipped for it. The Spirit does not shield him from the testing. The Spirit conducts him into it.

Led by the Spirit in the wilderness. Temptation was not an accident or a defeat; it was part of God’s plan. The wilderness of Judea is barren and rocky, falling away between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea, home of wild animals (Mark 1:13). It is the landscape of Israel’s failure and of the scapegoat sent away carrying sin (Leviticus 16:10). The Son goes out into it of his own will, led by the Spirit, because that is where the battle has to be fought.

For forty days. The number is not decorative. Israel was forty years in the wilderness and failed there repeatedly (Deuteronomy 8:2); Moses was forty days on the mountain without bread or water (Exodus 34:28); Elijah walked forty days to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8). Jesus goes where Israel went, on Israel’s terms, and does what Israel could not do.

Being tempted by the devil. The tense suggests continuous temptation throughout the forty days, coming to a head at the end. The devil (diabolos, the slanderer, the accuser) is a real, personal being, the enemy of God and of man, and the temptations he pressed on this real man were real.

And he ate nothing during those days. And when they were ended, he was hungry. Luke, the physician, understates it. Forty days without food takes a body to the edge of what it can survive, and the last sentence is almost comic in its restraint. Real hunger, from a real human body, near starvation. The attack comes at the point of greatest physical weakness, which is where such attacks generally come.

If God tempts no one, why does the Spirit lead Jesus into temptation? A difficulty sits in the very first line, and a thoughtful reader should not step over it. James says plainly that God himself tempts no one (James 1:13). The knot loosens once you see that one Greek word (peirasmos) covers two things English keeps apart. It can mean a test, a trial meant to prove and strengthen, the way God tested Abraham on the mountain (Genesis 22:1) and tested Israel forty years to know what was in their heart (Deuteronomy 8:2). And it can mean a temptation, an enticement whose whole aim is to make a person fall. The two can occupy the very same moment while pulling in opposite directions. From the Father’s side this is a test: the Spirit leads the Son into the wilderness to prove and display an obedience the world would need to see. From the devil’s side the identical event is a temptation: every word out of his mouth is designed to make Jesus fall. God ordains the testing; Satan supplies the enticing. They share the same forty days, and God never does the second.

Then what am I asking when I pray, lead us not into temptation? Not that God might otherwise tempt us. When God leads you into hard testing he is never trying to make you sin (James 1:13); he is proving a faith he fully intends to carry through, and he has bound himself to provide the way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13). The prayer is the prayer of people who know their own weakness and ask the Father to keep the test from ever becoming a fall: to spare them trials they could not bear, and to hold them in the ones he sends. The sinless Son did not need to pray it for himself. We do, every day.

Where Christians differ: could Jesus have sinned? Some say that if he could not have sinned, the temptation was not real. Others say that as God, he could not sin. Verdict: the historic view is that Jesus, being God, could not sin (he was “impeccable”), yet the temptation was real and fully felt. A strong bridge cannot fall, but the weight on it is real. A wall that cannot be breached still takes the full force of the siege. Indeed, only the one who never gave way knew the full force of temptation, because the rest of us give way before it reaches its height.

Is being tempted a sin? No, and this settles a question that torments sensitive believers. Jesus was tempted, really tempted, by a real enemy, at real cost, and he was without sin. The pull itself is not the fall. If it were, the Lord who was tempted as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), could not be our Saviour. What becomes sin is welcoming the thought, entertaining it, turning it over with pleasure, and acting on it (James 1:14–15). So when an ugly thought arrives uninvited, do not conclude that you are a hypocrite. Turn from it, at once, to the one who faced the same and stood. Feeling the pull is the battlefield, not the defeat.

In a sentence. Full of the Spirit, Jesus was led into the wilderness, where he fasted forty days and was tempted by the devil throughout, and at the end he was hungry.

On a Tuesday. Being full of the Spirit does not mean you will not be tempted. Expect it, especially when you are weak: tired, hungry, lonely, ill, or just after a high point. Notice which hour of the day and which state of body your worst temptations usually choose, and prepare for that hour beforehand, with Scripture you have already put away in your memory, and with someone you can be honest with. And when the hard season comes, do not read it as a sign that God has left you. The Spirit led Jesus into the wilderness. He may lead you into one, and he will be there.

For worship. The Spirit who had just come down on him at the Jordan leads him out into the waste places, and the beloved Son goes, alone and hungry, into the country of the scapegoat and the grumblers. He did not wait for us to find our way out of the desert; he walked into it, on our terms and at the point of our weakness, and he did not give way. Every temptation his people will ever meet has already been met at its full height by the one who now intercedes for them. He knows its weight from inside, and he never once set it down on the wrong side.

verseByVerse.quote: The devil said to him, 'If you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread.' And Jesus answered him, 'It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The devil said to him: if you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread. Jesus answered him: it is written, man shall not live by bread alone.

If you are the Son of God. The devil is not doubting it; the Greek form suggests since you are. The Father has just said it over the Jordan (3:22). He is proposing that a Son with a Father like that ought not to be this hungry, and that if the Father is not going to do something about it, the Son should. The temptation is: use your sonship for yourself. Use your power to meet your own needs, independently of your Father. Why should the Son of God go hungry?

Command this stone to become bread. Two things are being attacked at once. The first is obvious: hunger. And there is nothing wrong with bread. He will make it for five thousand people before this Gospel is much older (9:10–17), and he will hand it to his friends on the last night of his life. The temptation is not to a bad thing. It is to a good thing, taken by the wrong hand at the wrong moment. To do it now, for himself, at Satan’s suggestion, would be to step out of dependence on his Father, who had led him into the wilderness to hunger. It would also be to refuse the path of humiliation and weakness he came to walk (Philippians 2:7). He would not use his divine power to avoid the human condition he came to share.

The shape of temptation. It is worth naming, because this is the shape it usually takes. Temptation rarely opens by suggesting that God does not exist. It opens by suggesting that God is not looking after you, and that you had better see to yourself. In the garden the serpent did the same: has God really said? He is keeping something good from you. The lie is always about the Father’s heart.

It is written. Jesus answers with Scripture, three times. The Son of God, full of the Spirit, does not argue with Satan or rely on his own wisdom. He does not analyse the temptation or explain why it is wrong. He answers from the written word, the sword of the Spirit (Ephesians 6:17), and stops. And the Scripture he uses is not obscure; it is from a book any Jewish boy would have known. His weapon was available to every person in Israel and is available now. If Jesus needed Scripture to resist temptation, how much more do we.

Man shall not live by bread alone. Deuteronomy 8:3, and the context is the whole point. Moses reminded Israel that God let them hunger in the wilderness and fed them with manna, that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD. Israel was hungry, grumbled, and demanded. Jesus is hungrier, and quotes the lesson Israel refused to learn, in the same desert, about the same God. Physical bread matters, but life depends ultimately on God and his word. His food was to do the will of the one who sent him (John 4:34).

Does this mean physical needs do not matter? No. Jesus did not despise bread; he fed the hungry and taught us to pray for daily bread (11:3). The verse says not by bread alone. Bread keeps the body alive for a time; God keeps the whole person alive for ever, and it is God who gives the bread in the first place. The point is order and dependence. A real need is not to be met by stepping outside the Father’s will, because the Father who gives the command is also the one who gives the food. If a choice ever comes between obeying God and getting what you need, the need is safer in his hands than in yours.

In a sentence. The devil tempted the starving Jesus to use his power as Son of God to make bread for himself, but Jesus answered from Scripture that life depends on more than bread.

On a Tuesday. There will be a moment, perhaps this week, when a real need meets a wrong way of meeting it. Where it applies: money that could be had by a small dishonesty on an expense claim; comfort that could be had from a bottle or a screen at the end of a hard day; affection that could be had from someone else’s spouse who seems to understand you. The need is genuine. The hunger is not sinful. What is being offered is a way of feeding yourself that does not go through the Father’s hand. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: this is not a call to refuse ordinary provision, to stop working, or to neglect medicine and food in the name of trusting God. Jesus was led by the Spirit to fast; most of the time the Father feeds us through ordinary means, and we should take them with thanks. The question underneath is always the same one: is he actually going to look after me, or had I better see to it myself?

For worship. The Son of God went hungry so that hungry people could be fed with the bread that does not perish. He would not turn one stone into bread for himself, and on the last night he took bread and broke it and said, this is my body, given for you. The one who refused to feed himself in the desert makes himself the food of his people. Everything he would not take for himself, he gives to us.

parallels.desc: man does not live by bread alone

verseByVerse.quote: And the devil took him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, and said to him, 'To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whom I will. If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The devil took him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, and said to him: to you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whom I will. If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours.

The order. Matthew has the temple second and the kingdoms last (Matthew 4:1–11). Neither writer is mistaken, because neither claims a stopwatch account: Luke strings his scenes with and, the loosest connective in the language. He ends with Jerusalem and the temple because Jerusalem is the goal of his whole Gospel, which began in the temple and will end there (9:51; 24:53). The order is a signpost, not a clock.

Showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time. The second assault changes altitude. Luke does not say how; no mountain is mentioned, and the phrase in a moment of time suggests a vision rather than an ordinary view. Kingdoms of the oikoumenē: the inhabited world, the Roman Empire and beyond. Every empire, every capital, every throne, all the power and glory of human civilisation, laid out in an instant.

For it has been delivered to me. Is he lying? It matters, because if that sentence is simply false the temptation has no force at all, and Jesus does not treat it as false. He disputes the price, not the ownership. The New Testament will not let us dismiss the claim. Jesus himself calls Satan the ruler of this world, three times in John’s Gospel (John 12:31; 14:30; 16:11). Paul calls him the god of this world (2 Corinthians 4:4). John writes that the whole world lies in the power of the evil one (1 John 5:19). Since Adam’s fall, humanity has been under his dominion. Something real is being described.

Delivered by whom? Look at the word he uses: handed over. Not seized, not created, not owned outright, but held on licence from someone who can revoke it. The devil is a usurper administering territory that was never his, on a lease he did not write and cannot extend. Ultimately all authority belongs to God, who gives the kingdom of men to whom he will (Daniel 4:17), and Satan is a liar and the father of lies (John 8:44). His claim is true, and it is far smaller than it sounds.

If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours. Here is what makes this the subtlest of the three. What he offers is not something Jesus should not want. The kingdoms of the world are exactly what the Father has already promised him: ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage (Psalm 2:8). Every empire in that flash of vision is going to be his. The devil is offering him his own inheritance. What is being offered is a short cut: the nations without Gethsemane, the crown without the cross. Everything the Father promised, delivered this afternoon, at a price that looks small. It is the same temptation Peter would put to him, and Jesus would answer him as he answers Satan here (Mark 8:32–33).

In a sentence. In a vision of all the world’s kingdoms, the devil offered Jesus all their authority and glory, claiming they were his to give, if Jesus would worship him.

On a Tuesday. This temptation is rarely a straightforward invitation to do evil. It is the right thing by a wrong route. Where it applies: the church growth built on a manipulated figure or a softened gospel; the marriage entered by a compromise of faith; the promotion gained by the quiet betrayal of a colleague; the peace in a family bought by pretending an offence never happened. In each case the goal is good. The road is the problem, and the road is what Jesus was sent to walk. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: this does not mean that every success is suspect or that ambition is sinful. To seek a promotion honestly, to want a church to grow, to work hard for influence that can be used well, is not bowing to Satan. The question is not whether you want the kingdom but what you are willing to bow to in order to get it.

Does Satan really control the world, so that Christians should withdraw from it? No. His power is real but borrowed, limited and already broken. The earth is the LORD’s, and everything in it (Psalm 24:1). Satan blinds minds and holds people captive (2 Corinthians 4:4; 2 Timothy 2:26), and Christians must not be naive about him. But Jesus came to bind the strong man and plunder his house (11:21–22), and after the resurrection he declares that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him (Matthew 28:18). So Christians do not retreat from the world as enemy territory; they go into it as the King’s ambassadors, doing their work, raising their families and serving their neighbours under a better Lord.

For worship. He was offered the world for one bow, and he would not bow. And so the world came to him another way: through nails, a borrowed tomb and an empty one. He refused the throne from the usurper’s hand and received it from his Father’s, and it will never be revoked. Every knee will bow to him, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Philippians 2:10–11). He went the long way round, by the cross, because we were on that road, and he would not reach the kingdom without us.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s order of the temptations differs from Matthew’s; Luke ends at Jerusalem, the goal of his whole Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered him, 'It is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered him: it is written, you shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.

It is written. Again, Scripture. And notice what he does with the devil’s claim. He does not dispute it. He does not argue about who owns the kingdoms or on what terms. He goes straight past the whole question to the one word that decides it: worship.

You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve. Deuteronomy 6:13, and again the setting matters. It comes from the passage just after the Shema (Hear, O Israel), where Moses warns Israel about what will happen when they enter the land and find themselves suddenly comfortable: cities they did not build, wells they did not dig, vineyards they did not plant (Deuteronomy 6:10–12). The danger is not persecution; it is prosperity. Israel repeatedly bowed to idols for the sake of prosperity and security; Jesus will not. The commandment given for that moment is the one Jesus reaches for now.

Only. The word only is not in the Hebrew of Deuteronomy 6:13, but it is in the Greek Old Testament, and it is implied by the whole passage, which goes straight on: you shall not go after other gods (Deuteronomy 6:14–15). There is no room for divided worship. And that little word is the one that shuts the door. The offer was never really about territory. Strip away the vision and the glory, and what remains is a transaction: a moment of bowing in exchange for everything. Worship is not divisible. A man who worships two things worships neither; he simply has one master he admits to and one he obeys. No servant can serve two masters (16:13).

Jesus, who is God, worships God. As a man, he gives the Father the worship due to him. He who is the eternal Son, equal with the Father, has taken the form of a servant, and as the true man he does what every man was made for. This does not mean there are two gods, or that the Son is less divine than the Father. The eternal Son took a true human nature, and in that nature he lived the life of worship that every human being owes to God and none of us has given. He will receive all the kingdoms, but from the Father’s hand, through obedience and the cross (Philippians 2:8–11).

The hinge of all three. The first was about bread, the third will be about proof, but underneath every one of them is the same question: who is God here? Every temptation comes down to that, however small the surface of it looks. Behind the extra glass, the private message that should never have been sent, the figure adjusted on the form, is a very quiet transfer of allegiance: a moment in which something other than God is trusted to deliver what only God can give. Which means the test is not usually taken in the moment of crisis. It is taken beforehand, in the settled question of what a person actually worships when nothing is happening. Jesus came into that wilderness with the answer already fixed, and the devil found nothing in him to negotiate with (John 14:30).

How do I know what I actually worship? Here is a test that can be run without much difficulty. Not, what do I say I believe? But: what is the thing whose loss would make life feel unliveable? What do I daydream about when my mind is free? What do I spend money on without thinking, and what makes me angry when it is threatened? Whatever answers those questions is being worshipped, whether or not it has ever been called by that name. The answer may be a good thing: a child, a marriage, health, a reputation, a career. Good things become idols not by being loved but by being loved in God’s place. The cure is not to love them less but to love God more, and to bring them to him with open hands.

In a sentence. Jesus refused, quoting the command to worship and serve God alone.

On a Tuesday. Take the thing that came out of that test, the one whose loss you could not bear, and name it to God this week. Where it applies: if your mood for the whole day depends on what the bank balance, the scales or your child’s exam results say, something has taken a place that belongs to him. Thank him for it as his gift, ask him to keep it if it is his will, and tell him that you will trust him if he does not. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: this is not a call to stop loving your family or caring about your work, as though indifference were holiness. God gave them to be enjoyed. It is a call to hold them under him, not instead of him.

For worship. He would not bow, so that we might be set free from bowing to everything else. Here is the only man who ever gave God the whole of his worship with nothing held back, and he did it for us, as our representative. Our worship is divided and cold; his was single and burning, and in him the Father counts it ours. Worship the Lord your God, and him only: Jesus kept that commandment in a desert, starving, with the world on offer, and it is because he kept it that we, who have broken it every day, can come and worship at all.

parallels.desc: worship and serve the LORD alone

verseByVerse.quote: And he took him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him, 'If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here, for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you, to guard you,’ and ‘On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He took him to Jerusalem, set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him: if you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here, for it is written, he will command his angels concerning you, to guard you, and, on their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.

And he took him to Jerusalem. The third assault moves to the holy city, the place of the temple, and it comes with a Bible verse. Whether in a vision or physically, Luke does not say.

And set him on the pinnacle of the temple. The pinnacle (pterygion, little wing) was a high point of the temple complex, probably the south-eastern corner of the platform, where the ground falls away sharply into the Kidron valley, a drop of perhaps 450 feet (140 m), which the Jewish historian Josephus said made you dizzy to look down. Or it may be the roof of the royal colonnade. Below, the courts would have been full. This is not a private test. It is a proposal for a public one.

If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here. Prove your sonship; force God to act. A spectacular rescue in front of the temple crowds would also prove to everyone that he was the Messiah: a sign from heaven, the very thing his enemies would demand (11:16). And notice what the temptation actually is. Not to doubt the promise, but to use it: to manufacture a crisis that obliges God to act, and call the manufacturing faith. It is the most religious of the three, and the only one that comes with chapter and verse.

For it is written. Now Satan quotes Scripture too. Twice Jesus has answered, it is written. Very well: for it is written. The devil can quote the Bible, and he can quote it accurately.

He will command his angels concerning you. Psalm 91:11–12, a real psalm, a genuine promise about the protection God gives to the one who dwells in the shelter of the Most High. Nothing about the words is invented. Except that something has been left out, and it is the clause that would have ended the conversation. The psalm promises that he will command his angels to guard you in all your ways. In Luke’s account the devil quotes to guard you and lifts the promise out of its setting; Matthew’s version drops the guarding clause altogether (Matthew 4:6). Either way, in all your ways is the point he hides. God guards his people in the paths they walk in obedience to him. Jumping off a building to see whether he will catch you is not one of your ways. It is not a way at all. And the psalm goes on: you will tread on the lion and the adder (Psalm 91:13), the serpent Jesus is about to defeat. The devil quoted the verse just before his own sentence.

How Scripture is nearly always misused. Not by inventing a verse; anyone can check an invented verse. By quoting a true one with the qualifying clause removed, or the occasion changed, or the covenant context stripped off. Every cult, every ruinous proof text, every disastrous decision made on the strength of a verse lifted out of its paragraph has this shape. The words were accurate. The sentence they came from was not consulted. That is the strongest argument there is for knowing not merely verses but the shape of the whole book. The man who knows a hundred verses can be beaten by a hundred and one. The man who knows what God is doing in Scripture as a whole can hear a true verse being used against its own purpose and say so.

How do I read a promise in context? Ask four plain questions. Who is speaking, and to whom? What does the rest of the paragraph and chapter say? Is the promise for a particular person and occasion, or for all God’s people? And does my reading agree with the rest of Scripture, and with the way Jesus and the apostles used it? Psalm 91 promises real protection to those who trust God, and Christians may lean on it in danger. It does not promise that a believer will never suffer, since the same Bible shows faithful people imprisoned and killed (Hebrews 11:36–38). It promises that nothing will touch them outside their Father’s will, and that in the end no harm will undo them.

In a sentence. On the temple’s highest point, the devil tempted Jesus to throw himself down to prove he was God’s Son, quoting Psalm 91’s promise of angelic protection.

On a Tuesday. Scripture can be twisted, and the most dangerous twisting is the one that agrees with what we already want. Where it applies: when someone, including you, uses a verse to justify a decision that the rest of Scripture forbids, such as leaving a spouse because God wants you to be happy, or giving recklessly because God will multiply the gift. Read the verse in its chapter before you lean your weight on it. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: this is not a reason to distrust the promises or to read the Bible only with a commentary in hand. The promises are meant to be believed and claimed. Read them, rest on them, and let the whole Bible tell you what they mean.

For worship. He stood at the top of the temple and would not jump, and some years later he stood at the bottom of a hill outside the city and let them lift him up on a cross. He refused to throw himself down to make his Father prove his love; instead he gave himself up to prove his Father’s love to us. The angels who would have caught him at the temple were held back at Calvary, so that he could fall the whole way into death for our sake. There was no rescue for him, so that there would be rescue for us.
verseByVerse.note: The pinnacle was a high point of the temple complex, perhaps a corner of its outer wall.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered him, 'It is said, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered him: it is said, you shall not put the Lord your God to the test.

It is said. Jesus answers Scripture with Scripture. Scripture interprets Scripture; one verse is not to be set against the rest. The devil had a text; Jesus has the Bible.

You shall not put the Lord your God to the test. Deuteronomy 6:16, and Moses finishes the sentence with the place name that explains it: as you tested him at Massah. Massah is the incident in Exodus 17. Israel is thirsty in the desert; there is no water; and instead of asking, they quarrel and demand. The question they put is recorded because it is the question underneath all such demands: is the LORD among us or not? (Exodus 17:7).

What testing God is. It is not asking him for something. Scripture is full of people asking, urgently and repeatedly, and God never once objects. It is making his response the condition of believing him. It is setting up a situation in which he must act in a specified way or be found wanting, and then calling the arrangement faith. The line between trust and testing is fine to look at and absolute in practice. Trust says: he is good, and I will do what he has told me to do, and leave the outcome with him. Testing says: I will construct a circumstance that forces his hand, and I will read the result as a verdict on whether he loves me.

How it happens without our noticing. Most people who do this have no idea that is what they are doing. It is the bargain made silently at two in the morning: if this scan comes back clear, I will know he is with me. It is the resignation handed in without a plan, filed under stepping out in faith. And it is the terrible weight that settles when the scan is not clear, because a verdict was attached to it that God never agreed to. He does not owe us a demonstration. A God who could be summoned by staging the right circumstance would not be God, and a faith that needed him summoned would not be faith.

The Rock at Massah. Massah has a sequel that makes this answer shine. When Israel tested the LORD there, God did not strike the people. He told Moses to strike the rock, and said that he himself would stand before Moses on it, and water came out for the people to drink (Exodus 17:6). Paul says that the Rock was Christ, and warns the church not to put Christ to the test as some of them did (1 Corinthians 10:4, 9). So the Son standing in this desert is the very Lord whom Israel tested at Massah, and he refuses to do to his Father what Israel did to him. More than that: he will be the struck Rock. At the cross the blow falls on him, not on the people who quarrelled, and out of him flows the living water (John 7:37–39).

But God says through Malachi, put me to the test, and Gideon asked for signs. Yes (Malachi 3:10; Judges 6:36–40). Testing God in the forbidden sense means demanding that he prove himself on our terms, as Israel did at Massah and as Satan urged Jesus to do. Malachi’s call is God inviting his people to trust a promise he has made. Gideon’s fleece was a weak man’s request that God graciously answered; it is not a pattern for seeking guidance, now that God has spoken in his word.

Then how do I seek guidance without laying a fleece? Begin with what God has already said: is the choice in front of you commanded, forbidden, or left free by Scripture? If it is left free, pray for wisdom, which God promises to give (James 1:5). Think it through honestly; ask the counsel of mature Christians who know you; weigh your gifts, your responsibilities and the open doors in front of you; and then decide, trusting that God rules even your mistakes. You do not need a sign in the sky. A Christian who has prayed, consulted Scripture and sought counsel, and then chooses between two good paths, is not out of God’s will whichever he takes.

Is it wrong to ask God for evidence? No. God does not ask for blind faith. Luke wrote his Gospel so that his reader might have certainty (1:4), and the risen Christ gave his disciples many proofs that he was alive (Acts 1:3). What Jesus refuses here is something else: setting the terms on which God must perform before we will trust him. The sceptic who says, if God is real let him do this for me now, and the believer who says, if he loves me he will do this by Friday, are making the same demand. God has given evidence enough in Christ, above all in his resurrection. The question is whether we will come to it on his terms or insist on our own.

In a sentence. Jesus refused, answering from Scripture that we must not put God to the test.

On a Tuesday. Do not take reckless risks and expect God to bail you out; trust him in the path of obedience. Where it applies: driving after drinking because God will protect you; refusing a treatment your doctor urges because you have decided God must heal you without it; spending money you do not have because God will provide. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: obedience sometimes looks risky to the world, and that is not testing God. A missionary going to a dangerous place because Christ has called him, a believer refusing to lie at work and losing her job, a family taking in a child in need: these are not presumption but faith. The difference is not the size of the risk. It is whether God asked you to do it.

For worship. He could have jumped. The angels would have come; the promise was real. He declined to make his Father prove himself, and the reason he declined is that he did not need proving. He had heard the voice at the Jordan. He knew whose Son he was in the wilderness, hungry, with nothing whatever to show for it. And on the cross, when rulers and soldiers jeered at him to save himself (23:35–37), he stayed, and trusted his Father in the dark: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (23:46). Here is faith perfected, in a man who never once put God to the test, and who was tested in our place to the uttermost.

parallels.desc: do not put the LORD to the test

verseByVerse.quote: And when the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time.

When the devil had ended every temptation. Every kind: the arsenal was emptied. Whatever else the devil had, he used it, and none of it worked. That is worth stating plainly, because the wilderness is sometimes read as a warm-up. It was not. It was everything he had, brought against a man weak with hunger and forty days alone, and it failed completely. The three temptations represent the whole range: appetite, power and possessions, pride and presumption. John sums them up as the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life (1 John 2:16). The same three Eve faced, when she saw that the tree was good for food, a delight to the eyes, and to be desired to make one wise (Genesis 3:6). Where Eve took the fruit, the last Adam met all three, each at its strongest, and gave the enemy nothing. And so the devil departed from him, beaten: the first proof that the devil, resisted, flees (James 4:7).

Until an opportune time. Not merely a later date but a suitable one, the right moment. The enemy withdraws, and he withdraws to wait. Luke means this as a signal, and he will pick it up again exactly where he intends: Satan will return through opposition, and above all in the passion. The next time Satan moves openly against Jesus in this Gospel is as the Passover draws near: then Satan entered into Judas (22:3). And in the garden, when they come for him with torches, Jesus tells them what hour it is: this is your hour, and the power of darkness (22:53). The wilderness was the opening exchange. The opportune time was Gethsemane and the cross, and there the temptations came back in almost their original shapes: save yourself; if you are the Christ; if you are the King of the Jews (23:35–39).

The victory is real, and it is not yet final. That is a fact about the Christian life as well. There is a particular discouragement that belongs to the believer who genuinely settled something, who fought a thing through and prayed it through and thought it was dealt with, and then finds it standing in the doorway again eighteen months later, looking exactly as it did. The conclusion that suggests itself is that the earlier victory was not real, or that nothing has changed, or that this will simply go on for ever. The verse says something different. The enemy left because he had been beaten, and he came back because he had been beaten and had not stopped. A returning temptation is not evidence that the last resistance was fraudulent. It is evidence that the war is longer than the battle.

The opportune time is the hour of exhaustion. He chose the end of forty days without food, and later the last night, in the dark, when the friends were asleep. That is a good reason to be more careful, not less, when you are tired, and no reason at all to conclude, when it comes, that you have gone backwards.

If Jesus defeated Satan here, why does the devil still trouble me? Because his defeat comes in stages. Here, in the wilderness, he was beaten in single combat. At the cross he was disarmed and put to open shame (Colossians 2:15). At Christ’s return he will be thrown into the lake of fire for ever (Revelation 20:10). We live between the second and the third: the enemy is defeated and doomed but still active, like an army that has lost the decisive battle and fights on in the hills. He can tempt and accuse and harass you, but he cannot condemn you, and he cannot take you out of Christ’s hand (John 10:28).

In a sentence. Having tried every temptation and failed, the devil left Jesus until a more opportune time.

On a Tuesday. A victory over temptation today does not mean it will not return. Stay alert, especially when you are tired. If the old sin is back at the door this week, do not tell yourself that nothing ever changed; tell yourself that you are still in the war, and fight it with the same weapons. And take comfort: Jesus has already defeated your tempter.

For worship. The devil emptied his arsenal on the Son of God and went away with nothing. When he came back at the opportune time, in the garden and on the cross, he threw everything again, and again found nothing in him; and that time his defeat was total, because the death he arranged was the death that undid him. Our champion has met the enemy twice and won twice, once by refusing every temptation and once by bearing every sin. We fight a beaten foe, under a Captain who has never lost.

parallels.desc: your hour, and the power of darkness

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus returns from the wilderness “in the power of the Spirit” — the forty days have not depleted him but concentrated the anointing. He teaches through Galilee and is praised by everyone. Then he comes to Nazareth, where he grew up, and on the Sabbath stands to read.

He is handed the scroll of Isaiah and finds the place: Isaiah 61:1-2. “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor.” He reads it, rolls up the scroll, hands it back, and sits down. Every eye in the room is on him. And he says: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”

The passage is a Jubilee text — the year of the Lord's favour is the fiftieth year of Leviticus 25, when debts were cancelled, slaves freed, and lost land returned. Jesus announces that the true Jubilee has arrived. And he stops mid-sentence: Isaiah goes on to “the day of vengeance of our God,” and Jesus does not read it. The favour has come; the reckoning waits for a coming still ahead.

The congregation's first response is admiration — they marvel at his gracious words and say “Is not this Joseph's son?” It is simultaneously flattering and dismissive: impressed by the local boy, unprepared for the claim. Jesus reads the room and pre-empts the demand he can see forming: “Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, 'Physician, heal yourself.' What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here also.”

Then he does the thing that turns admiration into fury. He tells two stories from their own Scriptures: Elijah sent past every widow in Israel to a pagan widow in Sidon (1 Kings 17), and Elisha cleansing a Syrian general while Israel's lepers went uncleansed (2 Kings 5). In both, the prophet bypasses Israel and the blessing lands on an outsider.

The congregation hears it perfectly. The year of the Lord's favour is not automatically theirs; they could be the ones passed over. It is a challenge to every form of religious privilege, and the response of privilege threatened is exactly what one would expect. They drive him out of town to the brow of the hill, intending to throw him off. He passes through the midst of them and goes away — because the hour, and the place, and the manner of his death are not theirs to choose.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Isaiah text Jesus reads is a Jubilee text, and the Jubilee was Israel's built-in rehearsal of release: the trumpet, the cancelled debt, the freed slave, the restored land. Jesus announces that the ultimate Jubilee has arrived — not an economic reset but a cosmic one. The debt of sin cancelled, the captivity to Satan ended, the blind given sight, the oppressed set free.

This is why he can say “today.” Not soon, not when conditions improve, but today, in your hearing — and the “today” does not depend on the congregation's response. It depends on who has just sat down.

The rage at the Elijah and Elisha stories is the rage of religious privilege challenged. They wanted a Messiah for Israel who would bless Israel and defeat Israel's enemies, not one who would take the blessing to the enemies themselves.

Every generation of the church faces the same temptation: to want Jesus for itself, to treat the gospel as the property of those who already have it, and to be offended when grace reaches people who had been written off. The Nazareth synagogue is the permanent warning against a Christianity that has lost the scandal of grace.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” is the most decisive today in Luke's Gospel — and this Gospel is full of them: “unto you is born this day a Saviour” (2:11); “today salvation has come to this house” (19:9); “today you will be with me in Paradise” (23:43).

The gospel in Luke is always a present-tense announcement, never merely past-tense history or future-tense hope. The Scripture fulfilled in Jesus is not fulfilled in some spiritual realm remote from the present moment; it is fulfilled now, here, in the hearing of particular people in a particular room.

Jesus walking through the crowd that means to kill him (v. 30) is the first of several moments in Luke where he moves through danger untouched — not because violence is ineffective but because his hour has not come. His death must be the death he chooses, on the terms the Father has set.

And the scene is a warning about familiarity. Nazareth had thirty years of information about Jesus and was the one town where he could do almost nothing. The people who received him in this Gospel were, almost without exception, those who met him with no prior file: a centurion, a Samaritan, a woman with a bad name, a tax collector, a dying criminal.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through all the surrounding country. And he taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through all the surrounding country. He taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all.

And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit. Full of the Spirit (v. 1), led by the Spirit (v. 1), now in the power of the Spirit. He went into the wilderness full; he comes out in power. Forty days of hunger and assault have not depleted him. If anything, he is stronger. That is worth registering, because the usual assumption about hard seasons is that they take something out of a person and the best that can be hoped for is recovery. Luke reports the opposite. The testing did not drain the anointing; it proved it, and a proved thing carries weight that an untested thing does not. Luke stresses throughout that Jesus’ ministry is empowered by the Spirit (v. 18; Acts 10:38).

To Galilee. The northern region, where most of his ministry will take place (4:14–9:50). Luke compresses here. Between the wilderness and Nazareth there is a period of ministry he does not narrate. John’s Gospel fills in some of it, with the wedding at Cana and the first visit to Jerusalem (John 1–4), and Luke simply notes that word was spreading.

A report about him went out through all the surrounding country. His fame spread. This matters for reading what comes next, because Jesus will shortly refer to things he did at Capernaum that Luke has not yet described (v. 23). Luke told us at the outset that he was writing an orderly account (1:3), and that word means arranged in a followable sequence, not clocked to the day.

And he taught in their synagogues. Synagogues were local meeting places for prayer and for the reading and teaching of Scripture, in every Jewish town. They probably began during the exile, when the temple had been destroyed and the people were far from Jerusalem. Visiting teachers could be invited to speak, and Jesus, and later Paul, used them for preaching (Acts 13:15). The gospel began its journey in the ordinary weekly gatherings of ordinary people.

Being glorified by all. At first, universal acclaim. Hold that phrase against what happens fifteen verses later, when the congregation of his own village tries to throw him off a cliff (v. 29). Luke has set the two side by side deliberately. The universal early approval is real, and it is worth almost nothing, because it has not yet been tested by anything he actually came to say. A ministry, a message or a man can be widely admired right up to the first moment of genuine confrontation, and the admiration tells you nothing about what is underneath it. The crowds that praised him in Galilee were the same kind of crowds that would shout in Jerusalem three years later, and the second shout was not a change of mind. It was the first one, finally tested.

Is it wrong to want to be liked? No. Wanting the good opinion of others is natural, and Scripture commends a good name (Proverbs 22:1). Jesus himself grew in favour with God and man (2:52), and elders must be well thought of by outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7). What is dangerous is needing it: letting the crowd’s approval decide what you say, or measuring your faithfulness by your popularity. Be glad when people think well of you, and do not lean on it. The approval that will last is the one you will hear at the end: well done, good and faithful servant.

In a sentence. Jesus returned to Galilee in the Spirit’s power, and his fame spread as he taught in the synagogues to universal praise.

On a Tuesday. Popularity is fleeting. Jesus was praised by all, and before long his own town tried to kill him. If you are enjoying approval this season, at work, at church or in your family, enjoy it lightly and do not trim what you say to keep it. If you have lost it for doing right, you are in his company. Seek God’s approval, not the crowd’s. And if the Lord has brought you through a hard season, look for what it has strengthened in you, not only for what it has cost.

For worship. He came out of the desert stronger than he went in, carrying the Spirit without measure, and turned towards the villages of Galilee with good news. The crowd’s praise could not inflate him and their hatred would not deflect him. He was not working for their applause; he was working for their salvation. Here is a Saviour who cannot be flattered into silence or frightened into retreat, and who walked into every synagogue in Galilee knowing exactly what the cheering was worth, and loved them anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. And as was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and he stood up to read. And the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. As was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and he stood up to read. The scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written:

The programme of the ministry. Luke places this scene at the start of the Galilean ministry as a kind of manifesto, setting out what Jesus came to do. Mark and Matthew record a similar rejection at Nazareth later (Mark 6:1–6; Matthew 13:53–58). Luke may have brought it forward for its meaning, or it may be a different visit. Verse 23 implies that Jesus had already worked in Capernaum.

He came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. His home town, a small village in the hills of lower Galilee, where everyone knew him as the carpenter (Mark 6:3). He had grown up there, worked there, and been known there for nearly thirty years.

As was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day. Stay on that phrase, because four words are doing a great deal of work. This was his habit. Week after week, for something close to thirty years, the Son of God walked to a small building in an unremarkable village and sat through the service. Consider what was on offer there. A synagogue in Nazareth in the 20s meant a handful of families, the same faces, an attendant, a set of scrolls, prayers everyone knew by heart, and a teaching ministry that on any given week was probably very ordinary indeed. Whatever he received in that room, it was not instruction he needed. He had more of the Spirit than every teacher in Galilee combined. He went anyway, every week, including, on this particular Sabbath, to a congregation that would try to kill him before the morning was over. If the sinless Son of God worshipped with God’s people every week, so must we (Hebrews 10:25).

What if my church is weak, or the preaching is thin? That is a quiet rebuke to a very common piece of modern reasoning: that a person who is not being fed, or who finds the preaching thin, or who has outgrown the place, is thereby excused. Jesus had better grounds for that argument than anyone who has ever used it, and he did not use it. Go, and go as a giver as well as a receiver: to pray with others, to sing, to encourage the person next to you, to hear God’s word read even if the sermon is poor. If a church has abandoned the gospel itself, that is a different matter, and you may need to find one that preaches Christ. But dullness, weakness and ordinary faces are not reasons to stay at home. They are the setting in which Jesus worshipped for thirty years.

And he stood up to read. A synagogue service included the Shema, prayers, readings from the Law and the Prophets, a sermon and a blessing. Readers stood to read Scripture, out of respect, and sat to teach, and a visiting teacher could be asked to do both. The attendant handed him the scroll of Isaiah from its cupboard, a long roll of handwritten Hebrew columns.

He unrolled the scroll and found the place. Whether the passage was the appointed reading for that day or one he sought out, he handled the scroll like a man who knew where things were in it, which, given the eighteen unrecorded years, he did. He was handed the book he had inspired, in the village he had grown up in, and he found the sentence about himself.

In a sentence. At Nazareth, Jesus went to the synagogue on the Sabbath, as was his custom, stood to read, and found a chosen place in the scroll of Isaiah.

On a Tuesday. Make weekly worship with God’s people your custom, as it was his, not something you decide afresh each Sunday morning according to how you feel. A custom carries you on the weeks when desire does not. Plan your Saturday night so that Sunday morning is possible; sit near someone who looks alone; and between Sundays, read the Scriptures yourself, so that like him you know where things are in the book.

For worship. The Lord of the Sabbath kept the Sabbath, born under the law he had given, and he is himself the rest that every Sabbath had been waiting for (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). The one to whom every synagogue prayer was addressed stood among the villagers and prayed it with them. He did not despise the small congregation, the plain building, or the ordinary readings, because he was faithful in small things for thirty years before he did a single miracle. And when he unrolled the scroll, he found himself in it, because the whole book is about him. The Word who spoke the prophets’ words stood up in Nazareth to read them aloud, and every line was a promise he had come to keep.
verseByVerse.note: A synagogue service included readings from the Law and the Prophets; a visiting teacher could be invited to read and speak.

parallels.desc: Paul invited to speak after the readings

verseByVerse.quote: 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favour.

The passage. Isaiah 61:1–2, with a phrase from Isaiah 58:6, to set at liberty those who are oppressed. Luke, following the Greek Old Testament, brings the two together, and the effect is to sharpen the note of release. In Isaiah, the speaker is the Lord’s anointed servant, announcing the good news of return from exile and restoration. Jesus claims it as his own job description. And it is a job description: every clause names something the following chapters will contain.

The Spirit of the Lord is upon me. Luke has been building towards this since the Jordan. The Spirit descended at the baptism (3:22), led him into the wilderness, brought him back in power, and now the man on whom the Spirit rests reads out the passage about the man on whom the Spirit rests. Father, Son and Spirit are all in the first line: the Spirit of the Lord, upon me.

Because he has anointed me. Anointed (echrisen) is the verb behind Christ, and its Hebrew equivalent is behind Messiah. Prophets, priests and kings were anointed with oil; Jesus is the Anointed One, anointed not with oil but with the Spirit (Acts 10:38). He is reading his own title aloud.

To proclaim good news to the poor. The poor (ptōchois) are the destitute, the needy, and in the Old Testament especially the humble poor who depend on God (Psalm 34:6; Isaiah 66:2). The gospel comes first to those who know they have nothing (6:20; 7:22). Luke’s Gospel will be full of them: shepherds, a widow with two small coins, a beggar at a gate, a tax collector who could not lift his eyes. Both material and spiritual poverty are in view.

To proclaim liberty to the captives. Liberty (aphesis) is the same word Luke uses for forgiveness (1:77; 3:3; 24:47). Release from captivity and release from sin are the same word. That is what forgiveness is: a release. God cancels the debt our sins have run up and no longer holds it against us, and the guilty go free as surely as a prisoner walks out of an open cell (Colossians 2:13–14). Jesus sets free those bound by sin, by Satan and by disease (13:16).

And recovering of sight to the blind. From the Greek Old Testament of Isaiah 61:1. Jesus will heal the physically blind (7:21; 18:35–43), and open the eyes of the spiritually blind (Acts 26:18).

To set at liberty those who are oppressed. Isaiah 58:6. The oppressed are the crushed, the broken, those bruised under a weight they cannot lift.

To proclaim the year of the Lord’s favour. This is not a figure of speech. It is the Jubilee of Leviticus 25:8–55: the fiftieth year, when the trumpet sounded on the Day of Atonement, debts were cancelled, slaves walked free, and land sold off in hard times went back to the family that had lost it. Israel’s own calendar contained a rehearsal of release, and he stands up in a village synagogue and says the real one has arrived. The age of God’s favour, freedom and restoration has come.

Where he stopped. Isaiah’s sentence does not end where Jesus ends it. The prophet went on: and the day of vengeance of our God (Isaiah 61:2). Jesus reads the first half, rolls up the scroll, hands it back, and sits down, breaking off in the middle of a line. That is not carelessness. It is the most eloquent silence in the Gospel. His first coming is for salvation; the day of vengeance is still to come, at his return (21:22; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). Now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2). Everything in between, every year the world has had since that morning in Nazareth, including this one, is the unrolled length of that unread half sentence. Put plainly: the time between his first coming and his return is the year of favour, and it is still open, which is why the gospel is still being offered to you today.

Are these promises literal or spiritual? The question is badly put, and Luke will not let it be answered either way alone. Actual blind men receive actual sight in this Gospel; actual poor people are actually fed. And the same Gospel says that the deepest poverty is a man who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich towards God (12:21), and that the worst blindness is in people whose eyes work perfectly. Both are meant. A Christianity that spiritualises every one of these clauses has stopped doing what Jesus did; a Christianity that keeps them all material has stopped saying what he said.

What it does not mean. Not merely a programme of social or political liberation, as some liberation theologians have read it. Nor merely spiritual, with no care for the poor and sick. Jesus’ ministry addressed both: he forgave sins and healed bodies, preached to the poor and fed the hungry. But the deepest captivity is to sin, and the greatest liberty is forgiveness. A man can be freed from prison and remain a slave; a man can stay in chains and be free (Acts 16:25).

So is the church meant to fight poverty or preach the gospel? Both, in their order. The church’s distinctive task, which no one else will do, is to proclaim Christ and the forgiveness of sins (24:47). But the people who hear that message are given new hearts, and new hearts love their neighbours with food, money, time and justice (1 John 3:17; James 2:15–16). Mercy to the poor is not a substitute for the gospel and not an optional extra to it; it is what the gospel produces. A congregation that preaches release and ignores the widow down the road has misheard the sermon at Nazareth.

In a sentence. Jesus read Isaiah’s words of the Spirit-anointed one sent to bring good news to the poor, release to captives, sight to the blind, freedom to the oppressed, and the year of the Lord’s favour.

On a Tuesday. Think of yourself in the list before you think of anyone else: you were the poor man, the captive, the blind and the crushed, and he came for you. Then think of the people around you who are still there. Where it applies: the colleague trapped in a habit, the neighbour who is lonely and struggling, the family at church who cannot pay a bill. Bring them the news and bring them help. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: this is not a promise that every Christian will be lifted out of poverty or sickness in this life, nor a political manifesto for one party. The Jubilee has begun in Christ, and it will be complete only when he comes again.

For worship. Here is the trumpet of the true Jubilee, sounding in a village synagogue. The debts are cancelled, the slaves walk free, and the land comes home, because the anointed one has come to pay what was owed and break what held us. The prison doors are standing open, and the year of favour has not closed, and the one who stopped reading in the middle of the verse is the one holding it open. The day of vengeance is coming, and he will bear the sword; but first he came to bear the vengeance himself, so that for everyone who comes to him, the day of favour will never end.
verseByVerse.note: “The year of the Lord’s favour” recalls the Year of Jubilee, when debts were cancelled and slaves set free. Jesus stops before Isaiah’s next words, “the day of vengeance of our God.”

parallels.desc: to let the oppressed go free

verseByVerse.quote: And he rolled up the scroll and gave it back to the attendant and sat down. And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. And he began to say to them, 'Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He rolled up the scroll, gave it back to the attendant and sat down. The eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. He began to say to them: today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.

And he rolled up the scroll and gave it back to the attendant. The attendant was the hazzan, the synagogue official who looked after the scrolls. Luke slows the film down. Three ordinary actions, described one at a time, and then a silence.

And sat down. Sitting was the posture for teaching. So the room knows a sermon is coming, and the eyes of all are fixed on him: the local boy, back from wherever he has been, about to expound the great Servant passage. There will have been a rustle, and then nothing.

Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing. One of the most astonishing sentences ever preached. There may have been more (Luke says he began to say), but this is the whole of it in one line, and there is nothing else like it. Prophets said, thus says the LORD. Scribes said, Rabbi so-and-so taught. This man reads a seven-hundred-year-old prophecy about a Spirit-anointed liberator and says: that is about me, and it is happening now, in this room, while you are listening. Not one day, but today. The prophecy is fulfilled in Jesus. The Jubilee has begun.

There are only three possible responses. Either the man is deluded, or he is lying, or the year of the Lord’s favour has just begun in a small village. Being impressed is not one of the options. The one thing that cannot be done with a sentence like that is to admire the delivery, which is precisely what the congregation is about to attempt.

Today. The word is sēmeron, and it is one of Luke’s. Unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour (2:11). Today salvation has come to this house (19:9). Today you will be with me in paradise (23:43). Something in Luke’s Gospel refuses to let salvation be filed under history or postponed to the future. It keeps arriving in the present tense, at a particular address, on a particular afternoon. And notice what has to be true for that word to work. He does not say the Scripture will be fulfilled when the nation repents, or when the conditions are right, or when enough people believe. He says it is fulfilled in the hearing of a room that is about to reject him. The today does not depend on the response. It depends on who has just sat down.

How is the whole Old Testament about Jesus? Not that every verse is a hidden prediction, but that the whole story is heading towards him. Its promises are fulfilled in him (2 Corinthians 1:20); its sacrifices, priests and temple are pictures of what he would do; its kings and prophets point to the King and Prophet who would come; and its failures show why he was needed. After his resurrection he took the disciples through Moses and all the prophets and showed them the things concerning himself (24:27, 44). So when you read the Old Testament, ask not only what it meant then but where it leads: what does this show me of the Christ who was coming?

In a sentence. Jesus sat down to teach and, with every eye on him, declared that Isaiah’s prophecy had been fulfilled that day as they listened.

On a Tuesday. All Scripture finds its fulfilment in Jesus. Read your Bible looking for him, and when you finish a passage, ask: what does this show me of Christ? And hear his today as addressed to you. Whatever burden you are carrying, the release he announced is not for some future day when you are better; it is offered now, in your hearing, this week.

For worship. Every eye in that room was fixed on him, and they were right to look. Seven hundred years of longing had come down to a carpenter sitting in a synagogue and saying, today. Isaiah had heard the anointed one speak in the first person, the Spirit is upon me, and had never seen his face; Nazareth saw the face and heard the same voice. He did not come to explain the prophecy. He came to be it. And he still sits where the Scripture is opened, speaking to every hearer who has run out of time and hope the word Nazareth heard first.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers sat to teach.

parallels.desc: everything written about me must be fulfilled

verseByVerse.quote: And all spoke well of him and marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. And they said, 'Is not this Joseph's son?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
All spoke well of him and marvelled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. And they said: is not this Joseph’s son?

And all spoke well of him. Or bore witness to him. At first, admiration. They marvel, as the neighbours wondered after the shepherds came (2:18), and it means what it meant there. Wonder is not faith. It is what a person feels when something has been genuinely interesting and nothing has yet been decided.

And marvelled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. Gracious words are literally words of grace. Grace is God’s kindness given to people who have not earned it and deserve the opposite (Ephesians 2:8–9). Both his eloquence and the content: grace, favour, release. Grace is poured upon your lips, sang the psalmist of the King (Psalm 45:2). But notice what they are doing. He has just announced that the Jubilee has arrived in their village, and the congregation is appraising the performance.

And they said, Is not this Joseph’s son? The turning point. The compliment and the problem arrive in the same breath, and the second sentence cancels the first. At first the question is not hostile. It is the sound of a small community being pleasantly astonished by one of its own. They knew him at nine. They knew the family, the trade, the house, the brothers and sisters. They have watched him buy timber. And that is exactly the difficulty. It is not open unbelief; it is a settled framework into which the claim will not fit. They do not disbelieve the sermon so much as find the preacher already accounted for. He has been categorised, filed under people we know, and there is no category above it. Familiarity made it impossible for them to accept that God was at work in someone so ordinary. They did not know, as Luke’s readers do (3:23), that he was not really Joseph’s son. And Matthew and Mark record that they took offence at him (Mark 6:3).

Whose son is he? Luke has already given the reader the answer the synagogue lacked. Jesus was the son, as was supposed, of Joseph (3:23), and the angel had told Mary that the child would be called holy, the Son of God, and given the throne of his father David (1:32, 35). So the question is half right. He is Joseph’s son in law, and through that line the heir of David’s throne. He is not Joseph’s son in nature, for he is the Son of the Most High, the one the Father had just called beloved over the Jordan (3:22). That is why the words were gracious: they came from the Word who had become flesh, full of grace and truth (John 1:14).

The particular danger of everyone who has grown up near the things of God. Familiarity does not usually produce hostility. It produces a mild, pleasant, entirely unthreatened appreciation.
