The person who has heard the Christmas story every year since infancy has an account of Jesus in place before he ever hears a sermon, and the account is not wrong so much as too small, and it has the enormous advantage of never requiring anything. There is a way of knowing about someone which is the biggest single obstacle to knowing them. Nazareth had thirty years of information about Jesus Christ, and it was the one town in Galilee where he could do almost nothing. The people who received him in this Gospel were, almost without exception, people who met him with no prior file: a Roman officer, a Samaritan, a woman with a bad name, a tax collector up a tree, a criminal with a few hours to live.

I grew up in church. How do I stop Jesus becoming familiar? Familiarity itself is not the enemy; it is a great privilege to have known the gospel from childhood. The danger is assuming you already know what a passage says before you have read it. So read the Gospels slowly, as if for the first time, and ask what surprises you. Read them in a different translation. Notice the reactions of people who met him for the first time, and ask why you do not react the same way. Above all, pray: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). Only the Spirit can make the old story new, and he loves to do it.

In a sentence. The congregation admired his gracious words but then asked how this could be, since he was only Joseph’s son.

On a Tuesday. Do not let familiarity with Jesus blind you to who he really is. Take one Gospel scene you know well this week and read it aloud, slowly, asking at each verse: what does this show me about him that I have stopped noticing? And watch how you treat the ordinary Christian beside you. God often speaks through people we think we have already filed.

For worship. He grew up among them so quietly that they could not believe he was anything more than the carpenter. That is the glory of the incarnation: the eternal Son was so truly man that his neighbours mistook him for an ordinary one. He did not glow; he worked with wood and sawdust for years. And the words of grace that came from his mouth that morning are still coming, to people who think they know him already. He is more than our file on him. He is always larger, kinder and holier than we had thought.

parallels.desc: “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph?”

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, ‘Physician, heal yourself.’ What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here in your hometown as well.' And he said, 'Truly, I say to you, no prophet is acceptable in his hometown.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, physician, heal yourself. What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here in your home town as well. And he said: truly, I tell you, no prophet is acceptable in his home town.

Physician, heal yourself. Jesus answers the question they have not asked out loud. The saying is a proverb, found in Greek and Jewish writings: look after your own before you go looking further afield. Here it means: prove yourself. Do for your own people what you did elsewhere. If you claim to be the Messiah, show us. They wanted signs, not faith. On the cross they will throw the same taunt: he saved others; let him save himself (23:35).

What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here in your hometown as well. A reader tracking the narrative will stop here, because Luke has not told us about anything at Capernaum. That comes eight verses later (vv. 31–41). This is the clearest signal in the Gospel that Luke’s orderly account (1:3) means arranged, not strictly chronological. He has lifted the Nazareth visit out of its place in the sequence and set it at the head of the ministry, because it explains everything that follows: why Jesus is based at Capernaum and not at home, why the message goes to outsiders, and how it will end.

Is this the same visit as Matthew 13 and Mark 6? Matthew and Mark record a rejection at Nazareth much later (Matthew 13:54–58; Mark 6:1–6). Whether that is this visit told in its chronological place, or a second visit to a town that had not changed its mind, cannot be settled from the evidence; the details differ enough to allow either. What is certain is that Luke knew what he was doing when he put it first, and that none of the Gospels claims to give a diary.

The demand underneath. They want a miracle, and they want it on grounds of local loyalty. Not, show us you are the Messiah, but, do for us what you did for them. The claim underneath is one of entitlement: we knew you first, so we have first call. A miracle performed to satisfy a home town’s sense of ownership would establish nothing except that he could be leveraged. He has just come from forty days of refusing exactly this, do something spectacular to prove yourself, and the wilderness is still on his clothes.

No prophet is acceptable in his hometown. Acceptable (dektos) is the same word as favour in the year of the Lord’s favour (v. 19). A play on words: Jesus proclaims the acceptable year of the Lord, but he himself is not acceptable to his own. He is not complaining. He is placing himself in a line, and the line is not a comfortable one. Israel’s prophets were consistently rejected by their own people and killed by the people who had the Scriptures (Jeremiah 11:21; Acts 7:52). He knows what he is stepping into, says so at the start of his ministry, and goes on with it anyway.

Why would God not do a miracle for people who asked for one? Because they were not asking in faith; they were setting terms. Jesus never refused anyone who came to him in need and trust: the leper, the centurion, the blind beggar. What he refused was the demand for proof as a condition of believing, the very thing he had refused the devil (11:29). A sign given to people who have already decided what they will accept does not produce faith; it produces spectators. When God seems silent to your prayers, it is not because he is withholding favours from those who have not earned them, but sometimes because he is drawing you from wanting a display to wanting him.

In a sentence. Jesus anticipated their demand that he prove himself with miracles as he had elsewhere, and observed that no prophet is accepted in his home town.

On a Tuesday. If those closest to you are least willing to hear the gospel from you, you are in good company. Where it applies: the brother who still sees you as the teenager you were, the parents who smile at your faith as a phase, the old friends who know your faults too well. Keep faithful, keep loving, and let your life speak over years. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: their resistance is not always the prophet’s rejection. Sometimes they are rightly put off by our own pride, preachiness or inconsistency. Before you comfort yourself with this verse, ask honestly whether the offence is the gospel or you.

For worship. He was the one prophet who deserved to be received everywhere, and he was received least by those who had watched him grow up. He accepted that rejection without bitterness, because he had come to be rejected. He would be despised and rejected by men (Isaiah 53:3), so that we, who had rejected him, might be accepted in the Beloved. The one who was not acceptable in his home town proclaims to us the acceptable year of the Lord, and in him we are welcome.

verseByVerse.quote: But in truth, I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the heavens were shut up three years and six months, and a great famine came over all the land, and Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in truth, I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the heavens were shut up three years and six months and a great famine came over all the land, and Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian.

Two examples from Israel’s history. Now the two stories that turn admiration into a lynch mob, and it is important to see that Jesus chose them. He could have made his point about prophets and home towns and stopped. Instead he reaches for two episodes from Israel’s own Scriptures, both about the great miracle-working prophets, Elijah and his successor Elisha, and both about God going somewhere nobody expected.

Many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah. During the famine God sent in Ahab’s time (1 Kings 17–18), Israelite widows were starving in every village. Jesus gives three years and six months, as James 5:17 does; 1 Kings 18:1 says the rain came in the third year, probably counting from a different point, such as Elijah’s stay at Zarephath.

Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. 1 Kings 17:8–24. Zarephath was a Gentile town on the coast near Sidon, the very region of Jezebel, Israel’s great enemy and the homeland of the Baal worship Elijah was fighting. God sent his prophet past all the widows of Israel to a foreign widow, fed her through the famine with a jar of flour that did not run out, and raised her son from death.

And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian. 2 Kings 5. Syria (Aram) was the enemy. Naaman commanded the army that raided Israel’s borders; the little servant girl who told him about the prophet was a captive his own troops had carried off. He was healed when he humbled himself and washed seven times in the Jordan, and Israel’s lepers were not.

The point. Both stories are in their Bible. Neither is disputed. And put together they say something the congregation understands perfectly: the fact that the blessing is near you does not mean it is for you, and God has a settled habit of taking it past his own people to somebody they despise. Two Gentiles, an enemy’s widow and an enemy’s general, received God’s blessing, while Israel, in unbelief, did not. If Nazareth rejects its prophet, his blessings will go to others, to the Gentiles. This is the story of Luke and Acts in miniature (Acts 13:46; 28:28).

Grace is grace. Note what makes this so much worse than an insult. He is not saying they are unworthy and Gentiles are worthy. He is saying that grace is not owed to anyone, and therefore cannot be claimed by anyone, and therefore may land wherever God pleases. God’s grace is sovereign: not earned by birth or nationality or religious upbringing. Sovereign means that God is free and answerable to no one: he decides where his mercy goes, and no one can put him in his debt (Romans 11:35). The Nazareth congregation’s rage is the exact rage of the elder brother in Luke 15, and of the workers hired at dawn who grumbled that the latecomers were paid the same (Matthew 20:11–12). It is what religious people feel when they discover that the thing they thought they had earned is a gift.

A greater prophet than Elijah. Jesus does not pick these two men at random. He is telling Nazareth what kind of prophet is standing in front of them, and Luke goes on to show it. In chapter 7 Jesus meets a widow at Nain whose only son is being carried out to burial, raises him, and gives him to his mother, the very words the Greek Old Testament uses of Elijah at Zarephath (7:15; 1 Kings 17:23), and the crowd cries that a great prophet has arisen. In chapter 17 ten lepers are cleansed, and the only one who comes back to give thanks is a Samaritan, a foreigner like Naaman (17:15–18). Elijah and Elisha each reached one outsider, and Israel remembered it as a startling exception. Jesus is the prophet in whom that mercy stops being an exception and becomes the plan: a light for revelation to the Gentiles (2:32).

Is it unfair of God to bless some and pass by others? Fairness would mean everyone receiving what they deserve, and none of us wants that, because all of us deserve condemnation (Romans 3:23; 6:23). No widow in Israel had a claim on Elijah, and no leper had a right to be healed. That God shows mercy to any is grace; that he chooses where to show it is his right as God (Romans 9:15–16). The question that should astonish us is not why he passed by some but why he came to anyone at all. And the stories prove the door is open to the most unlikely: if a Sidonian widow and an enemy general were welcomed, no one who comes to Christ will be turned away (John 6:37).

In a sentence. Jesus reminded them that in the days of Elijah and Elisha, God sent his prophets past many in Israel to bless Gentile outsiders, a widow from Sidon and a Syrian general.

On a Tuesday. The test this passage sets is not difficult to state and is uncomfortable to answer. There is some category of person you have quietly written off: a nationality, a lifestyle, a political tribe, an individual with a name. Ask whether you would find it hard to be glad if God saved them tomorrow and left you exactly where you are. Whoever came to mind is your Naaman, and Naaman is the one the story is about. Pray for that person by name this week. No one has a claim on God’s grace by birth or background. Thank God that his grace reaches outsiders, including you.

For worship. God sent his prophet to the wrong address on purpose, to a widow in Jezebel’s country and a general of the enemy’s army, so that the whole world would know that his mercy is not a family inheritance. And then he sent his Son farther still, past every claim and every merit, all the way down to us. We were the foreigners, the enemies, the lepers outside the camp, and grace came looking for us. Blessed be the God whose kindness crosses every border we draw, and who loves to be found by those who were not looking for him (Romans 10:20).
verseByVerse.note: Both of these beneficiaries were Gentiles. Zarephath lay on the coast near Sidon.

parallels.desc: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath. And they rose up and drove him out of the town and brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, so that they could throw him down the cliff. But passing through their midst, he went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath. They rose up, drove him out of the town, and brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, so that they could throw him down the cliff. But passing through their midst, he went away.

All in the synagogue were filled with wrath. All of them. Six verses ago the same room was speaking well of him. Nothing has happened in between except two Bible stories. From admiration (v. 22) to fury in minutes. Why? Because Jesus suggested that God favoured Gentiles over them. National and religious pride was wounded. The thing that turned a congregation into a mob was not a miracle withheld, or a political provocation. It was the suggestion that God’s grace is free: free enough to go to a Sidonian widow and a Syrian general and past the people who had the Scriptures. The gospel had been preached in Nazareth for a few minutes and the response was attempted murder. The same reaction met Paul when he mentioned the Gentiles (Acts 22:21–22).

And they rose up and drove him out of the town. This is a Sabbath. These are worshippers. They have come from a service in which the Scriptures were read, and the congregation has become a lynch mob, marching a man to a precipice. The men doing the marching have known him since he was a boy. Somewhere in that crowd are people who taught him, sold to him, employed him, possibly his own relatives. Luke does not say they intended a trial. There was no trial. This is a village losing its temper so completely that it means to kill.

And brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built. Nazareth sits on a hillside, with steep drops nearby, and the plan was to throw him down the cliff. Stoning, the penalty for blasphemy or false prophecy, sometimes began by throwing the condemned down a drop. It is a foreshadowing of the cross: his own people would reject him and try to kill him. And it is worth noticing that the devil had just suggested he throw himself down from a height. He refused to do it for the devil, and he will not let them do it to him.

But passing through their midst, he went away. Eight words, and Luke offers no explanation whatever. Perhaps by his sheer authority, perhaps by a miracle; Luke does not say. He does not vanish, or strike anyone down, or call for angels, which, so soon after the temple pinnacle, is worth noticing. He simply walks through the middle of them and leaves. Whatever happened there, the reason it happened is the one the Gospels give again and again: his hour had not yet come (John 7:30; 8:59). No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord: that is John’s wording, but it is Luke’s conviction (John 10:18). He cannot be killed early, or in the wrong place, or by the wrong hands. He would die in Jerusalem, not Nazareth (13:33). His death is not something that will happen to him. It is something he has come to do, on a specified day, in a specified city.

The pattern of the whole Gospel. Grace offered, rejected by his own, and going on to others: the first congregation Jesus preached to tried to murder him, and he walked away and kept preaching. It is a fair warning to anyone who imagines that faithful preaching is chiefly a matter of being well received.

How can religious people become so violent? Because religion without grace makes people possessive of God. When a person’s standing rests on his heritage, his correctness or his good record, anything that suggests God might welcome outsiders on the same terms feels like theft. The more he has invested in his own goodness, the angrier he becomes. That is why the people who killed Jesus were not the irreligious but the devout. The cure is not less seriousness about God but a deeper knowledge of our own need. A person who knows he was saved by grace alone cannot be furious when grace saves somebody else.

In a sentence. Enraged that God’s grace had gone to Gentiles, the congregation drove Jesus out of town to throw him off a cliff, but he walked through the crowd and went away.

On a Tuesday. Grace offends those who think they deserve it. Receive God’s grace humbly, as an outsider. And if you find yourself irritated when someone with a worse past than yours is welcomed at church, or praised, or blessed, stop and recognise the voice of Nazareth in your own heart. Where it applies: the new believer with a messy history who is asked to give her testimony; the young man who came to faith last year and is already more zealous than you. Rejoice with them. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: this does not mean that a church should never question anyone’s profession or should hurry a new believer into leadership (1 Timothy 3:6). Wisdom is not envy. The heart test is whether you are glad.

For worship. They took him to the edge of a cliff, and he walked through them untouched, because his life was in his own hands and his Father’s, and not in theirs. Three years later he walked out of Jerusalem carrying his own cross, and that time he did not pass through their midst. He let them do it, because the hour had come. The one who could not be thrown from a cliff in Galilee chose to be lifted on a cross in Judea, for the very people who were shouting at him. He was never the victim of the crowd. He was always its Saviour.
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth is built on a hillside with steep drops nearby.

parallels.desc: Jesus hid himself and went out

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
From Nazareth, which rejected him, Jesus goes to Capernaum, which will be the base of the Galilean ministry. Within what appears to be a single Sabbath he teaches with authority, casts out an unclean spirit, heals Simon's mother-in-law, and at sunset heals a multitude brought to his door.

The contrast with Nazareth is complete. The hometown that had him from childhood loses him; the town that receives him gets a cascade of kingdom power — teaching, healing, and liberation.

The exorcism in the synagogue is Luke's first, and it raises a question that runs through the Gospel: what is the relation between the kingdom of God and the realm of demons? The demon's cry — “What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are, the Holy One of God” — is the first confession of Christ in his public ministry, and it comes from a demon. The powers of darkness identify him before anyone in Galilee does, and their knowledge saves them nothing. The demons believe and shudder (Jas. 2:19); they do not trust and rest.

Jesus silences it and casts it out with a single sentence. No ritual, no incantation, no procedure — which is exactly what a first-century reader would have found astonishing, since contemporary exorcists used elaborate techniques. Luke, the physician, adds that the man was left unharmed.

The healing of Simon's mother-in-law is narrated with the same economy: Jesus rebuked the fever, the same verb used of the demon, and it left her. The response is immediate — she rises and serves. That is the New Testament pattern: what is received is not kept. The restored woman becomes the one who provides.

The healings at sunset, when the Sabbath ended and the sick could lawfully be carried through the streets, are the kingdom in miniature: a whole town at one door, and Jesus laying his hands on every one of them, individually, into the night.

Then, at dawn, he leaves for a desolate place, and refuses the crowd's attempt to keep him: “I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.” The healings are real and they are not the mission. He was sent to announce a kingdom, and he goes to the next town.
verseByVerse.theology:
The demon's address, “the Holy One of God,” appears elsewhere in the New Testament, outside this scene and its parallel (Mark 1:24), only at John 6:69, on Peter's lips. The irony is severe: the demon confesses what the disciples will grasp only gradually and the religious leaders will refuse. The spiritual world sees what the natural eye misses.

But knowledge of who Jesus is, without submission to who he is, is not faith. The demons have impeccable Christology and it does them no good whatever. Right doctrine held in terror is still a lost condition.

Jesus's withdrawal at daybreak to a desolate place, and his answer to the crowd who would have kept him, establishes the missionary imperative of the ministry. The word “must” (dei) appears again — the same divine necessity that took him to the temple at twelve and will take him to Jerusalem.

And this is the first mention in Luke of the phrase that will dominate the rest of the Gospel: the kingdom of God. It is not a place or a programme but God's rule breaking into a world in rebellion, in the person of the King — which is why its arrival looks like demons evicted, bodies mended, and the poor given news.
verseByVerse.examples:
The demon's terror — “Have you come to destroy us?” — is the correct reading of what the kingdom of God means for the powers of darkness. Wherever the kingdom comes, the dominion of darkness gives ground.

That is the cosmic dimension of every healing, every exorcism, every act of forgiveness in the Gospels. It is not merely a personal benefit to the recipient; it is territory changing hands. The church that prays for the sick, that names fear and guilt and lies for what they are, and that proclaims forgiveness in the name of Jesus, is doing in its own place what he did in Capernaum.

The crowds “would have kept him from leaving them” (v. 42). The wish to possess Jesus — to keep him local, to make him the property of one congregation or one tradition — is a permanent temptation of Christian communities, and it is always well meant. Jesus consistently refuses it.

He came not to be kept but to be followed. The congregation that asks how to keep Jesus to itself has asked very nearly the wrong question. The right one is how to follow him to the next town.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee. And he was teaching them on the Sabbath, and they were astonished at his teaching, for his word possessed authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee. He was teaching them on the Sabbath, and they were astonished at his teaching, for his word possessed authority.

Following Mark. From here Luke follows Mark’s account closely (Mark 1:21–39), with his own touches. And the section that follows is one long day: a sermon, an exorcism, a healing in a house, a whole town at the door at sunset, and a departure at dawn.

And he went down to Capernaum. Down: from the hills of Nazareth to the lakeside, about 700 feet (200 m) below sea level. Rejected at home, he moves to a fishing town on the north-west shore of the Sea of Galilee, on the trade road, considerably larger than Nazareth and a good deal more mixed, with a customs post (5:27), soldiers under a centurion (7:2) and a synagogue. It became his base for the whole Galilean ministry (Matthew 4:13). The remains of a later synagogue, built on the foundations of an earlier one, and of a house thought to be Peter’s, can still be seen there. Luke calls it a city of Galilee, explaining for readers who had never seen the lake. The town that received him got him; the town that had him from childhood lost him.

And they were astonished at his teaching, for his word possessed authority. The word is exousia, and it is the key to everything that follows in this chapter. It means the right to act, backed by the power to do it. To feel the force of it you have to know what teaching normally sounded like there. A scribe taught by citation: Rabbi Hillel said this, Rabbi Shammai said that, and the weight of a teaching came from the chain of authorities behind it. Nobody expected originality; originality would have been a defect. The teacher’s whole business was to transmit accurately what had been handed down. Jesus does not do this. He quotes Scripture constantly (he has just quoted Deuteronomy three times in the desert) but he never props himself on a rabbi, and he will shortly be saying, I say to you, in a way no scribe on earth would have dared (6:27). His word is not commentary on the tradition. It is the thing the tradition had been trying to transmit. Put simply, the scribes passed on what others had said about God’s word; Jesus spoke as the one whose word it is.

The same authority in the sermon and the exorcism. Notice what Luke does with the word next. In four verses the crowd will use it again about something else entirely: with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits (v. 36). The authority in the teaching and the authority over the demons are the same authority. Luke has deliberately put the sermon and the exorcism in the same paragraph so that nobody separates them. What went out of his mouth in that synagogue is not a different order of thing from what went out of his mouth to the demon. The word that breaks a demonic hold and the word that is read on a Sunday morning are one word, and the reason preaching is worth anything at all is that it carries it.

In the flow. Nazareth heard the programme and would not have it (vv. 16–29). Capernaum now sees the programme carried out. The Spirit-anointed one said he was sent to proclaim good news and liberty to the captives (v. 18), and in the next few verses he preaches, sets a captive free from a demon, lifts a woman from her sickbed and heals a street full of the sick. Luke has set the rejected sermon and the day of power side by side so that we cannot miss it: the word one town drove out is the word that sets another town free.

Does a sermon today carry that authority? Only as far as it faithfully says what Scripture says. A preacher has no authority of his own; his opinions, illustrations and jokes carry none. But when he opens the Bible and explains truly what God has said, the word he speaks is the word of God, and the hearer is dealing with Christ, not merely with a man (1 Thessalonians 2:13). That is why you should test every sermon by the Bible (Acts 17:11), and why, when it passes the test, you should receive it not as advice to consider but as the Lord’s word to obey.

In a sentence. In Capernaum, Jesus taught on the Sabbath, and people were astonished at the authority of his word.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ word still carries authority. Read it as his word to you, not just interesting advice. When you open the Bible this week, before you read, ask: Lord, what are you saying to me? And when you read a command, notice whether your first instinct is to discuss it or to do it.

For worship. His word did not need footnotes. The Creator who said, let there be light, stood in a fishing town and taught, and the people heard in his voice something they had never heard from any rabbi: not a report about God but God speaking. The same word that made the world unmade a demon and healed a fever before nightfall, and it is still speaking from every page of Scripture: the one voice in creation that will still be speaking when creation itself has been rolled up like a garment.
verseByVerse.note: Capernaum was a fishing town on the north-west shore of the lake, and became Jesus’ base in Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice, 'Ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice: ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God.

A rescue in church. The first miracle Luke records in the public ministry is not a healing. It is a rescue, and it happens in the synagogue, on the Sabbath. A man has sat in that synagogue, presumably for years, with an unclean spirit, and nobody knew, until the presence of Jesus made it impossible to stay hidden. Whatever else that says, it says that a religious setting is no proof of a clean one, and that the arrival of Christ does not create trouble so much as reveal it.

A man who had the spirit of an unclean demon. Luke, writing for Gentiles, for whom demon could mean a neutral spirit, adds unclean: an evil spirit.

What is a demon, and does this still happen? A modern reader has no framework for any of this, so the plain question has to be faced. Scripture gives less than curiosity would like and enough to go on. Demons are personal, created, spiritual beings in rebellion against God, angels who fell (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). They are not equal and opposite to God; they are creatures, and Luke will shortly show one obeying a single command. They are not the explanation of ordinary sin, ordinary illness or ordinary sorrow: Luke, a physician, carefully distinguishes the demonised from the sick a few verses on (vv. 40–41). And they are real. The New Testament does not treat them as a first-century way of describing epilepsy. Does it happen now? Scripture never suggests the enemy has gone out of business, missionaries in many parts of the world report encounters they cannot explain any other way, and a person in the modern West is far likelier to be destroyed by respectable idolatry than by anything dramatic. Both errors are real: to see a demon behind every difficulty, and to have quietly stopped believing in the enemy at all. The second is much the commoner, and it suits him better.

What have you to do with us. The cry opens with Ha!, a shout of surprise, anger or dismay, or perhaps, leave us alone! The question is literally, what to us and to you?, a Hebrew idiom meaning: what do we have in common? Why are you interfering with us? (1 Kings 17:18). Us: the demon speaks for all the demons. The kingdom of God has invaded Satan’s territory.

Have you come to destroy us? They know their end is coming (Matthew 8:29; Revelation 20:10). Jesus has come to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8). The demon knows exactly what the arrival of this man means for him, and he is right.

I know who you are, the Holy One of God. That is the first confession of Christ in his public ministry, and it is made by a demon. Not by a disciple; the disciples have not been called yet. The powers of darkness identify him correctly before anybody in Galilee does, and their theology is impeccable. The Holy One of God: set apart by God, sinless, belonging to God (1:35). And it is this holiness the demon cannot bear. Unclean things have always found the presence of the holy God unendurable; even Isaiah, a godly man, cried out that he was lost when he saw the Lord (Isaiah 6:5). The demon is not interrupting the sermon by accident. It shrieks because absolute purity has walked into the room. It may be an attempt to gain power over Jesus by naming him, as was believed in ancient magic. And it saves them nothing. You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe, and shudder (James 2:19). Here is the proof in a sentence: right doctrine, held with terror, in a being that will be lost. Knowing who Jesus is and being willing to have him are two entirely different things, and this creature has the first and would die rather than have the second.

Can a Christian be possessed by a demon? A believer is indwelt by the Holy Spirit and belongs to Christ, and he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). The New Testament never describes a believer possessed, nor tells believers to cast demons out of one another. Christians can be tempted, deceived and attacked, and must resist the devil (James 4:7) with the armour God gives (Ephesians 6:10–18); but they cannot be owned by a demon.

Then what is the difference between my faith and the demon’s knowledge? The demon knows who Jesus is and hates him. Saving faith knows who he is and trusts him: it agrees that what God says about Christ is true, and it rests on him, personally, for forgiveness and life (Westminster 14.2). The demon says, have you come to destroy us? Faith says, you have come to save me. The test is not whether you can recite the creed, but whether you want him: whether you come to him, lean on him, and would rather have him than anything else. A frightened believer who clings to Christ has what this demon, for all its accurate theology, can never have.

In a sentence. In the synagogue, a man with an unclean spirit cried out, recognising Jesus as the Holy One of God who had come to destroy the demons.

On a Tuesday. Knowing correct facts about Jesus is not faith. Even demons know who he is. Trust him and follow him. And do not imagine that a church service is a safe place where nothing spiritual is at stake. When the word of Christ is preached, things are being revealed and battles are being fought. Pray before you go.

For worship. The demons know his name and tremble, and we know his name and sing. He is the Holy One of God, and hell recognised him the moment he walked into the room. What terrifies the powers of darkness is our comfort: he has come to destroy them, and he will. The one before whom unclean spirits shriek is the one who calls us his friends, and the holiness that is their doom is the holiness he shares with us.
verseByVerse.note: “The Holy One of God” is a title for the one set apart by God — the demon names who Jesus is.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus rebuked him, saying, 'Be silent and come out of him!' And when the demon had thrown him down in their midst, he came out of him, having done him no harm. And they were all amazed and said to one another, 'What is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!' And reports about him went out into every place in the surrounding region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jesus rebuked him, saying: be silent and come out of him! When the demon had thrown him down in their midst, he came out of him, having done him no harm. They were all amazed and said to one another: what is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out! And reports about him went out into every place in the surrounding region.

But Jesus rebuked him. Two commands follow, and the first is as striking as the second.

Be silent. Literally, be muzzled. The demon has said nothing false. It called him the Holy One of God, which is precisely what he is, and it said so out loud in a crowded synagogue where the truth had been in short supply. And he shuts it up. He will do it again six verses later, and repeatedly through this Gospel. He will not accept testimony from unclean spirits, however accurate. Partly because the messenger discredits the message; partly because a public identification at this stage would force the ministry into the wrong shape too early. His identity was to be revealed in God’s time and God’s way. But mostly because truth spoken by an enemy in terror is not witness. Witness comes from people who have been rescued and love him, and by the end of Luke’s second volume there will be thousands of them.

And come out of him! That is the whole exorcism. No ritual, no formula, no repetition, no objects, no appeals to other authorities, no contest. Jewish exorcists of the period used elaborate techniques and invoked greater powers; a first-century reader would have expected at minimum a lengthy procedure. Jesus uses one sentence, and it is finished.

Having done him no harm. A detail only Luke, the physician, records. The demon threw the man down on its way out, a last spiteful act by a creature that has lost, and Luke checks the man over and reports that he was unhurt. It is the note of someone who cared what happened to the person and not only to the story.

What is this word? Or, what is this message? Both his teaching and his command. The crowd’s reaction is exactly right. They do not ask what technique he used or where he trained. They ask about the word. They have grasped the connection Luke has been drawing since verse 32: the authority in the teaching and the authority over the spirits are one thing.

For with authority and power. Authority (exousia) is the right to command; power (dynamis) is the ability to enforce it. Jesus has both, and Luke often pairs them (9:1). Men may have authority without power, like a king in exile, or power without authority, like a thief with a gun. Jesus has the right and the might, perfectly joined.

He commands the unclean spirits, and they come out! The kingdom of God has come, and Satan’s power is being broken (11:20). Here is the beginning of the war, and here is how it goes. The strong man’s house is entered by someone stronger, and there is no struggle in the doorway (11:21–22).

Should Christians today try to cast out demons? The New Testament never gives believers a technique of exorcism, and Jesus’ authority here was his own. The apostles cast out demons in his name as signs of the kingdom, and what is now laid on every Christian is to resist the devil, firm in faith (James 4:7; 1 Peter 5:9), to put on the armour of God, and to pray. Where someone seems genuinely oppressed by evil, the right response is not drama but the gospel: patient prayer, the word of God, the elders of the church, and wise care, including medical care where illness may be part of the picture. The power is in Christ’s name and word, not in a ritual.

In a sentence. Jesus silenced the demon and commanded it to come out, and it left the man unharmed, while the people marvelled at the authority and power of his word.

On a Tuesday. No power of evil can stand against Jesus’ word. If you belong to him, you need not fear the devil. When you feel attacked, by dark thoughts, by accusation, by fear in the night, do not argue with the enemy for hours; do what Jesus did in the wilderness, and answer with the word. Speak a promise of Scripture aloud, and run to Christ in prayer.

For worship. Everything that holds a human being, the powers of darkness and death itself, is under orders it did not choose to take, from a voice that made it. He speaks once, and what has held a man for years lets go and goes out, and the man sits up unharmed on the floor of a village synagogue. There has never been a rival. There has only ever been a King, and a rebellion that had not yet been told it was over.

verseByVerse.quote: And he arose and left the synagogue and entered Simon's house. Now Simon's mother-in-law was ill with a high fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf. And he stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her, and immediately she rose and began to serve them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He arose, left the synagogue and entered Simon’s house. Simon’s mother-in-law was ill with a high fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf. He stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her, and immediately she rose and began to serve them.

And entered Simon’s house. Out of the synagogue and straight into a house. The authority that silenced a demon in public now walks into somebody’s kitchen. Simon, later called Peter, has not yet been formally called in Luke (5:1–11). Luke assumes his readers know him. It is another mark of his arrangement rather than his chronology, and it fits, because Simon must already have known Jesus before the boat scene in chapter 5, or the story there makes no sense.

Simon’s mother-in-law. Simon Peter was married. Paul mentions it in passing years later, noting that Cephas took a believing wife with him on his travels (1 Corinthians 9:5). The leader of the apostles had a wife and a mother-in-law, which hardly fits later teaching about compulsory clerical celibacy.

Ill with a high fever. Luke, the doctor, grades the fever. Only he says high (megalō), a medical term used by Greek physicians who distinguished great and small fevers. Mark says she had a fever; Luke says how bad it was.

And they appealed to him on her behalf. She did not ask. Somebody else did: a household asking on behalf of a woman too ill to ask for herself. That is intercession, and it is worth having by anyone who has ever sat by a bed with nothing to offer but a request.

And he stood over her and rebuked the fever. The same verb as for the demon (v. 35) and the storm (8:24): he rebuked it. Luke is not suggesting the fever was demonic; he is describing the same sovereign word applied to a different enemy. Jesus confronts illness as an enemy, part of the disorder sin has brought into the world, and he has authority over every power that harms. Sickness gets spoken to in the imperative.

And it left her, and immediately she rose and began to serve them. Immediately: complete healing, with no weakness or convalescence, which usually follows a high fever. She was well enough at once to serve the meal. And her first act with a restored body is to feed the people in her house. Serve (diēkonei) is the word for ministry. That is the shape of the thing all through Luke: what is received is not kept. She got up and put the meal on.

Why does God heal some people and not others? A chapter of instant healings will be read by somebody who has prayed for years and buried the person anyway. Luke is not describing the normal experience of God’s people, and he never says he is. Paul left a co-worker ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20) and had a thorn he asked three times to have removed, and it was not (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). What these days in Capernaum show is not a policy but a person: what he is like, what he will finally do, and what has already begun. Every fever he rebuked came back eventually and every person he healed later died. These are signs of the morning, not the noon. If your prayer was not answered with healing, it was not because you lacked faith or God lacked love. The full healing is still coming, at the resurrection (Revelation 21:4).

Does Christ still heal like this today? God still hears and answers prayer for the sick, sometimes with healing, often through ordinary means. But the healing miracles of Jesus and the apostles were signs that confirmed who he was and what they preached (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12). Many Christians believe the gift of healing continues; the more likely reading is that such sign gifts belonged to that foundational period. The church prays for the sick (James 5:14–15) and leaves the outcome to God.

In a sentence. At Simon’s house, Jesus rebuked the high fever of Simon’s mother-in-law, and she was instantly healed and got up to serve them.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the sick, as Simon’s family asked for her: by name, specifically, and more than once. Visit them, and ask what would help. And when Jesus has blessed you, in recovery, in an answered prayer, in an ordinary week of health, serve. Ask whom you could feed, help or visit this week with the strength he has given you.

For worship. The Lord of glory went home from the synagogue to a fisherman’s house and stood by the bed of an old woman with a fever. He did not think a kitchen too small for his authority or a mother-in-law too unimportant for his care. The word that silenced hell in the morning cooled a fever at lunchtime. Nothing in our lives is beneath his notice, and no illness is beyond his command; and one day he will stand over all his people and rebuke the last enemy, and we will rise and serve him for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Luke, a doctor, notes that it was a high fever. Simon (Peter) was married.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the sun was setting, all those who had any who were sick with various diseases brought them to him, and he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them. And demons also came out of many, crying, 'You are the Son of God!' But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the sun was setting, all those who had any who were sick with various diseases brought them to him, and he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them. Demons also came out of many, crying: you are the Son of God! But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ.

Now when the sun was setting. Luke gives the hour because it explains the crowd. The Sabbath ended at sundown, and carrying a burden, a sick relative on a mat, counted as work under the rules about carrying burdens (Jeremiah 17:21). So the whole town has been waiting, watching the light go, and the moment the sun is down the doors open all along the street.

All those who had any who were sick with various diseases brought them to him. Picture it. A single doorway in a fishing village, and a queue forming in the dark that stretches out of sight; families half-carrying people who have not been out of a house for years; the noise; and one man, who has already taught in the synagogue, fought a demon and healed a woman since dawn.

And he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them. That is the sentence to stop at. Only Luke says every one. He could have done it from the doorway. One word had emptied a man of a demon that morning; a word over a crowd would have been well within his power and would have taken about four seconds. He touched them one at a time. All of them. Every single person in that queue got his hands, his eyes, his attention, and given the numbers, that means hours of it, going on into the night, with the next face and the next and the next. Not mass healing, but individual care. And he healed every one.

The untouched. Some of those he touched had not been touched by anybody for years. Chronic and disfiguring conditions, the long-term sick: the conditions in that street were the kind that left a person at the margins, and the ceremonial law was not a cruelty, but it did leave people alone. He put his hands on every one of them. That is not efficiency. It is not even, strictly, necessary. It is what he is like.

But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ. The demons cry out, you are the Son of God, and Luke links Son of God and the Christ. It is not that they were wrong; it is that they knew, and he would not be announced by them. Testimony from demons would discredit him (11:15), and the popular understanding of Messiah was political and military. He would reveal his identity himself, in his own way, culminating in the cross.

Does Jesus still notice individuals, when millions pray to him? Yes, and this verse is the proof. He is not a crowd manager. He laid his hands on every one of them, and he has not changed (Hebrews 13:8). As the risen Lord he knows his sheep by name (John 10:3), and because he is God, his attention is not divided: he is not less present to you because he is also present to someone else. When you pray, you are not a number in a queue. You are one person, known completely, with his full attention.

In a sentence. At sunset the whole town brought their sick, and Jesus laid hands on each one and healed them, while silencing the demons who declared him the Son of God.

On a Tuesday. Jesus cares for people one by one. Bring the people you love to him, individually, in prayer, by name. And imitate him: in a busy week, choose one person who is easy to overlook, the housebound neighbour, the elderly member who no longer comes, the colleague nobody eats with, and give them your full attention, unhurried, for an hour.

For worship. The Son of God, who could have spoken once from a doorway and gone to bed, stood in a Galilean street after dark at the end of the first full day Luke records, putting his hands on one broken person after another until there was nobody left in the queue. He was not tired of them. He has never been tired of them. There is no one so far gone, so long untouched, or so far down the line that he works through the crowd and stops before he gets there.
verseByVerse.note: The Sabbath ended at sundown; only then could people carry the sick without breaking the Sabbath rules.

verseByVerse.quote: And when it was day, he departed and went into a desolate place. And the people sought him and came to him, and would have kept him from leaving them, but he said to them, 'I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When it was day, he departed and went into a desolate place. The people sought him, came to him, and would have kept him from leaving them, but he said to them: I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.

And when it was day, he departed and went into a desolate place. After a night like that, the first thing he does is leave. Luke does not say here what he went to do; Mark, telling the same morning, says he went to pray (Mark 1:35). It is the pattern Luke has already established at the Jordan and will keep returning to: before the Twelve are chosen, before Peter’s confession, on the mountain, in the garden (6:12; 9:18, 28; 22:41). Note when it happens. Not after a failure, not in a crisis, but the morning after the most spectacularly successful day of his ministry so far. The town is at his feet. That is the moment he walks out into the wilderness alone, which suggests that the hour of greatest danger is not the one that feels like it. Success has its own temptation: to begin living from the crowd’s need of us rather than from the Father’s love for us. Jesus went to his Father before the crowd could set the agenda.

And would have kept him from leaving them. This is not hostility. It is Capernaum at its best, a town that has seen what he can do and does not want to lose it. Yet notice the contrast: Nazareth drove him out; Capernaum tried to hold him in. Both wanted him on their own terms. He goes anyway.

I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God. There is the must again, dei, the divine necessity that first appeared on the lips of a twelve-year-old in the temple (2:49) and will drive him all the way to Jerusalem. And notice what it is attached to. Not to healing. To preaching. That is startling given the previous night, and it deserves saying plainly: the healings are real, and they are not the mission. He was sent to announce something, and the healings are the announcement made visible. Healing a body was good, but bodies die again. The word of the kingdom gives eternal life.

The kingdom of God. Here is the first mention in Luke of the phrase that will dominate the rest of the Gospel. It is not a place and it is not a programme. It is God’s reign, his rule breaking into a world in rebellion, in the person of the King, to save and to judge. Which is why its arrival looks like this: demons evicted, bodies mended, the poor given news, debts cancelled. Wherever he goes, the territory changes hands.

To the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose. Sent by the Father. His mission was wider than one town. The desire to keep him is a permanent temptation of Christian communities, and it is always well meant. A church that asks how to hold on to what God is doing among them has asked a natural question and very nearly the wrong one. He was not sent to be kept. He was sent to be followed, to the next town.

In the flow. The words I was sent pick up the language of the Nazareth reading: he has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives (v. 18). The chapter opened with the programme announced and closes with the programme pursued. Between them Luke has shown what the anointed one’s preaching meets when it is rejected and when it is received, and now he shows that it cannot be held in one place. This is the shape of the rest of the Gospel and of Acts: the word of the kingdom keeps moving outward, town after town, until it is preached openly in Rome (Acts 28:31).

Is it wrong to want our church to keep what God is doing? Not to be thankful and to want it to continue. What is wrong is to turn blessing inward, as though God’s work existed for us. A church blessed with gifted people, money and growth should ask not only how to keep them but where to send them: planting another congregation, supporting missionaries, releasing its best people to go. The church in Antioch, at the height of its blessing, sent away its two best teachers (Acts 13:1–3). Healthy churches give away what they have been given.

In a sentence. When the people tried to keep Jesus in Capernaum, he said he must preach the kingdom of God in other towns too, because that was what he was sent to do.

On a Tuesday. Jesus prioritised preaching the gospel. Do not let good things crowd out the main thing. And notice when he prayed: after success, not only before trouble. When a week goes well, take time alone with God before the next demand arrives. Where it applies: the Christian worker so busy meeting needs that the gospel is never spoken; the parent so busy with the children’s activities that they never hear about Christ at home. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: this does not make practical help unimportant. Jesus healed all night before he left. Do the good works, and do not let them silence the good news.

For worship. He prayed alone at dawn, after the greatest night of healing Capernaum had ever seen, because he lived from his Father and not from the crowd. And then he turned from the town that loved him to the towns that had never heard, because there were more lost sheep than one village. That must is the reason the gospel reached you. He would not stay where he was wanted, because he had been sent for those who did not yet know him, and he has been coming to the next town ever since.

verseByVerse.quote: And he was preaching in the synagogues of Judea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he was preaching in the synagogues of Judea.

And he was preaching in the synagogues of Judea. One sentence closes the chapter, and Luke uses it to widen the frame. The tense means he kept on preaching: a summary of an extended period of ministry.

Judea or Galilee? A reader with an older translation may find Galilee here instead, and the difference is a genuine textual one. The manuscripts divide, and the best manuscripts read Judea, which is also the harder reading. That is generally the stronger claim, since a copyist is far likelier to smooth a difficulty than to create one. Everything in this chapter has happened in Galilee, and Mark 1:39 has Galilee, so Judea looks like a slip and would have invited correction. But Luke uses Judea elsewhere for the whole land of the Jews, including Galilee, rather than the southern province alone (1:5; 6:17; 7:17; 23:5; Acts 10:37). On that usage there is no difficulty at all. He is saying that the preaching spread throughout the Jewish land.

Why put the sentence here. The chapter began with one man alone in a desert and ends with a preaching circuit across a nation. And at the end of it he is not consolidating Capernaum or building on a spectacular night. He is preaching, synagogue by synagogue, in the next town, which is exactly what he said he had been sent to do (v. 43).

In the synagogues. The ordinary weekly gatherings of ordinary Jewish people, the same institution whose Nazareth branch had just tried to kill him. He did not abandon the synagogue because a synagogue rejected him. He went to the next one.

Does a textual difference like this mean we cannot trust the Bible? No. Differences between manuscripts are real, and honest translations tell you about them in footnotes. But the great majority are tiny matters of spelling or word order, and none of them changes a single doctrine of the faith. Here, whichever word Luke wrote, the meaning is the same: Jesus preached throughout the land. We have far more early copies of the New Testament than of any other ancient book, and by comparing them scholars can recover what was written with remarkable confidence. God has kept his word.

In a sentence. Jesus went on preaching in the synagogues throughout the land of the Jews.

On a Tuesday. The good news must go to every town. Pray this week for a preacher you know by name, and for one place that has not yet heard; and give, if you can, towards the spreading of the gospel there. And if a door has closed on you somewhere, as Nazareth closed on him, do not conclude that God has finished with you. Go to the next one.

For worship. The trumpet of the Jubilee had sounded in one village and been shouted down. So he took it to the rest of them, and he has never yet stopped taking it to the next town, or run out of patience with congregations that will not have him, or decided that a place has heard enough. He came for the wilderness and the synagogue, the cliff edge and the kitchen, the queue at sunset and the empty place at dawn, and in all of them he was the same: the Son who would not bow, the King whose word cannot be resisted, the Saviour whose hands reached every one. Blessed be the Lord who keeps preaching good news to the poor, until every captive has heard.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Galilee. Luke sometimes uses “Judea” for the whole land of the Jews.

4.text: <sup>1</sup> And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness <sup>2</sup> for forty days, being tempted by the devil. And he ate nothing during those days. And when they were ended, he was hungry. <sup>3</sup> The devil said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread.” <sup>4</sup> And Jesus answered him, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone.’” <sup>5</sup> And the devil took him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time, <sup>6</sup> and said to him, “To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been delivered to me, and I give it to whom I will. <sup>7</sup> If you, then, will worship me, it will all be yours.” <sup>8</sup> And Jesus answered him, “It is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.’” <sup>9</sup> And he took him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here, <sup>10</sup> for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you, to guard you,’ <sup>11</sup> and ‘On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’” <sup>12</sup> And Jesus answered him, “It is said, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’” <sup>13</sup> And when the devil had ended every temptation, he departed from him until an opportune time. <sup>14</sup> And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through all the surrounding country. <sup>15</sup> And he taught in their synagogues, being glorified by all. <sup>16</sup> And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. And as was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day, and he stood up to read. <sup>17</sup> And the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written, <sup>18</sup> “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, <sup>19</sup> to proclaim the year of the Lord's favor.” <sup>20</sup> And he rolled up the scroll and gave it back to the attendant and sat down. And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. <sup>21</sup> And he began to say to them, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” <sup>22</sup> And all spoke well of him and marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth. And they said, “Is not this Joseph's son?” <sup>23</sup> And he said to them, “Doubtless you will quote to me this proverb, ‘Physician, heal yourself.’ What we have heard you did at Capernaum, do here in your hometown as well.” <sup>24</sup> And he said, “Truly, I say to you, no prophet is acceptable in his hometown. <sup>25</sup> But in truth, I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the heavens were shut up three years and six months, and a great famine came over all the land, <sup>26</sup> and Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow. <sup>27</sup> And there were many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian.” <sup>28</sup> When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath. <sup>29</sup> And they rose up and drove him out of the town and brought him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, so that they could throw him down the cliff. <sup>30</sup> But passing through their midst, he went away. <sup>31</sup> And he went down to Capernaum, a city of Galilee. And he was teaching them on the Sabbath, <sup>32</sup> and they were astonished at his teaching, for his word possessed authority. <sup>33</sup> And in the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out with a loud voice, <sup>34</sup> “Ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God.” <sup>35</sup> But Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent and come out of him!” And when the demon had thrown him down in their midst, he came out of him, having done him no harm. <sup>36</sup> And they were all amazed and said to one another, “What is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!” <sup>37</sup> And reports about him went out into every place in the surrounding region. <sup>38</sup> And he arose and left the synagogue and entered Simon's house. Now Simon's mother-in-law was ill with a high fever, and they appealed to him on her behalf. <sup>39</sup> And he stood over her and rebuked the fever, and it left her, and immediately she rose and began to serve them. <sup>40</sup> Now when the sun was setting, all those who had any who were sick with various diseases brought them to him, and he laid his hands on every one of them and healed them. <sup>41</sup> And demons also came out of many, crying, “You are the Son of God!” But he rebuked them and would not allow them to speak, because they knew that he was the Christ. <sup>42</sup> And when it was day, he departed and went into a desolate place. And the people sought him and came to him, and would have kept him from leaving them, <sup>43</sup> but he said to them, “I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.” <sup>44</sup> And he was preaching in the synagogues of Judea.

5.title: Calling, Cleansing, and the New Wine
5.overview:
Chapter 5 gathers five scenes that together define what it means to encounter Jesus: a miraculous catch of fish that produces not pride but prostration; the cleansing of a man whose disease had made him untouchable; the healing of a paralytic whose friends refused to be stopped by a crowd; the call of a tax collector from his booth; and a dispute about fasting that opens into the deepest question of the chapter — whether the new thing Jesus is doing can be contained in the old structures of Judaism. The answer is no. New wine requires new wineskins. What Jesus brings is not a reform of the old system; it is something genuinely, radically new.

The call of the first disciples (vv. 1–11) is Luke's fullest account of how Peter, James, and John came to follow Jesus — fuller than the brief summaries in Matthew and Mark, because Luke wants to show not just the what but the why. They did not follow a charismatic teacher because he seemed promising. They followed because they had encountered something that simultaneously exposed their unworthiness and compelled their trust. Peter's “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord” is the most honest response to the presence of holiness in the New Testament — the instinct that knows it cannot stand in the presence of what it has just encountered, and is answered not with departure but with the word: “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.”

The chapter closes with a theological dispute about fasting (vv. 33–39) that turns out to be the interpretive key to everything that has come before. The Pharisees and John's disciples fast; Jesus's disciples do not. The question is not merely about religious practice; it is about eschatology. Jesus answers with the image of a wedding: the bridegroom is present. The time of mourning is over; the feast has begun. This is not the time for old wineskins; the new wine of the kingdom — the presence of the Son of God himself — cannot be contained in the structures designed for a world still waiting for him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Jesus Calls the First Disciples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The call of the first disciples is set on the shore of the Lake of Gennesaret, where Simon Peter and his partners James and John have fished all night and caught nothing. Jesus borrows Peter's boat as a floating pulpit, teaches the crowd from the water, and then tells Peter to put out into the deep and let down the nets.

The instruction is professionally absurd. Fishermen who have worked the prime hours of the night without result do not take advice on technique from a carpenter, in daylight, with the nets already cleaned. But Peter obeys — “at your word I will let down the nets” — and the catch is so large that both boats begin to sink.

The miracle is not primarily about fish. It is about the person who commanded them. Peter, who knows these waters better than almost anyone alive, has just watched something no expertise can produce, and his response is immediate: he falls at Jesus's knees and says “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.”

That is the language of Isaiah's vision (“Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips,” Isa. 6:5), of Job before the whirlwind (Job 42:5-6), of John falling as dead at the feet of the risen Christ (Rev. 1:17). It is what happens when a creature with a conscience encounters holiness. Nothing had been said about sin; a boatload of fish had told him who was in the boat.

Jesus's answer to the confession of unworthiness is not agreement and not dismissal but a commission: “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.” The fear that holiness produces is not the end of the encounter; it is the beginning of the calling — because the calling was never going to rest on Peter's worthiness.

The verb is zōgreō, to take alive. Fishing is bad news for fish; this net means the opposite. The trade is the same and the direction is reversed.

“From now on” is one of Luke's phrases for a hinge. They bring the boats to land, leave everything — including the greatest catch of their lives, lying on the shingle — and follow him.

And this is not the first meeting. Jesus was in Simon's house a chapter earlier (4:38-39), and John records an earlier introduction at the Jordan (John 1:35-42). Matthew and Mark give the decisive moment; Luke shows what was behind it. Most people are called the way Simon was — not all at once, but finally.
verseByVerse.theology:
The miraculous catch authenticates the call. Jesus does not simply appear on the shore and invite Peter to follow; he first demonstrates, in the domain where Peter's competence is greatest, that Peter's competence is not the final authority over the natural world.

The one who commands the fish is the one who made them. Peter's professional knowledge is real and valuable, and it is relativised — not demeaned. In the presence of the maker of the sea, every human expertise finds its proper place, which is a genuine place and not the top one.

The commission “you will be catching men” describes a rescue rather than an occupation. The disciples are being called to pull people alive out of the water that was drowning them — which is why the calling that begins with a catch of fish reaches its first great haul at Pentecost, when three thousand are taken alive in a day (Acts 2:41), and has not stopped since.

And the pattern of the encounter is the pattern of every conversion: an approach from Christ's side, a demonstration that leaves the man with nothing to stand on, an honest confession of unworthiness, and a calling that does not depend on the confession being answered with reassurance.
verseByVerse.examples:
“At your word I will let down the nets” — spoken after a night of futile effort, in the daylight hours when fishing is least productive, on the instruction of someone who is not a fisherman — is the model of obedient trust.

It is not blind obedience. Peter states the professional futility of the exercise plainly and is entirely right to state it. But he has heard something that overrides his own competence, and the reason he gives is the only one he has: not that the strategy makes sense, but that the one who commands can be trusted.

“They left everything and followed him” (v. 11) is the most radical vocational change in the New Testament. James and John leave their father in the boat — not just a career but a family business and a family obligation. The “everything” is genuinely everything: livelihood, security, plans, and the future they had imagined.

Not every disciple is told to leave a trade; Luke's own Gospel sends several people home. But everyone who follows has a moment when something must be left on the beach — and it is very often the thing that had only just started going well.

verseByVerse.quote: On one occasion, while the crowd was pressing in on him to hear the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret, and he saw two boats by the lake, but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon's, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And he sat down and taught the people from the boat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On one occasion, while the crowd was pressing in on him to hear the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret. He saw two boats by the lake, but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon’s, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And he sat down and taught the people from the boat.

Meaning first. Luke 5 shows the authority of Jesus reaching into ordinary lives and calling them to himself. A fisherman lets down his nets at Jesus’ word, hauls in a catch that sinks two boats, falls on his knees confessing his sin, and is made a fisher of men. A leper is touched and cleansed. A paralysed man lowered through a roof is forgiven, and then healed to prove that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. A tax collector leaves his booth, and Jesus defends eating with sinners: a doctor goes to the sick. And the bridegroom is here, with new wine the old wineskins cannot hold. Here is the Lord whose holiness makes sinners tremble and whose grace makes them follow.

The setting. Only Luke tells the story of the great catch. Matthew and Mark record the call of these four men in a few brisk lines: Jesus walks past, says follow me, and they go (Matthew 4:18–22; Mark 1:16–20). Luke gives a whole morning, and he plainly does not think it is their first meeting, for Jesus has already been in Simon’s house (4:38–39). John fills in the earlier stage: Andrew met Jesus by the Jordan and brought his brother to him (John 1:35–42). So the call is a deepening: an introduction at the Jordan, an acquaintance in Capernaum, and then this morning, when acquaintance becomes the leaving of everything.

The crowd was pressing in on him to hear the word of God. Luke introduces the first disciples through a sermon, not a miracle. The crowd is pushing, physically crowding, and they came hungry for the word of God, Luke’s phrase for Jesus’ preaching. He needs a platform.

In the flow. Chapter 4 ended with Jesus insisting that he must preach the good news of the kingdom of God in other towns as well, because that is why he was sent (4:43). Chapter 5 opens with that preaching, and then shows what it does: it gathers people. In chapter 4 his authority drove out demons and fevers; here the same authority reaches into a working man’s life and claims him. Luke is beginning to show the company Jesus forms around himself, the men who will one day be his witnesses (24:48), and it starts with a sermon and a fisherman.

The lake of Gennesaret. Luke’s precise name for the Sea of Galilee, from the fertile plain of Gennesaret on its north-western shore. Luke, who had seen the Mediterranean, does not call a lake about 13 miles by 8 (21 by 13 km) a sea.

The fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. After a night’s fishing, nets had to be cleaned of weed and debris, mended and dried. It is the last job of a night shift, done by people who want to go home. Simon will say why in a moment: they caught nothing (v. 5). These are not prosperous boat owners at leisure. They are labourers at the end of a wasted night, and a teacher climbs into the boat and asks for a favour.

Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon’s. Jesus chooses Simon’s boat. He borrows what belongs to Simon, as a first step in claiming Simon himself. The relationship that will become the central human relationship of this Gospel begins as a practical arrangement between a preacher who needs a pulpit and a fisherman who has one going spare. Jesus enters their exhaustion and their disappointment before he asks anything of them, and he asks for something small before he asks for everything.

And he sat down and taught the people from the boat. A natural pulpit. Water carries sound, and the shore sloped like an amphitheatre; a boat pushed out a few yards turns a beach into an auditorium. Simon sat in the boat listening, while he held it steady. Before he is called, he is made to hear.

How does God usually call people? Most people are called the way Simon was: not all at once, but finally. A few Christians can name the hour they first believed; many cannot, and came to Christ over months or years, through a Christian home, a friend, a church, a slow dawning, and then a moment when it became their own. Both are real conversions. What matters is not whether you can date it but whether you are now following him. If your story is gradual, do not doubt it for that reason. God was at work in every stage, as he was with Simon at the Jordan, in his house, and in his boat.

In a sentence. With the crowd pressing to hear God’s word, Jesus got into Simon’s boat, asked him to push out a little, and taught from it.

On a Tuesday. Jesus often begins by asking for the use of something ordinary of yours: your car for someone without one, your kitchen for a meal with a new neighbour, your spare hour for the child who needs reading help, your living room for a Bible study. Let him have it. You may not see at first that he is not only borrowing the boat but coming for the boatman.

For worship. The Lord of the sea climbed into a borrowed boat, sat down among wet nets, and preached from it. He came to tired men at the end of a fruitless night, and he did not wait for them to be fresh or successful before he came near. He borrows our small things to give us great ones. The one who would soon ask Simon for everything began by asking for a few yards of water, and he is still coming to people in the middle of their ordinary work, patiently, until they are his.
verseByVerse.note: The lake of Gennesaret is the Sea of Galilee. Nets were washed and mended after a night’s fishing.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, 'Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.' And Simon answered, 'Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! But at your word I will let down the nets.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he had finished speaking, he said to Simon: put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch. Simon answered: Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! But at your word I will let down the nets.

Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch. Consider how that sounded. Simon has fished this lake all his working life. Fishing on the lake was done at night, when the fish came near the surface and could not see the nets, and he has just worked the whole of it for nothing. It is now morning, the worst time, and the gear has been cleaned and stowed. Daytime, in deep water, was the wrong time and the wrong place. And a carpenter from an inland village is telling a fisherman how to fish. Your nets is plural: the whole crew is to do it.

Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! Luke lets the objection stand. This is not a pious man swallowing his doubts; he states the professional reality plainly, and he is right: it makes no sense.
