Notice also what he calls him: Master (epistatēs), a word Luke alone uses, almost always on the lips of disciples, meaning someone in charge, a commander or superintendent. It is a real title, and it is not yet Lord. Three verses from now it will be. He knows enough to obey; he does not yet know who he is obeying. That is where most obedience begins, and there is no other way to start.

But at your word I will let down the nets. That is one of the great sentences of the Gospel, and its greatness lies in what it does not claim. Simon does not say he now expects fish. He does not say he has received an inner assurance, or felt a stirring, or reconsidered the science of it. He gives the reason, and there is exactly one: at your word. This is faith: acting on Christ’s word when it contradicts what we think we know. Not blind faith, but faith in a word, from a person he had begun to trust. And it is what faith looks like from the inside far more often than the confident version people imagine. Faith is not the disappearance of the objection. It is the objection stated honestly, and then the obedience anyway, because of who is speaking.

Whose word it was. Simon did not yet know it, but the word he leaned on was the word that had made the lake. By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and he spoke and it came to be (Psalm 33:6, 9). Luke has just shown that same word rebuking a demon and a fever (4:35, 39), and now it reaches under the surface of Gennesaret. Simon’s faith was small and his reasons thin; the one he trusted was neither. Faith does not save by its size but by its object, and a fisherman’s grudging at your word, spoken to the Creator, was enough to fill two boats.

The cost of obedience. It is easy to miss. The nets were clean. Letting them down again means hours more work at the end of a shift, in front of a crowd on the shore, at a time of day when everyone watching knows it will not work. Simon is not risking his life. He is risking looking a fool, which for most people is harder.

Does this mean I should obey any impression that comes to me? No. Simon obeyed a word spoken audibly by Jesus himself. For us, Christ’s word is Scripture, and that is where we must look for his commands (2 Timothy 3:16–17). A strong feeling or an inner voice is not the same thing, and should be tested by the Bible and by wise counsel, not obeyed as if it were the voice of Christ. But where Scripture does speak, to forgive, to give, to be honest, to keep a vow, to tell someone the gospel, Simon is our pattern: obey, even when experience says it will not work.

In a sentence. Jesus told Simon to go into deep water and let down the nets, and Simon, though they had caught nothing all night, obeyed because Jesus said so.

On a Tuesday. Where does Christ’s word tell you to do something that seems pointless by your own experience? Where it applies: forgiving the relative who has never changed; giving generously when the budget is tight; telling a friend about Christ when every past attempt fell flat; going on praying for a child who shows no sign of interest. Say with Simon: at your word, I will. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: this is not a licence for reckless schemes in the name of faith, such as quitting a job without a plan or ignoring a doctor because you feel God has told you something. Obey what he has actually said, and use the wisdom he has given you for everything else.

For worship. Here is the Lord whose word is worth more than a lifetime of experience. Simon knew the lake; Jesus made it. The man who had worked all night for nothing was about to learn that one word from this carpenter could do in a minute what all his skill could not do in a night. Blessed is the Master whose commands make no sense to us until we obey them, and who never once asks his people to let down their nets in vain.
verseByVerse.note: Fishing on the lake was done at night; daytime in deep water was the wrong time and place.

parallels.desc: a night of nothing, then a great catch

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had done this, they enclosed a large number of fish, and their nets were breaking. They signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. And they came and filled both the boats, so that they began to sink.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had done this, they enclosed a large number of fish, and their nets were breaking. They signalled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. They came and filled both the boats, so that they began to sink.

They enclosed a large number of fish. Luke does not describe the fish arriving. He describes the equipment failing. Not a lucky shoal, but a miracle of the Lord of creation, who appointed a great fish for Jonah (Jonah 1:17). Psalm 8 says God put all things under the feet of the son of man, even the fish of the sea, and Hebrews sees that psalm fulfilled in Jesus (Psalm 8:6–8; Hebrews 2:8–9). In this boat the fish of the sea are doing as he says.

And their nets were breaking. Literally, were beginning to break: overwhelming abundance. Torn nets, a shout across the water, two boats down to the waterline and going under. The miracle is reported from the point of view of men trying to cope with it.

They signalled to their partners in the other boat. James and John (v. 10): a small fishing business. The catch was so large that the second boat had to be called, and even then both crews together barely coped.

And filled both the boats, so that they began to sink. More than they could hold. God’s generosity overflows: after a night of empty nets, two boats full to sinking. That excess is the message. A moderate catch would have been a pleasant surprise and could have been put down to luck; a good fisherman has strange mornings. What happens here cannot be absorbed into anybody’s experience. The gear that was designed for this work cannot handle it, and neither can the boats. It is a picture of the harvest of people that the gospel would bring (v. 10; Acts 2:41).

In his own trade. It happens in the one arena where Simon is the expert, and that is not accidental. Jesus does not demonstrate his authority to these men in a synagogue, where they would have deferred to him anyway; he does it in their own trade, on their own water, at the exact point where their competence was greatest and had just failed. Simon’s professional knowledge is real, and it is not overturned so much as put in its place. In front of him is someone the fish obey.

The same lake at the end. This is the same lake, and some of the same men, Simon and the sons of Zebedee among them (John 21:2), on a morning after the resurrection in John’s Gospel, when a voice from the shore says, cast the net on the right side, and the net comes up full and unbroken (John 21:6, 11). Simon’s story begins and ends with a catch he did not earn, from a word he did not expect, in water he had already worked all night for nothing.

Will obeying Christ always bring visible success? No. Here obedience brought a spectacular catch, but Scripture is full of faithful people whose obedience brought prison, loss or apparent failure: Jeremiah preached for forty years and was largely ignored; Paul was beaten and imprisoned. The promise is not that obedience is always rewarded with results we can measure, but that it is never wasted (1 Corinthians 15:58). God sometimes gives the overflowing net to show what he can do; more often he asks us to keep letting down the nets and trust him with what comes up.

In a sentence. When they obeyed, they caught so many fish that their nets began to tear, and two boats were filled to sinking.

On a Tuesday. Obedience to Christ’s word may bring a blessing far beyond what you expected. Trust him with your empty nets: the ministry that has seen no fruit, the prayer that has had no answer, the work that has gone unnoticed. And when blessing comes, signal for the partners. Share it, and ask for help; the catches God gives are usually too big for one boat.

For worship. The Lord of the lake does not give by the cupful. One word from him, and nets that held nothing all night cannot hold what he sends; two boats settle to the waterline under the weight of his kindness. Here is the Creator who made every fish in Gennesaret and calls them where he pleases, giving to tired men who had earned nothing a morning they would remember all their lives. And here is the Saviour who would give, not fish, but himself, a gift no net, no boat and no heart was ever built to hold.

parallels.desc: the net full of large fish

verseByVerse.quote: But when Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, 'Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.' For he and all who were with him were astonished at the catch of fish that they had taken,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus’ knees, saying: depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord. For he and all who were with him were astonished at the catch of fish that they had taken.

He fell down at Jesus’ knees. Luke calls him Simon Peter, the only time he uses both names before 6:14, as if to mark the moment Simon became Peter. He falls in the boat, among the fish. He does not count the fish, or thank Jesus, or ask how it was done. He goes down on his knees in a sinking boat full of the largest catch of his life, in worship, and asks the man responsible to go away.

Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord. A surprising response to a miracle of blessing. Not thank you, but go away. Nothing has been said about sin. There has been no sermon on repentance, no accusation, no exposure of anything Simon has done. There has only been a boatload of fish. And the fish have told him something about the man in the stern that his conscience cannot survive standing next to. Simon suddenly saw who Jesus was. In the presence of divine holiness and power, he saw his own sinfulness.

The oldest pattern in Scripture. Isaiah sees the LORD high and lifted up and the first word out of him is: woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts! (Isaiah 6:5). Job argues for chapter after chapter, meets God, and says, now my eye sees you; therefore I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes (Job 42:5–6). John, who had leaned on Jesus’ chest at supper, sees him in glory and falls at his feet as though dead (Revelation 1:17). Not one of them is told to feel this way. It is simply what happens when a creature with a conscience gets close to holiness. And holiness is not first a rule but what God is: utterly pure, utterly other, a blazing goodness before which even the seraphim cover their faces (Isaiah 6:2–3). Simon saw a flash of it in a fishing boat, and it was enough to put him on his knees. The nearer we come to God, the more we see our sin. Conviction of sin is the beginning of true discipleship.

O Lord. Notice the title. Two verses ago he said Master. Now he says Lord, the title Israel’s Scriptures give to God himself. The fish have moved his vocabulary. He is a very long way from understanding, and he has understood the one thing that matters: the gap between himself and this man is not the ordinary gap between two men. And the whole crew felt it: astonishment (thambos) is awe, amazement and fear together.

The shame that wants to be left alone. Depart from me is a sentence a great many people have felt without ever saying aloud. There is a kind of shame that does not want to be forgiven so much as to be left alone: that finds the nearness of God unbearable and would genuinely prefer distance to exposure. Simon is not being falsely modest. He means it. What is worth seeing is that he is right about himself and wrong about what to do with it. He is a sinful man. That is the accurate diagnosis, and it is the reason Jesus got into the boat.

I feel more sinful now than before I was a Christian. Is something wrong? Usually, something is right. Growing in grace means seeing God more clearly, and the clearer the light, the more dust you see in the room. Paul near the end of his life called himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). A deepening sense of sin is not a sign that you are going backwards, provided it drives you to Christ and not away from him. The danger is not feeling your sin but concluding, as Simon did for a moment, that you must keep your distance. The right response to seeing your sin is the one Simon made next: to stay at Jesus’ knees and hear him say, do not be afraid.

In a sentence. Seeing the miraculous catch, Simon fell at Jesus’ knees and begged him to depart, because he was a sinful man in the presence of the Lord.

On a Tuesday. When God shows you something of yourself this week, through Scripture, a sermon, or a moment of his kindness that you did not deserve, do not run from it and do not hide from him. Say honestly what Simon said, I am a sinful man, and then stay where you are, on your knees and near him. Notice too that it was a blessing, not a rebuke, that broke Simon open. Let God’s goodness to you lead you to repentance (Romans 2:4).

For worship. Simon asked the Holy One to leave his boat, and the Holy One stayed. Among the slithering fish and the torn nets, with a sinner on his knees in front of him, he did not step back an inch. His holiness is not the kind that keeps its distance from the unclean; it is the kind that came all the way down to stand among them, and would go further still, to bear Simon’s sins in his own body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24). The nearness Simon dreaded was the very nearness that saved him.

parallels.desc: woe is me, for I am lost

verseByVerse.quote: and so also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. And Jesus said to Simon, 'Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.' And when they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. And Jesus said to Simon: do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men. When they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him.

James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. Business partners in the fishing trade. With Simon, they became the inner three, present at the raising of Jairus’ daughter and on the mountain of transfiguration (8:51; 9:28).

Do not be afraid. It is the fourth time in this Gospel. Gabriel said it to Zechariah, and to Mary; the angel said it to the shepherds; and now Jesus says it to a fisherman on his knees (1:13, 30; 2:10). The encounter with holiness always produces the fear, and the answer to the fear is always the same word. And note that he does not argue with the diagnosis. Simon says, I am a sinful man, and Jesus does not say, nonsense, or, you are being hard on yourself. He does not correct the self-assessment at all. He answers it with grace. A sinful man is exactly the kind of man he calls. He simply declines to leave, and gives the man a job.

From now on you will be catching men. From now on is a phrase Luke reserves for hinges. Everything before this morning was one kind of life; everything after it is another. And the word for catching is stronger than English lets on. Luke does not use the ordinary verb for fishing. He uses zōgreō, which means to take alive, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for sparing captives in battle rather than killing them (Numbers 31:18). Fishing, after all, is not good news for the fish; the net means death. This net means the opposite. Simon is not being told he will collect people the way he collected fish. He is being told he will pull them out alive, out of the water that was drowning them.

The same trade, reversed. Nothing of who he is gets discarded. The patience, the nerve, the long nights, the knowledge of when to move: all of it is taken up and turned round. Simon’s skills and hard work would be redirected to a new purpose. The first great haul comes on a morning in Jerusalem when about three thousand are taken alive in a day (Acts 2:41).

They left everything and followed him. Only Luke says everything, and everything includes the fish. That is worth stopping on. They had just landed the catch of a lifetime, enough money to change a family’s year, the best night’s work of their lives, and they beached the boats and walked away from it: boats, nets, fish, business. They did not sell it first. The greatest professional success of Simon’s life lasted about ten minutes and was abandoned on the shingle. Jesus was worth more. This is what following him means (14:33; 18:28).

Must every Christian leave his job to follow Jesus? No. Not everyone is called to leave a trade; Luke’s own Gospel is full of people sent home (8:39). Most Christians follow Christ as fishermen, nurses, accountants and parents, and serve him in that calling (1 Corinthians 7:17, 20). What every follower must leave is the claim of anything else to be first. Everyone who follows Christ has a moment where something has to be left on the beach, and it is usually the thing that had just started going well. For some it is a job; for others an ambition, a relationship, a habit, a way of spending money, or the right to run their own life.

Is every Christian meant to be catching people? Yes, though not all in the same way. The Twelve were called to a unique apostolic office, and some are called to preach. But every believer is part of a church that is sent into the world with the gospel (Matthew 28:19–20), and every believer is to be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in him (1 Peter 3:15). For most that means praying for people by name, living so that faith is visible, inviting friends to hear the gospel, and speaking of Christ when the door opens. You catch people alive by bringing them to the one who saves; you do not have to do the saving.

In a sentence. Jesus told Simon not to fear, for from then on he would catch people, and Simon, James and John left everything and followed him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus calls sinners to follow him and to fish for people. Ask honestly what is on the beach in your life: what you would find hardest to leave if he asked. Where it applies: the career ambition that has quietly become the centre; the evening hours that never have room for him; the savings you could not bear to share. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: this is not a call to neglect your family, walk out on your obligations, or despise ordinary work as second-class. Following Christ usually means serving him faithfully where you are. And this week, ask him for one person you might bring alive to him.

For worship. Do not be afraid: the first words Jesus spoke to the sinner at his knees were not a sentence but a calling. He took a man who wanted him to leave and made him a fisher of men and the first preacher of Pentecost. The Lord who could have sent Simon away instead sent him out. Grace does not deny the sin; it outbids it. And the net Simon would cast at Pentecost had been woven first around Simon himself, by the Lord who catches men alive.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A man “full of leprosy” comes to Jesus. The description is Luke's medical precision: this is not an early skin complaint but an advanced case. Leprosy in the ancient world covered a range of chronic conditions, all of which rendered the sufferer ritually unclean (Lev. 13-14).

The consequences were total. He lived outside the settlement, was required to warn others of his approach — “Unclean! Unclean!” (Lev. 13:45-46) — and was excluded from worship. He was the ultimate social and religious exile, and not because of anything he had done. He simply had a condition, and the condition put him outside.

His approach is itself an act of desperation and faith: he is in a city he may not enter, on his face in public, saying “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” He does not doubt the power. He is uncertain only about the will — which is exactly the right question to bring, and the answer is the most intimate thing in the chapter.

Jesus reaches out his hand and touches him: “I will; be clean.” The touch is the miracle inside the miracle. Any rabbi could have spoken healing from a safe distance; a word would have done it. Instead the hand lands on the one body in Galilee nobody had been permitted to touch for years.

Under the law, contact ran one way: touching a leper made you unclean. Here the direction is reversed. The holiness of Jesus is not contaminated by the leper; the leper is cleansed by the holiness.

The instruction to show himself to the priest and offer what Moses commanded (Lev. 14) is not legalism but pastoral wisdom. The priest's certificate was the man's ticket back into the community; without it, even a healed leper could not go home. Jesus heals the disease in a second, then walks the man through the process that heals everything else the disease had done to him — and the certificate stands in the temple records as “a proof to them.”

“Tell no one” is the recognition that a reputation as a healer will bury the preaching under a crowd of the desperate. It does, immediately. And Jesus's answer to growing fame is the one Luke keeps recording: he withdraws to desolate places and prays.
verseByVerse.theology:
The touch of the leper is the incarnation in miniature. The Son of God who became flesh did not keep a hygienic distance from the contaminated human condition. He entered it, touched it, took on himself what should have made him unclean, and transferred his own wholeness to the sufferer.

This is what Paul means: “he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Cor. 5:21). The direction of the transaction never varies. He takes what is ours; we receive what is his. The leper's healing is a parable of salvation performed on a real body.

The willingness Jesus expresses — “I will” — is the answer to every theology that doubts the desire of God to save. The leper's “if you will” is the question of everyone who has been told, explicitly or by implication, that God may not want them, that their case may be outside the scope of his grace, that they may be too far gone.

The reply is not merely “I can.” The power was never in question. It is “I will” — the desire, the purpose, the determination to cleanse, as absolute as the power.
verseByVerse.examples:
The leper models the prayer of humility. He falls on his face; he presumes nothing about Jesus's willingness; he makes no claim on his own account — and he comes. The combination of complete certainty about the power (“you can make me clean”) with complete submission about the will (“if you will”) is the posture faith takes before sovereign grace.

It is not the prayer of someone with low expectations. He expects everything. It is the prayer of someone who knows exactly what he is asking and knows he cannot command the answer. He can only ask, and trust the character of the one he asks.

Jesus's withdrawal to desolate places in the middle of growing popularity (v. 16) is the model of spiritual formation under pressure — and it was a habit, not an episode. The more the ministry succeeded by external measures, the more he went away.

The pattern refuses the assumption that fruitfulness makes prayer less necessary. For Jesus, fruitfulness was the reason to pray more, because fruitfulness creates demands that only communion with the Father can carry. The minister who cuts prayer in order to meet ministry demands has confused the cause with the effect.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was in one of the cities, there came a man full of leprosy. And when he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him, 'Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was in one of the cities, there came a man full of leprosy. When he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him: Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.

A man full of leprosy. Only Luke, the physician, says full: an advanced case, covered with it. Not early, not doubtful. Leprosy in the Bible (Hebrew tsara‘at) covers a range of chronic, disfiguring skin diseases, not only what we now call leprosy (Hansen’s disease). Leviticus 13–14 gives the rules. A person with it was ceremonially unclean. He had to wear torn clothes, leave his hair unkempt, cover his upper lip, and cry out, unclean, unclean, to warn people away. He shall live alone; his dwelling shall be outside the camp (Leviticus 13:45–46). No one could touch him without becoming unclean themselves.

A living death. No home, no synagogue, no temple, no work. Nobody has touched him in years: not a handshake, not an embrace at a funeral. He has been required, by the law of God, to announce his own contamination to anyone who came near, and he was not necessarily being punished for anything; the condition simply put him outside. And here he is in one of the cities, where he was not supposed to be, breaking every convention to get to Jesus.

Lord, if you will, you can make me clean. He falls on his face in front of a crowd, in desperate reverence, and prays one of the most exactly worded prayers in the Gospels, and both halves matter. You can is not a request; it is a statement. He has no doubt whatever about the power. He is not asking Jesus to try. If you will is where the uncertainty is, and it is not doubt so much as the absence of any claim. He does not tell Jesus why he deserves this. He does not bargain, or promise, or point to how long he has suffered. He puts the whole thing in the other man’s hands and leaves it there. And clean means not just healed but restored: to God’s people, to worship, to his own family.

The shape of real petition. It is not the prayer of low expectations; he expects everything. But he knows he cannot command it, and can only trust the character of the one he is asking. And underneath it is a fear a good many people carry and few say out loud. Not, is God able? But, is God willing, for someone like me?

Am I God, to make alive? The leper’s you can is a larger confession than he may have known. When Naaman arrived in Samaria asking to be cured, the king of Israel tore his clothes and said, am I God, to kill and to make alive? (2 Kings 5:7). The rabbis later counted the cure of leprosy as hard as raising the dead. Israel had no remedy for it, only a law to diagnose it and a camp to keep it outside. So a man who kneels to Jesus and says, Lord, you can, is ascribing to him what the Old Testament reserves for God. He is right. The one in front of him is the Lord who kills and makes alive, come in person to the place where the law could only say unclean.

Should I add if it is your will to every prayer? It depends on what you are asking. Where God has plainly promised something, such as forgiveness to those who confess (1 John 1:9), wisdom to those who ask (James 1:5), or the Spirit to his children (11:13), you need not pray if you will; he has told you he wills it. Where he has not promised, healing, a job, a spouse, a particular outcome, it is right to ask boldly and add, as Jesus did in Gethsemane, not my will, but yours, be done (22:42). That is not weak faith. It is trust in a Father who knows better than we do.

In a sentence. A man covered in leprosy fell before Jesus, confident that Jesus could make him clean, if he was willing.

On a Tuesday. Never doubt Christ’s power. And bring your request humbly: if you will. If the thing that makes you feel unclean is sin, the shame you hide, the habit you hate, the history you would never tell, bring that too, and do not wait until you feel worthy to come. He is always willing to cleanse those who come to him.

For worship. The man came with his whole life summed up in one word, unclean, and laid it down in front of Jesus with nothing to offer but a question about his will. And the Lord of glory did not turn away. No disease is too advanced for him and no outcast too far outside the camp. He is the one who went outside the camp himself, bearing reproach (Hebrews 13:12–13), so that those who were outside could be brought in. The question the leper asked, is he willing?, has been answered for ever at the cross.
verseByVerse.note: “Leprosy” in the Bible covers a range of skin diseases. A leper had to live apart and was ritually unclean.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, 'I will; be clean.' And immediately the leprosy left him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying: I will; be clean. And immediately the leprosy left him.

And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him. Read that again slowly, because it is the miracle inside the miracle and the most shocking detail in the scene. He did not need to. A word would have been enough; he will heal a centurion’s servant from a different part of town without going near him (7:7). A word from three feet away would have cleansed this man perfectly. Instead the hand goes out, and lands on the one body in Galilee that nobody had been permitted to touch for years. This man may not have felt a human touch since the day the priest declared him unclean.

Holiness is contagious in him. Under the law, touching a leper made a person unclean. The contamination ran in one direction, and everyone knew which. What happens here reverses it. Jesus is not defiled by the leper; the leper is cleansed by Jesus. The uncleanness did not pass to Jesus; the cleanness passed to the leper. The holiness is the stronger thing, and it moves outward. Here is the incarnation in a single gesture, and it is what Paul means: for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). The direction of the transaction never changes. He takes what is ours; we receive what is his.

I will; be clean. The answer to his question. Two words in Greek (thelō, katharisthēti), and they answer the exact thing the man was unsure of. He had not questioned the power; you can make me clean was said as settled fact. What he did not know was the will. And Jesus replies to precisely that, and to nothing else. Not, I can. The power was never in question. I will: the desire, the readiness, the glad determination to make this man clean. His will and his power are one.

And immediately the leprosy left him. Not gradually. Complete, instant cleansing: skin that had been diseased for years made whole in a moment. A sign that the Messiah had come: the lepers are cleansed (7:22).

A picture of salvation. Sin is like leprosy: it defiles, isolates, spreads and kills, and no human remedy can cure it. A whole life of exclusion had taught this man to expect a no, or at best a reluctant and distant maybe. What he got was a hand on the skin nobody would touch, and a word with not a hair’s breadth of hesitation in it.

Does I will mean that God always wills to heal every sick person who asks in faith? No. This healing was a sign that the kingdom had come in Jesus. Paul asked three times for his thorn to be removed, and was told, my grace is sufficient for you (2 Corinthians 12:9). Every prayer for healing is rightly prayed as the leper prayed, if you will.

What does it mean for me that Jesus touched the leper? It means there is nothing about you that makes him recoil. People who carry deep shame, from abuse suffered, from sin committed, from a body or a mind that does not work as it should, often feel untouchable, as if God would keep his distance if he really knew. This verse says otherwise. He comes nearest to what we hide. Bring him the thing you are most ashamed of, by name, in prayer; and if you can, tell a mature Christian, so that you hear his welcome spoken aloud. And then become his hand to others: notice who in your church or street is untouched, and go near.

In a sentence. Jesus reached out and touched the leper, saying he was willing, and commanded him to be clean, and the leprosy left him at once.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person in your circle whom others keep at a distance: the one with a contagious reputation, the awkward relative, the elderly neighbour who smells of neglect, the colleague everyone avoids after the scandal. Jesus could have healed from a distance and did not. Go near this week. A visit, a meal, a hand on the shoulder can say what words cannot.

For worship. For years no one had touched him, and the first hand to rest on his skin again was the hand that had made it. The Lord did not hold out a word at arm’s length and keep himself clean; he reached into the uncleanness, and it was the uncleanness that gave way. No reluctance, no weighing whether the case qualified, no recoil: only, I will. He has never once looked at someone who came to him and wished he had not been asked. And the will that went out to the leper is the same will that held him to the cross, where the clean one was numbered with the transgressors so that the unclean could be clean for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: And he charged him to tell no one, but 'go and show yourself to the priest, and make an offering for your cleansing, as Moses commanded, for a proof to them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He charged him to tell no one, but: go and show yourself to the priest, and make an offering for your cleansing, as Moses commanded, for a proof to them.

Two instructions that seem to cancel each other. Tell no one, and go and show yourself to the priest. They do not cancel. The second is a legal procedure, not a publicity campaign, and it is the thing the man most needs.

He charged him to tell no one. It is a restraint Jesus imposes repeatedly in Galilee, and the next verse shows why it was needed. Jesus did not want to be known mainly as a miracle worker. A reputation as a healer would bury the preaching under a crowd of the desperate, which is exactly what happens anyway (v. 15). He came to announce a kingdom, and the miracles were the announcement made visible, not a service he had come to provide.

Go and show yourself to the priest. Leviticus 14 lays down the ritual by which a healed leper is examined, declared clean and restored: the priest inspects him outside the camp; two birds are taken, one killed over fresh water, and the other, dipped in its blood, released alive into the open field; there is a week’s wait; and on the eighth day there are offerings, and the man is pronounced clean and may go home. Without that certificate, a healed man is still, in every practical sense, a leper. He cannot re-enter the town, or the synagogue, or his own family’s house. So Jesus heals the disease in a second and then sends the man through a week-long process to heal everything else the disease had done to him. He could have declared him clean on the spot with more authority than any priest in Israel; he sends him to the priest anyway, because the man needs to be received back by his community, and there is an appointed way for that to happen. Grace does not despise process: he could have skipped every step, and he walks the man through all of them.

The shadow and the substance. The law could examine a leper and pronounce him clean; it could never make him clean. The priest had a procedure for a healing he could not give. Jesus gives the healing, and then sends the man to the procedure, the shadow bowing to the substance it had been drawn from (Hebrews 10:1). The birds and lambs of Leviticus 14 could only declare a cleansing that had already happened. The sacrifice Jesus would offer does more: by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14).

For a proof to them. That phrase carries an edge. It is a testimony to the priests, and to the people, that he was truly clean. And since leprosy was rarely if ever cured, it was a testimony that the Messiah had come. If the man did as he was told, a priest had to examine someone who had been full of leprosy and declare him clean. The establishment that would shortly decide Jesus was a blasphemer had been handed, by its own procedure, a public proof of what he could do.

Why did Jesus tell people to keep quiet, when we are told to tell everyone? Because the moment was different. Before the cross, a reputation as a wonder worker would have drawn crowds who wanted miracles and a political Messiah, and would have obscured what he came to do. After the resurrection, when his identity and his saving work were complete, the command was the opposite: go and make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19). The silences of the Gospels are temporary. Now the whole story can be told, and must be.

In a sentence. Jesus told the man not to spread the news, but to go to the priest and offer the sacrifice Moses commanded, as proof of his cleansing.

On a Tuesday. Jesus respected the proper process and authorities. Follow through on what God requires, even after a great blessing. Where it applies: a person converted from a life of fraud still needs to pay back what he took and face the consequences honestly; a believer restored after a fall still needs the patient process of rebuilding trust with the church and family. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: this is not a call to add human rituals to the gospel or to make people jump through hoops before they can be welcomed to Christ. The cleansing is his gift, complete; the process is for restoring the life around it.

For worship. The Lord who healed in a moment cared about the week that followed. He sent the man home by the proper road, so that his family could have him back and his town could receive him. There is no part of our restoration he forgets. He cleanses the heart in an instant, and then patiently walks us back into every relationship that sin had broken. And the priest who certified the leper clean had no idea that the true High Priest had already done it, with a touch.

verseByVerse.quote: But now even more the report about him went abroad, and great crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed of their infirmities. But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now even more the report about him went abroad, and great crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed of their infirmities. But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray.

Even more the report about him went abroad. The instruction to keep quiet has failed, as such instructions generally do. Mark tells us the man disobeyed and spread the news everywhere (Mark 1:45).

Great crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed of their infirmities. Note the order: to hear first. Both, in that order, and Luke does not sneer at them. They want the word and they want their bodies mended, which is a perfectly reasonable pair of things to want.

But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray. Two sentences, set deliberately side by side, and the but between them is the whole point. Luke’s wording is worth having: he would withdraw. The tense means it was his habit: he kept on withdrawing. This was not a single retreat but a pattern. Again and again, the busier it got, the more he went away. Only Luke records this here. He goes back to the empty country on purpose. There is nothing there. That is what it is for.

It inverts the usual assumption. The natural reading of a growing ministry is that prayer becomes a luxury one can no longer afford. Jesus does the opposite. As the crowds increase, so does the withdrawal. He treats fruitfulness as a reason to pray more, not less. If the Son of God needed to pray, how much more do we.

The danger of crowds. A large and admiring crowd is not a neutral thing to stand in front of. It is one of the most dangerous places a person can be, and the pressure it exerts, to be what they want, to keep producing, to believe their estimate of you, is not resisted by good intentions. He met it by leaving. The crowd offered what the human heart craves, to be needed and admired, and he would not let it become his master. He took his sense of who he was from his Father’s voice, you are my beloved Son (3:22), not from theirs, and that is the only place where anyone is safe from the crowd.

Why did the Son of God need to pray? Because he was truly man, living in dependence on his Father, and because prayer is the communion of the Son with the Father, not a sign of lack. Hebrews says he offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears (Hebrews 5:7). He did not pray because something was missing in him as God. As a true man he lived each day by trusting his Father, and he showed us what a human life lived wholly towards God looks like.

I am too busy to pray much. What do I do? Begin by being honest that busyness is the reason to pray more, not the excuse to pray less. Then be practical. Choose a fixed time, even fifteen minutes, before the day’s demands begin, and guard it as you would a meeting with your employer. Find a place, as he did: a room, a car parked before work, a walk. Use Scripture to guide your prayers, a psalm or the Lord’s Prayer, so that you are not left staring at a blank wall. And pray in the gaps, briefly and often, through the day (1 Thessalonians 5:17). Small, regular prayer will do more than occasional heroic efforts.

In a sentence. As his fame spread and crowds came to hear him and be healed, Jesus regularly withdrew to lonely places to pray.

On a Tuesday. There is a plain diagnostic here for anyone, and especially anyone in Christian work, and it is uncomfortable. If prayer is the thing that gets cut when the demands rise, the demands are being served and the life is being hollowed out, because what the crowds actually needed from Jesus came out of the desolate places, and he never once let them have it on any other terms. When life is busiest, you most need to pray. Look at this week’s diary and put the time for prayer in first.

For worship. The one through whom all things were made went out alone into the empty places to speak with his Father. He lived on prayer. And the Son who prayed in the desolate places then still prays now: he always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). When the crowds pressed him, he went to the Father; when the pressure of our lives presses us, he is already there before the Father for us, and he has never once grown too busy to pray for his own.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
This is the first confrontation between Jesus and the religious authorities in Luke, and it is carefully staged. Pharisees and teachers of the law have come from every village of Galilee, and from Judea, and from Jerusalem — a gathering with the shape of an inspection. They are seated. And Luke notes, before anything happens, that the power of the Lord was with Jesus to heal.

Meanwhile four men are carrying a paralysed friend, and the crowd has made the door impassable. So they go up on the roof, take it apart, and lower the man on his mat into the middle of the room, through the ceiling, in front of everyone. It is rude, destructive and entirely out of order — and Luke calls it faith.

The faith Jesus sees is not the paralysed man's alone. It is “their” faith: the faith of friends who refused to be stopped. The man himself says nothing in the entire passage. His only contribution is to lie there and be carried, and everything that follows happens because other people would not leave him outside.

What Jesus then says is not what anyone came for: “Man, your sins are forgiven you.” Not “rise and walk.” The physical healing is four verses away; forgiveness comes first.

The scribes and Pharisees recognise the claim at once: “Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?” Their theology is entirely correct — only God can forgive sins against God. Their reasoning is impeccable and their conclusion is upside down. They have the premise right and the observation right, and instead of following the argument where it leads, they reach for blasphemy.

Jesus's challenge is pedagogical. “Which is easier, to say 'Your sins are forgiven you,' or to say 'Rise and walk'?” It is easier to say the first, because nothing visible follows and nobody can check. The second is the dangerous sentence. So he does the checkable one — as the credential for the claim that cannot be checked: “that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins.”

The miracles are never the message in this Gospel. They are the authentication of it.

And the man rises, picks up the mat he has spent his life lying on, walks out through the crowd, and goes home glorifying God — leaving a room full of people, dignitaries included, filled with awe and saying, “We have seen extraordinary things today.”
verseByVerse.theology:
Forgiveness before healing establishes the priority of Luke's whole Gospel: the deepest human need is not physical. The paralysis is real, the suffering is real, the exclusion from ordinary life is real — and Jesus removes all of it. But he deals first with something that would still have been wrong after the legs worked.

This is not a denigration of physical suffering, and it is emphatically not a suggestion that the paralysis was caused by the man's sin; Jesus explicitly rejects that reasoning elsewhere (John 9:3). It is a statement about what finally matters — the standing before God that sin destroys.

The scribes' objection is the most important theological sentence in the passage, and Jesus does not answer it by denial. He never says they are wrong about the exclusive divine prerogative. He acts on it, and offers the visible miracle as the proof.

“Son of Man” sounds modest in English and is not. It is Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man comes to the Ancient of Days and receives dominion, glory, and a kingdom that all peoples shall serve. In a room full of men who knew Daniel, that title while forgiving sins was the claim doubled — and “on earth” presses it further still. The authority is here, at ground level, exercised by a man they can see.
verseByVerse.examples:
The four friends are the model of intercessory persistence. They could not bring their friend by the normal route, so they found another. They could not get through the door, so they went through the roof. Their determination is not disrespect for the gathering; it is the overflow of confidence that Jesus can and will do what they believe he can.

This is what intercession looks like when it becomes serious: not eloquence, not technique, but the refusal to accept that the door is the only way, and a willingness to look foolish on somebody else's behalf.

“When he saw their faith” — the faith Jesus responds to is the faith of the group. That is a significant detail for understanding how the church actually works. The person who cannot bring themselves to pray, whose faith is exhausted or paralysed by their suffering, can be carried to Jesus by the faith of those around them.

People do get carried. There are seasons — grief, depression, shame, sheer exhaustion — when a believer will not get themselves into the room, and somebody else has to do the carrying. This passage says the carrying counts.

verseByVerse.quote: On one of those days, as he was teaching, Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem. And the power of the Lord was with him to heal. And behold, some men were bringing on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they were seeking to bring him in and lay him before Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
On one of those days, as he was teaching, Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem. The power of the Lord was with him to heal. And behold, some men were bringing on a bed a man who was paralysed, and they were trying to bring him in and lay him before Jesus.

Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there. The religious authorities appear in Luke’s narrative for the first time, and they are sitting down. Teachers of the law were the same as the scribes (v. 21), experts in the law of Moses. They have come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem: word has reached the capital, and the gathering has the shape of an inspection. They are seated, in the places of honour, while everyone else stands pressed in, and they are watching. The conflict that will run through the Gospel begins here.

In the flow. This is the first of five scenes in a row (5:17–6:11) in which Jesus’ authority meets the religious leaders: over sin, over the company he keeps, over fasting, and twice over the Sabbath. Each time the question underneath is the same, who is this?, and each time the opposition hardens, until the scribes and Pharisees are discussing what they might do to Jesus (6:11). The leper was told to keep quiet about his cleansing; this healing is done in front of the nation’s experts, and it opens the case that Luke will follow all the way to the cross.

Who were the Pharisees? A movement of devout laymen, perhaps six thousand strong at this time, who were zealous to keep the law of Moses in every detail of daily life, and who added a large body of oral tradition to guard it. They tithed even their herbs, fasted twice a week, and kept strict rules about purity, food and the Sabbath. Ordinary people respected them as the most serious believers in Israel. Their fault was not that they cared about God’s law, which was good, but that they trusted in their own keeping of it and looked down on others (18:9). Paul had been one (Philippians 3:5), and some came to faith (Acts 15:5).

And the power of the Lord was with him to heal. Luke adds a sentence that has no obvious grammatical business being there. He states it before anything happens, like a stage direction. The Lord here means God. Jesus’ healing power was the power of God, by the Spirit (4:14), and Luke has already given the reason: in Nazareth Jesus read, the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me, and said it was fulfilled in him (4:18, 21). Here is the Anointed One at work. The room is full of the men who decide what may be believed in Israel, the experts on what the Messiah would be, and the power of God is resting on the man they have come to examine, and not on them.

Some men were bringing on a bed a man who was paralysed. Luke’s and behold is the narrator turning the reader’s head. Outside, while the inspection proceeds, men are carrying a friend on a mat; Mark says four (Mark 2:3). A man who could not come himself, carried by friends. Consider what that took: somebody had to notice him and decide it was worth a day; four men had to carry a paralysed body through the streets on a pallet, slowly and in public; and at the end of the journey, a house so full that there was no way in.

They were seeking to bring him in and lay him before Jesus. They had one aim: to get him to Jesus. Luke says they were seeking: they kept trying. They did not arrive, see the crowd, and go home. They worked at it. The man on the mat has not said a word and will not say one in the whole passage. Everything that is about to happen to him happens because other people would not give up on getting him in front of Jesus.

How do I carry someone to Jesus today? First, in prayer: name them before God, regularly and specifically, for years if need be. Then in friendship: time, practical help, meals, lifts, honest conversation. Bring them where Jesus is spoken of, to church, to a Bible study, to a Christian friend who can answer their questions, and when the moment comes, tell them plainly about him yourself. Carry them together with others, as these four did; it is too heavy a load for one person. And remember that your task is to bring them, not to heal them. That is his part.

In a sentence. As Jesus taught, with Pharisees and teachers of the law from all over the land watching, some men tried to bring a paralysed friend to him on a mat.

On a Tuesday. Some people cannot come to Jesus on their own. Who can you carry to him in prayer and in friendship? Write down the names of two people this week, find one other Christian to pray for them with you, and do one practical kindness for each.

For worship. The power of the Lord was present to heal, and it was not in the honoured seats but in the one who sat among the crowd. The real authority in Israel was a carpenter from Nazareth, teaching in a borrowed house. He does not need the approval of the important to do his work, and he does not overlook the ones who must be carried. The great of the land came to inspect him; the helpless were brought to be healed by him; and he received them both into a room where God was at work.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers of the law were the same as the scribes, experts in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: but finding no way to bring him in, because of the crowd, they went up on the roof and let him down with his bed through the tiles into the midst before Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finding no way to bring him in because of the crowd, they went up on the roof and let him down with his bed through the tiles into the midst, before Jesus.

Finding no way to bring him in, because of the crowd. The crowd was an obstacle, as crowds often are to those who need Jesus most (18:39; 19:3).

They went up on the roof. Houses in Palestine had flat roofs, reached by an outside staircase or ladder. Stop and picture the actual logistics, because familiarity has made this scene charming, and it was not charming. An outside stair, four men, and a stretcher with a grown man on it. Then a roof, over a room that is at that moment packed with people, including religious dignitaries from Galilee to Jerusalem. And they begin taking it apart.

And let him down with his bed through the tiles. Dust and debris come down on the heads of the seated Pharisees, and somebody’s property is being damaged with no evidence that anybody asked the owner. It is rude, destructive and entirely out of order, and Luke, in the next verse, calls it faith. The four men did not have better theology than the men in the room; they had a friend they refused to leave outside. They could not get to Jesus by the obvious route, so they made a new one. The obstacle sent them upward.

Tiles or clay? One small detail draws the charge that Luke did not know Palestine. Mark says the men dug through the roof (Mark 2:4), which fits an ordinary Galilean house of beams, branches and packed clay; Luke says through the tiles. But tiled roofs were the normal Greek and Roman construction and had appeared in the towns of the region, and in any case Luke is writing for readers across the empire, who would picture a roof the moment he named its material. He is translating the scene into terms they could picture. Two witnesses describing the same hole from different sides of the Mediterranean is not a contradiction. Either way, they made a hole in someone’s roof.

Into the midst before Jesus. Every effort in the scene ends at one spot: in front of Jesus. Not in front of the teachers of the law from Jerusalem, who had the seats and the learning and no power to heal. Luke’s whole Gospel keeps moving the helpless to that same place: a sinful woman at his feet (7:38), a Samaritan leper at his feet (17:16), a dying thief beside him (23:42). Faith is not particular about the route; it is certain about the destination, because there is no one else to bring a paralysed man to. Peter will say it in Jerusalem: there is salvation in no one else (Acts 4:12).

The man who could do nothing. The man they lowered could do nothing at all. He could not walk to Jesus, could not push through a crowd, could not climb a stair. His entire contribution was to lie there. Whatever faith he had, Luke does not mention it separately; he says Jesus saw their faith, and the man’s part in the sentence is as the thing being carried. There is a whole doctrine of the church in that. People do get carried. There are seasons when a believer cannot pray, cannot come, cannot generate any momentum whatever, through grief, depression, exhaustion or shame, and the honest truth is that they will not get themselves into the room. Somebody else has to do the carrying, and the carrying counts.

I am the one who cannot pray right now. Am I failing? No. There are seasons of illness, grief and darkness when a Christian can hardly pray at all, and Scripture does not condemn him for it. The Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26), Christ intercedes for us at the Father’s right hand (Romans 8:34), and God gives brothers and sisters to carry us. Let them. Tell one or two trusted friends that you are struggling and ask them to pray for you. Keep coming to church if you can, even if you only sit there. You are not less a Christian because you are on the mat for now.

In a sentence. Unable to get through the crowd, they climbed onto the roof, removed the tiles and lowered the man on his mat right in front of Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Do not let obstacles stop you bringing people to Jesus. Be persistent and creative in love. Where it applies: when the friend you invited to church says no for the third time, try a meal at home; when a relative will not talk about faith, keep praying and keep loving; when a sick church member cannot come, take the service to them. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: creative love is not a licence to manipulate people, to trick them into a meeting, or to pressure them until they give in. The men broke a roof, not a person’s will. Bring people to Jesus; do not drag them.

For worship. Four men broke open a roof to bring their friend down to Jesus; he had broken open heaven to come down to us. He came by a lower road than any outside stair, into a crowded and hostile world, to lie where the helpless lie: in a manger, among the sick, at last in a borrowed tomb. We were the man on the mat, unable to move one muscle towards him, and he is the friend who would not leave us outside. Every rescue that ever ended at his feet began with his own descent.
verseByVerse.note: Luke speaks of tiles, the roofing his Greek readers knew; Mark describes digging through a roof of packed earth.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he saw their faith, he said, 'Man, your sins are forgiven you.' And the scribes and the Pharisees began to question, saying, 'Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he saw their faith, he said: man, your sins are forgiven you. And the scribes and the Pharisees began to question, saying: who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?

And when he saw their faith. Faith he could see, because it acted: a hole in the roof is faith made visible. The faith of the friends, and presumably of the man too. Jesus honours faith that brings others to him. Our faith and prayers can matter for others.

Man, your sins are forgiven you. Nobody in that room expected that sentence. Four men have gone to enormous trouble for one thing, and the whole audience is waiting for it. And Jesus looks at a paralysed man lowered through a hole in somebody’s ceiling and deals with his sins. He will heal the paralysis; it is four verses away. But he does the other thing first, and the order is deliberate. Jesus deals first with the deeper problem. The perfect tense means: your sins have been forgiven, and stand forgiven.

Was the man’s paralysis caused by his sin? Not necessarily, and the passage must be handled carefully because it can be heard cruelly. Jesus is not saying the paralysis does not matter; he removes it. He is not suggesting it was caused by the man’s sin; he says nothing of the kind here. Some Jews believed sickness was always caused by sin. Sometimes it is (John 5:14), though not always, and Jesus explicitly denies that reasoning about the man born blind (John 9:2–3). What he is doing is treating the deeper condition first, in a man who had not come about it and may not have known he had it. If you are ill, do not assume God is punishing you for something. All sickness belongs to a fallen world; your particular illness may have no link to any particular sin at all.

The deeper need. That is a hard word and a merciful one. A man who is healed and unforgiven has been given a working body and a few more decades, and the account is still open. The greatest need of every person is forgiveness. What does that actually mean? To be forgiven by God is to have the debt your sins have run up against him cancelled, not hidden. He does not bring it up again, now or at the judgement: as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us (Psalm 103:12).

Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Blasphemy is speaking against God, or claiming what belongs to him alone. The penalty was death by stoning (Leviticus 24:16). And notice where the charge is made: inwardly. They began to question, Luke says; they had not yet spoken it aloud (v. 22).

Who can forgive sins but God alone? Now this is important: their theology is correct. Entirely correct. All sin is ultimately against God (Psalm 51:4). A person can forgive a wrong done to himself, but only God can forgive sins against God. That is not a Pharisaic invention; it is the plain teaching of the Old Testament: I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake (Isaiah 43:25). Any faithful Jew in that room would have said the same. Their reasoning is impeccable and their conclusion is upside down. They have the major premise right: only God forgives sins. They have the observation right: this man has just forgiven sins. And instead of following the argument where it leads, they reach for blasphemy. If Jesus is not God, he is a blasphemer. He is not a blasphemer, because he is God. All through Luke, the people who reject Jesus are rarely those who understand him least; they are usually those who have grasped exactly what he is claiming.

Can someone else’s faith save a person? No. Luke does not say the paralysed man lacked faith, and the friends’ faith brought him to Jesus, which is what faith on behalf of others can do. We may carry others to Christ in prayer and witness, but each person must come to him in his own faith.

In a sentence. Seeing their faith, Jesus told the paralysed man his sins were forgiven, and the scribes and Pharisees thought this blasphemy, since only God can forgive sins.

On a Tuesday. Ask what you most want from God this week. If it is all about circumstances, health, money, a relationship mended, bring it to him; he cares. But ask also whether you have come to him for the deeper thing. Hear the word Jesus spoke to that man as spoken to everyone who trusts him: your sins are forgiven. And if someone has asked you to forgive them, remember that forgiving is the most God-like thing a person can do.

For worship. Only God can forgive sins, and Jesus does. The scribes were right about God and wrong about the man in front of them: the God who blots out transgressions for his own sake had come to Capernaum in human flesh, and spoke his pardon to a paralysed man on a mat. He did not ask for sacrifices; he was about to become the sacrifice. He spoke the pardon to a man who had not asked for it, and it stood. No one else in the universe has the right to say it, and he says it gladly.
verseByVerse.note: Blasphemy is speaking against God or claiming what belongs to him alone.

parallels.desc: I am he who blots out your transgressions

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answered them, 'Why do you question in your hearts? Which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins'—he said to the man who was paralyzed—'I say to you, rise, pick up your bed and go home.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answered them: why do you question in your hearts? Which is easier, to say, your sins are forgiven you, or to say, rise and walk? But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins (he said to the man who was paralysed), I say to you, rise, pick up your bed and go home.

When Jesus perceived their thoughts. They had not spoken. Luke says they began to question, inwardly, and Jesus answers the argument going on inside their heads, which is itself a demonstration of something only God does. Only God knows the heart (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10). Another sign of who he is.

Which is easier, to say, Your sins are forgiven you, or to say, Rise and walk? The question is sharper than it looks, and the answer is not the obvious one. Which is easier to say? Plainly the first. Anyone can announce that a man’s sins are forgiven, because nothing visible follows and nobody can check. Saying rise and walk to a paralysed man is the dangerous sentence: in three seconds everyone in the room will know whether it worked. In another sense, forgiveness is far harder, because it is a divine act, and would cost Jesus his life. Jesus will now do the visible, harder-to-say thing, to prove the invisible one.

That you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins. So Jesus does the checkable one, and he says exactly why. The healing is not the point. The healing is the evidence for the claim that cannot be verified: a visible miracle offered as the credential for an invisible one. That is the logic of miracle throughout the Gospels. The miracles are never the message. They are the authentication of the message. A Jesus who heals bodies and cannot deal with guilt would be a remarkable physician and no use at all at the end.

The Son of Man. This is Jesus’ favourite way of referring to himself, and the first time Luke uses it. It sounds modest in English; a son of man is just a human being. It was not modest. He is drawing on Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days and is given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations and languages should serve him, an everlasting dominion. In a room full of men who knew Daniel, choosing that title while forgiving sins was not a retreat from the claim. It was the claim, doubled.

On earth. Note the two small words in the middle. Everyone in that room believed sins were forgiven in heaven, by God, at the appointed time and through the appointed sacrifices. Jesus says the authority is here, at ground level, in a crowded house in Capernaum, exercised by a man they can see. God forgives from heaven; Jesus forgives on earth, as God in human flesh. Which means that the thing the whole temple system existed to deal with has walked into a room and dealt with it, in one sentence, freely, for a man who did not ask.

Rise, pick up your bed and go home. Three commands, impossible for a paralysed man. The word of Jesus gives the power to obey. As Augustine prayed, give what you command, and command what you will.

How can I know my sins are really forgiven, when I cannot see it? By the same logic Jesus used here. You cannot see forgiveness, but you can see the one who grants it, and he has given you evidence enough: his miracles, his death, and above all his resurrection, by which God declared his sacrifice accepted (Romans 4:25). Your forgiveness does not rest on your feelings, which rise and fall, but on his word: everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name (Acts 10:43). If you have come to him trusting him, you are forgiven, as surely as that man walked. Feelings of guilt may linger; take them to his promise, not his promise to your feelings.

In a sentence. Knowing their thoughts, Jesus healed the paralysed man before their eyes, so that they would know that he, the Son of Man, has authority on earth to forgive sins.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ visible works prove his invisible authority. If he can heal, he can forgive. Trust him for both. When an old sin comes back to accuse you this week, answer it the way Jesus answered the scribes: point to what he has done. The risen Christ is the proof that the debt is paid.

For worship. The Son of Man from Daniel’s vision, the one who rides the clouds of heaven and receives an everlasting kingdom, stood in a crowded room on earth and forgave a paralysed man. The King of all peoples bent down to a single mat. He read the hearts of his critics and answered their silent objections, and then he gave them proof they could see. And the forgiveness he spoke so easily that day was not cheap: it would be paid for at the cross. There is authority on earth to forgive sins, and it is in his hands.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Man” is Jesus’ favourite title for himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately he rose up before them and picked up what he had been lying on and went home, glorifying God. And amazement seized them all, and they glorified God and were filled with awe, saying, 'We have seen extraordinary things today.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately he rose up before them, picked up what he had been lying on, and went home, glorifying God. Amazement seized them all, and they glorified God and were filled with awe, saying: we have seen extraordinary things today.

And immediately he rose up before them, and picked up what he had been lying on. In front of everyone, including the sceptics. Luke lingers on the bed. The phrasing draws attention to it. That mat was the whole visible history of his life: what he was carried on, what he lay on, the thing other people had to lift. He walks out with it under his arm. The bed that had carried him, he now carried. And he walks out through the crowd: through the doorway they could not get him in by, past the seated dignitaries, into a street where everyone knew him. Whatever else that town discussed that week, it discussed this.

And went home, glorifying God. Only Luke records his praise. Forgiven and healed. And the man went home. That is where Jesus sent him: not into the travelling company, not into public ministry. Go home. There was a house somewhere in Capernaum where a family had been carrying this man for years, and that evening he walked in on his own feet, carrying the mat.

And amazement seized them all, and they glorified God. Amazement (ekstasis) is being beside oneself. Luke says it of the man, and then immediately of the crowd: they glorified God and were filled with awe. Not with admiration of a technique. With awe. All of them, which in that room includes the delegation from Jerusalem.

We have seen extraordinary things today. Extraordinary (paradoxa), from which comes paradox: things contrary to expectation, things that overturn the settled order. Today is Luke’s word again (4:21). And the thing most contrary to expectation was not finally the walking man. It was that God’s own prerogative had been exercised, out loud, by a man on earth. The paradox would deepen. The one with authority to forgive would be counted a blasphemer, crucified and raised on the third day, so that forgiveness of sins would be proclaimed in his name to all nations (24:46–47). The crowd saw the first page of it.

Amazed and unchanged. They are not converted. Luke does not say they believed; he says they were amazed and afraid, and by chapter 6 the scribes and Pharisees among them will be watching him to accuse him (6:7). It is entirely possible to witness the undeniable, glorify God out loud, and go home unchanged. Amazement is not faith. The man who went home with the mat had been forgiven; the men who went home with an anecdote had only been impressed.

In a sentence. The man got up at once, carried his mat home praising God, and everyone was amazed and glorified God, saying they had seen incredible things.

On a Tuesday. Do not settle for being impressed by Jesus. Many people admire him, as the crowd did, and go home unchanged. Ask whether what you have seen of him has reached you: whether you are carrying your mat home as a forgiven sinner. And then tell your household, as that man surely did, what God has done.

For worship. The man who had been carried in walked out carrying, and went home glorifying God, which is exactly where the Son of Man wanted the praise to go: every work he did turned eyes to his Father, and the Father was glorified in the Son. The four friends came for a pair of working legs and went home with a forgiven friend. And that street in Capernaum, loud with praise, is a foretaste of the morning when the lame will leap like a deer (Isaiah 35:6), every mat will be rolled up for the last time, and the whole forgiven company will glorify God for what the Son of Man has done.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
From the crowded house Luke moves straight to one of the most understated calls in the Gospel. Jesus sees Levi at his tax booth and says “Follow me.” And Levi left everything and followed him.

The form is identical to the call of Peter, James and John (v. 11) — an encounter, a bare imperative, and complete abandonment. But Levi's “everything” carries a different weight. Tax collectors in the Roman system had purchased the franchise; leaving the booth meant writing off a substantial investment with no prospect of return, and no possibility of going back. The fishermen could have returned to fishing. Levi could not return to a tax booth.

He was also, by the reckoning of every devout person who walked past him, beyond the pale: a collaborator with Rome, a legally protected extortioner, ritually unclean, inadmissible as a witness. Jesus called him without an assessment, a probation, or an interview.

Levi's first act as a disciple is to throw a great banquet and fill it with the only people he knows — a large company of tax collectors and others. He has no theology and no method. He has a house and a contact list, and he puts Jesus in the middle of them.

The Pharisees and their scribes complain, and they complain to the disciples rather than to Jesus: “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” The objection is not mere snobbery. Table fellowship in that world was a public declaration of acceptance and solidarity — closer to a signed statement than a meal — so this is a serious question about the boundaries of the people of God.

Jesus's answer is the programmatic statement of the whole ministry: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.”

The word “righteous” is ironic. Everyone in that house is sick; the difference between the two groups is entirely in what they know about themselves. A man who does not believe he is ill will not send for a doctor, however available the doctor makes himself. And the last two words are not decoration — he called sinners to repentance. The table at Levi's house is a doctor's visit, and doctors do not visit in order to agree with the disease.
verseByVerse.theology:
The call of Levi is Luke's announcement that the kingdom of God comes to the most unexpected people. Matthew's Gospel tells us this is Matthew himself (Matt. 9:9). The author of one of the four Gospels is a man whom the respectable religious society of his day considered beyond the reach of God's grace.

And of the four apostle lists in the New Testament, the only one that attaches “the tax collector” to his name is the one he wrote (Matt. 10:3). He never got over it.

“I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance” is not a statement about two classes of people — the righteous who do not need Jesus and the sinners who do. Scripture is unambiguous that there are no righteous: “none is righteous, no, not one” (Rom. 3:10).

It is a statement about two self-perceptions. The “righteous” are the self-righteous, whose assessment of their own spiritual condition is so favourable that they see no need of a physician. The tragedy of the Pharisees is not their theology, most of which was sound. It is their self-knowledge. They could not be called to repentance because they did not believe they needed to repent.
verseByVerse.examples:
Levi's banquet is the instinctive evangelism of someone who has just received grace and immediately wants the people he loves to meet the one who gave it. No training, no method, no strategy — he invites his friends to his house and invites Jesus to the same room.

The criticism this drew is the criticism grace-shaped evangelism has always drawn: it happens in the wrong places, with the wrong people, without sufficient concern for the reputation of those involved. Jesus's presence at that table is the answer to every objection of the kind.

“Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” is the perennial complaint of those who would like the church to be more selective in its welcome. The instinct to keep the table clean — to eat only with the already acceptable — is deeply human, and it rests on a real principle: that holiness is preserved by separation.

What it has not reckoned with is a holiness that works the other way round, which the same chapter has already shown at a leper's skin. Jesus's table is where the sick come for medicine, not where the well gather to congratulate each other on their health.

verseByVerse.quote: After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the tax booth. And he said to him, 'Follow me.' And leaving everything, he rose and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the tax booth. He said to him: follow me. And leaving everything, he rose and followed him.

A tax collector named Levi. Matthew’s Gospel calls him Matthew (Matthew 9:9); he had both names, as Simon was also Peter and Saul was also Paul. Levi probably collected tolls for Herod Antipas on goods passing along the trade route through Capernaum.

Sitting at the tax booth. At work, in the place of his sin. Capernaum sat on a trade route near a border, and the booth taxed goods in transit. The man in it collected for whoever held the contract, and kept whatever else he could extract. That was not an incidental abuse of the job; it was how the job worked. So Levi is three things at once to everyone walking past: a collaborator with the hated regime, a thief with legal protection, and ritually unclean from constant contact with Gentiles. Tax collectors were not accepted as witnesses in Jewish courts. He would not have been received in a synagogue in any meaningful way. And he was very probably rich.

Follow me. Two words in Greek, and no preliminaries whatever. Jesus walks past his table and calls him with the same bare command he used on the fishermen: no assessment, no probation, no interview. Nothing in Levi’s life made the call reasonable; the call made Levi. It is the voice that had just said rise to a paralysed man (v. 24), and it works the same way: the command carries the power to obey it. Levi does not rise because he has weighed an offer. He rises because the Son of Man, who has authority on earth to forgive sins, has chosen to spend it on him, in public, at the booth. The Pharisees had complained about forgiveness; now Jesus makes a tax collector a disciple.

And leaving everything, he rose and followed him. Luke uses the same phrase he used at verse 11, and for Levi it costs differently. The fishermen left boats and nets; boats and nets are still there tomorrow, and a man can go back to fishing, which several of them eventually did for a night (John 21:3).
