Levi leaves a lucrative post. There is no going back to a tax booth once you have walked away from one; someone else will be sitting in it soon enough. He gave up a lucrative career for good. He is burning the only asset he has, and he does it standing up. Money had been Levi’s security, and his compensation for everyone’s contempt. When Christ called, it lost its grip in a moment, because something greater had taken its place. That is how idols usually fall: not by being argued down, but by being outshone.

The man who wrote it down. Luke does not tell you this, and Matthew does. When the First Gospel reaches this same scene it names him Matthew (Matthew 9:9), and when it lists the twelve apostles it calls him Matthew the tax collector (Matthew 10:3), a description none of the other lists bothers to add. The man rising from that booth is the man the church has long believed wrote the Gospel that opens the New Testament, and the only apostle list that pins tax collector to his name is the one in the book bearing his name, as though he never got over it.

What did Levi do about the money he had taken? Luke does not tell us, but Zacchaeus, another tax collector, shows what repentance looked like for such a man: he gave half his goods to the poor and repaid anyone he had defrauded fourfold (19:8). Following Christ does not wipe out our obligations to people we have wronged. Grace forgives the sin before God freely and completely; it also makes us want to put right what we can. If you have cheated someone, the gospel does not ask you to earn forgiveness by repaying, but it will lead you, gladly, to repay.

In a sentence. Jesus called Levi, a despised tax collector, from his booth to follow him, and Levi left everything and followed.

On a Tuesday. No one is beyond Christ’s call. He calls people from the middle of their sin, and he calls you to leave whatever holds you. Think of the person you consider least likely to become a Christian, the cynical colleague, the relative in a crooked business, the neighbour who mocks faith. Levi was that man in Capernaum. Pray for them this week as for a future disciple.

For worship. He walked past the most despised table in town and stopped. No one in Capernaum would have chosen Levi; Jesus did, in daylight, in front of everyone who had ever paid him. The man who had spent his life taking from others met the one who had come to give everything away, and the booth was left standing empty. Such is the grace of the Lord who chooses what is low and despised in the world (1 Corinthians 1:28), so that no one may boast, and every forgiven tax collector may sing.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew’s Gospel calls Levi “Matthew.” Tax collectors were despised as collaborators and cheats.

verseByVerse.quote: And Levi made him a great feast in his house, and there was a large company of tax collectors and others reclining at table with them. And the Pharisees and their scribes grumbled at his disciples, saying, 'Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Levi made him a great feast in his house, and there was a large company of tax collectors and others reclining at table with them. And the Pharisees and their scribes grumbled at his disciples, saying: why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?

And Levi made him a great feast in his house. Levi’s first recorded act as a disciple is to throw a party. He has no theology yet, no training, no idea what is coming. What he has is a house, a large one evidently, and a contact list. A rich man, he gave a banquet: a celebration.

A large company of tax collectors and others. Luke’s polite way of describing the social world a man in that trade moved in. Levi’s friends were tax collectors and other outcasts; respectable people would not associate with him. So he fills the room with the only people he knows, and he puts Jesus in the middle of it. That is the instinct of somebody who has just been given something and immediately wants the people he cares about to meet the one who gave it. It is not a strategy. It is a man who cannot think of anything better to do with his house. The natural evangelism of a new believer.

Reclining at table with them. Table fellowship in that world was not a casual matter. To recline at a man’s table was to declare peace with him, to accept him, to be publicly associated with him. It was closer to a signed statement than to a meal.

And the Pharisees and their scribes grumbled at his disciples. Grumbled (egongyzon) means murmured, the word used of Israel grumbling in the wilderness (Exodus 16:7–8; Numbers 14:27). And notice who they complain to. Not to Jesus: they go round him to his disciples. It is the oldest form of religious criticism there is: raise it with the followers, where it will do most damage and cost least.

Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners? The objection is worth understanding rather than dismissing. The Pharisees kept themselves separate from sinners: those who did not keep the law as they interpreted it, and the openly immoral. Eating with them would make you unclean. The Pharisees are not complaining about the menu; they are asking a serious question about the boundaries of the people of God, and by their own logic they are entirely right to ask it. Their premise is that holiness is preserved by separation: that you keep clean by keeping away. It is not a stupid premise. It is much of the book of Leviticus, and it had kept Israel identifiable through centuries of pressure. What they have not reckoned with is a holiness that works the other way round. Luke has just shown it, and they had no category for it: a hand stretched out to a leper, and the cleanness travelling from the toucher to the touched (5:13). To the Pharisees, holiness meant separation from sinners. For Jesus, it meant going to them. The charge will come again (7:34; 15:2; 19:7).

But does the Bible not tell us to avoid bad company? Yes: bad company ruins good morals (1 Corinthians 15:33), and we are not to walk in the counsel of the wicked (Psalm 1:1). The difference is the direction of influence and the purpose of the friendship. Jesus ate with sinners as their physician, and he was never drawn into their sin; they were drawn to him. Paul says Christians must not keep close company with someone who calls himself a brother and lives in open sin, but he does not mean the immoral of this world, or you would need to go out of the world (1 Corinthians 5:9–11). So be a friend to unbelievers, with open doors and real love; but if a friendship is pulling you into sin rather than you drawing them to Christ, step back.

In a sentence. Levi held a great feast for Jesus with many tax collectors and outcasts, and the Pharisees grumbled to the disciples about eating with sinners.

On a Tuesday. Introduce your non-Christian friends to Jesus. Levi’s method is open to anyone: a meal, a house, and the people you already know. Where it applies: invite a neighbour and a Christian friend to dinner together; ask the colleague who is going through a hard time to lunch; open your home at Christmas to someone who would otherwise be alone. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: welcoming sinners is not approving sin, and it is not joining in. Jesus ate with them as the one who called them to repentance (v. 32). And do not let fear of criticism keep you from friendship with outsiders.

For worship. The holy Son of God reclined at a table crowded with tax collectors and sinners and was glad to be there. He was not slumming or making a point; he was at home among the people he came to save. And he still keeps that table. One day, in the kingdom, he will sit down to the great feast with people from east and west and north and south (13:29), and the guest list will be full of Levis. He receives sinners and eats with them (15:2), and every one of us is at his table only because he does.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, 'Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered them: those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.

Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. A proverb, especially apt from Luke the physician, and its force is that nobody can disagree with it. A doctor goes to the sick. That is his job. A doctor found among the sick is not compromising his profession; he is doing it. His presence in the ward is not evidence that he approves of illness. It is evidence that he is a doctor. He does not catch their disease; he heals it. Jesus is the doctor; sinners are the sick. Where else should he be? So the question, why do you eat with sinners?, answers itself the moment you know what he came for.

I have not come to call the righteous. The word righteous here is ironic, and everyone at that table knew it. Jesus is not conceding that the Pharisees are righteous and therefore outside his remit. Scripture is unambiguous that there are none: none is righteous, no, not one (Romans 3:10, quoting the Psalms). He is using their own self-description back at them. The Pharisees thought they were righteous, and so did not think they needed him. Jesus cannot help those who think they are well.

Everyone in the house is sick. This is the thing to hold. The difference between the two groups at Levi’s dinner is not their condition. Everyone in that house is sick. The difference is entirely in what they know about themselves. The tax collectors are aware of it; the men in the doorway are not. And a man who does not believe he is ill will not send for a doctor however available the doctor makes himself. That is the tragedy of the Pharisees. They were disciplined, serious, orthodox and self-denying, and they had a diagnosis of themselves that was wrong, and being wrong in that particular direction is the one condition that refuses treatment. No one is cured of it by argument. It takes God himself to open such eyes, as he later opened the eyes of a Pharisee named Saul, who came to count all his religious gain as loss for Christ (Acts 9:18; Philippians 3:4–9).

But sinners to repentance. Note the last two words, because they are easily lost. Only Luke adds to repentance. He does not say he came to call sinners and leave them as they were. He came to call them to turn round. Repentance means a change of mind that becomes a change of direction: agreeing with God about your sin, and turning from it to him (Acts 26:20). The table at Levi’s house is not an endorsement of anybody’s life. It is a doctor’s visit, and doctors do not visit in order to agree with the disease. Grace receives sinners and changes them.

Does that mean Jesus accepts me as I am? Yes, and he will not leave you as you are. He receives anyone who comes to him, however sinful, without first requiring that he be cleaned up; the leper came full of leprosy, and Levi came straight from the booth. That is why you need not wait until you are better to come. But the same Jesus calls you to repentance, and his acceptance is the beginning of a new life, not a seal of approval on the old one. You come as you are; you do not stay as you are. Both halves are love.

In a sentence. Jesus replied that, like a doctor who goes to the sick, he came to call not those who think they are righteous but sinners to repentance.

On a Tuesday. You qualify for Jesus only by admitting you are sick. Come to him as a sinner, and he will heal you. And watch for the Pharisee in yourself: the sense, after years of church, that you are basically well and that the gospel is for people with worse problems. Name, in prayer this week, one specific way you still need the physician.

For worship. The Great Physician makes house calls, and he goes to the worst cases first. He sat down among the sick, not because he loved disease, but because he loved the diseased, and he came with the only cure there is. And his remedy is costly in a way no earthly doctor’s ever was: by his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). The doctor took the sickness into himself so that the patients could go free. Blessed be the Lord who came, not for the righteous, but for sinners like us.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The question about fasting is deceptively simple — why do Jesus's disciples not fast like John's disciples and the Pharisees? — and the answer, in two images and an observation, reframes the whole relationship between the old covenant and the new.

The bridegroom image is the most significant, because it is a claim about identity. In the Old Testament there is one bridegroom, and he is God: “Your Maker is your husband” (Isa. 54:5); “I will betroth you to me forever” (Hos. 2:19; cf. Jer. 2:2). Israel is the bride, and every apostasy is described as adultery. To explain his disciples' behaviour by saying the bridegroom is present is to say who has arrived — and John the Baptist had already made the same identification, placing himself in the wedding party rather than at its centre (John 3:29).

The disciples do not fast because this is not the season for it. Fasting at a wedding is not more serious; it is out of time.

Then the shadow: “The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.” It is the first hint of the cross in Jesus's own teaching in Luke, dropped without warning into an argument about religious observance. Nobody at that table could have understood it.

The garment and the wineskin press the same point. A patch cut from a new coat ruins the new and does not match the old; new wine in a hardened skin bursts the skin and is lost. The kingdom Jesus inaugurates is not a reform of Judaism but its fulfilment — and fulfilment is not the same as continuation.

The new covenant is organically connected to the old; Jesus keeps the law, goes to the synagogue weekly, sends the leper to the priest. But what has arrived could not be contained by what preceded it, not because the old was worthless but because it was never designed to hold this.

And the last line is the sharpest: “no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, 'The old is good.'” It is not a compliment to the old wine. It is a description of a palate — and of the men in the doorway, who refused Jesus not because they had examined him and found him wanting but because they were comfortable, and he did not taste of what they were used to.
verseByVerse.theology:
The bridegroom language is one of the most significant implicit claims to deity in the Synoptic Gospels. In the prophets, the husband of Israel is the LORD himself, and the relationship between God and his people is consistently described in bridal terms.

Revelation carries the image to its conclusion — the marriage supper of the Lamb, the new Jerusalem coming down as a bride adorned for her husband (Rev. 19:7-9; 21:2-9). The fasting question in Luke 5 is a thread that runs all the way to the last page of the Bible.

The observation in v. 39 is not a sociological aside about wine preferences. It is a precise description of the spiritual condition of people who have grown comfortable in the old forms: they feel no need of new wine, because what they have is satisfying.

That is the condition of the Pharisees, and it was not a moral failure. The old wine of the law and the tradition was genuinely good — God gave it. This is the most dangerous spiritual position there is, because it requires a good thing to settle into: contentment with something genuinely good, in the presence of something better.
verseByVerse.examples:
The bridegroom's presence is the reason for the disciples' joy, and it remains the reason for Christian joy. The resurrection did not remove the bridegroom; it confirmed that he is alive and with his people until he returns.

So Christian fasting is not the fast of the men who asked the question. Jesus assumes his people will fast — “they will fast in those days,” and those days are these — but it is the fast of people who have known him, live between his going and his return, and want him back. Not a technique for getting God's attention. A body saying what the heart already knows: that the best thing is still ahead.

The new wineskins are a standing challenge to every Christian tradition, and the question has to be asked honestly. Not “is this old?” — age is no argument either way. But: is this form still carrying the life, or has it set hard around a shape the life has outgrown?

This is not a call to theological novelty. The wine is always the same wine, the gospel of the crucified and risen Christ, and it is the oldest thing there is. But a wineskin's only job is to hold wine, and the moment it begins to be valued for itself it has started to fail at the one thing it was for.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to him, 'The disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.' And Jesus said to them, 'Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said to him: the disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink. Jesus said to them: can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.

The disciples of John fast often and offer prayers. The third complaint of the section, and it is about fasting: yours eat and drink, as they had just been doing at Levi’s feast. The observation is accurate. The law commanded only one yearly fast, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29). But devout Jews fasted more. Pharisees fasted twice a week, on Mondays and Thursdays (18:12). John’s followers, in particular, were an austere group, following his austere life, and their teacher was in prison.

Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? He answers with a wedding. A Jewish wedding feast lasted up to a week and was a time of joy, and wedding guests were excused from certain religious duties, including fasting. Fasting expressed mourning, sorrow and longing. The point is not that fasting is wrong. It is that fasting at a wedding is absurd. It is not more serious; it is out of time. While Jesus is here, the time of longing is over.

The bridegroom. But the image is doing something much larger than settling a dispute about diet, and the men who asked would have felt it. In the Old Testament there is one bridegroom, and he is God. Your Maker is your husband (Isaiah 54:5); as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you (Isaiah 62:5); I will betroth you to me for ever (Hosea 2:19–20). Israel is the bride, and every failure of the nation is described as adultery. So when Jesus explains his disciples’ behaviour by saying that the bridegroom is present, he is not reaching for a pleasant metaphor about joy. He is saying who has arrived: another claim to be God. John the Baptist had already made the same identification and put himself in the wedding party rather than at its centre: the friend of the bridegroom rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice (John 3:29). The messianic wedding feast has begun.

The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them. Then the shadow. Taken away (aparthē) means removed. A bridegroom does not leave his own wedding feast; if he is taken away from it, he is taken by force. This is the first hint of the cross in Luke’s record of Jesus’ own teaching, and it is dropped into an argument about religious observance without warning or explanation (Isaiah 53:8). Nobody at that table could have understood it. He knew already.

And then they will fast in those days. After his departure, his disciples will fast (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). Fasting is right for Christians now, as we long for his return. But it is no longer a mark of mourning without hope, nor a means of earning favour.

Should Christians fast, and how? Jesus plainly assumes it: they will fast in those days, and those days are these. But it is not the fast of the men asking the question. It is the fast of people who have known the bridegroom, live between his going and his return, and want him back. Not a technique for getting God’s attention. A body saying what the heart already knows. In practice, fasting means going without food, or some meals, for a set time in order to give that time to prayer: before a big decision, in a time of repentance, in grief, or in longing for God’s work. Do it quietly, not for show (Matthew 6:16–18). Begin modestly, with one meal; take medical advice if you have a health condition; and never treat it as earning anything from God.

In a sentence. When asked why his disciples did not fast, Jesus answered that wedding guests do not fast while the bridegroom is present, but they will fast when he is taken away.

On a Tuesday. The Christian life has times of feasting and times of fasting. Rejoice in Christ’s presence, and long for his return. Where it applies: there are seasons to fast and pray, over a wayward child, a church decision, a besetting sin; and there are seasons to feast, at a wedding, a baptism, a birthday, with a clear conscience and a glad heart. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: do not make your own pattern of fasting a rule for others, or look down on Christians who do not fast as you do. That is exactly the error of the men who asked the question.

For worship. The bridegroom of Israel, the Maker who called himself her husband, came in person and sat down at a feast. And he knew, even as he spoke of the wedding, that he would be snatched away to a cross. He went to that cross for his bride, to wash her and present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). Our fasting now is the longing of a bride whose bridegroom has gone ahead, and our feasting is the foretaste of the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9), when he will never be taken away again.
verseByVerse.note: The law commanded one yearly fast, on the Day of Atonement. A wedding lasted days and was no time for fasting.

verseByVerse.quote: He also told them a parable: 'No one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new, and the piece from the new will not match the old.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He also told them a parable: no one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new, and the piece from the new will not match the old.

He also told them a parable. Three short parables (vv. 36–39) explain why Jesus’ disciples do not follow the old patterns.

No one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. Luke’s version of this saying is sharper than the others, and the sharpness is the point. Matthew and Mark speak of unshrunk cloth on an old garment (Mark 2:21); Luke has a man cutting up a new garment to patch an old one. So the loss is doubled. In Luke, you ruin the new garment by cutting a patch out of it, and the patch does not match the old one anyway. Both are spoiled.

The point. The question underneath is the one the whole section has been circling. Has Jesus come to repair Judaism? Is the kingdom of God a renovation of the existing arrangement: the same religion with better preaching, a bit of fresh material sewn over the worn places? The answer is no. What Jesus brings is not a patch to mend the old system. It is something entirely new: the kingdom of God, and the new covenant that he will seal in his own blood (22:20). It cannot be stitched onto the old ways of fasting and rule-keeping without ruining both. The gospel is not a supplement to religion; it is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17).

The old garment was not bad. The reason for the answer is not that the old garment was bad. God gave it. The law, the temple, the sacrifices and the priesthood were all his own design, and Jesus honours every one of them: he sends the leper to the priest, he goes to the synagogue weekly, he will keep the Passover. The old garment is not being criticised. It is being finished with, because what it was for has come.

How the saying is abused. This has to be held carefully in both directions, because the saying gets abused in both. It is abused by people who use it to junk everything old. New wine, they say, and away goes the creed, the confession, the twenty centuries of the church’s thinking, on the grounds that God is doing a new thing. But the newness in this parable is not new ideas. It is the gospel of the crucified and risen Christ, which is the oldest thing there is. And it is abused by people who cannot distinguish between the fabric and the pattern: for whom every inherited practice is a doctrine, and any change is apostasy. That is the Pharisees’ error exactly, and Jesus is answering it here. What is genuinely new is not a programme. It is a person, and a covenant sealed in his blood, and a Spirit poured out on ordinary people. Nothing that existed before could hold it: not because the old was worthless, but because it was never designed to.

In a sentence. Jesus said that no one cuts a patch from a new garment to mend an old one, since that ruins the new and does not match the old.

On a Tuesday. Do not treat Jesus as a patch on your old life: a little religion sewn over a life that is otherwise run by the same desires and the same self. He makes all things new. Where it applies: the person who adds church to his week but keeps his business dishonest, or adds prayer to his marriage but keeps his temper unchecked. Where it would be wrong to apply it that way: becoming new does not mean throwing away everything in your past, your family, your culture, your honest work and gifts. Christ does not discard those; he takes them up and makes them his.

For worship. He did not come to tailor a patch for a worn religion. He came with a whole new garment, and he cut it from his own life: the righteousness he wove in years of perfect obedience, given entire to people who had nothing to wear but rags, the robe of righteousness Isaiah sang of in the chapter Jesus read at Nazareth (Isaiah 61:10). The law that had clothed Israel for centuries was God’s own good work, and it was waiting for him. Now he wraps sinners from head to foot in what he alone has made, and not one thread of it is theirs.

verseByVerse.quote: And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins.

Wineskins. The same point, with a better image. Wine was stored in goatskins, made from whole hides, sewn and sealed. New wine is still fermenting, giving off gas and expanding. A new skin was supple and stretched with it. But a skin that had already been through one fermentation was set hard: it had done its stretching, and it had nothing left. Pour actively fermenting wine into it and the pressure has nowhere to go. The skin splits, and you lose both.

Both are lost. Notice what Jesus says is lost: the new wine will burst the skins and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. Both. This is not a saying about how the old is expendable. It is a warning that forcing new life into hardened forms wastes the life and wrecks the form.

The point. The new wine is the life of the kingdom that Jesus brings: joy, grace, the Spirit, the new covenant. The old wineskins are the Pharisees’ traditions and rituals, and they cannot contain it.

But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins. Must (blēteon): it is necessary. And that is the whole prescription. Not: throw away the wine. Not: pretend the old skin is fine. Get the wine into something that can move with it. The point is not that novelty is good. It is that living things expand, and whatever contains them has to be able to give. That was true of the first Christian generation in the most literal way. Within thirty years of this conversation the gospel had gone to Gentiles who did not keep the food laws, met on the first day of the week, had no temple and no priesthood, and were being told that the whole apparatus had been a shadow of what had now come (Colossians 2:17). Not because the shadow was false, but because the substance had arrived.

What it does not mean. Not that the Old Testament is bad or useless. Jesus came to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17). But the old covenant’s forms, the sacrifices, food laws, priesthood and temple, were shadows that pointed forward to Christ, and give way to the reality (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 8:13).

How do I tell a wineskin from the wine in my own church? Ask whether a thing is commanded in Scripture or chosen by people. The gospel, the preaching of the word, prayer, baptism and the Lord’s Supper, the ordering of the church and the moral law are given by God; they are the wine and must not move. The time of the service, the style of music, the order of worship, the building, the translation used, are human choices, wineskins; they may be good and well loved, and they may be changed when they no longer carry the life. Not, is this old? Age is no argument either way. But: is this form still carrying the life, or has it set hard around a shape the life has outgrown?

In a sentence. Jesus said new wine must go into new wineskins, because old ones would burst, meaning the new life of his kingdom cannot be contained in the old forms.

On a Tuesday. Is your faith so tied to familiar forms that you resist anything new God is doing? Hold to the gospel; hold forms loosely. A wineskin’s only job is to hold wine. The moment it starts being valued for itself, it has begun to fail at the one thing it was for. What must never move is the wine. Everything else is leather.

For worship. The new wine of the kingdom is Christ’s own life, poured out in the Spirit, and nothing made by human hands can hold it. It burst the old skins of temple and ritual and ran out into the whole world, to Gentiles and slaves and children, in every language under heaven. At Cana he turned water into the best wine, kept until last (John 2:10); at the Supper he gave the cup of the new covenant in his blood (22:20). He is the wine, and he is the one who pours it, and he has never run dry.
verseByVerse.note: Wineskins were goatskins. New wine is still fermenting; an old skin has lost its stretch and splits.

verseByVerse.quote: And no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, ‘The old is good.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says: the old is good.

Only Luke adds this saying. A wry, almost humorous comment on human nature, and the most quietly devastating sentence in the chapter. It is also frequently misread, because it sounds at first as though Jesus is conceding the point.

No one after drinking old wine desires new. Old wine is smooth and mellow; new wine is raw and harsh, still working. People who are used to the old prefer it, and will not even try the new. He is not commending old wine. He is describing a palate.

For he says, The old is good. Some manuscripts read better, but the best read good: the old is good enough. Why change? Jesus is not making a claim about the merits of the two covenants. He is stating a fact about human beings: having settled into something, we do not want the alternative, and we will always find a reason. The old is good. And so it is. And that is what makes it so hard to leave.

The point. Jesus explains why the Pharisees and many others reject him. It is not that they have tried the new and found it wanting. They are content with the old, and do not feel the need for what Jesus brings. Their problem was never that they had chosen something bad. Their problem was that they had something genuinely good, a real law given by God, a real tradition, hard won, real discipline, real reverence, real Scripture, and they were comfortable in it, and it had made the arrival of something better feel like a disturbance rather than a fulfilment.

The new wine was standing in front of them. What they refused to taste was not a recipe but a person. The bridegroom was at the table (v. 34), and the one of whom Moses and all the prophets had written was reclining at Levi’s feast (24:27). Their old wine was good because it had come from him, and it had been laid down for this very day. To prefer it to him was to prefer the promise to the one who kept it. The old covenant was never meant to be held against Christ; it was meant to make Israel thirsty for him.

The most dangerous spiritual position. It is not available to obvious sinners. It requires a good thing to settle into. Levi could be reached in two words at his tax booth; the men outside had spent thirty years acquiring a taste that made the new wine unpalatable. Nobody in this chapter refused Jesus because they had examined him and found him wanting. They refused him because they were comfortable, and he was not what they were used to.

In the flow. This saying closes the chapter, and it explains what has gone before. A fisherman, a leper, a paralysed man and a tax collector have all tasted the new wine, while the experts have questioned, grumbled and objected. The next two scenes (6:1–11) show the same palate at work over the Sabbath, the most treasured of the old forms, and they end in fury. Luke wants his reader to see that the dividing line runs not between the religious and the irreligious but between those who know they need what Jesus brings and those who are content without him.

Does this mean tradition is bad and new is always better? No. Jesus is not saying that whatever is new is from God; most novelties in the church’s history have been errors. The new wine is not a new idea but himself, the fulfilment of everything the old covenant promised. And Scripture tells us to hold fast to the traditions of the apostles (2 Thessalonians 2:15). The warning is against a heart so settled in its religion that it no longer needs Christ, or cannot hear him when he does not taste like what it is used to.

In a sentence. Jesus observed that those who are used to old wine do not want new, because they think the old is good enough, explaining why many rejected him.

On a Tuesday. Being content with your religion can keep you from Christ. Ask whether you are truly drinking his new wine, or just the old. Every long-standing Christian has an accumulated set of preferences, a way of worship, a style of preaching, a shape of church life, a period of hymnody, a translation, much of which is genuinely good and none of which is the gospel. The test is not whether we like the old. Of course we like the old. The test is what happens when God does something that does not taste of it.

For worship. He did not force his new wine on anyone. He set it out at Levi’s table and let the tax collectors drink, while the experts stood in the doorway saying the old was good enough. And he is patient still with palates set hard by long habit: he is the Lord who took a settled Pharisee from Tarsus and made him count all his old gain as loss for the surpassing worth of knowing him (Philippians 3:7–8). The wine he pours is forgiveness complete, the Spirit given, the Father’s welcome, and it does not run out. No one who has truly tasted it has ever found the old better.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke adds this saying — a wry comment on those content with the old ways.

5.text: <sup>1</sup> On one occasion, while the crowd was pressing in on him to hear the word of God, he was standing by the lake of Gennesaret, <sup>2</sup> and he saw two boats by the lake, but the fishermen had gone out of them and were washing their nets. <sup>3</sup> Getting into one of the boats, which was Simon's, he asked him to put out a little from the land. And he sat down and taught the people from the boat. <sup>4</sup> And when he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, “Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.” <sup>5</sup> And Simon answered, “Master, we toiled all night and took nothing! But at your word I will let down the nets.” <sup>6</sup> And when they had done this, they enclosed a large number of fish, and their nets were breaking. <sup>7</sup> They signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them. And they came and filled both the boats, so that they began to sink. <sup>8</sup> But when Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.” <sup>9</sup> For he and all who were with him were astonished at the catch of fish that they had taken, <sup>10</sup> and so also were James and John, sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. And Jesus said to Simon, “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men.” <sup>11</sup> And when they had brought their boats to land, they left everything and followed him. <sup>12</sup> While he was in one of the cities, there came a man full of leprosy. And when he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him, “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” <sup>13</sup> And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, “I will; be clean.” And immediately the leprosy left him. <sup>14</sup> And he charged him to tell no one, but “go and show yourself to the priest, and make an offering for your cleansing, as Moses commanded, for a proof to them.” <sup>15</sup> But now even more the report about him went abroad, and great crowds gathered to hear him and to be healed of their infirmities. <sup>16</sup> But he would withdraw to desolate places and pray. <sup>17</sup> On one of those days, as he was teaching, Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem. And the power of the Lord was with him to heal. <sup>18</sup> And behold, some men were bringing on a bed a man who was paralyzed, and they were seeking to bring him in and lay him before Jesus, <sup>19</sup> but finding no way to bring him in, because of the crowd, they went up on the roof and let him down with his bed through the tiles into the midst before Jesus. <sup>20</sup> And when he saw their faith, he said, “Man, your sins are forgiven you.” <sup>21</sup> And the scribes and the Pharisees began to question, saying, “Who is this who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God alone?” <sup>22</sup> When Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answered them, “Why do you question in your hearts? <sup>23</sup> Which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? <sup>24</sup> But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he said to the man who was paralyzed—“I say to you, rise, pick up your bed and go home.” <sup>25</sup> And immediately he rose up before them and picked up what he had been lying on and went home, glorifying God. <sup>26</sup> And amazement seized them all, and they glorified God and were filled with awe, saying, “We have seen extraordinary things today.” <sup>27</sup> After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi, sitting at the tax booth. And he said to him, “Follow me.” <sup>28</sup> And leaving everything, he rose and followed him. <sup>29</sup> And Levi made him a great feast in his house, and there was a large company of tax collectors and others reclining at table with them. <sup>30</sup> And the Pharisees and their scribes grumbled at his disciples, saying, “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?” <sup>31</sup> And Jesus answered them, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. <sup>32</sup> I have not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance.” <sup>33</sup> And they said to him, “The disciples of John fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.” <sup>34</sup> And Jesus said to them, “Can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? <sup>35</sup> The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days.” <sup>36</sup> He also told them a parable: “No one tears a piece from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new, and the piece from the new will not match the old. <sup>37</sup> And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins and it will be spilled, and the skins will be destroyed. <sup>38</sup> But new wine must be put into fresh wineskins. <sup>39</sup> And no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, ‘The old is good.’”

6.title: The Sermon on the Plain
6.overview:
Chapter 6 is Luke's equivalent of Matthew's Sermon on the Mount — shorter, sharper, and structurally parallel, though not identical. Before the sermon comes the choosing of the twelve and two Sabbath controversies that frame the sermon's radical ethics with a theological question: by what authority does Jesus define what is lawful, and what kind of community does that authority create? The Sermon on the Plain (vv. 20–49) is the charter of the kingdom community — the description of what it looks like to live under the reign of God when that reign runs against every instinct of the natural self.

The beatitudes and woes (vv. 20–26) are the most direct statement in the chapter: the kingdom reverses the world's value system. The poor are blessed; the rich are warned. The hungry are filled; the full are emptied. Those who weep now will laugh; those who laugh now will mourn. This is not a promise that poverty is virtuous or that comfort is sinful; it is a statement about the direction of the kingdom. God's attention, God's blessing, God's purposes consistently run toward those whom the world has left behind — and consistently challenge those who have arranged their lives to need nothing from anyone, including God.

The ethical core of the sermon (vv. 27–45) — love your enemies, do not judge, produce good fruit — is the most demanding teaching in Luke's Gospel, and it rests entirely on the character of God. Love your enemies because your Father is kind to the ungrateful and evil. Do not judge because you will be judged by the measure you use. Bear good fruit because the tree is known by its fruit. The final image — the house on the rock — is the sermon's warning: hearing these words is not enough. The one who hears and does not do is building on sand. The storm will come, and only the house that is built on hearing and doing will stand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Jesus Is Lord of the Sabbath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two Sabbath controversies open the chapter, and together they establish the claim that makes everything in the sermon possible: Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath.

The first is about disciples plucking grain as they walk through fields. Plucking ears from a neighbour's standing grain was expressly permitted (Deut. 23:25), so the objection is not theft; it is that plucking counts as reaping and rubbing as threshing, both forbidden on the Sabbath by the scribal fence built around the commandment.

That fence did not begin in wickedness. It began in a serious desire not to sin, by people whose nation had gone into exile for ignoring precisely this commandment. And it had become unbearable — a gift turned into an audit, a day given to relieve working people now governed by case law only the leisured could master.

Jesus's response reaches back to 1 Samuel 21:1-6. David, on the run and hungry, ate the bread of the Presence, which the law reserved for priests, and shared it with his men — and Scripture records it without a word of censure. The point is not that rules do not matter. It is that the law of God has an order of priorities inside it, and the ceremonial provision was never meant to override the life it was given to serve. Jesus is not appealing over the head of Scripture; he is appealing to Scripture against a reading of it.

The choice of precedent is not accidental either. Of all the cases available, he reaches for the one about God's anointed king, rejected and on the run, with his own small band of followers, doing what the authorities called unlawful.

Then the conclusion: “The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.” He does not argue that the Sabbath is unimportant. He claims that he is the one who determines its meaning — which, given that the Sabbath is rooted in creation, enshrined in the Ten Commandments, and named as the sign of the covenant between the LORD and Israel, is a claim about who he is.

The Pharisees are not wrong to take the Sabbath seriously. They are wrong to think their authority over it exceeds the authority of the one who instituted it.
verseByVerse.theology:
“The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath” is a divine claim in Jewish ears. The Sabbath is God's own institution — rooted in creation (Gen. 2:2-3), enshrined in the Ten Commandments (Exod. 20:8-11), and described as a sign of the covenant between the LORD and Israel for ever (Exod. 31:12-17).

To be Lord of the Sabbath is to exercise authority over the covenant sign of God himself. Jesus is not relativising the day; he is claiming to be its author. This is among the most compact and most decisive of the implicit claims to deity scattered through the Synoptic Gospels.

And the title he uses to say it is the one from Daniel 7:13-14 — the figure who comes to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion. It sounds modest in English and was not.

What is worth adding is what this lordship is for. He is not lord of the Sabbath in order to abolish rest, but to give it back. The day always pointed at a person, and the person has arrived.
verseByVerse.examples:
The complaint about grain-plucking is a case study in confusing the purpose of a law with the law itself. The Sabbath was given as a gift — a day of rest for those who worked, and a sign of trust that God would provide without their constant labour.

The Pharisees' elaborate hedge of regulations (the Mishnah tractate on the Sabbath runs to twenty-four chapters) had turned that gift into a burden. When a law loses contact with the grace and wisdom that gave it, it becomes oppression. Jesus does not abolish the Sabbath; he liberates it from the accretion that had buried what it was for.

The sequence is worth watching for, because it is not confined to the first century and does not require bad motives: a good practice, a rule to protect it, a further rule to protect the rule — and, three generations on, people who can tell you exactly what is forbidden and have entirely lost sight of the point.

The test is simple enough to apply. When a religious rule and a hungry person meet, which one does the rule-keeper find himself defending?

verseByVerse.quote: On a Sabbath, while he was going through the grainfields, his disciples plucked and ate some heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands. But some of the Pharisees said, 'Why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
On a Sabbath, while he was going through the grainfields, his disciples plucked and ate some heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands. But some of the Pharisees said: why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath?

Meaning first. Luke 6 shows the Lord of the Sabbath forming a new people and teaching them how to live. In two Sabbath conflicts, over hungry disciples picking grain and a withered hand healed in the synagogue, Jesus claims authority over God’s own law, and his enemies begin to plot. He answers with a night of prayer and the choice of twelve apostles, a new Israel gathered around himself. Then, on a level place, he preaches: blessings on the poor, the hungry and the persecuted, woes on the rich and the popular; love for enemies; mercy as the Father is merciful; no judging, no hypocrisy; a tree known by its fruit; and two houses, one on rock. The chapter shows who Jesus is, the Lord whose word is law, and the shape of life in his kingdom: mercy received from the Father, and mercy given to everyone else.

The Sabbath controversies. Two conflicts over the Sabbath (vv. 1–11) follow the conflicts over forgiveness, table company and fasting in chapter 5. The Sabbath, the seventh day of rest (Exodus 20:8–11), was one of the great marks of Jewish identity, along with circumcision and the food laws. The rabbis defined 39 categories of forbidden work, including reaping, threshing, winnowing and preparing food.

His disciples plucked and ate some heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands. Hungry men walking through a field, pulling heads of grain and rubbing the husks off between their palms as they go. It is the most ordinary thing in the chapter, and it starts a fight that ends at a cross. Only Luke mentions rubbing them in their hands, to remove the husks. Picking grain by hand from a neighbour’s field while walking through was explicitly allowed by the law: you may pluck the ears with your hand (Deuteronomy 23:25). Israel’s law had a built-in provision for the hungry traveller, and these hungry men are within it.

Why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath? The objection was not theft but the day. By the Pharisees’ rules, plucking was reaping, and rubbing was threshing and winnowing. Which sounds absurd until you understand where the reasoning came from, and it is worth being fair to them, because caricature makes the passage useless. The fourth commandment forbids work on the Sabbath and does not define work. So the rabbis, trying to obey, drew up definitions: thirty-nine categories of labour, of which reaping and threshing are two. And around those definitions they built what they called a fence: additional restrictions, so that a man would stop well short of the actual line and never break the commandment by accident. The Mishnah’s tractate on the Sabbath runs to twenty-four chapters. None of that began in wickedness. It began in a serious desire not to sin, by people who had watched their nation go into exile for ignoring precisely this commandment (Jeremiah 17:27).

A gift turned into an audit. And it had become unbearable. They had turned a day of rest and delight (Isaiah 58:13) into a burden of regulations. The day God gave to relieve working people had acquired a body of case law that only the leisured could master. And the sequence is not confined to the first century, nor does it require bad motives. It requires only this: a good practice, a rule to protect it, a further rule to protect the rule, and, three generations on, people who can tell you exactly what is forbidden and have entirely lost sight of what the thing was for. And underneath the rules a quieter danger grows in the heart. A man who can keep thirty-nine categories of labour can begin to feel that he has kept God, and then the rules stop being a fence around a gift and become a ladder to climb, with a good view of the people on the lower rungs.

Is it wrong to have church rules and customs that the Bible does not command? No. Every church needs some ordered customs: a time for the service, an order of worship, a way of receiving members. Wise guidelines can protect good things, such as a family deciding to keep Sunday free of sport so that they can worship together. The error comes when a human rule is treated as God’s law, binding other people’s consciences (Mark 7:8), or when the rule is kept at the expense of the very people it was meant to serve. Ask of any rule: does Scripture command this, or did we choose it? If we chose it, hold it gladly and lightly, and never let it stand between a hungry person and bread.

He answers for his men. The charge is laid against the disciples, but it is aimed at the one they follow: in Mark’s telling the Pharisees put it to Jesus himself (Mark 2:24), and in Luke it is Jesus who answers (v. 3). They did nothing in that field that their Master had not allowed, and he does not leave them to defend themselves. He steps between his hungry friends and their accusers and takes the question onto himself. That is the shape of his whole work. When the accuser speaks against his people, it is Christ who answers: who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is Christ Jesus who died, who was raised, who intercedes for us (Romans 8:33–34).

In a sentence. When Jesus’ disciples picked and rubbed some grain to eat as they walked through a field on the Sabbath, Pharisees accused them of breaking the Sabbath law.

On a Tuesday. Human rules can turn God’s good gifts into burdens. When a religious rule and a hungry person meet, notice which one you find yourself defending, and ask of the rules you are quickest to enforce on others whether they are God’s or yours.

For worship. The Lord of the harvest walked through a grainfield with his hungry friends, and let them eat. The law he had given was full of provision for the hungry traveller, because he is a God who feeds. The Pharisees saw a violation; he saw his own kindness at work. His commandments are not burdensome (1 John 5:3), and his yoke is easy: he never made a rule to keep bread from the hungry, and he never will.
verseByVerse.note: Picking grain by hand from a neighbour’s field was allowed; the objection was that plucking and rubbing counted as harvesting and threshing, work forbidden on the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, 'Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God and took and ate the bread of the Presence, which is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those with him?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered them: have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God and took and ate the bread of the Presence, which is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those with him?

Have you not read. A pointed question to experts in Scripture. Jesus answers from the Bible, and the way he introduces it has an edge: have you not read? To men whose life’s work was reading. The episode is 1 Samuel 21:1–6. David, fleeing from Saul, came with a handful of men and no food to the priest Ahimelech at Nob, where the tabernacle then stood, and asked for bread. The only bread was the holy bread.

The bread of the Presence. Twelve loaves, one for each tribe, set out on a golden table in the Holy Place before the Lord each Sabbath, and then eaten by the priests in a holy place (Leviticus 24:5–9). Only priests could lawfully eat it. The priest gave it to David. David ate it, and shared it with his men.

The argument. Scripture records without a word of censure that David, God’s anointed king, not yet on his throne, and his men ate the holy bread in a time of need, and David walks away fed. The ceremonial law gave way to human need. If David could do that, then the Son of David, the greater anointed king, and his followers can do much more. And if Scripture itself shows that ceremonial rules yield to need and mercy, the Pharisees’ rules certainly must. God desires mercy, not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6; Matthew 12:7).

What Jesus is arguing. Not that rules do not matter, and not that hunger dissolves the law. Something more precise: that the law of God has an order of priorities inside it, and that the ceremonial provision was never meant to override the life it was given to serve. He is not appealing over the head of Scripture. He is appealing to Scripture, against a reading of it.

Why David? There is a further thing in the choice of story, and the men listening would have felt it. Of all the possible precedents he reaches for the one about God’s anointed king, on the run, rejected, with his own small band of followers, doing something the authorities would call unlawful. The parallel is not accidental and it is not subtle. Here is another anointed king, gathering another company, being told by the officials of the day that what he does is not lawful. If David’s men could eat, so can his. Which means the argument is not chiefly about corn at all. It is about who this is, and Jesus is about to say so out loud: the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.

Does this mean I may break God’s commands when I am in need? No. The holy bread was a ceremonial law, about the use of sacred objects, and it was always meant to serve life. God’s moral law, do not steal, do not lie, do not commit adultery, is never set aside for convenience or need; David did wrong when he lied to the priest in this same chapter (1 Samuel 21:2). The lesson is not that hunger excuses sin, but that God’s law is kind, and that its outward ceremonies were never meant to be used against the hungry and the suffering.

In a sentence. Jesus answered from Scripture that David and his men, when hungry, ate the holy bread that only priests could lawfully eat.

On a Tuesday. God’s law is for human good. Use it to show mercy, not to load burdens on others.

For worship. David had to ask a priest for the holy bread, handed out through a door he could not enter. The Son of David asks no one. He is himself the Presence before whom those twelve loaves were laid, God with his people, walking the fields with his own company. And at the last he is the bread: on the night he was betrayed he took bread, broke it, and gave his own body to his apostles. What only priests could eat at Nob, he gives to every hungry sinner who comes to him. Blessed be the King who keeps open house, and sets his table with himself.
verseByVerse.note: The bread of the Presence was twelve loaves set before the LORD each Sabbath and eaten by the priests.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to them: the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.

The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath. An enormous claim, nine words in English, among the largest Jesus ever made. Consider what the Sabbath was. Not a custom, not a national tradition, not a piece of religious furniture that could be rearranged. God instituted it at creation: he rested on the seventh day and made it holy (Genesis 2:2–3). It stands in the Ten Commandments, spoken by God from the mountain in fire and thunder (Exodus 20:8–11). And it is named as the sign of the covenant between the LORD and Israel for ever (Exodus 31:17). There is no institution in Judaism more directly and personally God’s than this one. And a Galilean carpenter says he is its lord.

No soft reading. To be lord of the Sabbath is to have authority over God’s own law, to determine its meaning and use. Only God could claim that. He does not say the Sabbath is unimportant. He does not say his disciples were within the rabbinic rules after all. He says that the authority to determine what this day is and how it works belongs to him, which is to say that he stands where the Lawgiver stands. A man may say the Sabbath has been misunderstood. Only its author can say he is its lord. Jesus is not breaking the Sabbath; he is its Lord, who gives its true interpretation. Mark adds: the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27).

The Son of Man. The title he uses to say it is the one from Daniel 7 again: the figure who comes to the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion (Daniel 7:13–14). It sounds humble in English; it was not. So the quarrel over a handful of grain has arrived at the question the whole Gospel is about: not, what may be done on the Sabbath? but, who is this? The Pharisees are quite right to be alarmed. Somebody in that cornfield is either speaking blasphemy or telling the truth, and there is no third possibility on offer.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath today. Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists hold that Christians must keep Saturday. Many Reformed and Puritan Christians (following the Westminster Confession 21.7–8) hold that the Sabbath command continues, transferred to Sunday, the “Christian Sabbath”, to be kept by resting from work and recreation and devoting the day to worship. Others hold that the Sabbath was a sign of the old covenant fulfilled in Christ. Verdict: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, who gives the true rest it pointed to (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10); Christians are not bound to its ceremonial regulations (Colossians 2:16–17; Romans 14:5). Yet the Lord’s Day, the first day of the week, the day of resurrection, is the church’s day of gathering for worship (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10). It is a privilege and a gift, not a burden, and the principle of a regular day of rest and worship remains wise and good. This is held charitably toward those who keep a stricter Sabbath.

Lord in order to give rest. And see what this lordship is for. He is not lord of the Sabbath in order to abolish rest. He is its lord in order to give it back, and elsewhere he says what he means: come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28). The day always pointed at a person. The person has arrived, and he is not standing in the cornfield to take anything away. What does it mean that the Sabbath is fulfilled in him? The day pictured rest: God’s rest after his finished work, and Israel’s rest from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15). In Christ that rest is given in full. Whoever trusts him stops working to earn God’s favour, because Christ has finished the work, and rests from his works as God did from his (Hebrews 4:10).

So how should I spend Sunday? Begin with gathering: the Lord’s Day is first of all the day his people meet to hear his word, pray, sing and share the Lord’s Supper, and that should be the fixed point around which the day is arranged. Then rest: make room for what refreshes body and soul, family, a walk, a meal with others, visiting the lonely, reading. Christians who hold the stricter Sabbath view will set aside work and ordinary recreation for the whole day, and they are to be respected for it; others will use more freedom. Whichever conviction you hold, do not judge the brother who differs (Romans 14:5–6), and do not let the day become either a burden or just another day.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath, with authority over God’s own law.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath, and he gives true rest. Use the Lord’s Day as a gift: rest in him, and worship with his people.

For worship. The one who rested on the seventh day after making the world stood in a Galilean field and called himself its Lord. He made the Sabbath, he kept it perfectly, and he fulfilled it, resting in the tomb on the seventh day and rising on the first, so that his people could enter the rest that remains for the people of God (Hebrews 4:9). We do not work towards our rest; we begin from it, because he has finished the work. Lord of the Sabbath, Lord of the law, Lord of all: the rest we were made for has a name, and it is his.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — A Man with a Withered Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second Sabbath controversy involves a man with a withered right hand — which, in a manual economy, meant an inability to earn a living. Luke the physician notes which hand.

The scribes and Pharisees are watching to see whether Jesus will heal, “so that they might find a reason to accuse him.” The watching is calculated and hostile, and it is worth registering how ugly it is: they are in a house of God, on the day of God, hoping a disabled man will be healed so that they can bring a charge. His hand interests them only as evidence.

Jesus knows exactly what they are doing, and he does not avoid the confrontation — he creates it. He tells the man to stand up in the middle, where everyone can see, and puts a question to the room: “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it?”

That question is the interpretive key to his whole Sabbath theology, and it is why they cannot answer. They came prepared to argue that healing is work and that a hand withered for years can wait until sundown — a reasonable position on their own terms. Jesus refuses the terms. He removes the neutral square marked “wait until tomorrow”: to be able to relieve suffering and to decline is not inaction but a choice, and it belongs in the other column.

The Sabbath is not a day of inaction. It is a day defined by the character of its author — and the God who rested on the seventh day is the God who sustains life on every day. Their silence answers the question for them.

Then he heals without touching. The man is simply told to stretch out the hand he cannot stretch out, and the strength arrives inside the obedience. There is nothing to accuse.

And the response is fury — the first time in Luke that the religious leaders plot against him. It has taken six chapters, and the cause was a question they could not answer and a mercy they could not permit.
verseByVerse.theology:
The hardness that sets in at this point — “they were filled with fury” — begins the trajectory that ends at the cross. The fury is not primarily moral; it is theological. Jesus has publicly claimed authority over the Sabbath, healed in defiance of their interpretation, and refused to be intimidated by their watching.

Every confrontation confirms what they most fear: this man is either a blasphemer or he is what he claims to be. They have decided he is a blasphemer, and from that decision every subsequent action follows with a terrible logic.

Their fury is a rage that has stopped thinking. It is what a framework does when it has been exposed in public and its owners are unwilling to revise it. The alternative was to admit that a Galilean had understood the law of God better than the men who guarded it, and that admission would have cost them everything they were.

So these Sabbath controversies are not peripheral disputes about religious practice. They are the opening moves of the confrontation that will define history.
verseByVerse.examples:
The man with the withered hand is told to stand up and come out into the middle — to be visible, exposed, in front of everyone. He obeys, knowing his disability will be on display, and Luke records that he rose and stood there.

There is a kind of help that cannot be received privately. The person who keeps their need hidden, who manages a difficulty from the edge of the community, does not receive what the one standing in the middle receives. Jesus consistently calls his healings into the light.

And the command he gives is the one thing the man cannot do — stretching out that hand is the definition of his condition. The healing does not come first so that obedience becomes possible. He is told to do the impossible thing, and discovers in the doing that it is possible.

That is very often the order in the Christian life. The command comes before the strength to keep it, and the strength arrives inside the obedience — which is why so much of following Christ feels like being told to move a hand that does not work.

verseByVerse.quote: On another Sabbath, he entered the synagogue and was teaching, and a man was there whose right hand was withered. And the scribes and the Pharisees watched him, to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might find a reason to accuse him. But he knew their thoughts, and he said to the man with the withered hand, 'Come and stand here.' And he rose and stood there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On another Sabbath he entered the synagogue and was teaching, and a man was there whose right hand was withered. The scribes and the Pharisees watched him, to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might find a reason to accuse him. But he knew their thoughts, and he said to the man with the withered hand: come and stand here. And he rose and stood there.

On another Sabbath. A different day, a different setting, the same question, and this time the stakes are a man’s livelihood.

In the flow. Luke sets this second Sabbath scene straight after the claim that the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath (v. 5), and it shows that lordship at work. The first quarrel was about what the disciples did; this one is about what Jesus himself will do, and his critics are now watching him, not his men. The run of conflicts that began when he forgave a paralysed man (5:17–26) reaches its height here, in a synagogue, and ends with the first plotting against him (v. 11).

A man was there whose right hand was withered. Only Luke, the doctor, notes that it was the right hand: the working hand. In a manual economy that is not an inconvenience; it is the end of a man’s ability to earn. Withered means shrunken, paralysed. He is in the synagogue on the Sabbath, as he presumably is every week, with a hand that has not worked for years and no expectation that today will differ.

The scribes and the Pharisees watched him. Watched (paretērounto) means watched closely, spied on. They were there not to worship but to catch him out, and Luke tells us exactly why: so that they might find a reason to accuse him. They are in a house of God, on the day of God, hoping a disabled man will be healed so that they can bring a charge. The man’s hand is of no interest to them except as evidence. That is what religion becomes when it has stopped serving God and started defending itself. It can sit in a service, look at a suffering man, and see an opportunity.

To see whether he would heal on the Sabbath. By the rabbis’ rule, healing counted as work, and was allowed on the Sabbath only if life was in danger. A withered hand could wait until tomorrow.

But he knew their thoughts. Luke says it flatly, as he did when Jesus read the scribes who silently accused him of blasphemy (5:22). Only God searches the heart (Jeremiah 17:10), and Jesus reads these men as easily as he reads Scripture. So he walks into the trap knowing it is a trap. He knows that if he heals this hand the plotting will begin, and it does (6:11). He could protect himself by doing nothing until sundown. He will not buy his own safety with this man’s withered hand. Here, in one small room, is the whole pattern of his ministry: he sees exactly what mercy will cost him, and he chooses mercy, all the way to the cross.

Come and stand here. Literally, stand in the middle. Jesus does not avoid the confrontation. He makes the healing public, in full view of his critics. He could have healed the man quietly at the end of the service. Instead he puts him in the centre of the room.

And he rose and stood there. He has spent years managing a disability from the edge of the room, and he is now standing in the middle of it with his hand exposed and a row of officials staring. He does not know what is coming. There is a kind of help that cannot be received privately.

Should I deliberately provoke people who oppose me? No. Jesus did not seek conflict for its own sake; he sought the man’s good and the truth, and refused to let fear of critics hide either. Christians are to live peaceably with all, as far as it depends on them (Romans 12:18), and to answer opponents with gentleness (2 Timothy 2:24–25). What this verse forbids is the opposite fault: doing good only when no critic is watching, or abandoning what is right because someone is waiting to accuse you. Be quiet where quietness serves; be open where hiding would mean failing someone.

In a sentence. In the synagogue on another Sabbath, with scribes and Pharisees watching to accuse him, Jesus, knowing their thoughts, called a man with a withered right hand to stand in front of everyone.

On a Tuesday. Don’t let fear of critics stop you doing good openly.

For worship. He saw the man at the edge of the room whom everyone else had stopped noticing, and he called him into the middle, where mercy could be seen. That is what he does with us: he brings our withered places out of hiding, not to shame us but to heal us. No critic’s stare could stop him doing good, and no hiding place can keep us from his kindness.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke, the doctor, notes that it was the right hand. By the rabbis’ rule, healing a condition that was not life-threatening should wait until the Sabbath was over.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, 'I ask you, is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it?' And after looking around at them all he said to him, 'Stretch out your hand.' And he did so, and his hand was restored.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them: I ask you, is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it? After looking around at them all he said to him: stretch out your hand. And he did so, and his hand was restored.

Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm. The question is deadly, and it is worth seeing why they cannot answer it. They came prepared for a different argument. Their case was that healing is work, that this man’s condition is not life-threatening, and that a hand withered for years can perfectly well wait until sundown, which, on their own terms, is a reasonable position. Even their own tradition permitted saving a life on the Sabbath. Nobody’s life is at risk here. Jesus refuses the terms. He reframes the question: not, is healing work?, but, what is the Sabbath for? By pairing doing good with its opposite he removes the middle ground they were standing on. There is no neutral square marked, wait until tomorrow. To fail to do good when you can is to do harm.

To save life or to destroy it? Life (psychē) can also mean soul. And the irony: Jesus is doing good on the Sabbath, while his critics are plotting to destroy him on the Sabbath (v. 11).

Stricter, not laxer. That is the principle behind the whole of his Sabbath teaching, and it is not lax. It is stricter than theirs. Their rule asked what may be avoided. His asks what may be done, and a day designed by a God who never stops sustaining his creation cannot be a day for withholding mercy.

And after looking around at them all. A long, searching look. Mark says with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart (Mark 3:5). The look goes round the room, one face at a time, and in that silence they have already answered, and they know it.

Stretch out your hand. The very thing he could not do. Jesus did no work that could be charged: no touch, no medicine, just a word. And notice what is asked. Stretch out your hand is the one thing this man cannot do; it is the definition of his condition. The healing does not come first, so that he could then obey. He is told to do the impossible thing, and in the doing of it he discovers it is possible. The command brings the power to obey.

And his hand was restored. Made whole, as it had been. And that is very often the order. The command comes before the strength to keep it, and the strength arrives inside the obedience, which is why so much of the Christian life feels like being told to move a hand that does not work. Forgive, he says, to a heart that cannot; love your enemy, to a will that refuses; and the one who commands is the one who gives (Philippians 2:12–13).

But I cannot obey. What do I do with a command I have no strength to keep? Do what the man did: try, in dependence on Christ. Do not wait until you feel able; you may never feel able. Ask him for help, and then take the first small step he commands: the first sentence of the apology, the first prayer for your enemy, the first refusal of the old habit. God works in you both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13), and very often his strength is felt only in the moving. If you fail, confess it, receive his forgiveness, and stretch out your hand again tomorrow.

In a sentence. Jesus asked whether it was lawful on the Sabbath to do good or harm, to save life or destroy it, and then told the man to stretch out his hand, and it was restored.

On a Tuesday. Failing to do good when you can is not neutral. Look for the good you can do today.

For worship. He did not touch the hand. He spoke, as he spoke on the first day of the world, and it was so, because the one standing in that synagogue is the Word through whom all things were made (John 1:3). Sinews that had lain dead for years heard their Maker’s voice. And he said it in the face of men already planning his death: he saved life on the Sabbath while they sat counting how to destroy it, and in the end he let them destroy his, so that withered sinners might live.

verseByVerse.quote: But they were filled with fury and discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they were filled with fury and discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus.

But they were filled with fury. Fury (anoias) is literally mindlessness, a rage that has stopped thinking. And it is the response to a man’s hand being made whole. No law of Moses has been broken; Jesus did not so much as touch him. A disabled man in their own congregation can work again, and the reaction of the religious leadership is not joy but the beginning of a plot. Their religion had made them blind to mercy.

And discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus. The plotting begins. Mark says they began to plot with the Herodians how to destroy him (Mark 3:6). Luke’s wording is milder at this stage, but the direction is clear. From here the shadow does not lift. The cause was a question they could not answer and a mercy they could not permit.

Why such rage? Not because they were unusually wicked men. Because he had made their position untenable in public, and they were not willing to revise it. Fury is what a framework does when it has been exposed and its owners have decided to keep it. The alternative was to admit that a Galilean had understood the law of God better than the men who guarded it, and that admission would have cost them everything they were. So the mind goes past the argument to the arguer. If the position cannot be defended, remove the man who exposed it.

An ordinary mechanism. It does not require a council. It happens in churches and families, wherever somebody has said something true that cannot be answered, and the response is not to weigh it but to discredit the person who said it. The fury feels like conviction from the inside. It is nearly always the sound of a defence that has run out.

Hated for doing good. Here, for the first time, the leaders of Israel begin to plan against him, and the cause is not any wrong he did but the good. That is the mystery Luke wants us to feel. He is the one man who has ever lived without sin, and the nearer his goodness comes to sinners, the more it is resented, because light exposes (John 3:19–20). They hated me without a cause, he will say (John 15:25). Yet he does not withdraw his goodness to save himself. He goes on healing the people who will cry for his death, and he dies for enemies (Romans 5:10). The fury in this room is the first shadow of the cross, and the man it falls on is walking towards it of his own will.

How do I know whether my anger is righteous? Righteous anger is anger at what grieves God, for the sake of others, and it stays under control and seeks good.
