Jesus was angry in this very scene (Mark 3:5), grieved at hardness of heart, and he healed the man. Sinful anger is usually about me: my position, my pride, my being shown up, and it seeks to hurt. Ask: what exactly am I angry about? Would God be angry at it? Does my anger make me want to help someone, or to win? Be angry and do not sin (Ephesians 4:26); and if you find you are furious with someone who has told you the truth, stop and listen before you speak.

In a sentence. The scribes and Pharisees were filled with senseless rage and discussed what they could do to Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Religion without love can make people furious at the very goodness of God. Examine your reactions when God blesses people in ways you don’t expect.

For worship. They planned his destruction on the day he restored a man’s hand, and he knew it, and he went on doing good. The rage of men could not turn him aside, and their plot, when it ripened, became the means of our salvation. The wrath of man shall praise him (Psalm 76:10). What they meant for evil, God meant for good, and the hands they would nail to a cross are the hands that still restore the withered and the broken.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Before choosing the twelve, Jesus spends the whole night in prayer on the mountain. This is characteristic of Luke: the major decisions of the ministry are set in the context of prayer. And the placing is deliberate — Luke has just recorded the first plot against Jesus, and the next thing he records is a night on a hillside.

The choice of twelve from a larger body of disciples is not made lightly or impulsively. Luke gives the two stages precisely: he called the disciples, and from them he chose twelve.

The number is not convenient; it is theological. Israel had twelve tribes named for twelve sons, and no Jew could hear the number accidentally. Jesus is not assembling a staff. He is constituting a people — and at the end of the Bible the wall of the city has twelve foundations bearing these men's names (Rev. 21:14).

They are called apostles here for the first time in Luke — apostoloi, sent ones. They remain disciples, learners; but a disciple who has been given an errand is something more.

The list itself is a study in unlikely combinations. Peter, who a chapter ago asked Jesus to leave because he was a sinful man. Matthew, the tax collector from the booth. And Simon the Zealot — a man whose title points to zeal for Israel and the law, and very possibly to sympathy with armed resistance to Rome. In ordinary life Matthew and Simon would not have shared a road. They shared a purse and a mission for three years.

Several of the twelve are almost unknown — James the son of Alphaeus above all, of whom the Gospels record no words and no deeds, nothing but a name in the lists.

And the list ends with Judas Iscariot, “who became a traitor.” Luke will not let his reader meet him without the ending attached, and the wording matters: not who was a traitor but who became one. He was chosen after the night of prayer, with the others, and heard and saw everything they did.
verseByVerse.theology:
The apostles are distinguished from disciples by a specific function: they are sent ones, commissioned witnesses rather than merely learners. Their testimony to the life, death and resurrection of Jesus will be the foundation of the church's proclamation.

Paul will later say the church is “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone” (Eph. 2:20). The night of prayer before the choice establishes that this foundation is not a human selection but a divinely guided one, even though the divine guidance works through a human process.

Luke's parenthesis on Judas — chosen deliberately, after a night of communion with the Father, and yet becoming a traitor — is a weight the reader is not permitted to set down. Election to office is not the same as salvation, and proximity to Christ is no protection.

He handled the money, was sent out with power like the rest, and heard every word of the sermon that follows. The verb Luke chooses describes a process, not a category — which should sober anyone who has been near the things of God for a long time.
verseByVerse.examples:
The night of prayer before the choice models the principle that consequential decisions belong to God before they belong to us. Not every decision requires a night of prayer — but every decision that will shape the community of God's people belongs first to the Father.

The Jesus who spent a whole night praying before choosing twelve men puts a question to every leader, every elder board, every appointment committee: have we prayed as long and as seriously as this decision actually deserves?

And the composition of the twelve is a standing rebuke to congregations divided along political lines. Whatever holds a church together, it is not agreement about Rome, and the New Testament never once suggests it should be.

If a former agent of the Roman revenue and a man called the Zealot could eat from the same bag for three years, the divisions that currently make Christians unable to sit in the same room deserve a harder look than they usually get.

verseByVerse.quote: In these days he went out to the mountain to pray, and all night he continued in prayer to God. And when day came, he called his disciples and chose from them twelve, whom he named apostles:
verseByVerse.commentary:
In these days he went out to the mountain to pray, and all night he continued in prayer to God. When day came, he called his disciples and chose from them twelve, whom he named apostles.

He went out to the mountain to pray. Luke has just recorded the first plot against him. The next thing he records is a night on a hillside. Only Luke records this night of prayer. At a time of growing opposition (v. 11), and before a crucial decision, Jesus prays.

And all night he continued in prayer to God. The whole night, from dark to first light, alone. This is not a phrase to skim. Luke has shown us Jesus praying at the Jordan (3:21) and withdrawing to desolate places (5:16). This is the longest, and it comes before the largest decision of his ministry so far. The choice of the Twelve was so important that Jesus spent the night seeking his Father’s will. What he said out there for those hours we are not told, and it is better not to invent. What Luke gives us is the fact and the proportion: a whole night, for twelve men, and Judas among them.

He called his disciples and chose from them twelve. Two stages, and the wording matters. He called the disciples, a larger group of followers (Luke will mention seventy-two of them later, 10:1), and from them he chose twelve, an inner circle. This is selection, and it is his, and it comes out of the night. Twelve is not a convenient number. Israel had twelve tribes, named for twelve sons; a Jew could not hear it accidentally. Jesus is reconstituting the people of God around himself. He is not assembling a staff. He is constituting a people, and a man does not lay the foundations of Israel unless he is entitled to. The Twelve will sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes (22:30), and at the end of the Bible, the wall of the city has twelve foundations, and on them the names of these men (Revelation 21:14).

Whom he named apostles. Apostle (apostolos) means one who is sent, an envoy, an authorised representative, from the verb to send. A disciple is a learner, and they remain that. An apostle has been given an errand. They would be sent with his authority to preach (9:1–2), and after his resurrection, to be his witnesses to the world (24:48; Acts 1:8). Luke uses the title more than the other Gospels.

The apostles’ unique role. The apostles were eyewitnesses of the risen Christ (Acts 1:21–22), commissioned directly by him, and laid the foundation of the church through their teaching, which we have in the New Testament (Ephesians 2:20). There are no apostles in this sense today. Their teaching, in Scripture, is our foundation.

Two decisions. The men who decide he must be destroyed made their decision in fury, after a service. His was made alone, on a mountain, after a night of asking his Father, and it is the one that is still standing.

If Jesus prayed all night and still chose Judas, did his prayer fail? No. Jesus chose Judas knowingly: did I not choose you, the Twelve? And yet one of you is a devil (John 6:70). Prayer is not a way of getting a guarantee that everything will go smoothly; it is submitting our choices to the Father’s will, and the Father’s will included the betrayal, through which the Scriptures would be fulfilled and the world redeemed (Acts 2:23). So when you pray before a decision and it later brings pain, do not conclude that you missed God’s guidance. He may have led you exactly where he meant to, for purposes you cannot yet see.

In a sentence. After spending the whole night in prayer on a mountain, Jesus chose twelve of his disciples and named them apostles.

On a Tuesday. Pray before big decisions. If Jesus spent all night in prayer before choosing, how much more do you need to?

For worship. The Son of God climbed a mountain and spent a whole night with his Father before he named the men who would carry his gospel to the world. Every name was chosen in prayer, and every name was known. And the one who prayed over the Twelve prays still over all his people: I am praying for them, he said on the last night, for those whom you have given me, for they are yours (John 17:9). Before you ever chose him, he chose you, and he did it with his Father, in love.
verseByVerse.note: “Apostle” means one who is sent. Twelve matches the twelve tribes of Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Simon, whom he named Peter, and Andrew his brother, and James and John, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon who was called the Zealot, and Judas the son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon, whom he named Peter, and Andrew his brother, and James and John, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon who was called the Zealot, and Judas the son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.

Four lists. The Twelve are listed four times in the New Testament (Matthew 10:2–4; Mark 3:16–19; Luke 6:14–16; Acts 1:13). The order varies, but Peter is always first and Judas Iscariot always last. They fall into three groups of four, each headed by the same name (Peter, Philip, James son of Alphaeus). Luke sets the names down without comment. But look at who is in the list.

Simon, whom he named Peter. Peter (Petros, Aramaic Kēphas) means rock (Matthew 16:18; John 1:42). This is the fisherman who once begged Jesus to depart from him because he was a sinful man (5:8).

The one who gives new names. Luke says Jesus named him. In Scripture it is God who renames: Abram became Abraham, Jacob became Israel, each name a promise of what God would make of the man. Jesus does the same thing with the same authority. He calls Simon a rock before there is anything rock-like about him, and the rest of Luke’s two books show him keeping his word: the man who denies him three times by a fire in a courtyard stands up at Pentecost and preaches Christ to the city that crucified him. The list of the Twelve is a list of what Christ does with people. He takes them as they are, and names them for what his grace will make them.

Andrew his brother. Who first brought Peter to Jesus (John 1:40–42).

James and John. Sons of Zebedee, fishermen (5:10). James was the first apostle martyred (Acts 12:2); John wrote the Gospel, letters and Revelation.

Philip, and Bartholomew. Philip was from Bethsaida (John 1:44). Bartholomew (son of Tolmai) is probably the Nathanael of John 1:45–51, since he is paired with Philip.

Matthew. The tax collector at the booth in chapter 5, whom Luke calls Levi (5:27); Matthew’s own Gospel names the man at the booth Matthew (Matthew 9:9). A man who took money from his own people on behalf of the ruling power.

Thomas. The twin (John 11:16), remembered for his doubt and his great confession: my Lord and my God! (John 20:28).

James the son of Alphaeus. Possibly James the younger (Mark 15:40). Of him the Gospels record no words and no deeds, nothing but a name in the lists. Several of the Twelve are almost unknown. They gave their lives to this, and history kept only that they were chosen.

Simon who was called the Zealot. Zealot may mean zealous for the law, or a member of the nationalist movement that wanted to overthrow Rome by force. If so, he and Matthew, the tax collector who worked for Rome’s client, were political enemies, now united in Christ. Whatever precise stage the movement had reached by this date, the label meant a man of fierce conviction.

Enemies at one table. So in one company of twelve, Jesus may have put a former agent of the revenue and a man who believed such agents were traitors. In ordinary life these two would not have shared a road, let alone a purse and a mission. Luke does not tell us it was easy; he simply records that both names are there. Whatever holds a church together, it is not political agreement, and the New Testament never once suggests it should be. If Matthew and Simon could eat from the same bag, the divisions that make Christians unable to sit in the same room deserve a harder look than they usually get.

Judas the son of James. Probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark; the same man with two names. Also called Judas (not Iscariot) in John 14:22.

And Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor. And then the last name, with Luke’s terrible parenthesis. Became: he was not chosen as a traitor, but became one. He is in the list. He heard everything they heard, saw everything they saw, was sent out with power like the rest, and, John tells us, held the money bag (John 12:6). Luke will not let his reader meet him without the ending attached. He does not say who was a traitor. He says who became one, which is a sentence about a process, and it should sober anyone who has been near the things of God for a long time: outward closeness to Jesus is no guarantee of a true heart.

Could I become a Judas? Can a true Christian fall away? A true believer cannot finally be lost; those whom Christ has given eternal life will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28–29). Judas was never a true believer, though he looked like one; Jesus called him a devil while he walked with the Twelve (John 6:70), John tells us that Jesus knew from the beginning who would betray him (John 6:64), and Jesus said he was lost so that Scripture might be fulfilled (John 17:12). So the warning is not meant to terrify true believers but to wake up false ones. If you fear you are a Judas, that fear is itself a good sign: Judas did not fear it. Examine yourself (2 Corinthians 13:5), and run to Christ; no one who comes to him is cast out (John 6:37).

In a sentence. The twelve apostles were Peter, Andrew, James, John, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, Judas son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.

On a Tuesday. Jesus chose ordinary, very different, flawed men: fishermen, a tax collector, a zealot. He can use you. And he unites people who would otherwise be enemies.

For worship. Look at the list and marvel at the Lord who chose it. A man who would deny him, two brothers who wanted to call down fire, a doubter, a tax collector, a zealot, and several men we know nothing about, and he made them the foundation stones of his church. He chose the weak to shame the strong, the unknown to carry his name to the ends of the earth. And he has not changed his method. Your name, if you are his, is written in the Lamb’s book of life, from before the foundation of the world (Revelation 17:8; 21:27), by the same hand, in the same love.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s “Judas the son of James” is probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Sermon on the Plain begins with a declaration that sounds like a mistake on first reading: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.”

Luke's beatitudes are addressed directly to the disciples — “blessed are you” — unlike Matthew's more generalised forms. And they are paired with woes Matthew does not include. The poor are blessed and the rich are warned; the hungry are promised satisfaction and the full are warned of hunger; those who weep now will laugh, and those who laugh now will mourn.

The poverty is not romanticised. Luke does not say “poor in spirit” but simply “poor” — the destitute, those with nothing of their own who depend entirely on what others give. This is not a spiritualisation of poverty; it is the announcement that the kingdom belongs to those whose condition leaves no room for self-sufficiency. Not because poverty is virtuous, but because the poor have no resources to trust except God.

Set beside Matthew's “poor in spirit,” the two hold opposite ends of one truth, and neither is safe alone. Luke without Matthew makes an empty purse a ticket. Matthew without Luke lets “poor in spirit” be quietly spiritualised until it costs nothing. Matthew names the poverty God blesses; Luke names the room such people are usually standing in.

The woes are the other edge of the same blade. “Woe” (ouai) is the prophets' word, carrying grief as much as warning (Isa. 5:8-23; Amos 6:1-7). It is not a wish for harm but a declaration that those who have “received their consolation” have been paid already and have nothing further outstanding.

The last woe is the most searching: “Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets.” Israel's true prophets were consistently unwelcome; the popular ones were the ones who told the king what he wanted to hear.

And the final beatitude (vv. 22-23) is the only one about something the disciples bring on themselves. Four escalating forms of social death — hated, excluded, reviled, name thrown out as evil — and the command attached is not endurance but leaping.
verseByVerse.theology:
The beatitudes and woes together express the eschatological reversal — the biblical pattern in which the last days invert the present order. Mary sang it in the Magnificat: the mighty brought down, the humble exalted, the hungry filled, the rich sent away empty.

This is not a programme of economic analysis; it is a prophetic announcement about the direction of God's kingdom. Those whose present condition drives them to dependence on God are in the right position to receive what the kingdom gives; those who can be self-sufficient are in the wrong one.

Read through the whole gospel, these blessings and woes are far more than social reversal — they are anchored in Christ himself, who entered the very conditions he calls blessed. He became poor though he was rich (2 Cor. 8:9), hungered in the wilderness (4:2), wept real tears, and was hated, excluded and reviled for us.

The great reversal is therefore no abstract law of history but a sure thing purchased in him. We are not blessed for managing to be poor or hungry, but by being joined to the One who was made poor that we might be made rich, and who fills the empty out of his own fullness. And the woes are not cruelty but mercy raising its voice — a warning to the comfortable to loosen their grip on thin, passing riches before the day the tables turn.
verseByVerse.examples:
The beatitudes are often preached as comfort to those who suffer, and they are that. But they are also diagnosis and invitation. The question they put to every hearer is: in which column do you find yourself? The sermon does not allow a neutral answer; it creates a crisis of self-knowledge.

And the woes have to be applied honestly, because almost everyone reading them is, by any measure the world has ever used, among the rich. The question is not whether you enjoy good things but where your consolation actually comes from — what steadies you when the day has gone badly. A God who cannot be lost, or an arrangement that can?

“Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy” (v. 23) is the response Jesus commands to persecution — not stoic endurance, not grim determination, but leaping joy. The verb is the one used of the unborn John moving in Elizabeth's womb (1:41).

This is eschatological joy: the joy that knows how the story ends and can afford to leap because the future is secure. It is what Paul means in Romans 8:18 — the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed. The leap is only possible if the landing is sure.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came down with them and stood on a level place, with a great crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon, who came to hear him and to be healed of their diseases. And those who were troubled with unclean spirits were cured. And all the crowd sought to touch him, for power came out from him and healed them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came down with them and stood on a level place, with a great crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon, who came to hear him and to be healed of their diseases. Those who were troubled with unclean spirits were cured. And all the crowd sought to touch him, for power came out from him and healed them all.

The Sermon on the Plain. What follows (vv. 20–49) is Luke’s version of Jesus’ great sermon, shorter than Matthew’s Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7), with much of the same material. Luke’s version has less about the Jewish law, which would have interested his Gentile readers less, and it includes four woes that Matthew does not have.

In the flow. The order of the chapter matters. Jesus has just been rejected by the guardians of the old ways (v. 11) and has chosen twelve men as the foundation of a renewed Israel (vv. 12–16). Now he tells that new people how they are to live. The new wine of 5:37–39 is poured out here in words: blessing given before anything is asked, love for enemies, mercy like the Father’s. And the sermon ends with two houses (vv. 46–49), so that no one who hears it can treat it as a fine speech and nothing more.

One sermon or two? Luke says Jesus came down and stood on a level place; Matthew says he went up on the mountain and sat down (Matthew 5:1). What follows in each has obvious overlap, beatitudes, love of enemies, judge not, the tree and its fruit, the two builders at the end, and equally obvious differences. Matthew runs to three chapters where Luke runs to thirty verses; Luke adds four woes Matthew does not have; Matthew includes long stretches on the law, prayer and fasting that Luke places elsewhere. Both answers have been held by careful readers, and neither damages anything. Some take them as the same occasion from different angles: the phrase Luke uses need not mean flat ground at the foot of a hill; it can as easily mean a plateau or a shelf on the hillside. Others take them as two occasions, which is simply what travelling preachers do. Jesus spent perhaps three years saying these things village by village, and no teacher says a thing once. Either way the words are his, and the differences are not contradictions but the ordinary shape of a real ministry. The same voice is speaking in both, and it is asking for the same life.

And he came down with them. Jesus comes down from the mountain with the newly chosen Twelve, like Moses coming down from the mountain with the law. But Jesus brings the law of the kingdom.

From all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon. The crowd is enormous, and it is deliberately described. Jews from the south, the religious heartland, and people from the Gentile coastal cities of the north, pagan cities on the Phoenician coast, the country Elijah was sent to (4:26). Luke’s map is already the map of Acts: a foretaste of the gospel to all nations.

For power came out from him and healed them all. They came to hear him and to be healed, hearing first, as Luke always puts it, and both happen. The power of God (5:17), flowing from him (8:46). The word is dynamis: something goes out of him. Healing is not a technique he applies. So the sermon is not addressed to a neutral audience. Every person in earshot has just seen the demonised freed and the sick made well. When he says, blessed are you who are poor, he is saying it to people who have already had evidence.

Is the Sermon on the Plain a way to be saved, or a way to live? A way to live, for those who are being saved. It is addressed to disciples (v. 20), people who have already come to him, and it begins not with commands but with blessings: the kingdom is given before anything is asked. Its demands are real and searching, and no one keeps them perfectly; they show us how far we fall short and drive us to Christ, who kept them for us. But they are also the actual shape of the new life he gives. We do not obey this sermon in order to be accepted; we obey it because we have been, and because the one who preached it lives in us by his Spirit.

In a sentence. Jesus came down with the Twelve to a level place, where crowds from Judea, Jerusalem and the Gentile coast came to hear him and be healed, and power went out from him and healed them all.

On a Tuesday. Come to Jesus to hear him, as well as to receive from him.

For worship. Before he said a word of the sermon, he healed them all. Jews and Gentiles, the city crowd and the coastal pagans, every one of them who touched him went away whole. That is the order of the kingdom: grace first, then the call. The one who would ask them to love without return had just poured out his power on people who had nothing to give him. He came down from the mountain to the level place, to stand where we stand, and the power that came out of him then is the same power that has reached us now.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre and Sidon were Gentile port cities to the north. Luke’s sermon is given on a “level place”; Matthew’s similar sermon on a mountain.

verseByVerse.quote: And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said: 'Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said: blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.

And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples. The sermon is addressed to disciples, though the crowd hears it. It describes the life of those who follow him.

The Beatitudes. Luke gives four blessings (vv. 20–23) and four matching woes (vv. 24–26). Matthew gives nine blessings and no woes (Matthew 5:3–12). Luke’s are in the second person (you), spoken while looking at them, to actual people whose circumstances everyone standing there could see; Matthew’s in the third (those who).

Blessed. Makarioi: not happy in a shallow sense, but fortunate, in a good position before God, approved by him. The Hebrew equivalent opens the Psalms: blessed is the man (Psalm 1:1). It is God’s verdict, not a feeling.

Are you who are poor. Luke’s word is ptōchoi, which is not the word for someone of modest means. It means destitute: a beggar, a person with nothing of their own who depends entirely on what others give. Matthew says poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3). Luke speaks of the poor as they actually were. Many of Jesus’ disciples were literally poor, having left everything (5:11, 28). But in the Old Testament, the poor were also the humble, who had no one to depend on but God (Psalm 34:6; Isaiah 61:1; 66:2). Poverty is not itself a virtue, and not every poor person is blessed. But the poor are often more ready to receive the kingdom, because they know their need.

Luke and Matthew together. A reader who knows Matthew will stop here, because Matthew’s blessed are the poor in spirit and Luke’s flat blessed are you who are poor sound like different sentences. Did one of them adjust the Lord’s words? No: they hold two ends of one truth, and neither end is safe alone. Take Luke without Matthew and you get the error that poverty itself saves, as though an empty purse were a ticket. Take Matthew without Luke and you get the more respectable error: poor in spirit quietly spiritualised into a humble feeling entertained by comfortable people whose lives stay precisely as they were. Put them together and it stands clear. Matthew names the poverty God blesses: the poverty of a man who knows he has nothing to bring. Luke names where such people are usually found. It is far easier to know you have nothing when you actually have nothing, because money is extraordinarily good at hiding from us the emptiness we all have before him. Matthew names the empty hands; Luke names the room they are usually standing in.

For yours is the kingdom of God. Present tense: it is yours now. They have no earthly security, but they have God’s kingdom, the greatest wealth of all (12:32). Heaven keeps a different ledger from the one the world keeps. What does it mean to have the kingdom? The kingdom of God is God’s saving rule through his King. To have it is to live under that rule now, forgiven, cared for and belonging to him, and to inherit his new world when it comes in full (22:29–30).

Good news to the poor. Not long before, in the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus had read Isaiah’s words and claimed them: the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor (4:18). Now he does it. This beatitude is not a wise man’s observation about poverty; it is the Messiah’s announcement, made by the Anointed One himself. And that is why he can say yours is, and not yours will be. The kingdom is present because the King is present, standing on that level ground with his eyes on them. To have him is to have the kingdom. The poor are blessed not because their poverty is a virtue but because the King has come to them first, and given himself.

I am not poor. Is this beatitude for me? Yes, if you come the way the poor come. Before God every one of us is destitute: we have nothing to offer him that is not already his, and no righteousness of our own (Isaiah 64:6). The comfortable Christian must learn by grace what the poor man often knows by experience: that he lives entirely on what God gives. So hold your possessions as a steward, not an owner; receive salvation as a beggar, not a customer; and let your money flow towards the poor, so that it does not wall you off from them or from God. The kingdom is given to empty hands, whatever is in the bank.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples that they who are poor are blessed, because the kingdom of God belongs to them.

On a Tuesday. Come to God as one who is poor, with nothing to offer. The kingdom belongs to such people.

Where it applies: An elderly widow in your church lives on very little, and trusts Christ. Do not pity her as one who has missed out. She is rich in the kingdom, and you may learn more from her than she from you.

Where it would be wrong: Someone thinks poverty in itself makes a person right with God, or uses this verse as a reason not to help the poor, since they are blessed already. The poor Jesus blesses are those who look to God (Matthew 5:3), and the same Lord commands us to open our hands to them (1 John 3:17).

For worship. He looked at a crowd of day labourers and widows and beggars and said, yours is the kingdom. And he could say it because he had made himself poor: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). The King of heaven was laid in a manger and buried in another man’s tomb, so that the destitute could inherit everything. Blessed be the Lord who fills empty hands with a kingdom.

parallels.desc: has not God chosen those who are poor?

verseByVerse.quote: 'Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied. 'Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied. Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh.

Blessed are you who are hungry now. Two more blessings, both in the plainest terms, with a now attached that only Luke has: present hunger, future satisfaction. Luke means it as flatly as it sounds: people who did not eat enough yesterday. Real hunger, physical (the poor often went hungry), but also hunger for God and righteousness (Matthew 5:6). Mary sang: he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty (1:53). Hunger is not a virtue, and Jesus never says it is. What he says is that the condition which the world reads as God’s absence is, in his accounting, the condition of people who are about to be filled.

For you shall be satisfied. Future tense. At the messianic banquet (13:29; 14:15; Isaiah 25:6), and in a measure even now. Satisfied completely: the word is used of animals fed full. And the filling is not a metaphor. There is a table at the end of this book, and the guest list was drawn up from the streets and lanes (14:21).

Blessed are you who weep now. Those who grieve over suffering, over their own sin, and over the world’s rebellion against God. Those who mourn (Matthew 5:4). He does not tell them to stop, or suggest that the tears are a failure of faith. He lets the weeping stand and puts a date on it.

For you shall laugh. Joy will come. God will wipe away every tear (Isaiah 25:8; Revelation 21:4). And the promised end of it is not relief, or peace, or resignation. It is laughter, which is a startling word to use of the far side of grief, and he chose it. The psalmist had reached for the same thing: those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy (Psalm 126:5). Not a quiet settling. Shouting.

The pattern. The kingdom reverses present conditions: those who suffer now with Christ will rejoice with him later, which is the logic of the cross and resurrection. The hunger is now. The weeping is now. Neither is denied, minimised or explained. What is denied is that now is the last word about them.

Who is speaking. This is not a technique for feeling better, and it will not work as one. It is a claim about how the story ends, made by the only person entitled to make it. The one who promises to fill the hungry had gone forty days without food in a desert (4:2). The one who promises laughter to the weeping wept himself at a friend’s grave (John 11:35) and over Jerusalem (19:41). He is not calling out advice from the dry ground. He has been in the water.

Is it wrong for a Christian to grieve? No. Jesus blesses those who weep; he does not rebuke them. Paul does not tell the grieving Thessalonians to stop, only not to grieve as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Grief is love continuing after loss, and the psalms are full of honest lament. You do not have to pretend to be fine, or hurry yourself out of sorrow to prove your faith. Bring your tears to God; he keeps count of them (Psalm 56:8). The promise is not that you will stop feeling the loss tomorrow, but that the one who is with you in the weeping will one day turn it into laughter.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced blessed those who are hungry and weeping now, because they will be filled and will laugh.

On a Tuesday. If you are weeping now, take heart: Jesus promises you will laugh. Your present sorrow is not the end.

Where it applies: A friend has lost her husband, and three months on she is still crying in church. Do not tell her it is time to move on, or that a strong Christian would be rejoicing by now. Sit with her, let her weep, and remind her gently that Jesus calls her blessed, and that the morning is coming.

Where it would be wrong: A neighbour has no food in the house, and you tell him he is blessed and will be satisfied in the kingdom, and leave it there. This beatitude is never a reason to leave the hungry hungry. If a brother or sister is without daily food and you say, be warmed and filled, without giving them what they need, what good is that? (James 2:15–16). Bring the promise and the groceries.

For worship. On the evening of the first Easter, Luke tells us, the frightened disciples saw their Lord alive, and they disbelieved for joy (24:41). Then he asked for something to eat, and ate broiled fish in front of them. That room is this beatitude coming true in miniature: weeping turned to a joy too large to believe, and a table where the risen Christ himself sits down to eat. What he did for that grieving company on that night, he will do for all his people at the great supper of the kingdom. The now is real, but it is not long. The morning has already broken in him.

parallels.desc: those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy

verseByVerse.quote: 'Blessed are you when people hate you and when they exclude you and revile you and spurn your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man! Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven; for so their fathers did to the prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are you when people hate you and when they exclude you and revile you and spurn your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man! Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven; for so their fathers did to the prophets.

When people hate you and when they exclude you. The fourth beatitude is the longest, the most specific, and the only one about something that will happen to the disciples because they follow him. Four verbs, and they escalate. Hatred: the inward turn. Exclusion: being cut off from synagogue, family and community (John 9:22; 16:2). Reviling: insult to the face. Spurning your name as evil: your name, or the name Christian, treated as a curse (1 Peter 4:14–16). That is a complete social death, staged in four moves.

On account of the Son of Man! Not for being obnoxious, but for Christ’s sake. There is no promise here for the Christian who is excluded for being rude, or hated for opinions that have nothing to do with Christ. The clause is narrow on purpose. Persecution counts when it is about him. Suffering for wrongdoing has no blessing (1 Peter 4:15).

Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy. Not endure; not bear it patiently. Leap, like a lamb in spring, or like John in the womb (1:41, the same word). Jesus tells people who are about to lose their standing, their livelihood and their families to jump for joy on the day it happens. The apostles did exactly this: they left the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41).

For behold, your reward is great in heaven. The reason for joy: God sees, and will reward. Not that we earn heaven by suffering, but that God honours faithfulness. The joy is not about the circumstance; it is about the accounting. Something is being stored where none of this can reach it.

For so their fathers did to the prophets. Persecution puts you in the company of the prophets. It is a mark of belonging to God’s true servants (11:47–51; 13:34). Exclusion is company: look at who else was treated like this, and every one of them is now honoured by the descendants of the men who threw them out.

The landing is certain. The leap is only possible if the landing is certain, and nobody jumps in the dark. What makes this command sane rather than cruel is the phrase on account of the Son of Man. It binds the sufferer to Christ so closely that what is done to the one is done to the other. Years later, when Saul of Tarsus was hunting Christians from house to house, the risen Lord stopped him on the road with a question: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). The disciple who is thrown out for his name is never thrown out alone. He is held by the one whose name it is, the Son of Man who has received everlasting dominion, and the reward is with him.

How can I rejoice when it hurts? Rejoicing here does not mean pretending it does not hurt, or enjoying pain. It means looking past the hurt to what it means and where it leads. It means you belong to Christ; it means you stand with the prophets; it means a reward is being kept for you that no one can take. Paul could be sorrowful, yet always rejoicing (2 Corinthians 6:10). Begin by thanking God, honestly, even through tears, that you were counted worthy to share a little of his Son’s rejection. Then pray for those who wronged you (v. 28). Joy usually follows the thanks rather than coming before it.

In a sentence. Jesus called his disciples blessed when they are hated, excluded and insulted for his sake, and told them to leap for joy, because their reward in heaven is great, as the prophets’ was.

On a Tuesday. If you are mocked or excluded for following Christ, rejoice. You are in the company of the prophets, and God will reward you.

Where it applies: You are left out of a family group chat because you became a Christian. Do not answer with bitterness. Rejoice: you are in the company of the prophets.

Where it would be wrong: You are left out because you lecture everyone at family meals. That is not being hated for the Son of Man’s sake. Ask first whether the offence is Christ or your manner (1 Peter 3:15–16).

For worship. He was hated without a cause, excluded from his own town, reviled on the cross, and his name was spat out as the name of a deceiver. He went first down the road he describes, and he did it for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). Now the name men spurned is the name above every name. Those who share his rejection will share his glory, and on that day the leaping will be for ever.

parallels.desc: they will put you out of the synagogues

verseByVerse.quote: 'But woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. 'Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. 'Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep.

Woe. Only Luke records these woes, the mirror image of the blessings. Woe (ouai) is a cry of grief and warning, used by the prophets: Isaiah’s woe to those who join house to house (Isaiah 5:8–23), Amos’s woe to those who are at ease in Zion (Amos 6:1). Not a curse, and not a wish for harm, but a lament: how terrible for you. It is the sound a man makes looking at people walking towards a cliff.

Woe to you who are rich. Not that wealth is sinful in itself. But wealth tends to make people self-sufficient, satisfied with this world, and blind to their need of God (12:16–21; 16:19–31; 18:24–25). It is a great danger.

For you have received your consolation. Received (apechete) is a business word, used on receipts: paid in full. That is the whole argument in one verb. It is not that the rich are excluded. It is that they have already collected: the comfort has been drawn, and there is nothing further outstanding. Abraham said the same to the rich man: you in your lifetime received your good things (16:25).

Your consolation. The word for consolation is the one Luke used of old Simeon, who was waiting for the consolation of Israel (2:25), and found it when he took the infant Jesus in his arms. Israel’s consolation was a person. That gives the woe its edge. The rich are not condemned for having comfort but for having settled for a comfort that is not him. They have drawn their consolation in advance, in things, and feel no need of the one who stands in front of them as God’s comfort in flesh. Simeon was content to die once he had held Christ. The rich man in this verse can hold everything except Christ, and calls it enough.

Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. Those who are satisfied with this world’s goods, and feel no spiritual hunger. Each woe is the exact mirror of a blessing, and each turns on the same now.

Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep. Not innocent laughter, but the careless laughter of those who do not take God or sin or suffering seriously (James 4:9).

Almost everyone reading this is rich. By any measure the world has ever used, almost everyone reading this is among the rich, and it will not do to hurry past into a general remark about materialism. So let it be put as a question. Where is your consolation actually coming from? Not what you would say in church, but what actually steadies you when the day has gone badly. The danger these verses describe is not enjoying good things. It is being consoled by them, until the kingdom starts sounding like an optional extra for people whose lives are not working. A man who has been paid already does not come to collect.

How rich is too rich? Scripture sets no figure, and the question usually hides a hope of being just under the line. The better questions are these. Am I trusting my money for security instead of God (1 Timothy 6:17)? Could I give a large part of it away without feeling that my life was gone? Is my giving generous, regular and costly, or the leftovers? Do I know any poor people by name? Is my spending shaped by love for others or by keeping up with those around me? If those answers trouble you, the remedy is not guilt but generosity: begin giving more, and more joyfully, and let money become a servant again.

In a sentence. Jesus warned that the rich, the full and those who laugh now have had their comfort already, and will hunger and weep.

On a Tuesday. If you are rich, full and laughing, examine yourself. Is your comfort in this world, or in God? Hold your blessings with humility and generosity.

Where it applies: You have plenty. Give generously this month to someone who has little, and give thanks for what you have, holding it loosely.

Where it would be wrong: You look down on wealthy Christians, or feel guilty over every good meal. The woe is on those whose comfort is in their riches instead of God. Abraham, Joseph of Arimathea and Lydia were wealthy and faithful (Genesis 13:2; Matthew 27:57; Acts 16:14–15). Paul tells the rich not to hope in riches but to be rich in good works (1 Timothy 6:17–18).

For worship. The woes are spoken with grief, by the Lord who would later weep over Jerusalem (19:41) and who did not want anyone to be paid off with this world. And he took the woe on himself. He who was rich became hungry, mourned, and on the cross looked for comforters and found none (Psalm 69:20), so that people who had settled for a receipt might be given a river. His warnings are mercy too: he tells us where the cliff is because he would rather we came home.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke records these woes, the mirror image of the blessings.

parallels.desc: woe to those at ease in Zion

verseByVerse.quote: 'Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets.

When all people speak well of you. This is the most searching sentence in the sermon, and it is aimed squarely at anyone who speaks for God. Universal popularity is a danger sign. A faithful witness to Christ will always offend some (v. 22). If everyone is speaking well of you, either you have said nothing worth opposing, or you have said what people wanted to hear.

For so their fathers did to the false prophets. The logic is exact. Israel had true prophets and false ones, and there was a reliable way to tell them apart from the outside: not their doctrine, which took discernment, but their popularity. The true prophets were nearly always unwelcome. Jeremiah was thrown into a cistern. Micaiah was hated because he never prophesied good concerning the king (1 Kings 22:8). Amos was told to go and prophesy somewhere else (Amos 7:12). The false prophets, meanwhile, had access, standing and a hearing at court, because they told people what they wanted. Peace, peace, when there is no peace (Jeremiah 6:14; 1 Kings 22:13; Isaiah 30:10). The true prophets were persecuted; the false ones were praised.

When all spoke well of him. Luke has already shown us this verse lived out, by Jesus himself. In the synagogue at Nazareth, after he read Isaiah, all spoke well of him and marvelled at his gracious words (4:22). It was the moment every preacher dreams of. He did not stop there. He went on to say what they did not want to hear: that Elijah was sent to a widow of Sidon and Elisha cleansed a Syrian, and within minutes the congregation that had praised him was driving him to the edge of a cliff (4:24–29). He gave up the good opinion of his home town rather than shave a word off the truth. The one who warns against the praise of all is the one who, when he had it, let it go.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should try to be unpopular, or that being well thought of is always wrong (Acts 2:47; 1 Timothy 3:7). But seeking everyone’s approval will lead to compromising the truth. It is not a licence for being obnoxious. Some people are disliked for reasons that have nothing to do with Christ, and a man who has made himself unpleasant may console himself that he is being persecuted when he is only being avoided. The beatitude four verses earlier was carefully limited, on account of the Son of Man, and this woe carries the same limit. And Luke will shortly commend a centurion whom the whole town liked (7:4–5).

The temptation to shave the corners off. What the verse forbids is the pursuit of universal approval by someone who is meant to be carrying a message: finding the version of the truth that will not cost anything with this person, in this room. It works. Everyone speaks well of you. That is precisely what the false prophets did, and every one of them was wrong.

How do I speak the truth without being needlessly offensive? Separate the offence of the message from the offence of the messenger. The cross will offend some people whatever you do (1 Corinthians 1:23); your tone, timing and manner should offend no one. So speak when asked, or when love requires it, rather than at every opportunity. Listen first, and understand the person. Say the hard thing kindly, briefly and without contempt, and be honest about your own need of grace. Let your speech be gracious, seasoned with salt (Colossians 4:6). If people still object, let it be to Christ, not to you.

In a sentence. Jesus warned that being praised by everyone is a danger, because that is how people treated the false prophets.

On a Tuesday. Are you more concerned about pleasing people than pleasing God (Galatians 1:10)? Speak the truth in love, even when it is unpopular.

Where it applies: Your friends all approve of something Scripture calls sin, and expect you to cheer. Gently say what you believe, even if it costs you their good opinion.

Where it would be wrong: You take being disliked as proof that you are faithful, and do not care what outsiders think of you. Unpopularity proves nothing on its own. An elder must be well thought of by outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7), and Christians are to commend the gospel by honest, kind lives (1 Peter 2:12).

For worship. He lost the praise of his home town in one sermon and of his nation in one week, and he never bought it back with a softer word, nor ever spoke an unkind one. What he sought was the voice that had spoken over the Jordan: you are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased (3:22). And here is the wonder. The Son who bore the world’s evil word now shares his Father’s good word with all who are in him. Men may speak ill of us; God has spoken well of us in his Son, and that verdict is never revised.

parallels.desc: the prophets prophesy falsely, and my people love to have it so

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“But I say to you who hear: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you.” This is probably the most demanding ethical command in the New Testament, and it is not an aspiration but an imperative, repeated in four parallel forms.

All four are verbs of action, and none is a verb of feeling — which matters enormously for anyone who has read this and concluded they cannot do it. He does not command warm feelings; he commands treatment. And the four escalate in cost: do good can be done at a distance; bless requires words; pray for is hardest, because it cannot be done insincerely for long.

The natural instinct is reciprocity — love those who love you, do good to those who do good to you. Jesus points out that reciprocal love proves nothing: “even sinners love those who love them.” It requires no faith and no change of heart; self-interest produces it unaided. The question the passage forces is whether anything in a Christian's life could not have been produced by ordinary human decency.

The ground of the command is not the worthiness of the enemy. There is no suggestion that the enemy deserves love. The ground is the character of God, “for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.” The disciple who loves enemies is not performing an act of heroic willpower; he is showing a family resemblance.

The concrete instructions in vv. 29-30 — the cheek, the cloak, the beggar, the goods taken — have been read both as absolute commands and as radical illustrations of a disposition. What is certain is their subject: a backhanded blow was an insult to honour, and the cloak is taken by force. These are about personal affront and personal loss, and what is forbidden is the reflex of retaliation and the worship of one's own dignity.

They are not, and have never been, a command to remain within reach of violence. Jesus walked away from a crowd that meant to kill him (4:29-30); Paul invoked his citizenship against an unlawful flogging (Acts 16:37).

“Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful” (v. 36) is the summary — and mercy presupposes a real debt and then declines to collect it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The command to love enemies is the most radical expression of grace in the New Testament — and it is exactly what God has done towards his own. “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us… while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Rom. 5:8, 10).

The cross is the supreme act of love towards enemies. The disciple who loves an enemy is not doing something beyond what God has done; he is doing what has already been done to him, and doing it because he received it. The ethics of the sermon flow from its gospel: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

Luke's “be merciful, even as your Father is merciful” is a different formulation from Matthew's “be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5:48), and the difference is instructive. Matthew names the standard; Luke names the specific attribute this whole section reflects. In a passage about enemies, what perfection looks like is mercy.

And the order can never be reversed. Nobody loves their enemies into becoming a child of God. It is because he loved his enemies that there is anybody in the family at all — which is also why the sentence begins “your Father,” addressed to people who already hold the position they are being asked to display.
verseByVerse.examples:
The command to love enemies has been the most transformative teaching in Christian history — the basis of martyrdom (Stephen dying while forgiving, Acts 7:60), of peacemaking, of every real reconciliation in the church's story.

It has also been the teaching most frequently domesticated into something manageable: being pleasant to people who are slightly difficult, or to former enemies who are now friends. The test is not whether we are kind to the kind. It is what we do with the person who is actively hostile, who has genuinely wronged us, and who continues to wish us harm.

The Golden Rule (v. 31) has parallels in nearly every ethical tradition — and almost all of them state it negatively: do not do to others what you would not want done to you. A man can keep that rule perfectly by doing nothing at all.

Jesus states it positively, which cannot be kept by inaction. It requires initiative, imagination, and going towards somebody at your own cost without being asked. And there is a mercy in how he frames it: he does not ask for an abstract theory of the good but for the one piece of moral knowledge nobody lacks — how you would want to be treated — applied in the other direction.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But I say to you who hear, Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I say to you who hear: love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you.

But I say to you who hear. The woes were to outsiders; now Jesus turns back to his disciples. He is about to say the hardest thing in the sermon, and he marks off in advance the people who are actually listening.

Love your enemies. The heart of the sermon. Not just your neighbour, but your enemy. The love Jesus means (agapē) is not a feeling of liking, but a commitment to seek someone’s good, whatever they deserve. No ancient religion or philosophy taught this so radically.

Four commands, and one who kept them. Love is shown in action, in four rising steps: love (attitude), do good (deeds), bless (words), pray (prayer). Jesus kept all four towards his own enemies within a single night and day. He met the betrayer’s kiss with a question meant to wake him (22:48); he did good to one of them, touching and healing the ear a disciple had cut off (22:51); when he was reviled, he did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23); and from the cross, with the nails through his hands, he prayed: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (23:34). The sermon on the level place is his own life, described in advance. Stephen, dying under the stones, did the same (Acts 7:60), because the Spirit of Christ was in him.

Verbs of action, not feeling. None of the four is a verb of feeling. He does not command warm feelings towards a person who has wronged you; he commands treatment. You do not have to like your enemy to do good to him, and the command does not wait for the emotion to arrive.

The enemy is real. Luke gives three words for what this person is doing, hating, cursing, abusing, and none of them describes a mild difficulty. Jesus is not talking about a colleague who irritates you. He is talking about somebody who wishes you harm and is acting on it. Abuse (epēreazontōn) means mistreat, insult, harass.

The commands escalate in cost. Do good is an action, which can be done at a distance and without much of yourself. Bless requires words, and words about a person come out of somewhere. Pray for is the hardest, because it cannot be done insincerely for long: it is very difficult to keep asking God to be good to somebody and go on hating them. Nobody arrives at loving an enemy by working on their feelings. It generally goes the other way round: an act, then a word, then a prayer, and somewhere in the third the heart begins to move.

Does this forbid self-defence, military service or the state’s use of force? Jesus is speaking of personal retaliation and the way his disciples treat those who wrong them. The state’s sword is a different matter, given by God to restrain evil (Romans 13:4), and a Christian may serve in it (3:14). Protecting the weak from harm is not hating an enemy.

Is it not weak, or even unjust, to love people who are doing evil? No. Loving an enemy is not approving what he does, or pretending it is fine. It is refusing to become his mirror. It takes far more strength to do good to someone who is cursing you than to curse him back. And it does not give up on justice; it leaves justice with God, who says, vengeance is mine, I will repay (Romans 12:19). The Christian can afford to love his enemy because he trusts the Judge. And the one who gave the command kept it first, on the cross, for us.

What it does not mean. This is not a command to pretend nothing happened; forgiveness in Scripture never requires the pretence that the wrong was not a wrong. Nor is it a command to remain within reach of harm. What is forbidden is the natural, satisfying, entirely human project of returning what was given.

In a sentence. Jesus commanded his followers to love their enemies, do good to those who hate them, bless those who curse them, and pray for those who mistreat them.

On a Tuesday. Who is your enemy, the person who has hurt or opposed you? Do one good thing for them today, speak well of them, and pray for them by name.

Where it applies: A former friend is spreading unkind things about you online. Do not reply in kind. Pray for him by name, and do him good when you have the chance.

Where it would be wrong: The lie is serious: it accuses you of a crime, or it will lose you your job and hurt your family. Loving an enemy does not mean letting a damaging falsehood stand. Correct it calmly and truthfully, and if need be ask the platform or the law to deal with it. Paul defended himself against false charges more than once (Acts 24:10–21; 25:8–11).

For worship. We were not neutral strangers to him but enemies, hostile in mind and doing evil deeds (Colossians 1:21), and he did not wait for us to soften. He loved first, and his love did what ours never could: it turned enemies into children. Every believer is an enemy he has won. And now he puts that same love into our hearts by his Spirit, so that the command he gives is a likeness he is making in us. There is no enemy of yours so hard to love as you were to him.

verseByVerse.quote: To one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also, and from one who takes away your cloak do not withhold your tunic either. Give to everyone who begs from you, and from one who takes away your goods do not demand them back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also, and from one who takes away your cloak do not withhold your tunic either. Give to everyone who begs from you, and from one who takes away your goods do not demand them back.

Four illustrations. They are meant to shock. A blow to the face, a coat taken, a beggar’s hand, goods carried off, and in each case the response is the opposite of the reflex.

To one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also. The first needs its background. A slap on the cheek was more an insult than an injury: a contemptuous blow, the way a superior humiliated an inferior, or an argument was ended by putting a man in his place. Jewish law treated it under fines for damaged honour rather than damaged bodies. So to offer the other cheek is not to invite a beating. It is to refuse the humiliation on its own terms: to decline to be drawn into the exchange the insult was designed to start. Do not retaliate. Do not return insult for insult (1 Peter 2:23; 3:9). Absorb the wrong, rather than escalate it.

From one who takes away your cloak do not withhold your tunic either. The cloak was the outer garment, the tunic the inner one. If someone takes your coat, do not fight to get it back; let him have your shirt as well. Put people before possessions.

Give to everyone who begs from you. Generosity without discrimination. And from one who takes away your goods do not demand them back: hold possessions loosely, and do not live for revenge or recompense.

He gave his back to those who strike. Isaiah’s Servant said it centuries before: I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard (Isaiah 50:6). Luke records the fulfilment. The men guarding Jesus blindfolded him, struck him and mocked him (22:63–64), and at the cross they divided his garments by casting lots (23:34). He did not hit back, and he did not demand them back. Yet this was not weakness. He was holding still for a purpose, bearing an insult that was owed to us, with his face set towards finishing it. The disciple who turns the other cheek is walking a short way down a road his Lord walked to the end.

What this verse does not say to the abused. Something must be said plainly here, because few verses in the Bible have been so cruelly misused. Turn the other cheek has been quoted to battered wives, to abused children, to the bullied and the trafficked, to tell them Christ requires them to stay and keep absorbing the blows. He requires no such thing, and it is a wickedness to say he does. Look again at what he is describing: an insult to a man’s honour, and a coat taken by force. This is about personal affront and personal loss, the wound to pride and pocket that makes us itch to hit back and stand on our rights. What is forbidden is the reflex of retaliation and the worship of our own dignity. He is not handing a violent man a licence, and he is not telling his victim to hold still. Jesus himself walked away from a crowd that meant to kill him (4:29–30). Paul invoked his Roman citizenship against an unlawful flogging (Acts 16:37; 22:25) and let the believers lower him over a wall in a basket rather than be murdered (Acts 9:25). And the same love that will not retaliate for itself is fiercely bound to protect the weak, sometimes from the very person harming them.

If you are being harmed, hear this clearly. Getting to safety is not a failure of this verse. Removing yourself or a child from a violent home, calling for help, telling your pastor or elders, insisting that the law do its work: none of that is retaliation, and none of it is forbidden here. A church that tells an abused person to go back and submit to the abuse has disobeyed Christ, not obeyed him. What dies in these verses is the right to hit back for your own honour. Not the duty to keep the defenceless, including yourself, out of the reach of evil.

Where Christians differ: non-resistance. Some (Anabaptists, Quakers, Tolstoy) take these words literally and absolutely: Christians may never use force, serve in the army or police, go to court, or defend themselves. Verdict: these commands govern personal relationships and the disciple’s heart: no personal revenge, no retaliation for insult, generosity rather than grasping. They do not abolish the God-given role of the state to punish evil and protect the innocent (Romans 13:1–4), nor the duty to protect others, nor all legal redress (Paul appealed to Caesar, Acts 25:11). Jesus himself, when struck, did not offer the other cheek literally but protested the injustice (John 18:22–23). The principle is: never repay evil for evil; overcome evil with good (Romans 12:17–21). Giving to everyone who asks is to be exercised with wisdom, for their real good (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

Must I give to every beggar, even if the money will be misused? Jesus commands an open hand, a readiness to give rather than an instinct to refuse. He does not forbid discernment. Paul says that if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10), and the church cared carefully for genuine need (1 Timothy 5:3–16). Sometimes the most loving gift is food rather than cash, or time rather than money. What this verse rules out is the closed hand.

In a sentence. Jesus called his followers not to retaliate when insulted, not to cling to their possessions when wronged, and to give freely to those who ask.

On a Tuesday. When someone wrongs you today, resist the urge to hit back. Overcome evil with good.

Better to let it go: A friend borrowed your drill years ago and never gave it back. Let it go. You do not need to demand it back, or let it sour the friendship.

Wrong to let it go: Your house is burgled, or your employer stops paying your wages. Jesus forbids personal revenge and a grasping heart, not justice through proper means. Report the burglary to the police; pursue your wages, for withholding a worker’s pay is a sin God hears (James 5:4). And if others depend on you, you owe it to them.

For worship. They stripped him of everything, and he let it go. And then he did for us what this verse describes, beyond anything it could have meant on a Galilean road. To beggars who came with nothing he gave not a coin but himself. To sinners standing naked in their guilt he gave his own robe: he has clothed me with the garments of salvation (Isaiah 61:10), and all who were baptised into Christ have put on Christ (Galatians 3:27). We wear what was his. The Lord who was stripped is the Lord who clothes.
verseByVerse.note: The cloak was the outer garment, the tunic the inner one.

verseByVerse.quote: And as you wish that others would do to you, do so to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as you wish that others would do to you, do so to them.

The Golden Rule. One of the most famous sayings of Jesus, and it sits here for a reason: it is the engine of everything around it. The commands on either side are extraordinary and difficult; this is the principle that makes them intelligible rather than arbitrary. Others had stated it negatively: Rabbi Hillel, a generation earlier, said: What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour. Confucius and others said similar things. It is one of the few moral instincts that turns up everywhere. Jesus states it positively, which is much more demanding. Not just, do not harm others, but, do for others all the good you would want done for you. It requires active, imaginative love.

Why positive matters. The negative form can be satisfied by a man who does nothing at all: sit still, harm nobody, and you have kept it perfectly, which is why it is such a comfortable rule. The positive form cannot be kept by inaction. It requires imagining what you would want in that person’s position, and then going and doing it, at your own cost, without being asked. Consider what that means for the enemy, the one who struck you, the one who took your coat. The negative rule permits you to leave him alone, which is very nearly what you wanted to do anyway. The positive rule asks what you would want if you were him, and sends you towards him.

As you wish. We know what we want: to be treated with kindness, patience, respect, generosity and forgiveness. That is the measure of how we should treat others. And there is a hidden mercy in the way it is framed. Jesus does not ask you to work out a theory of the good. He tells you to use the one piece of moral knowledge nobody lacks: how you would like to be treated, and to apply it in the other direction.

What it does not mean. Not, treat others well so that they will treat you well, as a self-interested bargain. The motive is love, not return (v. 35).

He did not imagine our place; he took it. The rule asks for imagination: picture yourself where the other person stands, and act on what you see. The Son of God did not need to imagine. He came and stood there. He was made like his brothers in every respect (Hebrews 2:17), hungry, tired, misunderstood and tempted, so that he knows from the inside what we need and sympathises with our weakness (Hebrews 4:15). In Matthew, Jesus adds that this rule is the Law and the Prophets (Matthew 7:12), and Jesus said he came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfil them (Matthew 5:17). Here is the fulfilment: one life in which this sentence was never once broken, towards friend or enemy.

A test that is uncomfortably easy to run. Take the person you are currently having difficulty with, and ask what you would want from them if the positions were exactly reversed. The answer arrives immediately. It always does. That is the whole trouble with this verse.

What if what I would want is not good for me? The rule assumes a sensible, honest wish, not every passing desire. A man who wishes others would let him drink himself to death has not found a licence to supply someone else’s addiction. The rule is about the kind of treatment any reasonable person wants: honesty, fairness, patience, help in need, the benefit of the doubt, forgiveness, respect. Under all our particular wishes is the deeper wish to be truly loved, and true love sometimes says no. Ask, therefore, not only what you would like but what you would be grateful for in ten years’ time.

In a sentence. Treat others in every way as you would want them to treat you.

On a Tuesday. In every conversation today, ask: how would I want to be treated if I were them? Then do it.

Where it applies: You would want your manager to tell you plainly, but kindly, where your work falls short. Do that in your next review of someone else.

Where it would be wrong: A friend asks you for a glowing reference that you know is not true. The golden rule does not mean giving people what they ask for. The employer who will read the reference is also someone you must treat as you would want to be treated. Write honestly and kindly.

For worship. He had every right to be treated as the Holy One, and he treated sinners with the patience, honesty, welcome and healing he would have wished for in their place. Then he went beyond the rule altogether, for no one would ever wish to be treated as he chose to be. He who had no need of mercy came to give it; he who deserved honour took our shame. He let himself be treated as his enemies deserved, condemned, mocked and forsaken, so that his enemies might be treated as he deserves. Blessed be the Christ who kept the golden rule towards us, and then exchanged places with us.

verseByVerse.quote: 'If you love those who love you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. And if you do good to those who do good to you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. And if you lend to those from whom you expect to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to get back the same amount.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you love those who love you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. And if you do good to those who do good to you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. And if you lend to those from whom you expect to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to get back the same amount.

What benefit is that to you? Three questions, all the same shape, and each one dismantles a way of feeling good about yourself. Benefit (charis) is the word for grace, credit, thanks. What Jesus is asking, quite literally, is: what grace is there in that? And the answer is none, because grace by definition is unearned, and love returned for love is a transaction that has been earned.

For even sinners love those who love them. Love that is returned is just an exchange. The same move comes twice more, covering the three main forms of human exchange: affection, kindness, money. Do good to those who do good to you: a favour repaid.

Even sinners lend to sinners, to get back the same amount. Lending that expects repayment is business, not grace: credit extended against security. Each is perfectly respectable, and each is done by everyone.

The sting. Jesus’ comparison is not with wicked people but with ordinary people. Even sinners: a word that in this Gospel means the openly disreputable, the ones the Pharisees would not eat with. Even they manage reciprocal love. It requires no faith, no Spirit, no change of heart whatever. So the question is not, am I a decent person? Most people are, in this sense, and it proves nothing. The question is whether there is anything in your life that self-interest could not have produced.

A harder audit than it sounds. Reciprocity is very good at looking like generosity: the friendships that are mutually enjoyable, the kindnesses to people who will say thank you, the giving that goes where thanks will come back. None of it is wrong, and all of it would happen anyway. It establishes nothing about who you belong to. The test is not the warmth of your affections. It is whether anything you do costs you something that will never be returned.

Ten healed, and one came back. Jesus never asked this of his disciples without living it first. Luke will tell of ten lepers who cried to him for mercy and were all made clean, and of only one, a Samaritan, who turned back to give thanks (17:15–18). Jesus knew that would happen, and he healed the ten. Many of the people he fed and healed never followed him. He gave anyway, because his kindness was never an investment waiting for a return. It was grace, charis, love that does good to those who will not repay. That is what makes his love the one love in the world that self-interest could never have produced.

Is it wrong to enjoy friendships where love is returned? Not at all. Mutual love is one of God’s best gifts, and Jesus had close friends himself (John 11:5; 15:15). Marriage, family and Christian fellowship are meant to be full of love given and received. The point is not to despise reciprocal love but to refuse to stop there. Enjoy your friends with thanks; and then look beyond them, to the person who will never return your kindness, and love them as well.

In a sentence. Loving, doing good to and lending to those who will repay you is nothing special, since even sinners do it.

On a Tuesday. Is there anything about your love that could not be explained by self-interest? Do something today for someone who cannot repay you.

Where it applies: A single mother in your church cannot cover this month’s bills. Lend her what she needs, without setting a date, and be ready never to see it again.

Where it would be wrong: A relative wants you to co-sign a loan you could not repay, or keeps borrowing to cover gambling. Lending that feeds a destructive habit, or that puts your own family at risk, is not love (Proverbs 22:26–27; 1 Timothy 5:8). Give what you can afford to lose, and help in ways that actually help.

For worship. God’s love for us has no exchange in it anywhere, and that is why it is grace. He did not love us because we loved him; we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). He gave to people who had nothing to give back and lent to debtors who could never repay, and then he wrote off the whole debt at his own cost. Every Christian is living on a loan that was never called in, from the God whose love is pure charis.

verseByVerse.quote: But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return, and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return, and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.

But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return. The opposite of verses 32–34. The three questions are answered by repeating the three commands with the reciprocity stripped out. And the last phrase bites: not lending at generous rates, but lending with the expectation of repayment removed from the transaction, which, in plain terms, is giving with paperwork. In a society without banks, lending to the poor was a major act of charity.

Does this forbid charging interest or expecting repayment? The law forbade charging interest to a poor fellow Israelite (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 15:7–11), and Jesus goes further: when lending to someone in need, be ready to lose it. That is different from ordinary business lending and investment, which the Bible does not condemn. The heart of the command is generosity to the needy, even the ungrateful.

And your reward will be great. You will not lose by it. God will repay (14:14). Notice that Jesus has no embarrassment about reward.
