He does not say the disciple should want nothing; he says the disciple should stop expecting it from the debtor and start expecting it from God. The money is not written off. It is transferred to a different account.

And you will be sons of the Most High. This is the real payment, and it needs unpacking. You will show that you are God’s children by acting like him. A son resembles his father. In Hebrew idiom, to be called the son of something is to bear its character: sons of thunder, son of encouragement, sons of disobedience. To be a son of the Most High is to be recognisably like him.

The Son of the Most High. Luke has used this title once before, of one person. The angel told Mary that her child would be great and would be called the Son of the Most High (1:32). Now Jesus promises his disciples a share in the name. That is the gospel in a phrase. There is one Son of the Most High by nature, and he brings many sons to glory by grace (Hebrews 2:10), so that God is our Father because he is first his. And the family likeness is his likeness. He is the one who was kind to the ungrateful and the evil, and those who belong to him are being conformed to the image of the Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29).

For he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil. The whole theology of the sermon in ten words: common grace. Not kind to the deserving, but to the ungrateful, people who take what he gives and never once acknowledge where it came from. Kind to the evil, people actively opposed to him. Common grace means the goodness God shows to all people, believers or not: life, rain, food, family, beauty. It does not save anyone, but it is real kindness from a God who owes rebels nothing. He sends sun and rain on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17). He gives life, food and countless blessings to people who never thank him and who hate him. Every meal an atheist eats came out of the ground God keeps making fruitful. And beyond all common grace, he gave his Son for enemies (Romans 5:8). His children must be like him.

The family resemblance. So the command to love enemies is not an arbitrary height set for spiritual athletes. It is a description of the family likeness. And the order cannot be reversed. Nobody loves their enemies into becoming a child of God; that comes by grace through faith. It is because he loved his enemies that there is anybody in the family at all (Romans 5:10).

Is it wrong to want a reward from God? No. Jesus offers it here as a motive, and Hebrews says that whoever would draw near to God must believe that he rewards those who seek him (Hebrews 11:6). What is wrong is wanting the wrong reward, or wanting it from the wrong person: doing good to be admired, or to put others in our debt. The reward Jesus promises is God himself, his approval, and the joy of being like him, and these are rewards only a child would want. It is like a son who wants to please his father, not a hired hand bargaining for wages.

In a sentence. Love your enemies, do good and lend without expecting return, and you will be rewarded and will show yourselves children of God, who is kind to the ungrateful and evil.

On a Tuesday. God has been kind to you when you were ungrateful and evil. Thank him, and be like him toward others.

Where it applies: A neighbour who has complained about your children for years, and never said thank you for anything, has a burst pipe while his family is away. Turn off his water, let him know, and clear up what you can, and do not mention it again.

Where it would be wrong: A colleague who has repeatedly lied about you asks for access to your passwords or your accounts, promising to repay a favour. Kindness to the ungrateful does not mean handing a dishonest person the means to do more harm. Be shrewd as serpents and innocent as doves (Matthew 10:16). Do him good in ways that are good for him and safe for others.

For worship. Every sunrise is proof of his kindness to the ungrateful, and every harvest, and every breath drawn by a man who curses God. But the proof beyond all others has a name. The Son of the Most High came to the ungrateful and the evil, and they gave him a cross, and he gave them his Father. We were the debtors who never paid, and now we are called sons, with an inheritance that is not lent but given, and will never be called back. Our Father is the Most High, and his kindness has no bottom.

verseByVerse.quote: Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful.

Be merciful. The summary of everything Jesus has said about love, from verse 27 onwards. Merciful (oiktirmones) means compassionate, full of pity, feeling for others in their need and acting to help. Matthew has: you therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect (Matthew 5:48). Luke shows that the perfection of God is seen above all in his mercy. In a section about enemies, what perfection looks like is mercy.

What mercy is. Mercy is not being nice. It is not tolerance, and it is not the belief that the offence was minor. Mercy is what happens when someone deserves one thing and is given another; it presupposes a real debt, and then declines to collect it. Which means mercy can only exist where there is a genuine wrong. You cannot be merciful to someone who has not injured you; you can only be pleasant to them. The command therefore requires that the injury be named as an injury, and then not paid back. Any account of forgiveness that begins by minimising what happened has skipped the only step that makes mercy possible.

Even as your Father is merciful. God is the Father of mercies (2 Corinthians 1:3), merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love (Exodus 34:6). The standard is not other people, but God himself. Not as much as you can manage. Not proportionate to the offence. The measure given is God’s own conduct, which is the reason this command can never be marked complete. And the motive: you have received mercy; show it (Matthew 18:33).

The tender mercy of our God. What does the Father’s mercy look like? Luke has already told us. Zechariah sang that the coming of the Messiah was because of the tender mercy of our God, whereby the sunrise shall visit us from on high (1:78). The Father’s mercy has a face. It touched a leper, ate with tax collectors, and called a man with a withered hand into the middle of the room. To be merciful as your Father is merciful is, in practice, to watch the Son, because whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9). Every line of this sermon is a description of what the Father has already shown us in Jesus.

Why it is not crushing. The sentence begins with your Father. It is addressed to people who are already in the family, who have already received exactly the treatment they are being told to give. The mercy comes first, from him, at the cross, unearned and unasked. The command comes second, and it is not, be merciful in order to become his, but, you have seen how your Father behaves: do it like that. Nothing in this section is possible for someone who has not been on the receiving end of it. Everything in it becomes possible, slowly, for someone who has.

Does being merciful mean there should be no consequences? No. Mercy gives up the right to personal revenge and the desire to see someone suffer; it does not abolish justice or wise protection. A parent can forgive a child and still apply a consequence; a church can forgive a man who stole from it and still not give him the accounts; a victim can forgive an abuser and still give evidence in court. God himself is merciful and just. What mercy refuses is the grudge, the gloating, the long memory kept like a weapon, and it always leaves room for the person to be restored.

In a sentence. Be merciful, as your Father is merciful.

On a Tuesday. Reflect today on the mercy God has shown you. Let it overflow in mercy to others.

Where it applies: Your teenage son crashes the car after you told him to be careful. He is shaken and ashamed. Before you list the cost, put your arm round him; then, together, work out how he will help put it right.

Where it would be wrong: A church treasurer is found to have taken money for years. Being merciful does not mean hushing it up or leaving him in charge of the accounts because he says sorry. Forgive him, care for him and his family, and still remove him from that role and make the matter right (1 Corinthians 4:2). Mercy and wisdom walk together.

For worship. Our Father has never dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities (Psalm 103:10). And he did not do it by shrinking the debt. He laid the whole of it on his beloved Son, and the Son paid it to the last, and now the Father looks on his children with nothing but a father’s pity. Every mercy we show is a small reflection of that, and every mercy we have received is a drop from an ocean that will never run dry.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–45 — Judging Others and the Tree and Its Fruit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The teaching on judging (vv. 37-42) and on fruit (vv. 43-45) form one unit held together by the theme of discernment: how we assess others and ourselves.

“Judge not” is one of the most misquoted sentences in the Bible, taken to mean that no moral assessment of anyone is ever permitted. It cannot mean that. Four verses later Jesus tells his hearers to remove the log from their own eye so that they will see clearly to remove a brother's speck — an instruction to make a judgement, having first qualified oneself to make it. Two verses after that he explains how to tell a good tree from a bad one.

What is forbidden is not discernment about conduct but condemnation — pronouncing a verdict on a person, assigning their final worth and destiny. That work belongs to a court, and there is only one. The difference is felt easily enough: “that was a lie” assesses an act; “he is a liar” delivers a summary of a life, and requires access to motives and history that no human being has.

The image of the measure in v. 38 is from a grain market: filled, pressed down to compact it, shaken so the grains settle, then heaped until it spills over into the fold of a man's garment. It is not a level measure. It is a merchant who has decided to be ridiculous.

The blind guide and the log-and-speck follow, and the comedy is deliberate. A man with a plank in his eye leaning in to extract a splinter is an optical impossibility, and the audience can see it. Note that Jesus does not say “leave the speck alone.” The brother is still to be helped; what is corrected is the order. “First take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly.”

The tree-and-fruit teaching is the positive counterpart: character produces conduct. This is not moralism — it does not say “try harder to produce good fruit.” It is a statement about the direction of causation. The fruit reveals the tree; what a person does consistently reveals what they are.

And the source is the treasury of the heart: “out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks” — out of the overflow. Speech is not what a person decides to say; it is what spills when the container is full and nobody is watching.
verseByVerse.theology:
The measure-for-measure principle of v. 38 recurs across both testaments (Matt. 7:2; Rom. 2:1; Jas. 2:13). It is not mechanical karma but a reflection of God's character — the God who shows himself merciful to the merciful and severe to the severe (Ps. 18:25-26).

The warning is not that God will be unkind to those who judge. It is that a person who approaches God without mercy will meet his justice applied with the rigour they themselves used. Someone who has received grace and then withholds mercy has fundamentally misunderstood what grace is.

The word “hypocrite” at v. 42 needs care. In ordinary English it means a conscious fraud. But the man Jesus describes genuinely does not see the log — it is stated twice. The hypocrisy is not deliberate pretence but a failure of self-knowledge so complete that the man is entirely sincere.

Which is more frightening, not less. A conscious fraud could stop. This man is doing his best — and the blind guide of v. 39 is in the same condition, sincerely certain he knows the way, which is exactly why the pit is certain.
verseByVerse.examples:
The log-and-speck has a sharp application for every relationship involving authority: parents with children, leaders with congregations, employers with employees, elders with members. The right to speak into another person's life is not conferred by position; it is earned or forfeited by the quality of one's own self-examination.

The mentor who has faced his own worst and found mercy at the bottom of it can be trusted with somebody else's failure, because he is no longer using it to feel better about himself. There is a practical test before speaking: ask what this conversation will cost you, and whether you are looking forward to it.

“Everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher” (v. 40) is one of the most useful sentences in the New Testament for anyone choosing whom to learn from. Formation works. The ceiling of what you become is set by the person you follow, whether or not you intend it.

And “out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks” (v. 45) is the most usable diagnostic Jesus gave. Not what a person says when trying to impress, but what comes out when they are tired, unobserved, or talking about people who are not in the room. That is the overflow, and it is a straight readout of the treasury. Nor can it be fixed by monitoring speech — that produces a careful hypocrite. What must change is the treasury, and only one person restocks it.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Judge not, and you will not be judged; condemn not, and you will not be condemned; forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you. Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap. For with the measure you use it will be measured back to you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judge not, and you will not be judged; condemn not, and you will not be condemned; forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you. Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap. For with the measure you use it will be measured back to you.

Judge not, and you will not be judged. Four commands in a row, two negative and two positive, each with a consequence attached. Judge not is perhaps the most quoted saying of Jesus in the modern world, and usually quoted wrongly, to mean that no one may ever assess anyone’s conduct. It is not a ban on all judgement. Jesus tells us to recognise trees by their fruit (vv. 43–44), to rebuke a brother who sins (17:3), and to take the log out of our own eye so that we can see clearly to take out a brother’s speck (v. 42). Christians must discern right and wrong, and the church must exercise discipline (1 Corinthians 5:12–13). What Jesus forbids is a censorious, fault-finding, self-righteous spirit, that judges others harshly while excusing oneself, assumes the worst, and takes God’s place as judge (Romans 2:1; 14:4, 10–13; James 4:11–12).

The judge’s seat. Condemn not, and you will not be condemned. The distinction is practical and it is not hard to feel. There is a difference between, that was a lie, and, he is a liar; between assessing what a person did and delivering a summary of what they are. The first is often required of us. The second requires access to information, motives, history, what a person was given to work with, what they have resisted, that no human being has. To pronounce a final verdict on a person is a work that belongs to a court, and there is only one.

The Judge who says judge not. And here is the striking thing: the man who says these words is the one who will sit in that court. The Father has given all judgement to the Son (John 5:22), and God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed (Acts 17:31). When Jesus forbids us the judge’s seat, he is not speaking as one more sinner who knows he has no right to it. He is speaking as its rightful occupant, and telling us to get down from his chair. And the measure he promises to use is the measure he himself brings into the world: not the level scoop of strict desert, but the heaped and overflowing measure of a Saviour who came not to condemn the world but to save it (John 3:17).

Forgive, and you will be forgiven. Forgive (apolyete) means release, let go. A forgiving spirit is the mark of those God has forgiven (11:4; Matthew 6:14–15).

Give, and it will be given to you. Generosity is repaid by God’s generosity.

Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap. A picture from the grain market. Grain was poured into the lap, a fold of the robe held out as a bag. A generous seller filled the measure, pressed it down, shook it to settle the grain, and heaped it until it overflowed: a merchant who has decided to be ridiculous. God gives like that: generously, more than we could hold.

For with the measure you use it will be measured back to you. A principle of God’s dealings. The way you treat others is the way God will treat you. Harsh judgement brings harsh judgement; generous mercy brings generous mercy (James 2:13). That is not a transaction, and it is not karma. It is a description of how the same person meets God at both ends: the one who has understood mercy well enough to give it is the one who will know what to do with it when it comes.

What it does not mean. Not that we earn salvation by forgiving or giving, nor a prosperity gospel promise that giving money guarantees getting more money back. But God is no one’s debtor, and he repays generosity in his own way and time.

Is this a promise that giving money will bring financial return? No. The context is mercy, not judging, forgiving and generosity, and the measure returned is God’s generosity in kind. Paul says that whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully (2 Corinthians 9:6), but the harvest he means is righteousness and thanksgiving, not wealth (2 Corinthians 9:10–11).

If I struggle to forgive, does that mean God will not forgive me? No, not if you are struggling. The verse describes the settled heart of a forgiven person, not a test that a single hard battle can fail. Forgiveness of a deep wound is often a long road, chosen again and again, and God is patient with those who are walking it. What Jesus warns against is the heart that refuses to forgive at all, that holds the grudge and wants it held, because such a heart shows it has never understood its own forgiveness (Matthew 18:32–35). If you want to forgive but cannot yet feel it, ask God for help, decide not to take revenge, pray for the person, and keep going.

In a sentence. Don’t judge, condemn, or withhold forgiveness, but forgive and give, and God will treat you with the same measure, generously, overflowing.

On a Tuesday. Are you quick to judge others? Choose today to assume the best, to forgive and to give, and trust God to repay.

Where it applies: A family leaves your church, and rumours begin about why. Refuse to assume the worst. Think the best of them, and if you have reason to, ask them kindly.

Where it would be wrong: An employer must evaluate staff, a parent must decide which friends are safe, and a church must deal with open sin (1 Corinthians 5:12–13). Jesus forbids condemning and harsh judgement, not discernment or right decisions. And give, and it will be given to you is not a promise of money in return for giving: God repays in his own measure and his own way.

For worship. Our God is the merchant who heaps the measure until it spills into our laps. He gave his Son, and with him graciously gives us all things (Romans 8:32). He has not judged us as we deserve; he has forgiven us beyond all reckoning, pressed down, shaken together, running over. The one Judge who has every right to condemn took the condemnation himself, so that for those in Christ there is now no condemnation (Romans 8:1). Blessed be the God whose measure has no level brim.
verseByVerse.note: Grain was measured into a fold of the robe used like an apron; a generous seller pressed and shook it down so it held more.

verseByVerse.quote: He also told them a parable: 'Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit? A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He also told them a parable: can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit? A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher.

Can a blind man lead a blind man? Two short sayings, placed straight after the warning against judging, because they explain it. It is a joke with a knife in it. The picture is obviously absurd, and the audience would have laughed, and then stopped laughing, because they knew who it was aimed at. A judgemental person is blind to his own faults (vv. 41–42), and cannot guide others. Jesus applied this especially to the Pharisees (Matthew 15:14), who claimed to be guides of the blind (Romans 2:19). The men who had been watching him in the synagogue, hoping to build a charge out of a withered hand, were the recognised guides of Israel.

Will they not both fall into a pit? Teacher and follower alike come to ruin. Note that the blind guide is sincere. Nobody in the parable is lying. He genuinely believes he knows the way, which is exactly why the pit is certain. A guide who knew he was blind would stop. Choose your teachers carefully. And if you teach, make sure you can see.

A disciple is not above his teacher. Students cannot rise higher than their teachers. Follow a blind guide, and you will be blind.

But everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher. Fully trained (katērtismenos) means equipped, completed, mended: the word for mending nets (Mark 1:19). The claim is simply that formation works. A trained disciple ends up resembling the one who trained him, not partly, but characteristically, and the ceiling of what you will become is set by the person you are following, whether or not you intend it.

Whose voice is forming you? The first practical question is about intake. Not whose books are on the shelf, but whose sentences come out of your mouth when you are tired: the preacher you always listen to, the writer whose tone you have absorbed, the friend whose judgement you find yourself repeating, the voices on your phone every evening. You are going to end up like them. That is not a warning against having teachers; it is an argument for choosing them deliberately.

A warning to anyone who teaches. You are not merely passing on content. You are reproducing yourself, including the parts you would rather not pass on, and the reproduction will be more thorough than the instruction. Parents, Sunday school teachers, pastors and mentors teach most by what they are.

The one teacher worth becoming like. Which is why the sermon’s own answer to the whole problem is a person rather than a syllabus. Follow the right teacher, Jesus, and you will become like him: merciful, non-judgemental, loving even enemies. God has predestined his people to be conformed to the image of his Son (Romans 8:29). There is one teacher whose disciples, fully trained, will be like him, and that is the best news in the sermon.

How do I tell whether a teacher can see? Test what he teaches by Scripture (Acts 17:11): does he say what the Bible says, all of it, including the parts that are unwelcome? Look at what he says about Christ, whether he exalts him as Lord and Saviour or uses him for something else. Look at his life, his humility, his honesty about money and power, his treatment of people who cannot help him (1 Timothy 3:1–7). And look at his followers: do they become more like Christ, more loving, more holy, more humble, or more like the teacher, proud and quarrelsome? A teacher who can see will point away from himself.

In a sentence. Jesus warned that a blind guide leads his followers into a pit, and that disciples become like their teachers.

On a Tuesday. Who are you learning from? You will become like them. Make sure your teachers lead you to Christ.

Where it applies: You spend an hour every evening listening to a popular online preacher whose sermons are mostly about success and self-esteem, and you notice you have become impatient with your ordinary church. Turn him off for a month, and spend that hour in one of the Gospels instead.

Where it would be wrong: You decide no human teacher can be trusted, stop listening to anyone, and read the Bible only on your own terms. Christ gave pastors and teachers to his church for our good (Ephesians 4:11–13). The answer to blind guides is not no guides but faithful ones, tested by Scripture.

For worship. Here is the one Teacher who sees perfectly, who never led anyone into a pit, and whose every disciple, fully trained, will be like him. When he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). He mends us as a fisherman mends a torn net, patiently, knot by knot, until we are whole. Blessed be the Master whose school ends in glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? How can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me take out the speck that is in your eye,’ when you yourself do not see the log that is in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take out the speck that is in your brother's eye.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? How can you say to your brother, brother, let me take out the speck that is in your eye, when you yourself do not see the log that is in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take out the speck that is in your brother’s eye.

The speck and the log. A comic exaggeration, perhaps from the carpenter’s workshop. A tiny speck of sawdust, against a beam of timber. A man with a beam sticking out of his eye leans in with great concern to remove a speck from his friend’s.

The point. The critic is often guilty of a greater sin than the one he criticises, often the sin of judging itself. Our moral vision has astonishing resolution at range and is useless up close. We can detect an evasion in another person’s tone, or a self-serving detail in their account, with real precision, and walk about with structural failures of our own that everybody else can see from across a room.

You hypocrite. An actor, pretending to a righteousness he does not have. But in ordinary English a hypocrite is a conscious fraud, and the picture Jesus draws is of somebody who genuinely does not see the log. The hypocrisy here is a failure of self-knowledge so complete that the man is entirely sincere. Which is more frightening, not less. A conscious fraud could stop. This man is doing his best.

First take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly. Self-examination comes before correction of others. But Jesus does not say leave your brother’s speck alone. The speck is still to come out. The brother is still to be helped. What is being corrected is the order. Once you have dealt with your own sin, you are able, and responsible, to help your brother, gently and humbly (Galatians 6:1). Removing a speck from an eye requires great care. This passage is often quoted to mean that nobody may ever say anything to anybody. Jesus assumes the opposite: Christians are meant to help each other see, and he is telling you what qualifies you to do it.

The look that removed the speck. Only one man has ever stood with no log in his eye, and Luke shows us how he deals with a brother’s fault. In the high priest’s courtyard, as Peter denied him the third time and the rooster crowed, the Lord turned and looked at Peter (22:61). No speech, no pointing finger, no list. A look from the only clear eye in that courtyard, and Peter went out and wept bitterly. It broke him, and it began his mending, and on the third day the word went round among the disciples: the Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon (24:34). That is what clear sight does in the hands of perfect love. He sees the whole of our fault, and he looks at us in a way that heals.

The qualification is honest sight. Not moral superiority. A man who has faced his own worst and found mercy at the bottom of it is precisely the man who can be trusted with somebody else’s failure, because he is no longer using it to feel better. There is a practical test in it. Before speaking, ask what this conversation would cost you, and whether you are looking forward to it.

How do I find the log, if I cannot see it? Ask for help from outside, because the log is by definition in the eye you are using. Ask God: search me, O God, and know my heart, and see if there be any grievous way in me (Psalm 139:23–24). Read Scripture slowly and let it read you. Ask a spouse or close friend, and mean it: what do you see in me that I do not? Notice what irritates you most in others, because it is often a reflection of your own. And when you find the log, do not merely regret it; confess it, and ask the person you have wronged to forgive you.

In a sentence. Jesus warned against criticising others’ small faults while ignoring our own great ones, telling us to deal with our own sin first, so we can then help others clearly.

On a Tuesday. Before you correct someone today, ask God to show you the log in your own eye.

Where it applies: Before you speak to your teenager about time on the phone, look honestly at your own.

Where it would be wrong: You never correct anyone, because you are not perfect either. Jesus does not say leave the speck; he says take out the log first, then you will see clearly to take out the speck (v. 42). Humility makes correction gentle; it does not make it silent.

For worship. He alone could have stood over the human race with a pointing finger, for he alone had nothing in his own eye. Instead he came down to us and took the whole weight of our sin on himself, logs and specks together, and then gave us his Spirit so that we might begin to see as he sees. The one perfectly qualified to judge became the one who heals, and he still handles the eyes of his people with infinite care.

verseByVerse.quote: 'For no good tree bears bad fruit, nor again does a bad tree bear good fruit, for each tree is known by its own fruit. For figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor are grapes picked from a bramble bush. The good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure produces evil, for out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For no good tree bears bad fruit, nor again does a bad tree bear good fruit, for each tree is known by its own fruit. For figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor are grapes picked from a bramble bush. The good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure produces evil, for out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks.

For no good tree bears bad fruit. The sermon now shifts from conduct to cause, and the image is agricultural and inarguable. Nobody disputes this. You do not get figs off a thornbush. The nature of the tree determines the fruit. What a person does flows from what he is. The fruit does not determine the tree; it reveals it.

The direction of the passage. This could be read as a demand to try harder, produce better fruit or else, and it is the opposite. A tree does not decide what fruit to bear. It bears according to what it is. Which means the question this raises is not, what should I be producing? But, what am I?

For each tree is known by its own fruit. You can tell a tree by its fruit. And you can tell a person, and a teacher, by the fruit of their life (Matthew 7:15–20). This is right judgement, the discernment Jesus approves. Figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor grapes from a bramble bush.

The good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good. The heart is a storehouse, a treasury, the accumulated deposit. Whatever has been put in over the years is what comes out.

For out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks. Out of the overflow. Words especially reveal the heart. What overflows from your mouth shows what fills your heart (James 3:10–12). Speech is not only what a person decides to say. It is what spills over when the container is full and no longer being watched.

The most usable diagnostic. Not: what do I say when I am trying to make an impression? But: what comes out when I am tired, when the phone call has gone badly, when I am among people I do not need to impress? What is the tone of my speech about people who are not in the room? That is the overflow, and Jesus says it is a straight readout of the treasury.

The implication. To change the fruit, the tree must be changed. Outward reform cannot produce good fruit from a bad heart. A person needs a new heart, which only God can give (Ezekiel 36:26; 2 Corinthians 5:17). What does that actually mean? Not a new personality, but new desires at the root: God takes away a heart that loves sin and resents him, and gives one that loves him and wants what he wants (Ezekiel 36:27). Then good fruit follows. You cannot improve the fruit by working on the fruit, and you cannot change your speech merely by monitoring your speech; that produces a careful hypocrite, which is where this sermon started. What has to change is the treasury, and only one person restocks it.

What overflowed on the cross. There has been one heart whose treasury held nothing but good, and Luke lets us hear what came out of it under the worst pressure a man has ever borne. Nailed up, mocked by rulers and soldiers, with every reason for bitterness, his mouth spoke: Father, forgive them (23:34). To a dying thief: truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise (23:43). And at the last: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (23:46). Nobody was managing an impression on that hill. That was the overflow, mercy, promise and trust, and it is a straight readout of the heart of the Son of God.

One bad word does not prove a bad heart. The language is about what a tree bears, which is a pattern over seasons, not one morning’s crop. Every Christian says things they hate having said.

Then how is the treasury restocked? By God, through ordinary means he has given. The Spirit gives the new heart in the new birth, and then fills it over a lifetime as we take in his word: let the word of Christ dwell in you richly (Colossians 3:16). So fill your mind with Scripture, read and memorised; with prayer; with the worship and teaching of the church; with good books and good friends; and starve what feeds the old heart, the gossip, the bitterness, the screen that leaves you worse. Whatever you think about, dwell on what is true, honourable, just, pure, lovely (Philippians 4:8). Slowly, the overflow changes.

In a sentence. As a tree is known by its fruit, so a person’s words and deeds show what is stored in their heart.

On a Tuesday. Listen to what comes out of your mouth today. What does it reveal about your heart? Ask God to fill it with good.

Where it applies: You notice that whenever a certain colleague’s name comes up, you make a cutting remark. That is fruit, and it is telling you something about the root. Confess the resentment to God, pray for her by name, and say one good thing about her this week.

Where it would be wrong: You conclude that a Christian friend cannot be a believer because he lost his temper badly once at a football match. A tree is known by its fruit over seasons, not by one bad apple. Speak to him gently if need be, but do not pronounce on his soul from a single morning’s crop.

For worship. The good treasure was never ours to begin with. It is his, and he shares it. He is the true vine and we are the branches, and apart from him we can do nothing (John 15:5); joined to him, his own life runs into ours, and fruit appears that we could never have grown. The new heart is his gift, his Spirit is its treasure, and every gracious word that ever comes from a Christian’s mouth is overflow from the fullness of Christ, for from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace (John 1:16).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 46–49 — Build Your House on the Rock
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The sermon ends with two builders, two houses, and one storm — and everything hangs on a distinction that cannot be seen.

It is preceded by the question that makes the parable necessary: “Why do you call me 'Lord, Lord,' and not do what I tell you?” Jesus does not doubt that they call him Lord, or suggest they are insincere; the doubled address is the language of warmth. The problem is that the word has become detached from its meaning. Kyrios means owner, master, the one whose word settles the matter — and to call a man Lord while deciding independently what to do with his instructions is a contradiction in terms.

The parable is not a contrast between a man who heard and a man who did not. Both come to Jesus. Both hear his words. Both build. From the road, on a fine day, there is nothing to choose between them.

The difference is entirely underground. The wise builder “dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock” — two verbs describing the least rewarding work in construction. Nobody admires a foundation. It takes the longest, produces nothing visible, and the man who skips it gets his house up first.

Then the flood, and Luke is precise: the same stream breaks against both houses. The storm is not sent to test one and spare the other. It is weather, and it comes to everyone — which rules out the reading in which the obedient are protected from trouble. Both are hit equally. What differs is what happens next.

“Immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.” There is no gradual subsidence and no chance to shore it up. A life built on nothing does not fail by inches.

The storm is unspecified, and the vagueness is the point: bereavement, illness, betrayal, the slow attrition of a faith that was never load-bearing, and finally the judgement. Something always comes.

And the rock is not a set of principles. Jesus has spent thirty verses saying things no one can live out by admiration, and he ends by describing a man who hears my words and does them. The digging is obedience, and what it reaches is him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The eschatological note — the house that falls, and “the ruin of that house was great” — places the sermon's ethics in the context of final judgement. This is not moralism; it is eschatology.

The commands of the sermon are not useful guidelines for a better life. They are the description of the life that will stand on the day when every life is tested — which is why the sermon cannot be domesticated into a programme of self-improvement. It describes a life that is only possible through the transformed heart the kingdom produces, which is exactly what the tree-and-fruit teaching has just said.

And it is why the question at v. 46 is not an attack on assurance. It is a question about the relationship between what a person says about Christ and what they do about what Christ says. Every command in this chapter is checkable, and not one of them can be kept by admiring it.

The rock, finally, is not the sermon. It is the one who preached it. To hear these words and do them is to build on Jesus himself, and he is what the digging reaches.
verseByVerse.examples:
The parable of the two builders has been used in Christian preaching from the earliest centuries as the description of the difference between nominal and genuine faith. Both builders heard Jesus; both began to build; both appeared to be doing the same thing. The difference was invisible until the storm came.

This is Jesus's own warning against the self-deception that hears the word, feels its power, admires its truth, and then returns to a life built on other foundations. The church in every generation has members who have heard much and built little.

The wise builder “dug deep” — the effort of foundation-laying is not passive. It requires excavation, the removal of everything covering the rock, the work of getting down to what will hold. That is spiritual formation: not merely hearing but digging, through prayer and Scripture, through accountability, through obedience in small things, until the foundation is no longer mood and circumstance and social approval.

The digging is unglamorous and nobody sees it. The house is what people see. But the digging is what determines whether the house stands — and the way to start is not in general. Take one command from this chapter, with an actual name attached, and ask what it means this week.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and not do what I tell you?

Why do you call me Lord, Lord. Fourteen words, and there is nowhere to stand while reading them. Notice first what is not being questioned. He does not doubt that they call him Lord, and he does not suggest they are insincere in saying it. The doubling, Lord, Lord, is the language of warmth, even fervour; it is how you address someone you mean it about. The problem is not coldness.

And not do what I tell you? A contradiction. A lord is someone you obey. The word has become detached from its meaning. Kyrios means owner, master, the one whose word settles the matter. To call a man Lord and then decide independently what to do with his instructions is not merely a moral failure but a contradiction in terms. It is like calling someone your employer and never coming in. To call Jesus Lord and ignore his commands is hypocrisy. Words of worship without obedience are empty (Matthew 7:21–23; James 1:22). The test of whether Jesus is really your Lord is whether you do what he says, including everything in this sermon: love your enemies, don’t judge, give.

What I tell you. Hear who is speaking. The prophets never said, do what I tell you. They said, thus says the LORD, and pointed away from themselves. Jesus points to himself: my words (v. 47), what I tell you, and the whole sermon has been spoken in that voice, but I say to you (v. 27). He claims for his own commands the place that belongs to the commands of God, and he makes a man’s eternal safety hang on whether he does them. In the Greek Bible of the day, Lord (Kyrios) was the word that stood for the divine name. To call Jesus Lord is to acknowledge his authority, and in the full sense, his deity. Either he is mistaken about himself on a scale no prophet ever was, or he is the LORD speaking.

He asks why. The question is put as a genuine question. There is an answer, and every honest Christian knows roughly what it is: because the saying is warm and the doing is expensive; because the language of discipleship costs nothing and its substance costs everything; because it is entirely possible to love the person of Jesus in a general way and to have quietly arranged one’s life so that nothing he said in this chapter applies.

Why it comes exactly here. Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, give and expect nothing back, do not condemn, take the log out of your own eye: every command in this sermon is checkable, and none of them can be done by admiring it.

Does this mean I am not saved if I fail to obey? No. The verse is not an attack on assurance and it is not a demand for perfection. Every Christian fails to do all that Jesus says, every day, and the same Lord taught us to pray, forgive us our debts. The question is the direction of a life: whether you call him Lord and are trying, however falteringly, to do what he says, grieving when you fail and getting up again; or whether you call him Lord and have no intention of letting it change anything. The first is a weak disciple. The second is not a disciple at all. If you are troubled by your failures, that trouble is itself a sign that he is your Lord.

In a sentence. Jesus asked why people called him Lord but did not do what he said.

On a Tuesday. Which of Jesus’ commands in this sermon are you not doing? Take one, any one, and ask what it would mean this week, with an actual name attached. Then do it. That is the difference between two houses that look exactly alike.

Where it applies: You sing with real feeling on Sunday that Jesus is Lord of all, and on Monday you are still refusing to speak to your brother over an inheritance. This week, ring him, and begin the conversation Jesus told you to have.

Where it would be wrong: You are so afraid of being a Lord, Lord hypocrite that you stop singing, praying aloud or calling him Lord at all until your obedience is better. Jesus does not tell you to stop confessing him; he tells you to obey the one you confess. Keep calling him Lord, and let him make the words true.

For worship. He is Lord, and he is worthy of every word of worship we give him and of every act of obedience we owe him. The one who asks why we call him Lord and do not obey is the one who, being Lord, became obedient to the point of death (Philippians 2:8). He did all his Father told him, so that disobedient people who have called him Lord with empty words could be forgiven and made new. And one day every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, and every knee will bow, and none of it will be empty.

parallels.desc: if I am a master, where is my fear?

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, I will show you what he is like: he is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. And when a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it, because it had been well built. But the one who hears and does not do them is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the stream broke against it, immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, I will show you what he is like: he is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. When a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it, because it had been well built. But the one who hears and does not do them is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the stream broke against it, immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.

Two builders. The sermon ends with two builders, and everything hangs on a distinction that cannot be seen. Read the description carefully, because the usual telling gets it wrong. This is not a contrast between a man who heard Jesus and a man who did not. Both come to him. Both hear his words. Both build houses. From the road, on a fine day, there is nothing to choose between them. And Luke follows the sermon at once with a Gentile centurion who builds everything on Jesus’ word, trusting him to heal without even coming to the house (7:1–10): a living picture of a house built on the rock.

Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, he is like a man building a house, who dug deep. Three steps: come, hear, do. Only Luke says dug deep: hard work, below the surface, through the soil to the bedrock. Nobody admires a foundation. It takes the longest, produces nothing visible, and the man who skips it gets his house up first.

And laid the foundation on the rock. In the parable, the rock is hearing Jesus’ words and doing them (v. 47). Since they are the words of the Lord (v. 46), building on them means building on him: trusting and following him. The foundation is invisible once the house is built, but it determines everything.

The rock in the rest of Scripture. The text itself defines the rock as Jesus’ words heard and done, and then later Scripture shows why that is not a gospel of self-effort. Long before, God was the rock of his people: the Rock, his work is perfect (Deuteronomy 32:4); the LORD is my rock and my fortress (Psalm 18:2). Isaiah promised a tested stone laid in Zion, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation, and whoever believes will not be in haste (Isaiah 28:16). The apostles tell us who that stone is. Peter quotes Isaiah of Christ, the living stone, rejected by men but chosen by God (1 Peter 2:4–6). Paul says no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 3:11), and that the church is built on the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). So the reader should understand the parable rightly: the rock is not our obedience considered on its own, as if we built our own foundation. It is Christ himself, the Lord whose words these are. To dig deep is to come to him, hear him and do what he says; obedience is how a life rests its whole weight on him, and it is that resting, not the effort, that holds the house up.

And when a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it. In Palestine, wadis (dry stream beds) flood suddenly in the rainy season, with devastating force. The same stream broke against both. The parable is sometimes read as though the obedient are protected from trouble. They are not. Both houses are hit, equally, by the same water. What differs is what happens next.

Could not shake it, because it had been well built. The flood can be almost anything: bereavement, a diagnosis, a betrayal, persecution, the slow attrition of a faith that was never load-bearing, death, and finally the judgement of God. Jesus does not specify, and the vagueness is the point. Something always comes.

But the one who hears and does not do them is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. He has heard the same sermon; the difference is not in hearing but in doing. His way is easier, quicker, and in fair weather it looks just the same.

When the stream broke against it, immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great. The sermon ends with a warning: hearing Jesus without obeying him leads to ruin. Luke’s immediately is grim. There is no gradual subsidence, no chance to shore it up. The first serious pressure and it is over, and the wreckage is described as great, because a life built on nothing does not fail by inches.

What it does not mean. Not salvation by works. Jesus’ words begin with blessing for the poor and with the Father’s mercy (vv. 20, 36), so doing them starts with receiving mercy, not earning it. But true faith in Christ shows itself in obedience. Faith that does not obey is not saving faith (James 2:17).

How do I know whether I have dug deep? Look not at the outside of the house but at what you lean on when the water rises. When trouble comes, do you go to Christ, pray, open his word, and keep doing what he says, even through tears? Or does faith evaporate, and you reach for something else to hold you up? Look too at the ordinary weeks: is there a pattern, however imperfect, of hearing his words and doing them, in forgiveness, honesty, generosity, love for enemies? If you find you have built on sand, it is not too late while the sun is shining. Come to him now, hear him, and begin to dig.

In a sentence. Jesus ended by comparing those who hear and obey him to a man who built on rock and survived the flood, and those who hear and do not obey to a man whose house without foundations was swept away.

On a Tuesday. Storms are coming. Dig deep today: hear Jesus’ words and put one of them into practice.

Where it applies: You have heard this sermon many times, and you know you have been carrying a grudge against your former business partner for years. Dig today: tell God you forgive him, write the letter, and stop rehearsing the wrong. Do it now, in the dry season, before the flood comes.

Where it would be wrong: You treat digging deep as a programme of self-improvement, and measure how safe you are by how hard you are working at it. The rock is Christ, not your effort (1 Corinthians 3:11). Obey him, and rest your weight on him, not on your obedience.

For worship. Both men heard the sermon. Only one of them built on the man who preached it. And that man went down into the flood himself. The waters of God’s judgement broke over him at the cross, and he did not give way; the grave closed over him, and on the third day he rose. He is the rock the deluge could not move. Everyone who comes to him, hears him and does what he says rests on that, and when the last storm breaks over the whole world, not one house that stands on him will fall, because he cannot.
verseByVerse.note: Wadis (dry stream beds) flood suddenly in the rainy season.

6.text: <sup>1</sup> On a Sabbath, while he was going through the grainfields, his disciples plucked and ate some heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands. <sup>2</sup> But some of the Pharisees said, “Why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath?” <sup>3</sup> And Jesus answered them, “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him: <sup>4</sup> how he entered the house of God and took and ate the bread of the Presence, which is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those with him?” <sup>5</sup> And he said to them, “The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.” <sup>6</sup> On another Sabbath, he entered the synagogue and was teaching, and a man was there whose right hand was withered. <sup>7</sup> And the scribes and the Pharisees watched him, to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might find a reason to accuse him. <sup>8</sup> But he knew their thoughts, and he said to the man with the withered hand, “Come and stand here.” And he rose and stood there. <sup>9</sup> And Jesus said to them, “I ask you, is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to destroy it?” <sup>10</sup> And after looking around at them all he said to him, “Stretch out your hand.” And he did so, and his hand was restored. <sup>11</sup> But they were filled with fury and discussed with one another what they might do to Jesus. <sup>12</sup> In these days he went out to the mountain to pray, and all night he continued in prayer to God. <sup>13</sup> And when day came, he called his disciples and chose from them twelve, whom he named apostles: <sup>14</sup> Simon, whom he named Peter, and Andrew his brother, and James and John, and Philip, and Bartholomew, <sup>15</sup> and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon who was called the Zealot, <sup>16</sup> and Judas the son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor. <sup>17</sup> And he came down with them and stood on a level place, with a great crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the seacoast of Tyre and Sidon, <sup>18</sup> who came to hear him and to be healed of their diseases. And those who were troubled with unclean spirits were cured. <sup>19</sup> And all the crowd sought to touch him, for power came out from him and healed them all. <sup>20</sup> And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. <sup>21</sup> “Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied. “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh. <sup>22</sup> “Blessed are you when people hate you and when they exclude you and revile you and spurn your name as evil, on account of the Son of Man! <sup>23</sup> Rejoice in that day, and leap for joy, for behold, your reward is great in heaven; for so their fathers did to the prophets. <sup>24</sup> “But woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. <sup>25</sup> “Woe to you who are full now, for you shall be hungry. “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep. <sup>26</sup> “Woe to you, when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets. <sup>27</sup> “But I say to you who hear, Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, <sup>28</sup> bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you. <sup>29</sup> To one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also, and from one who takes away your cloak do not withhold your tunic either. <sup>30</sup> Give to everyone who begs from you, and from one who takes away your goods do not demand them back. <sup>31</sup> And as you wish that others would do to you, do so to them. <sup>32</sup> “If you love those who love you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. <sup>33</sup> And if you do good to those who do good to you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. <sup>34</sup> And if you lend to those from whom you expect to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to get back the same amount. <sup>35</sup> But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return, and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil. <sup>36</sup> Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful. <sup>37</sup> “Judge not, and you will not be judged; condemn not, and you will not be condemned; forgive, and you will be forgiven; <sup>38</sup> give, and it will be given to you. Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap. For with the measure you use it will be measured back to you.” <sup>39</sup> He also told them a parable: “Can a blind man lead a blind man? Will they not both fall into a pit? <sup>40</sup> A disciple is not above his teacher, but everyone when he is fully trained will be like his teacher. <sup>41</sup> Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? <sup>42</sup> How can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me take out the speck that is in your eye,’ when you yourself do not see the log that is in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take out the speck that is in your brother's eye. <sup>43</sup> “For no good tree bears bad fruit, nor again does a bad tree bear good fruit, <sup>44</sup> for each tree is known by its own fruit. For figs are not gathered from thornbushes, nor are grapes picked from a bramble bush. <sup>45</sup> The good person out of the good treasure of his heart produces good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure produces evil, for out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks. <sup>46</sup> “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you? <sup>47</sup> Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, I will show you what he is like: <sup>48</sup> he is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. And when a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it, because it had been well built. <sup>49</sup> But the one who hears and does not do them is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the stream broke against it, immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great.”

7.title: Faith, Doubt, and the Extravagance of Grace
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is one of the richest chapters in Luke's Gospel — four scenes that together compose a portrait of the grace of God operating at the edges of what respectable religion thought was possible. A Roman soldier sends word to Jesus about his dying servant; a widow's dead son is raised in a small village; the imprisoned John the Baptist sends messengers to ask if Jesus is really the one; and a woman known as a sinner anoints Jesus's feet with her tears and her perfume at a Pharisee's dinner table. In every scene, the expected is reversed: the Gentile soldier has greater faith than anyone in Israel; the dead man walks; the greatest prophet struggles with doubt; and the sinner, not the Pharisee, demonstrates the love that flows from forgiven debt.

The chapter's theological centre is the exchange between Jesus and John's disciples (vv. 18–35). John's question — “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” — is the most honest expression of faith-under-pressure in the Gospels. The forerunner who announced the Coming One from the womb, who saw the Spirit descend at the Jordan, who proclaimed the axe at the root of the trees — is now in prison, and the Coming One is not doing what John expected. Jesus's answer is not an argument but a recital: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor have good news preached to them. He is, in other words, doing exactly what Isaiah promised the Servant would do. Blessed is the one who is not offended by him — even when he does not do what you expected.

The sinful woman at Simon's house (vv. 36–50) is the chapter's most searching scene. She comes uninvited, she weeps, she wipes Jesus's feet with her hair, she anoints them with perfume. Simon, the Pharisee host, draws the obvious conclusion: if Jesus were really a prophet, he would know who was touching him, and he would not allow it. Jesus's response is the parable of the two debtors — one forgiven a small debt, one a large one; which loves more? And the answer overturns Simon's entire moral framework. The woman's extravagant love is not the cause of her forgiveness; it is the evidence of it. She loves much because she has been forgiven much. Simon's cool hospitality reveals that he considers himself forgiven little — which means he considers himself to owe little, which means he loves little.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Jesus Heals a Centurion's Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The centurion whose servant is sick is the first Gentile whose faith is commended in Luke's Gospel — and it is commended in the strongest possible terms: “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.”

He is a Roman military officer, commander of a hundred men, the local face of the occupying power in a garrison town. He has also built the local synagogue — an extraordinary act of generosity towards a community he was not part of, and towards a God who was not his. And Luke's first fact about him is that a dying slave was “highly valued by him,” which in a world that classified slaves as speaking tools tells you a great deal before the man opens his mouth.

The Jewish elders who come on his behalf argue from merit: “He is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue.” That is how human beings naturally think about who deserves help. The centurion contradicts every word of it.

“Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed.” The elders said he was worthy; he says he is not. Nothing he has done puts Jesus under any obligation.

Then the reasoning, and it is the most penetrating theology anyone has produced in the Gospel so far: “For I too am a man set under authority, with soldiers under me.” Note the first phrase. Not a man with authority but a man under it. He knows exactly why his orders are obeyed — when he speaks, Rome speaks — and that such authority operates through words, at any distance the words can travel.

He applies the framework to Jesus and concludes that illness is in the same position as a legionary: under orders. He is right, and he worked it out from his life in the army.

This is the faith the church has lived on since the ascension. Nobody now gets Jesus under their roof in the way the centurion declined. What is available is exactly what he asked for and received: the word, spoken at a distance, by one whose authority is not limited by where his feet are.
verseByVerse.theology:
The centurion's analogy is more profound than it first appears. He is not merely saying that Jesus is like a commanding officer. He is recognising that authority over illness has the same character as authority in a chain of command — it operates through words, at a distance, on the basis of what stands behind the speaker.

He knows that a soldier who refuses his order is refusing the emperor whose authority he carries. He perceives that the illness Jesus commands is in the same position, and he is right. The authority Jesus exercises over creation is the authority of its Creator, and creation obeys its Creator.

Jesus's amazement — “he marvelled at him” — is one of only two places in the Gospels where Jesus is said to marvel; the other is at the unbelief of Nazareth (Mark 6:6). Faith where none was expected, and unbelief where all was.

How the eternal Son can be surprised is answered the way Luke answered it at 2:52: two whole natures in one person. According to his divine nature he knows all things and learns nothing; according to his human nature he genuinely encountered this man and was genuinely moved. The wonder was real. He was not acting.
verseByVerse.examples:
“I am not worthy to have you come under my roof” is the model of the humility that genuine faith produces. By every external measure this man is among the most impressive people in the narrative — authority, resources, a reputation for generosity — and he is the one who says he is not worthy. The elders say he is; he says he is not.

It is not false modesty. It is the accurate perception of a man who has understood who he is asking for help, and the awareness of that distance is precisely what Jesus names as great faith.

And there is a quieter thing worth taking from him. Everything remarkable he says about authority he learned at work, in the army, in the ordinary business of command — not from the prophets and not in a synagogue. The best theologian in Galilee that morning was a soldier, and what qualified him was his job.

The centurion never came in person and received everything he asked for. The word of Jesus is not constrained by geography, and the authority he trusted across the streets of Capernaum is the same one trusted across continents in every generation of the church's praying.

verseByVerse.quote: After he had finished all his sayings in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum. Now a centurion had a servant who was sick and at the point of death, who was highly valued by him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After he had finished all his sayings in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum. A centurion had a servant who was sick and at the point of death, who was highly valued by him.

Meaning first. Luke 7 is four scenes, and in every one the kingdom of God turns up where respectable religion did not expect it. A Gentile officer asks Jesus only to speak, and Jesus finds no such faith in Israel. At the gate of Nain a funeral meets the Lord of life, and a widow is handed back her only son. From prison John the Baptist asks whether Jesus really is the one, and Jesus answers with the evidence Isaiah promised. At a Pharisee’s dinner a sinful woman weeps on his feet and hears that her sins are forgiven. The chapter shows who Jesus is, the Lord whose word heals at a distance, raises the dead and forgives sins, and what he is like: the friend of sinners, welcoming those everyone else has written off.

After he had finished all his sayings. The sermon ends and Luke turns immediately to a sickroom. He has told us what the kingdom requires; now he shows what the kingdom does, for outsiders (a Gentile soldier), the grieving (a widow), the doubting (John) and sinners (a woman of the city).

A house built on his word. The sermon closed with a man who built his house on the words of Jesus, and the very next thing Luke shows us is a man who does exactly that. A household in Capernaum is about to rest its whole weight on one sentence from the Lord’s mouth: say the word. The order is deliberate. The words just preached on the level place are not good advice from a teacher; they are the words of the one whose speech heals the dying at a distance and raises the dead. That is why a life can be built on them. The rock in the parable and the authority in this story are the same: Christ, whose word does what it says.

A centurion. A centurion commanded about a hundred men. He was the backbone of the Roman army: a career soldier, promoted on competence, the rank at which the empire actually worked. This one was a Gentile, probably serving Herod Antipas, whose forces were organised on the Roman model, stationed at Capernaum to keep order on the frontier. Whether his pay came from Rome or from Herod, he was the local face of foreign power. Every centurion in the New Testament is presented favourably (23:47; Acts 10:1–2; 27:3, 43), and Luke, writing for a Gentile world, seems to delight in showing that the soldiers of the empire were not beyond the reach of grace.

Had a servant. He is also, by the standards of the day, an owner of people. The word Luke uses is doulos, a slave, and that is the relationship the story turns on. Matthew uses a word that can mean boy (pais), which may tell us the slave was young, or simply that the centurion spoke of him with the affection of a household.

Who was highly valued by him. Highly valued means held in honour, precious, dear to him. It is not the vocabulary of a man protecting an asset, and a first-century reader would have felt the strangeness of it. Roman law classified a slave as property, and a Roman writer on farming could call him a tool that speaks. Nobody expected an officer to spend anything on a dying servant, and certainly not to go looking for a Jewish miracle-worker on his behalf.

The first evidence of his character. So before the man has said a word, Luke has told us something about him. He is a person of considerable power who has not used it in the ordinary way, and the first evidence of his character is not his religion but how he treats somebody who could not have made him do anything. What a person is really like shows most clearly in how they behave towards those who have no leverage over them at all. Everything else the centurion says will be extraordinary, but the thing that opens the door is simply that he loved a slave.

Why does Jesus not condemn slavery? Slavery in the Roman world was not the same as race-based chattel slavery, but it was still a system of ownership, and the Bible never praises it. Scripture regulates it and undermines it from within: masters are told they too have a Master in heaven (Ephesians 6:9), Paul urges Philemon to receive Onesimus no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16), and enslavers are listed among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10). The gospel’s teaching that every person is made in God’s image, and that slave and free are one in Christ (Galatians 3:28), is what eventually brought slavery down. Jesus heals this slave without first lecturing his owner, because the man in front of him is dying; but the very fact that he goes treats the slave as a person worth the journey.

Was the centurion a believer already? Not in the full sense, because the gospel of the cross and resurrection had not yet been preached. But he had plainly turned from the gods of Rome towards the God of Israel (v. 5), and he is about to show a faith in Jesus that Jesus himself calls extraordinary. Luke presents him the way he presents Cornelius in Acts 10: a Gentile whom God was already drawing, who responds to the light he has and is given more. That is how God usually works. Nobody comes to Christ unless the Father draws him (John 6:44), and the drawing often begins long before the person can name what is happening.

In a sentence. In Capernaum, a Gentile centurion’s slave, whom he valued dearly, was sick and about to die.

On a Tuesday. How do you treat those under your authority, and those who can do nothing for you? Think of one person this week who has no leverage over you at all: someone who works for you, serves you, or depends on you. Ask whether they would describe you as this slave would have described his master. Kindness to the powerless is not a side issue in the Christian life; it is one of the places where the reality of faith is tested first.

For worship. The Lord of glory let a Roman officer’s love for a slave be the doorway into this chapter, and he set out towards a house no rabbi would enter, for a man the law of Rome called property. That is what he is like. He who was rich became poor, and took the form of a doulos himself (Philippians 2:7), so that slaves and their masters alike could be brought into the household of God as sons.
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers. This one was a Gentile, probably serving Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and heal his servant. And when they came to Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying, 'He is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and heal his servant. When they came to Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying: he is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue.

He sent to him elders of the Jews. The centurion does not go himself. He sends a delegation of Jewish elders, the leading men of the local Jewish community and its synagogue, to ask on his behalf. That is not timidity. A Gentile officer of the occupying army approaching a Jewish teacher directly would put that teacher in an awkward position in front of his own people, so he uses the one channel that costs Jesus nothing.

He is worthy to have you do this for him. The elders make his case with real warmth, and their view is simple: he deserves it, because of his good works. Their word is worthy (axios), and their evidence is a track record: he loves us, he built us something. It is a case built on merit, which is exactly how human beings naturally think about who deserves help, and the centurion is about to contradict every word of it.

For he loves our nation. Some Gentiles in that world were attracted to the God of Israel, to Jewish morality and to synagogue worship, without becoming full converts. They were called God-fearers (Acts 10:2; 13:16), and this centurion was probably one. In a country occupied by Rome, a Roman officer who loved the people he was policing was rare enough to be talked about.

And he is the one who built us our synagogue. At his own expense: a wealthy and generous man. A Roman officer paid for the building in which the Scriptures were read and the God of Israel worshipped, in a town he was garrisoning: an extraordinary act of respect towards a conquered people’s God. At Capernaum today the remains of a white limestone synagogue from about the fourth century stand on the black basalt foundations of an earlier one, and it is entirely possible that the stones the centurion paid for are still there.

Only one is worthy. The elders say he is worthy. He himself will say he is not worthy (v. 6). The difference is the difference between two whole religions: one in which God is approached on the strength of a record, and one in which he is approached on the strength of his own goodness. And the gospel settles where that goodness comes to us. There is one person of whom heaven says, worthy are you (Revelation 5:9), the Lamb who was slain, and every sinner who is welcomed by God is welcomed on his worthiness, not his own. Christians do not bring God their synagogues. They come in the name of Jesus, with a righteousness that is not their own but comes through faith in Christ (Philippians 3:9). The centurion, without yet knowing the cross, stood in exactly the right place: unworthy, and asking.

One man or messengers? Matthew tells this same story and has the centurion come to Jesus and speak directly, with no elders and no friends in sight (Matthew 8:5–13). A reader who notices will want to know which it was. The answer is that this is how people have always reported such things, then and now. We say a king built a palace when he had it built, or that a firm wrote to us when a clerk typed the letter; what a man does through those he authorises to speak for him is credited to the man. Matthew, writing tightly, gives the centurion’s own words and leaves out the machinery of how they travelled. Luke, who told us he had carefully followed what the eyewitnesses handed down (1:2–3), keeps the machinery, and the extra detail sharpens Matthew’s point rather than softening it. The man is so persuaded he has no standing before Jesus that he will not even present himself. He sends others to say he is not worthy to come.

So do good works count for nothing? They count for a great deal before people, and nothing as a claim on God. The centurion’s generosity was real and good; it gave him friends who would speak for him, and it showed what his faith was already doing in him. But it did not put Jesus in his debt, and he knew it. Good works are the fruit of a heart that loves God and its neighbour, and they adorn the gospel (Titus 2:10). What they can never be is a bargaining chip. The moment we bring them to God as a reason he should help us, we have joined the elders and left the centurion.

In a sentence. The centurion sent Jewish elders to ask Jesus to heal his slave, and they urged Jesus to help because the man deserved it, loving the Jewish people and having built their synagogue.

On a Tuesday. Notice how you pray when you are desperate. Do you find yourself listing reasons God should help you: the years you have served, the giving, the times you said yes? That is the elders’ prayer. It is natural, and it is the wrong foundation. No one deserves God’s grace because of their good works. Bring the need, and plead God’s mercy and Christ’s merit instead. And meanwhile keep doing good to the people around you, because good works can open doors for others to speak for you, and for the gospel.

For worship. The God of Israel is not for sale, and he does not need to be. The centurion could build him a synagogue, but he could not buy his attention, and he did not have to: the Lord was already on his way. Every blessing God gives is given freely, out of the riches of his own kindness, so that no one may boast (Ephesians 2:8–9). We bring him nothing that obliges him, and he comes anyway.
verseByVerse.note: Luke tells us he sent elders; Matthew compresses the story as if he came himself. Some Gentiles admired Judaism and supported synagogues.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus went with them. When he was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends, saying to him, 'Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went with them. When he was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends, saying to him: Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed.
