And Jesus went with them. Five words. No enquiry into the man’s religion, no comment on slaveholding or the Roman occupation: a Jewish teacher sets off towards a Gentile officer’s house because a servant is dying. And then, before he arrives, a second message comes down the road.

Lord, do not trouble yourself. Do not go to the effort. The elders had said he is worthy. The centurion says, through his friends, that he is not. He is not being modest about his achievements. He is saying that the categories the elders were using do not apply.

For I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Worthy again, but a different word this time (hikanos, sufficient, fit). A devout Jew would not normally enter a Gentile house, because it would make him ceremonially unclean (Acts 10:28). The centurion knew this and spared Jesus the difficulty. But it is more than tact. He recognises Jesus’ greatness and his own unworthiness: a powerful Roman officer humbles himself before a Jewish teacher. It is a genuinely theological sentence, and it comes from a pagan soldier. He has understood something the men who built the case for him had not: that nothing he has done puts Jesus under any obligation, and that the distance between them is not measured in synagogues built.

Therefore I did not presume to come to you. He did not consider himself worthy even to approach Jesus. The reasoning is consistent all the way down. He did not come in person, not out of caution but out of conviction: a man who believes he has no standing does not push to the front.

But say the word, and let my servant be healed. He asks for nothing except a sentence. He does not need a touch, a ritual, a visit, or a sight of the patient. He believes that this man can say something in one place and have it happen in another, and he believes it firmly enough to stop the healer on the road and tell him not to bother coming. No one in Israel had shown this kind of faith.

The faith the church lives on. This is precisely the faith the church has had to live on ever since. Nobody now gets Jesus under their roof in the way the centurion declined. What is available is exactly what he asked for and got: the word, spoken at a distance, by someone whose authority is not limited by where his feet are. Every prayer offered for somebody in another country, every sermon trusted to do its work in a heart, rests on the thing this soldier worked out on a street in Capernaum.

Is it wrong to want Jesus to come close? No. The centurion is not teaching that we should keep Jesus at arm’s length; he is teaching that we do not need to see or feel him for his word to work. Jesus does come close to his people: he promises to make his home with those who love him (John 14:23) and to be with them always (Matthew 28:20). The point is that his nearness does not depend on our sensations. On the days you feel nothing, his word is exactly as powerful as on the days you feel everything.

In a sentence. As Jesus approached, the centurion sent friends to say he was not worthy to have Jesus enter his house, and asked him simply to speak the word of healing.

On a Tuesday. When you pray for someone far away (a child at university, a friend in hospital in another city, a missionary you have never met), you are standing where the centurion stood. You cannot be in the room, and you do not need to be. Pray as one unworthy, trusting the power of Christ’s word, and then leave it with him. That is the faith he honours.

For worship. The centurion’s words have entered Christian worship, and been said before the Lord’s Supper for centuries: Lord, I am not worthy that you should come under my roof; but only say the word. It is right that they should be, because they describe exactly how the King of heaven deals with us. We are not worthy that he should come under our roof, and he has come anyway, not only under our roof but into our flesh, and he has spoken the word over us that no illness and no death can disobey.
verseByVerse.note: A devout Jew would not normally enter a Gentile house.

parallels.desc: he sent out his word and healed them

verseByVerse.quote: For I too am a man set under authority, with soldiers under me: and I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I too am a man set under authority, with soldiers under me: and I say to one, go, and he goes; and to another, come, and he comes; and to my servant, do this, and he does it.

For I too am a man set under authority. Now the centurion explains his reasoning, and it is the most penetrating piece of theology anyone has produced so far in this Gospel. He does not say, I am a man with authority. He says he too is a man set under authority, and only then mentions the men beneath him. He understands authority from his military life. He is under authority (his commanders, ultimately the emperor), and therefore has authority over others.

With soldiers under me. When he gives a command, it is done. He does not have to be present; his word is enough. And the centurion knows perfectly well why his orders are obeyed, and it is not because he is personally impressive. It is because when he speaks, Rome speaks. The soldier who ignores him is not defying a man; he is defying the empire standing behind the man. His authority is real precisely because it is derived, and it operates entirely through words, at whatever distance the words can travel.

The reasoning. He applies that framework to Jesus, and the application is astonishing. If my word, backed by Caesar, is obeyed by soldiers and slaves, then your word, backed by God, is obeyed by sickness and death. Illness is in the same position as a soldier: it is under orders. Jesus stands under his Father’s authority and therefore wields God’s authority over every power. The centurion grasped what even the disciples were slow to understand: that Jesus’ word is the word of God, which does what it says and does not return empty (Isaiah 55:11).

A soldier taught by his job. He did not read it in the prophets. He worked it out from his life in the army and applied it to a man he had never met, and he was right. The authority Jesus exercises over sickness is the authority of the one who made the body, and creation obeys its Maker as reliably as a legionary obeys Rome, and more so. There is something in that for anybody who has ever felt their ordinary working life to be spiritually irrelevant. The best theologian in Galilee that morning was a soldier, and what qualified him was his job.

Does under authority mean Jesus is less than God? No. The centurion was reasoning from what he knew, and he had it exactly right as far as it went: Jesus does speak with the Father’s authority, because the Son came to do the Father’s will (John 5:19, 30). But the Son submits as the eternal Son, equal with the Father, not as a lesser being. The centurion saw that Jesus’ word carries God’s authority; the rest of the New Testament shows that it carries it because he is God the Son, the one through whom all things were made (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16). The soldier’s analogy was humble and true, and the truth was even greater than his analogy.

In a sentence. The centurion explained that, as a man under authority whose commands are obeyed, he knew Jesus’ command would be obeyed too.

On a Tuesday. Take the thing you are most afraid of this week, the diagnosis, the redundancy, the conversation, and say to yourself plainly: this too is under orders. Nothing in your life is outside the command of Christ. That does not mean he will always order it away; it means nothing reaches you that he has not permitted, and nothing stays one hour longer than he allows. And look at your own work with fresh eyes. Whatever you do all day may be teaching you something true about God, if you let it.

For worship. Every power in the universe stands to attention before the Son of God. Disease and demons, wind and wave, death itself: all of them are soldiers in his army, coming and going at his word. He upholds the universe by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3), and the same word that keeps the stars in place was spoken on a road in Galilee for a slave. Blessed be the Lord whose command nothing can disobey, and who uses that authority to heal.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him, and turning to the crowd that followed him, said, 'I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.' And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the servant well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus heard these things, he marvelled at him, and turning to the crowd that followed him, said: I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith. And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the servant well.

When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him. Jesus is astonished. There are only two occasions in the Gospels on which Jesus is said to marvel (Matthew tells of this one too, at 8:10), and they are exact opposites. Here he marvels at a Gentile’s faith. At Nazareth he marvelled at the unbelief of the people who had watched him grow up (Mark 6:6). He was surprised, both times, in the same direction: faith turning up where nobody expected it, and refused where everybody did.

How can the Son of God be surprised? The question is worth facing rather than dodging, and the answer is the one Luke gave at 2:52, where Jesus grew in wisdom. In the one person of the Son there are two whole natures. According to his divine nature he knows everything and learns nothing. According to his human nature he genuinely encountered this man, on that road, and was genuinely moved by what he heard. Jesus was truly human and could be astonished. The wonder is real. He was not acting.

Not even in Israel have I found such faith. He turns to the crowd and says it to them, which means it is not a private compliment but a deliberate lesson, delivered to a Jewish audience, comparing them unfavourably with a Roman officer. Israel, with the law, the prophets and the promises, should have had the greatest faith. Instead, a Gentile soldier outshines them all. It is the same point that emptied the synagogue at Nazareth in fury (4:25–27), and here it is again. It is a foretaste of the Gentile mission in Acts (Acts 10–11; 28:28), and Matthew adds the saying about many coming from east and west to sit at table with Abraham (Matthew 8:11).

What faith did Jesus commend? Not the man’s generosity, though it was real. Not his humility, though it was accurate. What Jesus names as faith is his confidence that the word of Christ is sufficient: that nothing further is required, no presence, no procedure, no leverage. Faith in the Bible is not a feeling of certainty or a force we generate. It is trust in a person, resting on what he has said. The centurion’s faith was great not because he felt strongly but because he saw clearly how great Jesus is.

And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the servant well. Healed by a word, at a distance. Jesus never saw him or spoke to him. Luke reports it flatly and from the messengers’ point of view. Nobody saw the healing happen. A man said something on a road, and in a house some distance away a dying slave stopped dying, and the only people who could testify to it walked in afterwards and found him up. The only other healing at a distance in the first three Gospels is also of a Gentile (Mark 7:24–30). The Gentiles receive the blessing of Christ without seeing him, as believers have done ever since (John 20:29).

How it often looks. That is very often how it looks from inside a Christian’s life. The word goes out, nothing visible happens where you are standing, and you come home and find that something has.

If I have great faith, will God always heal? No. The centurion’s faith was great, but the healing came from Jesus’ will and word, not from the size of the faith. Faith is not a lever that forces God’s hand. Paul, whose faith no one doubts, prayed three times for his own thorn to be removed and was told no (2 Corinthians 12:7–9), and he left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). We are to pray boldly for healing, and God often gives it. But when he does not, it is not proof that we believed too little. It means he has a better purpose, and his grace will be sufficient.

In a sentence. Jesus marvelled, declaring that he had not found such faith even in Israel, and the messengers returned to find the servant healed.

On a Tuesday. If you grew up in church, let this verse unsettle you a little. The people with the most privileges were outshone by an outsider. Ask whether your familiarity with Jesus has made you expect less of him than a newcomer does. And when you have prayed and seen nothing, remember the messengers walking back to the house. Keep walking; you may find that something has happened.

For worship. You have not seen Jesus, yet his word reaches you, as it reached a slave in a house he never entered. The Lord who marvelled at a soldier’s faith is the one who gave that faith in the first place, for faith is the gift of God. He delights to find it, and he delights to answer it. And the Gentile at Capernaum was the first of a great multitude, from east and west, who would trust a Christ they had never seen and sit down at his table.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–17 — Jesus Raises a Widow's Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The raising at Nain is one of the most tender scenes in Luke and one of the most deliberately crafted. Two crowds meet at the town gate: the crowd following Jesus, and a funeral coming out.

At the centre of the funeral is a widow carrying out her only son, and Luke underlines both facts because both are load-bearing. A woman's economic and legal standing ran through a man — father, then husband, then son. She has already buried the husband. She is now burying the son, and there is no fourth name on the list. This is not only the worst grief there is; it is destitution.

Nobody asks Jesus for anything. There is no centurion sending elders, no friends taking a roof apart. She has not prayed and does not know who he is. He simply arrives at the intersection of his journey and her grief.

“And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her.” Two things in that sentence. This is the first time Luke himself calls Jesus the Lord in his own narration — not a title on somebody's lips but the evangelist's own description, and he uses it in front of a coffin. And the compassion is something involuntary and physical — Luke uses the same words of the father seeing the prodigal (15:20) and the Samaritan seeing the man in the ditch (10:33).

He touches the bier, which under the law makes a man unclean for seven days (Num. 19:11) — and, as with the leper in chapter 5, the traffic runs the wrong way. Then one sentence to a corpse: “Young man, I say to you, arise.”

Luke, the physician, records the result in two clinical stages: he sat up, and he began to speak. And then the sentence that is the point of the whole scene — “and Jesus gave him to his mother” — which is almost word for word what is said of Elijah at Zarephath: he delivered him to his mother (1 Kgs. 17:23).

The crowd's response is fear, and then two acclamations: “A great prophet has arisen among us!” and “God has visited his people!” Both are true, and both fall short. Elijah prayed three times and God raised the boy; this man gave an order.
verseByVerse.theology:
The raising of the widow's son is a sign of the kingdom with both an immediate and an ultimate reference. Immediately it is the reversal of the most final of all reversals, accomplished by the one who will himself die and rise. Ultimately it points forward to the general resurrection, when the dead will rise at the voice of the Son of God (John 5:25-29; 1 Thess. 4:16).

Jesus does not raise this young man permanently; he will die again. What the miracle demonstrates is not the abolition of biological death but authority over death as a power — the authority that reaches its final expression in Jesus's own resurrection.

The echo of Elijah is deliberate, and Luke has been preparing it since 4:26, when Jesus preached about the widow of Zarephath at Nazareth and the town tried to kill him. Both prophets meet a widow whose only son has died; both speak; both give the son back to his mother in almost the same words.

The echo establishes Jesus as the fulfilment of the prophetic tradition rather than its continuation. Where Elijah stretched himself over the boy and cried out to the LORD three times, Jesus simply speaks. The authority has been concentrated. The prophet gives way to the Lord of the prophets.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus's compassion for the widow, unprompted and unsolicited, is the model of the grace that sees before it is asked. She did not pray. She did not seek him out. She was lost in her grief, and he saw her.

He was not the only person at that gate who could see her — the whole town was there. He was the one who looked at the woman rather than the coffin. The posture of compassion begins with seeing, and the Christian who prays to notice what God notices is asking to become like the man who walked into Nain and saw a widow in a crowd.

“Do not weep” — said to a woman at her only son's funeral — would be an outrage from anybody else. It is not a denial of her grief and not a rebuke; he wept himself at a friend's tomb. He says it because he is about to remove the reason.

That is the only circumstance in which the sentence is not cruelty, and it is the circumstance he was standing in. Nobody else may say it. He may — and one day, to everybody, he will (Rev. 21:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Soon afterward he went to a town called Nain, and his disciples and a great crowd went with him. As he drew near to the gate of the town, behold, a man who had died was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow, and a considerable crowd from the town was with her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Soon afterwards he went to a town called Nain, and his disciples and a great crowd went with him. As he drew near to the gate of the town, behold, a man who had died was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow, and a considerable crowd from the town was with her.

Soon afterward he went to a town called Nain. A village about 6 miles (10 km) south-east of Nazareth, on the slope of the hill of Moreh. Only Luke records this miracle. And the geography is not accidental. Nain is near Shunem, where Elisha raised a woman’s son (2 Kings 4:8–37), and further north, at Zarephath, Elijah had raised a widow’s only son (1 Kings 17:17–24). The crowd will draw the connection (v. 16).

As he drew near to the gate of the town. Two processions meet at a gate, and Luke has staged it deliberately. Coming up the road is Jesus, with his disciples and a great crowd: a company full of the energy of what happened in Capernaum, on their way into town. Coming out of the town is a funeral, with a considerable crowd of its own. One crowd is following the Lord of life into the town; the other is following a corpse out of it. The two meet in the gateway, and one of them is going to have to give way.

A man who had died was being carried out. Burial took place on the day of death, outside the town, because of the heat and because the dead made people unclean. The body was wrapped and carried on an open bier, with mourners, probably hired flute players and wailing women as was customary, moving towards the burial ground outside the walls.

The only son of his mother, and she was a widow. Luke describes the dead man in three steps, and each one closes a door. A man who had died: that is the first. Not sick, not sinking, but past every remedy anyone in either crowd could offer. The only son of his mother: that is the second. Not one of several, the only one. And she was a widow: that is the third, and it is the one that finishes her.

What those facts meant. A woman in the first century had no independent economic standing. Her security ran through a man: first her father, then her husband, then her son. This woman has already buried the husband. She is now burying the son. There is no fourth name on the list. So she is not merely a mother in the worst grief there is. She is, from that morning, facing destitution, with no income, no one to protect her in court, and no one to carry on the family name, walking behind the body of the last person who stood between her and the road.

Nobody asks. And notice what is completely absent from this story. Nobody asks Jesus for anything. There is no centurion sending elders, no friends taking a roof apart, no leper on his face in the road. Nobody in that funeral has heard of him or is looking for him. She has not prayed. She is, as far as Luke tells us, entirely lost in what has happened to her. He simply arrives at the intersection of his journey and her grief.

Did Jesus plan to meet her? Luke does not say he went to Nain because of the funeral, but the whole Gospel teaches that the Son did nothing by chance and that his Father governs every hour. Whether Jesus knew in advance or not, his Father did, and the timing that brought him to that gate at that moment was no accident. That is worth remembering in your own life. The meetings that change everything often look like coincidence from the inside.

In a sentence. At the gate of Nain, Jesus and his followers met a funeral procession carrying the only son of a widow.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone you know who is grieving and has stopped asking for help, perhaps because they do not believe anything can be done. They are like this widow: not praying, just walking behind the bier. You may be the one God uses to bring Christ to the gate. Go to them. And if you are that person yourself, take comfort: he came to this widow before she asked.

For worship. The Lord of life does not wait at a distance for the grieving to find him. He walks up the road into the gate of their sorrow. The God who is a father to the fatherless and protector of widows (Psalm 68:5) was walking into Nain in human flesh, and the procession of death was about to meet the one whom death cannot hold.
verseByVerse.note: Nain was a village south-east of Nazareth, near Shunem, where Elisha raised a widow’s son. A widow who lost her only son lost her means of support.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, 'Do not weep.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her: do not weep.

And when the Lord saw her. Luke has changed something, and a first-century reader would have caught it. Up to this point he has narrated Jesus by name. Here, for the first time in his story, Luke himself calls him the Lord, not as a title on somebody’s lips but as his own description of who this is. He does it at the gate of Nain, in front of a bier, at the very moment Jesus is about to show his power over death.

He saw her. There were two crowds and a body and a great deal of noise, and what he saw was the woman. She was not the loudest thing at that gate. She was a widow walking behind a bier among a crowd of mourners, and every person there had come for the son. He looked at her.

He had compassion on her. The verb is esplanchnisthē, from the word for the inward organs: the Greeks located the strongest feelings in the gut, and this is a word for something deep, involuntary and physical. It is the same word used of the father catching sight of the prodigal on the road (15:20), and of the Samaritan seeing the man in the ditch (10:33). It is not a decision to be kind. It is what happened inside him when he saw her. No one asked him. No one expressed faith. He simply saw her grief and was moved. This is pure grace.

The tender mercy of our God. And it is what Zechariah had sung about God himself: the tender mercy of our God, by which the sunrise would visit us from on high (1:78). The thing the old priest sang about in the abstract is now standing in a gateway, looking at a widow.

Do not weep. Those three words would be an outrage from anybody else. Said at a graveside to a woman who has lost her only child, it is the sort of thing that makes people leave the church. He is not telling her that grief is inappropriate; he does not say that anywhere, and he wept himself at a friend’s tomb (John 11:35). He is not offering perspective, or reminding her of the resurrection at the last day, or suggesting she is taking it badly. He is telling her to stop because he is about to remove the reason. It is the only circumstance in which the sentence is not cruelty, and it is the circumstance he is standing in. Nobody else may say it. He may, and one day, to all his people, he will, when he wipes away every tear from their eyes (Revelation 21:4).

So should Christians not grieve? Christians grieve, and should. Jesus wept, Paul speaks of sorrow upon sorrow (Philippians 2:27), and the Psalms are full of lament. What Scripture forbids is not grief but grief without hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Do not say do not weep to a grieving friend; only Christ has the right to say it. What you can say is what he has promised: that death is not the end for those who are his, and that the day is coming when there will be no more mourning. Weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15), and hold the hope for them until they can hold it themselves.

In a sentence. When the Lord saw the widow, he was filled with compassion and told her not to weep.

On a Tuesday. In a crowded room, who do you see? Jesus saw the one person nobody had come for. This week, at church, at work, at a family gathering, look for the person on the edge whose grief everyone else has forgotten, and go and sit with them. And if you are the one grieving, know that you are seen. You do not have to be the loudest voice in the room for him to notice you.

For worship. He looked at a mother following her only son to the grave, and he knew what lay ahead of him. Simeon had told his own mother that a sword would pierce her soul (2:35), and John tells us she stood by the cross (John 19:25). And the Father in heaven would give up his only Son, not to be handed back at a gate, but to be given for us. The compassion that turned over inside him at Nain is the compassion of the God who did not spare his own Son (Romans 8:32). It is not a mood that passes. He sees every widow still.
verseByVerse.note: This is the first time Luke calls Jesus “the Lord” in his narrative.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. And he said, 'Young man, I say to you, arise.' And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. And he said: young man, I say to you, arise. And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother.

Then he came up and touched the bier. Two things happen in that sentence, and both matter. He touched the bier, an open stretcher or plank on which the wrapped body lay. Under the law, contact with a corpse made a man unclean for seven days and required the water of purification, made with the ashes of the red heifer, to undo (Numbers 19:11–16). This is not a technicality; it is one of the strongest defilements in the law of Moses, and everyone in both crowds knew it. Mourners walked behind a bier; nobody who cared about purity laid a hand on one. He put his hand on it, and, exactly as with the leper two chapters earlier (5:13), the traffic runs the other way. Jesus is not defiled by death; death is undone by him.

And the bearers stood still. Nobody has told them to stop; the men carrying the body simply halt, startled, because a stranger has laid a hand on it. For a few seconds, at the gate of a Galilean town, a funeral is standing motionless in the road.

Young man, I say to you, arise. He speaks to a dead man, directly, as if he could hear, and he does. I say to you: on his own authority. There is no prayer here, and that is worth setting beside the obvious parallels. Elijah, faced with the widow of Zarephath and her dead son, stretched himself on the boy three times and cried out to the LORD, and God gave the child back (1 Kings 17:21). Elisha prayed and lay on the Shunammite’s son (2 Kings 4:33–35). The prophets prayed, and God raised. Jesus gives an instruction. He does not pray for power; he commands, because he is the resurrection and the life (John 11:25).

And the dead man sat up and began to speak. Proof that he was alive, and well. Luke, the physician, records it in two plain stages: he sat up; he started talking. Whatever the young man said, Luke does not tell us, and there is a restraint in that which is worth noticing. A later writer making things up would not have resisted supplying a report from the other side.

And Jesus gave him to his mother. Five words, and they are the point of the whole scene. Not, and the crowd was amazed; not, and the young man followed him. He handed the boy back to the woman he had looked at in the gateway. The miracle was for her. Jesus restores him to her, and her future with him. And the words are, almost exactly, what is said of Elijah at the end of the Zarephath story: he delivered him to his mother (1 Kings 17:23). Luke knew exactly what he was echoing. The prophet prayed three times and God raised the boy. Here the Lord of the prophets says a single sentence, and hands a son back to his mother, and walks on into the town.

What it shows. Jesus has power over death. This young man would die again; it was a restoration to this life, not the resurrection of the last day. But it was a sign of the final resurrection, when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out (John 5:28–29). What he did for one widow’s son at one gate, he will do for all his people at once.

Could he only have been unconscious? A sceptic may suggest it, but Luke leaves no room for it. He calls him a man who had died, his mother and a whole town were mourning him, and people who lived with death at close quarters were seized with fear at what they saw. A man in a faint does not sit up and speak at a stranger’s command at the very moment the command is given. In the end the question is not whether a physician could explain the scene, but who it was who spoke. Luke’s answer is the empty tomb: the Lord who raised this young man was himself raised, and his resurrection is the warrant for all the rest (24:6–7).

Why did Jesus raise some and not others? He did not empty every graveyard he passed. The raisings in the Gospels (this young man, Jairus’s daughter, Lazarus) were signs, pointing to who he is and to what he will do on the last day. They were not the final answer to death; the young man of Nain died again. The final answer came at the empty tomb, where Jesus himself rose never to die again, the firstfruits of all who belong to him (1 Corinthians 15:20–23). If you have buried someone you loved who trusted Christ, he has not passed them by. Their raising has been kept for the morning when it will be permanent.

In a sentence. Jesus touched the bier and commanded the dead young man to rise; he sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him back to his mother.

On a Tuesday. Next time you stand at a funeral of a believer, picture the bearers at Nain standing still. The procession you are in is not the last word. Let the hope change how you speak to the bereaved: not with cheap comfort, but with the solid promise that the one who said arise at Nain will say it again. And if you are tempted to keep away from the dying and the grieving because it is uncomfortable, remember that Jesus put his hand on the bier.

For worship. The one who spoke to the dead at Nain will speak to the dead on the last day, and they will hear. Death could not hold his word, and it could not hold him. He who laid his hand on a bier let himself be laid in a tomb, went down into death itself, and came out on the third day holding the keys of death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). The procession out of the gate has been turned round for ever. Since that morning, every funeral of his people is walking towards a resurrection.
verseByVerse.note: The dead were carried on an open bier and buried the same day. Touching it made a person unclean.

parallels.desc: he gave him to his mother

verseByVerse.quote: Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying, 'A great prophet has arisen among us!' and 'God has visited his people!' And this report about him spread through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying: a great prophet has arisen among us! and: God has visited his people! And this report about him spread through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding country.

Fear seized them all, and they glorified God. Fear first: holy awe. It is Luke’s consistent report of what the presence of God does to people (the shepherds in the field, the fishermen in the boat, the crowd after the paralytic), and it is not a defect in them. It is what sinful creatures feel when they realise that the holy God is not far away after all, and Peter’s cry in the boat, depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord (5:8), is what that fear sounds like. Something has happened at that gate which does not belong in the ordinary world, and the right first response is not delight but awe. And then praise. Luke records the two acclamations as two separate sayings going round the crowd.

A great prophet has arisen among us! They are entirely right, and they are working from the obvious precedent. A prophet, a widow, a dead only son, a boy given back to his mother: anybody who knew 1 Kings 17 would reach for Elijah, and they did. Perhaps, too, they thought of the prophet like Moses whom God had promised to raise up (Deuteronomy 18:15). It is the correct identification, and it is not enough. Elijah prayed and God raised the boy; this man gave an order. The crowd has recognised the category and missed that the category has been exceeded. Jesus is more than a prophet.

God has visited his people! This one is larger than the crowd knows. The verb is the one Zechariah used in his song: he has visited and redeemed his people (1:68, 78). It means God coming to see about his people with intent to act, the language of the exodus. They mean: God has taken notice of us again after all these years. What is actually true is that God has arrived in person and is walking through their gate, and the sentence they are saying is more accurate than they can possibly intend.

Incomplete theology, sound instinct. That describes most of what happens when God works among ordinary people. They knew they had seen God do something; they had not yet grasped who had done it. Nobody in this Gospel arrives at a full understanding of Jesus in one afternoon, and Luke does not despise the partial recognition. He records it, and moves the story on.

Through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding country. Judea here means the whole Jewish land, not only the southern province (4:44). The news travelled far enough to reach John the Baptist in Herod’s prison.

In the flow. The crowd’s verdict, a great prophet, sets the question that runs through the rest of the chapter. The news reaches John in prison, and he asks whether Jesus is the one who is to come (vv. 18–19). Jesus tells the crowd that John is a prophet and more than a prophet (v. 26). Simon the Pharisee decides that Jesus cannot be a prophet at all (v. 39), and his guests end by asking who this is who even forgives sins (v. 49). Scene by scene, Luke is leading his reader from prophet to Lord.

Is calling Jesus a prophet enough? It is true but incomplete. Jesus is a prophet, the greatest of them, the one Moses foretold (Acts 3:22). But many today are happy to call him a great prophet or a great teacher precisely to avoid calling him Lord and God. Luke will not let us stop there. The crowd at Nain said more than they knew; we are meant to say all of it. If Jesus is only a prophet, he cannot forgive sins (v. 49), and he cannot raise you on the last day. He is God come to visit his people.

In a sentence. Everyone was filled with awe and praised God, saying a great prophet had arisen and God had visited his people, and the news spread everywhere.

On a Tuesday. When God does something in your life, a prayer answered, a crisis turned, a heart changed, tell someone. The news from Nain spread because people talked. You do not need a complete theology to say: I have seen God do something. And let awe come before excitement. Ask yourself when you last felt the holy fear of being near God at work.

For worship. God has visited his people in Jesus, not to inspect but to redeem. The Lord who came down to Egypt when he heard his people groaning came down to Nain, and then to Golgotha, and he will come again. Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–35 — Messengers from John the Baptist
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
John is in prison — Herod arrested him for confronting the tetrarch's marriage (3:19-20) — and the imprisonment has raised the question that was always implicit in his ministry. He sends two disciples with it: “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?”

Take in who is asking. The man who leapt in the womb at Christ's approach (1:41), who saw the heavens open and the Spirit descend, who said “Behold, the Lamb of God” — this man, in a cell, in the dark, wondering whether he had been wrong. If he could come to the edge of that question, the presence of doubt is not proof that a faith was never real. It is very often the mark of a real faith under a real weight.

Jesus's answer is neither a rebuke nor a reassurance but a demonstration. First he works, in that very hour, in front of the messengers. Then: “Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them.”

The list is a mosaic of Isaiah — 26:19, 29:18, 35:5-6, 61:1 — the texts describing what it will look like when God finally comes to save. John knew every one by heart. Jesus is answering doubt not with an argument but with evidence, and the evidence is the Scriptures John built his life on, now enacted in front of his own men.

“And blessed is the one who is not offended by me” is a gentle warning that names John's actual difficulty without embarrassing him. He had announced an axe at the root and a winnowing fork (3:9, 17); what he is hearing about is healings and dinner parties. Everything promised is coming. Not everything is coming yet.

After the messengers leave — and only after — Jesus tells the crowd what he thinks of John: not a reed shaken by the wind, not a man in soft clothing, but a prophet, and more than a prophet, the messenger of Malachi 3:1. “Among those born of women none is greater than John. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.”

The section ends with the children in the marketplace. John came fasting and they said he had a demon; the Son of Man came eating and they called him a glutton. The objections were mutually exclusive, which proves the objections were never the reason.
verseByVerse.theology:
John's doubt from prison is the New Testament's most honest portrait of faith under pressure, and it is treated with complete respect. Jesus does not rebuke him, question his faith, or withdraw the commendation he is about to give. He answers the question with careful evidence.

That is the pastoral heart of the passage. Genuine doubt, honestly expressed, receives a genuine answer. A Christian tradition that treats doubt as a mark of spiritual failure has missed the model of Jesus himself. Honest wrestling with “is it really true?” is not the absence of faith; it is faith pushed to its limit by circumstance and still asking — and asking the right person.

The saying about the least in the kingdom is not a demotion of John but an elevation of the kingdom. It concerns position in redemptive history, not personal holiness or usefulness. John stood at the threshold: he announced the Lamb and did not live to see the Lamb slain, or raised, or the Spirit poured out.

The least believer in the kingdom has what John did not yet have — an accomplished redemption, a finished sacrifice, and the indwelling Spirit. Not because that believer is more faithful, but because he lives on the other side of the event John was pointing at.
verseByVerse.examples:
John's question is the question of every sincere believer facing a crisis of expectation: I believed this was true; this is not what I expected; am I wrong? And the answer Jesus gives is not “of course you are right, do not worry.” It is “look at the evidence.”

When faith is under pressure the antidote is not reassurance but the careful examination of what has actually happened — the Scriptures, the cross, the empty tomb, the testimony of those who met the risen Christ. Faith is not a leap in the dark; it is a step towards evidence that has been examined.

Notice too what John did with his doubt. He did not sit in the dark nursing it, and he did not broadcast it. He sent it to Jesus. That is the one move available to a man in a cell, and it is the right one.

And the parable of the children diagnoses a condition that is not confined to Pharisees. There is a way of engaging with the things of God in which one is always, sincerely, weighing an objection — the preaching is too demanding, or too soft; that Christian is a hypocrite, and that one a fanatic. Every objection may be individually reasonable. What gives the game away is that the seat is never vacated. The test is not whether you have a criticism, but whether anything has ever succeeded in getting you up.

verseByVerse.quote: The disciples of John reported all these things to him. And John, calling two of his disciples to him, sent them to the Lord, saying, 'Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?' And when the men had come to him, they said, 'John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, ‘Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples of John reported all these things to him. John, calling two of his disciples to him, sent them to the Lord, saying: are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another? When the men had come to him, they said: John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?

The disciples of John reported all these things to him. All these things: a centurion’s servant healed at a word, a dead man sitting up at a town gate. And John is in prison. Luke has already told us why (3:19–20). He confronted Herod Antipas about his marriage to his brother’s wife, and Herod locked him up, in the fortress of Machaerus, according to Josephus, on the far side of the Dead Sea. He has been there for months, and he will not come out.

Are you the one who is to come. The one who is to come (ho erchomenos) was a way of speaking of the Messiah, drawn from texts like Psalm 118:26 (blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD) and Malachi 3:1, where the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple. And John himself had used it: he had said that one mightier than he was coming (3:16).

Or shall we look for another? Read that slowly and take in who is asking. This is the man who leapt in his mother’s womb at the sound of Mary’s voice (1:41). Who was filled with the Spirit before he was born. Who baptised Jesus and saw the Spirit come down like a dove. Who said, of this very man, Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). That man is now asking whether he got it wrong.

Why did John doubt? Several things may be going on, and it is honest to say we cannot be certain which. He may be asking for his disciples’ sake rather than his own. More likely he is struggling with the shape of it. He had preached a Messiah who would come with the axe at the root and the winnowing fork in his hand, and with the fire of judgement (3:9, 17). What he is hearing about is healings and dinner parties with sinners, and no fire at all. And John was in prison, and the Messiah was supposed to proclaim liberty to the captives (4:18). Jesus did not fit his expectations. Or he may simply be in the darkness that a cell and a death sentence can bring on anybody. Even the greatest of the prophets had moments of doubt.

What it does not mean. Not that John lost his faith. He brought his doubt to Jesus, which is exactly what to do with doubt. And stay with it a moment longer, because there is more comfort here than a first reading gives. If this man, the greatest born of women by Christ’s own verdict a few verses later, could come to the edge of asking whether to look for another, then the presence of doubt is not proof that a faith was never real. It is very often the mark of a real faith under a real weight.

What he does with it. He does not sit in the dark nursing it, and he does not announce it to the world. He sends it to Jesus, and Luke tells it twice over: John sends, and then the men arrive and repeat the question word for word (v. 20).

The Lamb John had named. The answer to John’s question lay in his own earlier words. The Gospel of John records that the Baptist had pointed at Jesus and said, Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). A lamb does not come swinging an axe. It comes to be offered. The fire and the winnowing fork John preached were real, and the day of judgement will come, but the Messiah would first stand under that judgement himself. I have a baptism to be baptised with, Jesus says later in Luke, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished! (12:50). John was puzzled because the Coming One was not yet doing the thing he had foretold. He was doing something greater first: walking towards the cross where the fire would fall on him, so that it need never fall on those who trust him.

Is doubt a sin? Doubt is not the same as unbelief. Unbelief refuses to trust God; doubt is a believer struggling to hold on while something does not make sense. Scripture is full of believers who asked God hard questions: the psalmists (Psalm 13; 73), Habakkuk, Job, and here John. What they did not do was walk away from God; they took their questions to him. Doubt becomes dangerous when it is nursed in private, fed by resentment, and never brought to Christ and his word. Brought to him, it is very often the road to a stronger faith. Jesus did not rebuke John for asking. He answered him.

In a sentence. From prison, John sent two disciples to ask Jesus whether he really was the Messiah, or whether they should wait for someone else.

On a Tuesday. When Jesus does not act as you expected, and doubts come, take them to him. Write the question down, honestly, as John did, and bring it to God in prayer. Then go to his word, and if you can, to a mature Christian friend, rather than to the voices that will only feed the darkness. He does not despise honest questions.

For worship. The Lord did not leave his forerunner alone in the dark. John had spent his life preparing the way for Jesus; now it is Jesus who sends back down the road to John, with an answer for the cell. He is the Servant Isaiah promised, who does not snap the reed that is already bent or snuff out the wick that has burned low (Isaiah 42:3), and the same word he sent to Machaerus he sends to his people in their own darkest hours. Blessed be the Shepherd who does not scold his sheep for crying out in the night, but answers.
verseByVerse.note: John was in prison, held by Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: In that hour he healed many people of diseases and plagues and evil spirits, and on many who were blind he bestowed sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In that hour he healed many people of diseases and plagues and evil spirits, and on many who were blind he bestowed sight.

In that hour he healed many people. Before Jesus answers a word, he works, in that hour, while John’s two messengers stand there watching. Only Luke records this. The men were sent to ask a question about identity, and what they are given first is an afternoon: not an argument, but evidence.

Diseases and plagues and evil spirits. Luke, the physician, distinguishes the categories carefully, as he does throughout: diseases, chronic conditions; plagues (mastigōn, literally scourges), severe afflictions that lash a body; evil spirits, a separate category again, not collapsed into the medical ones.

And on many who were blind he bestowed sight. Then the blind, singled out and given their own clause, because they are about to matter. Of everything in the list Jesus is about to send back to the cell, sight to the blind is the one Isaiah repeats most often, and it is something no first-century physician could do. Bestowed (echarisato) means gave as a gift of grace. The word comes from charis, grace. Sight given freely.

The method. It is the same method Jesus will use after the empty tomb, showing his hands and feet. He does not defend himself by assertion. He does the thing, and lets the doing be the evidence. A man in a prison cell has asked whether the whole of his life’s work was pointed at the right person. The reply is not going to be, trust me. It is going to be a list of things his own messengers saw with their own eyes that afternoon: checkable, specific, and matching a text John had known since boyhood. That is how Christ handles honest doubt, and it has not changed. He does not scold it, and he does not ask for a leap in the dark. He points at what has actually happened.

Where is the evidence for me? You were not standing there that afternoon. But you have the same evidence John received, written down by eyewitnesses so that you may have certainty (1:4). You have the empty tomb and the witnesses to the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). You have the fulfilled prophecies. You have two thousand years of changed lives, and very likely some in your own church. And if you are a believer, you have the work of Christ in you: a love for him you once did not have. Faith is not a leap in the dark; it is trust resting on what God has done in history.

In a sentence. At that very time, Jesus healed many diseases, afflictions and evil spirits, and gave sight to many blind people.

On a Tuesday. When you doubt, look at what Jesus has done. Read one of the Gospels through, slowly, as evidence. Make a list of the ways God has kept his word in your own life. The evidence is there, and it is usually more than we remember.

For worship. The Lord does not ask us to believe in nothing. He bestows sight as a gift, and he has given us eyes to see his glory in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6). Every blind eye opened in Galilee was a preview of what he does in every heart he calls: he who said, let light shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered them, 'Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He answered them: go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.

Go and tell John what you have seen and heard. Report the evidence: eyewitness testimony. Not, tell John I am the Messiah. Not a rebuke, not a reassurance, not a word about how disappointing the question was. Jesus sends back a list of observable facts and lets John draw the conclusion. And the list is not merely a list of impressive works. It is a quotation.

The blind receive their sight, the lame walk. Jesus answers in the language of Isaiah’s promises about the coming of God to save: Isaiah 35:5–6 (the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then shall the lame man leap like a deer); Isaiah 29:18 (the deaf shall hear); Isaiah 26:19 (your dead shall live); Isaiah 61:1 (good news to the poor), which Jesus read at Nazareth (4:18). These are the passages describing what it will look like when God finally comes to save his people. John knew every one of them; he had built his ministry on the chapter that opens with the voice crying, prepare the way of the LORD (Isaiah 40:3). Jesus is saying: you know what the prophets said would happen when he came. Ask your messengers what they watched this afternoon. John would recognise it at once: these are the signs of the messianic age. Yes, I am the one.

Lepers are cleansed, the dead are raised up. Isaiah’s lists of signs never mention lepers, and only Isaiah 26:19 speaks of the dead living; Jesus adds both from his own works (5:12–13; 7:11–15), and they are greater still. The inclusion of lepers is its own argument: Israel had not seen a leper cleansed since Elisha and Naaman (4:27).

The poor have good news preached to them. The climax of the list. Preaching to the poor is placed after raising the dead, as the greatest sign. The gospel itself is the greatest miracle. A dead body raised will die again; a soul raised by the gospel lives for ever.

Where he stopped. As at Nazareth, Jesus leaves out the vengeance. Isaiah 35:4 says your God will come with vengeance; Isaiah 61:2 goes on to the day of vengeance of our God. The judgement John expected will come, but not yet. This is the time of grace. There is nothing in the list about an axe, or a winnowing fork, or fire, or a prison door opening. Everything John was promised is coming. Not everything is coming yet.

And blessed is the one who is not offended by me. Then the beatitude, and it is unmistakably meant for the man in the cell. Offended (skandalisthē) means caused to stumble, tripped up by something in the road. It is a gentle word and an honest one, and it names John’s actual difficulty without embarrassing him. It is a warning to John, and to all: do not stumble because I am not the kind of Messiah you expected. Blessed is the one who trusts me even when I do not fit his expectations.

Where believers stumble. This is exactly where a great many believers stumble, and the sentence is worth taking personally. The difficulty is rarely that Christ has failed to do what he said. It is that he has not done it in the order we assumed, or on the timetable we needed, or in the shape our expectations had already built for him. He does not promise John an explanation. He offers him the evidence, and a blessing for the man who can hold on when the answer is smaller than the question. And John, so far as the record goes, held on, and died in that cell, and was right all along.

Why did Jesus not get John out of prison? We are not told, and the silence is part of the lesson. Jesus could have opened the doors of Machaerus with a word, as he would later open a prison for Peter (Acts 12). He did not. John was beheaded (Mark 6:27). Faithfulness to Christ does not guarantee rescue in this life, and the gospel of the kingdom is not a promise of comfort now. What Jesus gave John was not freedom but the assurance that he had not been wrong, and a blessing on his faith. Some believers are delivered from the lions; others die by the sword, and Scripture honours them both (Hebrews 11:33–38).

In a sentence. Jesus told John’s messengers to report the signs Isaiah foretold for the age of salvation, and pronounced blessed the one who does not stumble over him.

On a Tuesday. Name the expectation you had of Jesus that he has not met: the healing that did not come, the marriage that did not happen, the prodigal who has not come home. Now look at what he has done, and let the list be as long as you can make it. Then pray the blessing over yourself: Lord, keep me from stumbling over you. Trust him as he is, not as you imagined him.

For worship. The Messiah came first not with the axe but with open hands: sight for the blind, feet for the lame, life for the dead, good news for the poor. The day of vengeance is real, and he has held it back so that sinners like us could be gathered in. Every opened eye in Galilee was a pledge of the last day, when the blind will see his face and the lame will run to meet him and the dead in Christ will rise. Blessed be the King whose first coming was all mercy.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus answers with the language of Isaiah’s promises.

verseByVerse.quote: When John's messengers had gone, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: 'What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are dressed in splendid clothing and live in luxury are in kings' courts. What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When John’s messengers had gone, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: what did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are dressed in splendid clothing and live in luxury are in kings’ courts. What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.

When John’s messengers had gone. The timing is one of the kindest details in the Gospel. Jesus waits until the two men are out of earshot, and only then tells the crowd what he thinks of John. The crowd might have thought less of John for his question; Jesus defends him. He could have sent the compliment back with the answer. He did not. John was to be given the evidence, not a testimonial, and the crowd was to be told the truth about a man who was not there to hear it and could not be embarrassed by it.

A reed shaken by the wind? Three rhetorical questions follow, each one demolishing something the crowd might have gone out to see. Reeds grew thick along the Jordan, tall, hollow, bending whichever way the air moved. It is a picture of a man with no fixed convictions, who goes with whatever is blowing. Was John that? No. He was unbending, a man of conviction, who rebuked a king and went to prison for it. His question did not make him a reed. There may be an edge in it, too: Herod Antipas had coins struck with a reed on them, and it was Herod who had John in a cell.

A man dressed in soft clothing? John wore camel’s hair and a leather belt (Mark 1:6). He was not a courtier. And Jesus adds the contrast himself: those who dress in splendid clothing and live in luxury are in kings’ courts. Which is precisely where John is at that moment, though not as a guest: in a dungeon below Herod’s palace. The crowds went into a desert to hear a man who could not be bribed, bent, or bought a better coat. That is what took them out there, and it is worth asking what takes people out now.

A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. The first two questions expected the answer no. This one expects yes, and then gets more than it asked for. John was the first true prophet in four centuries. And what is more than a prophet? A prophet speaks of what is coming. John was the only one who could point with a finger and say: that man. Every other prophet in Israel’s history described a horizon; John stood at the edge of it and named the person walking over. And there is a second thing that made him more: the prophets foretold the Messiah, and John was himself foretold, as the messenger sent ahead of the Lord (Malachi 3:1).

Did Jesus think less of John for doubting? No, and this passage is the proof. Jesus answered John’s question privately and then praised him publicly. The very doubt we might have used against him, Jesus did not mention to the crowd at all. That is how the Lord treats his struggling servants: he deals gently with the weakness, and honours the faithfulness. If you have been through a season of doubt, you need not fear that Christ has written you off. He judges a life by its direction and its faithfulness, not by its worst night in prison.

In a sentence. Jesus asked the crowds what they had gone out to see in John: not a wavering reed or a courtier, but a prophet, and more than a prophet.

On a Tuesday. When someone is absent, and the conversation turns to their weakness, be like Jesus here. Defend absent fellow believers, rather than criticising them. Speak of their faithfulness, not their worst moment. And in your own life, be unbending in truth, like John: not a reed moving with whatever the culture or your social circle is blowing this year.

For worship. How kind the Lord is to his servants. He knows our frame and remembers that we are dust (Psalm 103:14). The man in Herod’s dungeon never heard what Jesus said about him that day, but it was said, and it stands in Scripture for ever. So it is with all his people. We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1), who speaks for us when we cannot hear it, and on the last day the Judge of all the earth will say it aloud, before the whole universe: well done.

verseByVerse.quote: This is he of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’ I tell you, among those born of women none is greater than John. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is he of whom it is written: behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you. I tell you, among those born of women none is greater than John. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.

This is he of whom it is written. The quotation is Malachi 3:1, combined with Exodus 23:20, and there is something in it that ought to stop a careful reader. In Malachi, God is speaking about himself: I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me. The messenger goes ahead of the LORD, who is coming to his temple.

Before your face. Jesus quotes it with the pronouns changed: before your face, your way before you. Now God speaks to the Messiah about the forerunner who prepares his way. The one whose way is being prepared, in Malachi’s own words, is the God of Israel, and Jesus applies the text to himself and hands it to a crowd without further comment. John prepares the way for the Lord, and the Lord is Jesus.

Among those born of women none is greater than John. Not greater than the prophets: greater than anybody. Abraham, Moses, David, Elijah, Isaiah: none of them occupied a higher place in the purposes of God than the man currently sitting in Herod’s cell wondering whether he had been wrong. Why? Because of his unique role. He stood at the turning point of history, pointing directly to the Messiah. The prophets saw Christ from afar; John saw him and pointed: Behold, the Lamb of God (John 1:29).

Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he. It is not a demotion of John, and it is not about personal holiness or reward. Not greater in character, but in privilege: it is about which side of the cross a person stands on. John belonged to the age of promise and stood at its threshold. He announced the Lamb and did not live to see the Lamb slain, or raised, or the Spirit poured out.

What the least believer has. The least believer after the cross and resurrection has what John did not yet have: an accomplished redemption, a finished sacrifice, the forgiveness of sins actually purchased, and the Holy Spirit indwelling in the fullness of the new covenant. Not because that believer is more faithful (almost certainly he is not) but because he lives on the other side of the event John was pointing at. John saw the dawn; the least Christian lives in the full day. What does that actually mean? John was filled with the Spirit from the womb. But the least believer now receives the Spirit as the Spirit of the crucified and risen Christ, poured out because Jesus has been glorified (John 7:39), living in him for good and teaching him to call God Abba, Father, through a Son whose work is finished (Romans 8:15–16).

Is John in heaven, then? Yes. Being least in the kingdom or greater than John is not about who is saved. John was a man of faith, filled with the Spirit from the womb, and he is among those who will sit at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of God (13:28). Old Testament believers were saved by faith in the promised Christ, just as we are saved by faith in the Christ who has come (Romans 4; Hebrews 11). The difference Jesus speaks of is one of privilege and clarity, not of salvation: we know the name, the cross and the empty tomb that John died before seeing.

In a sentence. Jesus identified John as the messenger Malachi foretold, the greatest person ever born, yet said that the least in God’s kingdom is greater than he.

On a Tuesday. The temptation is always to measure ourselves against John’s heroism and despair. Measure instead what you have been given. Before you open your Bible this week, pause and remember that you are reading, in full, the story the prophets longed to understand (1 Peter 1:10–12). Do not treat as ordinary what John died longing to see.

For worship. The Lamb whom John pointed to has been slain, and raised, and has poured out his Spirit on the least of his people. The LORD whose way was prepared in Malachi has come in person, and he did not come to be admired from the threshold. The greatest man born of woman stood at the door and pointed, saying he was not worthy to untie the strap of his sandals (3:16). The least of his children has been brought all the way in, by that same Lord, and seated at his table, and given everything John died longing to hold.

verseByVerse.quote: (When all the people heard this, and the tax collectors too, they declared God just, having been baptized with the baptism of John, but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, not having been baptized by him.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
(When all the people heard this, and the tax collectors too, they declared God just, having been baptised with the baptism of John, but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, not having been baptised by him.)

When all the people heard this, and the tax collectors too. Luke drops in a parenthesis, which the ESV puts in brackets, explaining how the crowd took Jesus’ words about John. The ordinary people and the outcasts heard, and it is the tax collectors Luke singles out: the men whose profession was theft under licence heard John, agreed with God about themselves, and went into the water.

They declared God just. Literally, they justified God. That is not something people usually do. To justify God is to acknowledge that he is in the right about you: that his verdict on your life is accurate, that his judgement on sin is just, that his summons to repent was warranted, that when he says you need washing he is not exaggerating. They had admitted their sin and been baptised. And when God justifies a sinner, the same word runs the other way, which is the heart of the gospel. To be justified is to be declared righteous by God the Judge: not made sinless overnight, but pardoned and accepted, because our sin was counted to Christ and his righteousness is counted to us (2 Corinthians 5:21).

But the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves. Lawyers (nomikoi) were experts in the law of Moses. The purpose of God (boulē) is his plan, his will for them: here, the call to repent. The men who knew the Scriptures best refused it, to their own loss. And Luke’s phrasing is very exact: they rejected the purpose of God for themselves. They did not deny that God had purposes; they were entirely orthodox about that. They declined to be included. They thought they were righteous and did not need to repent (5:32).

Not having been baptized by him. Their refusal of John’s baptism showed their refusal of repentance. Baptism was the public sign of agreeing with God about your sin, and they would not be seen to need it.

Can God’s purpose be rejected? A reader who has been taught the sovereignty of God will feel a difficulty here, and it is worth facing rather than stepping round. Does this verse make his plan subject to a committee vote in Jerusalem? It does not, and Luke of all writers is the last person who thought so. This is the man who will record that Herod and Pilate and the Gentiles gathered to do whatever God’s hand and plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:28). The eternal purpose of God went forward exactly as decreed, and these men were not consulted. What they rejected was the purpose of God for themselves: the good and gracious call held out to them in John’s preaching, the invitation to repent and be washed. God’s call, as it comes to people in preaching, can be refused. They were offered it, and they would not have it, and the refusal was entirely their own. And God’s plan was not delayed by a single day. That is where the mystery sits in Scripture, and where it is left: God is sovereign, and people are responsible, and both are true.

The water Jesus entered. There is a further detail Luke has already given us that makes this refusal heartbreaking. When all the people were being baptised by John, Jesus too was baptised (3:21). The sinless Son of God went down into the same river as the tax collectors, standing with sinners in the water of repentance he did not need, because he had come to be numbered with them. And John’s baptism was always pointing past itself: John told the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus (Acts 19:4). So the purpose of God that the lawyers refused was, in the end, Christ himself. The water they would not be seen in was water the Lord had already entered for them.

Who did which. What is not mysterious is who did which. The men with nothing to protect said God was right about them. The men with a reputation to defend refused the water, and Luke records it in brackets, as though the thing were almost too sad to put in the main sentence.

In the flow. These two verses are a hinge. They explain why the crowd could hear Jesus praise John gladly and the leaders could not: one group had already said yes to God in the water, and the other had said no. They prepare the parable of the sulking children that follows (vv. 31–35), which describes the second group. And they set out in advance the two people at Simon’s dinner (vv. 36–50): a sinner who agrees with God about herself, and a Pharisee who sees no need to.

How do I justify God? By agreeing with him about yourself. When his word says you have sinned, you do not argue, minimise or compare yourself with others; you say, Lord, you are right. That is what confession is: saying the same thing as God (1 John 1:9). David did it after his adultery: you are justified in your words and blameless in your judgement (Psalm 51:4). The wonderful paradox is that those who justify God are justified by him, freely, through faith in Christ. Those who justify themselves, like the lawyer in 10:29, find that their own verdict is the one God will not accept.

In a sentence. The ordinary people and tax collectors, baptised by John, acknowledged God was right, but the Pharisees and lawyers, refusing John’s baptism, rejected God’s purpose for them.

On a Tuesday. The next time God’s word confronts you, in a sermon, in your reading, through a friend’s rebuke, notice your first reaction. Is it to defend yourself, or to agree with God? Agree with God about your sin. Those who justify God are justified by him; those who justify themselves reject his purpose.

For worship. God is right. He is right about our sin, right in his judgements, right in his call to repentance, and right in the remedy he has provided. He is just, and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). The tax collectors who went into the water discovered that the God they declared just was also the God who declared them clean.

verseByVerse.quote: 'To what then shall I compare the people of this generation, and what are they like? They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
To what then shall I compare the people of this generation, and what are they like? They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another: we played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.

To what then shall I compare the people of this generation? The people of this generation means especially the religious leaders who rejected both John and Jesus, and Jesus reaches for a scene everybody would have recognised.

Like children sitting in the marketplace. Children played games in the town square, imitating adults: weddings, with music and dancing, and funerals, with wailing. One group of children pipes, and the others are supposed to get up and dance. So they change the game and sing a lament, and the others are supposed to beat their breasts and wail. Whichever game is proposed, the second group sits there: sulky, contrary children whom nothing satisfies. It is a small, exact, slightly comic picture of the most exasperating thing in human relationships: the person who cannot be pleased, and who is never wrong, because the objection simply changes.

We played the flute for you, and you did not dance. The leaders are like that. They found fault with whatever God offered. Readers differ over which group of children stands for this generation: the ones calling out their complaints, or the ones who will not join in. The sentence works either way, because the sting is the same: whatever tune is played, the same people stay sitting down. Jesus goes on to name the two tunes that were actually played. John came with the dirge: fasting, camel’s hair, judgement, repentance. Jesus came with the flute: feasts, tax collectors, wine, a wedding. Between them they covered the whole range of what God can send to a nation. And the response to both was the same, dressed up in two different objections.

The bridegroom’s music. The flute was wedding music, and Jesus had already said whose wedding it was. When he was asked why his disciples did not fast, he answered: can you make wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them? (5:34). The joy around him was not carelessness. It was the celebration of the Bridegroom’s arrival, the Lord who had promised to betroth his people to himself for ever (Hosea 2:19), now present at their tables. To refuse to dance at that wedding is to refuse him. And he would sing the dirge too. As he came near Jerusalem he wept over the city, because it did not know the time of its visitation (19:41–44). He played both tunes himself, and wept when neither was answered.

Not confined to Pharisees. It describes a real and very common condition. There is a way of engaging with the things of God in which one is always, sincerely, weighing an objection: the preaching is too demanding, or too soft; the church is too formal, or too casual; that Christian is a hypocrite, and that one is a fanatic. Every objection may be individually reasonable. What gives the game away is that the seat is never vacated. The test is not whether you have a criticism. It is whether anything has ever succeeded in getting you up.

But is it wrong to criticise a church or a preacher? Not in itself. Scripture tells us to test everything (1 Thessalonians 5:21), and the Bereans were commended for checking Paul against the Scriptures (Acts 17:11). A church can be genuinely unfaithful, and a sermon can be genuinely wrong. The question this parable puts is not whether you ever disagree, but what your criticisms are doing. Do they lead you to a better obedience, a more faithful church, a deeper engagement with God’s word? Or do they keep you safely seated, so that nothing ever reaches you? Discernment moves a person towards God; this kind of objection keeps him at a distance.

In a sentence. Jesus compared his generation to sulky children in the marketplace who refuse to play either weddings or funerals.

On a Tuesday. Make a list of the reasons you have given in the last year for not responding to something God was saying: through a sermon, a friend, a passage. Read the list back. If the reasons contradict each other, too strict here, too loose there, you may be sitting in the marketplace. Beware of a spirit that will never be satisfied. Ask God for the grace to get up.

For worship. How patient God is with a sulky generation. He sent the prophet in the desert and his own Son to the wedding feast, and he did not stop calling when they would not dance. He has gone on playing for us, too, through every season of our resistance. The Lord is not slow to fulfil his promise; he is patient, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9).
verseByVerse.note: Children played at weddings and funerals; some refused whichever game was offered.

verseByVerse.quote: For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is justified by all her children.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine, and you say: he has a demon. The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say: look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners! Yet wisdom is justified by all her children.

For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine. Now Jesus names the two tunes, and the objections that met them. John was an ascetic, fasting, living on locusts and wild honey (Mark 1:6). His austerity was genuine, deliberate, and commanded before he was born (1:15). His was the funeral song, a call to mourn for sin.

And you say, He has a demon. Too strict. The verdict on John was not that he was mistaken but that he was possessed: a fanatic, not right in the head. Nobody argues with an ascetic; they diagnose him.

The Son of Man has come eating and drinking. At feasts, with sinners (5:29). The wedding music, the joy of the kingdom. Jesus went to dinner parties. He went to Levi’s house full of tax collectors, and he is about to go to a Pharisee’s.

And you say, Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard. Too loose. And that is what the other kind gets: the verdict that he was a man with no self-control and worse taste in company. The charge echoes Deuteronomy 21:20, where a rebellious son who was a glutton and a drunkard was to be stoned. It was not a joke; it was an accusation with a death sentence attached.

A friend of tax collectors and sinners! Meant as an insult, and it happens to be the finest description of him anyone produced in his lifetime. He is the friend of sinners. That is the gospel. They said it to shame him, and it is engraved on the hope of every person who has ever come to him ashamed.

The point. Two ministries, as different as they could be, both from God, both rejected, and the reasons given were mutually exclusive.
