They rejected John for being too severe and Jesus for being too relaxed. Which is the proof that the reasons were never the reason. The problem was not John or Jesus; it was their hearts. People who do not want God’s message will always find an excuse to reject the messenger.

Yet wisdom is justified by all her children. The saying picks up the language Luke used a moment earlier of the tax collectors, who justified God. Wisdom, in the Old Testament, is God’s own wisdom personified, calling in the streets and being ignored (Proverbs 1:20–33). Here she is vindicated, and the vindication comes from her children: the people who actually responded. God’s wisdom, in sending both John and Jesus, is shown to be right by those who respond to it: the tax collectors who went into the water, and the sinners who left his table forgiven. The proof is in the changed lives. The argument is not won by debate. You cannot argue a generation out of an objection that was never about the evidence. You can only produce the children.

Did Jesus approve of sin by eating with sinners? No. He ate with sinners as a physician goes among the sick (5:31–32), not to share the disease but to heal it. He was the friend of sinners, not the friend of sin. His company changed people: Levi left his tax booth, Zacchaeus gave back fourfold, the woman in the next scene left forgiven. Following him means going where sinners are, welcoming them warmly, and eating with them, while never pretending that sin does not matter. The church that keeps sinners at a distance has forgotten its Lord; the church that tells them sin is harmless has forgotten why he came.

In a sentence. The leaders rejected John as demon-possessed for fasting, and Jesus as a glutton and drunkard for feasting with sinners, but God’s wisdom is proved right by those who respond to it.

On a Tuesday. Who are the tax collectors and sinners in your world, the people your church crowd might be embarrassed to be seen with? Invite one of them for a meal this month. And if you have been holding someone at a distance because their life is a mess, remember who Jesus ate with, and remember that you were once at that table too.

For worship. No one has ever loved sinners as he did. He ate with them, defended them and forgave them, and in the end he was numbered with the transgressors (22:37) and died between two criminals, one of whom he took with him into paradise that same day. The friend of sinners did not only sit at their tables; he laid down his life for his friends (John 15:13), so that sinners might sit at his table for ever. The insult his enemies threw at him has become the name his people love best.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A Pharisee named Simon invites Jesus to dinner. Jesus accepts — which is worth registering, since two verses earlier they were calling him a friend of tax collectors and sinners. He ate with the disreputable and with the respectable, and seems to have refused nobody.

The setting explains the story. Guests reclined on low couches, propped on the left elbow, feet extending away from the table; and such meals were semi-public, with uninvited townspeople free to come in and stand round the walls. That is how she gets in.

She is “a woman of the city, who was a sinner” — no name, no history, and in that context the description almost certainly means she was publicly known for sexual immorality. She comes uninvited, stands behind him at his feet, weeps enough to wet them, wipes them with her hair, kisses them, and anoints them with ointment from an alabaster flask.

Every one of those acts is either socially ruinous or physically degrading. A respectable woman did not unbind her hair in public. The feet were the dirtiest part of a man in a sandalled country, and the anointing belonged on the head. She does not appear to notice any of it. She never speaks.

Simon's response happens entirely behind his face: “If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is.” The logic is tidy, and what he cannot conceive is the third possibility — that Jesus knows exactly what she is, better than Simon does, and is letting her touch him anyway. Jesus answers the unspoken thought, which settles Simon's question about prophetic knowledge before the conversation starts.

Then the parable of the two debtors, and Simon walks into it with a hedge that gives him away: “The one, I suppose.” Neither debtor could pay; the lender cancelled both; the one forgiven more loved more.

And then the mirror is turned on the table. No water for the feet, no kiss of greeting, no oil for the head — three ordinary courtesies any Galilean host provided without thinking, and Simon omitted all three. Against each, what she did, and each of hers is enormously larger. He withheld the cheap minimum; she gave the costly maximum at the lowest place in the room.

“Your sins are forgiven… Your faith has saved you; go in peace.” Not her love — her faith. The love was the fruit. The faith was what got her through the door.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable of the two debtors is the theological key to the scene and to the chapter. Forgiveness is the cause; love is the effect. This is the reverse of the moralism that says “love more, and God will forgive you more.” The gospel runs the other way: the more you understand what you have been forgiven, the more you will love.

Her love is extravagant because her sense of her cancelled debt is accurate and large. Simon's love is cool because his sense of his own debt is small — or rather, because he does not yet believe he has one. A man who considers himself basically righteous will never produce the love that flows from a woman who knows she was lost and is not any more.

Verse 47 is regularly misread, and the passage itself supplies three corrections. The parable Simon has just endorsed runs cancellation first and love after. Her forgiveness is what brought her into the house. And three verses later Jesus names what saved her, and it is her faith.

The “for” is the for of evidence, not of cause — as in “it rained last night, for the ground is wet.” The second half of the verse proves it: “he who is forgiven little, loves little.” Forgiveness is the input; love is the output.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman is the chapter's portrait of what it looks like to be genuinely overwhelmed by grace. She is not performing for the guests; she seems unaware of them. She is not observing social convention; she has left it behind. She is not managing her reputation; she forfeited it years ago.

What she is doing is the only thing she can think of in the presence of the one who has forgiven her — giving everything she has left, her tears, her hair, her perfume and her dignity, because what she has received is worth more than all of it together. The question the scene puts to every reader is whether we feel forgiven like that.

Simon's failure is the failure of good morality without grace-shaped self-knowledge. He is not a bad man. He is careful, observant, theologically serious, and he has kept his reputation intact. What he has never seen is the size of his own debt.

A person who does not see the depth of their own sin cannot be overwhelmed by the grace that forgives it, cannot produce the love that flows from it, and cannot understand a woman weeping on the floor. The church that produces more Simons than sinful women has failed at the most basic level of gospel communication: it has not helped people grasp what they have been forgiven.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him, and he went into the Pharisee's house and reclined at table. And behold, a woman of the city, who was a sinner, when she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster flask of ointment,
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him, and he went into the Pharisee’s house and reclined at table. And behold, a woman of the city, who was a sinner, when she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee’s house, brought an alabaster flask of ointment.

Wisdom’s children. Jesus has just been called, as an insult, a friend of tax collectors and sinners, and told the crowd that wisdom is justified by her children. Luke now shows both: the friend of sinners, and a sinner who responds to wisdom.

One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him. And he accepts, which is worth registering, because it settles something about him that is often got wrong. Jesus ate with Pharisees as well as with tax collectors (11:37; 14:1). He ate with the disreputable and with the respectable, and he is as willing to sit in Simon’s dining room as at Levi’s party. This Pharisee, Simon (v. 40), was curious, perhaps wanting to evaluate this new prophet.

And reclined at table. The setting needs picturing, because the story depends on it. At a formal dinner, guests did not sit on chairs. They lay on low couches arranged around a low table, propped on the left elbow, with their feet stretched out behind them, away from the food. A man’s feet were therefore at the outer edge of the room. So a woman could stand behind him at his feet without reaching the table. And such dinners were semi-public: the doors stood open, and uninvited people from the town could come in and stand round the walls to watch and listen. That was normal, and it is how she gets in.

And behold, a woman of the city, who was a sinner. Luke’s behold turns the reader’s head, and then he tells us almost nothing. No name. No history. Two descriptions: she is of the city, and she is a sinner. Applied to a woman and stated as her public identity, it most likely means she was known for sexual immorality, perhaps as a prostitute, though Luke does not say. That is what the room knew about her when she walked in, and very likely the only thing about her anybody could have told you.

Was this woman Mary Magdalene? No. Luke gives no name, and Mary Magdalene is introduced only in the next chapter, as one from whom seven demons had gone out (8:2), with nothing to link her to this story. The identification came much later, chiefly through a sermon of Gregory the Great in the sixth century, and it has no ground in Scripture. Mary Magdalene deserves to be remembered as what the Gospels say she was: a woman set free by Jesus, who supported his ministry, stood by the cross, and was the first to see him risen.

Is this the same anointing as the one at Bethany? Probably not (Matthew 26:6–13; Mark 14:3–9; John 12:1–8). This one happens in Galilee, earlier in the ministry, in a Pharisee’s house, by a woman known as a sinner, and the point is forgiveness. The other is at Bethany a week before the cross, by Mary of Bethany, and the point is his burial. That the host in both is called Simon is no difficulty: it was one of the commonest names in the land, and the New Testament alone has several men called Simon.

When she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee’s house. She came on purpose, at great risk of humiliation. She found out where he was, and went into the house of a Pharisee, the last building in that town where a woman like her would be welcome.

She came because he was there. Nothing else could have brought her through that door. Not the food, not the company, not the host. Luke gives one reason: she learned that he was there. Whatever she had heard him say or seen him do, it had persuaded her that this man would not drive her out, even in a Pharisee’s house. That is the pull of Christ on the guilty. The Pharisees’ holiness made sinners keep their distance; his holiness drew them in. The tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him, Luke says later (15:1), and this woman walks into enemy territory to reach him. His presence made the coldest room in town the one place she had to be.

Brought an alabaster flask of ointment. Perfume, expensive, kept in a sealed alabaster jar. She had already worked out what she was going to do before she got there.

Should a church welcome people like her? Yes, and gladly. If a woman known for sexual sin walked into your church on Sunday, the question is whether she would meet Simon or Jesus. Welcoming her does not mean pretending her past does not matter or that sin is harmless; Jesus is about to speak of her sins as many. It means receiving her as he did: with dignity, without flinching, and with the good news that her sins can be forgiven. Most people who have lived as she lived already know they are sinners. What they do not yet know is that there is a friend of sinners.

In a sentence. When Jesus was dining at a Pharisee’s house, a woman known in the town as a sinner came, bringing an alabaster jar of perfume.

On a Tuesday. No one is too sinful to come to Jesus. And no place is too respectable for sinners to seek him. If you have kept away from Christ, or from his people, because of what you have done, notice that this woman walked into the most hostile room in town because he was there. And if you are a regular in the respectable room, ask whether someone like her could come in where you are.

For worship. The Lord Jesus sat at the table of a Pharisee who despised him and was found there by a sinner who loved him, and he received both of them. He did not choose between the respectable and the ruined; he came for both, because both were lost. There is no house so cold and no past so dark that his grace cannot reach into it.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined on couches with their feet stretched out behind them, so a woman could stand at his feet. Doors were often open at such meals and onlookers could come in.

verseByVerse.quote: and standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head and kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head and kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment.

Standing behind him at his feet, weeping. Luke slows down and gives a run of actions in a single sentence, and every one of them is a scandal. Standing behind him at his feet: she takes the only position available to her, which is also the lowest place in the room. Weeping: Luke does not say why. She has not been rebuked, and nothing has yet happened; whatever this is, it started before she arrived. They are tears of repentance and of gratitude, which suggests she had already met Jesus, or heard him preach, and received forgiveness (v. 47).

She began to wet his feet with her tears. This is not a discreet tear or two. There are enough of them to wash the dust off a man’s feet, and they keep coming.

And wiped them with the hair of her head. Here the room would have gone very quiet. A respectable Jewish woman did not unbind her hair in public. It was done at her wedding, and after that in private, and to loosen it in front of men was so improper that it appears in later rabbinic discussion as grounds for divorce. She takes down her hair in a Pharisee’s dining room, in front of his guests, and uses it as a towel.

And kissed his feet. And kept on kissing them: Jesus will say she has not ceased (v. 45). Kissing the feet was a sign of deep humility, gratitude and reverence, given to a great benefactor or a king. And the feet were the dirtiest part of a man in a sandalled country, the part a slave washed.

And anointed them with the ointment. Perfume on the feet, not the head, which is where you anoint a guest of honour. Luke gives no reason, but it fits everything else she does: she takes the lowest place, as one who did not think herself worthy to anoint his head.

He did not stop her. Kissing the feet was homage, the kind of thing done before a king, and Jesus lets it go on and on. When Cornelius fell at Peter’s feet, Peter lifted him up at once: stand up; I too am a man (Acts 10:26). When John fell at an angel’s feet, the angel forbade it and said, worship God (Revelation 19:10). Jesus does not say either thing. He receives it, and then defends it to the host. The only explanation is the one the whole chapter has been building: he is the Lord, and the forgiveness she is weeping over came from him, so the gratitude belongs at his feet. She is not making a mistake about whom she owes. She has seen it exactly.

What she is not doing. Now the thing to see. Every one of these acts is either socially ruinous or physically degrading, and she does not appear to notice. She is not performing; there is no sign she is aware of the audience at all. She asks for nothing and says nothing. She is not trying to earn something: the debt was cancelled first, and this is what came after. She spends what is left of her dignity, in public, on a man’s feet, because she has been forgiven, and there is nothing else she can think of to do with it.

Do I have to be emotional to love Jesus? No. Tears are not the measure of love, and some of the deepest Christians are quiet people who rarely cry. What this woman shows is not a temperament but a direction: everything she had, poured out on Christ, with no thought for what it cost or who was watching. A reserved believer can love like that in his own way: in costly giving, in obedience nobody sees, in standing with Christ when it is embarrassing. The question is not whether you weep, but whether anything you have is held back from him.

In a sentence. Standing behind Jesus, she wept on his feet, wiped them with her hair, kissed them repeatedly, and poured perfume on them.

On a Tuesday. What is your alabaster flask: the thing of value you have been keeping back? It may be money, time, reputation, or a plan for your life. Love that knows it has been forgiven is extravagant. Ask what it would look like this week to pour something out on Christ, without calculating who will notice.

For worship. He is worthy of every tear and every flask. The feet she washed with her tears would soon be pierced for her, and after his rising he would hold them out to his friends: see my hands and my feet, that it is I myself (24:39). She poured out perfume; he poured out his soul to death (Isaiah 53:12). No love we give him can ever be extravagant beside the love he has given us.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself, 'If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner.' And Jesus answering said to him, 'Simon, I have something to say to you.' And he answered, 'Say it, Teacher.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself: if this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner. And Jesus answering said to him: Simon, I have something to say to you. And he answered: say it, Teacher.

Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself. Simon says nothing out loud. He is far too well brought up for a scene at his own table. The whole objection happens behind his face. But Jesus heard his thoughts.

If this man were a prophet. Some manuscripts read the prophet. The people had said Jesus was a great prophet (v. 16). Simon now concludes he is not.

He would have known who and what sort of woman this is. The logic is tidy and it is worth laying out, because Simon is not a fool. A prophet has supernatural knowledge; a prophet who knew what she was would not let her touch him, because touching a sinner would make him unclean; this man is letting her touch him; therefore either he does not know, or he does not care, and either way he is not a prophet. Simon thinks holiness means separation from sinners. What he cannot conceive is a third possibility: that Jesus knows exactly what she is, better than Simon does, and is letting her touch him anyway. Notice also the two words he uses of her: who and what sort. He wants Jesus to know not merely her name but her category. She is, in his mind, a type before she is a person, and the type is the whole of what needs to be said. Underneath the logic is something every religious person can feel. If my standing with God rests on my being better than her, then a welcome for her threatens me. That is why grace offends the respectable before it offends anyone else: it takes away the distance they have worked so hard to keep, and puts them on the same floor as the sinner.

And Jesus answering. Luke’s word is answering, though Simon has not spoken, and it is not the first time in this Gospel that Jesus replies to an unspoken thought (5:22; 6:8). Simon wanted to know whether this man had prophetic knowledge, and has just had a demonstration without noticing. Jesus knows exactly who she is, a forgiven sinner, and what Simon is thinking. Simon is the one who does not know what sort of woman she is, or what sort of man he himself is.

Simon, I have something to say to you. A gentle, personal approach. And observe how it is done. Not, I know what you are thinking, and it is disgraceful. He uses the man’s name and asks for permission to speak. There is no ambush and no humiliation in front of the guests: a courtesy, incidentally, that Simon had not extended to him.

Say it, Teacher. Simon is polite, and he is condescending. Teacher is a perfectly respectful word, and it is a good deal less than Lord, which is what the centurion called him in verse 6 without ever having met him.

Is it wrong to be wary of people with a bad reputation? Not always. Scripture warns against bad company (1 Corinthians 15:33), and wisdom takes care, especially where there is danger to others. Simon’s error was not caution but contempt. He saw a category and not a person; he assumed she could not change; and he assumed that his own holiness depended on keeping her at a distance. Jesus’ holiness is the kind that touches the unclean and makes it clean. Be careful with sin, especially your own, but never write a person off as a type.

In a sentence. Simon the Pharisee thought to himself that Jesus could not be a prophet if he let a sinner touch him, and Jesus, knowing his thoughts, said he had something to tell him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus knows your thoughts, including your judgements about others. Think of the person you have most quietly filed under a category: the colleague, the relative, the neighbour with the reputation. Let him speak to you about them. And when you need to correct someone, learn from his manner: use their name, speak privately, ask leave.

For worship. Nothing is hidden from him. He knows the thoughts we would never say aloud, and he knows the whole history of the sinner at his feet, and he is not shocked by either. All things are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account (Hebrews 4:13), and those eyes are the eyes of the one who loved us and gave himself for us. To be fully known by such a Lord is the safest place in the universe.
verseByVerse.note: Simon was a common name; this Pharisee is not Simon the leper of Bethany.

verseByVerse.quote: 'A certain moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. When they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both. Now which of them will love him more?' Simon answered, 'The one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt.' And he said to him, 'You have judged rightly.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
A certain moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. When they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both. Now which of them will love him more? Simon answered: the one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt. And he said to him: you have judged rightly.

A certain moneylender had two debtors. A simple parable, four sentences long, and it dismantles the room. It is told to make Simon judge himself, as Nathan made David judge himself (2 Samuel 12:1–7).

One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. A denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer. Five hundred denarii was more than a year and a half’s wages; fifty, less than two months’. A serious difference, and both are real debts. And sin is a debt to God (11:4; Matthew 6:12): an obligation we owed him and failed to pay. What does that actually mean? We owed God love with all our heart, and trust and thanks every day of our lives, and every day we have kept back part of it. Nothing we do tomorrow can pay for yesterday, because tomorrow’s obedience is owed already (17:10).

When they could not pay. Neither could pay. Both were bankrupt. This is the point Simon misses: he is a debtor too. The difference in the size of the debts made no difference whatever to the outcome, because fifty denarii a man does not have is as unpayable as five hundred.

He cancelled the debt of both. The cancelling is entirely the lender’s act. Nobody negotiated. Nobody offered instalments. Cancelled (echarisato) means forgave freely, graciously, as a gift. The word comes from charis, grace. He graced them both. Free forgiveness of an unpayable debt: that is the gospel.

Now which of them will love him more? Love is the response to forgiveness, in proportion to the sense of how much has been forgiven. Simon answers, the one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt, with a small hedge that gives him away: he can see that the answer is going somewhere he will not enjoy. You have judged rightly, says Jesus, and Simon has condemned himself.

Which way round. This is the theological hinge of the whole scene, and it is regularly got backwards. The love does not produce the cancellation. In the story, the cancelling comes first, and the loving comes after, and it comes in proportion to how much was cancelled. Love is the effect. Grace is the cause. Which means the question the parable leaves hanging over Simon’s dining table is not, who is the better person? It is: how big do you think your debt was? Simon is not being told that he is unforgiven. He is being told that his estimate of what he owed is the reason his welcome was so cool.

Who paid the debt? The lender in the parable simply cancels. But a cancelled debt is never free; someone absorbs the loss. The rest of the New Testament tells us who did. God did not wave our debt away as though justice did not matter. He nailed the record of debt that stood against us to the cross (Colossians 2:14), where Christ paid it in full. That is why forgiveness can be completely free to us and completely just in God: it was free because it cost him everything (Romans 3:24–26).

Am I the fifty-denarii debtor? If you have lived a fairly respectable life, you may feel that the woman’s debt was larger than yours. In terms of what people could see, perhaps it was. But the parable’s point is that both debtors were equally unable to pay, and both needed the same free cancellation. And anyone who looks honestly at his own heart before a holy God, at the pride, the coldness, the years of ingratitude, soon stops feeling like the small debtor. The Christians who love Christ most are usually not those with the most lurid past, but those who see most clearly what they were saved from.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a lender who freely cancelled two debts, one large and one small, and Simon admitted that the one forgiven more would love more.

On a Tuesday. Your debt to God is greater than you can pay. Have you let him cancel it freely? Take time this week to write down, honestly, what you have been forgiven: not only the dramatic sins but the daily ones. Then read Colossians 2:13–14 slowly, and give thanks.

For worship. He cancelled the debt of both. The God of all grace does not ask for instalments, does not negotiate, and does not cancel only the smaller sums. He forgives freely, because his Son has paid in full. There is no debtor so deep in arrears that the riches of his grace cannot clear the account.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer; five hundred denarii was more than a year’s wages.

verseByVerse.quote: Then turning toward the woman he said to Simon, 'Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. You gave me no kiss, but from the time I came in she has not ceased to kiss my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then turning toward the woman he said to Simon: do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. You gave me no kiss, but from the time I came in she has not ceased to kiss my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment.

Then turning toward the woman he said to Simon. Jesus turns to face her for the first time, since she has been behind him throughout, and he speaks to Simon. So she hears every word of what follows with his eyes on her.

Do you see this woman? Simon saw only a sinner. He had seen nothing but a category; he looked at her and read a file. Jesus asks him to look again, and then tells him what is actually there: a forgiven woman pouring out love.

Three contrasts. Water for the feet, a kiss of greeting, and oil for the head were ordinary courtesies to an honoured guest. Water after a dusty road was the minimum, a jug and a basin, usually handled by a servant. The kiss on the cheek was the equivalent of a handshake at the door. A little olive oil on the head was cheap and customary. None was legally required; all three were what any host in Galilee did without thinking. And Simon, who had invited this man to his own house in front of his own friends, omitted every one of them.

Water, kiss, oil. Against each omission, Jesus sets what she did, and every one of hers is enormously larger than the courtesy Simon skipped. Water: you gave me no water for my feet; she washed them with her tears and dried them with her hair. Kiss: you gave me no kiss of welcome; she has not stopped kissing my feet since she came in. Oil: you did not anoint my head with ordinary olive oil; she anointed my feet with costly ointment from an alabaster flask.

Not an oversight. Three courtesies are not forgotten by accident. Simon wanted Jesus at his table and was not prepared to honour him at it, and everyone in the room would have registered the small public slight. Each time, Simon gave less than the minimum; she gave far more than the maximum, at the lowest place in the room, to the dirtiest part of a man. The one who thought he had nothing much to be forgiven gave nothing much.

He came to his own. What makes the omissions so sad is who the guest was. Simon thought he was hosting a teacher of doubtful credentials. He was hosting the Lord whose word had just healed a centurion’s slave from a distance and raised a widow’s son at the gate of Nain. The one who made the water was given none for his feet. John says it of his whole coming: he came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (John 1:11). Simon’s cool dining room is that sentence in miniature. And the woman at his feet is the other half of it: to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God (John 1:12).

What does it look like to give Jesus the minimum today? It looks like a Christian life run on courtesies: attending, but not worshipping; reading a chapter, but not listening; giving what will not be missed; mentioning Christ only where it is safe. None of it is scandalous, and that is the point. Simon broke no law. Jesus’ diagnosis is not that we try harder, but that we look again at how much we owe him. Coolness towards Christ is cured not by guilt, but by grace seen more clearly.

In a sentence. Jesus contrasted Simon, who had not even given him water, a kiss or oil, with the woman, who washed his feet with tears, kissed them and anointed them with perfume.

On a Tuesday. Are you cool toward Jesus, giving him the minimum? Run the three questions through your own week. Did you welcome him (time with him that was more than a formality)? Did you show him affection (praise, thanks, worship that came from the heart)? Did you honour him (did anything cost you)? Then love him as she did, in whatever form that takes in your life.

For worship. The Lord sees everything given to him, the tears no one else noticed and the perfume no one thanked her for, and he will not let it go unnamed. And he sees what is withheld. But the same Lord, cold-shouldered at Simon’s table, went on, John tells us, to wash his own disciples’ feet (John 13:5), and then to give himself for them. He gives the costly maximum to people who give him the minimum. Who could not love such a Saviour?
verseByVerse.note: Water for the feet, a kiss of greeting and oil for the head were ordinary courtesies to a guest.

parallels.desc: let a little water be brought, and wash your feet
you anoint my head with oil

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven—for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little.

Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven. Jesus does not deny that her sins are many. He declares them forgiven. Are forgiven (apheōntai) is a perfect tense: an action completed in the past whose result stands in the present. Her sins have been forgiven and remain forgiven. That happened before she entered the house. It is why she came in.

For she loved much. This is one of the most misread verses in the New Testament, and it is worth taking slowly, because a great deal hangs on it. Read quickly, it sounds as though her love bought the forgiveness: that she earned it by the extravagance of what she did on the floor. That reading has a long history, and it is the natural sense of the English as it stands. It cannot be right, for three reasons drawn from the passage itself. First, it reverses the parable Jesus has just told and Simon has just agreed with: the debt is cancelled and then the loving follows. If love produced forgiveness here, the parable would have to run backwards. Second, the tense: her sins have already been forgiven. Third, three verses later he tells her plainly what saved her, and it is not her love: your faith has saved you.

The lender at the table. Look at where the parable puts Jesus. In the story the debtors love the lender who cancelled their debt. In the room the woman is pouring out her love on Jesus. The conclusion Jesus leaves Simon to draw is unavoidable: the man reclining at his table is the creditor. Her sins were debts owed to God, and the one she owes her love to is the one sitting in front of her. That is why he can say, on his own authority, I tell you, her sins are forgiven, and why nobody in the room misses the claim (v. 49). He is not a prophet passing on news of God’s pardon. He is the one whose pardon it is, and before long he will pay the debt himself.

The for of evidence. So what does for mean? It is the for of evidence, not of cause: her sins have been forgiven, as you can see from her great love. We use it constantly: it rained last night, for the ground is wet. Nobody thinks the wet ground made it rain. The wet ground is how you know. Her love is the evidence of forgiveness, not its price.

Where Christians differ: love and forgiveness. Some Roman Catholic interpreters, following the Latin, have taken this verse to mean that her love (as an act of contrition and charity) merited or brought about her forgiveness. Verdict: the parable (vv. 41–43) makes the order plain: forgiveness first, love second. Jesus will tell her that her faith, not her love, has saved her (v. 50). We are forgiven by grace through faith, and love is the fruit.

But he who is forgiven little, loves little. Aimed at Simon. Not that Simon’s sins were few, but that he thought they were. He did not see himself as a debtor at all. Feeling little need of forgiveness, he felt little love. And notice which way the causation runs in that clause. Not, he who loves little is forgiven little. The forgiveness is the input; the love is the output. Jesus has just used the same test to read the room: Simon’s cold hospitality was evidence of Simon’s small sense of debt, exactly as her tears were evidence of her large one. The person who thinks he needs little forgiveness will love Jesus little. Self-righteousness kills love.

Why it matters. This matters pastorally as much as theologically. If love earns forgiveness, then every anxious believer must ask whether they have loved enough, and the honest answer is always no. If love is the evidence of forgiveness, the question changes entirely, and the way to love more is not to squeeze harder but to look longer at what you have actually been forgiven.

My love for Jesus feels small, so am I really forgiven? Your forgiveness rests on Christ’s work and God’s promise, not on the size of your love. If you have come to Christ in faith, your sins are forgiven, however weak your love feels today. But a small love is a call to look again, not to despair. Love for Christ grows as we see more of our sin and more of his grace, and both are the Spirit’s work. Pray for eyes to see. Read the cross accounts slowly. Come to the Lord’s Table remembering what the bread and wine mean. Love is not manufactured; it is kindled.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that her many sins were forgiven, as her great love showed, while the one who thinks he has been forgiven little loves little.

On a Tuesday. If your love for Jesus is cold, do not begin by trying to feel more. Begin by looking at what he has forgiven you. Spend ten minutes this week with Psalm 103 or Romans 5:6–11, and let the size of the debt sink in. The love follows.

For worship. The grace is enormous: her sins, which were many, forgiven; our sins, which are many, forgiven; forgiven completely and permanently, the perfect tense standing over our lives for ever. No later failure can reach back and undo it, for it rests not on how much we have loved but on the one who loved us first and gave himself for us. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19), and every small flicker of that love is the evidence of a debt that has already been written off in his blood.
verseByVerse.note: Her love is the evidence of forgiveness, not its price, as the parable shows.

parallels.desc: we love because he first loved us

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to her, 'Your sins are forgiven.' Then those who were at table with him began to say among themselves, 'Who is this, who even forgives sins?' And he said to the woman, 'Your faith has saved you; go in peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to her: your sins are forgiven. Then those who were at table with him began to say among themselves: who is this, who even forgives sins? And he said to the woman: your faith has saved you; go in peace.

And he said to her, Your sins are forgiven. He has been speaking about her to Simon. Now he turns and speaks to her, and it is the first time anyone in the scene has addressed her at all. He speaks directly to her, publicly, so that everyone hears it and she knows it for certain.

Why say it out loud? She already knew. The thing was settled before she came through the door, and her tears were the evidence of it. So why say it? Because she needed to hear it said, in that room, in front of those people. A woman who has spent years as the town’s byword had just knelt at the feet of a rabbi at a Pharisee’s dinner party, and the whole room was watching to see what he would do with her. He tells her, where everyone can hear, that her sins are gone. It is an assurance of what was already true. She had been condemned by the town; now she is declared forgiven by the Lord, in front of the Pharisees.

Assurance spoken. There is a great deal of pastoral practice in that. Assurance is not merely a private transaction with God. People need to be told, in words, on the authority of Christ, that their sins are forgiven: which is a good part of what preaching, and the gospel spoken over a struggling friend, and the Lord’s Table are for.

Who is this, who even forgives sins? The same question as at the paralytic’s healing (5:21), and it is the right question. Only God can forgive sins committed against God; everyone at that table knew it. They have understood the claim perfectly and, once again, drawn no conclusion from it. The question hangs over the Gospel: who is he? He is the one who forgives sins, because he is God, and because he will pay the debt himself on the cross. And notice what Jesus does with the murmur: nothing. He does not turn to defend himself or argue the point. He has one more thing to say, and it is not to them.

Your faith has saved you. Not her love, not her tears, not her perfume: her faith. She trusted Jesus and came to him. Faith is the empty hand that receives forgiveness. Saved here means rescued from the guilt and judgement her sins deserved and brought into peace with God. The same word is used when Jesus heals (8:48), but nobody in this room is ill: it is her whole standing before God that has been put right. Her love flowed from it. The love was the fruit; the faith was the root: the trust that got her through a door she had no business entering, to the feet of a man she believed would not throw her out. And she was right about him. That is all her faith consisted of, and it was enough.

Go in peace. Literally, go into peace: into a new life of peace with God and wholeness, the Hebrew blessing shalom. She came weeping; she leaves in peace.

In the flow. The chapter ends where it began, with faith. The centurion trusted Jesus’ word for a dying body (v. 9); this woman trusts his word for her sins (v. 50), and the second is the greater gift. The question raised by the crowd at Nain and by Simon in his heart is answered here by Jesus himself: he is the Lord who forgives. And Luke at once shows women whom Jesus had healed travelling with him and providing for him out of their means (8:1–3): this is what a life lived in his peace looks like.

Can a pastor say your sins are forgiven? Only Christ forgives sins in his own right. But a minister of the gospel, or any Christian, may and should declare God’s forgiveness to those who repent and believe, because God has promised it. When Jesus gave the apostles authority to declare sins forgiven (John 20:23), it was the authority to proclaim his forgiveness, not to dispense it on their own account. When a Christian friend says to you, on the basis of God’s word, if you confess your sins he is faithful and just to forgive (1 John 1:9), that is the voice of Christ reaching you through his people. There is no priest standing between you and God, and no purgatory to pay off what remains: Christ’s forgiveness is complete.

What if I have done something worse than she did? There is no sin that Christ cannot forgive for anyone who comes to him in repentance and faith. Paul called himself the foremost of sinners, a blasphemer and persecutor, and said he was shown mercy precisely as an example to everyone who would believe (1 Timothy 1:15–16). Whatever is in your past, the question is not its size but where you take it. Bring it to the feet of Christ, as she did. He has never once turned away anyone who came to him (John 6:37).

In a sentence. Jesus told the woman publicly that her sins were forgiven, and that her faith had saved her, and sent her away in peace, while the guests wondered who could forgive sins.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone in your life who needs to hear the words of forgiveness said aloud: a friend crushed by guilt, a new believer unsure whether God could really forgive them? Say it to them, from God’s word. And if you are the one who needs it, hear Jesus’ words to you: your sins are forgiven; your faith has saved you; go in peace.

For worship. She came in with no name in the record, no standing, no argument and no words, into a room full of men who despised her, and put everything she had left on the feet of Christ. He did not flinch, did not distance himself, did not manage the situation. He received it, defended her to the man whose house it was, told her out loud that she was forgiven, and sent her out through the same door in peace. There has never been a sinner too far gone for that welcome, and there is not one now. He is the Lord, and the friend of sinners, and he is ours.

parallels.desc: who can forgive sins but God alone?

7.text: <sup>1</sup> After he had finished all his sayings in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum. <sup>2</sup> Now a centurion had a servant who was sick and at the point of death, who was highly valued by him. <sup>3</sup> When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent to him elders of the Jews, asking him to come and heal his servant. <sup>4</sup> And when they came to Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying, “He is worthy to have you do this for him, <sup>5</sup> for he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue.” <sup>6</sup> And Jesus went with them. When he was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends, saying to him, “Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. <sup>7</sup> Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed. <sup>8</sup> For I too am a man set under authority, with soldiers under me: and I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” <sup>9</sup> When Jesus heard these things, he marveled at him, and turning to the crowd that followed him, said, “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.” <sup>10</sup> And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the servant well. <sup>11</sup> Soon afterward he went to a town called Nain, and his disciples and a great crowd went with him. <sup>12</sup> As he drew near to the gate of the town, behold, a man who had died was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow, and a considerable crowd from the town was with her. <sup>13</sup> And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, “Do not weep.” <sup>14</sup> Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. And he said, “Young man, I say to you, arise.” <sup>15</sup> And the dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother. <sup>16</sup> Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying, “A great prophet has arisen among us!” and “God has visited his people!” <sup>17</sup> And this report about him spread through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding country. <sup>18</sup> The disciples of John reported all these things to him. And John, <sup>19</sup> calling two of his disciples to him, sent them to the Lord, saying, “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” <sup>20</sup> And when the men had come to him, they said, “John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, ‘Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?’” <sup>21</sup> In that hour he healed many people of diseases and plagues and evil spirits, and on many who were blind he bestowed sight. <sup>22</sup> And he answered them, “Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. <sup>23</sup> And blessed is the one who is not offended by me.” <sup>24</sup> When John's messengers had gone, Jesus began to speak to the crowds concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? <sup>25</sup> What then did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who are dressed in splendid clothing and live in luxury are in kings' courts. <sup>26</sup> What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet. <sup>27</sup> This is he of whom it is written, ‘Behold, I send my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way before you.’ <sup>28</sup> I tell you, among those born of women none is greater than John. Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.” <sup>29</sup> (When all the people heard this, and the tax collectors too, they declared God just, having been baptized with the baptism of John, <sup>30</sup> but the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves, not having been baptized by him.) <sup>31</sup> “To what then shall I compare the people of this generation, and what are they like? <sup>32</sup> They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.’ <sup>33</sup> For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’ <sup>34</sup> The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look at him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ <sup>35</sup> Yet wisdom is justified by all her children.” <sup>36</sup> One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him, and he went into the Pharisee's house and reclined at table. <sup>37</sup> And behold, a woman of the city, who was a sinner, when she learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster flask of ointment, <sup>38</sup> and standing behind him at his feet, weeping, she began to wet his feet with her tears and wiped them with the hair of her head and kissed his feet and anointed them with the ointment. <sup>39</sup> Now when the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself, “If this man were a prophet, he would have known who and what sort of woman this is who is touching him, for she is a sinner.” <sup>40</sup> And Jesus answering said to him, “Simon, I have something to say to you.” And he answered, “Say it, Teacher.” <sup>41</sup> “A certain moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. <sup>42</sup> When they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both. Now which of them will love him more?” <sup>43</sup> Simon answered, “The one, I suppose, for whom he cancelled the larger debt.” And he said to him, “You have judged rightly.” <sup>44</sup> Then turning toward the woman he said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. <sup>45</sup> You gave me no kiss, but from the time I came in she has not ceased to kiss my feet. <sup>46</sup> You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with ointment. <sup>47</sup> Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven—for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little.” <sup>48</sup> And he said to her, “Your sins are forgiven.” <sup>49</sup> Then those who were at table with him began to say among themselves, “Who is this, who even forgives sins?” <sup>50</sup> And he said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”

8.title: The Word, the Storm, and the Power of the Kingdom
8.overview:
Chapter 8 is organised around the question of hearing and responding to the word — the parable of the sower, the lamp under a jar, and Jesus's redefinition of family as those who hear the word and do it all converge on the same theme before the chapter moves into four great demonstrations of kingdom power. After the teaching section, the chapter becomes a series of astonishing encounters: Jesus calms a storm on the Sea of Galilee, casts a legion of demons into a herd of pigs, heals a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years, and raises Jairus's daughter from the dead. The four miracle stories are not loosely connected anecdotes; they form a theological argument. Jesus has authority over the forces of nature, over the powers of darkness, over the long suffering of a diseased body, and over death itself. Nothing is outside the reach of his word.

The opening note about the women who accompanied Jesus and provided for the ministry out of their means (vv. 1–3) is characteristic Luke — he notices and names women at a point in history when their testimony was not counted and their presence was not recorded. Mary Magdalene, Joanna the wife of Chuza, Susanna, and many others: they are not background figures but named participants in the mission, financing the ministry that will change the world. Luke's Gospel is consistently attentive to those whom history overlooks.

The parable of the sower (vv. 4–15) is the parable about parables — the key to how the whole teaching ministry of Jesus works. The word is the seed; the hearts of the hearers are the soil; the response to the word determines everything. But the parable also functions as a warning and a comfort simultaneously: a warning that most hearers will not bear fruit, for a variety of reasons; a comfort that some will — “an hundredfold.” The harvest is certain; it comes to those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart and bear fruit with patience.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke records that Jesus travelled through cities and villages proclaiming the kingdom of God, accompanied not only by the twelve but by a group of women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities.

The list is striking in its specificity: Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out; Joanna, the wife of Herod's household manager Chuza; Susanna; and many others. These women “provided for them out of their means” — out of their own money.

So the Galilean ministry was funded by women. Thirteen men walking from village to village for the better part of three years, eating every day, with no visible income — and Luke tells us in half a verse where the money came from.

The significance of the passage is easily underestimated. In a culture where women were excluded from the travelling company of a rabbi, Jesus's entourage included them as named, active participants — and it exposed him to precisely the accusation his enemies had already made (7:34). He did it anyway, and Luke records it without a word of defence.

Each woman is identified by what was done for her rather than by what she brought. The company around Jesus is not a collection of the promising; it is a collection of the rescued.

Mary Magdalene needs rescuing from a long misreading. Magdala was a fishing town on the lake, and the name says only where she came from. What Scripture tells us of her past is that seven demons came out of her — which is affliction, not scandal. She is not the unnamed woman of the previous chapter; the accident of neighbouring paragraphs invited that merger, and a sixth-century sermon fixed it in the Western imagination for a thousand years. There is no basis for it in the text.

Joanna is a court wife whose husband managed the estate of the man who had John the Baptist in a cell. Whatever her presence here cost her at home, she is named again at the empty tomb (24:10) — as is Mary Magdalene, who will still be there at the cross when the men have gone.
verseByVerse.theology:
The inclusion of women in the travelling band is a quiet revolution in the social world of first-century Judaism. Rabbis did not travel with female disciples; the association would have been scandalous, and Jesus's opponents were already looking for material.

His practice reflects the consistent pattern of including those the religious establishment excluded, and it anticipates the full participation of women in the life of the new covenant community (Acts 2:17-18; Gal. 3:28). The kingdom of God does not replicate the social hierarchies of the world it enters.

It matters, too, that the women are introduced immediately before the parable of the soils. Luke has just shown a company of people in whom the word took root and bore fruit — and their fruit was that they gave everything they had to keep the sowing going.

These same women are at the cross when the twelve have scattered (23:49), and at the tomb on the third morning (24:1-11). They are not peripheral figures. On the two occasions when the testimony mattered most, they are the witnesses Luke has.
verseByVerse.examples:
The women who supported the ministry “out of their means” are the New Testament's first and clearest model of financial stewardship in service of the gospel. They did not merely believe; they paid for it, and they kept paying.

The theology of giving that runs through Paul's letters (2 Cor. 8-9; Phil. 4:14-19) has its roots here: those who share in the blessings of the gospel share their resources with those who carry it forward. It is easy to romanticise the finances of the gospel and pretend they were not there. They were. Somebody bought the bread.

And notice what these women could not do. They could not preach in a synagogue, and there is no sign they tried. What they had was money and mobility, and they put both under the mission for years, and were named once and then never mentioned in that connection again.

There is a whole doctrine of unglamorous service in that. The four Gospels exist partly because a group of women paid the bills of an itinerant preacher and did not require anybody to notice.

verseByVerse.quote: Soon afterward he went on through cities and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. And the twelve were with him, and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Soon afterwards he went on through cities and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. The Twelve were with him, and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out.

Meaning first. Luke 8 is about hearing, and about the one whose word must be heard. Women Jesus had set free travel with him and the Twelve, paying for the mission themselves. In the parable of the sower one seed, the word of God, falls on four kinds of ground, and only the honest heart that holds it fast bears fruit; so take care how you hear, for his true family are those who hear God’s word and do it. Then four scenes show why his word deserves such hearing: Jesus rules the storm, a legion of demons, a disease no doctor could cure, and death itself. The disciples’ question hangs over the chapter: who then is this? The Lord of Psalm 107 is in the boat.

Soon afterward he went on through cities and villages. Luke gives the shape of the ministry in a sentence: town after town, on foot, saying the same thing. This was his main work, as he had said (4:43): I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well; for I was sent for this purpose.

Proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. Two verbs. Proclaiming (kēryssōn) is the word for a herald making a public announcement in the king’s name. Bringing the good news (euangelizomenos) is the verb behind our word gospel. He is not lecturing. He is announcing something that has happened: the King has come, and his reign has begun. What does the kingdom of God actually mean? Not a territory on a map but a reign: God himself stepping in as King to put right what sin and Satan have ruined. That is why, wherever Jesus goes, demons leave and the sick get up; as he says later, if it is by the finger of God that he casts out demons, the kingdom of God has come upon them (11:20).

The herald who is the news. A herald announces another man’s king and then steps aside. This herald cannot step aside, because the kingdom he proclaims has arrived in his own person: where he goes the sick are healed and the bound are freed, and the reign of God is seen walking a Galilean road. That is why Luke stops to describe the company behind him. The Twelve are the beginning of a renewed Israel (22:30). The women are the first spoils of his war on the strong man (11:21–22). Luke draws the procession like a king’s train after a victory, except that every captive in it is a captive set free, walking beside the one who freed them.

And the twelve were with him. Learning by being with him (Mark 3:14). The Twelve were trained less by lectures than by company: they watched him, walked with him, and heard the same message preached in a hundred villages until it was in their bones.

And also some women. Stop there, because a first-century reader would have. Only Luke records this, and it was remarkable in its culture. Rabbis had disciples, and disciples were men; one rabbi, in a saying preserved in later rabbinic writings, said it was better to burn the words of the law than to teach them to a woman. A travelling teacher whose company included women invited exactly the accusation his enemies had already made, that he was a friend of tax collectors and sinners (7:34). He did it anyway, and Luke records it without a word of defence, as he gives special attention to women throughout his Gospel.

Who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities. Notice how they are identified. Every one of them is described by what was done for her, not by what she brought. Their discipleship was a response to what Jesus had done for them, like the woman of 7:36–50. The company around Jesus is not a collection of the promising. It is a collection of the rescued.

Mary, called Magdalene. Then a name, and it needs rescuing from fourteen centuries of misreading. Magdala was a fishing town on the western shore of the lake, south of Capernaum, and the surname simply says where she was from. She stood at the cross when the men had gone (23:49; Mark 15:40), saw the burial (23:55), was at the tomb on the third morning (24:10), and was the first to see the risen Lord (John 20:11–18).

From whom seven demons had gone out. What Luke tells us about her is that seven demons came out of her: a severe case of possession, perhaps over a long time. Seven speaks of complete bondage, and of complete deliverance. It is affliction, not scandal, and it is the only thing Scripture ever says about her past. She was a woman under an oppression so total that Luke has to use a number for it, and she got free.

What it does not mean. Nothing in Scripture says Mary Magdalene was a prostitute. She is not the woman who wept at Jesus’ feet in the previous chapter. That woman, a few verses earlier, is deliberately left unnamed. The two stories simply stand side by side, and that accident is what first invited people to merge the two women. Then a sermon of Pope Gregory the Great in the sixth century identified Mary with the sinful woman of 7:37 and with Mary of Bethany, and fixed the idea in the Western imagination for a thousand years. There is no basis for it anywhere in the text. Luke introduces her here as a new character, freed from demons, not from immorality. She was a woman of means and devotion, and a witness of the resurrection.

Why does it matter who Mary Magdalene was? Because the truth honours both Christ and her. The legend turned her into a symbol of sexual sin repented, and in doing so it obscured what the Gospels actually say: that she was set free from a terrible bondage, that she gave her money and her life to Jesus, that she stayed at the cross, and that the risen Lord appeared first to her and sent her to tell the apostles. That is a greater story than the legend. And it is a warning to all of us: tradition, however old and beautiful, must always be tested by Scripture.

In a sentence. Jesus travelled through towns and villages preaching the kingdom, with the Twelve and with women he had healed, including Mary Magdalene, freed from seven demons.

On a Tuesday. Jesus welcomes all who have been freed by him to follow him. What has he freed you from? Name it, and let it lead to devotion. And look at the company you keep at church: if you find you are drawn only to the promising, remember that his company was made up of the rescued.

For worship. Seven demons once held Mary of Magdala, and not one of them could keep her when he spoke. Three years later the same Lord lay in a tomb, and death could not keep him either; and John tells us that the first person he showed himself to on the morning of his victory was this woman. That is the shape of his grace: the strongest bondage broken, the lowest given the highest honour, and a woman once owned by darkness sent to announce the light to the apostles themselves. Glory to the Lord who wins his battles for the bound, and then lets the freed carry the news.
verseByVerse.note: Mary Magdalene came from Magdala on the western shore of the lake. Nothing in Scripture says she was the sinful woman of chapter 7.

parallels.desc: from whom he had cast out seven demons

verseByVerse.quote: and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod’s household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means.

Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod’s household manager. Herod is Herod Antipas, and Chuza was his steward (epitropos), a high official over the royal household or estates: he managed the finances of the man who had John the Baptist in a cell and would have his head brought in on a platter. Joanna is a court wife, with status, money and a husband employed by the enemy, and she is walking round Galilee with an itinerant preacher from Nazareth. Luke does not tell us what conversations that produced at home.

Fed by those he feeds. The verb Luke uses for these women is the one Jesus will use of himself at the Last Supper: I am among you as the one who serves (22:27). Here the Servant of the Lord lets himself be served. He who in the next chapter will break five loaves for five thousand eats bread that Joanna paid for. That is the humility of the incarnation at its plainest: the Word made flesh became a man who needed a meal and a bed, and who took them gratefully from the hands of people he had healed. As Creator he needed nothing from them. As the Son become truly man he received their gifts, and so turned their giving into fellowship with himself.

The gospel in Herod’s house. The gospel reached even into Herod’s household. Acts 13:1 mentions Manaen, brought up with Herod, among the leaders at Antioch; and Paul sends greetings from the saints of Caesar’s household (Philippians 4:22). Joanna is named again at the empty tomb (24:10), so whatever it cost her, she was still there at the end. Perhaps she was one of Luke’s sources for the inside story of Herod (9:7–9; 23:8–12).

And Susanna, and many others. A name with no story at all, and then a crowd of women whose names nobody wrote down. Susanna is otherwise unknown. But she was known to Jesus, and her name is in Scripture for ever.

Who provided for them out of their means. Here is the detail that changes how the whole ministry looks. Provided (diēkonoun) means served, ministered, the root behind our word deacon, and the tense is continuous: they kept on providing, out of their own money. Thirteen men walked from village to village, eating every day and sleeping somewhere every night for the better part of three years, with no visible income, and Luke tells us in half a verse where much of the money came from. The Galilean ministry of Jesus Christ was funded, in large part, by women.

Somebody bought the bread. It is easy to romanticise the finances of the gospel. Somebody bought the bread, and the buyers are named here once and never again in connection with it. Women of means were patrons of Jesus’ ministry, as Lydia and others would be of Paul’s (Acts 16:14–15). They did not preach in the synagogues; they put their resources under the mission, quietly, for years.

Is giving money really ministry, or just a lesser support role? It is ministry, in the full sense of the word. Luke uses the same verb for these women that the New Testament uses for the service of deacons and for Christ’s own service (22:27). Paul calls the Philippians’ gift to him a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God (Philippians 4:18). Not everyone is called to preach, but everyone who belongs to Christ is called to serve, and putting your money under the gospel is one of the plainest ways to do it. The preacher in the pulpit and the giver in the pew are partners in the same work (Philippians 1:5).

How much should I give? The New Testament does not set a fixed percentage, but it gives clear principles. Set something aside regularly, in keeping with how God has prospered you (1 Corinthians 16:2). Give generously, because whoever sows sparingly will reap sparingly (2 Corinthians 9:6). Give cheerfully, not under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7). Give first to the work of the gospel in your own church, which supports those who teach you (Galatians 6:6), and then beyond it. Many Christians find the Old Testament tithe a helpful starting point, not a ceiling. The real question is not what is the least I can give, but what does this gift say about where my treasure is (12:34)?

In a sentence. Joanna, from Herod’s court, Susanna and many other women supported Jesus and the Twelve from their own resources.

On a Tuesday. Giving your money to support gospel ministry is serving Christ. Do it gladly, as these women did. Look at your bank statement for last month and ask what it says about the kingdom of God. And thank God this week for the quiet givers in your church, whose names no one mentions, who keep the bread on the table.

For worship. The cattle on a thousand hills are his, and he walked through Galilee eating bread bought with a steward’s household money. He became poor so that through his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9), and the poverty went further than borrowed bread: it went to a cross and a borrowed tomb. Now he reigns, owning everything again, and still he lets his people put their small coins under his work and calls it partnership. Nothing given to him in love is forgotten. Herod’s steward is a footnote; his wife’s name is written in the Gospel of the King she followed.
verseByVerse.note: Herod is Herod Antipas; Joanna came from his court.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–15 — The Parable of the Sower and Its Explanation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The parable of the sower is Jesus's own explanation of why his ministry produces such varied responses — and why his disciples should not be surprised or discouraged by it. He tells it publicly (vv. 4-8), then explains it privately (vv. 9-15), with a hard word about the purpose of parables in between.

Note when he tells it. Not to a disappointing turnout, but to a great crowd — and what he says is a story in which three-quarters of the sowing comes to nothing. He is telling the truth about crowds.

The picture was entirely ordinary. In that agriculture, sowing came before ploughing: a man walked the field broadcasting seed by the handful, and the ground was turned over afterwards. So the seed genuinely did fall everywhere. The sower is not careless; that is simply how the job was done, and it matters — the same generous scattering reaches all four kinds of ground.

The disciples ask what it means, and Jesus's answer is one of the most important passages in the Gospels on parabolic teaching: “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that 'seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.'” The quotation is Isaiah 6:9-10, the commission given after the vision of the throne — the hardening that follows persistent rejection of revelation.

This should not be softened, and three things hold it together. It is a judgement, and it falls on people who have already refused what they were given; Luke has shown a Nazareth that tried to kill him and a delegation plotting his death. A parable is also a door held ajar, hiding the thing from the casual and rewarding the man who comes back and asks — which is exactly what has just happened in verse 9. And it is mercy as well as judgement: to be told plainly and reject it plainly is a far more terrible position.

The explanation identifies the seed as the word of God, which settles a great deal. The variable in this parable is never the seed; it is the ground. The path is hardened by ordinary traffic. The rock is shallow soil over limestone, where the fastest growth in the field is the first to die. The thorns are already rooted and simply grow at the same time, for the same water and light. And the good soil holds the word fast in an honest heart and bears fruit with patience.

It is not a rigid psychological classification. It is a mirror, and every hearer is invited to hold it up.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable of the sower is the foundational parable — Mark records Jesus saying, “Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables?” (Mark 4:13). It establishes the principle governing all his teaching: the response to the word determines everything.

The seed does not change. It is the same word in all four soils, and the same generous hand scattering it. What varies is the condition of the heart it lands in — which is the basis of the New Testament's consistent call to prepare the heart through humility, through the removal of competing loves, through the patient reception of what has been given.

The description of the good soil — “an honest and good heart” — describes a heart that is not simply admirable. The heart he commends is not the morally superior one but the honest one: the heart that will let the word say what it says without negotiating, and does not flinch when the diagnosis is unflattering.

And the last word is patience, patient endurance. The rock soil was the fastest in the field; the good soil is the slowest. Fruit takes a season, and there is no arrangement by which it can be brought forward.
verseByVerse.examples:
The parable is a diagnostic tool. The question it puts to every hearer is not “have you heard the gospel?” but “what has happened to the word in you?”

Has it been taken away before it could go in — by distraction, by noise, by a life with no quiet in it? A footpath is not naturally hard ground; it is ordinary soil walked over so often that nothing can get into it, and the traffic that packed it down was perfectly innocent.

The rock soil frightens sincere believers, and it should be handled carefully. It describes someone who fell away — who is no longer there — not someone who is struggling and worried about it. Scripture is consistent that what God begins he finishes (Phil. 1:6; John 10:28), and John's own comment on those who left is that “they went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19). The remedy is never introspection; a plant cannot inspect its own roots. It is to go deeper, in the unspectacular disciplines nobody sees, before the drought arrives — because the sun in this parable is not a possibility. It is the weather.

The thorns are the most dangerous soil, because nothing appears to be wrong. And not one of the three Jesus names is a sin: cares, riches, and the ordinary pleasures of life. The choking of the word in a comfortable country is done almost entirely by legitimate things — which is exactly why it is so hard to see, and why the outcome is stated so precisely: their fruit does not mature. Not nothing at all. Perpetually promising, and never actually there.

verseByVerse.quote: And when a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable, 'A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable: a sower went out to sow his seed. As he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it.

In the flow. Luke has just shown two hearers of Jesus at one dinner: a Pharisee who heard nothing, and a forgiven woman who loved much (7:36–50). Now Jesus explains why the same word meets such different hearts. The parable opens a section about hearing (8:4–21) that ends with his true family, those who hear the word of God and do it, and the four miracles that follow show whose word it is. For the whole of Luke and Acts it explains what the reader will see again and again: the word goes out, and some are convinced while others disbelieve (Acts 28:24).

And when a great crowd was gathering. People are coming from town after town, and this is the moment Jesus chooses to tell a story in which three-quarters of the sowing comes to nothing. He is not looking at a discouraging turnout. He is telling the truth about crowds, and preparing his disciples for the years ahead and for every century since. The crowds were large, but how many truly heard?

He said in a parable. A parable is a story from everyday life that carries a spiritual meaning. It reveals truth to those who want to hear, and conceals it from those who do not (v. 10).

A sower went out to sow his seed. Every listener had watched it done. In that farming, it seems, sowing often came before ploughing: a man walked the field with a bag at his hip, flinging seed in wide arcs, and the ground was turned over afterwards. So the seed really did fall everywhere, on the path, on thin soil over limestone, into corners where last year’s thorns were still rooted. The sower is not careless; the same generous scattering reaches all four kinds of ground. Only Luke says his seed.

Some fell along the path. Footpaths ran through and around the fields, packed hard by generations of feet. The seed could not sink in. Only Luke adds that it was trampled underfoot, the detail of a careful reporter: before the birds even arrive, the ordinary traffic of ordinary life has walked over it, and then, lying on the surface, it is easy picking. Nothing has gone wrong with the seed. It never got below the surface, because the surface would not let it.

The sower is not named. One more thing governs how the whole parable is heard. Jesus identifies the seed (v. 11) and all four soils, and about the man with the bag he says nothing at all. That silence is a mercy to everyone who has ever tried to sow anything. The parable is not about the skill of the preacher, his technique, his timing or how the message was framed. The sower does one thing: he walks the field and scatters, generously, over ground he cannot control and mostly cannot even see.

The sower telling the story. Jesus does not name the sower, but the scene does. The first man with the bag is standing in front of this crowd, telling them what his own preaching will meet: hearts packed hard, hearts shallow, hearts already crowded. He knows most of the great crowd will drift away. He sows anyway, town after town, with the same open hand, because the seed is his Father’s word and the harvest is his Father’s business. The Son of God did not ration the word to the promising. He spent his ministry on Galilee knowing what Galilee would do, because somewhere among the paths and rocks were hearts his Father had prepared.

So does it not matter how we share the gospel? It matters, but not in the way we fear.
