We should speak clearly, kindly and wisely (Colossians 4:5–6), and Paul worked hard to remove needless obstacles (1 Corinthians 9:19–23). But the parable lifts from us the burden of thinking the harvest depends on our skill. Paul planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6). Your job is to scatter the seed faithfully and widely; the soil is in God’s hands. That frees you to share Christ without manipulation, and without despair when most people do not respond.

In a sentence. To a great crowd, Jesus told a parable of a sower whose seed partly fell on the path, where it was trampled and eaten by birds.

On a Tuesday. Being in the crowd around Jesus is not the same as truly hearing him. How are you hearing today? And if you are a parent, a Sunday school teacher, or a friend who has spoken of Christ and seen nothing, take heart: your task was to sow. Keep scattering.

For worship. Behind this one afternoon by the lake stands the whole patience of God, who sent prophet after prophet to ground that trampled them, and in these last days has spoken by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). The seed has never run out. It is living and abiding (1 Peter 1:23), the same word in every century, still scattered by ordinary hands over paths and rocks and thorns. Wherever it takes root, in a heart he himself has broken up, the harvest is his, and the Lord of it will not lose one grain.
verseByVerse.note: Seed was scattered by hand, and some fell on the hard footpaths between fields.

verseByVerse.quote: And some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.' As he said these things, he called out, 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. Some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold. As he said these things, he called out: he who has ears to hear, let him hear.

And some fell on the rock. Three more soils, and each fails at a different depth. This is not bare stone. Much of Galilee has limestone bedrock just under a thin layer of soil, and to a man walking the field it looks like the rest. Seed goes in, germinates fast, precisely because the shallow soil warms quickly, and comes up before anything else in the field. Then the sun comes, and the roots find rock instead of water. Only Luke mentions moisture: no depth, no water, no life. The fastest growth in the field is the first to die.

And some fell among thorns. Here nothing seems wrong. The soil is good, the seed goes in, the plant grows, and so does everything else. The thorns were not planted; their roots were already there from last year, unseen. They do not attack the wheat. They grow at the same time, for the same water and light, faster and stronger. Note the verb: choked. It is slow death by competition, and the crop is still standing when it happens.

And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold. Deep, clean, prepared ground. A hundred grains for one is an enormous return, an extraordinary harvest, far beyond what a farmer in that country would normally expect (compare Genesis 26:12, where Isaac reaped a hundredfold because the LORD blessed him). The figure is deliberately extravagant. Whatever the failures, the yield of the fourth soil is not merely adequate. It more than covers everything lost on the other three. The word of God bears abundant fruit in a good heart.

He who has ears to hear, let him hear. Luke says he called out, raising his voice over the crowd at the end. Everyone has ears; not everyone truly hears, and hearing in the Bible means listening, understanding and obeying. The sentence is itself a test. Anyone can hear a story about farming; he is asking for the hearing that goes past the surface and lets the thing in. A man who hears the parable of the soils and does not ask which soil he is has just shown the answer.

Ears for his voice. Whose voice is calling out over the crowd? In the Old Testament the summons to hear belongs to God: Hear, O Israel (Deuteronomy 6:4); incline your ear, and come to me; hear, that your soul may live (Isaiah 55:3). The prophets said, thus says the LORD, and pointed away from themselves. Jesus raises his voice and points the summons at his own words, as though hearing him and hearing God were the same thing. Luke will soon let the Father settle it from the cloud on the mountain: This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him (9:35). The hundredfold grows from his word, in those who hear him.

Can a person change from one soil to another? Yes, by the grace of God. The parable describes how people respond to the word at a given time, not a fixed caste they are born into. Hard ground can be broken up; God promises to take away the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26). Many Christians can look back on years when the word bounced off them, or sprang up and died, before God finally made the soil good. That is why we keep sowing, and why we keep praying for those who have heard and not yet believed.

In a sentence. Other seed fell on rock and withered, among thorns and was choked, and on good soil, where it yielded a hundredfold, and Jesus called out to those with ears to hear.

On a Tuesday. You have ears. Use them. Listen to Jesus’ word with your whole attention. Before you next hear a sermon, ask God to make your heart good soil, and afterwards ask yourself one honest question: what did that word ask me to do, and have I done it?

For worship. The harvest belongs to God, and it is glorious. Whatever is lost on the path, the rock and the thorns, the good soil yields a hundredfold, and the Lord of the harvest will not be disappointed in the end. A great multitude that no one can number will stand before his throne (Revelation 7:9), the fruit of seed scattered by hand across ordinary fields.
verseByVerse.note: Much of Galilee has limestone bedrock just under a thin layer of soil. A hundredfold would be an extraordinary harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: And when his disciples asked him what this parable meant, he said, 'To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that ‘seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
When his disciples asked him what this parable meant, he said: to you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.

And when his disciples asked him what this parable meant. This is the point of what follows. They do not assume they have understood; they come back and ask, and that asking is the parable enacted. The crowd heard a story about farming and went home; these men heard the same story and pressed for more. What separates them is not superior insight (Mark records Jesus telling them they had not understood it either, Mark 4:13). It is that they came back.

To you it has been given. A gift, by God’s grace. Note the passive: their understanding is not an achievement. Somebody handed it to them. Understanding the kingdom is not achieved by intelligence but given by God (10:21; Matthew 16:17).

To know the secrets of the kingdom of God. Secrets (mystēria) are mysteries: not puzzles, but truths once hidden and now revealed by God. Above all, the secret is that the kingdom has come in Jesus, in an unexpected form, like a seed, and not yet like a harvest (Ephesians 3:3–6).

The secret is a person. The secret given to the disciples is not a key for decoding stories but a person, sitting with them and explaining his own parables. Luke will say it outright two chapters later: no one knows who the Father is except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (10:22). The Twelve are not sharper than the crowd; they are closer to him, and the one who is himself the mystery of the kingdom opens it to those who stay and ask. Isaiah’s words hold a further wonder. John tells us Isaiah said them because he saw his glory and spoke of him (John 12:41): the Lord high and lifted up of Isaiah 6, whose holiness made the prophet cry out that he was lost, is the teacher answering fishermen’s questions.

So that seeing they may not see. This is one of the hardest sentences in the Gospels, and it should not be softened. Jesus is quoting Isaiah 6:9–10: the commission God gave Isaiah after the vision of the throne, sending him to a rebellious people who would hear and not understand, and telling him in advance that his preaching would harden them. Luke, unlike Mark, leaves out the end of the quotation (lest they turn and be forgiven), perhaps because he holds it back for the end of Acts (Acts 28:26–27).

Does God then deliberately blind people? Three things have to be held together. First, this is a judgement, and it falls on people who have already refused what they were given. Isaiah’s commission comes after generations of ignored prophets, and Luke has already shown us a Nazareth that tried to kill Jesus and experts plotting against him. The parables are a form of judgement on those who have already rejected the truth. They hear the stories without understanding, because they do not want to. To those who reject the light, more light is withheld (v. 18). Second, a parable is not merely a veil. It is also a door held ajar. It hides the thing from the casual and rewards the man who comes back and asks, which is precisely what has just happened in verse 9. The same story that closed the crowd’s ears opened these men’s, and the difference was whether they returned. Third, this is mercy as well as judgement. To be told plainly and to reject it plainly is a far more terrible position than to be told in a story you did not follow. A parable leaves the door open longer than a sermon does.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus was trying to keep people from salvation. He taught in parables also to draw people in, to provoke thought, and to make truth memorable. But for the hard-hearted, they confirm their blindness. The same sun melts wax and hardens clay. And what cannot be done with this verse is to use it to explain away one’s own dullness. The remedy is in verse 9, and it is not complicated. They asked.

If understanding is given, why do some get it and others not? Scripture answers with two truths and does not let us drop either. Understanding is God’s gift, given freely to whom he wills, so that no one may boast (Matthew 11:25–27; 1 Corinthians 4:7). And those who do not understand are not innocent victims; they are people who love the darkness and will not come to the light (John 3:19). God never blinds a willing seeker. If you want to understand, that wanting is itself the beginning of the gift, and the promise stands: ask, and it will be given; seek, and you will find (11:9).

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples that God had given them to know the mysteries of the kingdom, but for others they remain in parables, fulfilling Isaiah’s words about seeing without seeing.

On a Tuesday. When you read a passage you do not understand, do what the disciples did: come back and ask. Pray over it, read it again, look it up, ask your pastor or a mature friend. Do not let it slide off because it is hard. And pray by name for those you love who hear and do not see.

For worship. The mystery hidden for ages and generations is now revealed to his saints, and Paul gives it a name: Christ in you, the hope of glory (Colossians 1:26–27). That is where the secret of the kingdom was heading on the day the Twelve came back with their question. The one who explained the seed would come to dwell in them by his Spirit, so that fishermen, and every believer after them, would carry the King within. We did not find the secret. He gave it, and then he gave himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God. The ones along the path are those who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the parable is this: the seed is the word of God. The ones along the path are those who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved.

The seed is the word of God. That identification settles a great deal. The seed is the gospel message: not the preacher, the technique, the atmosphere of the meeting or the personality of the man scattering it, and it is exactly the same seed in all four soils. Its power is in the seed, not the sower (Isaiah 55:10–11; 1 Peter 1:23). The sower is first Jesus, and then everyone who spreads his word.

The variable is the ground. That is a hard word for anyone who preaches and a liberating one. Hard, because it removes the excuse that a poor response means the wrong method was used; liberating, because it removes the burden of believing that a better performance would have produced a better harvest. The sower cannot manufacture soil.

Then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts. The ones along the path hear, but the word makes no impression, and the birds are the devil. Two things deserve attention. The first is that there is an enemy, and Jesus names him. This is not a psychological account of inattention. Something intelligent and hostile is at work in the moment between hearing and believing, and its strategy is remarkably modest. It does not need to refute the word or produce an argument. It only needs to remove it before it goes in: by distraction, by doubt, by forgetfulness, by the next thing that comes along. The god of this world has blinded the minds of those who do not believe (2 Corinthians 4:4).

So that they may not believe and be saved. Only Luke adds this. That is what is actually at stake in a distracted hour. Jesus states plainly that Satan’s aim in taking the word away is to prevent faith and salvation. Faith comes from hearing the word (Romans 10:17); Satan’s strategy is to stop the hearing from taking root.

The one the devil could not rob. Luke’s readers have already watched the devil try this once. In the wilderness he came to Jesus with the same aim, to pry the word of God loose from a hungry man (4:1–13). Three times he tried, and three times Jesus answered, it is written, and the word stayed where it was. What every heart on the path loses, the Son of Man held. And he did not hold it for himself only. Within this chapter he will drive out a legion, and at the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities (Colossians 2:15), so that the enemy who snatches seed from the path has met one he cannot rob, and those who belong to Christ are kept by the stronger hand.

What a footpath is. A footpath is not naturally hard ground. It is ordinary soil walked over so often that nothing can get in, and the traffic that packed it was perfectly innocent. That is the danger of a life with no quiet in it. The word arrives on Sunday, and by the time the car is out of the car park there has been a conversation, a screen, a plan for the afternoon, and it is gone, and nobody did anything wrong.

Can the devil take the word from a Christian? He can steal a particular sermon from a believer’s attention, and he often does. But he cannot snatch a true believer out of Christ’s hand (John 10:28), because the word that saves has been planted by the Spirit, who keeps what he has begun. The path in this parable describes those in whom the word never went in at all. For the Christian, the warning is practical: guard the moment after hearing. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you (James 4:7).

In a sentence. The seed is God’s word, and the path represents those whose hard hearts let the devil snatch away the word before they can believe and be saved.

On a Tuesday. When you hear God’s word, do not let it lie on the surface. Think about it, pray over it, and let it sink in before the devil can take it. Try this next Sunday: before you speak to anyone after the sermon, take two minutes to name to God the one thing he said to you. On the drive home, talk about it instead of the weather. Protect the quiet.

For worship. The devil’s hurry is a confession. He does not trouble to snatch a seed that cannot grow; he swoops because the word of God is living and active (Hebrews 4:12), able to save the soul that receives it. And our God, knowing the birds are waiting, scatters it again, Sunday after Sunday, generation after generation, never weary of sowing what the enemy keeps stealing. Blessed be the Lord whose word outlasts every bird, and who has caused it to go down into hearts like ours and stay.

verseByVerse.quote: And the ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. But these have no root; they believe for a while, and in time of testing fall away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. But these have no root; they believe for a while, and in time of testing fall away.

And the ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. This soil frightens people and has hurt sensitive consciences, so it must be handled carefully. The response is real as far as it goes: they receive it with joy, and the joy is not called false. Something visible happened, perhaps more visible than in the good soil. But joy alone is not proof of genuine faith.

But these have no root. No depth: the word has not gone down into their heart and will. Root is precisely the part nobody can see, the underground work that nobody applauds and that only shows up in a drought. Only Luke says they believe for a while: a real but temporary belief, of the mind and the feelings, but not a heart transformed by God.

And in time of testing fall away. Testing (peirasmos) is the same word as at 4:13: trial, or temptation, the two senses English keeps apart and Greek does not. Matthew says, when tribulation or persecution arises (Matthew 13:21). When following Jesus becomes costly, they give up. Fall away (aphistantai) means depart, apostatise. The plant does not die because a wind blew it over. It dies because the sun came out and there was nothing beneath it to reach for water.

I have prayed for you. Testing is the word Luke uses again for the hour that came on the Twelve. On the night of his arrest Jesus told them to pray that they might not enter into temptation (22:40), and before it he told Peter that Satan had demanded to sift them like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail (22:31–32). Peter fell that night, and fell hard. Yet he did not fall away, because the root of his faith was not his own resolve but the prayer of his Lord. In plain terms: Peter kept believing after he had failed because Jesus had asked his Father to keep him, and the Father always hears the Son (John 11:42). That is the deepest difference between the rock and the good soil: the Son of God prays for his own, and he always lives to intercede for them (Hebrews 7:25).

Where Christians differ: can a believer fall away? Arminians take this as a believer who loses salvation. Verdict: the parable describes a faith that was never rooted, never the saving faith of the good soil. Its fruit never came. Scripture teaches that those whom God truly saves he keeps to the end (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6), and that those who fall away permanently show they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). This is the perseverance of the saints. But the warning is real: God keeps his people through warnings like this one, not in spite of them. Examine yourselves.

Is this me? Have I lost my salvation? The question presses on any believer who has ever gone through a bad season, and three things need saying, in this order. First, the passage is not describing someone who is struggling. It describes someone who fell away, who is no longer there. A person worried about this verse is by definition still asking the question, which is not what the rock soil does. Second, Scripture is consistent that what God begins he finishes. Paul was sure that the one who began a good work in the Philippians would carry it on to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6). No one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28). John’s own comment on those who left is not that they lost something but that they went out from us because they were not of us (1 John 2:19). The rock soil is not a Christian who was lost; it is a plant that never had root. Third, and this is the pastoral point, the remedy is never endless introspection. Staring at your own root system is exactly what a plant cannot do. What can be done is to go deeper: to put the word somewhere it can reach water, in the unspectacular disciplines that nobody sees, before the drought arrives. Because it will. The sun in this parable is not a possibility. It is the weather.

How do I put down roots? Roots grow in hidden places and over time. Read the Bible daily, not for information only but to meet God. Pray, especially when you do not feel like it. Sit under faithful preaching week by week, and come to the Lord’s Table. Join yourself to a church where people know you well enough to notice if you wither. Learn the great truths of the faith, so that when trouble comes you know what God has promised. And obey what you already know, because obedience is how the word goes down from the head into the will. None of it is dramatic. All of it is how God keeps his people.

In a sentence. The rocky ground represents those who receive the word with joy and believe for a while, but having no root, fall away when testing comes.

On a Tuesday. Enthusiasm is not enough. Let God’s word go deep. When testing comes, it will show whether you have roots. If you are a new Christian full of joy, thank God for the joy and give your attention to the roots. If you are leading others, do not measure a conversion by its excitement; walk with new believers through their first drought.

For worship. The Lord who calls is the Lord who keeps. Those whom he justified he also glorified (Romans 8:30), and not one of his sheep will be lost. He does not plant his people in shallow ground and leave them to the sun. He sends his Spirit as the deep water, and he himself is the root of their life, so that they are like a tree planted by streams of water, whose leaf does not wither (Psalm 1:3).

verseByVerse.quote: And as for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature.

And as for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear. This is the most dangerous soil in the parable, because it is the only one where nothing appears to be wrong. There is no bird here and no drought. The seed went in properly and the plant is growing; the man is still in the field, still green. What is happening is gradual and invisible until harvest, when it turns out there is nothing on the stalk.

But as they go on their way they are choked. Gradually, over time, not in a sudden crisis. There is no decision and no turning point. It happens over a decade, in the course of getting on with life, and the verb is strangled, slowly.

By the cares and riches and pleasures of life. Look at the three thorns Jesus names, because not one of them is in itself a sin. Cares: anxieties, worries about daily life, the future, money, health, a difficult child, an ageing parent, a job that may not last (12:22–31; 21:34). Riches: not theft, simply having things and the work of keeping them, and the love of money and possessions that so easily grows from it (12:15–21; 1 Timothy 6:9–10). Pleasures of life: only Luke adds this. Not vice, but the ordinary enjoyments; the word covers the perfectly innocent pleasures of an ordinary existence, good things that crowd out God.

The thorns are legitimate things. These are the thorns. Which means the choking of the word in a comfortable country is done almost entirely by legitimate things, and that is precisely why it is so hard to see. A man being strangled by an obvious sin usually knows it. A man being strangled by his mortgage, his hobbies and his family’s diary has nothing to repent of that he can name. Underneath, each thorn is a rival saviour. Worry quietly assumes that everything depends on me; riches promise a security God never promised through them; pleasures offer a happiness only he can give. The thorns grow wherever the heart has begun to trust them instead of him.

And their fruit does not mature. The outcome is stated with exact precision. Not, they bear no fruit at all. There is growth, perhaps even the beginning of fruit, but it never ripens. Perpetually promising and never actually there. A divided heart cannot bear the fruit of the kingdom. No one can serve two masters (16:13).

The one thing necessary. Luke shows the remedy for the thorns in a home in Bethany. Martha, whom Jesus calls anxious and troubled about many things (the same word as the cares of this verse), is busy with good work for Jesus; Mary sits at his feet listening to his word, and Jesus says that one thing is necessary, and that Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her (10:38–42). The thorns are not beaten by more effort. They are outgrown by a greater love. When Christ himself is the treasure, cares lose their grip, riches become tools, and pleasures become thanksgivings. The word does not ripen in a heart that merely resists the world; it ripens in a heart that has found someone better.

Are the thorn-soil hearers saved? The seed is choked and brings no fruit to maturity, and in the parable only the good soil bears a crop. The more likely reading is that they never truly believed: a faith that bears no fruit at all is not saving faith (compare John 15:2, 6). Some Christians read them as believers who are saved but fruitless. But a true believer may struggle with worries and riches and still bear fruit; the warning is not to let them choke the word.

Is it wrong to enjoy the good things of life? No. God richly provides us with everything to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17), and food, friendship, marriage, work and rest are his gifts. The thorns are not the pleasures themselves but the place they take. A pleasure becomes a thorn when it takes the time, the attention and the love that belong to God, when it becomes the thing you cannot give up. The test is not whether you enjoy things, but whether you could enjoy them less for Christ’s sake, and whether they lead you to thank him or to forget him.

In a sentence. The thorny ground represents those who hear, but whose faith is gradually choked by worries, wealth and pleasures, so that it never bears mature fruit.

On a Tuesday. Ask not, what sins am I fighting, but what has quietly become non-negotiable in my week, and when did I last examine it? Thorns are not planted; they are simply left. Pull one out this week before it chokes the word: cancel the thing that always crowds out prayer, give away what has begun to own you, or hand a named worry to God.

For worship. In his presence there is fullness of joy, and at his right hand are pleasures for evermore (Psalm 16:11); the pleasures that choke are thin and brief beside that. The cares that strangle us he bids us throw on him, because he cares for us (1 Peter 5:7), and he knows their weight: the Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head and carried a world’s sin, and his heart was never once divided. Every fruit of his obedience came to full ripeness, and that undivided obedience is counted to people whose hearts are divided still. Blessed be the Lord who was never choked, and who is untangling us.

verseByVerse.quote: As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience.

As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast. Every mark here is unspectacular. Hearing the word: the same word, from the same sower, that fell on all the other ground. Hold it fast (katechousin): keep it, grip it, refuse to let it go. It is active, and it is needed because things get taken; the bird came for the path soil. Mary treasured the word (2:19). The good hearer hangs on to it.

In an honest and good heart. Only Luke has this phrase (kalē kai agathē), which in Greek described a person of fine and noble character, and Jesus fills it with new content. The heart he commends is the honest one: open to God, not managing an impression, letting the word say what it says without negotiating. That is the one mark of good soil anybody can test in himself. Not, am I fruitful? That is not visible yet. But: when the word says something I do not like, do I let it stand?

Where does a good heart come from? Such a heart is itself God’s gift; he prepares the soil. The Lord opened Lydia’s heart to pay attention to what Paul said (Acts 16:14). No one is good soil by nature. Since the fall, every human heart is path, rock or thorns until God breaks it up and makes it new (Jeremiah 17:9; Ezekiel 36:26). If your heart has received the word and held it fast, give God the glory. And if you long for a better heart, ask him for it. That longing is already his work.

And bear fruit with patience. The last word is patience (hypomonē): endurance, steadfastness under pressure, the opposite of the rocky ground (v. 13), and the note the whole parable ends on. In a hurried Christianity that measures everything by immediate results, notice that the rock soil was the fastest in the field and the good soil the slowest. Fruit takes a season, whether or not anybody is watching, and it cannot be brought forward.

The ear that was never closed. There has been one hearer whose heart was wholly honest and good. Isaiah heard the Servant of the Lord say that morning by morning God wakened his ear to hear as one who is taught, and that he was not rebellious and did not turn back (Isaiah 50:4–5). Jesus held his Father’s word fast through the whole of his life, in Gethsemane and on the cross, and bore fruit with endurance to the end. And the good soil in his people comes from him. The heart that receives the word is the new heart he purchased. Purchased, because the new heart God promised (Ezekiel 36:26) is a gift of the new covenant, and Jesus said that covenant was made in his blood (22:20). And the patience in which it bears fruit is the endurance of the one who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2).

What is the fruit? The fruit is a changed life: the fruit of the Spirit, love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23); obedience and good works (Colossians 1:10); and, in God’s time, others brought to faith. It is not measured by size or fame. A hundredfold in the parable is the same seed reproduced, and the fruit of the word in you is Christlikeness. Do not compare your harvest with someone else’s; Jesus speaks elsewhere of a hundredfold, sixty and thirty, and all of it is good soil (Matthew 13:23).

In a sentence. The good soil represents those who hear the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and patiently bear fruit.

On a Tuesday. Hear, hold fast, and persevere. Fruit comes with patience. Do not give up. Choose one verse from Sunday’s sermon and carry it with you all week: write it down, repeat it, pray it. That is what holding fast looks like in an ordinary week. And when you see little fruit in yourself, remember that the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient about it (James 5:7).

For worship. The Lord of the harvest is in no hurry, and he is never late. He waits through the long seasons, and he does not abandon the ground he has broken up and sown. Every grain of honesty in our hearts he gave; every hour of endurance he supplies; and every ripened act of love will receive its commendation from him on the last day (1 Corinthians 4:5), as though it had been ours alone. Such is the generosity of God: he gives the seed, prepares the soil, sends the rain, and then rewards the harvest.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — A Lamp Under a Jar and True Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two brief teachings follow the parable, and both apply it.

The lamp saying comes first, and its placing is deliberate. Jesus has just explained a parable privately, to a small group, after saying that the secrets of the kingdom are given to some and not others. A disciple could easily draw the wrong conclusion: we have been let into something, and it is ours.

“No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light.” Both absurdities are exact: a jar smothers the flame for lack of air, and a lamp under a bed burns the house down. Neither preserves light; both destroy it while pretending to keep it.

And note the purpose clause — so that those who enter may see. Not so the lamp may be admired, and not for the household's benefit. The secrets of the kingdom were given to be put where strangers can see by them.

“For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest” cuts both ways. Forward, it is a promise: the gospel entrusted to twelve men in a house in Galilee will not stay in the house, and Luke is writing the second volume that proves it. But everything concealed also comes out eventually — which is terrifying for anyone hiding something, and one of the great comforts of Scripture for anyone who has been slandered or quietly written off.

“Take care then how you hear” is the imperative that gathers up the whole chapter. And the principle attached to it — to the one who has, more will be given — is not a cruelty but a description of how understanding actually behaves. Capacity grows by use, and atrophies without it. Luke alone adds the sharpest phrase: “even what he thinks that he has.” The man's holdings were never what he supposed.

Then Jesus's mother and brothers arrive, and he redefines family: “My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.” It is not a rejection of Mary. It is the good soil of verse 15, six verses on, given a family name — and it is the same hearing-and-doing that ended the sermon at 6:47-49.
verseByVerse.theology:
The lamp saying and the redefinition of family are the application of the parable to the disciples' own vocation. They have been given the secrets of the kingdom (v. 10) — not for private illumination but for public proclamation. The word they received is the lamp; the world they are being sent into is the stand.

The parable of the sower describes what happens when the word meets different soils. The lamp saying describes what those in whom it took root are to do with it.

And the family saying should be read alongside what Luke has already established about Mary. She is not being demoted; she is the founding member of the category. The woman who said “let it be to me according to your word” (1:38) heard the word of God and did it, and Jesus has just told a crowd of strangers that the door into his family is the one she walked through.

Nobody is in it by blood. Everybody is in it by hearing and doing — which is why the brothers standing outside at this point in the story, who did not yet believe in him (John 7:5), are outside in more senses than one.
verseByVerse.examples:
The redefinition of family as those who “hear the word of God and do it” is the basis of the extraordinary community the church creates across every natural human division. People who share nothing by blood, culture, language or class are family because they share the same word and the same response to it.

This is the sociological miracle of the first-century church, which drew together Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free, men and women, into a community the ancient world had no category for. It remains the miracle of every congregation that takes hearing-and-doing as its defining identity rather than any natural affinity.

“Take care then how you hear” is worth turning into a practical question, because the parable has just made hearing the decisive variable. Not what was preached, but what was done with it between the car park and Tuesday.

And “even what he thinks that he has” is aimed precisely at the person who is quite sure they are fine. Both the rock soil and the thorn soil had something, and both would have described themselves as having it, and neither had what they supposed — and each found out at the worst possible moment. There is a mercy in being told now, in a season of quiet, rather than in a season of testing.

verseByVerse.quote: 'No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light.

No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar. The saying is placed here on purpose. Jesus has just explained a parable privately, after telling the crowd that the secrets of the kingdom are given to some and not to others. A disciple could easily conclude: we have been let into something, and it is ours. The lamp saying shuts that down. A household lamp was a small clay bowl of oil with a wick, holding perhaps an hour or two of light, and you light it to give light, not to hide it.

Or puts it under a bed. The two absurdities are exact. A jar over it would smother it for lack of air, and a lamp under a bed would set the house on fire. Neither is a way of preserving light. Both are ways of destroying it while pretending to keep it.

But puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. Note the purpose clause. Not so that the lamp may be admired, nor so that the household may enjoy it, but so that those who enter, people coming in from outside, can see. The light of the gospel is meant to be seen (11:33; Matthew 5:14–16). The secrets of the kingdom were given to the disciples (v. 10) not for their private illumination, but to be put where strangers can see by them.

A light for the Gentiles. The lamp has a name in Luke. When old Simeon took the baby in his arms in the temple, he called him a light for revelation to the Gentiles (2:32). The light hidden for now in parables and in a house in Galilee is Christ himself, and the stand it was always meant for is the world. After the resurrection Jesus will open the disciples’ minds to see that the Christ should suffer and rise, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations (24:46–47). The ones who enter from outside are the nations, coming in to see by him. The disciples are not the light. They are the household that must not cover it.

For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest. This cuts two ways, and both are in the passage. Forward, it is a promise. The truth of the kingdom, now partly hidden in parables, will be fully revealed. What God has revealed is going somewhere; the gospel entrusted to twelve men in a house in Galilee will not stay in the house. Luke is writing the second volume that proves it.

Nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light. The sentence has a second edge. Everything hidden in human hearts will be exposed at the judgement (12:2–3; 1 Corinthians 4:5). There is no permanently private life, and the day is coming when the lighting is universal. For anyone hiding something, that is terrifying. For anyone who has been slandered or quietly written off, it is one of the great comforts of Scripture.

What if I have something hidden? Bring it into the light now, before God, and where needed before those you have wronged. The light that will one day expose everything is the same light in which there is forgiveness: if we walk in the light, the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). What is confessed to God is covered by Christ, and it will not be held against you on that day. The secrets that destroy are the ones we keep. A Christian has nothing to fear from the final light, because everything shameful in his life has already been dealt with at the cross.

In a sentence. As a lamp is lit to give light, not hidden, so the word must be made known, for everything hidden will be revealed.

On a Tuesday. Do not hide your faith. Let the light of the gospel be seen in what you say and how you live. Think of the one place in your week where no one knows you are a Christian, at work, at the gym, among a set of friends, and ask what it would look like this week to take the jar off.

For worship. The God who dwells in unapproachable light has not covered his lamp. He lit it in a manger, lifted it up on a cross where all could look, and raised it out of the darkness of a tomb, and it has never since gone out. Every hidden thing will one day come into that light, and for those who are his it will not be terror but homecoming: a city that has no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb (Revelation 21:23).
verseByVerse.note: A household lamp was a small clay bowl of oil with a wick.

verseByVerse.quote: Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away.

Take care then how you hear. This gathers up the parable section. Not what you hear but how: with an honest heart, holding it fast, obeying it. The four soils were not four kinds of seed, so pay attention to the way you are listening. Hearing is a moral act, with consequences.

For to the one who has, more will be given. Read at speed, it sounds like a cruelty: the rich get richer. It is a description of how understanding actually behaves, and everyone who has learned anything knows it. Capacity grows by use. A man who acts on what he has understood finds more opened to him; the next thing is intelligible because the last one was obeyed.

And from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away. A man who receives and does nothing loses even the ability to receive, not by an arbitrary penalty but by atrophy. Nothing is confiscated; it simply wastes, his superficial knowledge and his religious privilege with it. Neglected truth is lost.

Even what he thinks that he has. This phrase is easy to skim, and it is the sharpest in the sentence. Luke alone has it; Mark says simply what he has. Luke’s version is more disturbing: the man’s holdings were never what he supposed. He has been carrying a receipt for something that is not in the vault. That is the position of the rock soil and the thorn soil. Both had something, and both would have said they had it, and the discovery came at the worst moment, in the drought and at the harvest. So the warning is aimed not at the person who knows he is empty but at the one who is quite sure he is fine. And there is a mercy in being told now: a man can find out in quiet self-examination what he would otherwise find out in testing, and the remedy has not changed since verse 9. He can ask.

More will be given. What is the more? In Luke it is Christ himself, opened ever more fully. The disciples who listen so slowly in this chapter keep listening, and at the end the risen Lord walks with two of them and, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, interprets to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (24:27). That is where this principle leads: from a parable about seed to the whole Bible lit up with his face. And the one from whom even what he thinks he has is taken is the man who has the Scriptures without him. The scribes knew every line and refused to come to the one they were about (John 5:39–40).

What does good listening look like on a Sunday? Come prepared: pray before the service that God would speak, and come rested enough to listen. Listen expecting God, not merely a speaker, to address you (1 Thessalonians 2:13). Have your Bible open and test what you hear by it (Acts 17:11). Listen for yourself before you listen for others: what is this saying to me? Afterwards, talk about it, and decide on one thing to do. And keep listening when the preacher is not gifted; the seed is the word, not the sower.

In a sentence. Be careful how you listen, because those who receive and respond will be given more, while those who do not will lose even what they think they have.

On a Tuesday. Respond to what God shows you today, and he will show you more. Ignore it, and you will lose even that. Is there one thing God made clear to you months ago that you have still not acted on? Do it this week. The next door will not open until you walk through that one.

For worship. God is not stingy with light. From the fullness of his Son we have all received, grace upon grace (John 1:16), and that fullness is never drawn down: the more we receive, the more there is, for the riches of Christ are unsearchable (Ephesians 3:8). Eternity itself will be this verse fulfilled, an endless giving of more to those who have, as the Father shows his children the glory of his Son for ever. Blessed be the God whose generosity grows with every gift.

verseByVerse.quote: Then his mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. And he was told, 'Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, desiring to see you.' But he answered them, 'My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
His mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. He was told: your mother and your brothers are standing outside, desiring to see you. But he answered them: my mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.

Then his mother and his brothers came to him. Luke mentions the brothers without explanation; Mark names four of them, James, Joses (Joseph), Judas and Simon, and mentions sisters as well (Mark 6:3). John tells us plainly what they thought of him at this stage: not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5). They came to faith only after the resurrection (Acts 1:14; 1 Corinthians 15:7).

Why had they come? Luke is discreet; Mark is not, and records that his family set out to seize him, because people were saying he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21, 31–35). Whatever exactly is happening at the edge of this crowd, it is not a social visit, and they cannot even reach him because of the crowd.

My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it. This answer has troubled readers for centuries. Heard as a put-down of his mother, it would be startling; read carefully, it is nothing of the kind. He does not say he has no mother and brothers, and he does not refuse to see them. He loved his mother, and from the cross he provided for her (John 19:26–27). What he does is redefine the family, in public, at the very moment the claim of blood was pressed on him. A new family has come into being, bound not by blood but by obedience to God’s word, and it is closer and more lasting than the natural family.

The good soil with a family name. Notice what the definition is: those who hear the word of God and do it. That is the good soil of verse 15, six verses back, given a family name. It is the conclusion of the parables about hearing. It is also, almost word for word, the two builders at the end of the sermon (6:47–49). Luke has been circling this since chapter 6, and here he lands it.

Not a rejection of Mary. Which means the answer is not a rejection of Mary. It is an inclusion of everybody else on the terms Mary herself met first. The woman who said, let it be to me according to your word (1:38), is the founding member of the family. Even Mary’s blessedness lies chiefly in hearing and keeping God’s word (11:27–28). And Jesus has just told a crowd of strangers that the door into his family is the same one she walked through. Nobody is in it by blood. Everybody is in it by hearing and doing.

The family he makes. Who has the right to say who his mother is? Only someone who can make a family by his word. Jesus is not merely describing believers; he is founding a household around himself, and its centre is his person, for those who hear the word of God are the ones gathered round him hearing it from his lips. The brothers who thought him mad are later found among the praying disciples in Jerusalem (Acts 1:14), in the family by hearing, like everyone else. Their blood tie to Jesus gave them no head start. Grace gave them a place, and grace is the only door he has ever opened. So doing the word is not the entrance fee into the family; it is the family likeness. A child does not obey in order to become a child, but a child who truly hears his father begins to look like him (James 1:22–25).

Who were these brothers? The natural reading is that they were Mary’s later children, Jesus’ half-brothers (compare 2:7, where Jesus is her firstborn son; Mark 6:3). Roman Catholic and Orthodox Christians, holding that Mary remained a virgin, read them as cousins, since the Hebrew word for brother can be broad, or as Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage. But Scripture never suggests either, and the plain reading is the more likely.

Does following Jesus mean neglecting my family? No. Scripture commands us to honour father and mother (Ephesians 6:2) and says that anyone who does not provide for his own household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). Jesus himself cared for his mother to the end. What this passage teaches is priority, not neglect: when family claims and Christ’s claims collide, Christ comes first (14:26). For many believers, especially converts from other faiths, that collision is painful and real. For them the promise is precious: they gain, in the church, mothers and brothers and sisters a hundredfold (Mark 10:29–30).

In a sentence. When told his mother and brothers wanted to see him, Jesus said that his true mother and brothers are those who hear God’s word and do it.

On a Tuesday. If you hear and do God’s word, you belong to Jesus’ family. Treat other believers as your family. Who in your church has no family nearby, or a family that has rejected them for Christ? Invite them to your table this month. And if your own relatives do not yet believe, keep loving them as Jesus loved his brothers: patiently, until the day they too may come in.

For worship. The eternal Son of God is not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11). He has opened the family of God to people with no claim of blood, and adopted them through his own blood. Strangers in a crowd, Gentiles from the ends of the earth, sinners like us: all who hear the word of God and do it are his mother and brothers and sisters. What a family, and what an elder Brother.

parallels.desc: blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus and the disciples set out across the lake at his own initiative — “Let us go across to the other side.” They are in that boat, in that weather, because he told them to get in. The storm is not a consequence of any failure; obedience put them there.

He falls asleep. It is the only place in the Gospels where he is described as sleeping, and it is one of the plainest windows into his humanity: he had been preaching all day, and the moment the boat was under way he was unconscious in the stern.

Then a windstorm comes down on the lake. The geography explains it — the lake sits some two hundred metres below sea level in a basin ringed by hills, with ravines funnelling cold air off the heights into the warm basin without warning. A small, shallow lake goes from flat to lethal in minutes. It still does.

And these are professional fishermen who have worked this water all their lives. When they wake him with “Master, Master, we are perishing!” it is not landsmen panicking. These are the people you would want in the boat, and they have concluded they are going to drown — which is worth saying to anyone taught that fear is always a failure of faith. Sometimes fear is an accurate reading of the instruments.

He “rebuked the wind and the raging waves” — the same verb Luke used of the demon in the synagogue (4:35) and of a fever (4:39). There is no prayer. He speaks to the weather in the imperative.

“And they ceased, and there was a calm.” Luke's word is calm, a dead flat calm — and anyone who has been on water knows how strange that is. When wind drops, the swell runs on. Here the wind stops and the water goes flat in the same instant.

“Where is your faith?” is gentler than it looks. He does not ask why they have none; he asks where it has gone, which assumes they have some and mislaid it. What was missing was not courage but the conclusion they should have drawn from everything they had already seen.

And they were more frightened afterwards than during. The wind had threatened their lives; what came next threatened their categories. “Who then is this?”
verseByVerse.theology:
The stilling of the storm is the New Testament's most direct claim that Jesus exercises the prerogatives of the Creator over the natural world.

In the Old Testament only the LORD commands the wind and the sea. “He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed” (Ps. 107:29). “You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them” (Ps. 89:9). “Who shut in the sea with doors… and said, Thus far shall you come, and no farther?” (Job 38:8-11).

The disciples' question — “Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?” — has only one available answer, and every man in that boat had sung Psalm 107 since childhood. Luke leaves the question hanging; it will not be answered aloud until Peter's confession (9:20).

The sleeping is theologically as significant as the stilling. He is not asleep because he is unconcerned but because he is at peace — the one who will say “do not be anxious” (12:22) practising it in a sinking boat. And it is the fullest possible statement of the incarnation: the Lord of the storm, too tired to stay awake, four feet from men who thought they were dying.
verseByVerse.examples:
The disciples have Jesus in the boat and they are terrified. They have heard the sermon, seen the healings, received the explanation of the parables — and when the storm comes they are afraid and amazed.

That is the honest portrait of early discipleship, and of most later discipleship too. Knowing who Jesus is in the abstract is not the same as trusting him in the specific, wet, embodied crisis. Faith is very seldom lost in a crisis; it is mislaid — and “where is your faith?” is a search rather than an accusation.

The passage is not primarily about the disciples' failure. It is about the one who was in the boat with them. He did not abandon them in the storm and he did not scold them for waking him. He stilled it, and then invited them to examine where their faith had been — not to condemn but to grow.

And the sea does not negotiate. It does not respond to authority, or reputation, or courage; it has drowned better sailors than these. It heard a tired man speak from the back of a small boat, and it lay down.

verseByVerse.quote: One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them, 'Let us go across to the other side of the lake.' So they set out, and as they sailed he fell asleep. And a windstorm came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them: let us go across to the other side of the lake. So they set out, and as they sailed he fell asleep. A windstorm came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger.

Four miracles. Luke now records four great miracles (8:22–56): over nature, demons, disease and death. They show the authority of the one whose word the disciples are to hear. Having taught them how to hear, he now shows them who it is they are hearing.

Let us go across to the other side of the lake. Hold on to who said that, because it matters for everything that follows. The trip was not the disciples’ idea and it was not a detour. They are in that boat, in that weather, because Jesus told them to get in and where to go. He intended them to reach the other side. That disposes at the outset of a reading this story often gets: that the storm was a consequence of some failure. It was not. Obedience put them there.

As they sailed he fell asleep. This is the only time the Gospels tell us that Jesus slept, and Luke puts it with a doctor’s plainness: as they sailed, he dropped off. A day of preaching to crowds lies behind it. The Son of Man who will soon say he has nowhere to lay his head (9:58) finds a place in the stern of a fishing boat; Mark adds that it was on the cushion (Mark 4:38). This is not a lapse in the story. It is the incarnation, doing what a body does. And he sleeps in peace, trusting his Father: in peace I will both lie down and sleep (Psalm 4:8).

And a windstorm came down on the lake. Came down: the geography explains it. The Sea of Galilee lies about 700 feet (210 m) below sea level in a basin ringed by hills, with ravines funnelling down to the water from the heights to the east. Cold air off the heights drops into the warm basin without warning, and the lake, which is small and shallow, goes from flat to dangerous in minutes. It still does.

And they were filling with water and were in danger. Luke states the professional verdict plainly, and the men making it include four commercial fishermen who had worked this water all their lives. These are the people you would want in the boat, and they have concluded they are going to drown. Sometimes fear is simply an accurate reading of the instruments.

If I am obeying God, why am I in a storm? Because obedience does not exempt us from storms; sometimes it leads us into them. The disciples were exactly where Jesus told them to be. Paul was shipwrecked on a voyage God had appointed (Acts 27). A storm is not proof that you have taken a wrong turn. It may be the very path on which Christ means to show you who he is. The question is not whether storms will come, but who is in the boat with you.

In a sentence. As Jesus and the disciples crossed the lake, he fell asleep, and a violent storm struck, swamping the boat and endangering their lives.

On a Tuesday. Following Jesus does not keep you out of storms. He sent them into this one. If you are in one now, at work, in your health, in your family, do not conclude you are outside his will. And be honest about your fear; it may be an accurate reading of the instruments. Then remember who is asleep in the stern.

For worship. He slept in the storm because he was truly man; he stilled it because he was truly God. The Word made flesh grew tired, laid his head on a cushion, and slept in a fishing boat, sharing our weakness so that he could be our Saviour. He knows what exhaustion is. And the one who keeps Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4); even asleep in the stern, the Son of God had never stopped holding the sea.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden violent storms are common.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went and woke him, saying, 'Master, Master, we are perishing!' And he awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they ceased, and there was a calm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They went and woke him, saying: Master, Master, we are perishing! He awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they ceased, and there was a calm.

Master, Master, we are perishing! The doubled address is the sound of men shaking somebody awake. Luke’s version is gentler than Mark’s, where they say: Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing? (Mark 4:38). And their verdict is in the present tense: not, we are going to drown, but we are perishing; it is happening.

They wake him. Notice what they do underneath the panic. Whatever they expected of a carpenter in a storm, some instinct sent them to the back of the boat and not only to the oars. It is not much of a faith, and it is pointed in exactly the right direction, which is very often what faith looks like at three in the morning.

And he awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves. The verb is rebuked, and Luke has used it before in this Gospel: of the demon in the synagogue (4:35), and of Peter’s mother-in-law’s fever (4:39). It is the word for a sharp word of command to something that has no business behaving as it is. Jesus speaks to the storm as a master to a disobedient servant. And here is the thing to sit with. There is no prayer. He does not ask his Father to still the storm, as a prophet would have. He speaks to the weather, in the imperative.

And they ceased, and there was a calm. Instantly. What followed was a dead flat calm. Anyone who has been on water knows how strange that is. When a wind drops, the sea does not; the swell runs on for hours afterwards. Here the wind stops and the water goes flat in the same instant, and the boat is suddenly sitting still on a mirror with twelve soaked men in it. This calm was immediate and complete. What they had asked for was rescue. What they got was a demonstration.

Jesus does what God does. In the Scriptures these men learned as boys, exactly one person speaks to the sea like that. The LORD rebuked the Red Sea, and it became dry (Psalm 106:9); at his rebuke the waters fled (Psalm 104:7); he shut in the sea with doors and said, thus far shall you come, and no farther (Job 38:8–11). Luke’s single verb gathers it up. The same rebuke has silenced a demon and a fever and now the sea, because the one rebuking is Lord over every kind of disorder, in a soul, in a body, in the world itself. The one who does that is in the stern of their boat, and they had just woken him up.

Will Jesus always calm my storm? Not always in the way we ask. Sometimes he stills the storm; sometimes he stills his child in the storm, and carries him through it; sometimes he brings him home through it. Paul’s thorn was not removed, and many martyrs were not rescued. But this story shows what is always true: nothing in your storm is beyond his command, and you are never in the boat alone. Cry out to him, as the disciples did. He hears, and whatever he does, he will bring you to the other side he promised.

In a sentence. The terrified disciples woke Jesus, and he rebuked the wind and waves, and there was an instant calm.

On a Tuesday. When panic rises, do what the disciples did right: go to the back of the boat. Before you reach for the oars of your own solutions, cry out to him, honestly, even in a sentence. Then do the next sensible thing, trusting that the wind and the waves are under his command.

For worship. When the waters saw God, the psalmist sang, they were afraid (Psalm 77:16), and on Galilee they saw him again. The rebuke that once opened a road through the sea for Israel lays a storm flat for twelve frightened men, and one day it will still the last chaos of all, when the sea is no more (Revelation 21:1). There is no darkness in the world and no disorder in a human life that does not hear that voice. And the Lord who speaks it counts those who cry to him in a sinking boat as his own.

parallels.desc: he made the storm be still

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, 'Where is your faith?' And they were afraid, and they marveled, saying to one another, 'Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: where is your faith? They were afraid, and they marvelled, saying to one another: who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?

Where is your faith? The question is gentler than it looks in English. He does not say, why have you no faith? He asks where it has gone, which assumes they have some, and that it was mislaid rather than absent. That is the ordinary condition of most believers in most crises, and there is comfort in seeing it named without contempt. The question is not an accusation but a search: where did you put it?

What he is not rebuking. Not their fear of the storm; that was an accurate assessment by professionals. Not their waking him; that was the right instinct. What has gone missing is the conclusion they should have drawn from what they had already seen: that the person in the boat was not in the same category as the weather. His word, let us go to the other side, should have been enough, and he was in the boat. They had watched him command a demon and a fever with a word, and a dead man sit up at a town gate. The storm did not find them ignorant; it found them not applying what they knew.

And they were afraid, and they marveled. Luke is precise and slightly startling here. They were more frightened after the storm stopped than during it. A new fear: not of the storm, but of him. The wind had merely threatened their lives. What came next threatened their categories. The fear of the storm was replaced by awe at the one who controls it. This is what happens whenever sinful people find themselves close to the holy. Isaiah saw the Lord and cried that he was lost (Isaiah 6:5); Peter, in a boat on this same lake, fell at Jesus’ knees and begged him to depart, because he was a sinful man (5:8). The fear in the boat is not a failure of faith. It is the right response of creatures when God comes near.

Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him? There it is: the question this whole Gospel exists to answer, asked out loud for the first time by the men closest to him, sitting in a wet boat on a flat sea. They do not answer it. Luke leaves it hanging, and he will leave it hanging until the next chapter, when Peter finally says it (9:20). But everyone in that boat had sung Psalm 107 since childhood: then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress; he made the storm be still (Psalm 107:28–29). They are with the Lord himself.

Is fear always wrong for a Christian? No. There is a fear that is simply realism, and a fear that is reverence. The disciples’ first fear (of drowning) was natural; their second fear (of him) was the beginning of wisdom. What Jesus questions is not the feeling of fear but faith gone missing: forgetting who is in the boat. The answer to sinful fear is not to stop feeling, but to fear God more. When I am afraid, I put my trust in you (Psalm 56:3). The psalmist is afraid and trusting in the same breath.

In a sentence. Jesus asked where their faith was, and the disciples, filled with fear and wonder, asked who he could be, that wind and water obey him.

On a Tuesday. Where is your faith today? Put it in the one who commands the wind and water. When the next crisis comes, ask yourself his question: where did I put my faith? Then go and find it in what you already know: what he has said, what he has done, who he is.

For worship. The sea does not negotiate. It does not respond to authority, or reputation, or courage; it has drowned better sailors than these and will again. And it heard a tired man speak from the back of a small boat, and it lay down. There is only one who has ever been obeyed like that, and he had been asleep a few feet away from them the whole time. Who then is this? He is the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth and the sea, and he is in the boat with his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–39 — Jesus Heals a Man with a Demon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
On the far shore — Gentile territory, east of the lake, with pigs on the hillsides — a man possessed by a legion of demons meets Jesus and falls at his feet.

The description is harrowing and deliberate. He wore no clothes; he did not live in a house but among the tombs; he had repeatedly broken the chains put on him and been driven into the desert. Stripped of clothing, of community and of self-determination, he is not described as a man with a problem but as a site.

Two puzzles meet a careful reader here. Gerasa lay thirty miles inland, and Gadara six miles off; neither is on the shore. The likeliest answer is that Gergesa, modern Kursi, was the spot — a small place on the eastern shore where the hills drop sharply to the water — while Gerasa and Gadara were the well-known cities whose districts reached that coast. And Matthew names two men where Mark and Luke name one: Matthew adds a second, he does not subtract one, and the other two follow the man who spoke and who was left with a story to tell.

The demons recognise Jesus at once and their theology is impeccable: “Son of the Most High God” — a title Jews and Gentiles alike used of Israel's God, fitting on this side of the lake. But look at the verb. They beg. Three times in this scene the powers of darkness plead, which is Luke's way of showing how the balance of power stands the moment Jesus steps ashore.

“Legion” was nominally six thousand men, and a legion is not a crowd but an occupying force. The word would have had an edge in the Decapolis, where people had watched real ones march. And the answer comes from the occupation rather than the man: asked his own name, there is no I left to reply.

They beg not to be sent to the abyss — the sealed prison of rebel spirits (Rev. 20:1-3) — but into the pigs. Jesus permits it, and it is the demons who stampede the herd, doing to two thousand animals in a moment what they had done to one man for years. The lake full of drowned swine is the plainest possible evidence of what he had been living under.

The townspeople find him clothed, in his right mind, and sitting at the feet of Jesus — the posture of a disciple. And they ask Jesus to leave. The man himself begs to come along; that is the one request in the chapter that is refused. “Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.”
verseByVerse.theology:
This is the most comprehensive exorcism narrative in the Gospels, and it is performed in Gentile territory, on a Gentile man, before an audience of Gentile herdsmen. The geography is the theology: the kingdom of God does not stop at the borders of Israel.

The Gerasene man is the Gentile counterpart to the demonised man in the Capernaum synagogue (4:33) — both liberated by the same word, with the same authority, and neither able to put up the slightest resistance.

The restored man is “in his right mind” — sober, self-possessed — and he is sitting at Jesus's feet, where a disciple sits (cf. 10:39; Acts 22:3). The demonic occupation has not merely been evicted; the ground has been given to somebody else.

That distinction matters, because a deliverance that only removes does not hold. Jesus said so himself: a house swept and empty gets reoccupied (11:24-26). The sitting at the feet is not incidental colour. It is the theological point of the healing.
verseByVerse.examples:
The townspeople who ask Jesus to leave are the cautionary portrait of a community that values what it can calculate over what it cannot control. The pigs are gone; the man is well. The arithmetic should be straightforward.

But the fear is real, and Luke names it: something has happened here that they do not control. A lunatic in the tombs can at least be chained. Every generation of the church has had to decide whether to welcome the disruptive grace of God or manage it into something more comfortable — and Jesus does not argue with them. He gets into the boat and goes. He will not force himself on a community that has counted the cost and decided against him.

The man's desire to follow, and Jesus's refusal, is the missionary call in its most particular form: go to the people who already know you. That is a harder road than the boat. Everyone who has been converted where their old life is public knowledge understands it.

And he is sent to declare not a doctrine but a testimony — the one subject on which he is the world's leading authority. Then Luke does something quietly enormous and leaves it without comment: Jesus said “declare how much God has done for you,” and the man went and proclaimed “how much Jesus had done for him.” The two sentences sit side by side, and Luke sees nothing to explain.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they sailed to the country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. When Jesus had stepped out on land, there met him a man from the city who had demons. For a long time he had worn no clothes, and he had not lived in a house but among the tombs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They sailed to the country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. When Jesus had stepped out on land, there met him a man from the city who had demons. For a long time he had worn no clothes, and he had not lived in a house but among the tombs.

The country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. They land on the far shore, and everything about the place is foreign. This is Gentile territory: the region of the Decapolis, east of the lake, Greek-speaking, with pigs on the hillsides, which tells you at once that no Jewish community is farming here. Luke explains opposite Galilee for readers who did not know the geography.

Gerasenes, Gadarenes or Gergesenes? Two things about this crossing will stop a reader with a map, and both are worth settling. The first is the place. Some manuscripts read Gadarenes or Gergesenes. Gerasa lay some thirty miles inland; no herd could run from there down a bank into the lake. Matthew names the Gadarenes, and Gadara is about six miles off, still not on the shore. The likeliest answer is that Gergesa, perhaps modern Kursi, was the actual spot, a small place on the eastern shore where the hills drop sharply to the water, exactly as the story requires, while Gerasa and Gadara were the well-known cities whose districts reached down to that coast. Each writer named the region by the city his own readers would recognise, much as one might place a village in greater London. The steep bank is still there.

One man or two? The second is the number. Luke describes one man, and so does Mark; Matthew says there were two (Matthew 8:28). Neither denies the other. Matthew adds a second man; he does not subtract one. Where a pair is involved and only one does the talking and only one is left with a story to tell, a writer naturally follows him. Mark and Luke keep the camera on the man who spoke, who was called Legion, who begged to come along and was sent home instead. The same thing happens at Jericho, where Matthew has two blind men and Mark names only Bartimaeus.

For a long time he had worn no clothes. Then Luke sets out what was left of the man who met him, in three strokes. Only Luke mentions the nakedness. It is not an eccentricity but the loss of the most basic mark of human dignity, and Luke’s for a long time says this was his settled condition, not a crisis.

And he had not lived in a house but among the tombs. No house: no address, no household, no place at anybody’s table. Tombs were caves cut into the hillside, in a Jewish frame the last word in uncleanness, and in any frame a man living among the dead because the living will not have him. Here is Satan’s work: degradation, isolation, uncleanness, death. He is not described as a man with a problem. He is described as a site.

Liberty to the captives. At Nazareth Jesus read that he was anointed to proclaim liberty to the captives (4:18), then reminded his hometown that Elijah was sent to a widow of Sidon and Elisha cleansed Naaman the Syrian (4:25–27), and they tried to throw him off a cliff. Here he acts out that sermon. He crosses a storm to a Gentile shore and goes straight to the most bound man on it. The Lord of Israel has not forgotten the nations: the first person he meets in pagan country is a captive, and the first thing he does there is set him free. It is the mission of Acts in miniature, a generation early.

Was this man demon-possessed, or mentally ill? Luke, a physician, distinguishes healings from exorcisms (4:40–41), and this man’s condition had a demonic cause: the demons speak and are cast out into the pigs. Possession is real, and the New Testament does not say it has ceased. But most mental illness has ordinary causes and needs ordinary care. Christians should neither see demons behind every illness nor deny that the devil works. And the modern assumption that nothing personal and evil stands behind the darkness of the world is itself a belief, not a finding; Luke the doctor knew the difference between a fever and a demon, and he records both.

Can a Christian be possessed? No. The Holy Spirit dwells in every believer (1 Corinthians 6:19), who is sealed by him (Ephesians 1:13) and has been rescued from the domain of darkness (Colossians 1:13). A house cannot have two owners. A Christian can be tempted, attacked and deceived, and is told to resist the devil (1 Peter 5:8–9), but never to fear being taken over by him. The one who lives in you is greater than the one who is in the world (1 John 4:4).

In a sentence. On the eastern shore, in Gentile territory, Jesus was met by a demon-possessed man who had gone naked for a long time and lived among the tombs.

On a Tuesday. No one is too far gone, too degraded, too unclean for Jesus to reach. Think of the person in your town everyone has given up on: the addict, the man who sleeps rough, the relative no one mentions. Jesus crossed a stormy lake for a man like that. Pray for them by name, and ask what step of love you could take.

For worship. Satan strips, isolates and drives men among the dead; the Son of God clothes, restores and brings them home. He came to seek and to save the lost (19:10), and the man in this verse is as lost as a man can be: no clothes, no house, no living company. He is not beyond the reach of the one who would himself be stripped, numbered with the transgressors (22:37) and laid in a tomb, so that people who lived among the dead might live with him for ever.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Gadarenes, some Gergesenes. The region lay on the east side of the lake, Gentile country. Tombs were unclean places.

verseByVerse.quote: When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him and said with a loud voice, 'What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me.' For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. (For many a time it had seized him. He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the desert.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
