When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him and said with a loud voice: what have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me. For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. (For many a time it had seized him. He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the desert.)

When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him. He gets there first. Jesus has just stepped off the boat; the man comes at a run, screaming, and goes down at his feet. The demon recognises its master and submits. Whatever else is happening inside him, it is the posture of worship, forced out of an enemy.

What have you to do with me? The opening phrase is a stock formula of confrontation, literally what to me and to you?, the ancient equivalent of what do you want with me? The same words came out of the demon in the Capernaum synagogue (4:34).

Jesus, Son of the Most High God. And once again the theology is impeccable. Son of the Most High is the title Gabriel used to Mary (1:32). Most High God is a title often used by or to Gentiles for the God of Israel (Genesis 14:18–20; Daniel 3:26; Acts 16:17), a natural way for outsiders to name him. The demons know exactly who Jesus is.

I beg you, do not torment me. This is the first of four times in this scene that begging happens, and three of them come from the demons. The powers of darkness spend the whole passage pleading, which tells you how the balance of power stands the moment Jesus steps ashore. And they are not asking to be left alone. They are asking about timing, and they know there is a schedule; Matthew records them saying it outright: have you come here to torment us before the time? (Matthew 8:29). They have better eschatology than most of the people in this Gospel.

The Judge has come as Deliverer. Why do the demons speak of torment? Because they know who will judge them. The Father has given all judgement to the Son (John 5:22), and the demons recognise the Judge before the court has sat; this carpenter is the one appointed to judge the living and the dead (Acts 10:42). But the Judge has come first as Deliverer. He will bear judgement himself at the cross, for sinners, not for demons, and on this beach he spends his authority not on sentencing the man’s captors but on freeing their captive.

He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles. Luke adds a case history, as a doctor would: for many a time it had seized him. And the town had tried. Somebody bought chains and posted guards, again and again: a community attempting, in the only way it knew, to manage a man it could not help.

And be driven by the demon into the desert. The demon drove him, as a herdsman drives cattle, and each failed restraint sent him further out. That is what human management of a spiritual bondage looks like. Chains can stop a man harming anybody; they cannot give him back his mind.

Should Christians fear demons? No. This passage is written to cure that fear. The demons are the ones who are terrified; they fall down, beg, and know their doom. Christ has disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them at the cross (Colossians 2:15). Christians should take the devil seriously, be watchful and resist him, firm in the faith (1 Peter 5:8–9). But they should never be fascinated by him or afraid of him. The right response to the dark powers is not fear of them, but trust in the one before whom they tremble.

In a sentence. The man fell before Jesus, and the demon in him cried out, recognising him as Son of the Most High God and begging not to be tormented, for it had long controlled the man, defying every chain.

On a Tuesday. No human chain could hold this man. Only Christ could free him. Trust him with the bondages that human methods cannot break: the addiction that has beaten every programme, the anger that has outlasted every resolution. Use the help God gives through doctors and counsellors and friends, and bring it all to the one before whom every bondage must give way.

For worship. Heaven named him Son of the Most High before he was born, and now hell names him the same on a Gentile beach. Heaven and hell agree on who he is; only men argue. And what the demons confess in terror the redeemed will confess in joy, when every knee bows and every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:10–11). The one before whom darkness trembles is the one under whose wings his people shelter.
verseByVerse.note: “Most High God” is a title often used by or to Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then asked him, 'What is your name?' And he said, 'Legion,' for many demons had entered him. And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus then asked him: what is your name? And he said: Legion, for many demons had entered him. And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss.

Jesus then asked him, What is your name? It is the only question Jesus asks in the whole encounter, and it is worth asking why he asks it. Not for information. Perhaps to bring the man to awareness of his condition, or to expose the extent of the possession. But the likeliest reason is the simplest: a name is what a person has, and this man has not been addressed as a person in years. The town called him a danger; the tombs were his address. Jesus asks him who he is.

Legion. The answer is horrifying on two counts. First, what it means. A Roman legion numbered about 5,000 to 6,000 soldiers. Whether the number is literal or a way of saying an army, a legion is not a crowd. It is an occupying force: organised, under orders, in possession of ground, and in the Decapolis people had watched them march.

For many demons had entered him. That is Luke’s explanation of the name. And the second horror is who answers. The question was put to the man, and what comes out is the occupation speaking. He has been so comprehensively taken over that when asked for his own name he gives theirs. There is no I left to reply.

The real occupation. Israel longed for a Messiah who would drive the legions out of the land. Jesus meets a legion on this beach, and it is not Roman. Here is the occupation that really held the human race, and here is the King who really breaks it, not with a sword but with a word. The deliverance Israel hoped for was too small. Zechariah had sung of salvation from our enemies (1:71), and on a Gentile shore Luke shows how deep those enemies went and how complete the rescue would be.

And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss. Only Luke mentions the abyss (abyssos), the deep: in the Greek Old Testament it renders the waters of Genesis 1, and in later Jewish writing and in Revelation it is the bottomless pit, the prison of rebel spirits before their final judgement (Romans 10:7; Revelation 9:1–2; 20:1–3). They know where they are going, that he can send them there, and that they cannot stop him. The one thing they never attempt is resistance. From verse 27 to verse 31 there has been no struggle, only begging.

Why did Jesus not send them to the abyss at once? Because the time of their final judgement had not yet come (Matthew 8:29). Christ has defeated Satan decisively at the cross, but the final sentence will be carried out at his return, when the devil and his angels are thrown into the lake of fire (Matthew 25:41; Revelation 20:10). Until then, evil is real but bound and limited, able to do only what God permits (Job 1:12). We live between the victory and the final execution of judgement, which is why we must still resist the devil, and why we can do so with confidence.

In a sentence. Asked his name, the man said Legion, because many demons possessed him, and they begged Jesus not to send them to the abyss.

On a Tuesday. However many and powerful the forces of evil, they tremble before Jesus. Take courage. And remember that you have a name, given by him. Whatever has defined you, the addiction, the diagnosis, the failure, the label others have put on you, it is not who you are in Christ. He calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3).

For worship. A legion could not stand before one man from Nazareth. The army that had held a human soul for years asked for terms the moment he stepped on the beach, and the man it had renamed got his own name back. Our Lord is mighty, and his might is spent on mercy: one day he will shut the accuser away for good, and every one of his people will be known by the name written in the Lamb’s book of life (Revelation 21:27).
verseByVerse.note: A Roman legion numbered several thousand soldiers. The abyss is the place where evil spirits are confined.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission. Then the demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission. Then the demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.

Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside. Pigs were unclean animals under the law (Leviticus 11:7). This was Gentile territory, where pigs were raised. Mark says about two thousand (Mark 5:13).

And they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission. Even demons need Jesus’ permission. Two questions press on a thoughtful reader here: why did Jesus permit it, and what is the drowning meant to say?

Who does the drowning. Jesus does not command the pigs into the lake. He grants a request, and it is the demons who stampede the herd to its death, doing to a herd in a moment what they had been doing to one man for years. The destruction is theirs, and it unmasks them.

And the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned. Several reasons may be seen. It demonstrated visibly that the demons had left the man, and how many there were. It showed their destructive purpose: what they did to the pigs, they wanted to do to the man. The town had been looking at a naked man in the tombs and calling it madness. Now they have a hillside of evidence about what had been living in him, and it is impossible to misread. And unclean spirits went with unclean animals into the deep.

The arithmetic. Sceptics have long pointed to the drowned herd as proof that Jesus was careless of property and cruel to animals. Weigh the exchange as it stands. One human being, made in the image of God, somebody’s son, is pulled out of a living death; a herd of pigs is lost. Jesus refuses the calculation that counts the livestock and forgets the man. He will say in this Gospel that a man is worth more than many sparrows (12:7), and the scale holds here. A Saviour who would leave a man among the tombs to protect a herd would be no Saviour at all. And the ruined herd forced the district to a decision it could no longer avoid: it put a price on the table.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus was careless of property or of animals. Scripture says a righteous man regards the life of his beast (Proverbs 12:10), and God feeds the sparrows. He judged that the deliverance of one man was worth the loss. The townspeople judged otherwise (v. 37). Scripture does not linger over the owners’ loss, not because the loss did not happen, but because the point of the story is about to be standing there clothed and in his right mind. The pigs are the price tag the town could see. The man is the treasure it could not.

What a man is worth to him. The town weighed the man against the herd and found the herd heavier. Jesus weighed them the other way, and the cross shows how far his scale tips. One man’s freedom cost the owners a herd of pigs; the freedom of all his people cost the Son of God his own life. You were ransomed, Peter writes, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19). Nobody values a human being as highly as the one who paid for him.

In a sentence. Jesus permitted the demons to enter a large herd of pigs, which rushed down the bank into the lake and drowned.

On a Tuesday. One person is worth more than great wealth. Value people as Jesus does. Ask where your own spending of time and money shows that you value things more than people: the evening given to the project rather than the friend in trouble, the budget that has room for everything except mercy.

For worship. What is man, that you are mindful of him? (Psalm 8:4). The Lord of every herd on every hill looked at one ruined Gentile and counted him the treasure. Hebrews hears the psalm answered in Jesus, made for a little while lower than the angels and crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (Hebrews 2:6–9). He became the man of Psalm 8 so that men like this one, and like us, could be lifted up with him.
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean animals under the law.

verseByVerse.quote: When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and told it in the city and in the country. Then people went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. And those who had seen it told them how the demon-possessed man had been healed. Then all the people of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear. So he got into the boat and returned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and told it in the city and in the country. People went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. Those who had seen it told them how the demon-possessed man had been healed. Then all the people of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear. So he got into the boat and returned.

Then people went out to see what had happened. Luke sets the restoration against the ruin, item by item, and every term answers something in verse 27. He had worn no clothes: he is clothed. He had lived among the tombs, driven into the desert: he is sitting. He had been out of his mind: he is in his right mind.

Sitting at the feet of Jesus. And the fourth item is the one that is not merely a reversal: at the feet of Jesus. Sitting at someone’s feet was the posture of a disciple. It is where Mary of Bethany will sit (10:39), and where Paul says he sat under Gamaliel (Acts 22:3). The wild man who roamed the tombs now sits quietly as a learner. He has not simply been emptied. He has been re-seated. That distinction matters, because deliverance that only removes is not deliverance for long. Jesus said so himself: a house swept and empty gets reoccupied (11:24–26). What happened here is that the ground was taken back and then given to somebody.

Clothed, and in his right mind. No longer naked (v. 27); someone had given him clothes, perhaps from among the disciples. In his right mind is sōphronounta: sober, self-possessed, sane, at peace. A complete transformation, and the onlookers were not glad but afraid, because the power of God at work frightened them.

How the demon-possessed man had been healed. Healed (esōthē) is literally saved. The salvation is of the whole man: body, mind and soul. Luke uses the word that will run through the rest of the chapter.

Then all the people asked him to depart from them. This is the real indictment of the passage. The man everyone in that district had given up on, the one they had chained and guarded and finally left in the graveyard, is sitting quietly in his right mind, dressed, listening. It is the best thing that has happened there in years, and they want the man who did it to leave. Luke names one reason and implies another. The stated one is fear, for they were seized with great fear: something has come that they cannot manage, and that is more unsettling than a madman, because a madman can at least be chained. The unstated one is the hillside, and the herd in the lake that somebody has to account for. They preferred their pigs, their peace and their way of life to the presence of Jesus. Many still ask him to leave for the same reasons.

So he got into the boat and returned. Notice what Jesus does with the request. He does not argue, or press, or stay to reason with them. He does not force himself on people. He came a long way across a dangerous lake for one man, and when the district asked him to go, he went. That is a sobering mercy. He will not force himself on a community that has counted the cost and decided against him.

Can someone ask Jesus to leave for good? Jesus is patient, and he came back to the Decapolis later, where crowds received him (Mark 7:31–37). But this passage is a warning not to presume. The Gerasenes had one visit and sent him away. Scripture warns against hardening your heart today (Hebrews 3:15), because the day of opportunity does not last for ever. If you sense Christ calling you and you are inclined to send him off because he is disturbing or costly, do not wait. He may not cross the lake again on your timetable.

In a sentence. The townspeople came and found the man sitting at Jesus’ feet, clothed and sane; seized with fear, they asked Jesus to leave, and he did.

On a Tuesday. Is there anything you value more than Jesus’ presence, and would ask him to leave rather than lose? It may be a habit, a relationship, a way of making money, or simply a comfortable life he keeps disturbing. Name it before God. And when someone in your circle is changed by Christ in a way that unsettles everyone, be the one who rejoices.

For worship. Look at the man at his feet: clothed, quiet, in his right mind. Christ does not tidy the surface; he gives a man back himself and then a place at his feet. And he does it in a district that will ask him to go. The same Lord would one day be led out of Jerusalem to a cross, and answer by praying for those who put him there (23:34). There is a patience in Christ that outlasts our refusals, and the man at his feet is what that patience makes of anyone it will not give up.
verseByVerse.note: Sitting at someone’s feet was the posture of a disciple.

parallels.desc: Mary sat at the Lord’s feet

verseByVerse.quote: The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying, 'Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.' And he went away, proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying: return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you. And he went away, proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him.

The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him. This is the fourth begging in the passage, and the first that comes from a human being. The demons begged not to be tormented, begged not to go to the abyss, and begged to enter the pigs. The people only asked Jesus to leave. Now the man begs to go with him. The natural desire of the redeemed is to be with their Redeemer. And it is the only request in the scene from a human being that is refused.

A reasonable request. Consider what he was asking for and why it was reasonable. His neighbours had just told Jesus to leave. Every person in that district knew what he had been; there is no starting again in a place like that. The boat was leaving, and on it were twelve men who had also left their trades to follow, and he wanted a place among them. Given what he had come out of, it is difficult to imagine a more understandable request.

Return to your home. But Jesus sent him away, with two commands, and both cost him something. Not everyone is called to leave home; some are called to stay and witness where they are. Return to your home: back to the house he had not lived in, to relatives who had watched him deteriorate, to a town that had chained him and then given up. That is a harder road than the boat, as everyone converted where their old life is public knowledge knows.

And declare how much God has done for you. He is not sent to argue or to explain the kingdom of God; he has had perhaps an hour’s instruction. He is sent to tell people what happened to him, the one subject on which he is the world’s leading authority, and he becomes the first missionary to the Gentiles of the Decapolis. In Jewish territory Jesus often told people to keep quiet (8:56); here, where messianic excitement was less of a danger and where Jesus himself was not staying, he sends the man to tell. Everyone knew what he had been; now they could see what he was. That is worth holding on to by anybody who has ever felt disqualified from speaking: the first missionary to Gentile territory had no training and no theology, and he had a before and an after that a whole district had witnessed.

Proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him. And then Luke does something quietly enormous, and leaves it without comment. Jesus said: declare how much God has done for you. And the man went away proclaiming how much Jesus had done for him. He was told to speak about God. He spoke about Jesus. Luke sets the two sentences side by side and does not explain, because as far as he is concerned there is nothing to explain. What Jesus did, God did. Without saying so, Luke equates Jesus with God. He is the one the demons called Son of the Most High God (v. 28). And Mark adds that everyone marvelled (Mark 5:20). When Jesus later returned to the Decapolis, people brought the sick to him (Mark 7:31–37), perhaps in part the fruit of this man’s testimony.

How do I know whether to stay or go? Most Christians are called, like this man, to serve Christ where they already are: in their family, their street, their workplace. Some are called to leave for the gospel, and the church should test and send them gladly (Acts 13:1–3). Wanting to be with Jesus is right; but being with Jesus is not only a matter of geography. He goes with those he sends. If you are unsure, ask what doors God has opened, seek the counsel of your church, and remember that home is often the hardest and most fruitful mission field there is.

What should I say when I tell people about Jesus? Start where this man started: with what the Lord has done for you. Winning the argument is not your assignment. Tell honestly what you were, what Christ did, and what he is to you now (1 Peter 3:15). Then point beyond yourself to him: who he is, that he died for sinners and rose again, and that he receives all who come to him. Your story opens the door; his story is the message.

In a sentence. The healed man begged to follow Jesus, but Jesus sent him home to tell what God had done for him, and he proclaimed throughout the city what Jesus had done.

On a Tuesday. You are called to tell those around you what Jesus has done for you. Start at home. Write down, in three or four sentences, your own before and after, and pray for one person this month with whom you could share it.

For worship. The man who begged to go with him was sent home, and the boat left without him; yet he did not walk into that town alone, for the Lord who sends is with those he sends to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20). A district that had asked Christ to leave found it could not be rid of him: he left behind a living witness, clothed and sane, in its streets. Such is the persistence of our God’s mercy. Turned away at the shore, it walked back into the town on the feet of a man it had saved.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–56 — Jesus Heals a Woman and Raises Jairus's Daughter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The final section is Luke's most carefully interlaced double narrative — a healing folded inside a raising, with each story interpreting the other.

Jairus is a ruler of the synagogue: a lay official who organised the services and carried the community's respect, and a member of the class that had been watching Jesus with hostility since chapter 5. He falls at Jesus's feet in the road, in front of people who know exactly who he is. His only daughter, about twelve, is dying, and every consideration of position has gone.

Jesus goes with him. The crowd presses. And a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years — exactly as long as the girl has been alive — reaches through the crowd and touches the tassel on the corner of his garment.

Her twelve years had cost far more than health. Leviticus 15:25-27 put a woman in her condition under continuing ritual uncleanness, and not only her: anything she sat on, anyone who touched her. Twelve years without the synagogue, without normal contact, very likely without a husband — and none of it her fault. Luke, a doctor, records the failure of his own profession without flinching: she had spent everything and was no better.

Her approach is furtive because it had to be; by the law she understood, her touch would defile him. And once again the traffic runs the wrong way. The bleeding stops.

Jesus stops the whole procession to ask who touched him — a question he already knows the answer to. Peter's exasperation is reasonable and Luke lets it stand. But he will not take a transaction where a person is available: she had tried to take the gift and stay invisible, and that would have left her physically healed and socially exactly as she was. He makes her say it out loud, in public — which puts her restoration on the record where her whole town can hear it — and then calls her “Daughter,” the only time in the Gospels he uses that word to a woman.

And while he is still speaking, the message comes: “Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.” From where Jairus stands, the delay killed her. Somebody else's twelve-year problem was attended to first, and his child ran out of time.

“Do not fear; only believe.” Then the mourners are put out, the girl is taken by the hand — “Child, arise” — and her spirit returns. And the first thing Jesus says afterwards is that somebody should get her something to eat.
verseByVerse.theology:
The interlacing of the two stories is a masterpiece of narrative theology. The woman healed on the way to Jairus's house teaches Jairus — and the reader — that the delay did not diminish Jesus's power or exhaust his compassion. The one who felt power go out of him for her has more than enough for a dead girl.

Jairus is being taught, at his own cost and in real time, to resist the word that says “it is too late.” The “too late” of the messengers is not too late for the Lord of life, and Jairus had just watched, at close range, what this man does for somebody who ran out of options twelve years ago.

“She is not dead but sleeping” is not a correction of the diagnosis, and Luke — a physician — gives three signals that she was genuinely dead: the professional mourners had arrived, the crowd knew, and “her spirit returned.” Jesus is changing a category, not disputing a fact. Sleep is the condition from which you are expected to get up, and that is now what death is for those who belong to him (1 Thess. 4:13-15; John 11:11).

The woman's touch of the “fringe” may point to the tassels of Numbers 15:38-40, worn as a reminder of the commandments. Malachi 4:2 had promised that the sun of righteousness would rise “with healing in its wings,” and the Hebrew for wings is the word for the corners of a garment. She may have been reaching, knowingly or not, for exactly that.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman's twelve years, her exhausted resources, her uncleanness and her invisibility are the conditions in which she finally comes. She did not come while she still had options; she came when she had nothing left.

And Jesus's response — stopping in the middle of a crowd, insisting on finding her, calling her “daughter,” declaring her faith in front of everyone — is the public vindication of a person who arrived at the bottom of her resources. Her faith was ignorant in its theology, furtive in its method and frightened in its execution, and he calls it faith and commends it aloud.

Jairus's journey is faith pushed to its absolute limit. He did everything right: he found Jesus, he fell at his feet, he asked in time. Then the delay, and then the word that it was over. This has to be said plainly, because it is what a great many lives feel like and pious hurry past it is worthless.

“Only believe” is not a technique, and it is not an instruction to generate a quantity of faith sufficient to raise the dead — that reading crushes bereaved people. It is a word to a man who has just been told it is finished, asking him to keep hold of the person beside him for another ten minutes.

And the last instruction in the house is the one that could not have been invented. A girl has been raised from the dead, the room is beyond speech, and the Son of God says: get her something to eat. She is a child, and she has been ill, and she will be hungry.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. And falling at Jesus' feet, he implored him to come to his house, for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the people pressed around him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. Falling at Jesus’ feet, he implored him to come to his house, for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the people pressed around him.

Now when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him. The contrast is deliberate and painful. One shore, across the lake, had just asked him to leave; the other has been standing about waiting for the boat to come back, for they were all waiting for him.

And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. Luke gives us his name and his office, and both matter. A ruler of the synagogue was not a priest but a lay official: the man who organised the services, invited readers and preachers, cared for the building, and carried a good deal of the community’s respect. In a Galilean town he was somebody. He is also, by position, a member of the class that has been watching Jesus with increasing hostility since chapter 5. The Pharisees and teachers of the law who came from every village of Galilee and Judea to sit and observe (5:17) belonged to his world, and Luke will later show a synagogue ruler indignant at a Sabbath healing (13:14). Jairus set aside his dignity and his reputation.

And falling at Jesus’ feet, he implored him. He goes down in the road, in front of people who know exactly who he is. Whatever position he held, and whatever the synagogue authorities had been saying about this preacher, it is gone in a second. He has a dying child. That is one of the things suffering does, and it is not always a cruelty: it strips away the calculations we cannot ordinarily get past. Jairus did not come because his theology changed. He came because his daughter was dying and there was nowhere else.

At his feet, three times. Luke keeps putting people in the same place. The freed man sat at the feet of Jesus (v. 35); Jairus falls at his feet (v. 41); the healed woman will fall down before him (v. 47). A Gentile madman, a synagogue ruler and an unclean woman, as different as three people in Galilee could be, all end up on the same ground. That is where everyone ends who discovers who he is. These are the feet of the Lord, and Luke shows the kneeling beginning already among the desperate, long before the proud get there.

For he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. Luke’s detail is a physician’s and a storyteller’s at once. Only Luke says only, as with the widow’s son at Nain (7:12) and the boy of 9:38: he notices the depth of grief when an only child is lost. About twelve, in that culture, is the edge of womanhood, when a girl might soon be betrothed; she has had exactly one childhood, and it is ending. And twelve links her with the woman who had been ill for twelve years (v. 43): the girl had lived as long as the woman had suffered.

As Jesus went, the people pressed around him. Pressed (synepnigon) means crushed, nearly suffocated. It is the same word as the thorns that choked the seed (v. 14). The crowd that presses on him can be as much an obstacle as a help.

What if I only come to Jesus because I am desperate? Then you are in good company. Jairus came because his daughter was dying; the woman with the twelve-year bleeding came because every doctor had failed; the prodigal came home because he was starving. Jesus never once asked anyone whether their motives were pure enough before he helped them. Need is not a bad reason to come to Christ; it is the usual one. What matters is not why you first came, but that you came to him, and that you stay. Many who came to him for a healing found the Healer.

In a sentence. On his return, Jairus, a synagogue ruler, fell at Jesus’ feet begging him to come to his dying only daughter, aged about twelve, and Jesus went, with the crowd crushing around him.

On a Tuesday. Desperate need levels everyone. Whatever your position, fall at Jesus’ feet. Is pride, or the fear of what others will think, keeping you from asking for help, from God or from his people? Jairus let it go in a second. And if you are a leader in a church, remember that you will never be more useful than when you are on your knees.

For worship. One shore sent him away and the other was waiting for him, and he came, as he always comes, to those who wait. The ruler of a synagogue knelt in the dust before the Lord of the synagogue’s Scriptures, and the Lord did not ask for his credentials. The LORD is high, yet he regards the lowly, but the haughty he knows from afar (Psalm 138:6). The way to his heart has never been through a position. It has been through need, brought to his feet.
verseByVerse.note: A ruler of the synagogue organised its services and cared for its building.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and though she had spent all her living on physicians, she could not be healed by anyone. She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her discharge of blood ceased.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and though she had spent all her living on physicians, she could not be healed by anyone. She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her discharge of blood ceased.

And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years. Luke interrupts himself. Jesus is on his way to a dying child, the crowd is pressing, and the narrative stops for a woman nobody has noticed. Twelve: Jairus’s daughter has been alive for twelve years; this woman has been bleeding for exactly as long. Luke has set the two side by side on purpose: one has had a life, and the other has been losing hers, over the same span. It was probably continuous menstrual bleeding.

What those twelve years cost. Take in what they had cost her, because it is far more than a medical condition. Under the law, a woman with a chronic discharge was in continuing ritual uncleanness, and not only her. Anything she lay or sat on was unclean. Anyone who touched those things was unclean until evening (Leviticus 15:25–27). Which means twelve years unable to worship at the temple, twelve years cut off from normal contact, twelve years in which every human touch carried a consequence for the other person. If she was married when it began, she may well not be married now. She was physically ill, weak and probably anaemic, socially isolated, religiously excluded. And it is not her fault. She has done nothing.

And though she had spent all her living on physicians. Some manuscripts omit these words. Luke, a doctor, records the failure of his own profession without flinching, but he is gentler than Mark, who adds that she had suffered much under many physicians and had only grown worse (Mark 5:26). Luke says simply that she could not be healed by anyone. Twelve years of treatments, each one costing money and hope, and at the end of it she is bankrupt and no better.

She came up behind him. Secretly. Everything about this is furtive, and it had to be. She is ceremonially unclean in a dense crowd, touching a rabbi, and by the law as she understood it, her touch would defile him. She was not supposed to be in a crowd touching people. She has no right to be there at all.

And touched the fringe of his garment. The fringe (kraspedon) is the tassel the law told Israelite men to wear at the corners of their cloaks, to remind them of God’s commandments (Numbers 15:38–40). It is the furthest edge of him that a person crouching in a crowd could reach. Some believed the tassels of a holy man had power (Matthew 14:36). Her faith was mixed with superstition, but it was faith in Jesus.

And immediately her discharge of blood ceased. Luke uses the medical term for a flow stopping. After twelve years, in a moment. And once again the traffic runs the other way: instead of her uncleanness passing to Jesus, his healing passed to her. Wholeness travels from him to her.

Does Jesus accept a faith that is mixed with superstition? Yes, if it is reaching for him. Her understanding was confused; she thought the power was in the tassel. But Jesus did not wait for her theology to be corrected before he healed her. He honoured the faith, and then, in front of the crowd, he corrected the theology: it was not the cloth but your faith in me. That is how he still deals with new and weak believers. A trembling, half-informed faith in Christ saves; a well-informed faith in anything else does not. And he will not leave a weak faith where he found it.

In a sentence. A woman who had suffered bleeding for twelve years, incurable by any doctor, secretly touched the tassel of Jesus’ cloak and was instantly healed.

On a Tuesday. Even a weak and imperfect faith, if it reaches out to Jesus, finds his power. Reach out to him. If you have exhausted every other remedy, and spent all you had, come to him now, even if all you can manage is the edge of the garment. And think of the person in your church who has been sick or isolated for years. Twelve years is a long time to be forgotten.

For worship. Here is a holiness that is not threatened by our uncleanness but overcomes it. Under the law, the unclean defiled the clean; in Christ, the clean cleanses the unclean. He took our uncleanness upon himself at the cross, bearing our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24), so that power and wholeness could flow out from him to all who reach for him. No uncleanness is too great and no case too long for him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the words about the physicians. Her condition made her ritually unclean. The fringe was the tassel the law required on a garment.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said, 'Who was it that touched me?' When all denied it, Peter said, 'Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you!' But Jesus said, 'Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: who was it that touched me? When all denied it, Peter said: Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you! But Jesus said: someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me.

And Jesus said, Who was it that touched me? He is on his way to a dying child and he stops the whole procession to ask a question he already knows the answer to. Jesus knew. He wanted her to come forward, for her own sake.

Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you! Everyone denied it, at first even the woman herself, and then Peter spoke up. His exasperation was entirely reasonable, and Luke lets it stand. Hundreds of people are jammed against him; the question is, on the face of it, absurd. Everyone is touching you.

Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me. He distinguishes between the crowd’s pressing and this touch, and the distinction is the point. Hundreds were in physical contact with him. One person took something. Many touched him; one touched him in faith. There is a difference between jostling Jesus in a crowd and reaching out to him in faith. Many are near Jesus; few touch him. Power (dynamis) is the power of God, flowing from him, and Luke has used it before of the healing that flowed from him (5:17; 6:19). Whatever exactly it means, it was not automatic and it was not without cost. Something went out of him, and he felt it go.

Why stop? Now the real question. He knows what happened. She has what she came for. The child is dying up the road and every second matters. He stops because a healing is not the same as a person, and he has not come for transactions. She had tried to take the gift and remain invisible, which is entirely understandable for a woman in her position, and it would have left her exactly as she was in every way except the physical. Still unspoken of. Still, as far as her town was concerned, unclean. Still nobody’s daughter. He will not let her have it that way. He is going to bring her to say it out loud, in front of everyone, and then he is going to say something to her that she can carry for the rest of her life, and he holds up a dying child’s father in the road while he does it.

Does power going out of him mean Jesus has limited power? No. Jesus is fully God, and his divine power is infinite. The phrase tells us that the healing was a real act of his, consciously given, not a magic that leaked from his clothes without his knowledge. He perceived it because he is the source of it. It also reminds us that his healing was personal and costly: he did not dispense blessings like a machine. Every mercy we receive from Christ is given by him, knowingly, to us.

In a sentence. Jesus asked who had touched him, and when Peter protested that the whole crowd was pressing on him, Jesus said someone had touched him, for he had felt power go out from him.

On a Tuesday. Being in church, near Jesus, is not the same as touching him in faith. Reach out to him personally. On Sunday, in the crowd of familiar words and songs, ask yourself whether you are jostling him or touching him. And if you have received something from him in secret, an answered prayer, a burden lifted, do not be afraid to let him bring you into the open. He asks the question because he wants you, not only your need met.

For worship. In a crushing crowd he knew the one touch of faith. He knows yours too. The Lord who is surrounded by the worship of heaven and the noise of the whole earth notices the faintest reaching out of a frightened believer. He knows his sheep (John 10:14), one by one, and nothing that is done towards him in faith goes unseen.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. And he said to her, 'Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. And he said to her: daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.

And when the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling. Luke’s phrasing is exact. She did not come forward; she came when she saw that hiding had failed. She could not escape. And she is shaking. Why? Not, presumably, because she doubted the healing; she could feel it. She is frightened because of what she has just done. She was afraid of being rebuked for touching him while unclean: an unclean woman has touched a rabbi in public and taken something without asking. In front of a crowd, and a synagogue ruler, she is about to be exposed as both ceremonially defiling and presumptuous.

And falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people. Only Luke says in the presence of all the people. She tells the whole thing: why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. Twelve years of it, out loud, to a street full of strangers: the condition she has never been able to name in public, the money spent, the doctors, and what happened when she reached the tassel.

Why did Jesus make her do this? So that everyone would know she was clean. That is the confession he stopped the procession to get, and it is worth seeing why it was worth the delay. Her healing had been secret; her restoration had to be public. Her testimony is now on the public record. Everyone in that crowd has heard, from her own mouth, that she is well, which means she can go back to worship, and into her family’s kitchen, and into ordinary human contact, and nobody can say otherwise. After twelve years of exclusion, the whole town could now accept her. And so she would know that she had been healed not by magic but by Jesus, through faith. He did not merely stop the bleeding. He put her back into the community, and he did it by bringing her to speak.

Daughter. Luke loves to show Jesus bringing the excluded back into Abraham’s family with a single word. He will call a woman bent double for eighteen years a daughter of Abraham (13:16), and a despised tax collector a son of Abraham (19:9). Here, for a woman nobody could touch for twelve years, the word is simply daughter, without qualification, and it is spoken as his own claim on her. After twelve years of exclusion, the first word out of his mouth gives her a family.

Your faith has made you well. Made you well (sesōken) means has saved you. Not the tassel, but faith in Jesus. Body and soul. And notice what he says her faith did, and what it did not. It did not manufacture the power; that came out of him. Her faith was simply the hand that reached. It was ignorant in its theology, furtive in its method, and frightened in its execution, and he calls it faith and commends it in public.

Go in peace. As to the sinful woman (7:50). Peace is shalom: wholeness, everything put back in its right place. Not merely, you are cured. She came for one thing and he gave her the lot: her body, her standing, her place among people, and a name to be called by.

Do I have to tell people what Jesus has done for me? Not necessarily in a crowded street, but Christ does call his people to confess him openly. With the heart one believes, and with the mouth one confesses (Romans 10:10). For a believer, that confession is made in baptism, which is the public declaration that you belong to Christ, and then in a life of speaking of him. It is not a test you must pass to be saved; it is what Christ draws out of those he has saved, for their own good and for others. Like this woman, you may tremble. He will meet you there with peace.

In a sentence. Seeing she could not hide, the woman came trembling and told everyone what had happened, and Jesus called her daughter, said her faith had saved her, and sent her away in peace.

On a Tuesday. Jesus wants a personal relationship, not just a secret cure. Come to him openly and hear him call you son or daughter. If you have been a secret believer, consider what step of open confession he may be calling you to: baptism, church membership, a word to a friend. And when a trembling person tells their story in your church, receive it as the town should have received hers.

For worship. Daughter. The Lord of glory looked at a woman unclean for twelve years and called her his own. That is what he does for all who come to him: we who were far off are brought near, and the God of heaven calls us sons and daughters (2 Corinthians 6:18). He does not only heal; he adopts. Go in peace, for he is our peace.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, someone from the ruler's house came and said, 'Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.' But Jesus on hearing this answered him, 'Do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was still speaking, someone from the ruler’s house came and said: your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more. But Jesus on hearing this answered him: do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.

While he was still speaking. The timing is unbearable, and Luke means it to be. Jesus is in the middle of the sentence that gives the woman her peace, and the messenger arrives. Jairus came running with minutes to spare. Then the crowd slowed them. Then a woman touched a tassel, and Jesus would not move on until she had told her whole story in public, and while she was telling it, his daughter died. From where he stood, the delay killed her: somebody else’s twelve-year problem, which could surely have waited another hour, was attended to first. That has to be said plainly, because it is what many lives feel like, and a pious hurry past it is worthless. Jesus’ delays can seem cruel. But he had a greater purpose.

Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more. Hope is over. A teacher can heal the sick, but not raise the dead. And notice the messenger’s advice, which is kindly meant and entirely rational. There is nothing more to be done. The category has changed from illness to death, and everybody knows the difference. The word for trouble means to bother, to put to inconvenience: the man is being gently told to let the poor rabbi get on.

Do not fear; only believe. Jesus overhears the message and answers at once, cutting in before it can land and take root. Fear and faith are opposites; only believe means keep on believing. These words are not a technique. Jesus is not telling him to generate enough faith to raise the dead; that reading crushes bereaved people, and it is not what the sentence says. He is telling a man who has just been told it is over to keep holding on to the person standing next to him for another ten minutes. And here the woman’s healing was for Jairus as much as for her. He has just watched, at close range and at his own cost, what this man does for someone who had run out of options twelve years ago.

And she will be well. Only Luke adds this. Well (sōthēsetai) means saved, the same word as verse 48. It is the promise of Jesus, given after the worst news, not before it.

Why does God seem to delay when I pray? Scripture never pretends that God’s delays are easy; the psalms cry, how long, O LORD? (Psalm 13:1). But the story of Jairus, like that of Lazarus (John 11:6, 15), shows that his delays are never neglect. He was not too late for Jairus; he was exactly on time for a greater miracle. Your waiting may be for something God means to do that is greater than what you asked. That does not mean every prayer is answered as Jairus’s was. It means the one who makes you wait is the same one who loves you, and he has never once been late for his own purposes.

In a sentence. Word came that Jairus’s daughter had died, but Jesus told him not to fear but only to believe, and she would be saved.

On a Tuesday. When the worst news comes, the diagnosis, the phone call, the letter, there will be voices, often kindly, telling you not to trouble the Teacher any more. Do not listen to them. Hold on to Jesus for the next ten minutes, and then the next. And when you are the one bringing bad news to someone, bring Christ’s word with it.

For worship. Death sends its messengers to every house, and they always say the same thing: it is over, do not trouble him any more. Only one voice has ever answered them and been proved right. He went himself into the house of death, and on the third morning the women were asked why they sought the living among the dead (24:5). Because he lives, his word to Jairus is his word at every believer’s graveside, and no messenger has ever contradicted it: do not fear; only believe.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him, except Peter and John and James, and the father and mother of the child. And all were weeping and mourning for her, but he said, 'Do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping.' And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him except Peter and John and James, and the father and mother of the child. All were weeping and mourning for her, but he said: do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping. And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead.

And when he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him, except Peter and John and James. The inner three, who will also be on the mountain at the transfiguration (9:28) and, in Mark’s account, in Gethsemane (Mark 14:33), see him raise the dead, see him in glory, and see him on his face in the dirt. They are witnesses. And, tenderly, the parents are included, because this is their daughter and not a demonstration. Everybody else is put out.

And all were weeping and mourning for her. The house is full of noise: family and, it seems, professional mourners; Matthew mentions the flute players (Matthew 9:23). Mourning (ekoptonto) means beating their breasts. In that culture the mourning began immediately and it was loud; according to a later rabbinic rule, even a poor family was expected to provide flute players and at least one wailing woman, and the wailing was a formal, public performance of grief. It had started within the hour.

Do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping. Now, what does that mean? Because it is regularly used to argue that she was never dead: that this was a coma, and Jesus was correcting a medical error. That cannot be what Luke means, and Luke is a doctor. The messenger reported a death. The professional mourners had arrived, and they did not come for the unconscious. Luke’s own next sentence says the crowd knew she was dead. And when she revives, Luke writes that her spirit returned (v. 55), which is not the language of waking from a faint. Jesus does not deny that she is dead. He is not correcting a diagnosis. He is changing a category. Sleep is the condition from which you are expected to get up, and in his vocabulary that is now what death is: temporary, from which he can wake her. That is exactly how the New Testament will go on to speak of believers who die: those who have fallen asleep (John 11:11–14; Acts 7:60; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). Death is not the end for those Christ will raise. The word is not a denial of death. It is a claim about who is standing in the room.

And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead. Scornful laughter. Luke’s phrasing is careful and it is not kind to them: they laughed, knowing. This is not a misunderstanding; it is derision from people who were right about the facts. They knew she was dead. Luke makes it clear that this was a real raising from the dead, not a revival from a coma. They are the only people in this Gospel who are said to laugh at Jesus, and they had every reason. He said something absurd. And within minutes, the girl they had been paid to mourn got up and walked.

Does sleeping mean that the dead are unconscious? No. Jesus means that her death is not final; she will wake. The word describes the body awaiting resurrection, not the soul. Those who die in the Lord are with him at once, conscious and at rest (23:43; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). There is no soul sleep and no purgatory: the believer’s soul goes immediately into the presence of Christ, and the body sleeps in the grave until he raises it on the last day (Westminster 32.1).

In a sentence. At the house, Jesus took only the three disciples and the parents in, and told the mourners she was not dead but sleeping, and they laughed at him, knowing she was dead.

On a Tuesday. For those who belong to Christ, death is sleep, from which he will wake them. Grieve, but with hope. When you stand at the grave of a believer, use his word: she is not dead but sleeping. It is not a euphemism; it is a promise. And if people laugh at your hope, do not be surprised. They laughed at him.

For worship. To the Lord Jesus, death is a sleep from which he can wake anyone, as easily as a parent wakes a child. The last enemy has become, for his people, a bed. He went down into death himself, lay three days in the tomb, and rose, so that every believer’s grave is now a resting place to be left on the morning of resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: But taking her by the hand he called, saying, 'Child, arise.' And her spirit returned, and she got up at once. And he directed that something should be given her to eat. And her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Taking her by the hand he called, saying: child, arise. Her spirit returned, and she got up at once. He directed that something should be given her to eat. Her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.

But taking her by the hand. He takes her hand. Again, as with the leper, as with the bier at Nain, he touches what the law says will defile him. Touching a corpse made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11), and he reaches out and takes hold of a dead twelve-year-old. But Jesus touches the dead, and death gives way.

He called, saying, Child, arise. The word is a family word. Mark preserves it in Aramaic, Talitha cumi (Mark 5:41), the ordinary phrase a mother uses in the morning: little girl, get up. The greatest power in the universe is exercised in the tone of voice used to wake a child for school.

And her spirit returned. Only Luke says this. Her spirit had left her body at death (23:46; Acts 7:59), and came back: a clear statement that she had been dead, and that the human spirit lives on after death. And she got up at once. No process, no recovery, no gradual return of colour: she stood up.

And he directed that something should be given her to eat. This is the sentence that gives the passage away, and it is the reason no one could have invented it. A twelve-year-old has just been raised from the dead in front of her parents and three grown men. The room must be beyond speech. And the first instruction the Son of God gives, having conquered death in a bedroom in Galilee, is: get her something to eat. She is a child, and she has been ill, and she will be hungry. It is a practical, caring detail. She was really alive, in a real body, and hungry. After the resurrection Jesus himself would eat to show he was not a ghost (24:41–43). There is as much of what he is like in that instruction as in the miracle before it. The one who commands the wind and the abyss and the grave, and who has just called a girl’s spirit back into her body, is also the one who notices that nobody has thought about her supper.

Can a thinking person believe this really happened? The mourners are the first to tell us that dead girls do not get up; they laughed because they knew it. The real question is not whether death normally wins, but whether God exists and has come among us in Jesus. If he has, and if Jesus himself rose from the dead, then one girl raised in Galilee is no strain at all. Luke, a careful doctor, tells us he investigated everything from the beginning and wrote from those who were eyewitnesses (1:1–4), and details like the supper are the kind no legend invents. The deeper reluctance is often not the evidence but the cost: if this happened, Jesus has a claim on my life.

And her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened. Which is, on the face of it, impossible: a houseful of mourners is outside, and they had watched her die. Of course, everyone would know she was alive. But they were not to spread the story. He is not asking them to keep a secret so much as refusing to be turned into a spectacle, and Luke has recorded the same instruction before (5:14). Jesus did not want to be known as a wonder-worker, attracting crowds for the wrong reasons.

In the flow. This raising closes the four miracles of 8:22–56 at the deepest point: wind and waves, a legion of demons, a twelve-year disease, and now death itself. Each time Jesus’ word does what only God’s word can, and so the chapter answers the disciples’ question, who then is this? Chapter 9 picks it up at once. Jesus gives the Twelve his own authority and sends them out (9:1–2); Herod asks who this is of whom he hears such things (9:9); and Peter at last says that he is the Christ of God (9:20). And a girl raised to die again points ahead to the one who will rise, never to die again (24:6; Romans 6:9).

Why tell these parents to tell no one, when he told the Gerasene to declare it? The Gerasene lived in Gentile territory, where Jesus was not staying and where no crowd was waiting for a Jewish king. Here in Galilee, news of a girl raised from the dead would bring crowds wanting a wonder-worker or a political Messiah, and Jesus’ hour had not yet come. He was not hiding his glory; he was guarding his mission. The full truth of who he is could only be told rightly after the cross and resurrection, and then it was to be told to the ends of the earth.

Will Jesus raise my loved one who has died in him? Yes. This girl was raised to die again; what Christ promises his people is far greater. On the last day, all who are in the tombs will hear his voice (John 5:28–29), and those who belong to him will be raised imperishable, in bodies like his glorious body (1 Corinthians 15:42–44; Philippians 3:21). The same hand that took this girl’s will take theirs. Meanwhile, their spirits are with him. Grieve for them, but grieve as one who knows that the Lord who says arise has never yet been disobeyed.

In a sentence. Jesus took the girl by the hand and told her to rise, and her spirit returned and she got up at once, and he told them to feed her and to tell no one.

On a Tuesday. Let the tenderness of this scene shape how you care for people. After the great moments, prayer answered, crisis over, someone has to think about the meal. Be the one who notices. And whenever you hear of a death, remember the girl standing up in her parents’ house: that is a picture of the morning that is coming.

For worship. The hand that took a dead girl’s fingers in a Galilean bedroom was itself nailed to a cross, laid still in a tomb and raised on the third day, and it holds the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). One word from him called a child’s spirit back into her body. One word from him on the last day will call every sleeping believer out of the dust, and the Lord who remembered a hungry girl’s supper will sit them down at the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9). Almighty over the grave, and thinking of our hunger: that is our Lord.

parallels.desc: the child’s life came into him again

8.text: <sup>1</sup> Soon afterward he went on through cities and villages, proclaiming and bringing the good news of the kingdom of God. And the twelve were with him, <sup>2</sup> and also some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, <sup>3</sup> and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means. <sup>4</sup> And when a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in a parable, <sup>5</sup> “A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it. <sup>6</sup> And some fell on the rock, and as it grew up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. <sup>7</sup> And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it. <sup>8</sup> And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.” As he said these things, he called out, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” <sup>9</sup> And when his disciples asked him what this parable meant, <sup>10</sup> he said, “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for others they are in parables, so that ‘seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.’ <sup>11</sup> Now the parable is this: The seed is the word of God. <sup>12</sup> The ones along the path are those who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved. <sup>13</sup> And the ones on the rock are those who, when they hear the word, receive it with joy. But these have no root; they believe for a while, and in time of testing fall away. <sup>14</sup> And as for what fell among the thorns, they are those who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and their fruit does not mature. <sup>15</sup> As for that in the good soil, they are those who, hearing the word, hold it fast in an honest and good heart, and bear fruit with patience. <sup>16</sup> “No one after lighting a lamp covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. <sup>17</sup> For nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, nor is anything secret that will not be known and come to light. <sup>18</sup> Take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he thinks that he has will be taken away.” <sup>19</sup> Then his mother and his brothers came to him, but they could not reach him because of the crowd. <sup>20</sup> And he was told, “Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, desiring to see you.” <sup>21</sup> But he answered them, “My mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it.” <sup>22</sup> One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them, “Let us go across to the other side of the lake.” So they set out, <sup>23</sup> and as they sailed he fell asleep. And a windstorm came down on the lake, and they were filling with water and were in danger. <sup>24</sup> And they went and woke him, saying, “Master, Master, we are perishing!” And he awoke and rebuked the wind and the raging waves, and they ceased, and there was a calm. <sup>25</sup> He said to them, “Where is your faith?” And they were afraid, and they marveled, saying to one another, “Who then is this, that he commands even winds and water, and they obey him?” <sup>26</sup> Then they sailed to the country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee. <sup>27</sup> When Jesus had stepped out on land, there met him a man from the city who had demons. For a long time he had worn no clothes, and he had not lived in a house but among the tombs. <sup>28</sup> When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him and said with a loud voice, “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me.” <sup>29</sup> For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. (For many a time it had seized him. He was kept under guard and bound with chains and shackles, but he would break the bonds and be driven by the demon into the desert.) <sup>30</sup> Jesus then asked him, “What is your name?” And he said, “Legion,” for many demons had entered him. <sup>31</sup> And they begged him not to command them to depart into the abyss. <sup>32</sup> Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him to let them enter these. So he gave them permission. <sup>33</sup> Then the demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned. <sup>34</sup> When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and told it in the city and in the country. <sup>35</sup> Then people went out to see what had happened, and they came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone, sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. <sup>36</sup> And those who had seen it told them how the demon-possessed man had been healed. <sup>37</sup> Then all the people of the surrounding country of the Gerasenes asked him to depart from them, for they were seized with great fear. So he got into the boat and returned. <sup>38</sup> The man from whom the demons had gone begged that he might be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying, <sup>39</sup> “Return to your home, and declare how much God has done for you.” And he went away, proclaiming throughout the whole city how much Jesus had done for him. <sup>40</sup> Now when Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him. <sup>41</sup> And there came a man named Jairus, who was a ruler of the synagogue. And falling at Jesus' feet, he implored him to come to his house, <sup>42</sup> for he had an only daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the people pressed around him. <sup>43</sup> And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and though she had spent all her living on physicians, she could not be healed by anyone. <sup>44</sup> She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her discharge of blood ceased. <sup>45</sup> And Jesus said, “Who was it that touched me?” When all denied it, Peter said, “Master, the crowds surround you and are pressing in on you!” <sup>46</sup> But Jesus said, “Someone touched me, for I perceive that power has gone out from me.” <sup>47</sup> And when the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling, and falling down before him declared in the presence of all the people why she had touched him, and how she had been immediately healed. <sup>48</sup> And he said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace.” <sup>49</sup> While he was still speaking, someone from the ruler's house came and said, “Your daughter is dead; do not trouble the Teacher any more.” <sup>50</sup> But Jesus on hearing this answered him, “Do not fear; only believe, and she will be well.” <sup>51</sup> And when he came to the house, he allowed no one to enter with him, except Peter and John and James, and the father and mother of the child. <sup>52</sup> And all were weeping and mourning for her, but he said, “Do not weep, for she is not dead but sleeping.” <sup>53</sup> And they laughed at him, knowing that she was dead. <sup>54</sup> But taking her by the hand he called, saying, “Child, arise.” <sup>55</sup> And her spirit returned, and she got up at once. And he directed that something should be given her to eat. <sup>56</sup> And her parents were amazed, but he charged them to tell no one what had happened.

9.title: The Turning Point: Cross, Glory, and the Road to Jerusalem
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is the pivot of Luke's Gospel — the hinge on which the whole narrative turns. Everything before it is the Galilean ministry of proclamation, healing, and gathering; everything after it (from 9:51 onward) is the great journey to Jerusalem, the road that leads to the cross. Within this single chapter, the Galilean ministry reaches its theological summit and its geographical end. The chapter contains the feeding of the five thousand, Peter's confession, the first and second passion predictions, the transfiguration, the healing of the epileptic boy, and the setting of the face toward Jerusalem. It is the most theologically dense chapter in Luke's Gospel.

The pivot on which chapter 9 turns is v. 51: “When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem.” The phrase “set his face” is the language of prophetic determination — Isaiah uses it of the Servant who “set his face like a flint” (Isaiah 50:7) in the face of suffering and shame. From this moment, every step Jesus takes in Luke is a step toward the cross. The transfiguration (vv. 28–36), which precedes this turning point, is the divine confirmation of the way that is being chosen — Moses and Elijah appear and speak of “his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.” The Greek word translated “departure” is exodos. The cross is not a defeat; it is the Exodus, the supreme act of divine liberation toward which all of Israel's history has been moving.

The chapter's central theological contribution is the collision between two kinds of glory. The crowds see a miracle-worker; Herod is perplexed by a rumoured prophet; the disciples feed five thousand from five loaves; Peter confesses the Christ of God — and immediately Jesus reframes everything. The Son of Man must suffer. Anyone who wants to follow must take up their cross daily. Whoever tries to save their life will lose it. The glory of the transfiguration is flanked on both sides by the shadow of the cross — and that is exactly the point. The glory and the cross are not opposites; they belong together. The cross is the path to the glory; the glory is the validation of the cross.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Twelve Sent Out; Herod's Perplexity
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus calls the twelve together, gives them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and sends them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal. Two words, and not synonyms: power (dynamis) is the capacity, authority (exousia) is the right. Both are given, and neither is earned.

The instructions are deliberately spartan — no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, no second tunic. Between them those five items cover security, supply and comfort, and he takes all five away. The messengers are to depend entirely on the hospitality of those they visit, staying in whatever house first receives them and not moving on to a better one.

A reader comparing Gospels will find a difficulty: Mark records that they were to take nothing except a staff (Mark 6:8). Several explanations have been offered, and none is certain; what is plain is that both accounts fit the point of the list, which is not a uniform but a posture: do not equip yourself against the possibility that God will not provide.

Where they are not received, they are to shake the dust from their feet — the gesture a Jew used at the border when returning from Gentile territory, here applied to Jewish villages that refuse the kingdom's messengers. The old boundary has moved. It now runs not around the nation but around the message.

Luke reports the whole mission in one verse: they went, they preached, they healed, everywhere. What is absent is as striking as what is there — no account of the first house, the first refusal, the first demon. The instructions were not an ideal held up for admiration; they were the actual conditions under which twelve ordinary men walked into actual villages, and it worked.

Herod's perplexity closes the section. He has killed the greatest of the prophets and is now hearing that something greater is happening. The three theories on offer — John raised, Elijah appeared, one of the old prophets risen — are all respectful and all too small. His question, “who is this about whom I hear such things?”, is exactly the right question. And “he sought to see him” is the tragedy: he gets his wish at the trial (23:8), and Jesus does not answer him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The sending of the twelve is the first instance of the apostolic mission. The word apostle means simply one who is sent; it says nothing about the man's qualities and everything about his commission.

The authority they receive is delegated — the same authority Jesus has been exercising since chapter 4, now given to them to exercise in his name. This is the pattern that will run through Acts: the Spirit-empowered community carrying the same authority of the same word into the same world.

Note who receives it. These are the men who will shortly argue about which of them is greatest (v. 46), fail to cast out a demon (v. 40), propose incinerating a Samaritan village (v. 54), and desert him in a garden. He does not wait until they are ready.

And the errand has two halves held together: to proclaim and to heal. Luke will not let them come apart. A ministry that heals and says nothing has withheld the reason; a ministry that talks and touches nothing has announced a kingdom that apparently changes nothing.
verseByVerse.examples:
The instructions to take nothing are not a travel policy but a structural embodiment of dependence. The messengers carry no resources that would make them independent of those they are sent to, which creates a bond of mutual vulnerability: the messenger depends on the receiver, and the receiver depends on the message.

The rule about staying in the first house is more pointed than it looks. A travelling teacher who attracted interest could expect better offers as the week went on. A messenger who upgrades has begun to be paid — and the moment his comfort depends on the standing of his host, his message is for sale.

The shaking of the dust takes a refusal seriously enough to mark it, without bitterness and without a backward argument. Two instincts are common and both are wrong: to keep pressing until the gospel becomes an irritation attached to a person, or to shrug it off and privately conclude they were never going to anyway. The dust does neither.

And Herod is the standing warning that the right question is not enough. A man can be genuinely interested in Jesus Christ for years, ask exactly the correct question, and go to his grave having done nothing about the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He called the Twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal.

Meaning first. Luke 9 is the hinge of the Gospel. Jesus sends the Twelve out with his own power and authority, and Herod asks the question the whole chapter answers: who is this? In a desolate place Jesus feeds five thousand men, taking, blessing, breaking and giving, as he will at the Last Supper and at Emmaus. Peter confesses him the Christ of God, and at once Jesus says what kind of Christ he is: one who must suffer, be killed and be raised, and whose followers take up their cross daily. On a mountain three disciples see his glory, and the Father says, this is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him. Below, the disciples fail, argue about greatness and want fire on a Samaritan village. Then Jesus sets his face to go to Jerusalem, and nothing may come before him.

The setting. Chapter 9 is the climax of the Galilean ministry. It moves from the mission of the Twelve, through the question of who Jesus is (vv. 7–9, 18–20), to the first prediction of the cross and the transfiguration, and ends with Jesus setting his face toward Jerusalem (v. 51). From there, the great journey to the cross begins.
