verseByVerse.quote: But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.

But I tell you truly, there are some standing here. Some, not all. This is one of the hardest sentences in the Gospels, and sceptics have built a case on it. Jesus told the people in front of him that some of them would still be alive when the kingdom of God arrived. They all died. Therefore, it is said, he was mistaken.

Who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God. Luke leaves out Mark’s come with power (Mark 9:1), making it simpler: they will see the kingdom. Three answers are given, and they are not equally strong. The weakest takes see the kingdom of God as the second coming and then strains the words; the text does not bear it. The second, much better, takes the kingdom to mean what Luke consistently means: the reign of God breaking in. On that reading the promise was kept within the hearers’ lifetime, spectacularly: in the resurrection, when the King came out of a tomb; at Pentecost, when three thousand entered the kingdom in a morning; and as the gospel spread from Jerusalem to Rome. Men standing on that hillside saw all of it.

The answer eight days later. But the strongest answer is the one Luke himself supplies straight away: about eight days after these sayings Jesus took Peter and John and James up the mountain (v. 28). All three of the first Gospels put the transfiguration immediately after this promise, and none by accident. Some standing here, and eight days later exactly three of them are shown the Son of Man in his glory, with Moses and Elijah beside him and the voice of the Father over him. The fulfilment begins there, a preview of the kingdom, and continues in the resurrection, the ascension and Pentecost, all within their lifetime.

A mercy as well as a fulfilment. And the placing is a mercy. He has just told them he is going to be rejected, killed and raised, and told them all to pick up a cross. Then he takes three men up a mountain and lets them see, for a few minutes, what is on the other side of it. Which is more or less how it still works. Nobody gets the mountain permanently, and nobody is asked to walk to Jerusalem without ever having seen anything.

Is the kingdom here now, or still to come? Both. The kingdom of God came with Jesus: in his works, his death and resurrection, and the gift of the Spirit, God’s reign broke into the world, and every believer has been transferred into it (Colossians 1:13). But it has not yet come in its fullness; that awaits Christ’s return in glory, when every enemy will be put under his feet and the dead raised (1 Corinthians 15:24–26). We live between the two: citizens of a kingdom that is real now and will be visible then. That is why Christians can be joyful and longing at the same time.

In a sentence. Jesus promised that some standing there would see the kingdom of God before they died.

On a Tuesday. The cross is not the end. The kingdom is coming, and in Christ you already belong to it. When the cost of following feels heavy, remember the mountain: God gives his people glimpses, in his word, in answered prayer, in the fellowship of his people, to strengthen them for the road. Thank him for the glimpses you have had.

For worship. Some who stood on that hillside saw the King in his glory within eight days, saw him risen not long after, and saw his Spirit poured out fifty days after that. Not one of his words has fallen to the ground. The reign that broke in then has never been reversed, and the King who promised it is the King who will finish it, when the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign for ever and ever (Revelation 11:15).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
About eight days after the confession and the first passion prediction, Jesus takes Peter, John and James up a mountain to pray — and Luke alone tells us that is why he went. It happened while he was praying.

Luke is careful with his words. Mark and Matthew say he was transfigured; Luke, writing for Greek readers in a world full of stories about gods changing shape, describes what was seen: his face became different, his clothing turned a white that flashed. Nothing was added to him. This is not Jesus becoming something more than he was; it is the covering coming off something always there.

Moses and Elijah appear in glory — the Law and the Prophets. Both had met God on the same mountain, Sinai and Horeb; both had asked in their way to see him and been given a back and a whisper. Now they stand in the light, talking with him.

And Luke alone tells us the subject. They “spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.” The Greek word is exodos. The man who led the first one — out of Egypt, through the blood of a lamb, through the sea — is standing there while the word is applied to a death in Jerusalem. It is the interpretation of the cross, given from heaven, before it happens: not a defeat but a deliverance, accomplished by a lamb, on a fixed date, by a leader who goes ahead of his people. And the verb is accomplish, not suffer.

The three were heavy with sleep and nearly missed it — and Luke will find the disciples asleep again in Gethsemane (22:45). Peter's proposal to build three tents comes as Moses and Elijah are leaving: a man trying to stop something ending, and Luke's aside is candid and gentle, “not knowing what he said.” The proposal is wrong in a specific way: one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah, three equals.

The cloud interrupts him mid-sentence. It is the shekinah — the cloud of Sinai, of the tabernacle, of Solomon's temple, unseen in Israel for centuries — and the verb “overshadowed” is the one Gabriel used to Mary (1:35).

“This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!” Then the cloud lifts, and Moses is gone, and Elijah is gone, and there are not three figures on that mountain requiring three tents.
verseByVerse.theology:
The transfiguration is at once christological and eschatological — revealing who Jesus is, and what the coming kingdom will look like. What the disciples see is not a separate divine form he can put on and take off; it is the radiance belonging to who he always is, momentarily unrestrained. The humanity that veiled the glory at Bethlehem is for a few minutes transparent to it. This is what John means by “we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father” (John 1:14).

Moses and Elijah's conversation is the most extraordinary discussion never recorded — two of the greatest figures of the Old Testament speaking with the Son of God about the cross that will accomplish the ultimate Exodus. Everything either of them ever wrote or did had been leaning towards it.

Some Bibles read “my Beloved” at v.35 rather than “my Chosen One,” and the manuscripts do differ. “Chosen One” is very likely what Luke wrote, and it is the harder reading — a copyist would naturally smooth it to match the baptism and the parallel in Matthew. And the phrase is deliberate: “my chosen” is Isaiah's word for the Servant (Isa. 42:1). On a mountain where they have just discussed his exodus, the Father names him with the Servant's title.

“Listen to him” is the only imperative in the scene, and it is aimed with precision at three men who have spent eight days failing to accept one particular thing he said.
verseByVerse.examples:
Peter's desire to build three tents is the perennial temptation to institutionalise a moment of glory — to capture the experience, preserve it, replicate it. Every significant encounter with the living God carries it. The glory was never given to be housed; it was given for the road down.

And the road down is where nearly all Christian work is actually done. Jesus comes off that mountain the next morning into a crowd, a boy in convulsions, and a ministry that has failed. Moses came down Sinai carrying the tablets of God and found a golden calf.

“Listen to him” is the transfiguration's practical legacy. The disciples have been given an extraordinary visual confirmation, and are told the appropriate response is not to build but to listen. The Christian life is not primarily about spectacular experiences of divine glory, though God gives those in his mercy. It is about listening to the voice of the Son, in Scripture, in prayer, in the community of faith.

And the placing of it is a mercy as well as a fulfilment. He has just told them he will be rejected and killed, and told them all to pick up a cross. Then he takes three men up a mountain and lets them see, for a few minutes, what is on the other side of it. Nobody gets the mountain permanently, and nobody is asked to walk to Jerusalem without ever having seen anything.

verseByVerse.quote: Now about eight days after these sayings he took with him Peter and John and James and went up on the mountain to pray. And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became dazzling white.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About eight days after these sayings he took with him Peter and John and James and went up on the mountain to pray. And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became dazzling white.

Now about eight days after these sayings. Luke ties it to what came before. Eight days ago Peter said the Christ of God, and Jesus said the Son of Man must suffer, and everyone was told to take up a cross. Now three of them are going up a mountain. About eight days counts inclusively, and Luke says about; Matthew and Mark say after six days. There is no contradiction. Luke’s about is doing exactly the work it appears to do, and the two are the same span counted in the ordinary way people speak.

He took with him Peter and John and James. The inner three (8:51): the same three who were in the room when Jairus’s daughter was raised, and the same three who, in Mark’s account, are taken deeper into the garden at Gethsemane (Mark 14:33). They see a dead girl stand up, they see him in glory, and they see him on the ground with his sweat like drops of blood, and the third scene is unintelligible without the second.

And went up on the mountain to pray. There it is again, and Luke is the only one who says it. Matthew and Mark have him take them up the mountain; Luke says why he went. He did not go up to be transfigured. He went up to pray, and it happened while he was praying, as the voice at the baptism came while he was praying (3:21–22).

The appearance of his face was altered. Luke is careful with his verbs, and there is a reason. Mark and Matthew use metemorphōthē: he was transfigured, the word behind metamorphosis. Luke, writing for Greek readers in a world full of stories about gods changing shape, avoids it, perhaps because Greek readers would think of pagan myths. He describes what was seen: his face became different. But the meaning is the same. Matthew says his face shone like the sun (Matthew 17:2). As Moses’ face shone after being with God (Exodus 34:29–35); but Moses reflected a borrowed glory, and Jesus’ glory was his own, shining from within.

Not added, but uncovered. And his clothing became dazzling white (exastraptōn), flashing like lightning. Altered is the right sense. Nothing was added to him. This is not Jesus temporarily becoming something more than he had been; it is the covering coming off something that was there all along. The glory of God was, that evening, standing on a hillside in a human body, praying, and for a few minutes the body did not hide it. That is why the detail about prayer matters so much: in the communion of the Son with the Father on that mountain, the glory broke through the surface.

Where did the glory come from? From who he is. Jesus is the eternal Son, the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature (Hebrews 1:3). In becoming man he did not stop being God; he veiled his glory in our flesh (Philippians 2:6–7; John 1:14). On the mountain the veil was drawn back for a moment. It is also a preview of the glory he would enter after his suffering (24:26), and of the glorified body that believers will one day share, when he transforms our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21).

In a sentence. About eight days later, Jesus took Peter, John and James up a mountain to pray, and as he prayed his face changed and his clothes became dazzling white.

On a Tuesday. Pray. The transfiguration happened while Jesus prayed, and the great moments of his life all came out of prayer. You will not shine like the sun, but prayer is where the Christian is changed. Set aside a time this week longer than usual, and simply behold him in his word.

For worship. The carpenter from Nazareth, dusty from the roads, is the Lord of glory, and for a few minutes on a mountain he let it be seen. He did not keep it shining. He let the veil fall back, walked down the hill and went to Jerusalem, where the face that shone was spat on (18:32) and struck (22:63–64). That is the wonder: not only that the glory was there, but that he hid it for us, until the morning it could shine unhidden and draw us, beholding him, into the same likeness (2 Corinthians 3:18).
verseByVerse.note: “About eight days” counts inclusively; Matthew and Mark say “after six days.” Only Luke says Jesus went up to pray.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah, who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah, who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.

And behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah. Of all the figures in Israel’s history, these two. Moses, who gave the law; Elijah, the greatest of the prophets. Between them they are the Law and the Prophets: the whole Old Testament, standing on a hillside, in conversation. The Law and the Prophets bear witness to Jesus (24:27, 44). Both were expected before the end (Malachi 4:4–5).

Both met God on a mountain. They share a second thing that is not usually noticed. Both had met God on a mountain, Moses at Sinai and Elijah at Horeb, the same mountain, and each was hidden in a cleft or a cave while the glory passed by (Exodus 33:22; 1 Kings 19:9–13). Both had unusual ends: Moses died in Moab and God buried him where no one knows (Deuteronomy 34:5–6); Elijah was taken up in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11). Each once asked, in his own way, to see God, and was allowed a glimpse of his back and a low whisper. Now they appear in glory, standing in the light, talking with him.

And spoke of his departure. Only Luke tells us what they talked about, and his word is startling: exodos, exodus. Consider who is standing there while that word is used. Moses led the first exodus: through the blood of a lamb on a doorpost, through the Red Sea, toward the promised land. Now the word for what he did is applied, in his hearing, to a death in Jerusalem. Jesus will lead a new and greater exodus, through his death, resurrection and ascension, freeing his people from slavery to sin and death and bringing them home to God. That is the interpretation of the cross, given from heaven before it happens. It is not a defeat or an accident but a deliverance out of a slavery deeper than Egypt’s, accomplished by a lamb, through blood, by a leader who goes ahead of his people. The word also means death, departure from life (2 Peter 1:15).

Which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. And note the verb. Accomplish (plēroun) means to fulfil, complete. Not suffer. Not undergo. His death is not something that will happen to him, but something he will achieve. The cross is spoken of on that mountain the way a man speaks of a work he is going to finish. Jerusalem is the goal of the whole Gospel (v. 51; 13:33).

How did the disciples know who Moses and Elijah were? The text does not say; most likely it was given with the vision itself, or by what they heard them say. This is not a precedent for contact with the dead (compare 16:27–31). It was a unique revelation of the glorified state of God’s people and of the Law and the Prophets bearing witness to Christ’s departure.

Does this show the dead are conscious? It shows that Moses and Elijah were alive with God, centuries after they left the earth, and that they knew and cared about the work of Christ. That fits the rest of Scripture: God is not the God of the dead but of the living, for all live to him (20:38), and those who die in the Lord are with him at once (23:43; Philippians 1:23). There is no soul sleep. But Scripture forbids us to seek contact with the dead (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). This was God’s doing, once, on a holy mountain, for his Son’s sake.

In a sentence. Moses and Elijah appeared in glory and spoke with Jesus about his exodus, which he would accomplish in Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. The whole Old Testament points to the cross. Read it that way. When you read the Passover, the Red Sea, the wilderness, the prophets, ask how they lead to Calvary. And when you think of your own death, think of it as Luke does: for a believer, an exodus, a departure out of bondage into the presence of God.

For worship. Moses and Elijah are in glory, and they are not talking about glory. They have the attention of the Son of God on a mountaintop with the light of heaven on them, and what they discuss is Calvary. Everything either of them ever wrote or did had been leaning towards it, and now the road runs downhill from here to Jerusalem. The greatest of the saints in heaven are absorbed in the cross. So shall we be, for ever: worthy is the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:12).
verseByVerse.note: The word for “departure” is exodus — his death, resurrection and ascension as a new rescue of God’s people.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him. And as the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, 'Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah'—not knowing what he said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him. As the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus: Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah, not knowing what he said.

Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep. They almost missed it. Luke alone records this, and it is not a flattering detail. Perhaps it was night. The Son of God is shining, two of the greatest figures in the history of redemption have come to discuss the salvation of the world, and the disciples are struggling to stay awake. Luke tells us the same thing in Gethsemane, where Jesus finds them sleeping for sorrow (22:45). Twice, on the two most important nights of their lives, once in light and once in darkness, they cannot keep their eyes open. There is no rebuke here. They have climbed a mountain and it is late. It is simply what men are like.

But when they became fully awake they saw his glory. They did see it. Luke is careful to say so, because the testimony for this scene rests on these men. Peter himself would later write: we were eyewitnesses of his majesty, and we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain (2 Peter 1:16–18).

Let us make three tents. Booths, shelters, probably with the Feast of Booths in mind, when Israel lived in shelters for a week to remember the wilderness, a feast that looked forward to God dwelling with his people. Luke notes that Peter speaks as Moses and Elijah are parting from Jesus: the tents are a way of making them stay. Peter has grasped that this is a foretaste of the kingdom, and his instinct is to keep it. The proposal goes wrong twice. Three tents make three equals, Jesus level with Moses and Elijah; and a camp on the mountain means no road to Jerusalem, where the exodus they had just been discussing was to be accomplished. The answer, when it comes from the cloud, leaves Jesus standing alone.

Not knowing what he said. Luke’s comment is candid and gentle. Peter spoke from awe and confusion. He is not being wicked; he is doing what people do in the presence of something overwhelming, which is to talk, and to propose a project.

The tent God had already pitched. Peter offers to make a dwelling for Jesus, and does not see that Jesus is the dwelling. John says that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, using the verb for pitching a tent, and adds, we have seen his glory (John 1:14). The Feast of Booths looked forward to God living among his people; on this mountain the fulfilment is standing in front of Peter, shining. No shelter of branches could add anything to that. The tent of meeting has come in person, and the glory Peter wanted to shelter is the glory that shelters Peter.

Why can we not stay on the mountain? Because the glory was given for the road, not instead of it. Christians have high moments: a conference, a season of revival, a time of deep closeness to God in prayer. They are real gifts. But they are not meant to be housed and preserved, and trying to recreate them leads to disappointment or worse. The way to the final glory runs through Jerusalem: through faithful ordinary obedience, through suffering, through the cross. The mountain strengthens you for that; it does not excuse you from it. And one day there will be a dwelling that does not end, when God himself makes his home with his people (Revelation 21:3).

In a sentence. The drowsy disciples woke to see Jesus’ glory, and as Moses and Elijah were leaving, Peter suggested building three shelters, not knowing what he was saying.

On a Tuesday. We want to stay on the mountaintop. But glory comes through the cross. Follow Jesus down into the valley. If you are living on the memory of a past spiritual high, thank God for it, and then ask what obedience he is calling you to in the valley this week. And if your prayers often fight sleep, take comfort: so did Peter’s. Keep coming.

For worship. Peter wanted to keep the glory on the mountain, and the Lord of glory would not be kept. He came down, set his face to Jerusalem and went where no shelter could protect him, so that a home might be made for us: his Father’s house, with its many rooms, where he has gone to prepare a place (John 14:2). The tents Peter offered would have blown down in a winter. The dwelling Christ prepared by going down the mountain instead of staying on it will stand for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. And a voice came out of the cloud, saying, 'This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!' And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. And they kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. A voice came out of the cloud, saying: this is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him! When the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. And they kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen.

As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them. Peter is interrupted mid-sentence, and the cloud is the only answer his proposal gets. It is not weather but the cloud of God’s presence, the cloud of Sinai and of the tabernacle (Exodus 24:15–18; 40:34–35), unseen in Israel for centuries. Luke’s verb is the one he used at the annunciation: the power of the Most High will overshadow you (1:35). The presence that overshadowed Mary when the Son was conceived overshadows the mountain where the Son is revealed. And only Luke says they entered the cloud, and were afraid as they did: everything Israel knew said that men do not walk into that and come out.

And a voice came out of the cloud. In Luke the Father’s voice is heard twice, at the Jordan and here, and both times it is about his Son. At the baptism the words were spoken to Jesus himself (3:22); on the mountain they are spoken to the three disciples, about him. This is my Son: not one of three, but the Son, the answer to Peter’s three tents.

My Chosen One. Some manuscripts read my Beloved, as in Mark. Chosen One is very likely what Luke wrote, and it is the harder reading: a copyist would naturally smooth it to match the baptism and the other Gospels. And the phrase is deliberate. It echoes Isaiah 42:1, where God presents his servant, whom he upholds, his chosen, in whom his soul delights. Jesus is the chosen Servant of the Lord, who will suffer (Isaiah 53). On a mountain where they have just been discussing his exodus, the Father names him with the Servant’s title. And the rulers will mock this very title at the cross: if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One (23:35).

Listen to him! Then the only command in the whole scene. Not, look at him, though the light was extraordinary. Not, build for him. Listen. It echoes Deuteronomy 18:15: the LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you, and it is to him you shall listen. Jesus is that prophet, greater than Moses. And the command is aimed with precision at three men who have spent eight days failing to accept one thing he said: that the Son of Man must suffer and be killed and be raised. Listen to him, above all when he speaks of the cross. Moses spoke and Elijah spoke and Israel was to hear them; the Father says the listening now goes to his Son.

And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. Moses and Elijah gone. Jesus only. The cloud lifts. There are not three figures on that mountain requiring three tents. There is one, and he is the one they are to hear. The Law and the Prophets have said what they came to say and have stepped back, and what is left standing in the ordinary evening light is a man they are going to follow down the hill to Jerusalem.

And they kept silent and told no one in those days. Why did they tell no one? Jesus ordered them to tell no one until he had risen (Mark 9:9). Before the cross, the glory they had seen would only have fed the wrong hopes.

How do I listen to Jesus today? Through his word. The Son who spoke on earth now speaks through the Scriptures his Spirit inspired (Hebrews 1:1–2; 2 Timothy 3:16). There is no need for a new voice from a cloud, and we should not seek one; the canon is closed, and Scripture is sufficient. Listen when you read the Bible, slowly and with prayer. Listen when it is faithfully preached. Listen especially to the parts you would rather not hear, as the three needed to hear about the cross. And listen in order to obey, for hearing in the Bible always means doing.

In a sentence. The cloud of God’s presence covered them, and the Father declared Jesus his Son, his Chosen One, and commanded them to listen to him, and then Jesus was alone.

On a Tuesday. God’s command to you today: listen to my Son. Open his word and hear him. Before you open your phone in the morning, open his word. And when other voices, even good ones, crowd in, remember the mountain: Moses and Elijah stepped back, and Jesus was found alone.

For worship. The Father loved the Son before the foundation of the world (John 17:24), and on one evening in Galilee he let three fishermen overhear it. Every other voice in history steps back before that one. Moses and Elijah fade into the cloud, the Law and the Prophets having said their part, and Jesus only is left: our prophet, priest and king, who heard his Father’s delight on the mountain and carried it down into the valley and on to the cross. He is the Chosen One, and all who are in him were chosen in him (Ephesians 1:4).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “my Beloved” for “my Chosen One.”
