my chosen, in whom my soul delights

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–50 — Healing, Humility, and the Second Passion Prediction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Coming down from the mountain, Jesus meets a father whose only child is seized by a spirit that convulses him — and the disciples who were not on the mountain had tried and failed.

The father's description is clinical, and a modern reader will recognise it: sudden onset, a cry, convulsion, foaming, then flattened exhaustion. So was the boy ill or possessed? Luke is the last man in the New Testament who can be accused of not knowing the difference. He is a physician, and he consistently keeps the categories apart: those sick with various diseases, and demons also came out of many (4:40-41); a crowd healed of their diseases, and those troubled by unclean spirits (6:17-18). Jesus speaks the same way: “I cast out demons and perform cures” (13:32). Luke reports the symptoms as symptoms, and then tells us that in this boy something else was behind them.

Two errors do real harm and Luke's care rules out both — that every seizure or darkness of mind is the enemy's work, and that “demon” was merely the old word for a disorder we can now diagnose. But Jesus rebukes the thing, and it obeys and comes out. You do not reprimand a neurological condition and have it answer you.

“O faithless and twisted generation” is addressed to the whole scene, not the father — the word “twisted” is Moses' word for Israel in the wilderness (Deut. 32:5). And it is followed immediately by “Bring your son here.” He names the faithlessness and then heals the boy anyway.

Luke ends the miracle as he ended the one at Nain: “he gave him back to his father” (cf. 7:15). Not “the boy was healed.” A son handed back to the man who brought him.

Then, at the height of the crowd's enthusiasm, the second passion prediction — “let these words sink into your ears.” They did not understand, it was concealed from them, and they were afraid to ask. Afraid of the answer, almost certainly; Mark records Peter, after the first prediction, taking Jesus aside to rebuke him for it (Mark 8:32).

And what fills the silence is an argument about which of them is greatest. Jesus takes a child — a person with no legal standing and nothing to offer — and stands the child beside himself. Then John reports that they stopped a man casting out demons in Jesus's name, and gives his reason: “he does not follow with us.”
verseByVerse.theology:
The disciples' failure at v.40, after their success in vv.1-6, raises the question of what changed. Matthew records Jesus naming it as “little faith” (Matt. 17:20). The lesson is what the whole chapter teaches: the authority delegated to them is not their own. It flows from the one who gives it and is sustained by the relationship of trust with him.

“Delivered into the hands of men” — handed over. There is a bitter wordplay the English keeps: the Son of Man is handed over into the hands of men.

Luke's “it was concealed from them” is a passive without an agent, and probably deliberately so. Two things are true at once: there is a hiddenness God appoints (cf. 19:42; 24:16), and there is a hiddenness they are manufacturing, since the next verse shows exactly what they were thinking about instead.

On “the one who is not against you is for you” — a reader will notice the apparent opposite at 11:23, “whoever is not with me is against me.” The difference is in the pronouns. There the subject is a man's own relation to Christ, where there is no neutral ground. Here it is one servant's judgement of another. About my own standing, assume nothing; about another doing good in his name, assume the best.
verseByVerse.examples:
The child placed beside Jesus is a searching challenge to every form of Christian leadership measured by influence, platform, numbers or reputation. A first-century child had no legal rights, no property, no voice, and no capacity to confer honour on anybody — which is exactly why he was chosen for an argument about greatness.

So the test is not how a man behaves towards those above him; everyone is attentive upwards. It is how he treats those who cannot advance him, repay him, report him, or do him any good at all. The person who cleans the building. The member of the congregation whose conversation goes nowhere. The child in the room, who has nothing and is watching.

“I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not” is an honest report of ministry failure, said out loud, in front of a crowd, by the man it failed. It belongs in the Gospel and it is a comfort of a hard kind: the record of the church's work has always included the things that did not work.

And John's “he does not follow with us” — not “he does not follow you” — names the instinct precisely. It is the assumption that the boundary of my group is the boundary of the kingdom, and that work God is doing outside it is at best suspect and at worst competition. Christ has servants who do not attend your church, use your vocabulary, or share your history, and they are not to be stopped.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him. And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, 'Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him. And behold, a man from the crowd cried out: Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child.

On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain. From glory to need. The mountain was last night; this is the morning, and the crowd is waiting at the bottom. Luke has built the contrast deliberately, and it is the one Moses walked into. He came down Sinai carrying the words of God and found the people round a golden calf (Exodus 32). Jesus comes down with the voice of the Father still in the disciples’ ears, and finds a boy in convulsions and a ministry that has failed. That descent is where nearly all Christian work is done: not on the mountain, nor in the memory of it, but the next morning at the bottom of the hill, among people who were not there and have a problem that will not wait.

Teacher, I beg you to look at my son. Every word of what follows is a father’s, shouted over a crowd. He does not open with a theological claim or a request for a miracle; he asks Jesus to look at the boy. Look at means look upon with favour and compassion. He has stopped expecting anything and is asking for attention.

The God who looks. The father asks for what the desperate have always asked of God: look. Hannah prayed that the LORD would look on the affliction of his servant (1 Samuel 1:11), and Luke’s verb here is the very one Mary used when she sang that God had looked on the humble estate of his servant (1:48). The father asks it of Jesus, to his face, in a crowd. That is what the incarnation has made possible. The God who looks down from heaven has come close enough to be stopped on a hillside and asked to turn his eyes on one boy, and he does.

For he is my only child. And then the detail that does the work. Only Luke says only, and he has used that phrase twice already: the widow’s only son at Nain (7:12), Jairus’s only daughter (8:42). It is his way of saying there is nothing behind this. No other children, no second chance, and in that world no future for the family either. The depth of a father’s grief.

A father in a crowd. This man is not a disciple, and Luke does not tell us his name. He is a father in a crowd who has been living for years with a child who is destroyed in front of him at unpredictable intervals, and who has come, presumably having heard something, to a preacher’s followers, and been let down. Anybody who has cared for a severely ill or disabled child will recognise the exhaustion in the request. He does not ask for much. He asks to be looked at.

Does God see my child? Yes. The God who saw Hagar’s son crying under a bush in the wilderness (Genesis 21:17), and who looked on this boy through the eyes of his Son, sees every child and every parent. If you are caring for a child who is ill, disabled or far from God, you may feel unseen by everyone, including the church. Jesus is not like the crowd. Bring your child to him in prayer, as this father did, even if all you can manage is, Lord, look at my son. And ask your church family for help; they are meant to carry this with you (Galatians 6:2).

In a sentence. Coming down from the mountain, Jesus was met by a crowd and a father who begged him to look at his only son.

On a Tuesday. Bring your children to Jesus and ask him to look on them with favour. Pray for each one by name this week. And look out for the exhausted parents in your church, those caring for a sick or disabled child, and ask what one practical thing you could do for them.

For worship. The Son came down from the mountain of glory into a valley of need, and he has never stopped coming down. He came down from heaven to a manger, from the mountain to the crowd, from Jerusalem to a cross and a grave, and every descent was for someone who could not climb. The Father’s beloved Son left the cloud of glory to be stopped by a stranger’s cry, and he has never yet told a desperate parent to wait until he is less busy.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out. It convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and shatters him, and will hardly leave him. And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out. It convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and shatters him, and will hardly leave him. And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.

And behold, a spirit seizes him. An evil spirit. The father’s description is clinical, and a modern reader will recognise it: sudden onset, a cry, convulsion, foaming, and then the flattened exhaustion afterwards. The symptoms resemble epilepsy, but the cause was demonic (v. 42). It shatters him (syntribon: crushes, bruises, breaks), and even between seizures it will hardly let him go. Satan’s aim is destruction.

Ill or possessed? So was this boy ill, or was he possessed? And behind that sits the sharper question people actually mean: were these pre-scientific people simply calling a disease of the brain a devil? The answer comes from Luke himself, and it is worth having, because he is the last man in the New Testament who can be accused of not knowing the difference. He is a physician, and his Gospel is full of his clinical eye: the woman who had spent all she had on doctors (8:43), the high fever (4:38), the sweat like drops of blood (22:44). And he consistently keeps the two categories apart. He writes that they brought Jesus those who were sick with various diseases, and that demons also came out of many (4:40–41). He describes a crowd who came to be healed of their diseases, and those troubled by unclean spirits who were cured (6:17–18): two groups, named separately, in a single breath. Jesus himself speaks the same way: I cast out demons and perform cures (13:32). A man who thought every convulsion was a devil would not write like that. Luke reports the symptoms as symptoms, and then tells us that in this particular boy something else was behind them.

Two errors. Two errors do real harm here, and Luke’s own care rules out both. The first makes every seizure, every darkness of the mind, a work of the enemy: a cruelty this Gospel forbids by the plain fact that its author lists sickness and spirits as different things. A Christian with epilepsy is not in the devil’s grip; he needs good medicine and the love of his church, not an interrogation about hidden sin. The second is the fashionable error, that demon was merely the old word for a disorder we can now diagnose properly. But notice what happens in two verses’ time: Jesus rebukes the thing, and it obeys and comes out. You do not reprimand a neurological condition and have it answer you.

And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not. That sentence has to be sat with, because it is the honest report of a ministry failure, said out loud, in front of a crowd, by the man it failed. The nine disciples who stayed below had failed, though Jesus had given them authority over all demons (v. 1). These are the same men who came back a chapter ago full of what they had done. Whatever happened in those villages was real. And here, at the bottom of the mountain, with a father watching, nothing worked.

Why could the disciples not cast it out? Jesus calls it faithlessness (v. 41), and in Mark he adds that this kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer (Mark 9:29). The authority they had been given was real, but it was derived, and they had stopped depending on the one who gave it.

What his servants could not do. The failure at the foot of the mountain throws the whole weight of the scene onto one person. The nine had real authority, given in this same chapter, and it failed; the father’s hope now rests on Jesus alone. That is where Luke wants it. Every gift Christ gives his people remains his gift, and never becomes a power they own. The one thing that cannot fail in this story is not the ministry but the Master, and the boy’s rescue will come not from a better technique among the nine but from the Son of God walking down the hill.

What should I do when the church fails someone? Admit it honestly, as this father’s words force the disciples to. Churches and Christians do fail people: in counsel, in care, in prayer, in noticing. The answer is not to pretend otherwise, nor to give up on Christ because his people failed. The father did the right thing: when the disciples could not help, he took his son to Jesus himself. If you have been let down by Christians, do not let their failure keep you from the Lord. And if you are the one who failed, take it back to him in prayer, and learn dependence.

In a sentence. The father described how a spirit seized and convulsed his son, crushing him, and how the disciples had failed to cast it out.

On a Tuesday. Past success is no guarantee of present power. Every work of God needs fresh dependence on him. If you teach, lead, counsel or serve in any way, do not walk into this week on the strength of last week’s fruit. Pray before you begin, every time.

For worship. The thing that shattered this boy had beaten the disciples, the father and every year of the boy’s life, and it had never yet met the Son of God. He is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), and the uttermost includes what crushes a child and defeats a church. Blessed be the Lord of the mountain who is also the Lord of the valley, whose power is not borrowed and does not run out.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, 'O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.' While he was coming, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. And all were astonished at the majesty of God. But while they were all marveling at everything he was doing, Jesus said to his disciples,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered: O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here. While he was coming, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. And all were astonished at the majesty of God. But while they were all marvelling at everything he was doing, Jesus said to his disciples:

O faithless and twisted generation. It is one of the sharpest things Jesus says in this Gospel, and the first question is who it is aimed at. Not the father. The man has done nothing wrong; he came, he asked, and he told the truth about what happened. Not the boy. The address is to a generation: the crowd, the disciples, the whole scene at the foot of the mountain. Addressed to all, including the disciples. Twisted (diestrammenē) means perverse, crooked: the word Moses used of Israel in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 32:5).

How long am I to be with you and bear with you? And there is something in the tone worth noticing, because it is not simply anger. It is the sound of a man carrying something heavy: the weariness of the holy Son among unbelievers. He has come down from the light of his Father’s presence into a valley where nothing works, and he says so.

Bring your son here. Then, without pausing: and yet compassion. That is the whole answer to the question of whether the exasperation was the last word. He names the faithlessness and then heals the boy. He does not make the father’s help conditional on the crowd improving.

The demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. Its last attack, and it happens on the way. Luke wants it seen: the thing is at its worst in the final seconds before it is finished. That is not unusual, and it is worth knowing by anyone who has watched a besetting sin or a long oppression flare up hardest just as ground is being taken.

But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. Three verbs, and the third is the one Luke chose to end on. Luke tells it more briefly than Mark, but he keeps this. He gave him back to his father, exactly the phrase used at Nain, where he gave him to his mother (7:15). The same tender words. Not, the boy was healed; not, the demon departed. A son was handed back to the man who had brought him. Luke will not let a miracle be reported as an event when it can be reported as a gift, from one person to another, in front of witnesses.

And all were astonished at the majesty of God. Majesty (megaleiotēti) means greatness, magnificence. The crowd does not credit a technique or a healer. They saw God’s greatness in what Jesus did. The same word is used of the transfiguration (2 Peter 1:16). The majesty seen on the mountain is now seen in the valley: something of the size of God has been visible in a valley, in a boy who could stand up, in the arms of a father who had stopped hoping.

Does Jesus lose patience with me? He grieves over unbelief, and he says so; we should not pretend he is indifferent to it. But notice what he does with his weariness: he says, bring your son here. His patience is not endless in the sense that sin does not matter to him; it is endless in the sense that he goes on bearing with his people until he has finished his work in them. The same Lord who sighed over a faithless generation went to the cross for it. If you fear you have exhausted his patience, the very fear shows his Spirit is still at work. Bring your need to him.

In a sentence. Jesus lamented the faithlessness of his generation, then rebuked the spirit, healed the boy and gave him back to his father, and everyone was astonished at the majesty of God.

On a Tuesday. When the thing you are fighting flares up hardest, do not conclude you are losing. It may be the last throw of a defeated enemy. Keep bringing it to Christ. And when he answers, give him the glory: tell someone of the majesty of God you have seen.

For worship. The majesty of God was seen on the mountain in light, and in the valley in a gift. The splendour that shone beside Moses and Elijah stooped to lift a broken boy and put him back into his father’s arms. That is the greatness of our God: not only that he rules the universe, but that he hands sons back to fathers, and at the cost of his own Son is bringing many sons to glory (Hebrews 2:10).

verseByVerse.quote: 'Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.' But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. And they were afraid to ask him about this saying.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let these words sink into your ears: the Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men. But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. And they were afraid to ask him about this saying.

The second passion prediction. While everyone was marvelling at his power (v. 43), Jesus speaks of his weakness. The timing is the point. The crowd is at the height of its enthusiasm (a boy has been restored, God’s greatness is on everyone’s lips) and Jesus turns away from all of it to tell his disciples something that will spoil it. Popular amazement would not last. The disciples must not be swept up in it.

Let these words sink into your ears. Literally, put these words into your ears. Pay close attention. Remember this. Set them down there. He is not making an announcement; he is asking them to store something they will need later and cannot use yet.

The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men. This is the second passion prediction, much shorter than the first, and one word in it is new. Delivered (paradidosthai) means handed over, betrayed. It is the word that will be used of Judas throughout the passion, and the word Isaiah’s Greek text uses of the Servant who was handed over because of our sins (Isaiah 53:12). And there is a bitter play on words that the English keeps. The Son of Man into the hands of men. The one who came as the representative man is going to be handed over to men, by a man, and killed by them. The one who heals by his hands will be handed into human hands.

And it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. They did not understand, because they could not reconcile a suffering Messiah with what they believed. Only Luke adds that it was concealed. Concealed by whom? He does not say, and the passive is probably deliberate. Two things are true at once. There is a hiddenness that God appoints, not as punishment, but because the time for understanding had not yet come: Luke says the same of the Emmaus pair, whose eyes were kept from recognising him (24:16), until they were opened after the resurrection (24:31, 45). And there is a hiddenness the disciples make for themselves, for Luke shows straight afterwards what they were thinking about instead: which of them was greatest.

And they were afraid to ask him about this saying. There is the human half, stated plainly. They did not understand, and they did not ask, and Luke tells us why: they were afraid. Afraid of what? Almost certainly of the answer. There is a kind of not-understanding that is genuinely stuck, and there is a kind that has grasped enough to know it does not want the rest. Mark records Peter, after the first prediction, taking Jesus aside to rebuke him for it (Mark 8:32). They had understood more than they wanted to.

Why would God hide the meaning from them? For a time, and for their good. They could not yet bear the full truth of the cross, and they would understand it only in the light of the resurrection, when the risen Christ opened their minds to understand the Scriptures (24:45). God’s timing in revelation is wise. There are things in his word you may not understand yet, and some will become clear only through later experience, or in glory. That is no excuse for not asking; the disciples’ fear was their own fault. But it is a comfort when understanding is slow. He will finish teaching you.

In a sentence. While everyone marvelled, Jesus told his disciples to remember that he would be handed over to men, but they did not understand, because it was hidden from them, and were afraid to ask.

On a Tuesday. Do not be afraid to ask Jesus about the hard things in his word. Understanding is his gift. The question that most needs asking is very often the one nobody in the room will raise, not because it is difficult, but because everyone present suspects what the answer will cost. Ask it, in prayer and to people who know the Scriptures. And be wary of being carried along by enthusiasm without asking where Jesus is going.

For worship. The hands that had just lifted a broken boy would be handed over into the hands of men, and he told his friends so while the crowd was still marvelling. He was not caught by the cross; he walked toward it with open eyes, saying it aloud to men who did not want to hear. We understand now what they could not: that the handing over was love, that the Father did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32), and that the hands men pierced are the hands that hold us.

parallels.desc: they understood none of these things

verseByVerse.quote: An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child and put him by his side
verseByVerse.commentary:
An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child and put him by his side.

An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. Read that sentence with the previous one still in the air. He has just told them he is going to be handed over to men and killed. They did not understand it, and were afraid to ask. And what fills the silence is an argument about rank. Jesus speaks of being handed over; they argue about rank. Luke sets the two side by side without a word of comment, and the effect is devastating. The same argument will arise at the Last Supper (22:24).

What were they arguing about? The timing suggests an answer. Three of them had just been up a mountain and come back different, and would not say why (v. 36). Peter had been the one to name him the Christ. The nine had not managed to cast out the demon. Perhaps the choice of three for the mountain had stirred jealousy, or the failure of the nine. There was material for a dispute, and it was fresh. So this is not a general failing of ambitious men. It is what happened in the hours after the glory, among people who had been let in on something, which is precisely where this particular sin lives. Nobody argues about greatness who has not first been given something.

But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts. Luke does not say they told him. He knew what they were thinking (5:22; 6:8), and the phrase he uses is the reasoning of their hearts, which is where the argument actually was. Whatever was being said aloud, the thing being weighed was internal, and he could see it. That is worth pausing on before the child arrives. This is not a man detecting a squabble. It is the one who knew what was in man (John 2:25) reading the inner life of twelve people at once, including the parts they would not have admitted to each other.

Took a child and put him by his side. He does not answer the argument. He does not name a winner, or rebuke the ambition, or deliver a lecture on humility. He walks over, takes a child (paidion, a young one, small enough to be taken) and stands the child beside himself, in the place of honour. Children had no status in the ancient world. The picture is the argument. Twelve grown men are ranking themselves, and he places beside himself the one person present with no rank whatsoever.

Is it wrong to want to do well? No. Paul tells us to excel, to work heartily, to aim for the prize (1 Corinthians 9:24; Colossians 3:23). Ambition for God’s glory and for the good of others is a virtue. What Jesus exposes here is the desire to be thought greater than others: comparison, rank, the need to be ahead. The test is simple. Can you rejoice when someone else is honoured, chosen, or more fruitful than you (Romans 12:15)? Do you want to be great, or do you want Christ to be great? Pride hides easily in spiritual success, so watch especially after God has blessed you.

In a sentence. When the disciples argued about which of them was greatest, Jesus, knowing their thoughts, set a child beside him.

On a Tuesday. Pride is persistent, even in disciples. Watch for the desire to be thought greater than others. Notice this week when you mentally rank yourself against someone: a colleague, a fellow church member, a sibling. Confess it to God by name, and then do something to honour the person you were measuring yourself against.

For worship. While twelve men measured themselves against one another, the one who had just shone like lightning on a mountain was quietly making room at his side for a child. He who is the radiance of the Father’s glory has never needed to compete for anything. He gave rank away, all of it, on the road to being handed over, and he gives the place beside himself to those with no claim to it. Such is the King we serve: the greatest, at home with the least.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to them, 'Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For he who is least among you all is the one who is great.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And said to them: whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For he who is least among you all is the one who is great.

Whoever receives this child in my name receives me. To feel the force of this, set aside the modern picture of childhood. A first-century child was loved, certainly, but in law and society a child had no standing: no rights, no property, no voice, no capacity to confer honour on anybody. That is why Jesus chose one to stand beside him in an argument about greatness. Receives is the language of hospitality: to welcome, to take somebody in. So the question here is not, who is willing to be like a child? (that comes at 18:17), but: who will you make room for, when the person can do nothing for you? To welcome a person of no status, for Jesus’ sake, is to welcome Jesus himself.

And whoever receives me receives him who sent me. Then the chain, and it is startling. The child stands for Christ, and Christ for the Father who sent him, so that the person with the least standing in the room is joined, in two links, to the throne of God. It is not sentiment but a claim about where Christ has chosen to be found. Luke’s Jesus spends his ministry at the tables of the unimportant, and in his parable of the great banquet the servant is sent out for the poor and crippled and blind and lame (14:21). The welcome of the least is the shape of God’s own hospitality.

For he who is least among you all is the one who is great. And there is the answer to their argument, and it is not that the argument was about nothing. He does not abolish greatness. He tells them the measurement is inverted, and then leaves them holding it. Greatness in the kingdom turns the world upside down. The least is the greatest. Not the one who seeks to be great, but the one who becomes small: who welcomes the unimportant and serves without seeking recognition (22:26–27).

Making it concrete. This is easy to admire and hard to live. The test is not how a man behaves towards those above him; everyone is attentive upwards. It is how he treats the people who cannot advance him, cannot repay him, cannot report him, and will never be in a position to do him any good at all. The person who cleans the building. The member of the congregation whose conversation goes nowhere. The child in the room, who has nothing and is watching. Whatever is being said to them is being said to Christ, and whatever is being given them is going to the Father.

Does this mean children’s work in the church matters? Very much. Those who welcome, teach and care for children in Christ’s name are receiving Christ himself, though their work is often unseen and rarely thanked. The crèche rota and the Sunday school are not lesser ministries for those not gifted enough to preach. And the principle reaches further: the disabled, the elderly with dementia, the newcomer who does not fit, the person with nothing to give. A church’s greatness is measured by how it receives those who can do nothing for it.

In a sentence. Jesus taught that whoever welcomes a child in his name welcomes him and the Father, and that the least among them is the greatest.

On a Tuesday. Welcome someone today who can give you nothing in return. In them, you welcome Christ. On Sunday, speak to the child, the shy visitor, or the elderly member no one sits with. Thank someone who serves among the children. And if you are tempted to think your own hidden service is wasted, remember who is being received in it.

For worship. The God of glory has chosen to be found among the least. The Father sent his Son, the Son stood a child at his side and said, receive this one and you receive me, and so the welcome of a little one reaches the throne of heaven. He who was greatest became the servant of all, so that the least might be made great in him. There is no lowly door in his kingdom that does not open onto the Father’s house.

verseByVerse.quote: John answered, 'Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.' But Jesus said to him, 'Do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
John answered: Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us. But Jesus said to him: do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.

John answered, Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name. The word answered is odd, because nobody had asked John anything. He is responding to what Jesus has just said about receiving a child, and what he offers, apparently as a contribution, is an account of something they did. The timing is not accidental and Luke has left it exposed. Jesus has just placed a child beside himself and said the least is the greatest. John, one of the three who went up the mountain, immediately produces an incident in which the disciples enforced a boundary.

What John reports. Now look at what he actually reports, because it is carefully worded. The man was casting out demons. It was working. Successfully, when the disciples had just failed at precisely this a few verses earlier (v. 40). And he was doing it in your name: not in his own, not as a rival, but under the authority of Jesus.

And we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us. So the ground for stopping him is not that he was a fraud, and not that he was doing harm. John states the reason himself, and it is the only reason he has. With us: not one of our group. Not, he does not follow you. Us. The same pride as the argument about greatness, now as group pride.

For the one who is not against you is for you. Do not stop him: the correction is immediate and unqualified, and the principle is generous. Anyone genuinely working in Jesus’ name against Satan is on the same side. What is being corrected is a thoroughly religious instinct: the assumption that the boundary of my group is the boundary of the kingdom, and that work God is doing outside it is at best suspect and at worst competition.

The name that does the work. Israel had seen this scene before. When Eldad and Medad prophesied in the camp, outside the circle at the tent, Joshua begged Moses to stop them, and Moses answered that he wished all the LORD’s people were prophets (Numbers 11:26–29). John plays Joshua here. But the power at work is not Moses’ spirit shared out; it is Jesus’ own name. That is the real centre of the scene. Demons are leaving a man at the word of someone the Twelve have never met, because the name, not the group, does the work, and the name belongs to him.

Against or with? A reader will notice that Jesus says something apparently opposite two chapters later: whoever is not with me is against me (11:23). The two are not in conflict, and the difference is in the pronouns. There, the subject is a man’s own relation to Christ, and there is no neutral ground: no one is uncommitted where he is concerned. Here, the subject is one servant’s judgement of another, and the presumption runs the other way. The first is a rule for how to view others; the second, a test for oneself. About my own standing before Christ, assume nothing. About another man doing good in his name, assume the best. Do not exclude genuine fellow workers; but you yourself must be wholly with Christ.

What it does not mean. Using the name of Jesus does not make a man a true believer, and this is no licence to treat doctrine as unimportant (Matthew 7:22–23; Acts 19:13–16; Galatians 1:8). The issue here is group loyalty, not the truth of the gospel. The man in question was doing something unmistakably good in the name of Jesus. That is a long way from saying it does not matter what anyone believes.

How do I tell a fellow worker from a false teacher? Ask what he says about Christ and the gospel, not whether he belongs to your group. Does he confess Jesus as Lord and God, crucified for sinners and risen (1 John 4:2–3; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4)? Does he preach salvation by grace through faith, not by works (Galatians 1:6–9)? Does his life and teaching honour Christ? Where those are present, rejoice in his work, even if he baptises differently, governs his church differently or sings different songs. Where the gospel itself is denied, the name of Jesus is being used, not served, and love requires us to say so.

In a sentence. John told Jesus they had tried to stop an outsider who was casting out demons in his name, and Jesus forbade it, for whoever is not against them is for them.

On a Tuesday. Rejoice when Christ is served by believers outside your own circle. Think of a church or ministry in your town that is not yours but preaches Christ faithfully, and pray for it by name this week. Speak well of it. And watch for the moment when you are more pleased that your group succeeds than that Christ is honoured.

For worship. The name of Jesus is greater than any company that bears it. It was at work in a stranger’s hands, outside the circle of the Twelve, and it is at work now in places and churches we have never heard of. The Lord of the harvest is not confined to our circles. He will gather a people from every tribe and tradition to sing one song before his throne, and on that day the question will not be which group we followed with, but whether we followed him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 51–62 — The Face Set Toward Jerusalem; The Cost of Following
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem.” With that sentence Luke's narrative pivots. The Galilean ministry is over, and the journey that runs from here to 19:44 begins. Everything that follows — the parables, the healings, the controversies — happens on the road that leads to the cross.

“Taken up” reaches past the cross to the ascension. Luke has the whole arc in one word: the death, the rising, the going home.

“Set his face” is the language of the Suffering Servant: “I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame” (Isa. 50:7) — from a passage whose preceding verse reads, “I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard.” He is not swept toward the cross by events, or cornered by his enemies. He turns and starts walking.

The route runs through Samaria, which some Jewish pilgrims avoided by going round through the Jordan valley. He goes straight through. And the village refuses him precisely because his face is set toward Jerusalem — the ancient dispute over Gerizim and Jerusalem. On the first day of the journey to the cross, what he is rejected for is going to the cross.

James and John ask to call down fire, reasoning from Elijah (2 Kgs. 1:10-12), and reasoning badly: Elijah faced armed men sent to seize a prophet, and these two are facing a village that declined to provide beds. Jesus rebukes the disciples, not the Samaritans, and they go on to another village. Samaritan villages like it would be evangelised within a few years (Acts 8:5-8, 25), and no one there was burned.

Three encounters close the chapter. A man volunteers to follow anywhere and is told the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head — a saying that fits the refusal he has just met. A second is called and asks to bury his father first; in that world burial happened the same day, so the request may well mean “let me stay until my father dies,” an indefinite postponement. A third asks only to say goodbye — which is what Elisha was granted (1 Kgs. 19:20) — and is answered with a ploughing image, the difference being that Elisha destroyed his plough.
verseByVerse.theology:
The travel narrative beginning at 9:51 is Luke's unique structural contribution. Matthew and Mark move quickly from Galilee to Jerusalem; Luke devotes ten chapters to the journey. The structure is theological before it is geographical: to follow Jesus is to be on the road to Jerusalem, which is to say on the road to the cross. The whole of it is lived in the shadow of the set face of 9:51.

“Leave the dead to bury their own dead” is among the most shocking sayings in the Gospels — an apparent violation of the fifth commandment and of an obligation so weighty that the Old Testament names its absence as a mark of judgement (Jer. 22:18-19). It is not an abolition of family duty. It is a refusal of one word, and the word is first. And the saying is wordplay, not cruelty: let those who are spiritually dead attend to the socially necessary; you have been called by the one who gives life.

“Fit for the kingdom of God” is the language of usefulness. It is not a statement about whether such a man is saved. It is a statement about whether he is any use at the plough while facing the wrong way.

And the instinct James and John show — to destroy those who reject Jesus — is answered by the direction he is walking. The one who has set his face toward a cross does not call down fire on those who refuse him; he presses on toward the sacrifice that will make it possible for even Samaritans to receive him.
verseByVerse.examples:
The ancient plough was light, single-handled, and pulled through stony ground; it had to be held down with constant pressure and steered by eye on a fixed point ahead. A man who turns to look behind loses the line in a moment, and a crooked first furrow makes every furrow after it crooked, because they are all set by the first. The issue is not affection for home. It is that the eyes are not on the work.

The three would-be disciples represent three ways of not following. The first underestimates the cost — “wherever you go” sounds easy until it means homelessness. The second and third both say first. There will always be one more reasonable thing to finish before following becomes convenient, and the reasonable things are genuinely reasonable, which is exactly what makes them so effective at postponing everything.

Luke does not tell us what any of the three decided. He never does. The stories are left open, which is itself the point: the road is still going, and the question is still standing.

And a comfortable church needs the first exchange plainly, because a certain kind of preaching promises the opposite — that coming to Christ secures a settled life. The one making the offer had nowhere to sleep and was walking towards an execution, and he thought the volunteer was owed that information before signing.

verseByVerse.quote: When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. And he sent messengers ahead of him, who went and entered a village of the Samaritans, to make preparations for him. But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. He sent messengers ahead of him, who went and entered a village of the Samaritans, to make preparations for him. But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem.

The journey to Jerusalem. This is the hinge of Luke’s Gospel. Here Luke’s long account of the journey to Jerusalem begins, running to 19:44, ten chapters. Everything from here on happens on a road, and the road has one destination. Much of Luke’s unique material is here: the good Samaritan, the prodigal son, the rich man and Lazarus, Zacchaeus. The whole journey is lived in the shadow of the cross.

For him to be taken up. When the days drew near is literally, when the days were being fulfilled: time is running out on purpose, and it is being counted. Taken up (analēmpsis) is a noun used nowhere else in the New Testament. It reaches past the cross to the ascension, sharing its root with the verb in Acts 1, where he was taken up (Acts 1:2, 11, 22). Luke describes the whole arc of his departure in one word: the death, the rising, and the going home to the Father.

He set his face to go to Jerusalem. The phrase is Hebrew in shape, and Luke alone uses it here, then repeats it in the next breath, as if once were not enough. In the prophets, to set one’s face is the posture of a man sent with a hard commission: Ezekiel was told to set his face toward Jerusalem and preach against its sanctuaries (Ezekiel 21:2). Above all it is the Servant’s resolve in Isaiah, who sets his face like a flint in the same breath as he gives his back to those who strike and does not hide his face from spitting (Isaiah 50:6–7). So the face turned to Jerusalem already knows what waits there. He is not swept toward the cross by events, cornered by enemies or overtaken by a plot. He turns and starts walking, and nothing will turn him aside.

And he sent messengers ahead of him. To arrange food and lodging for a large group. The route from Galilee to Jerusalem ran through Samaria, and many Galilean pilgrims went round it, down the Jordan valley and through Perea, east of the river, adding days to the journey rather than cross that ground. He goes straight through.

A village of the Samaritans. Samaria lay between Galilee and Judea. The Samaritans descended from northern Israelites who intermarried with peoples settled there after the Assyrian conquest in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:24–41). Their Scriptures were the five books of Moses alone, and their holy mountain was Gerizim, not Jerusalem (John 4:20). The hostility was ancient and mutual.

But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem. He was going to worship at the temple they rejected, and Samaritans were often hostile to Jewish pilgrims passing through. So the refusal is not personal: a village sees a party of pilgrims heading for the wrong mountain and declines to house them. And notice the irony. What he is rejected for, on the first day of the journey to the cross, is going to the cross.

Did Jesus know everything that would happen in Jerusalem? Yes. He had already told the disciples twice (vv. 22, 44), and he would tell them again in detail: he will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and shamefully treated and spit upon (18:31–33). He did not go to Jerusalem hoping for the best. He went as the Lamb who knew the altar. That is what makes his resolve so overwhelming. Every step south was taken with full knowledge, and every step was chosen. He was not a victim of circumstances but the willing Saviour.

In a sentence. As the time of his departure approached, Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem, but a Samaritan village refused to welcome him because he was heading there.

On a Tuesday. Is there a hard thing God has made clear you must do: a conversation to have, a sin to confess, a duty to take up? Set your face. Do not wait for it to become easy. And when obedience costs you a welcome somewhere, remember that it cost him a bed on the first night of the road.

For worship. On the first day of the road the Lord of glory was refused a bed, for the very reason he was travelling. Nothing turned him aside: not the rejection of a village, not the failure of his friends, not the shadow of what was waiting. He looked past the cross to his taking up, to the throne and the glory, and walked toward both. Our salvation rests not on our resolve but on his, and his was fixed before the road began.
verseByVerse.note: Here Luke’s long account of the journey to Jerusalem begins. “Taken up” points to the ascension. Samaritans lived between Galilee and Judea and were often hostile to pilgrims heading to Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: I have set my face like a flint
Jews have no dealings with Samaritans

verseByVerse.quote: And when his disciples James and John saw it, they said, 'Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?' But he turned and rebuked them. And they went on to another village.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When his disciples James and John saw it, they said: Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them? But he turned and rebuked them. And they went on to another village.

James and John. Jesus called them Boanerges, Sons of Thunder (Mark 3:17). Here we see why, and it is difficult to read this verse without concluding that the name was earned.

Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them? And notice: they ask permission. They do not act. There is even a kind of deference in it, do you want us to?, which makes the request more disturbing rather than less, because they genuinely expect the answer might be yes. Their precedent is scriptural. Elijah, in this same region, called down fire from heaven on soldiers sent by the king of Samaria to arrest him (2 Kings 1:9–16). These two have recently come down a mountain where they saw Elijah in glory. And they had been given power (v. 1). Why not use it? They are not making it up; they are reasoning from the Bible, and reasoning badly. Because the situation is not the same at all. Elijah faced armed men sent by an idolatrous king to seize a prophet. James and John are facing a village that declined to provide beds.

But he turned and rebuked them. The one rebuked in this passage is not the Samaritans. Luke records no word to the village at all. The rebuke goes to the disciples. Jesus came to save, not to destroy. This is not the time for judgement, but for grace. The day of vengeance has not yet come (4:19).

Textual note. Some manuscripts add as Elijah did, and others add Jesus’ words: you do not know what manner of spirit you are of; for the Son of Man came not to destroy people’s lives but to save them. These are probably not original, but they capture the meaning. They are absent from the earliest and best manuscripts, and the modern versions put them in a footnote, which is why one Bible may be shorter than another at exactly this point. Two things are worth saying, and they pull in opposite directions. The words are almost certainly not what Luke wrote: a scribe appears to have supplied the content of a rebuke Luke deliberately left unstated, and once written in a margin it moved into the text. But the sentence that was added is entirely true, and it is true from Luke’s own pages. The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (19:10) is in this Gospel in Jesus’ own words. And within one chapter the hero of his most famous story will be a Samaritan (10:33). The copyist guessed the theology exactly right. He simply had no business putting his guess into the Gospel.

And they went on to another village. No revenge. He simply went elsewhere. That is the whole response to rejection: no fire, no argument, no curse. They walked on.

The fire that did come. And Jesus would later send his gospel to Samaria (Acts 1:8), where it would be received with great joy (Acts 8:5–8, 14–17), and John himself would go there with Peter to lay hands on Samaritan believers so they would receive the Holy Spirit. The fire would come down on Samaria: the fire of the Spirit, not of judgement. The man who wanted to burn a Samaritan village lived to pray for Samaritans to receive the Spirit.

Will God never judge, then? He will. The day of vengeance is real, and Jesus himself speaks of it often (17:26–30; 21:22). Those who finally reject him will face God’s just and eternal judgement (2 Thessalonians 1:7–9). But judgement belongs to God, not to us, and it belongs to the last day, not to this one. Now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2). Our task is to warn, to plead and to pray, never to wish destruction on those who reject us. Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord (Romans 12:19).

In a sentence. When James and John offered to call down fire on the Samaritan village, Jesus rebuked them, and they went on to another village.

On a Tuesday. When people reject you or the gospel, resist the desire for revenge. Jesus came to save, and so should you. Notice when you enjoy imagining the downfall of someone who has mocked your faith, or a political opponent, or a church that has hurt you. Turn the thought into a prayer for them. And be careful of using Bible verses to justify the anger you already feel.

For worship. The Lord who could have called down fire walked on to the next village, and the patience in that step reached all the way to Samaria’s salvation. He is slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love (Exodus 34:6), and he would rather walk another mile than burn a village that has shut its door on him. Every one of us was once such a village, and he did not send the fire. He came back with the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “as Elijah did,” and a further saying: “You do not know what manner of spirit you are of; for the Son of Man came not to destroy people’s lives but to save them.”

verseByVerse.quote: As they were going along the road, someone said to him, 'I will follow you wherever you go.' And Jesus said to him, 'Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they were going along the road, someone said to him: I will follow you wherever you go. And Jesus said to him: foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.

Three would-be followers. Three men now meet him on that road, in three short encounters about the cost of discipleship (vv. 57–62), and Luke puts them together because between them they cover most of the ways a person fails to follow. Each shows a different obstacle.

I will follow you wherever you go. The offer is unprompted, enthusiastic, sincere, and unlimited, but perhaps impulsive. Nobody called this man. He volunteers, and he volunteers everything: wherever you go. Matthew tells us he was a scribe (Matthew 8:19), which adds something: a trained man, used to attaching himself to a teacher, and probably expecting the arrangement to look like the ones he knew. Does he know where Jesus is going? To Jerusalem, to the cross.

Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests. Even animals have homes. It is not a refusal. It is a disclosure, and it is worth noticing that Jesus does not respond to enthusiasm by taking advantage of it. He gives the man the one piece of information his offer did not account for. The comparison is exact and slightly bitter. Foxes have dens. Birds have nests. The animals of the land he made have somewhere to sleep.

But the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head. The Son of Man does not. Jesus had left his home in Nazareth, and had just been refused lodging in Samaria. The timing matters: this is not only a general statement about his way of life; it fits the refusal he has just met. The man has said wherever you go on a road where the last village would not have him. Following him means giving up security and comfort. Count the cost first (14:28).

What a comfortable church needs to hear. A certain kind of preaching promises that coming to Christ secures a settled, prosperous life. The one making this offer had nowhere to sleep and was walking towards an execution, and he thought the volunteer was owed that information before signing. Luke does not tell us what the man decided, nor what any of the three did. The stories are left open, and the question is still standing, now for the reader.

Must every Christian give up their home? No. Jesus’ own followers included people with houses, like Martha (10:38), and Peter kept his house in Capernaum. Jesus was not laying down a rule that disciples must be homeless, but telling a volunteer the truth about the road. What every disciple must do is hold home, comfort and security loosely, ready to lose them if following Christ requires it, as many believers around the world do today. A Christian may have a home; he may not make it his foundation. The question is whether you would still follow if it cost you the house.

In a sentence. To a man who promised to follow him anywhere, Jesus warned that he, the Son of Man, had no home, unlike even foxes and birds.

On a Tuesday. Following Jesus may cost you comfort and security. Are you willing? Before you make a large promise to God, count what it may cost, and then make it anyway, leaning on his grace rather than your enthusiasm. And if you are helping someone come to faith, tell them honestly about the road.

For worship. The Lord of heaven and earth, for whom all things were made, had nowhere to lay his head. He who owned the foxes’ holes and the birds’ nests chose homelessness for our sake, and on the cross he bowed his head (John 19:30) in the only rest the world gave him. And he has gone to prepare a place for us, so that we who follow him on the road will have a home with him for ever (John 14:2–3).

verseByVerse.quote: To another he said, 'Follow me.' But he said, 'Lord, let me first go and bury my father.' And Jesus said to him, 'Leave the dead to bury their own dead. But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
To another he said: follow me. But he said: Lord, let me first go and bury my father. And Jesus said to him: leave the dead to bury their own dead. But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.

To another he said, Follow me. Jesus calls this one. He does not volunteer. He is called, with the same two words that were said to Levi at the tax booth (5:27), and to fishermen at a lakeside.

Lord, let me first go and bury my father. His reply sounds like the most reasonable sentence in the chapter. Burying a father was a sacred duty in Judaism, so important that it overrode other religious obligations, like reciting the Shema. A son who did not bury his father had failed at the commandment to honour him.

Was the father already dead? In that world burial happened the same day, or the next at the latest. If the father had just died, he would be burying him that day, at the tomb, not standing on a road listening to a travelling preacher. More likely, his father was still alive and the man meant: let me wait until my father dies, and I have my inheritance and have fulfilled my family duty, perhaps years from now. It is not a plea for three days off. It is a request for an indefinite postponement, a few years, perhaps many, until the duty is discharged and the inheritance settled and the man is free to go with nothing owing. Either way, he puts something else first. That is why the answer lands as it does. Jesus is not being cold about a coffin. He is refusing one word, and the word is first.

Leave the dead to bury their own dead. A shocking, deliberately paradoxical saying. It uses the word in two senses in a single line: let the spiritually dead bury the physically dead. Those who have not responded to the call of the kingdom can handle the affairs of this world. The village will manage the funeral. It cannot manage the proclamation. The kingdom is more urgent than even the most sacred family duty.

But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God. Your task is greater: to bring life to the spiritually dead. The commission is the reason for the severity. This is not a man being told to abandon his family for no purpose; he is being given a different one, and it is urgent.

The Lord who has the right to come first. Only God may claim a place ahead of father and mother. The fifth commandment stands under the first, and here Jesus claims the place of the first: no duty, however sacred, may stand in front of following him. A rabbi who said this of himself would be a blasphemer, unless he is the Lord of the commandments. And the one who claims it honoured his own Father perfectly, all the way to Gethsemane, where he prayed, not my will, but yours, be done (22:42). His claim is never a tyrant’s demand. It is the call of the Son who first put his Father before his own life.

What it does not mean. This gives no Christian leave to neglect his parents or stay away from funerals. Jesus condemned the Pharisees for using religion to avoid caring for parents (Mark 7:9–13). But no duty, however sacred, comes before Christ. Whatever you put first is your real lord.

What if my family really does need me? Then caring for them may be exactly the way you follow Christ. Scripture is clear that providing for your family and honouring your parents are Christian duties (1 Timothy 5:4, 8), and Jesus provided for his own mother from the cross (John 19:26–27). The man in this passage was not caring for his father; he was using his father as a reason to delay obeying Christ. The question to ask is not, do I have family duties?, but, am I using them to avoid something Christ has plainly told me to do? Duty done for Christ is following; duty used against Christ is the first that he refuses.

In a sentence. When a man called by Jesus asked first to bury his father, Jesus told him to let the dead bury their dead and go and proclaim the kingdom.

On a Tuesday. What do you want to do first, before following Jesus fully? Nothing should come before him. There will always be one more reasonable thing to finish before following becomes convenient, and the reasonable things are genuinely reasonable, which is exactly what makes them so effective. Name your first, and give it to him.

For worship. The Lord who calls is the Lord of life. He did not come to bury the dead but to raise them, and his call goes out to the spiritually dead with power to make them live. The kingdom does not take a place in the queue behind the rest of a life, because the King is worth more than everything else in the queue. He is the first and the last, and he gave his own first place up so that we could be brought in.
verseByVerse.note: Burying a father was a sacred duty; the man may have meant waiting until his father died.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet another said, 'I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home.' Jesus said to him, 'No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet another said: I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home. Jesus said to him: no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.

I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home. The third man volunteers like the first and asks for a delay like the second, and his request is the smallest of the three. He does not want to wait for a death or negotiate terms. He wants to go home and say goodbye. A reasonable request, it seems.

The precedent of Elisha. And there is a precedent for exactly this, which he may well have had in mind. When Elijah threw his cloak over Elisha at the plough, Elisha asked to kiss his father and his mother goodbye, and Elijah allowed it (1 Kings 19:19–21). He went back, slaughtered his oxen, burned his ploughing equipment for the fire, fed the people, and then followed. So the man is asking for what the prophet allowed. And this time the answer is no. Jesus demands more than Elijah, because he is more than Elijah.

No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back. Jesus answers with a ploughing image, which suggests the Elisha story is in view on both sides, and the difference is instructive: Elisha destroyed the plough; this man wants to keep the option of the house. Any farmer would have felt the picture. The ancient plough was light and single-handled, guided by one hand while the other held a goad, pressed down constantly and steered by eye on a fixed point ahead. A ploughman who turns to look behind loses the line in a moment. A divided heart, half looking back to the old life, cannot plough straight for the kingdom. Lot’s wife looked back (Genesis 19:26; Luke 17:32). The issue is not affection for home. It is that the eyes are not on the work.

Is fit for the kingdom of God. Fit (euthetos) means suitable, useful, well-placed for a purpose. Not that he cannot be saved, but that half-hearted discipleship is useless for kingdom work. It is a statement about whether he is any use at the plough while he is facing the wrong way.

The three obstacles. Comfort (v. 58), duty (v. 60), and family affection (v. 61). All good things. But none can come before Christ. Jesus demands undivided loyalty, because he is Lord. The first would not count the cost; the second and third both said first. None of them is told he cannot come.

Is it wrong to miss my old life? Not in itself. Feelings of loss are human, and Christ is not offended by honest grief over what following him has cost. The danger is the backward look that wants to return: the heart that keeps the old life as an option, in case Christ does not prove worth it. Paul’s remedy was to count everything loss compared with knowing Christ, forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead (Philippians 3:8, 13–14). The cure for looking back is not trying harder not to look, but fixing your eyes on what is ahead: on Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith (Hebrews 12:2).

In a sentence. When a third man asked first to say goodbye at home, Jesus warned that a ploughman who keeps looking back is not fit for the kingdom of God.

On a Tuesday. Are you looking back at your old life while trying to follow Christ? Fix your eyes forward on him. Is there an option you are keeping open, a relationship, a habit, a way back, in case following him does not work out? Close it this week, as Elisha burned his plough.

For worship. One man in this chapter put his hand to the plough and never looked back. Through the refusal of a Samaritan village, the failure of his friends, the agony of the garden and the darkness of the cross, he kept his eyes on Jerusalem until the work was done, and his last word there was a prayer of trust: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (23:46). Because he did not turn back, the furrow is cut, and people who have looked back a thousand times are counted fit in him.
verseByVerse.note: A ploughman had to keep his eyes forward to cut a straight furrow.

9.text: <sup>1</sup> And he called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, <sup>2</sup> and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal. <sup>3</sup> And he said to them, “Take nothing for your journey, no staff, nor bag, nor bread, nor money; and do not have two tunics. <sup>4</sup> And whatever house you enter, stay there, and from there depart. <sup>5</sup> And wherever they do not receive you, when you leave that town shake off the dust from your feet as a testimony against them.” <sup>6</sup> And they departed and went through the villages, preaching the gospel and healing everywhere. <sup>7</sup> Now Herod the tetrarch heard about all that was happening, and he was perplexed, because it was said by some that John had been raised from the dead, <sup>8</sup> by some that Elijah had appeared, and by others that one of the prophets of old had risen. <sup>9</sup> Herod said, “John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things?” And he sought to see him. <sup>10</sup> On their return the apostles told him all that they had done. And he took them and withdrew apart to a town called Bethsaida. <sup>11</sup> When the crowds learned it, they followed him, and he welcomed them and spoke to them of the kingdom of God and cured those who had need of healing. <sup>12</sup> Now the day began to wear away, and the twelve came and said to him, “Send the crowd away to go into the surrounding villages and countryside to find lodging and get provisions, for we are here in a desolate place.” <sup>13</sup> But he said to them, “You give them something to eat.” They said, “We have no more than five loaves and two fish—unless we are to go and buy food for all these people.” <sup>14</sup> For there were about five thousand men. And he said to his disciples, “Have them sit down in groups of about fifty each.” <sup>15</sup> And they did so, and had them all sit down. <sup>16</sup> And taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing over them. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd. <sup>17</sup> And they all ate and were satisfied. And what was left over was picked up, twelve baskets of broken pieces. <sup>18</sup> Now it happened that as he was praying alone, the disciples were with him. And he asked them, “Who do the crowds say that I am?” <sup>19</sup> And they answered, “John the Baptist. But others say, Elijah, and others, that one of the prophets of old has risen.” <sup>20</sup> Then he said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” And Peter answered, “The Christ of God.” <sup>21</sup> And he strictly charged and commanded them to tell this to no one, <sup>22</sup> saying, “The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.” <sup>23</sup> And he said to all, “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. <sup>24</sup> For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it. <sup>25</sup> For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world and loses or forfeits himself? <sup>26</sup> For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him will the Son of Man be ashamed when he comes in his glory and the glory of the Father and of the holy angels. <sup>27</sup> But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.” <sup>28</sup> Now about eight days after these sayings he took with him Peter and John and James and went up on the mountain to pray. <sup>29</sup> And as he was praying, the appearance of his face was altered, and his clothing became dazzling white. <sup>30</sup> And behold, two men were talking with him, Moses and Elijah, <sup>31</sup> who appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem. <sup>32</sup> Now Peter and those who were with him were heavy with sleep, but when they became fully awake they saw his glory and the two men who stood with him. <sup>33</sup> And as the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, “Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah”—not knowing what he said. <sup>34</sup> As he was saying these things, a cloud came and overshadowed them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud. <sup>35</sup> And a voice came out of the cloud, saying, “This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him!” <sup>36</sup> And when the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. And they kept silent and told no one in those days anything of what they had seen. <sup>37</sup> On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a great crowd met him. <sup>38</sup> And behold, a man from the crowd cried out, “Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, for he is my only child. <sup>39</sup> And behold, a spirit seizes him, and he suddenly cries out. It convulses him so that he foams at the mouth, and shatters him, and will hardly leave him. <sup>40</sup> And I begged your disciples to cast it out, but they could not.” <sup>41</sup> Jesus answered, “O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you and bear with you? Bring your son here.” <sup>42</sup> While he was coming, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit and healed the boy, and gave him back to his father. <sup>43</sup> And all were astonished at the majesty of God. But while they were all marveling at everything he was doing, Jesus said to his disciples, <sup>44</sup> “Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.” <sup>45</sup> But they did not understand this saying, and it was concealed from them, so that they might not perceive it. And they were afraid to ask him about this saying. <sup>46</sup> An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. <sup>47</sup> But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child and put him by his side <sup>48</sup> and said to them, “Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me. For he who is least among you all is the one who is great.” <sup>49</sup> John answered, “Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.” <sup>50</sup> But Jesus said to him, “Do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you.” <sup>51</sup> When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem. <sup>52</sup> And he sent messengers ahead of him, who went and entered a village of the Samaritans, to make preparations for him. <sup>53</sup> But the people did not receive him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem. <sup>54</sup> And when his disciples James and John saw it, they said, “Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?” <sup>55</sup> But he turned and rebuked them. <sup>56</sup> And they went on to another village. <sup>57</sup> As they were going along the road, someone said to him, “I will follow you wherever you go.” <sup>58</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” <sup>59</sup> To another he said, “Follow me.” But he said, “Lord, let me first go and bury my father.” <sup>60</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Leave the dead to bury their own dead. But as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.” <sup>61</sup> Yet another said, “I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home.” <sup>62</sup> Jesus said to him, “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”

10.title: The Seventy-Two, the Samaritan, and the Better Part
10.overview:
Chapter 10 gives us three of Luke's most theologically rich scenes — each one, in its own way, a complete world. The sending of the seventy-two (vv. 1–24) expands the mission beyond the twelve, shows what kingdom authority looks like in practice, and culminates in the most intimate expression of Jesus's joy in the entire Gospel. The parable of the Good Samaritan (vv. 25–37) is the world's most famous story about neighbourly love — and simultaneously one of its most searching challenges to religious self-justification. And the scene at the home of Martha and Mary (vv. 38–42) is the New Testament's most precise statement about the one thing that is necessary in a life pulled in every direction by legitimate demands.

The chapter is the opening movement of the great travel narrative (9:51–19:44) — the long road to Jerusalem during which Jesus pours himself into his disciples and into the crowds that gather around him. The sending of the seventy-two models the missional multiplication that will characterise the church after Pentecost. The Samaritan parable models the ethics of the kingdom in the most concrete possible terms. The Mary-and-Martha scene models the devotional centre that makes the mission and the ethics sustainable. Together, the three scenes answer three questions: What does the kingdom produce in the world? What does the kingdom demand of its citizens? And what does the kingdom require of those who would receive it?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Jesus Sends Out the Seventy-Two
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus appoints seventy-two others — beyond the twelve — and sends them ahead of him in pairs to every town and place he is about to go.

If your Bible says seventy, nothing is wrong: the manuscripts divide almost evenly here and at v. 17, and both figures carry the same symbolism. Moses appointed seventy elders to help carry a burden he could not carry alone (Num. 11:16), and two more prophesied in the camp (Num. 11:26); and the nations listed in Genesis 10 come to about seventy. Either way, the expansion from twelve signals that the mission is wider than the twelve tribes.

They go two by two — the two witnesses the law required (Deut. 19:15) — and they go ahead of him. They are not independent agents but an advance party, and everywhere they arrive he is coming behind them.

“The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few” inverts the instinctive picture. The field is not the problem; the field is ready. And faced with a labour shortage, Jesus does not say “go” but “pray” — and he says it to the seventy-two he is about to send out that hour. The crop is not ours, the field is not ours, and the shortage is not finally ours to solve: it is “the Lord of the harvest” and “his harvest,” twice in one sentence.

“Lambs in the midst of wolves” is candid. A lamb among wolves is food; there is no version of that scene where the lamb wins. Jesus does not promise safety, and the whole security of the arrangement is in the person doing the sending.

The instructions echo those to the twelve, with additions. “Greet no one on the road” is not rudeness but urgency — an Eastern roadside greeting could consume a large part of a day, and Elisha said the same to Gehazi on an errand that would not wait (2 Kgs. 4:29). The “son of peace” is a Semitic idiom for a person already prepared to receive what is being brought; and where there is none, the peace “returns” — nothing is wasted.

“Eat what is set before you” is far more than manners. It sends Jewish men into households whose kitchens were the daily boundary of the covenant, and it plants the seed of Peter's rooftop vision (Acts 10:14-15).

And the woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum are among the most severe words in Luke's Gospel — aimed not at pagan cities but at the three villages where most of the ministry had happened.
verseByVerse.theology:
The chain of representation in v.16 — “the one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me” — governs all Christian mission. It rests on the ancient principle that an authorised envoy carries the standing of the one who sent him: insult the ambassador and you have insulted the king.

The comfort in that is enormous. A believer stammering through an explanation to a colleague is not offering a private opinion; if the colleague hears, he has heard Christ. The messenger's inadequacy does not degrade what is carried.

The weight is equally real. There is no neutral response to the gospel faithfully spoken. But note the limit, or the verse becomes a tyrant: the chain runs through the message, not through everything a messenger happens to want. It has been used to shield leaders from criticism, as though disagreeing with the man were rejecting Christ. What could not be refused without consequence was a specific announcement: the kingdom of God has come near.
