The woes introduce graduated accountability — judgement proportional to light received. Paul develops it (Rom. 2:12-16), and Hebrews applies it to those who have known the covenant (Heb. 10:26-31). The privileged place in the kingdom is also the most exposed position under judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Chorazin appears in the whole New Testament exactly twice — here and in the Matthew parallel — and not one miracle done there is recorded anywhere in the four Gospels. Yet Jesus speaks of “the mighty works done in you” as though his hearers knew what he meant. It is a quiet reminder of how much is not in the books (cf. John 21:25): a town condemned for a history of miracles no evangelist thought to write down.

“It will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town” is not a claim that inhospitality outranks Sodom's sins. It is that Sodom never had this. Nobody stood in her streets announcing that the kingdom of God had come near.

And the last word a rejecting town hears is not a curse but the offer, repeated. “Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near” is almost word for word what the receiving towns were told (v. 9). The kingdom came as near to Chorazin as to anywhere — and nearness is not reception.

The principle bites hardest where most has been given (12:48), which in the modern world means anyone with a Bible on the shelf, a church down the road, and a lifetime of sermons behind them.

verseByVerse.quote: After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of him, two by two, into every town and place where he himself was about to go. And he said to them, 'The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of him, two by two, into every town and place where he himself was about to go. He said to them: the harvest is plentiful, but the labourers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers into his harvest.

Meaning first. Only Luke records the sending of the seventy-two. The Twelve were sent in chapter 9; now a wider circle goes out ahead of Jesus as he sets his face toward Jerusalem. The mission is not only for apostles. The chapter then moves from the field to the heart: the joy of names written in heaven, the Son’s own exultation in the Father, a lawyer who wants to know how little love he can get away with, and a woman at Jesus’ feet who has found the one thing necessary. Running through it all is a single question: what does it mean to have the kingdom of God come near, and what do you do when it is standing at your door?

Seventy or seventy-two? If your Bible says seventy where this one says seventy-two, nothing is wrong and nothing much hangs on it. The manuscripts divide almost evenly, here and again at v. 17, and translators go different ways. Either figure carries the same symbolism, because the Old Testament supplies both. The elders Moses appointed number seventy (Numbers 11:16), but two more were left in the camp and prophesied anyway (Numbers 11:26); and the table of nations in Genesis 10 comes to seventy in the Hebrew and seventy-two in the Greek. A copyist working from either tradition could easily tidy the other toward it. What the number says is the same on both counts. Moses’ seventy were appointed to carry a burden he could not carry alone. Genesis’ seventy are the nations of the world. Twelve for the tribes of Israel; seventy-two for the whole earth. This mission is larger than the Twelve, and it is pointed outward.

Two by two. Not only for company, though that helps on a dark road. Under the law a matter was established by two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and what these men are carrying is testimony. Pairs make them harder to discredit and harder to discourage. One can pray while the other speaks; one can lift the other when he falls (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10).

Into every town and place where he himself was about to go. They are not independent operators. They are an advance party, like John the Baptist preparing the way, and everywhere they go he is coming behind them. That is the whole shape of Christian mission, and it has not changed: the messenger arrives first, and the Lord follows into the place the message has opened. No believer ever goes anywhere for Christ where Christ is not already on his way.

The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Most of us picture evangelism as a thin crop in a resistant field. Jesus says the opposite: the field is not the problem. The field is ready (John 4:35–38). Harvest is also, in the prophets and in John the Baptist’s preaching, a picture of the end, when the wheat is gathered and the chaff burned (3:17). So the image carries both urgency and hope: the crop is ripe, and ripe crops do not wait.

Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest. Faced with a shortage of workers, he does not first say go. He says pray, to seventy-two men he is about to send out that very hour: the people being sent are told to pray for more of themselves. Pray earnestly (deēthēte) means beg, plead. And the one being begged owns the field: the Lord of the harvest, and his harvest, twice in one sentence. The crop is not ours, the field is not ours, and the labour shortage is not finally our problem to solve. It is his, and he has told us how to raise it with him.

The Lord appointed. Luke calls Jesus simply the Lord as the chapter opens, and the title is chosen with care. It is the Lord who appoints the seventy-two and sends them (v. 1), and in the next breath he tells them to pray to the Lord of the harvest to send out labourers. They are asking for the very thing the Son is doing in front of their eyes. The Father and the Son are one in this work: the harvest the Father owns is the harvest the Son has come to gather, and no one goes into it whom he has not first appointed by name. Mission begins in his choice, not in our enthusiasm.

To send out. The verb (ekballō) is literally to throw out, to thrust out; it is the word used for casting out demons. Workers do not usually drift into the harvest. They have to be pushed, by a God who overcomes their reluctance, rearranges their lives and sometimes uses hardship to get them moving.

What does praying for labourers look like in practice? Name real places and real people: your own church’s need for teachers and youth leaders, a missionary you know, an unreached people group, the street you live on. Pray for the sending of preachers and church planters, but also for ordinary believers in workplaces and families who will speak of Christ there. Pray for your own children and grandchildren to be among those sent, which is harder than it sounds. And hold your hands open while you pray, because the Lord of the harvest may answer by sending you, to the next room or the next continent.

In a sentence. Jesus sent seventy-two disciples ahead of him in pairs, telling them that the harvest is great but the workers few, and to pray to the Lord of the harvest to send out workers.

On a Tuesday. Pray today, by name, for God to send workers into his harvest, and be willing to be sent yourself. If you have stopped praying for the people around you because they seem uninterested, remember who said the field is ready. And if Christian work has become a weight you carry alone, hand the harvest back to its Lord: it was never yours to bring in by your own strength.

For worship. The Lord of the harvest is not short of anything. He owns the field, he ripened the crop, and he has a heart large enough to want the whole of it gathered in. He sent his Son into the field first, the true seed that fell into the ground and died so that it might bear much fruit (John 12:24). Every labourer he sends since then is following that Son into a harvest he has already secured, and the gathering in will be his glory, not ours.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read seventy. The number may recall the nations listed in Genesis 10, or the seventy elders who helped Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals, and greet no one on the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals, and greet no one on the road.

Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. It is one of the most candid sentences he ever spoke, and he says it as he sends them, not afterwards. A lamb among wolves is not an underdog with a fighting chance. It is food, and no shepherd ever put one there on purpose, which is exactly what he says he is doing. He does not promise that the wolves will be friendly or that the lambs will be made formidable. He says I am sending, and the whole security of the arrangement is in the person doing the sending: the Shepherd who will lay down his life for the sheep (John 10:11).

The design, not a fault. A comfortable church habitually softens this. The vulnerability of the mission is not a fault to be engineered out; it is the design, and it is his own. These men are sent ahead of a Lord who has just set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51) and has twice told them that he must suffer and be delivered into the hands of men (9:22, 44). The lambs walk the road the Shepherd is walking, a few miles in front of him. A church that has made itself safe, powerful and protected has not improved on the arrangement; it has stepped off his road. The gospel of a crucified Lord has always travelled best in the hands of people who could be hurt.

Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals. The list is even shorter than the Twelve’s (9:3): no purse, no traveller’s satchel, no spare sandals, the ancient equivalent of no wallet, no bag and no change of shoes for a journey on foot. The point is total dependence on God, shown in the plainest way possible. They will eat because someone feeds them, and they will be fed because God has gone before them into the houses.

And greet no one on the road. This sounds rude until you know what a greeting was. An Eastern roadside greeting was not a nod; it was an extended exchange of embraces, enquiries after family, health and business, and invitations to stay, and it could consume a large part of a day. There is a precedent almost certainly in view. Elisha, sending Gehazi urgently to a dead child, told him not to greet anyone he met on the way, or answer anyone who greeted him (2 Kings 4:29). So it is not a rule about manners but about urgency, and it is temporary and specific: one sweep through the towns he is about to visit, and the ordinary courtesies of the road must not eat the daylight.

Does this mean Christian workers today should go without money or supplies? No. These were instructions for one short, urgent mission inside Israel, where hospitality to travelling teachers was expected. Later Jesus deliberately reverses them: now let the one who has a moneybag take it, and likewise a knapsack (22:35–36), because the situation has changed. Paul travelled with funds, received gifts and sometimes worked with his hands. What carries over is not the packing list but the posture: go in dependence on God, do not let comfort set the terms of obedience, and do not let lesser things crowd out what is urgent.

In a sentence. Jesus sent them out like lambs among wolves, with no money, supplies or spare sandals, and no time to stop for long greetings.

On a Tuesday. There are seasons when the ordinary good things have to give way to something that will not wait, and knowing which season you are in is most of the skill. Think of the thing God has plainly given you to do, a conversation you owe a friend, a reconciliation, a call to a lonely relative, and ask what small courtesies, hobbies and screens keep eating the daylight. And if you feel exposed as a Christian at work or at home, remember you were never promised the wolves would be tame. You were promised a Shepherd.

For worship. The Shepherd who sent lambs among wolves went among the wolves himself, and let them have him. He became the Lamb, led to the slaughter and silent before its shearers (Isaiah 53:7), so that no lamb of his would finally be lost. He sends from a place of having already been where he sends us, and he holds every one of his sheep in a hand from which no one can snatch them (John 10:28).
verseByVerse.note: Travellers’ greetings could be long and elaborate; there was no time for them.

parallels.desc: if you meet anyone, do not greet him

verseByVerse.quote: Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house!’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. But if not, it will return to you. And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the laborer deserves his wages. Do not go from house to house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever house you enter, first say: peace be to this house! And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. But if not, it will return to you. And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the labourer deserves his wages. Do not go from house to house.

Whatever house you enter, first say, Peace be to this house! The greeting is shalom, and in Hebrew it never meant merely the absence of trouble. It means wholeness, everything in its right place, a life not at war with God or with itself. And in the mouth of a man sent by Jesus it is not a pleasantry. It is the peace the angels sang over the fields of Bethlehem (2:14), peace with God through the Messiah. Notice how the next sentence treats it: as something that goes somewhere, settles or does not, and can come back.

And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. “Son of peace” is a Hebrew idiom: a person characterised by the thing named, in this case one who belongs to the peace being offered and is ready for it. Somebody in that village has been prepared before the messengers arrive. Evangelism is not manufacturing interest out of nothing: the instruction assumes there is already a person in the street whose heart has been made ready by somebody else, and the work is largely to find him. Lydia’s heart was opened by the Lord before Paul finished speaking (Acts 16:14). The blessing is effective: God’s peace actually comes.

But if not, it will return to you. Nothing is lost. Like the dove sent out from the ark that found no place to rest and came back to Noah’s hand (Genesis 8:9), a blessing offered to a house that will not have it is not wasted; it comes back to the one who offered it. That is a quiet mercy for every believer who has spoken and been rebuffed and felt they had spent something they could not get back.

Peace to you. This is one of Luke’s great words, and it belongs to Jesus before it belongs to his messengers. The angels announced it at his birth (2:14). The crowds will shout it as he rides into Jerusalem (19:38), and he will weep that the city did not know the things that make for peace (19:42). Then on the evening of the resurrection he will stand among frightened disciples and say, Peace to you (24:36). The seventy-two speak a peace they cannot yet explain. It is his, and the day is coming when he will speak it himself, risen, to men who had failed him.

And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they provide. Stay put. Do not go from house to house. The rule is the same as the Twelve’s, and for the same reason: a messenger who trades up for better hospitality has begun to be paid, and a man whose lodging depends on the standing of his host will eventually trim his message to keep it. Be content with what you are given.

For the laborer deserves his wages. Paul quotes this phrase to Timothy as Scripture: for the Scripture says, you shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain, and, the labourer deserves his wages (1 Timothy 5:18). The first half is Deuteronomy 25:4; the second is this verse. So within Paul’s lifetime the words of Jesus recorded by Luke were set beside the Law of Moses under the single heading the Scripture says. That is not a later council conferring authority on a book. It is an apostle treating what Jesus said exactly as he treats what God said through Moses, because he could see no difference. The principle is plain: those who work for the gospel have a right to be supported by those they serve (1 Corinthians 9:14). It is not charity; it is wages earned.

Should I give to my church if I am not sure the money is well used? Give, and give gladly, because supporting those who teach you is obedience to Christ, not a favour to an institution (Galatians 6:6). But you are not asked to give blindly. A faithful church is open about its finances, and you may ask how money is spent. If you have real concerns, raise them with the elders, privately and kindly. What you should not do is let vague suspicion become a permanent excuse for keeping back what Jesus says the labourer deserves.

In a sentence. They were to greet each house with peace, which would rest on those open to it, and stay where they were welcomed, accepting food as a worker’s due wages.

On a Tuesday. Speak peace into the houses you enter this week, and mean it: a blessing on the household, a prayer for the family you visit, a kind word about Christ where the door is open. Watch for the person God has already prepared. And if you sit under faithful preaching, ask whether your giving treats your pastor as a labourer worthy of his wages or as a cost to be kept down.

For worship. The peace these men carried was not theirs to manufacture. It was bought at a price, by the one who made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), and it goes out still from his hand into ordinary houses. He is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). Every time it rests on a son of peace, a war that began in Eden ends in one more heart.
verseByVerse.note: A “son of peace” means a person open to God’s peace.

verseByVerse.quote: Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you. Heal the sick in it and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you. Heal the sick in it and say to them: the kingdom of God has come near to you.

Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you. It sounds like a rule about manners, and it is a great deal more. These Jewish men were going into towns where some kitchens were not kept by the purity laws, and the food laws were the daily, physical boundary of the covenant people. He tells them to eat what they are given. Luke, writing for a Gentile church, knows where that is going. In his second volume Peter, on a rooftop in Joppa, will protest that he has never eaten anything common or unclean and be answered: what God has made clean, do not call common (Acts 10:14–15); within days he will be in a Roman centurion’s house. The seed of that is here, in a travel instruction. Paul gives the same rule: eat whatever is set before you without raising questions on the ground of conscience (1 Corinthians 10:27).

Receiving the person. There is a plainer point too. To eat what a poor household puts in front of you, without inspecting it, is to accept the person. Anybody who has been served a meal by people who had very little will know that scrutinising it would have been the one unforgivable thing.

Heal the sick in it and say to them, The kingdom of God has come near to you. The two go together, and in that order: the touch and then the word. The healing is not a strategy to earn a hearing, and the word is not merely an explanation of the healing. They are one announcement made in two ways. The healings are signs of the kingdom: the King has arrived, and wherever he goes, sickness and death begin to retreat.

Has come near. The announcement is precise: not that the kingdom of God will come, but that it has come near. The perfect tense means the nearness is a settled state: it has arrived and it is standing there, which is exactly what a village would conclude on watching its sick get up. In Jesus, God’s reign is at your door. The kingdom is near because the King is near: these towns lay on his own route (v. 1), and the healings were his, done through men he had sent. It is close enough to be reached, and it demands a response.

Is “heal the sick” a command to the church today? It belonged to this particular mission, whose signs confirmed the arrival of the kingdom in Jesus. Many Christians hold that such healing gifts continue, and they should be heard charitably; the more likely reading is that the sign gifts belonged to that foundational time, when Christ and his apostles were establishing the word (Hebrews 2:3–4). But God still heals. The church still prays for the sick, the elders anointing and praying in faith (James 5:14–15), and God often answers, through medicine and sometimes beyond it. And the heart of the command, the message that the kingdom has come near, goes on until he returns.

In a sentence. In towns that welcomed them, they were to eat what was offered, heal the sick, and announce that the kingdom of God had come near.

On a Tuesday. The kingdom of God has come near in Jesus; tell someone today, simply. Pray for a sick friend by name, and visit if you can, because care for the body is part of the message. And when someone with little offers you hospitality, receive it gladly and without fuss. It is one of the ways the gospel crosses thresholds.

For worship. The kingdom that came near in Galilee came near in a Person. He touched lepers, ate with outcasts and made his home among the unclean, and the healings were the first light of a morning in which he will wipe away every tear and death shall be no more (Revelation 21:4). The Lord who sent word to Galilean villages that the kingdom had come near will one day bring it all the way: the dwelling place of God will be with man, and the nearness will never end.

parallels.desc: eat whatever is set before you

verseByVerse.quote: But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say, ‘Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near.’ I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say: even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near. I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town.

But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say. Notice that he does not tell them to leave quietly. He tells them to go out into the public street and make an announcement, which takes a good deal more courage than staying, and is the last thing a rejected messenger would naturally want to do.

Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. The gesture is the one the Twelve were given (9:5): the dust a devout Jew shook off at the border on returning from pagan ground. Performed in an Israelite street, it says something devastating: that this town has put itself outside, and the line no longer runs where they think it does. We want nothing of yours; you are under God’s judgement.

Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near. This is the same sentence they were told to say to the towns that received them (v. 9), almost word for word. The only real difference is the nevertheless. So the last thing a rejecting town hears is not a curse. It is the offer, repeated. Even in rejection the message stands: they cannot say they were not told, and it is a final warning that is still an invitation. The kingdom came near to that town exactly as near as it came to the village that took the messengers in, and nearness is not the same as reception. It came near, and they were standing there, and they said no. It walked up the street.

I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town. Sodom is the Bible’s byword for a place beyond saving, a city destroyed by fire from heaven, whose name became shorthand for the outer limit of wickedness (Genesis 19). And a Galilean village that declined to receive two travelling preachers will fare worse. The logic is not that hospitality outranks Sodom’s sins. It is that Sodom never had this. Nobody stood in the streets of Sodom announcing that the kingdom of God had come near, and nobody healed her sick in the market square. These towns did have it, and they had it in daylight, and they preferred not to. Judgement is according to light received (12:47–48).

The Judge who held back the fire. The one who speaks of Sodom here was himself refused by a Samaritan village a few verses earlier, and when James and John asked whether they should call fire down from heaven on it, as Elijah once had, he turned and rebuked them (9:52–55). He is not soft on judgement. He says I tell you, and claims to know what the last day will hold for every town in Galilee. But he will not bring that day early. He sends the offer instead, and has it repeated at the gate, because the Judge of that day is first on his way to Jerusalem.

Degrees of judgement. Note the phrase “on that day”: a fixed, known day, the day of judgement. Whatever else is true of the last day, it is not a single undifferentiated verdict. It is weighed. There are degrees of punishment in the final judgement, according to privilege and knowledge (Matthew 11:22–24; Romans 2:12). Every sentence is just, every sentence is conscious and eternal, and no sentence is the same as another, because the Judge knows exactly what each person was given.

Is it right for Christians to walk away from people who reject the gospel? The gesture was a solemn act by commissioned messengers on a short, urgent mission, not a licence to write people off. We still warn plainly, and we may move on from those who will not hear when there are others waiting (Acts 13:51; 18:6). But we do not stop praying, and we leave the door open, because Paul himself had once been on the rejecting side. With friends and family, keep loving, keep living the gospel, and speak again when God gives an opening. Judgement belongs to God, not to our frustration.

In a sentence. In towns that rejected them, they were to wipe off the dust as a sign of judgement, warning that the kingdom had come near, and Jesus said Sodom would fare better at the judgement.

On a Tuesday. Hearing the gospel is a great privilege and a great responsibility. Ask how many times the kingdom has come near to you: in your upbringing, in sermons, in a friend’s witness, in a crisis. Every one of those was mercy, and every one is remembered. Do not treat it lightly. Answer it today.

For worship. The God who keeps such exact accounts is the same God who sent the offer to the town that would refuse it, and repeated it at the gate on the way out. His justice weighs every grain of light; his mercy keeps knocking after the door has closed. And the judgement that rejecting towns will bear was borne in full by his Son for everyone who receives him: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1).

verseByVerse.quote: 'Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. But it will be more bearable in the judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. But it will be more bearable in the judgement for Tyre and Sidon than for you. And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades.

Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! Now the woes, among the most severe words in Luke’s Gospel, and it is worth being clear who is receiving them. Not Rome. Not the Sanhedrin. Not the towns that never heard. Three small towns at the north end of the Sea of Galilee, the places where he had lived and worked and where most of his ministry so far had happened.

The town with no recorded miracle. Chorazin appears in the whole of the New Testament exactly twice: here, and in the parallel in Matthew 11:21. Not one miracle done in Chorazin is recorded anywhere in the four Gospels. Yet Jesus speaks of the mighty works done in you as though everyone listening knew what he meant. It is a quiet reminder of how much is not in the books. John says as much at the end of his Gospel: there are also many other things that Jesus did (John 21:25). Chorazin is the evidence: a town condemned for a history of miracles that no evangelist thought to write down.

For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. Tyre and Sidon were wealthy pagan ports on the Phoenician coast, denounced by the prophets for pride and cruelty (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26–28); a Galilean would have filed them under hopeless. Sackcloth and ashes were the marks of mourning and repentance, as when the king of Nineveh came down from his throne (Jonah 3:6). And Jesus says they would have repented: not might have, but would have, long ago. So he knows what people would have done under circumstances they were never given. That raises questions no one can fully answer, but it gives no one an excuse, because the towns being addressed are the ones that did get the circumstances.

And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades. Capernaum was his base, the town he moved to after Nazareth threw him out (4:31), where he taught in the synagogue, healed Peter’s mother-in-law, and emptied a street of its sick in one evening. The most privileged town of all. And the language he uses about it is borrowed. It is the taunt Isaiah aimed at the king of Babylon, who said in his heart I will ascend to heaven and was told you are brought down to Sheol (Isaiah 14:13–15). The most privileged village in Galilee is addressed in the words written for the archetype of proud rebellion. Hades is the Greek name for the Hebrew Sheol, the realm of the dead; here it is the place of judgement. The ruins of Capernaum, Chorazin and Bethsaida still lie empty today.

The mighty works done in you. Everything in these woes turns on whose works they were. The miracles of Galilee were not displays to impress a crowd. They were the signs Isaiah said would mark God’s own coming to save: the blind seeing, the lame leaping, the deaf hearing (Isaiah 35:4–6). Jesus pointed John the Baptist to exactly those signs as his credentials (7:22). Chorazin and Capernaum had watched the Lord arrive in their streets and had gone on as before. That is why Sodom and Tyre come off better: the measure of judgement is nearness to Christ himself, and few towns on earth had stood nearer.

If Tyre and Sidon would have repented, why did God not send them these miracles? God gives light as he wills, and owes it to no one: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy (Romans 9:15–16). We are not told why he chose Galilee and not Phoenicia, and Scripture does not pretend to tell us. But we are told enough to stop us accusing him. Those who received more are judged more strictly, and those who had less are judged by what they had. The towns that saw and did not repent are condemned for their own refusal, not for a decree they were trying to obey. The secret things belong to the LORD our God (Deuteronomy 29:29); what is revealed is that the light came, and they would not walk in it.

Everyone to whom much was given. The principle underneath is stated plainly later: everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required (12:48). It cuts hardest at those who have had most, which in the modern world means anyone with a Bible on the shelf, a church down the road, and a lifetime of sermons behind them.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced woe on the Galilean towns that saw his miracles and did not repent, saying that pagan cities would have repented and would fare better at the judgement.

On a Tuesday. If you have grown up hearing the gospel, you have great privilege. Do not let familiarity harden you to it. Ask honestly whether the things that once moved you now leave you unmoved, and whether you have more light than you are walking in. Capernaum’s danger was not open hostility; it was a town that had seen it all and stayed exactly the same.

For worship. These woes are spoken by the one who wept over Jerusalem (19:41). He does not pronounce them from a distance, as a judge glad to be rid of a case; he pronounces them as the one whose miracles were refused and whose love was spurned, and then he goes on toward Jerusalem to die for sinners no better than Chorazin. The same Lord who weighs light so exactly gave the greatest light of all, himself, and still says to every town and every heart: come.
verseByVerse.note: Chorazin and Bethsaida were towns near Capernaum at the north end of the lake. Tyre and Sidon were Gentile cities. Hades is the realm of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: 'The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me.

The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me. One sentence, and it holds the whole doctrine of Christian mission in a chain of links. Follow it backwards, because that is the direction the authority runs. The Father sends the Son. The Son sends the seventy-two. So what is done to the seventy-two is done to the Son, and what is done to the Son is done to the Father. When Saul persecuted the church, the risen Lord asked him: why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4).

The envoy. This rests on something older than the Gospel. In the ancient world an authorised envoy carried the standing of the man who sent him; the rabbinic principle was that a man’s representative is as the man himself. Insult the ambassador and you have insulted the king, and every court in the world understood it. What Jesus does here is put ordinary men in that position, men with no money, no bag and no spare sandals, and connect them by a direct line to the throne of heaven.

A comfort and a weight. Two things follow, and they pull in opposite directions. The first is a great comfort. A believer stammering through the gospel to a colleague is not sharing a personal opinion; if the colleague hears, he has heard Christ, and nobody thinks less of a king because his letter arrived in the hands of a tired man. The second is a weight. There is no neutral response to the gospel faithfully spoken, and the person declining is not declining you. That should stop a rejected Christian from taking it as a verdict on himself, and from being casual about what has just happened in the conversation.

The authority of preaching. When the word of God is faithfully preached, Christ himself speaks: how are they to hear without someone preaching? (Romans 10:14–17); we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us (2 Corinthians 5:20). The preacher is not the source of the authority, but his message, if true to Scripture, carries Christ’s authority. The Second Helvetic Confession (1566) puts it boldly: the preaching of the word of God is the word of God.

What it does not mean. Notice one limit, or the verse becomes a tyrant. The chain runs through what the messenger says from Christ, not through everything a messenger happens to want. It has been used to protect leaders from criticism, as though disagreeing with the man were rejecting Christ. The seventy-two were carrying a specific message: the kingdom of God has come near. That is what could not be refused without consequence, not their preferences and not their opinions. A sermon carries Christ’s authority exactly as far as it says what Scripture says, and the Bereans were commended for checking Paul against it (Acts 17:11).

How do I tell when a preacher is speaking with Christ’s authority? Open your Bible during the sermon and ask whether the point is actually in the passage. Where it plainly is, receive it as Christ’s word to you, even if it is unwelcome and even if the preacher is not gifted. Where he adds his own views on politics, schooling or methods, weigh them as one man’s wise or unwise counsel. If he contradicts Scripture, speak to him privately, and if necessary to the elders. And do not treat a dull delivery as an excuse: the authority is in the word, not the voice.

In a sentence. Jesus told his messengers that whoever hears them hears him, and whoever rejects them rejects him and the Father who sent him.

On a Tuesday. When God’s word is faithfully preached on Sunday, listen as to Christ himself: come prepared, pray before, and decide afterward what you will do. And when you speak of Christ to a friend this week, remember whose message you carry. You do not need to be impressive. You need to be faithful, and the King will stand behind his own word.

For worship. The Father sent the Son, and the Son has never stopped sending. Through weak voices and tired messengers, the eternal Word still speaks into towns and kitchens and offices, and to hear the faithful word is to hear him. How kind of God, that the voice which called the worlds into being should be willing to be carried by such as us, and that he should count the welcome given to his smallest messenger as a welcome given to himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — The Return of the Seventy-Two
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The seventy-two return elated: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!” The word even gives them away — they expected the preaching to work and did not expect that. And they are careful about the mechanism: in your name.

“I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” is one of the most startling sentences in the Gospels. It may look back to the primordial fall, or forward to the cross and the final defeat (cf. Rev. 12:9); but the tense and the context favour a comment on what has just happened. They came back talking about demons submitting, and his answer begins “I saw.” He is telling them what their preaching tour looked like from where he was standing.

Seventy-two men had spent their tour in small towns nobody has heard of, saying an unimpressive sentence to farmers, with no money and no shoes. The Son of God, watching the same tour, saw the ruler of this world come down out of the sky like a strike of lightning. There is no ordinary Christian work — only work whose real scale is invisible from inside it.

Then the authority over serpents and scorpions, and the promise that nothing shall hurt them — both of which have been badly misused and both of which the passage itself guards.

And then the redirection: “do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” The joy was not wrong; it was aimed at the wrong thing. Authority is about what they can do, and anything resting on what a man can do rises and falls with his last performance.

Jesus then rejoices in the Holy Spirit — one of the very few places where Luke tells us what he was feeling, and it is exultation. The Son, filled with joy by the Spirit, speaks to the Father, and the occasion is a group of nobodies coming home from a preaching tour.

The prayer thanks the Father for a hiding as well as a revealing, and then makes one of the highest claims in the Synoptic Gospels: all things handed over, and a mutual knowing of Father and Son that admits no third party except by the Son's choosing.

Finally the private beatitude: “blessed are the eyes that see what you see.” Not blessed for perceptiveness — blessed for what happens to be in front of them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The joy of Jesus “in the Holy Spirit” is a Trinitarian moment: the Son's joy is given in the Spirit and directed to the Father in prayer. The mutual delight of Father, Son and Spirit overflows into the mission and into the lives of those who share in it.

Verses 21-22 have long been called the Johannine thunderbolt, because they drop into Matthew and Luke sounding exactly like the fourth Gospel. “All things have been handed over to me by my Father” is not authority in a defined area but everything. And the mutual knowing is not the language of a teacher who understands God better than others; it is a claim to stand inside the life of God, on the near side of a door only he can open. That he opens it is why the prayer is joy rather than terror.

“The wise and understanding” are not scholars in general — the man saying it is the finest interpreter of Scripture who ever lived, and Luke, who records it, is the most educated writer in the New Testament. They are the professionally religious who have watched everything and concluded he is a problem. And the “little children” are the seventy-two. The dividing line is not intelligence but whether a man will come with empty hands; learning is no obstacle to that, it simply supplies one more thing to hold onto.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Rejoice that your names are written in heaven” reorients the worker's identity from achievement to grace. The image is a citizen register — the book of life in which names are written (Ex. 32:32; Ps. 69:28; Dan. 12:1; Phil. 4:3; Rev. 21:27).

Every feature of it reverses what they were celebrating. The authority was given for a task; the name is written for good. The authority varies with the day; the writing was done before they were sent. The authority is theirs to exercise; the name was entered by somebody else — and it is in heaven, which is the one place nothing can be got at.

This belongs in the hands of every believer who measures himself by his usefulness. The minister whose standing before God rises and falls with the size of the congregation. The parent who reads his children's faith as a report card on himself. The Christian who has been ill for two years, can no longer do any of the things he used to do, and quietly suspects he has become surplus.

And the beatitude of vv.23-24 is a rebuke to the boredom that settles on people who have been in church a long time. Abraham died with one son of the promise and a burial plot. Moses asked to see God's glory and was shown a back. Isaiah described the Servant's wounds seven centuries early and never met him. Every one of them longed for this. Isaiah would have given everything he owned for an afternoon with a New Testament and a quiet room.

verseByVerse.quote: The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, 'Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!' And he said to them, 'I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventy-two returned with joy, saying: Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name! And he said to them: I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.

The seventy-two returned with joy. Joy is one of Luke’s great themes, from the angels’ good news of great joy (2:10) to the disciples returning to Jerusalem with great joy after the ascension (24:52). Here it is the joy of men who have seen God at work through their own unremarkable hands.

Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name! The word “even” gives them away, and it is delightful. They expected the preaching to work. They expected the healings, more or less: those they had been told to do (v. 9). They did not expect that. And they are careful about the mechanism: in your name. Whatever the exhilaration, they have not confused whose authority it was.

I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. The first question is when he saw it. It may look back to the primordial fall of the adversary, which Scripture gestures at rather than narrates (Isaiah 14:12 is often read this way). It may look forward to the cross and the final defeat, seen in advance (Revelation 12:9–11). Or it may describe what has just happened: as seventy-two unremarkable men walked through Galilean villages saying the name of Jesus, he watched the enemy’s position collapse. The context favours the third. They came back talking about demons submitting; his answer begins I saw. He is telling them what their tour looked like from where he stood. The kingdom of God is overthrowing the kingdom of Satan (11:20–22), and the decisive blow would fall at the cross, when the ruler of this world was cast out (John 12:31) and the powers were disarmed and put to open shame (Colossians 2:15).

Like lightning. The image is exact in two ways. Lightning is sudden: not a slow retreat but a fall. And lightning comes down; whatever height the adversary held, he is not holding it.

There is no ordinary Christian work. Seventy-two men had spent their tour in small towns nobody has heard of, saying an unimpressive sentence to farmers, with no money and no shoes. That is what they experienced. And the Son of God, watching the same tour, saw the ruler of this world come down out of the sky like a strike of lightning. There is no ordinary Christian work. There is only work whose real scale is invisible from inside it, which is why the report and the reply in these two verses hardly sound as if they belong to the same event.

If Satan is defeated, why is there still so much evil? Because he is defeated but not yet destroyed. The decisive battle was won at the cross, and his final end in the lake of fire is certain (Revelation 20:10). Between those two points he is like an enemy whose capital has fallen, still dangerous in retreat. He prowls like a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8), and we are to resist him, firm in faith. But he cannot take back one person Christ has rescued, and every time the gospel is believed, his kingdom shrinks again. We fight from victory, not toward it.

In a sentence. The seventy-two returned joyfully reporting that even demons submitted to them in Jesus’ name, and Jesus said he had seen Satan fall from heaven like lightning.

On a Tuesday. Satan is a defeated enemy; serve Christ with confidence. The Sunday school lesson you teach, the verse you share, the prayer you pray for a neighbour may look tiny from where you stand. You are not the one who sees the true size of it. Do the small faithful thing, and leave its scale to the one who watches from heaven.

For worship. The Son who saw Satan fall is the Son who made him fall. He bound the strong man and plundered his house; he went to the cross, where the serpent bruised his heel, and crushed the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15). The adversary who once stood in heaven to accuse the brothers has been thrown down, and they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb (Revelation 12:10–11). When seventy-two unknown men spoke his name in the villages of Galilee, heaven was already watching what the cross would seal.

parallels.desc: how you are fallen from heaven

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you.

Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you. Two things in that promise need guarding, because both have been badly misused. The language comes straight from Psalm 91:13: you will tread on the lion and the adder; the young lion and the serpent you will trample underfoot. Serpents and scorpions are standard biblical shorthand for hostile and demonic power, reaching back to the serpent in the garden (Genesis 3:15) and the wilderness of fiery serpents and scorpions (Deuteronomy 8:15). And the sentence explains itself in its own next clause: and over all the power of the enemy. The enemy is Satan. The promise is primarily spiritual: authority over the forces of evil.

What it does not mean. Set beside the longer ending of Mark, they will pick up serpents with their hands (Mark 16:18), this verse has been made the charter of the snake-handling churches, where believers lift live rattlesnakes in worship to demonstrate their faith, and where people have died doing it. But Jesus is describing the authority the seventy-two have just been exercising over demons, not issuing an invitation to pick up vipers. And there is a sharper point still, from Luke’s own pages. Psalm 91 is the very psalm the devil quoted in the wilderness, urging Jesus to throw himself from the temple because angels would catch him, and Jesus refused with a single line: you shall not put the Lord your God to the test (4:9–12). To engineer a danger in order to make God prove a promise is not faith; it is precisely the thing Jesus called temptation. A man who deliberately handles a rattlesnake to demonstrate his trust is not obeying this verse. He is repeating the devil’s use of Scripture.

And nothing shall hurt you. Read as bodily immunity, the phrase is contradicted by almost everyone who first heard it. James was killed with the sword (Acts 12:2); Stephen was stoned; Paul was beaten, stoned and shipwrecked, and by early tradition beheaded, though he once shook a viper into the fire unharmed (Acts 28:3–6), which shows that God can preserve, not that he always will. Luke himself puts both halves in one breath: some of you they will put to death, but not a hair of your head will perish (21:16–18). The promise is not that the body will be untouched. It is that the enemy cannot finally destroy them: no power can separate them from the love of God (Romans 8:35–39). Nothing done to a disciple’s body can undo what has been secured for his soul.

Does every believer have this authority over the enemy? The victory over Satan is real and secured (v. 18), and every believer is protected by Christ: he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4), and the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet (Romans 16:20). We resist the devil by faith, prayer and the word, and he flees (James 4:7). But the particular commission and signs given to the seventy-two belonged to their mission. A Christian does not need special formulas, shouted commands or rituals to be safe. And Jesus himself immediately points them away from the power to the greater thing: their names are written in heaven (v. 20).

In a sentence. Jesus gave his disciples authority over all the power of the enemy, so that nothing could ultimately harm them.

On a Tuesday. In Christ you have nothing to fear from the powers of evil. If you are troubled by fear of curses, spirits or the occult, or haunted by a dark past, take your stand on Christ’s finished work, renounce any involvement plainly, and pray in his name; you do not need to perform anything. And do not test God by courting needless danger; trust him in the dangers that come to you in the path of obedience.

For worship. He gives authority over serpents because he has already trodden on the serpent. In the wilderness he would not use the promise to save himself; on the cross he would not come down to save himself; and so he saved us. Nothing shall hurt you is a promise only he could make, because he let everything hurt him, and rose. Our safety is his wounds.

parallels.desc: you will tread on the lion and the adder

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.

Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you. He has just confirmed the authority in the strongest terms. Now he tells them not to build their happiness on it. Note that he does not say the joy was wrong. He says it was aimed at the wrong thing, which is a much finer correction and a much more necessary one. What they came back rejoicing in was real, granted by him, and worth being pleased about. It is simply not what a person can stand on.

Why not? Because it is about what they can do. And anything resting on what a man can do rises and falls with his last performance. There will be a day like the one at the foot of the mountain, where the disciples tried and nothing happened (9:40). There will be seasons when the work does not go. A joy founded on effectiveness is a joy on a schedule, and the schedule is not in your hands. Spiritual power can also feed pride, and there will be some on the last day who say, did we not cast out demons in your name?, and are told, I never knew you (Matthew 7:22–23). Power in ministry proves nothing about the heart.

But rejoice that your names are written in heaven. The perfect tense: they have been written and remain written. The image is a citizen register, the roll of a city listing those who belong to it. Scripture uses it repeatedly: the book of life, in which names are written (Exodus 32:32; Psalm 69:28; Daniel 12:1; Philippians 4:3; Revelation 20:12, 15; 21:27). And every feature of it is the reverse of what they were celebrating. The authority was given for a task; the name is written for good. The authority varies with the day; the writing was done before they were sent and is not being reviewed. The authority is theirs to exercise; the name was entered by somebody else, and, this is the part that carries the weight, it is in heaven, which is the one place nothing can be got at.

Election. The names are written by God, and written early: Revelation speaks of names written in the book of life before the foundation of the world (Revelation 17:8), and Paul says God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). Joy rests on grace, not on performance.

Who can read the register? Only someone who has seen it. A few sentences earlier Jesus said I saw Satan fall from heaven (v. 18); now he speaks of what is written in heaven as a man speaks of a room he has lived in. No prophet ever told anyone that his name was entered there. The Son can say it, because he came from the Father and knows the Father’s book, and because he is about to go up to Jerusalem to make the writing good. The seventy-two hear their eternal standing from the lips of the one on whom it rests.

For those who measure themselves by usefulness. This verse belongs in the hands of every believer who measures himself by his usefulness. The minister whose sense of standing before God rises and falls with the size of the congregation. The parent who reads his children’s faith as a report card on his own. The Christian who has been ill for two years and can no longer do any of the things he used to do for God, and quietly suspects he has become surplus. The word to all of them is that the thing worth rejoicing in was never the doing. It is a name, already written, in a book they cannot reach and cannot lose.

How can I know my name is written there? Not by trying to read the book, which God has not opened to us, but by looking at the Christ he has offered to you. The same Lord who told the seventy-two their names were written goes on, a few verses later, to reveal the Father to anyone he chooses (v. 22). Whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). If you have turned from sin and are trusting Christ alone, your trust is itself the sign of the writing, because no one comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). The fruit of the Spirit, love for other believers, and a growing hatred of sin confirm it (1 John 3:14). And if you are unsure, do not stare inward: come to him now. Nobody who comes is found missing from the roll.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples not to rejoice chiefly in their power over spirits, but that their names are written in heaven.

On a Tuesday. Notice what makes you happiest about your Christian life this week. If it is a good day of serving, a fruitful conversation, a well-received talk, thank God for it, and then lay it down beside the greater joy. And on the days when nothing goes well, when you are ill, or fruitless, or forgotten, rejoice anyway, because nothing about your name in heaven has changed since yesterday.

For worship. Before the seventy-two set out, before they were born, before the mountains were brought forth, a hand wrote their names. It is the hand of the Father who chose them in love, and the names stand in the book of the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 13:8), written in his blood and kept by his life. No failure on earth reaches that page. If you belong to Christ, your name is written in heaven, and the God who wrote it does not erase.

parallels.desc: blot me out of your book

verseByVerse.quote: In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, 'I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said: I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.

In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit. Luke stops to tell us what Jesus was feeling, which he almost never does. The verb is ēgalliasato: not quiet contentment but exultation, the verb of Mary’s song, my spirit rejoices in God my Saviour (1:47), and its noun is used when the child leaped in the womb (1:44). And it happens in the Holy Spirit; only Luke mentions the Spirit here. This is one of the clearest windows in the Gospels into the life of God. The Son, filled with joy by the Spirit, speaks to the Father: Father, Son and Spirit in one sentence, three persons, one delight. And the occasion for it is a group of nobodies coming home from a preaching tour.

I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth. Intimacy and sovereignty together. Father is the word of a son at home; Lord of heaven and earth is the title of the King of all things. Jesus holds both in one breath, and teaches us to do the same.

That you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children. He thanks the Father for a hiding as well as a revealing, and that has to be faced rather than smoothed. These things are what the seventy-two had just seen and heard: Satan falling, the kingdom arriving, and the identity of the one in whose name it happened. This is not a commendation of ignorance; the man saying it is the finest interpreter of Scripture who ever lived. The wise here are the professionally religious, men with the texts, the training and the standing, who have watched all of it and concluded he is a problem. The little children (nēpioi, infants) are the seventy-two, fishermen and farmers who could not have argued a point of law. So the dividing line is not intelligence but whether a man will come with empty hands. Learning simply supplies one more thing to hold onto, and pride blinds (1 Corinthians 1:18–31).

Yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. “Gracious will” (eudokia) is good pleasure, the same word as the angels’ song of peace among those with whom he is pleased (2:14). God reveals and hides according to his sovereign good pleasure. Jesus does not merely accept the Father’s arrangement or complain about it. He is delighted by it. Election is a cause of praise.

All things have been handed over to me by my Father. Scholars have long called this passage the Johannine thunderbolt, because it drops into Matthew and Luke sounding exactly like the fourth Gospel, and it is one of the strongest claims Jesus makes anywhere. All things: not some authority in a defined area. Everything, handed over.

No one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son. Then a mutual knowing that admits no third party: the Father knows the Son; the Son knows the Father; nobody else knows either except by the Son’s choosing. Only God can know God fully. That is not the language of a teacher who understands God better than others. It is a claim to stand inside the life of God, on the near side of a door that only he can open. It is one of the clearest statements in the first three Gospels of Jesus’ deity and his unique relationship to the Father.

And anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. The only way to know God is through the Son’s revelation, and the Son reveals the Father to whom he chooses. Knowing God is a gift of sovereign grace (John 6:44; 14:6; 17:6). And he opens the door. That is the last clause, and it is why this prayer is joy rather than terror.

Does God, then, choose who will understand? Jesus says so plainly: the Father has hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little children, for such was his gracious will, and the Son reveals the Father to anyone he chooses. The Reformed reading takes these words at face value: understanding is God’s gift, and no one can boast of having worked it out. Yet those who reject Jesus are responsible for it (vv. 13–16), and the invitation is to all: come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden (Matthew 11:28), which in Matthew follows these very words. Both are true. If you want to know God, that desire is already the Son at work, so come.

Can people of other religions know God without Christ? They may know that God exists, for creation declares his power (Romans 1:20), and their consciences bear witness. But they do not know him as Father, and they cannot be saved by that knowledge. The saving knowledge of God comes only through the Son: no one comes to the Father except through me (John 14:6). That is not narrowness for its own sake. It is the shape of reality, and it is why the church must go and tell, because the Son is willing to reveal the Father to anyone, from any nation, who comes to him.

In a sentence. Rejoicing in the Spirit, Jesus thanked the Father for revealing the truth to the humble rather than the wise, by his gracious will, and declared that only the Son knows the Father and reveals him to whom he chooses.

On a Tuesday. If you know God, it is because the Son chose to reveal him to you, and that leaves no room for looking down on anyone who does not yet see. Thank him today, by name, for opening your eyes. When you speak to a clever friend who scoffs, do not try to out-argue him into the kingdom; pray for him to be made a little child. And if you feel too ordinary to understand the Bible, take heart: these things are revealed to infants.

For worship. Beneath the noise of the world there is a joy that has never stopped: the Father delighting in the Son, the Son exulting in the Father, the Spirit filling the Son with gladness. For one hour on a Galilean road that joy broke the surface, and its occasion was seventy-two ordinary men, back from the villages, who now knew the Father because the Son had chosen to show him. The Lord of heaven and earth did not need us to complete his happiness. He opened the door anyway, and the gladness of God himself is the house we are brought into.

verseByVerse.quote: Then turning to the disciples he said privately, 'Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turning to the disciples he said privately: blessed are the eyes that see what you see! For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.

Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! Jesus turns and says it to the disciples alone, not to the crowd. Not blessed are you for being perceptive. Blessed are the eyes, for what happens to be in front of them. The blessing is entirely a matter of where they are standing in history, and they did nothing to arrange it. They are witnessing the fulfilment of everything the Old Testament promised: the Messiah, the kingdom, the defeat of Satan.

For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it. Put names to that and it becomes almost unbearable. Abraham, promised that all nations would be blessed through his offspring, died with one son of the promise and a burial plot, yet rejoiced to see Christ’s day (John 8:56). Moses asked to see God’s glory and was shown his back from a cleft in the rock. David, promised a son whose throne would stand for ever, went to his grave a thousand years before the child was born. Isaiah described the Servant’s wounds seven centuries early and never met him. Daniel saw one like a son of man receive an everlasting kingdom, and was told to seal the book and go his way. They spent their lives leaning toward something they were told they would not see, and all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen and greeted them from afar (Hebrews 11:13). And a group of Galilean labourers had been walking around with him, eating with him, and coming home to tell him how the trip went.

The boredom of proximity. There is a boredom that settles on people who have been in church a long time: the sense that the gospel is a known quantity, the Bible a familiar book, the whole thing slightly worn. It is not usually unbelief. It is simply the effect of proximity on the extraordinary. And it goes further. The disciples saw him before the cross and understood almost nothing of it; anyone reading this has the finished account of the death and the rising, the whole of the Scriptures, and the Spirit given. Daniel was told to seal up his book; ours lies open on the kitchen table.

My eyes have seen your salvation. Luke has already shown us one man who stood at the very end of that long line of longing and was allowed to see. Old Simeon took the infant in his arms in the temple and said that now he could depart in peace, because his eyes had seen God’s salvation (2:29–30). For Simeon salvation was not an idea; it was a child he could hold. That is what the blessed eyes of the disciples are looking at: not an experience or a doctrine, but a Person. Everything the prophets and kings strained toward has a face, and it is turned toward these men as he speaks.

Were the Old Testament believers worse off in salvation? No. They were saved by the same Christ, through faith in the promise, as we are through faith in the fulfilment (Romans 4; Hebrews 11). Abraham was justified exactly as a believer is today. What they lacked was not salvation but sight: they saw the dawn from a long way off, and we stand in the morning. Our advantage is in clarity and fullness, which is why it is ours to be more grateful, not more proud.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples privately that they were blessed to see and hear what many prophets and kings had longed to see and hear.

On a Tuesday. Open your Bible today as if the sealed book had just been handed to you, because it has. Read one Gospel passage slowly and say to yourself: prophets wanted to see this. If church has become routine, do not wait to feel differently; ask God to restore wonder, and keep looking at Christ until it comes.

For worship. The prophets and kings were not disappointed in the end. Abraham saw his day and was glad; Moses stood with him on the mountain and spoke of his departure (9:30–31); and all of them now see what they longed for, face to face. The Christ they strained toward has come, has finished the work, and has given us the whole story to hold in our hands. We live in the age every saint of old leaned toward. Blessed are our eyes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–37 — The Parable of the Good Samaritan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A lawyer — an expert in the law of Moses — stands up to test Jesus: “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” The wording gives him away twice over. What shall I do assumes the answer is an action; and an inheritance is the one thing nobody works for, since it comes by belonging to a family. He has put a doing-word and a receiving-word in the same sentence without noticing.

Jesus answers with two questions. “What is written in the Law?” asks for the text. “How do you read it?” asks for the man — and a reading is never neutral. The examination has quietly moved.

The lawyer's answer is superb: Deuteronomy 6:5 welded to Leviticus 19:18, the spine of the law in a sentence. And Jesus commends it: “You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.”

Which is perfectly true. Anyone who loved God with the whole heart, soul, strength and mind, and his neighbour as himself, without a lapse, from first breath to last, would indeed live. The catch is not in the offer but in the doer. Jesus is using the law as it was meant to be used — not a ladder to climb but a mirror to look into (Rom. 3:20; Gal. 3:24).

And it works. The lawyer does not go home content; he starts negotiating, “desiring to justify himself.” His question — “who is my neighbour?” — sounds like scholarly precision and is a search for a boundary. If neighbour has edges, there are people outside them, and a man can be entirely obedient and still walk past the rest. It was a live question with real answers on offer: neighbour was generally taken to mean a fellow Israelite, and the Qumran sect required its members to hate the sons of darkness.

The story refuses him a category from its first line: not a Jew, not a Gentile, just “a man.” Stripped and beaten unconscious, he has lost the two things — clothing and speech — by which anyone could have identified him.

A priest passes. A Levite passes. Every listener now expects the third man to be an ordinary Israelite; that is the shape of the joke. What arrives is a Samaritan — and the hostility was ancient, mutual and violent. It is only a chapter since a Samaritan village refused Jesus a bed and James and John asked to burn it.

Then the reversal: not “who is my neighbour?” but “which of these three proved to be a neighbour?” The lawyer cannot say the word. He says “the one who showed him mercy.”
verseByVerse.theology:
The usual defence of the priest is ritual purity: contact with a corpse made him unclean for seven days (Num. 19:11-13), and he could not tell from a distance whether the man was dead. But note the direction of travel — he was going down, away from Jerusalem, towards Jericho, where many priests lived between rotations. His duty is behind him, not ahead.

And the law he was protecting had a clause about exactly this. The same Torah commands a man to help even his enemy's fallen animal (Ex. 23:4-5), and forbids standing by the blood of your neighbour (Lev. 19:16) — two verses before the command the lawyer had just quoted.

Luke offers the priest and Levite no mitigation whatever. He simply says they passed by on the other side, and adds of the second that he “came to the place” — he got closer, looked from nearer, and crossed anyway. The Samaritan, by contrast, “when he saw him, had compassion.” The difference is not in the seeing. It is in what the seeing was allowed to do.

The parable has been read allegorically since Origen: the traveller is humanity, the robbers the devil, the priest and Levite the law and prophets that cannot save, the Samaritan Christ, the inn the church, the two denarii the sacraments. The reading is not without insight — Jesus is indeed the one who binds wounds, pays the debt and promises to return. But the surface command is non-negotiable: “Go and do likewise.”
verseByVerse.examples:
“Had compassion” — compassion felt physically, the thing that turns over inside a person. Luke uses the word at three great moments: of Jesus seeing the widow at Nain (7:13), of the father seeing the prodigal (15:20), and of the Samaritan.

The care is worth itemising, because Jesus itemises it. Bandages torn from his own clothing; his own oil and wine, the standard first-century treatment, now gone; his own animal, which means he walked; a night spent nursing a stranger; two denarii, two days' wages, enough for a fortnight's board; and then an open-ended undertaking — “whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.” A blank cheque, in a foreign town, for an unconscious man of the race that despised him.

“Go and do likewise” is not “go and feel compassion,” which is sentiment, or “go and have good intentions,” which are cheap. It is the specific, costly, schedule-wrecking, wallet-opening action of the Samaritan.

Which is unbearable if read honestly — and that is the moment it matters who is telling the story. One person has kept this command whole. He came down a far longer road, to where we were lying, when we were in no condition to ask; he paid what we could not, and he has promised to come back. The order is never mercy shown in order to earn mercy, but mercy received and then passed on (1 John 4:19). The command remains binding — and it is addressed to people who have already been picked up out of a ditch.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test, saying, 'Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?' He said to him, 'What is written in the Law? How do you read it?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test, saying: Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life? He said to him: what is written in the Law? How do you read it?

And behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test. A lawyer here is not an advocate in a court but an expert in the law of Moses, a scribe: a scholar of Scripture, a man whose whole training was in what God had said and what it required. And Luke tells us his motive before he opens his mouth. This is not an enquiry. It is an examination, conducted in public, by a professional, of a Galilean teacher with no formal qualifications. Students stood to ask a teacher a question, and the posture is respectful; the purpose is not.

Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life? The question is enormous, the most important question there is, and the rich ruler will ask it in the same words (18:18). But the wording gives the man away. What shall I do? The assumption is already in place before the answer arrives: eternal life is a thing achieved by an action, and what he wants is the specification. And there is a second thing buried in it that only shows up on a second reading. He asks what he must do to inherit. An inheritance is the one thing nobody works for. It comes by belonging to a family, and the beneficiary contributes nothing but a relationship. He has put a doing-word and a receiving-word in the same sentence and not noticed.

What is written in the Law? How do you read it? Jesus does not answer. He asks two questions back, and both are respectful: this man knows the law, and he is being invited to say so. Jesus always points to Scripture. But the second question is doing something the first is not. What is written asks for the text. How do you read it asks for the man. That distinction is worth having, because it is the difference between two things that are constantly confused. Two people in a disagreement about Scripture usually have the same words in front of them. What differs is the reading, and a reading is never neutral. It is done by a person, with a history and a set of interests, who wants some things to be true and others not to be. So Jesus has, in a handful of words, moved the examination. The lawyer came to test him on the content of the law. He is about to be tested on what he has been doing with it.

Beginning with Moses. Luke ends his Gospel with the same Teacher asking, in effect, the same question. On the Emmaus road the risen Jesus, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, interprets to two downcast disciples the things concerning himself in all the Scriptures (24:27). The lawyer is about to read Moses accurately and still miss the one standing in front of him, the only man who would ever do what Moses commands. A reading of the law can be correct in every word and still be wrong at the centre. The true reading of what is written ends at Christ.

What does eternal life mean here? Not simply living for ever, which in one sense everyone will do, in joy or in judgement. Eternal life is the life of the age to come, the life of God’s kingdom, beginning now and completed at the resurrection. Jesus defines it elsewhere: this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). So the lawyer is really asking how to belong to God for ever, and the answer will turn out to be a Person, not a performance.

In a sentence. A lawyer tested Jesus by asking what he must do to inherit eternal life, and Jesus asked him what the law said and how he read it.

On a Tuesday. When you have questions about God, go to his word: what is written? Then ask the second question of yourself: how do I read it, and what do I want it to say? Notice the passages you instinctively soften, and read those twice.

For worship. The inheritance the lawyer wanted to earn is held out by the Father to children who cannot earn it. If children, then heirs, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17). The Son came down to make outsiders sons, and the eternal life no one can buy is the gift of his own life, shared.
verseByVerse.note: A lawyer was an expert in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered, 'You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.' And he said to him, 'You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He answered: you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbour as yourself. And he said to him: you have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.

You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself. The lawyer’s answer is superb. He puts together Deuteronomy 6:5, from the Shema, which every Jew recited daily, and Leviticus 19:18, a single line in a chapter of miscellaneous statutes, and welds them into one command, as Jesus himself did elsewhere (Mark 12:29–31). Nobody had to teach him that. He has read the law and seen its spine. And the four terms are not a checklist of separate compartments; they are a way of saying all of you, with nothing held back.
