Heart, soul, strength, mind: the affections, the life, the effort, the thinking. There is no part of a man left over that is not commanded.

You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live. An echo of Leviticus 18:5: if a person does them, he shall live by them. And here is the question that ought to trouble anyone reading this with Paul in mind. Is Jesus really telling a man he can earn eternal life by keeping the law? Take the sentence at face value and it is perfectly true. Anyone who loved God with the whole heart, soul, strength and mind, and his neighbour as himself, without a lapse, from first breath to last, would indeed live. God has never said otherwise. The catch is not in the offer. It is in the doer, and there has never been one, apart from the man saying it.

Law and gospel. So Jesus is using the law exactly as the law was meant to be used: not as a ladder to climb but as a mirror to look into. This is the first use of the law, to convict of sin: through the law comes knowledge of sin (Romans 3:20); all who rely on works of the law are under a curse (Galatians 3:10–12); the law was our guardian until Christ came (Galatians 3:24). Its work is to bring a man to the end of himself so that he will look elsewhere. The perfect law demands perfect love. Only one man ever kept it, Jesus, and his perfect obedience is counted to those who trust him: by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous (Romans 5:19), for Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10:4–5).

Watch how well it works. Jesus says do this and you will live, and the lawyer does not say amen and go home content. The very next thing he does is start negotiating the terms, desiring to justify himself (v. 29). That is a man who has just felt the floor move. He asked how much he had to do, and has been handed a standard that leaves him nowhere to stand; and rather than fall, he reaches for a definition small enough to survive on. The parable that follows is not a softening of the demand. It takes his last handhold away.

If no one can keep the law, why should Christians still try to obey it? Because the law that could never save us now describes the life Christ has saved us into. Once we are justified by faith, the same commands become the shape of gratitude, and the Spirit writes them on our hearts (Jeremiah 31:33; Romans 8:4). We obey not to be accepted but because we are accepted, and our obedience, though imperfect, is pleasing to the Father for Christ’s sake. The law still shows us our sin daily and sends us back to Christ; and it still shows us the path of love. A Christian does not throw away the map because he has stopped trying to earn the journey.

In a sentence. The lawyer summarised the law as loving God with everything and one’s neighbour as oneself, and Jesus told him that if he did this, he would live.

On a Tuesday. Measure yourself honestly against these two commands, not against other people. Have you loved God with all your heart today, or with a corner of it? Have you loved your neighbour as yourself, wanting his good as eagerly as your own? If not, do not reach for a smaller definition. Flee to the one who kept them, and then ask him for grace to love a little more today.

For worship. There was once a man who loved the Lord his God with all his heart, soul, strength and mind, every hour of his life, and loved his neighbour so much that he died for him. He did this, and he lived; and then he gave his life away, so that those who had not done this might live in him. The great commandment was fulfilled by the great Commander himself, and his righteousness is the robe we wear.

parallels.desc: by doing them a person shall live

verseByVerse.quote: But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, 'And who is my neighbor?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus: and who is my neighbour?

But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, And who is my neighbor? Luke gives the motive again, and this time it is the hinge of the whole chapter. Desiring to justify himself: wanting to come out of this conversation still standing, still right, still able to say that he had done what was required. Perhaps also to justify his question, since he already knew the answer. Self-justification is the instinct of the human heart: to define God’s law in a way we can keep. Jesus will later say to the Pharisees, you are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts (16:15). The question that produces the world’s most famous story is asked by a man looking for somewhere to hide.

A clever question. It is not evasive on the surface at all. It sounds like precision, the reasonable request of a careful scholar wanting to know the scope of a term before he applies it. But run it out. If neighbour can be defined, then it has edges. If it has edges, there are people outside them. And if there are people outside them, then a man can love everyone inside the line, be entirely obedient, and walk past the rest with a clear conscience. That is what he is after. Not whom should I love? but whom am I permitted not to?

A live question. Teachers discussing Leviticus 19:18 leaned on its surrounding phrase, the sons of your own people, so neighbour was generally taken to mean a fellow Israelite, and some excluded sinners and enemies too. The sect at Qumran made it a rule to love those inside the community, the sons of light, and to hate the sons of darkness outside it. Every such definition gave a man a boundary and let him rest. The instinct does not present itself as wickedness but as realism: nobody can help everybody, so a line has to be drawn somewhere. And once a line is agreed, the people beyond it stop being a claim on anyone. Jesus is about to tell a story in which the line the lawyer most wanted, the racial and religious one, is crossed by the man he least wanted to admire. He will not answer the question as asked. He will turn it around.

The one who could have justified him. Luke uses the same word again a few chapters on. A tax collector who could only beat his breast and ask for mercy went home justified, and the Pharisee who listed his record did not (18:9–14). The lawyer is trying to do for himself the one thing that can only be done for him, and he is trying it in the presence of the one person who can do it. Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem to become the righteousness that sinners cannot produce. The man looking for a smaller law is standing beside the Lord who justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5).

In a sentence. Wanting to justify himself, the lawyer asked Jesus who his neighbour was.

On a Tuesday. Do you try to limit God’s commands so you can keep them? Listen for the sentences that begin with but surely: but surely I am not expected to love him; but surely that does not apply at work. Let his word define the terms, not you. Name the person you have quietly placed outside the line, and pray for him by name today.

For worship. We came to God with our definitions and our boundaries, wanting to know how little we owed. He came to us with no boundary at all. While we were still sinners, while we were enemies, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8–10). The God who is love never asked who his neighbour was. He crossed every line to make himself ours.

parallels.desc: those who justify yourselves before men

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus replied, 'A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus replied: a man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.

The parable of the good Samaritan. Only Luke records it, and it is one of the best-known stories in the world. That familiarity is its danger: a story so famous that its name has become a word for kindness has lost, for most readers, the shock it was built to deliver.

A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho. Note what we are not told. No name, no trade, no nationality, no religion. He is simply a man, and the omission is deliberate: the lawyer asked for a category, and the first thing the story refuses him is a category. The road is real, and it was notorious. Jerusalem sits about 2,500 feet above sea level; Jericho lies roughly 800 feet below it, some seventeen miles (27 km) away. The road drops over three thousand feet (900 m) through limestone gorges and blind bends, with caves and rocks all along it. Jerome, living nearby centuries later, says it was still called the red or bloody ascent, and it was known as bandit country.

He fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. Stripped, beaten and unconscious, unable to help himself, perhaps dying. Those details remove the only two things a passer-by could have used to identify him. Clothing told you a man’s nationality and status; speech told you the rest. Naked and silent, he is unclassifiable. He is a human being in a ditch, and there is no way to work out whether he is one of ours.

Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. Why? Perhaps fear of the robbers; perhaps ritual purity, since contact with a corpse made a priest unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11–13) and he could not tell whether the man was dead; perhaps simple indifference. Jesus gives no reasons; excuses do not matter. But note the direction: he was going down, away from Jerusalem, toward Jericho, where many priests lived between their weeks of service. His duty was behind him, so defilement would have cost him a week of inconvenience, not a turn at the altar. And the law he was protecting commands a man to help even his enemy’s fallen animal (Exodus 23:4–5), and forbids standing by while your neighbour’s life is in danger (Leviticus 19:16), two verses before the command the lawyer had just quoted.

So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side. Levites assisted the priests in the temple: religious, respectable, knowledgeable about the law. Luke adds a phrase for the second man: he came to the place. He got closer. He looked, from nearer, and crossed anyway. The two men who should have helped, who knew the law about loving one’s neighbour best, did nothing. Religion without love.

The shape of the story. And every listener now knows what comes next, because these stories run in threes and the third man is always the ordinary Israelite. Priest, Levite, layman. It is the familiar shape of every story anyone has ever told about the temple establishment failing while the common man does right. What arrives instead detonates the entire structure.

The same road, later. Luke will bring Jesus onto this very road. On his last journey he passes through Jericho and climbs toward Jerusalem (18:35–19:28). On the way a blind beggar shouts from the roadside, and the crowd tells him to be quiet; Jesus stops, has him brought, and gives him his sight (18:35–43). In Jericho itself he stops under a tree for a man the whole town had written off (19:1–10). The one telling this story does not pass by on the other side of the Jericho road. He stops for the man at the edge of it, on his way up to die.

Is it always wrong to pass by someone in need? Not every passing by is sin. There are real dangers, prior duties and needs you cannot meet, and sometimes the loving thing is to call for help rather than to stop yourself. A woman alone at night is not commanded to pull over on a dark road. But the priest and Levite had no such reasons that Jesus thought worth mentioning; they simply did not want the cost. The test is honest: am I unable, or merely unwilling? Has God put this person in my path, and is there something I can actually do? If so, the ditch is my business.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a man robbed and left half dead on the Jericho road, whom first a priest and then a Levite saw and passed by on the other side.

On a Tuesday. Who have you passed by on the other side? The colleague whose marriage is falling apart, the neighbour whose bins have not moved in a week, the widow at church who sits alone. Religious knowledge is no substitute for love, and a busy schedule of good things can make a very convenient other side of the road.

For worship. We were the man in the ditch, stripped and half dead, and no priest or Levite of the old order could lift us. The law passed by on the other side, not because it was evil, but because it had no power to heal. And then one came down the road from heaven to the place where we lay, and did not cross over. Blessed be the God who did not leave us there.
verseByVerse.note: The road from Jerusalem down to Jericho drops over 3,000 feet in about 17 miles through barren, rocky country, and was notorious for robbers. Touching a dead body made a priest unclean.

parallels.desc: no priest shall make himself unclean for the dead

verseByVerse.quote: But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion. He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he set him on his own animal and brought him to an inn and took care of him. And the next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying, ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion. He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he set him on his own animal and brought him to an inn and took care of him. The next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying: take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.

But a Samaritan. Jesus’ hearers expected the third man to be an ordinary Jewish layman. Instead, a Samaritan. The hostility was ancient, mutual and violent. Samaritans descended from the remnant of the northern kingdom mixed with settlers brought in after the Assyrian conquest; they had their own temple on Mount Gerizim, their own edition of the five books of Moses, and no use for Jerusalem, and Jews regarded them as heretics and half-breeds. Within living memory, Josephus says, Samaritans had scattered human bones in the temple courts at Passover to defile it. Jews had no dealings with Samaritans (John 4:9), and only a chapter earlier a Samaritan village had refused Jesus a bed (9:52–54). This is the man Jesus makes the hero, to a Jewish scholar of the law, in answer to a question about who counts as a neighbour.

And when he saw him, he had compassion. All three saw. Only one had compassion. The verb is esplanchnisthē, from the word for the inward organs: compassion felt physically, the thing that turns over inside a person. Luke uses it at three great moments: of Jesus seeing the widow at Nain (7:13), of the father seeing the prodigal on the road (15:20), and here. Compassion is the heart of the story. And note the sequence, because it is the same sequence the priest and Levite had and broke. They saw and crossed over. He saw and was moved and went to him. The difference is not in the seeing. It is in what the seeing was allowed to do.

He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Jesus itemises the care. He bound up his wounds, with whatever cloth he had, since there is nothing else on that road. He poured on oil and wine, the standard first-century treatment, wine to cleanse and oil to soothe, both of them his own travelling supplies, now gone. There is a quiet irony: oil and wine were also offerings in the temple the priest had just left. The Samaritan poured them out in the true worship, for I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6).

Then he set him on his own animal and brought him to an inn and took care of him. Setting him on his own animal means the Samaritan walked, at the pace of an injured man, in robber country, for however many miles remained. He brought him to an inn and took care of him: that is a night, spent nursing a stranger.

Two denarii. In the morning: two denarii, two days’ wages for a labourer, enough to cover board for perhaps a fortnight. Then the sentence that goes furthest of all: whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back. Without payment, a penniless guest could have been held as a debtor. He has just written a blank cheque, in a foreign town, for an unconscious man of the race that despises him, and bound himself to return.

Where Christians differ: Christ the Samaritan? From the early church onward (Origen, Augustine), many read the parable as an allegory of salvation: the man is Adam, the robbers are the devil, the priest and Levite are the law and the prophets, the Samaritan is Christ, the inn is the church, the two denarii the two commandments of love, and the return is the second coming. Verdict: the parable’s primary meaning, given by Jesus himself, is ethical: go and do likewise (v. 37). It answers the lawyer’s question, who is my neighbour?, and reading every detail as a code goes beyond the text. Yet there is a true echo: Christ is the supreme neighbour, who came to us when we were his enemies, half dead in our sins, and gave himself to save us (Romans 5:8–10). The parable both commands love and points to the love that makes it possible, and every Christian’s mercy flows from his.

What if helping someone could be dangerous or be taken advantage of? The Samaritan took a real risk, and love sometimes will. But wisdom is not the enemy of love. He did not hand the man his purse; he paid the innkeeper and arranged care, which is both generous and sensible. You may help through the right channels, involve others, set limits that protect your family, and decline to fund what would harm someone. What love may not do is use prudence as a disguise for indifference. Ask: what would genuinely help this person, and what part of that can I carry?

In a sentence. A despised Samaritan, moved with compassion, tended the man’s wounds, took him to an inn, cared for him, and paid for his ongoing care.

On a Tuesday. Love is costly and practical. Whose wounds can you bind up this week, whatever it costs? It may be an evening, a lift to hospital, a meal cooked, a bill quietly paid, a long conversation with someone whose politics or background you dislike. Notice whether there is a particular kind of person you would find it hardest to help, and ask God to make that the person you notice first.

For worship. The despised Samaritan is the clearest picture in the Gospels of the despised Saviour. He was despised and rejected by men (Isaiah 53:3); they called him a Samaritan and said he had a demon (John 8:48). He came to where we lay, was moved with compassion, bound up the broken-hearted, paid our debt with his own blood, and has promised: I will come back. Every act of mercy we do is a small copy of the mercy that found us on the road.
verseByVerse.note: Samaritans and Jews despised each other. Oil soothed wounds and wine cleaned them. The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage — two could cover some days at an inn.

parallels.desc: the captives clothed, anointed and carried on donkeys to Jericho

verseByVerse.quote: Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?' He said, 'The one who showed him mercy.' And Jesus said to him, 'You go, and do likewise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbour to the man who fell among the robbers? He said: the one who showed him mercy. And Jesus said to him: you go, and do likewise.

Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers? The question has been turned inside out, and that is the parable’s most important move. The lawyer asked, who is my neighbour?, which puts the other person under examination and the questioner safely in the chair. Jesus asks which of the three proved to be a neighbour, which puts the questioner in the road and asks what he did. It is no longer a question about the boundaries of obligation. It is a question about what kind of man is walking past. Neighbourliness is not defined by the other person’s status, but by my compassion.

He said, The one who showed him mercy. He cannot say it. The answer is a single word, the Samaritan, and he takes a whole phrase to avoid it. Luke leaves that exposed without a syllable of comment, and it is the most human moment in the chapter: a man who has understood the story perfectly and cannot get the word out of his mouth.

You go, and do likewise. And there the parable stops, which is unbearable if you have been reading honestly. The command is not lowered by an inch at the end. Stop asking whom you must love, and start loving whoever is in need, even your enemy. Go and be the Samaritan: cross a racial hatred, spend your own money, give your own time, take on an open-ended liability for a stranger who can never repay you. Anyone who finds that manageable has not understood it. Anyone who has understood it is standing exactly where the lawyer is standing, looking for somewhere to put his feet. If the lawyer is honest, he will find that he cannot love like this by his own strength. He needs a new heart. The law drives us to Christ.

Who is telling the story. Now it matters who is telling the story. One person has kept this command whole. He came down a far longer road than the one from Jerusalem to Jericho, to where we were lying, when we were stripped and half dead and in no condition to ask. He bound up the wounds at his own expense. He paid what we could not, and he has promised to come back. And he is on the road to Jerusalem as he speaks, to settle the account himself.

Does this mean I must help everyone in need? The parable defines a neighbour as the one who shows mercy to the person in front of him, whoever he is. It does not tell us how to meet every need in the world, nor is it a programme for the state. You cannot help everyone, and God does not ask you to. But it forbids us to decide that someone in real need, whom God has put in our path, is not our concern because of who he is. Begin with the household of faith and those nearest you (Galatians 6:10), and let your circle of mercy keep widening.

Mercy received, then mercy passed on. The order is never mercy shown in order to earn mercy. It is mercy received, and then mercy passed on: we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Go and do likewise remains a command, and it remains binding. But it is addressed to people who have already been picked up out of a ditch, and that is the only reason it is good news and not a sentence.

In a sentence. Jesus asked which of the three had been a neighbour, and when the lawyer answered that it was the one who showed mercy, Jesus told him to go and do the same.

On a Tuesday. Do not ask who your neighbour is. Ask whose neighbour you can be today. Look for the person in your path whom you would naturally file under not my concern, and do one concrete merciful thing for him. And when you fail, as you will, do not reach for a smaller definition. Go back to the Samaritan who picked you up, and let his mercy send you out again.

For worship. The lawyer could not bring himself to say the name of the one who showed mercy. God has said it for ever. To his Son, who humbled himself to the point of death on a cross for people who had despised him, he has given the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow (Philippians 2:8–10). The word that stuck in the lawyer’s throat will be on every tongue in heaven, and it will be a name of mercy.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter closes in a house in a village — Bethany, though Luke does not name it — and the placing is deliberate. The Samaritan has just poured out his time and money on a road, with “go and do likewise” still in the air. Now a woman does exactly that, and is gently told she has missed something.

Martha “welcomed him into her house” — her house, Luke says, which is unusual enough to notice, and she received him as an honoured guest. She is not a woman lacking spiritual interest. She is the one who let him in.

Mary “sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching,” and both halves of that would have struck a first-century reader. Sitting at a teacher's feet is the technical posture of a disciple — Paul describes his own training as being brought up “at the feet of Gamaliel” (Acts 22:3). And that place was not open to a woman. Mary sat down in it, Jesus let her, and in three verses he will defend her right to be there against her own sister. Luke reports it in a subordinate clause, as though it were ordinary — which, from now on, it is.

Martha is “distracted with much serving” — pulled around, dragged in different directions. It is not being busy but being torn. And the thing tearing her is service: she is doing exactly what the women of 8:3 were commended for.

Her complaint takes three steps and each goes further. She interrupts his teaching; she accuses her sister in front of the guests; and then she accuses him. “Do you not care?” is not a request but a charge, levelled at the Lord she has just welcomed in — and then “tell her,” which does not even ask him to intervene but tells him what to say.

Every word of it is what an exhausted person says, and she is not wrong about the facts. What has happened is that a service began as a gift and turned, somewhere between the door and the fire, into a grievance — and the sign of it is that she is now keeping score.

“Martha, Martha” is the address of someone who sees the whole of a person: the same register as “Simon, Simon” (22:31), “Jerusalem, Jerusalem” (13:34), “Saul, Saul” (Acts 9:4). And the diagnosis is not of her workload but of her interior — “anxious,” the worry he will forbid his disciples (12:22-26).
verseByVerse.theology:
Mary sitting at the Lord's feet is the posture of discipleship, and Luke has used the phrase once already of the Gerasene man restored to his right mind (8:35). In the first century women did not ordinarily receive rabbinic instruction, and the posture of female discipleship was itself a quiet revolution. Jesus does not redirect Mary to help; he defends her right to receive what he is giving.

“The good portion” plays on a word for a share at a meal — and Martha, of all people, would have felt it, since she is in the kitchen dividing portions while Mary has taken the one that matters.

“Which will not be taken away from her” carries the force of a promise. What Mary is receiving cannot be confiscated. The dinner will be eaten by nightfall and forgotten by the week's end; the word Mary is taking in is permanent, the living and abiding word of God (1 Pet. 1:23).

Some manuscripts read “few things are necessary, or only one” at v.42; the shorter reading is very likely original and the sense is unaffected either way. What lasts defines what is necessary, and what is necessary defines what must not be sacrificed to the urgent.
verseByVerse.examples:
The scene speaks to the perennial tension between doing and being. It does not abolish the tension; it orders it. Martha's service is not wrong — her anxiety is. And this is not a rebuke of practical work: Luke has just spent a chapter praising a man who bandaged a stranger and paid his bills.

It is a statement about order. Martha's work was needed. What was not needed was for it to be done by a woman who had stopped sitting down.

“Do you not care?” is worth naming for anyone who has prayed like it, because a good many have. It is the same accusation the disciples threw at him in the boat (Mark 4:38) — what resentment sounds like when it finally reaches God. And notice what he does with it: he does not rebuke her for the tone. He answers what is underneath it.

The Christian who serves without ever receiving will end up exactly where she is: efficient, indispensable, exhausted, and quietly furious with the people who are not helping — including, in the end, with the Lord it was all being done for. The cure is not less service. It is the recovery of the one thing that makes service a gift rather than a grievance.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. And a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. A woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. She had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to his teaching.

The placing. After the parable about doing, love your neighbour, comes a story about listening. The two belong together: loving God by hearing his word, and loving neighbour by serving. The chapter has just finished with a Samaritan pouring out his time and money on a road, and go and do likewise is still hanging in the air. Now a woman does exactly that, and is gently told she has missed something. Luke has arranged the two stories with care: Martha and Mary show the balance, and the order.

Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. Luke does not name it. John does: Bethany, two miles from Jerusalem, the home of Martha, Mary and their brother Lazarus (John 11:1; 12:1–3). Luke may leave it unnamed because in his ordering of the journey Jesus is not yet near Jerusalem.

And a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. It is her house; Luke says so, and it is unusual enough to be worth noticing. Martha was apparently the head of the household. And she welcomed him as an honoured guest. In a culture where hospitality was a sacred obligation, a travelling teacher with his disciples, perhaps thirteen or more people, meant a great deal of work, and Martha opened her door to the lot of them. This is not a woman being criticised for lacking spiritual interest. She is the one who let him in.

And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to his teaching. Sat at the feet is a technical phrase, the posture of a disciple under a rabbi; Paul describes being brought up at the feet of Gamaliel (Acts 22:3). Mary had taken a student’s place, and it was not normally open to her. Women were taught the law as it applied to their duties, and the formal relationship of teacher and student was a male arrangement. Mary sat down in it, Jesus let her, and within minutes he will defend her right to be there against her own sister. Luke reports it without a flourish, as though it were the ordinary thing; which, from now on, it is. And she listened: the tense means she kept on listening.

At the Lord’s feet. Luke keeps bringing people to this place. A sinful woman wept over his feet (7:38); the man freed from a legion of demons sat there, clothed and in his right mind (8:35); Jairus fell there (8:41); a healed Samaritan will fall there giving thanks (17:16). Mary sits where the forgiven, the rescued and the grateful sit, and Luke calls the one she sits before simply the Lord. A rabbi’s pupil sat at his teacher’s feet to learn the law. No rabbi ever said that listening to him was the one thing necessary. This Teacher will say it within the hour (v. 42), and only the Lord could say it truly.

Does Mary’s place at Jesus’ feet mean women may hold every office in the church? It means women are full disciples: called to learn, to know the Scriptures deeply and to sit under Christ’s word as fully as any man, which was a revolution in its day. That is the point Luke is making. The question of who may serve as an elder or preach to the gathered church is answered elsewhere, where the New Testament reserves that office to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7). This app holds that complementarian view, with headship understood as self-giving service, never domination. Mary’s example rebukes any church that keeps women from learning deeply. It does not settle the eldership question either way.

In a sentence. In a village, Martha welcomed Jesus into her home, and her sister Mary sat at his feet listening to his teaching.

On a Tuesday. Make time today to sit at Jesus’ feet: open his word and listen before you speak or serve. If you are the one who always opens the door and does the work, thank God for that gift, and then make sure you also take the student’s place. And if you are a woman who has been told, in so many words, that deep study of Scripture is not really for you, know that Jesus defended your seat.

For worship. The Lord of glory sat in an ordinary house and taught a woman who was not supposed to be learning, and called it the good portion. He is the Teacher who welcomes every disciple to his feet, and his word is life. How gracious of the Son of God, on his way to the cross, to stop in a village kitchen and give himself to whoever would sit and listen.
verseByVerse.note: John places Martha and Mary in Bethany, near Jerusalem. Sitting at a teacher’s feet was the place of a disciple.

verseByVerse.quote: But Martha was distracted with much serving. And she went up to him and said, 'Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Martha was distracted with much serving. She went up to him and said: Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me.

But Martha was distracted with much serving. The verb is periespato: literally to be pulled around, dragged in different directions. It is not a word for being busy. It is a word for being torn. And the thing tearing her is much serving, diakonia, the word that will become the church’s term for ministry. She is doing exactly what the women of 8:3 were commended for doing. Her service was good, and necessary. So the problem in this house is not that Martha chose work over devotion. The problem is what the work has become inside her: it pulled her away from Jesus. Luke marks the moment it surfaces.

Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? She went up to him and said it, and added: tell her then to help me. Three things in one sentence, each a step further than the last. She interrupts his teaching. She accuses her sister in front of the guests. And, this is the sharp one, she accuses him. Do you not care? That is not a request. It is a charge, and it is levelled at the Lord she has just welcomed into her house. They are almost the words the disciples threw at him in the storm: teacher, do you not care that we are perishing? (Mark 4:38). Anxiety turns into resentment, against others and against God. She has moved from serving him to reproaching him, and the distance between those two things was crossed in an afternoon, in a kitchen, doing a good thing. Then tell her: she does not even ask him to intervene. She tells him what to say. Busy, worried people often judge others who are not as busy.

Not hard on her. It would be easy to be hard on her, and it would be a mistake. Every word of her complaint is what an exhausted person says. She is not wrong about the facts: she is serving alone, and the meal does have to be produced, and somebody has to do it. What has happened is that a service began as a gift and turned, somewhere between the door and the fire, into a grievance, and the sign of it is that she is now keeping score. Do you not care? is what resentment sounds like when it finally reaches God. And notice what he does with it: he does not rebuke her for the tone. He answers what is underneath it.

Is it wrong to complain to God? Not to bring him your distress: the psalms are full of honest lament, how long, O LORD?, and he invites us to cast all our anxieties on him, because he cares for us (1 Peter 5:7). What Martha shows is the moment honest weariness hardens into accusation, when do you not care is said as a verdict rather than a cry. The cure is to tell him the truth about how you feel, and then to let him tell you the truth about himself. He does care. That is precisely why he will not simply give Martha what she asks.

The guest who serves. Martha thinks the serving in this house runs one way, from her kitchen to his table. Luke knows better. At the last supper Jesus will ask who is greater, the one at table or the one who serves, and answer: I am among you as the one who serves (22:27). He even promises that when he returns the master will dress himself for service and wait on his own servants at table (12:37). Mary has grasped what Martha has not. When this Lord comes into a house, he has come chiefly to give, and the first duty of his hosts is to receive.

In a sentence. Martha, distracted by her many preparations, complained to Jesus that her sister had left her to serve alone and asked him to tell Mary to help.

On a Tuesday. Even good service for Jesus can distract you from Jesus. Notice when busyness turns into resentment: the sigh as you clear up after the church lunch, the mental list of who never helps, the irritation at the person who seems to have time to pray. Those are signals, not proofs that you are wrong to serve. Stop, sit down for five minutes with him, and let him take the score card out of your hand.

For worship. The Lord whom Martha accused of not caring was on his way to the clearest proof of care the world has ever seen. In the garden he knelt and prayed in anguish (22:41); yet he did not charge his Father with neglect. He said, not my will, but yours, be done (22:42), and went on to serve disciples who had fallen asleep while he prayed. He kept no score. He knew the Father cared, and on the cross he made certain that we would know it too.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord answered her, 'Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord answered her: Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.

Martha, Martha. The doubled name is not impatience. Luke records the same double address at other moments, and the register is always the same: Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you (22:31); O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often would I have gathered your children (13:34); Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). It is the address of someone who sees the whole of a person and is about to say something she needs and will not enjoy. A gentle rebuke, from love.

You are anxious and troubled about many things. Two verbs, and neither is busy. Anxious is merimnas, the word for the worry Jesus forbids in 12:22–26, the same root as the cares that choke the word in the parable of the soils (8:14). Troubled (thorybazē) means agitated, in an uproar, flustered. He is not diagnosing her workload but her interior: these are words for a heart not resting in God. She is not too busy; she is worried, about many things.

But one thing is necessary. If your Bible has a footnote here, it is a real one: some manuscripts read few things are necessary, or only one, as if Jesus were saying that a simple meal would do. The shorter reading, one thing, is very likely original, and the sense is unaffected either way. Not just one dish, but the one thing that matters most: listening to Jesus. David knew it: one thing have I asked of the LORD, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD (Psalm 27:4). David’s one thing was the LORD himself. Here the one thing is to sit at Jesus’ feet and hear him, and he says it without apology. Quietly, in a village kitchen, he is standing where the LORD stands in the psalm.

Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her. Two words carry it. Portion (meris) is the word for a share at a meal, and there is a play on it that Martha, of all people, would have felt: she is in the kitchen dividing up portions, and Mary has taken the one that matters, the food of Jesus’ word. Man does not live by bread alone (Deuteronomy 8:3); Jesus said his own food was to do the will of the one who sent him (John 4:32–34). And “will not be taken away” is a promise: what Mary is receiving cannot be confiscated. The dinner Martha is making will be eaten by nightfall and forgotten by the week’s end. The word Mary is taking in is permanent. Jesus defends her.

What it does not mean. This is not a rebuke of practical service, and Luke has just spent a parable praising a man who bandaged a stranger and paid his bills. It is not a recommendation of contemplation over action, or of the monastery over the kitchen. And it is certainly not an instruction that meals should go uncooked. Martha was not wrong to serve. It is a statement about order. Listening to Jesus comes first, and is the source of true service. Martha’s work was needed. What was not needed was for it to be done by a woman who had stopped sitting down. Service without listening becomes anxious and resentful, and the Christian who serves without ever receiving will end up exactly where Martha is: efficient, indispensable, exhausted, and quietly furious with the people who are not helping, including, in the end, with the Lord she is doing it all for.

With young children, a job and an elderly parent, how can I possibly sit at his feet? The good portion is not measured in hours, and Jesus is not asking a mother of three to keep a monk’s timetable. It is a matter of where your heart rests. Take what you can: ten minutes with a Psalm before the house wakes, a passage read aloud at breakfast, a sermon listened to while you drive, a prayer while you wash up. Guard the Lord’s Day as a time to receive. And let the busy hours themselves be done at his feet, in the sense of being done for him and in dependence on him. Little and real is better than much and anxious.

In a sentence. Jesus gently told Martha that she was anxious about many things, but only one thing was necessary, and Mary had chosen the best portion, which would not be taken from her.

On a Tuesday. What are you anxious and troubled about today? Write the many things down, and then put them aside for a few minutes while you read one passage and pray. The list will still be there; you will not be the same person facing it. Before the next busy week of serving begins, sit down first.

For worship. The good portion is a Person, and nothing can take him away. The LORD is my portion, says my soul, therefore I will hope in him (Lamentations 3:24). Meals are eaten and forgotten; kingdoms rise and fall; but the word of the Lord remains for ever, and the Lord himself is the inheritance of everyone who sits at his feet. Martha’s dinner was gone by nightfall. Mary’s portion is still hers, and it is the same one offered to us.

10.text: <sup>1</sup> After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of him, two by two, into every town and place where he himself was about to go. <sup>2</sup> And he said to them, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest. <sup>3</sup> Go your way; behold, I am sending you out as lambs in the midst of wolves. <sup>4</sup> Carry no moneybag, no knapsack, no sandals, and greet no one on the road. <sup>5</sup> Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace be to this house!’ <sup>6</sup> And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him. But if not, it will return to you. <sup>7</sup> And remain in the same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the laborer deserves his wages. Do not go from house to house. <sup>8</sup> Whenever you enter a town and they receive you, eat what is set before you. <sup>9</sup> Heal the sick in it and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’ <sup>10</sup> But whenever you enter a town and they do not receive you, go into its streets and say, <sup>11</sup> ‘Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Nevertheless know this, that the kingdom of God has come near.’ <sup>12</sup> I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town. <sup>13</sup> “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. <sup>14</sup> But it will be more bearable in the judgment for Tyre and Sidon than for you. <sup>15</sup> And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You shall be brought down to Hades. <sup>16</sup> “The one who hears you hears me, and the one who rejects you rejects me, and the one who rejects me rejects him who sent me.” <sup>17</sup> The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!” <sup>18</sup> And he said to them, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. <sup>19</sup> Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall hurt you. <sup>20</sup> Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” <sup>21</sup> In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. <sup>22</sup> All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.” <sup>23</sup> Then turning to the disciples he said privately, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see! <sup>24</sup> For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.” <sup>25</sup> And behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test, saying, “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” <sup>26</sup> He said to him, “What is written in the Law? How do you read it?” <sup>27</sup> And he answered, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.” <sup>28</sup> And he said to him, “You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live.” <sup>29</sup> But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?” <sup>30</sup> Jesus replied, “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. <sup>31</sup> Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. <sup>32</sup> So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side. <sup>33</sup> But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion. <sup>34</sup> He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he set him on his own animal and brought him to an inn and took care of him. <sup>35</sup> And the next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying, ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.’ <sup>36</sup> Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?” <sup>37</sup> He said, “The one who showed him mercy.” And Jesus said to him, “You go, and do likewise.” <sup>38</sup> Now as they went on their way, Jesus entered a village. And a woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. <sup>39</sup> And she had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching. <sup>40</sup> But Martha was distracted with much serving. And she went up to him and said, “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her then to help me.” <sup>41</sup> But the Lord answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, <sup>42</sup> but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.”

11.title: Prayer, Darkness, and the Woes of the Pharisees
11.overview:
Chapter 11 divides into three movements of escalating intensity. It opens with the disciples' request — “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples” — and Jesus's response: the Lord's Prayer and two parables about persistent asking. It continues with the controversy over Beelzebul, where Jesus is accused of casting out demons by the power of the prince of demons, and responds with the parable of the strong man, the sign of Jonah, and a warning about the darkness that replaces expelled light. And it closes with the most sustained series of woes in Luke's Gospel — six pronouncements against the Pharisees and lawyers that are simultaneously the most confrontational and the most sorrowful words Jesus speaks in public.

The chapter's movement from prayer (vv. 1–13) to spiritual warfare (vv. 14–36) to religious condemnation (vv. 37–54) is not a random sequence. The prayer section establishes the relationship with the Father that makes spiritual life possible. The Beelzebul controversy shows what happens when the kingdom's power is at work in the world — it provokes opposition, demands decision, and warns against the neutrality that is actually a form of hostility. And the woes reveal what becomes of religious life when it loses the relationship with the Father — when the form of religion remains but the substance has been evacuated, replaced by the performance of piety for the wrong audience.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus is praying, and when he finishes one of the disciples asks: “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.” Of everything on offer in three years beside the Son of God — the healings, the stilled storm, the knowledge of men's thoughts — the one thing a disciple asked to be taught was how to talk to his Father.

Luke's version is shorter than Matthew's (Matt. 6:9-13), and that difference has unsettled readers who learned the prayer by heart as children. Where is “who art in heaven”? Where is “thy will be done”? An older Bible will have them at this very verse and a modern one will not.

There is nothing sinister in it. Luke's prayer was always the shorter of the two, but the version the church actually prayed aloud, week after week for centuries, was Matthew's — and scribes copying Luke knew that fuller wording by heart. Line by line, over generations, they filled Luke out to match what their lips already said. It is one of the most understandable corrections in the history of copying and one of the easiest to detect: the earliest manuscripts of Luke are short, and the additions match Matthew word for word. Nothing was lost. Every phrase you were taught is genuinely the Lord's; it is simply Matthew who recorded it.

And Luke's shorter form is worth having in its own right, because two versions tell us something one could not. Jesus plainly gave this prayer more than once, and not in identical words. Matthew says “pray then like this”; Luke says “when you pray, say.” Set them side by side and the conclusion is unavoidable: this was never handed down as a formula to be recited syllable-perfect on pain of not counting. It is a shape for praying — a floor to build on, not a ceiling.

The prayer opens with one word that was a revolution. The Old Testament calls God Father perhaps a dozen times, nearly always of his relation to Israel as a nation; what is almost entirely absent is an individual addressing him that way in prayer. The word Jesus himself uses in Gethsemane is the Aramaic Abba (Mark 14:36) — family vocabulary, and there is little or no evidence that Jews of that period addressed God with it in prayer.

Then five petitions: his name, his kingdom, our bread, our forgiveness, our protection. God first, then us — and the order is not decoration. A prayer that begins with God's honour can bring every human need afterwards without becoming a list submitted to a dispenser.
verseByVerse.theology:
The address “Father” is the theological revolution of this prayer. Paul will name what has happened: “you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'” (Rom. 8:15). The address is not a warmer name for the same relationship; it is a different relationship — the Son's own, opened to people with no natural claim to it.

“Hallowed be your name” asks that God be treated as holy, since his name cannot be made more holy than it is. A name in Hebrew thought is the person as he is known, so the petition asks that he be known, honoured and reverenced as what he actually is — first by the one praying, and then by everybody else. It is a request the person praying is volunteering to be part of the answer to.

“Your kingdom come” is the central petition and the shortest, and it cannot be prayed at a distance. To ask for God's rule to come is to ask for one's own to end, and there is no version of the sentence that leaves the person praying in charge of the parts he was hoping to keep. Every honest praying of it is a small abdication.

“Daily” bread — the ESV margin gives “our bread for tomorrow,” enough for the coming day. It is a small request, deliberately: enough for today, asked today, and again tomorrow.
verseByVerse.examples:
The “for” in “forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive” has troubled readers, and it must not become a bargain. God's forgiveness is not purchased by ours; the prayer has just called him Father, which nobody earns.

What the clause does is make our forgiving the evidence that his has landed — a diagnostic, not a transaction. A man who has grasped the size of what has been cancelled on his own account cannot go on with a ledger open against his neighbour; and if he can, the honest question is whether he has understood the first half of the sentence at all. Matthew makes the connection explicit (Matt. 6:14-15).

Note the tense, too: “we ourselves forgive,” present and continuing. Not “we forgave, once, years ago.” It is a standing policy.

And “lead us not into temptation” is not a fear that God might try to make us sin, which James forbids (Jas. 1:13). It is the prayer of a person who knows his own weakness well enough to ask not to be brought to the edge of it — which is a far more realistic prayer than asking for strength to survive the edge.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him, 'Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him: Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.

Meaning first. Luke 11 is a chapter about the God who hears and the people who will not. Jesus teaches his disciples to pray: the Lord’s Prayer, the friend at midnight, and the promise of the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Then, accused of casting out demons by Satan, he answers that the kingdom of God has arrived, that a stronger one is plundering the strong man’s house, and that there is no neutral ground. A sign-seeking generation is offered only the sign of Jonah. The chapter ends at a Pharisee’s table with six woes against religion that cleans the outside and leaves the heart full of greed, and with the scholars of the law beginning to hunt him. The thread through it all is the difference between knowing about God and knowing him as Father.

Now Jesus was praying in a certain place. Notice the order. He prays; they watch; and when he has finished, one of them asks. Luke shows Jesus at prayer more than any other Gospel: at the baptism (3:21), withdrawing to desolate places (5:16), all night before choosing the Twelve (6:12), before the great question about who he is (9:18), on the mountain where his face changed (9:28–29). He does not tell us what they saw in his praying, and he does not need to. Something about the way this man prayed was different enough that men who had grown up saying prayers several times a day concluded they did not know how.

Lord, teach us to pray. They had watched him still a storm, feed thousands, raise the dead, and send a legion of demons out of a man with a word, and some of them had just come back from a mission where preaching and healing were both happening. Yet of everything on offer in walking beside the Son of God, the one thing a disciple asked to be taught was how to talk to his Father. It is a wise request. Prayer must be learned; it does not come naturally to sinners, and the best teacher is the one who prays perfectly.

As John taught his disciples. Teachers and movements had characteristic prayers; they functioned as a kind of identity, a way of marking out what a group was for. John had given his followers one, and Jesus’ disciples want the same from him: not merely instruction in the discipline, but a prayer that belongs to them, that expresses who they are as his.

Why does prayer feel so hard? Almost every Christian who has been at it for a while will admit, if pressed honestly, that prayer is the part that never quite settles. It is the first thing to go in a busy week and the last thing to come back. Part of the reason is that prayer is the one Christian activity with no audience and no visible result in the moment; part is that our flesh resists dependence; and part is that the enemy hates it. The answer is not a technique, and it is not more determination. It is what the disciple did here: to say out loud, to the one person who can do anything about it, that he does not know how. Then to start small and keep going, using the words Jesus gives.

In a sentence. After watching Jesus pray, one of his disciples asked him to teach them to pray, as John had taught his disciples.

On a Tuesday. Make the disciples’ request your own today, in so many words: Lord, teach me to pray. Then give him five unhurried minutes, perhaps praying slowly through the prayer that follows. If you have let prayer slide for weeks, do not wait until you feel worthy to start again. The disciples asked because they could not, and that is exactly the qualification required.

For worship. The Son of God, who had the Father’s presence every moment, still went away to pray. He prayed for Peter that his faith would not fail (22:32), prayed in agony in the garden, prayed for those who crucified him, and he lives now to make intercession for us (Hebrews 7:25). The one who taught us to pray is praying still, and our stumbling words reach the Father on the strength of his.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers commonly gave their disciples a characteristic prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'When you pray, say: ‘Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: when you pray, say: Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come.

The Lord’s Prayer. Luke’s version is shorter than Matthew’s (Matthew 6:9–13). Jesus probably taught it on more than one occasion, in slightly different forms. Luke’s has five petitions; Matthew’s seven. The ESV notes that some manuscripts expand Luke’s version to match Matthew’s. It is both a prayer to pray, as the church has done ever since, and a pattern for all prayer. Notice the order: God’s concerns first, then ours.

Is this prayer a form to recite or a pattern to follow? Both. Luke says when you pray, say, and Matthew pray then like this (Matthew 6:9). Christians may pray these words together, as the church has done from the beginning, as long as they are prayed from the heart and not as empty repetition (Matthew 6:7). And they shape all our other prayers: praise before petition, God’s glory before our needs, forgiveness alongside bread. A believer who prays only these words has prayed well; a believer who never prays them has missed a gift.

Father. One word, and it was a revolution: simply Father, without our or in heaven. The Old Testament calls God Father perhaps a dozen times, nearly always of his relation to Israel as a nation (Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 63:16); an individual Israelite almost never addresses him so in prayer. The standard addresses were LORD, God of our fathers, King of the universe: titles that keep a proper distance. Behind Luke’s Greek stands the Aramaic Abba, the word Jesus uses in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). It is not baby-talk; grown men used it of their fathers. But it is family vocabulary, and there is little or no evidence that Jews of the period prayed to God with it. He hands it to them as the first word.

The Son’s own word, opened to us. Paul will later say exactly what has happened: you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, Abba! Father! (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). The address is not a nicer name for the same relationship. It is a different relationship, and it is the Son’s own, opened to people who have no natural claim to it whatsoever. We pray as children, adopted by grace. This is the privilege of the gospel: the holy God is our Father.

What if my earthly father was absent or cruel? Then the word may at first bring pain rather than comfort, and you are not wrong to feel that. But Jesus is not asking you to picture God as your father was. He is showing you what fatherhood was always meant to be, and what your father failed to be. God is the Father from whom every family is named (Ephesians 3:14–15): faithful, patient, never abusive, never absent. Many believers with wounded histories have found that learning to say Father to God slowly heals what an earthly father broke. Begin by reading how Jesus speaks of him, and let that, not your memory, fill the word.

Hallowed be your name. “Hallowed” (hagiasthētō) means sanctified, treated as holy, honoured. A name in Hebrew thought is the person as he is known: God’s name is God himself as he has revealed himself. And since God’s name cannot be made more holy than it is, the petition asks that he be treated as holy: known, honoured and reverenced as what he actually is, first by the one praying and then by everybody else (Ezekiel 36:23). That is a startling thing to put first. The prayer opens by asking that God’s reputation be honoured in a world that has trampled it, and it is a request the person praying is volunteering to be part of the answer to. Not first my needs, but his glory.

Your kingdom come. The central petition of the prayer, and the shortest. God’s reign, which has come in Jesus (11:20), is still to come in fullness (22:18). Pray for it to spread now, as people turn to Christ, and to come finally, when Christ returns. It was the prayer of the early church: Maranatha, our Lord, come (1 Corinthians 16:22; Revelation 22:20). And it cannot be prayed at a distance. To ask for God’s rule to come is to ask for one’s own to end, and there is no version of the sentence that leaves the person praying in charge of the parts he had been hoping to keep. Every honest praying of it is a small abdication.

In a sentence. Jesus taught his disciples to pray to God as Father, first asking that his name be honoured as holy and his kingdom come.

On a Tuesday. Begin your prayers with God, not yourself: his name, his kingdom. Before you list your needs today, spend a minute simply telling him who he is. Then pray your kingdom come over the specific places where you would rather keep your own rule: your money, your evenings, your temper, your plans for your children. And call him Father, out loud if you can.

For worship. The God whose name the seraphim cry holy, holy, holy has let us call him Father. It cost the Son everything to open that word to us, and Luke lets us hear him keep hold of it to the end: with his last breath he cried, Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (23:46). He held on to the word through the darkness of bearing our sin, so that rebels might be brought into his place at the Father’s table and say it after him. Hallowed be the name of the Father who adopted us, and come quickly the kingdom of the Son who made us heirs.
verseByVerse.note: Luke’s version of the Lord’s Prayer is shorter than Matthew’s; the ESV notes that some manuscripts add phrases from Matthew’s form. “Hallowed” means treated as holy.

parallels.desc: I will vindicate the holiness of my great name

verseByVerse.quote: Give us each day our daily bread, and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give us each day our daily bread, and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.

Give us each day our daily bread. Now the prayer turns to us, and asks for three things: bread, forgiveness and protection; body, past and future. The word behind daily is epiousios, so rare in surviving Greek that Origen, a native speaker, thought the evangelists had coined it. It may mean for today, or necessary for existence, or for the coming day. The point is clear: daily dependence on God, as Israel gathered manna day by day (Exodus 16:4). Not a year’s security or the removal of all uncertainty, but enough for today, asked for today, and again tomorrow (Proverbs 30:8).

A daily appointment. Anyone who has wished God would settle their finances once and for all, so the matter need never be prayed about again, has asked for something this prayer will not give. Israel in the wilderness got manna that rotted overnight if they hoarded it (Exodus 16:19–20), and it was not a punishment. It was a daily appointment. “Each day” is only in Luke: pray every day. And notice us and our: we pray for others’ bread as well as our own.

Should Christians save and plan, if we pray for daily bread? Yes. Joseph stored grain for seven years of famine; the ant prepares her bread in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8); Paul tells believers to provide for their households (1 Timothy 5:8). This petition does not forbid savings, insurance or a pension. It forbids trusting them. The man with a full barn still prays for daily bread, because the barn, the health to use it, and the next breath are all from God (12:16–21). Plan wisely, give generously, and pray this prayer as honestly with money in the bank as without it.

And forgive us our sins. Matthew has debts; Luke has sins, making the meaning clear for Gentile readers. We need forgiveness as much as bread, every day. A sin is something owed and not paid.

For we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. Here Luke keeps the image of debt. The word for in the middle must not become a bargain. God’s forgiveness is not purchased by ours; this same prayer has just called him Father, which no one earns. Our forgiving is the evidence that his has landed: a diagnostic, not a transaction. A man who has grasped the size of what has been cancelled on his own account cannot keep a ledger open against his neighbour, and if he can, the honest question is whether he has understood the first half of the sentence at all (Matthew 6:14–15; 18:21–35). The tense is present and continuing, a standing policy; and everyone means no exceptions.

The one who forgives. The man teaching this petition has already, in Luke, said to a paralysed man, your sins are forgiven, and proved his authority to say it by making him walk (5:20–24); he said the same to a weeping woman at a Pharisee’s table (7:48). And when Luke comes to the cross, he alone records Jesus doing the second half of the line under the greatest wrong ever done: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (23:34). The Lord who has authority to forgive sins on earth taught us to ask for forgiveness and to give it, and then gave it to the men who were crucifying him.

Does forgiving mean I must trust again or pretend it did not happen? No. Forgiveness means you release the debt: you give up the right to repay, and you hand the case to God, who judges justly (Romans 12:19). It does not mean the wrong was small, that consequences vanish, or that trust is instantly restored. Trust is rebuilt slowly, by changed behaviour. A victim of abuse may forgive and still rightly report the crime, keep away from the abuser and protect others; forgiveness never requires anyone to remain in danger, and abuse is never to be tolerated. And if the feelings lag behind, keep praying this prayer; forgiveness is often a decision renewed many times before the heart catches up.

And lead us not into temptation. The word (peirasmos) is the one used of Jesus in the wilderness (4:2), and it covers both testing and enticement: the trials that could draw us into sin or cause us to fall away. James insists that God tempts no one to sin (James 1:13); yet trials come under his hand. Luke gives this petition a second scene. On the Mount of Olives Jesus will twice tell his disciples to pray that they may not enter into temptation (22:40, 46), and within hours Peter will walk into a courtyard fire and deny him. So the prayer is: Father, I am weak; do not bring me to a test I cannot bear, or let me fall when tested (1 Corinthians 10:13). That is far more realistic than asking for the strength to survive the edge. Matthew adds: but deliver us from evil.

In a sentence. Jesus taught them to ask for daily bread, for forgiveness as they forgive others, and to be kept from temptation.

On a Tuesday. Bring your daily needs, your sins and your weaknesses to your Father every day. Name the person you are still holding a ledger against, and before you pray for your own forgiveness tonight, release him to God. And think of the particular situation where you know you are weak, the screen late at night, the colleague who provokes you, the shop where you overspend, and pray specifically not to be led there, and then do not walk into it.

For worship. The Father who feeds the ravens feeds his children day by day, and has never yet run out of bread. The Son who taught us to pray forgive us our sins never needed to pray it for himself; he bore our sins in his body on the tree, so that the debt we ask to be forgiven has already been paid. And the Lord who teaches us to pray lead us not into temptation went into the wilderness and the garden in our place, met the tempter at his strongest, and did not fall. Every line of this prayer rests on what he has done.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–13 — Ask, and It Will Be Given
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two illustrations follow the prayer, and both argue from the lesser to the greater.

The first is the friend at midnight. To feel it you have to see the house: one room, the family asleep together on a raised platform, a single door barred at night with a beam that cannot be lifted quietly. Getting up wakes everybody. And there is no bread in the house, because bread was baked daily and eaten daily.

The man banging on the door is not being inconsiderate. Hospitality in that culture was an obligation with the weight of law, and a traveller arriving at night was the whole village's guest; to fail him was a public disgrace. He asks a friend, at the worst possible hour, for three loaves — enough for one meal — and he asks to borrow them.

The sleeper's excuses are all true. The door is barred, the children are asleep, getting up will wake them. And he gets up anyway, “because of his impudence” — anaideia, shamelessness.

Whose shamelessness has been argued over. The traditional reading takes it as the asker's brazen persistence. A second reading, with a good deal to be said for it, takes it as the sleeper's — he rises to avoid the disgrace of being the man who had bread and would not open the door. Both land in the same place: if even this man gives, how much more the Father, who is neither asleep nor inconvenienced.

What the parable licenses is boldness. Most prayer dies of good manners, and this story was told to kill that.

Then “ask, seek, knock” — after that parable, keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking — and a promise unconditional in form: “everyone who asks receives.” Which raises the honest problem, because a great many people have read that verse and then buried someone they prayed for.

Jesus answers it with a picture of a father and a child. A fish and a snake are roughly the same shape; an egg and a coiled scorpion are roughly the same shape. What is described is not a father refusing his son but a father handing him something that looks like what he asked for and will hurt him — and no father does that.
verseByVerse.theology:
The three imperatives are in the present tense, implying continuous action: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. And there is a progression. Asking is words; seeking involves the feet; knocking is standing at a closed door that has not yet opened, and staying there.

On the difficulty in v.10, three things have to be said. Scripture itself never treats the promise as a blank cheque and says so in the same breath: “if we ask anything according to his will he hears us” (1 John 5:14), and “you ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (Jas. 4:3). Jesus himself prayed a prayer not granted in the form he asked it — “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me” (22:42). And the next three verses are his own commentary, which is where the weight lies.

A request denied is not a father who is deaf. It is a father who has looked at what was asked for and seen a snake where the child saw a fish. That does not make unanswered prayer painless, and it is not meant to. What it removes is the one conclusion that would be unbearable — that the silence means indifference.

And Luke's ending is his own. Matthew has “how much more will your Father give good things” (Matt. 7:11); Luke has “the Holy Spirit.” Luke's version tells you what good things finally means. The best thing the Father has to give is not a solution to a circumstance; it is himself, present, in a person.
verseByVerse.examples:
“You, who are evil” is dropped in without emphasis, as agreed common ground. He is talking to ordinary decent parents and takes it as obvious that they are bad — and that even so, they would not hand a child a scorpion.

The parable of the friend at midnight is also worth noticing for what the man needs. He is not asking for himself. He wants bread because someone has arrived and he has nothing to give them — which is the position of everyone who has ever tried to help another person and found himself empty.

And “give us each day our daily bread” has a hard edge for anyone who has wished God would settle their finances once and for all, so the matter could be closed and no longer prayed about. Israel in the wilderness got manna that rotted overnight (Ex. 16:19-20), and it was not a punishment. It was a daily appointment.

For anyone praying about something that has not moved in years, this is where the passage lands. Whatever else has or has not been given, the one gift explicitly promised to everyone who asks is God himself — and he is the only gift that cannot arrive in the wrong shape.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, for a friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’;
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him, friend, lend me three loaves, for a friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him.

Which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight. Only Luke records this parable, and to feel it you have to see the house. A Galilean peasant home was often a single room: the family asleep together on mats on a raised platform, the animals below, and one door barred at night with a heavy beam that could not be lifted quietly. Getting up meant waking everyone. Bread was baked in the morning and eaten through the day, so by midnight most houses had none, and neighbours knew who had baked. Travellers often journeyed at night to avoid the heat, so the late arrival was not unusual.

A friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him. Here is the pressure the parable turns on. Hospitality in that culture was not a courtesy. It was a sacred obligation, and it was not a private matter between host and guest; it was a village matter. A traveller arriving at night was in a sense the whole community’s guest, and to fail him was a public disgrace. So the man banging on the door is not being inconsiderate. He is doing what any neighbour would expect. And the request is modest and specific: three small flat loaves, enough for one meal, and lend: he will bake tomorrow and return them.

A friend’s door. Notice too that he asks a friend. There is an existing relationship, and he presumes on it at the worst possible hour, which is precisely what friendship is for. That is the picture Jesus chooses for prayer, immediately after teaching them to say Father: not a subject petitioning a distant monarch through the correct channels, but a man in the dark, out of bread, with somebody depending on him, walking round to a house where he knows he will be heard.

Asking for someone else. The need in the parable is also worth noticing. He is not asking for himself. He wants the bread because someone has arrived and he has nothing to give them, which is the position of everyone who has ever tried to help another person and found himself empty. The parent with a child in trouble, the friend sitting with someone grieving, the Sunday school teacher on Saturday night: I have nothing to set before him. That is not a reason to give up. It is the reason to knock.

You give them something to eat. The disciples hearing this had already stood where this man stands. As the day wore away in a deserted place, with five thousand hungry people and five loaves, Jesus told them: You give them something to eat (9:12–13). They had nothing to set before them. Then he took the loaves, looked up to heaven, blessed and broke them, and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd (9:16). Every one of the Twelve carried bread he had not made. That is the shape of all Christian giving: empty hands, a Lord who looks up to his Father, and bread passed on.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a man who went to a friend at midnight to borrow bread because an unexpected guest had arrived and he had nothing to offer.

On a Tuesday. When you have nothing to give others, go to God, who has everything. Before the hard conversation, the visit to the hospital, the lesson you feel unready to teach, say it plainly: I have nothing to set before him. Then ask for bread, for them, and expect to be given it.

For worship. We come to a Friend whose house is never dark and whose bread never runs out. Jesus is himself the bread of life (John 6:35), and he has called us friends (John 15:15). The door we knock at was opened from the inside, at the cost of his own body broken, and he has never once told a needy friend to go away.
