verseByVerse.note: Hospitality to a traveller was a sacred duty; villagers baked daily, and a household might have nothing left at night.

verseByVerse.quote: and he will answer from within, ‘Do not bother me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything’? I tell you, though he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he will answer from within: do not bother me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything? I tell you, though he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs.

Do not bother me; the door is now shut. The excuses are entirely accurate. The door is barred with its heavy bolt; the children are asleep on the mat beside him; getting up, unbarring it and stepping over them will wake the whole household. Every word of it is true, and my children are with me in bed is the clinching one. I cannot means I will not.

This man is not God. The parable is not a picture of a reluctant deity who has to be worn down. It is an argument from the lesser to the greater, and it works by contrast, not by comparison: if even this, how much more that. If a reluctant, sleepy neighbour will get up and give, how much more will God, who is not reluctant and never slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4), give to those who ask him. God is not like the sleeper; he is the opposite.

Yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs. The word is anaideia: literally shamelessness, the absence of the ordinary restraint that would stop a man knocking at midnight, and its sense here is argued over. The traditional reading makes it the asker’s: his brazen persistence wins, which fits what follows, keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking (v. 9). A second reading has much to be said for it. The shamelessness, or the avoidance of shame, belongs to the sleeper, who gets up to avoid the disgrace of being the man who had bread and would not open the door, in a village where everyone would hear of it by morning. Both readings land in the same place. Either the asker’s boldness prevails, or the host’s regard for his own name does; and in both cases, how much more the Father, who is neither asleep nor inconvenienced, and whose name is pledged to his promise.

Most prayer dies of good manners. What the parable licenses is the boldness of a man banging on a door in the dark because he has nothing and knows where the bread is. It is possible to be so respectful of God that nothing is ever actually asked for, and this parable was told to kill that. We do not have to wear God down. But we should pray with the persistence of someone who knows he has a real need and a friend who can meet it (18:1–8).

Borrowed boldness. Boldness at God’s door is not cheek; it is borrowed. Only the Son has an unbarred right to his Father’s house. Luke has shown him as a boy of twelve, telling his anxious parents that he must be in his Father’s house (2:49). Now he hands his disciples his own word for God, Father, as the first word of their prayers (v. 2). A sinner may knock without shame at midnight for the same reason a son may walk into his father’s house at any hour: the Son has brought him in and stands beside him at the door.

If God already knows what I need and wants to give it, why keep asking? Because prayer is not information for God; it is fellowship with him. He has chosen to work through the prayers of his people, as a father delights to hear his children ask even when he has already bought the gift. Persistent prayer also changes us: it clarifies what we truly want, exposes motives, deepens dependence, and keeps our eyes on him rather than on the problem. And Scripture simply commands it: pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17). We keep knocking not to change his mind but because he has told us to, and because he is worth talking to.

In a sentence. Even if the friend would not get up out of friendship, he would get up and give everything needed because of the man’s shameless persistence.

On a Tuesday. Pray boldly and persistently. God is not reluctant, but he loves to see his children keep asking. Pick one request you gave up on because it seemed too long unanswered, a prodigal child, a friend’s salvation, a besetting sin, and start knocking again this week, every day, plainly and without apology.

For worship. Our Father does not barricade his door against midnight callers. He neither slumbers nor sleeps; his ear is open to the cry of his children at any hour; and he has staked his own name on hearing them. The sleeper in the story gave three loaves to save his face. Our Father gave his own Son to save us, and a giver like that does not grudge bread at midnight.
verseByVerse.note: A peasant family slept together in one room; opening the barred door would wake everyone. The ESV notes that “impudence” can also be rendered “persistence.”

verseByVerse.quote: And I tell you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I tell you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.

Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. Three verbs, rising in intensity. Ask: make the request; that is words. Seek: search with effort; that involves the feet, what a man does when the thing is not lying where he can point at it. Knock: stand at a closed door that has not yet opened, and stay there, as the man in the parable did. The tense of each means keep on: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. That rules out the reading where a single well-formed request is submitted and the matter is closed. And three promises answer the three verbs: given, found, opened. God answers prayer.

For everyone who asks receives. Not a few privileged people, but everyone. Prayer is not reserved for the spiritual elite.

The honest problem. A great many people have read this verse and then buried someone they prayed for. The promise is unconditional in form, and a Christian who has asked for years for a marriage to be saved, a child to come home or a body to be healed, and seen none of it, may fairly put the verse and the experience side by side and ask what is going on. Three things must be said. First, Scripture never treats this as a blank cheque: if we ask anything according to his will he hears us (1 John 5:14); you ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly (James 4:3). Second, Jesus himself prayed a prayer that was not granted in the form he asked: Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me (22:42). If everyone who asks receives meant what the anxious reading takes it to mean, that sentence could not exist. Third, and this carries the weight, Jesus answers the question himself, at once, with a picture of a father and a child: no father hands his son a snake when he asks for a fish (vv. 11–13).

What it does not mean. It is not a blank cheque, as though God would hand over whatever we name. Jesus defines the gift himself within three sentences: the Father gives what is good, according to his will, and the best good is the Holy Spirit (v. 13). Sometimes the answer is not what we asked for but something better, as a wise father will refuse a child the thing that would hurt him. But no prayer of his child goes unheard or unanswered.

In a sentence. Jesus urged them to keep asking, seeking and knocking, promising that everyone who does so will receive, find and have the door opened.

On a Tuesday. What do you need to keep asking God for? Write it down, and keep knocking. And if a prayer you prayed for years has been answered with a no, bring that grief to him honestly as well. Asking again is not unbelief; it is exactly what he told you to do.

For worship. The God who says ask, seek, knock is not hiding behind his door. In Luke the great Seeker is God himself: the shepherd who goes after the one lost sheep, the woman who sweeps the house for the lost coin, the Son of Man who came to seek and to save the lost (15:4–10; 19:10). We seek because we were sought first. Every promise in this verse stands on the faithfulness of a Father who did not spare his own Son, and will with him graciously give us all things (Romans 8:32).

verseByVerse.quote: What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!

What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? A second argument from the lesser to the greater: from earthly fathers to the heavenly Father. Two pairs, and both are chosen with care. A fish and a water snake look roughly alike; an egg and a curled-up pale scorpion, about the size of a fist, look roughly alike too. What is being described is not a father refusing his son but a father handing him something that looks like what he wanted and will hurt him. And every parent listening knows the answer instantly. Nobody does that. It is not even a temptation.

Textual note. Some manuscripts add a bread-and-stone example, as in Matthew 7:9. It was probably added to match Matthew.

If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children. A striking aside, dropped in without emphasis, as an agreed fact: you, who are evil. Not you, who are imperfect, or you, who mean well. He is talking to ordinary decent parents, and he takes it as common ground that they are sinful, for human nature is sinful even at its best (Romans 3:10–12). And even so, they would not hand a child a scorpion.

How much more will the heavenly Father. Who is perfectly good. Here is the answer to the hardest question a praying person meets, why some requests are refused, and it is not a qualification of the promise but a description of who is keeping it. What a good father will not do is give a child something harmful that resembles what was asked for. So a request denied is not a father who is deaf; it is a father who has looked at what was asked for and seen a snake where the child saw a fish. That does not make unanswered prayer painless. It is not intended to. What it does is remove the one conclusion that would be unbearable: that the silence means indifference.

Give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him! Matthew’s version ends with good things (Matthew 7:11). Luke has the Holy Spirit, the greatest of all good gifts and the gift that includes all others, and so tells you what good things finally means. The best thing the Father has to give is not a solution to a circumstance but himself, present in a Person: to dwell in his children, to make them holy, to help them pray (Romans 8:26), and to empower them for witness (Acts 1:8). Whatever else has or has not been given, the one gift promised to everyone who asks is God himself, and he is the only gift that cannot arrive in the wrong shape.

The promise of the Father. Luke follows this promise to its fulfilment. The risen Jesus tells his disciples to stay in Jerusalem, because he is sending the promise of his Father upon them (24:49). At Pentecost Peter explains what the crowd is seeing: Jesus, exalted at the right hand of God and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, has poured him out (Acts 2:33). The Father’s best gift reaches his children through the hands of the Son, and only after the Son had gone to the cross and been raised. To ask the Father for the Spirit is to ask for what Christ died and rose to give.

If every believer already has the Spirit, why ask? This is not a promise of a second blessing for some Christians. Every believer receives the Spirit at conversion (Romans 8:9; Galatians 3:2). The disciples asking here were living before Pentecost, and the Father was eager to give. We ask now for his ongoing work: to be filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner being (Ephesians 3:16), for his fruit, and for his help in our weakness. You will never ask for that and be handed a scorpion.

In a sentence. If sinful fathers give their children good gifts, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him.

On a Tuesday. Ask your Father today for more of his Spirit: for love toward the person you find hardest, for self-control where you keep failing, for courage to speak of Christ. Ask specifically, and expect him to answer. And when he says no to something else you wanted, remind yourself out loud that he is not the father who hands out scorpions.

For worship. The Father who is asked for a fish has never once handed a child a serpent. What we deserved he handed to his own Son instead, who bore our sins on the cross, so that children who were evil might be given the Spirit, who is God himself, to dwell in them for ever. Earthly fathers at their best give good gifts and then die. This Father gives himself, and lives, and his giving has no end.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add a bread-and-stone example, as in Matthew.

parallels.desc: the gift of the Holy Spirit

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–28 — Jesus and Beelzebul; True Blessedness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus casts out a demon that has made a man mute, and the crowd marvels. Two responses come from the critics, and they are the only two available to anyone who does not want to accept him.

The first is the Beelzebul charge — that he works by the prince of demons. Notice what it concedes: nobody disputes that the man is speaking, and nobody suggests a trick. The miracle is granted and the source reassigned, which is in its way the strongest testimony in the chapter to the fact that it happened.

The second is a demand for “a sign from heaven” — a real one, not this business with a local demoniac. Made by people standing in the presence of the evidence, that is not scepticism; it is a way of postponing a decision indefinitely while appearing reasonable.

Jesus dismantles the charge twice over. A divided kingdom cannot stand, so Satan casting out Satan is destroying his own operation. And “by whom do your sons cast them out?” exposes a standard applied to him and not to their own exorcists — which means the objection is not the real reason.

Then his own account: “if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.” The phrase occurs three times in the Old Testament — Pharaoh's magicians conceding they are out of their depth (Ex. 8:19), and the tablets written by God's own finger (Ex. 31:18; Deut. 9:10). Deliverance from slavery and the giving of the covenant, in three words. And the verb is “has come upon you” — not near, as the seventy-two announced (10:9), but arrived.

The parable of the strong man is the interpretation of everything he has done. The strong man is fully armed, on his own ground, and while that holds his goods are safe. Then one stronger attacks, overcomes, strips the armour he trusted in, and divides the spoil. And the goods, in this context, are people.

The section closes with two warnings. Neutrality is abolished — “whoever does not gather with me scatters.” And the swept house: a life cleaned up and left empty is not a neutral state on the way to better. It is a vacancy, advertised.
verseByVerse.theology:
The warning about the returning spirit is the parabolic form of the New Testament's consistent warning against reformation without regeneration. Everything in the description is good news — swept, put in order, the mess dealt with, the habits sorted. One word is missing, and it is the whole point: nobody is living there.

Jesus's assessment of that condition is not “an improvement, as far as it goes.” It is “worse than the first,” because an empty swept house has been made attractive. The remedy is not more sweeping but occupation — and Luke has just named who is available, and how he is described: one stronger, who walks into an occupied house and takes it (v. 22). The Gerasene man was not left empty either; he was found sitting at the feet of Jesus (8:35).

“Whoever is not with me is against me” must be read alongside 9:50, “the one who is not against you is for you,” and the two sit together once you watch the pronouns. There the subject is you — the disciples' judgement of a stranger. Here it is me — a person's own standing before Christ. Generous outward, rigorous inward. Reverse those two and you get exactly the religion Jesus is about to spend fifteen verses dismantling.

And note what Jesus assumes in passing while making his argument: that the kingdom of darkness is a kingdom — organised, unified, under command, and pursuing an interest it will not act against. He says it as something too obvious to argue.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman's beatitude on Jesus's mother is well meant and entirely ordinary in that culture: praise the son by praising the woman who produced him. Elizabeth said something very like it in this Gospel's first chapter (1:42).

The word “rather” is doing careful work in the reply. It is not a contradiction but a redirection, and it refuses the assumption underneath the compliment — that blessedness is a matter of proximity. If that were true the whole thing would be closed to everybody else, since there is exactly one womb that bore him.

What he offers instead is open to the entire crowd: “hear the word of God and keep it” — two things anybody can do, in any century, at any distance from Nazareth. And Mary is the outstanding instance of exactly that: “let it be to me according to your word” (1:38). The correction takes nothing from her. It says that what made her blessed was not the biology, which nobody can share, but the faith, which everybody can.

And the swept-house warning is worth turning into a question by anyone whose Christianity consists mainly of things they have stopped doing. Not “what have you got rid of?” but “who lives there now?”

verseByVerse.quote: Now he was casting out a demon that was mute. When the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke, and the people marveled. But some of them said, 'He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons,' while others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was casting out a demon that was mute. When the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke, and the people marvelled. But some of them said: he casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, while others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven.

Now he was casting out a demon that was mute. Luke’s phrasing is compressed: the demon is named by its effect. The man could not speak, and when the demon went out he did. Matthew adds that he was blind as well (Matthew 12:22).

And the people marveled. The crowd’s reaction is the same as everywhere else: wonder, which is not the same as faith and never has been. Then come two responses from the critics, and they are the only two available to anyone who does not want to accept him.

He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons. Notice what this concedes. Nobody disputes that the man is speaking. Nobody suggests a trick. The miracle is granted and the source is reassigned, which is in its way the strongest testimony in the chapter that it happened. His enemies were reduced to explaining it, not denying it. Better to call God’s work demonic than to admit Jesus came from God.

The name. Beelzebul is a name for Satan, and it has a history. Baal-zebub was the god of Ekron whom a king of Israel once sent to consult instead of the LORD (2 Kings 1:2–3). The name probably means lord of flies, which Jews may have mocked into lord of dung; Beelzebul may also mean lord of the dwelling. By the first century it was a title for the chief of the demons. So the charge is as serious as a charge can be: not he is mistaken, but the power in him is the enemy’s, said of a man who has just given a mute person his voice back.

A tongue set free. Isaiah had said that when God came to save his people, the eyes of the blind would be opened and the tongue of the mute would sing for joy (Isaiah 35:4–6), and Jesus pointed John the Baptist to exactly such works as his credentials (7:22). A man who could not speak is speaking. The promise has arrived in a Galilean street, in the person of the one who did it. That is why the critics cannot simply wave it away. They are not debating a technique of exorcism. They are deciding what to do with the God of Isaiah’s promise standing in front of them, and they decide to call him the devil.

While others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven. The second response is subtler, and worse. They want a real sign, from the sky, spectacular and on their terms, not this business with a local demoniac. The demand for further evidence, made by people standing in the presence of the evidence, is not scepticism. It is a way of postponing a decision indefinitely while appearing reasonable, and there is always one more thing that could be asked for. Luke says they were doing it to test him, which is what Jesus refused, in the wilderness, to do to his Father (4:12). He will answer the demand with the sign of Jonah, and nothing else.

Is it wrong to want evidence for faith? No. Christianity is not a leap in the dark; God has given abundant evidence, and Luke wrote his Gospel so that Theophilus might have certainty (1:4). The resurrection was public, with many witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Honest questions are welcome, and Christians should answer them patiently. What Jesus refuses is the demand that God perform on our terms after he has already spoken. If you are genuinely seeking, read the evidence that exists, the Gospels themselves, and ask God to show you the truth. If you find you would not believe whatever you were shown, the problem is not the evidence.

In a sentence. When Jesus cast out a demon that made a man mute, some accused him of doing it by the power of Satan, and others demanded a sign from heaven.

On a Tuesday. People who do not want to believe will always find an explanation. Notice where you do it yourself: the conviction you explain away, the answered prayer you put down to coincidence, the clear command you are still waiting for more light on. Do not demand more evidence than God has given. Act on what you already know.

For worship. The Lord who opened a mute man’s mouth is the same Lord who will one day open every mouth to confess that he is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:11). His enemies could not deny his works, and they still cannot. He bore their slander patiently, and went on doing good, and the tongue he set free that day joined the praise that will never end.
verseByVerse.note: Beelzebul is a name for Satan.

verseByVerse.quote: But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them, 'Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls. And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul. And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them: every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls. And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul. And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.

But he, knowing their thoughts. Some made the Beelzebul charge, others demanded a sign; whether or not either was said to his face, Jesus answers what is in the room. Luke keeps noting this. Jesus knew the reasonings of the scribes over the paralysed man (5:22), the thoughts of the men watching his hand in the synagogue (6:8), and the argument in the disciples’ hearts about greatness (9:47). Solomon confessed that only the LORD knows what is in every human heart (1 Kings 8:39). The man accused of serving the prince of demons answers the accusation before it is spoken, and in doing so shows whose knowledge he has.

Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls. The first answer: the charge is illogical. He begins with a proposition nobody would dispute, drawn from politics and from family life, two things everybody in that crowd had watched fail. Civil war destroys a kingdom.

And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? The logic is simple and airtight. If the prince of demons is expelling demons, he is dismantling his own operation. No commander destroys his own positions. Notice what is assumed along the way, because it is easy to miss under the argument. Jesus takes it as given that the kingdom of darkness is a kingdom: organised, unified, under command, and pursuing an interest it will not act against (4:5–6). That is a good deal more than most modern readers assume, and he says it in passing as something too obvious to argue.

And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? The second answer: inconsistency. “Your sons” means your followers, your own people. Jewish exorcists were active at the time; Luke records an instance in his second volume (Acts 19:13–14), and the practice was not controversial among the Pharisees. So the critics have a standard they apply to Jesus and do not apply to their own. If you accept their exorcisms as from God, why not mine?

Therefore they will be your judges. Your own people’s practice condemns your double standard. And the shape of the thing is worth naming because it recurs. The objection is not being applied consistently, which means it is not really the reason. Something else is doing the work, and the argument has been assembled afterward to justify a conclusion already reached. There is a hard word here for anyone who has built a reason for refusing what he did not want to accept: the reasoning is usually sound. It simply is not what is actually going on.

In a sentence. Jesus answered that Satan would not fight against himself, and that their own exorcists exposed their double standard.

On a Tuesday. Look for the double standard in how you weigh other people’s ministries: the church across town whose fruit you dismiss while excusing the same weaknesses in your own, the preacher you criticise for what you praise in your favourite. And when you find yourself with an airtight argument against something God is plainly doing, ask what you are afraid of losing.

For worship. There is one kingdom that can never be divided. The Father plans, the Son accomplishes, the Spirit applies, and there is no seam between them for an enemy to prise open. Every kingdom raised against him will be laid waste in the end, but the love of the Father, the Son and the Spirit for the people they save is one love, and it cannot fall. His house stands, and those he has brought into it stand with it, answered with patience and truth by the Lord who saw through every argument they ever built against him.
verseByVerse.note: Other Jewish exorcists were active at the time; “your sons” means the critics’ own followers.

verseByVerse.quote: But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.

But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons. Matthew reads by the Spirit of God (Matthew 12:28), the same thing said plainly; Luke keeps the Exodus wording, which would have rung like a bell in that crowd. The phrase occurs three times in the Old Testament. The first is in Egypt. Pharaoh’s magicians have matched Moses trick for trick until the plague of gnats, which they cannot copy, and they tell Pharaoh: this is the finger of God (Exodus 8:19). Professional practitioners of the dark arts concede they are out of their depth. The other two are the tablets of stone, written with the finger of God (Exodus 31:18; Deuteronomy 9:10). So the phrase carries deliverance from slavery and the giving of the covenant, and Jesus applies it, in an argument with men who have just accused him of witchcraft, to what he has done for one mute man. It means the direct power of God. His exorcisms are as clearly God’s work as the plagues of Egypt, and like them they show God liberating his people from a tyrant.

Then the kingdom of God has come upon you. This is one of the most important sentences in Luke, and the verb (ephthasen) is the point: has arrived, has overtaken you. Not merely near, which is what the seventy-two were sent to announce (10:9), but landed, already here. The kingdom of God is not first a place or a programme or a future era. It is God reigning, and where the King acts, the reign is present, which is why the evidence for its arrival is not a throne or an army but a man who can suddenly talk. And it has come upon you, the people accusing him. They were standing in it.

Already and not yet. God’s reign has broken in. Satan’s kingdom is being invaded and overthrown. Yet the kingdom has not come in its fullness: we still pray your kingdom come (v. 2), and we still live among sickness, sin and death. This is the already and not yet of the kingdom. It came in the King’s first coming; it grows as the gospel spreads and hearts bow to him; and it will be complete when he returns and every enemy is put under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:24–26).

Where is the kingdom of God today, if not in exorcisms and healings? Wherever Christ reigns. It is present whenever a sinner repents and believes, because that is a captive set free; whenever the word is faithfully preached and the church lives under it; whenever a believer forgives, gives, or resists sin in Christ’s strength. It is not a political programme or a territory, though it will one day fill the earth. Look for it where people bow to Jesus, and pray for it there first.

In a sentence. If Jesus casts out demons by God’s own power, then the kingdom of God has arrived.

On a Tuesday. The kingdom of God has come in Jesus; live today as a subject of the King. When you face a temptation that has mastered you for years, remember that the finger of God is stronger than that habit. And when you pray for someone bound by addiction or despair, pray as one who believes the King has already invaded the enemy’s territory.

For worship. The finger that wrote the law on stone and humbled Pharaoh touched a mute man in Galilee, and he spoke. That same power raised Christ from the dead and is at work in all who believe (Ephesians 1:19–20). The kingdom has come in a Person, and it cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:28). The tyrant who held the world has met the finger of God, and the finger of God has a human hand.
verseByVerse.note: “The finger of God” is what Pharaoh’s magicians said of the plague of gnats, which they could not copy.

verseByVerse.quote: When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe; but when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him, he takes away his armor in which he trusted and divides his spoil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe; but when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him, he takes away his armour in which he trusted and divides his spoil.

When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe. A short parable, and it interprets everything he has just done. The strong man is Satan. He is not weak or asleep; he is fully armed, in his own house, guarding property he regards as his. And Jesus grants the premise: while that arrangement holds, his goods are safe, and his captives cannot escape by their own strength. The human race was not neutral territory awaiting instruction. It was occupied, the occupier was armed, and the goods were secure.

But when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him. The stronger one is Jesus, and Luke has prepared us for the word: John promised that one mightier than he was coming (3:16), and in Nazareth Jesus announced liberty to the captives (4:18). He has come to attack Satan’s kingdom, overpower him, and set his prisoners free. Four verbs follow, each worse than the last for the strong man. Attacks: the initiative is not his. Overcomes: it is not a contest; it is a result. This victory began in the wilderness (4:1–13), continued in the exorcisms, and was won decisively at the cross, where he disarmed the rulers and authorities (Colossians 2:15) and destroyed the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil (Hebrews 2:14–15).

He takes away his armor in which he trusted. The man is not merely beaten but disarmed, and Luke adds that this was armour in which he trusted, so what is removed is also his confidence.

And divides his spoil. The property is not merely recovered; it is distributed, handed out, given away. Isaiah said of the Servant: he shall divide the spoil with the strong, because he poured out his soul to death (Isaiah 53:12). Then note what the goods in this parable are. Not gold. The context is exorcism, and the thing carried out of the strong man’s house is a human being who could not speak. So this is what a healing means, seen from above. Every demon evicted, every sinner forgiven is plunder: property taken off an armed occupier by someone who walked in and was not stopped. The spoil is the people freed from Satan, who become Christ’s own.

No struggle recorded. No exorcism in this Gospel is a struggle. He speaks and it is over. The demons in Luke do not fight him; they beg (8:28, 31). The strong man in this parable never lands a blow, until the cross, where the blow he landed was his own undoing. Here, then, is what was actually happening in a village street while men argued about the source of his power. The house of the great occupier was standing open, the armour he had trusted in was on the floor, and the goods he had held for the whole of human history were being carried out and handed back.

Can a Christian be possessed by a demon? No. A believer belongs to Christ and is the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19); he has been delivered from the domain of darkness (Colossians 1:13). The strong man cannot move back into a house the stronger one now owns. Christians can certainly be tempted, deceived and oppressed by the devil, and must resist him (Ephesians 6:10–18), but not owned. If you are a believer troubled by dark thoughts or fears, you need not look for an exorcist. Confess any sin, renounce any occult involvement, and stand on what Christ has done.

In a sentence. Jesus compared Satan to a strong man guarding his palace, and himself to a stronger one who overpowers him, strips him of his armour and plunders his goods.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the people you love who are still in the strong man’s house, by name, as people the stronger one can carry out. And when your own past accuses you, remember whose property you are now. If you are a Christian, you are part of the spoil.

For worship. We were the goods in the strong man’s palace, safe in his keeping and hopeless in our chains. Then one stronger came. He walked into the house of death, broke its doors and stripped the enemy of every weapon he had trusted in. He poured out his soul to death, and so he divides the spoil, and the spoil is us: men and women who could not speak, now singing, his treasure, bought with his blood.

parallels.desc: he shall divide the spoil with the strong

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.

Whoever is not with me is against me. The middle ground is abolished in one sentence. Two groups have just been described. One accused him of working by Beelzebul; the other wanted a further sign. Neither has committed to anything. The second group in particular would have thought of itself as open-minded: not hostile, merely waiting for more evidence. Jesus tells them there is no such position. In the war between Christ and Satan there is no neutral ground. You are on one side or the other. Those who stand back and criticise are, in fact, on Satan’s side.

And whoever does not gather with me scatters. Gather and scatter are harvest words, and Luke has already named the harvest: plentiful, with few labourers (10:2). There is a gathering going on, and anyone not part of it is, by the simple fact of standing in the field doing nothing, part of the loss. That is the sharp edge of the saying, and it has nothing to do with hostility. Scattering does not require malice, only absence. Grain left ungathered is lost whether it was trampled deliberately or simply not picked up.

But did Jesus not say the opposite in 9:50? A reader with a good memory will object. Two chapters ago John reported that they had stopped a man casting out demons in Jesus’ name, and was told: do not stop him, for the one who is not against you is for you (9:50). The two sit together once you watch the pronouns. There, the subject was you: the disciples’ judgement of a stranger. Here the subject is me: a person’s own standing before Christ. And the two run in opposite directions on purpose. About somebody else, doing good in Christ’s name outside your circle: assume the best, and do not stop him. About yourself, in relation to Christ: assume nothing, because neutrality is not on offer. Generous outward, rigorous inward. Reverse those two and you get exactly the religion Jesus is about to spend fifteen verses dismantling.

In a sentence. There is no neutrality with Jesus: anyone not with him is against him, and anyone not gathering with him scatters.

On a Tuesday. Are you with Jesus, gathering with him? Ask what you are actually doing for the harvest: praying for the lost by name, supporting gospel work, speaking of Christ when the door opens, welcoming newcomers at church. Sympathetic spectating is not a third option. And be as generous to other believers as you are strict with yourself.

For worship. Christ is the great Gatherer. He came to gather the lost sheep of Israel and the scattered children of God from every nation into one (John 11:52), and he will not lose one of them. To gather with him is the highest honour a sinner can be given: to be taken into the work of the Lord of the harvest, whose kingdom is advancing and whose gathering will fill heaven.

parallels.desc: the one who is not against you is for you

verseByVerse.quote: 'When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order. Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person is worse than the first.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none it says: I will return to my house from which I came. And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order. Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person is worse than the first.

When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person. A strange little story, a warning that follows the point about neutrality, and one of the most searching things in the chapter. Deliverance from evil is not enough by itself.

It passes through waterless places seeking rest. Desert places were thought to be the haunt of demons (Isaiah 13:21; 34:14). Demons are restless; they want a home in a person. And note the pronoun the spirit uses when it decides to return: my house. It has been evicted and has not conceded ownership, and it comes back to inspect.

And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order. Everything in that sentence is good news, and that is what makes the story so unsettling. Swept: cleaned. Put in order: tidied, arranged, set right. This is not a person who relapsed. This is a person whose life visibly improved: the mess dealt with, the habits sorted out, the household running properly. And there is one word missing, which Matthew supplies: empty (Matthew 12:44). Reformed, but not occupied by anyone new. Nobody is living there. The person has been cleaned up, morally improved, but Christ has not come to live there.

Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself. Seven: complete possession. The house was not merely available. It had been made attractive.

And the last state of that person is worse than the first. The warning is aimed at something religion produces in quantity: reformation without regeneration. A man gives up the drink, or the affair, or the temper. He tidies the house, and everyone says he is better, which makes it harder rather than easier to see what has not happened: nobody has moved in. Jesus does not call that an improvement, as far as it goes. It is worse than the first. An empty swept house is not a neutral state on the way to something better; it is a vacancy, advertised. This applied to the people of Jesus’ generation, stirred by John and Jesus but never committed to him, as Matthew’s account spells out (Matthew 12:45), and it applies to anyone who makes a fresh start without Christ.

The remedy is occupation. The remedy is not more sweeping. It is occupation, and Luke has just told us in the same paragraph who is able to do it: one stronger, who walks into an occupied house and takes it (v. 22). The Gerasene man was not left empty either. He was found sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind (8:35). It is not enough to get rid of evil; the heart must be filled with Christ and his Spirit.

Can a Christian be repossessed? No. This parable describes a life cleaned up but left empty, someone reformed but not converted. A believer is not an empty house; the Holy Spirit lives in him, and what Christ has taken he keeps (John 10:28). But the warning is still for church members, because it is possible to sit in church for years, clean and orderly, without ever having received Christ. The question to ask is not whether you have stopped doing bad things, but whether Christ himself lives in you by faith.

In a sentence. Jesus warned that a person cleaned of an evil spirit but left empty will be reoccupied by worse spirits, ending worse than before.

On a Tuesday. Self-improvement is not salvation. Anyone whose Christianity consists mainly of things they have stopped doing should read this paragraph slowly. The question it puts is not what have you got rid of? but who lives there now? When you put off an old habit, ask what you are putting on in its place: prayer where there was the screen, generosity where there was grasping, fellowship where there was isolation. Do not just sweep your house clean; invite Christ to live in it.

For worship. Christ does not merely clean the house; he moves in, and he does not move out. The stronger one who took it from its armed owner keeps it by the same strength, and the Spirit he gives lives there as in a temple. Seven spirits, or seven thousand, cannot dislodge him. What was swept and empty is filled with the Lord himself, and the restless wandering of the desert is answered by a rest that cannot be lost.
verseByVerse.note: Waterless places were thought to be the haunt of demons.

verseByVerse.quote: As he said these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, 'Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed!' But he said, 'Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he said these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him: blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed! But he said: blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!

A woman in the crowd raised her voice. Only Luke records this. It is one of the most human interruptions in the Gospels: in the middle of an argument about demons and kingdoms, a woman shouts a blessing on his mother.

Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed! A common way of praising a man in that culture: praise the son by praising the mother who produced him. How blessed she must be to have such a son. It is entirely well meant, and it is also true. Elizabeth said something very like it, filled with the Holy Spirit (1:42), and Mary herself sang that all generations would call her blessed (1:48).

Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it! The word menoun means yes, but more than that: not a contradiction but a redirection. Jesus does not deny that his mother is blessed. He refuses the assumption under the compliment, that blessedness is a matter of physical nearness to him. There is exactly one womb that bore him, and nobody else can have it. What he offers instead is open to the whole crowd, including the woman who shouted: hear the word of God and keep it, two things anybody can do, in any century, at any distance from Nazareth. It is the same point as 8:21, where he named as his family those who hear the word of God and do it.

Mary heard and kept. Mary is, in fact, the outstanding example of the very thing he commends. When the angel finished speaking she said, let it be to me according to your word (1:38). Elizabeth called her blessed because she believed (1:45), and twice Luke tells us she treasured these things in her heart (2:19, 51). She heard the word of God and kept it. So the correction takes nothing from her. It says that what made her blessed was not the biology, which nobody can share, but the faith, which everybody can.

The word of God, from his lips. In Luke the word of God is what Jesus himself speaks. The crowds pressed on him by the lake to hear the word of God (5:1), and in the parable of the soils the seed is the word of God (8:11). So when he says blessed are those who hear the word of God, he is not pointing away from himself. The woman praised the body that bore him; he points her to the voice that is speaking to her. The blessing his mother had by birth is offered to everyone by hearing, and the way into Mary’s blessedness is to listen to her Son.

Where Christians differ: devotion to Mary. Roman Catholic and Orthodox devotion gives Mary a unique place of honour and intercession: praying to her, and calling her Queen of Heaven and Mediatrix. Verdict: Jesus himself redirects attention from his mother’s physical role to the blessing of obedience, which she shares with all believers. Mary is rightly called blessed, and is a great example of faith. But she is not to be prayed to or venerated. Christ alone stands between God and men as mediator (1 Timothy 2:5), and Mary herself rejoiced in God as her Saviour (1:47).

In a sentence. When a woman called Jesus’ mother blessed, he said that those who hear God’s word and keep it are more blessed still.

On a Tuesday. The blessing of hearing and keeping God’s word is open to you today. Read it, and do it. Choose one verse this morning and carry it into the day, and tonight ask yourself what difference it made. That small, repeated habit is the blessedness Jesus means.

For worship. How generous is this Lord, who will not let the greatest blessing be the privilege of one woman, but throws it open to everyone who hears and keeps his word. Mary bore the Word made flesh; every believer receives the same Word by faith and carries him in the heart. The blessedness of Nazareth is offered to the whole world.

parallels.desc: all generations will call me blessed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–36 — The Sign of Jonah; The Light in You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The crowds are increasing — and Luke notes it, because that is when Jesus says “this generation is an evil generation.” Popularity has never once altered what he told people.

They want a sign from heaven, and he refuses; but the refusal is not of evidence. It is of evidence on demand, produced to specification, for people who have already decided what would count. A sign given to someone resolved not to believe becomes one more thing to explain — which is exactly what happened fifteen verses earlier when an exorcism was credited to Beelzebul.

The sign of Jonah works two ways, and they are not rivals. Jonah himself was a sign to Nineveh: a foreigner walking into the greatest city of the ancient world with a single sentence of judgement and no miracle whatever, and the city repented (Jon. 3:4-9). And behind that stands what happened before he arrived, which Matthew makes explicit — three days in the belly of the fish, and three days in the heart of the earth (Matt. 12:40). Luke leaves it unstated and lets the reader who knows Jonah do the arithmetic.

Two witnesses are then called, and both are chosen to sting. The Queen of Sheba travelled over a thousand miles by camel, on a rumour, under no obligation to anybody's God. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria — the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom, a byword for a people beyond hope — and it repented at the preaching of a man who did not want to be there and was furious when it worked.

Neither had a fraction of the light this generation has. And twice the refrain: “something greater than Solomon is here… something greater than Jonah is here.” Not someone greater but something — broader and stranger. No prophet in Israel's history ever spoke about himself like that.

The lamp sayings close the section. The lamp is not hidden; it has been on a stand in Galilee for three years. So the problem cannot be the lighting — it is the window. “Your eye is the lamp of your body,” and its two conditions are not merely medical: Scripture speaks of “a bountiful eye” for a generous man (Prov. 22:9) and, as the ESV margin renders it, “a man whose eye is evil” for a stingy one (Prov. 28:22; cf. Deut. 15:9).
verseByVerse.theology:
The queen and the Ninevites will rise at the judgement and condemn this generation, because both responded to far lesser messengers. It is the graduated-accountability principle of the woes on Chorazin and Bethsaida, sharpened: it will not be the ignorant who are condemned by Nineveh, but the well-informed.

“Something greater than Solomon” is worth weighing. Solomon was the wisest man who ever lived, and Wisdom itself is standing in the street. Jonah was swallowed by the deep and given back, and the one who will actually break death is speaking. Jesus does not argue for it; he says “behold,” and leaves it there.

The eye sayings are not about eyesight or intellect. Ancient thinking often understood the eye as a window through which light entered and filled the person — so the picture is a house with a window: clear, and the house is bright; blocked, and the house is dark however strong the sun outside.

Which explains the whole chapter. The men in front of him are not short of information. They have the Scriptures, the traditions, and a mute man talking in the street. What they have is a blocked window, and the block is not ignorance. It is what they want. That is an uncomfortable diagnosis, because it means a person's capacity to see the truth is not independent of what he would prefer to be true — and nobody ever thinks that is happening to them.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Be careful lest the light in you be darkness” is the warning that ought to keep a religious person awake. It does not say “be careful in case you are in the dark” — a man in the dark generally knows it and can ask for a light. It says: be careful in case the thing you have been navigating by is itself darkness.

That is a different order of danger. It is not the traveller who knows he is lost; it is the traveller with a compass that is wrong, walking confidently in the wrong direction, and getting further away the harder he tries. Be careful — look carefully, examine. It is an instruction to inspect the instrument.

The context names who it is for. The next paragraph is a dinner party with a Pharisee that ends in six woes. The people at greatest risk are not the irreligious but those with the most exposure — long church attendance, real biblical knowledge, doctrine they could defend in an argument. All of that can be light, and all of it can be the darkness a man is steering by, and from the inside the two feel identical.

And then, after the warning, the promise, which is unexpectedly warm. “Having no part dark” is the condition — not a life with most of the rooms lit and one door kept shut. And the result is not an impressive person but a useful one: “as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.” A life fully lit becomes a lamp, and a lamp is not for the room it stands in.

verseByVerse.quote: When the crowds were increasing, he began to say, 'This generation is an evil generation. It seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. For as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so will the Son of Man be to this generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the crowds were increasing, he began to say: this generation is an evil generation. It seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. For as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so will the Son of Man be to this generation.

This generation is an evil generation. Luke marks the moment carefully: the crowds were increasing, and that is when he said it. Popularity does not impress Jesus; it has never once altered what he told people. This generation is evil because it does not repent, despite seeing God’s works.

It seeks for a sign. They had asked for a sign from heaven (v. 16). He refuses, and the refusal is instructive, because he has spent the chapter performing signs. A mute man is standing there talking. What is being refused is not evidence but evidence on demand, produced to specification, for people who have already decided what would count: a sign that would remove the need for faith. And there is a reason that request can never be satisfied. A sign given to someone who has resolved not to believe becomes one more thing to explain, which is precisely what happened earlier in this chapter, when an exorcism was credited to Beelzebul (v. 15).

But no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. Luke’s wording is that Jonah became a sign to the Ninevites, and there are two sides to that, which are not rivals. The first is the man and his message. Jonah walked into the greatest city of the ancient world, a foreigner with one sentence of judgement from a God they did not worship, and the city repented, king, nobles and commoners, in sackcloth (Jonah 3:4–9). They saw no wonder; they heard a word. The second is where he had been. He arrived as a man who had gone down into the deep and been given back after three days (Jonah 1:17; 2:6). Matthew’s account spells that out (Matthew 12:40). Luke leaves the reader who knows Jonah to see it.

So will the Son of Man be to this generation. Luke shows at the end of his Gospel how the sign is given. The risen Jesus opens the Scriptures and tells his disciples that it is written that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (24:46–47). That is Jonah’s story raised to its full height: a man given back from death, and a call to repent carried out to the Gentiles. The sign this generation is promised is not a wonder on demand. It is an empty grave outside Jerusalem and the word that goes out from it to the world, and it is enough.

How was Jesus three days and three nights in the earth if he died on Friday and rose on Sunday? In Jewish reckoning any part of a day counted as a day and night. Esther called for a three-day fast, night and day, and went in to the king on the third day (Esther 4:16; 5:1); an Egyptian had not eaten for three days and three nights and it was the third day (1 Samuel 30:12–13). Friday, Saturday and Sunday make three days. The phrase is an idiom, not a stopwatch, and the first readers would have heard no contradiction.

In a sentence. Jesus called his generation evil for demanding a sign, and said the only sign given would be the sign of Jonah: the Son of Man himself, and his resurrection.

On a Tuesday. You have the greatest sign of all: the risen Christ. If you are still waiting for God to prove himself in some more convenient way, the proof has been offered, once, in public, and it involved a tomb. And if you are praying for a friend who keeps asking for one more argument, do not despair: give him the Gospels, and pray that he will hear the message, as Nineveh did.

For worship. The sign of Jonah is the deepest mercy in the Bible. Jonah went down into the deep because he ran from God; Christ went down into death because he ran toward us, bearing the judgement Nineveh deserved and we deserve. And on the third day he came back, not reluctant and resentful, but rejoicing, to preach peace to the very city that rejected him. The empty tomb is God’s final answer to every demand for a sign.

verseByVerse.quote: The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The queen of the South will rise up at the judgement with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgement with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.

The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them. Two witnesses are called, and both are chosen to sting: a pagan queen and a pagan city. The queen of Sheba, probably from south-west Arabia, modern Yemen: a journey of well over a thousand miles by camel, undertaken on a rumour, by a foreign monarch under no obligation to anybody’s God. She came to test Solomon with hard questions, and she listened, and she said the half had not been told her (1 Kings 10:1–7). At the final judgement she will be a witness against them. She travelled a vast distance to hear Solomon; they had a greater one in their midst and would not listen.

Something greater than Solomon is here. The word is neuter: not someone greater but something greater, which is broader and stranger, the kingdom and the wisdom of God present in the person of Jesus. It is not merely that a better teacher than Solomon has turned up. The wisest man who ever lived is outranked by Wisdom itself, standing in the street. He is the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30), in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3).

The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, the empire that had destroyed the northern kingdom and deported ten tribes, whose armies were remembered for cruelty long afterward. If a first-century Jew had a byword for a people beyond hope, it was these. They repented at the preaching of a man who did not want to be there, who had run in the opposite direction, preached judgement with no promise of mercy, and was furious when it worked (Jonah 3:5–10; 4:1).

Something greater than Jonah is here. Jonah was swallowed by the deep and given back, and the one who will actually break death is speaking. He does not argue for it. He says behold, and leaves it there, and no prophet in Israel’s history ever spoke about himself like that. If pagans repented at Jonah’s preaching, how much more should Israel repent at his?

The point. Two Gentiles, a queen and a city, will condemn Jesus’ generation, and neither had a fraction of its light. Sheba had a rumour about a king’s wisdom. Nineveh had one sentence from an unwilling foreigner. The men listening to Jesus have him. Privilege increases responsibility, and judgement is proportional to light (10:13–15). It is not the ignorant who will be condemned by the Ninevites, but the well-informed: a pagan queen who travelled a thousand miles for a rumour of wisdom will stand up beside people who could not be troubled to cross a room.

Will the queen of Sheba and the Ninevites be in heaven? Jesus does not say, and we should not speculate beyond him. His point is not their final destiny but their response: they answered far smaller light with seriousness, and that response will expose those who answered the greatest light with indifference. The Ninevites’ repentance was real enough to turn away a temporal judgement (Jonah 3:10). Whether any of them came to saving faith in the God of Israel is known to God. What is certain is that no one is saved apart from the grace of God revealed in Christ, and that we, who have heard him, have no excuse.

In a sentence. The queen of Sheba, who travelled far to hear Solomon, and the Ninevites, who repented at Jonah’s preaching, will condemn this generation at the judgement, because one greater than Solomon and Jonah is here.

On a Tuesday. You have far more than Solomon’s wisdom or Jonah’s preaching: you have Christ, the whole Bible, and the Spirit. Ask what you would cross a thousand miles for, and whether you would cross the room for a Bible study or the road for a prayer meeting. Listen, and repent, and do it today.

For worship. Something greater than Solomon is here: the King whose wisdom made the worlds, whose throne is for ever, whose kingdom has no end. Something greater than Jonah is here: the Prophet who did not run from his mission but embraced it, who went down into death willingly and rose again. And this greater one has not stayed in a distant palace for us to travel to. He came all the way to us.
verseByVerse.note: The queen of the South is the queen of Sheba, probably in south-west Arabia. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria.

verseByVerse.quote: 'No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light, but when it is bad, your body is full of darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light, but when it is bad, your body is full of darkness.

No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand. The saying has been used before in this Gospel (8:16), and its placing here gives it a different edge. He has just said that something greater than Solomon and Jonah is here. That is the lamp, and it has not been hidden. It has been standing on a stand in the middle of Galilee, healing people in daylight, in front of crowds, with witnesses. So the problem in this generation cannot be the lighting. The problem is not lack of light but lack of sight.

Your eye is the lamp of your body. The image shifts, and it takes a moment to follow. The lamp on the stand is outside; now there is a lamp inside, and it is the eye. Ancient thinking about vision often pictured the eye as a window through which light entered and filled the person. So the picture is of a house with a window: if the window is clear, the house is bright; if it is blocked, the house is dark, however strong the sun outside. Spiritually, the eye is the heart’s ability to perceive God’s truth.

When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light. “Healthy” (haplous) means single, sincere, undivided, and in the wider usage of the day, generous: a single-minded focus on God. You receive the light and live in it.

But when it is bad, your body is full of darkness. “Bad” (ponēros) means evil, diseased. In Jewish idiom a bad or evil eye meant a grudging, envious, tight-fisted disposition (Deuteronomy 15:9; Proverbs 28:22; Matthew 20:15). So this is not really about eyesight or even about intellect. It is about whether a person is undivided and open-handed, or grasping and calculating, and Jesus says that condition determines what light can get in. A heart that is double-minded, greedy or hostile cannot see the light, however brightly it shines.

A blocked window. That explains the whole chapter. The men in front of him are not short of information. They have the Scriptures, the traditions, and a mute man talking in the street. What they have is a blocked window, and the block is not ignorance. It is what they want. That is an uncomfortable diagnosis, because it means a person’s capacity to see the truth is not independent of what he would prefer to be true. Nobody ever thinks that is happening to them.

How can I tell if my eye is bad? Watch for the things that make Scripture suddenly unclear to you. When a plain passage about money, sex, forgiveness or anger seems strangely complicated, ask whether the difficulty is in the text or in what obeying it would cost. Notice envy, which turns other people’s blessings into grievances, and greed, which makes generosity feel foolish. Then ask God to heal your sight: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). A single eye is not a perfect one; it is one turned wholly toward God and willing to see.

In a sentence. The light has been given openly, and a healthy, sincere eye lets it fill the whole person, but a bad eye leaves the whole person in darkness.

On a Tuesday. Is your eye single toward God? Pick one area where you have been calculating rather than trusting, and make one generous, open-handed choice there this week. Ask him to heal anything in your heart that keeps you from seeing his light.

For worship. God has not hidden his light. Zechariah sang of the sunrise from on high, visiting us to give light to those who sit in darkness (1:78–79), and old Simeon held that light in his arms, a light for revelation to the Gentiles (2:32). The lamp has been set on the stand for the whole world. And the God who lights it is the God who heals blind eyes to see it, so that the light and the sight are both his gifts.
verseByVerse.note: A “bad” eye was an idiom for stinginess or an evil desire.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness. If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness. If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.

Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness. Of all the warnings in Luke, this is the one that ought to keep a religious person awake. It does not say be careful in case you are in the dark; a man in the dark generally knows it, and can ask for a light. It says: be careful in case the thing you navigate by is itself darkness. It is the traveller with a faulty compass, walking confidently the wrong way and getting further off the harder he tries. Be careful means look, examine: inspect the instrument. The Pharisees thought they saw (John 9:39–41), and self-deception is the worst blindness.

Who is it for? The context answers. Luke goes straight from this saying to a Pharisee’s dinner table and six woes. The men being warned are the most religiously informed people in the country, men who could recite the law, tithed their garden herbs, and had built their whole lives around getting this right. So the people at greatest risk from this verse are not the irreligious. They are the ones with the most exposure: long church attendance, real biblical knowledge, doctrine they could defend in an argument. All of that can be light, and all of it can be the darkness a man is steering by, and from the inside the two can feel identical.

If I cannot tell from the inside, how can I ever be sure? Not by staring inward, but by letting something outside you test you. Measure yourself by Scripture, not by your feelings or your church’s customs. Invite honest friends to tell you what they see. Look at fruit: does your knowledge make you humbler, kinder and more prayerful, or prouder and colder? And above all, pray as David did: search me, O God, and know my heart, and see if there be any grievous way in me (Psalm 139:23–24). The man who asks God to show him his darkness is not the man this verse describes.

If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright. And then, after the warning, the promise, and it is unexpectedly warm. Having no part dark is the condition. Not a life with most of the rooms lit and one door kept shut; the whole of it, with nothing held back, no dark corner reserved.

As when a lamp with its rays gives you light. The result is not a person who has achieved something impressive. It is a person who has become useful: someone others can see by. The lamp is put on a stand so that those who enter may see, and a life fully lit becomes a lamp, which is not for the room it stands in.

Having no part dark. Only one life has ever met that condition in full. There was no room in Jesus kept shut and no corner reserved; his eye was single toward his Father from first to last. Luke has let us see it from the outside: on the mountain, as he prayed, the appearance of his face was altered and his clothing became dazzling white (9:29). What he warns the Pharisees about he never needed to fear for himself. And what he offers them is not a technique for self-inspection but himself, the light by which every other light is tested.

In a sentence. Jesus warned them to make sure that what they thought was light in them was not darkness, for a life fully open to the light will shine.

On a Tuesday. Ask God to search you and show you any part of your life you have kept dark: the room you never let anyone into, the habit you have never confessed, the attitude you have learned to call by a nicer name. Then open that door to one trusted believer this week. Light gets in where doors are opened.

For worship. The light that searches us is the light that saves us. The Lord who warned that a man’s light may be darkness went himself into the darkness that fell over the whole land at noon as he hung on the cross (23:44), so that people steering by broken compasses might be brought out into his day. He does not only show us our darkness. He takes it on himself, and gives us his light, until the whole of us is bright.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–54 — Woes to the Pharisees and Lawyers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A Pharisee invites Jesus to dine, and he goes. Luke records three such meals in this Gospel and every one ends badly — and Jesus accepts every invitation. Whatever is said in this room is said by a guest who came when he was asked.

He does not perform the ritual handwashing, and the omission may well be deliberate. That washing was not hygiene and it was not in the law of Moses; nothing in the Torah requires an ordinary Israelite to wash before eating. The Pharisees had taken the priestly standard and applied it to everybody, all the time — a serious and, in its way, admirable ambition. They wanted the whole nation to live as though it were serving in the temple.

His answer takes their own debating point about the cleansing of vessels and turns it on them. A cup polished outside and filthy within is not a partly clean cup; it is a cup nobody can drink from, and the polish makes it worse, because it gets the cup put back on the table. And the first word for what is inside is greed — the grasping that takes. Something is being taken.

“Give as alms those things that are within” is his prescription, and it is remarkable: they asked how to be clean and the answer is not a better ritual but to give the contents away. The remedy for greed is not scouring the cup; it is giving away what was grasped.

Then six woes — three against the Pharisees and three against the lawyers. The word itself needs setting straight: ouai is the prophets' word, a cry of grief as much as a verdict, the sound a man makes watching somebody walk towards a cliff. Jesus will weep over Jerusalem later in this Gospel (19:41).

They tithe mint and rue and neglect justice and the love of God — and “these you ought to have done” refuses to abolish the small duty. They love the best seat and the public greetings. They are unmarked graves. The lawyers load burdens they will not touch, build the tombs of prophets their fathers killed, and have taken away the key of knowledge.

And it hardens them. The chapter ends with respectable men following a guest out of a house, firing questions to get a sentence they can use.
verseByVerse.theology:
The tithing woe turns on a trade nobody consciously makes. The law required a tithe of grain, wine and oil (Deut. 14:22-23); it said nothing about the pot of mint on the windowsill. These were not lazy men — they were taking God seriously at a level of detail most people never attempt. And “these you ought to have done, without neglecting the others” is regularly ignored: he does not condemn the herb-tithing.

The mechanism is universal. The measurable duty is genuinely satisfying: it can be completed, checked off, and known to be done. Justice and the love of God can never be checked off — and a man who spends his religious energy on things that finish will find he has run out before he reaches the things that do not.

The unmarked-grave woe depends on a detail of the law. Contact with a grave made a person unclean for seven days (Num. 19:16), so graves were whitewashed each spring before Passover, conspicuously, so pilgrims could see them and go round. The marking was a public service; it kept people clean. An unmarked grave is the exact opposite — one a man walks straight over and finds out afterwards, if he finds out at all.

And “the key of knowledge” is the heaviest charge. The knowledge in question is not information about God but the thing the Scriptures exist to produce. These men were the keyholders legitimately — and they did not enter themselves, and they blocked the door for people who were already moving towards it.
verseByVerse.examples:
The lawyer's interruption — “in saying these things you insult us also” — is wonderfully revealing. He does not say “that is untrue.” He concedes the accuracy and objects to the tone, which is one of the commonest ways a person defends himself against a word he cannot answer: change the subject from whether it is right to whether it was polite.

The burdens woe puts a simple test to anyone who teaches. Does what you say make it harder or easier for an ordinary struggling believer to get up on Monday? There is a way of preaching high standards that lifts people and a way that flattens them, and the difference is usually whether the preacher has any intention of getting under the load himself. Set it against “my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:30).

The tomb-building is a way of being on the right side of a controversy that is safely over. It costs nothing to honour a dead prophet; he has stopped saying the things that got him killed. Meanwhile a living one is at the table, and they are about to arrange his death. Every generation of the church admires the awkward men of the previous one, whose battles are settled and whose statues are uncontroversial, and finds the equivalent figure in its own congregation intolerable. A dead prophet requires a subscription; a live one requires repentance.

And the key-of-knowledge woe puts a question to anyone who teaches anything to anybody. A teacher does not chiefly transmit doctrine; he transmits an impression of God, and people believe the impression long after they have forgotten the doctrine. Not whether what you say is correct, which is the easier test — whether someone who listened to you for a year would find the door easier to walk through, or harder.

verseByVerse.quote: While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him, so he went in and reclined at table. The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him, so he went in and reclined at table. The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner.

While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him. Two things to register before the confrontation starts. The first is that a Pharisee invited him, and he went. Luke records three such meals in this Gospel (7:36; here; 14:1), and every one of them ends badly, and Jesus accepts every invitation, as he accepted the tax collectors’. Whatever is about to be said in this room, it is being said by a guest who came when he was asked. That is worth holding on to when the woes arrive, because it decides how they should be heard. This is not a man denouncing his enemies from a safe distance. It is a man eating their food. The word for the meal is literally the morning or midday meal.

So he went in and reclined at table. Reclining tells you the kind of meal. Reclining on couches around a low table was the posture of a formal meal with guests, which means there was an audience, and the whole exchange took place in front of the Pharisee’s friends.

The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner. The washing was not hygiene but a purity ritual (Mark 7:3–4): water poured over the hands in a prescribed way to remove ceremonial defilement picked up in the day, especially from contact with people outside the observant community. It was not in the law of Moses, which required such washings only of priests handling holy things. It was the tradition of the elders. The Pharisees had taken the priestly standard and applied it to everybody, all the time, a serious and in its way admirable ambition: they wanted the whole nation to live as though it were serving in the temple.
