Deliberate. Jesus does not wash, and Luke says the Pharisee was astonished. It may well have been deliberate, to provoke the conversation that followed. Mark tells us his disciples had done the same in front of a delegation from Jerusalem, and he had defended them (Mark 7:1–5); he knew exactly what omitting it would say at a formal dinner. He is not being careless or rude. He is declining, in front of witnesses, to endorse a system, and he is about to explain why.

A guest at every table. In Luke, Jesus is forever at someone’s table: Levi’s, with a crowd of tax collectors (5:29); Simon the Pharisee’s (7:36); Zacchaeus’s (19:5–7). The grumble that follows him everywhere is that this man receives sinners and eats with them (15:2), and he accepts the Pharisees’ invitations on the same terms as the sinners’, because both need him. And the guest who sits down at their tables is the host of a greater one, where people will come from east and west, from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God (13:29).

Should a Christian accept invitations from people who disapprove of him? Jesus did, again and again, knowing the hostility at the table. Accept them where you can, and be a gracious guest; meals are one of the best places for real conversation. But do not buy peace by pretending to agree with what you believe is wrong. Jesus was courteous enough to come and honest enough to speak. You can be both: thankful for the food, kind to your host, and clear about Christ when the moment comes.

In a sentence. Jesus accepted a Pharisee’s invitation to dinner, and his host was surprised that he did not perform the ritual washing first.

On a Tuesday. Be careful about judging others by human traditions rather than by God’s word: how people dress for church, which translation they use, how they school their children, whether they raise their hands. Ask of each of your own standards: is this commanded, or only customary? Hold customs lightly and commands firmly.

For worship. The Holy One of Israel sat down unwashed at a Pharisee’s table, and he was the only clean person in the room. He needed no ritual, because he had no defilement. And he came to make the unclean clean, not by water poured on hands, but by his blood poured out for sinners, which cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7).
verseByVerse.note: The washing was a ritual of purity before a meal, not hygiene.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord said to him, 'Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also? But give as alms those things that are within, and behold, everything is clean for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord said to him: now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also? But give as alms those things that are within, and behold, everything is clean for you.

Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish. He answers the unspoken criticism with an image drawn from the table in front of him. The picture is exact, and it was not merely rhetorical. The Pharisees had detailed rules for washing vessels (Mark 7:4), and rabbinic law discussed whether the inside and outside of a cup could be clean or unclean independently of each other. Jesus takes their own debating point and turns it on them. They make the outside of their lives clean, ritually and morally, before people.

But inside you are full of greed and wickedness. A cup polished on the outside and filthy within is not a partly clean cup. It is a cup nobody can drink from, and the polish makes it worse rather than better, because it gets the cup put back on the table. And note the two words for what is inside. “Greed” (harpagē) is plunder, robbery, rapacity. It is a startling charge to bring against the most scrupulous men in the country, and it means the problem is not merely that they are inwardly unimpressive. Something is being taken. Religion that cares about appearances but not the heart is worthless.

You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also? “Fools” (aphrones) means senseless: a strong word. The argument is from creation, and it is unanswerable. The same God made the visible and the invisible parts of a man. He cares about both, and he sees the inside: the LORD looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). A religion that attends to one and not the other has not understood who it is dealing with, as though God could see the hands and not the heart.

The Maker at the table. The question is sharper than the Pharisee knew. The guest asking whether the Maker of the outside did not make the inside also is the one through whom all things were made (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16). He is not guessing at what God sees when he looks into a man; he is looking. The Lord who weighs the heart reclined at this table and saw exactly what the polish was covering, and he still stayed for the meal.

If Jesus warns against calling a brother a fool, how can he say it here? There (Matthew 5:22) he forbids the angry insult that despises a person. Here he gives the Lord’s verdict on teachers who ignore the God who made the inside as well as the outside (v. 40), as the prophets did before him. He is the Judge, and he sees hearts; we do not. So we may name folly in what people teach and do, but we must never use contempt as a weapon against a person, and never imagine that our anger shares his perfect knowledge.

But give as alms those things that are within. A genuinely difficult sentence, and translators differ. The likeliest sense is: give the contents of the cup and dish, the food and the wealth it stands for, to the poor, instead of grasping them. They had asked, in effect, how to be clean, and the answer is not a better ritual but give the contents away. It goes straight at the word he has just used: the inside is full of greed, and the remedy for greed is not scouring the cup but giving away what was grasped. Love for the poor is the inward cleanness God looks for (Micah 6:8). And there is a sharp practical test in this: it is entirely possible to be meticulous about religious observance and tight-fisted, and Jesus treats the second as the diagnosis and the first as the cover.

And behold, everything is clean for you. When the heart is right, the ritual rules do not matter. Mark notes that in teaching like this Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19).

Does this mean that almsgiving cleanses a person? No. The phrase is hard, and has been read as give the contents of your cups as alms or give from within, from the heart. On either reading Jesus is not teaching salvation by charity. He is telling men obsessed with outward purity that a heart turned outward in generous love is what God calls clean. Only the blood of Christ cleanses a sinner before God; but a heart he has cleansed will show it by opening its hands.

In a sentence. Jesus rebuked the Pharisees for cleaning the outside of the cup while their insides were full of greed, and told them to give generously from the heart, and then everything would be clean for them.

On a Tuesday. God sees your heart. Do not just look good on the outside; let him clean the inside. Look at your bank statement alongside your church attendance and ask which one tells the truer story about your heart. Then give something away this week that you would rather keep.

For worship. He who made the outside made the inside also, and he did not leave either to rot. The Creator came as Redeemer, to give us a new heart and put a new spirit within us (Ezekiel 36:26). He cleans from the inside out, and what he cleans, he fills with his own generosity: the generosity of the one who, though he was rich, for our sake became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9).

parallels.desc: to the pure, all things are pure

verseByVerse.quote: 'But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every herb, and neglect justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every herb, and neglect justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.

But woe to you Pharisees! Six woes follow, three on the Pharisees (vv. 42–44) and three on the lawyers (vv. 46–52), and the word itself needs setting straight before any of them are read. “Woe” (ouai) is not a curse and not an insult. It is the prophets’ word, Isaiah’s, Amos’s, Habakkuk’s, a cry of lament as much as a verdict of judgement. It is the sound a man makes looking at somebody walking toward a cliff. Jesus will weep over Jerusalem later in this Gospel (19:41), and the woe and the weeping come from the same heart.

For you tithe mint and rue and every herb. The law required a tithe, a tenth, of the produce of the field: grain, wine, oil, the fruit of the land (Deuteronomy 14:22–23). It said nothing about the pot of mint on the windowsill. The Pharisees, wanting to be certain they had not fallen short anywhere, tithed the garden herbs too, the tiniest plants, counting out every tenth leaf. There is something genuinely admirable in that, and it should be admitted before it is criticised. These were not lazy men. They were taking God seriously at a level of detail most people never attempt.

And neglect justice and the love of God. And there it is. The same men counting mint leaves were failing at the two largest things in the law, the weightier matters (Matthew 23:23). Justice: fair dealing with others, especially the poor. The love of God: loving him with the whole heart. The two great commandments (10:27). Careful about tiny details, careless about the heart of the law.

These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. This clause matters enormously and is regularly ignored. Jesus does not abolish the herb-tithing. He says they were right to do it. What he condemns is the trade: the quiet substitution of the small and achievable for the large and demanding. The small things must not replace the great ones.

How the trade happens. Nobody decides to swap justice for mint. The measurable duty is genuinely satisfying: it can be completed, checked off and known to be done. Justice and the love of God can never be checked off, and a man who spends his religious energy on things that finish will run out before he reaches the things that do not. Attendance is countable. Reading plans are countable. Positions on secondary matters are defensible. Whether I am just, and whether I love God, are neither, and they are the two things this verse says were being neglected.

Both, in one life. Only one man ever did the weightier matters and the smaller ones together, neglecting neither. Jesus kept the law his Father gave, down to its details, and in the same life proclaimed good news to the poor and liberty to the oppressed (4:18), and loved his Father with the whole heart from boyhood to the cross. The Pharisees at this table were looking at the very things they had neglected, sitting across from them in a body. Justice and the love of God were not, in the end, a programme. They were a Person.

Where Christians differ: the tithe today. Some teach that Christians must give a tenth of their income, as a binding law. Others say the tithe belonged to the old covenant, and the New Testament gives no fixed percentage. Verdict: the New Testament does not command a tithe for Christians, but calls for generous, cheerful, proportionate, sacrificial giving (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8–9). Jesus was speaking here to Jews under the law, before the cross. A tenth is a wise starting point, and many will give more. The heart matters more than the percentage, and the point of this verse is the weightier matters: justice and the love of God.

What does justice look like for an ordinary Christian? Paying your workers and your bills fairly and on time. Telling the truth in business, on forms and in references. Refusing to exploit someone’s weakness, ignorance or poverty. Speaking up for the person who is being treated unfairly at work or in church, especially the one with no voice. Treating the cleaner and the director with the same respect. And caring about the poor with your money and your time, not just your opinions (Proverbs 31:8–9). Justice is love in the shape of fairness, and it is checked daily, not annually.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced woe on the Pharisees for scrupulously tithing tiny herbs while neglecting justice and the love of God.

On a Tuesday. Are you careful about small religious details and careless about justice and love? Put first things first. Keep your quiet time, keep your giving, keep your church commitments; and then ask whether anyone you dealt with today was treated unjustly by you, and whether you loved God at your desk as well as in your pew.

For worship. The Pharisees counted out a tenth of every herb and kept the rest. Christ held nothing back. He gave not a tenth but all of himself, for people who had counted their leaves and forgotten their neighbours, and his righteousness now covers our careful tithes and our neglected weightier matters alike. What the law asked in small measures, he gave without measure; and the love of God that we failed to show is the love of God that came looking for us.
verseByVerse.note: The law required a tithe of produce; the Pharisees extended it to garden herbs such as mint and rue.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seat in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seat in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces.

Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seat in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces. The second woe is about seating arrangements, and it is more searching than it sounds. The best seat was a real and visible thing: a bench at the front, facing the congregation, near the chest where the scrolls were kept. To sit there was to be seen by everyone for the whole service, and to be seen in the act of being religious. And greetings in the marketplaces: the elaborate public respect, with honorific titles, paid to a recognised teacher in the open square, where the transaction could be observed by passers-by.

The word is love. Notice what is not being condemned. Not the seats: somebody has to sit at the front, and honouring teachers is not wicked. The word is love. What is diagnosed is an appetite: love of prominence and recognition. Their religion served their pride. They wanted to be seen and honoured by people (Matthew 6:1–5; 23:5–7). The problem is not the seat or the greeting, but the love of it.

The second audience. The appetite is not merely vanity. A man who loves the front seat has acquired a second audience, and the second audience is standing between him and the first. Every act of piety now has two possible payments, and one of them arrives immediately, which is precisely the problem Jesus names elsewhere: they have received their reward (Matthew 6:2). The reason this is a woe and not a scolding is that it is self-defeating in a way the man cannot see. He is doing genuinely good things and being paid for them in the wrong currency, and the payment is instant and pleasant and leaves nothing outstanding.

What if I recognise this in myself? Two things are worth saying. The first is that the desire to be well thought of is not curable by pretending not to have it. Public modesty about one’s own achievements is one of the front seats. The second is where the actual remedy lies, and it is not in trying harder to be humble. It is in the fact that a man who already has the approval he most needs stops shopping for the substitute. The prayer Jesus taught begins with the word Father, and a person who has heard that word settle on him has considerably less use for a bench at the front. Practise doing some good things in secret, where only he sees (Matthew 6:4), and let him be enough.

The lowest place. Three chapters later, at another Pharisee’s table, Jesus watches guests choosing the places of honour and tells them to take the lowest seat instead, for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted (14:7–11). He was describing his own road. The one who had the right to every seat of honour in heaven came to the bottom of the room: laid in a manger because there was no place for them in the inn (2:7), numbered with criminals at the end (22:37). And God has given him the highest place there is.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced woe on the Pharisees for loving the places of honour and public recognition.

On a Tuesday. Do you love recognition in church? Notice the small sting when your contribution goes unthanked, or the glow when your name is mentioned from the front. Do one helpful thing this week that no one will ever know about, and tell no one. Seek God’s approval, not people’s honour.

For worship. Before Jesus had preached a sermon or taken any seat at all, a voice from heaven said: You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased (3:22). He never needed a greeting in the marketplace, because he had that. And everyone who is in him is wrapped in the same pleasure. The Father who honours his Son honours those who belong to him, and beside that honour every bench at the front of every building on earth is a small thing that will not last.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without knowing it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without knowing it.

Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without knowing it. The third woe is the worst of the three, and it depends on a detail of Jewish law. Touching a grave made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16), one of the most serious defilements, which barred a man from worship until purification was complete. So graves were whitewashed each spring before Passover, so that pilgrims could see them and go round (compare Matthew 23:27). The marking was a public service that kept people clean. An unmarked grave is the exact opposite: a grave a man walks straight over, and finds out afterward, if he ever finds out at all.

Devastating in three ways. First, they are graves: whatever is on the surface, the contents are dead. He has said the inside of the cup is full of greed; now he says what is inside the man. Second, they defile. This is about the effect of their ministry on the people they teach: the self-appointed guardians of purity were in fact sources of defilement. Third, and worst, nobody can tell. There is no warning, nothing in their bearing or reputation to make a person step round. The damage is done precisely because they look entirely safe. People thought they were being led to holiness, and were being led to death.

Not obvious hypocrites. This is not a description of obvious hypocrites, who are much less dangerous because everybody eventually spots them. It is a description of respected men, whose seriousness about God is genuine, whose knowledge is real, whose lives are outwardly admirable, and who are quietly transmitting something that kills. What passes over the grave is very often the sincere. A young believer takes his cue from the most impressive religious person he knows, and if what that person actually has is scrupulosity without justice and knowledge without love, that is what he will catch, and he will catch it without any idea that a transfer has taken place.

The one who touched the dead. Under the law, contact with death spread uncleanness to whatever it touched. In Luke, when Jesus is involved, the movement runs the other way. At Nain he came up and touched the bier, and the dead young man sat up and began to speak (7:14–15); in Jairus’s house he took a dead girl by the hand, and her spirit returned (8:54–55). These Pharisees, without knowing it, passed death on to everyone who walked over them. Jesus touches death, and passes on life.

How do I protect myself and my children from unmarked graves? Test every teacher, however respected, by Scripture and by fruit (Matthew 7:15–20; 1 John 4:1). Watch whether a ministry produces love, humility and joy in Christ, or fear, pride and harshness. Be wary of anyone who cannot be questioned. Do not take your whole picture of the Christian life from one impressive person; let your children see many ordinary faithful believers. And where you find real spiritual abuse, name it and bring it into the light; protecting victims always matters more than protecting a reputation.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced woe on the Pharisees as unmarked graves that unknowingly defile those who walk over them.

On a Tuesday. Your influence affects others, more than you know. Think of the people who take their cue from you: your children, a younger believer, a colleague who knows you go to church. What are they catching from you, beneath the surface? Make sure it leads them to life, not defilement, and ask God to deal with what lies hidden before it spreads.

For worship. There was once a grave that defiled no one, because it could not hold its occupant. Christ entered the place of death and corruption and came out on the third day, and since then a grave is no longer the end for those who are his. He turns tombs into doorways. In him there is no hidden corruption, only life.
verseByVerse.note: Touching a grave made a person unclean; an unmarked grave defiled people without their knowing it.

parallels.desc: whoever touches a grave is unclean

verseByVerse.quote: One of the lawyers answered him, 'Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also.' And he said, 'Woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the lawyers answered him: Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also. And he said: woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers.

Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also. A revealing interruption. The lawyers were the experts in the law of Moses, the scholars behind the Pharisees’ practice, and many of them were Pharisees. Having listened to three woes aimed at somebody else, one of them points out that the criticism is landing on his profession too. Note what he does not say: not that is untrue, not you have misunderstood us, but you insult us, which concedes the accuracy and objects to the tone. It is one of the commonest defences against a word that cannot be answered: change the subject from whether it is right to whether it was polite. The interruption does not end it. It doubles it.

Woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear. The picture is of pack animals and their drivers. These men had built an elaborate structure of rulings around the law, the oral tradition that specified exactly how each command was to be kept, and the ordinary Israelite was expected to carry it. Countless rules made obedience impossible for ordinary people. Peter would later call the law as they handled it a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear (Acts 15:10).

And you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers. Either they found clever ways to avoid their own rules, or they did nothing to help others carry them. The heavier charge is the second: no allowance made, no weight shared, no interest in whether an ordinary man with a farm and five children could actually do it. They imposed burdens without compassion. Set that against Jesus, who two chapters later sees a woman bent double for eighteen years, lays his hands on her and straightens her, and is rebuked by the ruler of the synagogue for doing it on the Sabbath (13:10–17). The lawyers would not move a finger toward the load. He puts his hands on it. The contrast is the point of the woe.

Does this mean Christian teachers should not preach high standards? No. Jesus set the highest standard of all: be perfect, love your enemies, deny yourself. The difference is that his standards come with grace to keep them and forgiveness for failing them, and he himself carried the heaviest load. The test for anyone who teaches is uncomfortable and simple. Does what you say make it harder or easier for an ordinary struggling believer to get up on Monday? There is a way of preaching high standards that lifts people and a way that flattens them, and the difference is usually whether the preacher has any intention of getting under the load himself, and whether he points people to Christ who bears it.

In a sentence. When a lawyer protested, Jesus pronounced woe on the lawyers for loading people with impossible burdens while not lifting a finger to help them.

On a Tuesday. Do not load others with rules God has not given. Help them carry the burdens they have: the young mother overwhelmed by advice, the new believer drowning in expectations, the friend who feels he can never do enough. Lift a finger. And when you receive a hard word, ask first whether it is true before you ask whether it was gentle.

For worship. The lawyers would not touch the burdens with one of their fingers. Christ put his whole self under the heaviest burden there is. He bore our griefs and carried our sorrows (Isaiah 53:4), and the curse of a law no one could keep he carried to the cross and exhausted there. The experts left their hearers bent under rules. He straightens the bent and sets them walking, and the only weight he lays on them is the glad weight of being loved.
verseByVerse.note: A lawyer was an expert in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed. So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers, for they killed them, and you build their tombs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed. So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers, for they killed them, and you build their tombs.

Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed. The fifth woe has a sting that takes a moment to feel. Building and beautifying prophets’ tombs was a genuine piety of the period, and monuments to great figures of Israel’s past were being built in Jesus’ day. On the face of it, it is the most respectful thing imaginable: honouring the men their ancestors murdered, publicly, at their own expense. It seemed like repentance for their ancestors’ sin. And Jesus calls it complicity.

So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers, for they killed them, and you build their tombs. The logic is compressed, and there is a bitter play in it: the fathers put the prophets in the ground, and the sons put up the masonry over them. One buries, the other seals. The joint operation is complete. They honour dead prophets, but reject the living one, as their fathers did; and they will kill the greatest prophet of all.

Safely over. The real charge is deeper than wordplay: tomb-building is a way of being on the right side of a controversy that is safely over. It costs nothing to honour a dead prophet. He has stopped saying the things that got him killed; his words have been polished into Scripture and inscribed on the monument. Meanwhile a living prophet is sitting at their table telling them that their religion is an unmarked grave, and they are about to arrange his death. That is what makes the monument an endorsement rather than a repudiation. A man who says he would never have joined the mob, while queuing to join this one, has not broken with his fathers. He has simply arrived late.

The pattern in every generation. The pattern outlives the first century entirely. Every generation of the church admires the reformers, martyrs and awkward men of the previous one, whose battles are settled and whose statues are uncontroversial, and finds the equivalent figure in its own congregation intolerable. The reason is not always hypocrisy. It is that a dead prophet requires a subscription and a live one requires repentance. Honouring dead prophets is easy; listening to living ones costs.

Are there prophets today whom we must heed? Not in the sense of new revelation: the prophets and apostles laid the foundation once for all, and the canon of Scripture is closed (Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 1:1–2). But God still sends faithful preachers and believers who apply his word to us with uncomfortable accuracy: the pastor who preaches on the sin our church tolerates, the friend who tells us the truth. The test is not whether they claim a new word from God, but whether what they say is what Scripture says. When it is, we must not honour the Bible on the shelf while silencing the person reading it to us.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced woe on the lawyers for building tombs for the prophets their fathers killed, because by rejecting God’s messengers they share in their fathers’ guilt.

On a Tuesday. It is easy to honour the great Christians of the past while ignoring the uncomfortable message of God’s word today. Think of the last time someone applied Scripture to you in a way that hurt. Did you check whether they were right, or only whether they had the standing to say it? Go back to that word and weigh it honestly.

For worship. Every prophet the fathers killed was pointing to one Prophet, and when he came, he too was killed. But his tomb could not be sealed. The stone was rolled away, the grave was empty, and the one whom the builders rejected has become the cornerstone (Psalm 118:22). We do not build monuments to a dead Christ. We worship a living one.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore also the Wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles, some of whom they will kill and persecute,’ so that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, it will be required of this generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore also the Wisdom of God said: I will send them prophets and apostles, some of whom they will kill and persecute, so that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, it will be required of this generation.

I will send them prophets and apostles, some of whom they will kill and persecute. The quotation matches no known book exactly, and the likeliest explanation is the plainest: Jesus is speaking as the Wisdom of God, the one who sent the prophets, and summarising in his own words what that sending has always cost. Perhaps it means that God, in his wisdom, decreed this. Matthew puts the words directly in Jesus’ own mouth: I send you prophets (Matthew 23:34). Jesus is the Wisdom of God. And note the word apostles. He is not only reviewing history; he is looking at the men who will be sent after him. Some will be killed: Stephen (Acts 7:58–60), James (Acts 12:2).

So that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation. The generation that rejects the Messiah fills up the measure of all its ancestors’ guilt (Matthew 23:32). It is the climax of a long history of rejection.

From the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. The two names are the bookends of the Hebrew Bible. Abel is the first murder in Genesis (Genesis 4:8). Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the temple court, on the king’s orders, for rebuking the people (2 Chronicles 24:20–22); his is the last recorded murder in Chronicles, which stands last in the Hebrew ordering of the books. So from Genesis to Chronicles: from the first page to the last, the whole of the Old Testament. As he died, Zechariah said: may the LORD see and avenge! And he perished in the temple court, between the altar and the sanctuary.

Is God punishing men for what their ancestors did? That is the hardest question in the paragraph, and Scripture appears to forbid exactly that. The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father (Ezekiel 18:20); children shall not be put to death because of their fathers (Deuteronomy 24:16). If this verse meant inherited guilt, it would contradict the law and the prophets outright. It does not, and Jesus has already said why, one verse earlier: you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers (v. 48). Nothing is charged to these men that they have not personally ratified. The guilt is not inherited down a bloodline; it is incurred by choosing, in your own generation and with your own eyes open, to do the identical thing. And there is a reason the reckoning falls here. This is the generation to whom the Son himself has come, the one to whom every murdered prophet was pointing. A long account is closed not because these men are worse than their ancestors but because they have more light than any of them and are about to do worse with it. The judgement is proportional to the privilege, exactly as at Chorazin (10:13–15).

Which Zechariah? Matthew calls this Zechariah the son of Barachiah (Matthew 23:35), while 2 Chronicles 24:20 names his father as Jehoiada. Luke gives no father’s name. Jehoiada may have been his grandfather, or the name may reflect a confusion with the prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah (Zechariah 1:1). Either way, Jesus means the last murder in the Hebrew Bible’s order, as Abel’s was the first.

It will be required of this generation. This was fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 (19:41–44; 21:20–24), within forty years of these words.

What it does not mean. This verse and others like it have been quarried for centuries to justify appalling treatment of Jewish people. Note who is addressed: not a nation and not a race, but the scribes and lawyers in that room, whose conduct Jesus has just described. The speaker is himself a Jew, as are his disciples, as is every prophet whose blood he invokes, and later in this Gospel he will weep over this city rather than gloat over it (19:41). To take a rebuke that a Jewish prophet delivered to Jewish leaders about the killing of Jewish prophets, and turn it into a charge against Jewish people as such, is to misread it so completely as to end up standing exactly where the men being rebuked are standing. Christians owe Jewish people love, gratitude for the Messiah who came from them, and the gospel offered humbly.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that the generation which rejects God’s messengers will be held responsible for the blood of all the prophets murdered from Abel to Zechariah.

On a Tuesday. Rejection of God’s word accumulates. Each time you hear a clear word and set it aside, it becomes easier to do again. Do not harden your heart today. Name the truth you have been putting off, and obey it before the week is out.

For worship. Abel’s blood cried out from the ground for vengeance; Zechariah’s prayed that the LORD would see and avenge. There is another blood, shed by this same generation, that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24). It cries not for vengeance but for pardon. Father, forgive them, said the one whose blood it was. The account of all the prophets’ blood was settled in full, and for everyone who trusts him it is settled in mercy.
verseByVerse.note: Abel is the first murder in Scripture; Zechariah’s is the last in the Hebrew Bible’s order, which ends with Chronicles.

parallels.desc: Zechariah stoned in the temple court

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering.

Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. The last woe is the heaviest. There is a door, and behind it is the knowledge of God: not information about him, but the thing the Scriptures exist to produce, knowing him. These men were the keyholders by office, with the texts, the training and the languages; ordinary people came to them to learn what God had said. The key of knowledge is the right understanding of Scripture, which points to Christ (24:27, 44–45; John 5:39). And they have taken it away: not lost it, but removed it, locking with their traditions and false interpretations the door God had opened.

You did not enter yourselves. They had the key and never used it. They did not come to Jesus. A lifetime handling the Scriptures of the living God, and they never went in. That is possible, and it is possible in every generation, and it is one of the strangest facts about religious work.

And you hindered those who were entering. People were already on their way in, and these men got in the way. How? The whole chapter has shown it: by burying the law under rulings no ordinary person could carry (v. 46), by making the entry requirements ceremonial rather than moral (v. 39), by modelling a religion of counted herbs and front seats, and by teaching so that God came out looking like the sort of person these men were. That last is the real mechanism, and it is why this is the final and worst woe. A teacher does not chiefly transmit doctrine. He transmits an impression of God, and people believe the impression long after they have forgotten the doctrine.

How do I know whether my teaching opens or shuts the door? Ask whether people leave your teaching seeing Christ more clearly, and wanting him more. Ask whether you point to the cross and the empty tomb, or mainly to rules and techniques. Ask whether ordinary, struggling people find in you a way in or a wall. Teach the Bible as a book about Christ, not a manual of performance. And be in the room yourself: the surest way to open the door for others is to be someone who has gone through it and is still delighting in what is inside.

In a sentence. Jesus pronounced woe on the lawyers for taking away the key to understanding Scripture, neither entering the kingdom themselves nor letting others enter.

On a Tuesday. If you teach God’s word to anyone, a Sunday school class, your children, a small group, ask whether somebody who listened to you for a year would find the door easier to walk through, or harder. Make sure your teaching opens the door to Christ, not shuts it. And pray for faithful teachers in your church by name.

For worship. The lawyers took away the key; Christ turns it. On the evening of his resurrection he opened the Scriptures to two disciples on the Emmaus road until their hearts burned within them (24:32), and then opened the minds of the rest to understand them (24:45). The door the experts locked he unlocks from the inside, because everything behind it is about him. No keyholder on earth can lock out a sinner whom he has let in.

verseByVerse.quote: As he went away from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard and to provoke him to speak about many things, lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he went away from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard and to provoke him to speak about many things, lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say.

As he went away from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard. The dinner is over. He has said everything, and Luke records what it produced. Not repentance. Not even argument. Something colder. “Press him hard” (deinōs enechein) means to be bitterly hostile, to hold a grudge. The opposition hardens, and they provoke him to speak about many things, firing questions at him as a witness is pressed until he says something usable.

Lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say. The verbs end as hunting words: lying in wait is the vocabulary of an ambush, hunters setting traps for an animal. They were not seeking truth, but evidence against him. So the scene at the end of chapter 11 is a group of respectable men following a guest out of a house, not to learn anything but to get a sentence they can use. They will try again in Jerusalem, sending spies to catch him in something he said, and will fall silent, marvelling at his answer (20:20–26). This is a turning point. Up to now the opposition in Luke has been sceptical, then hostile, then organised. From here it is a hunt with a purpose, and it will run without interruption to a courtyard and a trial and a cross.

Truth softens or sets. This is one of the most sobering things in the Gospel. The word of God had been spoken to these men as clearly as it has ever been spoken to anybody, every woe accurate, delivered by a guest at their own table who had come when invited. And it hardened them. That is not a failure of the message. Scripture has said from early on that this happens: Pharaoh’s heart set harder with every plague; Isaiah was told that this people would hear and not understand (Isaiah 6:9–10); and in Luke the word falls on a beaten path where nothing can get in (8:12). The truth is never neutral. It softens or it sets, depending on what it lands on, and these men left the house looking for a way to kill him.

Why does the same word soften some and harden others? Because the word meets hearts in different conditions, and because God in his sovereign mercy opens some hearts (Acts 16:14) and in his justice leaves others to the hardness they have chosen (Romans 9:18). No one who hardens himself can blame God; no one who is softened can boast. The practical lesson is for us: when the word cuts, do not reach for a reason to resent the one who spoke it. Bring the wound to God and ask him to soften you. A heart that asks to be softened is already being softened.

In a sentence. After this, the scribes and Pharisees became fiercely hostile, firing questions to trap him in something he might say.

On a Tuesday. When you are criticised for faithfulness to Christ, remember that he was too. Speak the truth with wisdom, and do not be surprised when not everyone thanks you. And when the word of God corners you this week, notice the impulse to hunt for a flaw in the messenger, and let the word do its work instead.

For worship. They lay in wait to catch him in his words, and they never could, because he never spoke a false word. When at last they took him, it was not because he slipped, but because he gave himself up, the Good Shepherd laying down his life of his own accord (John 10:18). The hunters thought they had trapped him. In fact he was walking into the trap on purpose, to spring it on death itself, and to rescue the very men who were hunting him.

parallels.desc: to trap him in his talk

11.text: <sup>1</sup> Now Jesus was praying in a certain place, and when he finished, one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.” <sup>2</sup> And he said to them, “When you pray, say: ‘Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. <sup>3</sup> Give us each day our daily bread, <sup>4</sup> and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.’” <sup>5</sup> And he said to them, “Which of you who has a friend will go to him at midnight and say to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, <sup>6</sup> for a friend of mine has arrived on a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’; <sup>7</sup> and he will answer from within, ‘Do not bother me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything’? <sup>8</sup> I tell you, though he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his impudence he will rise and give him whatever he needs. <sup>9</sup> And I tell you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. <sup>10</sup> For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. <sup>11</sup> What father among you, if his son asks for a fish, will instead of a fish give him a serpent; <sup>12</sup> or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? <sup>13</sup> If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” <sup>14</sup> Now he was casting out a demon that was mute. When the demon had gone out, the mute man spoke, and the people marveled. <sup>15</sup> But some of them said, “He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons,” <sup>16</sup> while others, to test him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven. <sup>17</sup> But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and a divided household falls. <sup>18</sup> And if Satan also is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I cast out demons by Beelzebul. <sup>19</sup> And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges. <sup>20</sup> But if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. <sup>21</sup> When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe; <sup>22</sup> but when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him, he takes away his armor in which he trusted and divides his spoil. <sup>23</sup> Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. <sup>24</sup> “When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ <sup>25</sup> And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order. <sup>26</sup> Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there. And the last state of that person is worse than the first.” <sup>27</sup> As he said these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts at which you nursed!” <sup>28</sup> But he said, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it!” <sup>29</sup> When the crowds were increasing, he began to say, “This generation is an evil generation. It seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah. <sup>30</sup> For as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so will the Son of Man be to this generation. <sup>31</sup> The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. <sup>32</sup> The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here. <sup>33</sup> “No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on a stand, so that those who enter may see the light. <sup>34</sup> Your eye is the lamp of your body. When your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light, but when it is bad, your body is full of darkness. <sup>35</sup> Therefore be careful lest the light in you be darkness. <sup>36</sup> If then your whole body is full of light, having no part dark, it will be wholly bright, as when a lamp with its rays gives you light.” <sup>37</sup> While Jesus was speaking, a Pharisee asked him to dine with him, so he went in and reclined at table. <sup>38</sup> The Pharisee was astonished to see that he did not first wash before dinner. <sup>39</sup> And the Lord said to him, “Now you Pharisees cleanse the outside of the cup and of the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness. <sup>40</sup> You fools! Did not he who made the outside make the inside also? <sup>41</sup> But give as alms those things that are within, and behold, everything is clean for you. <sup>42</sup> “But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every herb, and neglect justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. <sup>43</sup> Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the best seat in the synagogues and greetings in the marketplaces. <sup>44</sup> Woe to you! For you are like unmarked graves, and people walk over them without knowing it.” <sup>45</sup> One of the lawyers answered him, “Teacher, in saying these things you insult us also.” <sup>46</sup> And he said, “Woe to you lawyers also! For you load people with burdens hard to bear, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers. <sup>47</sup> Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets whom your fathers killed. <sup>48</sup> So you are witnesses and you consent to the deeds of your fathers, for they killed them, and you build their tombs. <sup>49</sup> Therefore also the Wisdom of God said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles, some of whom they will kill and persecute,’ <sup>50</sup> so that the blood of all the prophets, shed from the foundation of the world, may be charged against this generation, <sup>51</sup> from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, it will be required of this generation. <sup>52</sup> Woe to you lawyers! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering.” <sup>53</sup> As he went away from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to press him hard and to provoke him to speak about many things, <sup>54</sup> lying in wait for him, to catch him in something he might say.

12.title: Fear, Greed, Anxiety, and the Coming Fire
12.overview:
Chapter 12 is one of the most urgent chapters in Luke's Gospel — a sustained call to a particular quality of life in the light of the coming judgment. Jesus addresses a massive crowd (v. 1 — “so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another”) and then moves between the crowd and the disciples in a series of teachings that together form a comprehensive call to undivided allegiance. Do not fear those who can kill the body; fear the one who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Do not covet or stockpile; the rich fool who planned bigger barns died the night he planned them. Do not be anxious about food and clothing; seek the kingdom first. Be dressed for action, with lamps burning, waiting for the master to return.

The chapter's emotional register is high throughout. Jesus speaks of fire he has come to cast on the earth and a baptism he has to undergo before it — and he is distressed until it is accomplished. He warns that he has not come to bring peace but division — a division that runs through the family. He rebukes the crowd for its ability to read the weather and its inability to read the present moment. And he calls everyone to settle accounts with their adversary before they arrive at the judge — because once you are before the judge, the outcome is fixed. The urgency is eschatological: the crisis of the kingdom's arrival is not a background hum; it is the defining emergency of every human life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Fear God, Not Man; Acknowledge Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The crowd is so large that people are being trampled — and in the middle of it Jesus turns his back on the thousands and addresses the handful. This is a word for those inside about a temptation specific to religious people.

“The leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.” Leaven was a lump of soured dough kept back from the last batch: small, invisible once mixed in, working by itself, changing everything it touches. And Luke alone gives us Jesus's own definition. Hypocrisy is not the same as failing to live up to what you believe, the condition of every honest Christian. It is playing a part.

The argument against it is not moral but practical: “nothing is covered up that will not be revealed.” The performance has a fixed run and a closing date. Whether that sentence is the most frightening in the chapter or the most liberating depends entirely on whether a person has anything he is currently maintaining.

The teaching on fear is the application. Do not fear those who kill the body — after that, Jesus says, they have nothing more. The threat runs out. What is commanded instead is a right ordering of fear, not a quantity of terror; and the effect is the opposite of paralysis, since a man who fears God properly has been made unafraid of everything else. Every tyranny in history has run on the fear of what can be done to a body, and this sentence cuts the supply line.

Which is why “fear him” is followed two verses later by “fear not.” The bridge is a bird nobody wanted: sparrows were the cheapest meat in the market, and Matthew's parallel prices them two for a penny (Matt. 10:29), so two pennies buys five — the fifth thrown in free, because it is not worth counting. Not one of them is forgotten.

Then the stakes rise. To acknowledge Christ before men is to be acknowledged before the angels of God; to deny him is to be denied. And then the hardest verse in the chapter — the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit — followed immediately by the promise that in the hour of trial the Spirit himself will supply the words.
verseByVerse.theology:
The word for hell is Gehenna, and it is not a mythological invention. It is a place: the Valley of Hinnom on the south side of Jerusalem, where children had been burned in sacrifice to Molech under two of Judah's worst kings (2 Kgs. 23:10; Jer. 7:31), and which the prophets turned into a byword for judgement. Everyone listening could have pointed at it.

The one to be feared is God, not the devil — Scripture never gives the enemy authority to cast anyone anywhere, and nowhere are believers told to fear him. And the whole force of the passage depends on the fact that the one who has authority over death is the same one who does not forget a sparrow and knows a number about you that you do not know yourself.

On the blasphemy against the Spirit, the context is decisive. This saying stands in Matthew and Mark immediately after the Beelzebul accusation — which Luke gave us in the previous chapter (11:15). Men had watched the Spirit of God work in the open and called it the devil, and Mark states the reason plainly: “for they were saying, He has an unclean spirit” (Mark 3:30).

It is not a word said in a bad moment. It is the settled, eyes-open decision to call the light darkness. And since the Spirit's work is to convict of sin and point to Christ (John 16:8-14), a man who has finally refused that work has stopped caring what the Spirit thinks. He is not troubled. The anxiety itself is therefore the disproof: nobody who has committed this sin is afraid of it.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light” uses the architecture everyone lived in. The “private rooms” are the windowless inner storeroom where valuables were kept — the one place a conversation could not be overheard; the housetops were flat, adjoining, and where public announcements were made. The most private place in the house, and the most public place in the town.

The saying cuts both ways, and the context decides which is uppermost. Much of what Christians say for Christ is said quietly, in rooms with no audience, and looks unrecorded; Jesus says it is being minuted. But the primary force here is the other: everything a man is when nobody is watching is going to be read out. And a man who has decided in advance that everything will be known has no further use for the machinery of managing an impression — which is a considerable amount of energy returned to him.

The confession sayings must not become a performance requirement, and the safeguard is in the Gospel itself: Peter denied him three times, in public, and was restored on a beach. What is described is a settled position, not a single failure of nerve. Yet it should not be softened into nothing either. Very few Western Christians will stand in a court; the moments that count are the conversation at work, the family gathering where silence is taken for agreement, the friendship of a decade in which the most important fact about your life has never been mentioned.

And “the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour” is not a licence for unprepared preaching — the situation named is arrest and interrogation — nor a promise that the defence will succeed. Stephen made the longest speech in Acts under exactly this promise and was stoned at the end of it. What is promised is not acquittal but that the right words will be there.

verseByVerse.quote: In the meantime, when so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another, he began to say to his disciples first, 'Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the meantime, when so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another, he began to say to his disciples first: beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known.

Meaning first. Luke 12 is Jesus teaching his disciples how to live in the open before God while the world presses in. Beware hypocrisy, because everything hidden will be revealed. Fear God, and then fear nothing, because the God who holds hell in his hand counts the hairs on your head. Guard against greed, as the rich fool learned on the night his soul was called in. Do not be anxious, because your Father delights to give you the kingdom. Be ready, because the Master comes at an hour you do not expect, and will put on an apron and serve his servants. And read the times: the baptism of the cross is near, and today is the day to settle with God on the road.

The setting. Chapter 12 gathers teaching on fearless faithfulness, money and anxiety, readiness for Christ’s return, and the urgency of the present time. Most is addressed to the disciples, with the crowds listening, and it follows straight on from a dinner that ended with the Pharisees and lawyers pressing him hard and lying in wait to catch him in something he might say (11:53–54).

When so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another. Literally tens of thousands. Luke sets the scene with a detail nobody would invent: the crowd is so large that people are being walked on. This is the height of his popularity, with his enemies still at his heels. Jesus is not impressed by numbers.

He began to say to his disciples first. In the middle of that crush, he turns from the thousands and addresses the handful. Not the Pharisees but the disciples are warned: this is a word to people already inside, and the first thing he says to them after watching what religion had done to the men at that dinner table. The disciples are not immune.

Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. Leaven in the ancient world was not a sachet of yeast but a lump of dough kept back from the last batch, left to sour, and worked into the new one. It is small, invisible once mixed in, works by itself, and changes everything it touches: a little leaven leavens the whole lump (1 Corinthians 5:6). Hypocrisy starts small and spreads through a life and a community. And Luke alone gives Jesus’ own definition: which is hypocrisy. A hypokritēs was a stage actor, speaking his lines from behind a mask. It is not the same as failing to live up to what you believe, which is the condition of every honest Christian. It is playing a part: pretending to be what you are not.

Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. The argument against hypocrisy here is not first moral but practical. He does not say it is wrong, though it is. He says it does not work: the performance has a fixed run and a closing date, and at the judgement everything behind the mask will be public (8:17; 1 Corinthians 4:5). That is either the most frightening sentence in the chapter or the most liberating, and which it is depends entirely on whether a person has anything he is currently maintaining.

The eyes that see through every mask. The one who says this is the one who will do it. When the Lord comes, Paul writes, he will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart (1 Corinthians 4:5). And Luke has shown him doing it already: he knew the thoughts of the scribes before they spoke (5:22), and read the heart of the Pharisee at whose table a sinful woman wept (7:39–40). So the warning in this crush is not an anonymous rule about honesty. It is the Judge himself telling his friends ahead of time what his eyes will one day uncover, while there is still time to come out from behind the mask and be forgiven.

If I struggle with sin I have not overcome, am I a hypocrite? No. A hypocrite is not a person who fails; he is a person who pretends. The believer who fights a sin, confesses it to God and perhaps to a trusted friend, and keeps getting up again is not acting a part. He is being honest about a war. Hypocrisy begins when you cultivate an image you know is false: hiding what you are, performing what you are not, and condemning in others what you excuse in yourself. The cure is not to stop striving for holiness until you are perfect. It is to walk in the light (1 John 1:7): honest before God, honest with someone, and humble about yourself.

In a sentence. With vast crowds around him, Jesus warned his disciples to beware of the spreading influence of the Pharisees’ hypocrisy, because everything hidden will be revealed.

On a Tuesday. Where are you tempted to seem more spiritual than you are? It is often in small things: the prayer said in a voice you never use alone, the Bible-reading habit described as more regular than it is, the marriage presented as better than it is. Be real before God and people. Tell one trusted believer the truth about where you actually are, and find how much energy it frees.

For worship. The Lord who warns us against masks wore none. What he was in public he was in private; what he said in the temple he said in the garden. And he came to save hypocrites, because he knew everything behind every mask and loved us still. On the day when all is revealed, those who are in him will not be found out. They were found out long ago, at the cross, and covered.
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) works invisibly through the whole lump; here it pictures hypocrisy.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light, and what you have whispered in private rooms shall be proclaimed on the housetops.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light, and what you have whispered in private rooms shall be proclaimed on the housetops.

Therefore whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light. Private words will be made public; every careless word will be judged (Matthew 12:36). The picture is precise, and it uses the architecture everyone in that crowd lived in. The private rooms are literally the inner rooms: the innermost storeroom of a house, the windowless space at the back where valuables were kept, and the one place where a conversation could not be overheard through a doorway.

Shall be proclaimed on the housetops. The housetops were flat, used for sleeping and drying grain, and in a village where the roofs adjoined, a man standing on his could be heard by the whole street. It was where public announcements were made, like a town crier. So: the most private place in the house, and the most public place in the town. What is said in the first is going to be repeated from the second. There are no secrets from God.

A double meaning. Which way does this cut? Both ways. It is an encouragement: the disciples are about to be hauled before synagogues and rulers (v. 11), and much of what they say for Christ will be said quietly, to individuals, in rooms with no audience. Jesus says it is being minuted, and will be preached publicly to the world. But the immediate context is hypocrisy, and the primary force is the warning. Everything a man is when nobody is watching, the private appetites, the things said about people not in the room, the self that exists only behind a closed door, is going to be read out.

Not done in a corner. The rooms where Jesus taught the Twelve were small: a boat, a house, a lonely place, an upper room. Within weeks of his resurrection Peter stood up in Jerusalem, and what had been said to a handful was proclaimed to thousands; Paul could tell King Agrippa that none of it had been done in a corner (Acts 26:26). The same law ran the other way at the cross. The bargain to betray him was struck in secret, with Judas looking for a chance to hand him over in the absence of a crowd (22:3–6), and God turned that whispered plot into the most public news in the world. What men arranged in the dark against the Son is now announced from every housetop as the place of mercy.

The gap is temporary. Most people keep a gap between the public self and the interior one, and manage it so habitually that they no longer notice. This verse says the gap is temporary. And a man who has decided in advance that everything will be known has no further use for the machinery of managing an impression, which returns a considerable amount of energy to him for better purposes.

Will my forgiven sins be broadcast at the judgement? Scripture’s emphasis for believers is that their sins are blotted out, cast into the depths of the sea, remembered no more (Hebrews 8:12; Micah 7:19). Whatever is opened on that day will be opened as the record of grace, not as evidence for condemnation, because there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). The warning here presses hardest on the hidden life that is being kept from God now. Bring it into the light today, in confession, and it will never be used against you.

In a sentence. Everything said in secret will be heard openly and announced from the rooftops.

On a Tuesday. Speak in private as you would if it were broadcast; God hears it all. Notice the conversation where you say about someone what you would never say to them, the message you would hate to see forwarded, the comment made only because the door is shut. And take courage from the other side of it: the quiet word for Christ to one person, which nobody else heard, has been heard in heaven.

For worship. The God who hears every whisper in every inner room is not a spy but a Father. He hears the gossip and the groaning alike, the curse and the prayer too deep for words. And the Son before whom every secret will be opened is the Son who already speaks for us in the highest court of heaven. Everything hidden will be revealed, and for those who are his, the last thing revealed will be how much they were loved.
verseByVerse.note: Flat roofs were public places; announcements were made from them.

verseByVerse.quote: 'I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. But I will warn you whom to fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him!
verseByVerse.commentary:
I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. But I will warn you whom to fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him!

I tell you, my friends. He has never called them that before in this Gospel; it is the only time in the first three Gospels that Jesus calls his disciples friends (compare John 15:14–15). The placing is deliberate. He is about to say the hardest thing in the chapter, preparing them for persecution, and he opens by naming the relationship it is being said inside.

Do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. Hypocrisy very often comes from fear of people, and Jesus addresses the root. He does not say persecution will not come. He says that when it does its worst, it will have reached the end of its resources, and its worst is death. They can kill a Christian. After that they have nothing more. The threat runs out, because death is not the end and they cannot touch the soul.

Fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Luke’s wording is exact: not merely power but exousia, authority, the lawful right to rule what lies beyond death. Some have taken this to be the devil, but Satan is never handed the keys of anyone’s final destiny, and believers are told to resist him (James 4:7), not to fear him. The one whose authority runs past the grave is God. The word for hell is geenna, Gehenna: the Valley of Hinnom, south of Jerusalem, where children had been burned in sacrifice to Molech under two of Judah’s worst kings (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31), and which the prophets made a byword for judgement. Everyone listening could have pointed at it. Jesus uses it of the place of final, conscious punishment.

Yes, I tell you, fear him! Repeated for emphasis. The fear of God drives out the fear of people: do not fear what they fear; the LORD of hosts, him you shall regard as holy, let him be your fear (Isaiah 8:12–13); the fear of man lays a snare (Proverbs 29:25). If you fear God, you need fear nothing else. And this awe is the beginning of wisdom.

Are Christians meant to be afraid of God? A sensitive reader will stop here. The answer is that this is spoken to my friends, and the two things are not in tension. The fear of God is not cringing terror for his children, but reverent awe of the one who holds all power, including over eternity. What is commanded is a right ordering of fear, not a quantity of terror. And the effect is the exact opposite of paralysis: a man who fears God properly has been made unafraid of everything else, because the worst any human power can do to him has been placed in its true proportion. A child can be in awe of his father’s strength and run into his arms in the same moment. That is why the next thing Jesus says is fear not.

The road to Jerusalem. The man who says this is walking to Jerusalem to be killed (9:51), and he lived the sentence before he asked it of anyone. A few weeks later, when Pharisees warned him that Herod wanted to kill him, he sent back word that he would go on casting out demons and healing, today and tomorrow, and finish his course (13:31–33). He feared his Father and no tetrarch. And when they did their worst, they found that what this verse says is true: they could kill his body, seal a tomb, post a guard, and after that they had nothing more that they could do. The friends he warns here are being invited to stand where he stands.

Cutting the supply line. Every tyranny in history has run on the same fuel, which is the fear of what can be done to a body. This sentence cuts the supply line. The martyrs who sang in the arena were not reckless. They had simply been told the truth about who held the final authority.

In a sentence. Jesus told his friends not to fear those who can only kill the body, but to fear God, who has authority to cast into hell.

On a Tuesday. Whose opinion do you fear most? Your manager’s, your family’s, the group chat’s? Name the person whose disapproval most shapes what you say about Christ. Then put that fear next to the fear of God, and watch it shrink to its true size. Fear God, and you will be set free from the fear of people.

For worship. The God who has authority to cast into hell sent his Son into the place of judgement for us. The fire that we feared fell on him; the One with authority over death went down into it and came out holding its keys (Revelation 1:18). So the God we fear is the God we flee to. He is holy beyond imagining, and he has called us friends.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” renders Gehenna.

verseByVerse.quote: Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? And not one of them is forgotten before God. Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? And not one of them is forgotten before God. Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows.

Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? Two verses after fear him comes fear not, and the bridge between them is a bird nobody wanted. Sparrows were the cheapest meat in the market, food for the very poor. Matthew records the price as two sparrows for a penny (Matthew 10:29); Luke says five for two pennies: buy four, and the fifth is thrown in free, the one with no value at all.

And not one of them is forgotten before God. Including that one. The form of the statement is unexpected. He does not say God feeds them, or watches them, or values them. He says none of them is forgotten, which is the language of memory, and it means that the death of a bird thrown in free with a purchase is registered. God’s care extends to the smallest and least valuable creature.

Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered. The perfect tense means the number is known and stands known: a figure that changes daily and is never out of date. It is the most useless piece of information imaginable, and that is the point. Nobody needs to know how many hairs are on a man’s head. That God does tells you not that the information is important but that the attention is total.

Fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows. The God to be feared (v. 5) is the God who cares; the same God. This is the answer to the fear of what men can do. Not that the danger has been overstated: he has just conceded that they can kill you. It is that the God who has authority over death is the God who does not forget a sparrow and knows a number about you that you do not know yourself. Even if they kill your body, it is not outside his care. Nothing happens to you that he does not know and allow, and he works all of it for the good of those who love him (Romans 8:28). The one to be feared and the one who counts the hairs are the same person, and the second fact is what makes the first bearable.

Priced at Calvary. How does a disciple know he is worth more than many sparrows? Not by looking in a mirror. The sparrow’s value was fixed in the market, a fraction of a penny. Ours was fixed at the cross: you were ransomed, Peter writes, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:18–19). The man telling his friends that they are of more value than many sparrows is the one who would pay that price for them. Their worth is not something they bring to God. It is what he has decided to spend on them, and he spent his Son.

If God cares so closely, why did he let this happen to me? Jesus does not promise that sparrows never fall; Matthew says not one falls to the ground apart from your Father (Matthew 10:29). The promise is not that nothing painful will happen, but that nothing will happen unknown, unnoticed or outside his purpose. You may not see the reason this side of glory, and Scripture does not ask you to pretend the pain is small. It asks you to trust the character of a Father who counts hairs, who did not spare his own Son, and who will one day wipe every tear away. Bring the question to him honestly; the psalms give you words for it.

In a sentence. God does not forget even the cheapest sparrow, and knows the number of hairs on your head, so do not fear, for you are worth more than many sparrows.

On a Tuesday. You are known and cared for by God in every detail. When you feel overlooked, at work, in church, in your family, look at a sparrow on a fence and remember that it is remembered. Face today without fear, and bring the smallest worry to him, because nothing about you is too small for his attention.

For worship. The Lord of the universe keeps a register of sparrows and a count of hairs, and the fifth bird, thrown in for nothing, is in it. A dying thief, worth less than that to the world that crucified him, turned his head on a cross and said, Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom (23:42). The Son of God, nailed beside him, answered with paradise. Nothing is beneath his notice and nothing beyond his power, and he has never forgotten one sinner who called on him.
verseByVerse.note: Sparrows were the cheapest birds sold for food; Matthew says two for a penny, Luke five for two, as if the fifth came free.

verseByVerse.quote: 'And I tell you, everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God, but the one who denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I tell you, everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God, but the one who denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God.

Everyone who acknowledges me before men. The word (homologēsē) means confesses, openly declares loyalty. The construction is literally confesses in me, an unusual phrase that suggests not merely stating a fact about him but declaring an allegiance to him. In the face of fear of persecution, the disciple publicly owns Jesus. And the setting for both halves is public: before men, then before the angels of God. So there are two courtrooms, and what happens in the second corresponds exactly to what happened in the first.

The Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God. At the judgement, Jesus will say: this one belongs to me. Jesus is the judge; his acknowledgement decides eternal destiny. And the promise on this side is worth as much as the warning. Whatever is said for him in a difficult room is said again, by him, in front of the angels of God. The other half is measure for measure: the one who denies him before men will be denied before the angels of God (compare 9:26).

What it does not mean. Not that a single failure means final rejection. The man who made the sharpest denial in the New Testament was forgiven and restored and became a leader of the church. Peter denied Jesus three times, in public, in a courtyard (22:57–62), and was recommissioned on a beach (John 21:15–19). So the saying is not describing a single failure of nerve. The warning is against a settled refusal to acknowledge him: the person who, over a life, will not own him. And the warning itself is one of the means God uses to keep us faithful.

The smaller moments. It should not be softened into nothing either. The disciples are about to be dragged before synagogues and rulers (v. 11), and the confession in view is the one made when it costs something. Very few Western Christians will ever stand in a court.
