The moments that count are smaller and more frequent: the conversation at work where it would be easier to say nothing; the family gathering where silence is taken for agreement; the friendship of a decade in which the most important fact about your life has never been mentioned. None of those is a courtroom denial. But a man can spend his whole life quietly declining to be identified, and never once decide to.

If I stayed silent when I should have spoken, have I denied Christ? Probably you failed, as Peter did, and the answer is the same as his: go back to the Lord, confess it, and be restored. He looked at Peter, and Peter wept, and that look was mercy (22:61–62). A single silence is not a settled life of denial. But do not leave it there: ask God for the next opportunity, and take it. Often the best repair is simply to go back to the person and say, I wanted to tell you what Christ means to me, and I did not. That is how a failure becomes a confession.

In a sentence. Jesus will acknowledge before God’s angels all who openly acknowledge him before others, and deny those who deny him.

On a Tuesday. Where can you acknowledge Jesus openly today, at work, with friends, online? Think of one friendship in which Christ has never been mentioned, and look for a natural way to mention him this week. It need not be a sermon. A plain sentence will do: I am a Christian, and this is why.

For worship. Before the angels of God, the Son of Man will speak our names. He was not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11), though we have so often been ashamed of him. He confessed the good confession before Pontius Pilate (1 Timothy 6:13), and went to the cross rather than deny the Father’s will. And on the last day, in front of the whole host of heaven, he will say of trembling, failing disciples: this one is mine.

verseByVerse.quote: And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.

Everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven. This is the verse that has caused more terror in sincere Christians than any other in the Bible, and it must be handled slowly. Start with what is being contrasted. A word spoken against the Son of Man is forgivable, and that is an extraordinary concession, since Jesus has spent this Gospel demonstrating who he is. Men can insult him, mock him, misjudge him, and be forgiven if they repent. Paul once blasphemed Jesus and persecuted the church in an organised way (1 Timothy 1:13). Peter denied him. Both were forgiven.

Spoken against, and praying. Why can a word against the Son of Man be forgiven at all? Because the Son of Man came to be spoken against. Simeon held him as a baby and said he was appointed for a sign that is opposed (2:34). He was called a glutton and a drunkard (7:34), accused of working by Beelzebul (11:15), mocked by soldiers, reviled by a dying criminal, and from the cross he prayed, Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (23:34). The forgiveness this verse holds out to his slanderers was bought by the very one they slandered. That is also why the other sin is beyond forgiveness: it refuses the Spirit who points to that blood, and there is no other blood to flee to.

But the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven. What is it? The context unlocks the verse. In Mark and Matthew this saying comes straight after the accusation that Jesus cast out demons by Satan (Mark 3:28–30; Matthew 12:31–32), and Luke has just given us that accusation (11:15). Men had watched the Spirit of God work through Jesus in the open and called it the devil; Mark gives the reason plainly: for they were saying, he has an unclean spirit (Mark 3:30). That is the sin: not a word said in a bad moment, but a deliberate, settled rejection of the Spirit’s testimony to Christ, in full knowledge, calling God’s light darkness.

Why can it not be forgiven? Not because God’s grace is insufficient, but because the Spirit is the one who brings people to repentance. His work is to convict of sin and to point to Christ (John 16:8–14). To reject him finally is to cut oneself off from the only way to forgiveness. It is not that someone wants to repent and cannot be forgiven, but that he no longer wants to repent. A man who has finally and permanently refused the Spirit’s work has, by definition, stopped caring what the Spirit thinks. He is not troubled. He does not lie awake. He has no interest in the question.

Where Christians differ, and a pastoral word. Some have taught that the unforgivable sin is a specific act, such as suicide or a particular blasphemous word. Verdict: it is not a single act or careless word, but a final, hardened rejection of the Spirit’s witness to Christ. Anyone who is worried that they have committed it has not, because the very worry shows the Spirit is still at work in them. Those who have committed it do not care.

The anxiety is the disproof. If you are reading this with your stomach tight, and have been for years, that tightness is not the symptom. It is the disproof. The Spirit produces the fear of having committed this sin, and he does not trouble hearts he has stopped working on. The unforgivable sin has never once been committed by a person who wanted to be forgiven.

What about blasphemous thoughts that come into my mind against my will? Many tender believers are tormented by sudden, horrible thoughts about God or the Spirit, which they hate even as they arrive. Those thoughts are not the sin Jesus describes; they are temptations or intrusive thoughts, and the distress they cause shows your heart is on God’s side. Do not argue with them endlessly or try to prove you did not mean them. Bring them to Christ, tell him you hate them, and turn your attention to his promises. If they are persistent and consuming, speak to a wise pastor, and do not be ashamed to see a doctor too.

In a sentence. Those who speak against Jesus can be forgiven, but those who finally reject the Holy Spirit’s testimony will not be forgiven.

On a Tuesday. If you fear you are beyond forgiveness, the fear itself shows you are not. Come to Christ, who forgives everyone who comes. And if you know someone haunted by this verse, do not leave them with it: sit with them, read John 6:37 aloud together, and remind them that the door is open.

For worship. Glory to the Spirit who does not give up easily. Fifty days after a Jerusalem crowd called for the death of the Son of Man, he cut men Peter could charge with crucifying him to the heart (Acts 2:23, 36–41), and about three thousand were baptised in the name of the one they had spoken against. He keeps convicting and drawing hard hearts for years, until they bow. The God who warns of the one sin never forgiven has forgiven every sin of everyone who comes to Christ, and he casts none of them out.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.

And when they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities. Not if. When. He tells them plainly that this is coming, and Luke’s second volume shows it happening repeatedly: Peter and John before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4), Stephen before the council (Acts 7), Paul before governors and a king (Acts 24–26). And note the range: synagogues, the religious courts, and rulers and authorities, the civil ones, Jewish and Gentile. Opposition will come from both, and sometimes from both at once.

Do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say. The word for defend yourself (apologēsēsthe) is the root behind apologetics, and in that world a technical term for a courtroom defence speech. A man in the dock had to make one, and men trained for years to do it well. They are told not to worry about it.

For the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say. The Spirit who is blasphemed by unbelievers (v. 10) helps believers. Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, spoke boldly before the council, and they were astonished at uneducated, common men (Acts 4:8–13). Stephen spoke with a wisdom they could not withstand (Acts 6:10).

The Son of Man standing. Stephen made his defence under this very promise, and at the end of it he saw the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:56). The one who had promised to acknowledge his confessors before the angels of God (12:8) was on his feet for the first martyr. Later in this Gospel Jesus repeats the promise in his own name: I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict (21:15). The Spirit who teaches in that hour is the Spirit of Christ, and the risen Lord is no spectator at his servants’ trials. He gives the words, and he watches from the throne.

What it does not mean. Two things need guarding, because this verse has been misused in both directions. It is not a licence for unprepared preaching or careless thinking. The situation named is precise: arrest, trial, an official interrogation about the faith. It has nothing to do with a man who has not opened his Bible all week and intends to trust the Spirit at eleven o’clock on Sunday. Paul, who lived through more of these trials than anyone, is also the man who told Timothy to do his best to present himself to God as one approved, rightly handling the word of truth (2 Timothy 2:15), and Peter tells every believer to be prepared to make a defence (1 Peter 3:15). And it is not a promise that the defence will succeed. Stephen made the longest recorded speech in Acts under exactly this promise and was stoned at the end of it. What is promised is not acquittal. It is that the right words will be there.

The ordinary comfort. The actual comfort is worth naming for a much more ordinary situation than a courtroom. The dread of not knowing what to say, at a hospital bedside, in a conversation that has suddenly turned serious, in front of someone hostile, is one of the commonest reasons Christians stay quiet. The promise here is not that you will be eloquent. It is that in the hour, and not before it, you will not be alone in the room.

In a sentence. When believers are put on trial for Christ, they need not worry about their defence, because the Holy Spirit will teach them what to say.

On a Tuesday. Pray for persecuted Christians standing trial today, that the Spirit would give them words; find one name or country and pray for it specifically. And when you dread a conversation about Christ, prepare what you can, then go into it trusting that you will not be alone. Short, true and kind is enough.

For worship. The Spirit who hovered over the waters, who spoke by the prophets, and who filled Jesus at the Jordan, stands beside the weakest believer in the dock. Christ himself stood silent before his accusers so that we might never stand alone before ours. The church has never lacked a defender, because its Defender is God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — The Parable of the Rich Fool
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A man interrupts a discourse on hell and martyrdom to ask for help with a family estate — and it was not an unreasonable request in that world, since rabbis routinely arbitrated inheritance disputes. But notice what he actually asks: not “settle the dispute between us” but “tell my brother.” He has already reached his verdict and wants it enforced.

Jesus refuses, and the address is cold — “Man,” not “friend” — with an echo of what was said to Moses when he intervened between two Hebrews in Egypt (Ex. 2:14). Then he diagnoses the plaintiff and says it to the whole crowd, so the man is not singled out: “be on your guard against all covetousness.” Not merely the greed a man would recognise as greed, but every form of it — including the perfectly legitimate-sounding conviction that one is owed what one is owed. This man had a case. He may well have been in the right.

The parable is not a warning against prosperity or against prudent planning. Notice how it opens: not “a rich man made a fortune” but “the land produced.” He did not do it. The harvest came out of soil he did not make, watered by rain he did not arrange — which is the first thing he forgets.

Then the pronouns. In three verses of soliloquy he says I or my eleven times, and God is mentioned by nobody but God. There is no wife in this man's head, no labourers, no neighbour, and above all no giver. The question “what shall I do?” had an obvious answer standing in plain sight in his own Scriptures, and he never considers it. There were poor people within a mile of that farm.

And then the strangest thing in the parable: he opens a conversation with his own soul, which is what a person does when there is nobody else — and tells it that its needs have been met by grain. Every clause is a category error. Ample goods; many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry. He is treating the ache of the soul as a supply problem.

The thing to see is that it very nearly works. He is not miserable. He had done it, and he was content, and he went to bed satisfied. And God's first word is “Fool.”
verseByVerse.theology:
“Fool” in Hebrew thought is not an insult about intelligence. The fool of the Psalms is the man who says in his heart “there is no God” (Ps. 14:1) — which is not a philosophical position but a working assumption. This farmer would have denied being an atheist. He simply ran his entire life without reference to anybody but himself.

“This night your soul is required of you” — demanded back, as a lender demands what is his. Which reframes everything he has said. He has spent the parable talking about what is his, and the soul he was addressing turns out to have been on loan the whole time.

And note the timing against his own words: he said “many years,” God says “this night.” The gap between those two is the whole distance between what a man can see and what is actually the case.

“Rich toward God” is the positive alternative and one of the most compact phrases in Luke. It is worth noticing that the alternative is not poverty. Jesus does not say “so is the one who is rich.” He says “so is the one who lays up treasure for himself” — rich in the wrong direction. To be rich toward God is to live in the awareness that every good thing was received and is to be used toward his purposes; the opposite is to treat what one has as one's own achievement, for one's own use, accountable to nobody.
verseByVerse.examples:
The man's problem is not the abundance; it is the accounting. He has a genuine agricultural difficulty and his solution is reasonable, practical, and completely self-oriented. There are exactly two things a man can do with a surplus — distribute it or store it — and he never considers the first. He demolishes serviceable barns to build larger ones, which is a considerable investment of time and money in the business of retention.

Watch also what happens to the ownership across the parable. It begins as “the land” producing. It becomes “my barns,” “my grain,” “my goods.”

“And the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” is left unanswered, and it is devastating precisely because everyone knows the answer is “somebody else's.” He tore down good barns for a harvest he would never eat, and by morning it belonged to people he had not thought about once in five verses.

Which leaves a test that takes about a minute and is uncomfortable. Not “how much have I got?” but: if my accumulation were described out loud by somebody else, in whose direction would it be pointing?

verseByVerse.quote: Someone in the crowd said to him, 'Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.' But he said to him, 'Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you?' And he said to them, 'Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Someone in the crowd said to him: Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me. But he said to him: man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you? And he said to them: take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.

Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me. It is one of the strangest interruptions in the Gospels. Jesus has just been talking about hell, martyrdom and the courts, and a man in the crowd wants help with a family estate. In that world it was not unreasonable: rabbis were sometimes asked to settle inheritance disputes, and the law gave the eldest son a double portion (Deuteronomy 21:17). But notice what he asks for. Not settle the dispute between us, but tell my brother. He has already reached his verdict and wants it enforced.

Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you? The address is cool, man, not friend, and the refusal is flat. And there is an echo in it of what was said to Moses when he intervened between two Hebrews in Egypt: who made you a prince and a judge over us? (Exodus 2:14). Why refuse? Not because the grievance was necessarily unjust; Jesus never enquires. He declines because this is not what he came to do. He did not come to sort out property disputes, but to deal with the heart, and becoming the arbiter of one man’s estate would have made him a functionary in somebody’s dispute rather than the Lord of both brothers. The man’s real problem is not his brother, but his greed.

Judge of the living and the dead. The man’s question, who made me a judge, has an answer he did not know: God did. Peter would tell Cornelius that Jesus is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead (Acts 10:42), and Stephen, recalling how the Hebrews sneered at Moses with these words, said that God sent the rejected man as ruler and redeemer (Acts 7:35). The pattern was coming true in the one standing in this crowd. He will not sit as arbitrator over one field, because he will one day sit as Judge over both brothers and every field on earth, and he came first to bring them both under a better rule than either had known.

Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness. He refuses the case, diagnoses the plaintiff, and then says it to the whole crowd, so the man is not singled out. The warning is doubled, the language for a threat that is not obvious. Covetousness (pleonexia) is the desire for more, and all covetousness includes the respectable kinds: not only the greed a man would recognise, but the legitimate-sounding conviction that one is owed what one is owed. It is forbidden by the tenth commandment (Exodus 20:17), and Paul calls it idolatry (Colossians 3:5). That is the sting. This man may well have been in the right. And what Jesus saw was not a wronged brother but a man whose grip had closed.

For one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions. Life is not measured by what you own. Possessions cannot give life, or keep it, or satisfy it. True life is found in God.

Is it wrong to seek justice in a money dispute? Not in itself. Scripture values justice, and Paul himself appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen (Acts 25:11). There are times when a fair settlement should be sought, especially to protect the vulnerable. But Jesus’ warning cuts close to every inheritance quarrel: ask what is happening in your heart. Is the money worth the brother? Christians should be slow to take one another to court (1 Corinthians 6:1–8), quick to seek reconciliation, and willing, sometimes, to be wronged rather than lose a relationship. Where you must pursue a claim, pursue it without bitterness, and be ready to let go of more than you think you can.

In a sentence. Asked to settle an inheritance dispute, Jesus refused and warned against all greed, because life does not consist in an abundance of possessions.

On a Tuesday. Is there a possession or an amount of money you think would make your life complete? Guard your heart against greed. Where this saying applies: the quiet resentment over who got what in a will, the endless browsing for the next upgrade, the sense that a little more would finally be enough. Where applying it would be wrong: using it to shame a widow for seeking what she needs to live, or to tell a poor family that wanting a decent wage is covetous. Greed is the grip, not the need.

For worship. The Lord who would not divide this man’s inheritance has given his people an inheritance that cannot be divided, an inheritance imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven (1 Peter 1:4). He is himself our portion. And he who owned everything became poor, so that brothers who quarrel over fields might become fellow heirs of a kingdom.
verseByVerse.note: Rabbis were sometimes asked to settle inheritance disputes. The law gave the eldest son a double share.

parallels.desc: a double portion to the firstborn

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them a parable, saying, 'The land of a rich man produced plentifully, and he thought to himself, ‘What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?’
verseByVerse.commentary:
He told them a parable, saying: the land of a rich man produced plentifully, and he thought to himself: what shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?

The land of a rich man produced plentifully. Only Luke records this parable of the rich fool, and the way it opens matters. Not a rich man made a fortune: the land produced. He may have ploughed and sown well, but the harvest came out of soil he did not make, watered by rain he did not arrange. God did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons (Acts 14:17). Every Israelite knew this; it is why firstfruits were brought to the temple and the edges of the field left for the poor (Leviticus 19:9–10). He was already rich, and God gave him more. It is the first thing the man will forget.

And he thought to himself. Literally he dialogued with himself: not with God, not with his neighbours, not with the poor. There is nobody else in this man’s head, no wife, no labourers who brought the harvest in, and above all no Giver. The whole discussion of an enormous surplus takes place inside one skull. He has more than he can hold and nobody to talk to about it, and that is what the surplus has done to him.

What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops? His problem is real. He is not a fraud or an oppressor; the parable gives him no vices at all. He is a competent farmer with a genuine logistical difficulty, and the question he asks is the sensible one. A good question, with a wrong answer. The question had an obvious answer standing in plain sight in his own Scriptures, and he never considers it. He could have shared with the poor (3:11); there were poor people within a mile of that farm. Notice: my crops. Everything is mine. In the three verses of his soliloquy he will say I or my again and again, and God will be mentioned by nobody but God.

A decent man. Jesus does not say the man was dishonest. He is not an oppressor, a swindler or a defrauder of labourers, which would have been the easy way to tell it, and would have let every hearer off. He is a competent farmer having a good year. That is the whole of his character, and it is precisely why the parable is dangerous. It removes every handhold a decent person might reach for.

Twelve baskets left over. Luke has already shown the opposite kind of life in the man telling this story. Before the great decisions of his ministry Jesus went out to talk with his Father, spending a whole night in prayer before choosing the Twelve (6:12). And Luke has shown what happens to a surplus in his hands. In a deserted place he took five loaves and two fish, gave thanks, and fed about five thousand men, and what was left over was gathered up, twelve baskets of broken pieces (9:17). The rich fool’s surplus went into barns; Jesus’ surplus went into baskets for others. All things had been handed over to him by his Father (10:22), and no one has ever been so open-handed.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a rich man whose land produced a huge harvest, who asked himself what to do with it.

On a Tuesday. When God blesses you with more than you need, ask him what to do with it, not just yourself. The pay rise, the bonus, the inheritance, the unexpected refund: before it is absorbed into a larger lifestyle, stop and ask God and someone wise what it is for. Notice too who is in your head when you make money decisions. If the answer is only you, invite others in.

For worship. Every good harvest is a letter from God, and the land that produced plentifully was writing it to a man who never read it. He sends rain on the just and the unjust, crowns the year with his bounty, and fills our hearts with food and gladness. And behind every field stands the Giver himself, who did not keep his greatest treasure in his own barn but gave his Son. The God of abundance is the God of open hands.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke records this parable of the rich fool.

parallels.desc: I must leave it to the man who comes after me

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, ‘I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. And I will say to my soul, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said: I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. And I will say to my soul, soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.

I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones. The solution is entirely rational and entirely revealing. He has a surplus. There are exactly two things a man can do with a surplus: distribute it or store it. He never considers the first. And note that he does not merely keep the barns he has and fill them. He demolishes serviceable buildings in order to construct larger ones, which is a considerable investment of time and money in the business of retention. And something has quietly happened to the ownership. It began as the land producing (v. 16). It is now my barns, my grain, my goods.

And I will say to my soul. This is the sentence the parable is built to reach, and it is the strangest thing in it. The man opens a conversation with his own soul, as if it could be satisfied with grain. That is what a person does when there is nobody else. He has been talking to himself for two verses, and now he addresses the last available party, and what he tells his soul is that its needs have been met.

Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry. Every clause is a category error. Ample goods: quantity, offered as an answer to a soul. Laid up for many years: a guarantee about a future he does not own. Relax, eat, drink, be merry: real goods, not one of which a soul can live on. It is the world’s philosophy: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die (Isaiah 22:13; 1 Corinthians 15:32). He treats the ache of the soul as a supply problem and answers it with more. And it very nearly works. There is no suggestion that he was secretly hollow. He was content, and he went to bed satisfied.

Something for the soul to eat. The man is right that his soul needs feeding, and wrong about the menu. Jesus never mocks the soul’s hunger; he came to meet it. In this Gospel he eats with tax collectors, tells of a father who kills the fattened calf so that a lost son may eat and celebrate (15:23), and at the last takes bread and says, This is my body, which is given for you (22:19). The barn-builder says to his soul: you have ample goods laid up. Christ says to the soul: I have been given for you. One is a store that will belong to someone else by morning. The other is a gift that death cannot recall.

Was his sin saving and planning ahead? No. Scripture commends the ant that stores up food in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8), and a man who does not provide for his family has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). The rich fool’s sin was not the barns but the heart: everything was my crops, my barns, my goods, his future taken for granted and God left out. Saving for old age is wise; living as if the savings were your life is folly.

Is it wrong to look forward to retirement? Not at all. Rest after a lifetime of work is a good gift, and age brings real limits. The question is what retirement is for. The rich fool’s plan was to stop being useful and start consuming. A Christian’s later years can be some of his most fruitful: time to pray, to serve the church, to help grandchildren and neighbours, to give generously, to mentor younger believers. Plan for rest, enjoy it with thanks, and keep asking how you can be rich toward God with the time and money you have saved.

In a sentence. The rich man planned to build bigger barns to store everything for himself, and then to tell his soul to relax and enjoy itself for many years.

On a Tuesday. Are your plans for the future all about I and my? Bring God and others into them. Look at your pension, your savings, your long-term goals, and ask a simple question: whom is this for? Where this applies: a plan that hoards, assumes many years, and leaves God out. Where applying it would be wrong: shaming a careful family for saving for their children’s needs or their own old age, which Scripture commends.

For worship. Blessed be the God who made the soul too large for any barn. He has put eternity into man’s heart (Ecclesiastes 3:11), so that no harvest could ever be enough, and then he filled the emptiness with himself. The rest he gives is not for many years but for ever, and the water he pours is a spring that never needs storing. Whoever comes to him shall not hunger, and whoever believes in him shall never thirst (John 6:35).

parallels.desc: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die

verseByVerse.quote: But God said to him, ‘Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’ So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But God said to him: fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be? So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.

But God said to him, Fool! The first word God speaks in this parable comes in the same breath as be merry. He had left God out of his plans; now God speaks. He is not called wicked but a fool, and in the Bible that is not an insult about intelligence. The fool says in his heart, there is no God (Psalm 14:1): not a philosophical position but a working assumption. This farmer would have denied being an atheist. He was clever, successful and prudent. He simply made every plan as if God did not exist, and as if he would never die.

This night your soul is required of you. “Required” (apaitousin) is a financial word: demanded back, as a loan is recalled. That reframes everything the man has said. He has spent the parable talking about what is his, and the soul he was addressing turns out to have been on loan the whole time, lent to him by God, and it is being called in tonight. Note the timing against his own words. He said many years. God says this night. The gap between those two is the whole distance between what a man can see and what is actually the case.

Into your hands. Set beside this night the night Luke records at the end of his Gospel. The rich fool’s soul is demanded back like a loan recalled; he had no say. Jesus, dying, cried out with a loud voice, Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! (23:46). Nobody took his life from him as a debt is collected. He gave it, into a Father’s hands, for fools like this one. And because he did, the soul of a believer is never simply required of him. Stephen, under the stones, prayed, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit (Acts 7:59). For those in Christ the night the soul is called in is not a creditor at the door. It is a Son receiving his own.

And the things you have prepared, whose will they be? The question is left unanswered, and it is devastating precisely because everyone knows the answer is somebody else’s. He cannot take any of it with him (Psalm 49:16–17; Ecclesiastes 2:18–19; 1 Timothy 6:7). He tore down good barns to build larger ones for a harvest he would never eat, and by morning it belonged to people he had not thought about once. Perhaps it went to the very kind of inheritance dispute that began this conversation (v. 13).

So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God. The two phrases define each other. For himself is the diagnosis; rich toward God is the alternative. And the alternative is not poverty. Jesus does not say so is the one who is rich. He says so is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God: rich in the wrong direction. To be rich toward God is to use what you have for him: for his kingdom, for the poor, for eternal treasure (v. 33; 1 Timothy 6:17–19). Not wealth itself, but wealth hoarded for oneself, is the folly.

What does being rich toward God look like? It begins with knowing God himself as your treasure, and then it shows in how you use everything else. It means giving regularly and generously to the church and to gospel work; caring for the poor and the stranger; being hospitable; supporting family members in need; and holding your possessions as a steward, ready to release them. It also includes being rich in good works (1 Timothy 6:18): time, attention and love spent on others. A poor widow with two small coins can be richer toward God than a millionaire (21:1–4).

In a sentence. God called the rich man a fool, for his life was demanded that very night, and his hoard would go to others, as it does for anyone who stores up treasure for himself but is not rich toward God.

On a Tuesday. If tonight were your last night, would you be rich toward God? Use what you have for his purposes today. A test that takes about a minute: if your accumulation were described out loud by somebody else, in whose direction would it be pointing? And make sure your will, your giving and your plans would read differently from the rich fool’s.

For worship. The God who called in the fool’s soul holds every breath we draw. And his Son was rich toward God as no one else has ever been: every hour he had, every word and every gift that passed through his hands went Godward and outward. He spent that wealth on fools, on men who had built their barns and told their souls to relax, so that they might be made rich toward God and rich in him. There is no fool so foolish that Christ cannot make him wise for salvation.
verseByVerse.note: In the Bible a fool is not unintelligent but one who lives as if there were no God.

parallels.desc: the fool says in his heart, “There is no God”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The “therefore” ties this to the barns. A man has just died with full storehouses, and the lesson drawn is not “store less” but “worry less” — aimed at a different group. The parable was for a crowd with a covetous man in it; this is for disciples, most of whom had nothing to store. And the two problems are the same underneath: both are attempts to secure a life by managing supplies.

Note what is named — food and clothing, not luxuries. This is spoken to people who might actually go hungry.

The ravens are chosen deliberately. They were unclean under the law (Lev. 11:15), they are scavengers, and there is a psalm about exactly this — “he gives to the beasts their food, and to the young ravens that cry” (Ps. 147:9; cf. Job 38:41). The argument is set at the lowest available point. And the ravens are not idle; they fly all day looking. What they lack is a storehouse.

“Which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?” is an audit. Anxiety presents itself as responsible — the alert mind doing necessary work — and the question exposes the claim. And then the sharper turn: he calls adding an hour to a life a small thing. From where we stand it is not small at all; it is what a person at a bedside would give everything for. He calls it the little end of the problem.

The lilies are probably the wild anemones that carpet the Galilean hillsides in spring, and the two activities they do not do — toil and spin — were the two halves of a household's labour. And the argument turns hard on where the grass ends up: gathered as fuel, because wood was scarce, and burned in a peasant oven within the week. God takes trouble over the appearance of something that will heat somebody's bread.

Then the alternative, and it is not serenity but a different pursuit: “seek his kingdom.” And behind it the tenderest address in the Gospel — “fear not, little flock” — with a gift that is not a wage but the kingdom itself, given because the Father enjoyed giving it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The argument from ravens and lilies is not an argument for passivity. The ravens still fly; the lilies still grow; the farmer still plants. What is addressed is not the activity of provision but the anxiety about it — the energy spent worrying about what worry cannot secure.

“O you of little faith” is a name Jesus uses only of disciples. It is never aimed at outsiders; nobody is called little-faith who has none. And the diagnosis is worth noting: not “you have too much to do” and not “your circumstances are difficult,” both of which may be true. The problem named is a shortage of faith in the character of a particular Father — which makes anxiety a theological condition rather than a temperamental one.

“Nor be worried” in v.29 names the mind that will not settle — up in the air, unanchored. Anybody who has lain awake at three in the morning will recognise the picture.

“The nations” is not an insult but a description of a real difference. The pagan world had a crowded pantheon of local deities who had to be managed — offerings at the right time, none of them notably fond of you, none reliable. Anxiety in that setting is not a failure of nerve; it is a rational response to the facts as understood. If nobody is certainly looking after you, somebody had better.

Against which stand seven words: “your Father knows that you need them.” Not a force, not a committee of powers. He knows — so it does not have to be brought to his attention, and a great deal of anxious praying is really lobbying. And the needs are not dismissed as unspiritual.
verseByVerse.examples:
Knowing that anxiety is useless does not cure it. Nobody was ever argued out of worry by being told it achieves nothing; anxious people generally know. What the argument does is clear the ground, so the question becomes the right one: not “how do I stop worrying?” but “what am I going to trust instead?”

“Little flock” is an honest name — a small group in an occupied province with the authorities already hunting their teacher. He does not tell them they are stronger than they look. He tells them who the shepherd is, and the word carries the whole weight of Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34, where God says “I myself will search for my sheep.” And “good pleasure” means it delighted him.

“Sell your possessions” must be faced, because it is not a metaphor — and Luke supplies the answer across his two volumes. Zacchaeus gives away half and salvation comes to his house that day (19:8-9). The women of 8:3 supported the ministry out of means they must therefore still have had. And Peter's rebuke to Ananias turns on it: “while it remained unsold, did it not remain your own?” (Acts 5:4). The selling was never compulsory; the sin was the lie.

So the command is a transfer of ownership, not a rule about percentages. What it can never mean is a Christian who has settled the matter, drawn a line, and considers the rest his own. Ask not what proportion you have given away, but whether there is anything left that you would refuse him.

And “where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” reverses the order everyone assumes. We think the heart chooses and the money follows. He says the heart goes after the treasure — which means the affections can be steered, and that there is a reliable way of finding out what you actually love. Not the confession of faith. The bank statement, and the diary.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to his disciples, 'Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on. For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds!
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to his disciples: therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on. For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds!

Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious. The therefore ties this to the barns. A man has just died with full storehouses, and the lesson drawn for the disciples, most of whom had nothing to store, is not store less but worry less. The rich fool trusted his possessions; the poor can be just as preoccupied with them through anxiety. The two problems look opposite and are the same: both try to secure a life by managing supplies, and both are forms of unbelief.

Do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on. “Anxious” (merimnate) means worried, divided in mind, distracted: the same word as Martha’s (10:41), and the same danger as the thorns that choke the word in the parable of the soils, the cares and riches and pleasures of life (8:14). Food and clothing are not luxuries but the two irreducible necessities, and for most of his hearers a genuine daily question. This is not a rebuke to the comfortable for fretting about trivialities. It is spoken to people who might actually go hungry.

For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. The rich fool has just shown the point from the other side. If the Creator has already given the great things, a living soul and a body, he is hardly going to withhold the small ones that keep them going. Whatever life is, it is not the sum of what sustains it, and the proof is that a man can have all the food and clothing he needs and be, as the last parable showed, a fool who dies that night.

Consider the ravens. “Consider”: look carefully, think about it. The choice of bird is not random and would have registered. Ravens were unclean under the law (Leviticus 11:15), scavengers, the least regarded. Matthew says birds of the air (Matthew 6:26); Luke names the bird nobody wanted. And there is a psalm about exactly this: he gives to the beasts their food, and to the young ravens that cry (Psalm 147:9); Job is asked, who provides for the raven its prey? (Job 38:41).

They neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Unlike the rich fool with his barns. So the argument is deliberately set at the lowest available point. If God feeds the birds nobody wants, on ground he owns, without a barn between them, how much more will he feed his children, who are of far more value than the birds.

Nowhere to lay his head. The one who says this lived it. He told a would-be follower that foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (9:58). He had no barn. He was supported by women who gave out of their means (8:3), and in the wilderness, starving, he refused to turn a stone into bread for himself, because man shall not live by bread alone (4:4). When he tells anxious disciples to consider the ravens, he is not a rich man advising the poor. He is the poorest man in the company, inviting them into the trust he lived in.

What it does not mean. Not that we should stop working or planning. Luke’s ravens are set against the rich fool’s barns, not against the farmer’s plough: the birds still go out after their food; they simply keep no reserve. Paul says: if anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10). The point is not idleness but trust: work, but do not worry. The verse is not against work. It is against the belief that security comes from the size of the reserve.

Is anxiety a sin, then, and is every anxious believer of little faith? Jesus is speaking to worry about food and clothing that springs from not trusting the Father. But some anxiety has roots in the body and the mind, and it is a real illness. Elijah despaired (1 Kings 19:4), the psalmist wrestled with his troubled soul (Psalm 77), and they were not cast off. Seeking help from a doctor or counsellor is not a lack of faith. The command still invites every anxious believer to bring the fear to the Father who knows what we need (v. 30).

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples not to worry about food or clothing, for life is more than these, and God, who feeds even the ravens, values them far more.

On a Tuesday. What are you anxious about? Consider the ravens: God feeds them; he will feed you. Where this saying applies: the late-night spiral about bills you have already planned for, the fear that God will not provide when he always has, the constant checking of a balance that has not changed. Where applying it would be wrong: telling someone with a diagnosed anxiety disorder that they simply need more faith, or telling a family with no food to stop worrying instead of helping them. The church is often the Father’s answer to the raven’s cry.

For worship. The Lord who feeds the ravens has never once forgotten a single bird. He opens his hand and satisfies the desire of every living thing (Psalm 145:16). He hears the young ravens that cry (Psalm 147:9), in a language nobody else heeds. And the Father who feeds scavengers fed his people in the wilderness with manna, and feeds them still with the true bread from heaven, his own Son, who gives life to the world (John 6:32–33).
verseByVerse.note: Ravens were unclean birds — yet God feeds them.

parallels.desc: he gives to the young ravens that cry

verseByVerse.quote: And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest?

And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? Having argued from the birds, he argues from the results, and the question is an audit. Anxiety presents itself as responsible, the alert mind doing necessary work, and it feels like preparation. What has it ever produced? The phrase can also be read a single cubit to his stature, about eighteen inches of height (the ESV notes this). Either way, nobody has ever managed it by worrying. If anything, worry shortens life.

If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest? And there is the second turn, the sharper one. He calls adding an hour to a life a small thing. Read that again, because it inverts the whole scale. From where we stand, an extra hour of life is not a small thing at all; it is precisely what a person at a bedside would give everything for. Jesus calls it the little end of the problem, and if a man cannot manage the little end, the anxiety about food and clothing is aimed at something he is even less able to control. Worry is useless. It does not change tomorrow; it only spoils today. And it forgets God, who controls what we cannot.

Clearing the ground. This is not exactly a comfort but a demolition. Anxiety is described as ineffective: a machine that runs continuously, burns enormous fuel, and produces nothing. Knowing that does not cure it; anxious people generally know. What the argument does is clear the ground, so that the question becomes the right one: not how do I stop worrying? but what am I going to trust instead? The answer is not a technique. It is a Father.

When the days drew near. Jesus measured his own life not by hours he could add but by an hour his Father had set. When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51). In the garden he did not try to buy time; he prayed, not my will, but yours, be done (22:42). And to the men who came with swords and clubs he said, this is your hour, and the power of darkness (22:53). The man who says worry cannot lengthen a life walked unhurried into the darkest hour there has ever been, because his times were in his Father’s hand, and he calls his friends into that same trust.

What is the difference between worry and responsible concern? Concern looks at a real problem, does what can be done, and then leaves the rest with God. Worry keeps turning the problem over long after anything can be done, and treats the turning as if it were doing something. A parent who books a doctor for a sick child is concerned; a parent who lies awake rehearsing every terrible outcome is worried. Paul’s cure is specific: do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God (Philippians 4:6–7). Do the next thing, pray about the rest, and give thanks.

In a sentence. Worry cannot add a single hour to your life, so if you cannot do something so small, why worry about anything else?

On a Tuesday. Has worrying ever changed anything? Take the thing you are anxious about and divide it into two lists: what I can do today, and what only God can do. Do the first list. Pray over the second, by name, and then deliberately give thanks for one thing. Give your worries to God in prayer instead.

For worship. Our days are numbered by God, not by us. He wrote every one of them in his book before one of them came to be (Psalm 139:16), and not one hour can be added or taken without him. The Lord who holds the span of our lives has given his people a life that no hour can end, for whoever lives and believes in him shall never die (John 11:26). Our times are in his hand, and his hand was pierced for us.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “a single hour to his span of life” can also be read “a single cubit to his stature.”

verseByVerse.quote: Consider the lilies, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass, which is alive in the field today, and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider the lilies, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass, which is alive in the field today, and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith!

Consider the lilies, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin. Consider: study them, take them in properly. The lilies are probably not the cultivated flower but the wild blooms that carpet the Galilean hillsides in spring with brilliant colour: anemones most likely, irises, poppies, scarlet and brief. And the two activities named are the two halves of a household’s labour in that world: men toiled in the field, women spun thread for cloth. The flowers do neither, which is to say they do not work for a living and they do not make their own clothes.

Yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. Solomon is the highest available standard, the richest, most splendid king in Israel’s history. His court was so magnificent that a foreign queen was left breathless (1 Kings 10:4–5), and the phrase in all his glory is the summit of what human wealth can dress a man in. And a weed on a hillside beats it: a flower that grew where the seed happened to fall, was dressed by nobody, and will be gone in a fortnight. His royal robes were nothing compared with the beauty God gives a wildflower.

But if God so clothes the grass, which is alive in the field today, and tomorrow is thrown into the oven. Now the argument turns hard, and the detail is deliberately unglamorous. Those hillsides dried out; the stalks were gathered as fuel, because wood was scarce, and a peasant’s clay oven was fired with dead grass and thorns. They last a day. So the sequence is: God takes trouble over the appearance of something that will be burned to heat somebody’s bread. Not preserved, not admired, not even noticed by most people who walked past. Burned, within the week.

How much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith! You are eternal; they are temporary. The rebuke is gentle, and it is a rebuke. Little-faith ones is a single word, one Jesus uses only of disciples; nobody is called little-faith who has none. Anxiety is a sign of small faith that does not take God at his word. And notice the diagnosis. Not you have too much to do, or your circumstances are difficult, both perhaps true, but a shortage of faith in the character of a particular Father. Anxiety is, at root, a theological condition and not only a temperamental one.

Greater than Solomon. A chapter earlier Jesus told this same crowd that something greater than Solomon is here (11:31). The greater than Solomon wore no royal robes. Herod and his soldiers dressed him in splendid clothing to mock him (23:11), and at the cross they divided his garments by casting lots (23:34). The King who robes the hillsides went to his death with less covering than a wildflower. So when he says, how much more will he clothe you, he says it as the one who would be stripped in order to keep that promise.

How can little faith grow? Not by staring at your faith, but by looking at God. Faith grows as it feeds on his promises and remembers his past faithfulness. Read the Psalms that recount what he has done. Keep a record of answered prayer. Sit under the preaching of his word. Take small steps of obedience that require trust, and watch him keep his word. And pray as the father of the epileptic boy did: I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24). Jesus did not reject that prayer. He answered it.

In a sentence. If God clothes short-lived wildflowers more beautifully than Solomon, how much more will he clothe his people, who have so little faith.

On a Tuesday. Look at a flower today and remember: your Father clothes it, and he will clothe you. When you worry about how you look, what you can afford, or whether your children will have enough, go and look at the hedgerow. Then say to him plainly what you are afraid of, and thank him for the last time he provided.

For worship. The God who paints anemones for a single week has clothed his people in something better than Solomon’s robes: the righteousness of Christ, a garment of salvation, a robe that will never wear out or be thrown in the oven. He takes delight in beauty, and he has determined to make his people beautiful for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Dry grass was used as fuel for clay ovens.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not seek what you are to eat and what you are to drink, nor be worried. For all the nations of the world seek after these things, and your Father knows that you need them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And do not seek what you are to eat and what you are to drink, nor be worried. For all the nations of the world seek after these things, and your Father knows that you need them.

And do not seek what you are to eat and what you are to drink, nor be worried. Do not make these the goal of your life. The word for worried is curious: meteōrizesthe, used in Greek of a ship tossed on the swell, or of something suspended in mid-air; it is where the English meteor comes from. To be up in the air, unanchored, in suspense, going wherever the next wave puts you. Anybody who has lain awake at three in the morning will recognise the picture with some precision. The mind is not thinking; it is being moved about.

For all the nations of the world seek after these things. The nations is the standard Jewish term for the Gentiles, used here as description, not insult. The pagan world had a crowded pantheon of deities to be managed, gods of harvest, weather and household, each requiring the right offering at the right time, none of them notably fond of you and none reliable. Provision had to be negotiated, and the negotiation never ended. In that setting anxiety is a rational response: if nobody is certainly looking after you, somebody had better. Worry about possessions is pagan, not Christian.

And your Father knows that you need them. Every word bears weight. Your Father: not a force or a committee of powers, but the name he taught them to pray with (11:2). Knows: so it need not be brought to his attention, and a great deal of anxious praying is really lobbying, as though the case had not yet been properly presented. That you need them: the needs are not dismissed as unspiritual. That is the whole answer, and it is not a technique for calming down. It is a fact about who is in charge of the supply.

Revealed by the Son. What makes the difference between the nations and the little band around Jesus? Not that the disciples were cleverer or more spiritual. It is that they had been brought to know God as Father, and Luke has told us how. All things have been handed over to me by my Father, Jesus said, and no one knows who the Father is except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (10:22). The anxious pagan could not say your Father, because no one had shown him the Father. The Son had come to do exactly that, and to make orphans into sons: God sent forth his Son, Paul writes, to redeem, so that we might receive adoption as sons and cry, Abba! Father! (Galatians 4:4–6).

If my Father already knows, why pray about my needs? Because he tells us to ask: give us each day our daily bread (11:3). Prayer is not briefing God; it is trusting him out loud. Asking reminds us that every meal is a gift, keeps us dependent, and turns anxiety into conversation. The difference between pagan prayer and Christian prayer is not that one asks and the other does not. It is that the pagan asks in order to persuade a reluctant power, and the Christian asks as a child whose Father already knows and already cares.

In a sentence. Do not make food and drink your goal or worry about them, as the pagans do, for your Father knows you need them.

On a Tuesday. Notice where your worries sound exactly like those of people who do not know God. Then talk to your Father about them as a child, not a lobbyist. Your Father knows exactly what you need. Thank him today, and trust him with tomorrow.

For worship. We are not orphans in a universe of indifferent powers, tossed like a ship on the swell. We have a Father in heaven who knows every need before we ask and has numbered our days. The gods of the nations had to be bargained with and never once came near. Our Father came near in his Son, and still he gives freely, and delights to.

verseByVerse.quote: Instead, seek his kingdom, and these things will be added to you. 'Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead, seek his kingdom, and these things will be added to you. Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.

Instead, seek his kingdom. Make God’s reign the goal and centre of your life. Matthew’s version adds and his righteousness (Matthew 6:33). Seeking it is not something extra special, but an ordinary life lived God’s way, asking first what he wants.

Not seek nothing. The energy is redirected, not switched off. He has just said the nations seek after food and drink, and uses the same verb: go after this instead. The alternative to anxiety here is not serenity but a different pursuit, and the man chasing the kingdom grows calmer because his attention has gone somewhere it can get purchase. The pursuit is ordinary: the next duty done for him, the next person loved because he loves them.

And these things will be added to you. Food and clothing, as extras: not riches, but what you need. Added is the language of a bonus on top of a transaction, not the object of the deal but not withheld either. It is not a promise that a Christian will never be hungry. Paul knew what it was to be in need (Philippians 4:12), and Hebrews remembers believers who were destitute (Hebrews 11:37). What is promised is that the Father who knows will not forget, not that provision will always look like comfort.

Fear not, little flock. Only Luke records this saying, and of all the things Jesus called his disciples, it is the tenderest. Little flock is an honest name: a small, weak, vulnerable group in an occupied province, with the religious establishment already hunting their teacher, like sheep among wolves (10:3). He does not tell them they are stronger than they look. He tells them who the shepherd is. The word flock carries the whole weight of Psalm 23, of Isaiah 40:11, where he gathers the lambs in his arms, and of Ezekiel 34, where God says he himself will search for his sheep. Jesus is their shepherd, and God is their shepherd.

For it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom. The verb (eudokēsen) means it pleased him, it was his glad decision, and Luke has used its root once before, when the voice from heaven said to Jesus at the Jordan, with you I am well pleased (3:22). The Father’s delight in his Son and his delight in giving the kingdom to the Son’s little flock are one delight. Luke shows how the gift travels: at the last supper Jesus tells the Twelve, I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom (22:29). It is not a wage or a supplement but the very thing they were told to seek. If he gives you the kingdom, will he not give you bread? He who did not spare his own Son, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? (Romans 8:32).

So what does seeking the kingdom look like on an ordinary day? Mostly it looks like the day you already have, lived under a different King. At breakfast it is thanking him and asking what he wants of you today. At work it is honest effort and fair dealing, done as for the Lord. At home it is patience with a tired spouse and time for a child. In money it is giving first and spending carefully. When you are wronged it is forgiveness; when you fail it is confession. It also means gathering with his people on the Lord’s Day and sharing Christ when the door opens. It rarely feels dramatic. It is ordinary walking in God’s will, one decision at a time, with his kingdom, not your comfort, as the question you ask first.

In a sentence. Seek God’s kingdom, and he will add what you need, so do not be afraid, little flock, for your Father delights to give you the kingdom.

On a Tuesday. Before your next decision today, a purchase, a reply, a plan for the evening, ask first: what does my King want here? Where this saying applies: the choice between a promotion that would swallow your family and church life and a slower path that keeps them; the decision to give before you spend. Where applying it would be wrong: thinking you must leave your job for full-time ministry to really seek the kingdom, or neglecting your family’s needs for a church project. The kingdom is sought in the ordinary calling God has given you.

For worship. The Shepherd who calls us little flock walked ahead of his sheep into the wolves’ jaws, and now holds the kingdom in his pierced hands to give away. We do not earn it, we do not bargain for it, we do not fight for it. We are given it, by a Father whose delight in his beloved Son overflows onto every sheep that Son has gathered, and who smiles as he gives.

parallels.desc: he will tend his flock like a shepherd
the kingdom given to the saints

verseByVerse.quote: Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.

Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. The command has to be faced, because it is not a metaphor. It is the opposite of the rich fool. Since God gives you the kingdom, you are free to give away earthly things, and some early Christians did exactly this (Acts 2:44–45; 4:34–37). Does the Lord require every Christian to liquidate everything?

What it does not mean. It is not a law that every believer must sell everything he owns, and Luke himself will not let it be read that way. But it does mean that every Christian must hold possessions loosely, give generously, and be willing to sell anything for Christ.

A transfer of ownership. Luke will not let us dodge the command, and he also supplies the answer across his two volumes. Zacchaeus gives away half his goods, and Jesus says salvation has come to his house (19:8–9): half, not all. The women of 8:3 supported the ministry out of means they must still have had. And when Ananias lies about a field, Peter’s rebuke turns on this: while it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? (Acts 5:4). The selling was never compulsory; the sin was the lie. So the command is not a rule about percentages. It is a transfer of ownership. The disciple stops being the owner, so that whatever is still in his hands is at the Master’s disposal. For one man that means selling the lot, as for the rich ruler whose possessions owned him (18:22). For another it means an open house, a funded ministry, a quietly emptied account. It can never mean a Christian who has drawn a line and considers the rest his own.

Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail. Leather purses wore out and got holes. He is not against investment; he is against bad investment. What is given to God and the poor is stored up in heaven, safe for ever (1 Timothy 6:18–19). Treasure in heaven is mostly ordinary: kindness, generosity, faithful work and care for others, done for Christ.

Where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. Wealth was often stored as fine clothing, which moths could eat, or as coins and goods, which thieves could steal. The purse that wears through, the thief and the moth are the three things that destroyed stored wealth in that world.

For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. The order is not what anyone expects. We assume the heart chooses and the money follows. He says the heart goes to where the treasure already is. That means the affections can be steered, and the steering wheel is a chequebook: a man who cannot make himself care about something can move his money into it and find, months later, that his heart has followed. It also gives a reliable way of finding out what you actually love, as distinct from what you say you love. Not the confession of faith. The bank statement, and the diary.

Where Christ is. Where, then, are the heavens in which this treasure is kept, and why should the heart want to go there? Because that is where the Lord is. Paul draws the line straight: if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God (Colossians 3:1). Treasure in heaven is not a private account in the sky. It is everything given away for love of him, laid up in the presence of the one who gave himself away first. So the heart that follows its treasure upward arrives, in the end, not at a vault but at a person.

How much should I give, and to whom? The New Testament sets no fixed figure, but it asks for regular, proportionate, cheerful and sacrificial giving (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 9:7). Begin with your own church, which feeds you; then the needy around you, especially fellow believers (Galatians 6:10); then gospel work further afield. Many find a tenth a wise starting point and grow from there. Give in a way that costs you something, plan it rather than leaving it to impulse, and do it quietly. If you are in debt or poverty, give what you can with a glad heart; the widow’s two coins counted most of all.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples to sell their possessions and give to the poor, storing up lasting treasure in heaven, because the heart follows the treasure.

On a Tuesday. Look at your bank statement. Where is your treasure? Give something away today, and see your heart follow. Where this applies: the possession you could not bear to lose, the account you never touch, the room full of things you have not used in years. Where applying it would be wrong: selling the family home without your spouse’s agreement, giving away what your children need to live, or treating a tired single mother’s modest savings as a sin. Hold everything open-handed, and let love, not guilt, decide what goes.

For worship. The Lord who told us to sell our possessions sold everything himself. He left the riches of heaven, had nowhere to lay his head, and was stripped of his last garment at the cross. And because he did, we have a treasure in heaven that does not fail, kept for us by him, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys, and a purse that will never wear through.
verseByVerse.note: Wealth was often stored as fine clothing, which moths could eat.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Three parables of readiness, and they describe the church living between the two advents.

“Stay dressed for action” is, as the ESV margin gives it, “let your loins stay girded” — the long outer robe pulled up and tucked into the belt, so that a man could run or work. It has a history: Israel ate the first Passover with belts fastened and sandals on, dressed to leave a country that night (Ex. 12:11). And the lamp kept burning through the dark hours required somebody awake to trim the wick — readiness is not a state achieved and possessed but maintained, hourly, by somebody who has not gone to sleep.

The servants are waiting on the night of somebody else's wedding feast, which could run for days. They have no timetable, and their whole readiness reduces to one small thing: whether the door opens at once. Not whether they achieved anything in his absence. Whether, when he knocked, somebody was still expecting him.

Then the sentence nothing in the ancient world prepares anybody for: he will gird himself, sit them at his table, and serve them. That does not happen — the whole architecture of that society rested on the distinction between those who recline and those who serve. And Luke proves it is not a flourish: “I am among you as the one who serves” (22:27), and on the same night John records him tying a towel round himself and washing feet (John 13:4-5).

The watches named are the second and third — roughly ten till two, and two till dawn. Not the early evening when staying up is easy, and not the last hour when the end is in sight. The dead middle, which is where most Christian waiting is actually done.

The thief image changes the register entirely: same arrival, opposite colour, and the difference is wholly in the state of the person inside. The walls were mud brick; a thief had no need to force the door.

Peter asks whether the parable is for the Twelve or for everyone, and gets no answer — only another parable, this one specifically about a man with responsibility over others. So the answer is yes, especially you, but not in the direction the question hoped.
verseByVerse.theology:
The returning master who serves his watching servants is the most counter-cultural image of authority in the ancient world. It is the enacted theology of the whole ministry — “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45) — and of the ascended Lord who gives the Spirit, intercedes, and prepares a place. He has never stopped serving those he loves.

The oikonomos of v.42 is a steward, usually himself a slave, placed over the household with the keys and the accounts. He owns nothing and can be dismissed. And his one named duty is not “increase the estate” or “keep order” but “give them their portion of food at the proper time” — which is the same commission Peter himself will receive on a beach: feed my lambs, tend my sheep, feed my sheep (John 21:15-17).

Two adjectives govern it. Faithful — trustworthy with what is not his; and wise — the practical sense to know what the household needs and when. Either without the other is useless.

The reward for faithfulness is startling in its logic: he is set over all the master's possessions. The reward for a job well done is a bigger job — not release from service, not a pension. Which cuts against a picture most people carry without examining it: the New Testament nowhere describes the life to come as retirement. Its images are of reigning, of serving, of being given cities to look after (19:17).

And the unknown hour is the arrangement, not an inconvenience in it. If the hour were knowable, readiness could be scheduled — and everyone would schedule it late, which is exactly what the wicked servant does when he concludes the master is delayed.
verseByVerse.examples:
The servant's ruin begins with a private conclusion about a timetable, said “to himself.” There is no moment of rebellion. And the conclusion is not even wrong — the master is delayed. What is wrong is what he does with an accurate observation.

Then two directions, and they are the two ways a leader goes bad. He turns on the household — and these are his fellow servants, not his property. Authority given to feed people is used to hit them, which does not usually involve fists: the pulpit used to settle a score, the discipline that is really about control, the counselling relationship in which one person is always the one who has to change. And he turns to himself: “eat and drink and get drunk,” an echo of the rich fool's “relax, eat, drink, be merry.” The food he was appointed to distribute is going down his own throat.

The two beatings settle something readers often pass over. Scripture does not teach that judgement is a single undifferentiated verdict falling equally on everyone; it teaches degrees (cf. 10:12-14). Perfect justice is exact, and exactness means proportion. But note what is not said: the second servant is not acquitted. Ignorance reduces the sentence; it does not produce innocence.

And the closing principle falls hardest not on the ignorant but on the well-taught. The wording — “was given,” “they entrusted” — points past the servant to the one who gave, which means every item is a deposit and not an achievement: a Christian upbringing, an open Bible, a church down the road, forty years of clear preaching. None of them is a reward. Every one raises the bar. A lifetime of good sermons is not a shelter; it is an account.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Stay dressed for action and keep your lamps burning, and be like men who are waiting for their master to come home from the wedding feast, so that they may open the door to him at once when he comes and knocks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stay dressed for action and keep your lamps burning, and be like men who are waiting for their master to come home from the wedding feast, so that they may open the door to him at once when he comes and knocks.

Readiness for Christ’s return. From possessions, Jesus turns to his return. The two are linked: those who store up treasure on earth are not ready for him, and those whose treasure is in heaven are already leaning toward the day it is opened.

Stay dressed for action. Two images, and both are physical. The first is literally let your loins stay girded, as the ESV notes. Men wore a long outer robe, and to do anything requiring movement, running, working, fighting, it had to be pulled up and tucked into the belt. To be girded was to be unable to lounge. The dress itself was a decision. And it has a history. Israel ate the first Passover with belts fastened, sandals on their feet and staff in hand (Exodus 12:11), dressed to leave a country that night. Jesus is putting his disciples in the posture of a people about to be brought out.

The exodus he accomplished. Luke has prepared us for this. On the mountain, Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about his departure, literally his exodus, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (9:31). The disciples are told to dress like Israel on the Passover night because a greater exodus is under way, and its Lamb is the one speaking: Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7). Israel left Egypt on the night the lamb died. The church waits, belts fastened, for the morning when the Lamb who died comes back to bring her home. The fastened belt is not the dress of people hoping to be rescued. It is the dress of people whose ransom has been paid and whose departure is certain.

And keep your lamps burning. The second image is a lamp kept burning through the dark hours, which required somebody awake to trim the wick and top up the oil. A lamp does not stay lit by itself, and that is the point of using it. Readiness is not a state a person achieves and then possesses; it is maintained, hourly, by somebody who has not gone to sleep.

And be like men who are waiting for their master to come home from the wedding feast. The picture is a household staff on the night of somebody else’s celebration. A wedding feast in that world could run for days, and there was no way to know which night the master would come back or at what hour. The servants have no timetable. What they have is a duty that continues regardless.

So that they may open the door to him at once when he comes and knocks. Not keeping him waiting. The whole of their readiness reduces to one small thing: whether the door opens at once. That is the test the parable sets, and it is a modest one. Not whether they achieved anything in his absence. Not whether they were impressive. Whether, when he knocked, there was somebody on the other side of the door who was still expecting him.

The delay is built in. It is worth noticing what this implies. There is a delay, it is unspecified, and it is long enough that staying awake is difficult. Jesus builds the waiting into the parable from the start. He never suggested it would be short.

What does being ready actually mean? Not living in a constant state of alarm, or giving up ordinary work to watch the sky. It means being a true believer, trusting Christ now, with nothing between you and him that you would be ashamed for him to find. It means keeping short accounts with God and others, confessing sin quickly and putting wrongs right.
