And it means being about your Master’s business: faithful in the work, the family and the church he has given you. A ready servant may be found asleep in bed at night; what matters is that he is the Master’s, and expecting him.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples to be dressed and ready with their lamps lit, like servants waiting to open the door at once when their master returns.

On a Tuesday. Are you ready for Christ’s return, if he came today? Ask what you would want to put right first, the unconfessed sin, the unreconciled friend, the neglected duty, and put it right now. Then go about your ordinary work with your belt fastened, as one who expects a knock.

For worship. The Master is coming home. He went away to prepare a place for us, and he will come again and take us to himself (John 14:3). The night is long and the lamps burn low, but the hand that will knock is a pierced hand, and the household it comes back for is one he bought with his own blood. The long night of waiting has a morning, and its first sound will be his.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the literal wording, “Let your loins stay girded” — the long robe tucked into the belt for work.

parallels.desc: your belt fastened, ready to leave

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them. If he comes in the second watch, or in the third, and finds them awake, blessed are those servants!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them. If he comes in the second watch, or in the third, and finds them awake, blessed are those servants!

Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake when he comes. Faithful, watchful. And then the sentence that ought to stop the reader, because nothing in the ancient world prepares anybody for it.

Truly, I say to you, he will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them. An astonishing reversal. The master ties up his own robe, the same girding the servants were told to do in v. 35, sits them at his table, and waits on them. Nothing like this happened in Roman households or Jewish ones. That whole society rested on the line between those who recline and those who serve; a master returning at midnight expects his meal (17:7–8). And the Truly, I say to you is Jesus flagging that he knows how this sounds.

Picture or promise? Both, and Luke shows it. At the Supper he says it about himself in plain words: who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines at table? But I am among you as the one who serves (22:27). And on the same night John records him rising from the meal, tying a towel round himself, and washing his disciples’ feet (John 13:4–5), girded, exactly as here. He came not to be served but to serve. So the image is not a flourish. It is what he is like, and it is what he did. The Lord of glory will serve his people at the banquet of the kingdom.

If he comes in the second watch, or in the third, and finds them awake, blessed are those servants! The second and third watches covered roughly nine in the evening to three in the morning: the hardest time to stay awake, and the least expected time to come. Not the early evening, nor the last hour when the end is in sight, but the dead middle. That is where most Christian waiting is done. Nobody finds the first years hard. What is hard is year twenty, in the dark, with no sign of anything, holding a lamp. And for those servants, the master will put on an apron.

Will Christ really serve us in heaven, rather than we serving him? Both. Scripture says his servants will worship him (Revelation 22:3), and we will gladly serve him for ever. But the deepest truth of the kingdom is that he serves us first and always: he feeds us at his table, wipes away our tears, and gives us himself. Our service is only ever a response to his. Heaven is not a place where Christ finally gets the reward of being waited on by us. It is the place where we discover the full extent of how he loves to give.

In a sentence. Blessed are the servants the master finds awake, for he himself will serve them at table, however late he comes.

On a Tuesday. If you are in the dead middle of a long night, a long illness, a long wait for a prodigal, a long season of dryness, keep your lamp lit for one more hour. Do the next small faithful thing. The Master who is coming is not a harsh inspector but the one who will tie on an apron and serve you.

For worship. The King of kings, before whom angels veil their faces, will tie up his robe and bring the dishes to tired servants who managed to stay awake. He has already served us once, at the cross, with his own body and blood. When the feast comes, the hands that pass the bread will still bear the marks of that first service. There is no master like this Master.
verseByVerse.note: The second and third watches covered the middle of the night.

parallels.desc: he dressed himself and washed their feet

verseByVerse.quote: But know this, that if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have left his house to be broken into. You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But know this, that if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have left his house to be broken into. You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.

But know this, that if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming. The register changes completely, and it is meant to. A few verses ago the arrival was a master coming home from a wedding, and the servants were waiting to open the door. Now the arrival is a burglary, and the householder is asleep. Same event, opposite emotional colour, and the difference is entirely in the state of the person inside. Thieves do not announce their arrival.

He would not have left his house to be broken into. Literally dug through, which is exact: the walls of an ordinary house were mud brick, and a thief did not force the door. He made a hole in the wall. And note where the argument sits. The householder is not blamed for being asleep at night, which is what nights are for. He is caught out because the one thing he needed, the hour, was the one thing unavailable.

You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect. Not that Christ is a thief, but that his coming will be as unexpected. The image is used elsewhere in the New Testament for the same event, and always the same way: the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10; Revelation 3:3; 16:15). It is never about his character. It is about the timing. No one can know the date (Mark 13:32). So be ready always.

Why the hour is hidden. If the hour were knowable, readiness could be scheduled, and everyone would schedule it late, as the servant in the next parable does when he concludes the master is delayed. The unknowability is not an inconvenience in the arrangement; it is the arrangement, and it makes readiness a way of living rather than a task done nearer the time. It is also the standing answer to every attempt to calculate the date: a man who has worked out when the thief is coming has not increased his readiness, he has explained why it can wait. And there is mercy in it. No Christian is ever asked to be ready later, only now, which is the only thing anybody can actually do.

The time of your visitation. Jesus speaks as one whose first coming was already being missed. Weeping over Jerusalem, he would say that its enemies would come because you did not know the time of your visitation (19:44). The city that read the prophets every Sabbath slept through the arrival of its King. But Luke has also shown us who was awake. Shepherds keeping watch over their flock by night heard the news first (2:8–11). Simeon was waiting for the consolation of Israel, and Anna spoke of the child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem (2:25, 38). The Lord who came once to a sleeping house and a few watchers is coming again, and he is telling his friends now which kind of household to be.

Will Christ come secretly first and take believers away before the end? This app holds that he will not. The New Testament describes one visible, public return of Christ at the end of the age, when the dead are raised, believers are gathered to him, and the world is judged (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). His coming is unexpected in its timing, like a thief, but not hidden in its manner: every eye will see him (Revelation 1:7). That is why the call is simply to be ready, all the time, for the day itself.

In a sentence. As a homeowner would guard his house if he knew when a thief was coming, so be ready always, because the Son of Man will come when you do not expect.

On a Tuesday. Live each day as if Christ might return today. When you hear someone predicting a date, do not be drawn in; ask instead what you would change if he came this afternoon, and change it. Unknown timing is not a reason for anxiety but for steady faithfulness.

For worship. The Lord who comes at an unexpected hour is the Lord who has never once been late. He came in the fullness of time; he rose on the third day as he said; he will return on the day the Father has fixed. We do not know the hour, but we know the One who is coming, and to those who love his appearing, his coming will be no thief’s surprise but a homecoming.
verseByVerse.note: Houses had walls of mud brick that a thief could dig through.

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said, 'Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all?' And the Lord said, 'Who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom his master will set over his household, to give them their portion of food at the proper time?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter said: Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all? And the Lord said: who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom his master will set over his household, to give them their portion of food at the proper time?

Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all? It is a very Petrine question, and Luke keeps it because of what it exposes. What is Peter actually asking? Almost certainly this: is the standard the same for the Twelve as for the crowd, or is there a separate arrangement for us? He has heard a warning about servants and unexpected arrivals, and he wants to know which category he is in.

Who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom his master will set over his household? Jesus does not answer the question directly. He does something better and more uncomfortable: he tells another parable, and this one is especially for people with responsibility over others. So the answer is yes, it does apply especially to you, Peter, but not in the direction the question was hoping. The manager is an oikonomos, a steward, often himself a trusted slave, but one placed over the whole household and its supplies, with authority to run it (16:1). He held the keys and the accounts. He was not the owner of anything, and he could be dismissed. The word is used of church leaders: stewards of the mysteries of God, of whom it is required that they be found faithful (1 Corinthians 4:1–2; Titus 1:7).

To give them their portion of food at the proper time. His one named duty is not what anyone would nominate: not to increase the estate, nor to keep order, but to feed the household. That is Christian leadership as Jesus states it: to feed God’s household with his word, faithfully and at the right time. It is the commission Peter himself will be given on a beach three times over: feed my lambs, tend my sheep, feed my sheep (John 21:15–17), and Paul and Peter will hand it on to the elders (Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:2).

Faithful and wise. Two adjectives govern it. Faithful: trustworthy with what is not his. Wise: the practical sense to know what the household needs and when. Either without the other is useless: a reliable man with no judgement will feed them the wrong thing, and a shrewd one who cannot be trusted will feed himself. And the whole thing turns on at the proper time. The steward is not asked to produce food from nowhere. He is asked to distribute what the master has provided, on time, to people who are hungry now.

A Son over the house. Behind every faithful steward stands the one the Master trusts most. Hebrews sets Moses and Christ side by side in exactly these terms: Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son (Hebrews 3:5–6). Jesus does not stand outside this parable as a supervisor. He is the steward who never once fed himself from the stores. He taught daily in the temple (19:47), and on his last night, with the cross hours away, he was still setting food before his disciples (22:14–20). Every pastor and parent who feeds others is handing out what he provided, and will answer to him.

If I am not a church leader, is this for me? Yes, in its own measure. Every Christian is a steward of something: a family to feed spiritually as well as physically, a Sunday school class, a friend who looks to you, gifts and money and time (1 Peter 4:10). Parents especially are managers of a household, given the task of feeding their children with God’s word at the proper time. The questions are the same for you as for a pastor: am I faithful with what is not mine, and wise about what the people in my care need now?

In a sentence. When Peter asked whom the parable was for, Jesus described the faithful and wise manager whom the master puts in charge of feeding his household.

On a Tuesday. Pray for those who lead your church, that they would be faithful managers, feeding God’s household; tell your pastor this week that you are praying for him. And ask who in your own household or circle is hungry for something from God that you could give them at the proper time: a verse, a prayer, an hour of your attention.

For worship. The Master of the house is himself the bread. He feeds his people with his own body and blood, given for them, and he appoints under-shepherds to set that bread before his household week by week. He never forgets the portion of the smallest servant, and in all the long night of his absence his household has never once been left without its food.
verseByVerse.note: A household manager was often a trusted slave put in charge of the other servants.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions.

Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. The blessing is not attached to results. So doing: not just watching, but still working faithfully at the thing he was left to do, on the day the master happens to arrive. That is a relief to anyone in Christian work, because it removes the metric most people quietly measure themselves by. The steward is not accountable for the size of the household or its enthusiasm, but for whether the food went out on time. Nor does he have to be found doing something impressive at the moment of arrival. The aim is not a heroic finish but an unbroken habit.

Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions. The reward is startling, and its logic is worth following. He was set over the household; he is now set over everything. The reward for having been trusted with a job is a bigger job. Not release from service, not a pension, not an easier post: more responsibility, and permanently (19:17). In the kingdom, faithful servants will share Christ’s reign (22:29–30; 2 Timothy 2:12; Revelation 3:21).

Not retirement. That cuts against a picture of heaven most people carry without examining it. The New Testament nowhere describes the life to come as idle retirement. Its images are of reigning, serving, being given cities to look after (19:17), and entering into the master’s joy, which is the joy of somebody still doing something.

All his possessions. The steward began as a slave with no property at all and ends with the run of the entire estate. Nothing has become his by right; everything has been entrusted to him. That is what being an heir means: if children, then heirs, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17). The man who was faithful with somebody else’s bread is handed the house.

Are rewards in heaven earned? No. Every reward is grace upon grace: God gives the gifts, the strength to use them, and then rewards the use as if it were ours (1 Corinthians 4:7; 15:10). Salvation itself is never earned; it rests on Christ alone. But Scripture does promise real, differing rewards to faithful servants, and Jesus means us to be encouraged by them. There will be no envy in heaven, because every servant will be full, and every crown will be cast at his feet (Revelation 4:10).

In a sentence. Blessed is the servant the master finds faithfully at work when he comes, for he will put him in charge of everything he owns.

On a Tuesday. What has the Master given you to do? Be found doing it when he comes. It is probably not glamorous: the nappies, the spreadsheet, the hospital visit, the Bible study preparation, the care of an ageing parent. Do today’s portion of it faithfully, and stop measuring yourself by results he has not asked you for.

For worship. The Master who rewards faithfulness is himself the faithful Servant, who finished the work the Father gave him to do and was set over all things. Every reward we receive is a share in his. And the God who could have run his household without us chose to entrust it to us, and then to make the stewards heirs. Such is the generosity of the Lord of the house.

verseByVerse.quote: But if that servant says to himself, ‘My master is delayed in coming,’ and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and put him with the unfaithful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if that servant says to himself: my master is delayed in coming, and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and put him with the unfaithful.

But if that servant says to himself, My master is delayed in coming. Everything that follows comes out of that one sentence, and it is worth noticing that it is said to himself. Nobody announces it. There is no moment of rebellion, no decision to become a tyrant. There is a private conclusion about a timetable. And the conclusion is not even wrong. The master is delayed: the whole point of the previous parables is that he takes longer than expected. What is wrong is what the servant does with an accurate observation. This is the danger of the delay of Christ’s return. People begin to think he will never come (2 Peter 3:3–4), and live accordingly.

And begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk. These are the two directions in which a leader goes bad. He turns on the household: authority given to feed his fellow servants is used to hit them. That is the permanent temptation of religious office, and it seldom involves fists: the pulpit used to settle a score, discipline that is really about control, counselling in which one person is always the one who has to change. And he turns to himself. Eat and drink and get drunk echoes the rich fool’s relax, eat, drink, be merry; the food he was appointed to distribute (v. 42) goes down his own throat. The delay does not cause either, but it makes both possible. A man who expects his employer within the hour does not start drinking the cellar.

The master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know. Sudden and unexpected.

And will cut him in pieces and put him with the unfaithful. The phrase is violent, and its exact sense is disputed, possibly meaning cut him off; but the verdict is not. The language shows how seriously God judges unfaithful leaders. He is put with the unfaithful, with unbelievers, which is the real sentence, and it means he is finally classified with the people he showed himself to be one of. He had the keys. He held the office. He was called a servant to the last line of the parable. And the accounting placed him where he had actually been standing all along.

Is this servant a true believer who loses his salvation? Luke’s own word answers it. He is put with the unfaithful, the apistoi, which also means unbelievers: he ends among the people who never trusted the master, because that is what he was. He is a professing servant, a leader in the household, whose conduct shows he never truly knew his master; Matthew says he is put with the hypocrites (Matthew 24:51). He held office in the household without ever belonging to its Lord, and his treatment of others exposed it. Cut in pieces is a picture of severe judgement, not of a believer’s fall from grace. A true servant may fail and be disciplined, but those who belong to Christ endure to the end because he keeps them.

The Master beaten in his own house. The parable came true against Jesus himself within months. In the high priest’s house, the men holding him blindfolded the Lord of the household and beat him, demanding that he prophesy who had struck him (22:63–64). Those whose office was to serve God’s people turned their authority on God’s Son. And he did not return the blows; he went on to the cross for servants like them. So the judgement at the end of this parable is not the anger of a master who has never been wronged. It is the verdict of one who knows in his own body what it is to be struck by those who should have served, and who will not let it stand in his house.

What should a church do about a leader who abuses those in his care? Take it seriously and act, because Jesus does. Abuse of any kind, physical, sexual, emotional or spiritual, must never be tolerated or covered up to protect a ministry’s reputation. Crimes should be reported to the civil authorities; victims should be believed, protected and cared for; and the leader should be removed from office while the matter is examined honestly (1 Timothy 5:19–20). A leader is a servant over the household, never its owner. A church that protects the powerful at the expense of the vulnerable has taken the side of the servant in this parable.

In a sentence. A servant who assumes his master’s delay means he can abuse others and indulge himself will be severely punished when his master returns unexpectedly.

On a Tuesday. The delay of Christ’s return is not a licence for unfaithfulness. He is coming; live accordingly. Ask where the long delay has made you careless: in your use of authority over others at home or work, in your appetites, in what you excuse because judgement feels far away. If you lead anyone, ask the people under you whether you serve them or use them, and listen to the answer.

For worship. The Master who will return is just. He sees every hand raised against the weak, every servant beaten in his house, every store wasted by those who should have fed his people, and he will put it right. He is also the Master who never once abused his authority, who used his power only to serve, and whose rule over his household is gentle and lowly in heart. Blessed are those who live under such a Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: And that servant who knew his master's will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating. But the one who did not know, and did what deserved a beating, will receive a light beating. Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required, and from him to whom they entrusted much, they will demand the more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That servant who knew his master’s will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating. But the one who did not know, and did what deserved a beating, will receive a light beating. Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required, and from him to whom they entrusted much, they will demand the more.

And that servant who knew his master’s will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating. Deliberate disobedience in full knowledge brings greater judgement.

But the one who did not know, and did what deserved a beating, will receive a light beating. Two servants, the same offence, different sentences, and the difference is what each knew. This settles something. Judgement is not a single undifferentiated verdict falling equally on everyone outside Christ. It has degrees. Jesus has already said it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon than for the Galilean towns that watched him work (10:13–14), and for Sodom than for a village that turned away his messengers (10:12). Perfect justice is exact, and exactness means proportion (Numbers 15:27–31; Romans 2:12). But the second servant is not acquitted. He did what deserved a beating, and receives one. Ignorance reduces the sentence; it does not produce innocence. Nobody in this parable gets away with it.

Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required. Privilege brings responsibility. The passive verbs are the reverent Jewish way of saying God gave without using the name, so every item on the list is a deposit, not an achievement: a Christian upbringing, an open Bible in your own language, a church down the road, forty years of clear preaching, health, education, money, time. Every one of them raises the bar. Those who know the Bible and those who lead in the church will be judged more strictly (James 3:1), and so will Christians in wealthy and free countries, who have so much.

An account, not a shelter. This word falls hardest not on the ignorant but on the well-taught. The man who has heard the gospel explained plainly for four decades and has never done anything about it is not in the safer category. He is the servant who knew his master’s will, and on the parable’s own reckoning he is nearer the severe beating than the light one. It is a strange thing to have to say, but there it is: a lifetime of good sermons is not a shelter. It is an account.

Does this mean people who never heard the gospel will be saved by their ignorance? No. The servant who did not know still receives a beating; ignorance lessens judgement but does not remove guilt, because all have sinned against the light of creation and conscience (Romans 1:20; 2:14–15). Salvation comes only through conscious faith in Christ (Acts 4:12; Romans 10:13–15), which is exactly why the church must send preachers. God will judge everyone with perfect fairness, according to what they knew. Infants who die in infancy, who cannot hear or believe, are in the hands of a merciful God, and we may trust that his elect among them are saved by Christ through the Spirit.

By his stripes. Both servants in this parable deserve a beating, and there is no third servant who does not. The gospel does not answer that with a lighter sentence but with a substitute. Pilate, finding no guilt in Jesus, still said, I will therefore punish and release him (23:16), and the one who knew his Father’s will perfectly and did all of it took the stripes owed to servants who knew and did not. Isaiah saw him wounded for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, bearing the punishment that brings us peace, so that by his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). Of the one to whom most was given, most was required, and he paid it.

Should I avoid learning more of the Bible so as to be judged less? That would be to choose darkness so as not to be blamed for it, which is itself a sin against light. The goal is not to know less but to obey what you know. Every truth learned is a gift to be lived, and the same God who requires much gives grace to do it. A believer who keeps learning and keeps obeying, however imperfectly, is not storing up judgement but growing in Christ.

In a sentence. Those who knew their master’s will and ignored it will be punished severely, those who did not know, less severely, for much is required of those to whom much is given.

On a Tuesday. You have been given much. Ask what God requires of you in return. List three things you have been given that most of the world has not: a Bible, a church, freedom, money, education. For each, ask one concrete question: what is this for, and what does my Master want me to do with it this week?

For worship. Our Master weighs every privilege and every refusal on scales that never tip unfairly, and not one person will receive a stroke more than justice allows. And the same Lord who requires much has given most: an open Bible, a church, a lifetime of grace, and beneath them all his Son, and then his Spirit to make his servants faithful. Everything he requires of us, he first gave.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 49–59 — Fire, Division, and the Urgent Hour
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chapter closes with three sayings of escalating urgency, and the first is the most emotionally exposed moment in Luke outside Gethsemane.

“I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled!” The fire is most likely the one John announced at the start of this Gospel — “he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (3:16) — and Luke's second volume opens with tongues of fire (Acts 2:3). It is also the fire of judgement and purifying, and the two are not separable: the same fire refines and consumes, depending on what it lands on.

“I have a baptism to be baptized with.” To be baptized is to go under — and it is not the Jordan, which is behind him. In the Psalms the waters are often death: “all your breakers and your waves have gone over me” (Ps. 42:7). He is talking about the cross, and calling it a drowning.

And “how great is my distress” is the cry of a man hemmed in, pressed on every side. Read the two verses together and the shape is precise: the fire cannot be lit until the baptism is finished, and the baptism is Calvary. Pentecost waits on Golgotha, and he is pressed between them.

Then the division saying, which shocks — not least because angels announced “on earth peace” over the fields outside Bethlehem (2:14). Both are true. What he brings is peace with God, which every human being needs and cannot manufacture. What he never promised is the peace of everybody getting along, which was only ever available while the question of who he is remained unasked. The household list is quoted from Micah 7:6, where it describes a society coming apart — and every pair is named in both directions.

Finally the weather. West of Israel is the Mediterranean, so cloud coming inland meant rain; a south wind off the desert meant the scorching sirocco. Two confident readings, and Jesus grants they are right. These people are competent. And they will not apply the skill where it matters.
verseByVerse.theology:
“How great is my distress until it is accomplished” is not a man dreading the cross and hanging back — Gethsemane will show that the dread was real, and this shows what was underneath it. He wants what is on the far side badly enough that the waiting is a torment. He went to that cross wishing it were already over, not because the pain was unendurable but because he could not wait to see the fire fall on the people he was dying for.

The charge of hypocrisy at v.56 is precise. It is not that the crowd is stupid; it is that they are perfectly capable of reading evidence and drawing conclusions, and have declined to apply the skill in the one place it matters. A man who cannot read anything is not a hypocrite but illiterate. A man who reads the sky every morning and cannot read what stands in front of him has made a choice and is pretending it was a limitation.

And the evidence he expects them to have read is not a secret sign. The “present time” is the whole visible situation: a preacher healing in the streets, demons evicted, the poor given good news, thousands following, and the authorities plotting a death.

“Why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?” assumes the resources for the judgement are already in their possession. It needs a guard — Scripture is emphatic that a man can be entirely convinced and entirely wrong (Prov. 14:12; Jer. 17:9) — so the question is not “why not decide what suits you?” It is narrower: given what you can already read, why have you not drawn the obvious conclusion? And the answer, in nearly every case, is that the conclusion would cost something.
verseByVerse.examples:
The division saying has real pastoral weight, because someone reading it is living inside it. He does not say the division is good. He says it is what happens — and he says it in advance, which is the mercy in it. A Christian whose family went cold when he was converted has very often concluded that he handled it badly, or that a wiser person would have avoided it. This verse says the fracture was in the nature of the case.

Every generation is expert at reading something — markets, politics, the mood of a culture, the trajectory of a career — and the skill is genuine. The same person who can tell you exactly where the country is heading has often never once asked what God is doing in his own lifetime, or in his own house. The evidence is not usually missing. What is missing is the decision to read it.

And “you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny” has carried theological weight it was never built to bear — one of the two verses historically cited for purgatory. But this is practical advice about a lawsuit used to illustrate urgency, and doctrine cannot be quarried from an illustration's scenery. A man in a debtors' prison could not earn, which was the point of the prison; “until you have paid the last penny” is the ordinary way of saying he is not getting out. And a doctrine supplying a further opportunity to settle after death removes the urgency of the only sentence that mattered. Settle now, on the road — and know that the settlement is not a schedule of payments but an amnesty, purchased at the judge's own expense (7:41-42; Col. 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: 'I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished!
verseByVerse.commentary:
I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! I have a baptism to be baptised with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished!

I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! For two verses Luke lets us hear what it was like inside him. What fire? In Scripture fire pictures judgement (3:9, 17), purifying (Malachi 3:2–3), and the Holy Spirit. John the Baptist announced that the Messiah would baptise with the Holy Spirit and with fire (3:16), and Luke’s second volume opens with tongues as of fire resting on each of the waiting disciples (Acts 2:3). The same fire refines and consumes, depending on what it lands on, and all of it would be set alight by his death and resurrection. Would that it were already kindled is an unfinished exclamation in the Greek, not a tidy sentence. It is a man wishing out loud.

I have a baptism to be baptized with. The word means to be plunged, immersed, submerged, and it is not the Jordan, which is behind him. To be baptised, in the Old Testament’s imagery, is to go under the waters, and the waters in the Psalms are often death: all your breakers and your waves have gone over me (Psalm 42:7); save me, O God, for the waters have come up to my neck (Psalm 69:1–2). He is talking about his death (Mark 10:38), and he is calling it a drowning: being overwhelmed, plunged into suffering, under the judgement of God against sin.

And how great is my distress until it is accomplished! “Distress” (synechomai) means to be gripped, hemmed in, pressed on every side. Luke uses it elsewhere of being seized by a high fever (4:38) and of a besieging army closing on a city (19:43). It is the word for something with no room left in it. A glimpse of Jesus’ inner anguish on the road to the cross, anticipating Gethsemane (22:42–44).

Pentecost waits on Golgotha. Read the two verses together and the shape is precise. The fire he longs for cannot be lit until the baptism is finished, and the baptism is Calvary. He cannot have the one without going through the other, and he is pressed between them. This is not a man hanging back. Gethsemane will show that the dread was real, and this shows what lay underneath it: he wanted what was on the far side badly enough that the waiting was a torment, because he could not wait to see the fire fall on the people he was dying for.

Does this baptism tell us anything about Christian baptism? Indirectly, yes. Jesus calls his death a baptism, and Paul says that believers are baptised into his death, buried with him and raised to walk in newness of life (Romans 6:3–4). That is why this app holds believer’s baptism by immersion: going under the water pictures union with Christ in the death he describes here, and coming up pictures resurrection. Our paedobaptist brothers see the same union signified in the baptism of infants, and we honour their faith. But the reality behind every baptism is this one, which Jesus endured alone.

In a sentence. Jesus longed for the fire he came to bring to be kindled, and was deeply distressed until his baptism of suffering was accomplished.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to treat your Christian life as routine, read these two verses and remember what it cost. Pray for the Spirit’s fire in your own heart and church: a holy love that burns away sin and warms cold faith. And when you are pressed by suffering you cannot escape, remember that your Lord knew what it is to be hemmed in, and went on for you.

For worship. Here the heart of the Son is laid open: hemmed in, pressed on every side, and still walking toward Jerusalem. He wanted the cross over, not to escape it but to reach what lay beyond it, a people set alight by the Spirit he would pour out. He went down into the flood alone, and he stands now on its far shore with all whom he carried through. The fire he longed to kindle was kindled, and it has never gone out.
verseByVerse.note: Fire can picture judgment or purifying; “baptism” here pictures being overwhelmed by suffering.

parallels.desc: the baptism with which I am baptized

verseByVerse.quote: Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division. For from now on in one house there will be five divided, three against two and two against three. They will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division. For from now on in one house there will be five divided, three against two and two against three. They will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.

Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? The sentence is meant to shock, not least because the angels announced on earth peace over the fields outside Bethlehem (2:14), and Zechariah sang that he would guide our feet into the way of peace (1:79). Both are true. Jesus brings real peace: peace with God, which every human being most needs and cannot manufacture (Romans 5:1), and peace among those who belong to him. What he never promised is the peace of the world, a peace without truth, which was only ever available while the question of who he is remained unasked.

No, I tell you, but rather division. The effect of his coming is to divide people by their response to him. Simeon said it over the infant: this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many, and a sword would pierce through his mother’s own soul (2:34–35). The division he brings ran first through his own family and his own heart, and he never asks a disciple to stand where he has not stood. Everyone must decide, and families split over him.

For from now on in one house there will be five divided, three against two and two against three. Five is a household: father, mother, son, daughter, and daughter-in-law, the son’s wife living with them. And the arithmetic is deliberately awkward. Three against two, then two against three: the same fracture described from both sides, because in a divided house both halves feel like the ones being left.

Father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law. The list is quoted, and the source matters. It is Micah 7:6, where the prophet describes a society coming apart in a time of judgement: the son treats the father with contempt, and a man’s enemies are the men of his own house. In Micah it is a picture of national breakdown. Jesus says it will happen because of loyalty to him. And note that every pair is named in both directions. There is no suggestion that the believing half will find it easy or behave well.

What it does not mean. Not that the disciple should go looking for a quarrel, sharpen every difference into a battle, or leave his family to fend for itself. Paul tells believers to live at peace with everyone as far as it depends on them (Romans 12:18), and Luke’s list names every pair in both directions for a reason: a great deal of family division is caused by Christians being insufferable rather than by Christ. But when others reject Christ, conflict may come, and loyalty to Christ must come first (14:26).

The mercy of a warning. Someone reading this is living inside it. Jesus does not say the division is good. He says it is what happens, and he says it in advance, which is the mercy in it. A Christian whose family went cold when he was converted often concludes that he handled it badly. When everything has been done gently and the division comes anyway, it is not evidence of failure. It is the thing he warned about, happening.

How do I love a family that opposes my faith? Honour your parents in everything that does not require disobeying Christ. Be the kindest, most helpful person at the family table, and let your life speak before your words. Do not preach at every gathering; do answer honestly when asked. Pray for them faithfully, sometimes for decades. Keep the door open, and refuse bitterness when they mock. Where there is real danger or abuse, you may need distance for safety, and that is not unloving. And remember that God has often used one believer’s patient faithfulness to bring a whole household to Christ (Acts 16:31–34).

In a sentence. Jesus said he came not to bring peace but division, which would split even families as people responded differently to him.

On a Tuesday. If following Christ has divided your family, he foretold it. Love them, pray for them, and stay faithful. Where this applies: the parent who disowns a child for being baptised, the spouse who mocks every prayer. Where applying it would be wrong: using it to excuse rudeness, harshness or neglect, or to justify cutting off a family that simply finds your faith strange. Ask whether the offence is Christ, or you.

For worship. The Prince of Peace accepted being the cause of division, because the only peace that lasts is peace with God, and it cannot be had on any terms but his. Mark tells us that his own family once thought he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21), and still he gathers into his family everyone who does the will of his Father. In him the lonely believer has a household that can never be divided.

parallels.desc: a man’s enemies are the men of his own house

verseByVerse.quote: He also said to the crowds, 'When you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, ‘A shower is coming.’ And so it happens. And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, ‘There will be scorching heat,’ and it happens. You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time?
verseByVerse.commentary:
He also said to the crowds: when you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, a shower is coming. And so it happens. And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, there will be scorching heat, and it happens. You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time?

When you see a cloud rising in the west. He turns from the disciples to the crowds, and begins with the weather, which in that country was entirely predictable if you knew the geography. West of Israel is the Mediterranean. Cloud building over the sea and coming inland meant rain, as Elijah’s servant saw from Carmel (1 Kings 18:44), and the peasant standing in his field did not need to think about it. A shower is coming, he says at once, and so it happens.

And when you see the south wind blowing. South is the Negev and the Arabian desert; a south wind meant scorching heat that could strip a crop in a day. Two signs, two confident readings, and Jesus grants that they are right: and it happens. These people are competent. They were good at reading the weather, and their instincts about the sky are reliable and hard-won.

You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky. The charge is precise. They are not stupid. They are perfectly capable of reading evidence, and have declined to apply the skill in the one place it matters. What makes it hypocrisy rather than error is that the failure is selective. A man who cannot read anything is not a hypocrite; he is illiterate. A man who reads the sky every morning and cannot read what is standing in front of him has made a choice, and is pretending it was a limitation.

But why do you not know how to interpret the present time? “The present time” (kairos) is this decisive moment, the time of God’s visitation. And notice what he expects them to have read. Not a secret sign. The whole visible situation: a preacher healing in the streets, demons evicted, the poor being told good news, thousands following, and the religious authorities plotting a death. The Messiah was among them, and he had said so in plain words at Nazareth: today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing (4:21). Any of it could have been interpreted by a man who reads clouds for a living. But they would not read it, and he will weep over Jerusalem because it did not know the time of its visitation (19:44).

Turning it on ourselves. Before this is enjoyed at their expense, turn it on ourselves. Every generation is expert at reading something: markets, politics, the mood of a culture, the trajectory of a career. And the person who can tell you exactly where the country is heading has often never once asked what God is doing in his own lifetime, or his own house. The evidence is not usually missing. What is missing is the decision to read it.

Does this mean I should try to match news events to Bible prophecy? Not in the way that often happens. Jesus’ point is that the decisive time had already arrived in his own coming, and his hearers were ignoring it. The present time, for us, is the age between his first and second comings: the day of salvation, when the gospel goes to the nations and he could return at any hour. Reading the times means recognising that, and responding with repentance, faith and readiness, rather than building charts of headlines. Discernment is spiritual, not speculative.

In a sentence. Jesus called the crowds hypocrites, because they could read the weather but would not read the signs of the time in which God was visiting them.

On a Tuesday. Can you read the signs of what God is doing? Take ten minutes and ask: where has God been at work in my life in the last year, in a trial, an answered prayer, a conviction that will not go away? Do not be skilled in everything except spiritual discernment.

For worship. The Lord of the seasons sends the rain from the west and the heat from the south, and he sent his Son in the fullness of time. He has never been unclear about his visitations; the clouds of mercy have been rising over this world since the manger. And the God who gave us eyes to read the sky has given us his Spirit to read his Son.
verseByVerse.note: Clouds from the west came off the Mediterranean with rain; the south wind blew hot off the desert.

verseByVerse.quote: 'And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?
verseByVerse.commentary:
And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?

And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right? One short question, and it assumes a great deal. He has just told them they can read the sky and will not read the times. Now he asks why they do not work it out themselves. You have the evidence; use your own judgement, honestly, and you will see who I am and what you must do. The time for decision is now.

Not for want of a teacher. They are not being told to go and consult somebody. The resources for the judgement are already in their possession. The verb is the one for reaching a verdict, and for yourselves puts the responsibility where the crowd would least like it. They had spent the chapter asking him to settle things: adjudicate my inheritance (v. 13), give us a sign (11:16), tell us whether this parable is for us (v. 41). He hands it back.

What it does not mean. This needs a guard, because it is not an invitation to make it up. Scripture is emphatic that the human heart is unreliable and that a man can be entirely convinced and entirely wrong (Proverbs 14:12; Jeremiah 17:9). The question is not why not decide what suits you? It is narrower and harder: given what is in front of you, the evidence you can already read, the conscience you already have, the Scriptures you already possess, why have you not drawn the obvious conclusion? And the answer, in nearly every case, is that the conclusion would cost something. The crowd’s problem is not a shortage of light but an unwillingness to act on what the light shows. That is why Jesus presses the question home with the picture of a man on his way to court, running out of road.

Who do you say that I am? The verdict Jesus wants them to reach for themselves is a verdict about him. He had put that question to his disciples in private, and Peter answered, The Christ of God (9:20). Nothing of the evidence was hidden from the crowd: they had seen the lame walk and the demons go, heard the poor given good news, and watched the lawyers fail to answer him. The judgement they are declining to make is not about a point of ethics but about a person. And there is a strange mercy in the question. The one who will one day judge them is asking them to judge him first, while a right verdict can still save them.

The habit of waiting to be told. There is a particular kind of religious passivity that this question is aimed at, and it survives well in churches. It is the habit of waiting to be told: of treating every question as one for the experts, so that nothing is ever settled and nothing therefore has to be done about it. Jesus calls it what it is by asking why.

Should I not rely on my pastor and church to tell me what is right? Listen to them, gratefully: God gives teachers to the church, and you should be humble enough to be taught (Hebrews 13:17). But no teacher can believe for you, repent for you or obey for you. The Bereans checked even Paul against Scripture (Acts 17:11). On the plain things, who Jesus is, what sin is, what he commands, you already know enough to act. Take your questions to your pastor, but do not hide behind them.

In a sentence. Jesus asked why they could not judge for themselves what was right.

On a Tuesday. Do not wait for others to decide for you. Weigh the evidence about Jesus for yourself, and act. Is there a question you keep postponing, whether to be baptised, whether to make things right with someone, whether to give up a known sin, because you are waiting for someone to tell you? You already know. Do it this week.

For worship. God has not left us in the dark. He has written his law on our hearts, set his creation before our eyes, given us his word in our hands and sent his Son into our world. The light is enough. And the God who asks why do you not judge? is the God who opens blind eyes to see and gives willing hearts to act.

verseByVerse.quote: As you go with your accuser before the magistrate, make an effort to settle with him on the way, lest he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer put you in prison. I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As you go with your accuser before the magistrate, make an effort to settle with him on the way, lest he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer put you in prison. I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny.

As you go with your accuser before the magistrate, make an effort to settle with him on the way. The picture is a lawsuit already in motion: a man on his way to court with a debt he cannot pay, and the case certain to go against him. The two parties are walking to court together, which is how it worked, the plaintiff bringing the defendant himself, and the road is the last stretch of time in which anything can be done. Make an effort is a strong verb: work at it, put yourself into it. Settle out of court while you still can. Once you reach the judge, it will be too late.

Lest he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer put you in prison. Three handovers in a row, and the man is passed down the chain like a parcel: debtors’ prison. Once the process starts, he has no further say in it, which is exactly the point. On the road he is a man who can negotiate. In the courtroom he is a case.

I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny. The penny (lepton) was the smallest coin in circulation. Every last coin.

The meaning. In context (vv. 54–57), this is a parable about the coming judgement of God. We are all on our way to court, with a debt we cannot pay. Now, on the way, is the time to be reconciled with God, through Christ. Once we stand before the Judge, it will be too late. And the debt cannot be paid by us; we would never get out.

Where Christians differ: purgatory. Roman Catholic teaching has sometimes cited this verse in support of purgatory, a place where souls pay for their sins after death before entering heaven. Verdict: the parable is about urgent reconciliation before judgement, not about a process of purification after death. Christ’s one offering has cleared the believer’s account completely (Colossians 2:13–14; Hebrews 10:14), and the believer who dies goes at once to be with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). For those who reject Christ, the debt can never be paid.

Three reasons the purgatory reading fails. With its parallel in Matthew 5:26, this clause is one of the verses historically cited for purgatory: until seems to promise a way out at the end of the paying, and a temporary prison is not hell. Three things make that reading impossible. First, this is practical advice about a lawsuit, used to illustrate urgency, and doctrine cannot be quarried from the scenery of an illustration. Push the method and the parable of the persistent widow would make God a judge who grants justice only to stop being pestered (18:1–8). The magistrate, officer, prison and penny are the furniture of the story, not a floor plan of eternity. Second, the idiom runs the other way. Nobody earned wages in a debtors’ prison; the cell existed precisely because the man had nothing and could get nothing. To say he will not get out until he has paid the last penny is the ordinary way of saying he is not getting out at all. Third, and most decisively, it reverses what the passage exists to say. Every line presses one point: act now, because afterward is too late. If there were a way to pay later, the advice to settle on the road would be optional.

An amnesty, not an instalment plan. And what of the debt itself? Luke answered that five chapters back, in a house where a woman wept over Jesus’ feet. Two debtors owed sums they could not repay, and when they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both (7:41–42). The record of debt that stood against us was not put on an instalment plan. It was set aside, nailed to the cross (Colossians 2:14). So take the urgency with full seriousness: settle now, on the road, while it is still called today. But know what the settlement is. It is not a schedule of payments. It is an amnesty, and it was purchased at the Judge’s own expense.

How do I settle with God? Not by offering to pay, because the debt is beyond you, and not by promising to do better, because that adds nothing to what is owed. You settle by agreeing with God about your sin, turning from it, and trusting Jesus Christ, who died to pay that debt in full and rose again. Tell him so, in your own words, today. Then you are no longer on the way to court as a debtor; you are walking home as a child. If you are already his, the parable also has a horizontal echo: where you have a quarrel with someone, settle it quickly (Matthew 5:23–25).

In a sentence. Jesus urged them to settle with their accuser on the way to court, before it was too late, a picture of the urgency of being reconciled to God before judgement.

On a Tuesday. Today is the day to be reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:20; 6:2). Do not wait until you stand before the Judge. Where this saying applies: anyone who has put off the question of God for years, assuming there will be time later; and, by its echo, a believer with an open quarrel he keeps meaning to resolve. Where applying it would be wrong: using it to frighten an assured believer into thinking he must keep paying for forgiven sin, or to pressure someone into a settlement that lets an abuser off. Christ has paid; settle by trusting him.

For worship. The Lord who warns of the debtors’ prison is the Lord who stood up in the synagogue at Nazareth and read that he had been anointed to proclaim liberty to the captives and the year of the Lord’s favour (4:18–19). He has not shortened anyone’s sentence. He has opened the doors, and the jubilee he announced has no end date. There is no purgatory for the forgiven, because there is not one penny left to pay. It is finished.
verseByVerse.note: The “penny” was the smallest coin in circulation.

12.text: <sup>1</sup> In the meantime, when so many thousands of the people had gathered together that they were trampling one another, he began to say to his disciples first, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy. <sup>2</sup> Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known. <sup>3</sup> Therefore whatever you have said in the dark shall be heard in the light, and what you have whispered in private rooms shall be proclaimed on the housetops. <sup>4</sup> “I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. <sup>5</sup> But I will warn you whom to fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him! <sup>6</sup> Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? And not one of them is forgotten before God. <sup>7</sup> Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows. <sup>8</sup> “And I tell you, everyone who acknowledges me before men, the Son of Man also will acknowledge before the angels of God, <sup>9</sup> but the one who denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God. <sup>10</sup> And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven. <sup>11</sup> And when they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious about how you should defend yourself or what you should say, <sup>12</sup> for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.” <sup>13</sup> Someone in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” <sup>14</sup> But he said to him, “Man, who made me a judge or arbitrator over you?” <sup>15</sup> And he said to them, “Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.” <sup>16</sup> And he told them a parable, saying, “The land of a rich man produced plentifully, <sup>17</sup> and he thought to himself, ‘What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?’ <sup>18</sup> And he said, ‘I will do this: I will tear down my barns and build larger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods. <sup>19</sup> And I will say to my soul, Soul, you have ample goods laid up for many years; relax, eat, drink, be merry.’ <sup>20</sup> But God said to him, ‘Fool! This night your soul is required of you, and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?’ <sup>21</sup> So is the one who lays up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.” <sup>22</sup> And he said to his disciples, “Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat, nor about your body, what you will put on. <sup>23</sup> For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing. <sup>24</sup> Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds! <sup>25</sup> And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? <sup>26</sup> If then you are not able to do as small a thing as that, why are you anxious about the rest? <sup>27</sup> Consider the lilies, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. <sup>28</sup> But if God so clothes the grass, which is alive in the field today, and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith! <sup>29</sup> And do not seek what you are to eat and what you are to drink, nor be worried. <sup>30</sup> For all the nations of the world seek after these things, and your Father knows that you need them. <sup>31</sup> Instead, seek his kingdom, and these things will be added to you. <sup>32</sup> “Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom. <sup>33</sup> Sell your possessions, and give to the needy. Provide yourselves with moneybags that do not grow old, with a treasure in the heavens that does not fail, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. <sup>34</sup> For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. <sup>35</sup> “Stay dressed for action and keep your lamps burning, <sup>36</sup> and be like men who are waiting for their master to come home from the wedding feast, so that they may open the door to him at once when he comes and knocks. <sup>37</sup> Blessed are those servants whom the master finds awake when he comes. Truly, I say to you, he will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them. <sup>38</sup> If he comes in the second watch, or in the third, and finds them awake, blessed are those servants! <sup>39</sup> But know this, that if the master of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have left his house to be broken into. <sup>40</sup> You also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect.” <sup>41</sup> Peter said, “Lord, are you telling this parable for us or for all?” <sup>42</sup> And the Lord said, “Who then is the faithful and wise manager, whom his master will set over his household, to give them their portion of food at the proper time? <sup>43</sup> Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. <sup>44</sup> Truly, I say to you, he will set him over all his possessions. <sup>45</sup> But if that servant says to himself, ‘My master is delayed in coming,’ and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk, <sup>46</sup> the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and put him with the unfaithful. <sup>47</sup> And that servant who knew his master's will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating. <sup>48</sup> But the one who did not know, and did what deserved a beating, will receive a light beating. Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required, and from him to whom they entrusted much, they will demand the more. <sup>49</sup> “I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! <sup>50</sup> I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished! <sup>51</sup> Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? No, I tell you, but rather division. <sup>52</sup> For from now on in one house there will be five divided, three against two and two against three. <sup>53</sup> They will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.” <sup>54</sup> He also said to the crowds, “When you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, ‘A shower is coming.’ And so it happens. <sup>55</sup> And when you see the south wind blowing, you say, ‘There will be scorching heat,’ and it happens. <sup>56</sup> You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of earth and sky, but why do you not know how to interpret the present time? <sup>57</sup> “And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right? <sup>58</sup> As you go with your accuser before the magistrate, make an effort to settle with him on the way, lest he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer put you in prison. <sup>59</sup> I tell you, you will never get out until you have paid the very last penny.”

13.title: Repent or Perish; the Narrow Door; Jerusalem's Lament
13.overview:
Chapter 13 is structured around the call to repentance and its refusal — three overlapping statements that together describe what happens when the opportunity for repentance closes. It opens with Jesus's response to news of a Galilean massacre and the fall of the tower of Siloam — two disasters that the crowd assumes were punishments for exceptional sinfulness. Jesus refuses the assumption and turns both events into a summons to universal repentance: “Unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.” Then he tells the parable of the fruitless fig tree — one more year of patient cultivation before the axe comes. Then on a Sabbath he heals a woman bent double for eighteen years, and the synagogue ruler objects, and Jesus names the synagogue ruler's hypocrisy before the entire crowd.

The middle section (vv. 18–30) moves through the parables of the mustard seed and the leaven — the kingdom's hidden but irresistible growth — to the question about the number of the saved, and Jesus's answer: “Strive to enter through the narrow door.” The door will close. The day will come when the master of the house rises and shuts the door, and those who knock and say “we ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets” will hear “I do not know where you come from.” Familiarity with Jesus is not relationship with Jesus; proximity to the gospel is not reception of it.

The chapter ends with one of the most heartrending passages in the Gospel: the lament over Jerusalem. Some Pharisees warn Jesus that Herod wants to kill him; Jesus refuses to be deflected (“I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem”). And then he speaks to the city itself: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” The willingness is on his side; the unwillingness is on theirs. And the house will be left desolate.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Repent or Perish; the Barren Fig Tree
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The massacre Pilate carried out on Galilean pilgrims is recorded nowhere else in ancient literature — which is itself telling, since this is exactly the kind of local atrocity that filled a province and left no trace in the histories. It fits everything known about the man.

The crowd assumes the victims' fate was a verdict on their exceptional sinfulness, and Jesus brings the assumption into the open before they can state it: “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners…? No, I tell you.” Flat, immediate, unqualified.

That was not a fringe view he was demolishing. It was the working theology of the ancient world — Job's friends spent most of a book on it, and the disciples will ask it about a blind man (John 9:2). It is the natural conclusion of anyone who believes God is just and in charge, and it is wrong.

He then supplies a second case himself, and the choice is deliberate because it is a different kind of disaster. The first was murder; the second is an accident — masonry giving way near the pool of Siloam. Between them the two cover the whole field: evil done by human beings, and evil that nobody did. And the answer is identical, word for word, twice, so that neither case is left open.

The parable of the fig tree extends the urgency and adds the intercession. The tree is planted in a vineyard — prime cultivated ground, occupying space that would otherwise carry vines. Three years is not impatience: a fig takes about three years to bear at all, and the law required the first three years' fruit to be left untouched (Lev. 19:23), so the owner has waited the full statutory period and then come three times on top of it.

And the charge is precise. Not that the tree has done harm, but that it is “using up the ground.” Barrenness here is not a neutral condition; a tree that produces nothing is consuming, and what it consumes belongs to somebody else.

The vinedresser disputes none of it. He accepts the whole case and asks for time — and offers to do the work himself: digging round compacted roots, and dunging. Heavy, unpleasant labour on a tree that has given him nothing.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus's answer refuses both the question and the assumption behind it. He does not say “God never punishes” — the Old Testament would contradict that. He says this is not the special punishment of especially sinful people. All are sinners; all face mortality; all need to repent.

So the disasters are not explanations of why those particular people died. They are reminders to the living that they are not exempt from the mortality those people have just experienced. The right response to someone else's death is not theological analysis of their sins but examination of one's own soul while there is time.

The fig tree and the vineyard together would have been unmistakable. Israel is the vineyard of Isaiah 5 — “he looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes” — and Israel is the fig tree in which God came looking and found nothing (Hos. 9:10; Jer. 8:13; Mic. 7:1). The one who stands between the tree and the axe, asking for another year and offering to do the digging himself, is standing in that room saying it.

But the intercession has a term. The vinedresser does not ask for indefinite reprieve; he names the period and concedes the outcome. Which puts this parable in its proper relation to the two disasters: those verses said the axe is real, and this one says the axe is being held — and by whom. Separating the two halves ruins the passage in one direction or the other. A gospel that is all axe produces terror; a gospel that is all delay produces a man who will still be intending to repent in fifteen years.
verseByVerse.examples:
Take this into the real world, because it will be needed there. When a wall comes down on a school, or a diagnosis arrives, or a driver crosses a line, two sentences will be offered and this passage forbids them both.

The first is the one Jesus is answering: they must have done something. He says no, twice, flatly, and about both kinds of death. Never say it, and never let it be said to the bereaved. The second is the modern one: God had nothing to do with it. He does not say that either — he does not remove these deaths from his Father's world; he refuses to let us read them as verdicts.

Between those two errors is where a Christian must stand, and it is a narrow place: God is not absent from the falling tower, and the eighteen who died under it were not worse than the crowd that survived it. The honest answer to why them? is that we are not told; the answer we are given instead is that our own footing is no firmer than theirs was.

And there is a sting in the wording. “You will all likewise perish” was heard by a generation that would watch Roman soldiers kill worshippers in the temple courts and walls come down on Jerusalem within forty years. It came true in the very forms they had just been discussing.

The vinedresser's response to three barren years is the model of patient labour with an apparently hopeless case — a church that has not grown, a child who will not turn. He neither writes the tree off nor pretends there is fruit. He asks for another year and goes and gets the spade.

verseByVerse.quote: There were some present at that very time who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. And he answered them, 'Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There were some present at that very time who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. He answered them: do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.

Meaning first. Luke 13 is a chapter about time running out and grace still running. Two disasters in the news are not verdicts on the dead but a summons to the living: repent, or you will likewise perish. A barren fig tree is given one more year because someone pleads for it. A woman bent double for eighteen years is straightened on the Sabbath. The kingdom starts as small as a seed and will fill the world, but its door is narrow, and one day it will be shut. And Jesus walks on towards the city that kills prophets, longing to gather it like a hen. Judgement is real, the patience is real, and the one who holds both is going to Jerusalem to die.

The setting. Jesus had just urged the crowds to read the signs of the times and be reconciled to God before judgement (12:54–59). Some in the crowd respond with a news item.

There were some present at that very time who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. The incident is recorded nowhere else, which is itself telling: this is the kind of local atrocity that left no trace in the histories. It fits everything known about Pilate, and Josephus records several riots he provoked and put down brutally. Some Galileans, perhaps suspected of rebellion, were killed in the temple courts while offering sacrifices, probably at Passover, when laymen slaughtered their own lambs. Men were killed at the altar, in the act of worship, by the governor of a pagan empire.

Why do they raise it? Luke does not say, and the silence is suggestive. They may be testing him. A Galilean teacher’s opinion on a massacre of Galileans would be useful to somebody: condemn Pilate and he is a rebel; say nothing and he has no sympathy for his own people. Perhaps they wanted him to say the victims deserved it. But the answer Jesus gives tells us what they were actually thinking.

Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way? There it is, and he brings it out into the open before they can say it. The assumption behind the report is that the manner of a man’s death is a comment on his life. That was not a fringe view. It was the working theology of the ancient world. Job’s friends spent most of a book on it (Job 4:7). The disciples will ask it about a blind man: who sinned, this man or his parents (John 9:2)? It is the natural conclusion of anyone who believes God is just and in charge, and it is wrong.

No, I tell you. Flat, immediate, unqualified. He does not say probably not, and he does not explore the possibility. Suffering is not always a sign of special guilt. The victims were not worse than others. The equation is broken.

But unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. And then the turn nobody was ready for. He does not merely deny that the dead were worse. He tells the living they are in the same position, and the only difference between them and the men on that temple pavement is timing. The real question is not why they died but whether you are ready to die. They brought a question about somebody else’s guilt, and he hands it back with their own name on it. And likewise may be meant quite literally. Forty years later, many Jews died at Roman hands in the temple courts during the siege of Jerusalem.

The same governor, the same feast. Within months another Galilean would die at Pilate’s hands at Passover time, and he is the one answering the question. When Pilate heard that Jesus was a Galilean, he sent him to Herod (23:6–7), and three times he declared that he found no guilt in him (23:4, 14, 22). His death would be no verdict on his own sins, for he had none. He was not a worse sinner than all the Galileans; he was the one sinless Galilean. His blood was not mingled with the sacrifices. It was the sacrifice, shed so that those who repent will never perish.

What does perish mean here? More than dying, since the Galileans have already died and his hearers will die too whatever they do. To perish is to be lost before God: to die unreconciled and come under his judgement, for ever (John 3:16, where perishing is the opposite of eternal life). Jesus is not threatening that the unrepentant will all be killed by Pilate. He is saying that what happened to the bodies of those men is a picture of what will happen to every soul that meets God without repentance: sudden, unprepared and final.
