That is why the warning is urgent and not merely sad.

What is repentance? Repentance is turning from sin to God. It begins by seeing your sin as God sees it, not only as harmful to you but as an offence against him, and grieving over it. It lays hold of God’s mercy in Christ, since sorrow with no hope in it only drives a sinner further from God. And it acts: by grace the sinner leaves the sin behind and sets out on a new obedience (Westminster 15.2). It is not a single event at conversion but the shape of the whole Christian life, and it is never too late to begin it while you are still breathing.

In a sentence. When told of Galileans killed by Pilate in the temple, Jesus denied that they were worse sinners than others, and warned that all must repent or perish.

On a Tuesday. When you hear of disasters, don’t ask what the victims did. Ask whether you are ready to meet God. Notice the reflex next time the news breaks: the faint relief that it was over there, the quick search for what they did differently. Jesus will not let that reflex stand. Let every report of sudden death send you, not into judging, but to your knees, and to the one honest prayer the news can produce: Lord, I am no safer than they were; have mercy on me.

For worship. The Lord of life does not use the dead to make the living feel secure. He tells the truth because he loves the people he is warning, and the warning is itself a door held open: perish is the word he speaks so that it need never be spoken over us. The one who said unless you repent is the exalted Saviour who gives repentance and forgiveness of sins (Acts 5:31), and there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents (15:10).
verseByVerse.note: This massacre is not recorded elsewhere, but it fits what is known of Pilate’s brutality. Many assumed disaster was punishment for a particular sin.

parallels.desc: who that was innocent ever perished? see: John 9:1–3 = who sinned, this man or his parents?

verseByVerse.quote: Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.

Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them. He supplies a second case himself, and it is a different kind of disaster. The first was murder, a cruel man doing wickedness on purpose. The second is an accident. Siloam was the area around the pool at the south end of Jerusalem (John 9:7); perhaps a tower in the city wall gave way, and eighteen people were underneath it. Again, it is recorded nowhere else. Between them the two cases cover the whole field: evil done by human beings, and evil that nobody did. Whatever a bereaved person’s loss, one of these two covers it.

Were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? The word for offenders (opheiletai) means debtors, the word Jesus taught them to use in prayer (11:4). Were they greater debtors to God? The question assumes there is a ledger, and that the falling masonry was the bailiff calling in one particular account. Jesus agrees there is a ledger. He denies that the tower was a reading from it.

No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. Word for word, twice, which is Jesus making certain that neither case is left open. Whether by human evil or natural disaster, death comes to everyone, often unexpectedly. The only safety is repentance.

Disasters and God. Scripture teaches that God is sovereign over all things, including disasters (Amos 3:6; Isaiah 45:7). But it does not teach that every disaster is a punishment for the particular sins of those who suffer. Rather, every disaster is a reminder that we live in a fallen world under the curse of sin (Romans 8:20–22), that life is short and death is certain, and that all of us need to repent.

Two sentences this passage forbids. When a wall comes down on a school, or a diagnosis arrives, or a driver crosses a line, two sentences will be offered. The first is the one he is answering: they must have done something. He says no, twice, flatly, about both kinds of death. Never say it, and never let it be said to the bereaved. The second is the modern one: God had nothing to do with it. He does not say that either. He does not remove these deaths from his Father’s world; he refuses to let us read them as verdicts. Between those errors is a narrow place where a Christian must stand: God is not absent from the falling tower, and the eighteen who died under it were not worse than the crowd that survived it.

Esteemed stricken. One death would be read exactly as Jesus forbids these to be read. At the cross the rulers sneered, He saved others; let him save himself (23:35), certain that God had passed sentence on him. Isaiah had foreseen the misreading: we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted (Isaiah 53:4). And the truth was stranger than the crowd’s theology. He was not crushed for his own sins, because he had none, yet he was crushed by the will of God, for ours. Of all the deaths in history, his is the one where God’s judgement truly can be read, and there it fell on the one man who had not deserved it.

So what may be said to the grieving? Very little about the dead, and a great deal to the living. The honest answer to why them is that we are not told. Do not offer explanations God has not given, and do not hurry anyone through their grief. Sit with them, weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15), pray with them, and speak of the God who is not distant from suffering because his Son entered it. The word Jesus gives here, that our own footing is no firmer than theirs, is not a change of subject but the only useful thing that can be said to people standing near a fresh grave and quietly assuming they are safe. It is usually a word for the preacher and for your own heart before it is a word for a widow.

And what about my own suffering? Is God punishing me? If you are in Christ, no. The punishment your sins deserved was laid on him, and there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). God does discipline his children, but discipline is a father’s training, not a judge’s sentence, and its aim is our holiness and good (Hebrews 12:5–11). You may not be able to say what a particular trouble is for. You can say what it is not: it is not God paying you back. It may be a call to search your heart, and it is always an invitation to draw near.

In a sentence. Jesus also denied that those killed when a tower fell in Siloam were worse sinners than others in Jerusalem, and repeated his warning to repent or perish.

On a Tuesday. Every news report of sudden death is a call to repentance. Are you ready? And there is a sting in the wording worth remembering when the headlines come. You will all likewise perish was heard by a generation that would watch Roman soldiers kill worshippers in the temple and walls come down on Jerusalem within forty years. The warning came true in the very forms they had just been discussing. The next disaster you read about is not a puzzle to solve. It is a mercy aimed at you, while there is still time.

For worship. God is sovereign over towers and governors, over accidents and atrocities, and nothing in this world falls outside his hand. He holds every stone in the walls of Jerusalem and every breath of the eighteen. And he is good: he does not leave us to guess our standing from what happens to us, but tells us plainly, in his Son, where safety lies, and opens the way himself. Blessed be the God who warns, and who saves.
verseByVerse.note: Siloam was the area around the pool of Siloam in the south of Jerusalem; the tower’s collapse is otherwise unknown.

parallels.desc: not wishing that any should perish

verseByVerse.quote: And he told this parable: 'A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none. And he said to the vinedresser, ‘Look, for three years now I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground?’
verseByVerse.commentary:
He told this parable: a man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none. And he said to the vinedresser: look, for three years now I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground?

A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard. Only Luke records this parable, and it explains the warning to repent: why the axe has not yet fallen, and why it will. A fig tree in a vineyard, not wild on a hillside, has been planted in prime cultivated ground, where it occupies space that would otherwise carry vines. That is the first half of the case against it: it has had every advantage. And the two images together were unmistakable to anyone who knew the prophets. Israel is the vineyard of Isaiah 5, where God looked for grapes and found wild grapes (Isaiah 5:1–7), and the fig tree in which God came looking and found nothing (Jeremiah 8:13; Hosea 9:10; Micah 7:1).

And he came seeking fruit on it and found none. Fruit means righteousness, justice, repentance and faith, the fruits in keeping with repentance that John the Baptist demanded at the start of this Gospel (3:8). Not leaves, not size, not a pleasant shape: fruit, which is the only thing a fig tree is for.

For three years now. Three years is not impatience. A fig takes some years from planting to bear at all, and the law required that the fruit of the first three years be left untouched in any case (Leviticus 19:23). So the owner has waited and then come three times on top of it. A fig tree that had not borne fruit after so long probably never would. Some see a reference to the length of Jesus’ ministry, though that is uncertain. What is certain is that this is a man who has given the tree every year it was owed and several it was not.

Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground? And here is the charge, stated exactly. Not that it has done harm, nor that it is diseased. It is using up the ground. The verb (katargei) means to waste, to exhaust, to make idle. A fruitless tree draws water and nutrients out of good soil, takes the light, and occupies a space where something fruitful could stand. Barrenness in this parable is not a neutral condition. A tree that produces nothing is not simply failing to help; it is consuming, and what it consumes belongs to somebody else. Judgement was deserved.

He came seeking fruit. Later in this Gospel Jesus tells another vineyard story, in which the owner sends servant after servant to collect his share of the fruit, and at last says, I will send my beloved son (20:13). The owner who comes looking on this fig tree is God, and in the man telling the parable he had come in person. For three years and more Jesus went through the towns and villages of Israel, preaching, healing, eating with sinners, looking for repentance and faith, and at the end he would weep over the city that would not have him (19:41). The owner’s visit is not a figure for some distant inspection. It is the Son standing in the vineyard, looking at the tree.

What fruit is God looking for in me? Not a religious performance, and not a quota of activity. Jesus means the life that grows from a heart turned to God: repentance, trust in Christ, and the fruit of the Spirit that follows, love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23), along with honest dealings and mercy to the poor (3:10–14). Fruit is quiet and grows over time. You will often see it more clearly in others than in yourself, and a believer who fears he has none is often bearing more than he knows. The barren tree in the parable is not a struggling Christian; it is a life that has had every privilege and given nothing back to God at all.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a vineyard owner who came for three years seeking fruit on a fig tree, found none, and ordered it cut down.

On a Tuesday. God has planted you in good soil, with every privilege: an open Bible, perhaps a Christian home, a church where the gospel is preached, the prayers of people who love you. What fruit is he finding in your life? Ask it of the last year rather than of your whole life, because the whole is too large to see. What has God’s word actually produced in you since this time last year? The question the owner asks is not whether the tree has done wrong. It is what the tree is for.

For worship. The Lord of the vineyard is not careless with his ground. He plants with purpose, he comes looking, and he has every right to expect fruit from what he has made. And he is astonishingly patient. Three years, and he comes again; generations, and he sends again. The God who seeks fruit is the God who gives the sap, the sun and the soil, so that every fig his people ever bear is grown from his own goodness and offered back to his glory.
verseByVerse.note: Fig trees were often planted in vineyards. The fig tree was a prophetic picture of Israel.

parallels.desc: the vineyard that yielded wild grapes

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered him, ‘Sir, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure. Then if it should bear fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he answered him: sir, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure. Then if it should bear fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.

Sir, let it alone this year also. The vinedresser does not dispute the verdict. He does not argue that the tree is fruitful, or that the owner has been hasty. He accepts the whole case and asks for time. It is a picture of intercession, and of God’s patience (2 Peter 3:9). And the identification is not difficult. The one who stands between the tree and the axe, asking for another year, is the one telling the story. Jesus intercedes for his people, and he is standing in that very crowd saying it.

Until I dig around it and put on manure. Notice what he offers along with the request. Not merely a delay: let it alone is only half his sentence. He undertakes to work: to dig round the roots, breaking up compacted ground so water can reach them, and to dung it. That is heavy, unpleasant, unglamorous labour on a tree that has given him nothing for three years, and he volunteers for it. Every possible help. God gives every opportunity to repent: his word, his messengers, his Son.

Then if it should bear fruit next year, well and good. The sentence in Greek is broken off: if it bears fruit next year, and then nothing, as if the outcome is left open. Will it? The translators supply well and good; Jesus leaves a silence.

But if not, you can cut it down. Patience has an end. The time of grace is limited. Judgement is delayed, not cancelled. And here the parable does something most of its readers would rather it did not. The intercession has a term. The vinedresser does not ask for indefinite reprieve; he names the period, and he concedes the outcome if nothing changes.

The point. God’s patience is great, but it is not endless. The extra year is a gift: use it to repent (Romans 2:4). The parable ends without telling us what happened, because the hearers must decide. And it stands in its proper relation to the two disasters that preceded it. Those verses said the axe is real. This one says the axe is being held, and by whom. Both halves are needed, and separating them ruins the passage in one direction or the other. A gospel that is all axe produces terror; a gospel that is all delay produces a man who will still be intending to repent in fifteen years’ time. Jesus puts them in the same paragraph.

Does this mean a Christian can be cut down and lost? The parable is spoken first to Israel, and then to everyone who has privilege without fruit: the person who has heard the gospel all his life and never truly turned. It does not teach that those who belong to Christ can be cut off. Jesus says his sheep will never perish and no one will snatch them out of his hand (John 10:28), and he who began a good work will complete it (Philippians 1:6). But it does warn that a fruitless profession is not safe, because fruit is the evidence of life (Matthew 7:16–20). If the warning troubles you, that is not a sign the axe is at your root. It is the vinedresser’s spade, and the right response is to turn to Christ now.

How do I pray for someone who seems hopeless? Like the vinedresser. His response to three barren years is not to write the tree off and not to pretend there is fruit. It is to ask for another year and go and get the spade. So pray specifically and persistently for the child who will not turn, the friend who shrugs, the church that has not grown. And add to your praying whatever digging is yours to do: the patient kindness, the honest conversation, the invitation, the Bible left open. The results belong to God. The asking and the labour belong to us.

In a sentence. The vinedresser pleaded for one more year to tend the tree, after which, if it still bore no fruit, it would be cut down.

On a Tuesday. God’s patience with you is a call to repent, not a reason to delay. This may be your extra year. If there is a sin you have been meaning to deal with, a reconciliation you have been putting off, a call to Christ you have been answering with later, the parable is talking to you, and its message is: now, while the ground is being dug for you.

For worship. The Son of God came down into the vineyard and took up the spade himself. He pleads for barren trees before the Father, and he works the soil of hard hearts with his own hands. And when the axe did fall, it fell on him: the one truly fruitful tree was cut down, hanged on a tree and made a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), so that barren trees might be spared and made fruitful. Every year of grace you have had has been bought by his blood and asked for by his prayers. He always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25).

parallels.desc: God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — A Woman with a Disabling Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke notes almost in passing that Jesus is teaching in a synagogue — the last time in this Gospel he is recorded doing so. The doors are closing.

The woman had been bent double for eighteen years and could not straighten herself. Luke the physician gives the clinical picture in a line. Consider what it means: she has not seen the sky except by turning her whole body, and has not looked another adult in the face in nearly two decades. She sees feet, floors, and the lower half of the world.

And she is in the synagogue. Nobody in that building had a better reason to have stopped coming — eighteen years of asking and receiving nothing, in a culture that read affliction as a verdict — and she is in her place. She asks for nothing when he arrives, which is what makes everything that follows one-sided.

Three things happen and all three are his: he saw her, in a crowded room, teaching, with a woman folded double probably out of everyone's sightline; he called her over, which made her healing public when it could have been quiet; and he touched her, which nobody had needed to do for a long time. “You are freed from your disability” — released, and the release stands; four verses later he calls it being “loosed from this bond.”

She stands up straight for the first time since the middle of another decade, and the direction she looks is the one she had been unable to look for eighteen years.

The synagogue ruler is indignant, and he does not address Jesus. He addresses the people — public instruction aimed sideways, delivered to an audience that is not the actual target. And his argument is not stupid: the fourth commandment says what he quotes. What he has done is classify a healing as work.

Which produces the sentence that gives the whole thing away: “come on those days and be healed.” He is proposing a schedule for a miracle, to a woman who has not been healed on any working day of any week for eighteen years.
verseByVerse.theology:
“A disabling spirit” should not be flattened either way. Luke does not call her possessed or record a demon being cast out; Jesus says Satan had bound her — and chapter 11 showed a stronger one overpowering the strong man (11:21-22). What is described is a physical condition with something darker underneath it: the fallen world's disorder, exploited.

“Daughter of Abraham” occurs nowhere else in the Gospels. Everyone in that synagogue would have called himself a son of Abraham without hesitation; the title is handed to a bent, unnamed, ceremonially awkward woman, and it means she is inside the covenant with every right that carries. Luke will pair it later with Zacchaeus — “he also is a son of Abraham” (19:9).

The argument from lesser to greater is unanswerable because it is drawn from their own practice. An animal tied in a stall cannot reach water, and leaving it thirsty for a whole day was not an option any farmer would entertain; the rulings of the period permitted untying and leading, because mercy to a beast was not counted as work. So the principle they already hold is that a knot may be untied on the Sabbath to relieve suffering.

And the final word is the one they thought was the problem: “on the Sabbath day.” Not in spite of it. Of all the days in the week, the day commemorating a people brought out of slavery is the day for a knot to be undone.
verseByVerse.examples:
The ruler's manoeuvre is worth naming because it is recognisable. Public instruction, aimed sideways, delivered to an audience that is not the target — the sermon everyone knows is about one person, the general remark about standards made in front of the one who fell short. It is cowardice dressed as teaching.

And underneath it is the real failure, which is not legalism exactly: he did not see her. A daughter of Abraham stood up straight in his building and what registered was a diary problem. There is a kind of religion that can watch God act and think first about procedure, and it does not feel like hardness from the inside. It feels like carefulness.

The woman glorifies God before anyone can tell her what she should feel — not the carefully considered religious expression calibrated for an audience, but the overflow of a life that has just been changed.

Two responses close the section, set side by side in a single verse: the adversaries put to shame, the people rejoicing. Nothing in the evidence separated them. They all saw a woman who had been folded double for eighteen years stand up, and what divided them was what they brought into the building. That is the pattern for the rest of this Gospel: the same act of God gladdens one man and humiliates another, and the difference is never in the act.

And there is a small mercy at the end. Being put to shame is not the end of a man; shame is the last stop before repentance for anyone willing to take it. Luke does not tell us what the ruler did next. The door was still open when the paragraph closed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. And behold, there was a woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years. She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. And behold, there was a woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years. She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself.

Now he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. Only Luke records this healing, and he notes the setting almost in passing. It is the last time in this Gospel that Jesus is recorded teaching in a synagogue. The doors are closing.

And behold, there was a woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years. The behold is Luke pointing. She is not mentioned by anyone else in the room. The phrase is literally a spirit of weakness. Her condition was caused by Satan (v. 16), though she is not described as possessed, and Luke does not say a demon was cast out of her. What is described is a physical condition with something darker underneath it: the fallen world’s disorder, exploited.

She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself. Luke the doctor describes it precisely, in a line, with the eye of a man who has examined such people. Perhaps a fusion of the spine. She is folded forward and cannot lift herself upright. Consider what that means for eighteen years of ordinary life. She has not seen the sky except by turning her whole body. She has not looked another adult in the face; every conversation of nearly two decades has been conducted with the top of her head. She sees feet, floors and the lower half of the world. Eighteen years is longer than a childhood.

And she is in the synagogue. That is the thing to sit with. Eighteen years bent double, in a culture that read affliction as a verdict, and she is still coming to worship on the Sabbath. Nobody in that building had a better reason to have stopped. She asks for nothing when Jesus arrives; she had probably stopped expecting anything. And nobody in that synagogue had done anything about her. She had become the settled furniture of the place: the bent woman at the back, whom everybody knew and nobody expected to change.

The first synagogue and the last. Luke opened Jesus’ public ministry in the synagogue at Nazareth, where he read that the Spirit of the Lord had anointed him to set at liberty those who are oppressed (4:18). Now, in the last synagogue scene Luke records, an oppressed woman sits at the back. The promise has not changed between those two Sabbaths, and here it is kept for one person nobody else had looked at. The synagogue had read the Scriptures over her every week for eighteen years. What it had not had, until this Sabbath, was the one the Scriptures were about, standing in the room.

Is sickness caused by Satan? Here Luke says this woman’s condition came from a spirit, and Jesus calls her one whom Satan bound (v. 16). But Scripture never teaches that every illness is demonic: the man born blind was not (John 9:3), and Paul’s thorn was a messenger of Satan that God used for his good (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). A believer cannot be owned by Satan, though God may permit him to be afflicted. The ordinary response to illness is prayer and medicine, not exorcism.

In a sentence. While Jesus was teaching in a synagogue on the Sabbath, a woman was there who had been bent double by a spirit of weakness for eighteen years.

On a Tuesday. She kept coming to worship through eighteen years of suffering; keep coming to God, whatever your burden. And look around your own church for the person who has become furniture: the one with the long illness, the one who comes alone, the one everybody knows and nobody expects to change. Jesus saw her. Ask him to give you eyes like his.

For worship. The Lord sees the ones who have stopped expecting to be seen. Eighteen years did not exhaust his attention, and a crowded room did not hide her from him. She had looked at the floor of that synagogue for most of two decades, and the Lord of glory walked across it to find her. He came into a building that had forgotten her, because he never had.

parallels.desc: another synagogue healing on the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus saw her, he called her over and said to her, 'Woman, you are freed from your disability.' And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight, and she glorified God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus saw her, he called her over and said to her: woman, you are freed from your disability. And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight, and she glorified God.

When Jesus saw her, he called her over. Three things happen in that half-verse, and all are his. She did not ask. He saw her, in a crowded synagogue, a woman folded double and probably out of the sightline of everyone facing the front; Luke uses the same verb of him seeing the widow at Nain (7:13), and it always precedes an action. He called her over, which meant she had to cross the room, slowly, bent, with every eye following her, and it made her healing a public event. Nobody in that building would be able to say afterwards that they had not seen it. He took the initiative, as he always does with those he saves.

Woman, you are freed from your disability. The verb (apolelysai) is a perfect passive: you have been released, set loose, and the release stands. It is the vocabulary of untying, and it is the same idea Jesus will use three verses later of the ox untied from its manger. He does not say be healed. He says the knot has been undone.

And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight. He touched her, which nobody may have done for a long time: a healing touch, and also a human one. After eighteen years she could stand upright and look up, and it took one sentence and a pair of hands. The Lord lifts up those who are bowed down (Psalm 146:8).

And she glorified God. The first thing she does with her new body, and the tense suggests she kept on doing it. Not only thanks, though presumably she thanked him; Luke records that the first use she made of standing upright was worship. For eighteen years she had not been able to lift her face towards heaven in a building built for lifting faces towards heaven. She stands up straight for the first time in nearly two decades, and the direction she looks is the one she had been unable to look all that time.

Why does Jesus heal some and not others, and should I expect healing? In the Gospels his healings are signs that the kingdom has come and that the one who will undo every curse is here. He did not heal every sick person in Israel, and he does not promise every believer healing in this life; Paul left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). God still heals today, in answer to prayer and through medicine, and we should ask him freely (James 5:14–15). But the miraculous gifts that marked the apostles were signs for the founding of the church, and we hold, charitably, that they are not given in the same way now. What every believer is promised is the final straightening: a resurrection body with nothing bent in it (Philippians 3:21). Ask boldly, and rest in that.

In a sentence. Seeing her, Jesus called her, declared her free, laid his hands on her, and she was straightened at once and praised God.

On a Tuesday. If you have been bent under something for years, an illness, a grief, a habit, a long loneliness, bring it to him again. You do not need to have the words; she had none. And when he lifts something off you, do what she did first. Before you tell anyone else, before you plan what to do with the freedom, look up and glorify God.

For worship. Glory to the Saviour whose first word to her was freedom and whose first gift was his hand. He saw her before she saw him, called her before she asked, and undid in a moment a knot Satan had tied for eighteen years. And the first thing the straightened woman did was the thing he had freed her for. One day the whole bent creation will stand up straight at his word, and his people will lift their faces, as she did, and see his.

parallels.desc: the LORD lifts up those who are bowed down

verseByVerse.quote: But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the people, 'There are six days in which work ought to be done. Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the people: there are six days in which work ought to be done. Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day.

But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath. The ruler of the synagogue was the man responsible for organising its services (8:41). A woman has just stood upright for the first time in eighteen years and is praising God at the front of his synagogue, and this man is angry. Not glad that a woman was freed after eighteen years, but angry that a rule had been broken. Religion without love.

Said to the people. Notice who he speaks to. Not to Jesus, who did it. To the people, and effectively to her, since she is the one being told when to come for healing. Too cowardly to rebuke Jesus directly, he lectures the congregation. That is a recognisable manoeuvre and it is worth naming: public instruction aimed sideways, delivered to an audience that is not the actual target. The sermon that everyone knows is about one person; the general remark about standards made in front of the one who fell short. It is cowardice dressed as teaching.

There are six days in which work ought to be done. He is quoting the fourth commandment (Exodus 20:9; Deuteronomy 5:13). And his argument is not stupid. He is right that the Sabbath forbids work, and he is not inventing a rule. What he has done is classify a healing as work. True, but misapplied.

Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day. Say it slowly and it collapses. He is telling a woman who has not been healed on any of the six working days of any week for nearly two decades to come back on Monday, as though healing were a service booked on weekdays and the only issue were the opening hours. Underneath that is the real failure, and it is not exactly legalism. He did not see her. A daughter of Abraham stood up straight in his building, and what registered was a diary problem.

Lord of the Sabbath. The ruler’s mistake is about the healer as much as the woman. He talks as if a healer had opened a clinic on the wrong day. But Jesus had already told the Pharisees, The Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath (6:5). The commandment the ruler quotes was given by the God whose Son was standing in his synagogue. Here was a man lecturing a congregation about the Lord’s day, with the Lord of the day beside him, telling the people to come back on a working day, while the Lord was doing the very work the day had always pointed to.

How do I know if I am like this man? There is a kind of religion that can watch God act and think first about procedure. It is not rare, and it does not usually feel like hardness from the inside. It feels like carefulness. Ask yourself what your first reaction is when God moves in an unexpected way: in a person you had written off, in a church tradition not your own, in a service that ran late. Is it gladness, or a list of objections? Order matters, and Scripture asks for it (1 Corinthians 14:40). But when your love for the way things are done is stronger than your joy that a sinner is helped, the rule has taken the place of the Lord who gave it.

In a sentence. The synagogue ruler, indignant that Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, told the people to come for healing on the other six days.

On a Tuesday. Don’t let love for rules make you angry at God’s grace. And if you have a grievance with someone, take it to that person, not sideways to everyone else (Matthew 18:15). The next time you feel the urge to make a pointed general remark, stop and ask whether you are teaching or merely hiding.

For worship. Our Saviour keeps no opening hours, and his mercy does not wait for Monday. He gave the commandment as a gift of rest, and he came in person to give the rest the commandment promised. The God who rested on the seventh day is the God who does not rest from doing good (John 5:17), and his grace overflows every timetable we try to set for it.
verseByVerse.note: A ruler of the synagogue organised its services.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Lord answered him, 'You hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the Lord answered him: you hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?

You hypocrites! The plural is deliberate. One man spoke; Jesus answers a whole way of thinking, and everyone in the room who agreed with him is included.

Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? The argument is unanswerable because it is drawn from their own practice, and everybody present did it. An animal tied in a stall cannot get to water, and animals could not go a day without it. Leaving a beast thirsty from Friday evening to Saturday evening was not an option any farmer would have entertained. Even the strictest rules of the period allowed livestock to be watered on the Sabbath; untying and leading were permitted, because mercy to a beast was not counted as work. So the principle they already hold is that a knot may be untied on the Sabbath to relieve suffering. Jesus is not asking them to adopt a new rule. He is asking them to apply the one they use every week of their lives.

And ought not this woman. Now the comparison, which is the sharpest thing in the chapter, and every term is chosen. The word for ought (edei) means must, it was necessary: the word of divine necessity that runs through Luke. It was not merely permitted to heal her; it was required. And this woman, set over against his ox or his donkey. The animal has an owner who will take trouble for it. The woman has been in that congregation for years.

A daughter of Abraham. The phrase occurs nowhere else in the Gospels. A member of God’s covenant people, an heir of the promises, like Zacchaeus, a son of Abraham (19:9). Everyone in that synagogue would have called himself a son of Abraham without hesitation. The title is being handed to a bent, unnamed woman, and it means she is inside the covenant with every right that carries. Of more value than an ox.

Whom Satan bound for eighteen years. The real cause. He names the one who tied the knot: the strong man of chapter 11, whom a stronger one overpowers (11:21–22). This is not merely a medical misfortune. It is an occupation, and someone is being dispossessed. Eighteen years, against the ox’s overnight thirst.

Be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day? A play on words: you untie your animals; should I not untie this woman? They untie; he unties. And the final word is the one they thought was the problem. Not in spite of the Sabbath, but on it. The Sabbath was the most fitting day for it. The Sabbath was given as a sign of God’s rest and of his liberation of Israel from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15). What better day to free a captive of Satan? Of all the days in the week, the day commemorating a people brought out of bondage is the day for a knot to be undone. The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ’s liberation.

Does the Sabbath still bind Christians? Christians who love the Bible answer this differently. Many, following the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the fourth commandment remains, moved by Christ’s resurrection to the first day, so that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, kept holy for worship and works of necessity and mercy (Westminster 21.7–8). Others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, the true rest, so that no day binds the conscience in itself (Colossians 2:16–17; Romans 14:5), while Christians gladly gather on the Lord’s Day as the apostles did. Verdict: the second view fits the New Testament best, and the Lord’s Day is a gift to be kept gladly, not a Sabbath law moved to Sunday. Both agree on what this passage teaches: the day of rest is a day of mercy, deeds of kindness are never a breach of it, and its meaning is found in Christ, who gives rest to the weary (Matthew 11:28).

In a sentence. Jesus called them hypocrites, since they untie their animals to water them on the Sabbath, and argued that a daughter of Abraham bound by Satan for eighteen years should certainly be freed on the Sabbath.

On a Tuesday. Look at the rules you live by, the good ones included, and ask whether you apply them more gently to your own convenience than to other people’s needs. Then think of the person in your church who is still bent under something, and ask what knot it is in your power to help untie this week: a visit, a meal, a lift, an hour of listening. Mercy is always in season.

For worship. The first day of the week has been a day of untying ever since Christ rose on it, having broken the bonds of death itself, and every Lord’s Day his people gather is a glad festival of that freedom. The knots of Satan cannot hold against his word. He counts a bent daughter of Abraham worth more than every ox in Israel, and he paid for his people’s release with his own life.
verseByVerse.note: Even the strictest rules allowed livestock to be watered on the Sabbath.

parallels.desc: he also is a son of Abraham

verseByVerse.quote: As he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things that were done by him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things that were done by him.

As he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame. One verse, two reactions, and Luke sets them side by side without comment. The adversaries are those set against him, opponents in a case; the synagogue ruler is no longer merely indignant, he belongs to a party. And they had no answer. Humiliated by exposure: not shouted down, but shown up. Nobody argued them into silence; the argument and the standing woman did it between them. It is an echo of Isaiah 45:16 in the Greek: all who are incensed against him shall be put to shame.

And all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things that were done by him. The ordinary people, who had nothing invested in a ruling about Sabbath work, saw it rightly and are simply delighted. The word (endoxois) is unusual for a healing. It is the word used of God’s mighty acts at the exodus (Exodus 34:10, in the Greek). They have not merely observed something useful. Something of the weight of God has been visible in their synagogue, and they know it. Jesus’ works are God’s works.

Two responses to one event. Nothing in the evidence separated these people. They all saw a woman folded double for eighteen years stand up. What divided them was what they brought into the building. That is the pattern for the rest of this Gospel: the same act of God gladdens one man and humiliates another, and the difference is never in the act. Luke will show the same split at the gates of Jerusalem: the whole multitude of his disciples rejoicing and praising God for all the mighty works they had seen, while Pharisees in the crowd tell him to rebuke them (19:37–39). Simeon had said it over the child: he is appointed for the fall and rising of many.

Is there hope for the man who was put to shame? Yes. Being put to shame is not the end of a man. Shame is what a person feels when he has been shown to be wrong, and it is the last stop before repentance for anyone willing to take it. Luke does not tell us what the synagogue ruler did next. The door was still open when the paragraph closed. If you have been shown up by Christ, in your pride or your hardness, the shame is not meant to drive you away from him. It is meant to bring you to him.

In a sentence. His opponents were humiliated, but the people rejoiced at all the glorious things Jesus did.

On a Tuesday. When God does something good that you did not plan, someone converted whom you had given up on, a gift in someone you had underrated, notice which reaction rises in you first. Make a habit of rejoicing out loud at the glorious things Christ does, in your home and in your church, so that gladness becomes your instinct rather than suspicion.

For worship. All glory to the Lord whose works carry the weight of the exodus. The power that split the sea and brought a nation out of slavery bent down in a village synagogue to straighten one woman’s back, and it was the same glory, and it rests on every sinner he lifts. His works are glorious because he is glorious. His enemies will one day be put to shame, and his people will rejoice for ever in all the glorious things that were done by him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–30 — Mustard Seed, Leaven, and the Narrow Door
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The “therefore” ties the parables to the healing. He has just untied one bent woman in a village synagogue, been attacked for it, and sent a happy crowd home — and it is a fair question whether that is what the kingdom of God amounts to.

The mustard seed was proverbially the smallest thing anyone handled. And it is sowed in his garden — deliberately put in the ground, which is a picture of a man doing something that could not possibly be worth the effort. Black mustard grows fast and reaches ten or twelve feet; calling it a tree is a stretch, and probably meant to be.

Because the image of a great tree with birds nesting in its branches is not invented here. It is Ezekiel's and Daniel's, and it always means a kingdom under whose shelter the nations live (Ezek. 17:23; 31:6; Dan. 4:12). Jesus takes the image of the imperial cedar and puts it on a garden herb. The empires of the world start large and end in ruins; this starts with a seed you could lose in the palm of your hand, and the nations end up living in it.

The leaven parable ought to bring a reader up short, since one chapter ago leaven was the picture of everything that ruins (12:1). That is its usual role in Scripture — scoured out before Passover (Ex. 12:15), and Paul's image for malice and evil (1 Cor. 5:6-8).

But the sentence refuses the warning reading. Jesus does not say the kingdom is threatened by leaven; he says it is like leaven — the identical construction he has just used of the mustard seed, as the matching half of a pair. Leaven is a picture of how a thing spreads, not a verdict on what is spreading, and everything that makes it a good image for hypocrisy makes it a good image for the kingdom.

Then someone asks whether the saved will be few, and gets no number. “Strive to enter through the narrow door” — strain, exert everything, as an athlete does in a contest. And the door is narrow: not locked, not hidden, not high. Narrow says nothing about how hard it is to open and everything about how much can be carried through it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The question “will those who are saved be few?” was a live one in the rabbinic schools, and notice how it is framed — a question about a number, and a number relating to other people. The man asking has placed himself outside the calculation.

That is one of the commonest ways of handling a subject that ought to be handled quite differently. There is a particular safety in the general: as long as the topic is the size of the saved population, the conversation can go on for a long time and cost nothing. And Jesus's reply is to them, plural, though one man asked.

If striving is required, is salvation earned? No — and notice what the striving is for. Not to become worthy, and not until enough has been done. Strive to enter. Everything in Luke pushes against the earning reading: the tax collector who can only beat his breast goes home justified (18:13-14), and the dying criminal with nothing to offer is told “today you will be with me in Paradise” (23:43). Nobody buys this door open — but plenty intend to go through it later, and later is a door that shuts.

“I do not know where you come from” is not a failure of memory. To know, in the Hebrew idiom, is relational (Amos 3:2), and “where you come from” is a householder's question about people at his door: whose are you, and what is your connection to this house?

The closing vision fulfils Isaiah's feast on the mountain for all peoples (Isa. 25:6-8) and the gathering from far off (Isa. 49:12). The seats do not stand empty; the table is full of people nobody in that synagogue expected to see there.
verseByVerse.examples:
The plea of those outside is entirely true and entirely beside the point. They had eaten in his company — very possibly at one of the meals Luke has been recording — and he had taught in their streets and they were there. These are not people making things up.

But every claim is about proximity. We were near you. We were in the room. We were in the town where you preached. Nobody says we trusted you — and a modern reader can produce the identical list without effort: I was at that church for thirty years; I sat under good preaching; I took communion. All of it true, and all of it a description of where a man was standing rather than what he did about it.

Which raises the question that keeps people awake: how do I know I am inside? The door is not a standard you climb to; in this Gospel it is a Person you come to, and Luke has been showing the entering all along in ordinary people. The centurion who says “say the word” (7:7). The woman told “your faith has saved you; go in peace” (7:50). The leper who came back (17:19). The blind man who would not stop shouting (18:38-39). Not one was admitted for being impressive; each came to Jesus himself, with nothing, and would not be turned aside.

And “some are last who will be first” should not be softened into a general maxim about the underdog. What determines the order is not disadvantage but grace — and grace can only be received by people with empty hands. Those most confident of their standing are the last to ask for mercy, and asking is the only way in.

verseByVerse.quote: He said therefore, 'What is the kingdom of God like? And to what shall I compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden, and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said therefore: what is the kingdom of God like? And to what shall I compare it? It is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden, and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.

He said therefore, What is the kingdom of God like? The therefore ties this to the healing. He has just untied one bent woman in a village synagogue, and been attacked for it, and the crowd went home happy. Now he explains what that was. In the light of the healing and of the opposition, the kingdom is present, in small beginnings, and it will grow. It is a fair question to have been asking. If this is the kingdom of God arriving, it does not look like much. One woman. One synagogue. One argument won against a minor official, and the establishment more hostile than it was that morning.

It is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden. The mustard seed was proverbially tiny, the standard picture of the negligible, and Jesus uses it that way himself when he talks about faith (17:6). The kingdom began with one man from Nazareth and a handful of followers, and seemed insignificant. And note that it is sown in his garden: not scattered in a field, not dropped by accident. Somebody deliberately put a thing that small into the ground, which is a picture of a man doing something that could not possibly be worth the effort.

And it grew and became a tree. The mustard plant by the Sea of Galilee can grow taller than a man, ten feet (3 m) or more, large enough for birds to perch and shelter in. Calling it a tree is a stretch, and is probably meant to be. There is a touch of exaggeration in the picture and it is doing work. A huge result from a tiny seed.

And the birds of the air made nests in its branches. The image is Ezekiel’s and Daniel’s, and it always means a kingdom under whose shelter the nations live (Daniel 4:12, 21; Ezekiel 17:23; 31:6). So Jesus takes the picture of the imperial cedar and puts it on a garden herb. That is the joke, and it is also the whole doctrine of how God works. The empires of the world start large and end in ruins. This starts with a seed you could lose in the palm of your hand, and the nations end up living in it. The birds are the Gentiles, and the church has grown from a handful in Jerusalem to every nation on earth.

The tender sprig. Ezekiel’s promise of the nesting birds is a promise about a king. The Lord himself takes a tender sprig from the top of the cedar, from a royal house of David broken and carried into exile, plants it on a high mountain, and it becomes a noble cedar under which birds of every sort will nest (Ezekiel 17:22–23). The kingdom grows from small to great because its King did. Isaiah saw him growing up before the Lord like a young plant, and like a root out of dry ground (Isaiah 53:2): a carpenter’s son from a village nobody rated, a teacher with a few fishermen, a body laid in a borrowed tomb. The one telling this parable is the sprig the parable is about.

Does this mean my church should be large? No. The parable is about the kingdom across the whole sweep of history, not a promise that every congregation will grow big. Many faithful churches stay small for generations, and many large ones are not faithful. What the parable forbids is despising the small and hidden as if God could not be at work there. The measure of a church is not its size but whether Christ is preached and his people are being changed. Small faithfulness is part of the great tree.

In a sentence. Jesus compared the kingdom of God to a tiny mustard seed that grows into a tree where birds nest, a small beginning that becomes great and shelters the nations.

On a Tuesday. Don’t despise small beginnings in God’s work (Zechariah 4:10). He makes great things from tiny seeds. The Sunday school class of six, the Bible study with three, the single conversation over a fence, the prayer meeting that nobody attends: these are mustard seeds, and the Gardener knows what he has planted. Sow, and leave the growing to him.

For worship. The kingdom of God does not need the world’s scale, because its King never needed a running start. The empires that were great cedars in Daniel’s day are dust, and the small thing sown in a garden in Galilee now shades the nations. Under its branches every kind of bird has found a home, and not one was too small or too far away to be welcome. The God who has never once planted a seed he did not mean to grow will not leave his tree half-grown.
verseByVerse.note: Mustard seed was proverbially tiny; the plant can grow taller than a man.

verseByVerse.quote: And again he said, 'To what shall I compare the kingdom of God? It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And again he said: to what shall I compare the kingdom of God? It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.

It is like leaven that a woman took and hid. The second parable ought to bring a reader up short, and if it does not, it is worth noticing why it should. Usually in Scripture leaven pictures a corrupting influence. One chapter ago, from this same speaker, it was the picture of everything that ruins: beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy (12:1). Israel scoured it out of the house before Passover (Exodus 12:15); the feast at the start of the passion is the feast of Unleavened Bread (22:1); and Paul takes the image for granted, a little leaven leavens the whole lump, and means malice and evil by it (1 Corinthians 5:6–8). Here, unusually, it is a positive picture: a small amount, working invisibly, spreading through the whole.

Why is leaven good here when it is bad elsewhere? Because the image is about the way leaven works, not about whether what it carries is good or evil. Some have concluded that Jesus must be warning of corruption spreading quietly through the church, but the sentence refuses it. He does not say the kingdom is threatened by leaven; he says the kingdom of God is like leaven, the identical construction he has just used of the mustard seed, as the matching half of a pair. Turn the second into a warning and you break the pair in half. Everything that makes yeast a good image for hypocrisy, that it is small, hidden, works from the inside and does not stop until the whole batch is changed, is exactly what makes it a good image for the kingdom. Luke’s own two uses prove the point: at 12:1 something false permeates a community; here something true permeates the world.

A man in the first parable, a woman in the second. Luke’s pairing again, the same care that set Simeon beside Anna and the shepherd beside the woman with the lost coin. And the woman hid it: the kingdom works hiddenly, invisibly, from within.

In three measures of flour. A very large batch, about 50 pounds (22 kg) of flour, enough to feed a hundred people and more. It is about what Sarah baked for her heavenly visitors (Genesis 18:6). An extravagant quantity, and an absurd amount for one woman to be kneading in a kitchen. The comedy is deliberate. A pinch of yeast, invisible the moment it goes in, and a mountain of dough; and the pinch wins.

Until it was all leavened. The whole lump is transformed. That is the answer to anyone who has looked at the size of the world and the size of the church and quietly concluded that the arithmetic is hopeless.

The two parables together. Luke sets them side by side as one lesson in two halves. The seed is seen from outside: something small in the ground becomes a thing the birds can find. The leaven is seen from inside: something small in the dough changes every part of it. One is the kingdom’s reach, the other its depth, and both are the work of one hand that does not stop until it is finished.

Christ in you. What is the hidden thing that works through the whole? The New Testament names it. The kingdom comes into a person not as a rule laid on the outside but as the King himself living within by his Spirit: the mystery hidden for ages and now revealed, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory (Colossians 1:26–27). Luke’s second volume shows it beginning. The risen and exalted Jesus poured out the Spirit (Acts 2:33) on a company of about a hundred and twenty in one city (Acts 1:15), and by the last page of Acts the kingdom of God is being proclaimed in Rome (Acts 28:31). Nobody watching that upper room could have seen the dough rise. It rose.

What it does not mean. Not that the whole world will gradually become Christian before Christ returns (postmillennialism), though some have read it that way. The parables promise growth and transformation, not universal conversion, and other passages speak of persecution and apostasy until the end (18:8; 21:12; 2 Timothy 3:1–5).

How does the kingdom work in me like leaven? Quietly and thoroughly. When Christ enters a life he does not stay in one compartment. He begins with the heart and works outward into habits, words, money, marriage, work, until nothing is left untouched. It is usually slower than we want and deeper than we notice. You may not see the change from one week to the next, any more than you can watch dough rise. But look back over years and you will often find that what once ruled you no longer does. That is the yeast at work, and the one who hid it will not stop until the whole is leavened (Philippians 1:6).

In a sentence. Jesus compared the kingdom to yeast that a woman hid in a large batch of flour until it had worked through the whole.

On a Tuesday. God’s kingdom is at work in your life and in the world, often invisibly. Trust its quiet power. Do the hidden work faithfully: the honest day’s labour, the kind word at home, the prayer no one hears. That is how leaven moves through a lump, and it is how the gospel moves through a street, an office and a family.

For worship. Glory to the King whose kingdom is not loud and cannot be stopped. He entered the world hidden in a virgin’s womb and grew up unnoticed in Nazareth, and he works now just as hiddenly, in kitchens and offices and hospital wards, wherever one of his people quietly lives by his word. No measure of flour is too large for him. He will not lay down his work until the whole is leavened and the earth is full of the knowledge of his glory.
verseByVerse.note: Three measures of flour is a very large batch — about what Sarah baked for her three guests.

verseByVerse.quote: He went on his way through towns and villages, teaching and journeying toward Jerusalem. And someone said to him, 'Lord, will those who are saved be few?' And he said to them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went on his way through towns and villages, teaching and journeying toward Jerusalem. And someone said to him: Lord, will those who are saved be few? And he said to them:

He went on his way through towns and villages, teaching and journeying toward Jerusalem. Luke reminds us where the road is going. He has been noting the direction of travel since 9:51, and it is not filler. Everything in these chapters is being said by a man walking towards his own execution, and the question about how many will be saved is put to the one person on that road who knows, because he is going to Jerusalem to save them.

Lord, will those who are saved be few? The question was a live one in the schools, and it was discussed with some relish. Jewish teachers debated how many of Israel would have a share in the age to come. Some said all Israel would be saved, with a few named exceptions; others were considerably tighter. And notice how the question is framed. It is a question about a number, and a number relating to other people. The man asking it has placed himself outside the calculation and is enquiring about the statistics. The questioner wants to discuss others, perhaps from curiosity.

The safety of the general. It is worth naming, because it is one of the commonest ways of handling a subject that ought to be handled quite differently. Questions like what about those who have never heard, are most people lost, what happens to those who die as infants, are genuine questions, and some of them have good answers. They are also very often a way of discussing eternity in the third person. As long as the topic is the size of the saved population, the conversation can go on for a long time and cost nothing.

And he said to them. Two small things before the answer itself. He does not tell him the number. Wherever in the Gospels curiosity presses for information God has not given, the times and seasons, who is greatest, what will happen to that man, the answer is a redirection, and it is never rude and never satisfies. And the reply is to them, plural, though one man asked. Jesus answers the crowd, and turns the question from theory to personal urgency. The questioner was not going to be allowed to receive it as a matter of general interest.

So will few be saved, or many? Scripture gives two answers that sound opposite and are both true. Looked at from the road, the way is narrow, and in any generation those who find it are few compared with the crowd on the broad road (Matthew 7:13–14). Looked at from the end, John sees a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, tribe, people and language (Revelation 7:9). God will save a vast people for his Son, and not one he has chosen will be lost (John 6:37–39). But you will not be in that number by being in a majority, a family or a church. Jesus’ answer is not a statistic. It is: make sure you are one of them.

In a sentence. As Jesus travelled toward Jerusalem, someone asked him whether only a few would be saved.

On a Tuesday. The question is not how many will be saved, but whether you will be. Notice when your conversations about God drift into the third person: other religions, other churches, people who have never heard. Those questions have their place. But before you leave them, ask the one Jesus asked back: and you?

For worship. The Lord of the harvest knows the number of his own, every name of them, and has written them in the book of life before the foundation of the world. He does not need our arithmetic. He walked to Jerusalem to secure that number with his own blood, and the multitude no one can count will stand at last before his throne crying that salvation belongs to our God and to the Lamb (Revelation 7:10).

verseByVerse.quote: 'Strive to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Strive to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able.

Strive to enter through the narrow door. The door leads into the kingdom feast (vv. 28–29), and the master of the house who shuts it is Jesus himself, who says, I do not know where you come from (vv. 25–27). So the way in is through him, by repentance and faith. John makes the picture explicit: I am the door (John 10:9).

The question that should have been asked. He does not answer the question asked. He answers the question that should have been asked, and it is not how many, but are you going in? Strive (agōnizesthe) is the root of our word agony, and in ordinary Greek it is what an athlete does in the games: to strain, to exert everything, to compete as though something depended on it. Something does.

The door is narrow. Not locked, not hidden, and not high. Narrow. Which says nothing about how hard it is to open and everything about how much can be carried through it. You cannot bring your own righteousness through this door, nor your pride, nor your claims on God, nor the sin you mean to keep. It is wide enough for any sinner and too narrow for any sinner’s baggage.

For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able. Why? Not because they wanted Christ and were refused, but because they came too late (v. 25), or on their own terms, wanting to enter without going through the narrow door. They seek, but not in the right way or at the right time. Nobody buys this door open. But plenty of people intend to go through it later, and he is telling them that later is a door that shuts.

What it does not mean. Not that we must earn salvation by effort. Salvation is by grace through faith (Ephesians 2:8–9). But entering requires urgency and wholeheartedness: repentance, faith, turning from sin, coming to Christ now. It is not a casual affair.

If I must strive, am I not earning my way in after all? No, and notice what the striving is for. He does not say strive to become worthy, or strive until you have done enough. He says strive to enter. The effort is not payment offered at the door; it is the urgency of a man who will not be talked out of going through it. Everything in Luke pushes against the earning reading. The tax collector who can only beat his breast goes home justified (18:13–14), and the dying criminal who has nothing whatever to offer is told he will be with Jesus in Paradise that very day (23:43). The striving is the striving of the drowning man for the rope, not of the labourer for his wages.

How do I know I am inside? The passage is about to be unsparing on false assurance, so it is worth saying plainly what genuine entering looks like. The door is not a standard you climb to; in this Gospel it is a Person you come to, and Luke has been showing us the entering all along in ordinary people. It is the centurion who asks Jesus only to say the word (7:7). It is the woman told that her faith has saved her and she may go in peace (7:50). It is the leper who came back (17:19), and the blind man who would not stop shouting (18:38–39). Not one of them was admitted for being impressive. Each came to Jesus himself, with nothing, and would not be turned aside. If that is what you are doing, you are not outside knocking. And the one who comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37).

What if I have doubts about whether I have really come? Doubt is not the same as being outside. Many true believers struggle with assurance, and the Westminster Confession says plainly that a true believer may wait long and conflict with many difficulties before he has it (Westminster 18.3). Do not look first at the strength of your faith; look at the Christ it holds. Come to him again today, as a sinner, with nothing in your hands, and you are doing exactly what this verse commands. Assurance usually grows as you keep coming, as you see the Spirit’s fruit slowly appear, and as you rest on his promise rather than your feelings.

In a sentence. Jesus told them to strive to enter by the narrow door, for many will seek to enter and not be able.

On a Tuesday. Don’t be casual about your salvation. Make sure you have come through the narrow door, Christ himself. If you have been meaning to settle things with God, do not let another week pass with the matter only intended. And if you are inside, strive still: in prayer, in the fight with sin, in pressing on to know him, because the door you came through is the beginning of the road, not the end.

For worship. Christ is the door, and he is open. To open it he was stripped of glory and stretched on a cross, so that the way into the Father’s house might be opened to sinners from every corner of the earth. No one who comes to him is too late while the door stands open, and no one who enters through him will ever be put out. Blessed be the Door, who is also the Shepherd and the Host of the feast.

verseByVerse.quote: When once the master of the house has risen and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and to knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, open to us,’ then he will answer you, ‘I do not know where you come from.’ Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.’ But he will say, ‘I tell you, I do not know where you come from. Depart from me, all you workers of evil!’
verseByVerse.commentary:
When once the master of the house has risen and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and to knock at the door, saying, Lord, open to us, then he will answer you: I do not know where you come from. Then you will begin to say: we ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets. But he will say: I tell you, I do not know where you come from. Depart from me, all you workers of evil!

When once the master of the house has risen and shut the door. The scene changes from a doorway to a house at night, and the decisive action has already happened before the verse begins. This is the day of judgement. There comes a time when the door is shut, and the opportunity is over (Matthew 25:10). He is not described as refusing to open it. He shut it, once, at a time of his choosing, and the shutting is presented as ordinary, what any householder does at the end of the day. Now it is open; one day it will be shut.

And you begin to stand outside and to knock at the door, saying, Lord, open to us. They call him Lord, but too late (6:46). They know the address. They know what to call him. They are at the right house, and they are asking the right person.

I do not know where you come from. It is a strange formula, and it is not a failure of memory. To know, in the Hebrew idiom, is relational: God knew Israel among all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2). And where you come from is the question of a householder about people at his door: whose are you, and what is your connection to this house? You do not belong to my household. I have no relationship with you. The answer is that there is none. They are the worst words anyone could hear (Matthew 7:23).

We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets. And here is the plea, and every word of it is true. They had eaten in his company, very possibly at one of the meals Luke records all through this Gospel. He had taught in their streets, and they had been there to hear it. These are not people making things up. Their credentials are entirely genuine. They are also entirely beside the point. Every claim is about proximity: we were near you, we were in the room, we were in the town where you preached. Nobody says we trusted you. They had contact with Jesus, but not a relationship. Proximity is not faith. Hearing sermons, attending church, being near Jesus, is not the same as belonging to him.

Depart from me, all you workers of evil! The words are from Psalm 6:8. Their lives showed they were not his. And the sentence lands hardest on the most religiously exposed people in any generation. A modern reader can produce the identical list without effort: I was at that church for thirty years. I sat under good preaching. I took communion. All of it true, and all of it a description of where a man was standing rather than what he did about it.

I have been in church all my life. Should this frighten me? It should make you honest, not hopeless. The question is not how long you have been near Jesus but whether you have come to him: whether you have owned your sin before him and trusted him alone to save you. If you have, being in church all your life is a great mercy, and you belong to him. If you are not sure, do not try to settle it by reviewing your attendance. Go to him now, in your own words, and ask him to receive you. The people in this parable are not those who came and were refused. They are those who never came, and assumed that being near was enough.

Does Jesus not know everyone? As God he knows everything about everyone, every thought and every deed (Psalm 139:1–4). But Scripture also uses know of the loving, saving knowledge he has of his own: the Lord knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19), I know my own and my own know me (John 10:14). That is the knowing these people lack. He is not saying he has no information about them. He is saying they were never his.

In a sentence. When the door is shut, those outside will plead that they ate with Jesus and heard him teach, but he will say he does not know them and send them away as evildoers.

On a Tuesday. Being familiar with Jesus is not enough. Does he know you as his own? Take one of the familiar things this week, the prayer before a meal, the hymn you sing without thinking, the sermon you half hear, and stop inside it long enough to speak to him rather than about him. And if you have children who have grown up near the gospel, pray that nearness will become belonging.

For worship. The master of the house is patient beyond all telling: he keeps the door open through long generations and calls and calls. And he is the Judge, whose word at the end is final and just. Those whom he knows, he knew before the world began, called by name, and will welcome into his house for ever. To be known by him is the glory of every believer, and it is entirely his gift.

parallels.desc: depart from me, all you workers of evil

verseByVerse.quote: In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God but you yourselves cast out. And people will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God. And behold, some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God but you yourselves cast out. And people will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God. And behold, some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last.

In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Weeping is grief and gnashing of teeth is anguish, and perhaps rage, so what is described may be not merely sorrow but sorrow with fury still in it. It is a picture of the misery of those shut out of the kingdom, for ever (Matthew 8:12; 13:42).

When you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God. The patriarchs and prophets, whose descendants Jesus’ hearers were proud to be. And the specific torment named is a sight. Whatever else exclusion means, this text says it involves knowing exactly what has been lost and who is at the table.

But you yourselves cast out. The shock: Abraham’s children shut out, because they did not share Abraham’s faith (3:8). Note who the people outside are. Not pagans. Men who could recite their descent from Abraham, and whose whole assurance rested on it, an assurance John the Baptist had already demolished at the start of this Gospel when he warned them not to begin to say that they had Abraham as their father.

Where Christians differ: is the punishment conscious and lasting? Some evangelicals hold that the lost are finally destroyed and cease to exist. Most Christians through history have held that the punishment of the lost is conscious and without end. Verdict: the punishment is conscious and lasting. This picture is of people who are present and aware of what they have lost, and Jesus elsewhere speaks of eternal punishment in the same breath as eternal life (Matthew 25:46), so that whatever one lasts, the other does. Hell is not annihilation but exclusion from the joy of God’s presence under his just judgement (2 Thessalonians 1:9). It is a terrible truth, and Jesus speaks it with tears, not relish.

And people will come from east and west, and from north and south. From all four points of the compass, which is the ancient way of saying everywhere: the Gentiles, from every nation (Isaiah 49:12; 59:19; Psalm 107:3). The seats do not stand empty. The table is full, and it is full of people nobody in that synagogue would have expected to see there.

And recline at table in the kingdom of God. The messianic banquet (Isaiah 25:6–8; Revelation 19:9), where Gentiles will sit with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Matthew 8:11). Christians differ on when it is spread. Premillennial brothers place it in a thousand-year reign on earth; this app holds, with the amillennial view, that it is the feast of the new creation after Christ’s one visible return.

At my table in my kingdom. Isaiah had foreseen it: on this mountain the LORD of hosts will spread a feast of rich food for all peoples, swallow up death for ever, and wipe the tears from every face (Isaiah 25:6–8). And Luke tells us whose table it is. Every meal in this Gospel, at a Pharisee’s table, in a tax collector’s house, on a hillside with five loaves, has Jesus at the centre of it, and at the last supper he says, I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God (22:16), and promises the Twelve that they will eat and drink at my table in my kingdom (22:30). The feast with Abraham is his feast. To recline was how guests lay at a banquet: not a snack at the door but a seat at the King’s own table, with nothing more to do but enjoy him.

And behold, some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last. The great reversal. Gentiles, last in privilege, will be first in the kingdom; Israel, first in privilege, many of them last. And within the church too: the proud will be humbled, and the humble exalted.
