This is Luke’s signature, running since the Magnificat, the mighty brought down and the humble exalted (1:52). But it should not be softened into a general maxim about the underdog. What determines the order is not disadvantage. It is grace, and the fact that grace can only be received by people with empty hands. Those most confident of their standing are the last to ask for mercy, and asking is the only way in.

Who are the first who will be last today? Anyone whose confidence rests on what he has rather than on Christ: a Christian upbringing, a good church, a long record of service, sound doctrine held at arm’s length. These are gifts, and the first in privilege can be first in the kingdom too, if they come as beggars. But privilege trusted becomes a wall. And the last who will be first are those who knew they had no claim at all: the convert from a wrecked life, the believer in a land that never heard the gospel until yesterday, the child with simple faith. The warning falls where it does because it is aimed at people who were sure they were near him.

In a sentence. Those shut out will weep in anguish when they see the patriarchs and prophets in the kingdom, and people from every nation feasting there, for the last will be first and the first last.

On a Tuesday. Hold your privileges with gratitude and with trembling. Thank God for every advantage you have had, and then come to him as though you had none, because in the only sense that counts you have none. Be glad, not jealous, when someone from far off is welcomed to the table before you expected, and look around your church for the stranger and the newcomer, who are guests of the same King.

For worship. Blessed be the Host who was himself shut out for us, crucified outside the city gate (Hebrews 13:12), so that strangers from east and west might sit down with Abraham and never be sent away. Gentiles who had no claim on Abraham’s table are guests at it, bought from every tribe and tongue by the blood of the Lamb, and not one seat will stand empty. The feast he has prepared is the one at which death itself is swallowed up for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined at a banquet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Some Pharisees warn him that Herod wants to kill him — the only occasion in the Gospels on which Pharisees warn Jesus of a danger, and their motive is genuinely uncertain. Not every Pharisee was an enemy; Luke records three who invite him to dinner. But Herod ruled Galilee, and a man frightened out of that territory would be driven towards Judea, where his real opponents were waiting.

“That fox” is contemptuous in a specific way. In Jewish usage the fox was not primarily crafty but the small predator set against the lion — a rabbinic saying speaks of being the tail of lions rather than the head of foxes. Herod is being called a nuisance rather than a power, which is what he was: Rome never let him be king, and he ended his days exiled to Gaul.

The reply is a timetable, and it belongs to somebody else. Herod does not set the date. “I finish my course” is the language of completion — the same English as the word from the cross, “it is finished” (John 19:30). And the last clause is grim irony: he is not saying Jerusalem is dangerous but that it is the appointed place, and that a prophet is therefore safe from Herod because he is booked in somewhere else.

Then the lament. “How often” is not the language of a man who has been in Jerusalem three or four times in three years. It is the language of someone who has been trying for a very long time — and behind it stands every prophet who was sent and killed. The one speaking is the one who sent them.

The image has a long history in Israel's Scriptures: the eagle stirring her nest (Deut. 32:11), the wings under which Ruth took refuge (Ruth 2:12), the shadow of the wings in the Psalms (17:8; 36:7; 57:1; 91:4). But a hen is not an eagle, and the difference matters. A hen has no talons and cannot fight; what she has is a body and a pair of wings, and the way she saves her chicks in a fire is to spread them and stay where she is. Farmers have found them afterwards, burnt through, with the chicks alive underneath.

That is the image he chose for himself, on the road on which he had set his face towards a city that was going to kill him.
verseByVerse.theology:
“Your house is forsaken” — and the first two words are the devastating ones. It had never been their house — Solomon built it and God filled it, and it is called “my house” in every prophet, as Jesus himself will say in that very building (19:46). To hand it back with the possessive changed is to say the owner has moved out.

Israel had seen it before. Ezekiel watched the glory rise from the cherubim, move to the threshold, and go out of the city to the mountain on the east (Ezek. 10:18-19; 11:23) — and the temple stood a few more years and was then flattened. A building God has left is not a temple; it is masonry.

The closing quotation is Psalm 118:26, sung by pilgrims arriving at the temple for the feasts, and the crowd will shout it over him within six chapters (19:38). Some read the promise as fulfilled there, and the words very nearly match; but the entry is one day, not an era, and what follows it does not look like a welcome. Others read it as pointing further on — to a day when the city that would not be gathered finally says it and means it, which is the hope Paul holds out (Rom. 11:26). The second fits the words better, since “Blessed is he who comes” is a welcome, not a cry of terror.
verseByVerse.examples:
The lament is the model of prophetic grief — the sorrow a faithful preacher feels for those who hear the word and do not receive it. It is not anger; it is love that has been refused, and the grief of knowing what the refusal costs.

Every pastor who has watched someone hear the gospel clearly and walk away, every parent who has prayed for a child who will not turn, every evangelist who has seen the door closing on someone who came so close, has tasted something of it.

“And you were not willing” is five words and the whole tragedy. Every verb before them is his — would I have gathered. The willingness was entirely on one side and the refusal entirely on the other. He does not say they were unable; he says they were not willing, which is worse, and it is the only thing standing between those chicks and those wings.

And what matters most about the last verse is its shape. It ends with until. He has just pronounced the most terrible sentence in the Gospel over the city he was born to save, and he did not stop at the desolation. He put a door in the last line — and the words on the far side of it are not a demand for reparations or a list of terms. They are a welcome, which is the one thing that city never gave him.

verseByVerse.quote: At that very hour some Pharisees came and said to him, 'Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you.' And he said to them, 'Go and tell that fox, ‘Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course.’ Nevertheless, I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that very hour some Pharisees came and said to him: get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you. And he said to them: go and tell that fox, behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course. Nevertheless, I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem.

At that very hour some Pharisees came and said to him, Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you. It is the only recorded occasion in the Gospels on which Pharisees warn Jesus of danger, and their motive is genuinely uncertain. Not all Pharisees were hostile. Luke records three who invite him to dinner, and John tells of Nicodemus, a Pharisee who came to him by night. Perhaps these were genuinely concerned. Or the warning may be a manoeuvre: perhaps they wanted him out of their area, or were sent by Herod to scare him away. A man frightened out of Herod’s territory would be driven towards Judea, which is where his real opponents were waiting. Luke does not tell us, and it is better not to decide.

For Herod wants to kill you. The threat is credible. This is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee and Perea, who had beheaded John (9:9) and has been wanting to see Jesus ever since. Jesus was probably in Perea at the time.

Go and tell that fox. The message is sent back to Herod personally, and it is not a compliment. In Jewish usage a fox was not only crafty; it was the small, destructive predator, set against the lion. A rabbinic saying advises being a tail to lions rather than a head to foxes. Herod is being called a nuisance rather than a power. Which is what he was. Rome never let him be king; he was a tetrarch, and he would end his days exiled to Gaul. Jesus is not afraid of Herod.

I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course. The reply is a timetable, and it belongs to somebody else. Today and tomorrow and the third day is an idiom for a fixed, short time, set by God, not by Herod. Jesus will go on doing exactly what he is doing until the work is finished. And the verb (teleioumai) means I am brought to completion, perfected, a thing brought to its proper end, which his work would reach at his death and resurrection in Jerusalem (Hebrews 2:10; 5:9). It is the same root as the word from the cross: it is finished (John 19:30).

Nevertheless, I must go on my way. There is the must again (dei), the divine necessity that has driven this Gospel since a boy in the temple said he must be in his Father’s house (2:49). Herod’s threats cannot change God’s plan.

For it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem. Bitter irony. Jerusalem, the holy city, had a long history of killing the prophets (Jeremiah 26:20–23; 2 Chronicles 24:20–22). Jesus would not die in Herod’s Galilee, but in Jerusalem. He is not saying merely that Jerusalem is dangerous. He is saying it is the appointed place: that the city which exists to bring men to God has a settled record of killing the men God sends, and that a prophet is therefore safe from Herod because he is booked in somewhere else.

Did Jesus insult a ruler? He spoke as a prophet with authority over Herod, giving God’s verdict on a cunning and destructive man. It is not a pattern for Christians to speak of rulers with contempt. Paul apologised for speaking against the high priest (Acts 23:5), and Peter tells believers to honour the emperor (1 Peter 2:17). We may and sometimes must speak plainly about injustice, and we must never be ruled by fear of the powerful. But our ordinary duty is to pray for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2) and to speak of them with respect, even when we oppose what they do.

What if someone is threatening me? Jesus did not ignore the danger, and he did not run from his calling either. He went on doing the work God had given him, in the place God had given it, until the time God had set. Take sensible precautions, seek help, and where there is abuse or real danger, go to those who can protect you; Scripture never asks you to stay under violence. But do not let fear decide your obedience. Your days are written in God’s book before one of them came to be (Psalm 139:16), and no Herod can add a minute to them or take one away.

In a sentence. Warned that Herod wanted to kill him, Jesus called Herod a fox and said he would continue his work until his appointed time, for a prophet must die in Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. No human power can cut short what God has planned for your life. Don’t be ruled by fear. Think of the thing you have been avoiding because of what someone might say or do: the honest word, the stand at work, the confession of faith in front of family. Do today’s work today, and tomorrow’s tomorrow, and leave the third day to your Father.

For worship. Jesus was never the victim of a schedule he did not set. Herod schemed, Pilate gave way, the crowds shouted, and through it all the Son walked steadily to the hour appointed by his Father, to lay down his life of his own accord and take it up again (John 10:18). His course was finished at the cross and crowned on the third day. The Lord who is not afraid of foxes holds every one of his people in the same unhurried, unbreakable hand.
verseByVerse.note: Herod is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, who had executed John. A fox was a picture of cunning and destructiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!
verseByVerse.commentary:
O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!

O Jerusalem, Jerusalem. The double address shows deep emotion, grief and love, the same register as Martha, Martha and Simon, Simon (10:41; 22:31). It is what he says when he sees the whole of someone and grieves.

The city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! This is what the city does, habitually, as a settled practice. And the charge is historical, not rhetorical. Zechariah was stoned in the temple court on the king’s orders (2 Chronicles 24:21). Jeremiah was thrown into a cistern to die (Jeremiah 38:6). Tradition held that Isaiah was sawn in two under Manasseh. And it is about to kill the greatest of the prophets.

How often would I have gathered your children together. How often is the phrase to stop at. Jesus had visited Jerusalem many times, as John records (John 2:13; 5:1; 7:10; 10:22). But this is not the language of a man who has been in the city a handful of times in three years. It is the language of someone who has been trying for a very long time, and behind it stands every prophet who was sent and killed. God had called Jerusalem through all the prophets. The one speaking is the one who sent them. Jesus speaks as God, who longed to gather his people.

As a hen gathers her brood under her wings. Luke sets this lament straight after the message to that fox, and the pairing is hard to miss: a fox is on the prowl, and a hen stands between it and her chicks. Matthew records the saying in the temple in the last week; Luke hears it on the road, with Herod’s threat still in the air. In the Old Testament God shelters his people under his wings: the eagle bearing her young on her pinions (Deuteronomy 32:11), the God of Israel under whose wings Ruth came to take refuge (Ruth 2:12), the shadow of his wings in the psalms (Psalm 17:8; 91:4). But a hen is not an eagle. She has no talons and cannot fight. What she has is a body and a pair of wings, and the way she saves her chicks is by spreading them and staying where she is, taking on herself what was coming for them. That is the image he chose for himself, on the road to a city that was going to kill him.

And you were not willing! Jerusalem refused. The tragedy of unbelief. Every verb before these words is his: would I have gathered. The willingness was entirely on one side and the refusal entirely on the other. He does not say they were unable. He says they were not willing, which is worse, and it is the only thing standing between those chicks and those wings.

Where Christians differ: God’s will and human refusal. Arminians take this verse to show that God wills all to be saved but that human free will can finally resist his saving purpose. Verdict: Scripture teaches both that God is sovereign in salvation (John 6:37, 44; Ephesians 1:11) and that he sincerely calls sinners and grieves over their refusal (Ezekiel 18:23, 32; 33:11). Reformed theology distinguishes God’s revealed will, what he commands and desires (that people repent and come), from his secret decree, what he has determined will happen. Jesus’ lament is genuine: God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. The responsibility for refusal lies entirely with those who refuse. Both truths stand; we should not cancel one by the other.

If God is sovereign, how can his tears be real? Because he means what he says. The Son who wept over Jerusalem is not acting a part. God truly delights in mercy, truly calls, and truly grieves when his call is refused, and none of that is pretence because he has also purposed what will come to pass. We cannot fit both truths into one neat sentence, and Scripture does not ask us to. It asks us to believe both: that no one comes to Christ unless the Father draws him (John 6:44), and that whoever refuses Christ does so freely and is answerable for it. The tears of Jesus are the clearest window we have into the heart of God towards sinners.

Can I still come? Yes. The wings that were spread over Jerusalem are spread still, and the invitation has never been withdrawn from anyone who will come. If you are afraid you have refused him too long, notice that the very fear is a sign he is still gathering you. Those who are finally lost are not those who wanted to come and were turned away. They are those who would not. Come to him today, and you will find there is room under his wings.

In a sentence. Jesus lamented over Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets, because he had longed to gather its people like a hen gathering her chicks, and they would not come.

On a Tuesday. Let the tears of Jesus shape the way you speak about those who reject him. Not with contempt, and not with indifference, but with longing. Pray for the people you know who have refused him, by name, with something of his grief. And if there is any part of your own life you have been unwilling to bring under his wings, bring it today.

For worship. Glory to the Lord God of Israel, who sent prophet after prophet into a city that killed them, and then came himself, the incarnate Son, grieving on the road. Centuries of refusal did not wear out his longing: how often is the voice of a love that kept count of every rejection and kept on calling. His wings are spread still, over sinners in every city on earth, and no chick that ran under them has ever been turned away. There is no tenderer heart in the universe, and no safer place.

parallels.desc: under his wings you will find refuge

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, your house is forsaken. And I tell you, you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, your house is forsaken. And I tell you, you will not see me until you say: blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!

Behold, your house is forsaken. Your house: the temple, or the city, or the nation. Two words, and they are devastating. It had never been their house. Solomon built it and God filled it, and it was called my house in every prophet, a house of prayer, as Jesus will say in that very building (19:46). No longer “my Father’s house” (2:49), but “your house”, abandoned by God. To hand it back with the possessive changed is to say that the owner has moved out. As in Jeremiah 12:7 (I have forsaken my house) and 22:5. God’s presence will leave, and the temple will be destroyed (19:43–44; 21:6). Fulfilled in AD 70.

Israel had seen this before. Ezekiel watched the glory of God rise from the cherubim, move to the threshold, and go out of the city to the mountain on the east (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:23), and the temple stood for a few more years and was then flattened. A building God has left is not a temple. It is masonry. And the glory that left in Ezekiel’s day had come back in person, a baby carried into the temple in Simeon’s arms (2:27–32), and was now being refused.

You will not see me until you say, Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! The quotation is Psalm 118:26, the psalm sung by pilgrims arriving at the temple for the feasts. When Jesus enters Jerusalem, the crowds will sing these words over him as he comes down the Mount of Olives (19:38). But the deeper fulfilment is at his return. The entry is one day, not an era, and what happens after it does not look like a welcome. And blessed is he who comes is a welcome, not a cry of terror.

Does this mean a future turning of Israel to Christ? Paul teaches that all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:25–27), which many understand as a future conversion of large numbers of the Jewish people before Christ returns. Others take it of the full number of God’s elect, Jew and Gentile. Either way, the verse holds out hope as well as judgement.

The shape of the sentence. What is certain is the shape of the sentence, and the shape is what matters. It ends with until. He has just pronounced the most terrible sentence in the Gospel over the city he was born to save, and he did not stop at the desolation. He put a door in the last line, and the words on the far side of it are not a demand for reparations or a list of terms. They are a welcome, which is the one thing that city never gave him.

How should Christians think about the Jewish people today? With love, gratitude and longing. Salvation is from the Jews (John 4:22): the patriarchs, the covenants, the Scriptures and the Messiah himself came through them (Romans 9:4–5). Paul had great sorrow and unceasing anguish for his kinsmen and prayed for their salvation (Romans 9:2–3; 10:1). Any contempt for Jewish people is a denial of the gospel, not a defence of it. At the same time the way of salvation is the same for Jew and Gentile: faith in Jesus the Messiah, the only name under heaven by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). So we pray, we love, and we tell the good news, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that Jerusalem’s house was forsaken, and that they would not see him until they welcomed him as the one who comes in the Lord’s name.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the Jewish people, that they would welcome Jesus as their Messiah. And ask whether your own life is a house he has been shut out of: a heart full of religious furniture, but no welcome for the Lord himself. Say it to him today, and mean it: blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.

For worship. The hen is still on the road, still walking towards Jerusalem, still saying how often would I have gathered you. And the sentence that ends her lament is not never. It is until. The Lord who left the temple will come again in glory, and every knee will bow, and a great multitude of his people, Jew and Gentile, will greet him with the song the pilgrims sang. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord: he came once to die, and he is coming again to reign.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD
this house shall become a desolation

13.text: <sup>1</sup> There were some present at that very time who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. <sup>2</sup> And he answered them, “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered in this way? <sup>3</sup> No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. <sup>4</sup> Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others who lived in Jerusalem? <sup>5</sup> No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.” <sup>6</sup> And he told this parable: “A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit on it and found none. <sup>7</sup> And he said to the vinedresser, ‘Look, for three years now I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I find none. Cut it down. Why should it use up the ground?’ <sup>8</sup> And he answered him, ‘Sir, let it alone this year also, until I dig around it and put on manure. <sup>9</sup> Then if it should bear fruit next year, well and good; but if not, you can cut it down.’” <sup>10</sup> Now he was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath. <sup>11</sup> And behold, there was a woman who had had a disabling spirit for eighteen years. She was bent over and could not fully straighten herself. <sup>12</sup> When Jesus saw her, he called her over and said to her, “Woman, you are freed from your disability.” <sup>13</sup> And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight, and she glorified God. <sup>14</sup> But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, said to the people, “There are six days in which work ought to be done. Come on those days and be healed, and not on the Sabbath day.” <sup>15</sup> Then the Lord answered him, “You hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it? <sup>16</sup> And ought not this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan bound for eighteen years, be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?” <sup>17</sup> As he said these things, all his adversaries were put to shame, and all the people rejoiced at all the glorious things that were done by him. <sup>18</sup> He said therefore, “What is the kingdom of God like? And to what shall I compare it? <sup>19</sup> It is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden, and it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.” <sup>20</sup> And again he said, “To what shall I compare the kingdom of God? <sup>21</sup> It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until it was all leavened.” <sup>22</sup> He went on his way through towns and villages, teaching and journeying toward Jerusalem. <sup>23</sup> And someone said to him, “Lord, will those who are saved be few?” And he said to them, <sup>24</sup> “Strive to enter through the narrow door. For many, I tell you, will seek to enter and will not be able. <sup>25</sup> When once the master of the house has risen and shut the door, and you begin to stand outside and to knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, open to us,’ then he will answer you, ‘I do not know where you come from.’ <sup>26</sup> Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.’ <sup>27</sup> But he will say, ‘I tell you, I do not know where you come from. Depart from me, all you workers of evil!’ <sup>28</sup> In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God but you yourselves cast out. <sup>29</sup> And people will come from east and west, and from north and south, and recline at table in the kingdom of God. <sup>30</sup> And behold, some are last who will be first, and some are first who will be last.” <sup>31</sup> At that very hour some Pharisees came and said to him, “Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you.” <sup>32</sup> And he said to them, “Go and tell that fox, ‘Behold, I cast out demons and perform cures today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course.’ <sup>33</sup> Nevertheless, I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following, for it cannot be that a prophet should perish away from Jerusalem. <sup>34</sup> O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! <sup>35</sup> Behold, your house is forsaken. And I tell you, you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’”

14.title: The Banquet, the Invitation, and the Cost
14.overview:
Chapter 14 is built around a dinner table — and it is one of the most dramatically productive dinner tables in the Gospels. Jesus is at a meal in the house of a prominent Pharisee, being watched carefully. A man with dropsy appears; Jesus heals him on the Sabbath and challenges the watching lawyers and Pharisees. He observes the guests scrambling for the best seats and tells a parable about table manners that is really about the kingdom's reversal of honour. He turns to the host and tells him who to invite to dinner — not the friends and family who will reciprocate, but the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, who cannot repay. And when a guest at the table says “Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God,” Jesus responds with the parable of the great banquet — the most complete statement of grace and rejection in the Gospel.

The chapter's second movement (vv. 25–35) shifts from the dinner table to the crowd following Jesus on the road, and the tone shifts from parable to direct confrontation. “Whoever does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, cannot be my disciple.” Two parables of counting the cost — the tower-builder and the king going to war — press the same point. “Any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.” This is not the Christianity of added benefits; it is the Christianity of total claim. The banquet of grace and the cross of discipleship belong to the same Gospel.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
On the Sabbath Jesus goes to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees — the third such invitation Luke records, and every one of them ends in confrontation. He kept going anyway.

“They were watching him carefully.” The verb is one used of keeping something under observation for a purpose; Luke uses it in Acts of men watching the gates day and night to kill Paul (Acts 9:24). It is not curiosity but surveillance. There is food on the table, a host at the head of it, and a set of guests whose real business is to collect evidence.

A man with dropsy is “before him.” Dropsy is what would now be called oedema: fluid retention, the limbs and abdomen swelling, usually a symptom of failing organs. And the ancient world understood something about it we might miss — a man with dropsy is swollen with water and desperately thirsty, which made it the standing image in Greek moralists for insatiable greed: a man consumed by wanting the very thing that is killing him. Worth holding, in a chapter about people at a table who cannot stop wanting the best seat.

Note the staging, too. Luke does not say how he came to be there; he may well have been put there to see what Jesus would do.

Jesus does not wait for the trap; he springs it himself, asking the question out loud before touching anybody — and framing it exactly as they would have framed it. Their silence is not puzzlement. They cannot say yes without undercutting their own position, and cannot say no with a swollen man standing in the room.

Then he heals him and sends him away, which is a mercy on its own: the man does not have to stand there for the argument that follows.

And the second question silences them completely — “a son or an ox” put in one sentence, as items in the same category, because that is where their practice puts them. They could not reply.
verseByVerse.theology:
The silence of the lawyers and Pharisees — both times — is the silence of people who know they have no answer and will not give the answer they do have. It is worth naming, because it is the commonest form cowardice takes among religious people: not denial, not opposition, but a careful and dignified silence held until the moment passes and the question can be treated as though it were never asked.

The argument is the same shape as the one in the previous chapter but sharpened in two ways. There, the animal was thirsty and being led to water; here something has fallen into a well and is drowning, and the word is immediately. This is an emergency, and nobody stands at the wellhead consulting a ruling.

The manuscripts vary slightly at v.5 and some read “a donkey or an ox,” which is the more expected pair and very likely why some copyists produced it. “Son or ox” is the harder reading and almost certainly what Luke wrote — and it is the one that does the work: if you would break the Sabbath for your child, and also for your livestock, on what grounds is a man with dropsy in a lower category than both?

They are beaten by their own practice, which is the only argument that cannot be got round. He has not quoted an obscure text or appealed to his own authority; he has described what every man in that room does on a Sabbath afternoon when something valuable falls down a hole.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus heals the man before making the argument. That is not bad pedagogy but the right order: the principle of Sabbath mercy is not established by syllogism and then applied — it is demonstrated in flesh and blood and then defended. The compassion leads the argument.

And there is a hard general truth in the second silence. Most people's real theology is not in what they say but in what they do without thinking, and the fastest way to expose a bad doctrine is very often to ask where its holder makes an exception for himself.

The two-tier system is the thing being dismantled: their own emergencies justify Sabbath flexibility, and somebody else's does not. That instinct did not die out in the first century. It is at work wherever a rule is applied rigorously to people at a distance and generously to oneself and one's own — and it is almost never noticed by the person doing it, because the exceptions feel like common sense.

Note also that Jesus sends the healed man away before the debate begins. He will not have a person used as an exhibit, even in an argument he is winning.

verseByVerse.quote: One Sabbath, when he went to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees, they were watching him carefully. And behold, there was a man before him who had dropsy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One Sabbath, when he went to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees, they were watching him carefully. And behold, there was a man before him who had dropsy.

Meaning first. Luke 14 happens around a table. At a leading Pharisee’s Sabbath dinner, watched by men hoping to catch him, Jesus heals a swollen man, tells grasping guests to take the lowest couch, and tells the host to fill his table with people who cannot repay. To a pious remark about the banquet of the age to come he answers with a parable: the feast is ready now, the invited make excuses, and the house is filled from the back streets and hedgerows. Then, to the crowds, he names the cost of following him: first place above every love, a cross, everything let go. The God of this chapter feasts those who cannot repay, and its Christ asks for everything because he is about to give everything.

The setting. The whole chapter is about banquets: who is invited, where they sit, who comes, and the great banquet of the kingdom. Jesus turns a dinner party into a lesson on grace and discipleship.

One Sabbath, when he went to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees. He accepted the invitation, the third time Luke has recorded it (7:36; 11:37), and every one of these dinners ends in confrontation. He kept going anyway. A ruler of the Pharisees is a leading Pharisee, perhaps a member of the Sanhedrin. Sabbath meals, prepared the day before, were the week’s occasion for entertaining guests, and Jesus is the one everybody has come to see.

They were watching him carefully. The verb is used of watching for a purpose, and in Luke’s second volume it is used of the plot to kill Paul, watching the gates day and night (Acts 9:24). It is not curiosity but surveillance (6:7). The invitation was a trap: food on the table, a host at the head of it, and guests whose real business is to collect evidence.

And behold, there was a man before him who had dropsy. Dropsy (oedema) is swelling of the body from fluid build-up, a sign of serious illness of the heart, liver or kidneys. The medical term (hydrōpikos) is Luke’s own, a physician’s word found nowhere else in the Greek Bible. Only Luke, the doctor, records this healing. And the ancient world understood one thing about the illness that we might miss. A man with dropsy is swollen with water and desperately thirsty: the more fluid he retains, the more he craves. It was the standing image among Greek moralists for insatiable greed, a man consumed by wanting the very thing that is killing him. Hold that detail, because the rest of this chapter is about people at a table who cannot stop wanting the best seat.

Was he planted there? He was before him, prominently placed, in a private house, at a formal dinner, on the Sabbath. Luke does not say how he came to be there, and a sick man would not normally be at such a table. He may well have been put there to test Jesus, a pawn in their game. Which means that the only person in the room who was treated as a person that evening was the one the others were using.

Why did Jesus keep accepting invitations from people who opposed him? Because he came to seek and to save the lost, and the self-righteous are lost too (19:10). He ate with tax collectors and with Pharisees alike; he never refused a table because of the company. That does not mean we must put ourselves under abuse or keep going where we are only mocked. But it does mean that hostility is not, on its own, a reason to withdraw. Some of the people who watch you most critically are the ones who most need to see Christ in you up close.

In a sentence. On the Sabbath, at the house of a leading Pharisee, with everyone watching him closely, Jesus was faced with a man suffering from dropsy.

On a Tuesday. Jesus went into hostile places, and still did good. Don’t avoid people because they watch you critically. Accept the invitation from the colleague who mocks your faith, sit at the table with the relative who thinks you are foolish, and be the same person there that you are at church. Being watched is not a reason to hide. It is an opportunity to be seen.

For worship. The Lord of glory sat at a table where he was not loved and ate food offered to trap him. He did not wait for a friendly room before he showed mercy. He came into a world that watched him carefully in order to kill him, and he kept coming, until the meal at which he gave himself as bread for the world. There is no table so hostile that his kindness cannot enter it.
verseByVerse.note: Dropsy is swelling of the body from fluid build-up, a sign of serious illness.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus responded to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, 'Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not?' But they remained silent. Then he took him and healed him and sent him away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus responded to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying: is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not? But they remained silent. Then he took him and healed him and sent him away.

And Jesus responded to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not? Luke says he responded, though nobody has said anything. He is answering their unspoken thoughts, what is in the room. And notice who moves first. They have set the trap and are waiting for him to walk into it; he asks the question himself, out loud, before touching anybody. There is nothing to catch him at, because he has put the whole matter on the table in advance. And the question is framed exactly as they would have framed it: is it lawful, the technical language of their own debates, addressed to the experts, inviting a ruling. If they say yes, they cannot object. If they say no, they show themselves heartless.

But they remained silent. And here is the answer, and it is the loudest thing in the chapter. They cannot say yes, because their whole position depends on saying no. They cannot say no, because there is a swollen man standing in the room and everybody can see him. So they say nothing, which is not neutrality. Silence is a decision, and this one has been taken in front of a suffering man.

The commonest form of cowardice. Among religious people it is rarely denial or opposition. It is a careful, dignified silence, held until the moment passes and the question can be treated as though it were never asked. The most learned men in that district have been asked a straight question about mercy, and every one of them has calculated that answering would cost him something.

Then he took him and healed him and sent him away. Three verbs. He took him: laid hold of him, which is contact with a diseased body at a Sabbath dinner in front of men obsessed with purity. He healed him. And he sent him away, which is a mercy on its own, perhaps to spare him further embarrassment. The man does not have to stand in that room for the argument that is coming. Whatever he was brought there for, he is not going to be used for it.

When should I speak up rather than stay silent? When someone is being wronged or a plain truth of God is being denied, and you are in a position to say something, silence is not safe ground. You do not need to speak about everything, and wisdom chooses its moment (Proverbs 26:4–5). But ask yourself honestly why you are quiet. If the answer is that speaking would cost you, the approval of the room, your standing at work, an awkward evening, that is exactly the silence Jesus exposed here. Say the true and kind thing, briefly and without heat, and leave the outcome to God.

In a sentence. Jesus asked the lawyers and Pharisees whether it was lawful to heal on the Sabbath, and when they said nothing, he healed the man and sent him home.

On a Tuesday. When doing good is right, don’t wait for others’ approval. Do it. And when you are asked a straight question about mercy or truth, at work, in a meeting, in a family argument, give a straight answer.

For worship. Christ is never silent when mercy is at stake. He asked the question no one wanted asked, and answered it with his hands. He took hold of a man no one else would touch and sent him home whole. The Lord who healed on the Sabbath is the Lord of the Sabbath, and his compassion is not governed by a calendar or a committee. Blessed be the Saviour who does not wait for permission to be kind.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Which of you, having a son or an ox that has fallen into a well on a Sabbath day, will not immediately pull him out?' And they could not reply to these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: which of you, having a son or an ox that has fallen into a well on a Sabbath day, will not immediately pull him out? And they could not reply to these things.

Which of you, having a son or an ox that has fallen into a well on a Sabbath day, will not immediately pull him out? The argument runs, as in the previous chapter, from what they already do to what they will not allow, but it is sharper. There the animal was merely thirsty (13:15). Here something is drowning, and the word is immediately: nobody stands at the wellhead consulting a ruling. Even strict Jews would rescue a son, or an animal, from a well on the Sabbath.

A son or an ox. The pairing is deliberately shocking. He puts them in one sentence, as items in the same category, because that is where their practice puts them. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read a donkey for a son, the more expected pair and very likely why copyists produced it. Son or ox is the harder reading and very probably what Luke wrote, and it does the work: if you would break the Sabbath for your child, and also for your livestock, on what grounds is a man with dropsy in a lower category than both? And there is a quiet irony in the case chosen. A man with dropsy was full of water; a man in a well is surrounded by it.

And they could not reply to these things. The second silence (13:17), and this time Luke reports it as inability rather than choice. They have been beaten by their own practice, the one argument that cannot be got round. He has simply described what every man in that room does when something valuable falls down a hole on a Sabbath afternoon. Of course you would pull it out. And will you not let me rescue a man?

The day made for release. The argument is not only clever; it rests on what the Sabbath was for and on who is standing in the room. Israel was told to keep the day remembering that the LORD had brought them out of slavery with a mighty hand (Deuteronomy 5:15). Jesus opened his ministry in Nazareth by announcing liberty to the captives (4:18), and a chapter earlier he called a bent woman a daughter of Abraham whom Satan had bound and asked whether she ought not to be loosed on the Sabbath day (13:16). The Lord of the Sabbath (6:5) is doing on the day of rest exactly what the day was meant to celebrate: pulling the drowning out of the well.

Where is my real theology? Most people’s real theology is not in what they say but in what they do without thinking, and the fastest way to expose a bad doctrine is very often to ask where its holder makes an exception for himself. Try it on yourself. Where are you strict with others and generous with yourself: about lateness, about money, about speech, about forgiveness? The place where your rules bend for you is the place where you will find what you actually believe.

And the Sabbath today? Christians who love the Bible answer differently. Many, following the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, to be kept for worship and for works of necessity and mercy (Westminster 21.8). Others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, so that no day binds the conscience in itself (Colossians 2:16–17), while gladly gathering on the Lord’s Day. Verdict: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest (Matthew 11:28), and the Lord’s Day is a gift, not a law about work. On what this passage teaches, both agree: works of mercy are always right on the day of rest, and human need is never an interruption to be ignored, on any day of the week.

In a sentence. Jesus asked which of them would not rescue a son or an ox from a well on the Sabbath, and they had no answer.

On a Tuesday. Show others at least the same compassion you would show your own family, or your property. Think of the effort you would make this week if your own child were in trouble, or your car broke down on the motorway. Then think of someone outside your circle who is in the well, and give them a fraction of that urgency.

For worship. The Son of God did not merely reach down into the well; he went down into it. He came into the pit of our sin and death, and drew us out, and set our feet upon a rock (Psalm 40:2). He counted us more precious than any son or ox, and he did it immediately, without waiting for us to deserve it. No argument can stand against such love, and every mouth is stopped before it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “a donkey” for “a son.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — Places of Honour; Inviting the Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus has been watching the guests arrive. Seating at such a meal was not casual — guests reclined on couches around a U-shaped arrangement graded by proximity to the host, a visible ranking of the room that everybody could read at a glance. Choosing your couch was choosing your public estimate of yourself. These men have just come from a Sabbath service, and their first act on arrival was to work out how important they were.

The parable begins as pure social advice, and the scenario would have made everyone wince. Honour in that culture was public and finite, gained and lost in front of witnesses. Follow the mechanics of the humiliation: the man is not merely demoted but has to get up and walk the whole length of the room, because the only seat left is the last one. And “begin with shame” is exact — the shame is not a moment; it starts, and goes on all evening.

Then the reversal, which would be shrewd manoeuvring if it stopped there. What closes the trap is the last verse: “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.” Neither verb says who does the humbling and the exalting, and neither needs to: God will do it. This is not about how the evening goes; it is about who runs the seating arrangements of the universe.

Which is what makes false modesty useless rather than merely distasteful. A man who takes the low seat in order to be moved up has exalted himself, and the verse has already seen it.

Jesus then turns to the host — at the host's own table, having eaten his food. The four categories he names are the entire ordinary guest list, and the objection is stated plainly: “lest they also invite you in return.” Hospitality in that world ran on reciprocal obligation; an invitation created a debt discharged by a return invitation of matching quality. A dinner party was a transaction with a settlement date.

The alternative list is the exact opposite: people who create no obligation because they can discharge none. And the reason given is not that they are more deserving — it is that they “cannot repay you.” The inability is the qualification.
verseByVerse.theology:
“He who humbles himself will be exalted” appears repeatedly in Luke (14:11; 18:14; and in substance in the Magnificat). It is the law of the kingdom inverting the law of the world, and it is grounded eschatologically: “you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.” The accounts are not settled in this life, but they are settled.

The parable cannot be obeyed as a technique. It can only be obeyed by somebody who has genuinely stopped competing — and there is exactly one thing that produces that, which is knowing what your actual standing is. The man who has understood where he stands before God is not being humble when he takes the low seat; he is being accurate. There is no lower place in that room than the one he already occupies before God, and he is at the table by invitation rather than merit.

Which is precisely why he is free. A person who is not defending a position cannot be demoted from it, and an evening at the bottom of the table costs him nothing.

And the promise on the other side is not a better seat at a dinner party. The one saying it is on his way to Jerusalem to take the lowest place there is, and Paul describes the outcome in the same two movements: “he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him” (Phil. 2:8-9).
verseByVerse.examples:
Read flatly, the instruction to the host bans Christmas dinner, and someone will read it flatly. Is a believer forbidden to have his own family round a table?

No — and the same chapter shows why. A dozen verses on, Jesus says a disciple must “hate” his father and mother (v.26), and everyone rightly understands that as the Semitic way of stating a comparison in absolute terms. The identical device is at work here. It is not never invite your friends but do not let your table be only that. Jesus himself ate with friends — at Levi's feast, in Martha's house, and at this very Pharisee's dinner while he says it.

So the practical question is not whether the family may come on Sunday. It is whether anyone else ever does. Put the two lists side by side and ask honestly which one your hospitality actually serves: the guests who will have you back, or the guests who cannot. Most of us have a table that runs entirely on exchange without ever having decided to make it so — and this is a command with a doorbell, not a principle to admire.

The host who invites only those who will invite him back has not given; he has traded. The host who invites those who cannot repay has given, and in doing so has imitated the God who invites sinners to his table knowing they have nothing to offer him. And note that the account is not cancelled but moved: what is on offer is a debt owed by God, payable at the resurrection, which is a far better security than a return invitation from a rich neighbour.

verseByVerse.quote: Now he told a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the places of honor, saying to them, 'When you are invited by someone to a wedding feast, do not sit down in a place of honor, lest someone more distinguished than you be invited by him, and he who invited you both will come and say to you, ‘Give your place to this person,’ and then you will begin with shame to take the lowest place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He told a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the places of honour, saying to them: when you are invited by someone to a wedding feast, do not sit down in a place of honour, lest someone more distinguished than you be invited by him, and he who invited you both will come and say to you, give your place to this person, and then you will begin with shame to take the lowest place.

Now he told a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the places of honor. The Pharisees watched Jesus; Jesus watched them. He has been watching them arrive. He saw them jostling for the best seats. So this is a room of men who have just come from a Sabbath service, at the house of a Pharisee, and their first act on arrival was to work out how important they were.

The seating. Guests reclined on couches ranked by closeness to the host, a visible ranking that everybody present could read at a glance. Choosing your couch was choosing your public estimate of yourself, in a culture where honour was gained and lost in front of witnesses.

A parable. Not just social advice, but a picture of how God deals with people. It opens as pure etiquette, the sort of thing a wise uncle might say, and it ends with a statement about who runs the seating arrangements of the universe.

Do not sit down in a place of honor, lest someone more distinguished than you be invited. Important guests often arrived last, so the scenario is entirely realistic and would have made everyone wince. Then comes the host’s word: give your place to this person. Follow the mechanics of the humiliation, because Jesus has thought it through. The man is not merely demoted. He has to get up, in front of everybody, and walk the length of the room.

And then you will begin with shame to take the lowest place. By then the middle places are taken, and every guest watches you go past to the very bottom. Begin with shame is exact: the shame starts, and it goes on for the rest of the evening. Proverbs had said it long before: do not put yourself forward in the king’s presence, for it is better to be told, come up here, than to be put lower in the presence of a noble (Proverbs 25:6–7). That is what the grasping actually costs, and the parable has not yet said a word about God.

Someone more distinguished than you. There was such a guest at that table, and nobody was jostling to give him their couch. The men scrambling for honour were doing it in the presence of the one whom David called Lord (20:41–44), the Son whom the Father had owned from heaven at the Jordan (3:22). And he did not scramble at all. Luke does not even tell us where he reclined. He was not competing, at a table where he had been invited only to be watched. The one who had every right to the top couch was the only man in the room who did not need it, because his honour came from his Father and could not be added to or taken away by the seating plan (John 5:41–44).

Is it wrong to want to be recognised? The desire to be honoured is not itself evil: God made us for glory, and he promises honour to those who seek it by patient well-doing (Romans 2:7). What Jesus condemns is seizing it, ranking yourself above others and pushing for the place. The question is who you want the honour from. If you live for the room’s estimate, you will always be anxious about the next guest through the door. If you live for God’s, you can sit anywhere, and let him do the honouring in his own time.

In a sentence. Seeing guests choose the best seats, Jesus told them not to take the place of honour, in case someone more important came and they were moved down in shame.

On a Tuesday. Don’t push yourself forward for recognition. Let others, and God, do the honouring. Notice the small seat-grabbing moves you make: steering the conversation to your achievements, needing to be thanked, quietly resenting the person who got the credit. Each is a scramble for a couch. Let it go.

For worship. The true guest of honour at that dinner had taken the lowest place long before he walked in. He left the highest seat in heaven and came down to the bottom of the table, laid in a manger because there was no other place for him, and he would go lower still. Every honour we scramble for, he laid aside, so that we might be called up to sit with him at his Father’s table.
verseByVerse.note: Places at a banquet were ranked by closeness to the host.

parallels.desc: better to be told, “Come up here,” than to be put lower

verseByVerse.quote: But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at table with you. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you: friend, move up higher. Then you will be honoured in the presence of all who sit at table with you. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.

But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, Friend, move up higher. The advice is exactly reversed, and the host honours the humble. And if it stopped here it would be a piece of shrewd manoeuvring: take the bottom seat as a tactic, and enjoy being moved up in front of everybody. Anyone who has read it that way has been outmanoeuvred by the parable, and the next verse is what closes the trap.

Then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at table with you. Real honour comes from the host, not from self-promotion. Only the one who gave the feast can say where you belong at it.

For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted. The principle. The passive voice means: humbled by God, exalted by God. This is not about how the evening goes. It is God’s own way with the world. It is a central truth of the kingdom, repeated in 18:14 (the Pharisee and the tax collector). Mary sang it (1:52). Jesus himself lived it: he humbled himself to the cross, and God highly exalted him (Philippians 2:5–11).

What it does not mean. Not false humility, a clever tactic to be noticed. Taking the lowest place in order to be promoted is pride in disguise. True humility is not thinking less of yourself, but thinking of yourself less, and leaving your honour to God (1 Peter 5:5–6).

Why humility is accuracy. Here the parable turns from advice into gospel. It cannot be obeyed as a technique, only by somebody who has genuinely stopped competing, and what produces that is knowing your actual standing. The man who has understood where he stands before God is not being humble when he takes the low seat. He is being accurate: he is at the table by invitation and not by merit. Which is precisely why he is free. A person who is not defending a position cannot be demoted from it.

Does humility mean I should never accept a responsibility or say I can do something well? No. Humility is not pretending to be less gifted than you are, and refusing a task God plainly calls you to is not modesty but disobedience. Paul could say he worked harder than all the apostles, and add at once that it was the grace of God with him (1 Corinthians 15:10). Humility is honest about gifts, because it knows they are gifts (1 Corinthians 4:7). It serves without needing the credit, rejoices when others are honoured, and does not grasp. You may sit at the head of the table if the host puts you there. Just do not put yourself there.

In a sentence. Take the lowest place, so that the host may call you higher, for whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

On a Tuesday. Where can you take the lower place today, and leave your honour in God’s hands? Let someone else have the parking space, the last word, the credit for the idea. Do one piece of good this week that nobody will ever know was yours.

For worship. The one who said this was on his way to Jerusalem to take the lowest place there is, lower than any couch: a cross between two criminals, with one of them asking to be remembered. And from that lowest place he answered as only the Host can: today you will be with me in paradise (23:43). He went to the bottom of the table so that a dying thief, and every sinner like him, could hear the word, Friend, move up higher. All our exaltation is his gift, and all the glory of it is his.

verseByVerse.quote: He said also to the man who had invited him, 'When you give a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said also to the man who had invited him: when you give a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbours, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.

He said also to the man who had invited him. Having dealt with the guests, he turns to the host, at the host’s own table, having eaten his food. It is one of the least comfortable moments in the Gospels.

Do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors. Not a prohibition of ever inviting family and friends. A Hebrew way of saying: not only these, but rather. The four categories are the entire ordinary guest list.

Lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. In that culture hospitality was a social exchange, building status and alliances. An invitation created a debt, discharged by a return invitation of matching quality: a transaction with a settlement date. That is not grace; it is business (6:32–34).

Invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind. These could never repay, and they were often excluded from religious gatherings, as the Qumran community excluded the lame and blind from its meals. They are the exact opposite of the first four: people who create no obligation because they can discharge none, and the very people God will bring to his banquet (v. 21).

And you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. The blessing is in giving without return. The reason given is not that they are more deserving. It is precisely that they cannot repay you: the inability is the qualification.

The guest list of his own ministry. Luke’s reader has heard this list before. When John’s disciples asked whether Jesus was the one who was to come, he answered by pointing to what was happening around him: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk, and the poor have good news preached to them (7:22). The host is being told to set his table the way Jesus has been setting his whole ministry. The poor, the crippled, the lame and the blind are not a charity project tacked onto the kingdom. They are the people the Messiah was anointed to reach (4:18), and every table that welcomes them is a small copy of his.

For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just. God will repay. The resurrection of the just is the resurrection to life of the righteous at the last day (Acts 24:15; John 5:29). Not you will not be repaid. The account is not cancelled; it is moved. And see what the host is being offered: a debt owed by God, payable at the resurrection, which is a far better security than a return invitation from a rich neighbour.

So am I forbidden to have my family round for Christmas dinner? No, and the same chapter tells you why. A dozen verses on, Jesus will say that a disciple must hate his father and mother (v. 26), and everyone rightly understands that as the Semitic way of stating a comparison in absolute terms. The identical device is at work here. It is not never invite your friends; it is do not let your table be only that. Jesus himself ate with friends, at Levi’s feast, in Martha’s house, and at this very Pharisee’s dinner while he said it. So the practical question is not whether the family may come on Sunday. It is whether anyone else ever does.

Does giving in hope of a heavenly reward spoil it? No. Jesus himself sets the reward before us, so it cannot be wrong to want it (Hebrews 11:6). What spoils giving is wanting the return from people: thanks, status, an invitation back. To give looking to God for your reward is to give freely to people, since you need nothing from them. And the reward itself is a gift of grace, not wages earned. God crowns in his children what his Spirit has worked in them, and the greatest part of the reward is the Giver himself.

In a sentence. Jesus told his host to invite to his feasts not those who could repay, but the poor and disabled who could not, and God would repay him at the resurrection.

On a Tuesday. Who could you invite to your home who could never invite you back? Put the two lists side by side, those your table has served this year and those Jesus names, and ask honestly which one your hospitality actually serves. Most of us have a table that runs entirely on exchange without ever having decided to make it so. Start with one name: the widower from church, the international student, the family that is struggling, the man nobody sits with.

For worship. God spread his table for people who had nothing to bring and could never invite him back. We were the poor, the crippled, the lame and the blind, and he did not wait for us to become worth inviting. The whole of salvation is a feast given to those who cannot repay, by a God who needs nothing from us and delights to give. And the one who tells the host to do it is the Host who has already done it, at the cost of his own body and blood.
verseByVerse.note: In that culture a meal created an obligation to invite in return.

parallels.desc: the Levite, sojourner, fatherless and widow shall eat

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–24 — The Parable of the Great Banquet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
A guest breaks the silence with something entirely correct: “Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!” The picture he invokes was the settled hope of Israel — the feast on the mountain, rich food for all peoples, death swallowed up (Isa. 25:6-8).

So why does Jesus answer with a parable about people who refuse an invitation? Listen to the sentence again. It is a beatitude in the third person and the future tense, and nobody in the room is implicated by it. Jesus has just told them to stop grasping for seats and to fill their tables with people who cannot repay them — both remarks about this table, tonight — and what comes back is a warm sentiment about a banquet in the age to come. It is the religious equivalent of saying what a wonderful idea in principle.

The parable changes the tense. And it turns on a custom: a formal banquet involved two invitations, the first well in advance so the host knew the numbers before he killed the animals, the second on the day to say it was ready. So these guests are not being asked whether they would like to attend. They accepted weeks ago, and the host has slaughtered on the strength of it.

“Come, for everything is now ready” is the gospel in six words. Not would you consider coming? The work is done, the cost has been met, and the only thing missing is the guests. And notice who carries it — not the host but a servant, sent on foot to men who outrank him, saying words that are not his own.

Then the excuses, and not one is disreputable. A field already bought; five yoke of oxen already bought; a new marriage. Property, work, family — every one a good thing, and not one a sin. Nobody says “I do not want to come.” They express regret, cite legitimate business, and stay at home.

Which is the form the rejection of the gospel almost always takes. Very few people ever say “I refuse Christ.” A great many say “not now — there is something I have to deal with first,” and go on saying it politely for forty years.
verseByVerse.theology:
The master's anger is the only emotion attributed to him, and it is easily made into something it is not. It is not the petulance of a man whose party has been spoiled. He has been given his guests' word and spent accordingly — and in that economy a great banquet meant slaughtered animals that could not be kept, so the cost was already unrecoverable. What has been refused is a gift already paid for, and the refusals were both unanimous and casual. Grace declined is not a neutral event that leaves the giver unmoved.

But the anger does not cancel the banquet; it redirects it. And the four categories the servant is sent to fetch are the same four Jesus gave the host eight verses earlier (v.13) — which is the parable's quiet accusation to a room that had just heard the instruction and let it pass. God does exactly what he told them to do.

The parable's geography follows the movement of Acts: the original guests, then the streets and lanes of the city, then the highways and hedges outside it — Jerusalem, then Judea and Samaria, then the ends of the earth. The original guests are the religious establishment that has had the invitation through the whole Old Testament and is declining it with polite excuses; the poor and lame of the city are the tax collectors and sinners responding to his ministry; the people beyond the walls are the Gentiles.

And the exclusion is stated without qualification: “none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.” The feast does not wait indefinitely, and the door does not stay open after the house is full.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room” is the most hopeful sentence in the parable. The servant has swept every street and every alley and brought in everyone he found, and the hall is not full. Whatever else this house is, it was built larger than the number of people who were ever likely to come.

One phrase has done real damage and should be handled plainly: “compel people to come in.” Augustine, pressed by the Donatist controversy, used it to justify the state coercing schismatics back to the church, and it was quoted for centuries afterwards in defence of forced baptisms and penal laws.

Which is exactly the opposite of force. Everyone actually compelled in this parable is somebody who thought himself too far outside to be wanted; the only people who stay out are those who were invited politely and had other plans. Nobody is dragged to this table against their will. If the verse presses anything on the church, it is urgency in persuading the people who assume the gospel cannot possibly be for them.

And “that my house may be filled” is the heart of it. Not that the food may not be wasted. He wants the room full.

verseByVerse.quote: When one of those who reclined at table with him heard these things, he said to him, 'Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When one of those who reclined at table with him heard these things, he said to him: blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!

Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God! Somebody breaks the silence, and what he says is entirely correct. A pious remark, perhaps to ease the tension, or to show his own piety. The picture he is invoking was the settled hope of Israel: the messianic banquet, the great feast at the end of the age, when the LORD of hosts would spread a feast of rich food for all peoples and swallow up death for ever (Isaiah 25:6–8), the feast Jesus had spoken of on the road (13:29). Every devout Jew at that table believed it and looked forward to it. He assumes he will be there. The parable that follows asks: will you?

Why does Jesus answer a true remark with a warning? Listen to the sentence again and the reason surfaces. It is a beatitude in the third person and the future tense: blessed is everyone who will eat. Nobody in the room is implicated by it. It is the kind of thing a man says at a dinner table when the conversation has become uncomfortable and he wants to return it to safe and elevating ground. And the timing gives it away. Jesus has just told this room to stop grasping for seats and to fill their tables with people who cannot repay them. Both remarks were about this table, tonight. What comes back is a warm sentiment about a banquet in the age to come. It is the religious equivalent of saying what a wonderful idea in principle.

The bread was already at the table. The guest spoke of eating bread in the kingdom as something far off, and he said it across the table from the one who would give that bread. On the night he was betrayed, Jesus would take bread, give thanks, break it and say, this is my body, which is given for you, and he would tell his disciples that he would not eat the Passover again until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God (22:16, 19). He would promise them that they would eat and drink at his table in his kingdom (22:30). The blessing the man admired from a distance was sitting opposite him, and it would be won at Jerusalem.

A manoeuvre worth recognising. Nothing false has been said, which is why it is hard to object to: the speaker has agreed with everything and moved the discussion somewhere it can cost him nothing. Jesus’ reply changes the tense. The parable is about a banquet that is ready now, a servant already at the door, and men who all had something else on. The man wanted to talk about the guest list of the kingdom. He is about to be told that the invitations have gone out and the replies are coming in.

In a sentence. One of the guests exclaimed how blessed are those who will eat at the feast in the kingdom of God.

On a Tuesday. It is easy to speak warmly about heaven. Make sure you have accepted the invitation. Watch for the moments when you change the subject to something true and general because the specific was getting close: a sermon applied to someone else, a conversation about the church’s needs that never reaches your diary. The kingdom is not only a hope to admire. It is an invitation to answer.

For worship. Blessed indeed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God, and the blessing is real because the King himself has made it so. Isaiah saw the menu and the miracle together: rich food and well-aged wine on the mountain of the LORD, and on that same mountain death swallowed up for ever and the tears wiped from every face (Isaiah 25:6–8). The LORD who promised that feast has spread it, and at it the guests will taste what the prophets only described, with every seat paid for by the Host.

parallels.desc: the marriage supper of the Lamb

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to him, 'A man once gave a great banquet and invited many. And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come, for everything is now ready.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he said to him: a man once gave a great banquet and invited many. And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited: come, for everything is now ready.

A man once gave a great banquet and invited many. The host is God, preparing the feast of the kingdom. Note the two stages, because the custom matters and the parable turns on it. In that world a formal banquet involved two invitations. The first went out well in advance, so that the host knew the numbers before he killed the animals. The second was sent on the day, when everything was ready, to tell those who had accepted that it was time to come. So the people in this story are not being asked whether they would like to attend. They said yes weeks ago. The host has bought and slaughtered on the strength of it. Israel had been invited long ago, through the prophets, and had said yes.

And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant. That is the second summons. And notice who carries it. Not the host. A servant, sent out on foot to the houses of men who outrank him, saying words that are not his own. In the story the servant is Jesus himself, and after him those who preach the kingdom. That is the shape of every gospel errand since. The servant does not prepare the feast, cannot add to it, and has nothing to offer but the message that it is ready, and the message is the whole of his commission.

Come, for everything is now ready. Hear what it actually says. Not would you consider coming, not are you free. Everything is now ready: the work is done, the cost has been met, the table is laid, and the only thing missing is the guests. All they need to do is come. That is the gospel in a sentence, and it is why the parable is not really about hospitality at all. The invitation Jesus brings is never an invitation to do something. It is the announcement that something has been done and is finished, and that the only remaining question is whether a man will come and sit down.

What made everything ready. When Jesus told this parable the most expensive part of the preparation was still ahead of him. He was on the road to Jerusalem, where the host’s great outlay would be made: not animals killed for a dinner, but the Son himself given up. The servant carrying the summons in the story is also the one whose body and blood would lay the table. So the word ready is a promise as well as a description. By the time the apostles carried the same invitation through the streets of Jerusalem at Pentecost, nothing at all remained to be done (Acts 2:38–39).

What does it mean for me to come? To come is to trust Christ: to stop relying on anything you bring and to rely on what he has done. It is not first a matter of feelings or of cleaning yourself up; the guests at this feast are fed, not inspected. You come by turning from your sin and resting on Christ, telling God in your own words that you have nothing and asking him to receive you for his Son’s sake. And having come, you keep coming: to his word, his table and his people. The banquet is ready today, and the invitation is addressed to you.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a man who gave a great banquet and, when it was ready, sent his servant to tell the invited guests to come, for everything was prepared.

On a Tuesday. If you speak to anyone about Christ this week, remember what you are carrying. Not a programme of self-improvement or a set of conditions, but news: everything is ready. You are a servant with a message, not a salesman with a pitch, and you need add nothing to it.

For worship. Come, for everything is now ready. The Father planned the feast before the foundation of the world, the Son paid for it with his own blood, and the Spirit goes out still with the summons, street by street. Nothing is left undone, nothing is left for the guest to bring, and nothing will ever need to be added. There is no gift more complete, no Host more generous, and no table more full.
verseByVerse.note: Guests were invited ahead of time and then summoned when the meal was ready.
