verseByVerse.quote: But they all alike began to make excuses. The first said to him, ‘I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Please have me excused.’ And another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them. Please have me excused.’ And another said, ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they all alike began to make excuses. The first said to him: I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Please have me excused. And another said: I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them. Please have me excused. And another said: I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.

But they all alike began to make excuses. All alike: with one accord, as though it had been arranged. And these are men who had already accepted. To refuse after accepting an invitation was a grave insult. And their excuses are flimsy. Three are given as samples, and the striking thing about them is that not one is disreputable.

I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Possessions. Nobody in that world purchased land unexamined, and the field would still be there tomorrow.

I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them. Business, and the same shape. Ten oxen mean a wealthy man farming on a substantial scale, and you would test them before buying, not on the evening of a feast.

I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come. Family, and this one is different in tone. The first two say please have me excused, which is at least polite. This one does not ask; he states it as a fact. He may be leaning on a legal provision: the law excused a newly married man from war and public duty for a year (Deuteronomy 24:5). But a banquet is not a war, and the law he is standing on was given to protect a marriage, not to excuse a man from a feast.

The point. Possessions, work, and family are all good things, and here they become excuses for refusing God’s invitation. Not wicked things but good things put first keep people out of the kingdom (8:14; 9:57–62). Which is why the parable is more searching than a story about wicked men would have been. Nobody here says I do not want to come. Nobody attacks the host. They express regret, cite legitimate business, and stay at home. That is the form the rejection of the gospel almost always takes. Very few people ever say I refuse Christ. A great many say not now: there is something I have to deal with first. And they go on saying it, politely, for forty years. Jesus classifies that answer without hesitation. It is not a postponement. It is the refusal.

The one who let nothing keep him away. Against these three excuses stands the man telling the story. Luke has shown him with his face set to go to Jerusalem (9:51), answering would-be followers who wanted first to bury a father or say farewell at home (9:59–62), and owning nowhere to lay his head (9:58). At twelve he had already said that he must be in his Father’s house (2:49). Jesus had a mother, brothers, a trade and a home town, and none of them became his apology. He came to the feast his Father appointed, and it was the cross. Every guest who will finally sit at the table is there because one man never sent an excuse.

But surely my family and work are things God gave me? They are, and that is exactly what makes them dangerous as excuses. God gives fields, oxen and wives so that we might enjoy them with thanksgiving under him (1 Timothy 4:4). Coming to Christ does not take them away; it puts them in their place, and they are better there. The trouble begins when a gift is used to keep the Giver at arm’s length. If your reason for not coming to Christ, or not following him fully, is something good, you are in precisely the position of these men. Bring the field and the oxen and the marriage with you to the feast. Do not send them as your apology.

In a sentence. The invited guests all made excuses: one had bought a field, another oxen, and another had just married.

On a Tuesday. What good thing in your life is your excuse for not coming fully to God? Listen for your own version of I must go and see it: the work that crowds out prayer, the weekend plans that keep you from worship, the family schedule that leaves no room for Christ. None of those is wicked. Any of them can be an apology sent to the King.

For worship. The God who gives fields and oxen and marriages is better than all of them, and he invites us to himself. How patient he is with polite refusals, how generous to keep his table spread after insults. The Son who told this story came to his own and was turned away by the guests his Father had invited, and he went on to the cross to make a place for people who had refused him before. Every one of us once sent our apology to that table, and the Host sent the invitation again.
verseByVerse.note: The law excused a newly married man from war for a year — but not from a feast.

parallels.desc: a newly married man free at home one year

verseByVerse.quote: So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his servant: go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame.

So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry. Rightly. His generosity had been insulted. It is the only emotion attributed to the host in the whole parable, and it is not the petulance of a man whose party has been spoiled. He had his guests’ word and spent accordingly; then, with the food on the table, every one of them sent back a message about a field. What has been refused is not an evening’s entertainment. It is a gift already paid for, and the refusals were both unanimous and casual.

Is God really angry with people who decline his invitation? Yes, and it would be a lesser God who were not. His anger is not a loss of temper but the settled response of holy love to generosity treated as an inconvenience. Grace declined is not a neutral event that leaves the giver unmoved. That is sobering for anyone who has been treating the gospel as an offer with no deadline. But notice what the anger does next. It does not cancel the feast. It sends the servant out again, to people nobody else wanted. God’s anger at refusal and his eagerness to fill his house stand together.

Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city. Then the astonishing turn: the anger redirects the banquet. Quickly, because the food is ready. The streets and lanes are the thoroughfares and the narrow back alleys where the outcasts lived. This is where a man goes to find people who have nowhere else to be: within Israel, the tax collectors, sinners and poor whom the religious elite kept out.

And bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame. Exactly the list of verse 13: God does what he told the host to do. That is the parable’s quiet accusation, delivered to a room that had just heard the instruction and let it pass. The people who cannot repay him are the ones who end up at the table, not as a second-best arrangement forced on him by circumstances, but because that was always the kind of guest list he wanted.

Where Jesus had been eating. The men at that dinner knew exactly where Jesus went when he was not at their tables. He had sat at Levi’s great feast with a large company of tax collectors (5:29), and the Pharisees had grumbled that he ate with sinners (5:30). Within a few verses they will grumble again: this man receives sinners and eats with them (15:2). The servant going into the back streets is no stranger to the scene. It is a picture of what the guests had watched Jesus do for three years, and he answered their complaint in a single line: he came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance (5:32).

What if I feel too broken to belong at God’s table? Then you are exactly the kind of guest this verse describes. The poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame were not brought in because they had recovered; they were brought in as they were. Your sense of unworthiness is not a barrier to coming. It is, in this parable, the very mark of those who are carried in. Come as you are, and he will make you what he wants you to be.

In a sentence. The angry master sent his servant to bring in the poor and disabled from the city streets instead.

On a Tuesday. Who in your town is in the streets and lanes: those who would never think a church was for them, those on the edges of your own congregation? Go to them quickly, with the same message the servant carried, and bring them in. Make your church a place where the poor and broken are not tolerated but wanted.

For worship. The King of glory fills his house with beggars and calls them his guests. He sent quickly, because he would not have the feast go cold while the poor waited in the alleys, and he did not ask anyone to tidy himself first. The blind are led to their places, the lame are carried, and the poor sit down to food they never paid for. And the joy of that feast is that every person there knows he had no right to be, and that the Host is glad he came.

verseByVerse.quote: And the servant said, ‘Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room.’ And the master said to the servant, ‘Go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled. For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant said: sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room. And the master said to the servant: go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled. For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.

Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room. The most hopeful sentence in the parable, and it is spoken by the servant. He has swept every street and alley of the city, and the hall is not full. God’s house was built larger than the number of people who were ever likely to come.

Go out to the highways and hedges. Now he is sent outside the town altogether, to the roads between towns and the hedgerows where travellers and vagrants sheltered. These are people with no address at all, and to the men listening they suggest outsiders: the Gentiles, beyond Israel. This is the mission of Acts, from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8; 13:46).

A light for the hedgerows. That outward sweep began with Christ himself. When the baby was carried into the temple, old Simeon took him in his arms and called him a light for revelation to the Gentiles (2:30–32). And the risen Lord, opening the Scriptures to his disciples, said that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (24:47). The servant goes out to the roads between towns because the Son has been given to the nations. Every stranger who comes in from the hedges comes in by his name, and the house is filled with people the first guests would never have thought to invite.

And compel people to come in. Compel means urge them strongly. In Middle Eastern culture a guest would politely refuse and have to be urged, and a man summoned from a hedgerow to a nobleman’s banquet would assume a mistake had been made, and would need pressing hard before he believed the invitation was meant for him. The compulsion in view is a servant taking a beggar by the arm and saying: no, truly, he means you. The invitation is so generous it must be pressed on people.

Where Christians differ: compel them to come in. Augustine used this verse to justify using the power of the state to force heretics (the Donatists) back into the church, and it was later used to justify forced conversions and persecution. Verdict: this is a grievous misreading. The compulsion is the urgency of love and persuasion, not force. Faith cannot be coerced. The gospel is to be pressed on people earnestly, but never by violence (2 Corinthians 5:11, 20). Everyone actually compelled in this parable is somebody who thought himself too far outside to be wanted; the only people who stay out are those who were invited politely and had other plans. Nobody is dragged to this table against their will.

How do I urge someone without being pushy? Urgency and respect belong together. Speak plainly about Christ, and do not be embarrassed to ask someone to come, more than once if need be: to church, to a Bible study, to Christ himself. Tell them the invitation is truly for them, especially if they think they are too far gone. But never manipulate, never bully, and never use pressure that bypasses the conscience; God opens hearts, and we only persuade (Acts 16:14). Pray before you speak, listen as much as you talk, and let your life make the invitation believable. Love presses; it does not coerce.

That my house may be filled. God is determined that his banquet will be full, and his purpose will not be thwarted by refusal. It is not merely that the food may not be wasted: he wants the room full. Every seat at that table has a name on it, and the Master will not rest until every one is taken (John 6:37–39).

For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet. Those who refused will be shut out (13:28), by their own choice. And the last line is spoken in the plural, to somebody other than the servant, which is Jesus stepping out of the parable and addressing the dinner party he is sitting at.

In a sentence. When there was still room, the master sent his servant to the country roads to urge people to come in until his house was full, declaring that none of the first guests would taste his banquet.

On a Tuesday. There is still room. Urge others to come to Christ, earnestly and lovingly. Think of the person you have assumed would never be interested, the one beyond the hedges of your usual circle, and tell them, kindly and plainly, that the invitation is for them. And pray for the missionaries who are going to the highways of the world where the name of Christ is still unknown.

For worship. Still there is room: the most hopeful words a sinner can hear. The Father’s house has many rooms, and the Son has gone to prepare them (John 14:2). His grace has run out to the hedgerows of the Gentile world and found us there, and it will not stop until the house is full. Glory to the God whose mercy is larger than all our refusals, and whose banquet will never be short of a single guest he has chosen.
verseByVerse.note: “Compel” means press them to come — the invitation is so generous it must be urged.

parallels.desc: we are turning to the Gentiles

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Great crowds are travelling with him, and he turns round and says the hardest thing in the Gospel — which is not what a man does who is trying to keep a following.

“Hate” is Semitic idiom for loving less by comparison, and the usage is well attested: Jacob “loved Rachel more than Leah,” and in the next verse Leah is described as “hated” (Gen. 29:30-31). Matthew records the same saying in the plainer form — “whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37).

The idiom explains the word, but the softer reading is not a rescue operation; it is the only one the rest of Scripture will allow. The same Lord upheld the fifth commandment with unusual severity — when the scribes devised Corban to avoid supporting aged parents, he called it making void the word of God (Mark 7:9-13), which is precisely the manoeuvre a literal reading of this verse would license. He kept the commandment himself in his last hours, giving his mother to John (John 19:26-27). And Paul states it flatly: a man who does not provide for his household “has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5:8).

And note the last name on the list, which governs the rest: “and even his own life.” Family is not being singled out for sacrifice; the self is on the same list, and it is the harder renunciation.

The cross image was not a metaphor to that crowd. A cross-bearer was a specific sight: a condemned man, already sentenced, carrying the beam of his own execution through the streets, with the jeering going on around him. It carries finality, shame, and submission — and the man saying it was going to do it himself within the year.

Then two parables, both beginning “sit down first.” The tower is probably a farm watchtower, not a monument, and the failure is public and permanent: an abandoned foundation sits in the field for as long as anybody remembers, and Jesus supplies the sentence the neighbours will say. The king's case adds a third option the builder does not have — sue for peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
The cost teaching is addressed to those already following, already enthusiastic, already in the crowd. They are not being warned before they commit; they are being warned that what they think they have committed to may not be what discipleship requires. The danger is not the uncommitted outsider but the enthusiastic follower who has not counted the cost.

He is not recruiting. He has just watched thousands attach themselves to his procession and his response is to tell them to stop and calculate — the exact opposite of every technique for gathering a following that has ever been used. A crowd that has not counted the cost is not an asset; it is a field full of abandoned foundations waiting to happen.

The king's parable changes the register. The builder's alternatives are to finish or be mocked; the king can send a delegation and ask for terms. And who is the greater king in that picture? A man weighing whether he can stand against a force twice his size is not being invited to conclude that he can manage it with effort. What is left is the delegation — going out, while there is still distance, and asking for terms. That is not defeat in this parable; it is the only wise move on the board, and it is what the counting of the cost is actually for.

“Renounce” is not primarily get rid of but let go of: a man at a door, releasing his hold on what he is leaving behind.
verseByVerse.examples:
What the hate-saying means is a matter of collision, not everyday temperature. Most of the time there is no conflict at all — loving Christ makes a man a better son, husband and father. The verse speaks to the moment when the two claims genuinely cannot both be honoured: when following Jesus will cost you your family's approval, or your inheritance, or your place at their table.

If you are living inside that collision, take two things from it. The cost is real and Jesus never pretends otherwise — he has already said he came to divide households (12:51-53), and he says this to a crowd, not to specialists; the grief you feel is not a sign you have done something wrong. And the command does not license coldness. Nothing here permits writing your family off, arguing at every meal, or making your faith a weapon. You go on loving them, and usually better than before; you simply stop letting their approval decide what you do with Christ.

“Renounce all that he has” is comprehensive in a way that goes past property — reputation, plans, the rights a man believes his circumstances have granted him, the future he has drawn up. Here is a test that is not about percentages: think of the thing you are most certain God would never ask you for. Not the hardest to lose — the thing quietly filed as not up for discussion. Whatever came to mind has not been renounced.

And the salt saying is the chapter's last word on what a half-committed disciple is for. The salt of Palestine was gathered from Dead Sea marshes and mixed with gypsum; if the sodium leached out with damp it left a white powder that looked exactly like salt and did nothing. Still in the jar, still the right colour, still called salt — and it has stopped working.

verseByVerse.quote: Now great crowds accompanied him, and he turned and said to them, 'If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now great crowds accompanied him, and he turned and said to them: if anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.

Now great crowds accompanied him. Jesus is not interested in crowds; he wants disciples. He has an enormous following, and he turns round and says the hardest thing in the Gospel, which is not what a man does who is trying to keep a crowd. He has been walking ahead and they have been following, and he stops the procession, deliberately, to tell them what following means.

If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother. A shocking statement. Hate here is a Hebrew idiom for loving less, a comparison. Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, and in the next verse the text says Leah was hated (Genesis 29:30–31; see also Malachi 1:2–3; Romans 9:13). Matthew’s parallel gives the plainer form: whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me (Matthew 10:37). Jesus demands first place, above every other love.

And wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life. The closest relationships are named one by one, so that no one can think his own case is the exception, and the last name on the list governs the rest. Family is not being singled out for sacrifice. The self is on the same list, and it is the harder renunciation of the two.

He cannot be my disciple. Not may not be a very good disciple, but cannot be. Jesus claims a loyalty that only God has the right to claim. Either he is God, or this is outrageous. No prophet ever said, love me more than your mother. Moses said, love the LORD your God with all your heart (Deuteronomy 6:5). Jesus puts himself where Moses put God.

Is this not a convenient softening? The idiom explains the word, but a reader may still suspect the explanation of being a rescue operation, a hard saying softened because we do not like it. It is not; it is the only reading the rest of Scripture will allow. The same Lord upheld the fifth commandment with unusual severity. When the scribes devised Corban, a way of declaring money dedicated to God so that it need not support aged parents, Jesus said they were making void the word of God by their tradition (Mark 7:9–13). That is precisely what a literal reading of this verse would license, and he condemned it. He kept the commandment himself at the last possible moment, giving his mother into John’s care from the cross (John 19:26–27). And Paul says that anyone who does not provide for his household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8).

What it does not mean. Not literal hatred, or neglect of family. Jesus commands honouring parents (18:20) and loving wives (Ephesians 5:25). But when love for family conflicts with loyalty to Christ, Christ must win. Compared with our love for him, every other love should look like hatred. And in fact, loving Christ most makes us love others better.

When does the conflict actually come? Most of the time there is no conflict at all: loving Christ makes a man a better son, a better husband, a better father. The verse speaks to the moment when the two claims genuinely cannot both be honoured. A convert from another faith whose family cuts him off. A believer whose spouse demands that she stop going to church. A son whose father insists he join a dishonest business. A parent who must choose between a child’s approval and the truth. In those moments Jesus must win, gently and without contempt, and with the door kept open. And where a family relationship involves abuse, putting Christ first never means submitting to it; it may mean seeking safety and help.

In a sentence. Jesus told the crowds that anyone who does not love him more than family and even his own life cannot be his disciple.

On a Tuesday. Who or what do you love more than Jesus? Put him first, and every other love will find its right place. Ask a hard question: if following Christ cost you the approval of the person whose approval you most want, would you still follow? Pray for the grace to answer yes, and then go home and love your family better than you did yesterday, for his sake.

For worship. Only one who is God can ask for this, and only one who loves like God would deserve it. Christ asks for first place because he gave up his first place: he left his Father’s side and laid down his own life for us. He is worthy to be loved above mother and father, wife and child, and life itself, because every one of those loves came from him. The mother we love was his gift, the children are his, and the life we hold is on loan from him. To put him first is not to lose them. It is to love them at their source.
verseByVerse.note: “Hate” here is a Hebrew idiom for loving less. Matthew’s parallel says “loves father or mother more than me.”

parallels.desc: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah — “Leah was hated”

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.

Whoever does not bear his own cross. He has said this before, after Peter’s confession (9:23), where it was daily. Here it is not take up but bear, the ordinary word for the sustained business of walking under a load, and not his cross but his own cross. There is no generic cross issued in one size; each man carries the one with his name on it.

What the image meant. To that crowd it was not a worn metaphor. A cross-bearer in the Roman world was a specific sight: a man already sentenced, carrying the beam of his own execution through the streets while the jeering went on around him. Many in that crowd had probably seen it. So the picture is not hardship. It is a man walking to his death in public, and it carries three things. Finality: nobody carrying a crossbeam is coming back down that road. Shame: crucifixion was designed to be degrading, reserved for slaves and rebels. Submission: a man carrying his cross has stopped fighting; he is going where he is being taken. To bear your cross is to accept rejection, shame and death for Jesus’ sake, as a way of life.

And come after me. Follow him on the road to Jerusalem and the cross. The cross is not carried in a circle; it is carried behind someone. Then the second cannot: there is no cross-less discipleship.

Behind Jesus. Luke has a picture waiting at the end of his Gospel that makes this verse visible. On the road out of Jerusalem the soldiers seized a man from Cyrene, coming in from the country, and laid on him the cross, to carry it behind Jesus (23:26). That is this verse, acted out in the street: a cross, a road, and a man walking after Christ. But on that day Jesus went in front to his own death, and the beam Simon carried was the beam on which the Lord would hang. Every disciple’s cross is carried behind the one cross that saves. Ours is borne in his company; his was borne for us.

Is my cross the illness or difficulty I have? Not exactly. Every Christian suffers the ordinary troubles of a fallen world, and God uses them; but the cross Jesus means is what comes to you because you follow him. It is the cost of saying no to yourself and yes to Christ: the career move declined because it meant dishonesty, the friendships lost because you would not join in, the mockery at work, the sin you go on refusing year after year, the persecution that in many lands means prison or death. A cross is chosen in the sense that you could put it down by abandoning Christ. Bearing it means you will not.

In a sentence. Whoever does not carry his own cross and follow Jesus cannot be his disciple.

On a Tuesday. What cross are you carrying for Jesus today? Name the place where following him costs you something this week, and do not quietly lay it down. And if nothing about your Christian life costs you anything at all, ask whether you are following closely enough to be noticed.

For worship. He never asks anyone to walk a road he has not walked first, and he walked this one condemned, shamed and submitting. He bore not only the wood but our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24), and what he carried was the full weight of the wrath we deserved. Our crosses are light beside his. And the road he calls us to does not end at the place of the skull, because he has already walked it to the end and out the other side, and he waits for his cross-bearers there, risen.
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution.

verseByVerse.quote: For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it? Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, saying, ‘This man began to build and was not able to finish.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it? Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, saying: this man began to build and was not able to finish.

For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost? Having said what discipleship costs, he insists that people work out whether they can pay. A tower might guard a vineyard (Isaiah 5:2) or be a farm building: an ordinary landowner’s project, not a civic monument. And the verb is sit down: stop, sit, and do the arithmetic before the first stone is laid.

This man began to build and was not able to finish. The failure is public and permanent. An abandoned foundation sits in the field, visible from the road, for as long as anybody remembers, and Jesus supplies the sentence the neighbours will say, which is what makes it sting.

The point. Before you follow Jesus, think about what it will cost, and do not start enthusiastically and give up halfway (8:13). The crowds were following without thinking.

He is not recruiting. With a great crowd attached to his procession, he tells them to stop and calculate whether they can afford it, the opposite of every technique for gathering a following. A crowd that has not counted the cost is a field of abandoned foundations waiting to happen. That is uncomfortable for any appeal that keeps the cost out of sight until the decision is made. Jesus does the reverse, in public, to the largest crowd he ever had.

The builder who finished. The one telling this parable had counted his own cost. When Herod was hunting him, Jesus sent word that he would go on casting out demons and healing today and tomorrow, and the third day I finish my course (13:32). He had set his face to Jerusalem knowing what was there (9:51; 18:31–33). No disciple’s tower is safe because the disciple is a good builder. It is safe because the Lord who lays the foundation of his people is the one man who never began anything he could not finish.

If I must count the cost, how can anyone afford it? No one can pay it in his own strength, and that is part of what the counting reveals; the next parable will say so. The cost is real: Christ asks for everything. But the one who calls also supplies. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6), and those who build on him are kept by his power, not their own (1 Peter 1:5). The counting is not meant to deter anybody. It is meant to make the commitment real, so that what begins actually gets finished, and so that the tower, when it is up, is a witness rather than a joke.

In a sentence. As a builder first counts the cost of a tower to make sure he can finish it, so a would-be disciple must count the cost of following Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Have you counted the cost of following Jesus? It is everything, and he is worth it. When you speak to others about Christ, tell them the cost honestly as well as the joy. And if you have stalled halfway, with a foundation laid years ago and little built since, come back to him today. He finishes what he starts.

For worship. At the cross the mockers thought they were looking at an abandoned foundation. The rulers scoffed that he saved others and should save himself (23:35), as though the builder had run out of means halfway. They were watching the last stone go in. Three days later the work stood complete, and it stands still, a tower no one will ever laugh at: our redemption, finished by the one who knew the cost before he began, and paid every part of it with joy.
verseByVerse.note: A tower might guard a vineyard or a farm.

verseByVerse.quote: Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? And if not, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? And if not, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace.

Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate? A second parable, and a greater matter: a war, not a building. The change of scale is deliberate, from a farmer with a half-built shed to a king with an army, from money to survival. Sit down first again: the same instruction as the builder’s. Do the sum before you move.

Whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? Outnumbered two to one. Not hopeless, but the kind of arithmetic that requires an honest man to face a difficult conclusion.

He sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace. Here the two parables part company. The builder can only finish or be mocked. The king has a third option: while the other is yet a great way off, he sends envoys and asks what the terms are.

The point. Two readings are possible, and both are true. First, as with the tower, count the cost of discipleship. Second, God is the king coming against you with superior force. You cannot win against him. Make peace with him now, while he is still far off, by surrendering everything to him (12:58).

Who is the greater king? A man weighing whether he can stand against a force twice his size, in a chapter about what it costs to follow Jesus, is not being invited to conclude that he can manage it with effort. He cannot. Nobody can. What is left is the delegation: going out, while there is still distance between you, and asking for terms. And that is not defeat in this parable. It is the only wise move on the board, and it is the one the king is commended for making. The disaster is not surrender; the disaster is a man who marches out with ten thousand against twenty thousand because he never sat down and did the sum. Which is what the counting of the cost is actually for. It is not to establish that you can afford discipleship. It is to bring you to the point of sending the delegation.

What are the terms of peace? Astonishingly generous. The King who comes against us does not demand that we make up our losses or pay reparations. He has already provided the peace himself. In Christ, God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and he has sent ambassadors to plead: be reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:19–20). The terms are unconditional surrender to his Son and trust in what his Son has done. We give up our arms; he gives us his friendship. Being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 5:1).

In a sentence. As a king facing a stronger army sits down to consider whether he can win, and if not, seeks peace while there is time, so a person must consider the cost and make peace with God.

On a Tuesday. You cannot fight God and win. Surrender to him on his terms, and find peace. Is there a part of your life where you are still at war with him: an area where you keep your own counsel, a command you resent, a providence you will not accept? Send the delegation today. Tell him you give it up, and ask for his peace.

For worship. The King who could have crushed us sent his own Son as the embassy of peace. We were the ten thousand marching out against twenty thousand, and he did not wait for our envoys; while we were still enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Romans 5:10). He made peace by the blood of his cross. There is no stronger King, and none more willing to receive those who lay down their arms. The war we could never win he has ended by losing his own life.

verseByVerse.quote: So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.

So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has. The so therefore ties this to both parables: this is the conclusion the builder and the king were drawn for. The verb (apotassetai) meant to take leave of somebody, to say goodbye, and Luke uses it of the man who wanted to say farewell to those at home (9:61). So it is not primarily get rid of but let go of. The picture is of a man saying goodbye at a door, releasing his hold on what he is leaving behind. It does not necessarily mean literally selling everything; it means giving up ownership of everything to Christ and holding it all at his disposal. Then comes the third cannot (vv. 26, 27, 33): Christ above family, above self, and above possessions.

Must I sell everything I own? No, and Luke himself will not allow that reading. Zacchaeus gives half and is told salvation has come to his house (19:8–9). The women of 8:3 funded the ministry out of means they must still have had. Peter’s rebuke to Ananias turns on the fact that the property was his to keep (Acts 5:4). What is required is that a man stop holding. Some are called to give up a great deal literally; all are called to hold everything open-handed, as stewards and not owners, ready to give whatever he asks. The test is not what percentage you give but whether anything you have is off limits to him.

What it does not mean. Not that discipleship earns salvation, or that only those who take a vow of poverty can be saved. But a disciple is someone who has surrendered everything to Christ, and will let go of anything he asks.

All that he has. The phrase goes past property to reputation, plans, rights and the future a man has drawn up: everything the sentence this is mine can be said about. Here is a test. Think of the thing you are most certain God would never ask you for. Not the thing you would find hardest to lose; the thing you have quietly filed as not up for discussion. Whatever came to mind has not been renounced. It is still being held, and this verse says so.

The one who let go first. Jesus asks for nothing here that he did not give up himself. Luke has shown him with no place to lay his head (9:58), living on the support of others (8:3), and at the end he was stripped even of his clothes, which the soldiers divided by casting lots (23:34). He renounced all that he had, down to the garment on his back, and he did it not to buy a disciple’s freedom from possessions but to buy the disciple. The command to let go is spoken by a Lord whose hands were emptied for us.

The freedom of letting go. There is a mercy in the severity, which the chapter has already supplied. A man who has let go of everything cannot be robbed, cannot be blackmailed, and cannot be moved from the low seat because he has nothing to defend. The renunciation is not a fee charged at the door. It is what makes a man free enough to walk through it.

In a sentence. Anyone who does not give up everything he has cannot be Jesus’ disciple.

On a Tuesday. Is there anything you have not yet surrendered to Christ? Give it to him today. Say it in prayer by name: my savings, my plans for retirement, my children’s futures, my reputation, my time. Then live this week as a steward of what you have handed over: give generously, hold loosely, and ask before you spend what is his.

For worship. Christ asks for all because he gave all. He said goodbye to heaven’s glory and to his own life, and in exchange he gives us himself and an inheritance that can never perish, spoil or fade. Everything a disciple lets go of at the door is already counted in his hands, and nothing laid down for his sake is lost (18:29–30). What we renounce for him is nothing beside what we receive from him, and he is the treasure for which a wise man sells everything with joy.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Salt is good, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile. It is thrown away. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Salt is good, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile. It is thrown away. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.

Salt is good. In that world salt was genuinely valuable: it kept meat, seasoned food, and in small amounts was scattered on the dunghill and dug into fields as fertiliser. The saying closes the chapter, and it is not a change of subject. The crowd has just been told what discipleship costs; this is what happens to a disciple who will not pay it.

But if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? Pure salt cannot lose its taste. But the salt of Palestine was not pure. Impure salt, collected from the Dead Sea marshes and mixed with gypsum and other minerals, could have its salt leached out by moisture and lose its taste, leaving a useless white powder. Which is the whole force of the image. This is not salt that has disappeared. It is salt that is still in the jar, still the right colour, still called salt, and it has stopped working.

It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile. Not even good enough to be mixed with manure as fertiliser. Luke’s detail is the sharpest of the three Gospels. Even the dunghill will not take it.

It is thrown away. It is worthless, and that is a fair description of what a half-committed disciple is for. Not wicked. Not an enemy of anybody. Simply useless for the one thing that was the point of him, because a follower who has kept his own life, his own family loyalties and his own possessions out of the arrangement has retained the appearance and lost the function.

The point. Discipleship that is not costly is not discipleship, and a church that has lost its distinctiveness is useless to the world.

Where Christians differ: can a true Christian lose his saltiness and be thrown away? Arminian Christians read the verse that way: a real disciple may fall away and be finally lost. Verdict: Jesus is warning those who follow at a distance without counting the cost. A disciple in name who will not carry his cross shows that he never truly had the salt (1 John 2:19; John 15:6). Those whom Christ has truly made his own he keeps to the end (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6). The warning is real, and it is one of the very means by which Christ keeps his true disciples faithful: they hear it, and they hold on to him.

He who has ears to hear, let him hear. This is serious. Jesus called out the same words after the parable of the soils (8:8), and it is the same demand. What is asked for is the hearing that goes past the surface and lets the thing in, and the sentence hands the whole chapter back to the reader. A man has counted a cost or he has not; a table serves people who can repay or people who cannot; a seat has been grasped or given up. The teaching has been given. What is left is the hearing.

I feel I have lost my saltiness. Is there hope? Yes. The very fact that you feel it and care about it is a sign that the Spirit is still at work in you. Salt that has truly lost its savour does not grieve over it. Return to Christ, confess where you have grown cold or compromised, and ask him to restore the joy of your salvation (Psalm 51:12). Saltiness is not something you manufacture by trying harder to be different. It comes from closeness to Christ, and it returns as you return to him: to his word, to prayer, to his people, and to the cost you had begun to avoid.

In a sentence. A disciple who loses his distinctiveness is like salt that has lost its taste: useless and thrown away.

On a Tuesday. Is your discipleship salty: distinctive, costly, wholehearted? Don’t lose your saltiness. Ask where your life has become indistinguishable from the people around you who do not know Christ: your speech, your spending, your entertainment, your ambitions. Choose one place this week to be different for his sake, quietly and gladly.

For worship. The Lord who warned about salt thrown away is the same Lord who said to Peter on the night of his denial, I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail (22:32). Peter lost his nerve and wept bitterly, and he was not thrown out; he was turned again and sent to strengthen his brothers. Christ was wholly given to his Father’s will, with nothing in him half-hearted, and he keeps his own by his intercession. His faithfulness is the reason ours does not fail, and the savour he gives he does not let go.
verseByVerse.note: Impure salt could have its salt leached out and lose its taste.

14.text: <sup>1</sup> One Sabbath, when he went to dine at the house of a ruler of the Pharisees, they were watching him carefully. <sup>2</sup> And behold, there was a man before him who had dropsy. <sup>3</sup> And Jesus responded to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not?” <sup>4</sup> But they remained silent. Then he took him and healed him and sent him away. <sup>5</sup> And he said to them, “Which of you, having a son or an ox that has fallen into a well on a Sabbath day, will not immediately pull him out?” <sup>6</sup> And they could not reply to these things. <sup>7</sup> Now he told a parable to those who were invited, when he noticed how they chose the places of honor, saying to them, <sup>8</sup> “When you are invited by someone to a wedding feast, do not sit down in a place of honor, lest someone more distinguished than you be invited by him, <sup>9</sup> and he who invited you both will come and say to you, ‘Give your place to this person,’ and then you will begin with shame to take the lowest place. <sup>10</sup> But when you are invited, go and sit in the lowest place, so that when your host comes he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will be honored in the presence of all who sit at table with you. <sup>11</sup> For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.” <sup>12</sup> He said also to the man who had invited him, “When you give a dinner or a banquet, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, lest they also invite you in return and you be repaid. <sup>13</sup> But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, <sup>14</sup> and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just.” <sup>15</sup> When one of those who reclined at table with him heard these things, he said to him, “Blessed is everyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!” <sup>16</sup> But he said to him, “A man once gave a great banquet and invited many. <sup>17</sup> And at the time for the banquet he sent his servant to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come, for everything is now ready.’ <sup>18</sup> But they all alike began to make excuses. The first said to him, ‘I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Please have me excused.’ <sup>19</sup> And another said, ‘I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to examine them. Please have me excused.’ <sup>20</sup> And another said, ‘I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come.’ <sup>21</sup> So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his servant, ‘Go out quickly to the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame.’ <sup>22</sup> And the servant said, ‘Sir, what you commanded has been done, and still there is room.’ <sup>23</sup> And the master said to the servant, ‘Go out to the highways and hedges and compel people to come in, that my house may be filled. <sup>24</sup> For I tell you, none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet.’” <sup>25</sup> Now great crowds accompanied him, and he turned and said to them, <sup>26</sup> “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. <sup>27</sup> Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple. <sup>28</sup> For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it? <sup>29</sup> Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, <sup>30</sup> saying, ‘This man began to build and was not able to finish.’ <sup>31</sup> Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? <sup>32</sup> And if not, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace. <sup>33</sup> So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple. <sup>34</sup> “Salt is good, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? <sup>35</sup> It is of no use either for the soil or for the manure pile. It is thrown away. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

15.title: Lost and Found: The Three Parables of Grace
15.overview:
Chapter 15 is the theological heart of Luke's Gospel — the chapter that more than any other earns Luke the title “the Gospel of grace.” It contains three parables told in response to a single complaint: the Pharisees and scribes grumble that “this man receives sinners and eats with them.” The three parables are Jesus's answer to the grumbling — not an argument but a story, or rather three stories that together form a single, overwhelming answer to the question: why does the Son of God eat with sinners? Because this is what God is like. He is the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to find the one lost sheep. He is the woman who lights a lamp and sweeps the whole house until she finds the one lost coin. He is the father who runs to meet his returning son while he is still a long way off.

The three parables form a crescendo: from a sheep (something lost through its own wandering nature), to a coin (something lost through its owner's carelessness, possibly), to a son (someone lost through deliberate, calculated rebellion). The lostness becomes more personal, more chosen, more culpable at each step — and the joy at the finding becomes more extravagant, more communal, more absolutely centred on grace rather than on the condition of the lost. The sheep does nothing to return; it is carried home. The coin does nothing; it is found. The son turns around and prepares a speech about his unworthiness — and the father interrupts the speech with the best robe and the ring and the sandals and the fatted calf. The grace always exceeds the repentance.

The chapter's most searching moment is the elder son (vv. 25–32) — the one who has never left, who has served faithfully, who is furious at the welcome given to the prodigal. He is the Pharisees in the parable — the ones whose complaint prompted all three parables. And the father's final words to him are the most tender and most open-ended in the chapter: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.” The chapter ends without the elder son's response. Luke does not tell us whether the Pharisees came in to the feast. The question is left open — which is where Jesus leaves the invitation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Parable of the Lost Sheep
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Everything in this chapter depends on the first two verses. Tax collectors and sinners are drawing near to hear him — a settled pattern rather than one occasion — and the Pharisees and scribes grumble.

Grumbling is what Israel did over and over in the wilderness (Ex. 16:2, 7-8). It is not argument; it is a noise made at the back of a crowd by people who have decided not to engage.

“This man receives sinners and eats with them” is meant as an accusation and is completely accurate. The charge is not that Jesus preaches to sinners — nobody objected to that. It is the table. A shared meal in that world was the single clearest social statement a person could make about who his people were, and he was making it, often enough for everyone to have noticed.

What follows is his answer: three parables, all about something lost, all ending in a party — and the charge is never denied. Luke calls them one parable (v.3), singular, which is worth noticing. They are one argument in three movements.

He begins by putting his critics inside the story. “What man of you” compels agreement: any shepherd here would do this. He is not defending an eccentric practice but describing their own instinct back to them, and then applying it to what they have just objected to.

The detail is realistic. A hundred sheep is a substantial flock, likely with hired help, so leaving the ninety-nine “in the open country” is not the recklessness it sounds. And a lost sheep is genuinely lost: sheep have no homing instinct, and a separated animal will lie down and refuse to move.

“Until he finds it” governs the whole search — there is no clause allowing the shepherd to come home empty. And he does not drive the animal back; an exhausted sheep cannot be herded, so he hoists seventy or eighty pounds across his shoulders and carries it home over the same country he searched, rejoicing.

Then he throws a party, over one sheep out of a hundred, quite possibly at a cost exceeding what the sheep was worth. The celebration is not incidental to the finding. It is what finding produces.
verseByVerse.theology:
The shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine is the most dramatic possible image of divine initiative. The sheep does not seek the shepherd; the shepherd seeks the sheep. This is the consistent pattern of grace: “we love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19); “no one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). The lost sheep contributes nothing to its rescue — it is found, lifted, carried.

Note also where the word repents falls. It appears in the application, not in the story. In the story the sheep does nothing except get lost and be carried. The repentance and the being-found are the same event seen from two sides.

The phrase “ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance” can be taken two ways and both are held by serious readers. It may be straightforward: there really are people already safe in the fold, and no slight is intended.

But remember who Jesus is answering. On the lips of the men grumbling at verse 2, “righteous persons who need no repentance” is exactly how they would have described themselves — and by the end of this chapter Jesus will paint one of them as an elder brother standing outside his father's house. Read against that ending, the phrase carries a dry edge: there is no joy in heaven over the ninety-nine, not because they are secure, but because nobody who believes he needs no repentance has yet given heaven anything to celebrate.
verseByVerse.examples:
The ninety-nine left “in the open country” looks irresponsible, and it reveals something about the community that belongs to the shepherd: they are safe in his care even while he is searching for the one. The gathered community is not threatened by the shepherd's pursuit of the wanderer; it is the context from which he goes and to which he brings the found sheep.

The church that begrudges the energy spent on the lost has misunderstood its own situation. It was once the one, and is now among the ninety-nine.

And the arithmetic of the parable is the thing to sit with, because it is deliberately disproportionate. Heaven does the sum the shepherd did. One sheep out of a hundred, and the whole neighbourhood is called in.

If you find yourself untroubled by this parable, it is worth asking which number you have quietly assigned yourself. The men it was told to were quite certain they were among the ninety-nine, and the parable was constructed so that they would agree with every word of it right up to the moment it closed on them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, 'This man receives sinners and eats with them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying: this man receives sinners and eats with them.

Meaning first. Luke 15 is Jesus’ answer to a complaint: this man receives sinners and eats with them. He does not deny it. He tells three stories of lost things found, a sheep, a coin and a son. In each the one who has lost goes looking or watching until the lost is home, and the finding produces a joy that must be shared: the shepherd carries, the woman sweeps, the father runs, and heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents. The last story turns to the son who never left, angry outside the feast, while his father comes out and pleads with him too. It shows the heart of God towards sinners of both kinds.

The gospel within the gospel. Chapter 15 has been called the heart of Luke’s Gospel, and all three parables answer the complaint of these two verses: why does Jesus welcome sinners? A reader who skips the complaint will misread the parables.

Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. The verb means they were drawing near and kept doing it. This is not one occasion. It is a settled pattern, and by this point in the ministry it has become the most conspicuous fact about him. Tax collectors were Jews who collected Rome’s revenue, regarded as traitors as well as extortioners. Sinners is broader: the openly immoral, but also, to the scrupulous, anybody who did not keep the purity code. And they came to hear him: not for bread or healing, but to listen to a preacher, the last thing anyone would have predicted of that crowd. Something in him made sinners feel welcome.

And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled. The verb (diegongyzon) means muttered among themselves, the word the Greek Old Testament uses over and over of Israel grumbling in the wilderness about the water and the bread (Exodus 16:7–8). It is not argument. It is a noise made at the back of a crowd by people who have decided not to engage.

This man receives sinners and eats with them. It is meant as an accusation, and it is completely accurate. Receives (prosdechetai) means welcomes, accepts, takes to oneself. And eats with them was the part that mattered most: to eat with a man was to accept him, his reputation attached to yours for the evening. Nobody objected to Jesus preaching to sinners. The offence was that he sat down with them. Their complaint is the gospel, and what follows is his answer, in which the charge is never denied.

The holy one at the sinners’ table. The scandal only makes sense if Jesus is who Luke says he is. A lax teacher eating with sinners would have surprised nobody. This is the one whom even the demons named the Holy One of God (4:34), whose touch made a leper clean instead of making himself unclean (5:13), and who had said plainly that he came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance (5:32). Holiness in him does not keep its distance; it comes close and makes clean. The Pharisees thought a holy man must be protected from sinners. Jesus is the holiness from which sinners need no protection, because it heals what it touches.

Does receiving sinners mean Jesus approves of sin? No. He receives sinners in order to save them, and the word that runs through the chapter is repentance (vv. 7, 10). The doctor sits with the sick because he means to heal them (5:31–32). Jesus never said to a sinner that what he had done did not matter; he said that their sins were forgiven, and called them to follow him, as he did Levi (5:27–28). His welcome is not an endorsement of the far country. It is the open door out of it. That is the pattern for his church: a table open to any sinner, and a gospel that calls every sinner home.

So should Christians spend time with people whose lives are a mess? Yes, gladly, as Jesus did, with the aim of drawing them to him. That means real friendship, meals, hospitality and patience, not a project kept at arm’s length. It also means wisdom: you go as one who belongs to Christ, not to join in the sin, and if a friendship is pulling you away from him rather than drawing them towards him, something needs to change (1 Corinthians 15:33). But the danger in most churches is not that we are too close to sinners. It is that we are as far from them as the Pharisees were.

In a sentence. When tax collectors and sinners crowded to hear Jesus, the Pharisees and scribes grumbled that he welcomed sinners and ate with them.

On a Tuesday. Who are the tax collectors and sinners in your world: the colleague with the scandalous life, the neighbour who has been in prison, the relative everyone avoids? Ask whether they would find you as approachable as they found Jesus. Invite one of them to eat with you.

For worship. This man receives sinners: his enemies meant it as a charge, and it has become the confession of every saint in glory. He did not keep his distance from us; he came and sat at our table, and then he spread his own table, broke the bread with his own hands and gave it to people who would deny and desert him that same night. He receives sinners still, and he will eat with them for ever, at the feast where no one will grumble at the guest list.
verseByVerse.note: Eating together signalled acceptance; that was the offence.

verseByVerse.quote: So he told them this parable: 'What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he told them this parable: what man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing.

So he told them this parable. He told it to the grumblers, and Luke calls it one parable, singular, though three stories are coming: one argument in three movements.

What man of you, having a hundred sheep. He begins by putting his critics inside the story. What man of you: the question is framed to compel agreement. Any shepherd would do this; the answer is obvious. Which is the move that traps them. He is not defending an eccentric practice. He is describing their own instinct back to them, and then applying it to what they have just objected to. Shepherds were despised by the Pharisees, but Jesus asks them to imagine being one, and God is the shepherd of Israel (Psalm 23; Ezekiel 34). A hundred sheep is a modest family flock.

If he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country? One percent, hardly worth worrying about, you might think. But a lost sheep is genuinely lost: sheep have no homing instinct. The ninety-nine are in pasture, presumably with other shepherds, so this is not the recklessness it sounds.

And go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? The shepherd takes the initiative. The sheep does not find its way back; the shepherd seeks it. Until he finds it: four words that govern the whole search. Not until dark. Not until it seems hopeless. There is no clause in this sentence that allows the shepherd to come home empty. This is God’s seeking love. God had promised through Ezekiel that he himself would search for his sheep and seek the lost (Ezekiel 34:11, 16). And Jesus: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (19:10).

I myself will search for my sheep. Put two sentences side by side and the parable shows who is telling it. Through Ezekiel, after Israel’s shepherds had failed, the Lord GOD promised: I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out, and I will seek the lost (Ezekiel 34:11, 16). In Luke, Jesus says of himself, the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (19:10). The God who promised to come looking in person has come, and he is the one sitting at the sinners’ table. That is why the parable is a defence of his conduct. When the grumblers object to Jesus seeking sinners, they are objecting to the very thing God swore he would do.

He lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing. A frightened, exhausted sheep will often lie down and refuse to move, and it cannot be herded, so the shepherd hoists it across his neck, front legs in one hand and back legs in the other, and carries it home over the same country he searched. No scolding, no punishment. And the word Luke attaches to that is rejoicing. The whole weight of the animal that caused the trouble is on his shoulders, and he is glad about it all the way home. Isaiah had seen it: he will gather the lambs in his arms (Isaiah 40:11).

If the shepherd does all the work, what do I do? You are found. In the story the sheep does nothing except get lost and be carried, and that is a true picture of salvation: God seeks us before we seek him, and we love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Our coming to him, our repentance and faith, is real, and we must do it; but it is the sheep’s response to the shepherd’s arms, not its own way home. If you have come to Christ, you can trace it back to his seeking. If you are still lost, know that he is the one who goes looking. Cry out to him, and you will find you have been sought.

What about the ninety-nine? Does God care less about faithful believers? No. The ninety-nine are not abandoned; they are left safe in the pasture. The parable is not ranking the sheep. It shows how much one lost sheep matters to a shepherd who already loves all of them. If you have been in the fold for years and feel overlooked, remember that you, too, were once the one he went after, and the joy over your finding was no less. The shepherd who carried you home has not put you down.

In a sentence. Jesus asked which of them, losing one sheep out of a hundred, would not leave the ninety-nine to search for it until he found it, and carry it home with joy on his shoulders.

On a Tuesday. Think of one person who has wandered: a friend who has stopped coming to church, a child who has turned away. Go after them, in prayer first and then in person, gently, without scolding. A phone call, a meal, a note: the shepherd’s work is often as plain as that.

For worship. The search cost this shepherd more than a day in the hills. John records him saying that the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), and Luke shows him walking towards Jerusalem to do it. He went into the open country of our ruin, and he did not come home until the lost was on his shoulders. And having lifted us, he does not set us down to walk the rest of the way. He carries us all the way home, rejoicing, and no sheep he has lifted will ever be dropped.

parallels.desc: I myself will search for my sheep
he will carry them in his bosom

verseByVerse.quote: And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost.’ Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbours, saying to them: rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost. Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.

And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors. Joy must be shared. He throws a party over one sheep out of a hundred, quite possibly at a cost exceeding what the sheep was worth. That is the detail nobody would predict, and it answers the grumbling of verse 2: the Pharisees object to a man who eats with sinners, and Jesus describes a man who recovers what was lost and calls in the neighbours for a meal. The celebration is not incidental to the finding. It is what finding produces.

The party at Jesus’ table. So the meals the Pharisees complained about are this party. When Jesus sat down with tax collectors, he was not lowering his standards; he was doing on earth what heaven was doing over the same people. Every meal with a repentant sinner was the shepherd calling in his neighbours. The grumblers were standing at the edge of heaven’s celebration and calling it a scandal.

Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost. My sheep: it belonged to him all along. It was his while it was lost, and that is why he went after it.

Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven. In heaven: a reverent way of saying God himself rejoices. The Pharisees grumble; heaven celebrates, doing the same disproportionate arithmetic as the shepherd.

Over one sinner who repents. The word repents appears here for the first time, in the application, not in the story. In the story the sheep is found; in reality the sinner repents. They are the same event seen from two sides.

Than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance. This is irony: there are no righteous people who need no repentance (Romans 3:10, 23). But the Pharisees thought they were such people (18:9). So heaven has no joy over them, because they will not repent. Righteous persons who need no repentance is exactly how the grumblers would have described themselves, and by the end of the chapter Jesus will paint one of them as an older brother refusing to come in. Nobody who believes he needs no repentance has yet given heaven anything to celebrate.

Does God really feel joy? Yes. Scripture does not picture God as cold or unmoved. The LORD your God will rejoice over you with gladness and exult over you with loud singing (Zephaniah 3:17). His joy is not like ours, needy or fluctuating; he is eternally blessed in himself. But he truly delights in mercy (Micah 7:18), and the repentance of a sinner is the occasion of real gladness in heaven. If you have come to Christ, you were the cause of God’s rejoicing. That is not sentiment. It is what Jesus said.

In a sentence. As the shepherd calls his friends to rejoice with him, there is more joy in heaven over one repentant sinner than over ninety-nine who think they need no repentance.

On a Tuesday. When a sinner repents, heaven rejoices. Share in God’s joy when someone comes to Christ. If you find yourself untroubled by this parable, ask which number you have quietly assigned yourself. And when you hear of someone converted, especially someone you thought unlikely, let your first response be gladness, out loud, rather than a question about whether it will last.

For worship. He called it my sheep while it was still lost in the hills. Before it was found it was already his, and that is why he went out after it, and why he came home singing. God is not grudging in mercy; he delights in it, and he delights in it as an owner delights in what was always his. Every conversion in the history of the church has been the Shepherd bringing home what the Father gave him, and his joy over his own will never end.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — The Parable of the Lost Coin
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second parable moves indoors, and the seeker is a woman — deliberate, and not likely to be accidental in the Gospel that records more about women than any other. God has just been pictured as a shepherd; he is now pictured as a housewife on her hands and knees.

The coins are drachmas, each roughly a day's wage. Ten is not a fortune, but for a peasant household it is ten days' living. It may be more serious still: in some parts of that world a woman's ten coins were her dowry, strung together and worn on her headdress — both her security and the visible sign of her marriage, so that the lost coin is a gap in something she wears.

Every detail of the search is exact for the house she lived in. A peasant home had few windows and a beaten earth floor, so even at midday the corners were dark — hence the lamp. And the sweeping is not tidying; it is dragging a broom across the floor to hear the coin move, because in that gloom you would find it by sound before you found it by sight.

“Until she finds it” is the shepherd's clause again, and the same refusal to stop. And the ending is the same: friends and neighbours called in, and a party quite possibly costing more than a drachma.

One difference from the first parable deepens the point. A sheep can wander; a coin can do nothing at all. It lies where it fell, in the dark, under something, and no amount of time will improve its position. Whatever contribution the sheep made to being found — and it made almost none — the coin makes less.

The application changes in two small ways. The tense moves from future to present: not “there will be joy” but “there is joy,” now, and every time. And the location becomes “before the angels of God” — which puts the angels in the position of onlookers, watching somebody else be glad.
verseByVerse.theology:
Whose joy are the angels watching? The phrasing leaves him unnamed, and both parables have already answered it. The shepherd rejoiced. The woman rejoiced. Every seeker in this chapter is God, and every one of them is delighted.

So the picture is this: somewhere a man nobody has heard of, at the end of a life he is ashamed of, turns round — and God is so pleased that the angels stop and watch him.

That is a very long way from the God the grumblers at verse 2 were defending, and a long way from the God many people privately imagine: correct, appeasable, and disappointed. Nothing in these parables is grudging. There is no reluctant pardon anywhere in the chapter, no probation, no interval in which the found thing has to prove itself. There is a search, and then there is a party.

The angels are elsewhere described as “ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation” (Heb. 1:14). They are not detached observers of the gospel; they are invested in its outcomes. The finding of one lost sinner is a cosmic event, celebrated at every level of the created order that understands what was lost.
verseByVerse.examples:
The woman's method is the model of the kind of prayer and pastoral work that refuses to give up. She does not glance round and conclude it is not there. She lights the lamp — creating the conditions for seeing clearly. She sweeps — removing what might be covering it. And she seeks diligently until the finding.

Intercession for the lost follows the same method: create the conditions for light, remove what obscures the gospel, and keep at it. And the sweeping is worth holding on to, because it is the least glamorous part and the part that actually finds the coin. It is repetitive, unremarkable work done on hands and knees in a dark room, and it is how the thing was recovered.

And the completeness of the coin's helplessness is a comfort rather than an insult. Anyone who has watched a person they love become entirely unable to help themselves — through addiction, or illness of the mind, or a hardness they cannot seem to break — is looking at the coin. It cannot call out. It cannot move towards the light.

What the parable says is that this changes nothing about the search.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbours, saying: rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.

Or what woman, having ten silver coins. The second parable moves indoors, and the seeker is a woman. Luke’s pairing again: a man and a woman (13:18–21). God has just been pictured as a shepherd; he is now pictured as a woman searching her house, on her hands and knees. Luke, who records more about women than any other evangelist, is not likely to have included it by accident.

The coins. The ESV notes that each coin was a drachma, roughly a day’s wage. Ten coins may have been her savings, or, as in some parts of that world, coins strung together and worn as her security and the sign of her marriage. Either way, losing one was a real loss for a poor woman.

Does not light a lamp and sweep the house. Every detail is exact for the house she lived in. A poor house had few or no windows, and a beaten earth floor, perhaps covered with straw, so even at midday the corners were dark: hence the lamp. And the sweeping is not tidying. Finding a small coin meant lighting a lamp and sweeping carefully, listening for the clink, because in that gloom you would find it by sound before you found it by sight.

And seek diligently until she finds it. The same until as the shepherd’s, and the same refusal to stop. Then the same ending: rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost, and a party quite possibly costing more than a drachma.

The difference. A sheep wanders away by its own folly; a coin is lost through no will of its own; a son will walk away deliberately. All lost; all sought; all found. And the coin deepens the point. A sheep can wander; a coin cannot do anything at all. It lies where it fell, in the dark, under something, and no amount of time will improve its position. Whatever contribution the sheep made to being found, and it made almost none, the coin makes less. It is simply lost, and then it is simply found, and everything in between was done by somebody with a lamp.

Salvation has come to this house. The grumblers did not have to imagine a searcher going through a house. A few chapters on, Jesus will stop under a tree in Jericho, call a chief tax collector by name and say, today I must stay at your house (19:5).
