The crowd will grumble with the very verb of this chapter (19:7), and Jesus will answer, today salvation has come to this house, for the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (19:9–10). The coin does not find itself, and Zacchaeus did not invite himself. The seeking in these parables is what Jesus was doing, house by house, in the towns where they lived.

Is it right to picture God as a woman? The parable pictures God’s searching love through a woman’s action, as Scripture elsewhere compares his care to a mother’s (Isaiah 49:15; 66:13), and Jesus has just compared himself to a hen (13:34). These are images of what God does, and they are precious. But Scripture never addresses God as mother or calls him she. He reveals himself as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and we name him as he has named himself. We can rejoice in every likeness Scripture gives, and still pray, as Jesus taught us, Our Father.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a woman who lost one of her ten silver coins and searched her house carefully until she found it, then called her friends to rejoice with her.

On a Tuesday. God searches diligently for the lost. Be part of his search: pray for and seek those who are lost. The lamp and the broom are ordinary tools; so are a Bible, a conversation and an open home. And if you feel as helpless as a coin under the furniture, unable to do anything to get yourself found, take heart: that is precisely the kind of lost thing this woman went looking for.

For worship. A coin cannot call out from under the straw. It does not know it is lost and cannot wish to be found. And the God who seeks sinners did not wait for us to ring out; he lit the lamp and bent down and went through the whole house, corner by corner, until we were in his hand. The coin was worth a day’s wage. He searched for us as though we were worth his life, and then he called his neighbours to rejoice over what he had found.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that each coin was a drachma, roughly equal to a denarius — about a day’s wage. Houses were dark, with small windows and earthen floors.

verseByVerse.quote: Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.

Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God. The same application as the sheep, with two changes. The tense: over the sheep there will be joy; here there is joy, now, every time. And the location: before the angels of God. Not exactly that the angels rejoice, though they surely do, but that there is joy in their presence, the joy of God himself, with the angels as onlookers.

Whose joy are they watching? The phrasing leaves him unnamed, and both parables have already told us. The shepherd rejoiced. The woman rejoiced. And in the parable still to come, a father will run down a road and kill the best animal on the farm. Every seeker in this chapter is God, and every one of them is delighted. So the picture is this. Somewhere a man nobody has heard of, at the end of a life he is ashamed of, turns round, and God is so pleased that the angels stop and watch him.

Good news of great joy. The angels have watched this joy before. On the night of Jesus’ birth an angel told shepherds, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people, for unto you is born this day a Saviour (2:10–11). That joy was announced over a manger; this joy breaks out over every sinner the Saviour finds. The heavenly host who praised God above Bethlehem belong to the same company before whom heaven now rejoices, one repentance at a time. What they announced at his coming, they now see fulfilled in each one he brings home.

Over one sinner who repents. The arithmetic never changes: one sheep out of a hundred, one coin out of ten, one sinner of no particular importance to anybody, whose repentance stops heaven in its tracks. That is a very long way from the God the grumblers were defending, and from the God many people privately imagine: correct, appeasable and disappointed. Nothing in these parables is grudging. There is no reluctant pardon anywhere in the chapter, no probation, no interval in which the found thing has to prove itself. There is a search, and then there is a party.

Do the angels know when someone is saved? The verse says there is joy in their presence, and Scripture elsewhere shows angels longing to look into the gospel (1 Peter 1:12) and serving those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14). It is natural to think they share heaven’s gladness. But we should not speculate beyond what is written, and the point is not the angels but the God before whom they stand. The joy that fills heaven at a sinner’s repentance is first and most of all his.

In a sentence. There is joy in the presence of God’s angels over every single sinner who repents.

On a Tuesday. If you think your repentance is too small to matter, or your life too ordinary to interest heaven, read this verse again. And when you pray for someone far from God, remember what you are asking for: an occasion of joy in the presence of the angels.

For worship. The God before whom the seraphim cover their faces is not too high to be glad over one sinner turning home. The angels who have seen his throne for ages still find something new to watch whenever a sinner repents, because each one is a fresh display of the manifold wisdom of God (Ephesians 3:10). His joy is not a reaction to our worth but the overflow of his love, and there is no repentance so small, no sinner so obscure, that it fails to make heaven glad.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–32 — The Parable of the Prodigal Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“There was a man who had two sons.” The story is announced as being about two — worth remembering, since it is usually preached as though it were about one.

The younger son's request is difficult to convey in its full shock. An estate passed at the father's death; a son had no standing to ask early, and the request carried an unmistakable meaning: I want what I will get when you are dead, and I do not want to wait for you to die. And he calls it “the share that is coming to me” — not a gift but something owed.

The father grants it without a recorded word. Note the plural: “he divided his property between them.” Two-thirds went to the elder son on the spot, and he never asked — which will matter enormously when he stands in a field complaining that he has never been given anything.

Liquidating that land was a public act. Land in Israel was the family's portion in the inheritance of God's people, with laws to keep it in the family (Lev. 25:23-28), so the whole district watched the transactions and drew the obvious conclusion. And the far country is not chiefly a place. It is wherever a man can go to be unobserved.

The descent is calibrated: the money goes, then a famine removes any possibility of recovery, then he attaches himself to a Gentile who sends him out of sight to feed pigs — the floor, for a son of Israel — and then he is hungry enough to envy the carob pods and cannot get them. “No one gave him anything.” The far country is generous to a man with a purse and has never once fed anybody without one.

“He came to himself” is exact. He does not become someone else; he comes round, the way a man does after a blow to the head — which says that everything from verse 12 onwards was the aberration, and repentance is sanity returning.

His prepared speech gets two things right and one wrong. He names it as sin, against God first and his father second. Then he proposes to work his way back as a hired labourer — he has understood his guilt and entirely misunderstood his father.

And the father, seeing him a long way off, runs.
verseByVerse.theology:
The father running is the most shocking thing in the parable. An elderly man of standing in a Middle Eastern village did not run; it required gathering up the robe and exposing the legs, which was humiliating, and dignity was the currency such a man lived on. He deliberately and publicly makes a fool of himself in front of the whole village.

And he may have had a further reason. The boy had sold family land to Gentiles and lost it, and could expect a hostile reception. The father reaches him first, on the road, before anyone else can get to him. The same logic runs through the fattened calf: everyone who comes to that meal has, by coming, accepted the father's verdict on his son, and it is very difficult to shun a man you have eaten fatted calf for.

Every gift is a specific restoration. The best robe is the finest in the house and probably the father's own — so anyone entering afterwards sees a son of the house and nothing else. The signet ring is authority, the instrument for sealing contracts in the father's name, handed to the one member of the family who has proved beyond argument that he cannot be trusted with money. Slaves went barefoot; the shoes settle the question the boy had rehearsed all the way home.

An objection has to be met here, because it is raised by critics and by thoughtful believers alike: there is no atonement in this parable. No sacrifice, no blood, no mediator — the father simply forgives. Some have built on that silence the claim that the doctrine of atonement was a later invention laid over a simpler gospel.

But the parable is not costless; we have been reading it from the son's side. The younger son's portion was real property, squandered and not coming back — the father is permanently poorer for having let him go. And the robe, the ring, the sandals and the calf all come out of what remains. The father does not forgive at no cost. He absorbs the entire cost himself, in silence, and never once mentions it.
verseByVerse.examples:
The boy did not come home because he missed his father. He came home because he was hungry, and the text is entirely candid about it — so a reader looks at his own conversion and goes cold. I turned to God when my marriage collapsed. I prayed because the results came back. Was any of that real?

Watch what the father does with it. He does not interrogate the motive or wait at the gate to establish whether the boy has come for love or for supper. He sees him a long way off and runs. Luke has been showing this all through: the tax collector who could not lift his eyes came out of sheer misery and went home justified (18:13-14); the criminal on the cross came with a few hours left and nothing else on earth to try (23:42-43).

Nobody's repentance is pure at the outset. Hunger is very often the first grace — the mercy that makes a man look up, because comfort never would have. What matters is not the elegance of the motive that got you onto the road, but whose house you are walking towards.

Then the elder brother, and the parable's real target. He describes his life in his father's house as service — “these many years I have served you” — and thinks he is stating a credential. He wanted a goat to celebrate with his friends; even his imagined party does not have his father in it. And the complaint is false: two-thirds of that estate had been legally his since verse 12, and he could have killed a goat any week he liked.

He cannot say “my brother.” The servant managed it without effort; the elder son says “this son of yours.” And he supplies the prostitutes, which Luke never mentioned and which he was several days' journey away from witnessing — resentment filling in the blanks in the worst available way and calling it honesty.

The parable then stops. A man standing in the dark outside a lit house, being begged by his father, with the music still playing. Jesus told this to the men who grumbled at verse 2, and left them on the doorstep. The ending was theirs to write.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, 'There was a man who had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.’ And he divided his property between them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said: there was a man who had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father: father, give me the share of property that is coming to me. And he divided his property between them.

There was a man who had two sons. Only Luke records this parable, and it is announced as being about a man and two sons, which is worth remembering when it is preached, as it usually is, as though it were about one. The younger son stands for the tax collectors and sinners (v. 1), the older for the Pharisees and scribes (v. 2), and the father for God. The story is left open at the end, because the older son, the Pharisees, must decide.

The Son who tells of the Father. It matters who is telling this story. Jesus had said that no one knows who the Father is except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (10:22). Here the Son draws the portrait. And he draws it to explain his own behaviour: he receives sinners because this is what the Father is like. Watch Jesus at a table with tax collectors and you are watching the father of the parable at the gate. Nobody had ever described God like this, because nobody had ever known him as the Son does.

Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me. It is difficult to convey how shocking that sentence was, and the shock is the doorway into the whole parable. A father normally divided his property at death. The younger son would receive one-third (the elder received a double portion, Deuteronomy 21:17). A father could distribute property early, but the son had no standing to ask. To ask for it now was like saying: I wish you were dead; I want your things, not you. And the words are careful: the share that is coming to me, his by right. He has not asked for a gift but for what he considers already owed.

And he divided his property between them. Astonishingly, the father agrees, without a recorded word, argument or condition. He does not force his son to stay. And note the plural: between them. The elder son receives his share too, and says nothing in defence of his father. That will matter at the end, when he stands in a field complaining that he has never been given anything. Everything both sons will need is already in their hands. This is what every sinner does to God: takes his gifts, life, health and abilities, and wants to live without him. Sin is not first breaking rules but breaking a relationship.

Why does God let people walk away from him? The father does not hold his son by force, and God does not drag sinners into his house against their will. He lets people have what they insist on, and sometimes that is the most terrible judgement there is (Romans 1:24). But the letting go is not indifference. The father’s eyes are on the road from the day the boy leaves. God’s patience gives a sinner room to discover what the far country is really like, and his providence, as the next verses show, is at work even there. If someone you love has walked away, the parable does not tell you to stop loving or praying. It tells you to keep watching the road.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a man with two sons, the younger of whom insulted his father by demanding his inheritance at once, and the father divided his property between them.

On a Tuesday. Are you enjoying God’s gifts while keeping him at a distance? That is the heart of sin. Look at the good things in your hands today, your health, your money, your time, your mind, and ask whether you are using them with him or without him. The request of verse 12 is rarely made out loud. It is made in the way we spend a Saturday.

For worship. Every good gift we have ever squandered came from a Father who gave it freely. He gave the younger son his share without a word, and he gives sun and rain to the just and the unjust, generous even to those who wish him gone. And the Son who told this story would one day stand in the place of rebels, despised and rejected, so that sons who had wished their Father dead might be brought home alive. There is no father like this Father, and no Son like the one who brings us to him.
verseByVerse.note: A father normally divided his property at death. The younger son would receive a third — the elder son had a double share.

parallels.desc: a double portion to the firstborn

verseByVerse.quote: Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country, and there he squandered his property in reckless living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country, and there he squandered his property in reckless living.

Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had. He did not even wait. He turned his share of the estate into cash, and selling family land was itself shameful: land in Israel was the family’s portion in the inheritance of God’s people, held in trust across generations (Leviticus 25:23–28). To sell up was a public act, and by the time he left the whole district knew what the boy thought of his father. Gathered all he had: everything convertible, converted, and nothing left behind that could bring him back.

And took a journey into a far country. Gentile land, far from his father, his family, his people, and his God. Distance was the point: a far country, where nobody had heard of his father and nobody would report on him. The far country is not chiefly a place. It is wherever a man can go to be unobserved, and every generation has its own version.

And there he squandered his property in reckless living. The verb (dieskorpisen) means scattered, like seed thrown to the wind, the verb Mary sang of God scattering the proud (1:51). Reckless (asōtōs) means literally unsavingly: without keeping anything back, the absence of any brake rather than a particular vice. Luke does not itemise. His brother will say: with prostitutes (v. 30), and Luke does not confirm it. Freedom from his father became slavery to his appetites.

Two sons, two prayers. Luke sets another Son beside this one. The younger son’s first words in the story are give me (v. 12): the Father’s goods, without the Father. The Son who tells the story will kneel on the Mount of Olives and pray, Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done (22:42), and his last words on the cross will be, Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (23:46). One son took his share and spent it on himself. The other gave up everything that was his and spent himself on his Father’s will, so that sons like the first could come home.

What is my far country? It may not involve travel at all. It is anywhere you go to be out of your Father’s sight, or so you think: the screen at midnight, the second life at a conference, the hidden spending, the resentment nursed in private, the corner of your heart where God is not consulted. It always begins with wanting the gifts without the Giver, and it always promises freedom. Name it honestly before God. The first step home is admitting where you are.

In a sentence. The younger son soon turned his inheritance into cash, went to a distant country, and wasted it all on reckless living.

On a Tuesday. The far country promises freedom, but delivers emptiness. Where is your far country? Notice the places in your life where you most want not to be seen, and ask why. Then bring them into the light, to God first, and if need be to a trusted Christian friend (James 5:16).

For worship. There is no country so far that the Father’s love does not reach it. He watched his son sell the land and take the road, and he never stopped being his father. The boy scattered everything, and the Father’s storehouse was not emptied; the boy forgot his home, and the Father did not forget his boy. The God we wronged in our far countries was keeping our place at his table the whole time, and his riches are still undiminished.
verseByVerse.note: A far country is Gentile land.

parallels.desc: a companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need. So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need. So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything.

When he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country. The sequence is ordinary and merciless. First the money runs out, which was always going to happen. Then the famine arrives on top of the spending, and the two together remove any possibility of recovery. He chose the far country and the spending; he did not choose the famine. Sin puts a man in a place where circumstance can destroy him, and circumstance does not ask his permission. God often uses hardship to bring sinners to their senses. And he began to be in need: from wealth to want.

He hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country. Literally glued himself, clung to him. This is not applying for a post. It is a starving man fastening himself to a Gentile who does not want him, and the employer’s response reads as a way of getting rid of him.

Who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. Pigs were unclean under the law (Leviticus 11:7), and a rabbinic saying pronounces a curse on the man who raises them. A Jew feeding pigs for a Gentile had fallen as low as a person could go: cut off from his people, his worship and his God.

And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate. Carob pods, the long dark seed pods of the carob tree, fed to animals and eaten by the very poorest in hard times. Coarse and barely nourishing, and he cannot get them. He is not eating them; he is longing to. He envied the pigs. He left home with a third of an estate, and he now ranks below the livestock.

And no one gave him anything. The far country does not care for its slaves. There were plenty of people around him while the money lasted. The far country is generous to a man with a purse and has never once fed anybody without one.

He has filled the hungry. Luke’s Gospel has been listening for this hunger since its first chapter. Mary sang of a God who has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty (1:53). Jesus pronounced a blessing on those who are hungry now, for you shall be satisfied (6:21), and in a desolate place he fed five thousand until everyone was full (9:17). The far country gives the hungry nothing. The Son who tells this story is the one in whom God fills them. The pigsty is exactly where his kind of mercy is aimed.

Is God behind the famine? God rules over famines as over everything (Psalm 105:16), and in this story the hardship is the very thing that turns the son homeward. That does not mean every hardship is a punishment for a specific sin, as Jesus has just insisted (13:1–5). But it does mean that the bottom of the pit is never outside God’s reach, and that he often uses empty hands to make a sinner look up. If you are at the bottom now, your misery may be the severe mercy that brings you home. Do not waste it.

In a sentence. When his money was gone and famine struck, he hired himself out to a Gentile to feed pigs, and was so hungry he longed to eat their food, but no one gave him anything.

On a Tuesday. Sin promises much and leaves you envying pigs. If you are at the bottom, the way home is still open. And if someone you love is in the pigsty, do not be in a hurry to rescue them from every consequence; pray that the famine will do its work, and be ready for the day they come to themselves.

For worship. The God who lets the far country show its true face is the God who never stops providing for those who come home. The far country gives nothing, not even the pods; he gives everything. And the Son, who had every right to the Father’s table, was hungry in the wilderness and despised outside the city for us, so that every pig-feeder who turns to him might sit down at that table and be satisfied.
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean under the law; a Jew feeding pigs for a Gentile had sunk as low as possible. The pods were probably carob pods, used as animal feed.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.'’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when he came to himself, he said: how many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.

But when he came to himself. One of the most exact phrases in the Gospels: came to his senses, woke up. He does not become someone else. He comes to himself, which is what we say of a man recovering from a faint, or coming round after a blow to the head. The implication is that everything from the request in verse 12 onwards was the aberration, and that this is the boy waking up. Sin is a kind of madness; repentance is coming back to sanity. It begins with seeing clearly: where I am, and where I could be.

How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! He remembers his father’s goodness, and he is honest about his own condition. His first clear thought is about bread, and about his father’s household, and the detail he remembers is that even the lowest grade of worker on the estate has more than enough. He is remembering the one thing he had never valued. Remembering God’s goodness draws sinners back (Romans 2:4).

I will arise and go to my father. Repentance is a decision, followed by action: turning around, going back. There is no agonising. He has been in the pigsty long enough.

Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. Against heaven: against God. All sin is first against God (Psalm 51:4). And against his father. Genuine confession, without excuses or blaming others. He does not blame the famine, or his friends, or his father. He names it as sin, not misfortune, and he names it against God first and his father second, which is the correct order.

Sin against heaven, pardon on earth. If sin is first against heaven, then only heaven can forgive it, and the scribes in Luke knew it: who can forgive sins but God alone? (5:21). Jesus answered them by healing a paralysed man, so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins (5:24). He said to a weeping woman at a Pharisee’s table, your sins are forgiven (7:48). The confession the boy rehearses in the pigsty is the confession sinners were bringing to Jesus, and they were receiving from him what only heaven could give.

I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants. True: he has forfeited every right. Hired servants were day labourers with no place in the family, paid at night. He plans to work off his debt. His repentance is real, but he has understood his guilt and entirely misunderstood his father.

Was his repentance real if he only came home because he was hungry? This troubles more honest Christians than almost any other question. The boy did not come home because he missed his father; the text is candid that he came because he was starving. So a reader looks at his own conversion and goes cold: I turned to God when my marriage collapsed; I prayed because the results came back. Was any of that real? The truth is that nobody’s repentance is pure at the outset. Hunger is very often the first grace, the mercy that makes a man look up, because comfort never would have. What matters is not the elegance of the motive that got you onto the road, but whose house you are walking towards. And motives are purified on the way, as the father’s embrace is about to show.

In a sentence. Coming to his senses, he remembered that even his father’s hired workers had plenty, and resolved to go home, confess his sin, and ask to be treated as a hired worker.

On a Tuesday. Come to your senses. Confess your sin to God, honestly and without excuse. And then go home. Make the confession specific: not I have not been very good, but the thing itself, by name. And notice if you are rehearsing a hired servant’s speech, planning how you will make it up to God. He is not looking for a labourer. He is looking for his son.

For worship. The Father’s goodness is so great that even the memory of it, in a pigsty, draws a ruined man home. His house is full of bread; his servants have more than enough; his mercy is from everlasting to everlasting. And the Spirit who brings sinners to themselves is the Spirit of the Father who has never stopped watching the road. Every homeward thought a sinner ever had was first a gift from him.
verseByVerse.note: Hired servants were day labourers, with no place in the family.

parallels.desc: against you, you only, have I sinned

verseByVerse.quote: And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.

And he arose and came to his father. He did what he said. Luke gives the journey half a sentence. Whatever it cost him to walk back into that village with the smell of pigs on him, past the neighbours who had watched him sell the land, it is not described.

But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him. Which tells you what the father had been doing. You do not identify a figure at that distance unless you are looking, and you do not look unless you have been looking for a long time. Nothing in the parable says the father knew he was coming. The old man had been watching a road for a boy who had every reason never to appear on it, and he saw his son before his son saw him.

And felt compassion. The word (esplanchnisthē) means moved in his innermost being, the compassion that turns over inside a person. It is the word used of Jesus at Nain (7:13) and of the good Samaritan (10:33): three great moments in Luke.

And ran. It is the most shocking thing in the parable. In that culture it was undignified for an older man to run: he would have to hike up his robe and show his legs, and dignity was the currency such a man lived on. So the father publicly makes a fool of himself in front of the whole village. There may be a reason beyond joy. Some have suggested that a son who lost his inheritance among Gentiles could be cut off by the village; the father reaches him first, taking the shame on himself and protecting his son.

And embraced him and kissed him. Literally fell on his neck, as Esau embraced Jacob (Genesis 33:4) and Joseph his father (Genesis 46:29). He is filthy, he stinks of a pig field, and he is ceremonially unclean. The father has him by the neck and kisses him again and again (the verb is intensive), the sign of reconciliation (2 Samuel 14:33), before the son can say a word of his confession.

The heart of God. This is the centre of the parable, and the answer to the Pharisees’ complaint. God is not a reluctant judge who must be persuaded to forgive. He is a father who runs to meet repentant sinners, while they are still far off. This is why Jesus receives sinners.

If God runs to forgive, does it matter how I live? It matters more, not less. The son who has been met on the road like this does not go back to the pigs; he has found his father’s heart, and the far country has lost its charm. Grace that is truly received produces a new life, because it changes what we love (Titus 2:11–12). Paul faced this objection directly: shall we go on sinning that grace may abound? By no means (Romans 6:1–2). The father’s running is not permission to leave again. It is the most powerful reason never to want to.

In a sentence. While the son was still far off, his father saw him, was filled with compassion, ran to him, threw his arms around him and kissed him.

On a Tuesday. If you have been putting off coming back to God because you think you must first clean yourself up, or because you dread the reception, look at this verse. The Father is already running. And when someone who has hurt you comes back, be quick to go out to meet them.

For worship. The God of all majesty set aside his dignity and ran. He did not wait at the door for an apology or send a servant to inspect the boy; he crossed the distance himself, in front of the village, and had the filthy son by the neck before the speech began. And behind the running lies a greater shame borne for us: the Son of God, stripped and lifted up outside the city, despising the shame (Hebrews 12:2), so that the Father could embrace sinners without compromising his holiness. No other god has ever run to meet a sinner.
verseByVerse.note: In that culture it was thought undignified for an older man to run.

parallels.desc: Esau ran to meet him and embraced him
you who once were far off

verseByVerse.quote: And the son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the son said to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.

Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son. He makes his confession even after the embrace. He is not embraced into a situation where nothing needs to be said; he says it, and both statements are entirely true.

What he does not say. He leaves out the last line of his prepared speech: Treat me as one of your hired servants (v. 19). Perhaps the father interrupts him. Perhaps, embraced and kissed, he realises he cannot bargain. Grace does not negotiate. You cannot earn your way back to a father who has already forgiven you. He comes as a son, or not at all.

Who makes the unworthy worthy? The boy is right: he is not worthy. The parable does not explain how a holy Father can call such a son his son without pretending that nothing happened, and it does not need to, because the one telling it was on his way to Jerusalem. There he would be numbered with the transgressors (22:37) and die between two criminals, the only Son who was ever worthy. The welcome at the gate costs the son nothing because it cost the Son everything. Sinners who say not worthy are received as sons in him.

Two readings, both worth having. He may have been interrupted: the next verse begins but the father said to his servants, like a man not waiting for the end of a sentence. Or he may have stopped himself, finding with his father’s arms round him that the offer had become absurd. Either way, the plan to work his way back never gets said out loud. Everything the son had worked out in the far country about how to be received is left unspoken, because it was answered before he opened his mouth.

Why confess, if I am already forgiven? Because confession is not payment; it is honesty. Grace is sometimes preached in a way that makes confession unnecessary, and the son shows otherwise: he says the words. What he does not get to do is set the terms on which he will be taken back. For the believer, daily confession is not a way of earning back a lost sonship. It is a child being truthful with his Father, and receiving again the assurance of a pardon already given (1 John 1:9). There is only one thing a returning sinner has to bring, and he brought it: an honest account of himself. Everything else in this scene is supplied by somebody else.

In a sentence. The son confessed his sin and unworthiness to his father, but did not finish his offer to become a hired worker.

On a Tuesday. When you confess your sins to God, stop at the end of the confession. Do not add the bargain: the promises to make up for it, the penance you set yourself, the quiet sense that you must earn your way back into favour. Say what is true, and let your Father answer.

For worship. His mercy is before our words, his embrace before our confession, his love before our coming. The speech the boy rehearsed in the pigsty ran out against his father’s shoulder, and the last line, the one about earning his keep, was never needed. So it is with every sinner the Father receives. We bring nothing but our sin and an honest account of it; he supplies the robe, the welcome and the name of son, and he does it with joy.

verseByVerse.quote: But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the father said to his servants: bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet.

But the father said to his servants, Bring quickly. He does not even reply to the confession. He acts, giving orders about clothing in which every item restores something specific. Quickly comes first and governs the rest: no delay, no probation, and nobody is sent to wash first.

The best robe. Literally “the first robe”: the finest in the house, perhaps the father’s own. It covered his rags and showed everyone in the village that he was restored to honour: a full, free welcome back, not a probation. Jesus does not say what the robe stands for, and the parable is about the Father’s joy over a returning sinner (vv. 7, 10), not about how forgiveness is achieved. But the Old Testament often pictures God clothing his people with salvation (Isaiah 61:10; Zechariah 3:3–5), and the rest of the New Testament shows that God clothes sinners with Christ himself (Galatians 3:27). So Christians have rightly heard in the robe an echo of the righteousness God gives in Christ, as long as we remember that this comes from the rest of Scripture, not from the parable alone.

And put a ring on his hand. A signet ring, used to seal documents, gave him authority to act on his father’s behalf (Genesis 41:42; Esther 3:10). Full restoration as a son, with a son’s rights. It is not jewellery. It is authority, handed to the one member of the family who has demonstrated beyond argument that he cannot be trusted with money.

And shoes on his feet. Sandals marked a free man; slaves went barefoot. It is a small detail and it settles the question the boy had been rehearsing all the way home. He had come to ask for a place among the hired men. Before he can propose it, his father has put shoes on him.

Three gifts at the gate. Between them they restore his standing, his authority and his freedom, immediately and without a single condition attached. Not one of them is deserved, and everybody watching knows it. The father does not restore him gradually as he proves himself. He restores him completely at the gate, before the boy has done one honest day’s work, and then lets him live the rest of his life as what he has been declared to be.

Is the prodigal a believer who fell away? The parable is aimed at the Pharisees’ complaint about tax collectors and sinners (vv. 1–2), and the younger son stands for sinners coming home to God. He is a son throughout; the father calls him my son (v. 24). It may also comfort a believer who has wandered for a season, but it does not teach that sonship can be lost and regained. If you are a Christian who has drifted, the way back is the same road: come to yourself, confess, and go home. You will find your Father has not changed.

In a sentence. The father ordered the best robe, a ring and sandals for him at once, restoring him fully to honour, authority and sonship.

On a Tuesday. If you are in Christ, live today as what you have been declared to be. You are not a hired servant on probation, anxiously working to stay in favour; you wear the robe, the ring and the sandals of a son. And treat returning sinners the same way: when someone comes back to church after years away, do not put them on probation. Welcome them as the Father welcomed you.

For worship. The Father does not merely let the boy back in; he dresses him so that no one can tell where he has been. Anyone coming into the feast would see a son of the house and nothing else. That is the gift God gives in Christ. The Son was stripped and his clothes divided by lot, so that we might be clothed; he took the form of a servant, so that we might wear the sandals of sons. Every gift at that gate was paid for by the Father’s own Son, and he gives them all at once.
verseByVerse.note: The robe honoured him, the ring gave him authority, and sandals marked a son, not a barefoot slave.

parallels.desc: Pharaoh gives Joseph his ring and garments

verseByVerse.quote: And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.’ And they began to celebrate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to celebrate.

And bring the fattened calf and kill it. A peasant household rarely ate meat, and a fattened calf was grain-fed and kept back for a single great occasion, a wedding or a visit from someone important, with enough meat to feed the whole village. The father throws a feast for the community, to restore his son publicly. The father is calling in the same village that had watched the boy sell his father’s land and leave. Which is a further piece of protection. Everyone who comes to that meal has, by coming, accepted the father’s verdict on his son. It becomes very difficult to shun a man you have eaten fatted calf for.

Let us eat and celebrate. Eating together is the very thing the Pharisees complained about (v. 2). Jesus eats with sinners because God celebrates their return.

For this my son was dead, and is alive again. My son: not a hired servant. The boy had just finished saying he was no longer worthy to be called it. The father does not argue the point. He simply uses the word. Dead and alive: the language of resurrection. In that culture a son who had done what this one did was reckoned dead to the family, and the father takes the household’s own language and reverses it. Repentance is passing from death to life (Ephesians 2:1–5; Colossians 2:13).

He was lost, and is found. Here the three parables close into one: a sheep, a coin and a boy, lost and found, and every one of them ending in a party.

And they began to celebrate. Luke’s phrasing is worth noticing: they began. The celebration is under way and is not finished when the chapter ends. It is still going on in the last verse, with music audible from the field, and one son standing outside it.

Where Christians differ: forgiveness without a cross? Some liberal theologians have argued that this parable shows God forgives freely, without any need for atonement: the father simply forgives, with no sacrifice. Verdict: a parable teaches one main point, not every doctrine. This one shows God’s welcome to repentant sinners, in answer to the Pharisees. It does not explain how forgiveness is possible for a holy God. The rest of Scripture does: Jesus came to give his life as a ransom (Mark 10:45), his blood is poured out for the forgiveness of sins (22:20; Matthew 26:28), and Luke ends with the Christ who must suffer so that forgiveness may be proclaimed (24:46–47). The father’s running, at cost to his own honour, is a hint of the cost God himself bore. And the one telling the story was on his way to Jerusalem to die.

Who paid for the calf? Somebody paid for it, and it was not the boy, who came up the road with nothing but the smell of pigs on him. Every single thing he receives in this scene is drawn from his father’s own resources, and the father never once mentions the cost. That is the gospel’s logic, and the cross is where the bill was met: God put Christ forward as a propitiation by his blood, to show his righteousness, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:25–26).

In a sentence. The father ordered the fattened calf killed for a feast, because his son had been dead and was alive, lost and was found, and they began to celebrate.

On a Tuesday. Make your church and your home a place where returning sinners are celebrated, not merely tolerated. When someone is baptised, or comes back after years away, show up, rejoice, and eat with them. And if you have never quite believed that God is glad you are his, read verse 24 slowly, with your own name in it.

For worship. Dead and alive again: the Father speaks of his son in the language of resurrection, and he has the power to make the words true. He raised Jesus from the dead, and in him he raises sinners who were dead in their trespasses. The music in that house has been playing since the first sinner came home, and it has not stopped. One day the whole family will sit down together at the marriage supper of the Lamb, and the joy that began on that road will fill the new creation.
verseByVerse.note: A fattened calf was kept for the greatest celebrations.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. And he said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. He called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. And he said to him: your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.

Now his older son was in the field. The story could have ended with the feast, but Jesus is telling it to the Pharisees (v. 2), and now comes their part. The older son is working, dutiful, as always. It is where he has been all day and every day. Whatever else is true of him, he is not a bad son by any ordinary measure. He is out working while his brother is being kissed at the gate.

He heard music and dancing. Celebration. He hears it before he understands it: music from his own house, and he has no idea why. That detail is doing work. It means nobody sent for him. A party is under way at his father’s expense, involving the whole village, and the elder son of the household learns about it by getting close enough to hear the band.

And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. He does not go in and ask his father; he stops outside, gets hold of a servant and interrogates him. Which is the first sign of the distance, and it is a considerable one. He is standing in his own yard, treating his own home as somewhere he needs to be briefed about before entering.

Your brother has come. The servant says your brother, without hesitation. The elder son will refuse the word in three verses’ time. The servant’s answer is entirely artless and entirely accurate, and it contains every fact the elder brother will later distort.

The brother who went looking. The elder son will not use the word brother, and he never went out to look for the boy. The parable leaves that gap, and the one telling it fills it. He is the Son who left his Father’s side to come and find his lost brothers, and who is not ashamed to call them brothers (Hebrews 2:11). Where the elder son counted the cost of the calf, this Son paid the cost of the feast. This is not a hidden meaning in the story, but the contrast it invites: the brother the younger son needed, and did not have, came in person to tell it.

Because he has received him back safe and sound. The word (hygiainonta) means healthy, whole. The father’s joy is simply that his son is back. That is the reason given, and it is worth weighing. Not because your brother has proved himself, not because he has paid anything back. The stated cause of the celebration is simply that he is home and he is well. A servant who has been in that house all his life has understood the father exactly. The son standing in the yard is about to demonstrate that he never has.

Can someone be in the church and still outside the feast? Yes, and this is the most searching part of the chapter. The older son lives on the estate, works the fields and keeps the rules, and he does not know his father’s heart. It is possible to grow up in a Christian home, serve faithfully for decades, hold sound doctrine, and still relate to God as an employer rather than a Father, and to grace as something for other people. The test is not how long you have been in the field. It is whether the music of grace makes you glad.

In a sentence. The older son, returning from the field, heard music and dancing, and was told his brother had come home and his father was celebrating his safe return.

On a Tuesday. When others come to Christ, do you join the celebration or stand outside asking questions? Notice your first reaction the next time you hear of someone’s conversion or restoration, especially someone who hurt others or who seems not to have paid for it. If it is suspicion, go in anyway, and ask God to tune your heart to the music.

For worship. The Father’s house is full of music because the Father is full of joy, and he needs no reason beyond this: the lost is home, safe and sound. Safe and sound is the Son’s report on all his people. He will bring every one the Father gave him through the far country and the famine and the dark, and on the last day present them whole before the Father’s face, without a single one missing, and the music will rise again.

verseByVerse.quote: But he was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him.

But he was angry and refused to go in. Neither verb is a passing mood. He was angry, a settled state like the Pharisees’ grumbling (v. 2), and he refused to go in, a public insult as great as the younger son’s demand, since every guest knows he is outside. The younger son had shamed his father by leaving; the elder is now shaming him by standing in the yard.

Two sons outside. The lost son is inside; the good son is outside, by his own choice. One went to a far country; one is standing just outside the door. The distance is not measured in miles.

His father came out and entreated him. For the second time in one evening the old man goes out to a son who has humiliated him. It is the same movement as the running in verse 20: he does not summon the boy or send a servant. He walks out of his own celebration and goes to find him. Entreated (parekalei) means urged, begged, pleaded. There is no command in it. The father, who has every right to order his son indoors, stands in the dark asking. God’s love pursues the self-righteous as well as the openly sinful. Jesus is pleading with the Pharisees, through this very parable.

Is God kind to sinners and severe to the religious? Not in this parable. The father goes out twice, and the second time is harder, because the second son does not want to be found. Whatever else the elder brother is about to say, he says it to a father who came out and asked. And there is a warning in the staging for anyone who has ever been the one outside. Standing in the yard feels like taking a position. It usually is just standing in a yard, in the dark, near a house where people are happy, waiting to be persuaded to enjoy something you have already decided not to enjoy. The father will not force him in. The door is open, the music is audible, the invitation has been delivered in person, and after that the yard is a choice.

In a sentence. The older son was angry and refused to go in, so his father came out and pleaded with him.

On a Tuesday. If you are standing in the yard about something, resentful of how God has blessed someone else, angry that grace has gone where you think it should not, recognise the father’s voice pleading with you. Go in. And if you lead or love someone who is standing outside, go out to them as the father did, gently and more than once.

For worship. The same love that ran down the road walks out into the dark yard. It is the love of the Son who wept over Jerusalem as he drew near to it (19:41), who had longed to gather her children as a hen gathers her brood (13:34), and who pleaded with the grumblers by this very story. There is no one too far gone for him, and no one too proud for him to plead with. Such is the patience of the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who does not want the elder son any more than the younger to be left outside.

verseByVerse.quote: but he answered his father, ‘Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he answered his father: look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!

Look, these many years I have served you. There is no respectful Father: the younger son began Father; the older son does not. The word (douleuō) means I have slaved for you. Not lived with, not worked alongside. He thinks of himself as a slave, not a son. He thinks he is stating a credential, and it is the whole tragedy in one verb: he has been a son for the entire story and has experienced it as employment. The younger son wanted to come back as a hired servant; the older son had been living like one all along.

And I never disobeyed your command. Outward obedience, like the rich ruler (18:21) and Paul before conversion (Philippians 3:6). But his heart was far from his father. He was as lost as his brother, though he never left home.

Yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. He wanted to celebrate, but with his friends, not his father. Even his imagined party does not have his father in it. A young goat is a modest animal, a small grievance carefully preserved, and the complaint is, as a matter of fact, false. Two-thirds of that estate had been his since verse 12. He could have killed a goat any week he liked. He had been living on his own property, asking permission he did not need, and resenting a father who had already given him everything. Self-righteousness is always resentful of grace.

But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes. Not my brother, but this son of yours: the servant managed the word without effort; the elder son cuts the boy out of his own family. And he announces the worst interpretation, because he wants his brother’s sin remembered. Luke never said that. Verse 13 says reckless living and nothing more. He does not know, and he reaches for the detail that will do the most damage. Resentment fills in the blanks in the worst available way and calls it honesty.

You killed the fattened calf for him! He cannot bear grace being given to someone who does not deserve it. This is the Pharisees’ complaint, this man receives sinners: not a complaint about justice, but about somebody else’s welcome.

A friend of tax collectors and sinners. The elder son will not call the sinner brother. His enemies had already given Jesus the opposite name. Look at him, they said, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners (7:34). It was meant as an insult, and he wore it. Where the elder son kept the record of his brother’s sins and refused the relationship, Jesus took the relationship and carried the record away. The name the grumblers threw at him is the best news the far country has ever heard.

How do I know if I am an older brother? Watch for the signs this verse gives. You keep score of your service and feel God owes you. You find obedience a grind, done for reward rather than love. You resent it when God is generous to people with worse records. You find it easy to remember other people’s sins in detail and hard to call them brother. You enjoy your friends more than your Father. Most of us find some of this in ourselves. The cure is not to try harder at being a good son. It is to see that you, too, have needed grace every day, and that everything the Father has was always yours as a gift.

In a sentence. The older son complained that he had slaved for his father for years without reward, while the father had killed the fattened calf for this son of his who had wasted everything on prostitutes.

On a Tuesday. Do you resent God’s grace to others? Do you obey God as a slave seeking wages, or as a son who loves him? Self-righteousness can keep you out of the feast as surely as rebellion. Think of one person whose sins you rehearse, aloud or in your head, and this week call them brother or sister in your prayers, and ask God to bless them.

For worship. The Father bears with the insults of both his sons, the one who wished him dead and the one who served him as a slave. He is not a hard master. He is the giver of every goat and every calf, the owner of the cattle on a thousand hills, and he gives himself to his children. And the true Son, who alone could have said I never disobeyed your command, and said it truly, did not resent the Father’s welcome of sinners. He died to make it possible.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to him: son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.

Son. The word (teknon) means child, the tender word, the one a parent uses. Despite the insult, the father speaks with love. After everything that has just been said in the yard, the father’s first word is an endearment.

You are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. Everything he wanted, he already had: his father’s presence, and the whole estate. He did not need to earn it. He only had to enjoy it as a son. He has had every day for years the one thing his brother threw away, nearness to his father, and he has been counting goats. And all that is mine is yours is a flat statement of fact that demolishes the complaint. The Pharisees had the Scriptures, the covenants, the temple, God’s presence (Romans 9:4–5), all theirs, but they lived as servants, not sons. And the sharpest thing in the parable is not aimed at the disreputable. A man can live in his Father’s house for forty years, keep every rule, resent the whole arrangement, and never once take anything out of a storehouse he has always owned.

It was fitting to celebrate and be glad. The word (edei) means it was necessary, it was right: the word of divine necessity Luke has used all through this Gospel of what God’s purpose requires. How could anyone not celebrate this? Not it was generous of me, and not I hope you will understand. Given what has happened, a party was the only proper response, and any other response would have been wrong.

The same must. Luke’s readers know this necessity from the lips of Jesus. The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected and be killed, and on the third day be raised (9:22). To Zacchaeus he will say, today I must stay at your house (19:5). After the resurrection he will ask, was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? (24:26). The party over a returning sinner is necessary in the same way the cross is necessary: both are what God’s purpose of mercy requires. The feast had to be held because the Son had to die.

For this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found. Not this son of yours, but your brother, and the refrain repeated. The father reminds him of the relationship he has disowned. He hands the word back, corrected. There is only one relationship in dispute here, and it is not the one between the father and the younger boy.

The open ending. Jesus does not tell us whether the older son went in. The story stops. Because the Pharisees and scribes, listening, had to decide: would they come in to the feast, and rejoice that sinners were coming home? Or would they stay outside? Every self-righteous person faces the same choice. Jesus has put the grumblers of verse 2 on the doorstep of a lit house, with the music still playing, and left them there. The ending was theirs to write. It still is.

What does all that is mine is yours mean for me as a Christian? It means that in Christ you are an heir, not a hired hand. All things are yours, Paul says, whether the world or life or death or the present or the future, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s (1 Corinthians 3:21–23). The Father’s presence, his promises, his Spirit, the riches of his grace, and an inheritance kept in heaven for you (1 Peter 1:4) are already yours, not as wages but as a son’s portion. So pray as a child who has access, give as one who cannot be impoverished, and serve as one who is already loved.

In a sentence. The father told his older son that he had always been with him and owned everything, but they had to celebrate, because his brother had been dead and was alive, lost and was found.

On a Tuesday. Take something from the storehouse today. Thank God for one specific blessing you have always had and never enjoyed. Spend time with your Father not because you must, but because you may. And when you hear that a lost brother or sister has come home, go in to the feast.

For worship. All that is mine is yours: the Father said it to a resentful son standing in the dark, and he says it to every child he has brought in. The Father who ran to the younger son and walked out to the elder is the God who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, and with him graciously gives us all things (Romans 8:32). His house is never full of servants only. It is full of children, every one an heir, and the music has not stopped.

parallels.desc: to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants

15.text: <sup>1</sup> Now the tax collectors and sinners were all drawing near to hear him. <sup>2</sup> And the Pharisees and the scribes grumbled, saying, “This man receives sinners and eats with them.” <sup>3</sup> So he told them this parable: <sup>4</sup> “What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? <sup>5</sup> And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing. <sup>6</sup> And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost.’ <sup>7</sup> Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance. <sup>8</sup> “Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and seek diligently until she finds it? <sup>9</sup> And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found the coin that I had lost.’ <sup>10</sup> Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.” <sup>11</sup> And he said, “There was a man who had two sons. <sup>12</sup> And the younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of property that is coming to me.’ And he divided his property between them. <sup>13</sup> Not many days later, the younger son gathered all he had and took a journey into a far country, and there he squandered his property in reckless living. <sup>14</sup> And when he had spent everything, a severe famine arose in that country, and he began to be in need. <sup>15</sup> So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs. <sup>16</sup> And he was longing to be fed with the pods that the pigs ate, and no one gave him anything. <sup>17</sup> “But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! <sup>18</sup> I will arise and go to my father, and I will say to him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. <sup>19</sup> I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Treat me as one of your hired servants.”’ <sup>20</sup> And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him. <sup>21</sup> And the son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ <sup>22</sup> But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring quickly the best robe, and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet. <sup>23</sup> And bring the fattened calf and kill it, and let us eat and celebrate. <sup>24</sup> For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.’ And they began to celebrate. <sup>25</sup> “Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. <sup>26</sup> And he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. <sup>27</sup> And he said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound.’ <sup>28</sup> But he was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him, <sup>29</sup> but he answered his father, ‘Look, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed your command, yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might celebrate with my friends. <sup>30</sup> But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your property with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him!’ <sup>31</sup> And he said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. <sup>32</sup> It was fitting to celebrate and be glad, for this your brother was dead, and is alive; he was lost, and is found.’”

16.title: Money, the Law, and the Great Divide
16.overview:
Luke 16 is one of the most challenging chapters in all the Gospels. It contains two sustained teachings — the Parable of the Dishonest Manager and the story of the Rich Man and Lazarus — that bracket a cluster of sayings about the law, divorce, and divine valuation. What holds it together is money as a spiritual diagnostic: how a person handles wealth reveals the true condition of their heart before God.

The Parable of the Dishonest Manager shocks its hearers because Jesus appears to commend a fraudster. The commendation, however, is carefully qualified: the manager is praised not for his dishonesty but for his shrewdness — his ability to think clearly about the future and use present resources to secure it. Jesus turns the parable into an indictment of disciples who exercise less practical wisdom in spiritual things than worldly people do in material ones.

The story of the Rich Man and Lazarus is the only parable in which a character has a proper name, and it closes the chapter with one of Scripture's most sobering statements: if people will not be persuaded by Moses and the Prophets, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead. This is both a claim about the sufficiency of Scripture and a prophecy about the response to Jesus's own resurrection.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Parable of the Dishonest Manager
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus tells this to his disciples while the Pharisees are also listening (v.14), which is why the chapter ends where it does.

The manager is an oikonomos — the steward of a large estate, usually a slave or freedman, who held the accounts, made contracts and ran the property in his master's name. And what he had been doing is what the prodigal did in the far country (15:13). The parable opens with a second man squandering another man's property.

Note the order of the dismissal: he is sacked first and the audit demanded second, which means he is finished and the paperwork is a formality. What that gives him is a gap — no longer trusted, not yet stripped of authority, the debtors not yet told, the seal still in his hand. The whole parable turns on that interval, and so does the application.

His options are closed: he cannot dig, and he will not beg — and the difference in the two clauses is a fair sample of the man. He is not able to dig; he is ashamed to beg. His pride survives his disgrace intact.

What he then buys is not money. He does not embezzle; what he wants is houses — an open door somewhere when he has nothing. He has worked out, at the last possible moment, that when the wealth goes the only thing left is relationships, and that the wealth can be converted into them while he still controls it.

The reductions are uneven — fifty per cent on oil, twenty on wheat — which is the clue. If he were simply defrauding his master the discounts would be arbitrary; that they differ by commodity suggests he is removing something that varied by commodity, and the obvious candidate is his own commission. On that reading he waives his fee and takes a large personal loss, which would explain the otherwise baffling commendation.

It cannot be settled with certainty and the parable does not require it. What is commended is neither the honesty nor the dishonesty but the structure of the act: he took a resource about to stop being his and spent all of it, immediately, on the only thing that would outlast the deadline.
verseByVerse.theology:
The commendation is careful about what it does and does not say. He is still called the dishonest manager. What is praised is his shrewdness: practical intelligence, the ability to see a situation clearly and act. A commander can admire an enemy's manoeuvre without approving the war.

“Sons of light” was a term the devout used of themselves — the Qumran community wrote a whole scroll about the war between the sons of light and the sons of darkness. Jesus grants the title and then says the other side is better at reading a situation and acting in time.

The observation is simply true, which is what makes it sting. A man will plan a pension he may never draw, take advice about a mortgage, insure a house he expects to keep. Set beside that the way the same qualities are deployed in the things of God by people who genuinely believe they will stand before him: the forward thinking stops, and a man who would never let a financial decision drift leaves the whole of his spiritual life to it.

The three descriptions of money in vv.10-12 are each deflating. It is unrighteous — the currency of a fallen order, and nobody's money is clean all the way back. It is a very little, said to people for whom it was the difference between eating and not eating. And it is another's. But the promise on the other side is easily missed: the true riches, and that which is your own. There is something coming that will actually belong to you.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 9 is the hardest sentence in the chapter and needs facing. Read flatly it appears to say a man can purchase his welcome into heaven — and it has been read that way in defence of almsgiving as accumulated merit.

Who are “they”? Three readings are held by careful Christians: the friends themselves, the angels, or — most likely — God himself, whose name the wording leaves unspoken.

And on whether salvation is for sale, the verse answers itself in three words that are easy to read past: when it fails. The money is explicitly the thing that runs out. Whatever else a currency guaranteed to become worthless may be, it is not the purchase price of eternity — and in this very chapter a rich man's fortune procures him not one drop of water.

What the verse teaches is that generosity is evidence, not currency. The paragraph ends four verses later with “you cannot serve God and money,” which is where the saying is travelling.

And that closing sentence is a statement about what is possible, not advice about priorities. A man may hold two jobs; nobody has ever had two owners. Note too that both outcomes are the same outcome — whichever way it falls, one master gets the loyalty and the other the contempt. Most people serving money would sincerely say they love God, and the conflict only becomes visible when the two masters give conflicting orders.

verseByVerse.quote: He also said to the disciples, 'There was a rich man who had a manager, and charges were brought to him that this man was wasting his possessions. And he called him and said to him, ‘What is this that I hear about you? Turn in the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
He also said to the disciples: there was a rich man who had a manager, and charges were brought to him that this man was wasting his possessions. And he called him and said to him: what is this that I hear about you? Turn in the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager.

Meaning first. Luke 16 is about money, and through money about the heart, eternity and the word of God. It has three movements: a dishonest manager who acts shrewdly before his dismissal takes effect (vv. 1–13); the money-loving Pharisees who sneer, and the permanence of God’s law (vv. 14–18); and a rich man and a poor man whose places are reversed at death (vv. 19–31). The puzzling first parable has a clear point: everything we hold belongs to Someone else, the arrangement is ending, and the wise use what they still control for what will last. The chapter ends at a grave someone was about to leave, with a Bible in the reader’s hands.

The setting. Chapter 15 answered the grumbling Pharisees with three stories of the lost being found. This chapter is spoken to the disciples, though the Pharisees are still listening (v. 14), which is why it ends where it does. One word ties the two chapters together: the manager is wasting, diaskorpizōn, scattering, his master’s possessions, the verb Luke used of the younger son squandering his inheritance in the far country (15:13). The prodigal was welcomed home by a father; the manager will have to find a welcome by his wits.

There was a rich man who had a manager. The manager is an oikonomos, the steward of a large estate, usually a slave or a freedman, who held the accounts, made contracts, lent goods, collected rents and ran the property in his master’s name. He had the seal and the keys, and with absentee landlords common in Galilee he could do a great deal of damage before anybody opened the books.

Charges were brought to him that this man was wasting his possessions. Whether by incompetence or dishonesty, the property was leaking away. And notice what the man does not do when he is confronted. He does not dispute the charges. Luke never says whether they were true, but the manager’s silence, and his immediate move to plan for unemployment, answer the question well enough.

Turn in the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager. The dismissal is announced first and the audit demanded second: he is finished, and the paperwork is a formality. What that gives him is a gap. He is no longer trusted and not yet stripped of authority; the debtors have not been told; the seal is still in his hand. The whole parable turns on that interval, and so does the application. Every person in this chapter is holding something on somebody else’s behalf, has been told the arrangement is ending, and has an unspecified amount of time left in which the seal still works.

The Steward who lost nothing. Set beside this manager the one who is telling the story. Jesus too had been entrusted with his Father’s house. Hebrews says that Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son (Hebrews 3:5–6). John records him saying that this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me (John 6:39). Every other steward in Scripture is accused of something sooner or later. This one never was, and when charges were brought against him at the end, they were false (23:2, 14).

Who is the manager meant to be? Not a cipher for any one person, and the parable does not need us to decide whether he stands for the Pharisees, for Israel’s leaders or for the disciples. He is a picture of every human being before God. Everything you have, your money, your body, your time, your gifts, your years, belongs to God, and you are its steward (1 Corinthians 4:2, 7). The notice of dismissal has already been served: it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment (Hebrews 9:27). The only open question is what you will do with the time in between.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a rich man who, hearing that his manager was wasting his property, dismissed him and demanded his accounts.

On a Tuesday. Look at your bank statement, your diary and your mirror, and say over each of them: this is not mine, I am managing it. Then ask the question the manager was forced to ask, the one that most people leave until a hospital corridor: when the books are handed in, what will they show? You do not need to be afraid to ask it. Asking it now, while the seal still works, is the whole point of the story.

For worship. The faithful Steward rendered his account in full, with nails in his hands, and it was found perfect. And the astonishing thing is that the account he rendered is the one God now reads over the wasteful stewards who trust him. When our books are opened, they show his faithfulness, not our waste. We scattered our Master’s goods; he gathered us, and the audit we dreaded has become the place where his perfect record is read out in our name.
verseByVerse.note: A manager (steward) ran an estate for his master, often with wide powers to make deals in his name.

verseByVerse.quote: And the manager said to himself, ‘What shall I do, since my master is taking the management away from me? I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg. I have decided what to do, so that when I am removed from management, people may receive me into their houses.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The manager said to himself: what shall I do, since my master is taking the management away from me? I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg. I have decided what to do, so that when I am removed from management, people may receive me into their houses.

And the manager said to himself, What shall I do? The parable now goes inside his head, which is where Luke has taken us twice already: the rich fool talking to his own soul (12:17), and the prodigal coming to himself in the pigsty (15:17).
