It is the same construction each time, and it is always a man at the end of his options. But this man, unlike the rich fool, thinks ahead.

I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg. Two doors, and both shut. A steward’s life was clerical, and he knows his back will not last a week of labouring. And note the difference in the two clauses: he is not able to dig, and he is ashamed to beg. The first is a limitation and the second is a decision, and it is a fair sample of the man. His pride survives his disgrace intact.

I have decided what to do, so that when I am removed from management, people may receive me into their houses. The tense suggests a flash of clarity: I know what I will do. There is the plan, and the thing to notice is what he is buying. Not money: he does not embezzle for himself. What he wants is houses, an open door and a place at a table when he has nothing. He has worked out, at the last possible moment, that when the wealth goes the only thing left is relationships, and that the wealth, while he still controls it, can be converted into them. That is the entire insight of the parable. What is striking is how late it comes: it took a dismissal notice to make him ask what any of it was for.

Who will receive me? The manager’s question has already been answered, one chapter earlier, in the complaint of the Pharisees: this man receives sinners (15:2). The man who has nothing left to trade, who can neither dig nor bring himself to beg, does not have to buy his way into a house. There is one who receives people precisely when they come with nothing. The manager schemes for a welcome because he does not know the Host. The sinners at Jesus’ table had found one without scheming at all.

Is it wrong to plan for my future, or to save for retirement? No. The manager is not blamed for planning; he is held up as an example of it. Scripture commends the ant that stores in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8) and calls a man who will not provide for his household worse than an unbeliever (1 Timothy 5:8). The rich fool of chapter 12 was not condemned for having barns but for being rich toward himself and not toward God (12:21). The question this verse presses is not whether you plan but how far ahead. Most people plan carefully for thirty years and not at all for eternity. Prudent saving is stewardship; a pension that has become your security in place of God is idolatry, and only you and he know which yours is.

In a sentence. The manager, unable to dig and ashamed to beg, came up with a plan to make people welcome him into their homes after he lost his job.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself the manager’s question, but further out: when I am removed, not from a job but from this life, who will receive me, and into what? Then notice whether you have actually given that question a single hour of the planning you have given your holidays this year.

For worship. The manager had to scheme for a house to receive him, and was ashamed to beg. We are received on other terms. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (9:58), was cast out of the city, and was laid in a borrowed tomb, so that the beggars who come to him with nothing are given a room in his Father’s house that he went ahead to prepare (John 14:2). We do not have to be shrewd enough to secure a welcome. He has secured it.

verseByVerse.quote: So, summoning his master's debtors one by one, he said to the first, ‘How much do you owe my master?’ He said, ‘A hundred measures of oil.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty.’ Then he said to another, ‘And how much do you owe?’ He said, ‘A hundred measures of wheat.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, and write eighty.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Summoning his master’s debtors one by one, he said to the first: how much do you owe my master? He said: a hundred measures of oil. He said to him: take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty. Then he said to another: and how much do you owe? He said: a hundred measures of wheat. He said to him: take your bill, and write eighty.

So, summoning his master’s debtors one by one. One by one, and quickly, before the news gets out. These are not petty debtors but tenant farmers who paid rent in produce, or merchants who had bought on credit, and they have serious contracts.

A hundred measures of oil. The ESV notes the size: a hundred measures of oil was about 875 gallons (3,300 litres), the yield of perhaps 150 olive trees. A hundred measures of wheat was about 1,000 bushels, the crop of something like a hundred acres. Each debt represents years of a labourer’s wages.

Take your bill, and sit down quickly and write fifty. The debtor writes it himself, in his own hand, on his own bond, which is important. What the manager produces is a document that looks entirely legitimate and carries no trace of him. The reduction on the oil is fifty measures, worth about 500 denarii, more than a year and a half’s wages; the reduction on the wheat, write eighty, is twenty measures, worth about the same. Each debtor now owes the manager a very large favour.

Was it dishonest? The reductions are curiously uneven: fifty per cent on the oil, twenty per cent on the wheat. That unevenness has led some scholars to suggest that the manager was removing something that varied by commodity: his own commission, the surcharge a steward customarily added to a contract, or the interest that the law forbade charging to fellow Jews (Deuteronomy 23:19). On that reading he is waiving his own fee to buy goodwill. But Jesus calls him dishonest (v. 8), and the simplest reading is that he cheated his master to make friends of the debtors, who would now be grateful and in his debt. It cannot be settled with certainty, and the parable does not require it to be. Jesus commends neither the honesty nor the dishonesty. What is commended is the structure of the act.

The structure of the act. He took a resource that was about to stop being his, and spent all of it, immediately, on the only thing that would still exist after the deadline. And notice the tempo, because it is part of what is being praised. Sit down quickly. He summons them one by one and gets it done before the news travels, because the window is measured in hours and he knows it. Nobody in this parable is described as clever. He is described as fast.

Five hundred, fifty, and nothing. Luke’s reader has met two debtors before. At a Pharisee’s table Jesus told of a moneylender with two debtors, one owing five hundred denarii and the other fifty, and when they could not pay, he cancelled the debt of both (7:41–42). Then he turned to the weeping woman and said, your sins are forgiven (7:48). The manager trims a bill by roughly that larger sum to buy a welcome for himself. Jesus is the creditor in person, and he does not trim. He cancels, and he does it for people who could never return the favour.

In a sentence. The manager called in his master’s debtors and quickly had them reduce their bills, making them indebted to him.

On a Tuesday. The world is quick about its own interests. A man who learns that his firm is closing does not drift; he updates his CV that night. Ask what you know about eternity that you have been treating as if there were all the time in the world. A reconciliation postponed, a sin you meant to deal with, a gift you meant to give, a conversation about Christ you meant to have with your father: write one down, and do it before the week is out.

For worship. The manager reduced other men’s debts to save himself; the gospel turns the picture inside out. Our Master did not trim our bill from a hundred to fifty. He took the record of debt that stood against us, with its legal demands, and set it aside, nailing it to the cross (Colossians 2:14). The cancellation that costs a creditor nothing on paper cost him his life. The manager wrote fifty to buy friends; Christ wrote nothing on our bond, because he paid everything, and then called us his friends (John 15:15).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the size of these debts: a hundred measures of oil was about 800–900 gallons, a hundred measures of wheat about 1,000–1,200 bushels. Cutting them won the debtors’ gratitude.

verseByVerse.quote: The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness. For the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness. For the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light.

The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness. The surprise of the parable, and the sentence is careful about what it does and does not say. He is still called the dishonest manager, literally the steward of unrighteousness, a man characterised by it. The commendation does not rehabilitate him. What is praised is that he acted phronimōs: with prudence, practical intelligence, the ability to see a situation clearly and act on it. A commander can admire an enemy’s manoeuvre without approving of the war, and that is roughly what is happening here. The master, a man of the world, recognised a clever move when he saw one, even at his own expense.

Who is the master who commends him? Most likely the rich man in the story, since Jesus speaks in his own voice in the next sentence and again in verse 9 (and I tell you). Some take it as the Lord himself. Either way, what is praised is the manager’s foresight, not his dishonesty.

For the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light. Here is the sting, and it is one of the most uncomfortable sentences Jesus ever spoke about his own people. The sons of this world are worldly people, who live for this age. The sons of light are God’s people (John 12:36; Ephesians 5:8; 1 Thessalonians 5:5). It was a title the devout used of themselves; the Qumran community wrote a whole scroll about the war between the sons of light and the sons of darkness. Jesus grants the title and then says the other side is better at this. Better at what, exactly? At dealing with their own generation: at reading a situation, seeing where it is going, and acting in time.

Sons of the light. The title is not a native quality. Zechariah sang that the sunrise from on high would visit us, to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death (1:78–79), and Simeon held that light in his arms (2:32). John records Jesus saying, while you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light (John 12:36), and in the same breath, walk while you have the light (John 12:35). A son of light is someone on whom Christ has risen. And the shrewdness Jesus asks of them is the shrewdness of people who know that the light is shining now and will not wait.

The ordinary competence of the world. The observation is simply true, which is what makes it sting. A man will take advice about a mortgage, insure a house, plan a career over decades. Set beside that the way the same people, who genuinely believe they will stand before God, approach the things of God. The forward thinking stops. A man who would never leave a financial decision to drift leaves the whole of his spiritual life to it. Jesus is not asking his disciples to become worldly. He is asking them to become as intelligent about eternity as they already are about money.

What it does not mean. Jesus is not commending dishonesty, or teaching that the end justifies the means. A parable can use a bad man to make a good point. Luke will do it again with the unjust judge, who gives a widow justice only to be rid of her (18:1–8). The argument in both runs from the lesser to the greater: if even a scoundrel acts decisively to secure a few years of comfort, how much more should the sons of light act for eternity. The point is the manager’s urgency and foresight, not his ethics.

How would I actually be shrewd about eternity? The same way a sensible person is shrewd about anything: by looking at where things are going and acting now. Shrewdness for the kingdom looks like setting your giving before you see what is left, not after. It looks like choosing a church, a house and a job with an eye on what they will do to your soul and your children’s, not only on salary and schools. It looks like investing in people, in friendships with believers, in hospitality, in the young, because people are the only part of this world that goes on into the next. And it looks like dealing with sin today rather than meaning to, because the window is not as wide as it seems.

In a sentence. The master praised the dishonest manager for his shrewdness, for worldly people are often shrewder in their affairs than God’s people are in theirs.

On a Tuesday. Pick one area of your life where you are clearly competent: your work, your finances, your garden, your fantasy football. Notice the planning, the attention, the willingness to act. Then put the same intelligence to one eternal thing this week: your prayer, your children’s souls, your giving, a neighbour who does not know Christ. Be as thoughtful, decisive and wise in eternal matters as worldly people are about money and career.

For worship. The wisest Son of Light who ever lived did not merely see a crisis coming; he walked into it on purpose. He set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51), knowing the hour and the cost, and spent everything he had, his reputation, his body, his life, on the one thing that would still exist after the deadline: a people for his Father. No one has ever been as shrewd for eternity as Jesus was for us.
verseByVerse.note: The master praises the manager’s shrewdness, not his dishonesty.

verseByVerse.quote: And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth, so that when it fails they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.

And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of unrighteous wealth. The application, and the hardest sentence in the chapter. Unrighteous wealth renders mammon, a Semitic word for money or possessions; literally, the mammon of unrighteousness. It does not necessarily mean wealth gained dishonestly. It means wealth that belongs to this unrighteous world, the currency of a fallen order, which so often leads to sin and is inevitably entangled with things God hates. Nobody’s money is clean all the way back. And Jesus says: use it. Use it wisely, to make friends, by giving to the poor and supporting the work of God.

So that when it fails. When money runs out, or when you die and it is useless to you. The money is explicitly described as the thing that fails, and a currency guaranteed to become worthless is not the purchase price of eternity.

They may receive you into the eternal dwellings. The manager made friends who would receive him into their houses; you can make friends who will welcome you into eternal homes. Who are they? Some take it of the friends themselves: those you have helped with your money, the poor and those who came to faith through the gospel you supported, standing at the door of the next life, glad to see their benefactor arrive. Some take it of angels, who will carry Lazarus a few verses later. And many take it as the Semitic way of saying you will be received without naming God directly, a reverent third-person plural. Luke has used the identical idiom already: this night your soul is required of you (12:20), where the Greek literally reads they require your soul, and nobody supposes a committee. Either way the point is the same: use money now with an eye on eternity. Lay up treasure in heaven (12:33).

Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. Luke’s second volume shows who stands at that door. As the stones fell on Stephen, he saw the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God, and he prayed, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit (Acts 7:56, 59). It is the same verb as the manager’s hope to be received. The friends made by generosity may be glad to see us, but the welcome itself belongs to the risen Christ. He is the one who receives his people into the eternal dwellings, and he does it as a host, not as a creditor collecting on the investment.

What it does not mean. Not that you can buy your way into heaven. Read flatly, the verse appears to say a man can purchase his welcome by spending money on the right people, and it has been read that way, in defence of almsgiving as a work that accumulates merit. Luke will not let that stand. The tax collector who could offer nothing but his beaten breast went home justified (18:13–14); the criminal a few hours from death bought nothing whatever and was told he would be with Christ in Paradise that day (23:43); and in this very chapter a rich man’s fortune procures him not one drop of water. If money could buy an eternal dwelling, the man in torment was the best-funded soul in the story. Salvation is by grace. But how you use money shows where your heart is, and true faith is generous. Generosity is evidence, not currency. The paragraph ends four verses later with you cannot serve God and money, which is where this saying is travelling: how a man treats his wealth shows which master owns him.

So how much should I give, and to whom? Scripture sets no fixed percentage for the Christian, but it sets a direction and a spirit. Give regularly and in proportion to what you have been given (1 Corinthians 16:2); give cheerfully, not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7); give first to the ministry of the word in your own church (Galatians 6:6) and to the poor, especially fellow believers (Galatians 6:10). Many Christians find a tenth a sensible starting place, not a ceiling. The test of this verse is simple: ten years from now, will there be people, in heaven or on the way there, who are there partly because of what you did with your money? If the honest answer is no, start this month with something that costs you.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples to use worldly wealth to make friends, so that when it runs out they will be welcomed into eternal homes.

On a Tuesday. Take your last three months of spending and divide it, roughly, into what will be gone when you die and what will not. A meal shared with a lonely widow, the support of a missionary, a gift to a struggling family in your church, a Bible for a new believer: these go on. Most of the rest does not. How could you use your money this week in a way that will matter in eternity?

For worship. There will be faces at the door. Heaven is not an empty hall but a household, and those who come in are greeted by people they once fed, helped or told about Christ. And over all of them is the Host himself, who had nowhere to lay his head and now has many dwellings to give. We spend the mammon that fails; he spent the riches that never fail, and spent them on us. Every eternal dwelling was bought with his blood, and every welcome at its door is an echo of his.
verseByVerse.note: “Unrighteous wealth” renders mammon, a Semitic word for money or possessions.

parallels.desc: rich in good works, storing up treasure

verseByVerse.quote: 'One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches? And if you have not been faithful in that which is another's, who will give you that which is your own?
verseByVerse.commentary:
One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much, and one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches? And if you have not been faithful in that which is another’s, who will give you that which is your own?

One who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much. The parable is finished and the application widens, and this is the principle underneath it. Character does not change with scale. The way a man handles a small thing is not a warm-up for how he would handle a large one; it is a sample of it. Faithfulness is not a matter of the size of the task.

Subject to them in Nazareth. Luke gives us almost nothing of Jesus between the ages of twelve and thirty, and what he gives is this: he went down with his parents to Nazareth and was submissive to them, and increased in wisdom and in stature and in favour with God and man (2:51–52). Those were the very little years, unrecorded, ordinary, obedient. And when they were over, before a single miracle, the Father spoke from heaven: you are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased (3:22). The one who says faithful in a very little had been faithful in a very little for most of his life.

And one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much. Small dishonesty reveals a dishonest heart. Which cuts against a very common self-assessment. Most people privately believe they would be generous if they had more, honest if the stakes were higher, disciplined if the work were more important. Jesus says the evidence is already in, and it is in the small things, and it has been all along. The expense claim rounded up, the hours padded, the change not returned, the excuse that was not quite true: none of these is small in what it reveals.

If then you have not been faithful in the unrighteous wealth, who will entrust to you the true riches? Three descriptions of money follow, and each is deflating. It is unrighteous wealth: the currency of a fallen world. It is a very little. That is an extraordinary thing to say to people for whom money was the difference between eating and not eating, and Jesus says it anyway. Whatever the sums involved, compared with eternal things they are small. And the true riches are the spiritual riches of the kingdom: God’s word, his grace, responsibility in his kingdom, eternal reward. How we handle money is a test of whether we can be trusted with greater things.

If you have not been faithful in that which is another’s, who will give you that which is your own? And money is another’s. Not yours. It belongs to God, and you are the steward of the parable, running an estate you did not buy, and the audit is coming. Then the promise on the other side, which is easily missed under the warnings: that which is your own. There is something coming that will actually belong to you, an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven (1 Peter 1:4). Everything held now is on loan and will be handed back; what is being trained for is an inheritance that cannot be taken away, and the training ground is a bank account.

Why would God care so much about money? It seems beneath him, and in one sense it is: he owns the cattle on a thousand hills (Psalm 50:10) and does not need a penny of yours. He is not interested in the money. He is watching what a man does with a small sum of somebody else’s cash, because that is the most reliable evidence available of what he would do with anything. Money is concentrated life: hours of work, choices, security, pleasure, power, all in a form you can count. What you do with it shows what you love, and God cares very much about what you love.

Does this mean I earn my place in heaven by being faithful? No. That which is your own is a gift, an inheritance, and an inheritance is never earned by the heir. But God is pleased to reward the faithfulness that his grace produces, and Scripture speaks plainly of rewards differing (19:17; 1 Corinthians 3:12–15). The believer is not saved by his faithfulness; he is saved for it, and then, in a kindness that is almost embarrassing, rewarded for what God himself worked in him. As Augustine said, when God crowns our merits he crowns nothing but his own gifts.

In a sentence. Faithfulness in small things like money shows whether someone can be trusted with the true riches of the kingdom, which will be their own.

On a Tuesday. Be faithful in small things: your money, your time, your promises. They reveal and shape your character. This week, put right one small dishonesty you have let stand, the overcharge, the borrowed thing not returned, the claim that was not quite accurate. Nobody else may notice. That is exactly why it matters.

For worship. He was faithful in much as well, in the greatest trust ever given: a world’s redemption placed in his hands, and carried all the way to the cross without one corner cut. Because of that, the true riches are now his to give, and he gives them to stewards who were unfaithful in a very little. That which is your own is waiting, and it is safe, because it is kept by the faithful One who never lost anything entrusted to him.

verseByVerse.quote: No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.

No servant can serve two masters. Servant here is oiketēs, a household slave, and that settles the argument before it starts, because a man may hold two jobs but nobody has ever had two owners. A slave’s time, body and will belonged wholly to one person. Two owners would make impossible, conflicting demands. So the sentence is not advice about priorities. It is a statement about what is possible.

For either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. Whichever way round it falls, one master ends up with the loyalty and the other with the contempt. Hate and love is the Hebrew idiom for preference (14:26): one will always come first. But the strength of the language is deliberate. Not prefer and neglect, but love and hate, devoted and despise. The divided man does not end up mildly disappointing one of his masters; he ends up with something like contempt for him.

The conflict that rarely surfaces. Most people who are serving money would sincerely say they love God. What Jesus describes becomes visible only when the two masters give conflicting orders. The promotion that would mean leaving a faithful church. The giving that would mean a smaller car. The Sunday shift that pays double. That is why so much of life passes without the conflict ever surfacing, and why, when it does, a man often discovers which master he had been serving all along. The division most people actually attempt, God at the centre and money in a firm second place, is not a compromise between two positions. It is one of them, held by a man who has not noticed which.

You cannot serve God and money. The ESV notes that money renders mammon, an Aramaic term for wealth or property, and Jesus treats it here as a name. Not a thing you own but somebody who owns you. He has personified it, and the personification is the point: money is not a neutral tool in this sentence. It is a rival lord, and it makes demands, and it has slaves. It promises security, power and happiness, the things only God can give. Then the flat impossibility: you cannot. Not should not, and not will find it difficult. Money is a wonderful servant, but a terrible master. You must choose.

Him only shall you serve. One man has made this choice without wavering. In the wilderness the devil showed Jesus all the kingdoms of the world and offered him their authority and glory if he would worship him, and Jesus answered from Scripture: you shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve (4:5–8). Every promise mammon makes, security, power and possession, was laid in front of him at once, and he refused it, hungry, alone and with nothing. The one who says you cannot serve two masters is the one Servant who never tried.

How do I know which master I serve? Ask what you worry about, because worry is the prayer we pray to the god we fear will fail us. Ask what you would find hardest to give up if God asked. Ask whether your giving is the first line of the budget or the last. Ask whether money decides where you live, what church you attend and how much time you have for your family, or whether God does. And ask how you feel when the markets fall. A Christian may feel the loss; but if a bad month on the statement shakes your peace more than a month without prayer, mammon has a stronger claim on you than you thought.

Is it wrong to be rich? No. Abraham was very rich, and he is the host at the banquet a few verses later. Joseph of Arimathea was rich and a disciple (Matthew 27:57). Paul tells the rich not to be haughty or to set their hopes on uncertain riches, but on God, and to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share (1 Timothy 6:17–18). It is not wrong to have money; it is fatal to serve it. But Jesus speaks of the danger of wealth far more than of its blessing, because wealth makes the service so easy to slide into and so hard to notice.

In a sentence. No one can be a slave to two masters, and so you cannot serve both God and money.

On a Tuesday. Which master do you serve? Your bank statement and your diary will tell you. Read last month’s as if they belonged to a stranger and ask what that stranger loves. Then do one thing this week that only a servant of God would do with money: give something away that you will notice.

For worship. There is a Master worth serving with everything, and he is not a hard one. Mammon takes everything and gives back anxiety; this Lord gave everything and gives back rest. He was sold by a disciple who chose the other master, and the chief priests were glad and agreed to give him money (22:5). He let himself be bought so that we might be bought back, and the slaves of mammon he redeems he does not take as slaves but calls his friends.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “money” renders mammon.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–18 — The Law, the Kingdom, and Human Exaltation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Pharisees are described as lovers of money, which is a blunt thing to say about the most respected religious men in the country. But it was not a secret vice among them and did not feel like a vice at all, because the theology of the day connected prosperity with divine approval. A wealthy Pharisee could regard his estate as a testimonial.

Their response is not argument. They ridiculed him, and that is the tell. There is no counter-exegesis, no appeal to Scripture. Ridicule is the cheapest defence available and the most effective: it requires no reasoning and lets a whole room off the hook at once by making the speaker faintly absurd.

Jesus goes past the laughter to the machinery underneath it. “You justify yourselves before men” describes the exhausting business of maintaining a verdict in front of an audience. And “abomination” is a heavy word, not chosen loosely — in the Old Testament it is a standard word for idols. He is not saying human and divine values sometimes differ. He is putting visible success, honour and social standing in the same category as an idol.

Then two verses that must be held together. “The Law and the Prophets were until John” dates an era, and John stands on the seam — the last of the old order and the herald of the new (cf. 7:28). But “not one dot of the Law” will become void: the dot is the tiny projecting stroke that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another, and Jesus says the cosmos will go before one of them does.

The word holding them together is fulfilment. The Law's era as the way God's people related to him has closed; the Law itself has been kept — by the man saying this — and its moral claim stands exactly where it stood. What has changed is not the standard but who has met it.

Which is why the divorce saying follows, and the placing is not a change of subject. He has just been accused, in effect, of relaxing things, by the party of permissive divorce rulings. He takes the point where their own tradition had quietly loosened the Law and shows who is actually relaxing it.
verseByVerse.theology:
“Everyone forces his way into it” is a strange phrase and the translations divide: everyone is pressing in, or, as the ESV margin gives it, everyone is forcefully urged into it. Either way the point stands and it is not gentle: since John announced the King, entering the kingdom is no polite formality. It is entered the way a man presses through a closing door (cf. Matt. 11:12).

There is a quiet rebuke in the word everyone, spoken to men who have just sneered. Tax collectors and prostitutes are shoving their way in through a door these men are standing beside, discussing.

The two verses guard against two opposite errors that are always with the church. One man reads “the Law and the Prophets were until John” and concludes the commandments no longer trouble him — that grace has made the moral law a historical curiosity. Verse 17 exists to stop him. Another reads verse 17 and concludes nothing has changed at all — that he is still under a covenant of works and must produce a righteousness of his own. Verse 16 exists to stop him: the good news is preached, and it is entered by people forcing their way in with nothing in their hands.

And the permanence of the Law is why the sexual ethic is not negotiable. The Pharisees were known for liberal divorce interpretations — Hillel's school allowed it for almost any reason — and Jesus reaffirms the original design of Genesis 2:24 as the Law's continuing moral claim, not as something the kingdom relaxes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Luke gives the divorce saying flat, with no exception attached, and a reader who has only Luke will conclude that every divorce and remarriage is adultery. Set the whole New Testament out and the picture fills in: Matthew records the same teaching twice with an exception for sexual immorality (5:32; 19:9), and Paul adds desertion by an unbelieving spouse (1 Cor. 7:15). On that basis the Reformed churches have historically recognised two grounds, and that is the position confessed in the Westminster standards.

Luke leaves the exception out because he is giving the rule, not the case law — which is how anyone states a principle. A doctor who says “never take this on an empty stomach” is not contradicting the note in the leaflet. The exceptions are narrow doors in a solid wall, not the wall itself.

But there is a further question, and it is the one that keeps people out of church: what about the man or woman already divorced and already remarried on no ground the New Testament allows? Notice how Jesus himself handles it. He tells the woman at the well that she has had five husbands (John 4:18) — he calls them husbands, names the truth exactly, and does not instruct her to go back and unpick it. A second marriage, once made, is a real marriage; it is not an ongoing act of adultery but a covenant that exists and carries real obligations.

Where there was sin it is to be confessed and forgiven like every other sin, and then left at the cross rather than dragged out every morning. Paul lists adulterers among those who shall not inherit the kingdom, and then writes the sentence that has rescued more consciences than almost any other: “and such were some of you. But you were washed” (1 Cor. 6:9-11).

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things, and they ridiculed him. And he said to them, 'You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things, and they ridiculed him. And he said to them: you are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God.

The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, heard all these things. Luke tells us two things and the second follows from the first. Lovers of money is philargyroi, literally silver-lovers, and it is a blunt thing to say about the most respected religious men in the country. Not all Pharisees were wealthy, but the love of money did not feel like a vice, because the theology of the day connected prosperity with divine approval. The covenant blessings promised full barns to the obedient (Deuteronomy 28:1–14), and it was a short step to reading the balance sheet as a certificate of righteousness.

And they ridiculed him. The verb is vivid: literally they turned up their noses at him. A poor teacher from Galilee, with nowhere to lay his head, telling them about money! And that is the tell. They do not argue or appeal to Scripture. They sneer, which is what people do when something has landed and cannot be answered. Ridicule is the cheapest defence available: it costs nothing and lets a whole room off the hook by making the speaker faintly absurd.

You are those who justify yourselves before men. He goes straight past the laughter to the machinery underneath it. They made themselves look righteous in people’s eyes; their wealth and religious reputation impressed others. To justify yourself before men is the effort of maintaining a verdict in front of an audience, which is exhausting, and which is the only thing sustaining the position they have just defended with a sneer. It is the opposite of the tax collector who will stand at the back of the temple two chapters later, with no audience and no defence, and go home justified by God (18:14).

But God knows your hearts. He sees through appearances: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10). The verdict of the audience and the verdict of God are two different courts, and only one of them is final.

The one who reads hearts. The men who sneered had already watched this sentence at work. Again and again Luke says that Jesus knew their thoughts: when they questioned his right to forgive (5:22), when they watched to see whether he would heal (6:8), when his own disciples argued about greatness (9:47). At the Pharisee’s Sabbath dinner he answered a question nobody had spoken aloud (14:3). The one who says God knows your hearts is himself reading theirs as he says it. They were not being judged by a Galilean teacher’s opinion, but by the searching gaze of God in the face of a man.

For what is exalted among men is an abomination in the sight of God. Abomination, bdelygma, is a heavy word and it is not chosen loosely. In the Greek Old Testament it is the standard term for idols and for the practices of the nations, the things that provoked God to jealousy, and it is used of the proud in heart (Proverbs 16:5). So he is not saying merely that human and divine values sometimes differ. He is saying that the thing this society most admires, visible success, honour, religious reputation, the standing these men had spent their lives accumulating, when it flows from pride and self-love, is in the same category as an idol.

Does God hate success, then? No. God gives wealth, skill and honour, and Scripture praises the man skilful in his work (Proverbs 22:29). What is an abomination is the exaltation: success turned into a throne, reputation turned into a righteousness, the applause of men treated as the verdict of heaven. The same promotion can be received with gratitude by one man and worshipped by another. The question is not what you have achieved but what you are leaning on, and whose praise you are living for (John 5:44).

Is it wrong to care what people think of me? Not entirely. A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches (Proverbs 22:1), and an elder must be well thought of by outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7). But reputation is a by-product of faithfulness, not its goal. The danger begins when the audience becomes the judge: when you would rather be thought generous than be generous, thought godly than be godly. A simple test: what do you do when no one will ever know? Jesus told us to give, pray and fast in secret, and promised that the Father who sees in secret will reward (Matthew 6:4).

In a sentence. When the money-loving Pharisees sneered at him, Jesus said that they justified themselves before people, but God knows their hearts, and what people prize is detestable to God.

On a Tuesday. Make a list of the three things you most admire in other people, the qualities that make you think, I wish I were like that. Then hold each one up to the cross and ask whether God values it. Money, looks, wit, influence and confidence may come out quite differently from humility, faithfulness, and kindness to people who cannot repay. And notice when you reach for ridicule. Mockery of something true is often the sound of a conscience defending its savings.

For worship. God knows your hearts. To the Pharisees that was a threat; to the broken it is one of the most comforting sentences in the Bible. The God who sees through every pretence also sees through every despair, and is not fooled by our failures any more than by our successes. He knows the heart, and he gives a new one. The Lord whom they sneered at was exalted by God to the highest place precisely because he refused every exaltation among men (Philippians 2:8–9). What men despised, God crowned.

parallels.desc: the LORD looks on the heart

verseByVerse.quote: 'The Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone forces his way into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone forces his way into it.

The Law and the Prophets were until John. A hinge verse, and it divides history in two. The Law and the Prophets names the whole Old Testament, and Jesus dates its era: until John. Not abolished at John, as the following sentence makes emphatic, but the time of promise has closed, because what it pointed to has come. John stands on the seam. He is the last of the old-covenant prophets and the herald of the new, the bridge between the ages, which is what Jesus meant when he said no one born of women is greater than John, and yet the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he (7:28).

Since then the good news of the kingdom of God is preached. A new era has begun: the time of fulfilment. The kingdom has come in Jesus. And notice how it comes. Not argued, not required: announced, as news is announced. The verb is euangelizetai, the gospel is preached. The kingdom is not a programme for people to implement but a report of what God has done, and its centre is a person. In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus read Isaiah’s words about the one anointed to preach good news to the poor, rolled up the scroll and said, today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing (4:18–21). The era of promise ended because the Promised One was standing in the room.

And everyone forces his way into it. A difficult phrase, because the Greek verb can be read more than one way. It may be middle voice: everyone is pressing urgently to enter, with the earnest striving of 13:24 (strive to enter through the narrow door), as the tax collectors and sinners are doing. Or passive: everyone is being urged in, pressed to come, like the guests compelled in from the highways (14:23); the ESV notes this in its margin. Or, as in Matthew 11:12, it may speak of the kingdom suffering violence from its opponents. In Luke’s context, the first is most likely: people of all kinds are pressing into the kingdom, while the Pharisees stay outside.

Entered like a closing door. Either way the point stands, and it is not gentle. Since John announced the King, entering the kingdom is no polite formality. It is not drifted into. It is entered the way a man presses through a closing door: with decision, urgency, and everything he has. And there is a quiet rebuke in the word everyone, spoken to the men who have just sneered. Tax collectors and prostitutes are pushing their way in through a door these men are standing beside, discussing.

Does this mean I get into the kingdom by my own effort? No. The kingdom is preached as good news, and good news is received, not earned. The striving here is not the effort that earns entry but the urgency of a man who will not let anything keep him from the gift: not pride, not fear of what people think, not the pleasures he must leave behind. Those who press in are precisely those who have stopped trusting their own righteousness. And behind every human pressing in is the God who draws: no one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him (John 6:44). The urgency is ours; the power is his.

In a sentence. The era of the Law and the Prophets lasted until John; since then the good news of the kingdom is preached, and people are pressing into it.

On a Tuesday. Turn this verse on any settled congregation, and on any settled heart. The kingdom in this verse is not a place people are gently ushered into over a lifetime of respectable attendance. It is somewhere people are visibly fighting to get. If you have been standing at the door for years, interested, sympathetic, attending, but never actually coming to Christ yourself, this verse is for you. Enter the kingdom with urgency. Do not stand at the door.

For worship. For centuries the Law and the Prophets stood at the window and looked down the road. Abraham rejoiced to see his day (John 8:56); the prophets searched and inquired what person or time the Spirit was indicating (1 Peter 1:10–11). And then he came. We live on the far side of the seam, in the age of the announcement, when what kings and prophets longed to see is preached in every village (10:24). The King has come, the door is open, and the most unlikely people in the world are pouring through it. Blessed are the eyes that see what you see.

verseByVerse.quote: But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one dot of the Law to become void.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one dot of the Law to become void.

But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one dot of the Law to become void. Immediately after saying that an era has ended, he says the Law is untouchable, and the but is there to stop exactly the conclusion a hearer would otherwise draw. Heaven and earth are the most permanent things imaginable, and Jesus says they are less secure than what God has written. The dot is the keraia, literally a little horn: the tiny projecting stroke that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another. In Hebrew script the difference between certain letters is a mark smaller than the head of a pin, and Jesus says the cosmos will go before one of them does. Not one word of God’s law will fail.

How the law continues. The two verses are held together by one word: fulfilment. Jesus did not come to abolish the law but to fulfil it (Matthew 5:17–18). The Law’s era has closed, but the Law itself has not been cancelled; it has been kept, by the man saying this. What has changed is not the standard but who has met it. Its moral demands remain, summed up in love for God and neighbour. Its ceremonial laws, such as the sacrifices, food laws and festivals, are fulfilled in Christ, who is their reality (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 10:1). Its promises are kept in him. Nothing of God’s word is lost; it all reaches its goal.

Must Christians, then, keep the Old Testament law? Reformed Christians distinguish three kinds of law in the Old Testament. Its ceremonial laws, the sacrifices, food laws and festivals, are fulfilled in Christ and no longer bind us (Hebrews 9–10). Its civil laws were given to Israel as a nation and expired with that nation, though their general equity still teaches wisdom (Westminster 19.4). Its moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, still guides believers, not as a ladder to climb to God but as the shape of the life he has given us (Westminster 19.5–6). Not a dot of the law fails, because Christ fulfils all of it, some by completing it and some by writing it on our hearts (Jeremiah 31:33).

Two opposite errors. One man reads the Law and the Prophets were until John and concludes that grace has made the moral law a historical curiosity; verse 17 exists to stop him. Another reads verse 17 and concludes that nothing has changed, that he must still produce a righteousness of his own; verse 16 exists to stop him. The good news of the kingdom is preached, and it is entered by people forcing their way in with nothing in their hands.

Why does Jesus turn straight from the law to divorce? The subject has not changed. He has just been accused, in effect, of relaxing things; the Pharisees who sneered at his teaching on money were also the party of permissive divorce rulings. So he takes the point at which their own tradition had quietly loosened the Law, and shows who is actually relaxing it. Verse 18 is an example of verse 17.

In a sentence. Heaven and earth would sooner pass away than the smallest stroke of God’s law fail.

On a Tuesday. God’s word is more permanent than the universe. Build your life on it. When a commandment is inconvenient this week, and one will be, notice the instinct to treat it as a dot that surely does not matter: a small lie, a small lust, a small theft of time. Then remember the One who kept every dot for you, and keep it for love of him.

For worship. Every stroke of the law pointed somewhere, and every one of them arrived. The lamb on the doorpost, the scapegoat in the wilderness, the bread in the holy place, the blood on the mercy seat: not one was a wasted pen stroke, because all were sketches of him. And the moral law, which condemned us to the last dot, was kept to the last dot by the Son, and its curse borne by him to the last drop. The sky over Galilee will be rolled up before one stroke of that obedience is undone. We stand on a foundation more stable than the ground, because it is the finished work of the one who wrote the law and kept it.
verseByVerse.note: The “dot” is a tiny stroke of a letter.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery.

Why here? An example of the permanence of God’s law (v. 17), aimed at the Pharisees, who used the law to allow easy divorce. Deuteronomy 24:1 permitted a man to give his wife a certificate of divorce if he found some indecency in her, and the school of Hillel read that so broadly that a burnt dinner could count, and Rabbi Akiva later added finding a prettier woman. They justified themselves (v. 15) by quoting Moses, while breaking the deeper intent of God’s law for marriage. And perhaps there is a pointed reference to Herod Antipas, who had divorced his wife to marry Herodias, his brother’s wife, and had imprisoned John for saying so (3:19–20).

Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery. In God’s eyes the marriage bond still holds, so remarriage is adultery (Mark 10:11–12). Divorce in that world was a man’s prerogative: he wrote the certificate, and she was put out. Jesus will not let the paperwork dissolve what God has joined. The man who discards his wife for another woman has not left a contract; he has broken a covenant.

And he who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery. The second husband too. The sin is not confined to the man who started it; it reaches everyone who treats the first marriage as though it had never been.

The exceptions. Luke, like Mark, gives the saying flat, with no exception attached. Set the whole New Testament out and the picture fills in. Matthew records the same teaching twice and both times includes an exception for sexual immorality (Matthew 5:32; 19:9). Paul adds a second case: if an unbelieving spouse insists on leaving, the believer is not enslaved (1 Corinthians 7:15). Why then does Luke leave the exception out? Because he is giving the rule, not the case law, which is how anyone states a principle. A doctor who says never take this on an empty stomach is not contradicting the note in the leaflet. Luke’s flat form is the shape of the thing: marriage is for life, and the exceptions are exceptions, narrow doors in a solid wall, not the wall itself.

Where Christians differ: may a divorced person ever remarry? Some Christians hold that there is no ground for remarriage while a former spouse lives, reading this verse without exceptions. Others allow divorce and remarriage on wider grounds, such as incompatibility or the breakdown of love. Verdict: the Westminster position (Westminster 24.5–6) is best: marriage is for life, and divorce is always a tragedy; but adultery, and wilful desertion that cannot be remedied by the church or the civil authority, are grounds on which the innocent party may divorce and, after the divorce, remarry as if the offending party were dead. Jesus himself allows divorce for sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9) and Paul for desertion by an unbeliever (1 Corinthians 7:15); Luke gives the principle, and Matthew and Paul give its exceptions. Those who have sinned in divorce and remarriage can find full forgiveness in Christ.

What about the person already divorced and remarried on no ground the New Testament allows? This is the question that keeps people out of church. Is every day of the new marriage a fresh sin? Is the only repentance available to break the second home apart? No. Notice how Jesus himself handles it. He tells the woman at the well that she has had five husbands (John 4:18); he calls them husbands, he names the truth exactly, and he does not instruct her to go back and unpick it. A second marriage, once made, is a real marriage. It is not an ongoing act of adultery but a covenant that now exists and carries real obligations to a real spouse and real children. Where there was sin, it is to be confessed and forgiven like every other sin, and then left at the cross, not dragged out and re-committed every morning. If that is your history, the word to you is not go back. It is be washed, and be faithful now.

Such were some of you. Paul lists adulterers among those who will not inherit the kingdom, and then writes the sentence that has rescued more consciences than almost any other: and such were some of you (1 Corinthians 6:9–11). He goes on to say that they had been washed, made holy and declared righteous, all in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit. The one who drew the line on marriage in this verse is the same Lord in whose name the adulterer is washed. None of this is a loophole, and it must not be heard as one. The fence stands exactly where Jesus put it, and he put it there to protect something, chiefly the wife who in that world could be dismissed at her husband’s convenience and left with nothing. But a fence is not a cage, and the gospel does not leave a man locked outside his own forgiveness.

What if my spouse is abusing me? Then this verse is not a chain to keep you in danger. Abuse is never to be tolerated, in the church or in the home, and nothing in Jesus’ words requires a husband or wife to remain under the same roof as someone who threatens, beats or terrorises them. Get yourself and your children to safety; tell your elders and, where a crime has been committed, the police (Romans 13:4). Separation for protection is not the sin this verse condemns. Whether persistent, unrepentant abuse has broken the marriage in the way Scripture recognises, by the abuser’s wilful abandonment of the covenant’s every duty, is a question to be weighed carefully with faithful elders, and many Reformed churches have judged that it can. What is never right is to tell a victim that God wants her to stay and suffer. Jesus’ words protect the vulnerable; they were never meant to be turned against them.

What if I was the one who sinned in my divorce? Yes, and the way is the same as for every other sin: confess it to God without excuse, put right what can still be put right, and receive his forgiveness fully. That may mean seeking reconciliation with a former spouse if both are unmarried and it is possible; it will certainly mean honesty, humility, and faithfulness to the obligations you still have, especially to your children. It does not mean living for ever under a cloud. David, who took another man’s wife and killed him to cover it, wrote the psalm the church still prays: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow (Psalm 51:7).

In a sentence. Jesus declared that a man who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, as does the man who marries a divorced woman.

On a Tuesday. Honour marriage as God designed it. If you are married, do one thing this week that strengthens the wall rather than tests the doors: an apology you owe, an evening together protected from screens, a prayer for your spouse by name. If you are unmarried, honour other people’s marriages in what you say and what you allow yourself to think. And if you have failed here, there is forgiveness in Christ, full and free, and a church that should be the first place to say so.

For worship. Behind this hard saying stands a Bridegroom who has never once divorced his bride. Israel went after other lovers, and the LORD said through Hosea that he would allure her and speak tenderly to her, and betroth her to himself for ever (Hosea 2:14, 19). The church is no better, and he gave himself up for her, to sanctify her, to present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:25–27). Every human marriage is a small picture of that one. When ours are broken, his is not. He hates divorce because he is faithful, and he is faithful to us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–31 — The Rich Man and Lazarus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The most extended treatment of life after death in the Synoptics, told as the direct sequel to the teaching on money.

Every detail of the opening is a price tag. Purple came from the murex shellfish and took thousands of them to colour a garment; the fine linen was a costly luxury cloth, and he feasted every day, not on feast days when ordinary people ate meat.

Lazarus was laid at the gate — passive, because he could not get there himself — and the gate is the great portal of a walled estate, which means the rich man could not enter or leave his own property without passing him. He wanted what fell: not a place at the table but the scraps on the floor. And he did not get them. The dogs are not a comfort but the final degradation — scavenging pariah animals reaching him when no human being would.

Then the reversal, and it is total. Lazarus is carried — the same passivity as at the gate, and he does nothing in either case. “Abraham's side” is, as the ESV margin gives it, his bosom: at a formal meal guests reclined on their left elbows, so the guest of honour lay with his head near the host's chest, which is the phrase John uses of the beloved disciple (John 13:23). The beggar who longed for what fell from a table is in the place of honour at the greatest table there is.

The rich man is buried — a few words, and the last good thing that happens to him. And the first thing he sees from Hades is Lazarus: the one face he had trained himself not to register, and he knows his name. He had always known his name.

Everything he then says shows that nothing has been learned. He pleads descent — “Father Abraham,” exactly what John the Baptist warned against (3:8) — and twice says “send Lazarus,” still treating him as somebody who ought to be running errands.
verseByVerse.theology:
The story teaches several interlocking truths. There is conscious existence after death, prior to the resurrection: the rich man sees, recognises, feels pain and argues. This is consistent with 23:43 and with Paul (2 Cor. 5:8; Phil. 1:23). The final state of the wicked involves real torment. And it is irreversible — the chasm “has been fixed,” established and standing established, and it is described as working in both directions. That second clause rules out something a sentimental reading would like: it is not that mercy is unwilling to reach him.

One caution on reading the scene rightly. Jesus is not drawing a surveyor's map of the afterlife. He speaks in the vivid imagery his hearers already knew to press home truths that stand however the scene is pictured: death settles our destiny beyond changing, the comforts and miseries of this life can be exactly reversed by God's justice, and no messenger from the dead will persuade those who will not hear Moses and the Prophets. The imagery serves the warning; it was never meant to be quarried for geography.

But the warning must not be softened by that caution — and the gulf of verse 26 is not a new thing. There was a gulf in verses 19 to 21 as well. It was a gate, and it could be crossed by anybody who chose to. One man had the power to cross it every day of his life and never did.

Abraham's “Child, remember” is tender and it is not an accusation. Nothing new is introduced; no list of sins is produced. He simply asks the man to recall a life in which he received his good things — got exactly what he had chosen, all of it, for as long as he lasted.
verseByVerse.examples:
One thing the parable never says needs saying out loud, because the story's shape invites the wrong conclusion. Lazarus is not said to have believed anything, and the rich man is not accused of any crime. Read carelessly this becomes a story in which poverty saves and wealth damns.

That cannot be right, and Luke has already guarded it: the beatitude at 6:20 blesses the poor because empty hands are where faith is usually found, not because an empty purse is a ticket. Abraham himself is in this parable, and Abraham was wealthy. Note also the one name in the story: the rich man, who had every name worth having in this life, is anonymous, and the beggar is called Lazarus — named, and known. What condemns the rich man is not his purple but the gate he walked past daily; what saves Lazarus is not his sores but the God who knew his name.

“They have Moses and the Prophets” is one of the most important sentences in Luke. They had not been left without warning: the Law commands provision for the poor at your gate (Lev. 19:9-10; Deut. 15:7-11), and the Prophets say almost nothing more often — Amos on those who lie on beds of ivory and are not grieved, Isaiah on fasting that does not share bread with the hungry (Amos 6:4-6; Isa. 58:6-7). The rich man heard it read every Sabbath of his life, walked home past Lazarus, and had dinner.

And the final line is devastating for two reasons. The problem is never a shortage of evidence but an unwillingness to hear — miracles do not create faith in a heart that has decided against it. And somebody did rise from the dead. When another Lazarus was raised at Bethany, the chief priests responded by planning to kill him too (John 12:10). The test was run, and it went exactly as he said.

verseByVerse.quote: 'There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously every day. And at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man's table. Moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously every day. And at his gate was laid a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man’s table. Moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores.

The rich man and Lazarus. Only Luke records this story. It illustrates the danger of wealth (v. 13), the reversal promised in the beatitudes and woes (6:20–26), and the sufficiency of Scripture (vv. 29–31). It also answers the Pharisees who had just sneered: they loved money and thought it a sign of God’s favour, and here is a man who had all of it.

There was a rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen. Every detail is a price tag. Purple dye came from the murex shellfish, and it took thousands of them to colour a single garment; it was so costly that some societies restricted it by law to royalty. The fine linen was a luxury cloth, worn by the very rich. And he is unnamed. Tradition calls him Dives, Latin for rich, but Jesus gives him no name at all. The man who had every name worth having in this life has no name before God.

And who feasted sumptuously every day. Not on feast days, when ordinary people ate meat, but every day, and the word suggests not just plenty but display: he made merry, splendidly.

And at his gate was laid a poor man. The verb is passive: he was laid there, thrown down, dumped, by somebody, because he could not get there himself. And the gate is not a garden gate. It is the great portal of a walled estate, which tells you the rich man could not enter or leave his own property without passing him. He was impossible to miss.

Named Lazarus. The only character in any of Jesus’ parables to be given a name. Lazarus, from Eleazar, means God helps, or God has helped. No one else did. The poor man has a name; the rich man does not. God knows the poor by name, and the name is the single hint the parable gives about where this man’s hope actually lay.

God has visited his people. The name says God helps, and the one telling the story is that help in person. Zechariah had blessed the God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people (1:68). When Jesus raised a widow’s only son at the gate of Nain, the crowd said, God has visited his people (7:16). In this parable no one at the rich man’s gate helps Lazarus. But the man speaking it had been stopping at gates all over Galilee, touching lepers and feeding the hungry. The hope hidden in the beggar’s name was walking the roads of Israel.

Covered with sores, who desired to be fed with what fell from the rich man’s table. Ulcerated, perhaps from malnutrition. He wants what falls: not a place at the table, the scraps that go on the floor, like the prodigal longing for the pigs’ pods (15:16). Diners used pieces of bread to wipe their hands and threw them under the table. Even those were not given to him.

Moreover, even the dogs came and licked his sores. The dogs are not a comfort. They are the scavenging street dogs of a Near Eastern town, unclean animals, and they can reach him when no human being will. He was too weak to keep them off. It is the final degradation, and Luke means it as one.

The rich man’s sin. Not that he was rich, nor that he had done anything to Lazarus. He did nothing. He walked past the poor man at his gate every day and ignored him. His sin was neglect, indifference, the failure to love his neighbour, and behind it the failure to love God, because a man who loves God cannot step over his image every morning.

What it does not mean. One thing the parable never says needs saying out loud, because the story’s shape invites the wrong conclusion. Lazarus is not said to have believed anything; the rich man is not accused of any crime. Read carelessly this becomes a story in which poverty saves and wealth damns, and a poor man is safe on the strength of his sores. That cannot be right, and Luke has already guarded it: the beatitude at 6:20 blesses the poor because empty hands are where faith is usually found, not because an empty purse is a ticket. Abraham himself is in this parable, and Abraham was a wealthy man. What condemns the rich man is not his purple but the gate he walked past daily. What saves Lazarus is not his sores but the God who knew his name.

Who is the Lazarus at my gate? Usually someone you pass so often you have stopped seeing him. It may be the homeless man outside the station, but it is just as often the widow two doors down who has not had a visitor in a month, the colleague whose marriage is collapsing, the asylum-seeking family at the back of church, the believer in your congregation who cannot pay the gas bill. Your gate is wherever your daily path brings you within reach of real need. You cannot meet every need in the world, and God does not ask you to. He asks you not to step over the one he has laid where you will see him.

Should I give to every beggar who asks? Not necessarily, and wisdom is not the opposite of love. Giving cash to someone feeding an addiction may not help him, and Scripture expects the able to work (2 Thessalonians 3:10). But the rich man’s problem was not careless giving; it was no giving and no seeing. A good rule is never to walk past without at least seeing the person: a word, a name asked, a meal bought, a referral to a church or charity that can do more than you can. And support, regularly, those in your church and town who do this work well. Love may be wise; it may not be blind.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a rich man who lived in daily luxury while a poor, sick man named Lazarus lay at his gate, longing for scraps, with dogs licking his sores.

On a Tuesday. Who is lying at your gate: someone in need whom you see every day and ignore? Walk your ordinary route this week with your eyes open, the commute, the school gate, the church foyer, the street where you park, and ask God to show you one person you have trained yourself not to register. Then learn his name.

For worship. There is a God who knows the names of those whom the world steps over. He counts the hairs of the beggar’s head and records the tears of the forgotten in his book (Psalm 56:8). The rich man had a name in every house in town and none in heaven; Lazarus had none in town and one that God himself kept. And the Son of God did not stay behind the walls of heaven’s estate. He came out to where we lay, and Matthew saw in his healings the word of Isaiah: he took our illnesses and bore our diseases (Matthew 8:17). The God who helps is not a hint in a name. He is a Man with scars.
verseByVerse.note: Purple dye was costly and fine linen a luxury — the clothing of the very rich. Lazarus, the Greek form of Eleazar, means “God has helped”; he is the only character in Jesus’ parables, apart from Abraham, who is given a name.

parallels.desc: whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor

verseByVerse.quote: The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side. The rich man also died and was buried, and in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side. The rich man also died and was buried, and in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side.

The poor man died. Luke does not say he was buried. A man in his condition, with nobody to claim him, would have gone into a common pit outside the walls, a pauper’s grave, and the parable simply passes over it, because something else was happening that nobody at the graveside could see.

And was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side. The same passivity as verse 20: he was laid at a gate by men, and he is carried through death by angels, and he does nothing in either case. The ESV notes that Abraham’s side is literally Abraham’s bosom, the language of a banquet, where the guest in the place of honour reclined with his head near the host’s chest, as the beloved disciple did at the Last Supper (John 13:23). It is a picture of paradise, the blessed rest of the righteous with the father of the faithful, at the messianic banquet where many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (13:28–29). So the beggar who longed for what fell from a table is now in the place of honour at the greatest table there is.

The rich man also died and was buried. It is the last good thing that happens to him: a funeral, which Lazarus did not get, presumably an impressive one. But his wealth could not save him, and the sentence moves straight past it.

And in Hades, being in torment. Hades is the Greek term for the realm of the dead, used in the Greek Old Testament for the Hebrew Sheol; here it is the place of punishment for the wicked. Torment, basanois, is torture, agony. And what the parable describes is conscious existence: he sees, he recognises, he is in pain, he will shortly argue. The reversal is complete: the rich man has nothing, Lazarus has everything. He has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty (1:53).

He lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side. He can see what he has lost. Then the detail that finishes him. The first person he picks out is Lazarus. The man he had walked past at his own gate, every day, for years, the one face he had trained himself not to register, is the first thing visible from where he now is. And he knows his name. He had always known his name.

Where Christians differ: parable or history? And what happens after death? Some argue this is a literal description of the afterlife; others that it is a parable using popular imagery, and should not be pressed for details. It begins like other parables, there was a rich man, but names Lazarus, which no other parable does. Some, holding soul sleep or annihilationism, deny that the dead have conscious existence, or that the lost suffer for ever. Verdict: it is a parable, and its details (seeing across the chasm, speaking, a drop of water) are pictures, not a map of the afterlife. But Jesus would not use a picture that taught falsehood. The story teaches clearly that at death there is conscious existence, that the righteous are comforted and the wicked suffer, immediately after death, that there is a fixed separation, and that destiny is settled at death. The fuller picture comes at the resurrection and final judgment, when Hades itself gives up its dead (Revelation 20:13–15) and the lost go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life (Matthew 25:46). The punishment is conscious and it is without end.

Hades and Abraham’s side. Hades here is the place of the dead before the final judgment, not yet the lake of fire, and Abraham’s side is the blessedness of believers with God, the same Paradise Jesus promised the dying thief that very day (23:43). The souls of the righteous, says the Westminster Confession, are received into the highest heavens, where they behold the face of God, and the souls of the wicked are cast into hell, where they remain in torments and utter darkness, reserved to the judgment of the great day (Westminster 32.1). Then the bodies are raised, and soul and body together enter their final state.

When a Christian dies, does he sleep until the resurrection? No. The body sleeps in the grave, which is why the New Testament can call death falling asleep (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). But the soul does not. Lazarus is carried at once to Abraham’s side; the thief is with Christ today; Paul says to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23), and to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Your believing mother, your child who trusted Jesus, the friend you buried last year: they are not unconscious and they are not waiting in some grey place. They are with Christ, awake, at rest and rejoicing, and they await only the resurrection of their bodies.

Is there a purgatory, a place where souls are cleansed before heaven? No. Lazarus goes straight from the gate to the banquet, and there is no third place in the story, only comfort and torment. Christ’s blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7), and by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14). Nothing remains to be paid off. Believers are made perfect in holiness at death and pass immediately into glory (Westminster 32.1). Purgatory would add our sufferings to Christ’s sacrifice, as though his were not enough. It was enough.

In a sentence. When Lazarus died, angels carried him to Abraham’s side, but when the rich man died, he found himself in torment in Hades, seeing Lazarus far off with Abraham.

On a Tuesday. Death reveals what was true all along. Where you spend eternity is decided by how you respond to God now. Think of the two funerals: one with no mourners and angels in attendance, one with every honour and none of the things that mattered. Then ask which of the two your life is preparing. And if you are grieving a believer this week, read this verse slowly. They were carried.

For worship. The angels who carried Lazarus are servants of the One who once lay in a manger while the heavenly host praised God above the fields. He is the true Host of Abraham’s banquet, the one at whose side the beloved disciple reclined, and he has prepared a table for his poor. He went down into death himself so that for those who are his it would no longer be a pit but a doorway. A pauper’s grave is not the end of a pauper who belongs to him. No believer dies unattended. No beggar of his is buried without being carried home.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Abraham’s side” is literally “Abraham’s bosom” — the place of honour beside the host at a banquet. Hades is the realm of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called out, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in anguish in this flame.’ But Abraham said, ‘Child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he called out: Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in anguish in this flame. But Abraham said: child, remember that you in your lifetime received your good things, and Lazarus in like manner bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in anguish.

Father Abraham, have mercy on me. Two things in that request tell you the man has not changed at all. The first is Father Abraham. He is pleading descent, which is exactly what John the Baptist had warned against at the start of this Gospel: do not begin to say to yourselves, We have Abraham as our father (3:8). Physically, yes; in faith, no. His claim is ancestry, and it is the only one he makes. And have mercy on me: he never showed mercy to Lazarus. Now he begs for it.

And send Lazarus. The second is worse. He knows the name, he can see the man in the place of honour beside Abraham, and his instinct is to have him fetched, like a servant, to bring water. Even now, he thinks of Lazarus as somebody who ought to be running errands for him. Nothing has been learned. Hell does not reform; it reveals.

To dip the end of his finger in water and cool my tongue. Note how small the request is: not release, not reversal, but a single drop. He who feasted every day now begs for one drop of water, the exact reversal of the scraps from his table, and even that is refused.

For I am in anguish in this flame. Fire is a picture of the suffering of the lost, used by John the Baptist and by Jesus himself (3:17; Mark 9:43–48). Whether or not the flame is physical, what it pictures is real, and Jesus chose the most terrible image available because nothing less would be true.

Child, remember. Abraham’s answer opens with Child. There is no cruelty in this scene, and no gloating; the word is tender.
