In a sentence. Jesus asked where the other nine were, and why only this foreigner had returned to give praise to God.

On a Tuesday. Make a list of God’s blessings this week, and thank him for each one. Begin with the ones you take most for granted: breath, sight, the people at your table, the Bible on your shelf, the church that will gather on Sunday. Then add the great one, the cleansing of your soul. You will find that the list does not end, and that the act of writing it turns you round.

For worship. He counted to ten on that road, and he knows exactly who came back. No mercy he gives is lost in a crowd; no face blurs into the nine. And when one turns round, heaven itself is glad: there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents (15:10). The Lord who asks where the nine are is the Lord who rejoices over the one, and he is not soured by the many who walk on. His joy, not his disappointment, is the last word on that road.

parallels.desc: they did not honour him as God or give thanks to him

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, 'Rise and go your way; your faith has made you well.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to him: rise and go your way; your faith has made you well.

Rise and go your way. He is not kept there. He is sent home like the others, on to the priests and to his new life, with a certificate no priest issued and a body no priest examined.

Your faith has made you well. Start with the difficulty, because it is a real one. All ten were cleansed; Luke says so twice (vv. 14, 17). So what is left for this man to get? The answer is in the verb. For made you well the ESV margin gives has saved you: sesōken. Luke has used the phrase twice before, and both times about something more than a body: to the woman weeping at his feet, who was forgiven (7:50), and to the woman who touched his garment (8:48). The word can mean physical healing and it can mean salvation, and Luke’s usage here is deliberate. Ten men were cleansed of leprosy. One was saved.

Physical blessing is not the same as salvation. The nine received physical healing; the Samaritan received more: salvation, a restored relationship with God through Christ. The difference was faith that returned in worship. The nine received a genuine, enormous, undeserved gift from Jesus of Nazareth and went home with it, and there is no suggestion that it was taken back. But a man can receive a great deal from Christ and never arrive at Christ, and this passage is the clearest picture of it in the Gospels.

What his faith consisted of. It is worth noticing, because it was not much. He shouted for mercy from a distance with nine other men. He obeyed an instruction that made no sense. And when he saw what had happened, he stopped, turned round, and went back to the one who did it. That is all of it. There is no impressive spiritual content anywhere in this man’s story. Saving faith is not a great achievement of the soul. It is an empty hand that comes back to Christ.

Can a person enjoy God’s blessings and still not be saved? Sadly, yes, and this is one of the most searching truths in the Gospels. Answered prayers, a healed body, a happy family, even religious experiences: all of these can be received from God by people who never bow to his Son (Matthew 7:22–23). The test is not what you have received but whether you have come back to the Giver. If you are uncertain, do what the Samaritan did. Do not wait to feel worthy. Turn round, go to Jesus, fall at his feet and thank him, and hear him say what he said to that man.

In a sentence. Jesus told the Samaritan to rise and go, for his faith had saved him.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself honestly: of all that God has given you, how much has actually brought you back to Jesus himself? Pick the blessing you are most grateful for and let it lead you to the Person, not just the gift. Spend ten minutes this week not asking for anything, only adoring him.

For worship. Ten were cleansed, and the cleansing was real; one was saved, and that is a gift of another order. The bodies the nine carried home would one day grow old and be buried. The salvation the Samaritan carried home could not be buried, because the One at whose feet he knelt was walking to Jerusalem to be counted unclean and cast out, and to rise. He gives his enemies good things in abundance; he gives his friends himself, and that gift outlasts the grave.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–37 — The Kingdom and the Coming of the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Pharisees ask when the kingdom is coming, and the question assumes a datable event that can be worked out by people currently standing outside it.

“Not coming in ways that can be observed” rules out surveillance for signs, which is precisely what men who study prophecy in order to date the end have always done.

“The kingdom of God is in the midst of you” has probably been misquoted more than any other line in Luke. The King James renders it “within you,” and that has been carried off to mean that the kingdom is an inner glow native to every human heart. The ESV margin allows “within you,” so the translation is not dishonest — what settles it is who he is addressing. He is answering the Pharisees, who have been lying in wait to catch him (11:53-54). He is not telling them the kingdom is glowing inside their hearts; he is telling them it is standing in the room.

Turning to the disciples, he warns of days when they will long to see one ordinary day of his presence and will not. The longing is named and allowed — and then he deals with the danger it creates, because a man who badly wants Christ to appear is exactly the man who will travel to where somebody says he has. The lightning settles it: nobody has ever been told where the lightning was.

Then, dropped into the middle of it, verse 25: first he must suffer. The Son of Man who comes like lightning is the same man about to be spat at and hung up outside a city wall, and he will be that first.

The Noah and Lot examples select, out of everything available, the ordinary: eating, drinking, marrying, buying, selling, planting and building. Not one is a sin. On its last morning, Sodom was a town where people were putting in orchards.
verseByVerse.theology:
The tension between “the kingdom of God is in the midst of you” and “the days of the Son of Man are coming” is the foundation of the New Testament's already-not-yet. The kingdom has come in the person and work of Jesus; it has not yet come in fullness. Believers live in the overlap.

“Revealed” at v.30 means unveiled — which says something precise about what is coming. It is not that the Son of Man will arrive from elsewhere like a visitor; he will be uncovered, and the implication is that he is not absent now, merely unseen. The day does not change where he is; it changes what can be seen.

On the missing verse 36: your Bible may go straight from 35 to 37, or may print a verse 36 reading “two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left.” Nothing has been removed. The line is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts of Luke and appears to have been copied in from Matthew 24:40 by a scribe who borrowed Matthew's “two men in the field” to bring Luke's two examples up to three. Modern versions drop it to a footnote and keep the old numbering rather than renumber the chapter, which is why the gap is visible — honest bookkeeping, with the workings printed rather than tidied away.

On “taken”: popular retellings fix the picture so that the taken are caught up to safety. But two paragraphs earlier the examples were Noah and Lot, and in both it was the judgement that did the taking — the flood swept them all away, and the fire fell on those who stayed in Sodom while Lot was left alive outside it.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Remember Lot's wife” is one of the shortest verses in Luke, and it does not need the story told. She had been brought out by the hand — the angels seized Lot and his wife and set them outside the city, “the LORD being merciful to him” (Gen. 19:16). She was rescued, physically, past the point of danger. And she looked back.

Her looking back was not curiosity. Everything she had was in that town — her house, her daughters, the whole shape of a life. She was out of Sodom and Sodom was not out of her.

Which is worth taking personally rather than eschatologically. There is a kind of Christian who has genuinely left something behind and spends the rest of his life half-turned towards it: the career surrendered and still mourned, the old life renounced and remembered fondly. He is walking forward; he is not looking forward. And Jesus does not say “remember Sodom.” He says remember the woman who got out and did not get away.

“Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it” is a statement about how reality is constructed rather than a piece of moral advice, and everybody knows a version of it. The parent who holds a child too tightly loses him; the man who protects his reputation above everything is left with nothing but a reputation. The grip is what loses the thing.

And the disciples' “Where, Lord?” is our instinct exactly. They have just been told that two people in one bed will be separated for ever, and what they want is the geography. He answers with a proverb that tells them nothing useful about location, and the uselessness is the sermon.

verseByVerse.quote: Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them, 'The kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed, nor will they say, ‘Look, here it is!’ or ‘There!’ for behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them: the kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed, nor will they say, look, here it is! or there! For behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you.

Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come. The question assumes a great deal, and the assumptions are what Jesus answers. It assumes the kingdom is a future event with a date; that the date can be worked out; and that the people asking are not currently in any relation to it except waiting. The Pharisees expected a visible, political kingdom, with signs announcing it: the defeat of Rome and the restoration of Israel.

The kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed. The word is paratērēsis, and it belonged to two vocabularies at once: the physician’s, for watching a patient for symptoms, and the astronomer’s, for observing the heavens. It means surveillance for signs. You cannot calculate it by signs. He is not saying the kingdom is invisible. He is saying it is not the kind of thing you detect by scanning for indicators, which is precisely what men who study prophecy in order to date the end have always done.

Nor will they say, Look, here it is, or there. It is not a place you can point to on a map. The pointing is the giveaway. Anything requiring a guide is not it.

For behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you. In its older wording this line has probably been misquoted more than any other in Luke. The King James renders it the kingdom of God is within you, and that has been carried off to mean something Jesus never said: that the kingdom is an inner spiritual glow native to every human heart, a divinity we already carry, needing no king outside us. The Greek entos can mean within, and the ESV notes that alternative. What settles it is who Jesus is talking to: the Pharisees, men who have been lying in wait to catch him (11:53–54), in whose hearts the kingdom certainly was not. So most scholars prefer in the midst of you, or among you. He is not telling them the kingdom is glowing quietly inside them. He is telling them it is standing in the room.

The King in front of them. The kingdom is present in the person of Jesus, the King, standing among them, and in his works: if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you (11:20). They are looking for signs, and the King is in front of them. The kingdom is not a feeling located by looking inward. It is a Person they have so far managed to look straight past, and they are asking him when he is going to arrive. And the kingdom is also present wherever God reigns in human hearts, because the King has taken his throne there by his Spirit.

Is the kingdom present or still to come? Luke holds both within a few verses. It is in the midst of them, because the King is in the room; and at once Jesus turns to his disciples and speaks of the day of the Son of Man still to come (vv. 22–37). The kingdom has begun in Christ and his people, and it will be revealed in its fullness at his return. Theologians call this the already and the not yet. We live between the two comings: the King has come, won his decisive victory at the cross and the empty tomb, and reigns now from heaven; and he will come again to finish what he began, raising the dead, judging the world and making all things new.

So is the kingdom of God a political programme? No. Christians should be good citizens, work for justice and love their neighbours in public life, and the gospel has transformed whole societies. But the kingdom is not built by votes, revolutions or legislation, and it is never identical with any nation, party or movement. My kingdom is not of this world, Jesus told Pilate (John 18:36). It comes where Christ is preached and believed, and it will come in fullness only when he returns. A church that confuses the kingdom with its politics will be disappointed by every election and will lose its message in the process.

In a sentence. Asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom would come, Jesus said it would not come with observable signs, for the kingdom of God was already in their midst.

On a Tuesday. Don’t look for the kingdom in political movements or spectacular signs. It is found where Jesus reigns. Look for it this week in the places it actually grows: a heart bowing to Christ in your small group, a quarrel ended in your family, a neighbour asking about your faith, the word preached on Sunday. And ask whether it is growing in you: where does Jesus reign in your life, and where are you still waiting for him to arrive?

For worship. The kingdom of God has a face. The rule of heaven, longed for by prophets and kings, did not come as a weather pattern or a political event but as a Man who could be touched, who ate with sinners and wept at graves. They were looking past him for signs, and he was the sign. And he is still among his people, wherever two or three gather in his name (Matthew 18:20). The King is here, and his kingdom cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:28).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the alternative “the kingdom of God is within you”; “in the midst of you” fits the setting — the King stood among them.

parallels.desc: the kingdom has come upon you

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to the disciples, 'The days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. And they will say to you, ‘Look, there!’ or ‘Look, here!’ Do not go out or follow them. For as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to the disciples: the days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. And they will say to you, look, there! or, look, here! Do not go out or follow them. For as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day.

And he said to the disciples. The audience changes. What follows is not for the Pharisees but for the men who will still be here when he is not. The kingdom is present (v. 21), but its fullness is still to come, at the return of the Son of Man.

The days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. A tender sentence and a bleak one. After Jesus’ departure, in times of persecution and waiting, his disciples will long for his presence, and it will not come as soon as they wish. Luke’s first readers were living in it. Not only the second coming; one of the days, an ordinary day of walking about with him. And they will not get it. He says so plainly rather than promising them a substitute.

For the believer who feels far from God. This is worth registering by anyone who has known a season of unusual nearness to God and now does not. The longing is not a fault, and it is not answered here with a technique for recovering the feeling. It is named, and allowed, and then he moves straight to what to do about the danger it creates. The Lord is not absent because you cannot feel him. He has promised to be with you always, to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20), and the longing itself is a sign of his Spirit in you. Keep to the means he has given, his word, prayer, the Supper, the fellowship of his people, and wait for him. He will come.

Do not go out or follow them. They will say to you, Look, there! or Look, here! Do not go out after them, because that is what longing makes a person vulnerable to. A man who badly wants Christ to appear is exactly the man who will get in a car and drive to where somebody says he has. These are false claims about Christ’s return, or false messiahs (21:8). The instruction is blunt and doubled: do not go out, and do not follow. Not weigh the claim carefully. Do not go.

For as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day. And there is the test, and it is beautifully simple. Nobody has ever been told where the lightning was. Nobody has ever had to travel to see it, or been let in on it by a teacher with special knowledge, or missed it because he was facing the wrong way. It fills the sky from one horizon to the other, and everybody in the country sees it at once. His return will be sudden, visible to all, unmistakable, universal. No one will need to tell you where he is. Every eye will see him (Revelation 1:7).

Anything that has to be pointed out is not it. Every claim that Christ has returned quietly, or secretly, or to a particular place or group, is refuted by one sentence about weather, issued in advance precisely so that his people would not spend the centuries chasing rumours. The cults that announced his invisible return in a particular year, the self-proclaimed messiahs in compounds and on screens, the date-setters with their charts: all are answered here.

What about people who predict the date of his return? Do not follow them. Jesus said that concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father only (Matthew 24:36), and that it is not for us to know times or seasons (Acts 1:7). Every date ever set has passed, and many who trusted them were shipwrecked in faith. The right posture is not calculation but readiness: live every day so that you would be glad to see him come that evening. Watchfulness is a way of life, not a reading of the news.

In a sentence. Jesus warned his disciples that they would long for his coming and should not be deceived by claims that he had appeared somewhere, for his coming would be as visible as lightning across the sky.

On a Tuesday. Don’t be taken in by anyone who claims to know where or when Christ will return. When he comes, everyone will know. If you find yourself drawn to the latest prophecy video or end-times chart, close it and open the Gospel instead. And if you are in a dry season, longing for one day back, tell him so. He hears, and he is not far.

For worship. He will not come quietly. The One who was laid unnoticed in a manger, who rode into Jerusalem on a borrowed colt, who was led out of the city to die between criminals, will come the second time in a glory that fills the sky from one horizon to the other. No rumour will be needed, no guide, no address. The longing of every lonely disciple will be answered in a single flash, and the face they waited for will be the one thing everyone sees. The lightning is his, and so is the day.

verseByVerse.quote: But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.

But first. Before the glory, the cross: one sentence dropped into the middle of a discourse about the end, and it changes the shape of everything around it.

He must suffer many things. Must is dei, the divine necessity, God’s plan, that has run through this Gospel since a boy in the temple said he must be in his Father’s house (2:49). The suffering is not a setback on the way to the glory. It is on the schedule (9:22). The way to glory goes through suffering: was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? (24:26).

And be rejected by this generation. Note who does the rejecting. Not Rome, though Rome will drive the nails. This generation: the people of his own time, including the Pharisees he was answering a few verses ago and the crowds who followed him from Galilee. Luke has recorded the prediction twice already (9:22; 9:44), and both times the disciples failed to take it in. Here it arrives without warning, in the middle of a different subject.

Why put it here at all? Because the disciples have just been told about a day of unmistakable, sky-filling glory, and a man can build a very attractive religion out of that alone. Jesus will not let the second coming be detached from the first. The Son of Man who comes like lightning is the same man who is going to be spat at, flogged, and hung up outside a city wall, and he is going to be that first. Any expectation of his return that skips the cross has the wrong person coming back.

A word about taste. There is a word here for the way Christians think about the future generally. It is possible to be genuinely thrilled by prophecy and entirely unmoved by Calvary: to find the trumpet stirring and the crown of thorns merely sad. That is a taste, not a theology, and this verse is placed exactly where it is to correct it.

Why must he suffer? Why could God not simply forgive? Because God is just as well as merciful, and sin is a real debt against a holy God. He cannot pretend it does not matter without ceasing to be good. At the cross the Son bore the penalty our sins deserved, so that God could be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). He was pierced for our transgressions, and the punishment that brought us peace was laid on him (Isaiah 53:5). The must is not a cruel necessity imposed on an unwilling Son; it is the plan of the Father and the Son together, freely embraced in love for us.

In a sentence. But before his glorious coming, the Son of Man must first suffer and be rejected by his generation.

On a Tuesday. If you think more often about the end of the world than about the cross, turn it round this week. Read one of the passion narratives slowly, Luke 22 and 23, and ask the Spirit to move you by the suffering as much as by the glory. And if you are suffering for Christ, remember the order: first the cross, then the crown, for him and for you.

For worship. The road to the day of the Son of Man runs through Jerusalem, and he was walking it while he said this. He knew the scourge and the spittle and the nails, and he did not slow his pace. The Lord of glory chose rejection by his own generation so that a rejected people could be received by his Father. And the One who will split the sky at his coming will still bear the marks of his first visit: when the lightning comes, it will light up the hands that were pierced.

verseByVerse.quote: Just as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man. They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man. They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all.

Just as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man. The first of two examples, from Genesis 6–7, and Jesus treats Noah and the flood as real history. The thing to notice is what he does not say about Noah’s generation. Genesis is not gentle about them: the earth was corrupt and filled with violence, and every intention of the thoughts of their hearts was only evil continually (Genesis 6:5, 11). Jesus could have made that the point. He does not.

They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage. Four activities, and not one of them is a sin. This is ordinary life in a village, a world doing nothing unusual at all. The problem was that they were absorbed in it and ignored God’s warnings through Noah, a herald of righteousness (2 Peter 2:5), living as if judgment would never come.

The warning people do not expect. The danger is not that the world will become monstrous and everybody will see it coming. It is that it will look exactly like this: supermarkets open, weddings booked, the school run, the football on Saturday.

Until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all. Two clauses, and the order is the point. The ark had been under construction for years, in public, by a man who preached while he built. Everybody knew. And then one day Noah went inside, and the LORD shut him in (Genesis 7:16), and the day he went in was the day it came. Sudden. Too late. The door was shut. Note the phrase destroyed them all. Luke does not soften it, and he will use the identical phrase about Sodom two verses later.

They were not short of warning. Noah’s generation had a preacher, a boat going up in their own neighbourhood, and decades to think about it, and they went on eating and drinking, not because they had weighed the evidence and rejected it, but because life was going on as it always had. That is the modern world’s position with respect to the return of Christ. Nobody in Noah’s village decided to drown. They simply had a normal week, and then another, until the last one.

The Son of Man in the place of the LORD. Notice whose days Jesus sets beside the flood. In Genesis it is the LORD who sees the earth’s corruption, who sends the waters, and who shuts the door of the ark (Genesis 7:16). Jesus calls the coming judgment the days of the Son of Man, his own days. He is not describing an event he will watch from the side; he is claiming the part God played in Noah’s generation. The one speaking is the Judge of all the earth, and he is warning his hearers of his own coming as plainly as Noah ever preached. That is why the warning is mercy: the Judge has come first to give it himself.

Is it wrong, then, to enjoy ordinary life? No. Eating, drinking and marriage are good gifts of God, to be received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4–5), and Jesus himself came eating and drinking (7:34). The Christian does not escape ordinary life; he lives it before God, with an eye on the door. The difference between Noah and his neighbours was not that Noah stopped eating. It was that he believed God’s word and built accordingly. Enjoy your meals, your marriage, your work; just do not let them become a reason to ignore the one who gave them, or the day he has appointed.

In a sentence. The Son of Man’s coming will be like the flood in Noah’s day, when people carried on with ordinary life until the flood suddenly destroyed them.

On a Tuesday. Are you so absorbed in ordinary life that you have forgotten Christ is coming? Look at your week: is there one hour in it given to getting ready for that day, in prayer, in the word, in speaking to someone who is not in the ark? And if you know someone who is not, do what Noah did: keep building and keep preaching.

For worship. There is an ark, and its door still stands open. The God who shut Noah in with his own hand has made a refuge from the wrath to come in his Son, who took the waters of judgment over his own head so that all who are in him rise above them. The patience that waited while the ark was being built (1 Peter 3:20) is waiting still, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). Every day the door stays open is another day of that patience, and the Judge who will one day close it is the Saviour who holds it wide.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot—they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building, but on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all— so will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot (they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building, but on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulphur rained from heaven and destroyed them all), so will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed.

Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot. The second example, from Genesis 19, and Jesus adds it because the first could be dismissed. Noah’s flood was a unique event at the dawn of history; Sodom was a town, in living memory of the patriarchs, in country his hearers could have walked to.

They were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building. Six activities this time, and again not one is wicked: commerce, agriculture, construction, the busyness of a prosperous city with no thought of God. Two of them, planting and building, are the most hopeful things a person can do, because both invest in a future. That is what makes the list so bleak. On its last morning, Sodom was a town where people were putting in orchards and laying foundations.

What Jesus selects. Sodom was notorious for its wickedness, and Genesis records it: the city is a byword for a particular sin, and elsewhere Scripture names its pride, excess of food, prosperous ease and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49). Jesus mentions none of it. What he selects, out of everything available, is the property market and the planting season. He emphasises its ordinariness.

But on the day when Lot went out from Sodom. The same structure as Noah, and the same hinge: the rescue of the righteous man and the arrival of the judgment are the same day. The moment the righteous were removed, judgment fell. Genesis is explicit that the angels could do nothing until Lot was out: escape there quickly, for I can do nothing till you arrive there (Genesis 19:22).

Fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all. Sudden and complete. The phrase is the same as for the flood, and the point is the same: no one in the city expected it that morning, and no one escaped who had not left.

So will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed. And there is the application, and one word in it is worth stopping at. Revealed, apokalyptetai: unveiled. It is not that the Son of Man will arrive from somewhere else, like a visitor. He will be uncovered, and the implication is that he is not absent now, merely unseen, reigning at the Father’s right hand. The day does not change where he is. It changes what can be seen. The world will be caught eating and drinking not because a stranger turned up unannounced, but because the one who was there all along stopped being hidden, and the judgment will be as sudden and complete as Sodom’s.

Will Christians be taken out of the world before the judgment, like Lot? Lot was rescued on the very day the fire fell, not years before it; Noah entered the ark on the day the flood came. That is the pattern of Christ’s return: one public day on which his people are gathered to him and the world is judged (2 Thessalonians 1:6–10). Believers are not promised escape from all suffering before that day; Jesus told them to expect tribulation (John 16:33), and they have always had it. But they are promised that not one of them will be lost when the day comes. The same Lord who took Lot by the hand will not forget a single one of his own.

In a sentence. The Son of Man’s coming will be like the destruction of Sodom, which fell suddenly on people busy with everyday business the day Lot left.

On a Tuesday. Business and building are not wrong. But don’t let them make you forget the day of the Lord. When you sign a contract, plant a garden or plan an extension this year, add a sentence to the plan: if the Lord wills (James 4:15). It changes nothing in the paperwork and everything in the heart.

For worship. When the veil is drawn back, the face revealed will be one his people already know. The Son of Man who will be unveiled to a busy world is the Lord who made himself known to two tired disciples at a table in Emmaus, when their eyes were opened in the breaking of the bread (24:30–31). For the world that day will be a terror. For those who love him it will be recognition: the One they have trusted without seeing, seen at last, and we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

verseByVerse.quote: On that day, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them away, and likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back. Remember Lot's wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On that day, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them away, and likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back. Remember Lot’s wife.

On that day, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them away. The picture is exact for a Palestinian village. Roofs were flat and reached by an outside stair; people slept, dried grain and sat in the cool up there. So a man on the roof can get to the street without entering the house at all, which is what makes the instruction possible and what makes it cost something. He must leave with what he is wearing.

Not this, but the end. Similar words in 21:21 and Mark 13:15–16 concern the flight from Jerusalem before its fall in AD 70. Here the point is different: on the day of Christ’s coming, there will be no time to save possessions, and no point. The pattern is the same; the event is the last. Attachment to things will be fatal.

And likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back. Luke sets this saying in the day of the Son of Man, and on that day nothing behind a disciple is worth a single step backwards. Nothing sinful is in view, only the field-worker’s instinct to go back and fetch one thing first, and on that day even that is too much. Jesus has already said in this Gospel that no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God (9:62), and this field is that plough’s furrow on its final day.

Remember Lot’s wife. Three words, and the shortest verse in Luke. He does not tell the story; he does not need to. She had been brought out by the hand: the angels seized Lot and his wife and daughters and set them outside the city, the LORD being merciful to him (Genesis 19:16). She was rescued, physically, past the point of danger. And she looked back to Sodom as she fled, and became a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:26).

What her looking back was. It sounds like a small thing punished enormously. It was not curiosity. Everything she had was in that town, the whole shape of a life, and to turn round was to have her heart still in it. She was out of Sodom, and Sodom was not out of her.

Half-turned. This is the warning to a disciple, and it is worth taking personally rather than only as prophecy. There is a kind of Christian who has genuinely left something behind and spends the rest of his life half-turned towards it: the career surrendered and still mourned, the relationship broken off and still visited in the imagination, the old life renounced and remembered fondly. He is walking forward. He is not looking forward. And Jesus does not say remember Sodom. He says remember the woman who got out and did not get away.

The face that was set. Luke has already shown us the opposite of Lot’s wife, and it is Jesus himself. When the days drew near for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51), and nothing on the road turned it: not a Samaritan village that refused him, not would-be followers with things to settle first, not his own clear knowledge of what waited in the city. Lot’s wife turned back towards the place of judgment because her heart was there. Jesus walked forward into the place of judgment because his heart was with the people he came to save. She looked back and was lost; he did not look back, and the lost are saved by it.

Can a true believer be lost like Lot’s wife? No one whom Christ has truly saved will finally perish (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6); God keeps his own to the end. But that promise does not make warnings like this unnecessary. They are among the very means by which God keeps us, waking us up when our hearts drift back. Lot’s wife shows what an outward rescue without an inward change looks like: someone who left Sodom with her feet but not with her heart. If this verse troubles you, that is a mercy. Turn your face to Christ, and keep it there.

In a sentence. On that day, no one should go back for possessions or turn back, but remember Lot’s wife, who looked back and was destroyed.

On a Tuesday. What are you tempted to look back to? Remember Lot’s wife, and fix your heart on Christ. Name it: the habit, the relationship, the ambition, the city you left. Then tell God what it is, ask him to break its pull, and do one thing this week that puts it further behind you.

For worship. Lot’s wife was brought out of Sodom by the hand, the LORD being merciful, and still her heart slipped back. Ours would do the same if our keeping were left to our own grip. But Christ has done more than lead his people out of the city. He has gone ahead of them along the road, and he turns their faces after his. The hand that holds them now was pierced to hold them, and it does not loosen when theirs does. No one he leads out will be left standing on the road behind him as a pillar of salt.
verseByVerse.note: Lot’s wife looked back and was turned into a pillar of salt.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it.

Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it. He has said this before, after Peter’s confession (9:24), where it followed the first passion prediction and the call to take up a cross daily. Here it follows a man on a roof told to leave his possessions and a woman remembered for looking back. The principle is the same; the application has moved from a lifetime to a moment. Lot’s wife tried to hold on to her old life, and lost everything.

Seeks to preserve. To secure as one’s own possession. The man on the roof who goes back for his goods is trying to preserve; so is Lot’s wife. What they are trying to keep is not merely property but the arrangement: the shape of a life that has been built and is now being taken away. And the sentence says the attempt is self-defeating. Not that it is wrong, or greedy, but that it does not work. The grip is what loses the thing.

How reality is built. This is a statement about how reality is constructed, not a piece of moral advice, and it applies well outside the day of the Son of Man. Everybody knows a version of it. The parent who holds a child too tightly loses him; the person who cannot bear to be disliked ends up with no friendships of any weight; the man who protects his reputation above everything is eventually left with nothing but a reputation.

But whoever loses his life will keep it. Keep is zōogonēsei: preserve alive, literally give it life, make it alive. Those who give up their lives to Christ gain eternal life. So the alternative is not a heroic sacrifice with nothing on the other side. It is the only route by which anything survives at all. The man who lets go is not choosing loss over gain; he is choosing the one grip that does not crush what it holds.

He saved others. Luke will show this sentence carried out to the letter. At the cross the rulers sneered, he saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One (23:35), and the soldiers and one of the criminals said the same. Every voice at Golgotha urged him to preserve his life, and he would not. He held nothing back: not his clothes, not his breath, not his spirit, which he committed into his Father’s hands (23:46). The man who refused to save himself is the reason anyone else is saved, and the one life that was wholly given up is the life that was given back on the third day.

What does losing my life look like for an ordinary Christian? Rarely martyrdom, though for some it is, and has been for millions. More often it is the daily surrender of what you would hold on to for yourself. It is choosing obedience when it costs you a promotion; telling the truth when it costs you a friend; giving away money you could have kept; opening your home when you would rather close the door; being known as a Christian at work. And at the end, it is dying in faith, letting go of everything into the hands of Christ. None of it is wasted. All of it is kept alive in him.

In a sentence. Whoever tries to save his life will lose it, and whoever loses it will preserve it.

On a Tuesday. What are you clinging to? Let go of it for Christ, and you will find true life. Open your hand, literally if it helps, in prayer, and name what is in it: your plans, your children, your health, your money, your reputation. Give each one back to him. You will find he does not take them away so much as hold them better than you could.

For worship. On the third morning the women came with spices to tend a body, and were asked, why do you seek the living among the dead? (24:5). The life he had let go of was not lost; it was kept, and raised, and now he holds the keys of death. Every disciple who lets go of a life for his sake lets it go into those hands, and it is hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3), where no thief, no grave and no day of judgment can touch it.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed. One will be taken and the other left. There will be two women grinding together. One will be taken and the other left.' And they said to him, 'Where, Lord?' He said to them, 'Where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed. One will be taken and the other left. There will be two women grinding together. One will be taken and the other left. And they said to him: where, Lord? He said to them: where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather.

I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed. One will be taken and the other left. The coming of the Son of Man will divide people who were closest: a household at night, husband and wife, or two companions. A sudden separation, with no warning. Outwardly the same, inwardly different.

There will be two women grinding together. Two women working side by side at a small hand mill, sitting opposite each other, grinding grain, a daily task done at dawn. Night and day: whenever he comes. The nearest possible proximity in both cases, and identical circumstances. And one of each pair is taken.

The child set for the fall and rising. What divides the two in one bed is nothing the eye can see. It is how each stands with the Son of Man. Luke announced this at the beginning, when old Simeon took the baby in his arms and said, Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel (2:34), and Jesus has said it himself: he came to bring not peace but division, even within one house (12:51–53). The separation of that night is the last unveiling of a line that already runs through households now, and he is the line.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 36: Two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left. The line is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts of Luke and appears to have been copied in from the parallel in Matthew 24:40 by a scribe who wanted to bring Luke’s two examples up to three. Modern versions put it in a footnote and keep the old numbering, which is why the gap is visible in some Bibles. Nothing has been hidden, and no teaching of Scripture depends on it.

Taken and left. A word on taken, because most readers arrive at this verse already certain which they would rather be. Popular retellings have fixed the picture: the taken are caught up to safety and the left are abandoned to disaster. That reading belongs to a particular scheme of the end times held sincerely by many Christians, and nothing here needs to be unkind about it. But notice what Jesus has just been talking about. A few verses earlier the examples were Noah and Lot, and in both, it was the judgment that did the taking. The flood came and destroyed them all (v. 27); the fire fell on those who stayed in Sodom while Lot was spared outside it (v. 29).

And they said to him, Where, Lord? Where will they be taken? And there it is: the disciples’ instinct, and ours. They have just been told that two people in one bed will be separated for ever, and what they want to know is the geography.

Where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather. A proverb, and it tells them nothing useful about location; the uselessness is the sermon. As certainly as vultures gather round a dead body, judgment will fall wherever there is spiritual death, as visibly as vultures circling, and nobody will have to be told where. Those taken are taken to judgment.

Where Christians differ: one taken, one left. Dispensationalists teach that one will be taken describes the secret rapture of believers before a tribulation, as in the novels and films about being left behind, reading it alongside the catching up of believers to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17) and his promise to take them to himself (John 14:3). Verdict: in context, the comparisons with Noah and Lot (vv. 26–30) show that those taken are taken in judgment, like those swept away by the flood, while those left are like Noah and Lot, spared. And the vultures (v. 37) show that being taken means death. There is no secret rapture here. Christ’s coming will be visible like lightning (v. 24), and will bring both the gathering of his people and judgment, at one public return. The point is the same on any reading: be ready, because no one will be warned in advance.

Then what do I make of the catching up in 1 Thessalonians 4? It is real and glorious, but it is not secret. Paul describes it with a cry of command, the voice of an archangel and the sound of the trumpet of God (1 Thessalonians 4:16), about as loud an event as can be imagined. At Christ’s one return the dead in Christ rise, the living believers are caught up to meet him in the air, and they come with him as he arrives in judgment, as citizens go out to meet a king and escort him into the city. Believers are not left behind, and they are not taken away years early. They are gathered to their Lord on the day the whole world sees him.

Will my believing spouse or parent save me on that day? No. Two in one bed, two at one mill: the nearest relationships on earth, and one is taken and the other left. You can sleep beside a believer, work beside one, be raised by one, and still be lost. Faith is personal: each must come to Christ himself. That is not a cold truth but an urgent invitation. If you have been sheltering under someone else’s faith, come to Christ for yourself today. And if you love someone who is not yet his, pray, and speak, while it is still today.

In a sentence. At the Son of Man’s coming, people side by side will be separated, one taken and one left, and judgment will come wherever it is due, as surely as vultures gather over a corpse.

On a Tuesday. Being near a believer will not save you. Make sure you are ready for his coming yourself. The question is not which group you would prefer. It is whether the day, arriving in the middle of an ordinary night, would find you facing the right direction. Tonight, before you sleep, tell the Lord where you stand with him, and if you are not sure, ask him to receive you.

For worship. The same night that brings the vultures brings the Bridegroom. For those who are his there is no terror in that separation, only a voice they have long been listening for. Not one of his own will be overlooked in the dark, in the bed or at the mill, because the Shepherd knows every one of his sheep by name. And the Judge at whose coming the earth will tremble is the Saviour who was judged in their place, so that the day which divides the world will unite his people with him for ever.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 36, “Two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left,” and that “vultures” may also be rendered “eagles.”

17.text: <sup>1</sup> And he said to his disciples, “Temptations to sin are sure to come, but woe to the one through whom they come! <sup>2</sup> It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were cast into the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to sin. <sup>3</sup> Pay attention to yourselves! If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him, <sup>4</sup> and if he sins against you seven times in the day, and turns to you seven times, saying, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive him.” <sup>5</sup> The apostles said to the Lord, “Increase our faith!” <sup>6</sup> And the Lord said, “If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you could say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you. <sup>7</sup> “Will any one of you who has a servant plowing or keeping sheep say to him when he has come in from the field, ‘Come at once and recline at table’? <sup>8</sup> Will he not rather say to him, ‘Prepare supper for me, and dress properly, and serve me while I eat and drink, and afterward you will eat and drink’? <sup>9</sup> Does he thank the servant because he did what was commanded? <sup>10</sup> So you also, when you have done all that you were commanded, say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have only done what was our duty.’” <sup>11</sup> On the way to Jerusalem he was passing along between Samaria and Galilee. <sup>12</sup> And as he entered a village, he was met by ten lepers, who stood at a distance <sup>13</sup> and lifted up their voices, saying, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.” <sup>14</sup> When he saw them he said to them, “Go and show yourselves to the priests.” And as they went they were cleansed. <sup>15</sup> Then one of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, praising God with a loud voice; <sup>16</sup> and he fell on his face at Jesus' feet, giving him thanks. Now he was a Samaritan. <sup>17</sup> Then Jesus answered, “Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine? <sup>18</sup> Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?” <sup>19</sup> And he said to him, “Rise and go your way; your faith has made you well.” <sup>20</sup> Being asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them, “The kingdom of God is not coming in ways that can be observed, <sup>21</sup> nor will they say, ‘Look, here it is!’ or ‘There!’ for behold, the kingdom of God is in the midst of you.” <sup>22</sup> And he said to the disciples, “The days are coming when you will desire to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it. <sup>23</sup> And they will say to you, ‘Look, there!’ or ‘Look, here!’ Do not go out or follow them. <sup>24</sup> For as the lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one side to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day. <sup>25</sup> But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation. <sup>26</sup> Just as it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man. <sup>27</sup> They were eating and drinking and marrying and being given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all. <sup>28</sup> Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot—they were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building, <sup>29</sup> but on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all— <sup>30</sup> so will it be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed. <sup>31</sup> On that day, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them away, and likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back. <sup>32</sup> Remember Lot's wife. <sup>33</sup> Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it. <sup>34</sup> I tell you, in that night there will be two in one bed. One will be taken and the other left. <sup>35</sup> There will be two women grinding together. One will be taken and the other left.” <sup>37</sup> And they said to him, “Where, Lord?” He said to them, “Where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather.”

18.title: Prayer, Humility, Children, Wealth, and Sight
18.overview:
Luke 18 is constructed around a series of contrasts: persistent widow versus unjust judge; Pharisee versus tax collector; those who would keep children from Jesus versus Jesus who receives them; a rich ruler who becomes very sad versus disciples who have left everything; a blind beggar who cries out versus those who rebuke his cry. In each pair, the unexpected person receives what they need — and the principle is always the same: those who come to God with empty hands receive; those who come convinced they already have what is required leave empty.

Luke tells us explicitly why Jesus told the opening parables. The widow-and-judge parable is told to show that “they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (v. 1). The Pharisee-and-tax-collector parable addresses “those who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt” (v. 9). Together they define authentic prayer: persistent, humble, directed entirely toward a God who can do what we cannot.

The final section (vv. 31–43) contains the third passion prediction — which the disciples cannot understand — and closes with a blind beggar, a man who cannot see physically but sees Jesus with perfect spiritual clarity: “Son of David, have mercy on me.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Persistent Widow and the Unjust Judge
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke tells us the point before the story starts — something he rarely does — which suggests he was not prepared to risk it being missed. And the two halves of the purpose are the same thing from two sides: “always to pray” and “not lose heart,” where the second word means to grow weary, to give out. The alternative to persistent prayer is not some other spiritual activity. It is quitting.

Note where it sits. The previous paragraph closed with a discourse about a day that comes without warning after a long wait. This parable is what to do in the meantime.

The judge is described comprehensively: he neither feared God nor respected man, which is the whole of the Old Testament's requirement for the office (cf. 2 Chr. 19:6-7). He is not corrupt — a bribe would be a lever, and a lever would work. He simply does not care, and Luke says so twice, once as narrator and once in the man's own mouth, so nobody can call it a hostile characterisation.

The widow is the other end of the scale. Without husband, father or male relative she had no standing in a court at all, no money for a lawyer and no influence. And the law was emphatic about her: God “executes justice for the fatherless and the widow” (Deut. 10:18), and cursed is the man who perverts it (Deut. 27:19). The one case this judge is most obliged to hear is the one he is refusing.

What she asks for is not charity but a verdict — “give me justice” — vindicate me. And the judge's phrase for what she is doing to him is violent: she will beat him down. He is not worn down by sympathy or shamed into it. He is being hit, repeatedly, in the same place.

So justice is done in that city for the worst possible reason, by a man who cared nothing about it, because one powerless woman would not go away. Which is the setup for the argument, and the argument runs by contrast: if even that produces justice, consider who you are actually dealing with.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer is not a mechanism for overcoming divine reluctance. The unjust judge is the contrast, not the model — this is an argument from the lesser to the greater, and every term in v.7 is set against him. He had no fear of God; this is God. The widow was a stranger; these are “his elect.” She was a nuisance at a door; they “cry to him day and night,” which is the language of the Psalms and of a people in exile.

And Jesus raises the delay himself rather than pretending it is not there. The parable assumes a widow who has been coming a long time. What is denied is not the delay but its meaning: the widow's problem was that her judge did not care, and that was the only reason for her wait. Whatever the reason for yours, it is not that one — because the one you are asking chose you.

“Speedily” does not promise a quick answer. It means without dawdling — that when God moves he does not drag his feet, and that nothing is being held up by reluctance at his end. And notice what the elect are crying for: not relief but justice, the setting right of all things, which arrives in full at the coming of the Son of Man named in the very next line. Some prayers are answered in this life; every prayer of God's people is answered at that day, and none of them a minute late.
verseByVerse.examples:
The parable ends with a question, and it is the reverse of the one everybody arrives with. We come asking whether God will keep faith with us; he settles that flatly and moves on. What he asks is whether he will find faith in us — and he leaves it open, which is more unsettling than any answer would have been.

The “nevertheless” is doing the work. Justice is certain; the perseverance of the people waiting for it is not. Which is exactly the danger the parable was told to address: the risk is not an unanswering God but a widow who stops coming.

So if you are still praying after eleven years and have concluded that the long silence is evidence of being ignored, read the last line again. The thing he says he will be looking for when he comes is the very thing you are doing.

And there is a word here for the man whose prayer life has quietly collapsed — who prays in a crisis but finds sustained daily prayer pointless, since God knows what he needs anyway. The purpose of persistent prayer is not to overcome divine ignorance. It is to keep the heart oriented toward the right Source, and to sustain the posture of a person who genuinely believes help is coming from outside himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart. He said, 'In a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart. He said: in a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected man.

Meaning first. Luke 18 is about how people come to God, and the answer is always the same: with nothing in their hands. A powerless widow keeps coming to a judge who does not care, and Jesus says God is nothing like him (vv. 1–8). A Pharisee lists his virtues, a tax collector begs for mercy, and only the second goes home justified (vv. 9–14). Babies are welcomed, and the kingdom is said to belong to such (vv. 15–17). A rich ruler goes away sad, and Jesus says salvation is impossible with man but possible with God (vv. 18–30). Jesus foretells his death and rising for the third time, and the Twelve understand nothing (vv. 31–34), while a blind beggar near Jericho sees exactly who he is (vv. 35–43).

The link. Jesus has just spoken of days when his disciples will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man and will not see it (17:22), and of a day that will come without warning after a long wait. How should they live in the meantime? This parable answers: by prayer.

And he told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart. Luke does something rare here: he gives the point before the story starts, as if he would not risk it being missed. Always means persistently, continually. The word for losing heart, enkakein, means to grow weary, to give out, to become discouraged. The two halves are one thing seen from two sides: the alternative to persistent prayer is not some other spiritual activity. It is quitting. Nobody stops praying because he has found something better to do with the time.

In a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected man. The description is devastating and comprehensive. The Old Testament asks two things of a judge: that he fear God and that he regard the people in front of him. Jehoshaphat charged the judges of Judah to consider what they did, for they judged not for man but for the LORD, and to let the fear of the LORD be upon them (2 Chronicles 19:6–7; compare Deuteronomy 16:18–20). This man has neither, and Luke says so twice, once here and once in the man’s own mouth (v. 4). He is the worst judge imaginable, and that is the point of him. He is in the story to be the opposite of somebody.

The teacher who never stopped praying. The one who tells this parable is the most persistent man of prayer in Luke’s Gospel. Luke alone records that heaven opened while Jesus was praying at his baptism (3:21), that he would withdraw to desolate places and pray (5:16), that he spent all night in prayer before choosing the Twelve (6:12), and that his face was transfigured as he prayed (9:29). He will kneel to pray in Gethsemane (22:41), and he will die praying (23:46). When he tells his disciples always to pray and not lose heart, he is asking them to walk a road he walked every day, and on which he never once gave up.

What does always to pray actually mean? It cannot mean doing nothing but pray, since Jesus also worked, ate, slept and taught. It means never giving up, and living in a settled habit of turning to God. Paul says the same: pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17). In practice that means fixed times, morning and evening, when you deliberately bring your needs and other people’s to God; short prayers through the day as things happen; and refusing to drop a request just because the answer is slow. It is not a feeling of constant devotion. It is a direction of the heart that keeps coming back.

In a sentence. Jesus told a parable to teach that his disciples should always pray and not give up, about a judge who neither feared God nor cared about people.

On a Tuesday. Have you given up praying for something? This parable is for you. Write down the request you have quietly stopped making, the prodigal, the illness, the marriage, the salvation of a parent, and put it back on your list this week, by name, every day.

For worship. Before Jesus says a word about the judge, he tells us that we ought to pray, and that alone reveals the heart of God. The Lord of heaven wants to be asked. He has not set the world running and left the weak to cope; he has opened his door and told them to keep knocking. And the prayers of tired disciples do not rise alone. The Son who prayed through the nights on earth lives for ever to make intercession for them (Hebrews 7:25), and every faint request is carried in on the strength of his.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a widow in that city who kept coming to him and saying, ‘Give me justice against my adversary.’ For a while he refused, but afterward he said to himself, ‘Though I neither fear God nor respect man, yet because this widow keeps bothering me, I will give her justice, so that she will not beat me down by her continual coming.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a widow in that city who kept coming to him and saying: give me justice against my adversary. For a while he refused, but afterwards he said to himself: though I neither fear God nor respect man, yet because this widow keeps bothering me, I will give her justice, so that she will not beat me down by her continual coming.

And there was a widow in that city. The other end of the scale. A widow in that world was the Bible’s shorthand for defencelessness: no husband to represent her, no money for a bribe, and unless a son or brother-in-law took up her case, little standing in court. And the law singled her out for protection: God executes justice for the fatherless and the widow (Deuteronomy 10:18; Exodus 22:22–24), and the prophets return to it constantly (Isaiah 1:17, 23). So the one case this judge is most obliged to hear is the one he is refusing.

Who kept coming to him and saying, Give me justice against my adversary. The tense means repeated, continual coming; her only weapon was persistence. The case may have been a debt, or her inheritance being stolen. What she asks for is not charity, leniency or revenge, but justice: vindicate me, settle my case. She believes she is in the right, and she is asking for a verdict rather than a favour.

For a while he refused, but afterward he said to himself. He had no reason to help her. And Luke takes us inside his head, and the man is entirely candid there. He repeats the narrator’s assessment of himself word for word, though I neither fear God nor respect man, which is a rare thing in Scripture and slightly chilling. He knows exactly what he is and it does not trouble him.

Yet because this widow keeps bothering me, I will give her justice. Not a love of justice, not compassion, but annoyance. He gives in, to get rid of her.

So that she will not beat me down by her continual coming. The verb hypōpiazē comes from the boxing ring: to strike under the eye, to give somebody a black eye; Paul uses it of disciplining his own body (1 Corinthians 9:27). Perhaps the judge means she will wear him out, or shame him publicly. Either way he is not moved by sympathy, or conscience, or argument. He is being hit, repeatedly, in the same place, and he gives her the verdict to make it stop. Justice is done in that city for the worst possible reason, because one powerless woman would not go away.

The widows’ Lord. Luke keeps putting widows in front of Jesus, and every time he is the opposite of this judge. At Nain he saw a widow following her only son’s bier, had compassion on her, and gave the boy back to his mother (7:12–15). In the temple he will single out a poor widow’s two small coins as the greatest gift of the day (21:1–4), and he will warn against the scribes who devour widows’ houses (20:47). The God who executes justice for the widow, in Deuteronomy’s words, has come into Israel’s towns in person. He needs no beating down. At Nain he saw the widow before she had said a word.

Does God answer only if I nag him? No, and the next verses say so. God is not the judge. The widow had to wear down a man who did not care; you come to a Father who does. Persistence in prayer is not a technique for overcoming God’s reluctance, because he has none. It is what faith looks like while it waits: it keeps coming because it believes there is Someone worth coming to. Jesus warned against heaping up empty phrases as if many words would earn a hearing (Matthew 6:7). Pray often, not because God is hard of hearing, but because you are dependent, and he loves to be asked.

In a sentence. A widow kept coming to the judge for justice, and though he refused for a while, he finally gave it to her just to stop her pestering.

On a Tuesday. Keep coming to God, as this widow kept coming. Persistence is not wasted. If you are fighting a long battle for justice in this world, against an employer, a landlord, an ex-spouse, a system that will not listen, take the widow as your companion. Pursue what is right by every honest means, and bring the case to the higher court every day.

For worship. The law of God was written with the widow, the orphan and the stranger in view, and that is a portrait of the Lawgiver. Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation (Psalm 68:5). He does not need to be worn down into caring. And in his Son he has come down into the courtroom himself, not as a judge who must be pestered, but as the Advocate who pleads our case (1 John 2:1), and wins it with his own blood.
verseByVerse.note: Widows had no one to plead their case; the law singled them out for protection.

parallels.desc: you shall not mistreat any widow

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord said, 'Hear what the unrighteous judge says. And will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night? Will he delay long over them?
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the Lord said: hear what the unrighteous judge says. And will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night? Will he delay long over them?

Hear what the unrighteous judge says. Listen to the point. Jesus tells them to listen to the villain, which is the instruction that unlocks the parable, and it is worth saying plainly what it does and does not mean. This is an argument from the lesser to the greater, like the father who gives good gifts (11:13), and such arguments work by contrast, not comparison. God is not the unjust judge; he is his opposite in every particular. The parable does not say God is reluctant, so keep pestering him. It says: if even that produces justice, consider who you are actually dealing with.

And will not God give justice to his elect. Every term is set against the judge. He had no fear of God; this is God. He is just, and he cares. The widow was a stranger to him; these are his elect, eklektōn, his chosen ones, the people he has bound himself to, against whom no charge can stand because God himself justifies them (Romans 8:33). The contrast is the point. If even this unjust judge gives justice to a widow he cares nothing for, how much more will God give justice to his chosen people, whom he loves?

Chosen in the Chosen One. Luke uses the word elect sparingly, and its centre is not us. On the mountain the Father’s voice said of Jesus, This is my Son, my Chosen One; listen to him (9:35). The elect are chosen in that Chosen One, loved with the love the Father has for his Son. So when Jesus promises that God will vindicate his elect, he is speaking of people bound to God through himself. Their cry is heard because it comes through him, and their vindication is sure because his was: the one the rulers mocked as a Chosen One who could not save himself (23:35) was raised and seated at the Father’s right hand.

Who cry to him day and night? She was a nuisance at his door; they cry to him day and night, which is the language of the Psalms and of a people in exile. And the verb for their crying is a strong one. This is not the recitation of a list. It is the sound people make when something is badly wrong and they know who to shout at. It is the persistent prayer of God’s people, suffering in a hostile world, longing for justice and for Christ’s return, the cry of the martyrs under the altar: how long, O Lord (Revelation 6:10).

Will he delay long over them? Or: will he be patient with them, or keep them waiting? The question is put to be answered, and it is worth noticing that Jesus raises the delay himself. He does not pretend it is not there. The parable assumes a widow who has been coming for a long time and elect who are crying day and night, which is to say, the waiting is written into the story. What is being denied is not the delay but its meaning. The widow’s problem was that her judge did not care. That was the reason for her wait, and it was the only reason. Jesus is telling people whose prayers have gone unanswered for years that whatever the reason for their wait, it is not that one, because the one they are asking chose them. God is patient (2 Peter 3:9), but he will not abandon his people.

What does elect mean, and why mention it here? The elect are those God chose in Christ before the foundation of the world, not because of anything in them but out of sheer love (Ephesians 1:4–5). Jesus mentions it here as the strongest possible ground for confident prayer. You do not have to wonder whether God is interested in you. He set his love on you before you existed, and the One who chose you will not ignore you now. Election is not a puzzle to make you anxious; it is a pillow for a weary pray-er. If you are crying to him day and night for his justice and his kingdom, that cry is itself the mark of his chosen.

In a sentence. Jesus said that if an unjust judge gave justice, how much more will God give justice to his chosen ones who cry to him day and night.

On a Tuesday. When you pray this week, begin by remembering whom you are speaking to. Not an indifferent official, but your Father, who chose you, who gave his Son for you, and who has already promised to hear. Say it out loud before you ask for anything: you chose me, and you love me. Then ask.

For worship. The elect do not plead with an unjust judge, but with a Father who chose them before they could cry at all. He did not keep back his own Son; he will not keep back justice from those he gave his Son to save. Each name is written in heaven (10:20), and each cry in the night is heard as if it were the only one. He is not the judge who must be beaten down. He is the Father who sees the returning son a long way off and runs (15:20).
verseByVerse.note: The argument runs from the lesser to the greater: if even this judge acts, how much more God.

parallels.desc: I cry out day and night before you

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, he will give justice to them speedily. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
I tell you, he will give justice to them speedily. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?

I tell you, he will give justice to them speedily. And there is the word that snags on real life. Speedily, en tachei: quickly, or suddenly. The person reading this has perhaps prayed for the same thing for eleven years: a marriage, a son who will not come home, a body that does not heal. So it is worth being honest about what the promise says. It does not promise a quick answer by our clocks; with the Lord one day is as a thousand years (2 Peter 3:8). It means that when God moves he does not drag his feet, and that nothing is being held up by reluctance at his end. And when justice comes, at Christ’s return, it will come suddenly.

What the elect are crying for. Notice what the elect in the parable are actually asking. Not relief; justice: the setting right of all things, which is precisely what arrives at the coming of the Son of Man named in the very next line, when the one who was denied justice in Pilate’s court returns as the Judge who sets all things right. Some prayers are answered in this life. Every prayer of God’s people is answered at that day, and none of them a minute late.

Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth? The parable ends with a question, and it is the reverse of the one everybody arrives with. We come to a passage like this asking whether God will keep faith with us. He settles that flatly and moves on. What he asks is whether he will find faith in us. Faith is literally the faith, this kind of persistent, praying faith. Will his people still be praying, still trusting, when he returns, or will they have given up? The question is not answered. It is put to each reader, and that is more unsettling than any answer would have been. The nevertheless is doing the work. Justice is certain; the perseverance of the people waiting for it is set before them as a question. Which is exactly the danger the parable was told to address. The risk here is not an unanswering God. It is a widow who stops coming.

Does this mean true believers might lose their faith? No. Scripture is clear that those whom God has truly called he keeps to the end (John 6:39; Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). But he keeps them through means, and one of those means is exactly a searching question like this. The warning is not meant to make the elect doubt their election. It is meant to keep them praying. A believer who hears it and says, Lord, keep me faithful, is doing what the question was asked to produce. The ones who finally fall away show that they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). The ones who keep crying day and night are the faith he will find.

For the one who has prayed for years. If you are still praying after eleven years, and have concluded that the long silence is evidence of being ignored, read the last line again. The thing he says he will be looking for when he comes is the very thing you are doing.

In a sentence. God will give his people justice quickly, but when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?

On a Tuesday. When Christ comes, will he find faith in you: still praying, still trusting? Keep praying today. Set a time tomorrow morning, even five minutes, and keep it every day this week. And when the old discouragement comes, the thought that it is pointless, answer it with this verse: he will give justice, and he is looking for faith.

For worship. The Son of Man is coming, and when he comes he is looking for something. He is not looking for successful people or impressive ones, but for faith: the widow still knocking, the old saint still praying for her grandchildren, the persecuted church still crying how long. That is what delights him. And the faith he looks for is the faith he gives, kept alive by the Spirit he sends and the intercession he makes. He is the Author of our faith and he will be its Finisher (Hebrews 12:2). When he comes, he will find what he planted.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — The Pharisee and the Tax Collector
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke names the target before the story begins, and the two clauses belong together as cause and effect. “Trusted in themselves that they were righteous” places confidence in something that can be inspected — and a righteousness that has to be maintained needs a scale, and a scale needs other people on it. The contempt is not an unfortunate trait attached to an otherwise sound position; it is generated by the position.

Note too that Luke does not say “to the Pharisees.” He says “to some who” — a description rather than a party, which leaves the door open for anybody to walk through.

The pairing is as wide as first-century Judaism could make it. A Pharisee was a serious man who took the law seriously enough to organise his life around it. A tax collector had contracted with the occupying power to extract money from his own people and was barred from giving evidence in court.

A word about the wording at v.11, since translations differ and something has been built on the difference. The phrase can attach either to the standing or to the praying — the ESV text has “standing by himself, prayed,” and its margin “standing, prayed to himself”; some older versions take the second, and preachers have made much of the idea that his prayer never got past his own ears.
