It is a fair possibility and not certain, and it should not carry weight the text will not bear.

What is certain is the content. The prayer opens correctly — thanksgiving, addressed to God — and then turns into a list of other people, the fourth of whom is standing in the same courtyard. And both claims are almost certainly true and both exceed what was required: the law commanded one fast a year, and he does two a week; the tithe was on produce, and he tithes everything.

This is not a fraud. He is doing more than God asked. Which is what makes the parable uncomfortable, because the natural reading is that his problem was insincerity, and it was not.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable is a pre-Pauline statement of justification by faith alone. The tax collector contributes nothing except his need and his cry — no promise of reformation, no religious performance, no favourable comparison — and he goes home justified.

His plea is worth pausing on. It is not “overlook my sin.” He is standing in the temple, very possibly at the hour when a lamb was being killed, asking for mercy on the only terms that building knew — sin dealt with by sacrifice. Paul will name what he was reaching for: Christ, “put forward as a propitiation by his blood” (Rom. 3:25).

And he names himself without qualification: “a sinner.” Which is what a man says when he has stopped comparing: the Pharisee could see four categories of people and himself above them, and this man cannot see anybody else in the building.

“Justified” is a courtroom word — a verdict entered in his favour, by somebody else, and standing. So a man who had defrauded his neighbours for a living walked out with a legal standing before God that the most religious man in the country did not have.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Rather than the other” is not “more than.” The Pharisee went home exactly as he arrived, which is the quiet tragedy of the parable: nothing happened to him at all. He came with a balance and took it away again.

And the closing principle needs one guard, because it can be turned into a technique. A man who humbles himself in order to be exalted has exalted himself, and the verse has already seen him. The tax collector was not performing humility; he was telling the truth, and it happened to be devastating — which is the only humility that has ever done anybody any good.

The parable also exposes what religious confidence actually costs. The Pharisee's problem was not that his facts were wrong but that his arithmetic required a comparison, and comparison requires somebody underneath. He had looked around the courtyard, found the tax collector, and put him in the prayer.

A man in a small group shares prayer requests — articulate, theologically sophisticated, focused on what he is doing for God. A woman prays: “Lord, I don't know what to say. I'm a mess. Have mercy.” Authentic prayer is measured not by eloquence but by honesty about need, and one of those two is a good deal closer to going home justified.

verseByVerse.quote: He also told this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt: 'Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He also told this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt: two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.

The second prayer parable. The first parable was about persistence in prayer; this one is about humility in prayer. And it is one of the clearest pictures of justification in the Gospels.

He also told this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous. Again Luke names the target before the story begins. Self-righteousness: trusting in one’s own goodness to be right with God. The confidence is placed in something they can inspect, which means it must be maintained. And a righteousness that has to be maintained needs a scale, and a scale needs other people on it.

And treated others with contempt. Treated with contempt, exouthenountas, means despised, counted as nothing, and it follows from the first clause as effect from cause. The contempt is not a personality trait attached to an otherwise sound position; the position generates it. A man who is sure of himself by comparison needs somebody to be worse. Note also that Luke does not say to the Pharisees but to some who: a description rather than a party, and it leaves the door open for anybody at all to walk through it.

The friend of sinners. The posture Jesus is exposing is the one he met wherever he went. When he ate with tax collectors, the Pharisees and scribes grumbled, this man receives sinners and eats with them (15:2), and they called him a friend of tax collectors and sinners (7:34). The contempt that looked down on the tax collector fell, sooner or later, on the one who sat beside him. Luke uses the same verb for Herod and his soldiers, who treated Jesus with contempt and mocked him (23:11). The Son of God took his place among the despised, and was despised with them, so that the despised could be received by God.

Two men went up into the temple to pray. Probably at the hours of prayer, the morning or afternoon sacrifice, when people gathered to pray (Acts 3:1), with the sacrifice being offered and a crowd in the court. It puts them in the same place at the same time.

One a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. The pairing is as wide as first-century Judaism could make it. A Pharisee was not a hypocrite in the popular sense but a serious man who organised his life around the whole law, respected in his community, by any ordinary measure the best sort of person available. A tax collector had contracted with the occupying power to extract money from his own people, and lived on what he could collect above the assessment (3:12; 19:7). To Jesus’ hearers the Pharisee was the obvious hero and the tax collector the obvious villain. Two men, one building, one God, and everybody listening knows which of them is going home right with him. Which is why the last verse detonates.

Who are the Pharisees today? Not a group you can point to across the street. The Pharisee is the person in any church who trusts in his own record and measures himself against others, and he is very often the person reading this. The trap is that reading this parable can produce a new kind of Pharisee: God, I thank you that I am not like that Pharisee. The parable is aimed not at a party but at a posture of the heart, and the only safe place to stand while reading it is where the tax collector stood.

In a sentence. To those who trusted in their own righteousness and despised others, Jesus told of a Pharisee and a tax collector who went up to the temple to pray.

On a Tuesday. Do you trust in your own goodness? Do you look down on anyone? This parable is aimed at you. Notice this week whom you mentally rank yourself above: the colleague whose language is coarse, the family member who never goes to church, the Christian with the messy life. Then ask whether your confidence before God rests on that ranking.

For worship. Two men went up into the temple, and the whole gospel was waiting for them there. God built that house not to display the righteous but to receive the guilty, with an altar of sacrifice in its court and blood carried to its mercy seat. And the true meeting-place of God and sinners has a name: the Lord Jesus, who came not to call the righteous but sinners to repentance (5:32). His door is lowest for those who know they deserve to be kept out, and it has never yet been shut on one of them.
verseByVerse.note: Pharisees were respected for their devotion to the law; tax collectors were despised as collaborators and cheats. Public prayers were offered at the temple morning and afternoon.

parallels.desc: the hour of prayer, the ninth hour

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisee, standing by himself, prayed thus: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I get.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisee, standing by himself, prayed thus: God, I thank you that I am not like other men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I get.

The Pharisee, standing by himself, prayed thus. A word first about the wording, because translations differ here and something has been built on the difference. The Greek phrase pros heauton can attach either to the standing or to the praying: standing by himself, prayed, or standing, he prayed thus to himself. Either he stood apart, so as not to be defiled by others, or his prayer was really addressed to himself. Probably both are true of him, though neither should carry weight the text will not bear. What is certain is the content, and the content settles the question without any help from the grammar.

God, I thank you. The opening is correct; it begins exactly as a good prayer should. But he thanks God for himself, not for God’s mercy. He asks for nothing; he does not think he needs anything. He uses I five times in two verses.

Another thanksgiving. Luke has already recorded a very different prayer that began the same way. When the seventy-two came back rejoicing, Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said, I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children (10:21). The Son thanked his Father for grace given to people with nothing. The Pharisee thanks God for himself, and for the distance between himself and the people with nothing. The two prayers open with the same words and face opposite ways: one looks up in delight at what God gives the small, the other looks down in satisfaction at what he has made of himself.

That I am not like other men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers. And then it turns, and it turns into a list of other people. He compares himself with notorious sinners, and of course comes off well.

Or even like this tax collector. Four categories, and the fourth is standing in the same courtyard. This tax collector: he has looked, identified him, and put him in the prayer. He looks at the man behind him with contempt.

I fast twice a week. The law required only one yearly fast, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29). Strict Pharisees fasted on Mondays and Thursdays. He does two a week. He did more than required.

I give tithes of all that I get. The tithe was on agricultural produce; he tithes everything that passes through his hands, including things somebody else should already have tithed (11:42). Again, more than required. This is not a fraud. He is doing more than God asked.

The problem. He was probably telling the truth about his outward life, and that is what makes the parable so uncomfortable. His problem was not insincerity, and not his deeds, but his heart: he trusted in them, compared himself with others rather than with God, and despised sinners. He came to God to report his goodness, not to seek mercy. He came to the temple with a credit balance, and he left with it, which is the one thing you cannot do anything with at that address.

Is it wrong to thank God that I am not living in some sin? Not in itself. If God has kept you from drunkenness or adultery, that is his grace, and you should thank him for it. The difference is where the thanks points. Grateful humility says: but for the grace of God, there go I, and it makes you gentler with the fallen. The Pharisee’s thanks said: look at me, and it made him harder. If your thanksgiving ends with you feeling superior to someone, it has turned into the Pharisee’s prayer. Paul, who could list more virtues than this man (Philippians 3:4–6), counted them all as loss, and called himself the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15).

In a sentence. The Pharisee prayed, thanking God that he was not like sinners or the tax collector, and listing his fasting and tithing.

On a Tuesday. When you pray, do you compare yourself with others? Compare yourself with God, and you will have nothing to boast about. Listen to your prayers this week, and count the I’s. Then pray once without mentioning anything you have done, only what God is and what you need.

For worship. There is only one Man who could have prayed the Pharisee’s prayer honestly: I am not like other men. Jesus was holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners (Hebrews 7:26). And he never once prayed it. Instead he stood with the tax collectors, was baptised in the line of sinners, and was numbered with the transgressors. The only one with a true credit balance gave it away to men with nothing, and went to the cross with our debts on his account.
verseByVerse.note: The law required only one yearly fast (the Day of Atonement); the Pharisee fasted twice a week and tithed even what the law did not require.

verseByVerse.quote: But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying: God, be merciful to me, a sinner!

But the tax collector, standing far off. Everything about him is measured in distance and refusal. Standing far off: at the edge, at a distance from the sanctuary, and from the Pharisee, as far into the court as he judged himself entitled to come. He feels he has no right to come near. The Pharisee had also stood by himself, and the two men are alone in the same building for opposite reasons.

Would not even lift up his eyes to heaven. The normal Jewish posture for prayer was standing, looking up, with hands raised. He is not adopting an alternative attitude of piety; he is failing to do the ordinary thing, because he cannot. He could not bring himself to look up: O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you (Ezra 9:6).

But beat his breast. Beating the breast was a sign of deep grief or remorse, and in that culture an unusual one for a man: it belonged to mourning, to funerals. Luke will record it once more, from the crowd walking home from Golgotha (23:48). He beats his heart, the source of his sin.

God, be merciful to me, a sinner! Six words in Greek, and the whole gospel in a prayer. Be merciful, hilasthēti, is not the ordinary word for mercy. It means be propitiated, be reconciled to me. It belongs to the family of hilastērion, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the mercy seat, the gold lid of the ark where the blood of atonement was sprinkled (Hebrews 9:5), and the word Paul uses of Christ in Romans 3:25. He is not asking God to overlook anything. He is asking God to accept the atoning sacrifice on his behalf and turn away his wrath, and he asks it standing in the temple, very possibly at the hour when a lamb was being offered.

The sinner. The second thing is a definite article the English cannot easily carry. He does not say a sinner. He says the sinner, tō hamartōlō. Not one among many, but the sinner, as if he were the only one. Which is what a man says when he has stopped comparing. The Pharisee could see four categories of people and himself above them. This man cannot see anybody else in the building. He does not compare himself with anyone. He brings nothing but his need.

What he does not say. He offers no undertaking. There is no promise to leave the profession, no schedule of restitution, no proposal that he will be different from tomorrow, all of which he might reasonably have thought were the price of being heard. He asks for mercy and stops talking. Seven words, and every one of them about God or about himself, and not one of them about what he intends to do next.

So does repentance not involve change? It does, and the change will come; Zacchaeus, another tax collector, will give back fourfold in the next chapter (19:8). But the change is the fruit of mercy, not its price. A man does not clean himself up in order to come to God; he comes to God to be cleaned. If you are waiting until you have sorted yourself out before you pray this prayer, you have reversed the gospel. Come as you are, with the prayer of the sinner, and let the God who justifies you begin to make you new.

In a sentence. The tax collector stood far off, unable to look up, beat his breast and prayed: God, be merciful to me, the sinner.

On a Tuesday. This is the prayer that God answers. Pray it today: God, be merciful to me, a sinner. Pray it on your knees, or in the car, or in the moment after you have lost your temper with your children. Christians who have walked with God for fifty years still pray it, and find it fresher every time.

For worship. The tax collector asked God to be propitiated, and God answered him, though not with anything on that day’s altar. The true Mercy Seat was walking towards Jerusalem while the parable was told, and soon the blood that every Day of Atonement had pointed to would be shed outside the city. Every sinner who beats his breast and asks for mercy is asking for the cross, and the cross has already been given. No prayer has ever been surer of an answer than a sinner’s plea for what God has already provided.
verseByVerse.note: Beating the breast was a sign of deep grief or remorse.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.

I tell you, this man went down to his house justified. A verdict on Jesus’ own authority, the kind that would make his hearers put their cups down. Justified, dedikaiōmenos, is a perfect passive participle and a courtroom word: declared right with God, acquitted, accepted as righteous. Not made morally perfect, and not improved or forgiven in a general way, but declared righteous by God the Judge, with a verdict entered in his favour by somebody else. The perfect tense means it is done and it stands: he went home in a state of being justified. A man who had defrauded his neighbours for a living walked out of that temple with a standing before God that the most religious man in the country did not have, having offered nothing except an accurate description of himself and a request for mercy.

Rather than the other. Not more than. The Pharisee was not justified. All his good works did not make him right with God, because he trusted in them. He went home exactly as he arrived, which is the quiet tragedy of the parable: nothing happened to him at all. He had come with a balance and taken it away again.

The doctrine of justification. Here, in a parable, decades before Paul wrote a word about it, is the doctrine he would set out in Romans and Galatians: a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law (Romans 3:28; Galatians 2:16). God justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5). Not by our righteousness, but by his mercy, through the atoning sacrifice that Christ would offer. The tax collector prayed for propitiation; Christ provided it (Romans 3:24–26; 1 John 2:2). The tax collector contributes nothing, and receives a verdict.

Where Christians differ: how are we justified? Roman Catholic teaching (Council of Trent, 1547) holds that justification is a process in which God makes us inwardly righteous by infusing grace, received through baptism and increased by good works and the sacraments; it can be lost through mortal sin and restored through penance. Verdict: the Reformers rightly taught that justification is God’s legal declaration that a sinner is righteous, on the basis of Christ’s righteousness imputed (credited) to him, received by faith alone (Romans 4:3–8; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9). The tax collector went home justified that day, at once, not after a long process of becoming righteous. Good works follow as the fruit of justification, never as its ground.

Can I be sure I am justified? Yes. Justification is not a feeling that comes and goes or a grade that rises and falls with your performance; it is God’s verdict, and God does not revise his verdicts. If you have come to him as the tax collector did, with nothing but your sin and his mercy in Christ, you went home justified too, and nothing can bring a charge against you (Romans 8:33–34). Your sense of it may waver, especially when you sin; then go back and pray the same prayer, and remember that the verdict rests on Christ’s righteousness, not yours, and his does not waver.

For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted. The principle of 14:11, and the two verbs again leave God unnamed as the one who does it. This is not a general observation about how life tends to work out. It is a statement about who is running the lift. The proud Pharisee is humbled; the humble tax collector is exalted.

Humility that is not a technique. The saying needs one guard, because it can be turned into a technique. A man who humbles himself in order to be exalted has exalted himself, and the sentence has already seen him. The tax collector was not performing humility. He was telling the truth, and it happened to be devastating, which is the only humility that has ever done anybody any good.

The one who went lowest. The saying has one perfect fulfilment, and it is Christ, who did not humble himself as a technique either. Though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and humbled himself to the point of death on a cross; therefore God has highly exalted him (Philippians 2:6–9). Luke tells the same story in the risen Lord’s own words: was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? (24:26). The tax collector goes down to his house lifted up because the Son went further down than any sinner, and was raised higher than every name.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that the tax collector, not the Pharisee, went home justified before God, for whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself exalted.

On a Tuesday. If you trust in Christ, you are justified: declared righteous before God, now and for ever. Live this week like a man who has been acquitted. When old guilt comes back, answer it with the verdict. When you are tempted to prove yourself to God or to anyone else, remember that the case is closed. And treat others, even the obvious sinners, as men and women who could go home justified today.

For worship. This is the strangest courtroom in the world: the guilty man walks out acquitted, and the Judge bears the sentence. The verdict the tax collector carried home did not ignore the law but honoured it, because the Son would stand where the guilty stood and be condemned on a hill outside the city. So the acquittal does not wear thin with time. It is entered in heaven, sealed in blood and upheld by the risen Lord. Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered (Psalm 32:1), and that blessing went home with a tax collector one afternoon and has never been taken back.
verseByVerse.note: “Justified” means declared right with God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke's word is infants, and it is precise: not children generally but babies. Matthew and Mark say children; Luke narrows it. These are infants in arms, and the parents want nothing except that he should touch them.

The disciples deserve a fair hearing. In this chapter he has been teaching about prayer, justification and the coming of the Son of Man, and in the last one he told them he must suffer many things and be rejected (17:25). The pressure is enormous and the time is visibly short — and a queue of mothers has formed with babies who cannot understand a word he says.

They are protecting his diary, and by every reasonable measure of importance they are right. Which is the thing worth sitting with, because the same judgement gets made constantly and never feels like a fault. The people with no standing, no urgency and nothing to contribute are the ones edged out of the schedule — not by hard men, but by conscientious ones with a great deal to get through.

“Do not hinder them” uses kōluein, a word with a history in Luke's second volume: the Ethiopian asks “What prevents me from being baptized?” (Acts 8:36); Peter asks “can anyone withhold water?” (Acts 10:47). It is the word used when somebody is being kept out who should be let in.

And the reason given is not what sentiment expects. Children are not held up as innocent, and Scripture nowhere claims it. What an infant in that world had was nothing — no legal standing, no property, no achievements, no capacity to give anything back. It can only be carried and received.

That is the model. Which is why the paragraph sits exactly where it does, between a tax collector who had nothing and a ruler who had a great deal.
verseByVerse.theology:
One further question needs asking, since this is one of the two texts most often brought to it: does “let the children come to me” support the baptism of infants? Honestly, it neither settles it nor is irrelevant to it.

Those who baptise infants point out that Jesus takes up children who can offer nothing, declares the kingdom theirs, and blesses them — and that God has dealt with families as units since Abraham, putting the covenant sign on children long before they could profess anything (Gen. 17:7; cf. Acts 2:39, “the promise is for you and for your children”). They add that the disciples who sought to exclude them are explicitly rebuked.

Those who baptise only believers answer, fairly, that Jesus blesses these infants and does not baptise them, and that every baptism recorded in Acts follows a profession of faith. That second point is the weightier, and the believer’s-baptism view is the better reading (see on Acts 2:39).

The text will not carry the whole argument by itself, and Christians who love the same Lord have divided over it for centuries without either side being able to close the case from this verse alone.

What the passage does say, and says with force, is the thing both sides should agree on: no one comes into this kingdom by contributing. If an infant can be blessed by Christ, then the door is not opened by understanding, or by maturity, or by anything a person brings — and every adult who enters comes in on precisely the same terms as the baby in his mother's arms.
verseByVerse.examples:
The verb Luke uses for the disciples' rebuke is a strong one; he used it of Jesus silencing a demon (4:35) and rebuking a fever (4:39). These men are not being gentle with the parents — and they are corrected in front of them.

Which is worth noticing again two dozen verses later, when the crowd tells a blind beggar to be quiet (v.39) using the same verb. The people nearest to Jesus are the ones clearing the road of those with nothing to offer, and it happens twice in one chapter.

A family brings their newborn to be presented at church, and the pastor wonders whether to spend time explaining the theological weight of it. This passage gives the content: this child is being presented to Jesus, exactly as the infants were in v.15, and Jesus's posture is not reluctance but welcome.

And the placing is the sermon. One verse after Jesus says the kingdom belongs to people who can do nothing, a ruler arrives asking what he must do — and ends very sad, still holding everything he came with.

verseByVerse.quote: Now they were bringing even infants to him that he might touch them. And when the disciples saw it, they rebuked them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now they were bringing even infants to him that he might touch them. And when the disciples saw it, they rebuked them.

The placing. Here Luke rejoins the order Mark follows (Mark 10:13), and the story fits after the tax collector: the kingdom belongs to those who come with nothing, like children.

Now they were bringing even infants to him. Luke’s word is brephē, and it is precise. Not children generally but babies: the same word he used of John leaping in Elizabeth’s womb (1:41). Matthew and Mark use the broader term; only Luke says infants. These are infants in arms, carried by parents who want nothing except that he should touch them. No question is being asked and no problem is being brought. They want their children in his hands.

That he might touch them. To bless them, as Jewish parents brought children to rabbis and elders for a blessing. Luke tells us nothing about the parents except what they wanted, and what they wanted was contact. They had no theology to offer and no request to make, only a conviction that whatever was in this man was worth getting their children within arm’s length of, even at the cost of being publicly told off.

And when the disciples saw it, they rebuked them. It is easy to be hard on the disciples, and the instinct deserves a fair hearing, because it was not cruelty. They had just heard teaching about prayer, about justification, about the coming of the Son of Man, and that he must suffer many things and be rejected (17:25). The pressure on him is enormous and the time visibly short, and a queue of mothers has formed with babies who cannot understand a word. The disciples are protecting his diary, and by every reasonable measure of importance they are right. But the verb for their rebuke is a strong one; Luke used it of Jesus silencing a demon (4:35). They are not being gentle with the parents, and they are about to be corrected in front of them.

The judgment that never feels like a fault. That is the thing worth sitting with, because the same judgment gets made constantly. The people with no standing, no urgency and nothing to contribute are the ones edged out of the schedule: not by hard men, but by conscientious ones with a great deal to get through. Children in a church service, the elderly, the disabled, the slow learner in the Bible study: it is very easy to treat them as interruptions to the real ministry. Jesus treats them as the ministry.

The baby who became the one they came to. Luke’s word carries its own wonder. He used it of the baby Jesus wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger (2:12, 16), and weeks later that baby was carried into the temple and lifted into old Simeon’s arms (2:28). Now the one who was carried in as a baby is the one to whom babies are carried. He has been small himself, wrapped and laid down and lifted by others, and he does not think smallness beneath the kingdom. The Son of God passed through infancy on purpose, and so infancy is not a waiting-room outside his concern; it is ground he has walked.

In a sentence. People were bringing even babies to Jesus for him to touch them, and the disciples rebuked them.

On a Tuesday. Never think a child is too small to be brought to Jesus in prayer. Bring your children, grandchildren, godchildren and the children of your church to him by name this week. And if you serve in a church, look at how you treat the crying baby in the service, the toddler at the door, the teenager on the edge. Make it easier, not harder, for them to come near.

For worship. The Lord of glory had time for babies. On his way to the cross, carrying the weight of the world’s salvation, he called the infants to himself. The hands their parents wanted on them were the hands of the one through whom all things were made (John 1:3), and before long they would be stretched out on a cross for children like these. No one is too small for him, too young to matter, too weak to be worth his time. The heavier his road grew, the lower he stooped.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus called them to him, saying, 'Let the children come to me, and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jesus called them to him, saying: let the children come to me, and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.

But Jesus called them to him. He calls them, the children, or possibly the parents; the wording allows either, and it hardly matters, since one comes with the other.

Let the children come to me, and do not hinder them. Do not hinder them: the language used when somebody is being kept out who should be let in. Nothing must stand between a child and Jesus.

For to such belongs the kingdom of God. Not the kingdom is like them, and not they may come in later. It belongs to them, and to such widens it past these particular babies to everyone of that kind: dependent, helpless, receiving as a gift.

Come to me. Notice where Jesus places the door of the kingdom. He does not say, let the children come to God, or to the temple, or to the teachers of the law. He says, let the children come to me, and in the same breath, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. Coming to Jesus and receiving God’s kingdom are, on his own lips, one movement. No prophet ever spoke like that. Moses pointed beyond himself; John the Baptist pointed beyond himself. Jesus points to himself, and calls the smallest people in the land to the place where the kingdom is given.

Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it. The reason is not what sentiment expects. Children are not held up as innocent; anyone who has raised one knows better, and Scripture nowhere claims it (Psalm 51:5). What an infant in that world had was nothing: no legal standing, no property, no achievements, no capacity to give anything back. A baby cannot ask a question, make a confession or demonstrate anything at all. It can only be carried and received. To receive the kingdom like a child is to receive it with no credentials, no negotiating position, and nothing whatever to bring.

Between the tax collector and the ruler. The Pharisee came as an adult with his achievements; the tax collector came as a child, empty-handed. The kingdom is received, not achieved. And this paragraph sits exactly between a tax collector who had nothing and a ruler who had a great deal, and it is worth noticing that the ruler is about to ask what must I do, one verse after Jesus has said that the kingdom belongs to people who cannot do anything.

Where Christians differ: does this passage support infant baptism? This is one of the texts most often brought to the question, and honestly it neither settles it nor is irrelevant to it. Those who baptise infants point out that Jesus takes up children who offer nothing, declares the kingdom theirs, and blesses them, and that God has dealt with families as units since Abraham, putting the covenant sign on children long before they could profess anything (Genesis 17:7; Acts 2:39). Those who baptise only believers answer, fairly, that he blesses these infants and does not baptise them, and that every baptism recorded in Acts follows a profession of faith. Verdict: the passage shows Christ’s welcome for children and the need to bring them to him, but does not mention baptism and cannot settle that question. The New Testament pattern of baptism following repentance and faith fits the credobaptist position (Acts 2:39), held charitably. The text will not carry the whole argument alone. What it does say, with force, is the thing both sides agree on: no one comes into this kingdom by contributing, and every adult who enters comes in on precisely the same terms as the baby in his mother’s arms. Brothers who baptise their infants do so out of a sincere desire to bring their children to Christ, and they are honoured here.

What of little children who die? Scripture gives no age of accountability and no explicit promise. But Luke’s own scene gives good ground for hope: these are infants who could profess nothing, and Jesus says the kingdom belongs to such. David, burying a baby son, said he would go to him (2 Samuel 12:23), and Abraham’s question still stands: shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just? (Genesis 18:25). The Westminster Confession states that elect infants dying in infancy are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when, where and how he pleases (Westminster 10.3). Salvation is still by grace through Christ alone; but grieving parents may entrust their child to the one who called little ones to himself, and many believers have found in this very verse the strength to bury a baby with hope.

How do we bring our children to Jesus today? Pray for them and with them, every day, from before they can understand. Read the Bible to them and tell them the stories of Jesus. Bring them to church, and let them see you love it. Live the gospel in front of them, including saying sorry when you sin against them. Talk naturally about God at the table and in the car (Deuteronomy 6:7). And when they come to trust Christ, as you pray they will, do not tell them they are too young to mean it. Their faith may be small and simple; so is everybody’s, at first.

In a sentence. Jesus called the children to him, saying the kingdom belongs to such as these, and that whoever does not receive it like a child will not enter it.

On a Tuesday. Come to God today as a child, receiving his kingdom as a gift. Stop bringing him your achievements or your excuses. Tell him you have nothing, and hold out your hands. And if there is a child in your life, take five minutes this week to pray with him, by name, and tell him that Jesus welcomes children.

For worship. The kingdom of heaven is not a prize for the competent but an inheritance for the helpless, and its King opened the door by calling for infants. He himself became a child, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons (Galatians 4:4–5). The Son who once could not walk or speak or feed himself has made every helpless sinner welcome. Because the eternal Son became a child, the children of men can become children of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke calls him a ruler, a man of official standing; Matthew tells us he was young, and all three Gospels that he was rich. He asks the best question in the Gospel, sincerely — Mark says he ran up and knelt (Mark 10:17), which is not the behaviour of a man laying a trap.

But listen to the shape of it: “what must I do to inherit?” The same collision Luke recorded from the lawyer at 10:25, a doing-word and a receiving-word in one breath. And it comes one verse after Jesus said the kingdom belongs to infants.

“Why do you call me good?” has been used to argue that Jesus denied his own deity, and it will not do the work. He does not say “I am not good”; he asks a question about a word. Either the title is loose — flattery paid to an admired teacher — or it is exact, and the ruler has said far more than he intended. Jesus does not resolve it. He leaves the man holding both halves.

The commandments he lists are all from the second table, and all observable. What is not quoted is the first table — nothing about other gods or idols — and nothing about the tenth commandment, the only one that is entirely interior. That omission is filled in at verse 22.

The man's claim deserves to be taken seriously, because Jesus does. Mark records that he looked at him and loved him. By any measure a first-century community could apply, this is an exemplary man — and that is precisely why the passage is so uncomfortable. He is not a warning about scandalous living but about a life that passes every test a person can be set. A man who has passed every test he knows about will not go looking for the one he has not been given.

“One thing you still lack” sounds like a small outstanding balance, which is how he would have heard it. It is not. The one thing is the whole thing.
verseByVerse.theology:
Is Jesus prescribing poverty as a universal requirement? No — the command was specific to this man, whose particular idol was wealth. He does not say it to Zacchaeus, who is also rich and gives away half (19:8-9); he does not say it to the women who funded the ministry out of their means (8:3). What has happened is that the first table of the law, quietly left out of the list two verses earlier, has been applied: you shall have no other gods before me, tested in the one area where it would cost him. It is a diagnostic instrument, precisely calibrated to one patient.

The camel and the needle should not be softened, and two softenings should be set aside. There is no evidence that “the eye of the needle” was a small gate in the Jerusalem wall — that story appears no earlier than the Middle Ages. And the suggestion that a copyist confused the word for camel with the word for rope is speculation about a text nobody has; a rope will not go through a needle either. Jesus picked the largest animal in the country and the smallest opening in common life, and the sentence means what it appears to mean.

The crowd's reaction — “then who can be saved?” — surprises modern readers, and the surprise is important. They shared the assumption Luke has been dismantling since chapter 16, that prosperity evidenced God's approval. On that theology the rich were at the front of the queue.

“What is impossible with man is possible with God” is the pivot of the whole chapter. The widow could not get justice; the judge gave it. The tax collector could not justify himself; God did. The infants could not come; they were carried.
verseByVerse.examples:
Peter's “we have left our homes” is easy to hear as boasting, and it is fairer to hear it as a question with the question mark missing. He has just watched a man grieve because he could not give up his possessions, and heard that entry is impossible for such a man — and Peter has done the thing the ruler would not. And “our homes” is understated: Luke has recorded boats, nets, a tax booth (5:11, 28).

Note the qualifying phrase in the answer: “for the sake of the kingdom of God.” This is not a promise attached to loss in general, and certainly not a licence for abandoning a family — Luke has already ruled that out (cf. 1 Tim. 5:8).

And what is returned is not usually the same currency. Mark's version specifies houses and brothers and mothers and children (Mark 10:30), which is not a promise of replacement relatives but a description of what the church turned out to be. A man who lost a family found himself in a hundred houses. Anyone who has watched a convert lose his relations and gain a congregation has seen this verse work.

But Mark adds two words Luke omits — with persecutions. The return is real and it is not comfortable, and Luke's silence should not be read as a promise of an easier settlement than his brother evangelist offers.

A wealthy member of a congregation serves faithfully — on the board, in generous giving, in every visible way — and there is one area he has never submitted to Christ's scrutiny. The rich ruler was, by most measures, exemplary. The issue was not what he had done but what he would not surrender.

verseByVerse.quote: And a ruler asked him, 'Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?' And Jesus said to him, 'Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A ruler asked him: Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life? And Jesus said to him: why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.

And a ruler asked him. After the infants who receive comes a man who wants to achieve. Luke calls him a ruler, a man of official standing, perhaps a synagogue leader or member of a council. Matthew tells us he was young (Matthew 19:20); all three Gospels tell us he was rich (v. 23). Rich, powerful, respectable. And he asks the best question in the Gospel, sincerely. Mark says he ran up and knelt (Mark 10:17), which is not the behaviour of a man laying a trap. Whatever is wrong here, insincerity is not it.

Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life? But listen to the shape of the sentence, because the whole problem is in it. It is the lawyer’s question (10:25), a doing-word and a receiving-word in one breath. He thinks of eternal life as something to be earned. And an inheritance is the one thing nobody works for. It comes one verse after Jesus said the kingdom belongs to infants.

Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. This has been used to argue that Jesus denied his own deity, and it will not do the work. He does not say I am not good. He asks a question about a word. Good Teacher was not a standard form of address; it reads as a compliment paid to a man whose approval the ruler wants. So the question is a challenge to think about what has just been said. Only God is good in the absolute sense. So either the title is loose, flattery, a pleasant thing to say to a teacher one admires, or it is exact, and the ruler has said far more than he intended. Jesus does not resolve it. He leaves the man holding both halves. And if only God is good, then the ruler is not good either.

Is Jesus denying that he is good, or that he is God? Neither. The title is true: Jesus is good because he is God, without sin (Hebrews 4:15). His question presses the man to think about what he is saying: if only God is good, and you call me good, what do you think I am? Jesus is not denying his own goodness or deity, but challenging the ruler’s shallow understanding of goodness. And there is a reason he starts here rather than answering the question. A man who hands out the word good that easily has a scale on which the word can be applied to people, and he is standing somewhere on it. Everything that follows is going to be about where.

In a sentence. A ruler asked Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life, and Jesus challenged his use of good, since only God is good.

On a Tuesday. Only God is truly good. Stop measuring yourself by your own standards. When you call yourself a good person this week, or think it, ask: good by whose measure? Then measure yourself against God’s goodness, and run to the only good Man who ever lived.

For worship. No one is good except God alone, and the good God stood on a road in Judea and was called Teacher by a man who did not know whom he was addressing. The goodness that made the stars, the source of every good gift (James 1:17), walked among us in sandals and answered questions. The ruler used the word lightly; heaven uses it with all its weight. In Christ that goodness has a face and a name, and it does not wait for us to become good before it speaks to us.
verseByVerse.note: Luke calls him a ruler; Matthew adds that he was young.

verseByVerse.quote: You know the commandments: ‘Do not commit adultery, Do not murder, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Honor your father and mother.’' And he said, 'All these I have kept from my youth.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
You know the commandments: do not commit adultery, do not murder, do not steal, do not bear false witness, honour your father and mother. And he said: all these I have kept from my youth.

You know the commandments. Note the assumption, and it is not a compliment. He does not teach him anything. This man knows. Jesus points him to the law.

The list. Adultery, murder, theft, false witness, honour to parents: the seventh, sixth, eighth, ninth and fifth commandments, all from the second table, the ones governing how a man treats his neighbour, and all observable, the kind a community can check. What is missing is the first table: nothing about other gods, idols, the name or the Sabbath. And nothing about the tenth, you shall not covet, the one commandment that is entirely interior and cannot be verified by anybody. That is where the ruler’s problem lies: his wealth is his god (Exodus 20:3), and he covets. The omission will be filled in at verse 22.

And he said, All these I have kept from my youth. Sincere, and outwardly perhaps true, and Jesus takes the claim seriously; nothing in the passage suggests the man is lying. By any measure a first-century community could apply, this is an exemplary man, and has been since boyhood. That is the position of a great many decent people, and it is why the passage is uncomfortable. The ruler is not a warning about scandalous living. He is a warning about a life that passes every test a person can be set, and a man who has passed every test he knows about will not go looking for the one he has not been given.

Another boy who kept the law. Luke has shown us one youth of whom the claim was simply true. At twelve the boy Jesus was found in his Father’s house, and then went down to Nazareth and was submissive to his parents, increasing in wisdom and in stature and in favour with God and man (2:51–52). He honoured his father and mother as no son ever has, and loved his Father in heaven with his whole heart. The ruler’s record was real by every outward test; Christ’s was real by every test, the heart’s included. The one man who could truly say all these I have kept was standing in front of the man who said it.

Was the ruler really blameless? Only by outward measure. He has not understood how deep the law goes: to the heart. No one keeps the law as God requires (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:10–11), and Jesus had taught that anger and lust break the commandments (Matthew 5:21–28). He has never seen himself as a sinner, unlike the tax collector. Jesus is not offering a ladder of law-keeping to eternal life; he is using the law to show the man his need. His next words expose that his wealth was his god (v. 22), and the answer comes at verses 26 and 27: what is impossible with man is possible with God.

Why does Jesus point him to the law, if no one is saved by keeping it? Because the law is the mirror that shows us our need of a Saviour. Through the law comes knowledge of sin (Romans 3:20), and the law was our guardian until Christ came (Galatians 3:24). A man who thinks he is healthy will not go to a doctor, so the Physician first shows him his disease. That is still how God brings people to Christ: the commandments, rightly understood, strip away every claim of our own and leave us looking for mercy. The ruler had measured himself by what he could see and had not yet found his limit. It is about to be located for him with a single sentence.

In a sentence. Jesus listed the commandments about others, and the ruler claimed to have kept them all since childhood.

On a Tuesday. Have you kept God’s law in your heart, not just outwardly? Ask God to show you. Take the tenth commandment this week, you shall not covet, and watch your heart for seven days: in shop windows, on the phone screen, at a friend’s house. You will find out quickly that you have not kept all these from your youth, and you will find yourself where the tax collector stood, which is the best place to be.

For worship. Christ’s perfect obedience was not kept for himself. Every commandment he honoured, first table and second, outward and inward, from the manger to the cross, is counted to everyone who trusts him. His record becomes ours. The ruler offered his own righteousness and was found wanting; the believer offers nothing but Christ, and is found complete in him (Colossians 2:10). The law that sent one rich man away sad has been satisfied on our behalf by the only man who ever kept it, and it has nothing left to say against his people.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus heard this, he said to him, 'One thing you still lack. Sell all that you have and distribute to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.' But when he heard these things, he became very sad, for he was extremely rich.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus heard this, he said to him: one thing you still lack. Sell all that you have and distribute to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me. But when he heard these things, he became very sad, for he was extremely rich.

When Jesus heard this, he said to him, One thing you still lack. After a lifetime of commandment-keeping, one item outstanding. It sounds like a small balance on an otherwise settled account, which is exactly how the man would have heard it. It is not. The one thing is the whole thing. His wealth had his heart, and he had broken the first commandment.

Sell all that you have and distribute to the poor. Jesus puts his finger on the one thing this man loved more than God. It is not a universal rule for disciples. He does not say it to Zacchaeus, who is also rich and gives away half (19:8–9), nor to the women who funded the ministry out of their means (8:3), nor to Martha, whose house he was glad of. Luke has been careful about this all through. What has happened is that the first table of the law, quietly left out of the list two verses ago, has just been applied. You shall have no other gods before me, and the man is being asked to show that he has none, in the one area where it would cost him. It is a diagnostic instrument, precisely calibrated to one patient.

And you will have treasure in heaven. Not a loss, but an exchange (12:33). Everything he gives up is banked where moth and rust do not destroy.

And come, follow me. The real goal, and the point of the other three imperatives. This is not mainly a command about money; it is a call to discipleship with an obstacle removed first. And see what Jesus sets in the place of the idol. He does not add a further rule; he names himself. The whole heart that the first commandment claims for God, Jesus claims as the one to be followed, because to follow him is to have God as God. Eternal life is not found in the selling. It is found in the Person the selling would free him to follow.

But when he heard these things, he became very sad, for he was extremely rich. Very sad, perilypos, is strong: deeply grieved. He does not argue. He is heartbroken, which means he understood exactly what was offered and what it cost. He wanted eternal life, but not more than his money, and Luke’s last clause is the diagnosis: for he was extremely rich. Matthew and Mark say he went away (Mark 10:22); Luke leaves him standing there, sad, in front of Jesus. He came with the right question, was offered treasure in heaven and the company of the Son of God, and could not do it. The contrast is with the tax collector, with the disciples who left everything (5:11, 28), and with Zacchaeus, who will give half his goods away (19:8).

Must I sell everything to follow Jesus? Not necessarily, as Zacchaeus and Mary and Martha show. But you must be willing to, and you must give up whatever Jesus puts his finger on. For one person it is money; for another a relationship, a career, a reputation, a grudge, a habit. The question is not whether you have possessions but whether they have you. A good test: if Jesus asked for it today, would you be sad, like the ruler, or glad, like the man who sold all he had to buy the field with the treasure (Matthew 13:44)? Whatever you cannot give up has become your god, and Jesus loves you too much to leave it there.

In a sentence. Jesus told the ruler that he lacked one thing: he must sell all, give to the poor, and follow him, but the ruler became very sad, because he was very rich.

On a Tuesday. What is the one thing that stands between you and wholehearted discipleship? Give it to Christ. You probably know already what it is; it came to mind as you read. Name it in prayer today, and take one concrete step to loosen its grip: give some of it away, cancel it, confess it to a friend, put it on the altar.

For worship. Mark records that Jesus looked at this man and loved him (Mark 10:21), and he asked for everything because he was offering everything. The one who said sell all that you have had already done it. He laid aside the riches of heaven and became poor for our sake (2 Corinthians 8:9), had nowhere to lay his head, and at the end was stripped even of his clothes while soldiers cast lots for them (23:34). He gave up all he had to purchase a people, and they are his treasure. Whatever he asks of us, he has already outgiven.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, seeing that he had become sad, said, 'How difficult it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! For it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, seeing that he had become sad, said: how difficult it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! For it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.

Jesus, seeing that he had become sad. Luke lets us watch Jesus watching him. The words that follow are not a general observation delivered afterwards; they are spoken over a grieving man who is still standing in front of him. And they come from the one who would weep over Jerusalem because it did not know the things that make for peace (19:41–42). The Lord who will not lower the price takes no pleasure in the man’s refusal. He tells the truth about riches with sorrow in his face, which is the only way the truth about riches has ever been told well.

How difficult it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! It is not that wealth is wicked, or that God objects to comfort. It is that this kingdom is entered with empty hands, and wealth is the most effective device ever invented for keeping them full. A rich man’s difficulty is not that he loves money more than a poor man does; that is often untrue. It is that his life is arranged so that he never has to depend on anybody, and the kingdom is entered only by people who have run out of alternatives.

For it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle. The image is deliberately absurd and it should not be softened. The camel was the largest animal in the land, the needle’s eye the smallest opening in common life. Jesus has picked the two extremes on purpose. It is deliberate, comic exaggeration, and the sentence means what it appears to mean: impossible. Luke, the doctor, uses the word for a surgeon’s needle (belonēs).

Two softenings to set aside. Over the centuries two softenings have been attempted. One is that the eye of the needle was a small gate in the Jerusalem wall through which a camel could pass on its knees with its load removed; there is no evidence that any such gate existed, the story appears no earlier than the Middle Ages, and it misses the point. The other is that the Greek word for camel is a near-miss for the word for rope, and a copyist confused them; that is speculation about a text nobody has, and a rope will not go through a needle either. The needle’s eye is not too small for a camel because God is stingy about the entrance. It is exactly the right size for a person carrying nothing.

Am I rich? By any global standard, almost everybody reading this is the camel. If you have a roof, more than one set of clothes, food for tomorrow, a phone in your pocket and some money put by, you are among the wealthiest people who have ever lived. So the danger in this verse is not for someone else. It is for you. The safeguard is not guilt but generosity and dependence: holding everything with an open hand, giving freely, and praying for daily bread as if you had none in the cupboard.

In a sentence. Seeing his sadness, Jesus said how hard it is for the rich to enter God’s kingdom, harder than for a camel to go through the eye of a needle.

On a Tuesday. By the world’s standards, you are probably rich. Don’t let your wealth keep you from the kingdom. Ask what in your life is arranged so that you never have to depend on God: the savings that mean you never pray about money, the comforts that mean you never feel your need. Then do something that makes you depend on him again, like giving away more than feels safe.

For worship. He does not shrink the needle. He does something far greater. He became the poor man who went through the narrowest gate of all, the gate of death, carrying nothing but the sins of others, so that rich and poor alike could pass through after him. And the compassion that looked on one sad ruler looks on every one of us who has loaded a life with things, and goes on calling us to put them down and come.
verseByVerse.note: The camel was the largest animal in the land; the picture is deliberate exaggeration.

verseByVerse.quote: Those who heard it said, 'Then who can be saved?' But he said, 'What is impossible with man is possible with God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who heard it said: then who can be saved? But he said: what is impossible with man is possible with God.

Those who heard it said, Then who can be saved? The reaction is not what a modern reader expects. We hear hard for a rich man and think: yes, wealth is a spiritual danger. They concluded that nobody could be saved at all, because they shared an assumption Luke has been dismantling since chapter 16: that prosperity was evidence of God’s approval. The rich had the means to give alms, to keep the law without economic pressure, to be visibly blessed. If they cannot be saved, who can?

The right question. So the question is despairing and it is entirely logical. It is also, at last, the right question, and it is the first thing anybody in this chapter has said that does not begin with I. The ruler asked what must I do? The crowd asks who can be saved? Passive, and with no candidate in mind.

But he said, What is impossible with man is possible with God. One sentence, and it is the gospel. He does not soften the diagnosis or produce a technique for wealthy disciples. He grants the whole objection: salvation is humanly impossible, for anyone, rich or poor. The camel does not get smaller and the needle does not get wider. What he adds is a different actor. Salvation is God’s work from start to finish: by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God (Ephesians 2:8). The camel can go through the needle if God takes it through.

The pivot of the chapter. Everything before this has been preparing for it. The widow could not get justice; the judge gave it. The tax collector could not justify himself; God did it. The infants could not come; they were carried. And a rich man cannot enter the kingdom, and God can put him there. Salvation, on this account, is not a difficult thing made possible by effort. It is an impossible thing done by somebody else.

How God does the impossible. Luke shows the answer in two steps, and both are Christ. A few verses on, Jesus tells the Twelve that he will be handed over, mocked, flogged and killed, and rise on the third day (vv. 31–33): that is the price of the impossible. And a chapter later a rich chief tax collector climbs a tree, Jesus invites himself to his house, and says that today salvation has come to it, for the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (19:9–10). What is possible with God does not arrive as a softer rule for wealthy men. It arrives as the Son of Man, walking in through a rich man’s front door on his way to die.

If salvation is God’s work, what part do I play? You repent and believe; but even that is his gift working in you. Faith is not your contribution that God rewards; it is the empty hand with which you receive what he gives. God does not drag people into the kingdom against their will; he changes the will, so that they come freely and gladly (John 6:44; Philippians 2:13). That is why no one in heaven will boast, and why you can pray with real hope for the hardest person you know. If God can bring a camel through a needle, he can save your brother.

In a sentence. When people asked who then could be saved, Jesus said that what is impossible for people is possible for God.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person you have privately given up on: the one you are sure will never believe. Write his name down, and under it write: possible with God. Then pray for him every day this week. And when you look at your own heart and despair of ever changing, read the same sentence over yourself.

For worship. Every saved sinner is an impossibility that God has done. He lifted a widow’s son off his bier, called a tax collector down from a sycamore, and turned Saul the persecutor into Paul the apostle. Ah, Lord GOD! It is you who have made the heavens and the earth by your great power; nothing is too hard for you (Jeremiah 32:17). The kingdom fills with rich and poor alike, and every one of them came in by the same door, a mercy no one could earn.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said, 'See, we have left our homes and followed you.' And he said to them, 'Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter said: see, we have left our homes and followed you. And he said to them: truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life.

And Peter said, See, we have left our homes and followed you. It is easy to hear this as boasting, and it is worth being fairer to Peter than that. He has just watched a man grieve because he could not give up his possessions. Peter has done the thing the ruler would not, and his sentence is less a claim to merit than a question with the question mark missing: we did it; is it all right? And our homes is understated. Luke has recorded what they left: boats, nets, a tax booth (5:11, 28).

There is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children. The answer is generous and it is exact. Only Luke includes wife (also 14:26). Peter was married (4:38), and his wife later travelled with him (1 Corinthians 9:5). Leaving here means putting the kingdom first, sometimes literally leaving family behind for mission.

The Son who made a new family. Jesus asks nothing here he has not lived. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (9:58). When his mother and brothers came and could not reach him for the crowd, he said, my mother and my brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it (8:21). He left his home to make a household. The many times more that he promises is the family he himself gathered, brothers and sisters drawn round him to hear the word, and every convert who loses a home finds a place at his table.

For the sake of the kingdom of God. The motive, and the qualifying phrase matters. This is not a promise attached to loss in general, and it is certainly not a licence for abandoning a family. What is in view is what discipleship costs when it costs something, and Scripture elsewhere rules out the reading that would make this an excuse for neglect: a man who will not provide for his own household has denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8).

Who will not receive many times more in this time. Not only in the age to come: something is returned now, though not usually in the same currency. Mark’s version names houses and brothers and mothers and children (Mark 10:30), not replacement relatives but a description of what the church turned out to be. A man who lost a family found himself in a hundred houses. Anyone who has watched a convert lose his relations and gain a congregation has seen this verse work. But Mark adds two words Luke omits: with persecutions. The return is real and it is not comfortable.

And in the age to come eternal life. The answer to the ruler’s question (v. 18), and what he was left without. Those who give up everything for Christ gain eternal life, not as a wage for leaving but as the inheritance of those who have found the treasure worth more than everything else.

What if following Christ has cost me my family? Then this promise is for you in particular, and Jesus knew exactly what he was saying. Many converts from other religions, and some from secular families, are cut off by parents or spouses for their faith. The church is meant to be the answer: real homes opened, real meals shared, real brothers and sisters who stand with you at weddings and funerals. If you are such a believer, tell your church what you have lost; and if you are a member of a church, look for such believers and become their family. Keep praying for those who rejected you. Many have later come to faith themselves.

In a sentence. When Peter said they had left everything, Jesus promised that anyone who leaves home and family for the kingdom will receive far more now and eternal life in the age to come.

On a Tuesday. If following Christ has cost you, look at the family of believers he has given you. And look ahead to eternal life. If it has cost you little, ask whom you could be family to this week: the student far from home, the convert disowned by his parents, the widow with no children nearby. Set an extra place at your table.

For worship. No one has ever outgiven Christ. Every disciple who has left anything for him has found it returned many times over, in brothers and sisters, homes and tables, peace and joy, and at the end, life without end. He himself left the Father’s side and the worship of angels for the sake of the kingdom, and he has not been short-changed either. On the last day he will stand before his Father with the whole household he gathered and say, Behold, I and the children God has given me (Hebrews 2:13), and not one of them will be missing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–43 — Third Passion Prediction and the Blind Man at Jericho
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The third and fullest of the passion predictions, and the only one that explicitly grounds the events in Scripture: “everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished.” What is coming is not a disaster overtaking a good plan; it is a text being fulfilled, and the text was written centuries before.

Every item can be traced. Isaiah's Servant gave his back to those who strike and did not hide his face from disgrace and spitting (Isa. 50:6); he was despised and rejected (Isa. 53:3-5). The psalmist is mocked and surrounded (Ps. 22:7-8). And “delivered over to the Gentiles” is new: the earlier predictions named the elders and chief priests.

Notice how much of the list concerns humiliation rather than pain — mocked, shamefully treated, spat on — and Luke will record every one of them happening.

Then the incomprehension, stated three times in one verse so the reader cannot soften it. Jesus has given six specific things in plain language with no parable attached, and twelve men who had been with him three years took in nothing.

And the juxtaposition that follows is deliberate and devastating. The disciples, who have eyes, cannot see what he has just told them plainly. A blind beggar outside Jericho, working from one sentence shouted at him by a stranger, gets the identity right — and “Son of David” is a messianic title, the first time in this Gospel that any human being has used it of him aloud.

The crowd tells him to be silent, using the same verb Luke used of the disciples turning away the babies two dozen verses earlier. And the people doing it are “those who were in front” — the ones nearest to Jesus.

He cries out all the more, and the widow at the top of the chapter would have recognised him exactly.
verseByVerse.theology:
A reader with three Gospels open will stop at v.35, and the difficulty is worth facing because sceptics have made a good deal of it. Luke has the healing “as he drew near to Jericho” and then has Jesus entering the town (19:1); Matthew and Mark both have it as he was going out (Matt. 20:29; Mark 10:46). Matthew reports two blind men where the others report one, and only Mark supplies a name.

The number and the name are the easy half. None of the three says only one, and one never denies two. Mark gives a name and a father's name — “Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus” — which is how you identify a man his readers could go and ask.

The harder half is most probably explained by the ground itself. There were two Jerichos in the first century, roughly a mile apart: the ancient city standing as a ruin on its old mound, and the splendid new town Herod the Great had built to the south with his winter palace, with the road running between them. A traveller on that stretch was leaving one Jericho and approaching the other in the same few minutes. Matthew and Mark date the event by the town at his back; Luke by the town ahead. Both are exactly true of one man on one road on one afternoon.

What looks like three writers contradicting each other is the ordinary signature of independent witnesses standing in different places. Three men copying one document do not produce discrepancies of this kind; three men who were there produce exactly these.
verseByVerse.examples:
Luke's threefold statement that the disciples understood nothing is a mercy to the reader as well as astonishing. These are the men who would shortly preach the resurrection, and the honest record of how slow they were is part of the case for their testimony. Nobody inventing an account of the founding apostles makes them this stupid, and nobody who had merely persuaded himself of a resurrection afterwards would write down that he had been told in advance and had not understood a word.

And there is something here for anyone who has read a passage repeatedly and got nothing from it. They heard this from the Lord himself, in person, three times, and it was hidden. Understanding did not arrive by effort or by proximity; it arrived after the resurrection, when he opened the Scriptures to them and then opened their minds (24:27, 45).

“And Jesus stopped” is worth the whole paragraph. He is on the last stretch to Jerusalem, has just described in detail what is waiting there, and the entire progress of the Son of Man towards his passion halts on a road outside Jericho for a beggar the people at the front had been trying to silence.

“What do you want me to do for you?” is on the face of it unnecessary — anybody could name the need. But being asked is itself a dignity, and this man has spent years being talked about over his head. And the mercy he shouted for has to be turned into a specific thing he is prepared to ask for out loud, in front of the crowd that had just told him to be quiet.

He was not told to follow, and he followed. The first thing he does with working eyes is fix them on Jesus, and the first road he walks is the one to Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: And taking the twelve, he said to them, 'See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished. For he will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and shamefully treated and spit upon. And after flogging him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Taking the Twelve, he said to them: see, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished. For he will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and shamefully treated and spat upon. And after flogging him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.

The third passion prediction. The last and fullest of these announcements (9:22, 44), and he takes the Twelve aside to give it. What follows is not for the crowd.

See, we are going up to Jerusalem. Jerusalem sits high, and pilgrims always went up to it; but the word carries more here, because Luke has had his face set that way since 9:51. This is the last stretch.

Everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished. Only Luke adds this. And the framing is prophetic. Not this will happen, but everything written will be accomplished, brought to completion. Which means what is coming is not a disaster overtaking a good plan. It is a text being fulfilled, and the text was written centuries before. The cross is the fulfilment of Scripture: Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, and much more. Jesus will explain it after his resurrection, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets (24:25–27, 44–46).

For he will be delivered over to the Gentiles. To Pilate and the Roman soldiers. Handed to Rome, which is new information; the earlier predictions named the elders and chief priests.

And will be mocked and shamefully treated and spit upon. Shamefully treated, hybristhēsetai: insulted, outraged, abused. Every item can be traced. Isaiah’s Servant gave his back to those who strike and did not hide his face from disgrace and spitting (Isaiah 50:6); he was despised and rejected, and with his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:3–5). The psalmist is mocked, surrounded, and has his garments divided (Psalm 22:7–8, 18). And notice how much of the list is about humiliation rather than pain. Mocked, shamefully treated, spat on: three of the six items concern what will be done to his dignity, and Luke will record every one of them happening.

And after flogging him, they will kill him. Roman scourging, with whips weighted with bone and metal, then crucifixion, the death Rome reserved for slaves and rebels.

And on the third day he will rise. Always the promise of resurrection. He has never once announced it without the rising in the same breath.

The turn in the verbs. One thing more is worth registering about the pronouns. Every verb in this list is passive or has somebody else as its subject. He will be delivered, mocked, treated shamefully, spat on, flogged, killed: things done to a man who is not doing anything. And then the last clause turns: he will rise. Active, and his own. Everything up to the grave happens to him; the thing after it is something he does.

If he knew all this, why did he go? Because he chose to. No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18). Luke shows it from start to finish: he set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51), prayed in the garden, not my will, but yours, be done (22:42), and on the cross committed his own spirit into his Father’s hands (23:46). He went up to Jerusalem not as a victim caught by events but as the Lamb walking to the altar, because the Father’s will and his own love were one. He knew every blow in advance and went anyway, for the joy set before him: the joy of bringing many sons to glory (Hebrews 2:10). The prophecy is not a fate he was trapped in; it is a promise he came to keep.

In a sentence. Jesus told the Twelve that in Jerusalem everything the prophets wrote about him would be fulfilled: he would be handed to the Gentiles, mocked, abused, spat on, flogged and killed, and rise on the third day.

On a Tuesday. Read Isaiah 53 this week, slowly, and then Luke 23, and put a mark beside every place where the one fulfils the other. Let the precision of it steady your faith: the God who kept these promises to the letter will keep every promise he has made to you.

For worship. Every detail of his suffering was written down centuries before: the handing over, the spit, the mockery, the whip. He knew those pages, and he knew whose name was on them. And still he kept walking. The Son of God went into the darkest chapter of the prophets with his eyes open, because on the far side of it was the third day, and on the far side of the third day was a people he had come to bring home.
