verseByVerse.quote: But they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was said.

But they understood none of these things. Three statements of the same fact in one verse: they did not understand, it was hidden, they did not grasp. That is Luke making certain the reader does not soften it. Not little, not imperfectly: none. The thing is astonishing, and Luke knows it. Jesus has just given a list of six specific things, in plain language, with no parable attached, and twelve men who had been with him for three years took in nothing.

This saying was hidden from them. A divine passive, as at 9:45. Luke does not say who hid it, but the phrase points to God, and the hiding was for a time. The same Gospel ends with the risen Christ himself lifting it. He walks unrecognised beside two disciples whose eyes were kept from recognising him (24:16), and beginning with Moses and all the Prophets interprets to them the things concerning himself (24:27); then in the upper room he opens their minds to understand the Scriptures (24:45). The cross is not explained by those who stand near it. It is explained by the one who hung on it, from the far side of the grave.

And they did not grasp what was said. It is worth asking what was actually blocking them, because it was not stupidity. These men had a settled picture of what Messiah meant, and it had no room in it for a crucifixion. The words went in and found nowhere to lodge. That is how most misunderstanding of Scripture works. Not a failure to hear the sentence, but a frame that will not accommodate it, and the frame is invisible to the person holding it.

A mercy to the reader. There is a second reason for the threefold statement. These men would shortly preach the resurrection, and the honest record of how slow they were is part of the case for their testimony. Nobody inventing an account of the founding apostles makes them this slow, or records that they were told in advance and understood not a word. When they did come to believe, it was not because they had been expecting it.

Why do I read the Bible and sometimes get nothing from it? The disciples heard this from the Lord himself, in person, three times, and it was hidden. Understanding did not arrive by effort or by proximity. It arrived after the resurrection, when he opened the Scriptures to them and then opened their minds (24:27, 45). So keep reading, and pray before you read: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). Ask what frame you might be bringing that the text does not fit. Read with others, and sit under preaching. The Spirit who wrote the word is the one who gives light to it, and he delights to answer that prayer, often in a quiet moment long after the reading.

In a sentence. The disciples did not understand any of this, because its meaning was hidden from them.

On a Tuesday. Before you open your Bible this week, pray the psalmist’s prayer for opened eyes. And be patient with others who do not yet see what you see. The apostles themselves heard the gospel three times from Jesus’ own lips and understood none of it, until God opened their eyes.

For worship. Every believer who understands the cross was once as blind to it as the Twelve, and no cleverer. The God who called light out of darkness on the first day has shone into hearts like theirs, and what the light shows is not a riddle solved but a face: the Son of Man, mocked, flogged, killed and risen, for us. To see the cross as love is a work of new creation, as great as the morning a blind beggar outside Jericho opened his eyes on the face of Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: As he drew near to Jericho, a blind man was sitting by the roadside begging. And hearing a crowd going by, he inquired what this meant. They told him, 'Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he drew near to Jericho, a blind man was sitting by the roadside begging. And hearing a crowd going by, he inquired what this meant. They told him: Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.

As he drew near to Jericho. Jericho lay some 17 miles (27 km) from Jerusalem by road, down in the Jordan valley, and from it the pilgrim road climbed steeply up to the city. A reader with three Gospels open will stop at this first line, and the difficulty is worth facing squarely. Luke says the healing happened as he drew near to Jericho, and then opens the next chapter with Jesus entering the town (19:1). Matthew and Mark both say it happened as he was going out of Jericho (Matthew 20:29; Mark 10:46). Matthew also reports two blind men where Mark and Luke report one, and only Mark supplies a name, Bartimaeus.

One man or two, entering or leaving? The number and the name are the easy half. None of the three says only one, and one never denies two. Mark gives not just a name but a father’s name, Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus, which is how you identify a man his readers could go and ask; he had evidently become known in the church, and both Mark and Luke follow the man who mattered to the tradition, while Matthew notes there were two. The harder half is most probably explained by the ground itself. There were two Jerichos in the first century, roughly a mile apart. The ancient city stood as a ruin on its old mound; Herod the Great had built a splendid new town to the south with his winter palace, and the road ran between them. A traveller on that stretch was leaving one Jericho and approaching the other in the same few minutes, and Jesus may have been between them. Matthew and Mark date the event by the town at his back; Luke by the town ahead. Both are exactly true of one man on one road on one afternoon.

Independent witnesses. What looks like three writers contradicting each other is the ordinary signature of independent witnesses standing in different places. Three men copying one document do not produce discrepancies of this kind; three men who were there, or who talked to people who were, produce exactly these. The Gospels are not identical because they are honest.

A blind man was sitting by the roadside begging. Pilgrims for Passover passed by in crowds, and were generous at festival time. For a blind beggar this road in this week was the best pitch of the year.

And hearing a crowd going by, he inquired what this meant. He cannot see, so he asks, and the detail is the point of him. He has to work out from sound alone that something is happening, and he does not let it pass.

They told him, Jesus of Nazareth is passing by. The crowd’s name for him. The description is accurate and small: a place and a name, what everybody knew. And the blind man is about to say something better with less information. And he is passing by: this was his one chance. As far as the Gospels tell us, Jesus never came that way again.

The man from Nazareth and the blind. The crowd’s label holds more than they knew. In the synagogue at Nazareth, at the start of his ministry, Jesus had read from Isaiah that the Spirit of the Lord had anointed him to proclaim recovering of sight to the blind, and had said, today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing (4:18–21). Nazareth threw him out that day. Now the man from Nazareth is passing a blind beggar on the Jericho road, and the promise he read aloud is about to be kept in front of a crowd. Jesus of Nazareth passing by means the Anointed One passing by, with the words of his first sermon in his hands.

In a sentence. Near Jericho, a blind beggar heard the crowd and was told that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by.

On a Tuesday. When Jesus passes by, don’t miss the moment. It may be a sermon that lands, a friend’s invitation, a crisis that opens your heart, a verse that will not leave you alone. Do not tell yourself there will be a better time. Behold, now is the favourable time (2 Corinthians 6:2).

For worship. Jesus of Nazareth passed by, and he passes by where the beggars sit. He took the Jericho road on purpose, through the poor and the blind and the shouting, on his way to give his life. The Lord of glory did not travel to Jerusalem by a private road, screened from need. He went through the middle of it, within earshot of every cry, and a beggar who could not go looking for him found that he did not need to. The Saviour had come to his roadside.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho lay about 17 miles by road east-north-east of Jerusalem. Mark names the man Bartimaeus; Matthew mentions two men.

verseByVerse.quote: And he cried out, 'Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!' And those who were in front rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, 'Son of David, have mercy on me!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he cried out: Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me! And those who were in front rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more: Son of David, have mercy on me!

And he cried out, Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me! He was told Jesus of Nazareth. What comes back is Son of David. That is a messianic title, the promised king from David’s line (2 Samuel 7:12–16), and it is the first time in Luke’s Gospel that any human being has used it of him aloud. Gabriel spoke of the throne of his father David (1:32); the genealogy runs through David; but no one in this book has looked at Jesus and said it until now. And it is a blind beggar sitting in the dust outside a town. The blind man sees what the crowd does not. And he knows what the Messiah was to do: give sight to the blind (Isaiah 35:5; 61:1).

The blind who see. Set that against the paragraph immediately before it. Twelve men who could see, who had been given the plainest possible account of what was about to happen, understood none of it. A man who cannot see, working from a sentence shouted at him by a stranger, gets the identity right. Luke has put the two side by side and he means it to hurt.

Have mercy on me! The tax collector’s prayer again (v. 13). A beggar, with no claim, only need. Not a diagnosis and not a request for anything specific: the same plea the tax collector made in the temple twenty-five verses ago. He asks for mercy and leaves the content of it to Jesus.

And those who were in front rebuked him, telling him to be silent. The same verb Luke used of the disciples turning away the infants (v. 15). The crowd is doing again what the disciples had just been corrected for doing: clearing the road of people with no standing so that the important business can proceed. And notice who they are: those who were in front. The people nearest to Jesus are the ones telling this man to be quiet.

But he cried out all the more, Son of David, have mercy on me! He does not lower his voice; he raises it. Nothing about his social position, his blindness or the public rebuke is enough to make him stop, because he has worked out that this is the only chance he is going to get and there is not going to be another crowd. He has the widow’s persistence (vv. 1–8), and she would have recognised him at once.

What if the people around me discourage me from coming to Jesus? Do what the blind man did: cry out all the more. Sometimes it is friends who mock, family who think you have gone too far, a culture that tells you faith is foolish. Sometimes, sadly, it is people in the church who make the needy feel unwelcome. Jesus is not like the people at the front. He hears the voice they tried to silence. And if you are one of those at the front, near Jesus, make sure you are not the one standing between him and someone crying for mercy.

In a sentence. The blind man cried out to Jesus as the Son of David for mercy, and when told to be quiet, cried out all the more.

On a Tuesday. Cry to Jesus for mercy, and don’t let anyone silence you. Bring him the need you have been embarrassed to mention, and keep bringing it. And look round your church on Sunday for the person on the edge whom no one is listening to, and be the one who brings him nearer.

For worship. The blind beggar called him by his true name, and heaven agrees. Jesus is the Son of David, the King of Israel, the Lord of the everlasting throne, and he is the King who has mercy. David’s greater Son does not rule from a distance; he rules from a roadside, from a cross, from the right hand of God, and everywhere he hears the cry of the poor. The LORD opens the eyes of the blind; the LORD lifts up those who are bowed down (Psalm 146:8).
verseByVerse.note: “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stopped and commanded him to be brought to him. And when he came near, he asked him, 'What do you want me to do for you?' He said, 'Lord, let me recover my sight.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus stopped and commanded him to be brought to him. And when he came near, he asked him: what do you want me to do for you? He said: Lord, let me recover my sight.

And Jesus stopped. Three words, and they are worth the whole entry. He is on the last stretch of the road to Jerusalem, and only a few verses ago he laid out for the Twelve, item by item, the mockery, the flogging and the death that lie ahead. There is a crowd around him, a procession moving, and a fixed appointment at the far end of it that everything in this Gospel has been travelling towards since 9:51. And he stops, because somebody is shouting. Luke does not decorate it. The entire progress of the Son of Man towards his passion halts on a road outside Jericho for one blind beggar the people at the front had been trying to silence.

And commanded him to be brought to him. Note who is now employed on the errand. Those who tried to silence him now bring him. Mark records them saying take heart; get up, he is calling you (Mark 10:49), which must have been a considerable adjustment.

And when he came near, he asked him, What do you want me to do for you? Which is, on the face of it, an unnecessary question. The man is blind and has been begging by a roadside; anybody could name the need. So why ask? Partly because being asked is itself a dignity, and this man has spent years being talked about over his head. Nobody in that town had put a question to him in a long time. But mostly because a request has to be made. Jesus asks him to say it. He will not heal him over his head either. The mercy he shouted for has to be turned into a specific thing he is prepared to ask for out loud, in front of the crowd that had just told him to be quiet.

Lord, let me recover my sight. And he asks. Plainly, without preamble, without qualifying it or hedging it or asking whether it is too much. Lord: he recognises Jesus’ authority. Simple, direct faith. It is worth setting that beside the ruler at verse 18, who came asking what he must do. The ruler wanted to do something; the blind man asks Jesus to do something for him. This man asks for what he needs.

If God knows what I need, why should I ask? Because he wants us to. You do not have, because you do not ask (James 4:2). Asking is not informing God; it is trusting him, and it brings our needs out of the vague background of worry into the light of his face. Jesus knew exactly what the blind man wanted and still made him say it, because the asking was part of the healing: a beggar who had always been spoken about was spoken to, and answered. So be specific in prayer. Name the thing. Your Father knows what you need before you ask him (Matthew 6:8), and he still loves to hear you say it.

In a sentence. Jesus stopped, had the man brought to him, and asked what he wanted, and he asked to see again.

On a Tuesday. Jesus asks you too: what do you want me to do for you? Tell him. Sit quietly this week, imagine the question put to you directly, and answer it honestly. You may be surprised what you say. Then say it to him, plainly, and leave it with him.

For worship. The question asked on the Jericho road is still asked from the throne. The same Jesus who asked a blind beggar what he wanted sits at the right hand of God, a high priest who can sympathise with our weaknesses, and the throne he sits on is a throne of grace, where the needy receive mercy and find help in time of need (Hebrews 4:15–16). The King of kings hears the specific request of the smallest of his people, the eyes, the rent, the son, the fear, and none is beneath his attention. Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears us up (Psalm 68:19).

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, 'Recover your sight; your faith has made you well.' And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to him: recover your sight; your faith has made you well. And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.

And Jesus said to him, Recover your sight. A word of command. No touch, no clay, no procedure. One word in Greek and it is done.

Your faith has made you well. And the second half is the phrase Luke keeps for the moments that go past the body: has saved you, sesōken, the same words spoken to the sinful woman weeping at his feet (7:50), to the woman with the bleeding in the crowd (8:48), and to the Samaritan leper who came back (17:19). The verb is sōzō, and it means both healed and saved. Body and soul. Something has happened here that is more than a pair of eyes.

What his faith was. It is worth examining, because there was not much of it and it was not sophisticated. He had heard a name, shouted a title, refused to be silenced, and asked for the obvious thing. That is the whole content. No theology, no track record, no promise about what he would do afterwards, and Jesus calls it faith and says it has saved him.

And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him. At once and completely. And then he follows, though he was not told to; Jesus had sent others home (8:39). This man simply falls in behind the procession, and everybody knows where it is going. The first thing he does with a pair of working eyes is fix them on Jesus, and the first road he walks is the one up to Jerusalem. The rich ruler would not follow (v. 22); the beggar does at once. He is a picture of true discipleship.

Glorifying God. As the Samaritan did (17:15). The gift turns into worship, and the worship is directed to God through the One who gave it.

And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God. His healing leads others to praise. The chapter that began with a widow being ignored ends with a whole crowd praising God, including the people who had told the man to be quiet.

The chapter’s pattern. Throughout chapter 18, those who come with nothing receive everything: the persistent widow, the tax collector, the infants, the blind beggar. The one who came with much went away with nothing.

Does Jesus still heal the blind today? He can, and God still answers prayer for the sick, sometimes wonderfully. But this healing was a sign of who Jesus is, the Messiah who opens blind eyes as Isaiah promised, and Scripture does not promise that every prayer for healing will be granted now. The gifts of miraculous healing given to the apostles confirmed their message and are not, in our judgment, the normal pattern for the church today (a cessationist view, held charitably towards brothers who see it differently), though God remains free to heal as he pleases, and we should pray for the sick in faith (James 5:14–15). The greater miracle, which he does every day, is the opening of blind hearts to see his glory. And the full healing of every believer’s body is certain, at the resurrection.

In a sentence. Jesus told the man to see, for his faith had saved him, and he saw at once and followed Jesus, praising God, and all the people praised God too.

On a Tuesday. If Jesus has opened your eyes, follow him, and let your life lead others to praise God. Tell someone this week what Christ has done for you, simply, like a man describing the day he first saw. And follow him where he is going, even when the road leads up to Jerusalem.

For worship. The Son of Man had set out for a city where he would be handed over, mocked, spat on, flogged and killed, and his friends had not understood a word of it. On the way he gave a beggar his eyes, and gained a follower who walked the rest of that road beside him. Nothing in Jerusalem was turned aside, and still there was time for one man nobody wanted him to hear. That is the grace of God in Christ: unhurried towards the cross, and never too hurried for a sinner on the way to it.

18.text: <sup>1</sup> And he told them a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart. <sup>2</sup> He said, “In a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected man. <sup>3</sup> And there was a widow in that city who kept coming to him and saying, ‘Give me justice against my adversary.’ <sup>4</sup> For a while he refused, but afterward he said to himself, ‘Though I neither fear God nor respect man, <sup>5</sup> yet because this widow keeps bothering me, I will give her justice, so that she will not beat me down by her continual coming.’” <sup>6</sup> And the Lord said, “Hear what the unrighteous judge says. <sup>7</sup> And will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night? Will he delay long over them? <sup>8</sup> I tell you, he will give justice to them speedily. Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?” <sup>9</sup> He also told this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt: <sup>10</sup> “Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. <sup>11</sup> The Pharisee, standing by himself, prayed thus: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. <sup>12</sup> I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I get.’ <sup>13</sup> But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’ <sup>14</sup> I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.” <sup>15</sup> Now they were bringing even infants to him that he might touch them. And when the disciples saw it, they rebuked them. <sup>16</sup> But Jesus called them to him, saying, “Let the children come to me, and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. <sup>17</sup> Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.” <sup>18</sup> And a ruler asked him, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” <sup>19</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. <sup>20</sup> You know the commandments: ‘Do not commit adultery, Do not murder, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Honor your father and mother.’” <sup>21</sup> And he said, “All these I have kept from my youth.” <sup>22</sup> When Jesus heard this, he said to him, “One thing you still lack. Sell all that you have and distribute to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” <sup>23</sup> But when he heard these things, he became very sad, for he was extremely rich. <sup>24</sup> Jesus, seeing that he had become sad, said, “How difficult it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God! <sup>25</sup> For it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” <sup>26</sup> Those who heard it said, “Then who can be saved?” <sup>27</sup> But he said, “What is impossible with man is possible with God.” <sup>28</sup> And Peter said, “See, we have left our homes and followed you.” <sup>29</sup> And he said to them, “Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, <sup>30</sup> who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life.” <sup>31</sup> And taking the twelve, he said to them, “See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished. <sup>32</sup> For he will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and shamefully treated and spit upon. <sup>33</sup> And after flogging him, they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.” <sup>34</sup> But they understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was said. <sup>35</sup> As he drew near to Jericho, a blind man was sitting by the roadside begging. <sup>36</sup> And hearing a crowd going by, he inquired what this meant. <sup>37</sup> They told him, “Jesus of Nazareth is passing by.” <sup>38</sup> And he cried out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>39</sup> And those who were in front rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>40</sup> And Jesus stopped and commanded him to be brought to him. And when he came near, he asked him, <sup>41</sup> “What do you want me to do for you?” He said, “Lord, let me recover my sight.” <sup>42</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Recover your sight; your faith has made you well.” <sup>43</sup> And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.

19.title: Zacchaeus, the Minas, and the Triumphal Entry
19.overview:
Luke 19 is a chapter of arrivals. Jesus arrives at Jericho and finds Zacchaeus — a chief tax collector who has climbed a tree to see him and who will descend, transformed, to receive salvation in his house. Then Jesus tells the Parable of the Ten Minas — a kingdom parable about accountability and fruitfulness during the time of the absent king. Then Jesus arrives at Jerusalem itself, riding on a colt, welcomed by his disciples with praise, weeping over the city as he approaches it, and then cleansing the temple. The chapter is a compressed journey from private transformation (Zacchaeus) to public confrontation (the temple), with the parable providing the theological framework for understanding the entire sequence.

Zacchaeus is one of Luke's most vivid portraits of salvation. He is a chief tax collector, wealthy, despised, short of stature, and apparently desperate to see Jesus. He runs ahead and climbs a tree — an undignified act for a man of his status. Jesus's response is overwhelming: “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.” The word dei (must) is a divine necessity — the same word used for the Son of Man's suffering. Salvation has come to this house; the Son of Man has come to seek and to save the lost.

The Triumphal Entry (vv. 28–44) contains one of the most emotionally powerful moments in all of Luke: Jesus weeping over Jerusalem. The parade of praise, the disciples crying out about the king who comes in the name of the Lord — and then Jesus stopping on the descent and weeping, because she did not know “the things that make for peace.” This is not despair; it is the grief of the shepherd for the sheep who will not come.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Jesus was passing through Jericho — not stopping. The whole story turns on that clause, and on a man who got in the way of it.

Zacchaeus is described with three details that should make him unsympathetic. He is a chief tax collector — architelōnēs, a word that appears nowhere else in surviving Greek literature and may be Luke's own coinage. It means he held the district contract and had other collectors under him, taking a percentage of each man's takings. And Jericho was no backwater: it sat on the trade route from the east, in a plain famous for balsam and dates, at the crossing into Judea. That customs post was one of the most lucrative in the country.

He is rich, and by this point in Luke that word has weight — a rich man in torment three chapters back (16:19-31), a rich ruler grieving one chapter back (18:23-25), and a camel that will not go through a needle. The disciples had asked, reasonably, “then who can be saved?” The next rich man in this Gospel is up a tree.

And he is small in stature, which the crowd exploits. A short man can usually reach the front of a gathering; a short and thoroughly hated man in the town where he holds the tax contract will find that nobody moves.

So he runs — humiliating for a man of standing, since it meant hitching up the robe — and climbs a fig-mulberry, which is a boy's activity in full view of the street. Dignity is the first thing that goes. It nearly always is.

Then Jesus stops, looks up, and uses his name. Nothing in the story explains how he knew it. He announces rather than asks — “I must stay at your house today” — which is a mercy, because a man in Zacchaeus's position does not issue invitations and had learned not to put himself where he could be refused.

The crowd grumbles, all of them. And Zacchaeus stands and gives away half of everything and repays fourfold, and Jesus says salvation has come to the house.
verseByVerse.theology:
The episode is a case study in sovereign grace. Jesus announces the visit before any repentance has occurred; the restitution follows the encounter and is the fruit of salvation received, not the ground of it. It is the exact pattern of chapter 15 — the shepherd finds the sheep, and the sheep does not find its way home.

A crux has to be faced at v.8, because a good many modern commentators press it. Both verbs are present — “I give,” “I restore” — and a present can describe a habitual practice. On that reading Zacchaeus is not promising but defending himself: I already give half away; the grumbling is unjust.

It is possible and should be rejected, for three reasons drawn from the passage. Luke has told us the man was rich, and a chief tax collector who gave away half his income and repaid fourfold every disputed claim would not have stayed rich for a season. Jesus's reply is “today salvation has come to this house,” which is a strange thing to say to a man who has just proved he was fine all along. And the present is also the ordinary form for a promise made on the spot — I give you my word, or a man at an altar saying I take you.

The numbers are not arbitrary either. Half is far beyond anything the law required, and fourfold is the penalty for the aggravated case, a stolen sheep slaughtered or sold (Ex. 22:1); ordinary restitution was the sum plus a fifth (Lev. 6:5). He sentences himself at the highest rate on the books.
verseByVerse.examples:
“Son of Abraham” is a deliberate provocation, because it is precisely what the grumblers would have denied. A tax collector had forfeited his place in the popular reckoning, and some rabbinic rulings treated his repentance as practically impossible, since he could never trace everyone he had defrauded. Jesus hands the title back — as he did six chapters earlier to a bent woman nobody had helped in eighteen years, “a daughter of Abraham” (13:16).

And v.10 is the sentence that gathers up the whole Gospel. It answers the grumbling completely: they objected that he had gone in to a sinner's house, and he replies that this is the errand. Not a regrettable necessity, not an exception made for a promising case — the stated purpose of the coming. The verbs are the shepherd's from chapter 15: to seek, and to save.

Zacchaeus climbed a tree to get a look at somebody who had come to that town looking for him.

The story is also addressed to the crowd. A man in a congregation has a reputation; everyone knows what he was before — the financial impropriety, the trail of damage. He is welcomed into membership and watched carefully, with a persistent sense that his inclusion is provisional. Those who murmur at Christ's table fellowship with notorious sinners share the theology of the men in this street. He does not.

verseByVerse.quote: He entered Jericho and was passing through. And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector and was rich.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He entered Jericho and was passing through. And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector and was rich.

Meaning first. Luke 19 ends the long road to Jerusalem that began in 9:51, and it gathers the whole Gospel into one chapter. In Jericho a hated, rich tax collector climbs a tree to see Jesus and finds that Jesus has come looking for him: salvation comes to his house, for the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (vv. 1–10). Because the crowd expects the kingdom at once, Jesus tells of a nobleman who goes away to receive a kingdom, leaves his servants to trade, and returns to reward the faithful and judge his enemies (vv. 11–27). He rides into Jerusalem on a colt as Zechariah’s humble King (vv. 28–40), weeps over the city that does not know the day of its visitation (vv. 41–44), and claims the temple as his Father’s house (vv. 45–48). The thread is the King himself, seeking the lost, going away and coming back, welcomed by some and refused by others.

The setting. This is the last stop before the city. Jericho lies about seventeen miles (27 km) from Jerusalem, and from here the road climbs through the desert to the Mount of Olives. Luke has just told of a blind beggar outside Jericho who shouted until he was heard, received his sight and followed Jesus glorifying God (18:35–43). So the crowd moving through the town is large, loud and celebrating, and Passover is near. Only Luke records the story of Zacchaeus.

He entered Jericho and was passing through. The whole story turns on the second clause. He was not stopping. Jericho lay on the pilgrim road up to Jerusalem, and he was walking through it on his way to a cross. Before he left, he would change a household, and he would do it by stopping where nobody expected.

Jericho. It was not a backwater. It was the city of palms in the Jordan valley, a winter resort for the wealthy, sitting on the trade route from the east, in a fertile plain famous for its balsam groves and date plantations, at the crossing point into Judea. Herod the Great had built palaces there, and his son Archelaus rebuilt them, a fact that will matter for the parable in v. 12. The customs post at Jericho was one of the most lucrative in the country. It was also the city whose walls fell to Joshua, whose name is the Hebrew form of Jesus. The first Joshua came to Jericho to destroy it; the second comes to Jericho to save a man in it.

And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus. The behold is Luke pointing, as he does whenever somebody is about to be noticed who would not otherwise have been. The name is Hebrew, Zakkai, which means pure or righteous. Whatever his parents hoped for when they gave it to him, the town had long since drawn its own conclusions. He is about to become what his name said, but not by any effort of his own.

He was a chief tax collector. The title, architelōnēs, appears nowhere else in Greek literature that has survived. It means he did not sit at a booth himself. He held the contract for the district, probably bought from the Roman authorities, and had other collectors under him, taking a percentage of everything each of them took. To his neighbours that made him two things at once: a traitor who worked for the occupying power, and a thief who grew fat on his own people.

And was rich. Luke states it flatly, and by this point in his Gospel the word has weight. Three chapters back a rich man was in torment and a beggar in Abraham’s side (16:19–31). One chapter back a rich ruler became very sad, and Jesus said it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God (18:23–25). The disciples asked, reasonably, then who can be saved? And Jesus answered, “What is impossible with man is possible with God” (18:27). Luke places the next rich man straight after that saying, and the next rich man is up a tree. Zacchaeus is the camel going through the needle, and this chapter shows how God does the impossible.

Why does Luke tell us he was rich? Because his money was the very thing that should have shut him out. The rich ruler had kept the commandments from his youth and still went away sad, because his wealth held him. Zacchaeus had broken the commandments for years and his wealth was dirty as well as heavy. If anyone was beyond the kingdom, it was this man. Luke wants us to see that the difference between them is not that one was better. The difference is that Jesus stopped at one man’s tree. Salvation is not the reward of the less sinful. It is the work of a God who does what is impossible with man.

The impossible walks into Jericho. Luke does not answer the question asked in 18:26 with a statement about divine power in general. He answers it with Jesus himself, entering Jericho on foot. The God for whom all things are possible is here in person, with a face and a road and a name, on his way to the cross that will pay for everything Zacchaeus ever took. That is how the impossible is done. The rich man does not shrink his fortune or his guilt until he fits. The Saviour comes to where he is, and the door that wealth had shut is opened from the other side.

In a sentence. As Jesus passed through Jericho, there was a rich man named Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person you would least expect to become a Christian: the colleague who mocks, the relative whose life is a wreck, the public figure whose name makes you wince. Pray for that person by name this week, and refuse the quiet conclusion that he or she is beyond it. The rich ruler and Zacchaeus stand side by side in Luke to settle the question. If you are the one who feels beyond reach, because of what you have done or what you have, this story was written with you in view. No one is too rich, too compromised or too hated for Christ’s grace.

For worship. The Son of God walked through the city of palms with a cross ahead of him and a crowd around him, and his eyes were on the one man Jericho had written off. Wealth that should have barred the door, guilt that should have sealed it and a town’s contempt that stood guard over it were no obstacle to him. What no rich man can buy and no sinner can earn, he gives on foot, in an afternoon, by coming. Blessed be the God of the impossible, who has a name, and whose name is Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho, near the Jordan, was a rich town on a major trade route. A chief tax collector oversaw other collectors and profited from all of them.

parallels.desc: how difficult for those who have wealth

verseByVerse.quote: And he was seeking to see who Jesus was, but on account of the crowd he could not, because he was small in stature. So he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was about to pass that way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was seeking to see who Jesus was, but on account of the crowd he could not, because he was small in stature. So he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was about to pass that way.

And he was seeking to see who Jesus was. The verb is continuous: he kept seeking, kept trying. And it is Luke’s own word for what will be said about Jesus seven verses later: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost. Two searches are running in this story and they meet under a tree. Notice what he wants. Not a healing; he is not ill. Not a favour. He wants to see who Jesus was. Perhaps he had heard that this teacher was called a friend of tax collectors and sinners (7:34), and that one of the Twelve was a former tax collector (5:27–28). Luke does not say whether it began as curiosity or something deeper. What he says is that the man kept trying.

But on account of the crowd he could not, because he was small in stature. The crowd is the obstacle, and it is worth asking whether that was entirely accidental. A short man can usually work his way to the front of a gathering. A short and thoroughly hated man, in the town where he holds the tax contract, is going to find that the people in front of him do not move. Nobody was going to make way for him. The crowd that surrounds Jesus can be the very thing that keeps people from him.

So he ran on ahead. Grown men of position did not run. It meant hitching up the long robe and showing the legs, and the same detail made the father’s run in chapter 15 so shocking (15:20). The richest and most powerful man in Jericho, in a robe worth more than most of the crowd earned in a year, sprints down the road ahead of a procession.

And climbed up into a sycamore tree. The tree is a sycamore in the old sense: not the plane tree of northern Europe but the sycamore-fig, a broad tree with a short trunk and wide, low branches, easy to climb and dense with leaves, common along the roads of the Jordan valley. And climbing a tree is worse than running. It is a boy’s activity, and it puts him where the whole street can see him. He was willing to look ridiculous in front of the people who despised him, because there was somebody he had to see. Dignity is the first thing that goes. It nearly always is.

Does a person have to seek Jesus before Jesus will find him? No. Zacchaeus’s seeking is real and Luke honours it, but the story is built so that his search turns out to be the smaller one inside a larger one. He thought he had found a way to see Jesus; in fact Jesus had come to Jericho to find him (v. 10). Scripture says that no one seeks God on his own (Romans 3:11), and that when anyone does begin to seek, it is because the Father is already drawing him (John 6:44). So the desire you feel to know Christ is not your achievement. It is the first sign that he is calling you. Follow it, and do not wait to be sure of your motives first.

In a sentence. Zacchaeus wanted to see Jesus, but was too short to see over the crowd, so he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore-fig tree on Jesus’ route.

On a Tuesday. What would you be unwilling to look foolish for? Some people never come to Christ because they cannot face what friends or family would say; some Christians never speak of him at work for the same reason. Name the specific embarrassment that is your tree, the thing you would have to be seen doing, and ask whether seeing Jesus is worth it. And if you are part of the crowd, a regular in church, ask whether anyone trying to reach Jesus finds you standing in the way: the newcomer nobody speaks to, the person with a past whom nobody quite trusts. Make room.

For worship. Christ had already chosen the tree before the man chose to climb it. The one who laid out the road through Jericho knew which branches would hold a desperate tax collector that afternoon. Every seeking soul is overtaken by a Saviour who was seeking first, and who will not be outrun.
verseByVerse.note: The sycamore here is the sycamore-fig, a tree with a short trunk and wide, low branches, easy to climb.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him, 'Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.' So he hurried and came down and received him joyfully.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him: Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today. So he hurried and came down and received him joyfully.

And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up. Zacchaeus climbed up to see. He had not expected to be seen. The crowd was moving, the procession had a destination, and Jesus stopped at exactly that tree. And the direction is beautiful: the Lord of glory, who came down from heaven, looks up into the branches at a sinner. He had to stoop to come to us at all, and here he lifts his eyes to find one man.

And said to him, Zacchaeus. He knew the name. Nothing in the story explains how. Nobody is described as telling him; there is no introduction. He walks to a particular tree in a town he is passing through, stops, looks up, and uses the man’s name. The good shepherd calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3). Zacchaeus had been called many names in Jericho, and none of them kind. Jesus uses the one his parents gave him, the one that means righteous.

Hurry and come down. There is urgency in it, and the urgency is on Jesus’ side. He is in a hurry for this man. All through Luke the one who searches is the one who hurries: the shepherd going after the lost sheep, the woman sweeping for her coin, the father running down the road.

For I must stay at your house today. Each word is startling. Must is dei, the word of divine necessity that Luke uses at every hinge of this Gospel, ever since a boy in the temple said he must be in his Father’s house (2:49). It has governed a preaching circuit (4:43), the prediction of the cross (9:22) and the journey to Jerusalem (13:33). Here it governs an evening in a tax collector’s dining room. This meeting was part of God’s plan. Today is Luke’s sēmeron, the word for the present moment of salvation (2:11; 4:21; 23:43), and it will come back four verses later. And notice that Jesus does not ask. He announces. To stay in a man’s house was a public sign of friendship and acceptance, and of all the houses in Jericho he chooses the house of the most notorious sinner.

Why does Jesus invite himself? It is a mercy, and anyone who has ever been the disreputable one in a room will see why. A man in Zacchaeus’s position does not issue invitations. He has learned not to put himself where he can be refused. If Jesus had waited to be asked, he would have waited under that tree until dark. So grace does not wait for us to work up the courage to invite it. It comes and says, I must stay at your house today. That is how every conversion begins: not with our invitation to Christ but with his claim on us.

So he hurried and came down and received him joyfully. He obeys both verbs, hurried and came down, and Luke adds a third. Received is hypedexato, welcomed as a guest. And joyfully: the joy of the found, the joy of the shepherd and the woman and the father in chapter 15 (15:5–7, 9, 32). The rich ruler went away sad; Zacchaeus receives Jesus with joy. Notice the order. Nothing has yet been said about sin, restitution or the tax contract. All that is coming, and it comes from Zacchaeus. What happens first is that a man who was up a tree is on the ground, and glad.

In a sentence. When Jesus reached the tree, he looked up, called Zacchaeus by name, and told him to come down at once because he must stay at his house today, and Zacchaeus hurried down and welcomed him with joy.

On a Tuesday. If Christ has claimed you, receive him as Zacchaeus did: quickly and gladly. Some believers treat Christ’s presence as an inspection to be endured rather than a guest to be welcomed. Today, in your home, at the table, among the people you live with, he is not a visitor checking the dust. Welcome him: read his word aloud at a meal, pray with the household, and let the joy show. And think of the person in your life who would never invite himself anywhere: the outsider, the one with a reputation. Christ went to his house. Go to theirs.

For worship. He knows your name. He knew it before the tree, before the road, before the world (Ephesians 1:4). He stopped at the place where you were hiding and looked up, and said that he must come in, today. There is no greater honour on earth than to have the Son of God insist on being your guest.

parallels.desc: I will come in to him and eat with him

verseByVerse.quote: And when they saw it, they all grumbled, 'He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner.' And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, 'Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they saw it, they all grumbled: he has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner. And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord: behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.

And when they saw it, they all grumbled. All of them. Not only the scribes and Pharisees this time, the grumblers of 15:2. Luke names no party. It is the whole crowd, including people who had been praising God about a blind man shortly before. The verb is the one used of Israel murmuring in the wilderness. A crowd can rejoice at a miracle of power and resent a miracle of grace in the same hour.

He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner. Accurate on every point, and meant as an indictment. To eat in such a house was, in their eyes, to share its uncleanness and to approve its owner. They were right that Jesus had joined himself to a sinner. They were wrong about which way the defilement would run. He is not made unclean by Zacchaeus. Zacchaeus is made clean by him.

And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord. He stood: probably rising at the meal, the posture of someone making a formal, public declaration rather than a private confession. And Luke calls Jesus the Lord, while Zacchaeus calls him Lord. The grumbling outside has been heard inside, and Zacchaeus answers it not with argument but with a changed life.

Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. Half is far beyond anything the law required, and nobody asked for it. Jesus told the rich ruler to sell everything (18:22) and he could not; Zacchaeus gives half, unasked. This is the camel going through the eye of the needle. Grace has changed his attitude to money in a single afternoon. The man who had spent his life taking now cannot wait to give.

And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold. If is not doubt; it is the form a man uses when he knows exactly what is coming. Defrauded is esykophantēsa, the word John the Baptist used to tax collectors and soldiers: do not extort by false accusation (3:14). And the numbers are not arbitrary. Fourfold is the law’s penalty for the aggravated case, a stolen sheep slaughtered or sold (Exodus 22:1). For fraud, the law required only the sum plus a fifth (Leviticus 6:5; Numbers 5:7). He sentences himself at the highest rate on the books. With half his goods given away and fourfold restitution paid from the rest, he would be left with little. He does not care.

Is Zacchaeus promising, or defending himself? Both verbs are in the present tense: I give, I restore. Some modern commentators read them as habitual, so that Zacchaeus is protesting that he already gives half and already repays, and that the grumbling is unjust. It is a possible reading of the grammar, but the passage itself points the other way. Luke has told us the man was rich (v. 2), and a chief tax collector who already gave away half and repaid fourfold would not have stayed rich for long. Jesus replies that today salvation has come to this house, a strange thing to say to a man who had been fine all along. And the present tense is also the ordinary form for a promise made on the spot, as a man at the altar says, I take you. So the best reading is that Zacchaeus is vowing a new life from this moment: from now on, I give; from now on, I restore.

What it does not mean. Not that his giving earned his salvation. Salvation came to his house when Jesus came (v. 9). Jesus pronounces it after the vow, but the vow is the fruit of a heart already changed by Jesus’ welcome, not the price of it (Ephesians 2:8–10). Grace came first; generosity followed. Nor does it mean that every Christian must give away half his goods. Jesus did not tell Zacchaeus to do this; Zacchaeus chose it freely, and he was undoing a fortune built on theft. The test for every believer is a loosened grip on money and an open hand.

Must a new Christian make restitution for past wrongs? Where it is possible, yes. Repentance includes putting right what we have wrongly taken or damaged (Exodus 22:1; Leviticus 6:1–5). It is not the ground of forgiveness, which is Christ’s blood alone, but it is how forgiven people behave. In practice: repay the money you took, return what you borrowed and kept, correct the false report you made, confess the lie to the person who was harmed by it. Where the person cannot be found, or repayment is beyond you, give what you can to the poor, as Zacchaeus did, and leave the rest with God. Take wise counsel where restitution might harm others, such as in a confession that would wound an innocent party.

In a sentence. When the crowd grumbled that Jesus had gone to a sinner’s house, Zacchaeus stood and declared he would give half his wealth to the poor and repay fourfold anyone he had cheated.

On a Tuesday. Is there anything you need to put right with someone you have wronged: money owed, a debt quietly forgotten, a reputation you damaged, an item you never returned? Name it, and take one step this week. And look at your giving: does it look like the giving of someone who has been found? Zacchaeus did not give because he was told to. He gave because the Son of God had come to his house, and money no longer seemed to matter much. Ask God for that kind of freedom.

For worship. Christ is the one who turns takers into givers. No law, no lecture and no crowd had ever moved Zacchaeus’s hand to open. One meal with Jesus did it. Such is the power of grace: it does not merely forgive the thief, it makes him generous. And he could give so freely because a greater restitution was about to be made for him. Christ repaid on a cross the debt that Zacchaeus could never have counted.
verseByVerse.note: The law required a thief to repay a stolen sheep fourfold; for ordinary wrongs, the amount plus a fifth.

parallels.desc: restore it in full and add a fifth

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, 'Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus said to him: today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.

Today salvation has come to this house. Today is one of Luke’s great todays, and together they form a spine through the Gospel: unto you is born this day a Saviour (2:11); today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing (4:21); this one; and, from a cross, today you will be with me in paradise (23:43). And notice what is said to have arrived. Not you have been forgiven, though he has been. Salvation has come, and it came up the road that afternoon and is sitting at the table. Salvation is not first a thing but a person. Simeon held a baby and said, my eyes have seen your salvation (2:30).

To this house. Not merely to Zacchaeus. The household is drawn into the blessing: the wife, the children, the servants, all of whom had lived on the proceeds and now live in a house where half of it has just been given away. Where Christ is welcomed, everyone under that roof is brought near to grace.

Does this mean his family and servants were saved with him? Salvation arrived in his home when Jesus came, and blessing spreads through a believing household. But each person must still believe for himself. At Philippi the jailer was told to believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household, and then Paul spoke the word to all who were in his house, and the household believed and rejoiced (Acts 16:31–34). Faith is never inherited. Children of believing parents have enormous privileges, and parents should pray and expect great things, but each child must come to Christ personally. For this reason this app holds to believer’s baptism, while honouring brothers who baptise the children of believers.

Since he also is a son of Abraham. A deliberate provocation, because it is precisely what the grumblers would have denied. In the popular reckoning a tax collector had forfeited his place in Israel. Some rabbinic rulings treated his repentance as practically impossible, since he could never trace everyone he had defrauded. Jesus hands him the title back. Luke has done this once before, for a bent woman nobody had helped in eighteen years: a daughter of Abraham (13:16). And it is more than a matter of birth. John had warned that God can raise up children for Abraham from stones (3:8). Zacchaeus is a son of Abraham now by faith as well as by blood, sharing the faith of Abraham, the father of all who believe (Galatians 3:7; Romans 4:11–12).

For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost. Here is the sentence that gathers up the whole Gospel, and Luke has been building to it for eighteen chapters. It answers the grumbling of v. 7 completely. They objected that he had gone in to a sinner’s house; he replies that this is the errand. Not a regrettable necessity, not an exception for a promising case: the stated purpose of his coming. The verbs are the shepherd’s from chapter 15, the lost sheep, the lost coin, the lost son. And they are the Lord’s own words through Ezekiel, when he condemned Israel’s faithless shepherds and promised to shepherd his flock himself: I will seek the lost (Ezekiel 34:11–16). The Son of Man says I came to do what the LORD promised to do. That is a claim to be the divine Shepherd in person.

Seek, save, lost. He came to seek: he takes the initiative, and his search was running long before Zacchaeus climbed his tree. He came to save: he does the saving, not merely offers it, and he will do it by giving his life as a ransom on the cross ahead. And the lost: not the righteous but sinners (5:32). The word lost means not only wicked but gone astray, out of place, missing from where one belongs, as a coin is lost from a purse. To be lost is to be missed. Heaven noticed Zacchaeus was gone.

Who are the lost? Everyone, until Christ finds them. The word does not describe a special class of very bad people; it describes all of us apart from him (Isaiah 53:6). The difference in this story is not between the lost and the found, as though the crowd were safe. It is between those who know they are lost and those who think they are not. The grumblers were as lost as Zacchaeus, and further from being found, because they did not know it. If you know you are lost, you are exactly the kind of person he came for.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that salvation had come to Zacchaeus’ house that day, for he too was a son of Abraham, and the Son of Man came to seek and save the lost.

On a Tuesday. Two applications, one inward and one outward. Inward: if you belong to Christ, remember this week that you were found, not that you found your way. It will kill your pride and steady your assurance, because he who sought you will not lose you (John 10:28). Outward: if the Son of Man came to seek the lost, his people cannot be content to wait in the building for them to arrive. Who is the Zacchaeus in your street or office, the one others avoid? Go to their house, or invite them to yours, and let them see what grace looks like at a table.

For worship. Zacchaeus climbed a tree to get a look at somebody who had come to that town looking for him. That is the gospel in one afternoon. The Shepherd of Israel left the ninety-nine, walked the road through Jericho and went up to a cross, so that the lost might be found and carried home. Blessed be the Son of Man, who came to seek and to save, and who never once came back from a search empty-handed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–27 — The Parable of the Ten Minas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke tells us exactly why the parable is given, and there are two reasons: they were near Jerusalem, and they supposed the kingdom was about to appear immediately. Seventeen miles from the city, at Passover, behind a man who raises the dead — every expectation they had was about to be fulfilled, and they were sure of it.

So everything in the parable is arranged to insert a delay where they expected a coronation: a departure, a long absence, an accounting on the return. And the shape is strange as a picture of the Messiah and exactly right — the King does not receive his kingdom in Jerusalem but in a far country, and comes back. Which is precisely what Luke's second volume describes (Acts 1:9-11).

Ten servants, ten minas — one each. Worth registering, because Matthew's cousin-parable of the talents distributes different amounts according to ability (Matt. 25:15). Where the sums differ, the story is partly about capacity; where they are identical, the only variable left is what each man did. And a mina was about three months' wages — modest, and that is the point.

The subplot of the rebel citizens is borrowed from living memory. In 4 BC Archelaus travelled to Rome to have his kingship confirmed, and a delegation of fifty Jews followed to argue against it (Josephus, Antiquities 17.11.1). They failed; he came back with power and dealt with them. Jericho of all towns would have felt it — Archelaus rebuilt it and had a palace there.

The first two servants are rewarded proportionately and without comparison. The third produces the mina intact, wrapped in a handkerchief, and explains that he was afraid — and his accusation is turned against him. If the master really were what he says, the sensible course would have been the bank.

And the parable ends with the enemies. It is the hardest sentence in Luke.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable teaches two related truths. The kingdom has a “not yet”: the King goes away and returns, and faithful servants must live faithfully in the in-between. And stewardship in the in-between is not optional maintenance — “engage in business” is a commercial verb, and it is not “look after this.”

“Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little” is worth weighing for the disproportion. The master calls the mina — everything the servant had for the whole absence — a trifle, and gives ten cities in return. The exchange rate is absurd, and meant to be.

And notice what the reward is: more responsibility, on an enormously larger scale. Not rest, and not a payment. Which says something about heaven that cuts against the popular picture, since Scripture's images run the other way — “his servants will worship him… they will reign forever and ever” (Rev. 22:3-5).

“To everyone who has, more will be given” is not a celebration of the rich getting richer. It is a description of how entrusted things behave: capacity grows by use and atrophies without it. And note the last clause carefully — “from the one who has not.” The third servant was still holding the mina when that was said. In the master's reckoning a coin wrapped in a cloth for a whole absence is not a possession but an absence dressed up as one.

A reader with Matthew open should also know this is not the parable of the talents, though the two are cousins. Matthew's setting asks what you did with what you were given. Luke's, told on the road up to Jerusalem, asks that and one thing more — whether you wanted the King at all.
verseByVerse.examples:
The third servant's fear is not reverence, though it wears the same clothes. Reverence produces obedience; this produced nothing. He was not too frightened to disobey — he was too frightened to act, which is a different thing entirely, and he had been calling it caution for the whole of the absence.

And his accusation is untrue, as the parable has already shown. This is a master who handed money to ten men with no supervision and no conditions, and who has just given a servant ten cities for a mina. The servant constructed a master he could justify doing nothing about.

The word “wicked” lands where a reader might not expect it. He has not stolen the money or wasted it or run off with it. He is called wicked for laying it away in a cloth — and there is a category of failure here that comfortable religion rarely counts as sin at all. Nothing bad was done; that is the whole defence, and it is exactly what is condemned. A life that has carefully avoided doing anything wrong has not on that account done what it was left here to do.

Verse 27 should not be hurried past. Two things keep it in place. These are words spoken by a character inside a parable, borrowed wholesale from a tyrant's homecoming, and not one command in this parable is addressed to the servants about the citizens; their whole task is to trade. And the horror of the image is the point rather than an embarrassment — Jesus is drawing a picture of what it is to refuse a king who is coming back anyway, and the tears of vv. 41-44 are fourteen verses off. A judgement described in terms this stark, by a man crying about it, is not bloodlust. It is the last warning of someone who would give anything to be heard.

verseByVerse.quote: As they heard these things, he proceeded to tell a parable, because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately. He said therefore, 'A nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they heard these things, he proceeded to tell a parable, because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately. He said therefore: a nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return.

As they heard these things, he proceeded to tell a parable. Luke, unusually, gives two reasons. The first is that he was near to Jerusalem, about seventeen miles (27 km) away: the end of the journey. It was Passover season, with a man who had raised the dead at the head of the procession and a crowd still talking about a blind man. Every expectation they had seemed about to be fulfilled, and they were sure of it.

And because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately. They expected Jesus to arrive in Jerusalem and set up the kingdom at once, throwing off Rome and taking David’s throne. They were wrong about the timing in a way that would nearly destroy them within the week. So the parable is corrective, and everything in it is arranged to insert a delay where they expected an immediate coronation: a departure, a long absence, work to do, and an accounting on the return. The kingdom will come in its fullness only after a period of absence.

A nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return. There is the shape of it. Before there is a kingdom there is a journey, and the throne is granted somewhere else. Jesus’ hearers would have known exactly where he got the picture. When Herod the Great died in 4 BC, his son Archelaus travelled to Rome to have his kingship over Judea confirmed by Caesar, and a delegation of fifty Jews followed him to argue against it (Josephus, Antiquities 17). Archelaus came back with a lesser title and took revenge on his opponents. And he had built a palace at Jericho, the very town Jesus is leaving. Everybody on that road knew the story.

The meaning. Jesus is the nobleman. Consider how strange that is as a picture of the Messiah, and how exactly it fits. The King does not receive his kingdom in Jerusalem. He receives it in a far country, and comes back. That is what happened. Through his death, resurrection and ascension he went to the Father, and like the Son of Man in Daniel’s vision he came to the Ancient of Days and was given dominion and glory and a kingdom (Daniel 7:13–14). Luke’s second volume describes it: a man taken up out of their sight, and a promise that he will come in the same way (Acts 1:9–11). He reigns now from heaven at the right hand of God, and he will return.

An error of timing, not of hope. Notice what Jesus corrects. He does not tell them the kingdom is a mere metaphor, or that they have misunderstood what a king is. He tells them it will come in its fullness later than they think, and that there is work to do meanwhile. Both halves have been lost in turn by the church. A Christianity that expects nothing has stopped believing there is a return. A Christianity that expects it next Tuesday, and sets dates, has generally stopped trading.

Where Christians differ: what kind of kingdom is the nobleman receiving? Some read the parable within a premillennial scheme: the nobleman receives the kingdom in heaven, but the kingdom itself is only set up on earth after his return, in a thousand-year reign in which the faithful servants govern actual cities. Others, the amillennial view, read it this way: the kingdom is received at the ascension and Christ reigns now, over his church and over all things for her sake (Ephesians 1:20–23); his return will bring not a further earthly stage but the final judgment and the new creation, in which his people share his reign for ever. Verdict: the second reading fits the parable and the New Testament best. Jesus says the kingdom was given to him in the far country, not that it would begin later, and Peter declares at Pentecost that Jesus has already been exalted to David’s throne (Acts 2:30–36). The return is one public event that brings reward and judgment together, as the parable itself shows (vv. 15–27), not a secret coming before the end. Brothers who hold other views of the millennium still confess the same returning King.

In a sentence. Because the crowds expected the kingdom to appear at once, Jesus told a parable of a nobleman who went to a distant country to be made king, and then return.

On a Tuesday. You live in the interval this parable describes. The King has been enthroned, and he is not here to be seen. Two dangers follow: to forget he is coming back, or to be so taken up with when that you neglect what. So hold both. Say to yourself each morning, he is coming, and today matters to him. And if you have been unsettled by prophecy charts and predictions, set them down. Jesus told this parable precisely to cool date-setting. Your task is not to calculate the day but to be found faithful on it.

For worship. The King went into a far country by way of a cross, and he received the kingdom. There is no vote left to be taken on the throne of the universe; it is filled. He who was despised in Jericho’s streets is seated at the Father’s right hand, and he will come back. Every Christian waits, not for a candidate who might be elected, but for a King who has already been crowned.
verseByVerse.note: Local rulers went to Rome to have their kingdoms confirmed. Herod’s son Archelaus did so in 4 BC, and a Jewish delegation went after him to oppose it.

parallels.desc: will you at this time restore the kingdom?

verseByVerse.quote: Calling ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas, and said to them, ‘Engage in business until I come.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Calling ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas, and said to them: engage in business until I come.

Calling ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas. They are his slaves, trusted to manage his affairs while he is away, and each receives one mina, which is worth registering. In Matthew’s cousin-parable of the talents, the master distributes different amounts to different men, each according to his ability (Matthew 25:15). Here everybody gets exactly the same. That changes what the parable is measuring. Where the sums differ, the story is partly about capacity. Where they are identical, the only variable left is what each man did.

A mina. A hundred denarii, about three months’ wages for a labourer. Not a fortune, and that too is the point. For a nobleman about to receive a kingdom it is a trifle. He does not hand over the estate. He gives each man a modest, manageable sum and goes away: a test of faithfulness in small things (16:10).

What is the mina? The parable does not say, and that has allowed many answers. Because each servant receives the same, it most likely pictures what all disciples equally receive: the word of the gospel, the knowledge of the King, and the calling to serve him while he is away. Particular gifts, money, time and opportunities differ from person to person and are better pictured by the talents in Matthew. Here the point is that no servant can say he was given nothing. Every believer has the gospel, and every believer is sent to trade with it.

Engage in business until I come. The verb is commercial: trade with it, invest it, put it to work. It is not look after this. And the instruction contains its own deadline. Until I come is both a promise that he will and a statement that the trading has an end date. So the servants are left with three things: a sum of money, an instruction to risk it, and a return that is certain but unscheduled. That is the situation of the church, stated in a sentence. The task of the disciple between Christ’s going and his coming is not idle waiting but work.

The freedom of the instruction. What was not given is detailed instructions. He does not tell them what business to engage in, set targets, or explain how he will assess them. He gives them the money and goes, and the freedom is real. That means the timid servant’s failure in a few verses is not a failure to follow a rule. It is a failure to believe the freedom was genuinely given, and that the master would be pleased with the attempt.

The commission of the departing King. The parable’s picture is not left to guesswork, because Luke records what the real King said before he went to the far country. The risen Jesus opened the Scriptures to his disciples, showed them that the Christ must suffer and rise, and told them that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (24:46–47). Then he was carried up into heaven (24:51). That is what the trading looks like: a crucified and risen Lord’s gospel, put into ordinary hands, with orders to spend it everywhere until he comes back.

In a sentence. The nobleman gave ten servants a mina each, telling them to put it to work until he returned.

On a Tuesday. Write down what Christ has entrusted to you: the gospel you understand, the people who live near you, the hours of this week, the money in your account, a skill you take for granted. Then pick one and ask what trading with it would look like before Sunday: a conversation in which you speak of Christ, an hour given to someone lonely, a sum given away, a gift offered to your church. Do not wait for a perfect plan. The master did not give one.

For worship. How generous the King is, to put his own money into the hands of slaves and go away without a contract, a target or a guard. He did not leave his people empty-handed when he went to his throne. He left his word, his name and his promise to come back, and he counts the stumbling trade of his servants as business done for a King. Nothing entrusted by him is ever wasted, and every coin of it is still his, waiting to be shown to him on the day he returns.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a mina was about three months’ wages for a labourer.

verseByVerse.quote: But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’ When he returned, having received the kingdom, he ordered these servants to whom he had given the money to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by doing business.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying: we do not want this man to reign over us. When he returned, having received the kingdom, he ordered these servants to whom he had given the money to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by doing business.

But his citizens hated him. A second plot enters the parable, and it has nothing to do with the servants and their money. These are the nobleman’s own people, as the Jews sent a delegation after Archelaus.

And sent a delegation after him, saying, We do not want this man to reign over us. He is walking toward the city that is about to say exactly this about him. Within days its leaders will cry, we have no king but Caesar (John 19:15). He says it out loud, in a shape they cannot miss, days before they prove it true. Notice the wording of the objection. Not this man is unfit, or we prefer another. We do not want this man to reign over us. The issue is not his credentials but his rule, and that has always been the issue. It is the cry of every human heart since Eden that will not have God for its King.

When he returned, having received the kingdom. Their delegation failed. That is the first thing the verse says, and it says it without comment: the objection was lodged, considered and overruled somewhere far away, and the kingdom was granted anyway. Every rebellion against Christ ends the same way. The nations rage, and the One who sits in the heavens laughs; he has set his King on Zion (Psalm 2:1–6). This is Christ’s return in glory, as King.

He ordered these servants to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by doing business. And the first thing he does on arriving with a kingdom is not to deal with the rebels. It is to send for his own servants and ask what they did with what he left them. Judgment begins with the household of God (1 Peter 4:17). All of us must stand before Christ’s judgment seat (2 Corinthians 5:10), and each of us will give an account of himself to God (Romans 14:12).

What it does not mean. The accounting is not a trial to decide whether the faithful servants belong to the master. They were his servants before he left. For believers, the question of acceptance was settled at the cross, and no condemnation awaits those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). What is examined at his return is what they did with what he gave them, and what is given is reward. That should make us serious, and not afraid.

Is it wrong to want rewards? No. Jesus offers them, and he offers them to motivate us (6:23, 35; 12:33). The desire to hear him say well done is not selfish ambition; it is love wanting to please the one it loves. What would be wrong is to think we earn heaven, or to serve for the reward rather than for the Master. But the two do not compete. The reward is mostly the Master himself: his pleasure, his presence and a share in his work.

In a sentence. His citizens hated him and sent a delegation saying they did not want him as king, but he returned as king and called his servants to account for what they had gained.

On a Tuesday. Where in your life are you saying, in effect, I do not want this man to reign over me? Rarely in words. Usually in a single room of the house kept locked: money, sexuality, a grudge, your ambitions, your time. The delegation was sent to a far country and lost its case. Yours will too. Open the room to him today, while he is still asking.

For worship. No delegation has ever unseated him. Kings and councils, empires and philosophies have sent their objections to heaven, and the answer has always come back the same: he has received the kingdom. And this King, who could crush every rebel, came first to Jerusalem on a donkey and gave himself for people who had said, we do not want this man.

parallels.desc: we have no king but Caesar

verseByVerse.quote: The first came before him, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made ten minas more.’ And he said to him, ‘Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first came before him, saying: Lord, your mina has made ten minas more. And he said to him: well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.
