The first came before him, saying, Lord, your mina has made ten minas more. Notice whose mina it is. Not I have made ten; your mina has made ten. The servant reports a result without claiming it, and there is no trace of a man presenting his own achievement. Paul said the same: I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me (1 Corinthians 15:10). The return is extraordinary: a thousand per cent, on three months’ wages, in a long absence. Whatever he did, he did it well.

Well done, good servant! It is the first thing the returning king says to anybody in the parable. Before any assessment of the estate, before the rebels are dealt with, the man who traded faithfully hears his master say good. There is no greater reward in heaven or on earth than that word from that mouth (Matthew 25:21).

Because you have been faithful in a very little. A very little: that is the master’s description of the mina, three months’ wages and everything the servant had to work with for the entire absence. He calls it a trifle. The reason given is faithfulness, not brilliance. The servant is praised not for being gifted but for being faithful with what he was given.

The one Servant who earned the word. Only one servant has ever heard the Father’s approval on his own merit. At the Jordan the voice from heaven said, You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased (3:22), and Jesus went on to do his Father’s will without a single failure, all the way to the cross. Every other well done is spoken over servants who have been joined to him. That is why the first servant says your mina and not my work: his trading was itself a gift, and his welcome rests on Another’s faithfulness. The King’s praise of his servants is the overflow of the Father’s delight in his Son.

You shall have authority over ten cities. And now the disproportion, which is the whole point. Set the very little against what is given in return. Not ten minas, not a hundred. Cities, with people in them, in the kingdom he has just been granted. The exchange rate is absurd, and it is meant to be. Whatever any Christian is trading with in this life, and it may look and feel like very little indeed, the parable insists on calling it small precisely to make the reward look impossible.

The reward is more responsibility. Notice what the reward actually is. Not rest, and not payment. It is a larger share in the King’s rule, on an enormously larger scale. The popular picture of heaven is largely of idleness, and Scripture’s images run the other way: his servants will worship him, and they will reign for ever and ever (Revelation 22:3–5). Believers will share in Christ’s reign (22:29–30; 2 Timothy 2:12; Revelation 2:26; 3:21). Whatever the life to come is, it is not retirement, and the training for it is going on now, in something the King calls very little.

Will we really rule cities? The parable uses the language of its story: a king’s servants rewarded with towns. The reality behind it is that the redeemed will share in Christ’s reign over the new creation, with real responsibility, real work and real joy, when he makes all things new (Revelation 21:1–5; 22:5). We are not told what that will look like in detail, and it is wise not to build a map from a parable. What we are told is enough: the faithfulness you show now is not wasted, and it is preparing you for something far greater than you can imagine.

In a sentence. The first servant had made ten minas from one, and the king praised him and gave him authority over ten cities.

On a Tuesday. You will probably not see great results this week. You will see a lunch box packed, an email answered honestly, a child put to bed with a prayer, a neighbour helped, a lesson taught to six children. The King calls that very little, and he is watching it. Do the small thing faithfully today, as if it mattered to him, because it does. And when something goes well, say aloud, your mina did this, and give him the credit.

For worship. The Lord is lavish. He takes the little we do with what he gave, calls it his servants’ work, and answers it with cities. He is not a grudging employer weighing hours, but a King who loves to share his reign, and who seats the faithful with him on a throne he won by a cross. A slave who began with three months’ wages ends by ruling ten cities, and the distance between the two is the measure of his heart.

verseByVerse.quote: And the second came, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made five minas.’ And he said to him, ‘And you are to be over five cities.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the second came, saying: Lord, your mina has made five minas. And he said to him: and you are to be over five cities.

And the second came, saying, Lord, your mina has made five minas. Two verses, and it would be easy to read them as a repetition. They are not, and what they add is one of the kindest things in the parable. The second man has produced exactly half what the first produced. Same starting sum, same length of absence, same instruction, and half the result. Less than the first, but still faithful.

And he said to him, And you are to be over five cities. There is no rebuke of any kind. Not a word about why he did not do better, no comparison with his colleague, no suggestion that five is disappointing. What he gets is five cities: a reward proportioned to the return, and every bit as real. There are degrees of reward in the kingdom (1 Corinthians 3:12–15), but there is no disgrace in having fewer cities than the man next to you.

No well done? The master’s reply to the second man is noticeably shorter. He gets the reward, and no well done is recorded. Some readers press that; it is probably better not to. Luke is compressing, as he does everywhere, and the parable’s contrast is not between the ten and the five. It is between both of them and the man with the handkerchief. What the two together establish is the principle: the King rewards what was actually done, at the rate it was done, without grading on a curve.

He came. There is one more thing in these two verses, and it is easy to walk past. The second servant came. He had a smaller result than the man in front of him and he came anyway, and said out loud in front of the whole court exactly what he had produced. That takes something. And it is the opposite of what the third servant will do in the next verse, which is to arrive with an explanation.

The Judge who counts small coins. The King who sets the five-mina servant over five cities without a word of reproach is the same Lord who, in a few days, will sit opposite the temple treasury, watch the rich put in their gifts and a poor widow put in two small copper coins, and say that she put in more than all of them (21:1–4). His arithmetic is not the world’s. He measures what was given against what was held back, and he never confuses a small return with an unfaithful one. The servant with five minas is safe in the hands of a Judge who sees like that.

What if I have done much less than other Christians I know? Then this verse is for you. You are not being measured against them. Faithfulness is judged by what you did with what you were given in the life God appointed you: your health, your circumstances, your years. A mother with three small children, a man caring for a dying parent, a believer with a long illness may trade quietly, and be over cities. Comparison is not the King’s method; do not make it yours. Bring him what you have, honestly, and expect his kindness.

In a sentence. The second servant had made five minas, and was given five cities.

On a Tuesday. Notice this week where you measure your Christian usefulness against someone else’s and go quiet: the friend who leads a ministry, the sibling whose children all walk with God, the Christian whose prayers sound so fluent. Stop. Ask instead whether you have been faithful with your own mina today. Then come to the Lord with whatever you have, and do not hide it because it is smaller than someone else’s.

For worship. The King does not despise the five. His kindness reaches the servant who did half as well, and sets him over cities with no reproach in his voice. The Lord who reigns over all things is gentle with the modest offerings of ordinary lives, and stoops to honour what the world would never notice. In his kingdom no faithful servant is despised. Each is rewarded beyond all deserving by a Master whose generosity is the one thing in the story that never varies.

verseByVerse.quote: Then another came, saying, ‘Lord, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a handkerchief; for I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. You take what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then another came, saying: Lord, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a handkerchief; for I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. You take what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow.

Then another came, saying, Lord, here is your mina. Literally the other, the third of the ten that Jesus describes, representing those who are unfaithful. He has it. That is the first thing, and it is what he thinks will save him. Nothing has been lost, nothing spent, nothing risked. He can put the coin on the table exactly as he received it. And note the difference from the others. They reported what the mina had made. He reports where he put it.

Which I kept laid away in a handkerchief. The handkerchief is a soudarion, a cloth for wiping the face, the same word used of the cloth over the face of Lazarus in the tomb (John 11:44). He wrapped the money in a rag and put it somewhere. It was not even a safe place for money. Burying it in the ground was the recognised secure method, and a man who did so was not liable if it was stolen. He did not even take proper care of it.

For I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. Now the reason, and he offers it as an explanation. It is in fact an accusation. Severe is austēros, the root of the English austere, used of unripe, sour fruit and of a man with no give in him: harsh, strict, exacting.

You take what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow. The two charges describe a profiteer: someone who collects where he has not invested and harvests fields he never planted. So the servant’s defence is that his master is grasping and unfair, and that his own inactivity was a rational response.

His fear was not reverence. It is not the fear of the Lord, though it wears the same clothes. Reverence produces obedience; this produced nothing. He was not too frightened to disobey. He was too frightened to act, and he has been calling it caution for the whole of the master’s absence. His fear was really unbelief.

His picture of the master was a slander. The accusation is also untrue, and the parable has already shown it. This is a master who handed out money to ten men with no supervision and no conditions, and who has just given a servant ten cities for a mina. Whatever he is, he is not a man who takes what he did not deposit. The servant has constructed a master he could justify doing nothing about. A false view of God is never harmless. It always leads somewhere, and very often it leads to a life of doing nothing for him.

The Master’s face. The slander is answered most fully by the one telling the story. The servant called his master a man who takes what he did not deposit. The Son who spoke these words was on his way to Jerusalem to give, not to take: to lay down his life and pour out his blood for his people (22:20). Whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9), and nothing in that face is austere. He wept over the city that rejected him and prayed for the men who crucified him. The servant’s fear was wrong because his picture was wrong, and the true picture walks through this chapter on the road to a cross.

What if I find myself afraid of God? There is a right fear and a wrong fear. The right fear is reverent awe of his holiness, combined with trust in his mercy, and it draws you toward him and makes you eager to please him (Psalm 130:4). The wrong fear sees him as a harsh taskmaster waiting to catch you out, and it drives you to hide. If that is your fear, the cure is not to try harder but to look again at who he is. Look at the cross: a God who gives his Son for his enemies is not severe. As you see his love, fear of punishment gives way to the reverent, glad fear of a child (1 John 4:18).

In a sentence. The third servant returned the mina he had wrapped in a cloth, saying he was afraid because his master was a harsh man who took what was not his.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself honestly what picture of God is behind your inaction. Do you avoid serving because you assume you will fail and he will be displeased? Do you keep your faith private because you think he wants you safe rather than fruitful? Write down one sentence that describes how you actually think of God when you are tired or anxious. Then test it against what Scripture says of him: compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love (Exodus 34:6). Change the picture, and the paralysis begins to lift.

For worship. God is not austere. He is kind to the ungrateful and the evil (6:35), he handed his servants his own treasure with no conditions, and he opened his hand widest of all in the gift of his Son. The servant hid a coin in a face-cloth because he thought his master grasping. The Master he slandered gives far more than he takes, and he has never reaped a single thing from his people that his own grace did not first sow.
verseByVerse.note: A handkerchief was not a safe place for money; burying it was safer.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to him, ‘I will condemn you with your own words, you wicked servant! You knew that I was a severe man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow? Why then did you not put my money in the bank, and at my coming I might have collected it with interest?’
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to him: I will condemn you with your own words, you wicked servant! You knew that I was a severe man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow? Why then did you not put my money in the bank, and at my coming I might have collected it with interest?

I will condemn you with your own words, you wicked servant! The master does not argue the description. He does not say, I am not severe. He takes the servant’s own account of him and turns it round. And the word wicked lands where a reader might not expect it. The servant has not stolen the money, or wasted it, or run off with it. He is called wicked for laying it away in a cloth. Not just lazy, but wicked: doing nothing with what God gives is sin.

You knew that I was a severe man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow? The logic is plain: very well, suppose I am exactly what you say. The master does not accept the description, but argues on its own terms.

Why then did you not put my money in the bank? There is the trap closing. Bank is trapeza, a table: the money-changer’s table. Banking existed and paid interest; the money-changers took deposits, and there was nothing exotic about it. It required no skill, no judgment and no courage. A man could walk in, hand the mina over, and walk out.

And at my coming I might have collected it with interest. So the servant’s own premise convicts him. If the master really were a hard man who reaped where he had not sown, the sensible response would have been to make certain he got something. The one course of action his stated fear cannot possibly justify is doing absolutely nothing. That exposes the fear as a cover story. He did not act on his belief about the master, because it was never the reason. It was the excuse he had ready. The unfaithful servant did nothing not because he was afraid of failure but because he did not care about his master’s interests.

Is the third servant a believer who loses reward, or an unbeliever who is lost? He belongs to the household outwardly. He was given a mina and called a servant. But his picture of the master as harsh shows that he never knew him, and in Matthew’s cousin-parable the worthless servant is cast into the outer darkness (Matthew 25:24–30). He represents those who receive God’s gifts and do nothing with them: outwardly religious, perhaps in church for years, but never truly serving Christ because they never truly trusted him. Faithfulness is not the ground of salvation; it is the fruit of knowing a gracious master. The servant who buries his gift shows that he does not know him.

Then can a true Christian lose his salvation? No. Those whom God has justified he will also glorify (Romans 8:30), and no one can snatch Christ’s sheep out of his hand (John 10:28–29). This parable does not describe a believer falling away. It describes someone who was near the master and never knew him, and it is a warning to search ourselves, not a threat hanging over those who trust Christ. A true believer may be weak, fearful and slow, and will still bring something, however small, because the Spirit is at work in him (Philippians 1:6). What the parable exposes is the settled heart that has never loved the master at all.

The Servant who left nothing undone. Nothing bad was done: that is the whole defence, and it is exactly what is condemned. The servant was not asked to avoid loss. He was asked to trade, and he did not. Set beside him the one Servant who did everything his Master asked. Jesus did not merely avoid sin. From the boy who said he must be in his Father’s house (2:49) to the man who set his face to go to Jerusalem, he did his Father’s will, until he could commit his spirit into his Father’s hands (23:46). That whole-hearted obedience is counted to everyone who trusts him (Romans 5:19), and it is the only righteousness that will stand when the King asks what was done with what he gave.

In a sentence. The king condemned the servant by his own words, asking why, if he thought his master so demanding, he had not even put the money in the bank to earn interest.

On a Tuesday. Doing nothing with God’s gifts is not neutral. What is the smallest step you could take today, the equivalent of putting the mina in the bank? Not a grand scheme: a text to a friend who is struggling, an offer to help with the children’s work, praying aloud at a meeting, giving to the work of the gospel, telling one person why you go to church. The servant’s own words show the bar was low. Do the least thing, and you will find it leads to more.

For worship. The Master is just, and his justice is clear. No one will be condemned by a law he did not know; every mouth will be closed by its own words (Romans 3:19). And the same Master who exposes the buried mina offers to every fearful servant who hears this parable a better word than condemnation: come to me, and see that I am not what you feared. Christ was condemned in place of those who trust him, so that their own words need never condemn them.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to those who stood by, ‘Take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has the ten minas.’ And they said to him, ‘Lord, he has ten minas!’ ‘I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to those who stood by: take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has the ten minas. And they said to him: Lord, he has ten minas! I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.

And he said to those who stood by, Take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has the ten minas. The idle man loses even what he had, and the man who traded best is trusted with what the idle man buried.

Lord, he has ten minas! The bystanders object, and it is the natural response, the one most readers share. Why give more to the man who already has most? It seems unfair.

I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given. The principle sounds harsh until it is read as what it is: not a rule for distributing prizes, but a description of how entrusted things actually behave. The saying has appeared before in this Gospel, attached to hearing: take care then how you hear, for to the one who has, more will be given (8:18). The mechanism is the same. Capacity grows by use. A man who trades finds he can trade more, because the trading made him a better trader. This is true of spiritual gifts, opportunities, and understanding of God’s word. The one who obeys what he knows is given to know more.

But from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. Notice the last clause carefully: from the one who has not. The third servant was still holding the mina when that was said. In the master’s reckoning a coin wrapped in a cloth for the whole of an absence is not a possession at all; it is an absence dressed up as one. He has nothing, because he has done nothing with it, and the removal of the coin is simply the paperwork catching up. And a man who hides away what he was given loses even the ability to use it, not only by confiscation but by atrophy. Nothing is more perishable than an unexercised gift.

The enthroned King still gives. The giving in this verse is a King’s, and Luke shows that King at work in his second volume. Exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit, Jesus poured him out on his waiting people at Pentecost (Acts 2:33). The nobleman who received a kingdom in the far country does not sit on it like a miser. He distributes from it, and he goes on giving more to those who use what he has given. Every increase of faith, understanding and fruitfulness in his servants is the overflow of his throne.

Is this the rich getting richer? No. The parable is not about money or social advantage; Luke has spent chapters warning the rich and lifting the poor (1:53; 6:20–24; 16:19–31). It is about the gifts of the King. In his kingdom those who use what he gives receive more of the same, and those who despise his gifts lose them. A poor widow who prays faithfully is the one who has, and a wealthy churchgoer who buries the gospel is the one who has not.

In a sentence. The king ordered the mina taken and given to the servant with ten, because those who have will be given more, and those who have nothing will lose even what they have.

On a Tuesday. Is there a gift you have let go dormant: a habit of prayer, a knowledge of Scripture, a talent for teaching, hospitality or music that you once used for Christ and have quietly shelved? Pick it up this week in one small way. Gifts revive by use, as they died by neglect. And when you hear God’s word on Sunday, act on one thing by Wednesday. That is how the one who has is given more.

For worship. The King’s treasury is never thinner for what it gives. He has emptied it into the hands of his servants for two thousand years, and it is as full as on the day he was crowned. Out of his fullness his people receive grace upon grace (John 1:16), and the servant who spends what he was given for his Master’s sake will never reach the bottom of it.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for these enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them before me.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as for these enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them before me.

But as for these enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them. The citizens of v. 14 return, and they are distinct from the unfaithful servant. He was idle. They are open rebels.

Bring them here and slaughter them before me. It is the hardest sentence in Luke, and it should not be hurried past. Readers recoil, and some have quoted the line as though Jesus were commanding violence against opponents. Two things keep it in its place.

Words inside a parable. First, these are words spoken by a character in a story, not an instruction issued to disciples. The king in the story is doing what such kings did, and the picture has been borrowed from Archelaus, whose reprisals after Rome confirmed him were remembered with horror. Nobody in that crowd would have heard it as a policy for them to carry out. Not one command in this parable is addressed to the servants about the citizens. Their whole task, from first to last, is to trade with what they were given. Christians are never to take up the sword against those who reject Christ (22:49–51).

The horror is the point. Second, the horror of the image is not an embarrassment to be explained away. Jesus is drawing a picture of what it is to refuse a king who is coming back anyway. The picture points first to the destruction of Jerusalem, which he will foretell with tears in a few minutes (vv. 41–44), and ultimately to the last judgment, when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven and those who do not obey the gospel suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:7–9). The parable and the tears over the city belong to the same person, fourteen verses apart, and a judgment described in terms this stark by a man about to weep over it is not bloodlust. It is the last warning of someone who would give anything to be heard.

Three groups. The faithful servants are rewarded. The unfaithful servant loses everything. The enemies are destroyed. Christ’s return will bring reward and judgment together, in one event, before all. There is no neutral fourth group. Everyone who hears of the King is either trading for him, burying what he gave, or refusing his reign.

This is not the parable of the talents. The two are cousins, but in Matthew the sums are enormous and unequal and there are no rebel citizens (Matthew 25:14–30). Jesus taught constantly and on the road, and reworked his material for the moment he was in. Luke’s parable, told a few days before a crowd shouted for his execution, asks what you did with what you were given, and one thing more: whether you wanted the King at all.

How can a loving Jesus speak of slaughter? Because love is not indifference. A King who did nothing about those who destroy his people and despise his rule would not be good. Final judgment is real and it is eternal; Jesus speaks of it more than anyone in the Bible. But notice who says this, and where he is going. He is on his way to Jerusalem to bear judgment himself, so that rebels who come to him will never face it. The same Jesus prayed for the men who crucified him, Father, forgive them (23:34). The door is open now. The parable is spoken so that no one need be found among the enemies when he comes.

In a sentence. The king ordered his enemies, who had refused his reign, to be brought and executed before him.

On a Tuesday. Rejecting Christ’s reign is not a neutral position, and it is not a private opinion that harms no one. If you have been keeping him at arm’s length, bow to the King now, while the far country is still between his throne and his return. And if you love someone who says, I do not want this man to reign over me, do not soften the warning, and do not stop praying. The same King who will judge his enemies is now receiving them as friends.

For worship. Blessed be the Judge of all the earth, whose every verdict will be right when every knee bows before him (Philippians 2:10–11). And blessed be the King who spoke of his enemies’ end on the same day that he sat at an enemy’s table. Before grace found them, every one of his people was among those who said, We do not want this man to reign over us. The chapter that ends with rebels summoned to judgment began with a chief tax collector welcoming the King into his house with joy.

parallels.desc: kiss the Son, lest he be angry

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–44 — The Triumphal Entry and Jesus Weeping over Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
He goes on ahead, leading — and “going up” is exact: Jericho lies 800 feet below sea level, Jerusalem 2,500 above, so the seventeen miles climb over three thousand feet through desert.

The Mount of Olives is not incidental scenery. Zechariah had said the LORD's feet would stand on it (Zech. 14:4), and from that ridge a king approaching Jerusalem first sees the city laid out below.

The instructions about the colt are startlingly specific, and Luke will not settle whether this is prior arrangement or foreknowledge. What it establishes is that nothing about the next hour is improvised. And “on which no one has ever yet sat” is not about comfort: an animal never worked was the requirement for sacred use — the cart that carried the ark (1 Sam. 6:7), the red heifer (Num. 19:2).

He has walked everywhere for three years. On the one occasion he rides, he sends for a specific animal, and the animal is the prophecy: “humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey” (Zech. 9:9). A king entering a capital rode a horse, and a horse was the animal of war.

The cloaks on the road are a coronation gesture, not enthusiasm — when Jehu was proclaimed king the officers put their garments under him on the steps and blew the trumpet (2 Kgs. 9:13). And a cloak was a poor man's blanket and often his most valuable possession, so protected in law that a creditor could not keep one overnight (Ex. 22:26-27).

Luke alone specifies who is shouting: “the whole multitude of his disciples.” And the reason is backward-looking — “for all the mighty works that they had seen.”

Then, at the point on the descent where the whole city comes into view at once, he weeps aloud.
verseByVerse.theology:
The disciples' shout alters Psalm 118:26. The psalm reads “blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD” — the greeting pilgrims received at the festivals. They insert one word: “blessed is the King who comes.” That is not a liturgical greeting any more but a public claim, at Passover, in earshot of Jerusalem — which is exactly why the Pharisees object. And it echoes what Jesus said at 13:35: they would not see him again until they said it.

“Peace in heaven and glory in the highest” closes a circle Luke opened in chapter 2. The angels sang “glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace” (2:14); the disciples sing it back with the terms reversed. Which is exact, and not sentimental. There will be no peace on earth this week — there will be a mob, a trial, a scourging and an execution. What is settled in heaven is another matter, and it is being accomplished by the very week that is about to look like total defeat.

“If these were silent, the very stones would cry out” has roots in Habakkuk, where the stone cries out from the wall against injustice (Hab. 2:11) — stones as witnesses that cannot be silenced. And there is a bitter appropriateness in the choice: he is looking at magnificent stonework, and within four verses will say not one of those stones will be left on another.

The prophecy of vv.43-44 was fulfilled with precision. In AD 70 Titus built a wall of circumvallation right round the city — some four and a half miles, thrown up in three days — to stop anyone getting out or supplies getting in. Josephus, who was there, describes it. The temple was burned and then dismantled, and the great platform stones were levered off the walls into the street below, where they are still lying.
verseByVerse.examples:
Luke's verb for the weeping is not the quiet one. Greek has two words: one for silent tears, used of Jesus at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:35), and this one — eklausen, to wail aloud, the word used of the mourners at Jairus's house (8:52) and of Peter after the cock crowed (22:62). So the sound coming from the middle of that procession is a man sobbing audibly, and the singing does not appear to have stopped.

And the sentence he speaks breaks off unfinished in Greek — an exclamation that starts and does not complete, exactly as a sentence does when the person speaking cannot finish it. “Even you” is emphatic and heartbreaking: of all the cities on earth, this one did not know the things that make for peace.

A pastor preaching this every Palm Sunday finds it tempting to stop at the shouting. The passage insists on including the tears. Palm Sunday is not unambiguously triumphant; it is triumphant and heartbroken at once.

“Visitation” is episkopē — God coming to see about his people, the word Zechariah used in the Gospel's first chapter: “he has visited and redeemed his people” (1:68). The visitation happened. That is what makes the sentence unbearable. And the word cuts both ways, because a visitation is an inspection as well as a rescue: the same coming that saves those who know it for what it is condemns those who do not — not by a change in God, but because there is nothing else left when the visit has been made and refused.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. When he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount that is called Olivet, he sent two of the disciples, saying, 'Go into the village in front of you, where on entering you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever yet sat. Untie it and bring it here. If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ you shall say this: ‘The Lord has need of it.’'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he had said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. When he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount that is called Olivet, he sent two of the disciples, saying: go into the village in front of you, where on entering you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever yet sat. Untie it and bring it here. If anyone asks you, why are you untying it? you shall say this: the Lord has need of it.

And when he had said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. Went on ahead: in front of them, leading, resolute, as he set his face to go to Jerusalem in 9:51 (Mark 10:32). Nobody is dragging him up that road. And going up is geographically exact as well as customary. Jericho lies far below sea level and Jerusalem about 2,500 feet (750 m) above it, so the seventeen miles are a climb of some 3,500 feet (1,000 m) through the desert. He has just told a parable about a king who goes away to receive a kingdom by way of a far country. He now walks toward the place where that departure will begin.

When he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount that is called Olivet. Villages on the Mount of Olives, just east of Jerusalem. Bethany was the home of Martha, Mary and Lazarus. The Mount of Olives is not incidental scenery. Zechariah had prophesied that on the day of the LORD his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives (Zechariah 14:4), and it was from that hill that a king approaching Jerusalem would first see the city and the temple laid out below him.

Go into the village in front of you, where on entering you will find a colt tied. The instructions are startlingly specific: the village, the animal, its condition, and what to say if challenged. Luke does not tell us whether this is prior arrangement or foreknowledge, and the text will not settle it. What it does establish is that nothing about the next hour is improvised. Jesus is in control of his own entry into the city where he will die.

On which no one has ever yet sat. That is not a note about comfort. An animal never put to ordinary use was the requirement for sacred purposes. The cart that carried the ark back from the Philistines was drawn by cows on which there had never come a yoke (1 Samuel 6:7), and the red heifer of purification had to be one on which a yoke has never come (Numbers 19:2). This colt is being set apart for a holy use. It will carry the King.

If anyone asks you, Why are you untying it? you shall say this: The Lord has need of it. Which is either a password arranged in advance or a claim of extraordinary boldness, and either way it is the only explanation offered. The Lord is ho kyrios: it could mean the colt’s master, and it means the Lord of all.

The animal is the prophecy. Notice what he is choosing. A conquering king entering a capital rode a horse; a horse was the animal of war. Zechariah had described the alternative: Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey (Zechariah 9:9). And Zechariah goes on: he shall speak peace to the nations, and his rule shall be from sea to sea (9:10). He has walked everywhere for three years. On the one occasion he rides, he sends for a specific animal, and the animal is the prophecy.

In a sentence. Jesus went on ahead toward Jerusalem, and near the Mount of Olives sent two disciples to bring an unridden colt, telling them to say the Lord needed it.

On a Tuesday. If the Lord has need of something you have, the only reason he owes you is that he needs it. Hold what you own with an open hand: your car on Sunday morning, your spare room for a visiting missionary, your evening for a grieving friend, your savings for the work of the gospel. Ask yourself which of your possessions you would struggle to untie if two strangers came and said these words. That is the one to offer first.

For worship. He walked up out of the Jordan valley in front of everyone, toward a cross, and sent ahead for the animal that would carry him the last stretch. Every step of his passion was ordered by his own will and his Father’s plan, down to a colt tied in a village. The King whom Zechariah saw coming, righteous and having salvation, chose the lowliest mount in Israel for the greatest entry in its history, and the Lord who prepared a donkey for himself prepares every step of the road for those he loves.
verseByVerse.note: Bethphage and Bethany were villages on the Mount of Olives (Olivet), just east of Jerusalem. An animal never ridden was fit for a sacred purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: So those who were sent went away and found it just as he had told them. And as they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, 'Why are you untying the colt?' And they said, 'The Lord has need of it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
So those who were sent went away and found it just as he had told them. And as they were untying the colt, its owners said to them: why are you untying the colt? And they said: the Lord has need of it.

So those who were sent went away and found it just as he had told them. Luke records the match on purpose, and he will record another when two disciples find the upper room exactly as described (22:13). The small fulfilment matters. For chapters the disciples have heard things they could neither understand nor test: that he must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and rise (18:31–34). Here is a prediction they can walk into a village and verify within the hour, and it holds to the last detail. The Lord who is right about a tethered colt can be trusted about a cross and an empty tomb.

And as they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, Why are you untying the colt? So the challenge came, precisely as he said it would. Notice the word owners, plural. Only Luke has it, and the Greek is kyrioi, literally lords. This is somebody’s animal, and they are standing right there, watching two strangers untie it.

And they said, The Lord has need of it. Six words in English, and the owners let it go. There is a play on words here that Luke surely intends: the lords of the colt ask, and the answer is that the Lord needs it. The lesser lords yield to the greater. The most likely explanation of how it worked is the simplest: Jesus was known in that area, he had friends in Bethany, and an arrangement had been made or the phrase was recognised.

The Lord who borrows. Do not lose what the sentence says while explaining how it worked. The one through whom every colt in Judea was made, who owns the cattle on a thousand hills (Psalm 50:10), sends two men to ask for the loan of a donkey. He came into the world in borrowed lodging, rode into his capital on a borrowed animal, ate his last meal in a borrowed room and was buried in a borrowed grave. He who was rich became poor for our sakes (2 Corinthians 8:9), and everything he used was lent to him by people who did not know what they were lending it for.

Why would the Lord of all need anything? He does not need anything in the sense of lacking it; he is served by human hands as though he needed anything only because he chooses to be (Acts 17:25). His need here is the need of a King who has decided to use ordinary things and ordinary people in his work. That is the dignity he gives us. He could have summoned angels. He asked for a donkey from a family in Bethphage, and their name is not recorded, and their colt is in the Gospels for ever.

In a sentence. The disciples found the colt as Jesus said, and when its owners asked why they were untying it, they answered that the Lord needed it.

On a Tuesday. Trust Christ’s word in small things, and you will learn to trust it in great things. Keep a simple record this month of promises in Scripture you have seen him keep: provision when money was short, peace in a hospital corridor, a prayer answered for a child. And if you have wondered whether what you have is of any use to God, this passage answers. He asks for ordinary things, from ordinary people, at short notice. Expect to be asked.

For worship. His word has never once missed. He spoke of a colt, and the colt was there; he spoke of a cross, and it came; he spoke of rising, and the tomb was empty. The Lord who named a village, an animal and the very question its owners would ask knows his people just as exactly, and orders the hour when each of them is asked for something. Blessed be the Lord who had need of a donkey, and who had no need of us at all, and loved us anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it. And as he rode along, they spread their cloaks on the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it. And as he rode along, they spread their cloaks on the road.

And they brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it. The cloaks go on first, over the animal’s back, because there is no saddle. And then they set Jesus on it: the disciples lift him up. It is a small domestic detail, and it is the last quiet moment before everything becomes public. The King mounts, a deliberate fulfilment of Zechariah 9:9. And there is a royal echo too. When David’s son Solomon was made king, he rode on David’s own mule down to Gihon to be anointed (1 Kings 1:33–40). The Son of David rides to his capital the same way.

And as he rode along, they spread their cloaks on the road. Now the gesture changes meaning entirely, because this one has a precedent every Jew would recognise. When Jehu was proclaimed king, the officers every man of them took his garment and put it under him on the bare steps, and they blew the trumpet and proclaimed, Jehu is king (2 Kings 9:13). Cloaks under the feet of a man are not enthusiasm. They are a coronation. Luke does not mention palm branches, and he does not need them.

What a cloak cost. Consider what a cloak was to a poor Galilean. It was his outer garment, his blanket at night, and often the most valuable thing he owned, so valuable that the law forbade a creditor to keep one overnight in pledge, for that is his only covering (Exodus 22:26–27). They are laying the most expensive things they possess in the dust of a road so that a donkey can walk over them.

What makes it worship rather than waste. Nothing is achieved by putting a coat under a colt. The road was passable; the animal was not troubled by stones. The gesture is pure declaration, a way of saying with the only material available: this man is the King, and nothing I own is too good to be walked on by him. Nobody in that procession got anything back except a dirty cloak. That is worship: not a transaction, but honour given because it is owed. John tells how Mary of Bethany poured out her ointment in the same spirit, and in Mark’s account Jesus calls it a beautiful thing (John 12:1–8; Mark 14:3–9).

On the road out. There is a further thing in the gesture that only shows on the way back down. Within the week, other men will take his clothes from him and cast lots for them at the foot of a cross (23:34). On the road into the city his own people threw down everything they had so that he could pass over it. On the road out, the last garment he owned was taken from him and divided by strangers. Of everyone in that procession, the only one who fully understood where it was going was the man on the donkey.

Why a donkey and not a warhorse? Because of the kind of King he is and the kind of victory he came to win. A horse would have announced a war against Rome, which is what many in the crowd wanted. The donkey announces a King who is humble, who comes in peace, and whose victory will be won not by killing his enemies but by dying for them. His kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36). That is still how he comes: not by force, but by the gentle power of the gospel, winning hearts rather than seizing territory. He will come once more in visible glory, but even then his first coming will have told us his heart.

In a sentence. They brought the colt, put their cloaks on it and set Jesus on it, and as he rode, people spread their cloaks on the road before him.

On a Tuesday. What is your cloak: the thing you value most that you could lay at his feet? It may be your reputation at work, your plans for retirement, your hold on a child who wants to go to the mission field, an evening a week. Worship is not only singing. It is laying down something costly because he is worth it, and expecting nothing back. Choose one thing this week and give it to him, not as a deal, but because he is King.

For worship. The humble King comes riding, and the road under him is carpeted with poor men’s cloaks. He is the Son of David going up to his capital, and the throne he goes to take is a cross. He received the homage of Galileans who had almost nothing, and counted their dusty garments a coronation. There is no King like him, so worthy of every honour that heaven and earth could give, and so gentle with the poor offerings of those who love him.
verseByVerse.note: Spreading cloaks on the road was a gesture of homage to a king.

parallels.desc: your king, mounted on a donkey

verseByVerse.quote: As he was drawing near—already on the way down the Mount of Olives—the whole multitude of his disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen,
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he was drawing near, already on the way down the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of his disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen.

As he was drawing near, already on the way down the Mount of Olives. Luke fixes the exact spot, and anyone who has stood there will know why. The road from Bethany crosses the shoulder of the Mount of Olives, and at a particular point on the descent the whole city comes into view at once: the Kidron valley below, the wall opposite, and the temple platform filling the eye, its white stone and gold catching the light. It is one of the great sights of the ancient world, and it arrives suddenly. That is where the shouting starts.

The whole multitude of his disciples. Luke is specific, and he is the only evangelist who is. Matthew and Mark have the crowds; Luke says it was his own followers: not just the Twelve, but the many who had come with him from Galilee, the women who had provided for him, the healed and the forgiven. Whatever the pilgrim crowd made of it, this is not a spontaneous public demonstration. It is the people who have been with him.

Began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice. Joy and loud praise, as at his birth, when the shepherds returned glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen (2:20). This is the joy of people who have seen God at work.

The same hillside. Luke will bring his readers back to this slope. After his resurrection Jesus leads his disciples out as far as Bethany, lifts up his hands and blesses them, and is carried up into heaven, and Luke’s second volume names the place: the mount called Olivet (24:50–51; Acts 1:9–12). Today the King comes down that hill amid praise, to be rejected and crucified. Then he will go up from it, crowned with glory, to the right hand of God, and his disciples will return to Jerusalem with great joy, continually in the temple blessing God (24:52–53). The road of this procession runs down to a cross and back up to a throne, over the same ground.

For all the mighty works that they had seen. The reason is entirely backward-looking. They are not praising him for what they expect on Friday. They are praising God for what they have already watched him do, and they have watched a great deal. Luke’s readers can supply the list, because they have just read it. A widow’s son sitting up on his bier. A legion evicted. Five loaves and twelve baskets. A leper who came back. A blind man at the gate of that very morning’s town, still with them in the procession and presumably shouting louder than anybody. These people have three years of evidence, and they are using it. They were wrong about the week ahead. They were not wrong about him, and the reasons they gave were sound.

What if I do not feel like praising? Then do what they did: remember. Praise in Scripture is rarely a feeling first. It is a telling of what God has done, and feeling usually follows the telling (Psalm 103:1–5). Begin with the mighty works you know for certain: the cross and the empty tomb, your own conversion, the prayers answered, the troubles survived. Say them aloud, or sing them with the church when you would rather stay silent. You are not being dishonest when you praise without strong emotion. You are telling the truth about God, which is always the right thing to do.

In a sentence. As Jesus came down the Mount of Olives, the whole crowd of his disciples began to praise God loudly for all the mighty works they had seen.

On a Tuesday. Make a list tonight of the mighty works you have seen God do: in Scripture, in your church, in your family, in your own life. Make it specific: names, dates, places. Read it aloud to God, and keep it for the week when nothing seems to be happening. And sing on Sunday with your whole voice. Loud praise is not a matter of personality. It is a matter of what he has done.

For worship. Blessed be the God of all the mighty works. He raised the widow’s son, fed the five thousand and opened blind eyes, and on the far side of that week he did the mightiest work of all: he raised his Son from the dead, and raised us with him. Every reason the disciples had on that hillside is ours, and the empty tomb besides. The praise that broke out on the slope of Olivet has never stopped since, and it never will.
verseByVerse.note: The road from the Mount of Olives descends into the Kidron Valley, with the city and temple in full view.

verseByVerse.quote: saying, 'Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saying: blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!

Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! The line is Psalm 118:26, one of the best-known sentences in Israel’s worship. Psalm 118 closed the Hallel, the psalms sung at the great festivals, and pilgrims arriving at Jerusalem were greeted with those words. But they have altered it, and the alteration is the whole point. The psalm reads, blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD. Luke’s disciples insert one word: blessed is the King who comes. That is no longer a liturgical greeting. It is a claim about the man on the donkey, made in public, at Passover, in earshot of Jerusalem, and it is precisely why the Pharisees will object in the next verse.

The words he said they would say. This is very nearly the sentence Jesus himself said they would not see him again until they said: you will not see me until you say, Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord (13:35). The condition he named is echoed on the road by his own disciples. Jerusalem as a whole will not say it this week. One day every tongue will.

Peace in heaven and glory in the highest! Here Luke closes a circle he opened in his second chapter. Over a field outside Bethlehem the angels had sung, glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased (2:14). Now human voices sing it back, with the terms reversed. The angels said peace on earth; the disciples say peace in heaven. Luke omits the word Hosanna, which his Gentile readers might not have understood, and gives us this instead.

Why peace in heaven and not on earth? Because that is exactly where things stand. There will be no peace on earth this week. There will be a mob, a trial, a scourging and an execution, and the man they are singing about will be dead within days. Peace on earth is about to be rejected by the city of peace (v. 42). What is settled in heaven is another matter. The reconciliation between God and sinners is being accomplished, and it is being accomplished by the very week that will look like total defeat. Through the blood of his cross God made peace (Colossians 1:20). Peace on earth will follow from peace in heaven: first in every heart that believes, and finally in a new creation where there is no more war.

The singers do not know how right they are. They think they are welcoming a king to a coronation. They are walking beside him to an altar, singing the anthem of a peace that will be made in blood on Friday afternoon, and it will hold for ever.

In a sentence. They praised Jesus as the blessed King who comes in the name of the Lord, and proclaimed peace in heaven and glory in the highest.

On a Tuesday. Peace with God comes before peace in your circumstances. If your week is full of conflict, at home, at work, in your own mind, remember that the most important peace is already settled in heaven, by the cross, and cannot be disturbed by anything that happens on earth (Romans 5:1). Start each day by giving thanks for that peace. Then go and be a peacemaker where you are, because the King of peace is your King.

For worship. The King who comes in the name of the Lord bears that name as his own. He came once on a donkey, to be refused by his city and to make peace in heaven by his blood, and he will come once more in a cloud with power and great glory (21:27), to a world that will have no song left but the one his disciples sang on the slope. Between the two comings the hillside choir has never fallen silent. Every generation of his people takes up the line, and every one of them is right about him.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD
glory in the highest, peace on earth

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him, 'Teacher, rebuke your disciples.' He answered, 'I tell you, if these were silent, the very stones would cry out.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him: Teacher, rebuke your disciples. He answered: I tell you, if these were silent, the very stones would cry out.

And some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him, Teacher, rebuke your disciples. It is the last time the Pharisees appear in Luke’s Gospel, and their final recorded words are a request to stop the worship. Their concern may have been partly genuine. A messianic acclamation at Passover, with Roman troops reinforced in the fortress overlooking the temple and the governor in town precisely because festivals produced riots, was a dangerous thing to be shouting. Men had died for less. But notice the address: Teacher. They will not use the word the disciples have just used. The disciples said King; the Pharisees say Teacher, and the whole dispute is contained in the gap between those two nouns. And notice what they ask for. Not that he deny the claim, but rebuke your disciples: silence them. It is enough for their purposes if nobody says it out loud.

I tell you, if these were silent, the very stones would cry out. The refusal is absolute, and the reason is not tactical. He says that if these voices stop, the created order will take over. That is a claim that the praise is not optional, not generated by enthusiasm, but owed. The time has come, and the King must be acknowledged. Creation was made by him and for him (Colossians 1:16), and it knows its Maker even when men do not.

The stones as witnesses. The image has roots. Habakkuk, denouncing the man who builds his house by injustice, says the stone will cry out from the wall (Habakkuk 2:11): stones as witnesses that cannot be silenced. And there is a bitter appropriateness in the choice. He is looking at a city of magnificent stonework, and within four verses he will say that not one of those stones will be left on another (v. 44). The stones will cry out. Within a generation they will be lying in a heap in the valley, and they will be saying something after all.

Is it wrong to worship loudly or emotionally? No. Jesus refused to silence it, and Scripture is full of shouting, clapping and singing with a loud voice (Psalm 47:1; 98:4). Nor is quiet worship less real. What matters is that praise is true, directed to Christ, and done decently and in order (1 Corinthians 14:40). The danger this passage exposes is not the noisy church or the quiet one. It is the person who is embarrassed that Jesus should be praised at all, or who would rather the claim that he is King were not made in public.

In a sentence. When some Pharisees told Jesus to silence his disciples, he said that if they were silent, the stones would cry out.

On a Tuesday. Where do you go quiet about Jesus because someone would rather you did not speak of him: at a family meal, in an office conversation, with a friend who has asked a direct question? Notice the pressure, and do not mistake it for wisdom. You do not have to shout. But you do not have to stay silent either. If the stones would cry out, a sentence from you about what Christ has done is not too much.

For worship. All creation owes him praise. The heavens declare his glory, and the stones of Jerusalem stood ready to cry out if his disciples fell silent. The Maker of every stone chose instead to be praised by the voices of Galilean fishermen and healed beggars, and by ours. He needs no one to be glorified, and he delights to be glorified by us, and the cry the stones were spared has been carried by redeemed voices into every nation on earth.

parallels.desc: the stone will cry out from the wall

verseByVerse.quote: And when he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it, saying, 'Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it, saying: would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes.

And when he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it. The shouting is still going on. He is on a donkey, surrounded by people singing that he is the King, at the summit of the only public acclaim he ever received, and he is crying. Only Luke records it. Wept is eklausen: not quiet tears but loud weeping, sobbing, the word used of mourners at a funeral. He has lamented over this city before, in the saying about the hen and her chicks (13:34). Now the lament becomes tears. He has been carrying this the whole way. Not for himself, though he knew he was riding to his death, but for the city that would reject him.

Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! The sentence breaks off. In Greek it is unfinished: an exclamation that starts and does not complete, exactly as a sentence does when the person speaking cannot finish it. Even you: the pronoun is emphatic, and it is heartbreaking. Of all the cities on earth, this one. The city of David, the place of the temple, the address to which every prophet was sent. Peace is eirēnē, and there is a play on the city’s name, which was popularly understood as city of peace. Jerusalem, of all places, did not know the things that make for peace.

The things that make for peace. They are Jesus himself, the King of peace riding on Zechariah’s donkey, and the peace with God he came to bring. On this day: the day of God’s visitation, the day the disciples are singing about. Now, at last, the King has come, and the city does not know him.

But now they are hidden from your eyes. There is the tragedy stated exactly. Not they were never offered. Hidden: now, at this point, after everything. Because they had rejected the light, it was now withdrawn from them. This is judicial blindness, the judgment that gives people over to what they have chosen (8:10; John 12:37–40; Romans 11:7–10).

Who hid these things from their eyes? Luke’s phrase points to God, who hides in judgment what people have refused to see (10:21; Isaiah 6:9–10; Romans 11:7–10). Yet Jerusalem’s refusal was its own, and Jesus weeps over it. Divine hardening and human responsibility stand together, and so do God’s judgment and Christ’s tears. We are not asked to reconcile them in a formula. We are shown both in the face of one man on a donkey, and that is enough to keep us from two errors: thinking God is helpless before human refusal, and thinking he is cold toward it.

Does this mean God is finished with the Jewish people? No. Jesus is weeping over the city that rejected him and foretelling its judgment in that generation, not announcing that no Jew can be saved. Within weeks thousands of Jews in this same city were converted at Pentecost (Acts 2:41), and Paul insists that God has not rejected his people (Romans 11:1–2). Christians differ on Romans 11:25–26: some expect a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return, others read all Israel as the full number of the elect from Israel and the nations. Both agree that Jews, like Gentiles, are saved only by faith in Jesus the Messiah, and that Christians should long and pray for it, as Jesus wept for it.

Can a person today reach a point where it is too late? Scripture warns that it is possible to harden yourself until God gives you over (Romans 1:24; Hebrews 3:12–15), and that is why today matters. But anyone who is troubled by the fear that it is too late shows by that very concern that God is still at work in him. The hardened do not weep over their hardness. If you want Christ, come to him; he will never cast out anyone who comes (John 6:37).

In a sentence. When Jesus saw Jerusalem, he wept over it, lamenting that it had not recognised on that day the things that would bring it peace, and now they were hidden from it.

On a Tuesday. Who do you know who is turning away from Christ: a child, a friend, a former churchgoer? Do you weep for them, or only worry about them, or have you quietly stopped thinking about them? Pray for them by name this week, with tears if they come. And let Christ’s tears shape how you speak to them. You are not to bring judgment with a hard face, but the warning and the invitation of a Saviour who wept.

For worship. Behold the heart of God. He is not indifferent to the ruin of people who would not have him. The King who could have ridden in as a conqueror rode in weeping, and the one who wept over the city was the one who would bear the judgment of sinners within the week. If he wept for those who rejected him, how great is his love for those he has brought home.

parallels.desc: that I might weep day and night

verseByVerse.quote: For the days will come upon you, when your enemies will set up a barricade around you and surround you and hem you in on every side and tear you down to the ground, you and your children within you. And they will not leave one stone upon another in you, because you did not know the time of your visitation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the days will come upon you, when your enemies will set up a barricade around you and surround you and hem you in on every side and tear you down to the ground, you and your children within you. And they will not leave one stone upon another in you, because you did not know the time of your visitation.

For the days will come upon you, when your enemies will set up a barricade around you. This prophecy of the destruction of Jerusalem is worth reading slowly, because within one generation every clause of it happened. In AD 70 the Roman general Titus besieged Jerusalem. When the defenders held out and the siege dragged on, he built exactly what this verse describes: a wall right round the city, nearly five miles (8 km) of it, thrown up in three days, so that no one could get out and no supplies could get in. Josephus, who was there, describes it in detail.

And surround you and hem you in on every side. The siege lasted about five months. The famine inside was appalling; Josephus records people eating leather and worse, and the dead were thrown over the walls into the valleys because they could not be buried.

And tear you down to the ground, you and your children within you. Tear down is edaphiousin, to dash to the ground. The verb is used in the Greek Old Testament of infants killed in a captured city (Psalm 137:9; Hosea 10:14). The horror is not softened. Huge numbers were killed, and many thousands of survivors were sold into slavery.

They will not leave one stone upon another in you. As Jesus will say of the temple (21:6). The temple was burned and then dismantled. The great stones were levered off the walls and thrown into the street below, and some of them are still lying there today, piled at the foot of the temple mount where they fell, with the paving cracked under them. He said it four verses after saying the stones would cry out. The prophecy was fulfilled precisely.

Because you did not know the time of your visitation. Here is the cause, and it is the only one given. Visitation is episkopē, God coming to see about his people, the word Zechariah used at the beginning of this Gospel: blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people (1:68, 78; 7:16). The visitation happened. That is what makes the sentence unbearable. God came to Jerusalem, on a donkey, weeping, and the city did not recognise the day. The judgment was the consequence of rejecting the Messiah.

A visitation cuts both ways. In Scripture a visitation is an inspection as well as a rescue. The same coming that saves the people who know it for what it is condemns the people who do not. Not by a change in God, but because there is nothing else left when the visit has been made and refused. There is no other Saviour to send.

Was AD 70 the final judgment? No, but it was a preview of it. The fall of Jerusalem was a real judgment in history on the generation that rejected the Messiah, and Jesus tells it in the language of the prophets who foretold the fall of the first temple. It also stands as a picture of the last day, when Christ will return to judge the whole world (21:25–28; Acts 17:31). Both are real. The first came on one city in one generation; the second will come on all. Nor does this give any Christian licence to despise the Jewish people. Jesus wept as he said it, and so should we.

In a sentence. Jesus foretold that Jerusalem’s enemies would besiege it, destroy it and its people, and leave no stone on another, because it had not recognised the time of God’s coming.

On a Tuesday. Don’t miss the time of God’s visitation. He visits through his word preached on Sunday, through a conscience that will not settle, through an illness or a loss that stops you, through a friend who keeps inviting you. If he is calling you, respond today, not when life is calmer. And if you are a Christian, look at the stones in Jerusalem and take your Lord’s warnings seriously. Every word he says comes true.

For worship. The Lord of history keeps his word, in judgment as in mercy. Not one of his warnings has failed, and not one of his promises will. And the same Jesus who foretold the stones thrown down gave himself to be torn down in our place, so that all who know the day of his visitation will be built into a temple that can never fall, made of living stones (1 Peter 2:4–5).
verseByVerse.note: The Romans besieged Jerusalem in AD 70, building a siege wall round it, and destroyed the city and temple. A “visitation” is God coming in mercy or judgment.

parallels.desc: I will encircle you with towers

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 45–48 — The Cleansing of the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke's account is the briefest of the four — one clause for the action, no overturned tables, no whip of cords. He is not interested in the drama. He gives the words.

The selling was in the Court of the Gentiles, the great outer platform, and it was not in itself illegitimate: pilgrims from a distance needed sacrificial animals, and needed foreign coinage changed into the Tyrian shekel required for the temple tax. Somebody had to provide both. What had happened was that the provision had taken over the place — and the place it had taken over was the one part of the temple where a non-Jew could come and pray.

The two quotations are not equally weighted. The first is Isaiah 56:7, and the full verse matters: “my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.” That is the promise the Court of the Gentiles existed to fulfil, and the cattle market was standing on it.

The second is Jeremiah 7:11, and it is a bomb. Jeremiah's temple sermon was preached at the gate of the first temple to people who believed the building guaranteed their safety — “the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD” — while cheating and oppressing outside it. It ended by announcing that God would do to that house what he did to Shiloh, which was to destroy it. So Jesus, two verses after prophesying that not one stone will be left on another, quotes the sermon that announced the destruction of the previous temple.

And note the exact charge. Not “you have made it a market.” A den of robbers is not where robbery happens; it is where robbers retreat to feel safe afterwards.

Then he stays. Having cleared the court he takes up residence in it, teaching daily — which is the behaviour of an owner, not a protester.
verseByVerse.theology:
The cleansing is a prophetic act, not a reform. Jesus is not trying to improve the temple's efficiency; he is enacting in symbol what he has just prophesied in words. The combination of texts is deliberate: Isaiah 56:7 describes the eschatological temple as a house of prayer for all nations, and Jeremiah 7:11 the corrupt pre-exilic temple. You were called to be one; you have become the other.

“A den of robbers” names a use religion has never stopped being put to — a system that people use to feel secure while their lives are indefensible. That is what Jeremiah's hearers were doing with the first temple, and it is the charge here.

The closing two verses describe the strangest week in history in a single sentence. The most powerful men in Jerusalem want a man dead and cannot touch him — not because he is hiding but because he is standing in the most public place in the city, in daylight, every day, surrounded by crowds who will not leave. Luke's phrase is worth having: the people were “hanging on his words,” suspended from him.

What finally breaks the deadlock is not a change in the crowd but a man on the inside who offers to hand him over quietly, away from the people (22:6). Which settles something about how this ends. The authorities did not overpower him, and Luke says so plainly.
verseByVerse.examples:
A church becomes known primarily for its events, its café, its networking and its programmes — all good things in themselves, which have gradually crowded out sustained corporate prayer. The cleansing is not a template for expelling coffee shops from church lobbies; it is a question every community of faith must ask about its primary purpose and what has displaced it.

And the specific displacement here is worth naming, because it was not frivolous. Everything in that court served the sacrificial system. The animals were for worship; the money-changing existed so that the temple tax could be paid in the right coin. This was religion crowding out prayer, not entertainment crowding out religion — which is much harder to see from the inside and a great deal more common.

It also matters where it happened. Of all the spaces on that platform, the trade had colonised the only one open to Gentiles — so the practical effect of a thoroughly religious arrangement was that the people furthest from God found the door blocked by the machinery of worship.

That is a question worth putting to any congregation. Not whether the activity is legitimate, but whether a stranger walking in could find room to pray.

verseByVerse.quote: And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold, saying to them, 'It is written, ‘My house shall be a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold, saying to them: it is written, my house shall be a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of robbers.

And he entered the temple. The King comes to his temple. The prophet had said it: the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple; but who can endure the day of his coming? (Malachi 3:1–2). He comes as its owner, not its visitor.

And began to drive out those who sold. Luke’s account is the briefest of the four, one clause for the action, with no overturned tables and no whip of cords (Mark 11:15–17; John 2:15). He is not interested in the drama. He gives the words. The selling was in the Court of the Gentiles, the great outer platform, and it was not in itself illegitimate. Pilgrims arriving from a distance needed sacrificial animals, and needed to change foreign coins into the shekels required for the temple tax. Somebody had to provide both, and the trade was under the control of the high priests. What had happened was that the provision had taken over the place, and the place it had taken over was the one part of the temple where a non-Jew could come and pray.

It is written, My house shall be a house of prayer. Two quotations, and the second is much sharper than the first. The first is Isaiah 56:7, and the verse in full says my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples. That is the promise the Court of the Gentiles existed to fulfil, and the cattle market was standing on it. And notice my house: the temple belongs to God, and Jesus claims it as his own.

But you have made it a den of robbers. The second quotation is Jeremiah 7:11, and it is a bomb. Jeremiah’s temple sermon was preached at the gate of the first temple to people who believed the building guaranteed their safety, chanting, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, while cheating and oppressing outside it. And it ended with the announcement that God would do to that house what he did to Shiloh, which was to destroy it. So Jesus, two verses after prophesying that not one stone will be left on another, quotes the sermon that announced the destruction of the previous temple.

The exact charge. Not you have made it a market. A den of robbers is not where robbery happens. It is where robbers retreat to feel safe afterwards. The accusation is that the temple has become a hiding place: a religious system that people use to feel secure while their lives are indefensible. The leaders used the temple as a safe haven while robbing the people, and judgment would follow, as in Jeremiah’s day. It is a use religion has never stopped being put to.

Was this the clearing John describes? Probably not. John places a clearing of the temple near the beginning of Jesus’ ministry (John 2:13–17), while Luke places this one in the final week. Two separate events is the likelier explanation: the Passovers differ, the words differ, and a trade driven out once would soon have crept back. Nor does this passage forbid every sale in a church building. The offence was that commerce had crowded out prayer in the one court open to the nations. And it was the Messiah acting with authority over his Father’s house, not a pattern for Christians to use force.

What does this mean for the church? The temple has given way to Christ and his people: the church is now God’s house, built of living stones (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:19–22). So the same two tests apply. Is it a house of prayer for all peoples, where the outsider and the stranger are welcomed to seek God? And is it a den, a place where people come to feel safe while refusing to repent? A church can fail either test without selling anything: by being closed to outsiders, or by offering comfort without holiness.

Did Jesus cleanse the temple once or twice? Most likely twice. John places a cleansing at the first Passover of the ministry (John 2:13–17), with different words spoken and a different setting, and the traders would soon have returned. Luke tells his briefly, as the King’s first act on arriving in Jerusalem, so that the Lord’s claim on his Father’s house stands at the head of the last week. Nor does the passage forbid every sale in a church building: the offence was that trade had crowded out prayer in the court open to the nations, and the act was the Messiah’s own authority over the house, not a pattern for Christians to use force.

In a sentence. Jesus entered the temple and drove out the traders, quoting Scripture: God’s house is a house of prayer, but they had made it a den of robbers.

On a Tuesday. Ask whether your church’s life crowds out prayer: busy programmes and polished services, and little time on our knees together. Go to the prayer meeting, even if it is small. And ask the sharper question of yourself: do you use church attendance as a den, a place where you feel safe about a life you are not willing to change? If so, the Lord who cleared the temple is not your enemy. He came to clear you of what does not belong, so that you can truly pray.

For worship. About twenty years earlier a boy in this temple had said he must be in his Father’s house (2:49). Now the Son returns to that house as its Lord, clears its outer court for the nations, and within days gives his body to be broken for the very sins that had made it a den. In him every nation may now come to God and pray. Blessed be the Son who made a house of prayer for all peoples by his blood.

verseByVerse.quote: And he was teaching daily in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes and the principal men of the people were seeking to destroy him, but they did not find anything they could do, for all the people were hanging on his words.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he was teaching daily in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes and the principal men of the people were seeking to destroy him, but they did not find anything they could do, for all the people were hanging on his words.

And he was teaching daily in the temple. Having driven out the sellers, he stays. This is not a raid. He cleared the court and then took up residence in it, teaching every day for the rest of the week (21:37–38). That is the behaviour of an owner, not a protester. He has just called it my house. The cleansed temple becomes a place of teaching, and the Word of God himself is its teacher.
