The chief priests and the scribes and the principal men of the people. Three groups, and between them they are the entire leadership of the nation: the temple establishment, the experts in the law, and the leading laymen, the elders. Together they made up the Sanhedrin, and Luke names them together.

Were seeking to destroy him. The plot that began in Galilee (6:11; 11:53–54) now becomes determined, and they kept on seeking. Note that the object is not to answer him or to discredit him. It is to destroy him. The decision has been taken; only the method is outstanding.

But they did not find anything they could do. They could not arrest him publicly. Here is the strangest week in history, described in one sentence. The most powerful men in Jerusalem want a man dead and cannot touch him: not because he is hiding, but because he is standing in the most public place in the city, in daylight, every day, surrounded by crowds who will not leave.

For all the people were hanging on his words. Hanging on is exekremato: literally hanging from him, suspended on his words, the picture of a crowd leaning in, spellbound. The people protected him, for now. Within days a crowd would be shouting, crucify him. For several days the two things run alongside each other. He teaches; they plot; nothing can be done. What finally breaks the deadlock is not a change in the crowd but a man on the inside who offers to hand him over quietly, away from the people (22:3–6).

He let them have him. That settles something about how this ends, as the chapter closes. The authorities did not overpower him. They could not, and Luke says so plainly. He walked into that city on a colt he had sent for, cleared the temple, and taught in it daily under the eyes of men who wanted him dead and could do nothing about it, until the hour came that he had been walking toward since chapter nine, and he let them have him. His death was not a defeat. It was an offering.

Why did the same crowd turn against him? Crowds are fickle, and Luke shows it. Many hung on his words for the excitement of a prophet who confounded the leaders, without bowing to him as King. When he did not overthrow Rome, and the leaders worked on them, they turned (23:13–23). It is a warning that enthusiasm for Jesus is not the same as faith in him. Hanging on someone’s words for a week is not the same as building your life on them (6:46–49). The test is what you do when following him becomes costly.

In a sentence. Jesus taught in the temple every day, and the leaders wanted to destroy him but could find no way, because all the people hung on his every word.

On a Tuesday. Hang on Jesus’ words today. Read them as if your life depended on them, because it does. Choose one of his sayings from this chapter, the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost, or the parable of the minas, and carry it through the day. And do more than admire it. Ask what obedience to it looks like before tonight, because the people who only hung on his words in the temple were shouting for his death by Friday.

For worship. His enemies wanted that voice silenced, and they thought a cross would do it. It did not. The Teacher who held the temple court spellbound for a week rose from the dead and has gone on teaching, every day, in every nation, through the word his apostles wrote down. People still hang on his words, and those words have outlived the temple, the council and the empire. Blessed be the living Word, who has never been silenced and never will be.

19.text: <sup>1</sup> He entered Jericho and was passing through. <sup>2</sup> And behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus. He was a chief tax collector and was rich. <sup>3</sup> And he was seeking to see who Jesus was, but on account of the crowd he could not, because he was small in stature. <sup>4</sup> So he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was about to pass that way. <sup>5</sup> And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for I must stay at your house today.” <sup>6</sup> So he hurried and came down and received him joyfully. <sup>7</sup> And when they saw it, they all grumbled, “He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner.” <sup>8</sup> And Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor. And if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.” <sup>9</sup> And Jesus said to him, “Today salvation has come to this house, since he also is a son of Abraham. <sup>10</sup> For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” <sup>11</sup> As they heard these things, he proceeded to tell a parable, because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately. <sup>12</sup> He said therefore, “A nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and then return. <sup>13</sup> Calling ten of his servants, he gave them ten minas, and said to them, ‘Engage in business until I come.’ <sup>14</sup> But his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’ <sup>15</sup> When he returned, having received the kingdom, he ordered these servants to whom he had given the money to be called to him, that he might know what they had gained by doing business. <sup>16</sup> The first came before him, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made ten minas more.’ <sup>17</sup> And he said to him, ‘Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.’ <sup>18</sup> And the second came, saying, ‘Lord, your mina has made five minas.’ <sup>19</sup> And he said to him, ‘And you are to be over five cities.’ <sup>20</sup> Then another came, saying, ‘Lord, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a handkerchief; <sup>21</sup> for I was afraid of you, because you are a severe man. You take what you did not deposit, and reap what you did not sow.’ <sup>22</sup> He said to him, ‘I will condemn you with your own words, you wicked servant! You knew that I was a severe man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow? <sup>23</sup> Why then did you not put my money in the bank, and at my coming I might have collected it with interest?’ <sup>24</sup> And he said to those who stood by, ‘Take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has the ten minas.’ <sup>25</sup> And they said to him, ‘Lord, he has ten minas!’ <sup>26</sup> ‘I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. <sup>27</sup> But as for these enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them before me.’” <sup>28</sup> And when he had said these things, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. <sup>29</sup> When he drew near to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount that is called Olivet, he sent two of the disciples, <sup>30</sup> saying, “Go into the village in front of you, where on entering you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever yet sat. Untie it and bring it here. <sup>31</sup> If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ you shall say this: ‘The Lord has need of it.’” <sup>32</sup> So those who were sent went away and found it just as he had told them. <sup>33</sup> And as they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, “Why are you untying the colt?” <sup>34</sup> And they said, “The Lord has need of it.” <sup>35</sup> And they brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it. <sup>36</sup> And as he rode along, they spread their cloaks on the road. <sup>37</sup> As he was drawing near—already on the way down the Mount of Olives—the whole multitude of his disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen, <sup>38</sup> saying, “Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!” <sup>39</sup> And some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, rebuke your disciples.” <sup>40</sup> He answered, “I tell you, if these were silent, the very stones would cry out.” <sup>41</sup> And when he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it, <sup>42</sup> saying, “Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes. <sup>43</sup> For the days will come upon you, when your enemies will set up a barricade around you and surround you and hem you in on every side <sup>44</sup> and tear you down to the ground, you and your children within you. And they will not leave one stone upon another in you, because you did not know the time of your visitation.” <sup>45</sup> And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold, <sup>46</sup> saying to them, “It is written, ‘My house shall be a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a den of robbers.” <sup>47</sup> And he was teaching daily in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes and the principal men of the people were seeking to destroy him, <sup>48</sup> but they did not find anything they could do, for all the people were hanging on his words.

20.title: Authority, Parables, and Traps in the Temple
20.overview:
Luke 20 records a sustained series of confrontations between Jesus and the religious authorities in the temple precincts during what we call Holy Week. Three major challenges are mounted: the question of authority (by what right does Jesus act?), the parable of the wicked tenants (Jesus's own counter-attack in story form), and a series of trick questions — the tribute to Caesar, the Sadducees' resurrection riddle, and the question about David's son. Each challenge is designed to trap Jesus; each is turned back on its questioners.

The chapter is a masterclass in Jesus's handling of religious and political hostility. He does not evade, capitulate, or compromise. He answers each question in a way that exposes the questioner's bad faith, defends the truth, and advances his own mission. The parable of the wicked tenants is the most sustained theological statement: it is a compressed history of Israel's relationship with God, a prophecy of Jesus's rejection and death, and an announcement of the judgment that will fall on those who reject the cornerstone.

The chapter closes with Jesus warning about the scribes — those who love the long robes and the best seats and the deferential greetings, who devour widows' houses and for a pretence make long prayers. The contrast with the genuine piety of the widow in 21:1–4 is deliberate and damning.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The chief priests, scribes and elders — between them, the Sanhedrin — approach Jesus while he is teaching in the temple and ask by what authority he does “these things.” The phrase is left unspecified and everyone knows what it means: he had ridden in as a king a few days earlier and then cleared the traders out of the temple court, and stayed.

The question is not unreasonable in itself. The temple was under their jurisdiction, and a man who takes public action in a place you are responsible for can properly be asked who authorised it. But the trap is well made and both jaws are shut: claim human authority and they can produce the records showing he has none; claim divine authority and they have a charge of blasphemy.

And notice the presumption underneath it. Nobody enquires whether the temple needed cleansing, or whether the trade had displaced the prayer it existed to serve. The question is entirely about credentials — which is the standard refuge of an institution that does not want to discuss the substance.

Jesus answers with a question, which was normal rabbinic practice and is not evasion. It is precision, because the two questions are the same question: John's ministry raised the identical issue, and they had never answered it. And the connection runs deeper — John had pointed at Jesus, so if John's baptism was from heaven, the man John pointed at needs no further credentials.

Which makes this more generous than a debating manoeuvre. He is giving a hostile delegation a genuine route to the truth that does not require them to capitulate in public.

They will not take it, and the reason is stated out loud by themselves. Luke lets us hear the huddle, and there is no question about truth in it anywhere — only about consequences. So they answer that they do not know, which is a lie, and Jesus declines to tell them what they have just refused to work out.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus's authority is not an administrative question but the central question of the Gospels. By what right does he cleanse the temple, teach, heal, forgive sins? The answer they are trying to avoid is divine right — the right of the Son sent by the Father.

Their counter-question strategy is itself an answer: those who cannot acknowledge John's prophetic authority cannot acknowledge the one John announced. Unwillingness to face the truth is not an epistemic failure but a moral one.

And the principle behind the refusal in v.8 runs right through Scripture. God does not supply further light to people who have refused what they already have — “to the one who has, more will be given” (8:18), and the reverse holds. A man who will not act on what he knows is not helped by being told more.

There is also a price the council paid that is easy to miss. These are the official teachers of Israel, and they have just declared publicly, in the temple, that they cannot tell whether a major prophetic movement was from God. Whatever they saved by that answer, they paid for it with the only thing their office was for. A man who will not risk being wrong ends up unable to say anything at all.
verseByVerse.examples:
The deliberation in vv.5-6 is worth reading twice for what is absent from it. Not one clause considers what John's baptism actually was. The entire discussion is about what happens to us if we say this or that.

The manoeuvre survives in every institution including the church, and it never feels like dishonesty from the inside. It feels like responsibility. There is always a reason why the honest answer would be unhelpful just now, and a man can spend a whole career calculating the reception of his answers without noticing that he has stopped asking whether they are true.

The test is simple and uncomfortable. When a hard question arrives, is the first thing that moves in you an assessment of what is true, or an assessment of what it will cost?

And v.8 bears on a common modern situation. There are people who genuinely do not know and are asking, and Jesus deals with them all through this Gospel with enormous patience — the centurion, the woman in the crowd, the thief on the cross. And there are people whose questions are a way of not arriving anywhere. The tell is not the difficulty of the question but what happens to the answers: whether each one is weighed, or simply replaced by the next question. Jesus can be asked anything. What he will not do is join a conversation designed never to end.

verseByVerse.quote: One day, as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the gospel, the chief priests and the scribes with the elders came up and said to him, 'Tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
One day, as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the gospel, the chief priests and the scribes with the elders came up and said to him: tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority.

Meaning first. Luke 20 is a day of questions in the temple in the last week before the cross. Israel’s leaders come at Jesus one after another, each with a trap: the Sanhedrin asks by what authority he acts (vv. 1–8), spies ask about tribute to Caesar (vv. 20–26), and Sadducees bring a riddle meant to make the resurrection absurd (vv. 27–40). Each attack is turned back, and each answer reveals more of who he is. Between them he tells of tenants who kill the owner’s beloved son, his plainest public claim to be the Son whom they are about to kill (vv. 9–19). Then he asks the question nobody can answer: how can the Messiah be David’s son if David calls him Lord (vv. 41–44)? He ends by warning against leaders who love honour and devour widows (vv. 45–47). Here is the King in his Father’s house, wiser than all his enemies, walking with open eyes toward the death he has just described.

The setting. These are Jesus’ last days of public teaching. He has entered Jerusalem on a colt, wept over the city, cleared the temple and taken up residence in it, teaching every day while the leaders look for a way to destroy him and cannot, because the people hang on his words (19:45–48). Chapter 20 records a series of challenges from those leaders, each meant to trap him, and each turned back on them.

One day, as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the gospel. That is where he is when they come for him: standing in the temple court, in the middle of a sentence, teaching. Luke has told us he was doing this daily (19:47), and the phrase preaching the gospel is his own addition. The word is euangelizomenou, Luke’s favourite word for announcing good news. Whatever else was going on in Jerusalem that week, the man at the centre of it was preaching good news, in the temple, to the very people whose leaders would hand him over. Even in the last week, it is gospel.

The chief priests and the scribes with the elders came up. Three groups, and between them they are the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council: the temple establishment, the legal experts and the leading laymen. This is not an individual objection. It is an official delegation.

Tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority. Two questions, and the second is the real one. These things is left unspecified and everyone knows what it means. He had ridden into the city as a king a few days earlier, then walked into the temple, the building they administered, and thrown out the traders. And he had stayed, teaching. So the question is not unreasonable on its face. The temple was under the high priest’s authority, and somebody who takes public action in a place you are responsible for can properly be asked who authorised it.

The shape of the trap. Look at it, because it is well made and both jaws are shut. If he claims human authority, a rabbi’s ordination or a sponsor, they can show he has none. If he claims divine authority, they have a charge of blasphemy. And notice the presumption underneath. They are not asking whether what he did was right. Nobody asks whether the temple needed cleansing, or whether the trade in the Court of the Gentiles had crowded out the prayer it existed to serve. The question is entirely about credentials, which is the standard refuge of an institution that does not want to discuss the substance.

Who gave Jesus his authority? The Father did, and the whole Gospel has been answering this question. The voice at his baptism called him the beloved Son (3:22). He forgave sins, and proved his authority to do it by healing a paralysed man (5:24). He commanded demons, winds and death, and they obeyed. He has already said that all things have been handed over to him by his Father (10:22). After his resurrection he will say that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him (Matthew 28:18). So the question the leaders ask in hostility is the question every reader must ask in earnest, and the answer changes everything. If his authority is from God, then his words are not advice to be weighed but commands to be obeyed, and his promises are as sure as God.

In a sentence. As Jesus taught and preached the gospel in the temple, the leaders of the Sanhedrin demanded to know by what authority he acted.

On a Tuesday. Every life has to settle what the Sanhedrin asked. Does he have the right to command you: your money, your sexuality, your time, your speech, your plans for next year? Most of us accept his authority in general and quietly question it in particular. Find the one area where you most often ask, in effect, who gave you this authority? and settle it with him today. And notice the leaders’ method in yourself: arguing about credentials when the real issue is that you do not want to change.

For worship. All authority belongs to him. The One who stood in the temple court being questioned by the Sanhedrin is the One before whom the Sanhedrin, and every council and court on earth, will one day stand. They asked who had given him the right to act in that house, and the answer was that it was his Father’s house, and he was the Son. He had every right to clear it and every right to judge them, and that week he used his authority to bring them good news.
verseByVerse.note: The chief priests, scribes and elders together made up the Sanhedrin, the ruling council.

verseByVerse.quote: He answered them, 'I also will ask you a question. Now tell me, was the baptism of John from heaven or from man?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He answered them: I also will ask you a question. Now tell me, was the baptism of John from heaven or from man?

I also will ask you a question. He answers a question with a question. That was an entirely normal move in rabbinic debate and it is not evasion. It is precision, because the answer to his question answers theirs.

Now tell me, was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? From heaven means from God. And the two questions are the same question. John’s whole ministry had raised the identical issue: a man with no priestly appointment and no institutional backing, baptising in the Jordan, calling the nation to repent. By what authority? They had faced it once already and had never given an answer. The alternatives are exhaustive. A prophetic ministry is either God’s or it is not, and every person in Israel had already made a private judgment about John.

The connection runs deeper. It is more than a debating parallel. John had said who Jesus was: he who is mightier than I is coming (3:16). And the answer to their question about authority had been given publicly at the Jordan by the voice from heaven (3:21–22). If John’s baptism was from heaven, then the man John pointed to needs no further credentials. The two stand or fall together.

A generous question. So this is not a clever deflection. It is Jesus offering them the answer, in the one form they could have accepted without losing face: by working it out themselves. He is giving a hostile delegation a genuine route to the truth that does not require them to surrender in public. And notice what the question exposes. He does not ask them about himself. He asks about a matter they had had years to settle, on which the evidence had been public. Their difficulty was never a shortage of information about Jesus of Nazareth. It was what they had already done with the last man God sent.

Is it right for a Christian to answer a question with a question? Sometimes, yes, when it is done as Jesus did it: not to dodge, but to bring the real issue into the light. Many hostile questions rest on a hidden assumption, and a good question can show it gently. If someone asks how you can believe in a God who allows suffering, you might ask what makes them so sure suffering is wrong. But Jesus also answered sincere questions directly and patiently. The skill is to tell the difference, and the aim is always to help the person to the truth, not to win.

In a sentence. Jesus answered with a question: was John’s baptism from God or from men?

On a Tuesday. Have you responded to the light God has already given you? Before asking him for more answers, ask whether you have obeyed what you know: the command you understood last month, the sin you were convicted of, the call to forgive that you put off. God’s further light usually comes to those who walk in the light they have.

For worship. Christ is the wisdom of God. He answers hostility with a question that opens a door, and he is patient enough to give his enemies a way back to the truth. Even in the trap they set for him, he was seeking them.

verseByVerse.quote: And they discussed it with one another, saying, 'If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why did you not believe him?’ But if we say, ‘From man,’ all the people will stone us to death, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
They discussed it with one another, saying: if we say, from heaven, he will say, why did you not believe him? But if we say, from man, all the people will stone us to death, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.

And they discussed it with one another. Luke lets us hear the huddle, and it is the most revealing paragraph in the chapter. Whether he had it from someone standing close enough, or from a member of the council who later believed, we are given the conversation. And its question is not what is true? but what is safe?

If we say, From heaven, he will say, Why did you not believe him? They see the trap instantly, and note what it consists of. Not a logical difficulty, but a personal exposure. They had rejected John (7:30). If John was from God, their failure to receive him is a public fact requiring explanation.

But if we say, From man, all the people will stone us to death. Only Luke records this fear. Stoning was the penalty for blasphemy and false prophecy, and the crowd might regard denying a true prophet as something close to it. John had been dead for some time, killed by Herod, and the popular verdict on him had hardened into reverence for a martyr. To deny him publicly, in a temple court full of Passover pilgrims, would have been physically dangerous. For they are convinced that John was a prophet: the people were convinced, and the leaders were calculating.

Truth is missing. Now read the whole deliberation again and notice what is absent from it. There is no question about the truth. Not one clause in either half considers what John’s baptism actually was. The whole discussion is about consequences: what happens to us if we say this, and what happens to us if we say that. These are the religious leaders of the people of God, standing in the temple, weighing a question about a prophet, and truth is not a factor in the deliberation.

The listener in the huddle. They spoke among themselves, but not out of his hearing in any sense that mattered. Luke has shown again and again that Jesus knew the reasonings of scribes and Pharisees before they said a word (5:22; 6:8; 9:47). The men calculating what was safe were doing it in the presence of the Mightier One whom John had announced (3:16), the Son on whom the Spirit came down at John’s baptism. Their question was never really about a dead prophet. It was about him, and the one thing they would not weigh was that the truth they were avoiding stood a few feet away and could read them.

How do I know if I am deciding by what is safe rather than what is true? Watch what moves first in you when a hard question arrives. If your first thought is what will people think? or what will this cost me?, you are in the huddle. Other signs: you find yourself changing your answer depending on who is asking; you avoid reading the parts of Scripture that would settle a matter you would rather leave open; you say I am still thinking about it for years. The remedy is to ask God, before anyone else, what is true, and then to trust him with the cost (Proverbs 29:25).

In a sentence. They reasoned that whichever way they answered, they would be trapped: either convicted of unbelief or stoned by the people.

On a Tuesday. Don’t decide what to believe by asking what is safe. Ask what is true. This week, when a question comes up at work, at home or in church where the honest answer will cost you something, say the true thing kindly and leave the result with God. The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe.

For worship. Christ never once calculated. He said what was true in the temple, before the council, before Pilate, knowing it would cost him his life. He is the truth, and he went to the cross rather than shade it. Because he did not seek his own safety, we are safe in him.

verseByVerse.quote: So they answered that they did not know where it came from. And Jesus said to them, 'Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they answered that they did not know where it came from. And Jesus said to them: neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.

So they answered that they did not know where it came from. It is a lie, and everybody present knows it. They knew exactly what they thought about John; they had been thinking it for years, and had just said it to each other. What they have done is take refuge in an agnosticism they do not hold, which is the safest position available, because it commits to nothing and cannot be attacked.

The price of the answer. These are the official teachers of Israel, whose duty was to judge true and false prophets. They have just declared publicly, in the temple, that they cannot tell whether the greatest prophetic movement of their age was from God. Whatever they saved by that answer, they paid for with the only thing their office was for. They disqualified themselves. A man who will not risk being wrong ends up unable to say anything at all.

And Jesus said to them, Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things. The refusal is not petulance, and it is not a debating victory being enjoyed. He had made them a real offer in v. 4: answer the question about John honestly and you will have the answer to your own. They declined, and not for want of information.

The principle underneath. It runs right through Scripture. God does not supply further light to people who have refused what they already have. Light that is used is increased, and light that is refused is withdrawn (8:18). Telling more to a man who will not act on what he knows does not help him.

And yet he does answer. He will not tell them in a proposition they can take to court. But he tells everyone in a story, in the very next breath: the parable of the tenants, in which the owner sends his beloved son (v. 13). The answer to their question is given after all, and given in a form that only an honest heart can receive.

What about people who genuinely do not know? Jesus deals with them all through this Gospel with enormous patience: the centurion, the woman in the crowd, the thief on the cross, the disciples themselves, who ask badly and are answered anyway. There are people who genuinely do not know and are asking, and there are people whose questions are a way of never arriving anywhere. The tell is not the difficulty of the question but what happens to the answers: whether each one is weighed, or whether it is simply replaced by the next question. Jesus can be asked anything. What he will not do is join a conversation designed never to end. If you are honestly unsure, tell him so, and keep reading what he said. He has never turned away an honest seeker.

In a sentence. They said they did not know, so Jesus refused to tell them the source of his authority.

On a Tuesday. I don’t know can be honest humility, or it can be evasion. Be honest about what you do know to be true about Jesus, and act on it. And if you are talking with a friend whose questions never land, it is right to ask gently: if I answered this, would it change anything for you? That is not unkind. It is the question Jesus asked.

For worship. The Lord is not mocked, and he is not played with. He gives light to those who walk in it, and he will not be drawn into games. Yet even here, refusing to answer the trap, he turns at once to tell a story that reveals his heart: a Father who sends his beloved Son. His silence toward the scheming is never silence toward the seeking.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–19 — The Parable of the Wicked Tenants
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
He turns from the delegation to the people and tells a story about the delegation, in their hearing — and they understand every word of it (v.19).

The opening line is a quotation. Isaiah's song of the vineyard ends with its own interpretation stated flatly: “for the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5:1-7). So the identifications come attached, from a passage everyone knew.

And the arrangement is entirely ordinary — absentee landlords letting estates to tenant farmers for a share of the crop were common in Galilee. But hold on to what it means: the tenants did not plant the vineyard, clear the ground, or build the winepress. Everything they work with was made by somebody else and handed to them on terms.

The escalation is exact: beaten; beaten and treated shamefully, which in that culture was the worse injury; then wounded and thrown out. And running alongside it is the stranger thing — a landlord who keeps sending. Any man with sense would have gone to law after the first assault. He sends a second, and a third, because he keeps wanting the relationship rather than the redress.

The servants are the prophets, and the compression is the point: “the LORD, the God of their fathers, sent persistently to them by his messengers… but they kept mocking the messengers of God” (2 Chr. 36:15-16). The men hearing this were standing in a building where some of it had happened.

Then the son — “my beloved son,” the phrase from heaven at the Jordan (3:22). And the tenants' reasoning, said aloud among themselves, is the oldest reasoning there is: remove the owner's representative and the property is ours.

Luke has the order deliberately: thrown out of the vineyard, and then killed. Jesus was crucified outside the wall (Heb. 13:12), and he is telling this three days before it happens, with the geography included.
verseByVerse.theology:
The parable is one of the most explicit statements in Luke of Jesus's divine sonship. The son is not one more servant in a long series but the heir — the beloved son, whose rejection is categorically different from the rejection of the prophets.

“Perhaps they will respect him” puzzles thoughtful readers and has been pressed into service to prove something it does not prove. Does it mean God did not know? Some have read it so. But the same Scripture says the Son was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23), and Jesus has already told his disciples three times how this would end.

The perhaps is spoken from the owner's side of the story — the language of a genuine appeal, not a report of divine ignorance. Its point is not what God did not know but what the tenants cannot claim: that the offer was real, that every possible envoy was sent, that the last was the owner's own beloved son. God knew exactly what they would do and sent the Son anyway — which is not a father caught out, but a love that kept knocking at a door it knew would not open, so that nobody could ever say the door was never knocked upon.

The verdict — the vineyard given to others — must not be misused. It is not a statement that God has finished with the Jewish people; Paul asks exactly that question after the resurrection and answers it flatly, “has God rejected his people? By no means!” (Rom. 11:1). The tenants are the leadership, and Luke names the men Jesus was looking at in verse 19.
verseByVerse.examples:
Psalm 118:22 is quoted from the same psalm the disciples had been shouting a few days earlier on the road down the Mount of Olives — verse 26 of it (19:38). He quotes their processional hymn back to the authorities, four verses earlier.

And the image is precise. The cornerstone sets the angle and the line for two walls at once, so everything built after it is squared by it; and a builder examining stones on site rejects the ones that will not do. So the picture is of professionals doing their job — men whose whole competence is judging stone, whose professional judgement was that this one would not do. Then the turn: it has become the cornerstone. Their verdict was simply overruled.

Verse 18 turns the image twice, drawing on Isaiah's stone of stumbling (Isa. 8:14-15) and Daniel's stone that grinds a statue to powder (Dan. 2:34-35). To fall on the stone is to trip over it and be broken — bad, and survivable, since broken things can be mended. When the stone falls on a man, it crushes him to dust. The stone cannot be avoided: it can be built on, tripped over, or fallen under, and nobody in this passage walks past it.

And the parable is fulfilled in the hearing of the parable. They grasped it immediately — which answers a question people often put to Scripture, why God does not simply tell people plainly what they are doing. He did, and it produced a decision to do it sooner.

verseByVerse.quote: And he began to tell the people this parable: 'A man planted a vineyard and let it out to tenants and went into another country for a long while. When the time came, he sent a servant to the tenants, so that they would give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He began to tell the people this parable: a man planted a vineyard and let it out to tenants and went into another country for a long while. When the time came, he sent a servant to the tenants, so that they would give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed.

And he began to tell the people this parable. Note who he turns to. Not the delegation, but the people. The council has just refused to answer him, so he tells the crowd a story about them, in their hearing, and the leaders will understand every word of it (v. 19).

A man planted a vineyard. The opening is a quotation, and every literate Jew in that court would have heard it. Isaiah’s song of the vineyard begins with a beloved friend who had a vineyard on a very fertile hill, who dug it and cleared it of stones and planted it with choice vines, and it ends with the interpretation stated flatly: the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel (Isaiah 5:1–7). So the identifications are not something a commentator has to supply. The parable comes with them attached, from a passage everyone knew. God planted his people and did everything to make them fruitful.

And let it out to tenants. The tenants are Israel’s leaders. The arrangement is ordinary: absentee landlords letting estates to tenant farmers for a share of the crop were common in Galilee. But the parable turns on what it means. The tenants did not plant the vineyard. They did not clear the ground or build the winepress. Everything they work with was made by somebody else and handed to them on terms.

And went into another country for a long while. Only Luke adds for a long while: the long centuries of God’s patience with his people.

When the time came, he sent a servant to the tenants, so that they would give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. Some of the fruit. Not the whole harvest; the owner’s share, which was the agreement. The servant is a prophet, one of God’s servants sent to call Israel back to fruitfulness and faithfulness.

But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed. That is not a rent dispute. Nobody argues about the percentage or pleads a bad season. They assault the man and send him back with nothing, and that is a declaration: we are not paying, and we are not discussing it. It is Israel’s long history of rejecting the prophets (2 Chronicles 36:15–16; Nehemiah 9:26).

What is the fruit God looks for? The fruit Isaiah’s vineyard should have borne was justice and righteousness (Isaiah 5:7): faith toward God, and lives of love, truth and mercy toward others. It is the fruit John the Baptist demanded (3:8), and the fruit of the Spirit Paul describes (Galatians 5:22–23). It is not a percentage of income or a level of church activity, though both may be part of it. God wants himself acknowledged as owner, and wants the life he has given returned to him in love and obedience. And he is looking for it in every life to which he has given anything.

The storyteller in the story. As the parable opens, nobody in the court yet knows where it is going, but the man telling it does. He is the beloved son who will be sent last, and he is standing in the vineyard as he speaks, in the temple, days before the tenants throw him out. Every servant in the story was sent to collect fruit and was refused. Jesus is about to describe his own coming as the owner’s final appeal and his own death as the tenants’ final answer, and he tells it with the men who will carry it out listening. No prophet ever told his own story like that. Only the Son could.

In a sentence. Jesus told of a man who planted a vineyard and let it out to tenants; when he sent a servant to collect the owner’s share, they beat him and sent him back with nothing.

On a Tuesday. God looks for fruit from what he has given you. What is he receiving? Look at your week as a tenant would look at his ledger: the time, the money, the abilities, the relationships, the Christian upbringing or the years of good teaching. Which of them are returning anything to the owner? Pick one and offer its fruit to him deliberately this week: an hour of your time, a gift, a kindness done in his name. And when his messenger comes to you, in a sermon, a Scripture or a friend’s rebuke, receive him, do not send him away empty.

For worship. The vineyard is his, every vine of it. He planted it, cleared the stones, built the tower and gave it into others’ hands, and he has never stopped caring about the harvest. The Lord is not an absent landlord. He is the beloved who sang over his vineyard, and his patience with it is longer than all its history.
verseByVerse.note: The vineyard is Isaiah’s picture of Israel. Absentee landlords commonly leased land to tenant farmers.

verseByVerse.quote: And he sent another servant. But they also beat and treated him shamefully, and sent him away empty-handed. And he sent yet a third. This one also they wounded and cast out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He sent another servant. But they also beat and treated him shamefully, and sent him away empty-handed. And he sent yet a third. This one also they wounded and cast out.

And he sent another servant. But they also beat and treated him shamefully, and sent him away empty-handed. Two things run in parallel through these verses, and both are extraordinary. The first is the escalation. Beaten. Then beaten and treated shamefully: Luke’s word means dishonoured, publicly humiliated, and in that culture the shame was the worse injury. Each envoy is treated worse than the last, and the tenants grow bolder because nothing has happened to them.

And he sent yet a third. This one also they wounded and cast out. Physical damage this time, and expulsion. In Luke’s telling no servant is killed until the son, which makes the son’s death the climax.

The sending. The second extraordinary thing is the sending. A landlord with any sense would have gone to law after the first assault. Instead, into a situation visibly growing more dangerous, he sends a second servant to men who have just beaten the first, and then a third. This is the patience of God set out as a plot, and in an ordinary landlord it would be unaccountable. He keeps sending because he keeps wanting the relationship rather than the redress.

The history in three sentences. The servants are the prophets, and the compression is the point: the whole tragic history of Israel and the men God sent to it, put into three sentences. The Chronicler’s summary of the centuries before the exile could stand as its caption: the LORD kept sending his messengers out of compassion for his people, and they kept mocking them and scoffing at his prophets (2 Chronicles 36:15–16). Jeremiah lowered into a cistern. Zechariah son of Jehoiada stoned in the court of this very temple (2 Chronicles 24:20–22). The men listening were standing in a building where some of it had happened, hearing their own history read back to them in the third person.

The ownership is the problem. There is something in the tenants’ behaviour that explains a great deal about religious opposition generally. They do not argue with the owner. There is no letter disputing the terms, no counter-claim, no attempt to renegotiate. They simply will not have anyone come from him. The messenger is attacked before the message is heard, every time, because the message is not the problem. The ownership is.

How often would I. The patience in this parable has a face. Only a little earlier on the road Jesus had cried, O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! (13:34). How often would I: he speaks of the city’s whole history as one who had been reaching for it all along. Father and Son share one heart toward the rebellious vineyard, and the patience that kept sending prophets now stands in the temple court in person, telling the tenants their own story one last time.

Why is God so patient? Because patience belongs to his very name: merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love (Exodus 34:6). He is not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9). His long sending is not weakness, and it is not that he does not care. Every servant sent was another invitation, and it left the tenants more and more without excuse. If God has been patient with you, through years of half-hearted faith or outright rebellion, it is not because he does not care. It is because he has been sending, again and again, to bring you home.

In a sentence. The owner sent a second and third servant, and the tenants beat, insulted, wounded and threw them out.

On a Tuesday. Think of the messengers God has sent to you: a parent who prayed, a friend who spoke up, a preacher who said the thing you needed to hear, a verse that would not leave you alone. How did you receive them? If you treated any of them shamefully, thank God that he sent another, and go and thank the person if you can.

For worship. Who is a God like him, who does not retain his anger for ever, because he delights in steadfast love (Micah 7:18)? Three servants came back bruised, shamed and wounded, and still the owner did not send soldiers. He sent again. Every century of Israel’s story, every prophet in a cistern or a dungeon, is the record of a mercy that would not take no for an answer, and that same mercy has sent, and sent again, to us.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the owner of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.’ But when the tenants saw him, they said to themselves, ‘This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the owner of the vineyard said: what shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him. But when the tenants saw him, they said to themselves: this is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours.

Then the owner of the vineyard said, What shall I do? Only Luke records this deliberation. The question is not helplessness; it is deliberation made audible. The owner has exhausted the ordinary options and is deciding. Here is the heart of God, pondering how to reach his rebellious people.

I will send my beloved son. Every word has been chosen. My beloved son is ton huion mou ton agapēton, the exact phrase spoken from heaven at the Jordan: you are my beloved Son (3:22), and from the cloud on the mountain, this is my Son, my Chosen One (9:35). There is no possibility that Luke’s readers, or the men in the courtyard, are meant to miss it. And so Jesus answers the question of his authority after all. He is not another servant. He is the beloved Son. And the logic is a father’s rather than a landlord’s. He has run out of servants; he will send the one person left, and the one person he cannot replace.

Perhaps they will respect him. The phrase puzzles thoughtful readers: was heaven hoping for an outcome it could not foresee? But the same Luke records that the Son was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23), and Jesus has already told his disciples three times, in detail, how this would end. He is not guessing.

Did God not know what would happen? He knew. The perhaps is spoken from the owner’s side of the story, the language of a genuine appeal, not a report of divine ignorance. Its point is not what God did not know but what the tenants cannot claim: that the offer was real, that every possible envoy was sent, that the last was the owner’s own beloved son, and that their rejection was therefore without excuse. God knew exactly what they would do and sent the Son anyway. That is not a father caught out. It is a love that kept knocking at a door it knew would not open, so that nobody could ever say the door was not knocked upon. It is the extraordinary hope of love.

Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours. When the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves, this is the heir. There is the reasoning, said aloud among themselves, and it is the oldest reasoning there is. They recognise him, and they kill him for that reason. Remove the owner’s representative and the property is ours. It is what the serpent offered in a garden: you will be like God. The leaders wanted to keep control of God’s people for themselves. And Jesus foretells his own death to their faces, three days before it happens.

Did the leaders know Jesus was the Son of God? Not in the full sense, or they would not have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8; Acts 3:17). But they knew enough. They saw his works, heard his claims and understood this parable (v. 19), and their opposition was not ignorance but refusal. In the parable they recognise the heir and kill him because he is the heir. That is the heart of all unbelief: not a lack of evidence, but an unwillingness to let God be God. People do not reject Christ because they cannot see who he is, but because they see enough to know he would claim them.

In a sentence. Finally the owner sent his beloved son, hoping they would respect him, but the tenants decided to kill the heir and seize the inheritance.

On a Tuesday. Where are you saying, in small ways, let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours? It is the impulse to take God’s gifts and push the Giver out: to enjoy your family, career, health or comfort while keeping him at the edge. Name one gift you treat as your own possession, and give thanks to the owner for it today. The inheritance is only ever safe in the Son’s hands.

For worship. The Father asked, What shall I do? and the answer was the costliest gift in heaven. He did not send a better servant or a sterner one. He sent the Son he loved into the hands of those who would kill him, so that the death they meant as a theft of the inheritance became the way the inheritance was given away. The heir they killed has made heirs of rebels, fellow heirs with him of everything the Father has (Romans 8:17).

verseByVerse.quote: And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.' When they heard this, they said, 'Surely not!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others. When they heard this, they said: surely not!

And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. Luke’s order is deliberate: cast out first, then killed. Mark puts the killing first; Luke and Matthew keep the sequence that matches what was about to happen, for Jesus was led out of the city and crucified beyond its wall. The letter to the Hebrews draws out the meaning: Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:12–13). He is telling this in the temple, days before it happens, with the geography included.

What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? He asks the crowd for the verdict. In Matthew’s telling the hearers supply the answer and condemn themselves out of their own mouths; here Jesus gives it, and the effect is the same.

He will come and destroy those tenants. Judgment on the leaders, and it landed within a generation. The destruction came in AD 70, in the terms he had wept over in the previous chapter (19:41–44).

And give the vineyard to others. The tenancy transferred: to new leaders, the apostles whom Christ appoints over his people, and through them to the Gentiles (Acts 13:46; 28:28). The vineyard is not destroyed. God’s people continue, under new tenants, and it is now a vineyard gathered from every nation, Jew and Gentile together in Christ (Ephesians 2:11–22). That would have been the most offensive part of the whole story: the covenant privileges passing to people who were not in the room.

When they heard this, they said, Surely not! Only Luke records this. Literally may it not be!, the phrase Paul uses again and again in Romans. The crowd’s reaction is horror. They have understood it. They can see where the story is pointing, and the thought of judgment on Israel and of the vineyard being given to others is unbearable. Within days a crowd in this city will call for the death of the son and get it.

Has God finished with the Jewish people? No, and this parable has been misused to say so. Paul, writing after the resurrection, asks exactly this question: has God rejected his people? By no means! (Romans 11:1). The tenants in the parable are the leaders, and the men Jesus is looking at are named in v. 19. Many Jews believed: the apostles, the first church of thousands in Jerusalem, Paul himself. Christians differ on what Romans 11 expects for the Jewish people in the future. Some look for a great turning of Israel to Christ before his return; others understand all Israel as the whole number of the elect from Jews and Gentiles. All agree that there is one vineyard and one way into it, through faith in Jesus the Messiah, and that Christians should long and pray for Jewish people to come to him.

In a sentence. The tenants killed the son, so the owner will destroy them and give the vineyard to others, and the people were horrified.

On a Tuesday. Privilege is no guarantee. What God gives, he can give to others if it bears no fruit. A Christian heritage, a gospel-preaching church, a home where the Bible is read: all of these are mercies, and all of them make us more accountable. Do not trust your church’s history or your family’s faith. Ask whether the vineyard in your own care is bearing fruit for its owner, and pray for the churches of your land that have the name but have lost the gospel.

For worship. The judgment Jesus pronounced was real, and it fell on the tenants within a generation. Yet the same story holds a mercy they could not see. The vineyard was not destroyed, only given to others, and the others are a people gathered from every nation, strangers who had no claim on it and were brought in by the death of the Son. God’s judgment and his mercy meet in the one who was thrown out, so that those who were outside could be welcomed in.

verseByVerse.quote: But he looked directly at them and said, 'What then is this that is written: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he looked directly at them and said: what then is this that is written: the stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone?

But he looked directly at them. Luke stops the narrative for a look. The verb means to fix the eyes on someone, the same word used of Jesus turning and looking at Peter in the courtyard after the rooster crowed (22:61). The parable was told to the people (v. 9). The look is for the men who came with the question. It is a penetrating look, and both times Luke uses it, it is a look that could have broken a heart open.

The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. Jesus introduces it with a question: if judgment on Israel cannot happen, as the crowd has just cried, what then is this that is written? He answers from Psalm 118:22, a word they all accepted, and the psalm is chosen with care. His disciples had sung from it on the descent of Olivet a few days before, hailing the King who comes in the name of the Lord (Psalm 118:26; 19:38). Now he takes the same hymn, four verses earlier, and hands it to the authorities.

The builders and the stone. The cornerstone sets the angle and the line for two walls at once, so that everything built after it is squared by it: the most important stone in the building. The picture is of professionals doing their job. Men whose whole competence is judging stone look at this one, assess it, and throw it on the discard pile as unfit. That is exactly what was happening in that courtyard. The chief priests and scribes were the builders, trained and appointed to recognise what God was doing. They examined the stone, and their professional judgment was that it would not do.

Has become the cornerstone. Then the turn. Not somebody else used it. It was taken up and set at the corner by an authority above the builders, and their verdict was simply overruled. This is the LORD’s doing; it is marvellous in our eyes, the psalm goes on (Psalm 118:23). It was fulfilled in the resurrection. The early church seized on this verse and could not let it go. Peter quotes it to the Sanhedrin itself (Acts 4:10–12) and again in his letter (1 Peter 2:4–8). It became the standard text for what the resurrection did to Friday’s verdict.

Why does it matter that the experts rejected him? Because it means the verdict of the experts is not the last word. In every generation scholars, institutions and cultured voices have looked at Jesus and set him aside, and some Christians are shaken by it. This verse expected it. The rejection of the stone by the builders is part of the prophecy, not a refutation of it. God has always overruled the builders. The question is not what the professionals think of Christ, but what God has done with him: he raised him and set him at the corner, and everything is now squared by him.

In a sentence. Looking straight at them, Jesus quoted Scripture: the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.

On a Tuesday. Is Christ the cornerstone of your life, the stone everything else is squared by? Test it. When you make a decision about money, work, marriage or where to live, is the first question what fits with Christ? or is he fitted in afterwards? Choose one decision you face this week and lay it against him first.

For worship. Men threw the stone away, and God set it at the head of the corner. Every age has its builders who examine Christ and set him aside, and in every age their verdict is overruled from heaven. The whole house of God, from every nation and century, is squared by the stone they rejected, and it will stand when every rival structure has fallen. Nothing in all the works of the LORD is more marvellous than the rejected Son raised to the corner.

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.

Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces. The image turns, and it turns twice. The stone has just been the foundation. Now it is something that can be tripped over, and something that can fall on you, and the two halves describe two quite different disasters. Both come from the prophets. Isaiah had said the LORD of hosts would be a sanctuary and a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling to both houses of Israel, and many shall stumble on it, they shall fall and be broken (Isaiah 8:14–15). To fall on the stone is to stumble over it: those who reject Jesus will be broken.

And when it falls on anyone, it will crush him. Daniel had seen a stone cut out by no human hand, striking the great statue of the world’s kingdoms and grinding it to dust, and becoming a great mountain that filled the whole earth: the kingdom of God (Daniel 2:34–35, 44–45). The verb Luke uses means to winnow, to reduce to dust and blow away. Christ will come in judgment and crush all who oppose him. Nothing is left to repair.

Broken or crushed. Note the difference. To fall on the stone is to trip over it while walking along. That is bad, and it is survivable: broken things can be mended, and Scripture is full of people whose first encounter with Christ knocked them off their feet. Saul of Tarsus fell on this stone on the Damascus road and was broken, and rose an apostle. The second is not survivable. When the stone falls, it is the last day, and there is nothing left to mend.

The point. No one can be neutral toward Jesus. This stone cannot be avoided. It can be built on, tripped over or fallen under, and there is no fourth option. The same stone is foundation, obstacle and instrument of judgment, and which it turns out to be is determined by what a person does when he meets it. Only Luke records this saying here, though some manuscripts of Matthew include it too.

If I have stumbled over Jesus, is it too late? No. The men listening had already stumbled, and what the sentence holds out, terribly and graciously, is that a stumble is not yet the end. Many who once mocked Christ, or walked away, have been broken by him and then healed by him. Peter preached to the very builders who rejected the stone, and thousands of them believed (Acts 2:36–41). But there is a day coming when the stone is no longer lying in the road. The time to fall on him in repentance is now, before he falls in judgment.

In a sentence. Everyone who stumbles over the stone will be broken, and anyone it falls on will be crushed.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is either your foundation or your judge. If you have been stumbling over something in him, his exclusive claims, his teaching on sin, his demand for your whole life, do not keep walking around the stone. Fall on him: bring your offence to him honestly, in prayer and in his word, and let him break your pride. He breaks in order to rebuild.

For worship. The stone cut without hands is filling the earth. The kingdoms of this world rise and fall, and his kingdom grows until it fills everything. Blessed is the one who builds on him, and blessed is the one who falls on him broken, because the stone that breaks the proud is the rock that holds the humble for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very hour, for they perceived that he had told this parable against them, but they feared the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very hour, for they perceived that he had told this parable against them, but they feared the people.

The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very hour. Not later, after deliberation. They wanted him seized on the spot. And there is the whole tragedy of the passage in one sentence. They have just heard a story in which tenants kill the owner’s son, and been told it is about them, and their response is to try to arrest the son. They are doing exactly what the parable described. The parable is being fulfilled in the hearing of the parable.

For they perceived that he had told this parable against them. They understood it. Luke says so plainly, and it settles something about the parables in general. They are not a code that only insiders can break. The men who came off worst in this one grasped it immediately. Their problem was not understanding. It was the will.

Why does God not simply tell people plainly what they are doing? He did. There is no gentler or clearer way to say you are about to kill me and you will be judged for it than the story he had just told, and it produced a decision to do it sooner. Clarity alone does not change a heart. Only the Spirit of God, opening blind eyes and giving a new heart, can do that (Ezekiel 36:26; 2 Corinthians 4:6). That is why we pray as well as speak when we share the gospel.

But they feared the people. Luke has now said this three times in two chapters: they could find nothing they could do, for all the people were hanging on his words (19:48); the fear of stoning in v. 6; and here. The most powerful men in Jerusalem cannot touch a man standing in the open in their own building, because of a crowd. And note what fear is running the council. Not the fear of God, which would have stopped them entirely, and not the fear of being wrong. The fear of the people: of a riot, of losing position. It has governed every decision they have made in this chapter, and it will govern the one they finally take, which is to arrange the arrest at night, away from the crowd (22:6).

In a sentence. The leaders wanted to arrest him at once, knowing the parable was against them, but feared the people.

On a Tuesday. When God’s word exposes you, repent rather than resent it. Notice your reaction the next time a sermon or a passage of Scripture lands too close: is it humility, or anger at the preacher? The leaders understood perfectly and hardened. Understanding is not the same as yielding. Ask God for a soft heart, and when the word cuts, say yes to it before you say anything else.

For worship. The Lord rules even over the plots of his enemies. They wanted him that very hour, and they could not have him until his hour came. Not one of his enemies can move a finger against him except as the Father allows, and the Father allowed it only when it would save us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–26 — The Question about Tribute to Caesar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The direct approach has failed twice, so the tactics change. Spies are men planted, and they “pretended to be sincere” — actors playing devout enquirers. Luke gives the object before the question: a capital charge Rome will act on, because Pilate does not care about blasphemy.

The flattery is a trap in itself. If he is a man who “shows no partiality,” he cannot now give a diplomatic answer — they have publicly committed him to fearless speech before asking the dangerous question. And the terrible thing is that every word of the compliment is true. They have described him accurately as a means of destroying him, which is only possible for people who know exactly who he is and have decided against him anyway.

The tribute was the poll tax, a denarius a head, levied since Judea became a Roman province in AD 6 — and it had provoked an armed revolt at the time. Say yes and he endorses the occupation before a Passover crowd of patriots; say no and there are witnesses ready to report a man inciting tax refusal, which is exactly the charge they will eventually bring (23:2).

He asks for a coin, and does not have one — the man they are trying to trap on taxation has to borrow the currency from his accusers. And somebody produces one immediately, in the temple. The denarius bore the head of Tiberius with an inscription naming him son of the divine Augustus, and Pontifex Maximus on the reverse: a portrait, which offended the second commandment, and a claim of divinity in writing.

“Caesar's” is the only possible answer and it concedes the whole question. The trap has been sprung without a word of doctrine, and it took one question about a coin.
verseByVerse.theology:
The verb in v.25 is not give but render — pay what is owed. It is the word for settling a debt, not making a donation, which quietly answers the first half: if the coin is Caesar's, handing it over is returning property.

But the weight falls on the second clause. He has just established the principle by which ownership is determined — whose likeness and inscription does it bear? So the question the second half silently asks is: what bears the image of God? And every person listening knew the answer from the first page of their Scriptures (Gen. 1:27).

The coin is stamped with Caesar and belongs to Caesar. The man holding it is stamped with God.

Two things follow, and the church has often held one without the other. The civil authority is legitimate — Jesus does not tell them to stop paying, and Paul develops it at length (Rom. 13:1-7). And the civil authority is bounded: Caesar gets what has his image on it and nothing more, so the moment he asks for worship, conscience, or the ultimate allegiance of a life, he is asking for property that is not his.

The “two kingdoms” principle drawn from these verses has been foundational for Reformed political theology. But the passage presses beyond institutional analysis to the personal: if you bear God's image, you belong to God — completely, with no reservation, because the image is not stamped on part of a man.
verseByVerse.examples:
A Christian facing a regulation he considers unjust can think clearly from this. There is a legitimate sphere of civil authority, and there is an authority that is absolute. The question is not whether to comply with any government but whether the specific demand crosses into what belongs exclusively to God.

Note also what the borrowed coin exposes. The men who came to catch him on faithfulness to God were carrying Caesar's portrait and Caesar's divine title in their purses, in the temple courts, and one of them had it out in seconds. Whatever the question was really about, it was not scruple.

And “marveling at his answer” is a surprising word for men who came to destroy him. It is possible to admire the truth and remain entirely unmoved by it — Herod was glad to see Jesus and questioned him at length (23:8-9). There is a way of appreciating the quality of an answer that functions as a substitute for obeying it, and it is common among people who take religion seriously enough to enjoy a good argument about it.

Which is a hard lesson for anyone who assumes a sufficiently good answer will settle a matter. Jesus gave the best answer anyone ever gave to a hostile question, in public, and the men who heard it admired it, went quiet, and had him killed on Friday.

verseByVerse.quote: So they watched him and sent spies, who pretended to be sincere, that they might catch him in something he said, so as to deliver him up to the authority and jurisdiction of the governor. So they asked him, 'Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and show no partiality, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they watched him and sent spies, who pretended to be sincere, that they might catch him in something he said, so as to deliver him up to the authority and jurisdiction of the governor. So they asked him: Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and show no partiality, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not?

So they watched him and sent spies, who pretended to be sincere. The direct approach has failed twice, so the tactics change. Watched is the word for lying in wait. Spies is enkathetous, men hired and planted. And pretended to be sincere is literally that they pretended themselves to be righteous: actors playing devout enquirers, hypocrites in the old sense of the word.

That they might catch him in something he said, so as to deliver him up to the authority and jurisdiction of the governor. Luke tells us the object before we hear the question, and only Luke states their aim so plainly. This is no longer about winning an argument in the temple. They want a political charge that Rome will act on, and Pilate does not care about blasphemy.

Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and show no partiality, but truly teach the way of God. The flattery is thick, and it is a trap in itself. They are not merely being pleasant; they are building a fence. If he is a man who shows no partiality, he cannot now give a diplomatic answer. They have publicly committed him to fearless speech before asking the dangerous question. And the terrible thing about the compliment is that every word of it is true. He does speak rightly, he does show no partiality, he does teach the way of God. They have described him accurately as a means of destroying him, which is possible only for people who know well enough who he is and have decided against him anyway.

Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not? The tribute was the poll tax, a denarius a head, paid directly to Rome by every adult in Judea since it became a Roman province in AD 6, and bitterly resented. It had provoked the armed revolt of Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:37). So the question is live and dangerous. Say yes, and he endorses the occupation in front of a Passover crowd of patriots and loses them. Say no, and there are witnesses standing ready to report a man inciting tax refusal to Pilate. And the irony is that they will bring exactly that charge anyway, falsely: we found this man forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar (23:2).

How should a Christian respond to flattery? With gratitude for kindness, and with a guarded heart. Flattery is praise with a purpose: it wants something from you, and it is often the prelude to a request you would otherwise refuse (Proverbs 29:5). Jesus was not moved by it at all, because he did not live for human approval (John 5:41). The more you need to be thought well of, the easier you are to manipulate. So when someone praises you before asking something hard, pause, pray, and answer the request on its merits, not on the warmth of the introduction.

In a sentence. The leaders sent flattering spies to trap Jesus into a statement they could report to the governor, asking whether it was lawful to pay tribute to Caesar.

On a Tuesday. Beware of flattery that leads into a trap, and beware of using it. Notice this week when you are tempted to soften someone up before asking for something, or to praise a person in front of others to box them in. Speak plainly and kindly instead. And when you face a question designed to make you lose either way, ask God for wisdom before you open your mouth (James 1:5).

For worship. Christ was the one man who could not be flattered, because he needed nothing from men. He stood in his Father’s house surrounded by actors and spies, and was moved neither by their praise nor by their threat. His heart was not for sale, and his words could not be bought or bent. The Lord who would not be steered by compliments is the Lord who cannot be turned against his people by any accuser, and whose love for them was settled before a word was said to him.
verseByVerse.note: The poll tax was paid directly to Rome and bitterly resented. “Yes” would anger the people; “no” would be treason before the governor.

parallels.desc: forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar

verseByVerse.quote: But he perceived their craftiness, and said to them, 'Show me a denarius. Whose likeness and inscription does it have?' They said, 'Caesar's.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he perceived their craftiness, and said to them: show me a denarius. Whose likeness and inscription does it have? They said: Caesar’s.

But he perceived their craftiness. Craftiness is panourgian: cunning, trickery, the quality Paul ties to the serpent in Eden (2 Corinthians 11:3), whom Genesis calls more crafty than any other beast of the field (Genesis 3:1). He is not taken in for a moment. The one who knows what is in man (John 2:25) sees through the actors at once.

Show me a denarius. He does not answer. He asks for a coin, and there is something in that request that is easy to miss. He asks them for one. The man they are trying to trap on the subject of taxation has the currency produced by his accusers, which tells you a good deal about the relative interest each party had in Caesar’s money. And somebody produces one immediately. In the temple. A denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer.

Whose likeness and inscription does it have? That matters more than it looks. The denarius was a silver coin bearing the head of the emperor Tiberius, and around the head an inscription calling him Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus, with the title high priest on the reverse. It was a portrait, which strict Jews regarded as a graven image forbidden by the second commandment, and it carried a claim to divinity in writing. The men who had come to catch him on a point of faithfulness to God were carrying it in their purses, in the temple courts, and one of them had it out in seconds.

They said, Caesar’s. That is the only possible answer, and it concedes the whole question. They have just testified, in public, that they are in Caesar’s economy and using his money. And a man who uses a currency, and benefits from the roads, order and trade it pays for, has accepted the authority that mints it.

The method. The trap has been sprung without a word of doctrine, with one question about a coin, and they have been made to say the awkward thing themselves. There is a lesson in the method, because Christians in hostile conversations reach for the wrong tool almost every time. He does not weigh the arguments about Roman taxation or find a form of words careful enough to survive being quoted. He asks for an object and asks what is written on it. The answer comes out of their own pockets and their own mouths, and by the time they have given it the argument is over. Nothing has been conceded and nobody has been insulted.

In a sentence. Seeing their trick, Jesus asked for a denarius and whose image and inscription it bore, and they said Caesar’s.

On a Tuesday. Wisdom often lies in looking carefully at what is in front of you. When you are drawn into a heated argument, at work, online or at a family gathering, slow down. Ask a simple question that brings the real issue into view, rather than rushing to defend yourself. And look honestly at your own purse: are there things you condemn in public while quietly benefiting from them?

For worship. The Lord sees through every disguise. No craftiness has ever outwitted him, from the serpent in the garden to the spies in the temple. And the same eyes that read the hearts of his enemies read ours, and he still came to save. There is nothing hidden from him, and nothing in us that his grace cannot reach.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage. The coin bore the emperor’s head — probably Tiberius — and his titles.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, 'Then render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: then render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.

He said to them, Then render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s. Render is apodote: pay back, hand over what is due, the language of a debt settled rather than a gift made. If the coin carries Caesar’s face, giving it to him is not a betrayal of God; it is returning what is his. Civil authority is legitimate. Jesus does not tell them to stop paying, and Paul will develop it at length: let every person be subject to the governing authorities, and pay to all what is owed to them, taxes to whom taxes are owed (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17). Taxes are owed, and paying them is not idolatry.
