And to God the things that are God’s. The weight falls on this second half. Jesus has just made ownership a matter of image: whose likeness and inscription does it bear? The coin wears Caesar’s face, so it goes to Caesar. The clause leaves a second question hanging in the air: what bears the image of God? Every listener knew the answer from the first page of the Scriptures. God created man in his own image (Genesis 1:26–27). The coin is stamped with Caesar and belongs to Caesar. The man holding it is stamped with God.

A far larger answer. That makes this a far larger answer than the tax question deserved. Caesar may have the metal; he has a genuine claim, and it is limited to things with his face on them. God’s claim is on the person, and not on a portion of the person, because the image is not stamped on part of a man. Give Caesar his coin; give God yourself, wholly. And Caesar’s claims are bounded by God’s. Caesar is owed taxes, not worship. The moment he asks for what belongs to God, worship, conscience, the ultimate allegiance of a life, he is asking for property that is not his, and the answer is the apostles’: we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

The Image who rendered everything. Only one man has ever given God all that is God’s. The one who said these words is himself the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15), the true likeness that Adam’s children bear only in broken form, and his whole life was a rendering of himself to the Father. Within days he would hand over the last thing a man has. Father, into your hands I commit my spirit, he cried from the cross (23:46). The coin went to Caesar; the Son gave himself to God, entire, and by that offering he redeems those who have kept back from God what was always his.

Where Christians differ: how do the two claims relate? Some have read this verse as dividing life into two equal and separate realms, a sacred one where God rules and a secular one where the state rules, each sovereign in its own sphere and neither answerable to the other. Others read it as placing Caesar’s realm inside God’s: the state has real authority, but only as a servant of God, accountable to him and limited by his law. Verdict: Jesus does not make God and Caesar equal partners. All authority is under God; the governing authorities exist because God has instituted them (Romans 13:1), and even Pilate had no authority except what was given from above (John 19:11). Christians should be good citizens, paying taxes and honouring rulers, praying for them (1 Timothy 2:1–2), but their final loyalty is to God alone.

What if my government uses my taxes for things I believe are wrong? Pay them anyway, as a rule. The tax Jesus told them to pay funded a pagan empire that crucified people, kept armies of occupation and supported idol temples, and Paul wrote Romans 13 under Nero. The responsibility for misuse lies with those who spend the money, not with the citizen who obeys God by paying what is owed. Use every lawful means to work for justice: vote, write, speak, protest peacefully. The line is crossed only when the state commands you yourself to do what God forbids, or forbids what God commands. Then obey God, and accept the consequences without violence.

In a sentence. Jesus said to give Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and God what belongs to God.

On a Tuesday. Pay your taxes honestly: no cash-in-hand work kept off the books, no invented expenses, no quiet rounding in your own favour. That is rendering to Caesar. Then ask what it would mean today to render to God what bears his image: your body, mind, time and affections. Begin the morning by offering yourself to him (Romans 12:1), and end it by asking where you kept something back.

For worship. Every human face carries God’s likeness more deeply than Caesar’s face was struck into silver. When sin defaced that image, the Maker did not throw the coin away. He came to recover it himself, and he is renewing his people in knowledge after the image of their Creator (Colossians 3:10), until they bear the likeness of his Son. Caesar’s coins wore thin within a generation. The image God is restoring in his people will shine for ever, and every one of them is his twice over, by making and by purchase.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were not able in the presence of the people to catch him in what he said, but marveling at his answer they became silent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were not able in the presence of the people to catch him in what he said, but marvelling at his answer they became silent.

And they were not able in the presence of the people to catch him in what he said. Three things in one sentence, and each is worth having. In the presence of the people: Luke keeps saying it. The crowd is the reason nothing can be done, and it is the reason the question had to be public. They needed witnesses to a seditious answer, and instead they have witnesses to a devastating one. Catch is a hunting word: to take hold of, to seize. It is the second failed attempt in this chapter, and a third is coming.

But marveling at his answer they became silent. Marvelling is the surprising word. These men came to destroy him. They had rehearsed the flattery, planted the spies and framed a question with no safe answer, and when the answer came, something in them responded to it. Jesus is the wisdom of God, and even his enemies could see it.

Marvelling in the temple again. Luke has shown us this scene once before. When Jesus was twelve he sat in this same temple among the teachers, listening and asking questions, and all who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers (2:46–47). Now the boy has come back as a man, and the teachers of Israel are amazed again, this time against their will. The wisdom that astonished them in his childhood has not changed; only their hearts have. The one standing in the court is the Son who said then that he must be in his Father’s house, and he is still there, still answering, and still beyond them.

Admiration is not faith. It is possible to admire the truth and remain entirely unmoved by it. Herod was glad to see Jesus and questioned him at length (23:8–9). Agrippa asked Paul whether in so short a time he would persuade him to be a Christian (Acts 26:28). There is a way of appreciating an answer that works as a substitute for obeying it. They became silent. Not persuaded: silenced. And the silence is not repentance. It is the end of a line of attack, and they will send the Sadducees in next.

Why did the best answer not convert them? Because the problem was never the quality of the answers. Set this beside v. 7, where the same men said we do not know. Twice now this delegation has been reduced to saying nothing, once by choosing not to answer and once by having nothing left to say. There is a hard lesson in that for anyone who assumes that a good enough answer will settle the matter. Jesus gave the best answer anyone ever gave to a hostile question, in public, and the men who heard it admired it, went quiet, and had him killed that week. Answers matter, and Christians should give them well (1 Peter 3:15). But only God can change a heart that does not want to be changed.

In a sentence. They could not trap him in front of the people, and, amazed at his answer, they fell silent.

On a Tuesday. Do you admire Christ’s teaching without obeying it? It is easy to enjoy a fine sermon, nod at a sharp point and walk out unchanged. After the next sermon you hear, write down one thing to do, and do it before the week is out. And if you are trying to persuade an unbelieving friend, do your best to answer well, and then pray, because the decisive work is not yours.

For worship. The cleverest men of his nation set their best trap and came away marvelling, and that wisdom has never been caught out since. Every treasure of wisdom and knowledge lies hidden in him (Colossians 2:3). Every question ever laid before him, hostile or sincere, has found him ready, and the mind that silenced the spies in the temple is the mind that governs every detail of his people’s lives.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–47 — Sadducees on Resurrection, the Son of David, and Scribal Warning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Sadducees were the aristocratic party — the chief priestly families and wealthy landowners who ran the temple and managed the relationship with Rome. They accepted the five books of Moses and treated the rest as secondary, and from that drew the conclusions Acts states fully: “the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit” (Acts 23:8). Which limits the field for Jesus: he cannot answer from Daniel 12 or Isaiah 26, and will have to find the resurrection in Moses.

Their riddle rests on a good law. Deuteronomy 25:5-10 provided that if a married man died childless his brother should marry the widow, and the first son would carry the dead man's name and inherit his portion — so no family line or allotted land in Israel would be extinguished. It is the law behind Boaz and Ruth, and it was designed to protect a widow from destitution.

They turn it into a joke. Seven brothers, one after another, each obeying Moses, each dying childless. And notice what the story does to the woman: she is unnamed, unnumbered, given no words, and exists purely as contested property. The question at the end is not “what became of her?” but “whose will she be?”

The argument is a reductio, and it rests on one assumption the Sadducees have never noticed they are making — that the age to come is this age carried on, the same arrangements made permanent. So the answer is not a solution to the puzzle. Jesus dismantles the premise and the puzzle goes with it.

He then proves the doctrine on their own ground, from the burning bush; the scribes commend him; and nobody dares ask anything further. Which leaves him free to ask his own question, about Psalm 110 — and to close with a warning about the men who had been asking all day.
verseByVerse.theology:
“They cannot die anymore” is the reason marriage does not continue. Marriage in this age carries the future of the race: where people die, people must be born. Remove death and the mechanism for replacing the dead is no longer needed — the way scaffolding is no longer needed. And “equal to angels” does not mean disembodied; the resurrection is precisely of the body, and Luke's own last chapter has the risen Christ eating fish to prove it (24:41-43). The comparison is specifically to deathlessness, and Jesus says so in the same breath.

The argument from Exodus 3:6 turns on a tense. God does not say “I was the God of Abraham” but “I am” — four hundred years after Abraham was buried. And to be somebody's God is covenant language: to have bound yourself to a person and promised him a future. So if God is still Abraham's God, then either the covenant is with a handful of dust, which is no covenant at all, or Abraham is alive.

Note what the argument does not rest on. Not the immortality of the soul, which is a Greek idea and appears nowhere in the reasoning. It rests entirely on the character of God: he does not enter a binding relationship with a man and then let death end it, because that would make him unfaithful. The ground of resurrection hope is not something in us but something in him — which is why the last clause is one of the great sentences of Scripture: “for all live to him.”

Psalm 110:1 became the most quoted Old Testament text in the New (Acts 2:34-35; 1 Cor. 15:25; Heb. 1:13; 10:12-13). In that world honour ran upward — a man addressed his forebears as “my lord,” never the reverse — so a psalm in which David calls his own descendant “my Lord” is upside down, unless the descendant is more than a descendant.
verseByVerse.examples:
All of the resurrection teaching is true, and none of it is what the widow in the third pew is asking. She has buried a husband she loved for forty years, reads “neither marry nor are given in marriage,” and hears the one thing she was most afraid of.

For marriage was never the destination. Paul says the whole thing was pointing somewhere: “this mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church” (Eph. 5:31-32). Every good marriage has been a signpost, and nobody keeps reading the signpost after arriving at the city. What waits at the end of this age is a wedding (Rev. 19:6-9) — and marriage is not carried into it because it was too little, not too much. It was the picture; that is the reality.

The chapter closes with predation rather than vanity. Long robes and good seats are appetite; devouring widows' houses is theft — and the two halves of v.47 belong together, because the long prayers are not a separate failing but the instrument. The reputation for piety is what gets a man access to a widow's confidence and her accounts. The prayer is the cover.

Which is a word for anybody holding spiritual standing over others. It is possible to use the things of God to get things from people, and Scripture reserves its severest language for it. And Luke sets the next scene immediately: a widow at the treasury, putting in everything she had (21:1-4).

verseByVerse.quote: There came to him some Sadducees, those who deny that there is a resurrection, and they asked him a question, saying, 'Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man's brother dies, having a wife but no children, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There came to him some Sadducees, those who deny that there is a resurrection, and they asked him a question, saying: Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies, having a wife but no children, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.

There came to him some Sadducees. The third delegation of the day, and Luke supplies the label a reader needs. The Sadducees were the priestly, aristocratic party: the chief priestly families and the wealthy landowners, the men who controlled the temple and managed the relationship with Rome. They were fewer than the Pharisees and far more powerful, and they were conservative in a particular way. They accepted the five books of Moses as fully authoritative and treated the rest of the Scriptures as secondary.

Those who deny that there is a resurrection. Luke explains, for his Gentile readers. From their narrow view of Scripture they drew the conclusions Acts states more fully: the Sadducees say there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit (Acts 23:8). Their argument was that these doctrines are not in the Pentateuch and are therefore later inventions. That matters for what follows, because it limits the field. Jesus cannot answer them from Daniel 12 or Isaiah 26, both of which teach the resurrection plainly. He will have to find it in Moses, and he does.

Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies, having a wife but no children, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. The law they cite is real, and worth understanding before the riddle is built on it. Deuteronomy 25:5–10 provides that if a married man dies childless, his brother should marry the widow, and the first son of that marriage would carry the dead man’s name and inherit his portion. The purpose was twofold: to stop a family line being blotted out in Israel, and to keep a piece of the promised land in the family to which it had been allotted. It is the law behind the book of Ruth, where Boaz acts as redeemer for Naomi’s line, and through it comes the line of David and of Christ. It is a good and compassionate law.

A true text used falsely. And it is about to be turned into a joke. The Sadducees are not misquoting Moses; every word of their citation is accurate. They are using a true text to make a doctrine they dislike look ridiculous, a technique available to anybody with a Bible and a grievance. A passage is quoted correctly, pushed to an extreme its author never envisaged, and the resulting absurdity is laid at the door of the belief rather than the method.

In a sentence. Some Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, came with a question based on Moses’ law that a man should marry his dead brother’s childless widow.

On a Tuesday. Scepticism about the resurrection is nothing new. It sat in the temple, wore priestly robes and quoted Moses. If you meet it in a friend, a lecturer or a book, do not be alarmed, and do not assume it is new or unanswerable. Jesus’ answer still stands. And watch your own use of Scripture: do you ever quote a verse to win a point rather than to learn what God means?

For worship. The Lord of the resurrection stood in the temple and let the deniers of the resurrection bring their best argument. He was not threatened by it, because he was about to answer it with an empty tomb. Death is not the end of God’s people, because it was not the end of God’s Son.
verseByVerse.note: The Sadducees, the priestly party, denied the resurrection. Levirate marriage kept a dead man’s name alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife, and died without children. And the second and the third took her, and likewise all seven left no children and died. Afterward the woman also died. In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife will the woman be? For the seven had her as wife.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife, and died without children. And the second and the third took her, and likewise all seven left no children and died. Afterwards the woman also died. In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife will the woman be? For the seven had her as wife.

Now there were seven brothers. The case is constructed, not reported. Nobody claims this happened. It is a thought experiment, probably a standard argument the Sadducees used to ridicule the Pharisees’ belief in the resurrection, and the number seven is chosen because it is the number of completeness and makes the situation as absurd as possible.

The first took a wife, and died without children, and the second and the third took her. Luke compresses what Matthew and Mark spell out, and the effect is a kind of grim comedy: seven brothers, one after another, each obeying Moses, each dying childless. And likewise all seven left no children and died. Afterward the woman also died.

What the story does to the woman. Notice her. She is the one person in it who is not named, not numbered and given no words. She exists in the riddle purely as a piece of contested property, the thing seven men had a claim on. And the question at the end is not what became of her? but whose wife will the woman be? That tells you something about the men asking. They have taken a law given to protect a widow and used it to build a puzzle in which the widow is an object.

In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife will the woman be? For the seven had her as wife. There is the question, with its last clause driving the point home. The argument underneath is a reductio: if the resurrection were true, and Moses’ law were true, you would end up with an insoluble situation in the age to come; therefore the resurrection cannot be true. Moses could not have believed in it.

The hidden assumption. It is a clever argument and it rests entirely on one assumption, which is never stated because the Sadducees have never noticed they are making it. They assume the age to come is this age carried on: the same arrangements, the same institutions, the same questions, only permanent. That is why the answer will not be a solution to the puzzle. Jesus is not going to tell them which brother gets her. He is going to dismantle the premise, and the puzzle will go with it.

Seven graves and an empty tomb. Notice what the riddle is made of: seven funerals and then an eighth. Every brother obeys the law, death wins every round, and the woman follows them into the ground. The Sadducees offer this as the last word on human life, and in their scheme it is. But they put it to the one man in history who would not stay in a grave. Within the week Jesus would die and rise, so that by dying he might break the power of the one who held the power of death, and free those whom the fear of death had kept in slavery all their lives (Hebrews 2:14–15). The chain of graves in their story was about to be broken from the inside.

In a sentence. They told of seven brothers who married the same woman in turn and died childless, and asked whose wife she would be in the resurrection.

On a Tuesday. Clever objections often rest on false assumptions. Look for the assumption. When an argument against the faith seems unanswerable, ask what it takes for granted: that God is like us, that the future must be like the present, that what we cannot imagine cannot be. And notice the people in the story. The woman was a person, not a puzzle. Never let a debate about doctrine make you careless of the human beings it concerns.

For worship. In the Sadducees’ riddle the woman has no name and no voice; she passes from brother to brother like an heirloom. The God of the resurrection is not like that. He knows each of his people by name, numbers the hairs of their heads (12:7), and will raise them as persons, not as pieces in somebody’s argument. The age he has prepared is not this tired age stretched out, but a new creation where no one is owned, no one is passed on, and no one is ever buried again.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, 'The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage, but those who are considered worthy to attain to that age and to the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they cannot die anymore, because they are equal to angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them: the sons of this age marry and are given in marriage, but those who are considered worthy to attain to that age and to the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they cannot die any more, because they are equal to angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection.

The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage. He begins by naming a category the Sadducees did not have. This age and that age: two orders of existence, and marriage belongs to the first. It is good, given by God in Eden, and it belongs to this present age.

But those who are considered worthy to attain to that age and to the resurrection from the dead. Only Luke has this fuller form. That age is the age to come. Considered worthy is a verdict God gives, through grace, not a merit earned (2 Thessalonians 1:5, 11). Such people neither marry nor are given in marriage: resurrection life is not this life continued, and marriage’s purposes are fulfilled.

For they cannot die anymore. There is the reason, and only Luke gives it. Marriage in this age carries the future of the race. Where people die, people must be born, and the institution that provides for that is marriage. Remove death and the mechanism for replacing the dead becomes unnecessary, not abolished by decree, but no longer needed, the way scaffolding is no longer needed once the building stands. In the resurrection there is no death, and so no need for levirate marriage. The Sadducees’ whole puzzle falls apart.

Because they are equal to angels. Like angels, immortal, not that they become angels. Equal to angels does not mean disembodied. The resurrection is precisely of the body, and Luke’s own last chapter has the risen Christ eating broiled fish to prove it (24:39–43). The comparison is specifically to deathlessness, and Jesus says so in the same breath.

And are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection. Children of God by resurrection, sharing his life. We wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies (Romans 8:23), and when he appears we shall be like him (1 John 3:2).

Who are those who are considered worthy? Jesus is speaking of the resurrection to life of God’s people, those whom God counts worthy through faith in Christ. Elsewhere he says that all the dead will rise, those who have done good to the resurrection of life and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment (John 5:28–29). No one is worthy in himself. The worthiness is Christ’s, credited to those who trust him.

What it does not mean. All of this is true, and none of it is what the widow in the third pew is asking. She has buried a husband she loved for forty years, and she reads neither marry nor are given in marriage and hears the one thing she was most afraid of: that she will not have him again. So let the verse be read to her properly, because it does not say that. Jesus says the institution ends: the marrying, the giving in marriage, the arrangement by which this age replaces its dead. He does not say the people end, and he does not say the love ends. Married love is not lost or forgotten; it is taken up into something greater. You will not know your husband less there. You will know him better than you ever managed here, without the tiredness and the half-attention that got between you every day of the forty years.

Marriage was a signpost. Marriage was never the destination. Paul says the whole thing was pointing somewhere: the one-flesh union of husband and wife is a profound mystery, and it speaks of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). Every good marriage has been a signpost, and nobody keeps reading the signpost after arriving at the city. And what waits at the end of this age is a wedding: the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:6–9). Marriage is not carried into it because it was too little, not too much. It was the picture. That is the reality.

What about those who never married, or whose marriages were unhappy? This verse is good news for them too. The single believer is not missing out on the final reality; he or she is heading for the same wedding as everyone else, the marriage of Christ and his church, and will lack nothing there. Jesus himself never married. And for those whose marriages were marked by pain, or by a spouse who did not believe, the age to come will not prolong what was broken. Every relationship will be healed in its proper place, and every believer will be satisfied in Christ.

In a sentence. Jesus answered that marriage belongs to this age, but those raised to the age to come do not marry, because they can no longer die, being like angels and children of God.

On a Tuesday. If you are married, love your spouse today as a signpost to Christ: serve, forgive and speak kindly, because your marriage is preaching a sermon about him and his church. If you are single, widowed or divorced, do not believe the lie that you are missing life’s main event. The main event is still to come, and you are invited. And if you grieve someone who died in Christ, take comfort: you will see them again, and know them better.

For worship. Blessed be the Son of God, raised first, the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29). His people are sons of the resurrection because he is the Son who rose, and the life they will share is his own deathless life, which no grave can interrupt and no age can end. Death has no future for them. The God who made marriage to picture his love will give them the reality, and they will be his, and he theirs, for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: But that the dead are raised, even Moses showed, in the passage about the bush, where he calls the Lord the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob. Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But that the dead are raised, even Moses showed, in the passage about the bush, where he calls the Lord the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob. Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him.

But that the dead are raised, even Moses showed, in the passage about the bush. Having dismantled the riddle, he now proves the doctrine, and he does it on their ground. They accepted Moses. Very well: Moses. The passage about the bush is Exodus 3, the burning bush. Before chapter and verse numbers existed, passages were located by their subject like this.

Where he calls the Lord the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob. The reference is Exodus 3:6, one of the best-known sentences in the Pentateuch, spoken centuries after the patriarchs died. God introduces himself to Moses by naming his relationship to three men who had been dead for hundreds of years. He still calls himself their God.

Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living. The argument turns on the relationship. God does not say, I was the God of Abraham. He says, I am the God of your father, four hundred years after Abraham was buried at Machpelah. Now, what does it mean to be somebody’s God? It is covenant language. It means to have bound yourself to a person: to be his shield and his very great reward, to have promised him a future (Genesis 15:1; 17:7). So if God is still Abraham’s God, then either the covenant is with a handful of dust, which is no covenant at all, or Abraham is alive. A covenant relationship with God cannot be broken by death. If God is their God, they live to him, and he will keep his promises to them, body and soul.

The ground of hope is in God. Note what the argument rests on. Not the natural immortality of the soul, which is a Greek idea and appears nowhere in the reasoning. Not the resilience of the human spirit. It rests entirely on the character of God. He does not enter into a binding relationship with a man and then let death end it, because that would make him unfaithful. The ground of resurrection hope is not something in us. It is something in him.

For all live to him. Only Luke adds this, and it is one of the great sentences of Scripture. It proves the resurrection from God’s faithfulness to his covenant. It also implies that those who have died in the Lord are alive to God now, as other texts say plainly (23:43; Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Romans 14:8). They await the resurrection of the body, but they are with him. Whatever the state of the dead in Christ, they are not gone from God’s side of it. Nobody who belonged to him has ever been lost track of, and the graves of the patriarchs did not interrupt a single conversation.

The God of Abraham raised his servant Jesus. Within weeks Peter stood in this same temple, in Solomon’s Portico, and used the very words of the bush. The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, he said, had glorified his servant Jesus, whom they had killed and God had raised from the dead (Acts 3:13–15). The argument Jesus made to the Sadducees from Moses was answered in his own body. The covenant God who will not be the God of dead men did not leave his Son among the dead. On Easter morning the angels asked the women why they were seeking the living among the dead (24:5), and the first fruits of the resurrection Jesus defended in the temple was Jesus himself.

Are the dead asleep until the resurrection? Not in the sense of being unconscious. Scripture uses sleep as a gentle picture of the believer’s death, because the body rests and will wake (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14). But the person is not extinguished or unaware. Jesus told the dying thief that today he would be with him in paradise (23:43); Paul said to depart is to be with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23). So the believer who dies goes at once, consciously, into the presence of the Lord, and waits there with joy for the resurrection of the body at Christ’s return (Westminster 32.1). There is no purgatory in between. All live to him.

In a sentence. From the burning bush Jesus proved the resurrection: God still names himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, he is God of the living, and all live to him.

On a Tuesday. If God is your God, you will live for ever, and that changes how you face death: your own, and the deaths of those you love in Christ. At the next funeral of a believer, say it to yourself: he is not God of the dead, but of the living. And let it change how you read the Bible. Jesus found the resurrection in a single verb. Read Scripture slowly and believe every word, because God’s promises hang on them.

For worship. Blessed is the God of the living. He called himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob over their graves, and he calls himself the God of his people over theirs. He does not lose those who are his. The God who spoke from the bush that burned and was not consumed keeps his own through the fire of death, and will raise them on the last day.
verseByVerse.note: “The passage about the bush” is how a passage was located before chapter and verse numbers existed.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob

verseByVerse.quote: Then some of the scribes answered, 'Teacher, you have spoken well.' For they no longer dared to ask him any question.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then some of the scribes answered: Teacher, you have spoken well. For they no longer dared to ask him any question.

Then some of the scribes answered, Teacher, you have spoken well. An unexpected moment, and Luke alone records it. These are scribes, and most scribes were Pharisees, who believed in the resurrection and had been arguing with the Sadducees about it for generations. They have just watched a rival party demolished on a doctrine they hold, and they cannot help themselves.

The approval of those who agreed. You have spoken well. It is genuine as far as it goes. Not you are the Christ. Not even we will follow you. It is the approval of men who agreed with the conclusion. They came to this chapter to destroy him, and here they are commending him, because on this particular point he was on their side. That is a familiar thing, and it is not the same as faith. It is entirely possible to be delighted by a preacher who demolishes a position you already disliked, and to walk out having received nothing at all. The test of whether a person is listening to Christ is not whether he applauds when Christ attacks somebody else. These same scribes are back within two chapters, seeking how to put him to death (22:2).

For they no longer dared to ask him any question. Luke closes the day’s interrogation with a verdict, and it covers all three delegations. The chief priests came with a question about authority and ended by saying, we do not know. The spies came about the tribute and became silent. The Sadducees came with the seven brothers and are not recorded as replying at all. Three attacks, each carefully prepared by men who did this professionally, and after the third nobody would risk a fourth. Every trap has failed.

Nobody defeated him in argument. What is left is the arrest, and it will happen at night, with a bribe, away from the crowd, the only method remaining to men beaten in the open. That settles something about the trial to come. Three organised attempts were made by the best-qualified men in the country, on their own ground, at a time of their choosing, and all three collapsed in public. What happened to him that Friday did not happen because the case against him was strong.

In a sentence. Some scribes praised his answer, and no one dared ask him any more questions.

On a Tuesday. Christ’s answers are sufficient. Bring your questions to him in Scripture: your doubts about suffering, the afterlife, his goodness, your own future. Read the Gospels with a question in mind and see how he answers. And check your applause. Are you as glad when Christ’s word corrects your side, your views, your habits, as when it corrects others?

For worship. No one could answer him, and no one can now. The wisest men of Israel fell silent before the teacher from Nazareth, because he is the Word made flesh. All the questions of the world come to rest in him, and he has never been out-argued. He went to the cross not because he lost the argument, but because he chose to save those who lost it.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to them, 'How can they say that the Christ is David's son? For David himself says in the Book of Psalms, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he said to them: how can they say that the Christ is David’s son? For David himself says in the Book of Psalms: the Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand.

But he said to them, How can they say that the Christ is David’s son? Now he asks. Three delegations have questioned him and failed. He has one question of his own, the decisive one, and it is about who he is. Note first that he is not denying the premise. That the Messiah would be a descendant of David was not a rabbinic guess but a promise: I will raise up your offspring after you, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom for ever (2 Samuel 7:12–16); there shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1). A blind beggar had been shouting Son of David at him outside Jericho (18:38). So the question is not whether the Christ is David’s son. It is whether that is the whole of it.

For David himself says in the Book of Psalms. The quotation is Psalm 110:1, and it was universally taken to be David’s and about the Messiah. Jesus’ argument depends on both: that David wrote it, and that it speaks of the Christ. It became the Old Testament verse most quoted in the New, in Peter’s sermon at Pentecost, in Paul, and repeatedly in Hebrews (Acts 2:34–35; 1 Corinthians 15:25; Hebrews 1:13; 10:12–13). The early church could not stop returning to it, and this is where they learned to.

The Lord said to my Lord. In the Hebrew the two words are different. The first is the covenant name of God, Yahweh, which English Bibles print as LORD in small capitals. The second is adoni, my lord, an ordinary word for a master or superior. So it reads: the LORD said to my lord. God speaks to David’s Lord. In the Greek that Luke’s readers had, both come out as kyrios, which is why English needs the capitals to keep them apart.

Sit at my right hand. An invitation to share the throne of God, extended to a figure distinct from the one speaking, and the position is not honorary. The right hand is the place of supreme honour, where the authority is exercised. It is a coronation psalm that every scribe in the courtyard could recite, and he is asking them about a text they had known since childhood. The material for recognising him had been in their hands the whole time. What was missing was not information.

Gabriel had already answered it. The reader of Luke does not have to wait for the riddle to be solved, because the angel solved it in the first chapter. Gabriel told Mary that her son would be given the throne of his father David, and in the same breath that he would be called the Son of the Most High, conceived by the Holy Spirit and so called holy, the Son of God (1:32–35). He is David’s son by human birth, born into David’s house (1:27). He is David’s Lord because he is the eternal Son of God. That is how David could call his own descendant Lord: the child of Mary was the Lord whom David worshipped, come in David’s flesh.

In a sentence. Jesus asked how the Messiah could be David’s son, when David himself in Psalm 110 calls him Lord, seated at God’s right hand.

On a Tuesday. Is your view of Jesus too small? You can believe true things about him, a good teacher, a great example, a helper in trouble, and still believe too little. Read Psalm 110 this week and ask what it means that the one you pray to is seated at God’s right hand now, ruling. Let it change how you pray: not timidly, as to a distant friend, but boldly, as to the reigning King.

For worship. Jesus is seated at God’s right hand now. The LORD said to him, Sit, and he sat down, his work finished, his enemies being placed beneath his feet. The one who stood in the temple court asking this question was the Lord David adored a thousand years before he was born, and the right hand of God, where all authority is exercised, has been his seat since he rose. There is no throne above his, and no prayer of his people that does not reach it.

verseByVerse.quote: until I make your enemies your footstool.’ David thus calls him Lord, so how is he his son?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Until I make your enemies your footstool. David thus calls him Lord, so how is he his son?

Until I make your enemies your footstool. The image is from the ancient world’s pictures of conquest: a victorious king with his feet on the necks of the defeated, and Egyptian and Assyrian carvings show it literally. Joshua had the commanders of Israel put their feet on the necks of five kings (Joshua 10:24). It is a picture of total victory. Christ reigns now, and must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet; the last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Corinthians 15:25–26). And the word until is not a limit on the reign. The sitting does not stop when the enemies are subdued. What stops is the interval in which they are still standing.

David thus calls him Lord, so how is he his son? There is the question, and its whole weight rests on a social fact so obvious that nobody in that courtyard needed it explained. In that world, honour ran upward. A son honoured his father; a descendant honoured his ancestor. A father did not call his son lord, and the further back the ancestor, the greater the honour due. David was the greatest king Israel ever had, and every Jew traced honour toward him. So a psalm in which David calls his own descendant my Lord is upside down. It cannot happen, unless the descendant is something more than a descendant. If David calls the Messiah Lord, the Messiah must be greater than David.

The answer. Jesus does not supply it. He leaves the question standing, and Luke records no reply. But the answer is not obscure, and every reader of this Gospel has had it since chapter one. The Messiah is David’s son and David’s Lord because he is both: descended from David by human birth, and the eternal Son of God who was there before David and made him. Paul states it in exactly those two halves: descended from David according to the flesh, and declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:3–4). Fully man and fully God. Jesus is pointing to himself.

A true expectation that is too small. That is why the question was asked at all. The scribes had a Messiah who was David’s son and nothing more: a king, a deliverer, a national restorer. Their expectation was true and it was too small, and a man with an expectation that is true and too small will reject the reality when it arrives, because it does not fit. He was standing in front of them, and the psalm they recited was about him.

Why does it matter that Jesus is both God and man? Because only such a Saviour could save us. As man, he could take our place, obey the law we broke and die the death we deserved, for he shared our flesh and blood (Hebrews 2:14–17). As God, his obedience and his death have infinite worth, enough to pay for the sins of all who believe, and he has power to conquer death and to keep his people for ever. A Saviour who was only man could not save; one who was only God could not die. Jesus is both, in one person, for ever.

In a sentence. Since David calls the Messiah Lord, who will rule until all enemies are under his feet, how can he be merely David’s son?

On a Tuesday. Bring both truths into your day. When you are tempted or weary, remember that he is David’s son: a real man who knows hunger, grief and temptation, and can sympathise with your weakness (Hebrews 4:15). When you are afraid or overwhelmed, remember that he is David’s Lord, reigning until every enemy, including the one you fear, is beneath his feet. Pray to him as both.

For worship. Jesus is both David’s son and David’s Lord, the root and the offspring of David (Revelation 22:16): before David he made him, and after David he was born of his line. The Son of David reigns with his enemies already being laid beneath his feet, and the last of them, death itself, will lie there too. Every grave of every believer is on the list of things he will put under his feet, and the King who has already risen will see to every one.
verseByVerse.note: A conquered king’s neck could be used as a footstool — a picture of total victory.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the hearing of all the people he said to his disciples, 'Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes, and love greetings in the marketplaces and the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts,
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the hearing of all the people he said to his disciples: beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes, and love greetings in the marketplaces and the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honour at feasts.

And in the hearing of all the people he said to his disciples. Luke marks the audience carefully, and the arrangement is deliberate. The words are addressed to his disciples and spoken in the hearing of all the people: a warning given to one group in front of another, publicly, so that both hear it.

Beware of the scribes. The verb is the one for watching out for a danger. And it is worth registering how startling the sentence is. The scribes were the Bible teachers, the men who copied, studied and expounded the Scriptures, and the ordinary person’s assumption was that they were the most reliable guides available. He tells the crowd to be careful of them. It is a warning against their example, as at the Pharisee’s table (11:43).

Who like to walk around in long robes. Four marks follow, and they are all about being seen. The long robes were the full-length garment that marked out men of learning and rank. And the phrase is walk around in them: not wearing one to a function but promenading, which is a small and perfectly recognisable vanity.

And love greetings in the marketplaces. The respectful titles due to a teacher, paid in the open square where they could be observed. Note the verb: not receive greetings, which they could not help, but love them.

And the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts. The bench at the front, facing the congregation, a seat that makes a man visible for the whole service. And the couches nearest the host, exactly what Jesus had watched the guests scrambling for at a Pharisee’s dinner (14:7).

The appetite to be seen. Not one of these is a sin in itself. Somebody has to sit at the front; robes and greetings are not wicked. What is diagnosed, four times over, is an appetite, and the appetite is for being looked at while being religious. That is a hazard of the office and not only of the men. Any position in which a person is watched being godly carries it, and it does not announce itself. It feels like enjoying one’s work.

The Teacher who took the lowest place. The man warning against the scribes had told a dinner party that everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted (14:11), and he was about to live it to the end. The Lord of the temple wore no robe of rank and sought no seat at the front. Within days he would take the lowest place there is, numbered with the transgressors and crucified between two criminals (22:37; 23:33), and God would raise him to the highest. Every scribe who loved the best seat was standing in the presence of the only one who deserved it, and who gave it up.

Is it wrong for church leaders to have titles or be honoured? Not in itself. Scripture tells churches to respect and honour those who labour among them, and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work (1 Thessalonians 5:12–13; 1 Timothy 5:17). The sin is in loving the honour. Leaders should test themselves: would I be content to serve unseen? Do I resent it when I am not thanked? And churches should guard their leaders, not feeding vanity with flattery, but praying for them and holding them to the example of Christ, who came not to be served but to serve (Mark 10:45).

In a sentence. Jesus publicly warned his disciples against the scribes, who love fine robes, public honour and the best seats.

On a Tuesday. Watch your heart for the love of recognition, especially if you serve in church. Notice the small pleasure when your name is mentioned from the front, and the small sting when it is not. Do one piece of service this week that no one will know about, and give thanks to God for the freedom of it.

For worship. Only once in the Gospel is Jesus dressed in a splendid robe, and it is put on him in mockery, when Herod and his soldiers treat him with contempt and send him back to Pilate (23:11). The only man with a right to the long robe and the first greeting wore one as a joke and went on to the cross without complaint. To him now belong every greeting, every title and every seat of honour, and he alone wears them rightly.
verseByVerse.note: Long robes marked out men of learning and rank.

verseByVerse.quote: who devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who devour widows’ houses and for a pretence make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.

Who devour widows’ houses. The register changes completely. Long robes and good seats are vanity; this is predation. How did scribes devour widows’ houses? Scripture does not say, and several means were available in that world. Scribes were not supposed to charge for teaching the law, and so depended on the hospitality and gifts of the devout, of whom widows were a notably generous group. A scribe might be appointed to manage a widow’s estate and take a fee from it, or manage it dishonestly. He might accept board and lodging from a woman who could not afford it. He might simply encourage a level of giving that ruined her. What all of these have in common is that none is illegal. They are the abuse of religious standing to extract money from people who trusted the standing.

The most vulnerable. And the victims are chosen with care. Widows in that society had no earning power, little legal protection and nobody to complain to. God’s law had singled them out for special protection for that very reason: you shall not mistreat any widow or fatherless child; if you do mistreat them, my wrath will burn (Exodus 22:22–24). The prophets returned to it constantly. And these are the men entrusted with teaching that law.

And for a pretense make long prayers. The two halves belong together, which is the horror of the verse. The long prayers are not a separate failing; they are the instrument. The reputation for piety is what gets a man access to a widow’s confidence and her accounts. The prayer is the cover for the theft: long public prayers to appear holy, while robbing the defenceless.

They will receive the greater condemnation. The principle has run through this Gospel since chapter twelve: everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required (12:47–48). The sentence is heavier because the position was higher, the knowledge greater, and the trust betrayed deeper, and because they used religion to cover their sin. Not many of you should become teachers, James warns, for we who teach will be judged with greater strictness (James 3:1). There are degrees of punishment as there are degrees of reward, and Scripture reserves its severest language for those who use the things of God to get things from people.

The link. Luke sets the next scene immediately: a poor widow at the treasury, putting in everything she had (21:1–4). She may well have been one of the victims of such men. The chapter that began with the leaders questioning Christ’s authority ends with Christ exposing theirs, and the next scene shows whose side he is on.

What if this has happened in my church? Then it must be named and dealt with, not hidden. When a leader has used his position to exploit the vulnerable, whether financially, emotionally or sexually, the church’s duty is to protect the victims, tell the truth, involve the civil authorities where the law has been broken, and remove the offender from leadership (1 Timothy 5:19–21). Protecting the institution’s reputation at the victims’ expense is to repeat the scribes’ sin. And if you have been harmed by someone who used God’s name to do it, know that Christ is not on their side. He saw the widows, and he warned the whole temple about the men who devoured them.

In a sentence. The scribes exploit widows and pray long prayers for show, and will receive greater condemnation.

On a Tuesday. Never use religion to cover selfishness. God sees and will judge. Ask whether there is any place where your reputation for being a Christian gives you an advantage over someone weaker: an elderly relative’s finances, an employee who trusts you, a friend who defers to you. Handle it as before God. And look out for the widows of your church: visit, help with practical needs, make sure no one is exploiting them.

For worship. God is the defender of widows and the father of the fatherless (Psalm 68:5), and his Son stood in the temple courts and took their side against the most respected men in the nation. He sees every hidden injustice, and he will right it. And he is the true High Priest, who does not devour the houses of the poor but gave his own life for them, and whose prayers for his people are never a pretence (Hebrews 7:25).

parallels.desc: you shall not mistreat any widow

20.text: <sup>1</sup> One day, as Jesus was teaching the people in the temple and preaching the gospel, the chief priests and the scribes with the elders came up <sup>2</sup> and said to him, “Tell us by what authority you do these things, or who it is that gave you this authority.” <sup>3</sup> He answered them, “I also will ask you a question. Now tell me, <sup>4</sup> was the baptism of John from heaven or from man?” <sup>5</sup> And they discussed it with one another, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why did you not believe him?’ <sup>6</sup> But if we say, ‘From man,’ all the people will stone us to death, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.” <sup>7</sup> So they answered that they did not know where it came from. <sup>8</sup> And Jesus said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.” <sup>9</sup> And he began to tell the people this parable: “A man planted a vineyard and let it out to tenants and went into another country for a long while. <sup>10</sup> When the time came, he sent a servant to the tenants, so that they would give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed. <sup>11</sup> And he sent another servant. But they also beat and treated him shamefully, and sent him away empty-handed. <sup>12</sup> And he sent yet a third. This one also they wounded and cast out. <sup>13</sup> Then the owner of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.’ <sup>14</sup> But when the tenants saw him, they said to themselves, ‘This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours.’ <sup>15</sup> And they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them? <sup>16</sup> He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.” When they heard this, they said, “Surely not!” <sup>17</sup> But he looked directly at them and said, “What then is this that is written: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’? <sup>18</sup> Everyone who falls on that stone will be broken to pieces, and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.” <sup>19</sup> The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very hour, for they perceived that he had told this parable against them, but they feared the people. <sup>20</sup> So they watched him and sent spies, who pretended to be sincere, that they might catch him in something he said, so as to deliver him up to the authority and jurisdiction of the governor. <sup>21</sup> So they asked him, “Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and show no partiality, but truly teach the way of God. <sup>22</sup> Is it lawful for us to give tribute to Caesar, or not?” <sup>23</sup> But he perceived their craftiness, and said to them, <sup>24</sup> “Show me a denarius. Whose likeness and inscription does it have?” They said, “Caesar's.” <sup>25</sup> He said to them, “Then render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's.” <sup>26</sup> And they were not able in the presence of the people to catch him in what he said, but marveling at his answer they became silent. <sup>27</sup> There came to him some Sadducees, those who deny that there is a resurrection, <sup>28</sup> and they asked him a question, saying, “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man's brother dies, having a wife but no children, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. <sup>29</sup> Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife, and died without children. <sup>30</sup> And the second <sup>31</sup> and the third took her, and likewise all seven left no children and died. <sup>32</sup> Afterward the woman also died. <sup>33</sup> In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife will the woman be? For the seven had her as wife.” <sup>34</sup> And Jesus said to them, “The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage, <sup>35</sup> but those who are considered worthy to attain to that age and to the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, <sup>36</sup> for they cannot die anymore, because they are equal to angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection. <sup>37</sup> But that the dead are raised, even Moses showed, in the passage about the bush, where he calls the Lord the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob. <sup>38</sup> Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him.” <sup>39</sup> Then some of the scribes answered, “Teacher, you have spoken well.” <sup>40</sup> For they no longer dared to ask him any question. <sup>41</sup> But he said to them, “How can they say that the Christ is David's son? <sup>42</sup> For David himself says in the Book of Psalms, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, <sup>43</sup> until I make your enemies your footstool.’ <sup>44</sup> David thus calls him Lord, so how is he his son?” <sup>45</sup> And in the hearing of all the people he said to his disciples, <sup>46</sup> “Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes, and love greetings in the marketplaces and the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts, <sup>47</sup> who devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.”

21.title: The Widow's Offering and the Olivet Discourse
21.overview:
Luke 21 opens with a scene that provides the perfect contrast to the scribes condemned at the end of chapter 20: a widow who puts into the temple treasury two small copper coins — “everything she had to live on.” Then, as Jesus leaves the temple and a disciple admires its magnificent stones, he delivers the Olivet Discourse — his most extended eschatological teaching, covering the destruction of Jerusalem, the sufferings of the disciples, the fall of the city, and the coming of the Son of Man.

The Olivet Discourse in Luke (parallel to Matthew 24 and Mark 13) is notable for several features. Luke emphasises the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 more explicitly than the other Gospels, and the discourse includes several passages that apply specifically to that historical event. At the same time, the coming of the Son of Man in glory transcends any single historical event — it is the final, universal, unmistakable arrival of the Kingdom in its fullness.

The chapter closes with a pattern that defines the final days of Jesus's ministry: he teaches in the temple by day; the people come early to hear him; at night he goes out to the Mount of Olives. This is the rhythm of the last week — teaching, opposition, and solitary prayer, all moving toward the cross.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Chapter 20 ended with Jesus warning about scribes who devour widows’ houses and for a pretence make long prayers. Chapter 21 opens with a widow whose house has been devoured, giving away the last of it. Luke has put the two paragraphs side by side on purpose.

Jesus is sitting in the Court of the Women, where thirteen trumpet-mouthed chests stood against the wall, built so that a coin rang all the way down. He looks up and watches the rich putting in their gifts — nothing is said against them, and nothing should be read in. Then he sees a poor widow put in two lepta, the smallest coin minted, together worth about a sixty-fourth of a day’s wage.

His verdict is that she has put in more than all of them, and the reason he gives is arithmetical: they gave out of their abundance, their overflow, what they would not miss; she gave out of her poverty, and she gave all she had to live on. The measure is not the size of the gift but the size of what remains.

There is a real difficulty in the sequence, and it is worth facing rather than smoothing over. Jesus has just condemned the men who run this temple, and five verses later he will say the building is coming down to the last stone. Is he praising a woman for handing her last coin to a doomed and corrupt institution? Some read the passage as a lament rather than a commendation. But his own words settle it — this poor widow has put in more than all of them is praise, not mourning. He is not endorsing the temple. He is telling us what God saw at the treasury.

Which is the comfort in it for every believer who has given, served and poured out small resources inside a church that was flawed, or failing, or would not outlast them. The worth of the gift was never in the soundness of the institution that received it.
verseByVerse.theology:
This is the divine valuation of giving, and it runs on a different ledger from ours. The rich men’s gifts are not condemned; they are revalued. What looked large is revealed to be cheap, and what looked negligible is revealed to be everything, because heaven measures the cost to the giver and not the benefit to the fund.

Behind that lies a deeper principle: God does not need our money. The temple did not stand or fall on the widow’s two coins, and the kingdom does not advance on donations. What God seeks in giving is the giver — which is why proportion tells the truth about a heart and totals do not.

And the scene is a small portrait of the cross, days before it. She gave her whole livelihood; he was about to give his whole life. She trusted God for the next meal with nothing left in reserve; he would go into the dark with nothing held back either. Complete self-giving is not a heroic exception in the kingdom of God. It is the shape of the King.
verseByVerse.examples:
The test in v. 1 is easy to run and hard to survive. Think of the last thing you gave to God’s work, and ask not how much it was but what you went without because of it. If nothing in the month changed, the answer has already been given.

A church announces the total of a giving campaign with celebration — a large figure, mostly from prosperous members. The pastor privately knows the costliest single gift came from a widow on a fixed income who gave her entire discretionary fund for the month. He has to decide whether the celebration names the total or the sacrifice, and this passage tells him which one heaven has already recorded.

And for anyone whose giving is small: she is remembered in every language on earth two thousand years later, and the names of the wealthy donors that morning are gone without trace — because the Lord noticed, and said so. Nothing done for him is unwitnessed.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus looked up and saw the rich putting their gifts into the offering box,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus looked up and saw the rich putting their gifts into the offering box.

Meaning first. Luke 21 is Jesus’ last public teaching before the cross, given in the temple. A poor widow puts two tiny coins into the treasury, and Jesus says she has given more than all the rich (vv. 1–4). When some admire the temple, he foretells its destruction, and his answer to their question gives no date (vv. 5–7). He warns against false messiahs and against panic at wars and disasters, and promises words, wisdom and safety under persecution (vv. 8–19). He foretells the fall of Jerusalem, which came in AD 70 (vv. 20–24), and beyond it his visible return in glory, when his people will lift up their heads (vv. 25–28). He ends with a call to watch and pray (vv. 29–38). Luke carefully distinguishes the fall of Jerusalem from the coming of the Son of Man, with the times of the Gentiles between them.

The link. Straight after the warning about scribes who devour widows’ houses (20:47), Jesus sees a widow. Luke puts the two scenes side by side on purpose. The men who loved the best seats are condemned; the woman nobody noticed is praised.

Jesus looked up and saw the rich putting their gifts into the offering box. Mark tells us he was sitting opposite it (Mark 12:41), and he had been teaching in the temple every day that week (v. 37). The offering box was probably one of the collection chests in the Court of the Women, the large paved court that ordinary Israelites could enter. Around its walls stood thirteen chests, shaped like trumpets, narrow at the mouth and widening below, so that a coin dropped in rang all the way down. A small gift made a small sound; a handful of silver made a noise the whole court could hear. And the rich are walking past, and it is ringing.

He looked up. Luke says it deliberately. Jesus is not glancing about; he stops what he is doing to watch what people put in. That is the fact that gives the whole scene its weight. The offering is observed. Not audited: observed. There is Someone at the treasury whose interest is not in the total. He watches how people give. He still does.

The Lord who came to his temple. Malachi had promised that the Lord whom Israel sought would suddenly come to his temple, and that he would come as a refiner of silver, purifying the priests until they brought offerings in righteousness (Malachi 3:1–3). Luke has already told us who the messenger sent before him was (7:27). So the man watching the offering chests is not a visitor with opinions about stewardship. He is the Lord of the house, come to his own temple as the refiner, testing what is brought into it. The rich are weighed and the widow is weighed, and his verdict, in the next breath, will overturn every reckoning the court has made.

Nothing is said against the rich. Their gifts were real, and the temple ran on them. Jesus does not call them hypocrites or say a word to them at all. His reckoning will not be a rebuke of their giving but a revaluation of it, and that is the more searching thing. It is easy to guard against hypocrisy; you know when you are performing. It is much harder to discover that a gift made in good faith was, on the ledger that finally matters, worth very little, because it cost you nothing.

In a sentence. Jesus looked up and watched the rich putting their gifts into the temple offering chests.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last thing you gave to God’s work, and ask not how much it was but what you went without because of it. If the standing order leaves and the month proceeds exactly as it would have done anyway, you have learned what heaven saw when your coin rang in the trumpet. The Lord looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7).

For worship. The chests were built to ring, and the rich made them ring. Above the noise was the One whose ear is not tuned to the sound of silver. He is the Lord of the temple and the owner of every coin in it, and still he stoops to weigh what each hand lets go. Nothing given to him is lost in the din, and nothing loud impresses him. Blessed is the refiner who sees through the gleam to the heart, who weighs us truly, and who then gives himself to make us pure.
verseByVerse.note: The offering box was probably one of the collection chests in the Court of the Women.

verseByVerse.quote: and he saw a poor widow put in two small copper coins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he saw a poor widow put in two small copper coins.

And he saw a poor widow. Poor is penichran: needy, of very little means. And Luke says he saw her. That is the second time in two verses that the verb is one of sight, and it is the hinge of the paragraph. It is a small sentence with a great deal behind it. In a crowded court, in the loudest week of the religious year, with the wealth of Jerusalem filing past a row of collection chests, the eye of the Son of God rested on a woman nobody was looking at, holding a sum nobody would have counted, and it stayed there.

A widow. In that economy the word described destitution, not merely bereavement: no husband and so no wage, little legal standing, no way of earning beyond gleaning and charity. The law had commanded Israel to care for her (Deuteronomy 14:29; 24:19), and Jesus had just said what the religious establishment actually did with women like her: it devoured their houses (20:47). She may well have been one of its victims. She is the wronged party in the very institution she is about to fund.

Put in two small copper coins. The coin was the lepton, the smallest in circulation, a tiny copper coin worth about a hundred and twenty-eighth of a denarius. Two of them together came to perhaps a sixty-fourth of a day’s wage. In a trumpet-mouthed chest they would have made almost no sound at all: a tap, and then nothing. She could have kept one. She gave both, walking up in the same queue as the men with the silver.

The widow at Zarephath. Jesus himself had preached on her at Nazareth: of all the widows in Israel in Elijah’s time, the prophet was sent to one in Zarephath (4:25–26). She gave him the last of her flour and oil before feeding herself, and the jar did not run dry (1 Kings 17:12–16). Now one greater than Elijah stands in the temple, and again the eye of heaven passes over the great and rests on a widow. The sermon that nearly had him thrown from a cliff is being lived out in the Court of the Women. His mission, from Nazareth to the treasury, has always moved towards the overlooked.

Does God really notice small things? Yes, and this verse is the proof. Jesus noticed two coins worth almost nothing, in a crowd, in the week of his death. He says the very hairs of your head are numbered (12:7), and a cup of cold water given in his name will not lose its reward (Matthew 10:42). So the small, hidden faithfulness of an ordinary life is not wasted: the prayer no one hears, the care of an elderly parent, the coins given from a pension. He sees it. Because he spoke about her, this woman is known in every language on earth, while the names of that morning’s wealthy donors are gone without trace.

In a sentence. Jesus saw a poor widow put in two tiny copper coins.

On a Tuesday. No gift is too small to be seen by God. If you have little to give, money, time or strength, give it anyway and do not be ashamed. And look around your church for the poor widows: the people who give quietly out of very little, whom no one thanks. Thank them, and help them, and make sure no one is taking advantage of them.

For worship. The Lord of glory, days from the cross, with the weight of the world’s sin pressing on him, was watching a poor woman drop two thin coins into a box. He was not too preoccupied, and he was not too exalted. That is the eye that is on his people. Nothing done for him is unwitnessed, and nothing witnessed by him is small.
verseByVerse.note: Her two coins were the smallest in circulation, a tiny fraction of a day’s wage.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, 'Truly, I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty put in all she had to live on.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said: truly, I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty put in all she had to live on.

Truly, I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them. More than all the rich together. God measures not the amount but the cost and the heart. By heaven’s arithmetic she has given more than all the wealthy donors combined, because the measure is not the size of the gift but the size of the trust.

For they all contributed out of their abundance. The Greek word behind abundance is perisseuontos: their overflow, what was extra, what they would not miss. From their surplus.

But she out of her poverty put in all she had to live on. The widow gives from her hysterēmatos: her lack, her deficit, the thing she cannot spare. All she had to live on is literally her whole life, her whole livelihood. She trusted God for her next meal. It is an act of utter abandonment to God’s provision. She loved God with all her strength (10:27). And she pictures what Jesus is about to do in a few days: give his whole life. She who gives everything at the treasury points to him who will give everything on Golgotha.

Where Christians differ: praise or lament? The arrangement of Luke’s text raises a real question. Only a few verses earlier Jesus condemned the scribes who devour widows’ houses (20:47); a few verses later he says the temple whose treasury she is filling will be torn down to the last stone (21:6). So some readers conclude that Jesus is not praising her at all but lamenting her, mourning a religious system that has taught a penniless widow to give away her last means of living. It is an honest reading, and the sequence that suggests it is not accidental. Verdict: as in Mark’s account (Mark 12:43–44), the context of corruption is real (20:47; 21:6), but Jesus’ words are clearly praise of her faith and devotion. This poor widow has put in more than all of them is commendation. He is not endorsing the temple, and he is not saying her coins repaired anything; within a generation the whole apparatus would be ash. He is telling us what God saw at that treasury: not the sums, but a heart holding nothing back. The worth of her gift was never in the soundness of the institution that received it. It was in the trust of the one who gave it, and God received it even though the building it was dropped into was under sentence. That is a mercy for everyone who has given and served inside a church that was flawed or failing or would not outlast them.

Does Jesus mean that every believer should give away everything? No. He commends her trust and her gift; he does not command everyone to give away all they live on. Paul says a gift is acceptable according to what a person has (2 Corinthians 8:12), and a believer must provide for his own household (1 Timothy 5:8). And no church may press the poor to give beyond their means; Jesus has just condemned those who devour widows’ houses (20:47). What he does ask of everyone is what she showed: a heart that trusts God more than money, and a gift that costs something.

How much should I give? The New Testament gives no fixed percentage, but it gives clear principles. Set something aside regularly, in keeping with your income (1 Corinthians 16:2). Give generously, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:6–7). Give first, not from what is left over. Many Christians find the Old Testament tithe, a tenth, a helpful starting point, and many in comfortable circumstances give more. The widow’s question is not what is the least I must give? but what does it cost me to trust God here? Start where you are, and let your giving grow as your trust grows.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that the widow had given more than all the rich, because they gave from abundance and she gave all she had to live on.

On a Tuesday. Does your giving cost you? Look at your bank statement this month and ask what it says about where your trust lies. If your giving would not change your life at all, consider one step that would: a regular gift you will feel, a cut in some comfort to support a missionary, a gift to a struggling believer. Give as an act of trust and worship, and see whether God lets the jar run dry.

For worship. The rich gave out of their abundance and the widow out of her poverty. Christ alone gave out of both. Out of the infinite riches of the Son of God he gave, and what he gave was not a portion of his wealth but his very self, until nothing was kept back. Her two coins outweighed the silver of Jerusalem; his one offering outweighs the sins of a multitude no one can number. He emptied himself to make beggars heirs, and every gift his people bring is a coin from his own treasury, given back.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–19 — The Temple, the Signs, and the Cost of Witness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Someone admires the temple — the noble stones and the offerings fixed to its walls — and it was worth admiring: white limestone blocks over forty feet long, a gold-plated front that Josephus says a man could not look at in the morning sun, a golden vine over the entrance with clusters the height of a man. Jesus replies that not one stone will be left on another. In the year 70 Titus besieged the city, the temple burned, and soldiers levered the stones apart to get at the gold that had run molten into the joints.

The disciples ask the natural question — when, and what sign? He never answers it. What he gives instead is a series of instructions for living in the meantime.

First, do not be led astray: many will come claiming to be the one, and many more will announce that the time is at hand. Second, when you hear of wars and tumults, do not be terrified — these things must happen, and the end will not be at once. Third, the ordinary catastrophes of history — nation against nation, earthquake, famine, pestilence, terrors from heaven — are the weather of this long age, not the signal that it is over.

Then the turn that dominates the section: but before all this. Before any of the cosmic disturbances, the disciples themselves will be seized, delivered to synagogues and prisons, and brought before kings and governors. Luke’s second volume then records every item happening in order — Acts 4:3, 9:2, 5:18, 24, 25, 26.

And that, Jesus says, is their opportunity to bear witness. They are not to rehearse a defence; he will give them a mouth and wisdom their adversaries cannot withstand — a promise Luke shows kept, in the same vocabulary, when Stephen’s opponents could not withstand the wisdom with which he spoke (Acts 6:10).

The cost is named without softening: betrayal by parents, brothers, relatives and friends; some put to death; hatred from all for his name’s sake. And then, two verses after saying some of them will be killed, he says not a hair of their heads will perish, and that by endurance they will gain their lives.
verseByVerse.theology:
The apparent contradiction between v. 16 and v. 18 is the theological centre of the section, and it is not a contradiction. Not a hair of your head is a Hebrew idiom for total preservation, and Jesus has already used it in this Gospel in exactly this setting (12:7). What enemies can do to a believer is real and can be final in every visible respect, and it cannot reach the person himself. Stephen was stoned, and not a hair of his head perished.
