This is providence applied to persecution. The disciple is not promised safety; he is promised supply — words when words are needed — and security that no execution can touch. Endurance is remaining under. It is not gritted teeth or heroic reserves; it is staying at the post today, on grace that arrives daily and never in advance.

Note also the qualifier attached twice to the suffering: for my name’s sake. Not every kind of unpopularity a Christian achieves is covered by these promises. The test is whether the hostility would disappear if the name of Christ were subtracted from the situation.
verseByVerse.examples:
A believer in a country where conversion is punishable by imprisonment reads vv. 12–19 and finds that Jesus does not promise he will avoid arrest. He explicitly promises the opposite, and then promises something more reliable than safety: words at the moment they are needed, and a life that cannot finally be taken.

For readers who will never see a courtroom, the principle needs no handcuffs. The awkward silence after you said where you were on Sunday, the promotion that went elsewhere, the family meal that went quiet — those feel like loss and are being counted as testimony, because a watching colleague learns more from what your faith costs you than from anything you could say when it was free.

Verse 15 also answers a common anxiety that has nothing to do with persecution: the dread of the question at work, the thirty seconds at the kitchen table, the lying awake afterwards composing what you should have said. Settle it therefore in your minds is a phrase about laying something down. The rehearsal was never the preparation; it was the anxiety.

And for those whose faith has cost them a family: it was foreseen, it was foretold, and the one who foretold it had brothers who did not believe in him either. The promise attached to it in this Gospel is not replacement but enlargement — many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life (18:29–30).

verseByVerse.quote: And while some were speaking of the temple, how it was adorned with noble stones and offerings, he said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
While some were speaking of the temple, how it was adorned with noble stones and offerings, he said:

The Olivet Discourse. Here begins Luke’s version of Jesus’ teaching about the future (Mark 13; Matthew 24). In Luke it is spoken in the temple (vv. 5, 37). It answers two questions: when will the temple be destroyed, and what will happen at the end? Luke is especially clear in distinguishing the fall of Jerusalem (vv. 20–24) from the coming of the Son of Man (vv. 25–28), with the times of the Gentiles between them (v. 24).

And while some were speaking of the temple, how it was adorned with noble stones. They were not being foolish. The temple Herod built was one of the wonders of the ancient world, and everyone who saw it said so. Herod the Great had rebuilt it on a vast scale. Josephus, who had stood in it, describes its stones as white and strong, and some foundation stones still in place today are over forty feet long and weigh hundreds of tons. The front was plated with gold, and Josephus says that when the morning sun struck it a man had to look away, and that from a distance the building looked like a mountain covered with snow.

And offerings. Votive gifts dedicated to God and displayed. Over the entrance hung a golden vine, with clusters of grapes said to be as tall as a man, added to cluster by cluster by worshippers as offerings. The temple had been under construction for forty-six years by the first Passover of his ministry (John 2:20). It was completed in the early sixties, and within a few years of completion it was gone.

Admiration is not idolatry. This is the admiration any of us would have felt: men from the country standing in the most impressive building they had ever seen. The thing admired was genuinely magnificent, genuinely God-ordained and genuinely doomed, and nothing in the stonework told them which of the three was about to matter.

The temple of the LORD. Jeremiah had met the same instinct six hundred years earlier and named it exactly. God told him to stand in the gate and say to the people coming to worship: do not trust in these deceptive words, this is the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD (Jeremiah 7:4). They were not chanting a lie. It was the temple of the LORD. They were resting on a building instead of on the One who had asked for it, which is a different sin and much harder to see in yourself.

The glory of this latter house. When this second temple was first rebuilt, the old men who remembered Solomon’s wept (Ezra 3:12), and God answered through Haggai that the latter glory of this house would be greater than the former (Haggai 2:9). Herod’s gold never made that true. What made it true was a child forty days old carried up its steps and taken into an old man’s arms as God’s salvation (2:22–32), a boy of twelve calling it his Father’s house (2:49), and now a man teaching in its courts day after day. The disciples are admiring the frame while the picture stands beside them. The glory Haggai promised has come, and the stones they praise will soon have nothing left to do.

Is it wrong to love a beautiful church building? No. Beauty is God’s gift, and the tabernacle and temple were made beautiful at his command (Exodus 28:2; 1 Chronicles 22:5). Caring for a building where God’s people gather is good stewardship. The danger is trusting in it, or in any institution: assuming that because the building, the denomination or the tradition is old and impressive, God must be pleased with what happens inside it. The church is not the building. It is the people of God gathered around Christ, and that church will survive any building’s fall.

In a sentence. When some people were admiring how the temple was decorated with beautiful stones and gifts, Jesus spoke.

On a Tuesday. Take the nearest thing: the church you attend, the denomination you trust, the institution whose survival you quietly assume. Ask what would remain of your faith if it were gone. That is not cynicism. It is the question Jesus is about to put to the men beside him, because in forty years they will need to have been asked it already.

For worship. Over the temple door hung a golden vine, and worshippers added golden grapes to it, gift by gift, for generations. It was a fitting emblem, for Israel was the vine God brought out of Egypt and planted (Psalm 80:8). The true Vine (John 15:1) walked beneath it that week, unadorned, and in a few days he would be cut down. Yet from him, and not from the gold, grows the fruit God sought in every age: branches joined to him, living, bearing fruit that no Roman torch can reach. Glory belongs to the Vine, and every cluster is his.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great had rebuilt the temple on a vast scale, with gleaming white stone and gifts displayed by donors.

verseByVerse.quote: 'As for these things that you see, the days will come when there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for these things that you see, the days will come when there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.

As for these things that you see, the days will come. A prophetic formula of judgment, the language of Jeremiah and Amos. He points at the most permanent things in their world and puts a term on them.

When there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down. It is hard to overstate how violent this sentence sounded: this was the one place on earth where sacrifice could lawfully be offered, where sin was dealt with, where God had put his name. To say the temple would fall was to say that the whole system of Israel’s approach to God was coming to an end. Men had been threatened with death for saying less. Jeremiah was nearly killed for it (Jeremiah 26:8–11), and a version of a saying about the temple would be brought against Jesus at his own trial (Mark 14:58).

The fulfilment. About forty years later, in AD 70, Titus besieged Jerusalem through spring and summer; the city fell and the temple burned. Josephus, who was in the Roman camp, says Titus tried in vain to stop the fire. The great platform survived, including the Western Wall that pilgrims visit today, but that wall belongs to the platform, not the sanctuary. Of the sanctuary itself, exactly what Jesus said is what is there: nothing.

Was this prophecy written after the event? Some scholars argue that Luke must have written after AD 70 and shaped the saying to fit. It is worth meeting rather than dodging. Many conservative scholars note that Acts, Luke’s second volume, ends with Paul alive in Rome, and says nothing about the fall of Jerusalem, the death of Paul or the death of James, events a Christian historian writing later would have been unlikely to leave out of a history of the early church. And the prediction is not detailed in the way invented prophecy tends to be; it does not mention the fire. But the deeper answer is simpler. Jesus is the Son of God, and the God who declares the end from the beginning (Isaiah 46:10) is able to tell his servants what will happen.

The perishable and the imperishable. What Jesus does say is worth hearing as the men in the courtyard heard it. He looks at the most permanent thing in their world and puts a date on it. Everything they could see, weigh and lean on had a term, and he knew what it was. He will say the counterpart to this later in the chapter: heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away (v. 33). Between those two sentences the whole discourse is held. The visible is perishable and the spoken word of Christ is not, which is the exact reverse of how the world grades reality (Isaiah 40:8).

Why did God allow his own temple to be destroyed? Because its work was done. The temple was a shadow; Christ is the substance. He is the true temple, where God dwells with man (John 2:19–21), and his death is the one sacrifice to which all the temple’s sacrifices pointed (Hebrews 9:11–12; 10:11–14). When the veil was torn at his death (23:45), the old way was finished. The fall of the temple in AD 70 was also a judgment on the generation that rejected the Messiah (19:41–44). After that, no one could imagine that animal sacrifices were still the way to God. There is one way now, and it is open to every nation: Jesus himself.

In a sentence. Jesus predicted that the day would come when not one stone of the temple would be left on another.

On a Tuesday. The most magnificent human works will pass away: buildings, careers, reputations, nations, savings. Build on what cannot be shaken (Hebrews 12:27–28). Look at what you are most proud of, or most anxious to protect, and ask how it will look in a hundred years. Then invest something this week in what will last: the word of God, the souls of people, the kingdom of Christ.

For worship. Not one stone was left on another, and not one of his words has fallen to the ground. The prophet who pronounced the temple’s end was himself the temple God had always meant: thrown down at Golgotha, raised on the third day, standing now where no army can lay siege. The house of stone kept worshippers at a distance behind a curtain; the house of his body opens the way into the holiest for everyone who comes in his name. The sanctuary on Mount Zion is gone, and the true Sanctuary reigns.
verseByVerse.note: The Romans destroyed the temple in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: And they asked him, 'Teacher, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when these things are about to take place?' And he said, 'See that you are not led astray. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he!’ and, ‘The time is at hand!’ Do not go after them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They asked him: Teacher, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when these things are about to take place? And he said: see that you are not led astray. For many will come in my name, saying, I am he! and, the time is at hand! Do not go after them.

And they asked him, Teacher, when will these things be? Two questions, and both are about timing: when, and how will we know it is close. In Luke, the question is specifically about the temple’s destruction. It is the most natural response in the world, and it is what any of us would have asked.

And what will be the sign when these things are about to take place? Notice what he does not do. He does not give a date. Not here, and in Luke not anywhere: there is no date in this chapter, and no formula for calculating one. What he gives instead is a series of instructions about how to live in the meantime, and the very first is a warning about people who will answer the question he has just declined to answer.

See that you are not led astray. Jesus’ first concern is not a timetable but protection from deception. The verb is planaō, from which comes the English planet, the wandering star, the light that does not keep its place among the fixed ones. To be led astray is not to be argued out of the faith by an opponent. It is to drift off course while still believing you are travelling in a straight line.

For many will come in my name, saying, I am he! Claiming to be the Messiah, or taking to themselves the divine name. Acts and Josephus both record such men in the decades that followed, and every century since has had them.

The name worth stealing. Counterfeiters copy only what is valuable. No one forges a worthless coin, and no one comes in a nobody’s name. That false christs would arise for centuries, all borrowing his title, is itself a testimony to the One they imitate. Peter has already confessed who the true one is: the Christ of God (9:20). And within days, before the council, Jesus will answer the question himself: you say that I am (22:70). Every impostor must claim what Jesus simply is, and must keep claiming it, because it was never his. The test of every voice is whether it points away from itself to him.

And, The time is at hand! Only Luke adds this. False prophets announcing that the end is about to come. These are two different claims. The first is a claim about a person: someone stands up and says he is the one. The second is a claim about a clock: someone announces that the hour has arrived. A great many people who would never make the first claim make the second every decade, and Jesus puts them in the same warning.

Do not go after them. The history of the church is littered with the wreckage of announced dates, and the wreckage is always made of people: farms sold, savings given away, and then the morning after, when the sun came up as usual. Every one of those movements was led by someone quoting this very chapter.

How can an ordinary Christian tell whether a teacher is leading people astray? Jesus gives the test in the sentence itself, and it is beautifully simple: do not go after them. Watch where the teaching takes the people who follow it. Teaching from God sends a person back to ordinary obedience: his work, his family, his prayers, his neighbour, his local church, and above all to Christ himself. Teaching that leads astray gathers a following around a teacher, doing something exceptional at his direction, on a timetable he supplies. Test every spirit (1 John 4:1). The mark of the false is that it makes you dependent on a man who claims to know something Christ declined to tell you (Acts 1:7).

In a sentence. Asked when the temple would fall and what sign would come first, Jesus warned them not to be deceived by false messiahs or by people claiming the end was at hand.

On a Tuesday. Ignore anyone who claims to know the date of the end. Jesus warned against them. If a book, video or preacher you follow keeps announcing that the end is about to come, at a particular date or through a particular event, put it down. And if you are anxious after reading such things, return to Jesus’ own words: no date, no panic, and faithful work while you wait.

For worship. Christ is the faithful shepherd who warns his sheep before the wolves come. He does not leave his people to the mercy of every voice that claims his name. He has told us beforehand. And he himself is the fixed star by which every wandering light is judged, the same yesterday and today and for ever (Hebrews 13:8).

verseByVerse.quote: And when you hear of wars and tumults, do not be terrified, for these things must first take place, but the end will not be at once.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when you hear of wars and tumults, do not be terrified, for these things must first take place, but the end will not be at once.

And when you hear of wars and tumults. Take the verbs in order, because the pastoral care in this verse is in the sequence. When you hear: not when you suffer, but when you hear. Jesus is speaking about the effect on the soul of news from elsewhere: the report of a war in a country you will never visit, the account of an uprising among people you have never met. He knew, twenty centuries before the phone on the bedside table, that a person can be crushed by events that are not happening to him. Tumults is akatastasias: revolutions, disorder, the breaking up of settled things.

Do not be terrified. Not ordinary fear, but being startled out of your senses, the panic of a flushed bird, the mind scattering. He is not forbidding grief, and he is not forbidding concern; the man who reads of a famine and feels nothing has a worse problem than anxiety. He is forbidding the state in which fear has taken over the controls. Wars are not signs that the end has come.

For these things must first take place. Must is dei, Luke’s word for the settled purpose of God, the very word Jesus used of his own suffering: the Son of Man must suffer many things (9:22). He puts the same word under the wars. They are inside the plan, not outside it: not caused by God in the way that good is caused by him, but not loose either. And the cross shows what that word means in God’s mouth. The worst thing men ever did was also a must, and it became the salvation of the world (24:26). The One who says the wars must come is the One who set his face to go to Jerusalem because he must, and the hands that hold the plan were pierced for those who live through it.

But the end will not be at once. This sentence removes what makes catastrophic news unbearable. What crushes a person watching the world convulse is the conclusion drawn from it: that history is unravelling and there is nothing after this. Jesus flatly denies the inference. Wars are the weather of a long age, and he says so in advance so that nobody has to work it out during the storm.

What should I do when the news frightens me? Not look away, but refuse the false interpretation. When the headline arrives, the question is not is this the end? He has told you it is not. The smaller and more answerable question is: what does love require of me today, in this street, with this news in my head? Pray for the people in it, by name if you can. Give if you can. Then do your work and go to bed. And limit what you take in: no one is helped by a mind fed with disaster every hour. God is our refuge and strength, therefore we will not fear though the earth gives way (Psalm 46:1–2).

In a sentence. When they heard of wars and revolutions, they were not to be terrified, for these must happen first, but the end would not come at once.

On a Tuesday. Notice this week how much news you consume and what it does to you. Turn one anxious moment into a prayer for the people affected, and then turn back to the task in front of you. That is faith, not denial.

For worship. The news arrives faster now and from further away, but it never arrives first at his throne. He heard every rumour of war before it was spoken, and he told his friends of it before it came, so that their hearts would be held when it did. He is not the anxious watcher of a world coming apart. He upholds all things by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3), he has told his people how the story ends, and his voice, not the headline, has the last word over the night.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to them, 'Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be great earthquakes, and in various places famines and pestilences. And there will be terrors and great signs from heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he said to them: nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be great earthquakes, and in various places famines and pestilences. And there will be terrors and great signs from heaven.

Then he said to them, Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. Wars on a large scale. Four categories follow, and between them they cover everything that can go wrong on a planet. War, which men cause. Earthquake, which nobody causes. Famine and plague, which are often both: a failed harvest made deadly by somebody’s decisions. And then the sky.

There will be great earthquakes, and in various places famines and pestilences. Pestilences are plagues and epidemics, and only Luke includes them. There was a severe famine under the emperor Claudius in the forties, which Luke himself records (Acts 11:28), and major earthquakes in the sixties. But these have marked every generation since. They are the beginning of the birth pains (Mark 13:8), not signs of a specific date.

And there will be terrors and great signs from heaven. Only Luke has this. Josephus records strange portents before the fall of Jerusalem: a star like a sword over the city, a comet, visions of armies in the sky, the great eastern gate of the temple opening by itself at night.

Not signs of the end. The list is so vivid that the main point is easy to miss. Jesus is not giving signs of the end here. He has just said the opposite: these things must happen, and the end will not be at once (v. 9). He is describing the ordinary content of the long age between his ascension and his return, in advance, so that his people will not misread it. Not one item on the list is unprecedented.

The temptation every generation has felt. The plague years of the fourteenth century produced a certainty that the end had come. So did the wars of the twentieth century, and so does whatever is on the news this month. A man who thinks he is watching the last act does not plant trees. Jesus takes the false interpretation away as a kindness.

The Lord of everything on the list. Read the list against the Gospel Luke has already written. The man who speaks of earthquakes and terrors is the one who rebuked the wind and the raging waves until there was a calm (8:24). The one who speaks of famine fed five thousand in a desolate place with five loaves (9:12–17). The one who speaks of plagues laid his hands on the sick of every kind and healed them (4:40). Every disaster he names is a territory he has already entered as its master. He does not foretell these things as a spectator, and none of them is a coded message about the date. He foretells them as the Lord who will one day end each of them for good.

Why does God allow earthquakes, famines and plagues? Scripture does not give a full answer, but it gives enough to trust him. These things are the fruit of a world under the curse of sin (Genesis 3:17–19; Romans 8:20–22), not usually the punishment of particular sufferers for particular sins (13:1–5). They are warnings that this world is not our home and that judgment is coming, calling all people to repentance. And God is not absent from them: his Son entered this groaning world, suffered in it, and will make all things new (Revelation 21:4–5). Meanwhile, they are occasions for the church to show the love of Christ.

In various places. There is a mercy in this phrase that is easy to walk past. The suffering is distributed, not universal. That is why the church has always been able to answer it. When the famine is in one place, the harvest is in another, and the collection can be taken and carried, which is exactly what the believers in Antioch did when they heard of the famine in Judea (Acts 11:29–30). The geography of trouble is the opportunity of the body of Christ.

In a sentence. Jesus foretold wars between nations, earthquakes, famines, plagues, terrors and great signs from heaven.

On a Tuesday. These things remind us that this world is groaning, waiting for its redemption (Romans 8:22). So expect them, do not try to read dates from them, and send help. When the next disaster comes, give through a trusted Christian relief agency or your church, and pray for believers in the affected region. That is what the church at Antioch did, and it is still the right response.

For worship. The earth shakes, and he is not shaken. Harvests fail, and his storehouse is not poorer. Plagues spread, and he is neither afraid nor absent. The groaning of creation is real, but it is labour, not death throes, and the first of the new creation has already been born: the Son who went down into the grave and came up alive on the third day, the firstborn from the dead (Colossians 1:18). Every tremor in the world is the old order loosening its grip on a creation he has already begun to make new.

verseByVerse.quote: But before all this they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, delivering you up to the synagogues and prisons, and you will be brought before kings and governors for my name's sake. This will be your opportunity to bear witness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But before all this they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, delivering you up to the synagogues and prisons, and you will be brought before kings and governors for my name’s sake. This will be your opportunity to bear witness.

But before all this. Two words carry this paragraph, and the first is before. Luke stresses the order: persecution of the disciples comes first, before the wars and signs. Before the cosmos does anything, the authorities will. The disciple’s experience of the last age begins not with a sign in the sky but with a hand on his arm.

They will lay their hands on you and persecute you, delivering you up to the synagogues and prisons. Luke, alone among the Gospel writers, went on to write the sequel, and every item on this list happens in Acts. Hands laid on them: Peter and John arrested (Acts 4:3). The apostles beaten (Acts 5:40). Stephen stoned (Acts 7). James killed with the sword (Acts 12:2). Delivered to the synagogues for discipline (Acts 9:2), and to Roman prisons (Acts 5:18; 12:4; 16:23). The Gospel makes the prediction and Acts records its fulfilment, item by item.

And you will be brought before kings and governors for my name’s sake. Paul stood before the governors Felix and Festus and before King Agrippa (Acts 24–26), and finally appealed to Caesar. And the cause is named: not for being difficult, or political, or strange, but because they belong to Jesus.

Before a governor and a king. The Master would go first. Within days Jesus himself would be seized, delivered up and brought before a governor, Pontius Pilate, and, as Luke alone records, before a king, Herod Antipas (23:1–12). There he made the good confession (1 Timothy 6:13). Every disciple who has since stood before a magistrate for his name has stood where the Son of God stood, in a courtroom he had already made the place where the truth was told. The first witness of the faith was the faithful witness himself (Revelation 1:5), and the disciples’ opportunity was his before it was theirs.

This will be your opportunity to bear witness. The second word turns the paragraph over: opportunity. The Greek says it will turn out for you as testimony. And testimony is martyrion, from which comes the word martyr, though here it still means simply the evidence a witness gives. So God does not merely bring good out of an arrest afterwards. The arrest is the appointment. The courtroom becomes a pulpit. There was no other way for a fisherman from Galilee to get a hearing before a Roman governor, and the Lord arranged it.

Paul saw it so. Writing from prison, he says what reads like a commentary on this verse: what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel, so that it has become known throughout the whole imperial guard that my imprisonment is for Christ (Philippians 1:12–14). He would never have reached those soldiers any other way.

What if I never face a courtroom? The principle does not require handcuffs. It requires only that following Christ has cost you something in front of other people: the awkward silence when you said where you were on Sunday, the promotion that went elsewhere, the family meal that went quiet when you would not laugh at the joke. Those moments feel like loss, and they are counted as testimony. A watching colleague learns more from what your faith costs you than from anything you could have said when it was free. And remember the believers today for whom this is not a metaphor at all: in many countries Christians are arrested, beaten and imprisoned for the name of Jesus exactly as he said.

In a sentence. Before all this, the disciples would be arrested and persecuted and brought before kings and governors for Jesus’ name, giving them opportunity to bear witness.

On a Tuesday. Opposition to your faith can become an opportunity to speak for Christ. Look for it. The next time you are mocked, passed over or questioned because you are a Christian, ask before you react: what does this person now have the chance to see? Then answer gently and with respect (1 Peter 3:15–16). And pray today, by name if you can, for one persecuted church.

For worship. Christ rules even the courtrooms of his enemies. Kings and governors think they are trying his servants, and they are being preached to. He turns chains into an open door for the gospel. What the world takes from a Christian, it takes in public, and he makes the taking itself a witness to his name.

verseByVerse.quote: Settle it therefore in your minds not to meditate beforehand how to answer, for I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Settle it therefore in your minds not to meditate beforehand how to answer, for I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict.

Settle it therefore in your minds. Decide it now, in advance, and lay it down: put it in your heart once and cease to carry it. What you are to settle is that you will not be anxious.

Not to meditate beforehand how to answer. The verb is promeletan, a technical word from the law courts: to rehearse a defence speech in advance, as a defendant would. Jesus is not talking about study or thinking hard about Scripture, which Luke’s own heroes do constantly. He is talking about the anxious drafting of testimony before a hearing. It is not a ban on preparation but a promise for persecution.

Does this verse forbid preparing sermons or Bible studies? No. Paul settles it by example. This is the man who reasoned in the synagogue from the Scriptures for three Sabbaths (Acts 17:2), who quoted Greek poets in Athens, who asks Timothy to bring the books, and above all the parchments (2 Timothy 4:13), and who also, standing before Agrippa, plainly received something he had not written. Preparation and this promise are not rivals. One is the ordinary work; the other is the extraordinary supply at the moment when the ordinary work has been taken away. Prepare diligently when you can. When you cannot, trust him.

For I will give you a mouth and wisdom. Notice the I. In 12:12 it is the Holy Spirit who will teach them what to say; here it is Jesus himself. The risen Christ gives his Spirit, and the Spirit speaks Christ’s words. Two gifts are promised, and they are not the same. Wisdom is what to say. A mouth is the ability to say it, which is the part most people actually lack. Plenty of Christians know exactly what the truth is and cannot get it past their teeth when it matters.

Which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict. Luke shows the promise landing. Of Stephen before the synagogue: they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he was speaking (Acts 6:10). Same verb, same claim. And the council, seeing the boldness of Peter and John, uneducated, common men, was astonished (Acts 4:13–14).

Does this mean Christians will always win the argument? Not in the sense that their opponents will be persuaded or that they will be acquitted. Stephen’s hearers could not withstand his wisdom, and they stoned him. The promise is that the truth spoken by Christ’s witnesses will not be refuted, that their testimony will stand, and that God will be glorified in it. The result is in his hands. Your task is to be faithful; his is to give the words and to use them as he wills.

In a sentence. They were to resolve not to worry beforehand about their defence, because Jesus would give them words and wisdom their opponents could not resist.

On a Tuesday. The anxiety this verse addresses is rarely about courtrooms. It is the man who dreads the question at work, the mother whose adult child asks something at the kitchen table, the believer who lies awake composing what he should have said. The command is not try harder but settle it. Pray before the conversation, say what you know simply, and leave the rest with him.

For worship. He who made man’s mouth (Exodus 4:11–12) has promised to fill it. He has never yet sent a witness into a room and failed to arrive himself. Blessed be the Lord whose wisdom no adversary can withstand, and who puts that wisdom on the lips of fishermen.

parallels.desc: they could not withstand the wisdom of Stephen

verseByVerse.quote: You will be delivered up even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and some of you they will put to death. You will be hated by all for my name's sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will be delivered up even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and some of you they will put to death. You will be hated by all for my name’s sake.

You will be delivered up even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends. The list moves outward from the innermost circle a human being has, and the innermost is named first. Delivered up means handed over into the power of someone who intends harm. This is not an argument at a family gathering. It is a father telling the authorities where his son is. The deepest betrayal is by those closest, as the prophet foresaw: a man’s enemies are the men of his own house (Micah 7:6; 12:52–53).

Delivered up, as he was. The verb Jesus uses here is the one Luke keeps for his own passion. The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men, he had said (9:44); and within days Judas, one of the Twelve, who had shared his table, would look for an opportunity to deliver him up (22:4–6) and do it with a kiss (22:48). So when Jesus warns his disciples that friends will hand them over, he is not describing a road he will watch them walk. He is describing the road he is already on. Every disciple betrayed by those closest to him walks where his Master walked first.

And some of you they will put to death. Not all, but some. Martyrdom. He does not say which, and there is a terrible tenderness in that, because he is speaking to his disciples and he knows the answer for each of them. James would be first, killed with the sword by Herod within about a dozen years (Acts 12:2). John would die old.

You will be hated by all for my name’s sake. All: by all kinds of people. Hatred from a few can be borne with a clear conscience; hatred that seems universal makes a person suspect the fault is his. But the ground of it is stated twice in six verses: for my name’s sake.

Not every unpopularity. Jesus is not blessing every unpopularity a Christian can achieve. It is entirely possible to be disliked for being rude, superior or tactless, and a person suffering that has not been promised anything here. The test is simple and searching: subtract the name of Christ from your situation, and see whether the hostility goes with it. If it would remain, the cause is not Christ, and the remedy is repentance.

What if my family has turned against me for following Christ? Then this verse is for you, and two things in Luke are true for you. First, Jesus said this would happen. The silence at the other end of the phone is not evidence that God has abandoned your family or that you made a mistake. It was foreseen and foretold, by someone whose own brothers did not at first believe in him (John 7:5). Second, he attached a promise to it: there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children, for the sake of the kingdom of God, who will not receive many times more in this time, and in the age to come eternal life (18:29–30). The family is not replaced. It is enlarged, in the church now, and you should let the church be family to you. Keep loving and praying for your relatives, honour them where you can without denying Christ, and leave the door open. Many have come later.

In a sentence. They would be betrayed even by family and friends, some would be killed, and they would be hated by everyone because of Jesus’ name.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for Christians betrayed by their families for following Christ. If there is such a person in your own church, invite them for a meal this week and be family to them. And if your faith has strained relationships at home, examine yourself honestly: is it the name of Christ that offends, or something in you? Repent of the second, and stand firm in the first.

For worship. The Son who was handed over by a friend has become the Friend who hands over no one. He knows the silence at the end of the phone and the empty chair at the table, and he answers them with a household: his mother and his brothers are those who hear the word of God and do it (8:21). No disciple disowned for his name is left without a family, and none is left without an elder Brother at the Father’s right hand, who calls him by name and is not ashamed of him.

verseByVerse.quote: But not a hair of your head will perish. By your endurance you will gain your lives.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But not a hair of your head will perish. By your endurance you will gain your lives.

But not a hair of your head will perish. This is the sharpest apparent contradiction in the chapter. Two verses earlier he said some of you they will put to death (v. 16). Both sentences are his, addressed to the same men in the same breath. Neither is exaggeration; they are measured on different scales, and the second is the true measure. They may lose their lives, but they will not perish.

The idiom. Not a hair of your head is an established Hebrew way of speaking of complete preservation, used when a life is under threat and God or a king intervenes (1 Samuel 14:45; 2 Samuel 14:11; Acts 27:34, again in Luke’s own writing). It means that down to the last and smallest detail, nothing of you is lost. Jesus has used it once already in this Gospel, and the setting there is decisive: even the hairs of your head are all numbered; fear not, you are of more value than many sparrows (12:7). That saying, too, comes in a passage about being dragged before the authorities and killed.

The person is safe. So the promise is not that the body is spared but that the person is kept. What his enemies do to a Christian can be final in every visible respect, and it cannot reach the man himself. Stephen was stoned to death, and not a hair of his head perished. Luke wrote both sentences.

Why both sentences can be true. The man who spoke them was himself about to be put to death, and on the third day he stood among these same disciples and showed them his hands and his feet: it was he himself, and a spirit does not have flesh and bones as he had (24:39). That is the ground of this promise. Death did to Jesus everything it can do, and it could not keep him, and his people are joined to him. The martyr does not perish because his Lord did not stay dead. Not a hair of your head will perish is, in the end, a promise of resurrection, sealed on the first Easter morning by the One who made it.

By your endurance you will gain your lives. Endurance is hypomonē: steadfastness, perseverance under pressure (8:15). The word is a compound of under and remain: to remain under the load, like a beam still bearing the weight in the morning. Gain your lives means win your souls, eternal life. And the verb is gain, not keep. The life that is handed over in the losing is handed back larger.

Does my salvation depend on my endurance? Endurance is the evidence and fruit of God’s keeping, not the ground of salvation. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6), and no one will snatch Christ’s sheep out of his hand (John 10:28). True faith perseveres, and God preserves it. This is the perseverance of the saints: God keeps his people, and they keep going. The call to endure is real, and God uses it as one of the means by which he keeps his people enduring. So the warning and the promise belong together. You must endure; and if you are his, you will, because he will hold you.

What if I do not think I have it in me to last? That is the quieter fear this verse raises in most Christians, and it is not the fear of martyrdom. It is: I do not think I can keep going. Not thirty more years. Not through what is coming. You are not asked to last thirty years at once. Endurance is not a store of strength held in reserve; it is remaining under, today. Nobody is given the grace for a decade in advance. The saints who endured to the end did it the way anyone does: the next morning, and then the one after that, on mercies that are new every morning (Lamentations 3:22–23) and grace that is sufficient for the day (2 Corinthians 12:9).

In a sentence. Yet not a hair of their heads would perish, and by their endurance they would gain eternal life.

On a Tuesday. Remain under the load today, just today. If you are facing a long trial, an illness, a hard marriage, a hostile workplace, a grief that will not lift, do not try to carry next year. Ask for today’s grace, do today’s faithful thing, and lie down tonight trusting the One who numbers your hairs. Tomorrow’s grace will come with tomorrow.

For worship. The God who numbers every hair on his children’s heads holds the whole of them in hands that were pierced for them. Their life is hidden with Christ in God (Colossians 3:3), in a place no sword can find and no fire can reach, and when he appears they will appear with him in glory. The enemies of the church can take everything that can be seen. They have never once taken a saint out of the hand of his Shepherd, and they never will.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–28 — The Fall of the City and the Coming of the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Where Matthew and Mark speak of the abomination of desolation and add let the reader understand, Luke gives his Gentile readers the plain meaning: armies around Jerusalem. Then three commands, all of them counter-intuitive — flee Judea, leave the city, and do not go in. Under a normal siege the countryside empties into the walls. Jesus tells them to do the opposite, and the history bears him out: the horror of that siege was concentrated inside. Eusebius records that the Jerusalem church, warned beforehand, withdrew to Pella across the Jordan.

He then names what is happening theologically. These are days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written — covenant language, and a quotation. Isaiah 61:2 speaks of the year of the LORD’s favour and the day of vengeance of our God, and that is the passage Jesus read at Nazareth in 4:19, where he stopped mid-sentence and left the vengeance unread. Here he finishes it.

And in the same breath he grieves: Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days. The judgment is deserved and it is agonising, and the one announcing it had already wept over this city (19:41).

Verse 24 adds the clause found only in Luke: Jerusalem trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled. Readings of that phrase differ, but every reading rests on the same word. Gentile dominion is real, permitted, and bounded.

Then the scene widens from a city to a world. Signs in sun and moon and stars; nations in perplexity, with no way through; people fainting with fear at what is coming — strength leaving the body over an event that has not yet happened.

Against that backdrop, one figure: the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory — Daniel 7:13. And one instruction to his people, and it is physical: straighten up, and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.
verseByVerse.theology:
How the destruction of Jerusalem (vv. 20–24) relates to the coming of the Son of Man (vv. 25–28) is one of the most discussed questions in the Gospels. Three approaches are held by serious readers: that both refer to the events of that generation; that both refer to the final end; or that the fall of Jerusalem is a real judgment which is also a pattern and foretaste of the last one. The third fits the language best — vv. 25–28 are cosmic in scope, and v. 28 is addressed to disciples of every generation — and it has the advantage of taking both halves seriously.

Luke’s own contribution to the question is v. 24, and it is decisive: he alone writes an interval of unspecified length into the discourse, between the trampling of the city and the appearing of the Son of Man. The reader who takes that clause seriously will not be troubled by the objection that Jesus predicted a return that did not come.

The cloud in v. 27 is not weather. In the Old Testament the cloud is where God is — the pillar in the wilderness, the glory filling the tabernacle. And they will see anchors the Christian hope in something public: he was seen born, seen killed, seen ascending, and will be seen returning. The dominion Daniel saw handed over was always going to be handed to a crucified man.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 21 raises an honest question: is fleeing not simply cowardice? Jesus says no, and it helps to have a Lord who will say so. Paul was let down the wall in a basket and thought no less of himself. Flight is cowardice only when it abandons a post you were given, and nobody was given the post of dying inside those walls. For anyone facing a collapse they cannot prevent — a business, a church, a marriage — faithfulness sometimes means staying and sometimes means going, and the Lord does not leave his people without direction.

Verse 23 answers a question people really carry: does God take satisfaction in judgment? The answer stands in the temple court with tears not yet dry, grieving in advance for infants not yet conceived — and within the week the wrath he is describing falls on him.

Verses 25–26 describe the commonest suffering in a comfortable country: not disaster, but dread. The mortgage that has not failed, the scan that has not come back, and the strength going out of the body over a thing that has not happened. Jesus does not scold it; he names it with medical precision, and then tells his own people to lift their heads — the one thing no frightened person ever thinks to do.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near. Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and let those who are inside the city depart, and let not those who are out in the country enter it,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near. Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and let those who are inside the city depart, and let not those who are out in the country enter it.

But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies. Luke speaks plainly of Jerusalem surrounded by armies, where Mark and Matthew speak of the abomination of desolation standing where it ought not, with the aside let the reader understand (Mark 13:14). Luke, writing for Gentile readers who might not catch an allusion to Daniel, gives the plain meaning instead. It was fulfilled when the Romans surrounded Jerusalem, first under Cestius Gallus in AD 66, and then under Titus in AD 70.

Then know that its desolation has come near. Desolation is the destruction and abandonment of the city, as Daniel had foreseen (Daniel 9:26–27).

Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. Three commands follow, startlingly ordinary: get out of Judea, get out of the city, do not go back in.

And let those who are inside the city depart, and let not those who are out in the country enter it. The third is the strangest and the most revealing. Under any normal siege, the countryside empties into the walled city, because that is where the walls are. Jesus tells them to do the opposite of the sensible thing, and history records why. Many fled into the city for refuge and were trapped, and the horror of that siege was concentrated inside the walls, where famine and fighting between rival factions did more than the Romans.

The church heard him. The church historian Eusebius records that the Christians of Jerusalem, warned by a prophetic word given to their leaders, left the city before the war reached its height and settled at Pella, in the hills east of the Jordan. Many think this happened when Cestius Gallus unexpectedly withdrew in AD 66, giving a window to escape. The tradition has been questioned, but it fits what plainly happened: a movement whose leadership had been centred in Jerusalem was not destroyed when Jerusalem was. They took their Lord at his word, forty years in advance, and lived.

He went in so that they could go out. There is a striking contrast in this command. Jesus tells his disciples to get out of Jerusalem and not go back in, and he says it in the week he himself has entered it with his face set (9:51), knowing that a prophet cannot perish away from Jerusalem (13:33). He enters the doomed city so that his people can leave it. Outside its walls he would bear a wrath far deeper than any Roman siege, and because he did, his people need not be found under judgment when it falls. The command to flee comes from the One who, a few nights later, would refuse to flee himself.

Is fleeing not simply running away? A thoughtful reader will feel the question. Should the disciples not have stayed and prayed for the city, and died with it if necessary? Jesus says no, and it is good to have a Lord who will say so. There is a time to stand and a time to go, and the difference is not measured by how brave it feels. Paul was let down the Damascus wall in a basket (Acts 9:25) and thought no less of himself for it. What decides the answer is not courage but calling: flight from danger is cowardice only when it is flight from a post you were given. Nobody was given the post of dying inside those walls. The same applies to Christians facing persecution today: it is not wrong to flee if God opens a way, and it is not wrong to stay if he calls you to.

In a sentence. When they saw Jerusalem surrounded by armies, they would know its destruction was near, and must flee rather than take refuge in the city.

On a Tuesday. There is a comfort here for anyone facing a collapse they cannot prevent: a business, a marriage, a church. Faithfulness sometimes means staying and sometimes means leaving, and the Lord does not leave his people without direction. Seek it in his word, in prayer and in godly counsel, and when it is clear, act.

For worship. He spoke forty years ahead, and his people carried his word for forty years: through arrests and stonings, through the first rumours of revolt. When the armies came, his word was already waiting for them, and, as the church remembered it, they went over the Jordan into the hills and lived. That is the Lord we have. His word does not age, it does not need revising, and it reaches his people at the hour it was meant for, not one day late.
verseByVerse.note: Luke speaks plainly of Jerusalem surrounded by armies, as the Romans did in AD 66–70; Matthew and Mark speak of “the abomination of desolation.”

verseByVerse.quote: for these are days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written. Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For these are days of vengeance, to fulfil all that is written. Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people.

For these are days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written. Two things are said here that a modern reader instinctively wants to separate, and Luke has bolted them together. The first is that this is judgment. Days of vengeance is not Roman policy described from outside; it is covenant language, God’s judgment on Jerusalem for rejecting her Messiah (19:43–44). And it is quoting. Isaiah 61:2 speaks of the year of the LORD’s favour and the day of vengeance of our God, and that is the very passage Jesus read in the synagogue at Nazareth (4:18–19), where he stopped reading in the middle of the sentence, rolled up the scroll and sat down, having announced the favour and left the vengeance unread. Seventeen chapters later he finishes the sentence.

To fulfill all that is written. The prophets had warned of judgment on unfaithful Jerusalem: the curses of the covenant, with siege and famine so terrible that parents would eat their children (Deuteronomy 28:49–57); the city and sanctuary destroyed after an anointed one is cut off (Daniel 9:26); Zion ploughed as a field (Micah 3:12). God does what he has said.

Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! The second thing is that this is grief. The word is ouai, often translated woe and often heard as a threat. It is not a threat here. It is the sound a man makes over something unbearable, and it is aimed at the least guilty people in the city: a woman eight months pregnant, a mother with a baby at the breast, on the day the siege begins. That is Jesus’ compassion, spoken in the middle of a prophecy of wrath.

For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people. Upon the earth may mean upon the land of Israel, and the wrath is God’s. Josephus describes horrors of famine and slaughter during the siege that are hard to read.

Judgment and tears together. So the same paragraph says the judgment is deserved and that it is agonising. Both. And the one who says the first is weeping as he says it, which we know because Luke has already shown him doing it, riding toward this city with the crowd shouting, and stopping, and crying over it (19:41–42). That is the character of God: he does not judge half-heartedly, and he does not judge coldly. I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord GOD; so turn, and live (Ezekiel 18:32).

Does God enjoy judging people? No. That is the question underneath this passage, and people really carry it. The answer is standing in the temple court with tears not yet dry, describing a siege forty years off, and grieving in advance for infants not yet born. His judgment is real and it is just, because sin is real and he is holy. But he takes no pleasure in it. And within the week the wrath he is describing will fall in its fullness on him, so that everyone in that city and every sinner in the world who turns to him might not have to bear it. There is no vengeance in Scripture that God has not first been willing to bear himself for those who trust him (Isaiah 53:5; Romans 5:9).

In a sentence. These would be days of God’s vengeance, fulfilling Scripture, terrible for pregnant women and nursing mothers, with great distress and wrath on the people.

On a Tuesday. If you have grown casual about sin, read this passage slowly and let it sober you. And if you are afraid of God’s wrath, look at who is speaking: the one who wept over the city and went to the cross for it. Run to him, not away from him. There is no safer place.

For worship. At Nazareth he rolled up the scroll before the day of vengeance, and he has held it rolled for everyone who will come. The day did fall on Jerusalem, and a greater day is coming on the world, yet the year of the Lord’s favour is still being proclaimed in his name to every nation. The Judge who weeps is also the herald of grace, and the patience that kept the scroll closed at Nazareth is the patience that has kept the door open for us.

parallels.desc: the days of punishment have come

verseByVerse.quote: They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.

They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations. Josephus says over a million died in the siege, probably an exaggeration, though the scale was vast, and that ninety-seven thousand were taken captive, many sold as slaves, sent to the mines or made to die in the arenas of the empire.

And Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles. Under Gentile control. After the second Jewish revolt (AD 132–135), the Romans rebuilt Jerusalem as a pagan city, Aelia Capitolina, and banned Jews from entering it. Empire after empire has held it since.

Until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled. Only Luke has this clause, and Christians who love the Bible read it in different ways. Start with what every reading agrees on: the word is until. Gentile dominion over Jerusalem is real, it is permitted, and it is bounded. God has written an end into the very sentence that describes the trampling. Jerusalem’s judgment is not the end of God’s purposes for Israel. And the times of the Gentiles are also the times of Gentile mission: Paul uses the same shape when he says a partial hardening has come upon Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in (Romans 11:25).

A light for the Gentiles. The phrase has a history in Luke. Over the infant Jesus in this same temple, Simeon had sung of a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to your people Israel (2:32). And the risen Christ will send his apostles to proclaim repentance and forgiveness of sins in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (24:47). So the times of the Gentiles are not empty time between two catastrophes. They are the age in which the light Simeon held in his arms goes out to every people, while the city that rejected him lies trampled. The age named after the Gentiles belongs to him.

Where Christians differ: the times of the Gentiles. Many Reformed interpreters take the phrase to mean the age of Gentile ingathering and Gentile dominance, running from the fall of Jerusalem to the return of Christ, in which the gospel goes to the nations. Dispensationalists, including teachers many readers have been helped by, understand it as a defined period of Gentile political domination of Jerusalem, and many have seen the founding of the modern state of Israel (1948) and the capture of Jerusalem (1967) as the end of the times of the Gentiles and a sign of the imminent end. Their instinct is a sound one in this respect: they are trying to let the word until mean something, and to take seriously that God has not finished with the people to whom he made the promises. Verdict: Jesus gives no such timetable, and warns against date-setting (vv. 8–9). The times of the Gentiles is the age of Gentile mission and Gentile dominance between the fall of Jerusalem and Christ’s return. This fits Luke’s own flow, where Acts carries the gospel out to the nations, and Romans 11:25 measures the term by the ingathering of the Gentiles, not by who governs a city. Paul holds out hope of a future turning of Israel to Christ (Romans 11:25–27), but that is a work of grace through the gospel, not a political event to be calculated.

Is the modern state of Israel the fulfilment of prophecy? Christians hold different views, and they can be held charitably. What this verse will not bear is a calendar. It gives a boundary without a date, deliberately, and every attempt to turn it into arithmetic has expired. The New Testament’s focus is not on territory but on the gospel: the promises to Abraham are fulfilled in Christ, the true offspring (Galatians 3:16, 29), and Jews and Gentiles alike are saved only by faith in him. Christians should pray for the peace of Jerusalem and for all its people, Jewish and Arab, and long for them to know the Messiah. They should not treat the news from the Middle East as a timetable for Christ’s return.

A horizon behind the trampling. The sentence does not deny the trampling or promise it will not hurt. It puts a horizon behind it. The occupying power is standing on ground it does not own, on a clock it did not set, and the word until is God’s, not theirs. That is true of every trampling. There is no oppression in this world that Scripture describes without an end.

In a sentence. Many would die by the sword or be taken captive, and Jerusalem would be trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are complete.

On a Tuesday. You live in the times of the Gentiles, the age of mission: support the work of taking the gospel to the nations, and pray for Jewish friends and neighbours by name. And if you are suffering under some trampling of your own, remember the word until. God has set its limit.

For worship. The city that rejected him was trampled, and the King it rejected went on reigning. From his throne he sends his gospel to the ends of the earth, and people who were once without hope and without God in the world have been brought near by his blood (Ephesians 2:12–13). The same Lord has not forgotten the people to whom the promises were made, for his gifts and calling are irrevocable (Romans 11:29). History is not an empty corridor between two disasters. It is the long harvest of a Saviour who is gathering his own from every nation.

parallels.desc: the nations have come into your inheritance
until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in

verseByVerse.quote: 'And there will be signs in sun and moon and stars, and on the earth distress of nations in perplexity because of the roaring of the sea and the waves, people fainting with fear and with foreboding of what is coming on the world. For the powers of the heavens will be shaken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And there will be signs in sun and moon and stars, and on the earth distress of nations in perplexity because of the roaring of the sea and the waves, people fainting with fear and with foreboding of what is coming on the world. For the powers of the heavens will be shaken.

And there will be signs in sun and moon and stars. Now the end. After the fall of Jerusalem and the times of the Gentiles, Jesus speaks of his return, and the discourse moves from a city to the world. Sun, moon, stars, the shaking of the heavens, the roaring sea: every image here comes from the prophets, who used it in a settled way for great acts of God’s judgment. When Isaiah foretold the fall of Babylon, he spoke of stars withholding their light and a sun darkened at its rising (Isaiah 13:10). Ezekiel darkens the stars over Egypt (Ezekiel 32:7). Joel has the sun turned to darkness and the moon to blood (Joel 2:30–31), which Peter quotes at Pentecost (Acts 2:20).

Literal or picture? This language, in the Bible’s own usage, is the language of God arriving in judgment and of an old order ending, and it is used both of historical catastrophes and of the last day. Whether the sun will literally go dark is not something this passage settles, and a reader should not be told it does. What it plainly announces is that the created order itself will register the coming of its Maker, and that the registering will be terrifying.

The sun’s light failed. Luke has a foretaste of these signs only days away. On the day Jesus died, a darkness lay over the whole land from noon until three in the afternoon, and Luke alone gives the reason in so many words: the sun’s light failed (23:44–45). The heavens that will be shaken at his return went dark at his death, because the One being judged there was their Maker, bearing the sin of his people. That is why a believer can read this verse without terror. The judgment these signs announce has already fallen once, at noon on Golgotha, on the Son of God in the place of all who trust him.

And on the earth distress of nations in perplexity because of the roaring of the sea and the waves. Then Luke turns from the sky to the faces. Distress of nations is worldwide anguish, nations not knowing where to turn. The word for perplexity is aporia: literally no way through. It is the state of a person who has run out of options. And the sea, in Scripture, is a picture of chaos and evil (Psalm 46:3; Isaiah 17:12; Revelation 13:1). Creation is in turmoil.

People fainting with fear and with foreboding of what is coming on the world. The verb is apopsychō, used of a body giving out, strength simply leaving. And foreboding is prosdokia, expectation: not fear of what is happening, but fear of what is coming. Luke describes a world in which the anticipation does more damage than the event, and that is the commonest suffering in a prosperous country: the scan that has not come back, the redundancy not yet announced, the strength going out of the body over a thing that has not happened. Jesus does not scold this. He knows what dread does to a person.

For the powers of the heavens will be shaken. Haggai heard God say, once more I will shake the heavens and the earth (Haggai 2:6), and Hebrews explains that the shaking removes what is made, so that what cannot be shaken may remain (Hebrews 12:26–27). The whole created order will be shaken by the coming of its Maker.

Should these verses frighten a Christian? They should sober us, but not terrify us. They describe what the world will feel when its Maker comes in judgment, and they are meant to warn the unbelieving and wake the sleepy. But for those who belong to Christ the same events are the prelude to joy, for Jesus at once tells them that while others faint, they are to lift up their heads. You do not need to fear the day of the Lord if you are hidden in the Lord of the day. If you are not, these verses are his kind warning to come to him now.

In a sentence. There will be signs in the heavens, nations in anguish at the roaring sea, people fainting with fear, as the powers of heaven are shaken.

On a Tuesday. When everything is shaken, those who belong to Christ have an unshakeable kingdom. If you are exhausted by what has not yet happened, name the dread to God this week, specifically, and hand it over (Philippians 4:6–7). Then do today’s duty. The future that matters most is already settled: the King is coming, and he is yours.

For worship. The sun he made will darken at his word, and the sea that roars is his. The powers of the heavens, which keep the stars on their courses, will be shaken by the approach of the One through whom they were made, and they will bow to him as they did on the first day. What makes the nations faint makes his people glad, for the One who comes over the shaken heavens is the Lamb who was slain, and the face the world dreads is the face his church has longed to see.
verseByVerse.note: Prophets used cosmic images like these for great acts of God’s judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. Now when these things begin to take place, straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. Now when these things begin to take place, straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.

And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. Daniel saw, in the night, one like a son of man brought on the clouds before the Ancient of Days and handed a kingdom that would never be destroyed (Daniel 7:13–14). From that vision Jesus took the title he used of himself more than any other. He came first in weakness, laid in a manger; he will come again with power and great glory.

In a cloud. Luke alone has the singular, a cloud, and Luke alone wrote the two scenes that explain it. On the mountain a cloud overshadowed the disciples and a voice from the cloud said, this is my Son, my Chosen One (9:34–35). At the ascension a cloud took him out of their sight, and the angels said he would come in the same way as they had seen him go (Acts 1:9–11). In Scripture the cloud is the robe of God’s presence, the glory that filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34–35). To come in a cloud is to come clothed in the visible presence of God, as only God comes.

They will see. This is why the Christian hope can never be reduced to an inner experience. He was seen when he was born, when he was killed and when he went up, and he will be seen coming back: every eye will see him (Revelation 1:7). The gospel is a report about a Man, and the report ends with him visible.

There is no secret coming. Some Christians have been taught that Christ will first come secretly to remove the church from the world, and later come visibly in glory. This passage, like every other New Testament description of the return, speaks of one coming, public, glorious and seen by all. The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel and the trumpet of God (1 Thessalonians 4:16); nothing could be less secret. The gathering of his people, the resurrection of the dead and the judgment of the world come together at that one appearing (Matthew 24:30–31; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). So Christians are not told to expect to be removed before trouble, but to endure through it and lift their heads at his coming.

Where Christians differ: is this the Second Coming, or the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70? Some interpreters read this coming as Christ’s vindication, made visible when the temple fell, pointing out that in Daniel 7 the son of man travels to the Ancient of Days to receive his kingdom rather than down to the earth. Verdict: in Luke the far horizon is in view here. Luke has already set the times of the Gentiles between the fall of the city and these signs (v. 24), and what he describes reaches far beyond AD 70: signs in sun, moon and stars, anguish among the nations of the whole earth, and the redemption of God’s people drawing near (v. 28). The fall of Jerusalem (vv. 20–24) was a real judgment and a foretaste. This is the final, visible return of Christ.

Hold the picture. Hold it as Daniel drew it: a figure like a son of man, brought before the throne, and every people and nation and language given into his hands. And it is the same figure who is standing in a temple courtyard, tired, days from being flogged, describing what is coming to men who will run away from him before the week is out. The dominion in Daniel’s vision was always going to be handed to a crucified man, because that is who he is.

Now when these things begin to take place, straighten up and raise your heads. Two commands, and they are physical. Straighten up: the word is used of a bent body made erect, and Luke has used it once before, of the woman bent double for eighteen years who could not straighten herself until Jesus laid his hands on her (13:11–13). Raise your heads: lift the chin, which is what nobody under threat ever does. Fear curls a person up. So while the world is fainting at what is coming, the Christian is told to do the opposite of the natural thing with his own body.

Because your redemption is drawing near. Redemption is apolytrōsis: release on payment of a price, the word for bringing a slave out. Here it is full and final deliverance, including the resurrection of the body (Romans 8:23; Ephesians 4:30). It is yours, and it is drawing near while the shaking is going on. The events that terrify everyone else are, for the believer, the sound of the door opening. The world sees the end of everything. The church sees him.

How should I think about Christ’s return day to day? As the believer’s great hope, not a subject of dread or calculation. It means that history is going somewhere; that every injustice will be put right; that the dead in Christ will rise; that our bodies will be redeemed; that we will see him face to face. Paul calls it the blessed hope (Titus 2:13). It should make you watchful in holiness, steady in suffering and generous with this world’s goods, because they are not your final treasure. And it should put the prayer of the early church in your mouth: come, Lord Jesus (Revelation 22:20).

In a sentence. Then all will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and glory, and when these things begin, believers should stand up and lift their heads, because their redemption is near.

On a Tuesday. Practise the posture. When the news is bad, or your body is failing, or the church seems weak, physically and spiritually lift your head. Say to yourself: my redemption is drawing near. Let it change one thing today: the fear you will not feed, the grudge you will let go, the thing you will give away because it is not your treasure.

For worship. The hands that once straightened a woman bent double for eighteen years will one day straighten a whole bowed creation. He paid the price of our release with his own blood, and he is coming to claim what he bought, body and soul. The world will see him and mourn; his people will see him and stand up straight as they never have before. Blessed is the King who comes in a cloud, not to destroy his own but to take them home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–38 — The Fig Tree, the Weight on the Heart, and the Daily Rhythm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The parable is deliberately ordinary. Trees come into leaf, and everybody knows summer is near; nobody consults an expert about it. Luke adds a phrase the others do not — and all the trees — which quietly rules out reading the fig tree as a coded symbol requiring decipherment. The signs are meant to be legible from your own doorstep. And note what the application says is near: not the end, not the judgment, but the kingdom of God.

Then the most debated sentence in the chapter: this generation will not pass away until all has taken place. Taken with v. 24, Luke’s structure is straightforward — the things the disciples asked about in v. 7 all happened within forty years, and v. 24’s interval of Gentile times stands between that and the Son of Man’s appearing. And the ground under everything is v. 33: heaven and earth will pass away, but his words will not. The visible is the perishable thing; his speech is not.

Then, after the cosmos, the kitchen. Watch yourselves — not the sky. Three weights are named, running from the obvious to the invisible: dissipation, the heaviness of the morning after; drunkenness, the night that produced it; and the cares of this life. The third is not a sin in the ordinary sense, which is exactly why it is the deadliest. Nobody will ever be rebuked for it.

The verb is physical — weighed down, like a ship low in the water or eyes too heavy to stay open, as the disciples' were on the mountain (9:32). An overloaded heart does not become wicked. It becomes slow. And a trap works on one principle: the animal is looking at something else.

The remedy is not detachment but prayer: stay awake at all times, praying for strength to escape and to stand before the Son of Man. That is the entire practical conclusion of the discourse.

Then Luke closes with a timetable. Teaching in the temple by day, sleeping on Olivet by night, and the people coming early to hear him. The mount that had seen his tears (19:41) would see his agony (22:39), his arrest, and his ascension (Acts 1:12).
verseByVerse.theology:
Watchfulness in the New Testament is not scanning the news for prophetic fulfilment. It is the settled attention of people who know that today is lived under eternity. That is why Jesus ends a discourse about the end of the world with two verbs — stay awake, pray — and no preparations, no place to go, no date.

The phrase at all times rules out the pattern every generation falls into: intense watchfulness when the news is bad, and none when it is good. Wakefulness that responds to headlines is not wakefulness; it is nerves.

And to stand before the Son of Man is courtroom language. The Psalms ask it directly: if you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, who could stand (Ps. 130:3)? The answer of this verse is that the strength to stand is not mustered but asked for, and asked of the very one before whom we shall stand. He is not the examiner waiting to see whether we managed it. Jude puts the ground plainly: to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy (Jude 24).
verseByVerse.examples:
A test for v. 34, and it is uncomfortable because it is easy to run. Count the hours of the last week spent turning over a practical worry — money, a diagnosis, a difficult colleague. Then count the minutes spent thinking about the return of Christ. The ratio is the answer.

None of this is a call to care less about your family or your work. It is a diagnosis: what will finally leave a Christian unready for glory is very unlikely to be a scandal. It will be a diary.

And vv. 37–38 give the pattern for anyone overwhelmed by what is coming — not a technique but a rhythm. This man has just announced the fall of the temple, the arrest of his friends, the shaking of the heavens and his own return in glory, and he knows he will be crucified within the week. What he does with the days that remain is teach in the morning, sleep on a hillside, and get up and do it again. No frenzy, no last campaign, no scramble to secure the movement. Work in the day, withdraw at night, be found where the people who need you can find you, and do the next ordinary faithful thing.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them a parable: 'Look at the fig tree, and all the trees. As soon as they come out in leaf, you see for yourselves and know that the summer is already near. So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that the kingdom of God is near.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He told them a parable: look at the fig tree, and all the trees. As soon as they come out in leaf, you see for yourselves and know that the summer is already near. So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that the kingdom of God is near.

And he told them a parable: Look at the fig tree, and all the trees. There is a small phrase here that is entirely Luke’s and worth noticing: and all the trees. Matthew and Mark have only the fig tree. The fig tree is sometimes read as a coded symbol for the nation of Israel, and whole systems of date-calculation have been built on that reading; the prophets do use figs of Israel (Jeremiah 24; Hosea 9:10). But Luke’s and all the trees makes it plain that the point is not symbolic botany. Trees come into leaf before summer, and everybody knows it.
