As soon as they come out in leaf, you see for yourselves and know that the summer is already near. Signs are readable. You do not consult an expert to know that summer is coming; you look at a branch. The knowledge is immediate, unanxious and available to a child. That, he says, is how the signs are meant to work: not as a cipher for the initiated, but as a season a Christian can read from his own doorstep.

What the fig tree does not tell you. It gives no date. Nobody has ever looked at a bud and said summer begins on the fourteenth. It tells you the direction of travel and the nearness of the thing, and it refuses to tell you more. That is precisely the amount of information Jesus has been giving all through this chapter, and precisely the amount that produces watchfulness rather than arithmetic.

So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that the kingdom of God is near. These things are the events he has described, beginning with the fall of Jerusalem. And the wording is easy to read past: not the end is near, not the judgment, but the kingdom. Everything in this discourse has been dark: armies, betrayal, famine, dread, a city under sentence. And the thing all of it announces is the reign of God arriving in its fullness. The signs are not the symptoms of a world dying. They are leaves on the branch.

The kingdom is the King. In Luke the kingdom of God is never an abstraction. It came near when he came near. Within days he would tell the Twelve that he assigns them a kingdom, as his Father assigned one to him (22:29), and a dying thief would ask, Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom (23:42). So the summer the leaves announce is not finally a season of history but the face of the King. When Christians read the branches, they are not reading the weather of the world. They are watching for him, and every leaf says the same thing: the One who came once in humility is on his way back in glory.

If the kingdom is already here, how can it be near? Both are true. The kingdom came in Jesus: the King was among them, healing and forgiving, and he reigns now from heaven (17:21; Acts 2:33–36). But it has not yet come in its fullness, when every enemy is defeated, the dead are raised and the creation renewed. Christians live between the two: the kingdom has come, and the kingdom is coming. The events of history are like leaves on the tree, telling us that the full summer of his reign is on the way.

In a sentence. As the leaves on trees show that summer is near, so the events Jesus described would show that God’s kingdom is near.

On a Tuesday. When you read of the world convulsing, is your emotion dread or expectancy? The difference is not temperament. It is whether you believe the thing on the far side of the shaking is a ruin or a King. Practise expectancy this week: when bad news comes, pray, help where you can, and then say quietly, the kingdom is near.

For worship. Winter has never once been the last season, and it will not be now. The Lord who made the fig tree put summer into its branches before anyone saw a leaf, and he has written his own return into the branches of history in the same way. The world sees bare wood and storms; his people see buds. He who came first as a child in a manger is coming again in the full summer of his reign, and on that day nothing that is his will be left unripened.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all has taken place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all has taken place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.

Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all has taken place. This generation, taken naturally, means Jesus’ contemporaries, the generation alive as he spoke. All means the events leading to and including the fall of Jerusalem, which happened within forty years. Sceptics press the point: Jesus has just spoken of the Son of Man coming in a cloud (v. 27), so if all includes the return, that generation passed away and he did not come. It is the standard charge that Jesus was a mistaken prophet, and it should be answered.

Luke’s answer is eight verses earlier. Where Matthew and Mark keep the fall of Jerusalem and the end of the age closely braided, Luke pulls them apart and names the gap: Jerusalem will be trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled (v. 24). That clause is an interval of unknown length, written into the discourse by Jesus himself, standing between the city’s fall and the Son of Man’s appearing. The all that must take place is what the disciples asked about in v. 7: the stones thrown down, the siege, the captivity. Every one of them happened within forty years. Then comes an age of unknown length in which the gospel goes to the nations. Then the end.

Where Christians differ: what does this generation mean? Some take it to mean the Jewish race, which will last until the end. Others take it to mean the generation alive when the final signs appear. Some critics claim that Jesus was simply mistaken. Verdict: the best reading (compare Mark 13:30) is that Jesus’ contemporaries would see the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, the event the disciples had asked about (v. 7), and they did. Elsewhere in Luke this generation means the people of Jesus’ own day (7:31; 11:29–32). The day of his final coming itself remains unknown, as Mark records Jesus saying (Mark 13:32). Jesus was not mistaken by a single day.

The opposite error. This also disposes of the commoner error in our own time. Because v. 24 sets a limit on Gentile dominion and v. 32 attaches a generation to fulfilment, people have bolted the two together to calculate a date: a political event in Jerusalem is declared the end of the times of the Gentiles, a generation is priced at forty years, and the arithmetic is published. Every such attempt has expired quietly. When the apostles asked the risen Christ one last time, he declined the question outright: it is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority (Acts 1:7). A man who has worked out the date does not need to stay awake. That is precisely why we are not given it.

Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. Jesus sets his own sayings against the whole visible universe and says the universe will give way first. Israel’s prophets claimed that permanence only for the word of the LORD: the grass withers and the flower fades, but the word of our God stands for ever (Isaiah 40:8). Jesus claims it for what he himself says, with no thus says the LORD in front of it. Earlier in Luke he had said that whoever hears his words and does them builds on rock (6:47–48), and after Easter he would point the disciples back to the words he had spoken while he was still with them (24:44). Either he is deluded or the LORD is speaking, and the temple stones, lying where he said they would lie, have given their verdict.

How can I trust words spoken two thousand years ago? Because they have been tested and have never failed, and because of who spoke them. Within a generation the temple fell as he said. He said he would rise on the third day, and he did. He said the gospel would go to the nations, and you are reading this. And the Spirit who inspired the Scriptures still bears witness to them in the hearts of those who read (John 16:13; 2 Timothy 3:16). The words of Jesus are not old in the sense of outdated. They are older than the world and will outlast it. Build on them.

In a sentence. Jesus solemnly said his generation would not pass away before all these things happened, and that his words would outlast heaven and earth.

On a Tuesday. Take one of his promises this week, I will never leave you, come to me and I will give you rest, my words will not pass away, write it down and carry it. When you are tempted to trust what you can see more than what he has said, take it out and read it again.

For worship. The heavens will vanish like smoke and the earth will wear out like a garment, but his word endures for ever. He who spoke the universe into being spoke these words in the temple, and they will still be standing when the stars have gone out. Blessed be the Word made flesh, whose words are spirit and life, and whose every promise is yes in him.

verseByVerse.quote: 'But watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly like a trap. For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of the whole earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly like a trap. For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of the whole earth.

But watch yourselves. After the cosmos, the kitchen. The discourse has built through wars and sieges and the shaking of the heavens, and now Jesus names the things that will actually cost his disciples their readiness, and not one of them is on the news. Only Luke has this application. Watch yourselves: not the sky, not the headlines.

Lest your hearts be weighed down. Made heavy, dull, sluggish. The verb is physical: think of a ship low in the water, or eyes too heavy to stay open, as Peter and those with him were heavy with sleep on the mountain while Jesus prayed (9:32). Notice what happens to a heart with too much on it. It does not become wicked. It becomes slow.

With dissipation and drunkenness. Three weights are named, and the order runs from the obvious to the invisible. Dissipation is kraipalē, an old medical word for the heaviness in the head the morning after: the hangover, precisely, or the carousing that brings it. Drunkenness is the night before that produced it: self-indulgence.

And cares of this life. Then the third: anxieties about ordinary things (8:14; 12:22). Not the great questions but the small ones: bills, rotas, the boiler, the appointment, the form that has to go back by Friday. And that one is not a sin at all in the ordinary sense, which makes it the deadliest item on the list. No elder will visit about it. A man can be entirely sober, faithful to his wife, honest in business, in church every Sunday, and be so occupied with things that will not exist in a hundred years that the return of Jesus Christ is, in practice, no part of how he thinks about Thursday. Two opposite dangers, self-indulgence and anxiety, both make the heart heavy and blind it to eternity.

The night the warning was tested. Within days this warning would be tested on the same hillside. In the garden Jesus found the disciples sleeping for sorrow (22:45): not drunk, not careless, simply weighed down by grief until their eyes closed. And there, under a weight no one else has ever carried, he himself stayed awake and prayed: not my will, but yours, be done (22:42). The heart that was most burdened in all history was the one heart that was not dulled. He watched when his friends could not, and he lives to intercede for those whose eyes keep closing (Hebrews 7:25).

And that day come upon you suddenly like a trap. A snare does not work because the animal is stupid, but because it is looking at something else, head-down in a perfectly reasonable activity, when the cord closes.

For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of the whole earth. No one will escape it. Isaiah had warned of terror and the pit and the snare for the inhabitants of the earth (Isaiah 24:17). The return of Christ is not a local event that some will miss. It will come on everyone, and the only question is whether it finds them ready.

Does this mean I should care less about my family and work? No. The remedy Jesus gives at once is not detachment but prayer. Jesus does not tell you to stop paying the bills or caring for your children. He tells you not to let them weigh down your heart. The difference is whether your ordinary duties are done before the face of the coming King, or whether they have crowded him out. Cast your cares on him (1 Peter 5:7), do your work as for the Lord (Colossians 3:23), and let the thought of his coming lighten the load rather than add to it.

In a sentence. Jesus warned them not to let their hearts be dulled by self-indulgence or the worries of life, so that the day would not catch them suddenly like a trap, for it will come on everyone.

On a Tuesday. Think back over the last week and count the hours you spent turning over a practical worry: money, health, the difficult person at work. Now count the minutes you spent thinking about the return of Christ. The ratio is your answer, and almost nobody likes it. What will finally make a Christian unready for glory is very unlikely to be a scandal. It will be a diary. Put one minute of looking for his coming into each day this week.

For worship. The Lord who is coming is not a trap for his people but their deliverer. He has warned us so that the day will not take us by surprise. He bears our burdens daily (Psalm 68:19), and he invites the weighed-down heart to come to him and find rest. Blessed be the Saviour who lifts our heads and lightens our hearts.

parallels.desc: like a thief in the night

verseByVerse.quote: But stay awake at all times, praying that you may have strength to escape all these things that are going to take place, and to stand before the Son of Man.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But stay awake at all times, praying that you may have strength to escape all these things that are going to take place, and to stand before the Son of Man.

But stay awake at all times. The whole discourse, the falling stones, the wars, the arrests, the trampled city, the shaken heavens, funnels into one sentence with two verbs in it: stay awake, and pray. No preparations to make, no place to go, no date to mark. At all times is not decoration. It rules out what every generation of Christians tends to do instead, which is to become intensely watchful when the news is bad and forget entirely when it is good. Wakefulness that responds to headlines is not wakefulness. It is nerves.

Praying that you may have strength to escape all these things that are going to take place. Prayer is the means of watchfulness (22:40, 46). And the escape is asked for in prayer, not announced as automatic. It is coupled with strength, which is language for endurance rather than absence. Not escape from the world, but from the judgment, and from being swept away by deception and fear.

Where Christians differ: does strength to escape mean a rapture before the tribulation? Many Christians have been taught to hear in this phrase the promise of a removal: that the church will be taken out of the world, secretly, before the worst arrives. Others read the escape as being kept safely through rather than being spared. Those who hold the first view are not careless readers; they are trying to give full weight to the word escape. Verdict: the more likely reading is that it means being kept faithful through what is coming, so as to stand before the Son of Man at the end, not being removed beforehand. Jesus has just said his followers will be persecuted and some put to death (vv. 12–16), and promised that by their endurance they will gain their lives (v. 19). The escape is paired with standing before the Son of Man, which is plainly the final scene, and the New Testament knows only one, public return of Christ (v. 27). There is no secret rapture. Whatever a reader concludes, the verse gives him something to do, and what it gives him is prayer.

And to stand before the Son of Man. To stand is legal language. It is what a man does when the case is called and his name is read. To stand before him at his coming means to be unashamed and accepted (1 John 2:28), not to fall in judgment but to stand in his presence. The psalm asks the question directly: if you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? (Psalm 130:3).

He stood where we could not. The Son of Man before whom his people will stand is the one who, within days, would himself stand bound before the council, before Pilate and before Herod. Pilate found no guilt in him, said so three times, and handed him over anyway (23:4, 14–15, 22–25). That is why the guilty can stand on the last day. The Judge has already stood in the dock in their place, and the sentence they deserved was carried out on him.

Will I be able to stand? That is the fear this verse leaves in many sincere hearts: have I watched enough, prayed enough, endured enough? Read the verse again and see where the strength comes from. It is not mustered; it is asked for. The prayer is not that we might be strong but that we might have strength given, and the one being asked is the one before whom we shall stand. He is not an examiner waiting to see whether we managed it. He is the one supplying the answer to his own examination. No one has ever stood before the Son of Man on his own record. The psalm that asks who could stand answers at once: but with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared (Psalm 130:4). The standing is his doing.

What does staying awake look like in practice? Not sleeplessness or constant anxiety. It means a life awake to God: regular prayer, morning and evening; reading Scripture; gathering with his people; confessing sin quickly rather than letting it settle; living each day as if it could be the day, and planning as if he might not come for a hundred years. It means asking often: if he came today, would he find me doing what he left me to do? Watchfulness is simply faithfulness that remembers he is coming.

In a sentence. Stay alert and pray always for strength to escape what is coming and to stand before the Son of Man.

On a Tuesday. Build one habit of watchfulness into this week. It might be a prayer each morning, Lord, keep me faithful today and ready for your coming; or a moment before sleep to confess the day’s sin and hand tomorrow to him. Small and daily is the point. Wakefulness is not a burst of zeal when the news is bad, but a rhythm that keeps going when nothing seems to be happening.

For worship. When the Son of Man comes, his people will not crawl to his throne. They will stand before it, upheld by the One who sits on it. He gives power to the faint, and the strength by which they stand on that day will be his gift, asked for in a thousand small prayers and answered in one great morning. They will look up into the face of their Judge and find there the face of their Saviour, and they will stand, and never fall again.

verseByVerse.quote: And every day he was teaching in the temple, but at night he went out and lodged on the mount called Olivet. And early in the morning all the people came to him in the temple to hear him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every day he was teaching in the temple, but at night he went out and lodged on the mount called Olivet. And early in the morning all the people came to him in the temple to hear him.

And every day he was teaching in the temple. Luke ends the greatest prophetic discourse in his Gospel with a timetable, and it is quietly astonishing. This man has announced the destruction of the temple he is standing in, the siege of the city he is standing in, the arrest and death of the friends beside him, the shaking of the heavens and his own return in the glory of God. He knows that within days he will be flogged, mocked and crucified. He knows which of the men around him will betray him and which will deny him. And what he does with the days that remain is: teach in the morning, sleep on a hillside, and get up and do it again.

But at night he went out and lodged on the mount called Olivet. Olivet is the Mount of Olives. Pilgrims crowded Jerusalem at Passover, and many camped outside. Jesus may have stayed at Bethany (Mark 11:11), or in the open, at the place where he often went to pray (22:39), which is where Judas would find him. He had said it himself: foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (9:58). In the last week of his life it was still true. And the mountain he slept on was the one from which he had wept over the city (19:41), the one where he would pray in agony and be arrested, and the one from which he would ascend (Acts 1:12).

And early in the morning all the people came to him in the temple to hear him. Eager crowds, at dawn. There is no frenzy in him, no last campaign, no scramble to secure the movement. He teaches, as he had for three years, available to whoever comes, and the leaders could not touch him in public.

The rhythm of a man who knows the future. Work in the day. Withdraw at night to pray. Be found in the morning where the people who need you can find you. That is what perfect knowledge of a terrible future looked like when it was lived out in an actual week by an actual man, and it looked like peace: not the peace of someone who does not know what is coming, but of someone who knows exactly and is not afraid, because the Father who holds the whole of it is his Father and has never once been late.

How can I have peace when the future is uncertain? Your future is less known to you than Jesus’ was to him, but it is just as fully known to your Father. Peace does not come from knowing what will happen. It comes from knowing who holds what will happen, and from doing today what he has given you to do. Jesus’ last week shows that faithfulness and peace go together: he did not escape the cross by worrying about it, and he did not lose his peace by facing it. Bring each day to the Father, as he did on the Mount of Olives, and you will find that the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guards your heart (Philippians 4:7).

In a sentence. Each day Jesus taught in the temple and each night stayed on the Mount of Olives, and early each morning all the people came to hear him.

On a Tuesday. Begin your day by hearing Jesus in his word. The crowds got up before dawn to hear him in the temple; you can hear him at your kitchen table. Set aside the first part of the morning, even fifteen minutes, before the phone and the news, to read a passage of the Gospels and pray. Then go and do the day’s ordinary work in peace, and give the evening back to God.

For worship. He is teaching in the temple he has just condemned, sleeping on the hill where he will be arrested, and there is no tremor in him anywhere. That is the Lord of the Olivet Discourse. He did not merely predict the shaking of heaven and earth; he slept under those heavens, on that earth, days before the worst of it fell on him, and rose early to teach whoever came. Blessed be the calm and faithful Son, who walked into his last week with open eyes, for us.
verseByVerse.note: Olivet is the Mount of Olives. Pilgrims crowded Jerusalem at Passover, and many camped outside it.

parallels.desc: as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives

21.text: <sup>1</sup> Jesus looked up and saw the rich putting their gifts into the offering box, <sup>2</sup> and he saw a poor widow put in two small copper coins. <sup>3</sup> And he said, “Truly, I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all of them. <sup>4</sup> For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty put in all she had to live on.” <sup>5</sup> And while some were speaking of the temple, how it was adorned with noble stones and offerings, he said, <sup>6</sup> “As for these things that you see, the days will come when there will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.” <sup>7</sup> And they asked him, “Teacher, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when these things are about to take place?” <sup>8</sup> And he said, “See that you are not led astray. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he!’ and, ‘The time is at hand!’ Do not go after them. <sup>9</sup> And when you hear of wars and tumults, do not be terrified, for these things must first take place, but the end will not be at once.” <sup>10</sup> Then he said to them, “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. <sup>11</sup> There will be great earthquakes, and in various places famines and pestilences. And there will be terrors and great signs from heaven. <sup>12</sup> But before all this they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, delivering you up to the synagogues and prisons, and you will be brought before kings and governors for my name's sake. <sup>13</sup> This will be your opportunity to bear witness. <sup>14</sup> Settle it therefore in your minds not to meditate beforehand how to answer, <sup>15</sup> for I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to withstand or contradict. <sup>16</sup> You will be delivered up even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and some of you they will put to death. <sup>17</sup> You will be hated by all for my name's sake. <sup>18</sup> But not a hair of your head will perish. <sup>19</sup> By your endurance you will gain your lives. <sup>20</sup> “But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near. <sup>21</sup> Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and let those who are inside the city depart, and let not those who are out in the country enter it, <sup>22</sup> for these are days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written. <sup>23</sup> Alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people. <sup>24</sup> They will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled. <sup>25</sup> “And there will be signs in sun and moon and stars, and on the earth distress of nations in perplexity because of the roaring of the sea and the waves, <sup>26</sup> people fainting with fear and with foreboding of what is coming on the world. For the powers of the heavens will be shaken. <sup>27</sup> And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. <sup>28</sup> Now when these things begin to take place, straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.” <sup>29</sup> And he told them a parable: “Look at the fig tree, and all the trees. <sup>30</sup> As soon as they come out in leaf, you see for yourselves and know that the summer is already near. <sup>31</sup> So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that the kingdom of God is near. <sup>32</sup> Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all has taken place. <sup>33</sup> Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. <sup>34</sup> “But watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly like a trap. <sup>35</sup> For it will come upon all who dwell on the face of the whole earth. <sup>36</sup> But stay awake at all times, praying that you may have strength to escape all these things that are going to take place, and to stand before the Son of Man.” <sup>37</sup> And every day he was teaching in the temple, but at night he went out and lodged on the mount called Olivet. <sup>38</sup> And early in the morning all the people came to him in the temple to hear him.

22.title: The Last Supper, Gethsemane, and the Arrest
22.overview:
Luke 22 covers the most theologically concentrated night in human history. It begins with Judas's betrayal agreement and the preparation of the Passover meal, moves through the institution of the Lord's Supper, includes a remarkable dispute among the disciples about greatness, records Jesus's prediction of Peter's denial and his commissioning of Peter to strengthen the brothers, narrates the agony in Gethsemane, and ends with the arrest, Peter's denial, and Jesus before the Sanhedrin.

Luke's account of the Last Supper has several distinctive features: he records two cups (v. 17 and v. 20), emphasises the kingdom dimension of the meal (“I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God”), and includes the unique account of the disciples' dispute about greatness followed immediately by Jesus's teaching about servant leadership. The contrast between the disciples' argument about rank and Jesus washing their feet (in John) — and more immediately, serving them with his body and blood — could not be sharper.

The Gethsemane account in Luke is distinctive for the appearance of an angel strengthening Jesus (v. 43) and for the detail that “his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground” (v. 44) — a possible description of hematidrosis, a rare condition in which extreme distress causes capillaries to rupture into the sweat glands. Luke the physician may be noting what he understood as a medical phenomenon of extreme psychological anguish. The cup Jesus prays about is not merely the physical suffering of crucifixion but the cup of God's wrath that he will drink on behalf of sinners.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Conspiracy, Preparation, and the Last Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Luke lays two sentences on top of each other and makes the reader hold both. The Passover — the feast of the lamb whose blood turned the destroyer aside in Egypt — draws near; and in that week the chief priests are looking for a way to kill the Lamb of God. Their reasoning is entirely practical: they feared the people. A crowd-control problem, being managed during a busy festival, by men who had no idea what they were aiming at and hit it exactly.

Then the most disturbing sentence in the chapter: Satan entered into Judas — who was of the number of the twelve. Luke offers no psychology. But his next sentence makes the responsibility plain: Judas went, conferred, agreed a figure, consented, and began looking for a moment without a crowd. Every verb is his. Matthew gives the price, and it is the compensation the law set for a slave killed by an ox, and the sum weighed out to the rejected shepherd in Zechariah.

The preparation is handled the way the colt was handled in chapter 19 — two disciples sent, a sign described in advance, everything found just as he said. A man carrying a water jar would stand out in that crowd, since water-carrying was women's work. Whether Jesus had arranged it quietly or knew it prophetically, the effect is the same: nothing about this night is happening to him.

At the table he says he has earnestly desired this meal, and then looks past his suffering to a Passover still owing in the kingdom of God. He takes the Passover cup and the unleavened bread, both of them fifteen centuries old, and fills them with himself: this is my body, which is given for you; this cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood. Jeremiah's promise, unfulfilled for six hundred years, is claimed at a supper table.

And then, only after the bread and the cup have been handed round, the betrayer is named — his hand on the same table. The Son of Man goes as it has been determined, and woe to the man by whom he is betrayed. Both, in one breath, unreconciled.

The disciples begin questioning one another, and not one of them looks at Judas.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord's Supper is memorial, proclamation and anticipation at once. Memorial: do this in remembrance of me — remembrance of the kind Passover itself was, never bare recollection but an act that brought a past deliverance into the present of the people keeping it (cf. Exod. 12:14). Proclamation: you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes (1 Cor. 11:26). Anticipation: he will not eat or drink it again until the kingdom of God comes, so every communion table is an unfinished meal.

Four views are held on what happens at that table. Rome teaches transubstantiation — the substance becomes the body and blood while the appearances remain. Luther held the body is present in, with and under the elements. Zwingli held the elements purely symbolic, the Supper a remembrance and a pledge. The Reformed position, with Calvin and the Westminster standards, is that the bread remains bread and Christ is nonetheless truly given: by his Spirit the believer really feeds on Christ, not with the teeth but by faith. The strongest argument for it is that his body was in front of them, unbroken, when he said the words — and he habitually spoke this way: I am the door, I am the vine.

Note the two words in both sayings: for you — on behalf of, in the place of. Substitution, spoken by the substitute the night before he was substituted.

And vv. 21–22 set divine determination and human guilt side by side without reconciling them. This is the settled pattern of Scripture — Joseph's you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, and Peter's delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 3 frightens some believers, who wonder whether they could be handed over like Judas. The fear is itself the answer. Judas is never recorded as afraid of what he was becoming; he was calm, he negotiated, he ate the supper, he came with a kiss ready. A conscience that recoils in horror at the thought of betraying Christ is not being handed over — it is being held. And the man in this chapter who did deny his Lord out loud, three times, was being prayed for while he did it.

Verses 4–6 supply a test that needs no theological training. Every part of that transaction required the absence of a crowd. Is there any part of what you are arranging that has been arranged so that it happens where you will not be seen?

Verse 20 answers the fear that keeps some believers away from the table — that they are not good enough to come. The cup does not commemorate anyone's fitness. It was poured out for a table that contained a traitor, a denier, and ten men who would run before morning.

And v. 23 is quietly searching. When a sin is named from a pulpit, notice who comes to mind first. The eleven looked inward before they looked around, and they were right to. When Judas asked it, he already knew the answer (Matt. 26:25).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Feast of Unleavened Bread drew near, which is called the Passover. And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to put him to death, for they feared the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Feast of Unleavened Bread drew near, which is called the Passover. And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to put him to death, for they feared the people.

Meaning first. Luke 22 is the last night before the cross. The leaders plot, Judas sells his Lord, and Jesus, in command of every detail, keeps the Passover with his apostles and turns it into the Lord’s Supper: bread that is his body given for them, a cup that is the new covenant in his blood (vv. 1–23). At the table the disciples argue about rank; he shows them greatness as service, promises them a kingdom, and tells Peter he has prayed for him (vv. 24–38). Then come the prayer on the Mount of Olives and the cup, the betrayal with a kiss, the healing of an enemy’s ear, Peter’s denials and the Lord’s look, and the dawn trial where Jesus declares that the Son of Man will be seated at God’s right hand (vv. 39–71). The one being handed over is the one in charge.

The setting. Chapters 22 and 23 tell the passion: the supper, the arrest, the trials and the death of Jesus. No story was told more often in the early church, and every Gospel slows down here, as if to say that everything before was leading to this.

The Feast of Unleavened Bread drew near, which is called the Passover. Unleavened Bread was the week-long feast that began with the Passover meal (Exodus 12:15–20), and Luke explains for Gentile readers that the two were spoken of as one. Passover was the feast of the lamb. Every family in Israel that could afford one brought a year-old male without blemish to the temple, and on the fourteenth of the month, between the afternoon and the evening, it was killed. Josephus, who had reason to know, reckoned the lambs slaughtered at a single Passover in the hundreds of thousands. The city smelled of it. And the whole ritual existed to keep one night alive in the nation’s memory: the night in Egypt when the blood went on the doorposts and the destroyer passed over the houses that had it (Exodus 12). That is the week the chief priests choose to kill the Lamb of God, who is our Passover lamb, sacrificed for us (1 Corinthians 5:7).

The chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to put him to death. The plot has been building for days (19:47; 20:19). They do not know what they are really doing, and that is the point of putting the two sentences together. They think they are managing a political problem, and their reasoning is entirely practical.

For they feared the people. Not God; the people. They needed a quiet arrest, away from the crowds who hung on his words (21:38), at a festival when the city’s population multiplied several times over and Rome was watching. Notice how small it is. The men entrusted with the worship of Israel are conspiring against the salvation of Israel, and the thing governing their deliberations is a public-order risk assessment.

Behind them a purpose is running to time. Seven weeks later Peter would set the two truths side by side before a crowd in this same city: Jesus was delivered up by the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and they had killed him by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). Luke records both and lets neither swallow the other. The scheming was theirs, freely chosen and fully culpable. And it was the means by which the Lamb was brought to the feast in the very week the lambs died, the week the Scriptures had been pointing at for fifteen hundred years. The priests were thinking about crowds. God was keeping an appointment.

Does God cause people to do evil, then? No. God never puts wickedness into a heart or approves it (James 1:13). The leaders hated Jesus because they wanted to, and they will answer for it. But God is never a spectator who has to improvise around human sin. He governs it, restrains it, sets its limits and turns it to his own good ends, as he did with Joseph’s brothers (Genesis 50:20). That is why the cross can be at once the worst crime ever committed and the best thing that ever happened. Hold both: the evil is real and blameworthy, and it is never out of God’s hand.

In a sentence. As Passover approached, the leaders looked for a way to kill Jesus without provoking the people.

On a Tuesday. When your own circumstances look as if they are being decided by people with small motives, very often they are. A department is restructured because someone wanted a title. A church divides because two men could not back down. Naming those motives honestly is not cynicism. But their reach is not what it appears. Bring the thing to God today, tell him plainly what the people involved are doing, and then do the next right thing in front of you, knowing that the one who used a crowd-control decision to bring his Son to the cross is not defeated by a reorganisation.

For worship. Blessed be the God who chose the lamb before the priests chose the date. Fifteen centuries of Passovers were rehearsals for one afternoon, and every lamb that died in Egypt and in the temple courts was a finger pointing at his Son. Men plotted in the dark, and he had already written the ending in the light: the blood on the doorposts, the destroyer passing over, a people brought out free. The Lamb was chosen before the world began, and there is no plot of men or devils that does not end by serving him.
verseByVerse.note: Unleavened Bread was the week-long feast that began with Passover; the two names were used together.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Satan entered into Judas called Iscariot, who was of the number of the twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Satan entered into Judas called Iscariot, who was of the number of the Twelve.

Then Satan entered into Judas called Iscariot. Luke says it without preamble, and it is the most disturbing sentence in the chapter. After the temptation in the wilderness the devil departed from Jesus until an opportune time (4:13). Now is that time. He does not attack Jesus directly; he works through a man at his side. John says the same, placing it at the supper (John 13:2, 27). Luke does not tell us why Judas did it. Preachers have supplied a hundred theories about disappointed political hopes. Luke supplies none of them. He names a spiritual event: the enemy of God entered a man who had been walking beside Jesus for three years.

The stronger man. Jesus had already told the parable of this night. When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own palace, his goods are safe; but when one stronger than he attacks him and overcomes him, he takes away his armour and divides his spoil (11:21–22). The devil has come back at his opportune time, but he has come to fight the stronger man, and he has chosen as his weapon the very death by which the stronger man will strip him. Satan enters Judas to destroy Jesus. Jesus lets Judas deliver him up, so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death (Hebrews 2:14).

Who was of the number of the twelve. This is the clause that makes it unbearable. Not a hanger-on, not a stranger: one of the Twelve, chosen after a night of prayer (6:12–16), sent out with authority to preach and to heal (9:1–2), who had come back and told Jesus all they had done (9:10). Whatever else this verse teaches, it teaches that nearness to Jesus is not the same as belonging to him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Judas was not responsible. Luke’s next sentence answers that: Satan entered him, and then he went away and conferred. He walked to the meeting, opened the negotiation, named his terms and took the money. Every verb belongs to Judas, and Jesus calls the betrayal a woe upon the man who commits it (v. 22), which would be monstrous if the man were a puppet. Satan does not manufacture desires that were not there. He finds them, feeds them and hands the man the opportunity. Judas had already given way to greed (John 12:6). What entered him found a door already unlocked, and Judas had been turning the key, quietly, for a long time: a coin here, a resentment there, a growing private conviction that he understood things better than his master. And even Satan’s work serves God’s purpose (v. 22; Acts 2:23). The cross that Satan plotted would be his own defeat (Colossians 2:15).

Could Satan enter me like that? Not if you belong to Christ. A believer is indwelt by the Holy Spirit (Romans 8:9), and he who is in you is greater than he who is in the world (1 John 4:4). Satan can tempt a Christian, accuse him, and sift him hard, as this chapter will show with Peter, but he cannot take possession of one whom Christ has bought. Judas was never one of Christ’s sheep (John 6:64, 70; 17:12). Yet the warning still stands for every Christian: do not give the devil a foothold (Ephesians 4:27). Unconfessed sin, nursed resentment and secret greed are exactly the open doors he looks for.

I am afraid I might be a Judas. Some believers are frightened by this verse: they wonder whether the sin they cannot shake is the beginning of a betrayal. The fear itself is the answer, and it should be said plainly. Judas is never once recorded as being afraid of what he was becoming. He was calm; he negotiated; he ate the supper; he came to the garden with a kiss ready. A conscience that recoils in horror at the thought of betraying Christ is not a conscience being handed over. It is a conscience being held. And the man in this very chapter who did deny his Lord, out loud, three times, was being prayed for while he did it (v. 32), and was fully restored. Judas went out to a meeting. Peter went out and wept. The difference between them was not the size of the sin (2 Corinthians 7:10).

In a sentence. Satan entered into Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve.

On a Tuesday. Sin left unchecked opens a door. Ask yourself which private grievance or habit you have been feeding while telling yourself it is under control: the resentment you rehearse on the drive home, the money that is never quite accounted for, the opinion that you see more clearly than the people God has put over you. Name it to God today, specifically, and shut the door by repentance before anyone else walks through it.

For worship. Jesus once saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven (10:18), and on this night the fallen one made his last throw. He entered a traitor, gathered priests and soldiers, and arranged the darkest afternoon the world has known, and every move he made ran straight into the purpose of God. The cross he plotted became the throne from which Christ triumphs over him. Strong as the enemy is, the Lord is stronger, and the trembling sheep who fear they might fall are held by the hand that conquered him.

verseByVerse.quote: He went away and conferred with the chief priests and officers how he might betray him to them. And they were glad, and agreed to give him money. So he consented and sought an opportunity to betray him to them in the absence of a crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He went away and conferred with the chief priests and officers how he might betray him to them. And they were glad, and agreed to give him money. So he consented and sought an opportunity to betray him to them in the absence of a crowd.

And conferred with the chief priests and officers. Read the whole sentence slowly, because Luke has written it as a sequence of ordinary business, and the flatness is deliberate. He went. He conferred. They were glad. They agreed a figure. He consented. He began looking for a window. There is no struggle recorded, no hesitation. It reads like the minutes of a meeting, and that is more frightening than a scene of tormented decision. The officers were the captains of the temple police, who would make the arrest (v. 52). It is a meeting between the religious executive and the head of security, with an informant, about an operational difficulty.

How he might betray him to them. The verb is paradidōmi, to hand over. It is the word Jesus had used in his predictions (9:44; 18:32), and the word Paul will use of the Father who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32). Judas hands him over for money; the Father hands him over for love; the Son gives himself up (Galatians 2:20). Three handings-over in one act, and only one of them was wicked.

And they were glad. Luke will not let that pass. These men had been unable to touch Jesus because of the crowds, and now the solution has walked in the door by itself, wearing the face of one of his own friends. Their gladness is a small and squalid emotion, and it is recorded so that we can see what the leadership of Israel had become: relieved, at a problem solved.

And agreed to give him money. Matthew tells us the figure: thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:15). It is not an arbitrary sum. It is the compensation set in the law of Moses for a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32), and it is the sum weighed out to the rejected shepherd in Zechariah’s strange prophecy, the lordly price at which God himself was priced by them (Zechariah 11:12–13). That is the value the guardians of his own house placed on the Son of God: the going rate for a dead slave.

In the absence of a crowd. This last phrase is the tell. At night, in a quiet place, with an insider to show them where. Both parties want the same thing: darkness. The priests want it because their power cannot survive daylight, and Judas wants it because betrayal cannot be done in front of witnesses. Sin has a settled preference, and this is it. Not one thing in this transaction could have been done at noon in the temple court (John 3:20; Ephesians 5:11–13).

How could anyone sell Jesus for money? Very easily, and by degrees. John tells us Judas kept the common purse and used to help himself to it (John 12:6). He did not wake one morning and decide to betray the Messiah; he had spent months letting money matter more than the Master, and when the offer came the decision was already mostly made. That is why Paul calls the love of money a root of all kinds of evils (1 Timothy 6:10). Most of us will never be offered silver for Christ. But every week we are offered small trades: a dishonest claim, a hidden purchase, a Sunday given up for overtime we do not need. Each one teaches the heart what it values.

In a sentence. Judas went to the chief priests and temple officers to arrange to betray Jesus, and they gladly agreed to pay him, so he looked for a chance to hand Jesus over away from the crowds.

On a Tuesday. Here is one of the few tests of conduct that is genuinely reliable and takes no theological training to apply: is there any part of what I am doing that I am arranging so that it happens where I will not be seen? The message deleted, the receipt not kept, the route home chosen so no one asks. Whatever needs the absence of a crowd usually needs it for a reason. Bring that thing into the light today, with God first and then, if it is needed, with one trusted person.

For worship. The leaders were glad over a bargain; heaven is glad over a ransom. The one they bought cheaply, in an office by lamplight, had already resolved to buy them at a price no treasury could hold: not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with his own precious blood (1 Peter 1:18–19). Men agreed a sum for the Son of God and thought they had settled his worth. God had settled the price of our redemption before the foundation of the world, and he paid it in full, in the Son they sold.
verseByVerse.note: The officers were the captains of the temple police. Matthew says the price was thirty pieces of silver.

verseByVerse.quote: Then came the day of Unleavened Bread, on which the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed. So Jesus sent Peter and John, saying, 'Go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then came the day of Unleavened Bread, on which the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed. So Jesus sent Peter and John, saying: go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat it.

On which the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed. The lambs were sacrificed at the temple on the afternoon of 14 Nisan, before the meal that evening, by the thousands. Three words carry more weight than they seem to: had to be. The Greek is edei, from dei, it is necessary, it must. Luke uses this word all through his Gospel for the fixed purposes of God. The Son of Man must suffer many things (9:22). It was necessary that the Christ should suffer and enter into his glory (24:26). Here it is used of the lamb. Luke means first that the law required it on that day, and that is the plain sense. But he has chosen the word he uses for divine necessity, and used it about a lamb being killed, on the day the true Lamb would be killed, in a chapter about a death he keeps calling determined. Luke does not do this by accident. The law required the lamb, and the purpose of God required the Lamb.

So Jesus sent Peter and John. Only Luke names them. They are the two who will stand at the centre of Luke’s second volume, together in the temple in Acts 3, before the council in Acts 4, sent to Samaria in Acts 8. Their partnership begins here, running an errand.

Go and prepare the Passover for us. What an errand it was. Preparing a Passover meant securing the room, buying the lamb, taking it to the temple court to be killed in the afternoon rush, carrying the carcass back, roasting it whole, buying the bitter herbs, mixing the fruit paste, and setting out the unleavened bread and the wine. It was a whole afternoon of ordinary labour, and Jesus asked two of his closest friends to do it on the last day of his life. There is a whole doctrine of vocation in that, for anyone who has felt that their own tasks are too small to be part of anything. Peter and John spent the afternoon before the Lord’s Supper buying groceries.

That we may eat it. Not that you may eat it. He includes himself in the meal, and he is looking forward to it: he will tell them he has earnestly desired to eat this Passover with them (v. 15).

Was this a Passover meal? Luke, with Matthew and Mark, says so plainly. John seems at first to put the Passover a day later (John 18:28; 19:14). The more likely explanation is that John’s Passover there means the meals of the festival week, and Preparation means the Friday before the Sabbath of Passover week. The Last Supper was a Passover meal, and Jesus is the true Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Should Christians keep the Passover today? Christians are free to learn from a Passover meal, and many find that seeing one explains the Lord’s Supper wonderfully. But we are not bound to keep it. The Passover was a shadow of the things to come, and the substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 10:1). The lamb has been slain once for all, and Jesus gave his church a new meal to keep until he comes, which is the Lord’s Supper. To treat the old feast as necessary would be to go back to the shadow when the light has risen.

In a sentence. On the day the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed, Jesus sent Peter and John to get the meal ready.

On a Tuesday. Jesus planned his last meal with his friends; he wanted to be with them. And he put two apostles to work on shopping and cooking. If your own day is mostly errands, lists and ordinary work, do it today as service to him, not as time stolen from serving him. The jobs that look smallest are often the ones that lay a table for something you will not see until later.

For worship. Peter and John went to the temple that afternoon to buy a lamb and see it killed, and the Lamb who sent them was waiting in the city to be killed the next day. They carried a carcass home; he would carry the sin of the world. Every lamb that bled in those courts died once and stayed dead, and was never enough. He would die once and rise, and be enough for ever. Blessed is the Host who sent his friends to prepare a meal, and then gave himself for the life of the world.
verseByVerse.note: The lambs were sacrificed at the temple on the afternoon before the Passover meal.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, 'Where will you have us prepare it?' He said to them, 'Behold, when you have entered the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house that he enters
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said to him: where will you have us prepare it? He said to them: behold, when you have entered the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house that he enters.

Where will you have us prepare it? A reasonable and slightly anxious question. Jerusalem at Passover was overwhelmed, its population swollen several times over, and rooms went early and to the connected.

A man carrying a jar of water. The answer is a sign that will pick itself out of a crowd of thousands. Carrying water was usually women’s work, done in the morning and evening by the women of the household. Men carried wineskins; women carried water jars. A man with a jar on his shoulder would stand out at once.

Had Jesus arranged this beforehand, or did he know it prophetically? Luke does not say, and both are entirely possible. The parallel is the colt in 19:29–34: two disciples sent, a sign described, a password given, and everything found as told. Jesus may well have made quiet arrangements. What both explanations agree on is the thing Luke is certainly saying: nothing about this night is happening to Jesus. He is arranging it.

Follow him into the house that he enters. A secret arrangement, very likely so that Judas would not know the place in advance and could not betray Jesus before the meal. A man who knew the city was full of people wanting to arrest him had good reason to keep the location of his last evening out of Judas’s hands until the last possible hour.

He is not being taken. He is going. Everything from here to the tomb will look like a man being carried along by other people’s decisions: arrested, tried, condemned, executed. Luke opens the sequence by showing you a man who knows what a stranger will be carrying on his shoulder that afternoon. No one takes my life from me, he had said, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18).

Does Jesus guide me in the details like this? He does, but usually not in this way. The same Lord governs every detail of your life by his providence, down to the hairs of your head (12:7), and he guides his people through his Word, through wise counsel and through the ordinary sense he gives. He does not promise us coded signs about which street to take, and we should not demand them or treat every coincidence as a message. Pray about the details, read the Scriptures, ask advice, decide with a clear conscience, and then trust that the one who knew about a water jar is not absent from your house move or your job interview.

In a sentence. Jesus told them that in the city they would meet a man carrying a water jar, and should follow him into the house he entered.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is in control of every detail. Take the decision you are anxious about today and pray over it specifically. Then take the next step that is plainly right, even if you cannot see the step after it. Peter and John were not told the whole evening; they were told to follow a man with a jar.

For worship. The priests had silver, soldiers and an informer, and they could not find out where he would eat. He kept the room hidden until the hour, not to save his life, which he had already resolved to give, but to keep the supper safe until he had placed it in his friends’ hands. Nothing would be taken from him before he had given it. The Lord who ordered every street and stair of that city that afternoon orders every step by which he brings his people to his table still.
verseByVerse.note: Carrying water was usually women’s work, so a man with a jar would stand out.

verseByVerse.quote: and tell the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says to you, Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ And he will show you a large upper room furnished; prepare it there.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And tell the master of the house: the Teacher says to you, where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples? And he will show you a large upper room furnished; prepare it there.

The Teacher says to you. The message is a phrase, not an explanation. No name is given. Whoever this householder was, he needed only that much, which tells you the arrangement was already understood between them, and that there was at least one man in Jerusalem that week who counted it an honour to be trusted with something and asked no further questions. He is never named. He appears for one sentence in the history of the world and disappears, and the room he lent has been remembered for two thousand years.

Where is the guest room. The word is katalyma, the same word as the inn at Bethlehem where there was no place for them (2:7). At his birth there was no room; at his death a room is ready. The world that had no space for him in the manger has one large furnished room for him on his last night, and he fills it with a gift the world has fed on ever since.

A large upper room furnished. Larger houses had an upper room reached by an outside stair. Furnished means spread and laid out: carpets down, the low couches arranged around the table, cushions in place. Somebody had already done the work. It may have been the same upper room where the disciples gathered after the ascension (Acts 1:13), and possibly the house of Mark’s mother (Acts 12:12), though we cannot be sure.

It was the room. This unnamed man gave not a sermon, not a miracle, not a martyrdom, but a furnished room for an evening, and in it the Lord’s Supper was instituted, the meal the church has kept in every century since. That is the encouragement for every believer whose service is practical: someone opens the building, someone sets out the chairs, someone drives the elderly member to church. The householder had no idea what he was providing space for, and that is the ordinary condition of Christian service.

Where I may eat the Passover with my disciples. Notice the possessive. On the eve of the night when every one of them will fail him, one betraying, one denying, the rest scattering, he calls them my disciples. He knows exactly what they are going to do. And the room is booked for them, the meal is prepared for them, and they are still his. Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end (John 13:1).

What if my home or my gifts seem too ordinary to matter? Then you are in exactly the householder’s position, and he is one of the quiet heroes of the Gospels. Hospitality is not a minor virtue in the New Testament; it is required of elders and commended to all (Romans 12:13; 1 Peter 4:9). A kitchen table where a struggling believer is fed, a spare room for a missionary, a lift to church: these are rooms lent to Christ. Do not wait until you have something impressive to offer. Offer what you have, and let him decide what it is for.

In a sentence. They were to ask the owner, on the Teacher’s behalf, for the guest room, and he would show them a large furnished upper room.

On a Tuesday. Make room for Jesus in your home and life. Think of one practical way your home, car, time or skill could serve someone in your church this week, and offer it without waiting to be asked. Then do not mention it.

For worship. The Lord of heaven and earth borrowed a room, and in it he gave away everything. He asked a stranger for cushions and a table so that he could put into his friends’ hands the bread and the cup of the new covenant. He took a guest’s place in a borrowed house so that we, who were strangers, might be given a son’s place in his Father’s house, where he has gone to prepare rooms that will never be lent and never be taken back (John 14:2). We lent him an upper room for one night. He gives us a home for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Larger houses had an upper room reached by an outside stair.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they went and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.

Just as he had told them. A single short sentence, and Luke uses the same construction he used of the colt: they went, and found it just as he had told them (19:32). He is building a pattern in his reader’s mind on purpose, and the pattern is about to be tested to destruction. What has been said so far is easy to trust. A room, a signal, a stranger with a jar: the words of Jesus proved reliable in a small domestic matter. Within hours the same two men will hear things that are impossible to receive: that one of them will betray him, that Peter will deny him before dawn, that he himself will be numbered with criminals. By the following afternoon they will be looking at a body. If he could be trusted about a man with a water jar, he could be trusted about his death and resurrection.

The last easy verification. This is the last easy verification any of them will get; everything afterwards has to be believed in the dark. That is the ordinary shape of a Christian life. There is a stretch where the promises are checkable, a prayer answered plainly, a provision at the right hour, and then a season in which nothing is confirmable and all you have is that the same voice was accurate before. That does not make the silence pleasant. It makes it survivable, because the silence of a proven friend is not the silence of a stranger.

And they prepared the Passover. This is where the disciples’ part lies. He told them where; they did the work. Foreknowledge in this Gospel never replaces obedience; it directs it. They found it as he said, and then they went and roasted a lamb, not knowing that they were laying a table for the end of the world’s long night.

Does this mean everything I want will turn out as I hope? No. What comes true is what Jesus has said, not what we have wished. He told these men about a room, and also about betrayal, denial and his own death, and all of it came true. His promises to every believer are many and certain: forgiveness, his presence, the Spirit, the resurrection of the body, a place in his kingdom. He has not promised you the job, the healing or the outcome you are praying for, though you may and should ask. Trust him for what he has said, and leave what he has not said in his hands.

In a sentence. They found everything just as Jesus had said, and prepared the Passover.

On a Tuesday. Think of one thing God has actually done for you that you could not have arranged, the sort of thing you have told other people about. Then hold it up against the situation in which he is currently saying nothing. The one who was accurate then is the same one now. Write that answered prayer down somewhere you will see it this week, and do the plain duty in front of you while you wait.

For worship. He was right about a stranger with a jar, and he was right about the cross, and he was right about the third morning. Not one of the good promises the LORD made to Israel failed (Joshua 21:45), and the One who stood behind them all was reclining in a borrowed room, about to keep them in his own body. The water jar and the empty tomb came from the same mouth, and that mouth has never yet had to take back a word.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the hour came, he reclined at table, and the apostles with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the hour came, he reclined at table, and the apostles with him.

And when the hour came. In one sense it means the appointed time for the Passover meal, which began after sunset. But this is the Gospel in which Jesus has been walking towards something with his face set (9:51), and the chapter in which he will say to the arresting party, this is your hour, and the power of darkness (v. 53). John makes the theme explicit: his hour had not yet come, and then at last it had (John 13:1). Luke says it more quietly. The hour came, and he sat down to dinner.

He reclined at table. Not upright on chairs behind a long table, as in the paintings, but lying on their left sides on low couches around a low table, propped on the left elbow, eating with the right hand. That is why John could lean back against Jesus (John 13:23), and why a woman could once reach his feet without crawling under anything (7:38). Reclining had its own meaning. Free men reclined; slaves stood and served. The first Passover was eaten standing, ready to leave Egypt (Exodus 12:11), but by Jesus’ time reclining had become the custom, to celebrate freedom. You eat this meal lying down, at ease, because you are no longer slaves.

And the apostles with him. All twelve, including Judas. Luke has told us in v. 3 what one of them has done, and he places him here without comment, reclining with the rest.

Composure that is real. The hour has come, the hour he has been moving towards since the first page, and what he does with it is lie down among his friends in the posture of a free man at a feast of deliverance, on the last evening of his life, with the man who has already sold him lying somewhere along the same table. He is going to be flogged before this time tomorrow, and he is at table, at peace, keeping the feast. Whatever composure is, this is what it looks like when it is real: not the absence of dread, for the garden will show you the dread, but the refusal to let dread eat the hours that are still good.

Does it matter whether we sit, stand or kneel at the Lord’s Supper? Scripture does not prescribe a posture, and churches do it differently with clear consciences. Some sit at a table, as the disciples did, to show that we are guests welcomed to a family meal; some come forward; some kneel. What matters is that the posture of the heart is right: humble, because we are sinners, and at rest, because we are free. A believer may come to that table as these men came, as guests whom the Master has invited, not as slaves earning a place.

In a sentence. When the hour came, Jesus reclined at the table with the apostles.

On a Tuesday. You may have a hard thing coming this week, a hospital appointment, a difficult conversation, a deadline you dread. Do not let it eat the good hours before it. Sit at your own table tonight with the people God has given you, give thanks for the food, and be present. The Lord who reclined on the night before the cross is with you in the evening before yours.

For worship. He who would bear the curse lay down at a feast of freedom, and made his last evening a welcome. You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies (Psalm 23:5): the shepherd-king of that psalm is reclining in an upper room with his enemies already moving in the dark, and he spreads the table anyway. Jesus still invites his people to his table, slaves made free, and bids them recline.
verseByVerse.note: The Passover was eaten after sunset, reclining.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I tell you I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I tell you I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.

I have earnestly desired. The English is polite. The Greek is not. Epithumia epethumēsa, literally with desire I have desired: a Hebrew way of speaking that doubles the word to intensify it. It is the language of aching for something, the word used of Jacob longing greatly for his father’s house (Genesis 31:30). Only Luke records it.

To eat this Passover with you. And the object of the longing is this: an evening with eleven ordinary men and one traitor, in a borrowed room, eating roast lamb. He is not saying he was resigned to the meal, or glad of company on a hard night. He had ached for it: of everything available to the Son of God in the last hours of his earthly life, he had set his heart on being at a table with them. These are the men who will, before morning, argue about rank, fall asleep on him, draw a sword he did not want, deny him and run. He knows all of it. The longing is not based on a misreading of their quality.

Before I suffer. Then, immediately, the shadow. The word is pathein, from the same root as the church’s old name for these events, the Passion. He is not merely aware that suffering is coming. He is dating the meal by it. This was a Passover meal, and the last before his suffering, and he knew.

For I tell you I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God. Having named the suffering, he looks straight past it. That is a startling thing to say at that table. It assumes there is a far side. The Passover pointed forward, and its meaning would be filled full first in his death, the true Passover sacrifice, and finally in the banquet of the kingdom (13:29; 14:15): the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9), the mountain feast of rich food that Isaiah saw, where the covering cast over all peoples is swallowed up and God wipes away tears from all faces (Isaiah 25:6–8). The meal looks back to Egypt, forward to the cross, and beyond the cross to the feast.

Will there really be a feast in the kingdom? Yes, and it is more solid than we imagine, not less. The kingdom’s fulfilment comes when Christ returns, the dead are raised bodily, and God makes all things new. Scripture pictures that renewed creation with a table, food and wine, faces and fellowship (Isaiah 25:6; Matthew 8:11). We need not press every detail, but we must not make it thin and ghostly either. Those who rise will have real bodies, as Jesus did when he ate fish after his resurrection (24:42–43). Whatever the feast is, it is not less than the best meal you have ever eaten with the people you love, and he will be at the head of the table.

Why would Jesus long to be with people like me? Because his love was never based on our quality, and so our failures do not cancel it. He longed for that table knowing every denial to come. The same is true of you. He does not tolerate your company while hoping for better; he has set his heart on you, which is what it means to be chosen in him before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). When you come to the Lord’s Supper feeling unworthy, remember that the first table was laid for men who were about to fail him, and he had ached to share it with them.

In a sentence. Jesus told the apostles how deeply he had longed to eat this Passover with them before his suffering, for he would not eat it again until it was fulfilled in God’s kingdom.

On a Tuesday. On the evening before your church next shares the Supper, read this verse and let the order of desire sink in: he longed for it first. Come with longing too. And this week, eat a meal with someone in your church whom you would not naturally choose. That is a small, true rehearsal of the table he is preparing.

For worship. With desire he desired it. The Son, who had the Father’s company from all eternity and the praise of angels, longed to eat lamb with fishermen. That is the heart of our God: he wants his people near him. And every communion since has faced two ways, back to a death and forward to a meal still owed. He has kept a place at that table for every one of his own, and his longing will not be satisfied until the last of them is home.

parallels.desc: the marriage supper of the Lamb

verseByVerse.quote: And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he said, 'Take this, and divide it among yourselves. For I tell you that from now on I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he said: take this, and divide it among yourselves. For I tell you that from now on I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.

He took a cup. Readers sometimes stumble here because Luke has a cup before the bread and another after it (v. 20), and it looks like a muddle. It is neither, once you know the shape of the meal. The Passover was structured around several cups of wine, traditionally four, each with its place in the liturgy: a cup at the opening, a cup after the telling of the Exodus story, the cup of blessing after the meal, and a cup of praise at the end with the singing of the psalms. Luke records what happened in order. This first cup belongs to the earlier part of the evening, before the bread; the cup in v. 20 is the one after supper, almost certainly the cup of blessing (1 Corinthians 10:16). So Jesus did not invent a new ceremony out of nothing. He took a cup that already had fifteen centuries of meaning and filled it with himself.

And when he had given thanks. Over wine a Jewish host blessed God as King of the universe, who creates the fruit of the vine. So on the night of his betrayal his first recorded word over the cup is thanksgiving.

Take this, and divide it among yourselves. He did not drink it and pass it on; he gave it to be shared. The Supper is corporate at its root. Nobody at that table received it alone, and nobody does now. It is a meal of the family, not a private devotion.

I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes. He is fasting. Having said in the previous breath how deeply he longed for this meal, he announces that he is setting the cup down and will not lift it again until the kingdom has come. The abstinence is not asceticism. It is the vow of a man with unfinished business. He will not sit down to the feast until his people can sit down with him, and there is a death between here and there. So the cup he pushes away at this table is the measure of the cup he accepts in the garden. He declines the wine of the feast in order to drink the cup of wrath, so that when the kingdom comes there will be somebody there to drink with.

But did he not drink sour wine on the cross? He was offered it, and John records that he received it just before he died (23:36; John 19:29–30). That was not the festive fruit of the vine at the table of the kingdom. It was the cheap sour wine of soldiers, moistening the lips of a dying man so that he could cry out that it was finished. The vow stands: he has not yet drunk the cup of celebration with his people. He is waiting for the whole family to be gathered home.

Wine or grape juice at communion? Faithful churches differ. Jesus used wine, and many churches use it for that reason. Others use unfermented grape juice to protect those who struggle with alcohol, and point out that Jesus calls it simply the fruit of the vine. Both seek to honour him, and neither should despise the other. What matters is what the cup means: his blood poured out, and the feast to come.

In a sentence. Jesus gave thanks over a cup and told them to share it, for he would not drink wine again until the kingdom of God came.

On a Tuesday. When you next share the cup at church, look around at the people sharing it with you. They are your family at his table, the ones with whom you will drink it new in the kingdom. If there is someone there you are estranged from, go and be reconciled before then (Matthew 5:23–24).

For worship. He gave thanks over the cup on the night he was betrayed. Before the garden, before the kiss, before the scourge, his first word over the wine was blessing to the Father, and even with the darkest cup of all in view he did not stop praising. The King who fasts at this table is keeping the feast for the day when the whole family sits down together. Then the One who gave thanks in the shadow will rejoice in the light, with all his people around him, and the wine will be the best, kept until last (John 2:10).
verseByVerse.note: The Passover meal included several cups of wine; Luke mentions a cup before the bread and another after supper.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying, 'This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying: this is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.

He took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them. The four actions are the same as at the feeding of the five thousand (9:16) and at Emmaus (24:30): took, blessed, broke, gave. The bread he hands them is the bread of the hand that fed the crowds, and the same hand will be recognised breaking bread on the evening of the resurrection.

This is my body. At this point in the Passover the host held up the unleavened bread and spoke of it as the bread of affliction the fathers ate in Egypt (Deuteronomy 16:3). Every man at that table had heard it every year of his life. Jesus says something else. This bread now speaks of his own body, about to be given in death. He broke it before anyone broke him. He gave it before anyone took him. Nothing about that night was extracted from him.
