Which is given for you. Only Luke and Paul record these words (1 Corinthians 11:24). The preposition is hyper: on behalf of, in the place of. Not merely for your benefit, but in your stead. This is substitution, spoken by the substitute the night before, in the plainest words he ever used about his own death. His death is a sacrifice for his people.

Do this in remembrance of me. Only Luke and Paul record the command. Jesus institutes an ongoing practice. As Israel remembered the exodus at Passover, the church remembers Christ’s death at his Supper. The word is anamnēsis, and in the Old Testament remembering of this kind is never a private effort of memory. It is a public act that brings the past event into the present of the people doing it. Each generation ate the Passover as though it had itself come out of Egypt. So the Supper is more than mental recall: it is a living proclamation of his death until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26) and a renewal of the covenant. He takes the oldest memorial of the covenant, puts himself where the lamb had been, and hands it to men who have not the faintest idea yet what they are holding, and the church has been holding it ever since.

Where Christians differ: the Supper. Four words have divided the church for five hundred years, and the reader is entitled to know what the argument is about. Roman Catholics hold transubstantiation: at the priest’s word the substance of the bread becomes the actual body of Christ, though everything observable remains bread, and the Mass is offered as a sacrifice. Lutherans reject that but hold that Christ’s body is genuinely present in, with and under the bread. Those who follow Zwingli hold that the bread signifies the body and the Supper is a memorial and a pledge. Calvin and the Reformed churches hold a real spiritual presence: the bread remains bread, and yet Christ is truly given, so that by his Spirit the believer really feeds on him, not with the teeth but by faith. Verdict: Calvin’s view is best. This is my body is a sacramental sign, spoken while his body was at the table, unbroken, in front of them, which settles what kind of sentence it is: he spoke as he always spoke, I am the door, I am the vine. Yet the Supper is more than a memory. The cup of blessing is a participation in the blood of Christ, and the bread a participation in his body (1 Corinthians 10:16): believers truly feed on Christ by faith through the Spirit, who joins us to the risen Lord in heaven. Nor is it a sacrifice offered again. Luke’s word is remembrance, not repetition: Christ was offered once for all (Hebrews 9:25–28; 10:10–14), and the Supper receives that offering rather than renewing it. Westminster, which the 1689 Baptist Confession follows here, puts it carefully: worthy receivers, inwardly by faith, really and indeed, yet not carnally, receive and feed upon Christ crucified (Westminster 29.7).

What does it mean to feed on Christ by faith? Think of how food works. You do not admire bread; you take it into yourself, and it becomes your strength. At the Supper, as the bread and cup are taken with the mouth, the believer’s heart takes hold of Christ himself, crucified and risen, as the one whose body was given for him. The Holy Spirit makes that real: he lifts our hearts to Christ where he is, and Christ strengthens our faith, assures us of forgiveness and binds us to him and to one another. It is not magic, and it is not merely thinking hard. It is communion with a living Saviour, through means he has appointed.

What if I feel nothing when I take communion? Then you have still received what was given. The Supper does not depend on the strength of your feelings but on the faithfulness of Christ who promised himself in it. Some Sundays the heart is warm; some Sundays it is numb with tiredness or grief. Come anyway, trusting his word: given for you. A child fed by his father is nourished whether or not he notices the taste. And if the numbness persists for months, speak to your pastor; it may be weariness, sorrow or sin that needs care, but it is never a reason to stay away from the means of grace.

How often should we take the Lord’s Supper? Scripture does not fix it. The early church seems to have broken bread often, perhaps each Lord’s Day (Acts 2:42; 20:7), and many churches celebrate weekly; others monthly or quarterly, to guard against it becoming routine. Calvin wished it to be weekly. What Scripture does require is that it be kept, regularly, with self-examination and faith, until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26).

In a sentence. Jesus gave thanks for bread, broke it and gave it to them, saying it was his body given for them, and told them to do this in remembrance of him.

On a Tuesday. Prepare for the next Lord’s Supper on the days before it. Read one of the accounts (this one, or 1 Corinthians 11:23–32), confess the sins you know of, put right what you can with others, and come hungry. When the bread is broken, say to yourself the two words he put at the heart of it: for you.

For worship. He asked to be remembered by a meal, not a monument. The Lord of glory, hours from being forsaken, chose bread, the commonest thing on the table, and put into it the most uncommon promise: given for you. Kings are remembered in marble; he is remembered at plain tables in cathedrals, prison cells and village halls, wherever his church breaks bread in his name. And the One who asked to be remembered never forgets his own. He feeds them with himself by his Spirit, and he will remember them on the day he comes.

verseByVerse.quote: And likewise the cup after they had eaten, saying, 'This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And likewise the cup after they had eaten, saying: this cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.

The cup after they had eaten. Probably the third Passover cup, the cup of blessing (1 Corinthians 10:16), drunk after the main meal.

This cup that is poured out for you. For a table of Jewish men, the word blood in connection with a cup was very close to unthinkable. The law forbade the drinking of blood absolutely, on the ground that the life is in the blood and God had given it for atonement on the altar (Leviticus 17:11–14). Blood belonged on the altar, not in the mouth. Which is exactly why the words work. He is not inviting them to drink blood; he is telling them what the cup means, and the meaning is atonement. Poured out is altar language, the blood of a sacrifice poured out at the base of the altar (Leviticus 4:7). And for you, as with the bread: in your place.

Is the new covenant in my blood. This is a quotation, and every man there would have caught it. Jeremiah, six centuries earlier, in the ruin of everything, heard God promise a new covenant, not like the one their fathers broke. This one would be different in three ways: the law written on the heart rather than on stone; every member knowing God personally, from the least to the greatest; and the ground of it all forgiveness, for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more (Jeremiah 31:31–34). That promise had stood unfulfilled for six hundred years. Israel came home from exile, rebuilt the temple, resumed the sacrifices, and no one saw a new covenant. Now a man at a supper table lifts a cup and says: here it is, and it is in my blood.

Covenants are sealed with blood. Every covenant in Scripture is ratified with blood: Noah’s with sacrifice, Abraham’s with divided animals, Sinai’s with Moses throwing blood on the people and saying, behold the blood of the covenant (Exodus 24:8). The pattern never varies, because a covenant is a bond made at the cost of life. What is new here is not the mechanism but the victim. The old covenant at Sinai was sealed with the blood of animals; the new covenant is sealed with Jesus’ own blood. God is not asking for a bull. His death establishes a new relationship between God and his people, resting on complete forgiveness and a new heart (Hebrews 8:6–13; 9:15–22).

Textual note. Some ESV readers will see a note that a few manuscripts omit the end of v. 19 and v. 20. The longer text has overwhelming support, and the same words are found independently in Paul (1 Corinthians 11:23–25) and in Matthew and Mark. No doctrine rests on Luke’s wording alone.

Who may come to the Lord’s Table? Those who belong to Christ: baptised believers who trust him and are willing to turn from sin. Paul tells each to examine himself and then eat (1 Corinthians 11:28). It is not a reward for being good enough; it is for sinners who need Christ. But it is not for unbelievers, nor for those living in unrepentant sin under the church’s discipline. Baptist churches, holding believer’s baptism, ask that those who come should first have been baptised as believers, and many gladly welcome to the table believers from paedobaptist churches who love the same Lord, recognising them as brothers and sisters in Christ.

I am struggling with a sin, so should I stay away? Not if you are fighting it. This fear keeps some believers from the table: they are not good enough to come. But the cup does not commemorate your fitness. It commemorates the death that made you fit, and it is offered by the one who poured it out for a table that included a traitor, a denier and ten men who would run. Examine yourself, confess the sin to God, and come as a sinner holding on to Christ. The person who should hold back is the one who has decided to keep a sin and stop fighting it; for him the Supper is a call to repent first, today, and then to come.

Does God really forget my sin? He chooses not to remember it against you. God knows all things, but in the new covenant he binds himself never again to bring your forgiven sins up as a charge, to hold them over you, or to treat you as they deserve (Hebrews 10:17–18). They were remembered once, fully, at the cross, and laid on Christ. When your conscience digs them up again, answer with the cup: this was poured out for me, and God has promised to remember my sin no more.

In a sentence. After supper Jesus took the cup, saying it was the new covenant in his blood, poured out for them.

On a Tuesday. If a forgiven sin from years ago keeps returning to accuse you, write down Jeremiah 31:34 and Hebrews 10:17 and read them aloud the next time it comes. Then thank God, out loud, that he has bound himself to remember it no more. Live today as a member of the new covenant: the law on your heart, God known personally, and your record clean.

For worship. For six hundred years the promise of a new covenant waited in Jeremiah’s scroll, and on this night it was poured into a cup. The covenant made at Sinai was sealed with the blood of bulls and broken by the people within weeks. This one is sealed with the blood of God’s own Son, and so it rests not on our faithfulness but on his. Nothing his people do can spill what he has poured out, and no accusation can reach behind it. The cup is full, and it is for them.

verseByVerse.quote: But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. For the Son of Man goes as it has been determined, but woe to that man by whom he is betrayed!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. For the Son of Man goes as it has been determined, but woe to that man by whom he is betrayed!

But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. Matthew and Mark have the announcement of the betrayal before the bread and the cup. Luke puts it after, and the effect is devastating. Not among you, but on the table. In that culture the shared dish was the sign of covenant friendship; to eat with a man was to pledge yourself to him. Psalm 41 had already given words to the wound: the trusted friend who ate the psalmist’s bread and lifted his heel against him (Psalm 41:9). In the Son of David that psalm reaches its fullest meaning, and John records Jesus applying it to this very night (John 13:18).

Did Judas receive the bread and cup? Luke’s order makes it look as if he did. But Matthew and Mark put the warning about the betrayer before the Supper, and John has Judas leave after the morsel (John 13:30). Luke often arranges events by subject, and the more likely reading is that Judas left before the cup was shared. Either way, he sat at the table with Jesus and betrayed him.

For the Son of Man goes as it has been determined. The word is hōrismenon: marked out, fixed, appointed by God (Acts 2:23; 4:28). The cross is not a catastrophe that overtook the plan; it is the plan. Nothing that happens between here and the tomb is an accident, an unlucky turn, or an escape that failed. Goes is the language of a man on a journey, walking a road he has chosen.

But woe to that man by whom he is betrayed! And the betrayal, though it fulfils a determined purpose, remains entirely the betrayer’s own, and the guilt of it is his. Two things are asserted in one breath which the human mind cannot fit together, and Jesus makes no attempt to reconcile them. It is the settled pattern of Scripture rather than an isolated puzzle: the same combination appears in Joseph’s words to his brothers (Genesis 50:20) and in Peter’s Pentecost sermon (Acts 2:23). God’s sovereignty and human responsibility together: God determined it, and Judas is guilty. And woe here is grief as well as doom: the cry of a friend over a man walking to ruin.

If it was determined, how can Judas be blamed? Because he did exactly what he wanted to do. Nobody forced Judas; God did not put a single wicked desire into his heart. He chose freely, for his own reasons, and God in his wisdom used that free choice to accomplish redemption. Scripture never explains fully how both are true, but it insists on both, and so must we. If God were not sovereign, the cross would be an accident; if Judas were not responsible, there would be no sin for the cross to deal with. A man is judged for what he intends, and Judas intended betrayal (Genesis 50:20).

Could Judas have repented? Yes. The offer was real to the very end. Jesus warned him at this table, washed his feet, and in the garden asked him a question that held the door open (v. 48). Judas did not repent because he would not. Nothing in God’s decree stopped a man who wanted to come back; the tragedy is that he did not want to. Scripture calls him the son of destruction (John 17:12), and his end shows a remorse that never turned to God. No one who truly comes to Christ is ever turned away (John 6:37).

A word for the wronged. There is a pastoral use for this verse, which is where many readers actually need it. People who have been badly wronged live between two temptations. One is to conclude that the wrong was outside God’s reach, which makes the world random and God small. The other is to conclude that because God had a purpose in it, the person who did it was not really guilty, a false comfort that leaves the victim unable even to name what happened. This verse refuses both. God’s purpose stood, and the man who did it is answerable. You are permitted to say that what was done to you was wicked, and that God was not absent from it, and you are not required to make those two sentences into one. Where the wrong was abuse or a crime, it must be named, reported and stopped; trusting God’s purpose never means covering it up.

In a sentence. Jesus said that his betrayer was at the table, and that though the Son of Man goes as God has determined, woe to the one who betrays him.

On a Tuesday. God’s sovereignty never excuses your sin. When you catch yourself saying, it must have been meant to happen, about something you chose to do, stop and own it before God instead. And if you are carrying a wrong done to you, try saying both sentences in prayer today: Lord, this was evil; and Lord, you were not absent. Then leave the judging of it with him.

For worship. He sat at supper with the hand that would betray him resting on the same table, and he did not withdraw his own. He grieved over the traitor and went on to the cross for the rest. The woe that hung over Judas is the woe every sinner has earned, and the One who pronounced it went out that night to bear it for all who would believe. No betrayal of ours is beyond the reach of a Saviour who shared his table with the man who sold him, and then died for the friends who ran.

parallels.desc: according to the definite plan of God

verseByVerse.quote: And they began to question one another, which of them it could be who was going to do this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they began to question one another, which of them it could be who was going to do this.

Which of them it could be. A short verse, easily skipped, and one of the most searching sentences at that table. Consider what did not happen. Nobody looked at Judas. Eleven men, three years in his company, sharing every meal and every road, and when a betrayer is announced, not one of them can identify him. Matthew adds that each asked, Is it I? (Matthew 26:22).

Judas was not obvious. He was so entirely unsuspected that every other man in the room thought the traitor was more likely to be himself. Serious spiritual defection does not announce itself in advance. It is generally invisible until it is complete, sometimes even to the person concerned.

The eleven looked inward first. They had heard things all evening that they had not understood, but they had grasped this much: if the Lord says one of us is capable of it, I had better start with myself. It was a sound instinct, the last sound instinct several of them would show that night. And each knew, in some measure, that he was capable of it. That is the exact opposite of the reflex most of us have, which is to run an accusation across everyone we know and stop just short of our own door. It explains why Paul, writing about this very table, tells the Corinthians to examine themselves before eating (1 Corinthians 11:28), not to examine each other, which is what that church was busy doing.

The one who knew. Only one man at that table knew the answer, and he did not give it. Jesus had read hearts all through this Gospel, knowing the thoughts of the scribes before they spoke (5:22; 6:8), and he knew Judas’s. Yet he did not point, did not name him to the eleven, did not set the others on him. The Lord who sees every heart chose to shield the traitor from exposure and to leave the door of repentance open to the last moment.

How do I examine myself without becoming morbid? Examine yourself to find sin and bring it to Christ, not to find a reason to despair. Ask honest, simple questions: Am I trusting Christ, or something I have done? Is there a sin I have stopped fighting? Is there someone I refuse to forgive? Then take what you find straight to the cross and confess it. Do not keep digging once you have looked; the purpose of looking at yourself is to look away to him. The eleven asked, Is it I?, and then they stayed at the table. Self-examination that ends in fleeing from Christ has gone wrong. Self-examination that ends at his feet has done its work.

In a sentence. The disciples began to ask each other which of them would do this.

On a Tuesday. When you hear a sermon that names a sin, notice who comes to mind first. If it is reliably someone else, a spouse, a colleague, a member who really does need to hear it, that is worth knowing about yourself. This week, the next time a warning lands, turn it on yourself before anyone else, and pray Psalm 139:23–24 over it: search me, O God, and know my heart.

For worship. The men who asked in fear whether it could be they were not the ones who did it. The Lord who knew every heart at that table knows his people’s hearts better than they know them, and he did not send the trembling eleven away. He is the searcher of hearts and the keeper of hearts at once. What he finds in us he does not hold as evidence for the prosecution; he carries it to his cross, and what he has begun in his own he will finish.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–38 — Greatness, Sifting, and the Turning Season
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The bread has been broken and the betrayal announced, and in that room an argument breaks out about rank. It was a love of winning, and they had done it before (9:46). It is not a failure peculiar to them: a congregation can have a moving communion service and a dispute about who was asked to serve at it in the car park afterwards.

Jesus describes the world they know. Gentile kings play the lord, and those in authority are called benefactors — a formal honorific, voted by cities and inscribed on stone, claimed by rulers who had done real good and intended it remembered. So the mechanism of worldly power is not brute force. It is force that has arranged to be thanked.

But not so with you. He does not abolish leadership — he distinguishes the greatest from the rest in the same sentence in which he redefines them. The greatest becomes as the youngest, who in that world ran the errands and was interruptible. And then: I am among you as the one who serves, said while reclining at his own table, having handed round the bread himself.

Then he satisfies the ambition he has just corrected. You are those who have stayed with me in my trials — said to men who will scatter within hours, and said accurately, because three years of staying is not cancelled by one night of failure. He assigns them a kingdom on the same terms his Father used with him: a table to eat at, and thrones.

To Peter, by his old name and doubled: Satan demanded to have you — the plural you, the whole barn — that he might sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, singular, that your faith may not fail. Not that the sifting be cancelled, nor the fall prevented, but that the faith itself hold. And the commission comes before the failure, with when and not if: when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.

Peter contradicts him and is told the number and the deadline. Then the season turns: the disciples who once went out with no moneybag and lacked nothing are told to take the bag, and the sword saying arrives — which the next two verses immediately defuse.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verse 32 is the doctrine of perseverance in one sentence, and it is not a claim about the strength of Christians. Peter's faith survived because Christ was praying, and he prays still: he always lives to make intercession for them (Heb. 7:25). The scene behind Satan's demand is Job 1 — the accuser must ask, is given a limit, and cannot exceed it.

The teaching on greatness in vv. 25–27 is not a management philosophy but the application of the incarnation to the question of authority. The one holding the basin is the eternal Son by whom all things were made, and within a day the serving goes further than a towel. Authority in the kingdom is real and it exists for those under it.

Verses 35–38 must be read as a unit or they will be abused. Jesus quotes Isaiah 53:12 — numbered with the transgressors — which is precisely why the swords must go: a man being arrested as a criminal cannot be defended by force without becoming one. Two swords for a band of disciples facing an armed detachment is absurd for a fight, and it is enough is not a quartermaster approving the arsenal but a teacher closing a conversation that has gone wrong. Both the crusading reading and the absolute-pacifist reading are more than the passage will carry.
verseByVerse.examples:
A test for anyone who leads anything, and it is sharper than asking whether you serve, since everyone believes they serve. When did you last do something for your church that carried no credit whatever, that nobody would notice was done, and that could not be mentioned afterwards without losing the point? That is the youngest man's work, and Jesus took it.

Verse 28 is one of the most reassuring things in the Gospel about how Christ assesses a life. He is not scoring the worst night. He looks at eleven men hours from failing him completely and says: you stayed.

Verses 33–34 are for anyone who has made God a promise they did not keep — the resolve after a hospital ward, the change that lasted eleven days. Peter's sincerity was real, his self-confidence was misplaced, his failure was total, and none of it surprised Jesus or altered anything he had decided about the man. Being told in advance is what made restoration possible: the denial could only ever mean he knew, and prayed for me anyway.

And v. 35 is worth answering out loud, as the disciples had to. Not has life been easy, but the narrower question: has God ever actually let you go without what you needed? Most Christians, made to say it aloud, arrive at the same word they used.

verseByVerse.quote: A dispute also arose among them, as to which of them was to be regarded as the greatest. And he said to them, 'The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, and those in authority over them are called benefactors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A dispute also arose among them, as to which of them was to be regarded as the greatest. And he said to them: the kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, and those in authority over them are called benefactors.

A dispute also arose among them. The placing is almost unbearable, and Luke means it to be. The bread has been broken. The cup has been passed. The betrayal has been announced. And in that room, minutes later, an argument breaks out about rank. Only Luke places it here. It was probably about seating, who would lie nearest to Jesus, and the word is philoneikia, literally a love of winning. Not a disagreement they fell into but an appetite they indulged.

Which of them was to be regarded as the greatest. The old argument. They had had it before (9:46), and had been answered then with a child set in front of them. The honest response is not shock but recognition. A church can have a deeply moving communion service and a quarrel in the car park afterwards about who was asked to serve at it, and the two things do not feel connected from the inside. Jesus does not shame them. He describes a world they know.

The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them. They play the lord. The world’s model of greatness is power over others, and it has never needed to be taught.

And those in authority over them are called benefactors. This is the sharper observation. Benefactor, euergetēs, was not a compliment paid spontaneously. It was a formal honorific, voted by cities, inscribed on stone and on coins, and claimed by rulers who had done something for the public and intended everyone to remember it. Ptolemy III of Egypt took it as his official title, Euergetes. So Jesus has named the mechanism by which worldly power sustains itself, and it is not brute force. It is force that has arranged to be thanked. The tell is not whether a person does good, but whether the doing of good has been arranged so that it is seen, credited and remembered.

He went about doing good. The verb from this word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke’s own second volume, and it is used of Jesus. Peter, telling Cornelius about Jesus of Nazareth, says that he went about doing good, literally benefacting, and healing all who were oppressed by the devil (Acts 10:38). The one true Benefactor never took the title. He took a towel, and then a cross. The kings of the Gentiles had their goodness carved in stone so that it would come back to them. His came back to him as thorns and nails, and he gave it anyway.

Is ambition wrong? Not in itself. Jesus does not tell them to stop wanting greatness; in the next breath he tells them how to have it, and then gives them a kingdom (vv. 26–29). Paul calls it a noble thing to aspire to oversight in the church (1 Timothy 3:1). What is wrong is ambition for yourself: to be seen, ranked and thanked. The test is simple. Would I still want this work if nobody ever knew I did it, and if someone else got the credit? Godly ambition wants Christ to be great and the church to be served, and it is content to be the youngest at the table while that happens.

In a sentence. When the disciples argued about who was greatest, Jesus said that Gentile kings lord it over their people and like to be called benefactors.

On a Tuesday. Watch for the desire to be recognised as great, even in serving. Notice this week where you mention, or want someone to notice, the good you have done: the extra hours, the gift, the help. Then do one thing for someone that cannot be traced back to you, and tell no one, not even in a hint.

For worship. At the very table where he had just given them the bread and the cup, his friends quarrelled over seats, and he did not take the gift back. He answered their love of winning with a love that had already chosen to lose everything for them. No plaque bears his name in the room where he gave the Supper, and none is needed. His name is written on every forgiven heart that has ever sat at his table, quarrelsome and unworthy, and been fed.
verseByVerse.note: “Benefactor” was an official title that rulers loved to claim.

verseByVerse.quote: But not so with you. Rather, let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves. For who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines at table? But I am among you as the one who serves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But not so with you. Rather, let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves. For who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines at table? But I am among you as the one who serves.

But not so with you. Five words, and they carve the church out of the world. Whatever else the Christian community is, it is to be the one place on earth where the usual arithmetic of status does not operate. Notice what he does not say. He does not abolish leadership. He distinguishes the greatest from the rest and the leader from those led in the same sentence in which he redefines them. The New Testament is full of appointed elders and real authority. What is forbidden is not office; it is what office is used for.

Let the greatest among you become as the youngest. In that world the youngest at a gathering was not merely the least honoured; he did the menial jobs. He fetched. He was interruptible. Everybody’s needs came before his plans for the evening.

And the leader as one who serves. Leadership in the kingdom is service (Mark 10:43–45). The leader is the one who carries the most weight for others, not the one who is carried.

Who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Jesus asks a question with an obvious answer and gives the obvious answer himself, which is a way of making sure nobody escapes into cleverness. Everyone in the room knew: the man lying down. By the world’s standards the guest is greater than the waiter, and in every society that has ever existed the served outrank the servers.

But I am among you as the one who serves. He says it while reclining, at his own table, having handled the bread and the cup and put them into the hands of men who had just been arguing about precedence. On the same evening, John tells us, he got up, took a towel and washed their feet (John 13:4–15), including the feet of the man who had already agreed to betray him. This is where the passage stops being about management and becomes about God. The one speaking is not a good leader modelling humility to inspire imitation. He is the eternal Son, by whom all things were made, holding a basin. And within a day the serving will go further than a towel: the hands that poured the water will be nailed through. Luke does not record here the ransom saying that Mark sets beside this teaching (Mark 10:45). He shows it instead, at a table, the night before the ransom was paid. The Lord of all is the servant of all, and his followers must be the same.

Does servant leadership mean leaders have no real authority? No. Elders are to be respected and obeyed (Hebrews 13:17), and parents and others hold real authority from God. Jesus himself is Lord while he serves. The point is the direction in which authority flows: it is given for the good of those under it, never for the comfort of the one holding it. A servant leader still decides, still teaches, still corrects, but he does it as a man carrying others, and he expects to give an account to God for them.

What does this mean in a marriage and a home? The same pattern applies, and it is the key to Christian headship. Scripture calls a husband the head of his wife, and in the same breath tells him to love her as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:23–25). So headship is not a right to be served; it is a call to lead in self-giving love, taking the first step in prayer, in apology and in sacrifice, protecting and providing and putting her good before his own. A man who uses headship to control, belittle or frighten his wife has turned it upside down into the Gentile model. Abuse is never tolerated in Christ’s church; a wife in danger should seek safety and help at once, and the church must stand with her.

In a sentence. Jesus told them not to be like that: the greatest must become like the youngest and the leader like a servant, for he himself was among them as one who serves.

On a Tuesday. If you lead anything, in a church, a business or a family, do not ask whether you serve; everyone believes they do. Ask when you last did something for these people that carried no credit whatever and that nobody would notice. That is the youngest man’s work, and Jesus took it. Find one such task today and do it.

For worship. Once he told a parable no one else would have dared to tell, of a master who comes home in the night, finds his servants awake, and dresses himself for service, has them recline at table, and comes and waits on them (12:37). At this table the Master was already doing it, and he has never stopped. He serves his people now from the throne, interceding, feeding, upholding, and on the last day the Lord of glory will still be the one who serves. There is no God like this God: the highest is the lowliest, and the King of all things waits at his own table.

verseByVerse.quote: 'You are those who have stayed with me in my trials, and I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom,
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are those who have stayed with me in my trials, and I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom.

You are those who have stayed with me in my trials. Having corrected their ambition, he now satisfies it, which is not what anyone expects, and it tells you something important about how Jesus handles wrong desires. He does not tell them to want less. He tells them they have been wanting the right thing in the wrong shape. Read that sentence in the light of what is about to happen and it is almost incredible. Within hours they will fall asleep on him, then scatter into the dark, and one will deny three times that he ever knew him. And on the evening before all of it Jesus looks round the table and says: you stayed.

He counts the staying. He is not being sentimental, and he is not unaware. He is describing three years accurately. They did stay: through the hostility in the synagogues, the accusations of working with demons, the plots, the crowds falling away when the teaching got hard (John 6:66), the long homeless walk to Jerusalem. The failure that is coming is real and he has already named it, and it does not cancel what preceded it. This is one of the most reassuring things in the Gospel about how Christ assesses a life. He is not scoring the worst night. He sees the whole thing, and he counts the staying. Grace sees the good in weak disciples.

And I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom. The verb is diatithemai, the word used for making a will, disposing of an estate, and the verb behind the noun covenant (diathēkē). He is bequeathing. A man about to die is settling his affairs, and what he has to leave is a kingdom. And the chain of it is the astonishing part: as my Father assigned to me. The Father has given the kingdom to the Son (Daniel 7:14); the Son gives it to his disciples (12:32), by the same verb, on the same terms. They will share his reign. They argued about greatness; Jesus gives them a kingdom.

A scramble by heirs. This recasts the whole dispute. They were fighting over a portion of something that was already being left to all of them in full. That is nearly always the shape of status-hunger in the church: a scramble for a slice, conducted by heirs. If we are children, then heirs, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17).

Does Jesus really count my faithfulness when I keep failing? He does, because he sees what is really there. A Christian’s faithfulness is not erased by his falls, any more than these men’s three years were erased by one night. That is not because the failures do not matter; Jesus names them honestly. It is because your perseverance is itself his work in you, and he will not despise what he has made (Philippians 1:6). He remembers the cup of cold water given in his name (Matthew 10:42). If you are still following him after many stumbles, he calls that staying.

In a sentence. Jesus told the apostles that because they had stood by him in his trials, he was granting them a kingdom, as his Father had granted one to him.

On a Tuesday. Next time you are tempted to measure your Christian life by your worst week, measure it as he does: over years. Write down three ways you are still with him that you were not five years ago. Then thank him, because the staying was his gift. And look for one weak believer this week whose faithfulness you can name to his face.

For worship. The Father gave the Son a kingdom, and the Son, on the night of his betrayal, wrote his failing friends into the will. A will takes effect only when the one who made it dies (Hebrews 9:16–17), and within hours he would die to make this one good. They came to him quarrelling over crumbs, and he left them a kingdom, and then he rose again to see that they received it.

parallels.desc: he himself has suffered when tempted
if we endure, we will also reign

verseByVerse.quote: that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

That you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom. Two pictures, and the church has generally been much happier with the first than the second. He has just said he will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes (v. 18), and now he says what the resumption looks like. The meal is not over; it is adjourned. The same table, the same host, the same men, and this time nobody is arguing about seats and nobody leaves in the dark. This is the messianic banquet, fellowship with Christ for ever (v. 16).

Heaven is a table. Take that concretely, because heaven is usually left vague and should not be. It is not a sensation, and it is not a choir practice that never ends. It is, in his own image, a table: food, drink, faces, conversation, and the person you most want to be near presiding over it. Everyone who has ever sat at a long meal with people they love and felt the evening going too fast has been given a small, accurate sample of it.

And sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel. The Twelve correspond to the twelve tribes; they stand for the renewed people of God. The word judging carries the sense it has in the book of Judges, to govern, to rule, to put right, rather than merely to pass sentence. This is not a promise of a courtroom rota. It is real authority in the world to come (Matthew 19:28; Revelation 21:12–14). And all believers will share in some way in his reign. Paul says it in passing to a church that was suing itself, as though everyone already knew it: do you not know that the saints will judge the world (1 Corinthians 6:2–3; Revelation 3:21)?

What are these thrones? Christians read this in different ways, and the reader should know them. Premillennial Christians see a future earthly reign over a restored Israel. Matthew places it in the new world (Matthew 19:28), the renewed creation. The more likely reading is that the apostles share in Christ’s rule over his people, the true Israel of all who believe, which begins now through their word, the apostolic foundation on which the church is built (Ephesians 2:20), and will be complete in the new creation. Whatever God has still in store for ethnic Israel, which Christians present differently from Romans 11, the promise here is of the apostles’ share in Christ’s reign.

The future is not passive. Christians are not going to be looked after for ever; they are going to be trusted with something, as in the parable of the minas, where the faithful servant is given authority over ten cities (19:17). And the men handed this promise were not a shortlist of the impressive but provincial men who had spent the last few minutes squabbling about precedence and would spend the next few hours failing.

Will I really rule with Christ? Yes, in the way that fits you and that he appoints. Scripture says those who endure will reign with him (2 Timothy 2:12), and that the redeemed will reign on the earth (Revelation 5:10). We do not know the details, and we should not imagine a crowded court of rival kings. But it means that the work you do faithfully now, in small things, is training for responsibility in the new creation, and that heaven will not be idleness. It will be service without sin, weariness or rivalry, under a King we love.

In a sentence. They would eat and drink at his table in his kingdom, and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

On a Tuesday. Live today in that hope. Do the small responsibility in front of you, the class, the accounts, the care of one child or one elderly neighbour, as if it were practice for ruling a city, because in a sense it is. And at your next meal with Christian friends, say out loud that this is a foretaste of the table to come.

For worship. He knew what they were, and he set a table for them anyway and wrote thrones into the promise. The one who was about to be crowned with thorns was handing out crowns, and every one he gives was bought with his blood. At that table no one will argue about seats, because the highest honour any of his people will ever hold is the honour of eating with the King who served them.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.

Simon, Simon. The doubled name is how Scripture speaks when something enormous is about to be said to one person: Abraham, Abraham; Moses, Moses; Martha, Martha (10:41); Saul, Saul. It is tender and urgent, the sound of a hand on the shoulder. And notice which name. Not Peter, the rock, the name Jesus gave him. Simon, his old name, the name he was born with. He is being addressed as the man he still is, as he is about to fail.

Satan demanded to have you. Asked formally, demanded a person be handed over. There is only one other place in Scripture where this happens in the open: the first chapters of Job, where the accuser appears before God, asks for a man, is granted a limit, and cannot exceed it by a hair (Job 1:6–12; 2:1–6). That is the scene behind this sentence. Satan does not have free access to God’s people. He has to ask. And the ESV notes that this you is plural in the Greek: he demanded to have all of you. Satan asked for the whole barn.

That he might sift you like wheat. Sifting is violent: the grain thrown and shaken in a sieve until what is not grain is separated out. Satan’s aim was not to shake the chaff out of Peter but to demonstrate that Peter was chaff, to shake them until their faith fell apart. The intended verdict was that there was nothing there.

But I have prayed for you. Here the you is singular: for Peter specifically, who was about to fall most heavily. Satan asked for them all; Jesus names one man. And the one who prayed for Peter on earth now intercedes for his people at God’s right hand (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25).

That your faith may not fail. Sit with what he did not pray. He did not pray that Peter would be spared the sifting; the sifting comes. He did not pray that Peter would not fall; Peter falls within hours, three times. He prayed for the one thing underneath all of it: that the faith itself would not give out, that the man would go down and not stay down. Peter fell, but did not fall away. Judas fell away. The difference is not that Peter was stronger. Jesus prayed for Peter. This is the ground of the perseverance of the saints: not the strength of our faith but the prayer of our Saviour (John 17:11–15). He always lives to make intercession for them (Hebrews 7:25).

And when you have turned again. Repented, returned. The word is when, not if. Jesus knows Peter will fall, and he knows Peter will come back. The restoration is settled before the fall has happened.

Strengthen your brothers. His failure will become the means of his usefulness. The man about to be the worst failure in the room is appointed to hold up everyone else, and he will be able to, because a man who has been carried back knows the way. Restored, he strengthened others (John 21:15–17), and years later he wrote to suffering churches about the devil who prowls like a roaring lion, and about the God of all grace who will himself restore, confirm, strengthen and establish you (1 Peter 5:8–10). He had been sifted, and he knew.

Does strengthen your brothers make Peter the head of the church? No. The commission is personal and pastoral: Peter, restored after his fall, would strengthen the others, as he did in Acts and in his letters. Nothing in it speaks of an office passed to successors, and Paul later rebuked Peter to his face (Galatians 2:11–14).

Why does God allow Satan to sift his people at all? Because God means the sifting for good while Satan means it for harm. Satan wanted to prove Peter was chaff; God used the same night to burn away Peter’s self-confidence and make him a humble shepherd. Trials test faith so that it is found genuine, more precious than gold refined by fire (1 Peter 1:6–7). God sets the limits, and nothing exceeds them (1 Corinthians 10:13). That does not make the sifting painless, but it means it is never pointless, and never outside the reach of Christ’s prayers.

Does Jesus pray for me personally? Yes. His high-priestly prayer reaches beyond the apostles to those who will believe through their word (John 17:20), and he lives to intercede for all who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). He does not pray for the church in a vague mass; he knows his sheep by name (John 10:3). When you are being shaken and cannot pray well yourself, the Son is praying for you, and the Father always hears him (John 11:42).

In a sentence. Jesus told Simon that Satan had asked to sift them all like wheat, but that he had prayed for Simon that his faith would not fail, and when he turned back, he must strengthen his brothers.

On a Tuesday. If you are in a season of being shaken, say this to yourself today, aloud if you can: Jesus is praying for me, that my faith may not fail. Then think of one fellow believer who is struggling, and do what Peter was told to do: strengthen them, with a visit, a message, a Scripture, a meal. Your past failures, now forgiven, may be exactly what qualifies you to help.

For worship. John the Baptist had said that the winnowing fork is in Christ’s hand, and that he will gather his wheat into his barn (3:17). Satan may shake a disciple, but he does not hold the fork, and he does not give the verdict. The One who does had already looked at Simon, the man about to deny him three times, and counted him wheat, and prayed over him, and appointed him to strengthen the rest. The accuser asks; the Son decides; and what the Son has gathered no sifting will scatter.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the first “you” is plural — Satan asked for all of them — while in verse 32 it is singular: Jesus prayed for Peter. Sifting shook wheat in a sieve to separate it.

parallels.desc: Satan asks leave to test Job
shake Israel as one shakes with a sieve

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said to him, 'Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death.' Jesus said, 'I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow this day, until you deny three times that you know me.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter said to him: Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death. Jesus said: I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow this day, until you deny three times that you know me.

Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death. Peter is not lying. He means it entirely. Before the night is out a disciple will strike the high priest’s servant with a sword in front of an armed crowd, and John tells us it was Peter (John 18:10); and Peter will follow into the high priest’s courtyard when the others have gone. His love and courage are real. What he lacks is any accurate knowledge of himself. Jesus has just said, when you have turned again, which is to say, you are going to fall, and Peter contradicts him. He heard a warning and answered with a list of his qualities. One day he would go to prison (Acts 12:3–5) and, by early tradition, to death by crucifixion in Rome (John 21:18–19). But not yet. Now he relied on his own strength.

I tell you, Peter. The only time in the Gospels Jesus calls him Peter directly. The rock is about to crumble, and the name he was given is spoken over the moment he will least resemble it.

The rooster will not crow this day, until you deny three times that you know me. The reply is exact. This day. Three times. Before the rooster crows, that is, before dawn. No hedging, no you might. Jesus does not say Peter is weak in general; he tells him the number and the deadline.

Why tell him in advance? It cannot be to prevent the denial, because it does not. It cannot be to humiliate him, because Jesus has just promised to restore him. The reason is in the words before: when you have turned again. If Peter had denied Christ without warning, the collapse would have been total. He would have concluded that Jesus had misjudged him, that his discipleship had been a mistake from the start, that there was nothing to go back to. Judas made an inference of that kind, and it killed him. Because he was told in advance, the denial could only ever mean one thing: he knew. He knew, and he prayed for me anyway, and he told me I would come back.

Did the rooster crow once or twice? Mark says the rooster would crow twice (Mark 14:30). Luke gives the general warning, before cock-crow; Mark, writing from Peter’s own memory, gives the precise form. There is no contradiction.

Should I stop making promises to God? No, but make them leaning on him rather than on yourself. Vows and resolutions are not wrong; Scripture is full of people pledging themselves to God. Peter’s mistake was not his devotion but his self-reliance, and his refusal to hear the warning. So make your promises as prayers: Lord, I want to be faithful in this; keep me, for I cannot keep myself. And when you break one, do not conclude that the whole thing was a sham. Confess it, get up and go on. A broken resolution is a reason to trust Christ more, not to stop following him.

In a sentence. Peter declared he was ready to go to prison and death with Jesus, but Jesus told him that before the rooster crowed that day, he would deny three times that he knew him.

On a Tuesday. Think of a promise you made God and did not keep: the habit you were going to give up, the resolve after a conviction that lasted eleven days. The pattern is nearly always the same: sincerity, self-confidence, collapse, and then the conviction that the whole thing was a sham. Peter’s case says otherwise. Bring that broken promise to Christ today, and replace it with a humbler prayer: keep me. Don’t trust your own strength. Trust the one who prays for you.

For worship. Peter promised to go with him to prison and to death, and could not. Jesus went to both alone, that night and the next day, and he went for Peter. Because he did, the boast that failed beside a courtyard fire was one day made good: Peter did go to prison for his name, and, as the church remembered it, to a cross, held up by the Lord who had once gone there without him. Our promises collapse; his never do, and in the end he even makes good the promises we could not keep.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'When I sent you out with no moneybag or knapsack or sandals, did you lack anything?' They said, 'Nothing.' He said to them, 'But now let the one who has a moneybag take it, and likewise a knapsack. And let the one who has no sword sell his cloak and buy one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: when I sent you out with no moneybag or knapsack or sandals, did you lack anything? They said: nothing. He said to them: but now let the one who has a moneybag take it, and likewise a knapsack. And let the one who has no sword sell his cloak and buy one.

When I sent you out with no moneybag. He begins with a question about the past, and he makes them answer it out loud. The reference is to the missions of chapters 9 and 10, when he sent them out deliberately unprovisioned, no bag, no money, no spare sandals (9:3; 10:4), into a countryside that received them.

Did you lack anything? Their answer is one word: nothing. God had provided through people’s hospitality. It is a good question to be made to answer, and worth answering yourself before reading on. Not, has life been easy? but the narrower and more testable one: has God ever actually let you go without what you needed? Most Christians, made to say it aloud, arrive at the same word the disciples used, and are surprised by it.

But now. Something has changed, and the change is not in God’s care but in the world’s welcome. The season of open doors is closing. Israel is about to reject her Messiah, and the men at this table will go out into a world that will treat them accordingly, with the arrests and courtrooms he described in the previous chapter (21:12). So the instructions are reversed. Take the bag, take the money. They will face hostility, not welcome, and will need to provide for themselves.

The Lord who sent them. It was Jesus who sent them out with nothing, and his name that opened the doors: the seventy-two came back rejoicing that even the demons were subject to them in his name (10:17). Their lack of nothing was his doing. And the reason the season is changing is himself. The world that welcomed his messengers is about to reject their Master, and the hostility they will meet is the hostility he meets first, tonight. Disciples share their Lord’s welcome, and they share his rejection (John 15:20).

Let the one who has no sword sell his cloak and buy one. This is one of the hardest sentences in the Gospels, and the honest thing is to say what it plainly means before saying what it does not. The sword saying is a vivid warning of the hostility ahead, not a call to armed resistance. In that world a cloak was a man’s most necessary possession, his coat by day and his blanket by night, so basic that the law forbade keeping it overnight as a pledge because he had nothing else to sleep under (Exodus 22:26–27). To sell the cloak for a sword is to say: the danger ahead is now greater than the cold. Things will be desperate. It is a picture of how sharply conditions are about to change, put in the most arresting terms available, and his own response, when they produce two swords and later when one is used, shows beyond argument that it is not a licence for the disciples to fight.

Does this verse teach that Christians may carry weapons or use force in self-defence? It is not really about that question, and it should not be made to settle it. Jesus is speaking figuratively of the danger ahead, and when a disciple took him literally he said, enough, and later stopped the sword and healed the wound (vv. 38, 50–51). Christians differ on personal self-defence, and Scripture elsewhere gives the governing authority the sword to punish evil (Romans 13:4). What this passage settles is that the gospel and the kingdom of Christ are never to be advanced or defended by the sword (John 18:36).

In a sentence. Jesus reminded them that on their earlier mission they had lacked nothing, but said now they would need money, supplies, and even a sword, so great would the hostility be.

On a Tuesday. Be prepared for opposition. Following Christ in a hostile world is not always welcome, and a workplace, a family or a culture that once tolerated your faith may turn cold. Prepare as he told them: soberly and practically, without panic, by knowing what you believe, keeping close to other Christians, and being wise with what you have. And keep a record of the times God has met your needs, so that when the season turns you can still answer, nothing.

For worship. The Lord who provisioned them so completely in the easy season is the same One preparing them for the hard one, and he does not pretend the second is like the first. He tells his people in advance when the weather is about to turn, and then he walks into the storm ahead of them. Every disciple who has gone out into a cold world with a thin cloak has found that the One who asked, did you lack anything?, is still asking, and that at the end of every season the answer is the same.
verseByVerse.note: The sword saying is a vivid warning of the hostility ahead, not a call to armed resistance, as verses 38 and 51 show.

verseByVerse.quote: For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in me: ‘And he was numbered with the transgressors.’ For what is written about me has its fulfillment.' And they said, 'Look, Lord, here are two swords.' And he said to them, 'It is enough.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in me: and he was numbered with the transgressors. For what is written about me has its fulfilment. And they said: look, Lord, here are two swords. And he said to them: it is enough.

This Scripture must be fulfilled in me. Must, dei: the divine necessity again. Not merely a prediction that happens to come true, but the fixed purpose of God written in advance and now arriving.

And he was numbered with the transgressors. He quotes Isaiah 53:12, the last line of the Servant Song, about the servant who poured out his soul to death and was numbered with the transgressors, yet bore the sin of many and makes intercession for the transgressors. It is the only direct quotation of Isaiah 53 by Jesus in the Gospels, and it is the lens through which he reads his own arrest. He will be taken like a criminal, tried as a criminal and killed between two of them (23:32–33): counted in the same column, entered on the same list. And by quoting it he identifies himself as the servant of Isaiah 53, who bears sin for others. That is also the reason the swords must go. A man being arrested as a criminal cannot be defended by force without becoming one.

For what is written about me has its fulfillment. Literally has its end: is reaching its goal. Everything written about him is being fulfilled. Jesus reads Isaiah 53, finds his own name in it, and goes out to the garden to make it true.

Look, Lord, here are two swords. They take him literally. Two short swords or large knives, perhaps used for preparing the Passover lamb. He was telling them the friendly season was over; they heard sword and reached for iron.

It is enough. Not that two swords are enough to fight, which would be absurd against an armed detachment, and Jesus knows it. Rather: enough of this, the weary words of a teacher closing a conversation that has gone wrong (Deuteronomy 3:26). And when the iron did come out in the garden, he stopped it with a word and mended the only casualty of the night with a touch (vv. 50–51).

Buy a sword, then put it away, so which is it? Down the centuries the church has misread this in both directions. Some have taken v. 36 as a divine licence for the sword and built crusades and holy wars on it. Others have taken v. 51 as an absolute ban on any force whatever, in any hands, for any cause. The passage will carry neither load. The key is the detail easily missed: two swords for twelve men about to be surrounded is not enough for a fight, and Jesus says, it is enough. The single sword-stroke of the whole passion was struck by a disciple, against Christ’s will, and Jesus reversed it. That is Luke’s last word on swords in the kingdom.

What does numbered with the transgressors mean for me? It means he was counted where you belonged so that you could be counted where he belonged. On the cross he was listed among the lawless, and God treated him as the sin-bearer. God made the sinless one to be sin for us, so that in him we might become his righteousness (2 Corinthians 5:21). That exchange is the whole gospel. When your conscience reminds you that you belong in the column of transgressors, answer that Christ has already stood in it, and you have been moved, by grace, to his.

In a sentence. Jesus said that the Scripture about being counted among the lawless must be fulfilled in him, and when the disciples produced two swords, he said: enough.

On a Tuesday. When someone misunderstands what you meant about your faith, follow his example: say enough, kindly, and let your actions explain it later. And when you are tempted to defend Christ by being harsh, sarcastic or forceful in an argument online or at work, remember the two swords. His kingdom is not served by that kind of strength.

For worship. He was numbered with the transgressors, and he made the most of the company. Hanging between two of them, he heard one ask to be remembered, and he answered with paradise that very day (23:42–43). The Servant who was entered on the criminals’ list used his place on it to take a criminal home. Blessed is the Lord who stooped low enough to be counted among the lawless, and stayed close enough to them to save.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
He goes to the Mount of Olives as was his custom — which is why Judas knew where to look, and why he had a path to walk on the worst night of his life. The habit was already worn smooth. And his instruction to the disciples is not that they pray for him but that they pray for themselves: pray that you may not enter into temptation, the petition from the prayer he taught them.

A stone's throw away he kneels, which was not the customary posture, and prays Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done. The cup is not a general image of suffering. In the prophets it is fixed: the cup of the wrath of God, which the wicked drain to the dregs (Ps. 75:8; Jer. 25:15; Isa. 51:17).

Luke adds two details the others do not: an angel strengthening him, and sweat like great drops of blood. Both verses carry a note in modern Bibles — some manuscripts omit them, as the ESV margin says — because the manuscript evidence is genuinely divided — including the real possibility that early scribes removed them because a Christ who trembled embarrassed them.

He finds the disciples asleep, and Luke alone says why: for sorrow. They were not indifferent; grief of that weight shuts a body down. He wakes them without rebuke and gives them the smallest possible next action: rise and pray.

Then, while he is still speaking, the torches. Judas leads them and comes to kiss him, and Jesus names it to his face — using his name, in a question, which is a door held open to the last second. A disciple strikes and takes an ear, and Jesus stops his own arrest to heal a member of the arresting party.

To the officials who came out at night with clubs, he points out that he had been in their temple every day that week and they had not touched him. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness — real authority, genuinely theirs, and lasting exactly an hour.
verseByVerse.theology:
Not my will, but yours, be done is the perfect alignment of a human will with the divine, and it required agony to reach — which is what makes it obedience rather than indifference. Both wills are real: he genuinely did not want the cup. Gethsemane is the counterpart of Eden. In one garden a man said my will, not yours and the world broke; in another the second Adam said it the other way round.

The unanswered request is itself doctrine. If the Father would not spare his own Son a single mouthful of that cup, there was no other way for sinners to be saved. The silence after if you are willing is the measure of what the cross was for.

Verse 51 is the last healing before the cross and it is performed on an enemy, unasked, by the prisoner. He had said love your enemies and do good to those who hate you (6:27), and here he does it with his own disciple's blade still wet.

And this is your hour, and the power of darkness concedes two things and withholds a third. The hour is genuinely theirs; the authority is real and belongs to darkness. What is withheld is any suggestion that it is more than an hour. Luke has used that clock before — the devil departed from him until an opportune time (4:13).
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 39 is for anyone who has tried to pray in an emergency and found nothing there. The crisis is a terrible time to begin; what carries a person through a night like that is a path already trodden, and paths are made in the ordinary weeks when nothing is wrong.

Verse 42 settles a question many carry: is if you are willing a failure of faith? A woman facing a diagnosis, told that Christian prayer should always be confident and specific, wonders whether her honest conditional is weakness. The Son of God prayed exactly that prayer, in those words, on the worst night in history. Telling God plainly what you want and then leaving it with him is the highest thing faith ever does.

Verse 44 ends another argument — the idea that visible distress proves weak faith. The sinless Son, in perfect communion with his Father and doing exactly his will, was in such distress that his body gave way under it.

And vv. 45–46 name one of the least-discussed experiences in the Christian life: the point at which grief makes prayer impossible. Bereavement, depression, exhaustion after months of caring — and the believer finds the one thing he most needs to do is the thing he can no longer make himself do, with the accusation following that a real Christian would be praying. Look at who is standing over these men. He knows exactly why they are asleep, he has just been through worse, and he wakes them gently and tells them to pray. They were kept that night, and it was not by their own watchfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came out and went, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples followed him. And when he came to the place, he said to them, 'Pray that you may not enter into temptation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came out and went, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples followed him. And when he came to the place, he said to them: pray that you may not enter into temptation.

As was his custom. Luke has already told us this was the pattern of the week: teaching in the temple by day, lodging on the Mount of Olives by night (21:37). It is a small phrase with two large consequences. The first is that Judas knew where to find him. John says so: Judas knew the place, because Jesus often met there with his disciples (John 18:2). Jesus goes, on the one night when his habits are lethal, to the one place his betrayer would look. He did not hide.

A path already trodden. The second consequence is about prayer, and it is the more useful one for most readers. The worst night of his life did not send him somewhere new. He went where he always went. The habit was already in place, worn smooth by years of use, and when the crisis came he did not have to invent a practice; he had only to keep one. The hour of crisis is a hard time to begin. What carries a person through a night like that is a path already trodden, made in the ordinary weeks when nothing is wrong and prayer feels unnecessary.

When he came to the place. Gethsemane (Mark 14:32), an olive grove on the slope of the Mount of Olives; the name means oil press. Luke does not name it. He simply calls it the place, as if every reader knew where the Lord prayed.

Pray that you may not enter into temptation. It is not what he might have asked for. He does not ask them to pray for him. He is about to enter the deepest agony any human being has known, and what he asks of his friends is that they pray for themselves. The words are lifted straight out of the prayer he taught them: lead us not into temptation (11:4). Temptation, peirasmos, is the trial that is coming, testing as well as enticement, which could make them fall. It is a prayer to be kept from the place where faith is put under a pressure it cannot bear, a plea born of the self-distrust these men lack. And he does not say, watch for Judas, or arm yourselves. The danger closing in on that garden was real and armed, and the only defence he issued was prayer. He says it at the beginning of the scene and again at the end (v. 46).

Does God lead us into temptation? God tempts no one to sin (James 1:13), but he does bring his people into testing. The prayer asks to be kept from falling when the test comes; and God promises that he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation will provide the way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13).

How do I build a habit of prayer like this? Start small, regular and fixed, rather than large and occasional. Choose a time and a place, as Jesus had the Mount of Olives: a chair, a walk, the first ten minutes after the children leave. Use the Lord’s Prayer as a frame, the Psalms as words when you have none, and a short list of people to pray for. Expect it to feel dry some days; the habit is not for the good days but for the night when you will need a worn path. Pray with others too, in your church’s prayer meeting, because it is easier to keep a path that others walk with you.

In a sentence. Jesus went as usual to the Mount of Olives with his disciples, and told them to pray that they would not enter into temptation.

On a Tuesday. What testing are you facing, or likely to face, this week: a conversation, a temptation that comes at a certain hour, a weariness that makes you sharp? Pray about it before it comes, naming it specifically, and ask God to keep you from entering it. Then fix tomorrow’s time and place for prayer tonight.

For worship. He is walking into the worst hour in history, and his last instruction before he kneels is a warning for their sakes. He went to the place his betrayer knew, because he was not fleeing from the cup but walking to it. The Shepherd thought of his sheep while the wolves were climbing the hill, and he still does. Jesus knows the hour of our testing before we do, and he has already prayed.

verseByVerse.quote: And he withdrew from them about a stone's throw, and knelt down and prayed, saying, 'Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he withdrew from them about a stone’s throw, and knelt down and prayed, saying: Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.

About a stone’s throw. Near enough to be seen and heard, far enough to be alone, perhaps thirty yards. Luke measures the distance, which is the kind of detail a man includes when he has spoken to someone who was there.

And knelt down. The customary posture for Jewish prayer was standing. Kneeling was for extremity, a sign of intensity and submission. In Mark he falls on the ground (Mark 14:35).

Father. Whatever else is about to be said, it begins there, and the address never wavers. Even in agony, the intimate name.

If you are willing, remove this cup from me. The cup has to be identified correctly, because everything depends on it. In the prophets the cup is a fixed image, and it is not an image of pain in general. It is the cup of the wrath of God: the LORD holds a cup of foaming wine that the wicked of the earth must drain to its dregs (Psalm 75:8); the cup of the wine of wrath for the nations (Jeremiah 25:15); the cup of staggering (Isaiah 51:17). So what makes him shake is not the nails. Thousands of men were crucified in that province and some faced it with composure; there were Jewish martyrs who went to terrible deaths singing. If Jesus were merely facing execution he would be less brave than his own martyrs, which is absurd. What is in front of him is the cup: the undiluted judgment of God against sin, to be drunk in the place of sinners by the only man who never deserved a drop of it. Here is a real human shrinking from the horror.

If you are willing. He does not presume. He asks, and the asking is real: if there is another way, let there be another way. There was not, and the silence that followed that request is the measure of what the cross was for. If the Father would not spare his own Son a single mouthful of it, there was no other way for you to be saved.

Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done. The heart of the prayer: total submission. Two wills are in that sentence, and both are real. He genuinely did not want the cup. That is not a flaw in his obedience; it is what makes it obedience rather than indifference. His human will submitted to the Father’s. Where Adam said my will in a garden, Christ says your will in a garden. And this obedience is our salvation: by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous (Romans 5:19; Hebrews 10:7–10).

Did Jesus have two wills? Yes. He is one person, the eternal Son, with two natures, divine and human, and each nature has its own will. As God he shares the one will of the Father and the Spirit. As man he has a true human will, which recoiled from the cup as any holy human will must, and which he freely and perfectly bent to the Father’s purpose. The church confessed this against those who said Christ had only one will (Constantinople, 681), because a Saviour without a human will could not offer human obedience in our place. Gethsemane is where you see it: a real man choosing, at the cost of everything, to obey.

Is it weak faith to pray if it is your will? No. The Son of God prayed it, in those words, on the worst night in history. Telling God plainly what you want and then leaving it with him is not a failure of faith; it is the highest thing faith ever does. Pray boldly for healing, for a marriage, for a child: ask, and say what you long for. Then add what Jesus added, not as a hedge but as trust. It is not lack of faith that says, your will be done. It is faith in a Father who knows better than you, and who did not spare his own Son.

In a sentence. Jesus withdrew a short distance, knelt and prayed that, if the Father was willing, the cup would be taken from him, yet asked that not his will but the Father’s be done.

On a Tuesday. For the reader praying an if you are willing prayer over something they are terrified of, a diagnosis, a marriage, a child: pray it today as he did. Say the whole of what you want, without dressing it up. Then say the second half, nevertheless, not my will but yours, and if you cannot yet mean it fully, ask him to make you mean it.

For worship. A few hours earlier he had handed his friends a cup and called it the new covenant in his blood, poured out for them. Now, on his knees in the dark, he is shown the other cup, with no mercy mixed in it, and he takes it. That is the exchange at the heart of the gospel: he drank the cup of wrath to the dregs so that the cup his people hold is the cup of salvation (Psalm 116:13). Behold the obedience that saved us, a man on his knees under the night sky, saying, Father.
verseByVerse.note: A stone’s throw is a short distance. The “cup” pictures God’s judgment poured out.

verseByVerse.quote: And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him.

And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. The Father does not remove the cup. He sends someone to help his Son drink it. Take that in before anything else, because it is the pattern of answered prayer through the whole of Scripture, and it is what most people need to know about their own unanswered prayers. God rarely removes the furnace. He goes into it. The angel does not come to rescue Jesus from the cross; the angel comes so that he can get to it. That is often how God answers prayer: not by removing the trial but by strengthening us in it (2 Corinthians 12:7–10). As after the temptation in the wilderness, angels came and ministered to him (Matthew 4:11; Mark 1:13).

He needed strengthening. Notice what this says about the Son in his humanity. Not metaphorically: he needed strength. The one who made the angel is being ministered to by it. He was made like his brothers in every respect (Hebrews 2:17), including the need for help from heaven in the hour of weakness.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit verses 43 and 44. The evidence really is divided. The two verses are missing from some early and important manuscripts, and present in many others; they were known to early writers like Justin Martyr and Irenaeus in the second century. Some copies mark them with a sign showing the scribe knew there was a question. Careful people hold two explanations. Either Luke wrote them and some scribes cut them, or they preserve a true early memory later written in. The first has real force. Some readers in the early centuries were embarrassed by a Jesus who sweated, shook and needed an angel, thinking it made him look too weak, and a scribe who removed these lines would have thought he was defending Christ’s dignity. He would have been removing the proof of his humanity. Many scholars think they are original.

How then should they be read? Read them, and rest nothing on them that rests nowhere else. Nothing in them is unique to them. The agony in the garden is in Matthew and Mark without these verses. Angels attending Jesus after a great trial is already in the record (Matthew 4:11). And a Christ who prays in anguish is not a fragile idea propped up by two disputed lines; it is the settled teaching of the New Testament: in the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears (Hebrews 5:7). They are true in any case to what we know of Gethsemane.

Do angels help believers today? Yes, though usually unseen. Angels are ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14), and the angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him (Psalm 34:7). But Scripture never tells us to pray to angels, seek them, or build our comfort on stories of them. The angel in the garden pointed Jesus to the cup, not away from it.
