Our strength comes from God, by his Spirit and his Word, and whether he uses angels to give it is his business.

In a sentence. An angel from heaven appeared to Jesus and strengthened him.

On a Tuesday. God may not take away your trial, but he will give you strength to bear it. Ask him today, plainly, not only for the trial to be removed but for strength to walk through it if it is not. Then look for the strength he sends: a verse that lands, a friend who calls, the next hour that turns out to be bearable.

For worship. The church has never had a Saviour who suffered at a comfortable distance, and the rest of the New Testament says so with no question of text. He was made like his brothers in every respect, and because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18). Our High Priest knows from the inside what it is to need help in the dark. So the throne he sits on is a throne of grace, where the weak are always welcome to find mercy and help in time of need (Hebrews 4:16).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit verses 43 and 44.

verseByVerse.quote: And being in agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And being in agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground.

And being in agony. The word is agōnia, and it does not mean misery. It comes from the arena. The agōn was the contest, and agōnia was the state of a man at the point of maximum exertion in it: the struggle of an athlete, intense conflict. This is not despair. It is a battle of the will, at the limit of what a body can do.

He prayed more earnestly. Look at what the agony produced. That is the reverse of the usual direction. Under that kind of pressure the human instinct is to stop praying, because prayer needs an attention that terror takes away. He went the other way: the worse it got, the harder he prayed. Strengthened by the angel, he prayed more, not less. Strength from God leads to deeper prayer.

And his sweat became like great drops of blood. The detail only the physician records. Careful readers have long noticed the word like, and Luke may mean that the sweat fell in thick, heavy drops, the way blood falls. But there is a rare documented condition, hematidrosis, in which extreme distress ruptures the small vessels near the sweat glands so that blood is mixed with sweat. Luke was a doctor, and if he was told of something of that kind he described it as a doctor would. Either way the point is not clinical. The point is that it went that far, and it shows the intensity of his anguish as he faced the wrath of God.

Falling down to the ground. In a garden, on the ground. Adam was cursed to eat bread by the sweat of his face until he returned to the ground (Genesis 3:17–19). Here the second Adam’s sweat falls on the ground of a garden, and the curse of Adam’s sin is borne by the one who came to undo it. There is blood on the ground of that garden before a single soldier has laid a hand on him.

Is anxiety or deep distress a sign of weak faith? Not in itself. There is a strain of Christian teaching that treats visible distress as evidence of weak faith: a believer facing something terrible ought to be calm, and fear is failure. This verse ends that argument. The sinless Son of God, in perfect communion with his Father, doing exactly the Father’s will, was in such distress that his body gave way under it. Anxiety can become sin when it turns to unbelief or grumbling, and we are told to cast our anxieties on God (Philippians 4:6; 1 Peter 5:7). But fear and anguish carried to the Father in prayer are not failure. They are exactly what Jesus did. And if anxiety has become a constant illness, seeking medical help is wisdom, not lack of faith.

In a sentence. In his anguish, Jesus prayed even more earnestly, and his sweat fell to the ground like great drops of blood.

On a Tuesday. When pressure rises this week, notice whether your instinct is to stop praying. Do the opposite, even if it is only a sentence: Father, help me; your will be done. And if you are ashamed of how badly you are coping with something, bring the shame to the one who sweated like this. He is not puzzled by human dread.

For worship. Whatever the precise history of these words, the sorrow they describe is certain. Mark records him saying that his soul was very sorrowful, even to death (Mark 14:34), and he had not yet been arrested, tried, flogged or nailed. He went further into dread than any of his people will ever go, and he went in freely, for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). That joy was his Father’s glory and a people brought home, and he counted it worth the cup.
verseByVerse.note: Luke, a doctor, describes the extreme anguish; “like great drops of blood” may be a comparison or describe a rare medical condition.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he rose from prayer, he came to the disciples and found them sleeping for sorrow, and he said to them, 'Why are you sleeping? Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he rose from prayer, he came to the disciples and found them sleeping for sorrow, and he said to them: why are you sleeping? Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation.

And found them sleeping for sorrow. Matthew and Mark record that the disciples slept. Only Luke tells us why: from grief. That is a physician’s observation and it is a kindness. They were not bored or indifferent. They had spent an evening being told that one of them was a traitor, that their leader was going to die, that Peter would deny him, and grief of that weight does something to a body. It does not keep you awake. It shuts you down. Anyone who has sat with the bereaved knows the heaviness that comes over people in the days after a death, the sleep that is not rest. Luke is gentle with the disciples, mentioning only one return where Mark has three.

Why are you sleeping? There is no long rebuke in those words, and no discussion of their failure at all. Mark records a sharper word to Peter (Mark 14:37), but Luke gives us this: a gentle question.

Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The same command as v. 40. The testing is about to come up the path. He does not say, feel better, or stop grieving. He says, rise and pray, which is the smallest possible next action, and the only one available. They will fail, because they did not pray.

When grief makes prayer impossible. This names one of the commonest and least-discussed experiences in the Christian life. Bereavement, depression, a marriage coming apart, exhaustion after months of caring for someone, and the believer finds that the very thing he most needs to do is the thing he can no longer make himself do. He opens the Bible and reads the same paragraph four times. He kneels and falls asleep. And then, on top of the sorrow, comes the accusation: a real Christian would be praying. Look at who is standing over these men. He knows exactly why they are asleep, he has just been through something immeasurably worse, and his response is to wake them gently and tell them to pray, not to inform them that they have forfeited anything.

What if I cannot pray at all right now? Then pray the smallest prayer you can, and lean on others and on the Spirit. A groan, a single line, the Lord’s Prayer said slowly, a psalm read aloud: God hears all of it. The Spirit helps us in our weakness, for we do not know what to pray for as we ought, and he intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words (Romans 8:26). Ask a friend or your pastor to pray for you and with you. Rest and sleep are not sins; Elijah was fed and allowed to sleep before he was spoken to (1 Kings 19:5–8). And remember that Christ is praying for you while you cannot.

In a sentence. Rising from prayer, Jesus found the disciples asleep from grief, and told them to get up and pray that they would not enter into temptation.

On a Tuesday. Sorrow can make you spiritually sleepy. If you are grieving, do not wait to feel able before you pray. Set a tiny, achievable practice: one psalm a day, read aloud, and one sentence of prayer after it. And if you know someone who is grieving, pray for them by name today, and tell them you did.

For worship. He had asked them to pray for themselves, and they could not, and all the while he had been praying a stone’s throw away. The disciples were kept that night, and not by their own watchfulness. The Keeper of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps (Psalm 121:4), and that night he knelt in the dust in a human body, awake in anguish while his friends slept in sorrow. He is awake still, and the sleepers he woke so gently he has never given up.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, there came a crowd, and the man called Judas, one of the twelve, was leading them. He drew near to Jesus to kiss him, but Jesus said to him, 'Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was still speaking, there came a crowd, and the man called Judas, one of the Twelve, was leading them. He drew near to Jesus to kiss him, but Jesus said to him: Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?

While he was still speaking. The warning and the danger arrive in the same breath. He was mid-sentence telling them to pray, and the torches were already coming up the hill. The temptation arrives.

The man called Judas, one of the twelve, was leading them. Luke, who has already told us in v. 3 who this man was, says it again as though it still cannot be believed. He is at the front. He is not being brought along as a witness; he is guiding an armed party to a place only an insider knew. The one who had followed Jesus now leads his enemies.

He drew near to Jesus to kiss him. In that world a kiss was not a small or private gesture. It was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher, an act of honour and affection performed in public. So the sign agreed with the arresting party was the gesture of love, used to identify Jesus in the dark. He could have pointed. He chose the one movement that means, I am yours, and used it as a marker for the temple police. That is what sin does when it is finished: it takes what is good and makes it the instrument. Worship offered to be seen, truth told to wound, affection used as a lever.

Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss? Only Luke records these words. Jesus uses his name. This is the last recorded word of Jesus to Judas, and it is not a curse. It is a question, and it is his name, the same name he had spoken on the mountain when he chose him (6:13–16). It exposes the obscenity: betrayal with a sign of love. And still he calls himself the Son of Man, the one who will come in glory (Daniel 7:13). It is better read as what it plainly is: a last door held open, a last appeal to Judas’s conscience. He puts to Judas the thing Judas is doing, in words, at the moment of doing it, and the question hangs there waiting for an answer. This is how the Lord deals with a man walking into ruin: not by ambush, but by naming it to his face while there is still a second in which to stop.

Why did Jesus choose Judas if he knew? Jesus knew from the beginning who would betray him (John 6:64, 70), and chose him all the same, so that the Scripture would be fulfilled (John 13:18; Psalm 41:9). That choice did not make Judas a traitor; it gave a man every privilege, three years of Jesus’ company, his teaching, his miracles and his love, and Judas turned them all down. His story is a warning that nearness to holy things does not save, and a proof that Christ’s love was offered even to the one who sold him.

Was Judas ever truly a believer who lost his salvation? No. Jesus says that of those the Father gave him he lost none except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled (John 17:12), and he had said early on that one of the Twelve was a devil (John 6:70). Judas shared the outward life of a disciple but never belonged to Christ; his faith was never real, and his end showed it (1 John 2:19). The true believer may fall terribly, as Peter did, but Christ’s sheep never perish (John 10:28).

In a sentence. Judas arrived leading a crowd and came to kiss Jesus, and Jesus asked whether he would betray the Son of Man with a kiss.

On a Tuesday. Outward signs of love for Jesus can hide betrayal. Ask where you use good things as tools: a kind word to get your way, a Bible verse to win an argument, church service to be noticed. Let your love for him be real. And if you have been walking the wrong way and his Word is asking you a question today, answer it now, while the door is open.

For worship. The traitor came with a kiss, and the Lord met him with his name. Even then the One being betrayed was the One doing the seeking, holding open a door the other man was closing. And when the question went unanswered, he did not turn back from the cross. He went with them, and within the day he died for sinners exactly like the one who kissed him, for at the right time Christ died for the ungodly (Romans 5:6).
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: And when those who were around him saw what would follow, they said, 'Lord, shall we strike with the sword?' And one of them struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear. But Jesus said, 'No more of this!' And he touched his ear and healed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When those who were around him saw what would follow, they said: Lord, shall we strike with the sword? And one of them struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear. But Jesus said: no more of this! And he touched his ear and healed him.

Lord, shall we strike with the sword? They ask the question and then do not wait for the answer, which is the whole trouble with them in one line. They had two swords (v. 38) and had misunderstood. Before the reply comes, a sword is out and a man is bleeding.

And one of them struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear. John names them both: Peter with the sword, and the servant Malchus (John 18:10). Only Luke and John say it was the right ear. Peter was a fisherman, not a swordsman, and the fact that he took an ear rather than a head suggests a wild stroke that the man ducked. It is a serious wound and, in the circumstances, suicidal: eleven Galileans and two swords against an armed detachment.

No more of this! Or, let them do this, allowing the arrest. Either way, Jesus stops the violence. Four words, and they are the last command he gives before he is bound. Consider what he is stopping. Not an enemy, but a friend. Not cowardice, but reckless courage performed out of love for him. Peter is the only man there willing to die for Jesus at that moment, and Jesus tells him to stop. Because the kingdom does not come that way, and never has. He would say it under interrogation the next morning: if my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting (John 18:36). The one thing he would not permit in his own defence was the thing his followers have most often reached for since.

And he touched his ear and healed him. Only Luke, the doctor, records it, and it is one of the most extraordinary sentences in the Gospels. Jesus is minutes from being bound and led away. Torches are in his face, weapons are drawn, his own men are about to run. And in the middle of it he stops his arrest in order to repair the injury his disciple has done to one of the men who came to take him. Malchus went to work that night to arrest a man and came home whole. The last miracle of healing before the cross was performed on a member of the arresting party, by the prisoner, without being asked. He loves his enemies (6:27), even at the moment of betrayal. That is who he is when everything is against him: not merely non-retaliating, but actively mending.

Was Peter wrong to defend Jesus? His love was right and his method was wrong. He wanted to protect Jesus from the cross, which is exactly what Jesus had come to embrace, and he reached for the world’s weapon to do it. Christians make the same mistake whenever they try to defend Christ with anger, force, manipulation or political power. The way we stand up for Jesus is by speaking the truth in love, suffering wrong patiently, and doing good to those who oppose us (1 Peter 2:23; 3:15–16).

Does Jesus still heal like this? Christ still heals, often in answer to prayer, and we should pray for the sick with confidence (James 5:14–15). But the instant miracles of his earthly ministry and of the apostles were signs confirming the new revelation of the gospel (Hebrews 2:3–4), and this commentary holds, with many Reformed Christians, that such sign gifts ceased with the apostolic age. Brothers and sisters who believe otherwise are to be loved and listened to. Either way, every healing, through medicine or prayer or both, is his gift, and the greatest healing he gives is the forgiveness of enemies.

In a sentence. When a disciple cut off the right ear of the high priest’s servant, Jesus stopped the violence, touched the man’s ear and healed it.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person you are most at odds with this week. Do not merely refrain from striking back; look for a way to repair something for them: a kind word to someone who insulted you, a practical help for the colleague who undermined you. Love your enemies, and do good to those who hate you (6:27).

For worship. The prisoner healed the man who came to bind him. The hand that touched that ear would be nailed within hours, and from that wounded hand healing has gone out ever since to enemies who came against him armed. We too were his enemies, and he reconciled us to God by his death (Romans 5:10). He healed the servant unasked, and he came to us unasked. The last healing before the cross is the pattern of every one after it: grace to the undeserving, given first.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke, the doctor, records that Jesus healed the ear. John names the servant Malchus and the swordsman Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus said to the chief priests and officers of the temple and elders, who had come out against him, 'Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs? When I was with you day after day in the temple, you did not lay hands on me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jesus said to the chief priests and officers of the temple and elders, who had come out against him: have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs? When I was with you day after day in the temple, you did not lay hands on me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.

The chief priests and officers of the temple and elders. He speaks to the officials, not to the muscle. Luke names them: the leadership itself had come out to the garden at night. They wanted to see it done.

Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs? A robber here, lēstēs, is not a pickpocket but a bandit or an insurgent: a man with a weapon and a hillside. So the question is precise. They treat him as a dangerous criminal: have you come out equipped for an armed rebel? And within hours Luke will show a real insurrectionist, Barabbas, set free while the man they treated as one is condemned in his place (23:18–25).

When I was with you day after day in the temple, you did not lay hands on me. The fact convicts them without a word of accusation. He was there every day of that week, in the open, in their own building, teaching in front of thousands. If he were a danger to public order, that was the moment. They chose the olive grove, at night, with a paid informant and a crowd carrying clubs, and the choice tells you who believed his own case would survive daylight. Their night-time arrest exposed their cowardice.

But this is your hour, and the power of darkness. Only Luke records these words, and they are among the darkest Jesus ever said. Two things are conceded and one is withheld. He concedes the hour: this is genuinely theirs, the time God has permitted them to act, and what follows is not a puppet show in which the participants only pretend to arrest him. And he concedes the power: exousia, real authority, and it belongs to darkness, which means the authority of Satan (Colossians 1:13; Acts 26:18). What he withholds is any suggestion that this is more than an hour. Luke has used that clock before: the devil departed from him until an opportune time (4:13), and here is the time. It gets an hour. That is the lease. Darkness seems to triumph. But it is only an hour, and it is God who has given it.

What is the power of darkness today? It is the same enemy, still working through human hearts and systems: lies, cruelty, false religion, persecution, and the ordinary pull of the world against God. Christians are not to be naive about it (Ephesians 6:12). But for believers it is a defeated power. God has rescued us from the domain of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of his beloved Son (Colossians 1:13). Satan’s hour ended at the empty tomb, and what remains is a beaten enemy’s rage before the end. We resist him with the truth, the gospel, faith and prayer (Ephesians 6:13–18), never with fear.

In a sentence. Jesus asked the leaders why they came against him with weapons as if he were a bandit, when they had not arrested him in the temple, and said this was their hour, and the power of darkness.

On a Tuesday. When darkness seems to be winning, in the news, in your family, in your own heart, remember that it looks permanent from inside. It looked permanent to the eleven men running down that hillside, and by Sunday morning it was over. Say it aloud today about the darkest thing you face: this is an hour, and God has set its length.

For worship. He is being arrested, and he is the only one present who knows what time it is. The men with the torches thought they had taken him. They had been given an hour, by him, and they used it exactly as he said they would. Evil has its hour, but only an hour, and only by God’s permission, and the Lord of the hours has already appointed the dawn. Three days later the hour of darkness ended at an empty tomb, and the day that dawned there will have no evening.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 54–71 — The Denial and the Trial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Peter follows at a distance — more than anyone else managed, and still far enough to be nobody. In the courtyard a fire is kindled and he sits down among the men who arrested his Lord. It was cold, and there is nothing sinful about wanting to be warm; but this is how a fall actually happens. He did not decide to deny Christ. He decided to stay warm.

The accuser is a servant girl, the person of least standing in that yard, and her charge is about as mild as an accusation can be: this man also was with him. Peter answers, Woman, I do not know him — denying not a fact but a person.

Luke keeps the clock running: a little later, then an interval of about an hour. This is not a moment of panic; Peter had an hour to get up and leave. And the denials deteriorate — first the person, then the fellowship (I am not), then the subject itself (I do not know what you are talking about). The third accuser has evidence nobody can argue with: his accent. The very voice denying Christ was proving him a follower with every word.

Then the rooster, mid-sentence — the most ordinary sound in the world, and enough, because it had been named in advance. And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. It was not a look of contempt; a man looked at with contempt remembers the contempt, and Peter remembered the saying of the Lord — which included I have prayed for you and when you have turned again. He went out and wept bitterly.

Inside, the guards fill the night with a game: blindfold him, strike him, and demand he name the hand. While they demand a prophecy, three of his prophecies are being fulfilled in that building.

At daybreak the council reconvenes to give the night's work a lawful appearance, and asks its one question. He declines to perform — if I tell you, you will not believe — and then makes a claim larger than the question: from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God. They ask if he is the Son of God. He affirms it, and they need nothing further.
verseByVerse.theology:
Peter's fall and Judas's ruin are the two halves of the same night, and the difference between them is the most important distinction in the chapter. Both men were sorry. Matthew says Judas was seized with remorse and threw the money back; then he hanged himself. Peter wept and lived. Paul named the difference exactly: godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death (2 Cor. 7:10). The test is not the intensity of the grief but its direction.

Verse 69 is one of the most explicit claims of identity in the Synoptic Gospels, and it welds two Scriptures together: Psalm 110:1, the Lord seated at God's right hand, and Daniel 7:13, the Son of Man receiving an everlasting dominion. The right hand is not geography but authority, and the sitting means the work is finished — under the old covenant the priests stood, because it never was (Heb. 10:11–12). And the timing is the audacity: from now on, said with his hands tied.

The council's reaction disposes of the notion that Jesus never claimed divinity and the church invented it. His enemies, in his own language, drew exactly that conclusion and put it to him, and he affirmed it in the recognised idiom of assent. They convicted him under exactly the right law. They got one thing wrong, and it was the identity of the defendant.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 54 gives a better test than a resolution. Not would I deny Christ under pressure — everyone answers no, and Peter answered no out loud a few hours earlier. Ask instead: where do I habitually sit, whose fire am I warming myself at, and what have I already agreed, without saying so, never to bring up there? The distance always comes before the denial.

A Christian leader fails publicly — not a considered defection but a collapse of nerve under social pressure — and concludes he has forfeited his calling. Peter is the specific answer. The man who denied Jesus three times within earshot of him was restored, commissioned, and preaching Christ in that same city within seven weeks. The look did not end his ministry; it began it.

Verses 63–65 describe the commonest kind of cruelty, which has nothing ideological in it: a man who was available and could not retaliate, and it passed the time. He could have named every man in that room and the day of each one's death. He said nothing, and the power that made the hands striking his face was restrained by nothing but his own will to be struck.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they seized him and led him away, bringing him into the high priest's house, and Peter was following at a distance. And when they had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat down among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they seized him and led him away, bringing him into the high priest’s house, and Peter was following at a distance. And when they had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat down among them.

Then they seized him and led him away, bringing him into the high priest’s house. John records a first hearing before Annas, the former high priest, and then before Caiaphas (John 18:13, 24). Luke gives us the denial first, then the mocking, then the morning council.

And Peter was following at a distance. The phrase deserves both halves. He was following, which is more than most of the others managed; they had fled. Whatever is about to happen to him happens to the bravest man there. And he was at a distance: close enough to see, far enough to be nobody. It is the exact position of a man who cannot bear to leave and cannot afford to be counted. Most Christians recognise that distance: not apostasy, and not confession either, but the conversation where you did not lie about your faith and did not mention it.

Led away alone. Luke keeps the camera in the courtyard, but the reader is not allowed to forget who is inside. The Shepherd has been struck and the sheep are scattered, as Mark records Jesus foretelling from Zechariah (Mark 14:27; Zechariah 13:7). He enters the high priest’s house without one friend at his side. And even the little that Peter manages, following far behind, he owes to the Lord who had prayed that night that his faith would not fail (v. 32).

They had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard. It was cold; Jerusalem nights in spring can be cold, and John notes it (John 18:18). There is nothing sinful about wanting to be warm. But look at the picture. Inside the house his Lord is being interrogated. Outside in the yard Peter sits shoulder to shoulder with the men who brought him there, faces lit by the same fire, waiting to see what happens.

Peter sat down among them. Among the servants and guards, in the light of the fire. This is how the fall actually occurs, and it almost never happens the way people expect. Peter did not decide to deny Christ. He decided to stay warm. He drifted to the safest available place, sat down with people whose questions he had no intention of answering honestly, and the denial came out of his mouth as the natural consequence of where he was sitting. Nobody plans the third denial. They choose the fire.

Is it wrong to spend time with people who are not Christians? No. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners and was criticised for it (15:1–2), and we are sent into the world, not out of it (John 17:15–18). The danger in Peter’s case was not where he sat but why: he sat there to hide. Be among unbelievers as yourself, a follower of Jesus, friendly, honest and unashamed. The question is not whether you share their fire, but whether you have agreed, without saying so, to keep Christ out of the conversation in order to keep your seat.

In a sentence. They seized Jesus and took him to the high priest’s house, and Peter followed at a distance and sat down with others around a fire in the courtyard.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test more useful than a resolution. Not, would I deny Christ under pressure? Everyone answers no, and Peter answered no out loud a few hours earlier. Ask instead: where do I habitually sit? Whose fire am I warming myself at, and what have I already agreed, without saying so, not to bring up there? Following Jesus at a distance puts you in danger. Stay close: this week, in one setting where you have kept quiet, let it be known, simply and kindly, that you belong to Christ.

For worship. Peter followed at a distance, and the Lord went the whole way. Into the high priest’s house, before the council, up the hill outside the city, he went the entire distance that sin had put between God and his people, and he went it alone. Because he did, those who were once far off have been brought near by his blood (Ephesians 2:13), not to a fire in an enemy’s courtyard but to the warmth of the Father’s house.
verseByVerse.note: John records a first hearing before Annas, the former high priest.

verseByVerse.quote: Then a servant girl, seeing him as he sat in the light and looking closely at him, said, 'This man also was with him.' But he denied it, saying, 'Woman, I do not know him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then a servant girl, seeing him as he sat in the light and looking closely at him, said: this man also was with him. But he denied it, saying: woman, I do not know him.

A servant girl. Luke has arranged the details so that the reader cannot miss how small the pressure was. The accuser is a servant girl, a young female slave, the person with the least standing of anyone present. She commanded nothing, could arrest no one, and her word carried no legal weight whatever.

Seeing him as he sat in the light and looking closely at him. He had put himself where the fire was, and the fire showed his face. He was recognised because he was warm. Looking closely, atenisasa, is staring intently. That is all. There is no interrogation, no threat, no soldier.

This man also was with him. Her charge is about as mild as an accusation can be. Not, he is one of the ringleaders. Not, he drew a sword in the garden, which was true and would have been dangerous. Merely: he was with him. Yet with him is the very essence of discipleship (8:1; Mark 3:14), and that is exactly what he now disowns.

Woman, I do not know him. The first denial, a flat lie, and a few hours earlier he had said he was ready to go to prison and to death (v. 33). Not, I was not there, which would have been a lie about a fact. He denies the person. Three years of it, the boat, the storm, the mountain, the loaves, you are the Christ of God (9:20), and the sentence that comes out is that he does not know who the man is.

The one he could not unknow. Peter says he does not know him, and the one fact in that courtyard no lie could touch is that Jesus knew Peter. He had called him from his boat (5:10), named him (6:14), prayed for him by name that very night (v. 32) and foretold this very sentence (v. 34). Peter could disown the relationship with his mouth. He could not dissolve it, because it had never rested on Peter’s hold on Jesus. It rested on Jesus’ hold on Peter, and that held through the denial.

The gap between intention and action. Here is what this passage is for, and it should be said without softening and without despair. The gap between what Peter sincerely intended and what Peter did was total, and the force needed to open that gap was one stare from a slave girl. That is why self-confidence is not a Christian virtue. Peter did not overestimate his love; his love was real. He overestimated what love can do on its own in a cold yard at night. And it is why the previous instruction was, pray that you may not enter into temptation (v. 40). He did not pray. He slept, then he sat down at the fire, and then a girl looked at him.

I have denied Christ by silence, so what now? Then you are where Peter was, and the way back is the same. Name it to God honestly, without excuses. Remember that Christ was not surprised and has prayed for you. Then, where it is possible, take the next opportunity in the same company to own him plainly. Peter, who denied Jesus before a servant girl, later stood before the very council that condemned him and said, we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard (Acts 4:20). Silence can be forgiven, and courage can be given.

In a sentence. A servant girl stared at Peter in the firelight and said he had been with Jesus, but Peter denied knowing him.

On a Tuesday. Denials of Christ often happen in small moments, before unimportant people: the joke you laugh at, the question about your weekend you answer vaguely, the moment someone asks whether you are religious. Before work today, pray for courage for exactly those moments, and decide now one simple sentence you could say if asked.

For worship. While Peter said, I do not know him, the Lord inside the house was being condemned for confessing who he was. The disciple denied the Master to save his skin; the Master did not deny the disciple, though it cost his life. A servant girl stared at Peter and he hid. The high priest questioned Jesus and he told the truth, and the truth he told that night is the ground on which Peter, and every denier who comes back, is received.

verseByVerse.quote: And a little later someone else saw him and said, 'You also are one of them.' But Peter said, 'Man, I am not.' And after an interval of about an hour still another insisted, saying, 'Certainly this man also was with him, for he too is a Galilean.' But Peter said, 'Man, I do not know what you are talking about.' And immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A little later someone else saw him and said: you also are one of them. But Peter said: man, I am not. And after an interval of about an hour still another insisted, saying: certainly this man also was with him, for he too is a Galilean. But Peter said: man, I do not know what you are talking about. And immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed.

You also are one of them. A little later, the second accusation, from someone else. Luke keeps the clock running, and the times are the point.

Man, I am not. The second denial. And watch the denials themselves, because each one is worse than the last and the movement is instructive. The first denied the person: I do not know him. The second denies the fellowship: I am not one of them, I have no part in that group. The third will deny the subject altogether: I do not know what you are talking about. He goes from disowning his Lord, to disowning the church, to pretending the whole matter is unintelligible to him. Sin does not stay the size it started. The second lie exists to protect the first, and the third to protect the second, and each costs less to tell than the one before.

After an interval of about an hour. Only Luke notes the time. This is not a moment of panic. It is a long, cold, deteriorating night, and Peter had an hour to think, to get up, to walk out, to repent. He stayed.

For he too is a Galilean. The third accuser has evidence, and it is the sort no one can deny for long. Matthew adds that his accent gave him away (Matthew 26:73). Galileans spoke with a recognisable regional accent, mocked in Jerusalem. Peter could control what he said. He could not control how it sounded. The very voice denying Christ was proving him a follower with every word.

Man, I do not know what you are talking about. The third denial, and immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed. He is mid-sentence. Luke does not even let him finish. The lie is still in the air when the sound comes across the courtyard, and it is the most ordinary sound in the world, the sound that had woken him a thousand mornings on the lake. God did not send an earthquake or a voice from heaven to stop Peter. He used a bird doing at dawn what birds do at dawn, and it was enough, because it had been named in advance (v. 34).

The Lord of the rooster. The Lord who knew where a colt was tied (19:30) and who would be carrying a water jar into the city (22:10) knew the hour a bird would crow, and tied his warning to it. Even the most ordinary sounds of creation keep time with his word. Peter’s lies were running to their own schedule, and the rooster was running to Christ’s.

Who accused Peter? The Gospels differ in who accused Peter: a servant girl, another girl, a man, the bystanders. In a crowded courtyard several people likely spoke at each turn, and each writer records the voices he chose. All four agree on the threefold denial and the rooster.

Is denying Christ an unforgivable sin? Not for one who comes back. Peter denied him three times, with oaths (Matthew 26:74), and was forgiven and restored. The sin Scripture calls unforgivable is the settled, knowing rejection of the Spirit’s witness to Christ, calling his work evil (Mark 3:28–30), and such a person does not want to repent. Hebrews warns of those who fall away and never return (Hebrews 6:4–6). But anyone grieving over a denial and longing to come back is plainly not in that condition. The rooster was not the end of Peter’s story. It was the alarm that woke him.

In a sentence. Peter denied it twice more, the last time an hour later, when someone noticed his Galilean accent, and while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed.

On a Tuesday. Notice the first small lie or compromise you are tempted to protect with a second one this week, and stop at the first. Confess it while it is still small. And when an ordinary thing pulls you up short, a verse on a calendar, a hymn on the radio, a child’s question, consider that it may be the rooster.

For worship. He had said this day, and three times, and before the rooster crows, and every word landed in a yard where no one was watching but the One who had said it. God is not man, that he should lie (Numbers 23:19), and the Son kept even the hardest of his words to the hour. And the same mouth that foretold the fall had foretold the turning again (v. 32). The warning came true at cock-crow, and the promise came true when the risen Lord appeared to Simon (24:34), and it is still coming true for every fallen disciple he brings home.
verseByVerse.note: Galileans spoke with a recognisable regional accent.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the saying of the Lord, how he had said to him, 'Before the rooster crows today, you will deny me three times.' And he went out and wept bitterly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the saying of the Lord, how he had said to him: before the rooster crows today, you will deny me three times. And he went out and wept bitterly.

And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. Only Luke records the look, and it may be the most affecting sentence in his Gospel. How it happened is not explained. Most likely Jesus was being led across the courtyard between hearings, or could see Peter from where he was held, and the timing put him within sight of the fire at the instant the rooster sounded. Luke simply says: the Lord turned, and looked at Peter. And he calls him the Lord. Even as a prisoner, he is Lord.

What was in that look? Everything depends on it, and the text tells us by what it produced. It did not produce despair or self-justification. It produced memory, and then tears. So it was not a look of anger or contempt. A man looked at with contempt does not remember a promise; he remembers the contempt. What Peter remembered was words, and surely the ones that came just before the prediction: I have prayed for you, and when you have turned again. So the look said something like: I told you. And I knew. And nothing between us has changed. A look of grief and love, and Peter never forgot it. Jesus does not speak. He is bound, mocked and about to be beaten, and he has no opportunity to cross a courtyard and put a hand on his friend’s shoulder. All he has is a turn of the head. It was enough.

And Peter remembered the saying of the Lord. The word of Jesus came back to him. That is how the Lord still restores his people: by bringing his word back to mind at the moment it is needed.

And he went out and wept bitterly. Bitter tears of repentance. Peter went out into the night, as Judas had gone out from the supper (John 13:30), but their nights ended differently. Matthew tells us that Judas, seized with remorse, returned the silver and took his own life (Matthew 27:3–5). Peter wept, and lived. Both regretted what they had done; only one turned with his regret towards the Lord he had wronged. That is Paul’s distinction between a grief that leads to repentance and salvation and a grief that ends in death (2 Corinthians 7:10). What matters is not how hard a man weeps but which way he faces when he does. And Jesus had prayed for him (v. 32). His faith did not fail. He would turn again, and be restored (24:34; John 21:15–19).

How do I know if my sorrow over sin is godly sorrow? Look at which way it faces. Worldly sorrow is mainly about me: what I have lost, how I look, what it will cost, and it either hardens into excuses or sinks into despair. Godly sorrow is about God: I have wronged him, and I go to him. It grieves the sin itself, not only its consequences; it confesses; it hopes in Christ’s mercy; and it turns, slowly but really, from the sin. You do not need to measure the size of your tears. If your sorrow drives you towards Christ rather than away from him, it is the godly kind.

Does Jesus look at me like that when I fail? Yes. If you belong to him, his look at your failure is the look Peter received: knowing, grieved, and full of love. He is not surprised by your sin and he has already prayed for you. The look is meant to bring his word back to you and to lead you to tears that end in restoration, not to drive you away. There is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1), and his kindness is meant to lead you to repentance (Romans 2:4).

In a sentence. The Lord turned and looked at Peter, and Peter remembered his words, went out and wept bitterly.

On a Tuesday. When you have failed Jesus, do not hide from his look. Go somewhere quiet today, as Peter went out, and tell him plainly what you did. Let yourself grieve, then read his promises of forgiveness (1 John 1:9) and get up. And if there is someone you have wronged, go to them too.

For worship. Bound and about to be beaten, the Lord still had eyes for a failing friend. Seven weeks later the man who had wept in the dark stood up in the same city and preached Christ to thousands (Acts 2:14–41). The look that broke his heart had begun to heal it, and it did not end his ministry; it began it. The eyes that turned towards Peter across a courtyard have never once looked at one of their own who has fallen and looked away.
verseByVerse.note: Only Luke records that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the men who were holding Jesus in custody were mocking him as they beat him. They also blindfolded him and kept asking him, 'Prophesy! Who is it that struck you?' And they said many other things against him, blaspheming him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The men who were holding Jesus in custody were mocking him as they beat him. They also blindfolded him and kept asking him: prophesy! Who is it that struck you? And they said many other things against him, blaspheming him.

Mocking him as they beat him. These are not the council and not the Romans. They are the guards, the men holding him overnight, with hours to fill and a prisoner nobody would ask about. Jesus had foretold it: he will be mocked and shamefully treated (18:32). It is the commonest kind of cruelty, with nothing ideological in it. He was simply available and unable to retaliate, and it passed the time.

They also blindfolded him. And kept asking him to prophesy who had struck him. A cruel game, with a rule: blindfold him, hit him, and demand that he name the hand. The mockery aims at the one thing they had heard about him, that he was a prophet. And Luke has built the chapter so that his reader sees the irony: in the very hours these men demand a prophecy, three of his prophecies are being fulfilled. Judas has betrayed him with a kiss, as foretold. Peter has denied him three times before the rooster, exactly as foretold; Luke has just told us so (vv. 34, 61). And the Son of Man is being numbered with the transgressors, as he said from Isaiah at the table. He is a true prophet. They blindfold the only man in the room who can see anything, and then ask him to prove he can see. Isaiah had heard the Servant say it: I gave my back to those who strike (Isaiah 50:6).

And they said many other things against him, blaspheming him. The word is blasphēmountes. They will condemn him for blasphemy (v. 71), but they are the blasphemers, insulting the Son of God.

He does not answer. That is the thing to hold. He could have named every man in that room, their fathers, their homes and the day of their deaths. He says nothing. He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth (Isaiah 53:7). Consider what is being held back. Not merely a retort but legions of angels (Matthew 26:53). The power that made the hands striking his face was under perfect control, restrained by nothing but his own settled will to be struck.

Why did Jesus not defend himself? Because he had come to suffer, not to win the argument. His silence was not weakness but chosen obedience: he was the Lamb led to the slaughter, bearing in his body the punishment our sins deserved. Had he spoken, he could have silenced them; had he struck back, he could have destroyed them; but then there would have been no sacrifice and no salvation. Peter, who watched it, later wrote that he answered insult with no insult and suffering with no threat, but handed himself over to the One who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23).

How should I respond when I am mocked for my faith? With the same trust, though not always the same silence. Jesus did speak when the truth required it (v. 69), and we too should be ready to give a reason for our hope, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). But we need not answer every taunt, defend our dignity, or repay insult with insult. Leave your reputation with God. Count it an honour to share a little in his reproach (Acts 5:41), and pray for those who mock you, as he did for those who crucified him (23:34).

In a sentence. The guards mocked and beat Jesus, blindfolded him and taunted him to prophesy who hit him, and insulted him in many other ways.

On a Tuesday. Notice this week the small, casual cruelties of a group: the joke at the expense of the person who cannot answer back, the colleague everyone mocks behind his back. Do not join in. And if you are the one being laughed at, bring it to the one who was blindfolded and struck, and let him carry it.

For worship. In Isaiah the Servant who gave his back to the smiters also said that he had set his face like a flint, knowing he would not be put to shame (Isaiah 50:6–7). Luke had told us long before that Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51), and here, under a blindfold and a rain of blows, that face is still set. They covered it and struck it, and it did not turn from them. One day it will shine like the sun before every knee, and even behind the blindfold it was turned towards their salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: When day came, the assembly of the elders of the people gathered together, both chief priests and scribes. And they led him away to their council, and they said, 'If you are the Christ, tell us.' But he said to them, 'If I tell you, you will not believe, and if I ask you, you will not answer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When day came, the assembly of the elders of the people gathered together, both chief priests and scribes. And they led him away to their council, and they said: if you are the Christ, tell us. But he said to them: if I tell you, you will not believe, and if I ask you, you will not answer.

When day came. The daylight session was not an accident of scheduling; it was a repair. Jewish legal tradition held that capital cases should not be tried at night. A night hearing had no legal standing, so at first light the council met formally to give the outcome a lawful appearance and confirm the verdict. This is a formal body following a procedure arranged around a verdict decided days before (v. 2). The most respectable machinery in Israel is being operated correctly in order to kill the Son of God.

The assembly of the elders of the people, both chief priests and scribes. The Sanhedrin, Israel’s supreme council, under the high priest.

If you are the Christ, tell us. The direct question. It sounds like an inquiry and it is not one. Luke records no charge read and no evidence presented; Matthew and Mark tell how the false witnesses failed to agree. The council does not want information. It wants a sentence it can take to Pilate.

If I tell you, you will not believe. Two clauses, entirely without bitterness and quite unanswerable. This is not a guess; it is a description of a settled state. They had already decided (20:1–8). They had seen the blind receive sight and the lame walk, and when Lazarus came out of a tomb their response was to plan another death (John 11:53). A further sentence from him was not going to move anything.

And if I ask you, you will not answer. A direct reference to what had already happened. Earlier that week in the temple he had asked them whether the baptism of John was from heaven or from man, and they had refused to answer (20:7). So he declines to perform. He will not supply an answer to men who have shown that answers make no difference to them. But he does not stay silent, and what he says next is not a defence. It is a claim so large that the council will need nothing else.

Was the trial of Jesus illegal? By the standards of the later Jewish law code it broke several rules: a night hearing, a hurried verdict, no defence, the judges as accusers. We cannot be sure every rule was in force then, but the Gospels plainly show a trial whose verdict was settled before it began. The deeper point is that the court was right about the law and wrong about the man. God allowed injustice to condemn the just so that the unjust could be justified (1 Peter 3:18).

What if someone I love keeps asking but never believes? Keep answering with patience, but recognise what Jesus saw: some questions are not requests for truth but defences against it. You cannot argue anyone into the kingdom; only God opens hearts (Acts 16:14). So pray for them more than you debate them, live the gospel in front of them, and give them the plain claims of Christ, as he did here. Then leave them with God. He changed the heart of one member of that very council (23:50–51), and of a young Pharisee named Saul.

In a sentence. At dawn the council met and demanded that Jesus tell them if he was the Christ, and he said they would not believe him if he did.

On a Tuesday. If you have already decided against Jesus, no evidence will convince you; open your heart. And examine yourself here too: is there something Jesus says that you keep treating as a debate to be prolonged rather than a matter to be settled? A command you keep questioning so that you do not have to obey it? Settle it with him today.

For worship. The council sat in judgment on the Judge of all the earth, and he let them. He who answered every honest seeker in Galilee would not argue with men who had already decided, and then spoke the truth that cost his life. That is the patience of God in the dock. He stood an unjust trial so that, on the last day, all who trust him will stand in his court with nothing left to answer, because every charge against them was heard and settled in that room, against him.
verseByVerse.note: A night hearing had no legal standing; the council met formally at daybreak.

verseByVerse.quote: But from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God.

But from now on. He has just told them that answering their question is pointless. Then he answers it, and gives them far more than they asked. From now on: from this very moment, through his death, resurrection and ascension. Not after some distant vindication, but from this room, with his hands tied and his face bruised and a death sentence being drafted.

The Son of Man. The title comes from Daniel’s vision of one like a son of man, brought on the clouds before the Ancient of Days and given an everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:13–14). Jesus has used it all through Luke’s Gospel; here, before the highest court in Israel, he speaks it with the whole vision in view.

Shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God. Psalm 110:1, the LORD says to my Lord, sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool, the psalm he had used to silence the scribes that same week (20:41–44). Two Scriptures are folded into one sentence, and every man in that room would have heard both. Put together, they make a claim no mere Messiah could make. Israel expected a deliverer. Israel did not expect a man to sit down on God’s own throne. Jesus claims the place of supreme authority beside God, sharing his throne. The prisoner before them is the judge of all.

Seated, because the work is finished. The right hand is not about geography. It is the position of the one who exercises the king’s authority, and to be seated there is to have the business settled. Under the old covenant the priests stood daily, offering sacrifices that could never take away sins; there were no chairs in the tabernacle, because the work was never finished. Hebrews draws the contrast: the priests stand, but Christ, having offered one sacrifice for sins for all time, sat down at God’s right hand (Hebrews 10:11–12). Luke omits the coming on the clouds that Mark records (Mark 14:62) and emphasises the present enthronement, which begins at the ascension (Acts 2:33–36; 7:55–56).

What is Jesus doing at the right hand now? Reigning and interceding. He rules all things for the good of his church (Ephesians 1:20–22), and he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25). His reign is not postponed to a future age; it is happening now, from heaven, as the gospel goes to the nations and the Spirit gathers his people. And he prays for those who are his (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25). One day he will come again visibly, in glory, to judge the living and the dead and make all things new. Until then the throne is occupied, and nothing in your life is outside his rule.

In a sentence. Jesus declared that from now on the Son of Man would be seated at the right hand of God’s power.

On a Tuesday. When the world feels out of control, in politics, illness or your own circumstances, say Psalm 110:1 to yourself and remember who is seated. Then do your duty today as a subject of that King: honestly, bravely, without anxiety, because the throne is not empty.

For worship. They thought they were trying him; he told them the throne was already his. The bound man from Galilee is the one Daniel saw, whose dominion is everlasting, and the road to his seat ran through Golgotha, and he walked it on purpose. He said it to men who would kill him for saying it, it was true when he said it, and he has not left that throne since. Every court that has sat in judgment on him since has sat beneath his feet.

verseByVerse.quote: So they all said, 'Are you the Son of God, then?' And he said to them, 'You say that I am.' Then they said, 'What further testimony do we need? We have heard it ourselves from his own lips.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they all said: are you the Son of God, then? And he said to them: you say that I am. Then they said: what further testimony do we need? We have heard it ourselves from his own lips.

Are you the Son of God, then? They heard it. That is the first thing to note, and it disposes of a modern idea that will not survive this paragraph: that Jesus never claimed to be divine and the church invented it later. His enemies, sitting in front of him, in his own language, drew exactly that conclusion from what he had just said, and put it to him as a question. The then does real work: so it follows that. They have understood v. 69 correctly. A man who takes the seat at God’s right hand is claiming a relation to God that no creature has. The one seated at God’s right hand must be God’s Son.

You say that I am. English readers sometimes hear evasion in that, and it is not. It is a recognised way of saying yes: those are your words, and they are correct (Matthew 26:64). The council’s own reaction settles it: if the answer had been a dodge, they could not have said, we have heard it ourselves from his own lips. They took it as a yes because it was one. There may be more in it. The final words are egō eimi, I am, the words that echo God’s own name given to Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:14), and the words Jesus had used before in a way that made men pick up stones (John 8:58).

What further testimony do we need? The trial ends without proof of any crime, because there was never one. In Luke no witness is called; in Matthew and Mark the false witnesses fail to agree. No act is established. They have their charge: blasphemy.

We have heard it ourselves from his own lips. The only evidence the court ever had was his own confession. That is the deepest irony in Luke’s passion narrative, and he lets it stand without comment. The charge is blasphemy, a creature claiming the honour of God. The charge would be entirely just, and the sentence entirely correct, if the man in the dock were anyone else. They convicted him on exactly the right law. They got only one thing wrong, and it was the identity of the defendant. Either he was a blasphemer, or he is the Son of God. There is no third option.

Does Son of God mean only that Jesus was a very godly man? No. Israel’s kings could be called God’s sons, and believers are sons by adoption, but that is not what the council heard or what Jesus meant. He claimed to sit at God’s right hand and to be the Son in a unique sense: the eternal Son, one with the Father (John 10:30), who shares the Father’s nature and glory, became man without ceasing to be God. That is why they called it blasphemy. A merely good man claiming that would not be good.

Who was responsible for Jesus’ death? A small group of leaders handed him over, and Rome executed him; Jew and Gentile together, as the church confessed (Acts 4:27–28). Behind them all stood God’s plan, and the sins of everyone he came to save. It gives no ground for blaming the Jewish people as a whole, and Peter, preaching to Jerusalem, said they had acted in ignorance (Acts 3:17).

In a sentence. When they asked whether he was the Son of God, Jesus said that they said he was, and they declared they needed no more testimony, having heard it from his own lips.

On a Tuesday. Decide what you will say when someone tells you that Jesus never claimed to be God: point them here, to his enemies, who understood him perfectly and killed him for it. And ask yourself the question the council asked: are you the Son of God? If your answer is yes, then confess him today, by word and deed, wherever it costs you a little.

For worship. The innocent was condemned by the guilty on his own true testimony, so that the guilty might be acquitted on his. He could have said less and lived. He told them the truth about himself, knowing what it would cost, because the truth about himself was the reason he had come. Before the council of his own people he said, I am, and they called it blasphemy. On the last day every tongue will confess what he said that morning, and the court that condemned him will hear its verdict reversed by the Judge it condemned.

22.text: <sup>1</sup> Now the Feast of Unleavened Bread drew near, which is called the Passover. <sup>2</sup> And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to put him to death, for they feared the people. <sup>3</sup> Then Satan entered into Judas called Iscariot, who was of the number of the twelve. <sup>4</sup> He went away and conferred with the chief priests and officers how he might betray him to them. <sup>5</sup> And they were glad, and agreed to give him money. <sup>6</sup> So he consented and sought an opportunity to betray him to them in the absence of a crowd. <sup>7</sup> Then came the day of Unleavened Bread, on which the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed. <sup>8</sup> So Jesus sent Peter and John, saying, “Go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat it.” <sup>9</sup> They said to him, “Where will you have us prepare it?” <sup>10</sup> He said to them, “Behold, when you have entered the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house that he enters <sup>11</sup> and tell the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says to you, Where is the guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ <sup>12</sup> And he will show you a large upper room furnished; prepare it there.” <sup>13</sup> And they went and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover. <sup>14</sup> And when the hour came, he reclined at table, and the apostles with him. <sup>15</sup> And he said to them, “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. <sup>16</sup> For I tell you I will not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.” <sup>17</sup> And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he said, “Take this, and divide it among yourselves. <sup>18</sup> For I tell you that from now on I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.” <sup>19</sup> And he took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” <sup>20</sup> And likewise the cup after they had eaten, saying, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood. <sup>21</sup> But behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me on the table. <sup>22</sup> For the Son of Man goes as it has been determined, but woe to that man by whom he is betrayed!” <sup>23</sup> And they began to question one another, which of them it could be who was going to do this. <sup>24</sup> A dispute also arose among them, as to which of them was to be regarded as the greatest. <sup>25</sup> And he said to them, “The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them, and those in authority over them are called benefactors. <sup>26</sup> But not so with you. Rather, let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves. <sup>27</sup> For who is the greater, one who reclines at table or one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines at table? But I am among you as the one who serves. <sup>28</sup> “You are those who have stayed with me in my trials, <sup>29</sup> and I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom, <sup>30</sup> that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel. <sup>31</sup> “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, <sup>32</sup> but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.” <sup>33</sup> Peter said to him, “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death.” <sup>34</sup> Jesus said, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow this day, until you deny three times that you know me.” <sup>35</sup> And he said to them, “When I sent you out with no moneybag or knapsack or sandals, did you lack anything?” They said, “Nothing.” <sup>36</sup> He said to them, “But now let the one who has a moneybag take it, and likewise a knapsack. And let the one who has no sword sell his cloak and buy one. <sup>37</sup> For I tell you that this Scripture must be fulfilled in me: ‘And he was numbered with the transgressors.’ For what is written about me has its fulfillment.” <sup>38</sup> And they said, “Look, Lord, here are two swords.” And he said to them, “It is enough.” <sup>39</sup> And he came out and went, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples followed him. <sup>40</sup> And when he came to the place, he said to them, “Pray that you may not enter into temptation.” <sup>41</sup> And he withdrew from them about a stone's throw, and knelt down and prayed, <sup>42</sup> saying, “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” <sup>43</sup> And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. <sup>44</sup> And being in agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground. <sup>45</sup> And when he rose from prayer, he came to the disciples and found them sleeping for sorrow, <sup>46</sup> and he said to them, “Why are you sleeping? Rise and pray that you may not enter into temptation.” <sup>47</sup> While he was still speaking, there came a crowd, and the man called Judas, one of the twelve, was leading them. He drew near to Jesus to kiss him, <sup>48</sup> but Jesus said to him, “Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” <sup>49</sup> And when those who were around him saw what would follow, they said, “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?” <sup>50</sup> And one of them struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear. <sup>51</sup> But Jesus said, “No more of this!” And he touched his ear and healed him. <sup>52</sup> Then Jesus said to the chief priests and officers of the temple and elders, who had come out against him, “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs? <sup>53</sup> When I was with you day after day in the temple, you did not lay hands on me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.” <sup>54</sup> Then they seized him and led him away, bringing him into the high priest's house, and Peter was following at a distance. <sup>55</sup> And when they had kindled a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat down among them. <sup>56</sup> Then a servant girl, seeing him as he sat in the light and looking closely at him, said, “This man also was with him.” <sup>57</sup> But he denied it, saying, “Woman, I do not know him.” <sup>58</sup> And a little later someone else saw him and said, “You also are one of them.” But Peter said, “Man, I am not.” <sup>59</sup> And after an interval of about an hour still another insisted, saying, “Certainly this man also was with him, for he too is a Galilean.” <sup>60</sup> But Peter said, “Man, I do not know what you are talking about.” And immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed. <sup>61</sup> And the Lord turned and looked at Peter. And Peter remembered the saying of the Lord, how he had said to him, “Before the rooster crows today, you will deny me three times.” <sup>62</sup> And he went out and wept bitterly. <sup>63</sup> Now the men who were holding Jesus in custody were mocking him as they beat him. <sup>64</sup> They also blindfolded him and kept asking him, “Prophesy! Who is it that struck you?” <sup>65</sup> And they said many other things against him, blaspheming him. <sup>66</sup> When day came, the assembly of the elders of the people gathered together, both chief priests and scribes. And they led him away to their council, and they said, <sup>67</sup> “If you are the Christ, tell us.” But he said to them, “If I tell you, you will not believe, <sup>68</sup> and if I ask you, you will not answer. <sup>69</sup> But from now on the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God.” <sup>70</sup> So they all said, “Are you the Son of God, then?” And he said to them, “You say that I am.” <sup>71</sup> Then they said, “What further testimony do we need? We have heard it ourselves from his own lips.”

23.title: The Trial, the Cross, and the Tomb
23.overview:
Luke 23 is the passion narrative — the most carefully and deliberately structured chapter in the Gospel, in which every detail carries theological weight. Jesus is tried before Pilate, sent to Herod, returned to Pilate, condemned, led to Golgotha, crucified between two criminals, and buried in a borrowed tomb. Through it all, Luke maintains a single consistent emphasis: Jesus is innocent. Pilate declares it three times (vv. 4, 14, 22). Herod finds no crime worthy of death (v. 15). The criminal on the cross confesses it (v. 41). The centurion declares it at his death (v. 47). This is the innocent One dying for the guilty.

Luke's crucifixion account is distinctive in several ways. He records Jesus's prayer for his killers: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (v. 34). He preserves the remarkable conversion of the dying criminal — the most compressed account of salvation in the Gospels: a man with minutes to live, who can offer nothing but a confession and a request, receives from Jesus the promise of paradise this very day. And he records the moment of Jesus's death as a prayer of trust: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit” — drawn from Psalm 31:5, later used in Jewish tradition as a prayer before sleep, now spoken by the Son into the Father's hands in the sleep of death.

The chapter ends in mourning and waiting. The women from Galilee follow and see the tomb; they return and prepare spices and ointments; they rest on the Sabbath. The darkness before the dawn of resurrection is total — and in the silence, everything depends on whether the one who said “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit” was speaking to Someone who was listening.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Trial before Pilate and Herod
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The Sanhedrin cannot execute — only Rome can — so the charge has to change. In their own chamber they convicted him of blasphemy; before Pilate they produce three fresh charges built for a Roman ear: subversion, tax revolt, and a claim to a throne. The middle one is a flat lie, and they knew it when they said it: they had asked him that very question in the temple and heard him answer render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's (20:25). The third is not a lie at all, and it is the one that will kill him.

Pilate goes straight to the only charge that concerns him, hears a qualified affirmation, and reaches the correct verdict at once: I find no guilt in this man. He was not a soft man — Judea had already made him notorious for handling unrest badly — and he had crucified rebels before. He looks at this one and says there is nothing here.

The accusers press, mentioning Galilee as an aggravating detail, and Pilate hears in it an escape route: Galilee is Herod's jurisdiction. It is not a legal necessity; it is a door. Herod is delighted, because he has wanted to see Jesus for a long time (9:9) and is hoping for a sign. He questions him at length and gets nothing — the one occasion in Luke on which Jesus is asked a direct question by a ruler and answers not a word. Herod counts him as nothing, has him arrayed in a bright robe as a joke, and sends him back. And two enemies become friends over him that day, which is the world's unity at its truest: a peace built on a shared contempt.

Pilate then convenes a public assembly and states his finding for the record — not guilty of any charge, and neither did Herod find anything — and follows it, in the same breath, with I will therefore punish and release him. Flogging an innocent man as a concession is the hinge of the chapter, and it fails, as such compromises do.

The crowd asks for Barabbas: an insurrectionist and a murderer, guilty of precisely what Jesus was falsely accused of. Three times Pilate declares the innocence; three times the shouting overrules him. And their voices prevailed. He releases the guilty man and delivers Jesus over to their will.
verseByVerse.theology:
Luke's repeated declarations of innocence are the theological spine of the chapter: Pilate three times (vv. 4, 14, 22), Herod by implication (v. 15), the dying criminal (v. 41), the centurion (v. 47). This is not a deserved death, and the innocence is not a tragic detail — it is the point, because a guilty man dying settles nothing for anybody. Only an innocent one has a life to spare.

The Barabbas exchange is the atonement enacted in the street before it is accomplished on the hill. He is not pardoned and not reviewed; nothing about him changes. He is guilty when he goes into the cell and guilty when he walks out, and he goes free because another man dies in his place that day. He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us (2 Cor. 5:21).

Verses 23–25 must hold two truths at once. These men are entirely guilty — Peter says so to their faces at Pentecost. And behind the crowd stands the settled purpose of God, who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Rom. 8:32) — and Paul can say of the Father's act what Luke says of Pilate's: he was delivered up for our trespasses (Rom. 4:25). Pilate surrendered him to pressure; the Father gave him in love. The same handing over, and the difference is everything.
verseByVerse.examples:
Pilate's sin is not brutality but procedure. He never once says he believes Jesus guilty; he simply never gets round to acting on the fact that he is not. Every institution has that move and most of us have used it — refer it upward, wait for the review, ask for another opinion. The test is simple: is the referral a way of finding the right answer, or a way of not having to act on the answer you already have? Responsibility does not transfer. The man who tried hardest not to be involved has had his name said in the creed every Sunday for eighteen centuries.

Verse 5 is the oldest complaint made against Christ and his people, and it alleges no crime — only disturbance. Honesty requires admitting that some of the trouble Christians attract is their own manner and not the gospel, and it is worth asking which before claiming this verse. But when the charge is that a man taught the truth and people were changed, the disturbance is real and the complaint is a compliment.

Herod is the frightening figure here, and not for the reason people assume. He had already had his word from God in John the Baptist and had killed him; what he wanted now was a trick. But the believer who fears that God has gone silent on him is answered by the shape of the case: Herod was not troubled about it. He was very glad. Anxiety about God's silence is itself evidence that he has not gone.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the whole company of them arose and brought him before Pilate. And they began to accuse him, saying, 'We found this man misleading our nation and forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole company of them arose and brought him before Pilate. And they began to accuse him, saying: we found this man misleading our nation and forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.

Meaning first. Luke 23 is the day of the cross. Jesus is declared innocent again and again by Pilate and Herod, yet handed over to be crucified while Barabbas, a rebel and murderer, walks free (vv. 1–25). On the way he warns the weeping women of judgment coming on Jerusalem; on the cross he prays for his killers, is mocked as a king who cannot save himself, and promises a dying thief paradise today (vv. 26–43). Darkness falls at noon, the temple curtain is torn, and Jesus commits his spirit to his Father and dies; a centurion praises God, and a councillor buries him while the women watch (vv. 44–56). Luke’s great theme is the innocence of the one who died: the righteous for the unrighteous, the King enthroned on a cross, opening paradise to the guilty.

The setting. The council has condemned Jesus at dawn for claiming to be the Son of God (22:70–71). But under Roman rule it could not carry out a death sentence (John 18:31), so the whole case must now be taken to the governor, and made to sound like something a governor would care about.

The whole company of them. The Sanhedrin, the council of seventy, arose together: a formal delegation of the highest religious body in Israel, marching a bound prisoner across the city to a Gentile. And the charge has to change, because the one they convicted him on is useless here. In their own chamber the charge was blasphemy. A Roman governor would have thrown that out before lunch; provincial religion was not his business.

Three charges. So they make three fresh charges, each designed for a Roman ear: sedition, tax refusal and treason. Misleading our nation means stirring up rebellion, the word a governor most feared to hear at a festival.

And forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar. A flat lie, and they knew it when they said it. It was they who had come to him in the temple with that exact question, hoping to trap him, and he had answered: render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s (20:25).
