They had been standing there, and Luke recorded it three chapters ago. And notice what the lie is made of. It is not invention out of nothing; it is his own words turned upside down. He had said pay it; they report that he forbade it. That is how false witness usually works: not fabrication, which is easy to disprove, but a true thing rotated until it points the other way.

And saying that he himself is Christ, a king. They translate Messiah into king, a rival to Caesar. This third charge is the interesting one, because it is not false. He is the Christ. He is a king. He had told them so a few hours earlier, and it was the reason they wanted him dead. Half true, deliberately twisted: Jesus is a king, but not the kind Pilate feared. They accuse him of it in the confidence that Pilate will hear the word king and stop listening. So the Son of God is brought before the empire on two lies and a truth, and the truth is the one that will kill him.

Is it wrong to defend myself when I am falsely accused? No. Paul defended himself before councils and governors (Acts 24–26), and calmly correcting a lie is often right, especially when others will be harmed by it. Jesus was silent at points in his trial because his hour had come and he had chosen to suffer, not because silence is always the godly answer. The question is your spirit. Speak the truth plainly and without bitterness, refuse to answer lies with lies, and then entrust your name to God, who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). You do not have to win to be vindicated.

In a sentence. The council brought Jesus to Pilate and accused him of subverting the nation, forbidding taxes to Caesar, and claiming to be the Messiah, a king.

On a Tuesday. Jesus was falsely accused, and bore it. If someone is twisting your words this week, at work, at church, online, resist the urge to twist theirs back. Say what is true once, clearly. Then pray for the person, and leave the outcome with God.

For worship. They came for a man they could not execute and found a wording that would do it for them, and every word was chosen by men who knew better. Malicious witnesses rise up; they ask me of things that I do not know (Psalm 35:11). And the one they slandered stood still and let them, because the charge sheet that really mattered was not theirs but ours, and he had come to have it nailed to the cross (Colossians 2:14). Blessed be the King who was accused of being a king, and was.
verseByVerse.note: The charges are framed for a Roman governor: sedition, tax refusal, and a rival king. The tax charge was false.

verseByVerse.quote: And Pilate asked him, 'Are you the King of the Jews?' And he answered him, 'You have said so.' Then Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, 'I find no guilt in this man.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate asked him: are you the King of the Jews? And he answered him: you have said so. Then Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds: I find no guilt in this man.

Pilate. Pontius Pilate governed Judea from about AD 26 to 36, known for brutality and contempt for the Jews (13:1). He had provoked a crisis by bringing imperial standards into Jerusalem, and put down a protest over an aqueduct with clubs. He knew what a rebel looked like; he had crucified some.

Are you the King of the Jews? Pilate goes straight to the only charge that concerns him. Sedition and tax revolt are secondary; a claimant to a throne inside a Roman province is a matter for the governor personally. Notice the phrasing. No Israelite said the Jews when speaking of his own nation; it is an outsider’s term. Pilate is asking a political question in political language, and he means: are you a pretender to a throne?

You have said so. The same idiom he used before the council: an affirmation, not a dodge. But it is a guarded yes, true but not in the sense you mean, and the qualification is the whole difference between the truth and what Pilate has in mind. John fills in what Luke compresses: my kingdom is not of this world; if it were, my servants would have been fighting (John 18:33–38). It is a yes with the sword taken out of it.

I find no guilt in this man. And Pilate believes him, which is the striking thing. He looks at this man and says there is nothing here. That verdict is the first of three from Pilate in this chapter, and Luke means you to count them as he builds his case. Pilate says it here (v. 4). He says it again in public after Herod (v. 14). He says it a third time under pressure (v. 22). Herod finds nothing (v. 15). A dying criminal says it (v. 41). A Roman officer says it (v. 47). Six declarations of innocence, and the execution proceeds. And Luke’s readers in the Roman world would learn something else: that the founder of Christianity was no political threat, and his followers need not be treated as one.

If Jesus was innocent, why did God let him die? Because only an innocent man could die for the guilty. Nothing about the cross is a miscarriage that God later put right. The innocence is not a tragic detail; it is the point. A guilty man dying would settle nothing for anybody, because he would only be paying for himself. Christ, who had no sin of his own, bore the penalty of ours in our place: he died not for his own crimes, but for the sins of others, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Peter 3:18). God did not merely permit it; he willed it, out of love (Isaiah 53:10; John 3:16).

In a sentence. Pilate asked Jesus if he was King of the Jews, Jesus said that he had said so, and Pilate declared he found no guilt in him.

On a Tuesday. Read the six verdicts of innocence in this chapter (vv. 4, 14, 15, 22, 41, 47) and then say to yourself, aloud, the verdict God has given you in Christ: no condemnation (Romans 8:1). The innocent one was condemned so that you, who are guilty, could be declared righteous. Live today as someone acquitted.

For worship. I find no guilt in this man: a pagan governor said it of Jesus, and on the last day the holy God will say it of everyone who is in him. Pilate’s verdict was simply true. He was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15), and he carried that spotless innocence to the cross and laid it down under the sentence that belonged to us. Now he clothes the guilty in his own righteousness, so that the Judge of all the earth, looking at those who trust his Son, finds nothing to condemn. Glory to the Lamb whose acquittal has become ours.
verseByVerse.note: Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36.

verseByVerse.quote: But they were urgent, saying, 'He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, from Galilee even to this place.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they were urgent, saying: he stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, from Galilee even to this place.

But they were urgent. The verdict was not what they came for, so they change tactics. Urgent means insistent, pressing hard, refusing to accept the verdict. The ESV uses the same English again at v. 23, when the pressing turns into shouting.

He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, from Galilee even to this place. Judea here means the whole Jewish land (4:44). From Galilee to Jerusalem: the whole course of his ministry. Calling him a rabble-rouser, they unwittingly summarise Luke’s Gospel. But notice the geography. That is not a description of a teaching itinerary; it is a threat assessment. Galilee was the province that produced insurgents. The revolt of Judas the Galilean was still remembered in Jerusalem; a member of this very council would name him in a speech a few years later (Acts 5:37). To tell a Roman governor that a Galilean has been stirring people up all the way to the capital is to say the word rebellion without having to prove it. And the mention of Galilee gives Pilate an idea.

One word that is not a lie. Teaching. That is exactly what he had been doing, every day of that week, in the temple, in the open, in front of them. So here is the accusation stripped down: he has been teaching, in public, and people have listened. They cannot produce an act. They can only produce an effect. It is the oldest complaint made against Christ and his people. Nobody has to allege a crime. It is enough to allege disturbance: that the message is divisive, that it upsets people, that things were calmer before (Acts 17:6).

How do I know whether the offence is the gospel’s or mine? Sometimes the charge of stirring up trouble is fair, and honesty requires saying so. Christians can be needlessly abrasive, and a good deal of the trouble some believers attract has nothing to do with Christ and everything to do with the manner of the man carrying his name. So ask: Am I being offensive in tone, timing or pride? Have I spoken the truth with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15)? Am I more eager to win than to love? If you can honestly say that the only thing that offended was the truth about Christ, spoken kindly, then the disturbance is real and the complaint is a compliment.

In a sentence. They insisted that he was stirring up the people with his teaching throughout the land, from Galilee to Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. Faithful teaching will sometimes be called stirring up trouble. Before you claim this verse, check your manner. This week, if you speak about Christ to someone who disagrees, make sure the only stumbling block is the cross, not you.

For worship. He stirred up the people, and he did it by telling them the truth, and it is still the only thing he has ever been guilty of. I came to cast fire on the earth (12:49), he had said. The rulers were right about the effect and wrong about everything else: Judea was not the same, and neither is the world. Blessed be the Teacher whose words turn hearts upside down, and whose truth no council could silence.

verseByVerse.quote: When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was a Galilean. And when he learned that he belonged to Herod's jurisdiction, he sent him over to Herod, who was himself in Jerusalem at that time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was a Galilean. And when he learned that he belonged to Herod’s jurisdiction, he sent him over to Herod, who was himself in Jerusalem at that time.

When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was a Galilean. Only Luke records the trial before Herod. He may have learned of it from Joanna, wife of Herod’s steward (8:3), or from Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod (Acts 13:1). The accusers meant Galilee as an aggravating detail. Pilate hears it as an escape route, a way out of a difficult case.

He belonged to Herod’s jurisdiction. Galilee was the territory of Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, a client ruler under Rome, and he was in Jerusalem for the Passover. So there is a defensible administrative argument: the accused is another ruler’s problem. It is not a legal necessity. The offence, if there were one, was alleged to have happened in Judea, and Pilate had every authority to try it. He is not applying a rule. He is looking for a door.

He sent him over to Herod. Pilate tries to pass the problem to someone else, and perhaps pays a diplomatic courtesy at the same time. What makes this so recognisable is that the door is entirely procedural. He does not release Jesus, which his own verdict required. He does not condemn him, which the evidence would not support. He transfers the file. That is the characteristic sin of this chapter, and it is not brutality. It is the sin of a man who knows exactly what is right, does not want to pay for it, and finds a mechanism that postpones the decision. Pilate never says, I believe this man is guilty. He simply never gets round to acting on the fact that he is not.

The one who took what was not his. Set Pilate beside the prisoner he is passing on. Pilate holds a responsibility that is truly his, and spends the morning trying to put it down. Jesus stands before him carrying a burden that was never his, the guilt of his people, and he will not put it down for a moment. Pilate looks for a door; Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem (9:51) and will not take one. Pilate wants the decision to belong to someone else; Jesus had already said in the garden, not my will, but yours, be done (22:42). The whole trial is a man refusing what is his, before the Man who has taken on himself what is ours.

Responsibility does not transfer. Pilate tried to get the case off his desk, and the church has said his name in the creed for centuries: suffered under Pontius Pilate. The man who tried hardest not to be involved is the one whose name is fixed to it for ever. Whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin (James 4:17).

Can I avoid making a decision about Jesus? No. You can postpone it, refer it, wait for more information or hand it to someone else, but not deciding is a decision. Pilate tried every route around the question and was left holding it. Every person must answer for himself who Jesus is and what he will do with him; a parent’s faith, a spouse’s faith or a church’s faith cannot answer for you. If you have been putting it off, ask the question honestly today, read one of the Gospels through, and ask God to show you the truth.

In a sentence. Learning Jesus was a Galilean, under Herod’s jurisdiction, Pilate sent him to Herod, who was in Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. Every institution has this move, and every one of us has used it: refer it upward, wait for the review, ask for another opinion. It is sometimes genuine diligence. The test is simple, and worth applying honestly to one thing on your desk this week: is the referral a way of finding the right answer, or a way of not having to act on the answer you already have?

For worship. He sent the case away and kept the guilt. And the prisoner he passed from hand to hand walked between the palaces in silence, the Lord of all being treated as an administrative inconvenience. He who will judge the living and the dead let himself be shuffled between judges, so that on the last day those who trust him will not be passed between courts but welcomed home. You cannot pass Jesus off to someone else, and blessed be God, he does not pass his people off either.
verseByVerse.note: Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and was in Jerusalem for Passover. Only Luke records this hearing.

verseByVerse.quote: When Herod saw Jesus, he was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him. So he questioned him at some length, but he made no answer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Herod saw Jesus, he was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him. So he questioned him at some length, but he made no answer.

He was very glad. Herod Antipas is delighted, not by Jesus but by the prospect of entertainment, and Luke has prepared this moment for a long time. This is the man who had John the Baptist arrested, kept him in prison, liked listening to him (Mark 6:20), and then had him beheaded to save face at a birthday feast.

For he had long desired to see him. Since 9:9, when reports of Jesus reached him and he was perplexed: John I beheaded, but who is this about whom I hear such things? And he sought to see him. He got his wish on the last morning of Jesus’ life.

He was hoping to see some sign done by him. There is the whole man in one clause. He does not want teaching, and he certainly does not want repentance; he has had that offered and killed the man who offered it. He wants a display: a miracle, a trick, a performance. Curiosity, not faith. Jesus has been reduced, in the mind of a king, to an entertainment that has finally been booked.

So he questioned him at some length, but he made no answer. Not one word. Herod is the only person in the Gospels to whom Jesus says nothing at all, and this from the Christ who answered scribes, Pharisees, Sadducees, lawyers, a Samaritan woman, a Roman centurion and a thief. The silence is not sulking and it is not fear. It is the answer. Herod had already had his word from God, in the greatest prophet born of woman, and had put him in a cell and then in a grave. Herod had silenced the voice of God in John; now God is silent to him. There was nothing further to be said, and the mercy of God does not perform on request. Like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth (Isaiah 53:7). Jesus will not perform for the curious.

Does God ever stop speaking to a man? He does, and Scripture says so more than once (Proverbs 1:24–28; Romans 1:24). But the fear a sensitive believer carries, that this has happened to him, is answered by the very shape of the case. Herod was not anxious about it. He was very glad. A man who is troubled that God may have gone quiet has, in that trouble, the evidence that he has not. If you are worried that you have hardened your heart beyond hope, the worry itself is the Spirit still at work. Come to Christ now; he has never turned away anyone who comes (John 6:37).

Is it wrong to want to see a miracle? Not in itself; God did signs to help people believe (John 20:30–31), and we may ask him to act in power. What is wrong is Herod’s spirit: wanting a show while refusing the message, demanding proof on our terms while ignoring the evidence already given. Jesus called it an evil generation that seeks a sign (11:29). If God has given you his Word, the testimony of the apostles and the empty tomb, you have been given the greatest sign of all, and the right response is not to ask for another but to repent and believe.

In a sentence. Herod was delighted to see Jesus, hoping to see a miracle, and questioned him at length, but Jesus said nothing.

On a Tuesday. If you come to Jesus only for entertainment or curiosity, he may be silent. Come in faith. Look at how you approach him this week: in your Bible reading, in church, in prayer. Are you hoping to be impressed, or ready to obey? Come to listen, not to audit.

For worship. The Word through whom the worlds were made stood before a king and said nothing, and even his silence was holy. He would not perform for the man who had silenced John, yet he walked out of that hall to die for scoffers and killers, and a man brought up with this very Herod would one day be among the prophets and teachers of the church at Antioch (Acts 13:1). He was silent before Herod so that he might speak for us before the Father, for he always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). His silence to the proud is never his last word to the humble.

verseByVerse.quote: The chief priests and the scribes stood by, vehemently accusing him. And Herod with his soldiers treated him with contempt and mocked him. Then, arraying him in splendid clothing, he sent him back to Pilate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests and the scribes stood by, vehemently accusing him. And Herod with his soldiers treated him with contempt and mocked him. Then, arraying him in splendid clothing, he sent him back to Pilate.

Vehemently accusing him. The chief priests have followed him across the city. They are not going to let the case out of their sight. Vehemently suggests strain: men raising their voices, pressing, working at it fiercely and relentlessly. They have to work at it, because the accused is not helping. There is nothing to answer, so the volume has to do what the evidence cannot.

And Herod with his soldiers treated him with contempt and mocked him. Disappointed, Herod turned to mockery, and it is worse than a verdict. He does not condemn Jesus; he finds him ridiculous. The Greek is exouthenēsas, to count as nothing, to reckon at zero. It is not hatred, which at least concedes that its object matters. It is the judgment of a bored man who was promised a miracle-worker, received a silence, and decided the whole thing was beneath him. He was despised and rejected by men (Isaiah 53:3).

Arraying him in splendid clothing. Bright, shining, gorgeous: a royal robe thrown over a prisoner as a joke, because he had been accused of claiming a throne. This is the first of the mockeries, and every one that follows has the same shape. The soldiers will offer him sour wine and call him king (v. 37). Pilate will nail a title over his head (v. 38). Matthew records a crown of thorns and a reed for a sceptre. In every case the mockery consists of treating him as what he actually is.

He sent him back to Pilate. Herod found no grounds to condemn him either (v. 15). And Jesus walked back across Jerusalem in the mocking robe, without taking it off or saying a word.

How should I feel when Jesus is mocked today? Grieved, but not surprised and not afraid. Christ has been mocked from the first, and the mockery has always come from people who think they are cleverer than he is. Do not answer with mockery, and do not imagine that his honour depends on you. Pray for the mockers; some of them, like many in Jerusalem, may yet beat their breasts and believe. And let the mockery remind you that every taunt aimed at him is a backhanded confession of who he truly is.

In a sentence. As the priests and scribes fiercely accused him, Herod and his soldiers mocked him, dressed him in a splendid robe, and sent him back to Pilate.

On a Tuesday. When you notice yourself treating something holy as small, a sermon as a performance to be rated, prayer as a box to tick, the Lord’s Supper as a routine, that is Herod’s contempt in miniature. Stop and repent of it. And when you are counted as nothing for Christ’s sake, remember who was counted as nothing first.

For worship. They put a bright robe on the King of kings in order to laugh, and every thread of it was true. He was a king. He was going to a throne. The one who counted him as nothing was standing before the one by whom all things were made, and he made himself nothing, taking the form of a servant, and therefore God has highly exalted him and given him the name above every name (Philippians 2:7–9). The soldiers who laughed have long since gone to dust; the one they dressed as a stage king is robed in majesty at the Father’s right hand, and every knee will bow to him.

parallels.desc: a similar mockery by Pilate’s soldiers

verseByVerse.quote: And Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day, for before this they had been at enmity with each other.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day, for before this they had been at enmity with each other.

Became friends with each other that very day. A single sentence, easily read as a footnote, and Luke has put it there because he wants it seen. We are not told the cause of the quarrel; perhaps it was Pilate’s massacre of Galileans (13:1), perhaps something in the long friction between a Roman governor and a client ruler sharing a border. Luke does not care about the cause. He cares about the cure. What healed it was Jesus. Not his teaching, and not any appeal for peace. Pilate sent the prisoner over as a courtesy, Herod sent him back with a joke attached, and united by their contempt for Jesus, the two men discovered they could work together.

Contempt makes friends. That observation has not dated. Two people who agree on nothing will warm to each other instantly over a third party they both find absurd, and the friendship feels genuine while it lasts, because the pleasure is genuine. Office politics runs on it, and so does a good deal of family and public life.

The fulfilment. Luke knows exactly what he is recording. Peter and John would quote the psalm in prayer a few weeks later, naming both men: why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed (Psalm 2:1–2). They go on: truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:25–28). The psalm says gathered together, and here is the gathering: a governor and a tetrarch who could not stand each other, reconciled over the body of the Son of God, on the day they killed him. But the psalm does not end with the plotting. It goes on: as for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill (Psalm 2:6). The gathering of rulers was the very road by which the Anointed went to his throne, and within three days the one they had sent back and forth between them would be raised, declared the Son of God in power (Romans 1:4).

Does this mean rulers and governments are always against God? No. Scripture tells us that governing authorities are appointed by God for our good, and calls us to pray for them and honour them (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Timothy 2:1–2). Psalm 2 describes what rulers do when they set themselves against Christ, and it ends by calling them to kiss the Son and be wise. The point here is that even when the powerful unite against him, they plot in vain. The one enthroned in the heavens laughs (Psalm 2:4), and their plans end up serving his.

In a sentence. That day Herod and Pilate, formerly enemies, became friends.

On a Tuesday. Opposition to Christ unites strange allies, but God rules over them all. Notice this week where you are bonding with someone over shared contempt for a third person: the boss, the in-law, the other political party, the difficult member at church. Stop the conversation, or turn it. A friendship that needs a common enemy is a poor kind of peace.

For worship. Two rulers found a friendship in despising him, and the price of it was already being carried up a hill outside the city. Yet the true peace made that day was not theirs. By the blood of that same cross God reconciled to himself all things, making peace (Colossians 1:20), and turned enemies into friends, not by a shared contempt but by a shared mercy. Herod and Pilate were joined against the Son; sinners are joined to the Son, and in him to one another, Jew and Gentile, ruler and thief, one new man where there had been two (Ephesians 2:15).

parallels.desc: the kings of the earth set themselves against the LORD’s Anointed

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate then called together the chief priests and the rulers and the people, and said to them, 'You brought me this man as one who was misleading the people. And after examining him before you, behold, I did not find this man guilty of any of your charges against him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate then called together the chief priests and the rulers and the people, and said to them: you brought me this man as one who was misleading the people. And after examining him before you, behold, I did not find this man guilty of any of your charges against him.

Pilate then called together the chief priests and the rulers and the people. Pilate convenes a formal assembly and puts his finding on the record, and he does it with unusual care. And now the people are involved: the crowd is drawn into the decision.

After examining him before you. A formal Roman hearing. He restates their charge in their own words, states the procedure, and delivers the finding. Before you: the examination was not held in a back room. They were present and heard it, and no one can afterwards claim the governor rushed it. This is a man building a defensible file, and he is doing it because he already suspects he is going to need one.

I did not find this man guilty of any of your charges against him. The second declaration of innocence (v. 4). And here is the tragedy of Pilate in one motion. He is scrupulous about the record and careless about the man. Everything he does from here is aimed at making sure that when this goes wrong it will not be attributable to him, and none of it is aimed at the only thing his own verdict required, which was to open the door and let an innocent man walk out. A Roman prefect held the power of the sword and answered to the emperor, not to a crowd. Nothing prevented him from dismissing the case except the calculation of what it would cost him.

What is the fear of man, and how do I fight it? The fear of man is letting other people’s approval or anger decide what you do, even when you know what is right. It lays a snare, says Proverbs, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe (Proverbs 29:25). Pilate’s fear was of the crowd and of Caesar (John 19:12). Ours is usually smaller: the colleague’s raised eyebrow, the family’s disapproval, the online pile-on. The cure is not bravado but a bigger fear: the fear of God, who sees and judges and also loves. Ask, in the moment, whose verdict on me matters most? Then act for an audience of one.

In a sentence. Pilate summoned the leaders and the people and told them that after examining Jesus, he found him not guilty of any of their charges.

On a Tuesday. There is a difference between not knowing what is right and knowing it and pricing it. Pilate knew. He held a hearing, reached the correct conclusion, announced it publicly, and then began negotiating with people who had no standing to negotiate with him. The moment a man starts asking what the right thing will cost, the answer has usually already been decided, and the asking is the decision. Is there a right thing you already know you should do this week? Do it before you start counting.

For worship. Pilate kept a careful record to protect his own name, and the prisoner made no effort to protect his. He who knew no sin let his condemnation be filed by a man counting the cost, because he had counted a far greater cost and chosen to pay it. If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? But with you there is forgiveness (Psalm 130:3–4), and this is how: the record that should have been kept against us was charged to him. The governor’s file is lost to history; the believer’s debt is lost for ever.

parallels.desc: I find no guilt in him

verseByVerse.quote: Neither did Herod, for he sent him back to us. Look, nothing deserving death has been done by him. I will therefore punish and release him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neither did Herod, for he sent him back to us. Look, nothing deserving death has been done by him. I will therefore punish and release him.

Neither did Herod, for he sent him back to us. Two rulers, two verdicts of innocence: the two witnesses that the law required to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15). Nothing deserving death has been done by him is the plainest verdict spoken by anyone that day, and the high-water mark of the trial.

I will therefore punish and release him. And then, in the same breath, without any transition at all, this. The joint between the two halves is where the whole chapter turns. The word is therefore: he has established innocence, and the conclusion he draws from innocence is a flogging. The verb is paideusas, literally to discipline or instruct, a chillingly domestic word for a beating lighter than the full scourging before crucifixion, meant as a warning. But Roman flogging was no formality; men were badly injured by it. Pilate offers it as a concession, so that the crowd will accept the release. There is no version of justice in which this is defensible, and Pilate knows it. He is bargaining, and what he has put on the table is somebody else’s back.

The chastisement that brought us peace. Pilate’s word belongs to the same family as the word the Greek Old Testament uses in Isaiah 53:5: upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace. Pilate meant a beating to buy off a crowd, an innocent man punished to keep a guilty city quiet. God meant something infinitely greater by the same innocent suffering: the Servant bearing the punishment due to others, so that those who deserved it might have peace with God. Pilate’s compromise was wicked; the Servant’s substitution was righteous, and it was the only exchange that day that worked.

How decent men do monstrous things. It is almost never a single decision to do evil. It is a series of small settlements, each presented as the reasonable middle course. He will neither release the prisoner nor condemn him; the something in between is to have an innocent man beaten. The compromise fails, as compromises with this kind of pressure always do, and for a reason worth naming. Once Pilate conceded that innocence was no protection, there was no principle left in the room to stop at. If the man can be flogged though innocent, the argument against crucifying him though innocent is only a matter of degree, and the crowd could do arithmetic.

What should I do when I am pressured to compromise at work or in my family? First, see the compromise for what it is: not a middle way between two goods but a smaller wrong offered to avoid a cost. Then decide what is right before the pressure peaks, and say it calmly and early, as Pilate should have done. Find out what you actually can and cannot be made to do; often the threat is larger than the reality. Seek counsel from a wise Christian. Be willing to lose something, a promotion, a friendship, a peaceful Christmas, rather than your integrity. And remember that the Lord who stood before Pilate knows what that pressure costs.

In a sentence. Pilate said that neither he nor Herod found Jesus guilty of anything deserving death, so he would have him flogged and release him.

On a Tuesday. Look for one place where you are offering half of something to avoid giving all of it: half the truth to a customer, half an apology to your wife, half obedience to God. Give the whole.

For worship. Pilate offered them half of an innocent man to save the other half, and within ten verses they had all of him. Yet no one took his life from him; he laid it down of his own accord (John 10:18), the whole of it, back and hands and side and soul. He would not be a half-measure Saviour, and he does not save by halves: all that he bore he bore in full, so that all we owed is paid in full. Blessed be the Lord who gave his back to those who strike (Isaiah 50:6), and whose mercy holds nothing back.
verseByVerse.note: To “punish” here means a flogging.

verseByVerse.quote: But they all cried out together, 'Away with this man, and release to us Barabbas'— a man who had been thrown into prison for an insurrection started in the city and for murder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they all cried out together: away with this man, and release to us Barabbas, a man who had been thrown into prison for an insurrection started in the city and for murder.

Away with this man. Literally, take this one: get rid of him. They all cried out together. It is the same cry the crowd would raise against Paul in this same city (Acts 21:36; 22:22). And release to us Barabbas appeals to the Passover amnesty, the custom of releasing one prisoner at the feast, which Matthew, Mark and John all record (Mark 15:6).

Textual note. A reader following in a modern Bible will notice the text jumps from verse 16 to verse 18, with verse 17 printed only as a note: Now he was obliged to release one man to them at the festival. Nothing has been removed from Scripture. Verse numbers are not inspired; they were added in the sixteenth century. Since then far older copies have been found, centuries closer to the apostles, and in the oldest of them this sentence is not there. It appears in later copies and looks very much like a helpful explanation of the Passover custom, written in the margin by a scribe and then copied into the text. So the translators keep the number, print the words in the note, and tell the reader exactly what the evidence is. What is displayed here is not damage to the text but the care with which it has been kept. And nothing in the account depends on it; the custom is attested independently by the other Gospels.

A man who had been thrown into prison for an insurrection started in the city and for murder. Luke will not let the reader past the choice without naming what Barabbas was. Insurrection is exactly the crime Jesus had been falsely accused of in v. 2. Pilate is being asked to release the man who had actually done what the innocent man is accused of doing. The crowd picks the guilty man, and the Son goes to the cross that had been prepared for the other. Barabbas, of all men, could say literally: Jesus died for me.

Am I really like Barabbas? Yes, and that is the best news you will ever hear. You may never have led a revolt or killed anyone, but Scripture says every one of us has rebelled against God, our rightful King (Isaiah 53:6; Romans 3:23), and that hatred in the heart is murder in his eyes (Matthew 5:21–22; 1 John 3:15). We stood under a just sentence. Christ was condemned in our place, and we were let go. The difference is that Barabbas was released without being changed, while all who trust Christ are not only set free but made new and declared righteous. Seeing yourself in Barabbas is not humiliation for its own sake; it is the door to gratitude.

In a sentence. The crowd shouted for Jesus to be taken away and for Barabbas, a rebel and murderer, to be released.

On a Tuesday. Next time you are tempted to think of yourself as one of the decent people who would never have shouted with that crowd, picture instead the cell. Then thank God, specifically, for the substitution: he went to the cross that was meant for me. Let that make you gentle today with someone who is plainly guilty.

For worship. Away with this man, they cried, and the Father let him be taken away, out of the city and out of the sight of the holy place, so that we who once were far off might be brought near by his blood (Ephesians 2:13). The crowd chose a rebel and rejected the King, and the King went quietly to the place the rebel had earned. All we like sheep have gone astray, and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53:6). He was sent away so that the guilty would never be sent away from God.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 17: “Now he was obliged to release one man to them at the festival.” Barabbas means “son of the father.”

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate addressed them once more, desiring to release Jesus, but they kept shouting, 'Crucify, crucify him!' A third time he said to them, 'Why? What evil has he done? I have found in him no guilt deserving death. I will therefore punish and release him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate addressed them once more, desiring to release Jesus, but they kept shouting: crucify, crucify him! A third time he said to them: why? What evil has he done? I have found in him no guilt deserving death. I will therefore punish and release him.

Crucify, crucify him! Pilate addressed them once more, desiring to release Jesus, and they kept shouting: it did not stop. The repetition shows the frenzy. And what they shout has stopped being an argument. There is no charge in it, no accusation, no reasoning. Two words, repeated. A crowd in this state is not being persuaded and cannot be answered, because it is no longer making a case. Crucifixion was the most shameful death in the Roman world, kept for slaves and rebels.

A third time. Three times Pilate declared him innocent (vv. 4, 14, 22), as Peter had denied him three times. Three declarations of innocence from the bench, three refusals from the floor.

Why, what evil has he done? It is the right question. It is the only question. And nobody answers it: not in Luke, not in Matthew, not in Mark, not in John. The question hangs in the middle of the loudest morning in Jerusalem’s history and no one supplies a reply, because there was none. So consider what has actually defeated the governor of Judea. Not evidence, which does not exist. Not law, which is entirely on the other side. Not force, since he commands the only soldiers present. Noise. He is beaten by volume, and he knows it, and he gives way anyway.

How do I stand against a crowd? Most people will never face a mob, and almost everyone will face its smaller relatives. A room in which one view is being expressed loudly and confidently exerts a pressure that has nothing to do with whether the view is true, and it works on people who can see perfectly well that it is not true. So decide what you believe before you enter the room. Speak early and simply, before the noise builds. Look for one other person who agrees, and stand with them. You shall not fall in with the many to do evil (Exodus 23:2). And remember that the question is not, can I see what is right? Pilate saw it three times. It is whether you can still say it when it is expensive.

In a sentence. Pilate appealed again to release Jesus, but they kept shouting that he should be crucified, and a third time he asked what evil Jesus had done, declaring him not guilty.

On a Tuesday. The crowd had no answer to what evil has he done? He did none. He bore yours. This week, in some conversation where everyone seems to agree on something you know is wrong, ask Pilate’s question quietly: why? Then wait for the answer, and do not fill the silence by giving in.

For worship. Why, what evil has he done? The question still stands, and neither earth nor hell has ever answered it. Of all who have lived, here is the one against whom no charge could be found: he committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth (1 Peter 2:22). And the spotless one, hearing his own people roar for his death, called down no fire and summoned no angels. He heard them shout crucify, and he went, because the evil that was not his had been laid on him, and he had come to carry it away.

verseByVerse.quote: But they were urgent, demanding with loud cries that he should be crucified. And their voices prevailed. So Pilate decided that their demand should be granted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they were urgent, demanding with loud cries that he should be crucified. And their voices prevailed. So Pilate decided that their demand should be granted.

And their voices prevailed. They were urgent, demanding with loud cries: the same insistent pressing as in v. 5, now become a roar. And then four words, among the bleakest in the Gospel. Not the evidence, not the law, not the verdict given three times by the only man with authority to give it. The voices. Prevailed means overpowered, had the mastery, and the mastery belongs to a crowd.

So Pilate decided that their demand should be granted. The word is epekrinen: he pronounced sentence. Luke’s phrasing is almost administrative, and the flatness is the point: a judicial murder processed as a granted application. Pilate chose his position over justice (John 19:12).

Two things held together. They must be held together or the passage will be misread. The first is that these men are entirely guilty. Not one of them is excused by anything that follows. Peter would say so to their faces at Pentecost, you crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23), and he was not being rhetorical. Pilate bears real guilt. The second is that behind the crowd, behind Judas’s price and the council’s hatred and Pilate’s cowardice, stands the settled purpose of God, who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32; Acts 4:27–28). And Paul’s verb there is the very verb Luke uses of Pilate in the next breath: paradidōmi, to hand over. Pilate handed him over to a mob. The Father handed him over for us. The same act, and the difference is everything: one was a surrender to pressure, the other was love with nothing forced about it at all.

Was Pilate less guilty than the leaders who handed Jesus over? Less, but still guilty. Jesus told Pilate that he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin (John 19:11): the men who knew the Scriptures, saw the signs and still demanded his death sinned against greater light. But Pilate had the power and the knowledge to stop it and did not. Scripture never lets anyone off because someone else was worse. Each will give an account for what he knew and did (12:47–48), and the creed still names Pilate.

In a sentence. They kept loudly demanding crucifixion, their shouts won, and Pilate gave the sentence they demanded.

On a Tuesday. If someone has handed you over, abandoned you to a situation they had the power to stop and would not pay the cost of stopping, take comfort here. That is exactly what happened to him, and he knows it from the inside. Bring it to him today, by name.

For worship. Their voices prevailed in the courtyard for an hour, but the counsel of the LORD stands for ever (Psalm 33:11). Beneath the roar a quieter will was being done, and it was love. Blessed be the Father who did not spare his own Son, and the Son who did not spare himself. And if God gave the greatest gift when the world was shouting for his Son’s blood, he will not withhold the lesser ones from those who now call on his name: how will he not also with him graciously give us all things (Romans 8:32)?

verseByVerse.quote: He released the man who had been thrown into prison for insurrection and murder, for whom they asked, but he delivered Jesus over to their will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He released the man who had been thrown into prison for insurrection and murder, for whom they asked, but he delivered Jesus over to their will.

He released the man who had been thrown into prison for insurrection and murder. Luke has already told us who Barabbas was, and he tells us again, in the same sentence as the release, with the same two words. He wants no reader to reach the end of the trial without knowing exactly who walked out of that building alive, and how plainly unjust it was.

For whom they asked. They chose a murderer. Peter would say it to them in the temple: you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, and killed the Author of life (Acts 3:14–15).

He is not pardoned. Picture it, because it happened to a real man on a real morning. A condemned prisoner lies in a cell in Jerusalem waiting to be crucified. He hears a crowd outside and cannot make out the words. Then a door is unlocked, a soldier tells him he is free to go, and he walks out into the daylight past a beam being carried the other way. Be exact about it. Nobody has said he is innocent, nobody has reviewed his case, and nothing about him has changed. He is guilty of insurrection and murder when he goes in and guilty when he comes out, and he goes free because another man is going to die in his place. There is no better picture anywhere in Scripture, and it happens in the street before it happens on the hill. Barabbas walked free because Jesus took his place; sinners walk free because Jesus took their sin, and with it their sentence.

But he delivered Jesus over to their will. Luke places it at the very end, where it will be felt. Delivered over is the word used throughout the passion predictions (9:44; 18:32): the Son of Man handed over into the hands of men. Not to justice, not to a sentence, but to their will, the most complete abandonment a court can perform. From this point until a centurion speaks at the end of the chapter, no authority in Jerusalem stands between the Son of God and whatever men want to do to him. And behind it, the Father’s will (Romans 8:32).

Does this passage blame the Jewish people as a whole? No. Luke names the actors: a handful of leaders, a crowd stirred up by them, Pilate and his soldiers. Jesus himself, his apostles and the first thousands of believers were Jews. The charge of collective or inherited guilt, used for centuries to justify hatred of Jews, has no ground here, and Christians must repent of it wherever it appears.

Did Barabbas ever believe? We are not told. Scripture leaves him at the prison door, and any tradition about his later life is guesswork. Perhaps that is deliberate. His story stops at the moment of release so that every reader can step into it. The question is not what Barabbas did with his freedom but what you will do with yours.

In a sentence. Pilate released the rebel and murderer they asked for, and handed Jesus over to their will.

On a Tuesday. Live today as a released prisoner. Freedom you did not earn should make you grateful, humble and generous. Think of someone whose guilt you find easy to see, and remember the cell you walked out of. Then treat them with the mercy you were shown.

For worship. They asked for a man who took life and handed over the one who gives it, and the Author of life let himself be traded for a murderer. The exchange was wickedness on their side and grace on his: the Holy and Righteous One delivered to the will of sinners, so that sinners might be delivered from the wrath they had earned. Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Peter 3:18). The door that opened for Barabbas that morning has stood open ever since.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–43 — The Way of the Cross and the Crucifixion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Simon of Cyrene is seized out of the crowd — coming in from the country, with plans for the day, compelled by a soldier as any provincial could be. Luke says he carried it behind Jesus, which is the posture Jesus had described for discipleship in 9:23. He did not volunteer. He is the only human being who ever carried the cross of Christ, and Mark's readers in Rome evidently knew his sons by name.

Women follow, mourning and wailing, and Jesus turns round on the way to his own execution to speak to them about their future: do not weep for me, but for yourselves and your children. What is coming to Jerusalem will be so terrible that barrenness — the standard image of shame in that world — will be called a blessing, and people will ask the mountains to fall on them (Hos. 10:8). Then the proverb: if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?

At the place called The Skull he is crucified between two criminals, one on his right and one on his left — the arrangement two disciples had once requested for themselves (Mark 10:37), and the fulfilment of numbered with the transgressors (22:37). Luke records the execution in four words and describes none of it.

The first word from the cross is a prayer for the men driving the nails: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do, while the squad gambled for his clothes exactly as Psalm 22:18 had said they would.

Three groups mock, and all three say the same thing: the rulers (let him save himself), the soldiers (if you are the King of the Jews — the wilderness temptation in its original form), and one of the criminals. Above his head Pilate's notice states the only charge ever proved against him: that he is the King of the Jews.

And the other criminal turns. He fears God, agrees with his own sentence, declares Jesus innocent, and asks only to be remembered. He is told he will be accompanied — today you will be with me in paradise.
verseByVerse.theology:
Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do raises the question of how far ignorance mitigates. It is real and partial: they knew they were killing a man, not that they were killing the Author of life. The plea is not an acquittal — if it acquitted them no forgiveness would be needed — but a ground on which to ask. And Luke shows the prayer answered in his own second volume: Peter tells that same city you acted in ignorance (Acts 3:17), and three thousand are forgiven in a day.

The mockery of v. 35 states the atonement with perfect accuracy and no understanding. He could not save himself and save others; not for lack of power, since legions were available for the asking, but because the two were mutually exclusive. To come down would leave the work undone and everyone he came for still under sentence. He saved others; himself he did not save.

The dying criminal answers works-based salvation and deathbed scepticism at once. He cannot be baptised, cannot make restitution, cannot demonstrate any fruit, and has no time in which to try. He brings a verdict on himself, a recognition of who Jesus is, and a request. And the reply exceeds it at every point: not someday but today; not somewhere but with me. There is no purgatory in that sentence and no room for one.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 26 is one of the most useful in the chapter, because most crosses in a Christian life are not chosen. People speak of taking up a cross as a decision, and sometimes it is — but the diagnosis was not chosen, nor the redundancy, nor the decade of caring for a parent. It was laid on. Simon is not recorded as willing, and he may have resented every step, and he is the man who walked closest behind the Son of God.

Verses 27–28 correct the commonest sentiment attached to the cross: a devotion that consists mostly of feeling sorry for Jesus, dwelling on the physical agony, producing much sympathy and no repentance. He declines it on the road. And grief that fastens on someone else's situation can be a way of not looking at your own — it is far easier to weep over a tragedy on the news than to face one's own household.

Verses 39–40 demolish the assumption that suffering makes people better. Two men, identical pain, identical distance from Jesus and from death, and Matthew says both began by reviling him. One changed. Proximity to Christ saved neither of them; one of them looked at him.

And v. 43 is for anyone who thinks it is too late — the man in a hospice, raised near the church and never committed, wanting to know whether there is time. There was no baptism, no restitution, no probation, no changed life, because there was no life left in which to change. There was a confession and a request, and Jesus took him home that afternoon.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they led him away, they seized one Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid on him the cross, to carry it behind Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they led him away, they seized one Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid on him the cross, to carry it behind Jesus.

As they led him away. Out of the city to the place of execution. A condemned man carried the crossbeam himself: not the upright, which stood permanently at the execution ground, but the beam, a heavy timber lashed across the shoulders. That a stranger had to carry it suggests what the flogging had already done to him. Jesus, weakened, could not carry it further.

Too weak to carry the beam. Pause on the fact that he needed help at all. The one who upholds the universe by the word of his power (Hebrews 1:3) could not lift a beam of wood up a hill. That is not play-acting. It is the measure of how truly he became man, and of how much he had already suffered for us before the nails. He did not use his divine power to spare his human body. He went to the cross in real flesh, as weak as ours, so that he would be a high priest able to sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), and no sufferer who has run out of strength would ever think him far away.

They seized one Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country. So a soldier picks a stranger out of the crowd, a man arriving with plans for the day. Cyrene was a city in North Africa, in what is now Libya, with a large Jewish community; Simon may well have come a great distance for this Passover. A Roman soldier could compel any provincial to carry a load, and did. Simon had no say whatever. He did not volunteer and was not asked.

To carry it behind Jesus. They laid the crossbeam on a stranger’s shoulders. Only Luke says behind Jesus, and he chooses the words with care. That is the posture Jesus had described for discipleship: if anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me (9:23; 14:27). Luke has recorded the metaphor; now, on the road, he shows a man doing it literally, and against his will.

Most crosses are not chosen. This is where the verse becomes one of the most useful in the chapter. People speak of taking up a cross as though it were a decision, and sometimes it is. But the illness was not chosen. The child’s diagnosis was not chosen. The redundancy, the parent who needs care for a decade, the marriage that became a long endurance: none of it was volunteered for. It was laid on. Simon says nothing in the Gospels. He may have resented every step. And apart from Jesus himself, he is the only man who ever carried the cross of Christ.

Simon’s family. Mark adds a detail that reads like a signature: Simon was the father of Alexander and Rufus (Mark 15:21), which means that when Mark’s readers heard the names they knew the family. Paul greets a Rufus in Rome, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who had been a mother to Paul too (Romans 16:13). It may be the same family. If so, the man pressed into service that morning did not stay a bystander.

What does it mean for me to carry my cross? It means following Jesus wherever he leads, accepting the cost of belonging to him, and saying no to self when self and Christ conflict (9:23–24). Sometimes the cross is chosen: you give up a sinful relationship, tell the truth at a price, take a stand that costs you. Often it is laid on you: a suffering you did not seek, which you carry not with resentment but behind Jesus, trusting him with it. Your cross is never his cross. He alone carried our sins; we carry only what comes from following him, and he walks ahead.

In a sentence. As they led Jesus away, they forced Simon of Cyrene to carry the cross behind him.

On a Tuesday. Name the load you did not choose and would put down if you could. Today, before you ask God to remove it, ask him to help you carry it behind Jesus: with your eyes on him, step by step, as part of following him rather than as an interruption of it.

For worship. He set out for a festival and was handed a load he had not asked for, and it turned out to be the nearest any man has ever walked behind the Son of God. And the one who walked ahead of Simon was carrying a weight no one else could lift: the sin of the world. Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows (Isaiah 53:4). Simon carried the wood for a few hundred yards; Christ carried our curse all the way, and he never asks us to carry anything he has not first carried himself.
verseByVerse.note: Cyrene was a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community.

verseByVerse.quote: And there followed him a great multitude of the people and of women who were mourning and lamenting for him. But turning to them Jesus said, 'Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There followed him a great multitude of the people and of women who were mourning and lamenting for him. But turning to them Jesus said: daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.

A great multitude of the people. Not all were hostile. The walk itself is easy to picture and hard to hold. He has been awake all night, beaten by the temple guard, mocked by Herod’s soldiers, flogged by Pilate’s. He is walking through his own capital carrying nothing now, because a stranger has the beam, towards a place where he will be nailed down.

And of women who were mourning and lamenting for him. Only Luke records this. The words describe formal, audible grief, beating the breast and wailing, as at a funeral. Perhaps these were the women of Jerusalem who traditionally mourned for the condemned. There is no hint that Jesus thinks it insincere, and he does not rebuke them for it.

Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me. Even on the way to the cross he thinks of others. He turns round to speak to a group of women about their future. Not because his suffering is not worth weeping over, but because theirs is nearer than they think, and pity is not what he needs from anyone. That corrects the commonest sentiment attached to the cross. There is a kind of devotion that consists mostly of feeling sorry for Jesus, a Good Friday emotion that dwells on the physical agony and produces a good deal of sympathy and no repentance at all. He declines it here, on the road. He did not go to Golgotha to be pitied.

But weep for yourselves and for your children. Weep for the judgment coming on Jerusalem (19:41–44; 21:20–24). Their children would see the siege and destruction of AD 70. And the redirection is sharper than it looks. Grief that fastens on someone else’s situation can be a way of not looking at your own. It is far easier to weep over a tragedy on the news than to face the state of one’s own household, and the tears are real either way, and only one kind costs anything.

Is it wrong to be moved by the sufferings of Christ? No. It would be strange to read of the cross and feel nothing, and the church has always sung of his wounds with tears. The question is where the feeling leads. If it ends in a pleasant sadness, it has missed the point. If it leads you to see the seriousness of sin, to repent of your own, to trust him and love him, it is exactly what the cross is meant to produce. Do not weep for him as a victim. Weep over the sin that put him there, and then rejoice that he chose to go.

In a sentence. A large crowd followed, including women who mourned for him, but Jesus turned and told them not to weep for him but for themselves and their children.

On a Tuesday. Pray today, by name, for your children or the children you know, that they would know Christ and escape the judgment to come. Then look honestly at one thing in your own home that you have been avoiding.

For worship. He is on the way to be crucified, and what occupies him is what will become of the women crying at the roadside and the children holding their hands. Even the last mile is spent on somebody else. Jesus wept at the grave of a friend (John 11:35) and over a city that rejected him (19:41), and now, bleeding, he grieves for its daughters. This is the heart of our Lord: in his own agony, still the shepherd.

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, the days are coming when they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren and the wombs that never bore and the breasts that never nursed!’ Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall on us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us.’
verseByVerse.commentary:
For behold, the days are coming when they will say: blessed are the barren and the wombs that never bore and the breasts that never nursed! Then they will begin to say to the mountains, fall on us, and to the hills, cover us.

Blessed are the barren. To understand how terrible this is, you have to know what childlessness meant in that world. It was the standard image of grief and shame. Sarah, Rachel and Hannah wept over it, and Elizabeth, at the start of this very Gospel, says the Lord has taken away her reproach among people (1:25). Jesus says a day is coming when women will be congratulated on it. That is not a statement about the value of children. It is a measurement of horror: a day so bad that the worst thing that could happen to a woman will look like an escape, because she will not have to watch her children suffer and die. What is being described is a siege, the siege of the year 70, when the mothers inside those walls watched what happened to their children before it happened to them. He is not saying it with satisfaction. He wept over this city on the way in (19:41), and he is grieving over it on the way out.

They will begin to say to the mountains, Fall on us, and to the hills, Cover us. A quotation from Hosea 10:8, spoken over the northern kingdom on the eve of its destruction. It is a cry of despair, people who would rather be crushed than face what is coming. And John heard it again at the end of all things, from kings and the great and the slave and the free, hiding in the rocks from the face of him who is seated on the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb (Revelation 6:16). That tells you what the fear really is. Being buried under a mountain is not the thing they are fleeing. It is the alternative they prefer.

Is Jesus speaking about AD 70 or about the final judgment? Both, in the way prophecy often works. The nearer fulfilment came within forty years, when Roman armies besieged and destroyed Jerusalem, as he had foretold (21:20–24). But the words he uses, and Revelation’s use of the same cry, show that the fall of Jerusalem was a foreshadowing of the last day, when all who have refused Christ will face the holy God. The first came exactly as he said, which is a sober warning that the second will too.

In a sentence. Jesus warned that days would come when childless women would be called blessed, and people would beg the mountains to fall on them.

On a Tuesday. Do not let this passage stay in the first century. Think of one person you love who is outside Christ, and pray for them today. Then ask whether there is a way to speak to them of him this month.

For worship. There is a day coming when men will find the presence of God unbearable, and the terror of it is not that he is cruel but that he is holy and they are not. And the one who spoke of that day was walking towards a hill to make sure the people crying by that road would never have to say those words. The wrath of the Lamb is real; so is the blood of the Lamb, and whoever hides in him will never need to hide from him.

parallels.desc: they shall say to the mountains, “Cover us”

verseByVerse.quote: For if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?

For if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry? It has the sound of a proverb, and it probably was one. Green wood is living wood, full of sap; it resists a fire and has to be forced to burn. Dry wood is dead, and goes up at a spark. So the question argues from the lesser to the greater, a form the rabbis used constantly: if this is what happens in the unlikely case, what will happen in the likely one? The application is not stated, which is why readers have taken it two ways, and both are worth having.

Two readings. The first reads the green wood as Jesus himself, innocent, before Rome. If Rome and the temple authorities together will do this to a man who is entirely innocent, the living wood, the one who gave no cause at all, what will they do when the city is full of genuine rebels and the case against it is real? Jerusalem burned forty years later. The second reading goes deeper and does not exclude the first. If God allows this to happen to his innocent Son, what will happen to those who reject him? If judgment falls like this on the green wood, the one man in history who never deserved a stroke of it, what will it be when it falls on the dry? If judgment begins at the household of God, what will be the outcome for those who do not obey the gospel (1 Peter 4:17–18)? What is happening on that hill is the wrath of God against sin, absorbed by a substitute, and even so it produced three hours of darkness and a cry that has never stopped echoing.

Is God’s judgment not out of all proportion? This is a question people ask honestly and often: would a loving God really deal with sin so severely? Look at what he was prepared to do to his own Son rather than overlook it. Nobody who has understood Calvary can go on thinking that God takes sin lightly or deals with it cheaply. Sin is not a small thing because it is committed against an infinitely holy God, and the punishment of those who refuse his mercy is conscious and eternal (Matthew 25:46). The cross is not evidence that judgment is mild. It is the fullest evidence available of how serious it is, and, in the same act, the reason a sinner need never face it.

In a sentence. If they do this to green wood, what will happen to dry?

On a Tuesday. The next time you are tempted to call a sin small, look at the cross and measure it there, and then name that sin to God and turn from it.

For worship. He was led out to be burned as the green wood, so that the dry might be spared the fire. Behold the severity and the kindness of God (Romans 11:22) in one tree: the severity that would not overlook a single sin, and the kindness that laid all of it on his Son. The fire that should have consumed us consumed the living wood, and for all who are in him there is no fire left.
verseByVerse.note: A proverb: if this is done to the innocent (green wood), what will happen to the guilty (dry wood, ready to burn)?

parallels.desc: every green tree and every dry tree

verseByVerse.quote: Two others, who were criminals, were led away to be put to death with him. And when they came to the place that is called The Skull, there they crucified him, and the criminals, one on his right and one on his left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two others, who were criminals, were led away to be put to death with him. And when they came to the place that is called The Skull, there they crucified him, and the criminals, one on his right and one on his left.

Two others, who were criminals. Fulfilling Isaiah 53:12, which Jesus had quoted at the table only hours before: he was numbered with the transgressors (22:37). Here is the numbering, carried out by a Roman work detail who thought they were simply executing three men that morning.

The place that is called The Skull. Luke gives the meaning rather than the Aramaic name, for readers who would not know it: the Aramaic is Golgotha, and the Latin, Calvary. Nobody now knows for certain why it was called that.

There they crucified him. Luke, like the other Gospels, describes it in a single word. No account of the nails, no description of the pain, nothing of what the writers could easily have supplied and every one of them declined to. They were writing for a world that knew exactly what crucifixion was. Cicero called it the most cruel and disgusting penalty, and said the very word should be kept far from the ears of Roman citizens. Its purpose was not death, which could be achieved faster, but public degradation over hours. Every reader could fill in the detail, and Luke’s restraint is a kind of reverence.

One on his right and one on his left. That is exactly the arrangement James and John had once asked for: grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory (Mark 10:37). They had no idea what they were requesting. When the places either side of him were finally filled, they were filled by convicted criminals on crosses. He is not placed near them. He is placed among them, in the middle, the place one would give a ringleader.

Why did Jesus have to die by crucifixion? Because crucifixion was a death under curse. The law said that a man hanged on a tree is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23), and Paul explains that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). It was also the most shameful death the world knew, and he despised the shame (Hebrews 12:2), taking the lowest place so that none of his people would be beneath his reach. And it was public: lifted up, as he said, to draw all people to himself (John 12:32).

In a sentence. Two criminals were led out with him, and at the place called the Skull they crucified Jesus between them.

On a Tuesday. If you think there is someone too far gone for Christ, remember where he chose to die: in the middle of the guilty. Pray today for one person you have mentally written off. And if that person is you, look at the two crosses either side of his.

For worship. What was in the middle of that row was not a criminal among criminals. It was the Lord of glory, put in the worst place on the hill by men who were guessing, and it was the right place, because he had come to stand exactly where the guiltiest stands. He was crucified among criminals, counted as one of them, so that sinners could be counted righteous. Blessed be the King whose throne was a cross and whose courtiers were thieves.
verseByVerse.note: Luke uses the Greek name, “The Skull”; the Aramaic is Golgotha.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said, 'Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.' And they cast lots to divide his garments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus said: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do. And they cast lots to divide his garments.

Father, forgive them. The first of Jesus’ words from the cross in Luke, and it is a prayer for the men holding the hammer. Father: even on the cross. Nothing these men are doing to him has changed one syllable of how he addresses God. Forgive them: the soldiers, the leaders, the crowd, all who had a part. He practises what he taught: love your enemies, pray for those who abuse you (6:27–28). It is the intercession of a high priest, begun before he is dead, for people who have not asked and are not sorry. Stephen would pray the same as he died (Acts 7:60); he had heard where it came from.

For they know not what they do. The ignorance is real and it is partial. They knew they were killing a man; they did not know they were killing the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8), the Author of life (Acts 3:15, 17). That is not offered as an acquittal. Ignorance does not remove guilt; if it did, no forgiveness would be needed. But it is a ground on which to plead, and it made forgiveness possible. And the prayer was answered. Peter stood up in that same city, before some of the same people, and said you crucified him, and then, I know that you acted in ignorance (Acts 3:17), which is exactly the ground Jesus pleaded here. Thousands of those who crucified him repented and were forgiven at Pentecost (Acts 2:36–41), and a centurion at the foot of the cross praised God (v. 47).

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the prayer. It is missing from some important early copies and present in many others. But it is very early, widely attested, and fits Luke perfectly; no evangelist is more preoccupied with forgiveness. Some have suggested that a later scribe, looking back on the destruction of Jerusalem, thought the prayer had gone unanswered, or that the Jews should not be forgiven, and let it fall. If so, he stopped reading too soon, because Luke wrote a second volume telling what became of it. Most scholars accept it as an authentic saying of Jesus.

And they cast lots to divide his garments. A condemned man’s clothes were the perk of the execution squad, a small bonus at the end of a shift. And it is Psalm 22:18 happening in front of them, word for word: they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots. The soldiers gambled for his clothes at the foot of the cross, the very men he was praying for.

Were they forgiven even if they did not repent? No. Jesus prayed that they would be forgiven, and God answered that prayer by bringing many of them to repentance and faith. Forgiveness is always received through turning to Christ (Acts 2:38; 3:19). Those who went on rejecting him were not forgiven by a blanket pardon. But the prayer shows the heart of Christ towards his enemies, and it means that no one who had a part in his death, and no one today who has despised him, is beyond the reach of his mercy if they come.

Must I forgive someone who has not said sorry? You must let go of revenge and bitterness, and wish them good, even before they repent. That is what Jesus did here: he prayed for them, and gave up any desire to repay. Never avenge yourselves (Romans 12:19). But full reconciliation, the restoring of trust and relationship, needs repentance on their side (17:3–4), and forgiveness does not mean pretending nothing happened or putting yourself back in harm’s way. Where there has been abuse or crime, forgiveness and reporting it go together; you can forgive from the heart and still let the authorities do their God-given work. Start where he started: pray for them by name, and ask God to forgive them.

In a sentence. Jesus prayed for his Father to forgive those crucifying him, for they did not know what they were doing, while the soldiers gambled for his clothes.

On a Tuesday. Jesus prayed for his killers. He prayed for you. Who do you need to forgive? Name them before God today, and pray this exact prayer for them: Father, forgive them. If you cannot yet mean it, pray it anyway and ask him to make you mean it.

For worship. Nailed to a piece of wood by men who were dividing his clothes before he was dead, the Son of God spent his first breath asking his Father to let them off. If he prayed like that for those who drove the nails, there is no sinner he will refuse who comes to him. Father, forgive them: those three words are the gospel in the mouth of the dying Lamb, and every forgiven believer since has been an answer to them.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the prayer “Father, forgive them.”

verseByVerse.quote: And the people stood by, watching, but the rulers scoffed at him, saying, 'He saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people stood by, watching, but the rulers scoffed at him, saying: he saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One!

And the people stood by, watching. Luke separates two groups, and the distinction will matter by the end of the chapter. No mockery is attributed to the people. They are silent, and they will go home beating their breasts (v. 48). The people watch; the rulers scoff.

But the rulers scoffed at him. The word is exemyktērizon: they turned up their noses, sneered. All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads (Psalm 22:7).

He saved others; let him save himself. And what they say is true; that is the extraordinary thing about it. He saved others: they do not dispute it. They concede his miracles in the middle of a taunt, as an agreed fact not worth arguing about. Then the sneer. They think they have found the flaw. A saviour who cannot get himself off a cross is no saviour, and the logic feels unanswerable. It will be repeated by the soldiers in two verses and by one of the criminals in four. It is the settled assumption of the whole hill: real power rescues itself.

Exactly wrong, and exactly right. The logic is exactly wrong. He could not save himself and save others. Not because the power was lacking, for he had told Peter that legions were available for the asking (Matthew 26:53), but because the two things could not both be done. To come down would be to leave the work undone and every person he came for still under sentence. So the mockery states the gospel with perfect accuracy and no understanding whatever. The great irony: they admit he saved others, and because he would save others, he would not save himself. That is not a taunt. It is the doctrine of the atonement, put into words by his enemies, at the foot of the cross, on the day it was accomplished.

If he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One! They gave him a title too, without meaning it. They use Peter’s confession, the Christ of God (9:20), and the Father’s word at the transfiguration, this is my Son, my Chosen One (9:35), in mockery. Chosen is Isaiah’s word for the Servant: behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights (Isaiah 42:1). They were quoting the Father’s own delight in his Son back at him as an insult. Their words are true. He is God’s Chosen One, and he is saving others by not saving himself.

Could Jesus really have come down from the cross? Yes, in power. He was the eternal Son, and nothing held him there but his own will and his love for the Father and for us.
