No one takes my life from me, he said; I lay it down of my own accord, and I have authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again (John 10:18). That is what makes his staying so glorious. It was not the nails that kept him on the cross. It was the will to save.

In a sentence. While the people watched, the rulers sneered that he saved others and should save himself if he was God’s Christ, his Chosen One.

On a Tuesday. The world still says that real strength protects itself. This week, when you have the chance to defend your rights or your comfort at the expense of someone else’s good, choose the way of the cross: give something up so that another may be helped. That is power as Jesus defines it.

For worship. They flung the Father’s own word at him, his Chosen One, and it was true. The Father had chosen him before the foundation of the world, and on the cross the Chosen One was choosing too: choosing the shame, and choosing us. Because he is the Chosen, all who belong to him were chosen in him (Ephesians 1:4), and the delight the Father has in his Son now rests on them. The rulers sneered that God’s Chosen could not save himself. He did not need to. On the third day the Father raised him from the dead, and now he saves all who call on his name.

verseByVerse.quote: The soldiers also mocked him, coming up and offering him sour wine and saying, 'If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The soldiers also mocked him, coming up and offering him sour wine and saying: if you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!

The soldiers also mocked him. A different group, a different reason, the same sentence. Jews and Gentiles together. The rulers mocked him theologically; they cared what he claimed. The soldiers have no theology in it at all. They are an execution detail, they have done this many times, and this is how they pass the afternoon.

Offering him sour wine. Sour wine was the cheap, vinegary wine soldiers drank. Offering it to a crucified man was a joke about hospitality: here you are, your majesty, a toast to the king. And this too was written: for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink (Psalm 69:21).

If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself! If you are: the phrase has been said to him before, in the wilderness, by a voice that knew perfectly well the answer: if you are the Son of God, command this stone to become bread; if you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here (4:3, 9). Luke closed that scene with a sentence he clearly meant his reader to keep: the devil departed from him until an opportune time (4:13). This is that time. Three times on the cross he is told to save himself (vv. 35, 37, 39), as he was tempted three times in the wilderness. The temptation in the wilderness and the temptation at Golgotha are the same, in the same grammatical form: prove it by using your power on your own behalf. And the answer is the same both times: he will not use his power for himself. In the wilderness he answered with Scripture; on the cross he answers with silence.

If God loved me, would this be happening? It is what a Christian hears in a hospital corridor, in a marriage gone cold, in the fourth month of looking for work: if you really were what you claim to be, you would not be in this position; if God loved you, this would not be happening. The shape of that temptation is universal even when the stakes are small. Answer it from the cross. The beloved Son, in whom the Father delighted, was in the worst position any man has ever been in, and it was not because God did not love him but because God was doing the greatest good through it. Suffering is never proof that you are not loved. For the Christian it is always held inside the love that gave the Son (Romans 8:32, 35–39).

In a sentence. The soldiers also mocked him, offering him sour wine and taunting him to save himself if he was the King of the Jews.

On a Tuesday. When that voice says, if God loved you, this would not be happening, answer it out loud today with Romans 8:35–39. Write the verse on a card and keep it where the doubt usually comes.

For worship. The Son of God heard it at the beginning of his ministry and at the end of his life, and both times he declined to prove anything, and he was never once not the Son of God while he was being told he might not be. The soldiers raised a mocking toast to the King, and he drank instead the cup the Father gave him. He will drink the fruit of the vine again with his people in the kingdom; and they will not be mocking then.
verseByVerse.note: Sour wine was the cheap wine soldiers drank.

verseByVerse.quote: There was also an inscription over him, 'This is the King of the Jews.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was also an inscription over him: this is the King of the Jews.

An inscription over him. The board carrying the charge, posted on the cross as was the Roman custom, either hung round the condemned man’s neck on the walk or fixed above him at the site, so that everyone who passed knew what he was dying for and thought twice. So this is a legal document. It states the crime.

This is the King of the Jews. And the crime, as recorded by the Roman government, is that he is the King of the Jews. Meant as mockery and a warning, and true. Which means the only formal charge ever proved against Jesus of Nazareth is that he is who he said he is. Pilate wrote it as a sneer at the men who had forced his hand. John records the sequel: the chief priests asked him to change it to this man said, I am King of the Jews, and Pilate refused with the flattest sentence he ever spoke: what I have written I have written (John 19:21–22). He had lost every round of that morning; he won this one, the only thing he got right. John also tells us it was written in Aramaic, in Latin and in Greek (John 19:20): the language of the people, the language of the government, the language of the world’s trade and learning. Every kind of person in that crowded festival city could read it in his own tongue. Without meaning to, Pilate proclaimed to the world who Jesus is: he reigns from the cross.

Why do the Gospels give different wordings? A careful reader comparing them will spot it. Matthew has this is Jesus, the King of the Jews; Mark, the King of the Jews; John, Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews. This is what happens when four witnesses report a sign written in three languages: each gives the substance, and the substance is identical in every one. It is the ordinary variation of honest testimony, and a set of accounts that agreed word for word would be more suspicious, not less.

In what sense is Jesus a king now? In the fullest sense. He was not only King of the Jews but is King of kings and Lord of lords (Revelation 19:16), raised and seated at God’s right hand, with all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18). He rules now over all things for the sake of his church, gathers his people from every nation through the gospel, and will return visibly to judge and make all things new. His kingdom does not advance by armies or elections, but no throne on earth is outside his rule. To be a Christian is to be his willing subject.

In a sentence. Above him was the notice: this is the King of the Jews.

On a Tuesday. Ask today which areas of your life you have quietly kept outside his kingship: money, ambition, speech, a relationship. Put one of them under the sign today. Say, Jesus is King here too, and make one concrete change that shows it.

For worship. Above his head, in the great languages of that world, the government of Rome published the truth about him, refused to withdraw it, and left it there until he died: a proclamation to the nations, written by a pagan who did not believe a word of it. The King’s first herald was his judge, and his first throne was a cross. And the day is coming when the same truth will be told in every language without a trace of irony, when every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:10–11).

verseByVerse.quote: One of the criminals who were hanged railed at him, saying, 'Are you not the Christ? Save yourself and us!' But the other rebuked him, saying, 'Do you not fear God, since you are under the same sentence of condemnation?
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the criminals who were hanged railed at him, saying: are you not the Christ? Save yourself and us! But the other rebuked him, saying: do you not fear God, since you are under the same sentence of condemnation?

One of the criminals who were hanged railed at him. Two men, the same distance from Jesus, the same distance from death, in identical pain, hearing identical words. And they go opposite ways. Railed is eblasphēmei: he blasphemed. Even a dying criminal joins the mockery. Matthew and Mark report both men reviling him at first (Matthew 27:44; Mark 15:32), so the difference between them emerged during those hours, on the wood. Perhaps the second changed his mind as he watched Jesus die and heard him pray for his enemies. Only Luke records what follows.

Set for the fall and rising of many. Luke has prepared us for this scene since the temple courts, where old Simeon took the baby in his arms and said that this child was appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that is opposed (2:34). Here is that word in its starkest form: one Saviour, a cross on either side, and humanity divided by the man in the middle. Nothing separated the two criminals except what each made of Jesus. Even while he is dying, he is the hinge on which every human destiny turns.

Suffering does not make people better. That demolishes something people believe without examining it: that suffering softens people, or that a man facing death will naturally turn to God. These two were nailed up on the same morning by the same soldiers for the same kind of crime. Suffering did not soften one of them. Only grace did that.

Save yourself and us! The first man has repeated the rulers’ sneer and added a request entirely about his circumstances: get me down. He wants rescue from the cross, not from sin, and shows no interest in Jesus beyond what he might do about the nails. That is a real form of religion and a very common one. It appears in hospital wards and financial crises, and it is perfectly sincere at the time. It wants God to change the situation. It has no view at all about God.

Do you not fear God. Then the second man, and his first recorded words are not about Jesus and not about himself. There it is, the beginning of everything. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10), and here is a dying criminal, hours from the end, with no religious education anyone knows of, arriving at the one thought that no amount of pain had produced in the man on the other side. Facing death, he fears God.

Since you are under the same sentence of condemnation? He is not lecturing from above. He includes himself. We are all dying; how can you mock? The whole rebuke rests on this: we are both getting what we deserve, which is a thing almost nobody says about himself.

What does it mean to fear God? It is not cringing terror before a tyrant, but a deep reverence and awe before the holy God who is our Judge, joined, for those who know his mercy, with love and trust. It means taking him seriously: knowing that he sees, that sin matters to him, and that we will stand before him. Those who fear him are drawn to him, not driven away, because with him there is forgiveness, that he may be feared (Psalm 130:4). The thief feared God, and that fear sent him to Christ. That is always where true fear of God leads.

In a sentence. One of the criminals mocked Jesus to save himself and them, but the other rebuked him for not fearing God when he was under the same sentence.

On a Tuesday. Facing death clarifies what matters. Do you fear God? Look honestly at your prayers this week. Are they mostly requests to change your circumstances, or do they include God himself: his glory, his will, your sin, his mercy? Add one prayer today that asks for nothing but to know him.

For worship. Two men hung within arm’s reach of the Saviour of the world, and nearness alone saved neither of them. What turned one of them was grace, and the grace came from the cross in the middle. When I am lifted up from the earth, he had said, I will draw all people to myself (John 12:32), and the first one he drew was hanging beside him. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him (John 6:44). Blessed be the God who draws the dying to his dying Son, and does not wait for the Son to be finished before the drawing begins.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew and Mark report both men reviling him at first.

verseByVerse.quote: And we indeed justly, for we are receiving the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong.' And he said, 'Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we indeed justly, for we are receiving the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong. And he said: Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.

And we indeed justly. What this man says in two sentences is a more exact statement of the gospel than most Christians could manage on a good day, and he is dying while he says it. He confesses his guilt. He does not minimise, excuse, blame his upbringing or plead circumstances. He says the sentence is right. Whatever he had done, he agrees with the court: we are receiving the due reward of our deeds. That is true repentance, and it speaks as David did: you are justified in your words and blameless in your judgment (Psalm 51:4).

But this man has done nothing wrong. One more witness to Jesus’ innocence, alongside Pilate and Herod, and this from a man who has nothing to gain by saying it: the only declaration in the chapter made by someone who was himself dying.

Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom. Astonishing faith. Consider what he is looking at while he says it. Not a miracle-worker surrounded by crowds. A man nailed to a beam a few feet away, bleeding, mocked by everyone present, visibly dying, with a Roman notice over his head calling him a king as a joke. And he calls him by his name, Jesus, which means the Lord saves, with no title, and asks to be included in a kingdom that not one visible thing on that hill supports the existence of. He sees a dying man and believes he is a king who will come into his kingdom. Not even the disciples believed that at this moment.

Faith with everything stripped off it. He has no Bible, no baptism, no church, no time, and no capacity to do a single good work; he cannot even come down and be useful. He has nothing to bring except an honest verdict on himself and a conviction about who the man beside him is. And notice how modest the request is. Not save me, not give me a place. Just remember me: do not let me be forgotten when you come into what is yours, as Joseph once asked the cupbearer to remember him (Genesis 40:14). He has nothing to offer. Only faith in Jesus.

Is a deathbed conversion real? It can be, and this man is the proof. Salvation is by grace through faith, not by the length of a Christian life (Ephesians 2:8–9). If someone truly turns to Christ at the end, they are as fully saved as one who believed as a child. But this is one thief, and one is enough so that none need despair, and only one, so that none should presume. Many who plan to repent later find their hearts hardened or their time gone. If you are hearing the call of Christ today, do not wait for your last hour. Today is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2).

Do I need to be baptised to be saved? Baptism is commanded by Christ for every believer (Matthew 28:19), and a Christian who refuses it is disobeying his Lord. But baptism is not what saves; Christ saves, through faith. The thief was never baptised, because he could not be, and he was in paradise that day. Baptism is the sign and confession of a salvation already received, which is why this commentary, with the 1689 Baptist Confession, holds that it is for those who have believed, while honouring paedobaptist brothers and sisters who see it differently. So if you have come to faith, be baptised, gladly and soon; but never think that the water does what only the blood can do.

In a sentence. The second criminal admitted they deserved their punishment, declared that Jesus had done nothing wrong, and asked Jesus to remember him when he came into his kingdom.

On a Tuesday. Measure your own prayers against this one. Many Christians pray carefully and apologetically, working out in advance whether they have the standing to ask. This man had no standing whatever, and asked anyway. Pray the thief’s prayer today, in his words, when you are most aware of your failure: Jesus, remember me.

For worship. Everyone else on that hill was talking about him; one man, guilty and out of time, talked to him, and asked only to be remembered. Joseph once begged a cupbearer to remember him, and the cupbearer forgot him for two whole years (Genesis 40:23; 41:1). This King answered at once. While we were still weak, at the right time, Christ died for the ungodly (Romans 5:6), and he has never forgotten one of them. Blessed be the dying King whose memory is mercy, who remembers the sinner and remembers his sins no more (Hebrews 8:12).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, 'Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to him: truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.

Truly, I say to you. A solemn promise. He asked to be remembered. He is told he will be accompanied. Take the answer in its parts, because each gives more than was requested.

Today. Not at the resurrection, not after an interval of waiting, not once something further has been done about him. Before the sun goes down on the worst day of his life, this man will be somewhere else entirely. Today is Luke’s great word of present salvation: unto you is born this day (2:11); today this Scripture has been fulfilled (4:21); today salvation has come to this house (19:9). There is no purgatory in that sentence and no room for one: the same day, straight through, from a Roman cross to paradise.

You will be with me. That is the heart of it, and the heart of heaven: being with Jesus. Paradise is not described, and it does not need to be. Paul says the same thing when he thinks of his own death: his desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better (Philippians 1:23); away from the body and at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Whatever else heaven contains, its content is a person, and the man who has him has everything in it.

In paradise. The word is Persian in origin and means a walled garden, a royal park. The Greek Old Testament uses it of the garden of Eden (Genesis 2:8), and the New Testament of the place of the blessed dead with God: Paul was caught up into paradise (2 Corinthians 12:4), and the tree of life is in the paradise of God (Revelation 2:7). Eden restored. So the last promise Jesus makes to anyone before he dies is that the garden is open again, and he says it to a criminal. The thief would be with Christ that very day, in the presence of God.

What it shows. Salvation is by grace through faith alone. The thief had no good works, no baptism, no communion, and no time for any of them. He was saved by trusting Jesus. And at death, believers go immediately to be with Christ, conscious and blessed, awaiting the resurrection of the body.

Where Christians differ: purgatory and soul sleep. Roman Catholic teaching holds that most of the saved must pass through purgatory after death, to be purified before they enter heaven. Others teach soul sleep: that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. And some have tried to move the comma, reading I say to you today, you will be with me, so that today describes when Jesus spoke rather than when the man would arrive. The Greek carries no punctuation, so the question is fair. But truly I say to you is a fixed formula on Jesus’ lips, used scores of times in the Gospels, and not once does it take a trailing today; and it would be a pointless thing to say, since the man could hardly have supposed he was being answered on some other day. Verdict: today goes naturally with you will be with me, as Luke uses the word elsewhere. The thief, a criminal with no time for penance, went straight to paradise with Christ. There is no purgatory: Christ’s sacrifice is sufficient, for by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14), and the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). And there is no soul sleep: believers who die are with the Lord at once, consciously, which is why Paul could call it far better (Philippians 1:21–23), and why the souls under the altar speak (Revelation 6:9–10). The Confession puts it carefully: the souls of men neither die nor sleep, and the souls of the righteous, being then made perfect in holiness, are received into the highest heavens, where they behold the face of God, waiting for the full redemption of their bodies (Westminster 32.1).

Where was Jesus between his death and resurrection? His body lay in the tomb, and his soul went to the Father: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit (v. 46). That is why he could promise the thief today. The creed’s phrase he descended into hell has been read in different ways; the Heidelberg Catechism (Question 44) understands it as the anguish he suffered on the cross, and others as his remaining under the power of death until the third day. It does not mean he went to suffer further after he had said that it was finished, nor that he gave a second chance to the dead.

Are my loved ones who died in Christ aware and happy now? Yes. They are with the Lord, conscious, at rest from their labours, and blessed (Revelation 14:13). They are not asleep in the sense of being unaware; when Scripture calls death sleep (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14), it speaks of the body resting until it is raised and of death’s gentleness for the believer, not of the soul’s unconsciousness. We are not told what they know of us, and we must not try to contact them (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). But we can grieve with hope, because they are with Christ, which is far better.

If they are already in paradise, why do we still need the resurrection? Because God made us body and soul, and he will not leave half of us in the grave. The state of believers between death and resurrection is blessed but not yet complete. Paul longs not to be unclothed but further clothed (2 Corinthians 5:4). At Christ’s return the dead in Christ will be raised with glorious bodies like his (1 Thessalonians 4:16; Philippians 3:21), and the paradise the thief entered that day will become a whole new creation. The thief’s body went into a criminal’s grave; it will come out as Christ’s did.

In a sentence. Jesus solemnly promised the criminal that he would be with him in paradise that very day.

On a Tuesday. Read this verse to anyone who thinks it is too late: a man raised near the church but never committed, dying in a hospice, wanting to know whether there is time. This verse is the answer, and it is unqualified. There was no baptism, no restitution, no probation, no evidence of a changed life, because there was no life left in which to change. There was a confession, a recognition and a request, and Jesus took him home that afternoon. And if you belong to Christ, take this verse to bed with you tonight: whatever day you die, it will be today, with him.

For worship. In Luke’s account the last person Jesus speaks to before he commits his spirit to the Father is a convicted criminal, and he speaks to him about a garden. The first Adam was driven out of paradise, and cherubim with a flaming sword guarded the way back (Genesis 3:24). The last Adam, dying on a tree, opened it with a word, and walked a thief in. The sword that barred the gate had awoken against the Shepherd (Zechariah 13:7), so that the garden could stand open to the guilty; and for everyone who trusts him, the day of death is simply today, with him.
verseByVerse.note: “Paradise” is a Persian word for a walled garden, used for the dwelling of God’s people after death.

parallels.desc: the tree of life in the paradise of God

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 44–56 — The Death of Jesus and the Burial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
From noon until three the land goes dark — not an eclipse, which is impossible at Passover full moon and never lasts three hours, and Luke names no mechanism, only that the sun's light failed. The Old Testament supplies the meaning: I will make the sun go down at noon (Amos 8:9), and the three-day darkness over Egypt, the plague just before the night the firstborn died. This is the sign of judgment, falling this time on one man.

And the temple curtain tears — a woven hanging some sixty feet high, guarding the room nobody entered but the high priest, once a year, with blood. Matthew and Mark record the direction: from top to bottom, where no hand could reach.

Then, with a loud voice — which is not how crucified men died — Father, into your hands I commit my spirit. It is Psalm 31:5, which later Jewish tradition used as a prayer before sleep, with one word added: Father. And he breathes his last.

The centurion praises God and says certainly this man was innocent. The crowds who came for a spectacle go home beating their breasts — the gesture of the justified tax collector in 18:13. And his acquaintances and the women from Galilee stand at a distance, watching, having been there through all of it.

Joseph of Arimathea, a council member who had not consented to the verdict and who was waiting for the kingdom of God, goes to Pilate and asks for the body — a request that publicly identifies him with a man executed for treason. He takes it down, wraps it in linen, and lays it in a rock-cut tomb where no one had ever been laid.

It is the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath is beginning. The women see the tomb and how the body was laid, go home and prepare spices against the clock — and then, with the jars ready by the door, rest according to the commandment.
verseByVerse.theology:
The darkness is judgment language, not grief. The blow that fell on Egypt and was promised on Israel falls here on the Lamb, in the middle of the day, in the dark, so that it need not fall on anyone else.

The tearing of the veil is the architecture of the atonement. For fifteen centuries the message of that room was not yet, and not you. Hebrews states the consequence exactly: we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Heb. 10:19–20). It was torn from the top and has never been mended.

A reader who knows Matthew and Mark will notice that Luke has no cry of dereliction. He has not softened the death. No Gospel records the horror more directly — the agony, and the sweat like blood and the strengthening angel that are Luke's alone. He shows the abandonment in Gethsemane and chooses trust for the last moment, and both are true. Stephen would die with almost the same words on his lips (Acts 7:59).

And the burial is not an appendix. Paul lists it among the four facts of first importance — died, was buried, was raised, appeared (1 Cor. 15:3–5) — because it proves he was dead and supplies the address at which he stopped being dead. A rock-cut tomb with one entrance, previously unused, its location known to a named councillor and to the women watching. Isaiah had written it: and with a rich man in his death (Isa. 53:9).
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 47 rewards a reader who compares Gospels. Mark's centurion says truly this man was the Son of God; Luke's says certainly this man was innocent. A man watching an execution says more than one sentence, and each writer keeps the one that serves his account. Luke is building a case for a Roman reader who will shortly read a second volume full of Christians before magistrates: the founder of this movement was examined by every competent authority, pronounced innocent by all of them, and executed anyway.

Verse 49 is for anyone whose service to Christ has been the kind nobody records. The women who had followed him from Galilee had been funding the ministry out of their own means (8:2–3). The twelve are gone; the women are still on the hillside. They see him die, they see where he is buried and how, and they are the first human beings on earth to hear that he is alive — and in that world their testimony would not have been admitted in a court.

Verse 54 leaves a gap that the church has never quite known what to do with, and a great deal of Christian life is lived in it: not the crisis and not the deliverance, but the flat interval afterwards when nothing whatever is moving and prayers appear to land nowhere. Nothing here suggests that gap means abandonment. The most decisive work in history had just been finished, and from the outside on the Saturday it looked exactly like defeat.

And vv. 55–56 describe faithfulness with no feeling left in it. The spices are made up, the tomb is a walk away, every instinct says go — and the commandment says rest, so they rest a whole day with the jars by the door. Anyone who has kept turning up, praying with nothing in it, holding the line in the dark, is standing where those women stood, and should notice how their Saturday ended.

verseByVerse.quote: It was now about the sixth hour, and there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour, while the sun's light failed. And the curtain of the temple was torn in two.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was now about the sixth hour, and there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour, while the sun’s light failed. And the curtain of the temple was torn in two.

It was now about the sixth hour. The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about three in the afternoon. So this is not evening coming on early. It is darkness at the brightest part of the day, for three hours.

There was darkness over the whole land. The Old Testament had already supplied the meaning. Amos, prophesying judgment: I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight (Amos 8:9). And Egypt had a darkness that could be felt for three days (Exodus 10:21–22), the plague immediately before the Passover lamb. So the sign is not merely grief. It is judgment, and the reason for the darkness is the reason the sky went black over Egypt: God is dealing with sin. Only this time the blow does not fall on a nation. It falls on one man, in the middle of the day, in the dark. The judgment against sin was falling on the Son.

While the sun’s light failed. Not an eclipse, and it is worth saying so, because the suggestion is sometimes made and it will not work. Passover falls at full moon, and a solar eclipse cannot happen at full moon; besides, no total eclipse lasts more than a few minutes. Luke says only that the sun’s light failed, and leaves the mechanism alone. It was a supernatural darkness.

And the curtain of the temple was torn in two. The second sign happens across the city, where nobody at Golgotha could see it. The curtain separated the Most Holy Place, the place of God’s presence, from the rest of the temple. Behind it nobody went: one man, one day a year, with blood, and not without trembling (Leviticus 16; Hebrews 9:7). The whole architecture of Israel’s worship was a statement that the way in was closed. Matthew and Mark note the direction of the tear: from top to bottom (Mark 15:38). Nobody could reach the top. That is not vandalism; it is a verdict, passed from above. Torn: the way into God’s presence is open through the death of Christ. We have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Hebrews 10:19–20). And it was a sign that the temple system was ending. Luke places the tearing before Jesus’ death, Mark after it; Luke groups the signs together.

Can I really come to God directly, without a priest? Yes, through Christ, and only through him. The curtain is torn for everyone who trusts in Jesus. There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and he is our great high priest. You do not need a human priest to confess to, a saint to plead for you, or a holy building to stand in. You may pray to the Father, in Jesus’ name, anywhere, at any hour, about anything. Pastors are given to teach and care for you, and fellow believers to pray with you, but none of them stands between you and God. The way in is open, and it is open because of blood.

In a sentence. From noon until three, darkness covered the land as the sun failed, and the temple curtain was torn in two.

On a Tuesday. If you have been keeping God at a distance, praying only through set words, or only in church, or not at all because you feel unworthy, come directly today. Go into a room, shut the door, and speak to your Father plainly, in Jesus’ name. The curtain is torn; you do not need to knock on it.

For worship. For fifteen centuries the message of that curtain was: not yet, and not you. In one afternoon, while the sky was dark and a man was dying outside the walls, God tore it from the top and left it hanging open, and it has never been mended. The darkness fell on the Son so that the light of the holy place could stream out to sinners. He went out into the dark so that we could walk into the presence, and the God who once dwelt behind a veil now meets his children at a throne of grace (Hebrews 4:16).
verseByVerse.note: The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m. The curtain separated the Most Holy Place from the rest of the temple.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus, calling out with a loud voice, said, 'Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!' And having said this he breathed his last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jesus, calling out with a loud voice, said: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! And having said this he breathed his last.

Calling out with a loud voice. That is not how crucified men died. Death on a cross came by exhaustion and suffocation, and the end was a fading, not a shout. Every observer on that hill would have known the difference. He chose the moment of his death (John 10:18).

Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! The words are a quotation: Psalm 31:5, into your hand I commit my spirit. Later Jewish tradition used that verse as an evening prayer, said before sleep, the last thing said before the dark. Jesus dies with a bedtime prayer, trusting his Father. And he added one word to it. The psalm says, into your hand. He says, Father. The relationship is unbroken. Commit is paratithemai, to deposit, to place something valuable into safe keeping. It is not resignation but a deliberate entrusting. Stephen, dying, would say almost the same words, addressed to Jesus (Acts 7:59), because that is what the first Christians did with this sentence: they took it as the pattern for how to die.

Where is the cry of dereliction? A reader who knows Matthew and Mark will notice something missing, and it should be faced rather than passed over. In those Gospels the cry from the cross is, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me (Mark 15:34), and Luke does not have it. Has he softened the death? He has not, and the answer is in what he has already given. No Gospel records the horror of that night more directly than Luke’s: the agony in the garden, the sweat like blood and the angel sent to strengthen him, which are his alone. Luke has shown the anguish; he shows it in Gethsemane. What he chooses for the last moment is the other true thing about it, and both are needed. The cry of dereliction tells you what the cross cost. This word tells you how it ended. It is the word of perfect trust, the work finished. After the darkness, after whatever passed in those three hours that no writer describes, the last sentence out of his mouth is the one a child says to a father he is sure of.

And having said this he breathed his last. He died. Truly. Not a swoon, not an appearance of death, but the separation of his soul from his body. The Son of God died.

How can I die well? By learning to say this prayer before you need it. Jesus did not invent new words at the end; he used a psalm he had known all his life. So fill your memory now with Scripture and with prayers of trust: Psalm 23, Psalm 31, Romans 8, John 14. Settle your trust in Christ while you are well. Put your affairs in order, forgive those you need to forgive, and tell those you love that you belong to him. And when the time comes, whether slowly or suddenly, you may commit your spirit to the Father with confidence, because Jesus has gone ahead of you and is waiting to receive you (Acts 7:59).

In a sentence. Jesus called out loudly, Father, into your hands I commit my spirit, and died.

On a Tuesday. Pray his prayer tonight before you sleep: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit. Teach it to your children. Then make it the pattern of your days as well: hand over to him the things you cannot hold.

For worship. He was not overcome. He called out, in a strong voice, at the moment of his choosing, in the words of a child going to sleep, and then he gave up his spirit, which nobody was able to take from him. The Prince of life laid down his life with a prayer, and because he did, death for every believer is only this: placing our spirit in the Father’s hands, and being at once with him, received by the one who went that way first.
verseByVerse.note: Later Jewish tradition used Psalm 31:5 as an evening prayer.

parallels.desc: into your hand I commit my spirit

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the centurion saw what had taken place, he praised God, saying, 'Certainly this man was innocent!' And all the crowds that had assembled for this spectacle, when they saw what had taken place, returned home beating their breasts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the centurion saw what had taken place, he praised God, saying: certainly this man was innocent! And all the crowds that had assembled for this spectacle, when they saw what had taken place, returned home beating their breasts.

When the centurion saw what had taken place. The first voice after the death belongs to the officer in charge of killing him. A centurion commanded a century, nominally a hundred soldiers and in practice about eighty, and had generally served for years to get there. This one had run executions before; it was routine duty for the garrison. He is the last man on that hill who could be moved by sentiment.

He praised God. A Roman soldier praising God at the cross. Luke loves that response; it is how his Gospel greets every mighty work of God (2:20; 5:25; 7:16; 18:43). Even here, at a death, someone glorifies God.

Certainly this man was innocent! The Greek is dikaios: righteous, or innocent, depending on the setting. In Mark he says, truly this man was the Son of God (Mark 15:39); a man watching an execution says more than one sentence, and each writer has kept the one that serves his account. Luke’s choice is the key to his whole passion narrative. Count the verdicts: Pilate three times (vv. 4, 14, 22); Herod (v. 15); the dying criminal (v. 41); and now the officer commanding the execution squad, the last voice, and a Gentile one. Luke is building a case for a Roman reader. Theophilus is about to read a second volume in which Christians are dragged before magistrates and the charges keep collapsing, so Luke establishes that their founder was pronounced innocent by every competent authority, and executed anyway. That is not a smaller confession than Mark’s. It is the same verdict from the other side: Mark tells you who he was, and Luke tells you what Rome could not find in him. The righteous one has died for the unrighteous (1 Peter 3:18).

And all the crowds that had assembled for this spectacle returned home beating their breasts. They came for a spectacle, a show, and they go home beating their breasts in grief and remorse. That gesture has appeared once before in this Gospel, and it is worth remembering where. A tax collector, standing far off, who would not even lift his eyes to heaven, beat his breast and said, God, be merciful to me, a sinner, and Luke says that man went home justified (18:13–14). Here is the beginning of repentance, and it would bear fruit at Pentecost, when the people were cut to the heart (Acts 2:37).

What did the centurion actually understand? Probably not everything. He saw how Jesus died: the prayer for his killers, the promise to the thief, the darkness, the loud cry of trust, and he knew this was no criminal. Whether he believed in Jesus as Lord we are not told. But he praised God, and in that moment he spoke truer words than the council. God often begins with a person there: an honest recognition that Jesus is not who the world says he is. Pray for that beginning in those you love, and do not despise it when you see it.

In a sentence. The centurion, seeing what had happened, praised God and declared Jesus innocent, and the crowds went home beating their breasts.

On a Tuesday. Stand at the cross with the centurion and the crowd. Read Luke 23:32–49 slowly this evening. Then do two things: praise God for what you see there, and beat your breast in repentance for what put him there. End with the tax collector’s prayer: God, be merciful to me, a sinner.

For worship. Certainly this man was righteous: the soldier who killed him said it, and heaven had said it first. And the Righteous One did not die to keep his righteousness to himself. By his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous, and he shall bear their iniquities (Isaiah 53:11). The officer glorified God at a death, because this death was the mightiest of all God’s works, the one Luke’s whole Gospel of praise had been waiting for. And some of the crowd who went home striking their chests would be in Jerusalem seven weeks later, cut to the heart, and then washed clean.
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded a century, nominally a hundred soldiers but in practice about eighty. Beating the breast was a sign of grief or remorse.

verseByVerse.quote: And all his acquaintances and the women who had followed him from Galilee stood at a distance watching these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all his acquaintances and the women who had followed him from Galilee stood at a distance watching these things.

All his acquaintances. His friends, perhaps including some of the disciples. At a distance: Luke used that phrase of Peter in the high priest’s courtyard (22:54), and he uses it again here of everyone who loved him. They are there, which is more than can be claimed for most of the men: Luke does not put a single apostle at the foot of the cross by name. Whoever these acquaintances were, they stayed until it was over, watching someone they loved die slowly without being able to do anything at all. And they stood at a distance, which is where soldiers keep the friends of a condemned man, and where grief itself often stands. My friends and companions stand aloof from my plague, and my nearest kin stand far off (Psalm 38:11).

Alone in the middle of a crowd. Luke’s phrase at a distance echoes the Greek of the psalms of the suffering righteous (Psalm 38:11; 88:8), and the echo is deliberate: the righteous sufferer is dying, and his friends cannot come near. The one who touched lepers, took children in his arms and let a sinful woman wash his feet dies with no one who loves him within reach. He bore the distance as well as the nails. And because he was left alone, none of his people will ever be: I will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5).

And the women who had followed him from Galilee. Luke names their qualification. He has told us about them before, in one of the least-noticed sentences in his Gospel: Mary called Magdalene, Joanna the wife of Herod’s household manager, Susanna, and many others, who provided for them out of their means (8:2–3). They had travelled with him for the length of the ministry, and they had been paying for it. And they are still there. The Twelve are gone, the crowds have gone home, the rulers have said their piece and left, and the women who came down from Galilee are standing on a hillside outside Jerusalem watching the end of everything they had given three years to.

Stood at a distance watching these things. Watching: eyewitnesses. Luke is quietly building something, and the payoff is a few verses away, and again at dawn on Sunday. They see him die. They see where he is buried, and how (v. 55). They come back with the spices. The unbroken chain of witness that runs from the cross to the empty tomb is held, in this Gospel, by women, whose testimony in that world carried little weight in a court. God chose them anyway.

What does this say about women in the church? It honours them highly. In the Gospels women were the most faithful followers at the cross, the witnesses of the burial and the first to hear of the resurrection. They supported Christ’s ministry, served him, and were sent to tell the apostles. This commentary holds, with the complementarian reading of the New Testament, that the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church are given to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), and that this is a pattern of order, not of worth. Women and men are equally made in God’s image and equally heirs of grace (Galatians 3:28; 1 Peter 3:7), and every church should value, use and thank its faithful women as Luke does.

In a sentence. All who knew him, and the women who had followed him from Galilee, stood at a distance watching.

On a Tuesday. Faithfulness sometimes means simply staying, watching, not running away. If you are sitting beside someone in a long illness or a grief you cannot fix, your presence is not nothing; it is the ministry of the women at the cross. Stay. And thank someone this week whose quiet service has held your church together.

For worship. They funded a ministry, walked its roads, watched its founder die, buried him, and were the first human beings on earth to hear that he was alive. The Lord who noticed a widow’s two coins noticed these women, and wrote their faithfulness into the Gospel. He is not ashamed of those the world overlooks; he gives them the best news first.

parallels.desc: my friends stand aloof from my plague

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man named Joseph, from the Jewish town of Arimathea. He was a member of the council, a good and righteous man, who had not consented to their decision and action; and he was looking for the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a man named Joseph, from the Jewish town of Arimathea. He was a member of the council, a good and righteous man, who had not consented to their decision and action; and he was looking for the kingdom of God.

A man named Joseph, from the Jewish town of Arimathea. Luke introduces him carefully, the way you introduce a witness whose credentials matter. Arimathea was a town of Judea, perhaps Ramathaim, Samuel’s birthplace.

He was a member of the council. The Sanhedrin, the very body that had condemned Jesus a few hours earlier, so the man about to take the body down belonged to the court that condemned him. Yet Luke calls him a good and righteous man, as he described Zechariah and Elizabeth (1:6) and Simeon (2:25) at the start of the Gospel.

Who had not consented to their decision and action. Only Luke records this. Not every member of the council agreed. Luke goes out of his way to clear him, and the phrasing is precise: not the decision only, but the action. Perhaps Joseph was absent from the night hearing, or voted against it. But the passage does not hide the honest question: where was the dissent when it might have mattered? John says Joseph was a disciple, but secretly, for fear of the Jews (John 19:38). He was a good man who had kept his convictions private in a chamber where they would have cost him everything, and by the time he acts, the man he might have defended is dead. He is neither hero nor coward, but something more recognisable: a believer who was afraid, whose silence had a real cost, and who then did the bravest thing still available at the moment he had left.

And he was looking for the kingdom of God. Waiting for it, as Simeon waited for the consolation of Israel and Anna for the redemption of Jerusalem (2:25, 38). The Gospel begins and ends with faithful people waiting. And here is what Joseph’s waiting had come to on that Friday afternoon: the man he had privately hoped was the answer was hanging dead outside the city, and his own council had arranged it.

Waiting for a kingdom that had just come. Joseph thought his waiting had ended in failure. In fact it had ended in the very thing he was waiting for. A few yards from the cross a dying thief had asked Jesus to remember him when he came into his kingdom, and had been promised paradise that day. The kingdom of God was not defeated on Friday; it was won, by a King who reigned from a tree and conquered by dying. Joseph went to Pilate believing he was burying the hope of Israel. He was laying in the tomb the King who would walk out of it.

Am I a secret disciple? Many believers are at times: you love Christ, but in some setting, at work, with certain friends or family, nobody would know. Joseph’s story is both a warning and a hope. A warning, because silence when it matters has a cost, and Jesus says that whoever is ashamed of him, he will be ashamed of (9:26). A hope, because Christ did not reject Joseph, and gave him a magnificent act of courage at the end. If you have been hiding, the way forward is not despair but a step into the open: one clear, kind word that shows whose you are.

In a sentence. Joseph from Arimathea, a member of the council, a good and righteous man who had not agreed to their decision, was waiting for the kingdom of God.

On a Tuesday. If there is a committee, a board, a family decision in which you have kept quiet about something wrong, speak up this week, gently and clearly, before it is too late to matter.

For worship. A frightened disciple who had kept silent in the council found his courage only when it seemed too late, and the Lord he had failed to defend wasted none of it. Joseph’s late, trembling love was taken up into God’s plan and made the means by which the tomb, its place and its emptiness were put on the record for ever. Such is our Lord: a bruised reed he will not break (Isaiah 42:3), and the faintest flame of love he fans rather than snuffs out. He receives the courage of the fearful, and turns their last decent act into a witness to his resurrection.
verseByVerse.note: Arimathea was a town of Judea. The council is the Sanhedrin.

verseByVerse.quote: This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then he took it down and wrapped it in a linen shroud and laid him in a tomb cut in stone, where no one had ever yet been laid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Then he took it down and wrapped it in a linen shroud and laid him in a tomb cut in stone, where no one had ever yet been laid.

This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. Consider what that request cost him. Crucified bodies were not usually surrendered. The whole point of the penalty was public and continuing degradation, and Roman practice was often to leave the corpse or throw it into a common pit. To go to the governor and ask for the body of a man executed for treason was to identify yourself, on the record, with the treason. Mark says Joseph took courage and went (Mark 15:43), hours after his own council had procured the execution. Whatever he had been keeping quiet, he is not keeping it quiet now.

Then he took it down and wrapped it in a linen shroud. And then the ordinary, terrible work. Somebody had to draw the nails and take the weight of the body as it came free, and Joseph, a wealthy councillor by Matthew’s account (Matthew 27:57), did it, or stood there while it was done, and the body was wrapped in a burial cloth. John adds that Nicodemus came too, with a great weight of spices (John 19:39).

And laid him in a tomb cut in stone. Every clause from here does quiet evidential work. A tomb cut in stone: not a shallow grave that could be disturbed, but a chamber hewn out of rock, the kind wealthy families had, with one entrance, sealed with a large stone. And Isaiah had put it in writing seven centuries before, in the same breath as the transgressors: and with a rich man in his death (Isaiah 53:9).

Where no one had ever yet been laid. A new tomb (John 19:41). So that on Sunday morning there could be no confusion about whose body was missing, and no possibility that some other occupant was being mistaken for him. Like the colt on which no one had ever yet sat (19:30), it was set apart for him. And its location was known to a named member of the council, and to the women watching from a few yards away, and therefore checkable by anyone in Jerusalem who cared to walk out and look.

Did Jesus really die, or did he only faint? He really died. Roman executioners were experts in death, and the centurion confirmed it to Pilate (Mark 15:44–45). John saw a soldier pierce his side, and blood and water came out (John 19:34). His friends handled his body, wrapped it and laid it in a tomb, and his enemies sealed and guarded it (Matthew 27:62–66). A half-dead man, flogged and crucified, could not have rolled away the stone, overpowered guards, and then persuaded his disciples that he was the conqueror of death. The burial is in the creed and in Paul’s summary of the gospel (1 Corinthians 15:3–4) precisely because it is the proof that he was dead.

In a sentence. Joseph asked Pilate for Jesus’ body, took it down, wrapped it in linen and laid it in a new tomb cut from rock.

On a Tuesday. The burial is not a sad appendix to the crucifixion. Paul lists it among the facts of first importance: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day, and that he appeared (1 Corinthians 15:3–5). When you stand at a graveside this year, as most of us will, remember that the Lord has lain in one, and that graves are not permanent addresses for those who belong to him.

For worship. They laid the Lord of glory in a rich man’s tomb, in a hurry, before sundown, and rolled the stone across a room that would be famous for being empty. The hands that had made the rock were wrapped in linen and laid on it. He went down into our grave, the last enemy’s own house, and lay there as one of us, so that the grave of every believer might become a resting place for the body until the morning, and the stone over it a door that opens only one way.
verseByVerse.note: Rock tombs were sealed with a large stone.

verseByVerse.quote: It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was beginning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was beginning.

It was the day of Preparation. One short sentence of chronology, and it explains the haste of everything around it. The day of Preparation was Friday, the day on which everything for the Sabbath had to be done, because from sunset nothing could be: food cooked, lamps lit, work finished.

And the Sabbath was beginning. The Sabbath began at sundown. Literally, the Sabbath was dawning, perhaps referring to the lamps being lit, or the first evening star. So Joseph and whoever helped him are working against a clock. There is no time to wash the body properly, no time for the full anointing, no time for anything but linen and stone and a rolled door. The women watching are noting exactly where it is, because they can see it is unfinished and they intend to come back. Then the sun goes down, and nothing more can be done, and nothing more is done for a day and a half.

The Sabbath rest. On the seventh day God rested from the work of creation (Genesis 2:2). Now the Son rests in the tomb on the seventh day, his work finished (John 19:30). On the first day of the week, the new creation would begin.

The emptiest space in the Bible. That silence is worth staying in, because Luke does not hurry past it. Between the last verse of this chapter and the first verse of the next lies the emptiest space in Scripture. God had become man, and was dead, and was in a grave, and it was the Sabbath, and nobody knew anything. There is a great deal of Christian life lived in that gap. Not the crisis, and not the deliverance: the flat interval afterwards, when the worst has already happened and nothing is moving, and prayers go up and seem to land nowhere, and the only thing available is to keep the ordinary rules of an ordinary day while your heart is in pieces. Nothing in this chapter suggests that the gap is a sign of abandonment. The most decisive work in the history of the world had just been finished, and from the outside, on the Saturday, it looked exactly like defeat.

How is Friday to Sunday three days? In Jewish reckoning any part of a day counted as a day (compare Esther 4:16 with 5:1), so three days and three nights (Matthew 12:40) and on the third day mean the same span. All four Gospels say Jesus died on the day of Preparation, the day before the Sabbath (Mark 15:42), and theories of a Wednesday or Thursday crucifixion have arisen only to fit a literal count of hours.

In a sentence. It was Friday, the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was about to begin.

On a Tuesday. If you are living in a Saturday, after the loss and before any sign of hope, keep the ordinary rules of the ordinary day: get up, pray even if it feels empty, go to church, do the next duty. That is not hypocrisy; it is faith keeping the commandment in the dark. Sunday is coming.

For worship. The Sabbath came on, as it did every week, and the Lord of the Sabbath lay still and kept it. It was the stillest day in the history of the world, and the most secure: nothing remained to be paid, nothing to be added, and no power in heaven or earth could reopen the account. There remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, for whoever has entered God’s rest has also rested from his works as God did from his (Hebrews 4:9–10); and we enter it because he rested first, in a tomb, with everything done.
verseByVerse.note: The day of Preparation was Friday; the Sabbath began at sundown.

verseByVerse.quote: The women who had come with him from Galilee followed and saw the tomb and how his body was laid. Then they returned and prepared spices and ointments. On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The women who had come with him from Galilee followed and saw the tomb and how his body was laid. Then they returned and prepared spices and ointments. On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.

Followed and saw the tomb and how his body was laid. The last three verbs of the chapter: they saw, they prepared, they rested. Luke is being a historian again. They did not merely know which tomb; they watched the laying out, so that they would know what had been done and what had not. They were eyewitnesses of the burial, and on Sunday they would not go to the wrong tomb.

Then they returned and prepared spices and ointments. To anoint the body properly after the Sabbath. This is Friday evening, in the shrinking minutes before sunset, and they go home and start grinding and mixing. Stay with what that means, because it is one of the most affecting details in the Gospel. They are preparing to anoint a corpse. They expected a dead body. They did not expect a resurrection. Everything they are doing is the work you do when hope is finished. And they do it beautifully, at speed, with care, for a man who cannot thank them.

The word they had forgotten. The spices are the measure of how completely they had missed what he said. He had told them plainly that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be killed, and on the third day be raised (9:22), and again on the road up to Jerusalem (18:31–33). Their grief was real and their love was real, but their plans had no room for his promise. And the promise did not depend on their remembering it. While they ground spices, the word of the Son of God was quietly on its way to fulfilment, and on the third day it would keep itself.

On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment. Faithful Jews, keeping the law even in grief (Exodus 20:8–10): obedience with nothing left to fuel it. The spices are made up and sitting in the house. The tomb is a walk away. Every instinct they have is to go, and the commandment says rest, so they rest, for a whole day, with the jars ready by the door. There is a kind of faithfulness that has no feeling in it at all. Nobody is watching. Nothing is being achieved. The obedience produces no comfort and changes nothing, and it is done because it is commanded and God is God.

Does this mean Christians must keep the Sabbath? These women lived under the old covenant, and Christ had not yet risen, so their example does not settle the question by itself. Christians hold different views. Many Reformed and Baptist Christians, with the Westminster and 1689 Confessions, hold that the Sabbath command continues, moved by Christ’s resurrection to the first day of the week as the Lord’s Day, to be kept holy for worship, rest and mercy (Westminster 21.7–8). Others hold that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10), while the church gladly gathers on the first day, the day of resurrection, without Sabbath rules. Verdict: the second view fits the New Testament best; the first day is set apart gladly, out of joy and wisdom, not as the fourth commandment transferred to Sunday. Both seek to honour the Lord of the Sabbath, and believers should not judge one another over it (Romans 14:5–6). All agree that the day of rising is a gift, and that weekly rest and worship are wise and good.

In a sentence. The women from Galilee saw where and how the body was laid, went home to prepare spices, and rested on the Sabbath as the law commanded.

On a Tuesday. Anyone who has kept going through a season like that, turning up, praying with nothing in it, holding the line on a Monday in the dark, is standing exactly where these women stood, and should know how their Saturday ended. Keep doing the faithful thing this week, even if it feels like grinding spices for a tomb.

For worship. They rested on the Sabbath with the spices ready, and every one of those jars was wasted, because before they could use them he was up and out, and angels were asking why they sought the living among the dead. Their love brought ointment for a corpse; his love brought them a living Lord. Blessed be the God who lets his people’s faithful grief be overtaken by his joy, and whose answer to the tomb is the third day.

23.text: <sup>1</sup> Then the whole company of them arose and brought him before Pilate. <sup>2</sup> And they began to accuse him, saying, “We found this man misleading our nation and forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king.” <sup>3</sup> And Pilate asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” And he answered him, “You have said so.” <sup>4</sup> Then Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, “I find no guilt in this man.” <sup>5</sup> But they were urgent, saying, “He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, from Galilee even to this place.” <sup>6</sup> When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was a Galilean. <sup>7</sup> And when he learned that he belonged to Herod's jurisdiction, he sent him over to Herod, who was himself in Jerusalem at that time. <sup>8</sup> When Herod saw Jesus, he was very glad, for he had long desired to see him, because he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him. <sup>9</sup> So he questioned him at some length, but he made no answer. <sup>10</sup> The chief priests and the scribes stood by, vehemently accusing him. <sup>11</sup> And Herod with his soldiers treated him with contempt and mocked him. Then, arraying him in splendid clothing, he sent him back to Pilate. <sup>12</sup> And Herod and Pilate became friends with each other that very day, for before this they had been at enmity with each other. <sup>13</sup> Pilate then called together the chief priests and the rulers and the people, <sup>14</sup> and said to them, “You brought me this man as one who was misleading the people. And after examining him before you, behold, I did not find this man guilty of any of your charges against him. <sup>15</sup> Neither did Herod, for he sent him back to us. Look, nothing deserving death has been done by him. <sup>16</sup> I will therefore punish and release him.” <sup>18</sup> But they all cried out together, “Away with this man, and release to us Barabbas”— <sup>19</sup> a man who had been thrown into prison for an insurrection started in the city and for murder. <sup>20</sup> Pilate addressed them once more, desiring to release Jesus, <sup>21</sup> but they kept shouting, “Crucify, crucify him!” <sup>22</sup> A third time he said to them, “Why? What evil has he done? I have found in him no guilt deserving death. I will therefore punish and release him.” <sup>23</sup> But they were urgent, demanding with loud cries that he should be crucified. And their voices prevailed. <sup>24</sup> So Pilate decided that their demand should be granted. <sup>25</sup> He released the man who had been thrown into prison for insurrection and murder, for whom they asked, but he delivered Jesus over to their will. <sup>26</sup> And as they led him away, they seized one Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid on him the cross, to carry it behind Jesus. <sup>27</sup> And there followed him a great multitude of the people and of women who were mourning and lamenting for him. <sup>28</sup> But turning to them Jesus said, “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children. <sup>29</sup> For behold, the days are coming when they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren and the wombs that never bore and the breasts that never nursed!’ <sup>30</sup> Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall on us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us.’ <sup>31</sup> For if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?” <sup>32</sup> Two others, who were criminals, were led away to be put to death with him. <sup>33</sup> And when they came to the place that is called The Skull, there they crucified him, and the criminals, one on his right and one on his left. <sup>34</sup> And Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.” And they cast lots to divide his garments. <sup>35</sup> And the people stood by, watching, but the rulers scoffed at him, saying, “He saved others; let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, his Chosen One!” <sup>36</sup> The soldiers also mocked him, coming up and offering him sour wine <sup>37</sup> and saying, “If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself!” <sup>38</sup> There was also an inscription over him, “This is the King of the Jews.” <sup>39</sup> One of the criminals who were hanged railed at him, saying, “Are you not the Christ? Save yourself and us!” <sup>40</sup> But the other rebuked him, saying, “Do you not fear God, since you are under the same sentence of condemnation? <sup>41</sup> And we indeed justly, for we are receiving the due reward of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong.” <sup>42</sup> And he said, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” <sup>43</sup> And he said to him, “Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.” <sup>44</sup> It was now about the sixth hour, and there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour, <sup>45</sup> while the sun's light failed. And the curtain of the temple was torn in two. <sup>46</sup> Then Jesus, calling out with a loud voice, said, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” And having said this he breathed his last. <sup>47</sup> Now when the centurion saw what had taken place, he praised God, saying, “Certainly this man was innocent!” <sup>48</sup> And all the crowds that had assembled for this spectacle, when they saw what had taken place, returned home beating their breasts. <sup>49</sup> And all his acquaintances and the women who had followed him from Galilee stood at a distance watching these things. <sup>50</sup> Now there was a man named Joseph, from the Jewish town of Arimathea. He was a member of the council, a good and righteous man, <sup>51</sup> who had not consented to their decision and action; and he was looking for the kingdom of God. <sup>52</sup> This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. <sup>53</sup> Then he took it down and wrapped it in a linen shroud and laid him in a tomb cut in stone, where no one had ever yet been laid. <sup>54</sup> It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was beginning. <sup>55</sup> The women who had come with him from Galilee followed and saw the tomb and how his body was laid. <sup>56</sup> Then they returned and prepared spices and ointments. On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.

24.title: Resurrection, Recognition, and Commission
24.overview:
Luke 24 is one of the most carefully constructed chapters in the New Testament. It moves through three episodes — the empty tomb, the road to Emmaus, and the appearance to the disciples in Jerusalem — each building on the last, each advancing the disciples' understanding from confusion to recognition to burning conviction to mission. The chapter does not merely report the resurrection; it shows how the resurrection makes sense of everything that has come before and commissions everything that comes after.

The Emmaus account (vv. 13–35) is Luke's unique contribution to resurrection narrative, and it is one of the most theologically rich passages in the entire Gospel. Two disciples, walking away from Jerusalem in bewilderment, encounter the risen Jesus — who does not reveal himself immediately but walks with them, opens the Scriptures to them, and is recognised only in the breaking of bread. The entire sequence is a model of Christian formation: Scripture opened, heart burning, Jesus recognised in the meal, and immediate return to the community to testify.

The final appearance in Jerusalem includes Jesus's most explicit post-resurrection teaching: that everything written about him in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms has been fulfilled; that repentance and forgiveness of sins are to be proclaimed in his name to all nations; that the disciples are witnesses; and that they must wait in Jerusalem for the power from on high. The chapter — and the Gospel — ends with the ascension and with the disciples returning to Jerusalem with great joy, continually in the temple blessing God. Luke's Gospel that began in the temple (Zechariah at the altar of incense, 1:9) ends in the temple. The story is complete — and about to begin again in Acts.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The previous chapter ended with jars of spices standing ready while the Sabbath was kept. This one opens with them being carried out at first light. Nobody grinds spices for a man they expect to be alive — which disposes of the theory that the resurrection was something wishful people talked themselves into. These women were carrying embalming materials, and their only practical worry was who would move the stone.

It was already moved. Luke describes no rolling, no earthquake, no angel heaving at it; he simply reports the state of things on arrival. And the stone was not moved to let him out — a body that would enter a locked room that evening needed no doorway. It was moved to let them in.

Then the first fact of the Christian faith, arriving as an absence: they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. Luke uses that full title here for the first time in the Gospel, and writes it over an empty shelf.

Two men in dazzling apparel ask the finest opening question in the New Testament: Why do you seek the living among the dead? It is not a rebuke but a reorientation — they have come to the right place with the wrong category. And the phrasing claims more than he is alive again: the living is a class, a permanent condition.

The remedy the angels give for bewilderment is not new information. It is old information that was not believed: remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee. He had — three times, plainly, with the details (9:22; 9:44; 18:31–33).

They remember, and that is the first act of Easter faith on record: they believe a promise before any appearance at all. Then they run to the eleven — the men who had abandoned him — and hand over the best news in the world, and are told it is an idle tale.

Peter gets up and runs. He sees the linen cloths lying by themselves, which no grave-robber ever left behind, and goes home marvelling — which Luke is careful not to call believing.
verseByVerse.theology:
The resurrection is a bodily event in space and time, and Luke is meticulous about the physical detail — the stone, the body, the cloths — because what is claimed is not the survival of a spirit but the raising of the one who died. Paul builds everything on it: if Christ has not been raised, faith is futile; if he has, death is defeated and the future of the universe is different (1 Cor. 15:14–20).

That women are the first witnesses is one of the strongest historical arguments the Gospels contain. In that world a woman's testimony carried little weight in court, and pagan critics would later sneer at a religion resting on it. Every instinct of a forger would put the discovery in the hands of a respected man. Luke names the women, reports that the apostles dismissed them as hysterical, and leaves it standing. Nobody invents a story that embarrasses their own leadership and undermines their own witnesses.

And the angels' remember is the hermeneutical key to the whole chapter. The failure to understand the resurrection is a failure to have believed the word already given. Everything that happened had been announced in advance; the only question was whether those who heard it would take it seriously.
verseByVerse.examples:
The women's walk to the tomb is obedience with no expectation attached. They were not going out to meet a risen Lord; they were going to finish a burial. A great deal of faithful Christian service has exactly that shape, and it does not make it less faithful — it was the people carrying the spices who were first at the empty tomb.

Verses 6–8 supply the most practical test in the chapter. Think of the thing that frightens you most at present, and ask what God has actually said about it in Scripture — not what you feel, but the words. Most Christians discover they know the verse, could quote it, and have not once thought of it since the trouble began. Faith rarely fails for lack of material. It fails for lack of memory.

Verse 11 is for anyone who has told the truth about Christ and been treated as a fool. They were right, they were disbelieved, and the disbelief did not alter the fact by one degree.

And v. 12 names a real place on the road that is not a disqualification. Peter looked at the strongest evidence anyone had yet seen and went home wondering. Marvelling is not believing — but nobody who ran to the tomb stayed outside it for long.

verseByVerse.quote: But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they went to the tomb, taking the spices they had prepared. And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb, but when they went in they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the first day of the week, at early dawn, they went to the tomb, taking the spices they had prepared. And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb, but when they went in they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus.

Meaning first. Luke 24 is the first Easter Sunday, all of it one day in Luke’s telling. The women find the tomb empty and hear from angels that Jesus has risen; the apostles call it nonsense, and Peter runs to look (vv. 1–12). On the road to Emmaus the risen Lord opens the whole Old Testament to two downcast disciples and is known in the breaking of the bread (vv. 13–35). That evening he shows the eleven his hands and feet, eats before them, opens their minds to the Scriptures, and sends them to preach repentance and forgiveness to all nations, once clothed with power from on high (vv. 36–49). Then he blesses them and is carried up into heaven, and they worship him with great joy (vv. 50–53). The crucified one is alive in his body, the whole Bible is about him, and the Gospel that began in the temple with a silent priest ends in the temple with a blessing that never stops.

The setting. The chapter before ended with jars of spices standing ready in a house while the Sabbath was kept (23:56). This one opens with the jars being carried out of the door. It is the climax of the Gospel.

On the first day of the week. The first day of the week is Sunday. From then on the day of resurrection became the Lord’s Day, when Christians gather (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10). A whole new week of history began on that morning.

At early dawn. As soon as the law allowed and there was light enough to see the path. Nobody asked them to; the burial had been done, hurried but done. This is simply what love does when it has been made to sit still for thirty-six hours.

Taking the spices they had prepared. To anoint a dead body (23:56). Every step of that walk was taken in the belief that they were going to a corpse. Hold on to that, because it disposes of the theory that the resurrection was a story wishful people talked themselves into. Nobody grinds spices for a man they expect to be alive. These women were not primed for a miracle; they were carrying embalming materials, and their only practical worry, Mark tells us, was who would roll away the stone (Mark 16:3). They did not expect a resurrection.

And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb. Luke does not describe the rolling. He gives no earthquake, no angel heaving at it, none of the drama a storyteller would have supplied. He reports the state of things when they arrived: it was open, and it had been done by somebody else, before they got there. Matthew tells us an angel of the Lord did it (Matthew 28:2). And the stone was not moved to let him out. The risen Lord who would vanish from a table at Emmaus that evening (v. 31) did not need a doorway. It was moved to let the witnesses in.

But when they went in they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. That is the first fact of the Christian faith, and it arrives as an absence. Not a vision, not a voice, not a shining figure: an empty shelf in a rock chamber, and a few bewildered women holding jars they no longer have any use for. And note the title Luke chooses at exactly this point: the Lord Jesus. It is the only time in this Gospel that the full title is used. He writes it over the empty place where the corpse was supposed to be. The crucified one is the Lord.

Could the body simply have been stolen? Consider who could have taken it. His enemies had every reason to keep it and produce it the moment the apostles began preaching in the same city weeks later, and they never did.
