His friends were hiding, frightened and disbelieving; men do not go to their deaths, as many of them did, for a story they know they made up. Grave robbers leave the body and steal the valuables; here the linen was left and the body gone (v. 12). And the tomb could not explain the appearances: to the women, to Peter, to two on a road, to the eleven, to more than five hundred at once (1 Corinthians 15:6). The simplest explanation of the empty tomb is the one the angels gave.

Why do Christians gather on Sunday? Because this is the day he rose. The first Christians, most of them Jews who had kept the seventh-day Sabbath all their lives, began meeting on the first day of the week (Acts 20:7), and John calls it the Lord’s Day (Revelation 1:10). Christians differ on whether that day is the Christian Sabbath, carrying over the fourth commandment, or a day of joyful worship without Sabbath rules. This commentary holds that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, and that the Lord’s Day is his gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest rather than kept as a law of rules, while honouring those who hold the Westminster and 1689 view. All agree that every Sunday is a small Easter, a weekly announcement to the world that the tomb is empty.

In a sentence. At dawn on Sunday, the women went to the tomb with spices, found the stone rolled away, and went in but did not find the body of the Lord Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Make next Sunday morning an Easter. Before you go to church, read Luke 24:1–12 and remind yourself why you are gathering. And notice the careful arrangements you are making this week for a situation you have already decided is dead. God may already have acted.

For worship. They came with spices for a corpse and found an open door, and the first fact of the new creation arrived as an absence. The Lord Jesus had kept the Sabbath in the grave and risen on the first day, and the week has never been the same since. Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures; he was buried; he was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). The grave that held the Lord of life was emptied by the Father’s hand, and it stands open for ever as the pledge that every grave of his people will open too.
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: While they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them in dazzling apparel. And as they were frightened and bowed their faces to the ground, the men said to them, 'Why do you seek the living among the dead?
verseByVerse.commentary:
While they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them in dazzling apparel. And as they were frightened and bowed their faces to the ground, the men said to them: why do you seek the living among the dead?

While they were perplexed about this. Confused, at a loss: the word Luke used of the nations in perplexity in the Olivet discourse (21:25), with no way through. They are standing in an open grave with no explanation, and Luke says the messengers came while they were in that state, not after they had worked something out. Their first thought was not resurrection.

Two men stood by them in dazzling apparel. Angels: later the disciples call it a vision of angels (v. 23). Luke calls them men because that is what they looked like, and every reader knows what they were. Two, the two witnesses the law required (Deuteronomy 19:15). Like the two men in glory with Jesus at the transfiguration (9:30), and the two men in white at the ascension (Acts 1:10).

Do the Gospels disagree about the angels? Matthew has one angel, Mark a young man, and Luke and John two; the women named and the times differ a little too. Each Gospel is a selective, independent report, and one does not deny two: Matthew and Mark focus on the spokesman. The women seem to have come in more than one group, and Luke himself says some of those who were with us went to the tomb (v. 24). All agree on the empty tomb, the women first, and the message that he had risen. Accounts that agreed word for word would look rehearsed; these look like witnesses.

And as they were frightened and bowed their faces to the ground. Awe before heavenly messengers. The terror is the ordinary response. Every angelic appearance in this Gospel has begun with a frightened human being: Zechariah at the altar, Mary in Nazareth, shepherds on a hillside. Here the women go face down on the floor of the tomb.

Why do you seek the living among the dead? The finest opening line in the New Testament. It is a gentle rebuke, but more a reorientation. They have come to the right place with the wrong category. Tombs are where the dead are, and everything about their errand was correct except its central assumption. And the phrasing carries a claim no other sentence had yet made. Not, he is alive again, which would put him back where he was. The living: a description, a permanent condition. He has not returned to life like Lazarus, to die again. He has passed into a life that death has no further business with. I am the living one; I died, and behold, I am alive for evermore (Revelation 1:18). Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again (Romans 6:9).

Where might I be looking for Jesus among the dead? The question turns outward, and it has been doing its work on readers ever since. Many people take Jesus seriously as a teacher, an example, a great moral figure of the past, and would be embarrassed to be thought unserious about him, and every one of those categories is a tomb. It is possible to hold him in the highest regard and still be looking for him among the honoured dead, where he cannot be found. Christians can do it too, treating him as a memory, a doctrine or a tradition rather than as a living Lord to speak to today. Seek him where he is: risen, reigning, present by his Spirit, speaking in his Word.

In a sentence. As the women stood perplexed, two angels in dazzling clothes appeared and asked why they were looking for the living among the dead.

On a Tuesday. Speak to Jesus today as someone who is alive, not as the subject of a memory. Tell him what you are doing, ask him for help, thank him, as you would someone in the room. That is the difference between honouring a dead teacher and following a living Lord.

For worship. Two men in dazzling light stand in a grave at first light and ask the question that has rung through every age since: why seek the living among the dead? Every other great name in history is found among the dead, honoured and still. He alone is found among the living, and he makes the dead live. The women brought spices to a tomb, and the tomb became the doorway of life; because he lives, all who are his will live also (John 14:19).

verseByVerse.quote: He is not here, but has risen. Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee, that the Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men and be crucified and on the third day rise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is not here, but has risen. Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee, that the Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men and be crucified and on the third day rise.

He is not here, but has risen. Seven words, and everything turns on them. Has risen, ēgerthē, is literally has been raised, by God. The New Testament often puts it as something done to him, because the resurrection is the Father’s verdict on the Son. God vindicated him. The tomb was not broken out of; it was opened from the throne. This is the heart of the gospel (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee. Having announced the greatest news ever delivered, the messengers do not explain it. They tell the women to remember. Jesus had said it, three times in this Gospel, plainly, with the details: the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected and be killed, and on the third day be raised (9:22); again after the transfiguration, let these words sink into your ears (9:44); again on the road to Jerusalem, with the mockery and spitting named in advance (18:31–33). The women were among those who heard. Luke notes that the disciples did not understand, and that the saying was hidden from them. So the angels’ remedy for bewilderment is not new information. It is old information that was not believed when it was given.

The Son of Man must be delivered. Must, dei: divine necessity, God’s plan. The Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and on the third day rise. All of it happened exactly as he said.

Faith fails for lack of memory. This is the most practical sentence in the chapter. The women are in the worst confusion of their lives, and what they are handed is not an explanation of the present but a reminder of a promise made in Galilee, months earlier, on an ordinary afternoon, which they had heard and filed away. Faith very rarely fails for lack of material. It fails for lack of memory, which is why God fills his book with commands to remember, and gives his people bread and wine and says, do this in remembrance of me.

Why does it matter that Jesus was raised bodily, and not just that his spirit lives on? Because everything depends on it. If Christ has not been raised, says Paul, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins (1 Corinthians 15:17). The resurrection is the Father’s public declaration that the sacrifice was accepted and the debt paid: he was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Romans 4:25). It proves he is who he said (Romans 1:4). And it is the firstfruits of our own resurrection; his body raised is the pledge that ours will be (1 Corinthians 15:20). A spirit living on would prove none of this. An empty tomb proves all of it.

In a sentence. The angels said Jesus was not there but had risen, and reminded them of his words in Galilee that he must be handed over, crucified and raised on the third day.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test, and it is uncomfortable. Think of the thing that is frightening you most just now. Ask what God has actually said about it in Scripture: not what you feel, but the words. Most of us find we know the verse and have not once thought of it since the trouble began. Write it down today and say it aloud.

For worship. He told them in Galilee, on the road, in the plainest words he had, and they were standing in an empty tomb before it occurred to them that he had meant it. And he had. The Son of Man went into the hands of sinful men, and came out of the hands of death, exactly as he said. His people forget his promises; he never does. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away (21:33).

verseByVerse.quote: And they remembered his words, and returning from the tomb they told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they remembered his words, and returning from the tomb they told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest.

And they remembered his words. Five words, and they are the first act of Easter faith recorded by anyone. Nothing has been proved to them. They have not seen him. What they have is an empty tomb, a message from two figures they could not identify, and a sentence from Galilee suddenly coming back with everything in it that they had missed the first time. And it is enough. They believe a promise, on the strength of a word already given, before any appearance at all. The beginning of faith: remembering what Jesus said, and seeing it fulfilled.

Returning from the tomb they told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest. No reflection, no waiting to see, no discussion of whether they would be believed: they remembered, and they went, to the eleven. The eleven are not named at the cross. They had slept in the garden, Peter had denied him, and none of them had come to the tomb. The women had every human reason to nurse a grievance, and none of it appears. They ran to the men who had abandoned him with the best news in the world and handed it over. The first witnesses of the resurrection were women, and they became the first messengers of the risen Lord, who let the news of his victory go first to the men who had run away, carried by those who had stayed. The first proclamation of the Christian era was made to a room of disillusioned men who did not want to hear it, and every proclamation since has had roughly the same shape.

Faithful in the background. Luke has tracked this group across three chapters without once putting them in the foreground. They funded the ministry (8:3), watched the crucifixion when the men had gone (23:49), marked the tomb (23:55), rested with the spices ready, and came at dawn. They had been there for everything, and they were the first to be told, and the first to tell.

May every Christian share the good news, women included? Yes, gladly. These women were sent with the message, and in Acts the whole church, men and women, went about speaking the word (Acts 8:4), Priscilla with Aquila explaining the way of God to Apollos (Acts 18:26). Every believer is a witness to Christ, at home, at work, among friends. The New Testament reserves the office of elder and the authoritative teaching of the gathered church to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7), but that does not silence anyone from telling a neighbour, a child or a colleague that Jesus is risen.

In a sentence. The women remembered his words, returned from the tomb, and told everything to the eleven and the others.

On a Tuesday. Tell what you know of the risen Christ, even if you are not sure you will be believed. Think of one person who has let you down, or who is far from God, and ask whether you have kept good news from them because of the hurt. Take it to them anyway.

For worship. Before a single apostle believed, a few women believed a promise, and the risen Lord has built his church on that footing ever since: his word, remembered and trusted. Nothing had been proved to them, and nothing more was needed, because the word was his. Such is the King of Easter: his first heralds were the overlooked and his first hearers the ashamed, and he has never ranked his messengers by anything but love. Blessed be the Lord whose spoken promise is as sure as his opened grave.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it was Mary Magdalene and Joanna and Mary the mother of James and the other women with them who told these things to the apostles, but these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was Mary Magdalene and Joanna and Mary the mother of James and the other women with them who told these things to the apostles, but these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them.

Mary Magdalene and Joanna and Mary the mother of James. Luke names them, and the naming is deliberate. In a document of this kind, names are checkable. Mary Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out (8:2). Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod’s household manager (8:3), a woman of position whose husband worked in the palace of the man who had mocked Jesus two days earlier; only Luke names her. Mary the mother of James. These were living people, with addresses, when Luke wrote. Named eyewitnesses.

But these words seemed to them an idle tale. Luke reports the apostles’ reaction without softening it. The word is lēros, and in Greek medical writing it is used of the babbling of a delirious patient. It appears nowhere else in the New Testament. The apostles did not simply doubt the report; they dismissed it as the raving of women unhinged by grief. They were not gullible.

And they did not believe them. Two things follow. The first is that this is one of the strongest arguments the Gospels contain: nobody inventing a resurrection story in the first century would do this. A woman’s testimony carried little weight in court at the time, and a pagan critic would later sneer at the whole religion as resting on the word of a hysterical woman. Every instinct of a forger would be to put the discovery in the hands of a respected man. Luke puts it in the hands of women whose report was rejected by the apostles themselves, and he names them. Nobody makes up a story that embarrasses their own leaders and undermines their own witnesses. The second is pastoral, for anyone who has told the truth about Christ and been treated as a fool. They were right, and they were disbelieved, and the disbelief did not alter the fact by one degree. Within the hour some of those same men would be running to a tomb.

Unbelief met by the Lord himself. Luke does not leave the apostles in their scorn. That same evening the Lord would stand among them, show them his hands and feet and eat in front of them (vv. 36–43). He sent no rebuke by the women; he came himself. Their unbelief was met not with a lecture but with his own presence, wounds and all, and that has been his way with doubting disciples ever since.

Is it wrong to have doubts? Doubt is not the same as unbelief. The apostles began here as sceptics, and Jesus dealt with them patiently and with evidence (vv. 38–43). Many sincere Christians go through seasons of honest questions. The right response is not to hide them or to feed them, but to bring them into the light: read the evidence, talk to a mature believer, pray as the father did, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24). What Scripture warns against is not the struggling doubter but the settled refusal to believe what God has made plain. Be merciful to those who doubt (Jude 22), including yourself.

In a sentence. The women told the apostles, but the apostles thought their words were nonsense and did not believe them.

On a Tuesday. If a friend tells you the resurrection is a fairy tale, do not be rattled: the first people to say so were the apostles. Offer to read Luke 24 and 1 Corinthians 15 with them, and look at the evidence together.

For worship. The apostles called the gospel nonsense on Sunday morning, and in later years they would die for it. God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise (1 Corinthians 1:27): the testimony of women a court would not hear, delivered to men who would not believe it, about a crucified man the world had finished with. And through that foolishness the living Christ has gathered his church from every nation, so that the idle tale of one morning has become the hope of the world.
verseByVerse.note: A woman’s testimony carried little weight in court at the time; no one inventing the story would have made women the first witnesses.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter rose and ran to the tomb; stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths by themselves; and he went home marveling at what had happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter rose and ran to the tomb; stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths by themselves; and he went home marvelling at what had happened.

But Peter rose and ran to the tomb. Everyone else stayed sitting. Peter ran. This is the man whose last recorded act was to weep bitterly in a courtyard after denying three times that he knew Jesus. He has not been restored yet; that comes later in the day, in a meeting Luke will mention and refuse to describe (v. 34). He has spent two days with the worst thing he ever did sitting on his chest, and the moment he hears the tomb is open, he is out of the door. John tells us that another disciple ran with him (John 20:3–10). And Peter could run because of a prayer: Jesus had prayed for him that his faith would not fail, and that when he had turned again he would strengthen his brothers (22:32). That tells you something true about repentance. Shame’s instinct is always to withdraw, and if the report were true, Peter would have to face the man he had disowned. He ran anyway. Real sorrow for sin moves towards Christ, not away from him; that is the whole difference between Peter and Judas, and it is visible here in a pair of running feet.

He saw the linen cloths by themselves. Stooping to look in through the low entrance, he saw the linen, not disturbed, not gone, not taken: the wrappings lying there without a body in them. This was not the scene of a robbery. Anyone stealing a corpse takes it as it lies; nobody unwraps a body in the dark and carries it out naked, leaving the valuable linen behind. Something had happened.

And he went home marveling at what had happened. Not yet believing fully. Luke is precise, and the honesty is a mercy. Peter looked at the strongest physical evidence anyone had yet seen and walked home wondering, with the thing not yet settled in him. Later that day the Lord would appear to him (v. 34).

Textual note. Some manuscripts omit this verse, as the ESV notes, but it is well attested in the earliest and best copies, and John tells the same story at greater length (John 20:3–10).

What if I am still at the marvelling stage? Then you are in a real place on the road, not a disqualified one. Something has begun to move in you; the old explanations no longer fit; and settled faith has not yet arrived. Do what Peter did next: stay near the other disciples, keep listening to the word, and wait for Christ to show himself. Read a Gospel through, slowly. Ask God plainly to make him real to you. Marvelling is not believing, but nobody who ran to the tomb was left outside it for long.

In a sentence. Peter ran to the tomb, looked in, saw only the linen cloths, and went home amazed.

On a Tuesday. Go and look at the evidence for yourself. It will lead you to wonder, and to faith. And if you have failed Christ recently, do not let shame keep you away from him. Run towards him today, in prayer and in his Word, as Peter ran to the tomb.

For worship. The denier ran, and grace had already reached him before he knew it: the Intercessor who had prayed for him was alive, and was about to find him. Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation (2 Corinthians 7:10), and its feet run towards Christ. Blessed be the risen Lord, who left the linen lying in the tomb and went looking for Simon.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
On the same Sunday, two disciples walk seven miles out of Jerusalem, going over the events again and again the way grief does. Jesus draws near and walks with them, and their eyes are kept from recognising him — deliberately and temporarily, until in v. 31 they are opened.

He asks what they are discussing, and they stop dead in the road, downcast. Cleopas's reply is one of the great ironies in Scripture: are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know what has happened? He is addressing the only person alive who knows what actually took place on that hill, and Jesus does not correct him.

Their summary of him is entirely accurate and completely insufficient: Jesus of Nazareth, a prophet mighty in deed and word, delivered up by our own chief priests, crucified. Every clause is true. The sum of it is a dead prophet and a walk home. And then the saddest tense in any language: we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel — followed by it is now the third day, the very fact that should have sent them running back, offered as the closing argument for despair.

They have the empty tomb, the angelic message and independent corroboration, and they are walking away. So he gives them not more evidence but the key: beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interprets in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself — making a foreign language intelligible.

At the village he acts as if he were going farther. He will not force the door. They press him — stay with us, for it is toward evening — and at their table the guest becomes the host: he took the bread, blessed, broke and gave it, the same four actions as on the hillside and in the upper room. Their eyes are opened, they recognise him, and he is gone.

Then, and only then: did not our hearts burn within us? And they rise that same hour and walk the seven miles back in the dark — to find the room already alight with news that the Lord has appeared to Simon.
verseByVerse.theology:
Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? Necessary — the divine must that governs this Gospel. Their whole difficulty inverts here: they thought the crucifixion was the reason he could not be the Christ, and are told it is the reason they should have known he was. The suffering was never a detour from the plan; it was the plan, and the glory is entered through it rather than after it.

Verse 27 is the hermeneutical claim on which the church has read its Bible ever since. The Old Testament is not religious literature with some predictions in it. It is one book with one subject: the seed of the woman, the ram in the thicket, the lamb at the door, the serpent on the pole, the goat driven out, the servant who said nothing, the son of man receiving a kingdom. To read it without him is to miss what it is about.

And the sequence of the afternoon is the pattern the church has followed since: Scripture opened, then bread broken, and Christ known in both. This is not the Lord's Supper — it is an ordinary meal in a private house — but the Reformers' insistence stands: Word and Table belong together, and neither is complete without the other.
verseByVerse.examples:
Verse 16 describes a real and common condition of the Christian life: he is nearer than at any point you could identify, and you cannot see him, and the not-seeing is preparation rather than abandonment. These men later said their hearts had burned the whole way. At the time they would have told you they were walking home from a funeral with a stranger.

Verse 21 is for anyone currently living inside a we had hoped. Their hope was not disappointed; it was being fulfilled beyond anything they had asked, on the very day they gave it up, and the redemption they wanted for Israel turned out to be a redemption for the world.

Verses 19–20 describe a position a great many decent people hold: Jesus was remarkable, his teaching profound, his death unjust, the world would be better if people lived as he said. All true, all sincere, and it is a description of a corpse.

And v. 32 answers a question honest Christians carry privately — what do I do when the Bible feels dead? Not try harder, and not a better method. The burning came from a person, and the response is a prayer he grants: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Ps. 119:18). Note also the reverse error: they had burning hearts and were still walking the wrong way. Feeling is a gift, not a verdict.

verseByVerse.quote: That very day two of them were going to a village named Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, and they were talking with each other about all these things that had happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That very day two of them were going to a village named Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, and they were talking with each other about all these things that had happened.

That very day two of them were going to a village named Emmaus. The same Sunday. The tomb has been found open that morning, the report has been made and dismissed, Peter has been and come back, and two disciples are walking out of the city. Only Luke records this story, one of the most beautiful in the Bible. Two of them: not apostles, but disciples of the wider company. One is named Cleopas (v. 18); the other never is. It has been suggested that the unnamed one was his wife, since they arrive at a shared home and press the stranger to stay, and it is a reasonable guess and no more.

About seven miles from Jerusalem. About sixty stadia, as the ESV notes, around two hours on foot. Where Emmaus was is not certainly known; several sites have been proposed and none is secure. That is a small mark of honesty: a legend attaches itself to a famous place, not to a village nobody can now find. They are not fleeing. They are going home, away from Jerusalem, because it is over, to pick life up again.

The Shepherd goes after them. Luke’s whole Gospel has been travelling towards Jerusalem since Jesus set his face to go there (9:51). Everything has been accomplished in that city, and these two are walking away from it. But the risen Lord does not wait for them to come back. The Shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to go after the one that is lost (15:4) goes after two, on foot. The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (19:10), and the resurrection has not changed his ways.

Talking with each other about all these things that had happened. The crucifixion, the empty tomb, the women’s story. This is what grief does on a long walk: it recounts, as every family does in the week after a death, turning the events round and round, trying to make a shape of them that does not hurt so much, and getting nowhere.

Why did the risen Jesus not appear to everyone? He appeared to chosen witnesses, as Peter later said: God made him to appear, not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose (Acts 10:40–41). The resurrection was not a show to compel belief from the hostile; Jesus had said that those who will not hear Moses and the Prophets will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead (16:31). He gave his church reliable eyewitnesses and sent them to tell the world, so that we who have not seen may believe through their word (John 17:20; 20:29).

In a sentence. That same day two disciples were walking to Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, talking about everything that had happened.

On a Tuesday. Talk about Jesus with other believers, especially when you are confused. He often draws near in such conversations (Malachi 3:16). If you are walking away from something, a church, a hope, a calling, because it seems over, talk it through with another Christian before you settle into the village.

For worship. Two ordinary disciples walked away from Jerusalem on the greatest day in history, discussing a defeat that had not happened. And the risen Christ, with death conquered and every claim in the universe on his time, chose to spend his afternoon on a dusty road with two people whose names history barely kept. The King of the new creation is never too high for the lowly nor too busy for the discouraged, and the first glory of his risen life was his gentleness.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the distance is about sixty stadia; the location of Emmaus is uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: While they were talking and discussing together, Jesus himself drew near and went with them. But their eyes were kept from recognizing him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While they were talking and discussing together, Jesus himself drew near and went with them. But their eyes were kept from recognising him.

Jesus himself drew near and went with them. Luke puts the emphasis on the person: Jesus himself. Not a messenger, not a vision. And the verb is entirely undramatic: he came alongside and walked with them, as any traveller does who catches up with people going the same way. The first act of the risen Lord recorded in this part of the Gospel is to join two disappointed people on a walk and let them talk.

But their eyes were kept from recognizing him. A divine passive: God kept them from recognising him, until the right moment (v. 31). This is not a failure of observation and not a disguise. It is deliberate, temporary, and lifted later by the same hand. Mary Magdalene also did not recognise him at first (John 20:14). His risen body was the same, yet changed.

He withheld himself to give them more of himself. Why? The answer is in what the next fifteen verses contain. If he had made himself known at the roadside, there would have been joy, and there would have been no Bible study. They would have had the fact and not the meaning. Instead he keeps his face hidden long enough to walk them through Moses and the Prophets, so that when recognition came they would understand what they were looking at, and would learn to know him first through the Scriptures.

Is Jesus with me when I cannot sense him? Yes. This verse describes a real and common condition of the Christian life: he is closer than at any point you can identify, and you cannot see him, and the not-seeing is not abandonment but preparation. He has promised, I am with you always (Matthew 28:20), by his Spirit who dwells in every believer. These two later said their hearts had been burning the whole way. At the time they would have told you they were walking home from a funeral with a stranger. Your feelings are not the measure of his presence; his promise is.

In a sentence. As they talked, Jesus himself came and walked with them, but they were kept from recognising him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus walks with you, even when you don’t recognise him. Look back over the last hard stretch of your life and ask where he was quietly present: a verse, a friend, a provision, a strength you did not know you had. Thank him for it by name today.

For worship. The Lord of glory, hours out of the grave, matched his pace to two people who had given up on him, and walked with them for two hours while they explained his death to his face. Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it (Genesis 28:16). He is not a distant king who waits for us to find our way to him; he is the Lord who comes down the road and falls into step beside us.

parallels.desc: the disciples did not know that it was Jesus

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'What is this conversation that you are holding with each other as you walk?' And they stood still, looking sad. Then one of them, named Cleopas, answered him, 'Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in these days?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: what is this conversation that you are holding with each other as you walk? And they stood still, looking sad. Then one of them, named Cleopas, answered him: are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in these days?

What is this conversation that you are holding with each other as you walk? He asks a question he does not need the answer to, as he has throughout this Gospel. Where is your faith? Who was it that touched me? What do you want me to do for you? He is not gathering information. He is opening a door and letting them walk through it in their own words, drawing them out.

And they stood still, looking sad. One of Luke’s small masterpieces of observation. The question stops them dead in the road. Grief that has been talking freely between two people cannot always survive being asked about by a third; something in the stranger’s question brings the whole weight back, and they cannot walk and hold it at once. Sad is skythrōpoi: the look of someone who has stopped expecting anything.

One of them, named Cleopas. He may be the Clopas of John 19:25, whose wife Mary stood at the cross. If so, perhaps she was the other disciple. An early tradition says Clopas was Joseph’s brother, which would make him Jesus’ uncle by law, but we cannot be sure.

Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in these days? One of the great ironies in Scripture. He is addressing the only person in the world who truly knows what happened. Everyone else in that city had watched from outside: the crowd saw an execution, the council a problem solved, the soldiers a shift completed. One man knew what had actually taken place on that hill, and he was standing in the road being asked whether he had heard the news. And he does not correct him. He does not say, I was there. He asks another question and lets Cleopas go on. That is the patience of Christ. He listens to a mistaken account of his own death from a grieving man without interrupting to put the record straight, because the man needs to say it more than he needs to be corrected, and everything Cleopas gets wrong will be answered properly a few minutes later.

Is it all right to tell God that I am sad and disappointed? Yes. He asked these two to tell him, and he listened. A third of the psalms are laments: honest prayers of grief, confusion and complaint, poured out to God (Psalm 13; 42; 88). Honesty with God is not unbelief; it is faith speaking to the only one who can help. What turns lament into sin is accusing God of wrong or turning away from him. Tell him the whole thing, in your own words, as Cleopas did. Then let him answer you from his Word.

In a sentence. Jesus asked what they were discussing, and they stopped, downcast, and Cleopas asked if he was the only visitor in Jerusalem who did not know what had happened.

On a Tuesday. Tell Jesus what is troubling you. He already knows, but he wants you to tell him. Take ten minutes today, go for a walk if you can, and tell him the thing you have been going over and over in your head, from the beginning, as if he had not heard it.

For worship. He asked them what they were talking about, and stood in the road, and let two heartbroken people tell him he must be the only man in Jerusalem who had not heard. How gentle he is with our confusion. He knows our frame (Psalm 103:14), and he is never too great to listen to the small, wrong, sad story of a disciple.
verseByVerse.note: Cleopas may be the Clopas of John 19:25.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'What things?' And they said to him, 'Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, a man who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people, and how our chief priests and rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to them: what things? And they said to him: concerning Jesus of Nazareth, a man who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people, and how our chief priests and rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him.

Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, a man who was a prophet mighty in deed and word. What things? Two words from him, and he has them telling the story. What follows is a small creed, and it is worth taking seriously as what these disciples actually believed on Easter afternoon, because everything in it is true, and it is not enough. Jesus of Nazareth: the right man, correctly identified. A prophet: true; Moses had said one would come (Deuteronomy 18:15). Mighty in deed and word, and in that order, which is how Luke has told the story. Before God and all the people: his ministry was public, and God attested it (Acts 2:22). A good description, but limited. Not yet the Son of God.

And how our chief priests and rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him. The history, accurate to the last detail. They do not blame Rome, which would have been the easy account; they say our leaders did this, and use Luke’s word for Pilate’s act, delivered him up (23:25). So here is a man with the facts entirely straight and no gospel at all. Every clause is correct, and the sum of it is a dead prophet and a walk home. Notice the word missing. They call him a prophet. They do not call him the Christ, and they are about to be told by the man walking beside them that they had it in the Scriptures all along.

What is the difference between knowing about Jesus and knowing him? A great many people are not hostile to Christianity in the least. Jesus was a remarkable man; his teaching was profound; he was killed unjustly; the world would be better if people lived as he said. All of that is true, and it will not save anybody, because it describes a corpse. Knowing Christ means trusting him as the living Saviour who died for your sins and rose again, and Lord to whom you belong. This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). You can tell the difference by asking: do I speak about him, or to him? Do I admire him, or depend on him?

In a sentence. They told him about Jesus of Nazareth, a mighty prophet in word and deed, whom their leaders had handed over to be crucified.

On a Tuesday. Knowing the facts about Jesus is not the same as understanding them. Ask him to open your eyes. If you grew up in church and could recite every fact, ask yourself honestly today whether he is to you a prophet of the past or the living Lord of your Tuesday. Then speak to him as the second.

For worship. The most accurate account of Jesus of Nazareth ever given by people without the gospel was given on that road, and the man it was given to had to spend two hours explaining what it left out. He was a prophet mighty in deed and word; he is far more: the Lord of glory, the Son of the Father, the Christ who had to suffer and enter his glory. He is more than our best words for him, and he is patient until we see it.

parallels.desc: a man attested to you by God

verseByVerse.quote: But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel. Yes, and besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel. Yes, and besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened.

But we had hoped. The saddest words in the story. There is no sadder tense in any language. Not we hope, which is alive; not we never hoped, which is safe. We had hoped is the tense of a thing once real and now over, and everyone who has prayed for something and watched it not happen knows its exact weight. Hope had died.

That he was the one to redeem Israel. It was not a small or foolish hope. To redeem, lytrousthai, is to ransom, to buy out of slavery, the language Zechariah used in the first chapter of this Gospel when he sang that God had visited and redeemed his people (1:68), and that Anna used of all who waited for the redemption of Jerusalem (2:38). They wanted the promises kept and the occupation ended. They understood redemption mainly as liberation from Rome, and a crucified Messiah seemed a contradiction. They were not wrong to want God to act. They were wrong about the shape and the timing, and that is nearly always where hope goes wrong.

It is now the third day since these things happened. The more remarkable sentence. They know it is the third day. They say so. He had told them again and again that the Son of Man would rise on the third day (9:22), and here are two disciples reciting the timetable as the reason their hope is finished. The very fact that should have had them running back to the city is offered as the closing argument for despair. That is what unbelief does with evidence. It does not ignore it. It files it on the wrong side of the ledger.

What do I do when my hopes are dashed? First, tell God, as they told the stranger. Then ask whether what you hoped for was God’s promise or your own picture of how he should keep it. These two had the right God and the wrong expectation. God does not always give what we hoped for; he always keeps what he has promised, and often in a far larger way (Ephesians 3:20). Go back to his actual words, as Jesus took these two back to Moses and the Prophets. And remember Romans 8:28: not that every disappointment is good in itself, but that God works all things together for good for those who love him.

In a sentence. They said they had hoped Jesus would redeem Israel, and now it was the third day since it all happened.

On a Tuesday. Name one thing you are living inside a we had hoped about. Take it to him today, and ask him to show you what he has promised, rather than what you assumed.

For worship. They said we had hoped to the face of the risen Son of God, three days into a rescue so much larger than the one they had prayed for that they could not recognise it while it was happening to them. Their hope was not disappointed. It was being fulfilled beyond anything they had asked, on the very day they gave it up. The redemption they wanted for Israel was walking beside them, and it was a redemption for the world. Blessed be the God of Zechariah, who has visited and redeemed his people.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, some women of our company amazed us. They were at the tomb early in the morning, and when they did not find his body, they came back saying that they had even seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive. Some of those who were with us went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not see.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moreover, some women of our company amazed us. They were at the tomb early in the morning, and when they did not find his body, they came back saying that they had even seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive. Some of those who were with us went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not see.

Some women of our company amazed us. They report the evidence: the empty tomb, the angels, the message. Read what they have and then read where they are going, because the gap between the two is the point.

They came back saying that they had even seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive. The message they had heard, but could not believe. The women had seen angels, but what mattered was what the angels said: he is alive. In this retelling the sight survives and the message is held at arm’s length, and once a report is filed under that heading it requires nothing of anybody.

Some of those who were with us went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said. Peter and John (v. 12; John 20:3–10). Confirmed. They have three separate strands: the empty tomb, reported by named witnesses of their own company; the announcement of angels; and independent corroboration. All pointing one way. And they are walking to Emmaus.

But him they did not see. That is honest, and it is the sticking point: they have decided in advance what would count. Only a sighting will do. The empty tomb is a puzzle, the angelic word is a rumour, and the promise from Galilee has not entered the conversation at all. That is why the answer Jesus is about to give them is not what anyone would expect. He does not say, look at me. He spends two hours in the Old Testament, because their problem was never a shortage of evidence, and giving them more of the same kind would have left the real defect untouched. Facts do not interpret themselves.

Is evidence enough to bring someone to faith? Evidence matters, and God has given a great deal of it; the apostles appealed to it constantly (Acts 2:32; 1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Christianity is not a leap in the dark. But evidence alone does not change the heart. These two had all the facts and were walking the wrong way. What they needed was the Scriptures opened and their eyes opened by Christ himself. So give people the evidence, gladly and honestly, and also give them the Word, and pray, because only God can open eyes (2 Corinthians 4:6).

In a sentence. They told him that some women had found the tomb empty and seen angels saying he was alive, and others had confirmed the tomb was empty, but had not seen him.

On a Tuesday. If you are waiting for one more proof before you trust him, ask whether you have decided in advance what would count. Then read his Word, and ask him to open your eyes.

For worship. They were carrying the news of the empty tomb in their own mouths, walking in the wrong direction, and the answer to it was matching their stride. He did not leave them with their evidence and their sadness. He did not even give them first the sight they had demanded: he gave them the Scriptures, and then himself, and in himself the meaning of everything. Blessed be the Lord who is not content that we should know the facts about him, and will not rest until we know him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to them: O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?

O foolish ones. It sounds severe in English and it is gentler in Greek. Foolish is anoētoi, literally un-minded: without understanding, not thinking, not stupid but not putting together what they have (Galatians 3:1).

And slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Not slow of mind, but slow of heart: the word you would use of someone who takes a long time to be persuaded of something he already half knows. And notice what he does not correct. He does not say slow to believe the women, or the empty tomb. He says slow to believe all that the prophets have spoken. Their failure is not that they doubted the evidence of that morning. It is that they had a Bible. They believed parts of the prophets, the glorious parts, but not all, and especially not the suffering parts. The glory was easy to find: a throne, a kingdom, an everlasting dominion. The suffering was on the same pages and had been left unread: the servant despised and rejected, wounded for our transgressions, led like a lamb to the slaughter (Isaiah 53); the man of Psalm 22 with hands and feet pierced and garments divided; the shepherd struck (Zechariah 13:7). It was all there, and nobody had wanted it.

Was it not necessary. Edei, divine necessity again. The cross was not a defeat that ruined God’s plan; it was the plan. Consider how completely that inverts their position. They think the crucifixion is the reason he cannot be the Christ. He tells them the crucifixion is the reason they should have known he was.

That the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory? Suffering first, then glory (1 Peter 1:11): the pattern of the whole Bible. The Messiah had to suffer to redeem Israel, not by defeating Rome but by dying for sin. And enter into his glory is not a consolation offered after the suffering; it is a destination reached through it. The word is one of movement, of going in by a door, and the door was a cross.

Why was it necessary, and could God not simply forgive? God is love, and he is also just. He cannot pretend that sin does not matter, or treat evil as if it were good, without ceasing to be the holy God. The cross is how he can be both just and the one who justifies the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:25–26). The punishment our sins deserved was laid on Christ, our substitute, so that God’s justice was satisfied and his mercy set free. That is why it was necessary: not because God was reluctant to forgive, but because he would not forgive at the cost of his justice, and so he paid the cost himself, in his Son.

Is my suffering a detour from God’s plan? This verse answers the question a suffering Christian most often asks, though it does not remove the pain. If suffering was necessary for the Christ on the way to glory, it is not evidence of a mistake in anyone else’s case either. The same pattern holds for his people: we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him (Romans 8:17). Your hard road is not God having lost the thread. It may be the very door to the glory he has prepared.

In a sentence. Jesus rebuked them for being slow to believe all the prophets had said, asking whether it was not necessary for the Messiah to suffer and then enter his glory.

On a Tuesday. Which parts of the Bible do you skip? This week, read one of them: Isaiah 53, or Psalm 22, slowly, and look for Christ in it.

For worship. He had been raised from the dead that morning, and on that road he spent his risen voice opening the Scriptures to two people who had stopped believing them. Every page they had skipped was written about him: the pierced hands, the silent lamb, the struck shepherd, and beyond them all the glory. The sufferings and the glories were never two stories but one, and the one who lived them both was walking beside them. Worthy is the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:12).

parallels.desc: it was necessary for the Christ to suffer

verseByVerse.quote: And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.

Beginning with Moses and all the Prophets. Moses and all the Prophets means the whole Old Testament. Every preacher has wished for a transcript. There is none, and Luke does not think one is needed, because the whole New Testament is written by men who had this lesson or were taught by those who did. Beginning with Moses: so he started at Genesis. The offspring of the woman who would crush the serpent’s head and be struck in the doing of it (Genesis 3:15). The promise that in Abraham all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). A ram caught in a thicket on the mountain where God would provide, dying in the place of a son (Genesis 22). A lamb slaughtered and its blood on the doorposts so that death would pass over the house (Exodus 12). A bronze serpent lifted on a pole, so that anyone dying of the bite could look and live (Numbers 21). A tabernacle with a curtain and a mercy seat and blood carried in once a year by one man. A scapegoat driven into the wilderness carrying the sins of the people on its head. And all the Prophets: a servant pierced for our transgressions, on whom the LORD laid the iniquity of us all (Isaiah 53); a shepherd struck and the sheep scattered (Zechariah 13:7); a son of man coming with the clouds to receive a kingdom that shall not pass away (Daniel 7); a new covenant, written on the heart, with sins remembered no more (Jeremiah 31). And the kings, the Son of David, and the psalms of suffering and vindication (Psalms 22; 16; 110).

He interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. The greatest Bible study ever given. The word is diermēneusen: he explained, he translated. It is the word for making a foreign language intelligible. The Scriptures were not new to these men; they had heard them read every Sabbath of their lives. What they had never had was the key. And the claim is enormous: the Old Testament is not a collection of religious literature with some predictions in it. It is one book, with one subject, and the subject was walking down a road to Emmaus explaining himself. Jesus is the key that unlocks the Scriptures. You search the Scriptures, he had said, and it is they that bear witness about me (John 5:39, 46).

How to read the Old Testament. This verse teaches Christians how to read the Bible: with Christ at the centre. Not by forcing Jesus into every verse, but by seeing how every part points to him, prepares for him, or is fulfilled in him. Everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished, he had said on the way up to Jerusalem (18:31), and on this road he showed them that it had been.

Where should I start, if the Old Testament feels like a closed book? Start where Jesus started, with the big story, and read it with a few signposts. Genesis 1 to 3, 12 and 22; Exodus 12 and 20; Leviticus 16; Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12; Psalms 2, 22 and 110; Jeremiah 31:31–34. As you read, ask three questions: What does this show me about God? What does it show me about our need? How does it point forward to Christ? Use a reliable study Bible, and read the New Testament passages that quote the Old, especially Hebrews, which is in large part a commentary on Leviticus. Over time the shape of the whole becomes clear.

In a sentence. Starting with Moses and all the prophets, Jesus explained to them what all the Scriptures said about himself.

On a Tuesday. Choose one Old Testament passage this week, perhaps Genesis 22 or Exodus 12, and read it slowly with this question: how is this about Jesus? Write down what you see. Then read Hebrews 11:17–19 or 1 Corinthians 5:7, and see how the apostles read it.

For worship. The Author of the book had come to read it aloud. For fifteen hundred years every altar, every lamb and every promise in Israel had been pointing down the centuries at one person, and on the afternoon of the third day that person walked down a road and showed two travellers his own face on every page. The Scriptures were never a puzzle with Christ as one of the pieces; they were his portrait, drawn in advance by the love of the Father. Blessed be the Word made flesh, who is himself the meaning of every word God spoke.
verseByVerse.note: “Moses and all the Prophets” means the whole Old Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: So they drew near to the village to which they were going. He acted as if he were going farther, but they urged him strongly, saying, 'Stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is now far spent.' So he went in to stay with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they drew near to the village to which they were going. He acted as if he were going farther, but they urged him strongly, saying: stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is now far spent. So he went in to stay with them.

He acted as if he were going farther. Readers sometimes find this uncomfortable, as though it were a pretence unworthy of him. It is not. He is a traveller who has reached the point where his companions turn off, and the courteous thing, the only thing that leaves them free, is to keep walking unless he is asked. He does not force himself on them. He had joined them uninvited and given them two hours they would never forget, and at the gate of the village he leaves the next move to them.

But they urged him strongly. And they make it. They pressed him, took hold of him in the ordinary way of eastern hospitality, and would not let him go on. Hospitality to travellers at nightfall was a duty, and the roads were not safe after dark. But more: they wanted him to stay. Something in those two hours had made them unwilling to let this man walk away, and they would tell each other later what it was: their hearts had been burning (v. 32). They could not have named it at the gate. They only knew they did not want the conversation to end.

Stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is now far spent. Their reason is practical. They are not asking for more teaching; they think they are doing a kindness to a man with nowhere to sleep. The invitation that changed their lives was, on the face of it, ordinary courtesy: the great moments of the Christian life rarely announce themselves in advance. And the sentence has been the prayer of Christians ever since, for the reason they first said it: the day is far spent and the light is going. It is in the old hymn: Abide with me, fast falls the eventide.

So he went in to stay with them. He accepts the invitation. He went as far as the door and would not go in until he was wanted, and the moment he was asked he came in and sat down.

If Jesus waits to be invited, does salvation depend on my asking? Our asking is real, and he does respond to it: behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in (Revelation 3:20). But notice who began this whole afternoon. He drew near to them first, unasked, on the road, and it was his words that set their hearts burning so that they wanted him to stay. That is how grace always works. God’s call is effectual: he opens the heart, and the heart, opened, gladly invites him in (Acts 16:14; John 6:44). So we must ask, and when we do, we find that he gave us the desire to ask. Do not wait to feel sure you are chosen. Ask him in; that you want to is the sign of his work.

In a sentence. When they reached their village, Jesus made as if to go on, but they urged him to stay with them because evening was coming, and he went in.

On a Tuesday. Invite Jesus to stay with you. He will come in. Tonight, as the day ends, pray their prayer in your own home: Lord, stay with us. And look for a practical way to open your home this month to someone who would otherwise be alone at evening.

For worship. The Lord of heaven stood at the gate of a village at dusk and waited to be asked, and when two tired disciples pressed him, he went in. He who fills all things accepted a night’s lodging in a disciple’s house. And the evening they feared was the evening he chose to show himself, for even the darkness is not dark to him (Psalm 139:12). The day is far spent for every one of us, and the light is going; and the Lord who stayed at Emmaus has promised to be with his people always, to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20).
verseByVerse.note: Hospitality to travellers at nightfall was a duty.

verseByVerse.quote: When he was at table with them, he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. And he vanished from their sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he was at table with them, he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognised him. And he vanished from their sight.

When he was at table with them, he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. Look at who is doing what. It is their house. They invited him in as a guest, and at the table he takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it and gives it to them. The guest becomes the host. That happens wherever he is welcomed, and it is never announced. Four actions, and Luke has recorded them twice before: once on a hillside with five thousand men on the grass (9:16), and once in an upper room three nights earlier, with a cup and a new covenant (22:19). Whether these two had been in that upper room we are not told. What is certain is that they had seen those hands do this before, and that the hands were now marked.

And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. Another divine passive: God opened their eyes, the reverse of v. 16, by the same hand. He had held their sight; now he releases it. Perhaps they recognised the way he broke bread, or saw the wounds in his hands. Recognition, from first to last in this account, is a gift and not an achievement. It came in fellowship at the table, after the Scriptures had prepared them.

And he vanished from their sight. The instant they see him, he is gone. His risen body was not bound by ordinary limits. This has struck readers as cruel, and it is the opposite. He does not leave them with nothing. He leaves them with everything they now need, and no longer requires them to have him visible in the room. Once they knew him, they did not need to see him. He would be known through the Scriptures and the breaking of bread. And the way they behave next proves it: they do not sit down and grieve his going. They get up and run.

Word and table. The pattern of Emmaus became the pattern of Christian worship: the Scriptures opened, then the bread broken. This is not itself the Lord’s Supper; it is an ordinary meal in a private house, and the passage should not be pressed into a doctrine it does not carry. But the church’s settled instinct here is right. Christ is known in word and sacrament. The Word preached and the Supper given belong together, as the Reformers insisted, and neither is complete without the other.

Why do I not seem to recognise Christ in worship? Sometimes because, like these two, we come with our eyes held by grief or tiredness or distraction. Sometimes because we come expecting only a performance, not a meeting. Recognition is his gift, so ask for it before you go: Lord, open my eyes to see you in your Word and at your table. Come prepared, having read the passage if you can. Listen to the preaching as Christ speaking through his servant. And remember that he was present with these two long before they saw him. A dull Sunday is not an absent Lord.

In a sentence. At table Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it and gave it to them, and their eyes were opened to recognise him, and he vanished.

On a Tuesday. At your own table tonight, before the meal, give thanks as he did. Make the ordinary meal a reminder that he is the host of your life. And at the next Lord’s Supper, come having heard the Word, and ask to see him.

For worship. He had walked seven miles and preached the whole Old Testament, and it was when he broke the bread that they knew him. The Lord whose body had been broken for them broke bread for them, and then was gone, leaving them not empty but full. He gives himself still where his people make room for him, and the bread he gives at last is himself, the living bread that came down from heaven, given for the life of the world (John 6:51).

parallels.desc: he took bread and broke it

verseByVerse.quote: They said to each other, 'Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said to each other: did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?

Did not our hearts burn within us. They say it afterwards, which is the first thing to notice. Nobody said at the time, my heart is burning. It was only when they knew who he was that they understood what had been happening to them for two hours. That is very often the shape of it: a Christian looks back on a stretch of road or a hard year and sees that God was at work in him unnoticed. Even before they recognised him, his words had set their hearts on fire. Jeremiah knew the feeling: there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones (Jeremiah 20:9). In Scripture the heart is not merely the emotions; it is the whole inner person, thinking, willing, loving. So this is not a mood. It is a man saying that something caught light in him.

While he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures. Two clauses, worth separating, because most people run them together. While he talked to us on the road: the person. While he opened to us the Scriptures: the book. Neither alone did it. A stranger’s company would not have set a heart burning, and the Scriptures had been read to these men every Sabbath without producing this. It was Christ, in the Scriptures, opening them. And opened, diēnoigen, is the same word as their eyes were opened (v. 31) and he opened their minds (v. 45). Christ opens the Scriptures, opens eyes, and opens minds.

What do I do when the Bible feels dead? This is a question many honest Christians carry privately. The answer this verse gives is not, try harder, and not, find a better method. The burning came from a person, and the request that follows is a prayer rather than a technique: that the one the book is about would open it. Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). So pray before you read. Read a whole passage, not a fragment, and look for Christ in it. Read with others sometimes. Keep reading on the dull days; the fire is his to give. And add this, because the reverse error is real: they had burning hearts and were still walking the wrong way. Feeling is not the test. The fire is a gift, not a verdict.

In a sentence. They said to each other that their hearts had burned within them as he talked on the road and opened the Scriptures to them.

On a Tuesday. Before you open your Bible tomorrow, pray Psalm 119:18 in your own words. Then read one Gospel passage slowly, and stop to talk to Christ about what you read. Do it again the next day, whether or not your heart burns.

For worship. Two men who had given up on him sat in a house at nightfall and realised they had been on fire since mid-afternoon, and had thought it was only a good conversation. That is how the risen Lord kindles faith: quietly, through his own words, long before we know his name is on them. He who opened the Scriptures on the road opens them still, and walks beside his people in his Word, and his voice still sets cold hearts alight.

parallels.desc: a burning fire shut up in my bones

verseByVerse.quote: And they rose that same hour and returned to Jerusalem. And they found the eleven and those who were with them gathered together, saying, 'The Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!' Then they told what had happened on the road, and how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They rose that same hour and returned to Jerusalem. And they found the Eleven and those who were with them gathered together, saying: the Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon! Then they told what had happened on the road, and how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread.

They rose that same hour and returned to Jerusalem. The meal is abandoned. It is dark, they have already walked seven miles that day, the roads are dangerous, and the reason they gave for pressing him to stay, that the day was far spent, applies with equal force to them. They go anyway, back over the same seven miles they had walked out in despair, at night, without hesitation, because there are people in Jerusalem who need to hear this tonight. Nobody told them to. Their sadness turned to joy, and their direction reversed.

The Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon! And they arrive to a room that is already alight. Before they can say a word, the news is shouted at them. Risen indeed, ontōs: really, truly. It has become the ancient Easter greeting: The Lord is risen! He is risen indeed! And Simon: not Peter the rock, but the old name, the one Jesus used in the upper room when he warned him (22:31). Somewhere in that Sunday, between the run to the tomb and this moment, the risen Christ met privately with the man who had denied him three times. The Lord went first to Peter, to restore him.

The meeting no one described. Luke does not describe it. Neither does anyone else. Paul confirms it happened and names Peter first among the witnesses: he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve (1 Corinthians 15:5). That is all the record there is, and it is hard not to feel the tact of it. Whatever passed between those two stayed between them, and the only trace of it is a room full of people repeating a name. That is worth knowing by anyone whose own worst failure has been dealt with quietly, without a public account ever being given. The church heard that the Lord had appeared to Simon. It never heard what was said.

And how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread. Then the Emmaus pair tell their story, and Luke’s summary of it is the shape of the whole afternoon: what had happened on the road, and how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread. That phrase would become Luke’s term for the church’s fellowship meal and the Lord’s Supper (Acts 2:42, 46; 20:7).

Does God make public everything I have confessed to him? No. Some sins must be confessed to people we have wronged, and some public sins need public repentance, but much of our dealing with Christ is private, as Peter’s was. You do not have to tell everyone everything to be fully forgiven. What God has covered, he has covered (Psalm 32:1). And what he says to you in that private meeting, his forgiveness, his restoration, your new commission, is as real as if it were announced from the housetops.

In a sentence. They immediately returned to Jerusalem and found the disciples saying the Lord had really risen and appeared to Simon, and they told how they had recognised him when he broke the bread.

On a Tuesday. The Lord is risen indeed! Say it to another believer today, in words or a message. And if you have news of what Christ has done for you, do not wait for a convenient time. These two walked seven miles in the dark to tell it.

For worship. Two men who had walked away in the morning came back at night, and before they could tell their news they heard it: the Lord has risen indeed. It was the church’s first confession of Easter, called across a crowded room, and it has never stopped being said since, in every language and every century, by sinners who have met him. The one who appeared to Simon the denier still comes to the ashamed by his word and Spirit, and every restored sinner becomes another voice in that room.
verseByVerse.note: Simon is Peter.

parallels.desc: he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–53 — Jerusalem, the Commission, and the Ascension
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
He arrives mid-sentence into a locked room, and the first word of the risen Christ to the gathered church is peace — spoken to men who had failed him in the garden and the courtyard, by the one who bought it on Friday. Their response is not faith: they think they are seeing a ghost. The ancient world had a settled category for the appearance of the dead, and it was apparitions, not resurrection. Nobody in that room was expecting this.

So he offers evidence, which is a remarkable thing for the risen Son of God to bother doing. See my hands and my feet — the identification runs through the wounds. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have. And then, while they are disbelieving for joy, he asks whether there is anything to eat, and eats a piece of broiled fish in front of them.

Then he sends them back to the book. The Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms is the standard threefold division of the Hebrew Scriptures — the whole Bible they possessed, listed by its own sections. And he opened their minds to understand it: the third opening of the day, after their eyes at the table and the Scriptures on the road, all three by the same hand.

The commission follows, and it is still inside thus it is written: repentance for the forgiveness of sins, in his name, to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem — the city that had just killed him. You are witnesses of these things. And then a command nobody expects at the end of a commission: stay in the city and do nothing until you are clothed with power from on high.

Finally Bethany, and hands lifted in the priestly posture of Leviticus 9:22 — hands with holes in them. He parts from them while he blessed them, in the middle of the blessing, and is carried up.

They worship him — Jewish monotheists, on their faces, before a man they had eaten with in those forty days — and return to Jerusalem with great joy, continually in the temple blessing God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verses 39–43 close off an entire family of misunderstandings. The resurrection is not the survival of a soul, nor a vision granted to grieving friends, nor a cause living on. It is a body, with hands and feet, that can be handled and that eats. A reader who knows 1 Corinthians 15 may feel a difficulty, since Paul calls it a spiritual body — but Paul is describing not what it is made of but what governs it, as when he calls a person spiritual without meaning immaterial. Paul's argument is that ours will be like his, and Luke has just shown his eating fish.

And the wounds are kept. He did not leave the marks in the tomb as an unpleasantness now finished with; the Lamb in John's vision stands in the middle of the throne looking as though it had been slain (Rev. 5:6).

Verse 45 carries a whole doctrine. These men had the text, had heard it since childhood, and had just spent an evening with the risen Christ expounding it — and still needed their minds opened before they could take it in. Understanding Scripture is not finally a matter of intelligence or access (1 Cor. 2:14; Acts 16:14). That is humbling, and it is freeing: the right response to a Bible that will not open is to ask the one who opens it.

And the ascension is not the end of the story but the beginning of the reign — seated at the right hand of the Majesty on high (Heb. 1:3), exactly as he told the council would begin from that moment (22:69). The disciples' worship of him is the first unambiguous worship of the risen Jesus in this Gospel, given by monotheists, with nobody correcting them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Disbelieved for joy is the commonest form of unbelief among genuine Christians: not doubt that the gospel is true, but the inability to take it personally — believers who can recite justification and cannot quite accept that they are forgiven. Jesus neither rebukes it nor argues with it. He asks for something to eat. Their joy was too big to be trusted, so he made the moment small enough to be believed.

Beginning from Jerusalem is the measure of the thing announced. Any ordinary movement starts where it is welcome and works back to hostile ground later. The risen Christ orders the reverse: the first offer of forgiveness goes to the people who killed him, in the city where they did it, carried by men who watched. Three thousand of them took it in a day.

Verse 48 defines what any Christian is actually asked for. Not to have the answers to every question, and not to argue anyone into the kingdom — simply to say what he has seen of Christ, accurately, and let it be weighed. And it was entrusted to eleven men who had all failed him within the previous seventy-two hours.

Verse 49 is for anyone in a season of enforced waiting. There is a stillness that is disobedience and a stillness that is obedience, and the difference is not how it feels — both feel like wasting time. These men went nowhere and did nothing, on orders, until the power came. Zeal without the Spirit was what Peter had already shown in the garden with a sword.

And v. 52 speaks to anyone who half wishes he had been there instead of here. These men had the choice between seeing him in the room and having him enthroned with the Spirit about to come, and they went home with great joy.

verseByVerse.quote: As they were talking about these things, Jesus himself stood among them, and said to them, 'Peace to you!' But they were startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they were talking about these things, Jesus himself stood among them, and said to them: peace to you! But they were startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit.

As they were talking about these things, Jesus himself stood among them. He arrives mid-sentence, into a room where he is being discussed, suddenly. John adds that the doors were locked for fear of the authorities (John 20:19). There is no entrance described. One moment the room contains a dozen frightened people arguing about reports; the next it contains him.

Peace to you! The first word of the risen Christ to the gathered church is peace. It was the ordinary greeting, shalom. But consider who is saying it and to whom. The last time most of these men saw him, he was being arrested in a garden while they ran. Peter had denied him. If ever there was a moment for a reckoning, this was it, and what he says is, peace to you. And it is not a mere courtesy, because of where he has come from. Peace with God through the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20) was bought on Friday; on Sunday evening the one who bought it stands in the room and says the word. The angels announced peace on earth at his birth (2:14). The risen Lord delivers it in person.

But they were startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit. They have just been shouting that the Lord is risen. He appears, and they conclude they are looking at a ghost. That is not a flattering detail, which is why it is worth trusting. The ancient world had a settled category for the appearance of the dead, and it was not resurrection; it was apparitions. Everyone believed in those, and nobody thought they had bodies. So the disciples’ instinct here is exactly the instinct of their culture, and the opposite of what they are about to be made to accept. Nobody in that room was expecting a resurrection. They were expecting a haunting, and they were terrified.
