What does it mean to have peace with God? It means the war is over. By nature we were God’s enemies, under his just wrath because of our sin (Romans 5:10; Ephesians 2:3). Through Christ’s death that hostility is ended for everyone who trusts him: since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 5:1). It is not first a feeling, though it brings calm; it is a status, a settled relationship, which does not rise and fall with your mood. And from it flows the peace of God that guards the heart in anxious times (Philippians 4:6–7).

In a sentence. As they talked, Jesus stood among them and greeted them with peace, but they were terrified, thinking he was a ghost.

On a Tuesday. If you are carrying guilt over a failure you have already confessed, hear the first word of the risen Christ to his failed disciples: peace to you. Receive it today. Then carry it to someone else: make peace with one person you are at odds with this week.

For worship. He stood among men who had abandoned him and were now afraid of him, and the first word out of his mouth was the one he had bought for them on Friday. He himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14): not a truce he negotiates but a peace he is, made in his body on the cross and spoken by his risen mouth. Deserters heard it first, so that no one who has failed him need ever wonder whether it is meant for them. Glory to the Prince of Peace, who came back from the dead to say it.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, 'Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.' And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said to them: why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have. And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet.

Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? He does not scold the doubt. He asks about it, and then he answers it with evidence, which is a remarkable thing for the risen Son of God to bother doing. Gently, he deals with their doubts.

See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Why the hands and the feet? Because that is where the nails went. He is not simply proving that a body is present; he is proving whose. The identification runs through the wounds. The risen Lord is the same Jesus, the crucified one. And the resurrection body is glorious, imperishable, no longer subject to death, and it is scarred. He did not leave the marks behind in the tomb as an unpleasantness now finished with. He carried them out, and he carries them still: the Lamb standing in the midst of the throne, as though it had been slain (Revelation 5:6). The only man-made things in heaven are the scars of Christ.

Touch me, and see. Physical evidence. Not just a vision, but a body that can be handled. John would write years later of what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we looked upon and have touched with our hands (1 John 1:1).

For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have. That sentence closes off a whole family of misunderstandings. The resurrection is not the survival of a soul, not a vision granted to grieving friends, not a symbol of a cause living on, not merely his spirit living on. It is a body, with hands and feet, in a room, that can be handled. Jesus’ body was raised, transformed but real (1 Corinthians 15:42–44).

But does Paul not call it a spiritual body? A reader who knows 1 Corinthians 15 may feel a difficulty here, because Paul calls the resurrection body a spiritual body, and that sounds like the opposite of flesh and bones. It is not. Paul is not describing what the body is made of but what it is ruled and animated by, as when he calls a person spiritual without meaning that he has no body (1 Corinthians 2:15). A spiritual body in Paul’s sense is a body wholly governed by the Spirit of God: imperishable, glorious, powerful. It is not a ghost. Paul’s whole argument in that chapter is that ours will be like Christ’s, and Luke has just shown us his eating fish.

Where Christians differ: a spiritual or bodily resurrection? Some modern theologians speak of the resurrection as spiritual only: a vision, or the disciples’ renewed faith, or Jesus living on in their memory and mission. Verdict: Luke goes out of his way to insist on bodily resurrection: flesh and bones, wounds, touch, eating. The empty tomb, and Jesus’ own words, rule out a merely spiritual resurrection. As he rose bodily, so will his people: he will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21).

What kind of body will I have in the resurrection? A real body, continuous with this one, but transformed. Sown perishable, raised imperishable; sown in dishonour, raised in glory; sown in weakness, raised in power (1 Corinthians 15:42–43). No more sickness, ageing, disability or death. Recognisably you, as Jesus was recognisably himself, yet changed in ways we cannot fully picture. And the Christian hope is not the escape of the soul from the body. It is the redemption of the body (Romans 8:23), in a renewed earth, and the ground of it is standing in a room in Jerusalem holding out his hands.

In a sentence. Jesus asked why they doubted, showed them his hands and feet, told them to touch him, and said a ghost does not have flesh and bones as he had.

On a Tuesday. If you live with a body that is failing, in pain or limited, read 1 Corinthians 15:42–44 today and say it about your own body: raised in power. Then treat your body, and other people’s, as something God intends to keep for ever: with care, with purity, with respect.

For worship. He showed his friends his wounds as his signature, and he has never put them away. The hands that were pierced now hold the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18), and the body that was laid in the tomb is the firstfruits of every grave his people will leave. When we see him, we shall know him by the marks of the love that bought us. Blessed be the Lamb, risen in the flesh, who wears his scars in glory.

parallels.desc: which we have looked upon and touched

verseByVerse.quote: And while they still disbelieved for joy and were marveling, he said to them, 'Have you anything here to eat?' They gave him a piece of broiled fish, and he took it and ate before them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And while they still disbelieved for joy and were marvelling, he said to them: have you anything here to eat? They gave him a piece of broiled fish, and he took it and ate before them.

While they still disbelieved for joy. One of the truest phrases in Scripture, and only a very honest writer would have set it down. The fright has passed. What holds them back now is the paralysis of a person offered something too good to be true: not scepticism, but the fear of letting yourself accept a thing in case it turns out not to be so.

Disbelieving for joy among Christians. It is the commonest form of unbelief among genuine Christians. There are believers who can recite the doctrine of justification and cannot quite accept that they personally are forgiven, not because they think the gospel untrue, but because they cannot make themselves take it. That is disbelieving for joy, and Jesus’ response to it here is worth studying, because he does not rebuke it and he does not argue with it. He asks for something to eat.

Have you anything here to eat? It is the most ordinary sentence in the chapter and the most disarming. The Son of God, three days out of a grave, with the powers of the age to come in his body, asks whether there is anything in the house. More evidence.

They gave him a piece of broiled fish, and he took it and ate before them. Leftovers, plainly. He did not need it; nothing suggests the resurrection body requires food. He ate because they needed to watch him do it. A ghost cannot chew. Whatever they were prepared to believe about apparitions, none of it survived a man sitting down with a piece of fish. Peter would later preach that they ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead (Acts 10:41). And there is something almost unbearably homely in it. Their joy was too big to be trusted, so he made the moment small enough to be believed.

I believe the gospel, but I cannot feel forgiven, so what should I do? Look at what Jesus did here. He did not demand that they feel more; he gave them something solid to look at. Do the same with your own heart. Look away from your feelings to the facts: Christ died for sinners; he rose; he has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37); God declares the one who trusts in Jesus righteous (Romans 3:26). Come to the Lord’s Supper, where he gives you bread and wine to take into your hands. Let a trusted Christian remind you of the promises. Feelings often follow facts slowly. Keep looking at him until joy lets itself believe.

In a sentence. While they were still struggling to believe for joy, Jesus asked for food, and ate a piece of broiled fish in front of them.

On a Tuesday. Name the promise of God that seems too good to be true for you. Write it down, and next to it write the evidence that God keeps his word: the cross, the empty tomb, the answered prayers of your own life.

For worship. The Lord of glory ate a scrap of cold fish to settle the hearts of eleven men who were too happy to think straight. He who had fed five thousand on a hillside let his friends feed him, so that their joy could find its feet. He will stoop to the smallest kindness to help his people believe the greatest news, and he is as gentle still with every heart that is afraid to let itself be glad.

parallels.desc: who ate and drank with him

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to them, 'These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he said to them: these are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.

These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you. There is a small phrase here that repays attention: while I was still with you. He is with them at that moment, in the room, eating. So he is marking off a period that has now ended, the years of walking Galilee together, and speaking from the other side of it. A new arrangement has begun. And what he does first in it is what he did on the road: he sends them back to the book. He had told them, many times (9:22, 44; 18:31–33).

Everything written about me. Not a few verses, but everything. Hold the claim up to the light and it is breathtaking. A man stands in a room in Jerusalem and says that the Bible, the whole of it, is about him: the garden and the flood, the altar on Moriah and the blood on the doorposts, the tabernacle and the throne of David, the laments and the love songs, the exile and the promised return. No one else in history has said that of any book and been believed. He says it of the book God wrote, and it is true, because he is the eternal Word through whom God has always spoken.

In the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms. That is not a loose gesture at religious literature. It is the threefold division of the Hebrew Bible: the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings, here named after their best-known book, the Psalms. In other words, the whole Bible they possessed, listed by its own sections, with nothing left out.

Must be fulfilled. Dei, divine necessity again, the word that has governed this Gospel from the boy in the temple who must be in his Father’s house (2:49) to the Son of Man who must suffer. Scripture cannot be broken (John 10:35). So the claim is total. Not that the Old Testament contains some prophecies he happened to satisfy, the way a candidate meets criteria, but that the whole of it, in every division, is about him, and that it had to come out this way.

What am I to do with all the Old Testament? Every new Christian eventually asks it: genealogies, sacrifices, a tabernacle measured in cubits, kings who mostly failed, prophets shouting at a nation that would not listen. Read it as the setting-up of a story whose ending you already know. It is not a different religion stuck on the front of yours. It is the same God, working towards the same person, for two thousand years before he arrived.

Is every Old Testament passage about Christ? The whole Old Testament leads to him: its promises, its patterns and its law find their goal in him. But each passage has its own meaning in its own setting, and that must be read first. Finding Christ is not a matter of hunting for hidden symbols in every detail; it is tracing how each part of the story moves towards him, shows our need of him, or is fulfilled in him.

In a sentence. Jesus reminded them that he had told them that everything written about him in the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.

On a Tuesday. Pick one of the three sections and read a chapter from it this week with Christ in mind: Exodus 12 from the Law, Isaiah 53 from the Prophets, Psalm 22 from the Writings. Ask: what did this mean then, and how does it reach its goal in him?

For worship. All of it was for him and about him: every sacrifice smoking on an altar, every king anointed with oil, every psalm sung in the dark, every prophet’s cry of not yet. The Bible is one song in many voices, and every line of it resolves on one name. And the one in whom it all comes to rest is not a theme or an idea but a living Lord, with the marks of the nails in his hands, who sat with his friends and told them the story was his. Blessed be the Christ in whom every word of God finds its Amen.
verseByVerse.note: The Law, the Prophets and the Psalms (the Writings) are the three divisions of the Hebrew Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures.

Then he opened their minds. Nine words in English, and a whole doctrine in them. The verb is diēnoixen: he opened thoroughly, he unlocked. Luke has used it twice already in this chapter, and the repetition is deliberate: their eyes were opened at the table (v. 31), the Scriptures were opened on the road (v. 32), and now their minds are opened in the room. Three openings in one day, by the same hand. What was hidden from them before (9:45; 18:34) is now revealed.

To understand the Scriptures. The Old Testament, read in the light of Christ. And the sequence corrects an assumption almost everyone makes. These men had the text. They had heard it since childhood. Two of them had just spent an afternoon with the risen Christ expounding it. And they still needed something done to them before they could take it in. Understanding Scripture is not finally a matter of intelligence, education or access. It is a matter of a closed mind being opened by God, and he does the opening. Paul says the same from the other side: the natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned (1 Corinthians 2:14). The veil is removed only through Christ (2 Corinthians 3:14–16). And Luke shows it happening again in Acts, in almost the same words: the Lord opened Lydia’s heart to pay attention to what was said (Acts 16:14). Understanding Scripture is a gift of the risen Christ, by his Spirit.

Two consequences. The first is humbling. Nobody reasons himself into the kingdom by being clever with a text. If you understand the gospel, someone opened your mind, and you did not do it. The second is freeing, and it is where this verse belongs in a Christian’s practice. If the opening is his work, then the right response to a Bible that will not open is to ask him. It is a request this verse says he grants.

Can an unbeliever understand the Bible? He can understand its words, its history and its arguments, sometimes very well; many scholars who do not believe have explained the text accurately. What he cannot do without the Spirit is receive it as true, see the glory of Christ in it, and believe it savingly. That is why we share the Scriptures with unbelievers and pray for them at the same time. The Word is the means; the Spirit is the one who opens.

In a sentence. Then Jesus opened their minds to understand the Scriptures.

On a Tuesday. Pray before you read the Bible: Lord, open my mind to understand. Make it a habit, the first words before every reading this week. And pray it for one friend or family member who does not yet believe, by name.

For worship. He had risen from the dead, shown them his wounds and eaten fish in front of them, and none of it was enough by itself; so he reached into their minds and opened them. The same risen Lord opens minds today, by his Spirit, through his Word. Every Christian who has ever understood the gospel has been touched by that same hand. Blessed be the Christ who is not only the subject of the book but its interpreter.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to them, 'Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And said to them: thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead.

Thus it is written. Everything the risen Christ says about himself in this room is anchored to a text. He might have argued from what had just happened, and it would have been unanswerable: the wounds, the fish, the empty tomb. He argues instead from Scripture, which tells you what he intends the church to stand on when the eyewitnesses are gone. This is the heart of what the Scriptures teach.

That the Christ should suffer. That is the half nobody had wanted. Christ means the anointed King, and a suffering King was not what Israel was watching for. It was in the book all the same: in Isaiah’s servant (Isaiah 53), in the psalms of the righteous sufferer (Psalm 22), in the one whom they have pierced (Zechariah 12:10) and the shepherd struck (13:7).

And on the third day rise from the dead. A fair question: where exactly is that written? No verse in the Old Testament says in so many words that the Messiah will rise on the third day. The apostles answered it two ways. They pointed to particular texts. Peter at Pentecost quotes Psalm 16:10, you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption, and argues that David died and was buried and his tomb is still here, so he was speaking of another (Acts 2:25–31). Isaiah’s servant, after being cut off, sees his offspring and prolongs his days (Isaiah 53:10–12). Hosea speaks of being raised on the third day (Hosea 6:2), and Jonah supplied the pattern, as Jesus himself said (Jonah 1:17; Matthew 12:40). But the deeper answer is the one this chapter has made since the road: it is written not in one verse but in the shape of the whole. A story that runs from a garden lost to a people redeemed by blood, from exile to return, from a valley of dry bones to an army standing up, does not end in a tomb.

In a sentence. He told them that Scripture says the Messiah would suffer and rise from the dead on the third day.

On a Tuesday. Learn to say the gospel in one sentence from Scripture, so that you can give it to someone this week: Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, he was buried, and he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Memorise it today.

For worship. Thus it is written: the risen Lord rested the whole weight of his death and his rising on the page, and the page held. What the prophets saw in fragments, the servant cut off who yet prolongs his days, the Holy One who would not see corruption, the shepherd struck and the flock gathered again, met in one body raised from one tomb on the third day. God wrote the story before the world was old, and then came into it and lived it to the last line. Glory to the Christ who suffered as it was written, and rose as it was written, and reigns as it is written still.

parallels.desc: on the third day he will raise us up

verseByVerse.quote: and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.

And that repentance for the forgiveness of sins. Notice where this sentence sits. It is still inside thus it is written. The mission of the church is not an application drawn from the resurrection; it is part of what the Scriptures foretold, on the same footing as the suffering and the rising. This is the message, and a great deal gets preached in its place: moral improvement, respectability, a technique for a better life. Repentance, a change of mind that turns the whole person round from sin to God; and forgiveness of sins, the gift won by Christ’s death, which is the thing a guilty person actually needs and cannot obtain for himself (1:77; 3:3). They are the same words as John the Baptist’s preaching, now grounded in the cross.

Should be proclaimed. Also written: the mission is part of the Scriptures’ plan. I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth (Isaiah 49:6).

In his name. That is the authority and the ground: on his authority, by his power, through faith in him (Acts 2:38). Not in the name of the church, and not on the strength of anyone’s sincerity. Peter would put it flatly: there is salvation in no one else (Acts 4:12).

To all nations. The scope is the world, and it is the climax of Luke’s great theme. All flesh shall see the salvation of God (3:6). Simeon held a baby and called him a light for revelation to the Gentiles (2:32). Luke traced his genealogy back not only to Abraham but to Adam (3:38).

Beginning from Jerusalem. The clause to stop at. Jerusalem: the city that had just done it. The place where the crowd shouted crucify, where the council condemned him, where the soldiers blindfolded and beat him, where the cross went up outside the wall. Any ordinary movement would start where it was welcome; the risen Christ orders the exact opposite. The first offer of forgiveness goes to the people who killed him, in the city where they did it, offered by men who watched them do it. That is the measure of the thing being announced. And when Peter did preach there, about three thousand people of that city and its pilgrims were forgiven in a day (Acts 2:41). The book of Acts follows this exact plan: Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth (Acts 1:8).

Must people hear of Christ to be saved? Yes. Salvation is through conscious faith in Christ, and there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). That is why the risen Lord sends his church to all nations: how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard (Romans 10:14)? The church has always held that God may save elect infants who die in infancy, and those unable to understand, by his Spirit, through Christ alone, in ways we are not told. But for all who can hear, the gospel must be preached, which is why missions are not an optional extra for keen Christians. They are the reason the church is still here.

What does repentance actually look like? Repentance is turning from sin to God, with grief for sin and hope in his mercy (Westminster 15.2). It begins by seeing your sin as God sees it, not only as harmful but as offensive to him. It lays hold of mercy in Christ, for grief over sin with no hope of pardon only drives a sinner further from God. And it turns: you forsake the sin and set yourself to walk with God in new obedience. In practice that means naming the specific sin to God, putting right what can be put right, removing what feeds it, and starting again the next time you fall. It is not only the first step of the Christian life but the shape of the whole of it.

In a sentence. Scripture also says that repentance for the forgiveness of sins must be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. Choose one practical thing this month: learn about one unreached people and pray for them by name; give regularly to a missionary; welcome an international student; or speak of Christ to the person in your own Jerusalem, the one nearest you, who seems least likely to listen.

For worship. He was crucified in Jerusalem on Friday, and on Sunday he told his friends to take the forgiveness there first. The blood his killers shed became the blood that could cleanse them, and the city that cast him out was the first to be offered his name. The gospel goes to the guilty, and the guiltiest first, and from there to the ends of the earth. Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost (1 Timothy 1:15), wrote a man who had once hunted his church. Blessed be the King whose commission from the empty tomb began with mercy for his murderers.

verseByVerse.quote: You are witnesses of these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are witnesses of these things.

You are witnesses. Six words in Greek and English alike, and the whole church rests on them. A witness is not an advocate and not a theorist. He is a person who was present and can say what he saw. That is the entire qualification and the entire limitation: a witness may not embellish or speculate. The word is martyres, and English has narrowed it, because so many of the men in that room died for their testimony. But here it means only what it says: you saw it; say so. The apostles were eyewitnesses of his life, death and resurrection, and their testimony is the foundation of the church (Acts 1:8, 22; 2:32; Ephesians 2:20). We believe through their word (John 17:20).

Of these things. His suffering and resurrection, and the message of forgiveness. Christianity is not in the first instance a philosophy or a set of values. It is a report: that a particular man, in a particular place, under a named Roman governor, was executed and buried, and three days later was alive, and here are the people who saw it. Paul argued exactly this way and staked everything on it: he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve, then to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive (1 Corinthians 15:5–6). That is not the language of a man offering a spirituality. It is a man saying: go and ask them.

Look at who is commissioned. These are the men who fell asleep in the garden, denied him in a courtyard, dismissed the women’s report as nonsense, and were standing in that room minutes ago convinced they were seeing a ghost. Not one has a record to be proud of. Every one is about to be sent to the ends of the earth on the strength of what he saw. They will not be asked to be impressive. Only truthful.

I did not see the risen Christ, so am I a witness? Not in the apostles’ unique sense: they were eyewitnesses, and their testimony, written in the New Testament, is the foundation that cannot be repeated or added to. But every Christian is a witness to what Christ has done for him, and to the truth of the apostles’ report, which he has believed. You do not need to have the answers to every question, or to argue anyone into the kingdom. You are asked simply to say what you know of Christ, accurately, and let it be weighed (1 Peter 3:15). The blind man in John 9 could not answer the theologians, but he could say: one thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see.

In a sentence. Jesus told them they were witnesses of these things.

On a Tuesday. Prepare it now: three or four sentences about what you were, what Christ did, and what he means to you. Then pray for an opening this week, and when it comes, say it simply.

For worship. He entrusted the report of his own resurrection to eleven men who had all failed him within the previous seventy-two hours, and he has never taken it back. The word they carried was true because he was alive, and it is true still, passed from witness to witness for two thousand years until it reached us, with the same living Lord standing behind every faithful telling of it. Blessed be the Christ whose resurrection needs no improving, only telling.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, I am sending the promise of my Father upon you. But stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And behold, I am sending the promise of my Father upon you. But stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.

I am sending the promise of my Father upon you. The promise of the Father is the Holy Spirit, poured out at Pentecost (Acts 1:4–5; 2:1–4, 33), promised long before in the prophets: I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh (Joel 2:28–29); I will put my Spirit within you (Ezekiel 36:26–27). And notice that Jesus himself sends the Spirit (John 15:26; 16:7). Only God can send the Spirit of God. Another claim to divine authority, made almost in passing.

But stay in the city. He has just given them the message, the authority, the scope and the starting point, and then he tells them to do nothing at all. Wait in Jerusalem. Consider how hard that was. They had the greatest news in the world and were forbidden, for the moment, to take it anywhere, and forbidden to leave the one city where every person who wanted them dead was still in office. There is a kind of stillness that is disobedience and a kind that is obedience, and the difference is not how it feels; both feel like wasting time. These men were not idle; Acts says they devoted themselves to prayer (Acts 1:14). But they went nowhere, on orders, until the power came.

Until you are clothed with power from on high. A striking image: the verb is the one used for putting on a garment. Power, dynamis, is the power of the Spirit (Acts 1:8). It comes from outside and is put on. It is not a capacity discovered within, and it is not the disciples becoming better men. It is something they will wear. They cannot be witnesses in their own strength. Mission needs the Spirit. Zeal without the Spirit was exactly what Peter had shown in the garden with a sword.

Stay in the city, or go to Galilee? A reader comparing Gospels will notice a difficulty, which sceptics have pressed for a long time. Here Jesus says, stay in the city; but at the tomb in Matthew and Mark he is going ahead of them to Galilee, and Matthew’s great commission is given on a mountain in Galilee. The objection only bites if all of this happened on one evening, and it did not. Luke’s own second volume says Jesus appeared over forty days (Acts 1:3). Restore that span and the accounts unfold in order: appearances in and around Jerusalem on Easter Day and the week after; then Galilee, where Matthew’s mountain and John’s breakfast on the shore belong; then back to Jerusalem for the last days before Pentecost. Luke compresses the forty days. Stay in the city was given and repeated at their end (Acts 1:4), and it governs the last days before Pentecost.

Should Christians today wait for the Spirit as the disciples did? No. Their waiting was for one unrepeatable event, the coming of the Spirit at Pentecost, which marked the new age. Now every believer receives the Spirit when he believes (Romans 8:9; 1 Corinthians 12:13; Acts 2:38–39). Some Pentecostal and charismatic Christians teach a later baptism in the Spirit, to be sought after conversion, often with speaking in tongues. This commentary, holding that the sign gifts ceased with the apostles, does not believe Scripture teaches a second baptism for all believers, and holds that view charitably towards brothers and sisters who see it otherwise and often shame us by their zeal. We are not waiting for the Spirit to come; we are asking him to fill us (Ephesians 5:18), and depending on his power in everything.

In a sentence. Jesus promised to send them what the Father had promised, and told them to wait in the city until they were clothed with power from on high.

On a Tuesday. Before your next act of service, the class, the visit, the conversation about Christ, stop and ask for the Spirit’s power, plainly and specifically. And if you are in a season of enforced waiting, of illness or delay or a closed door, use it as they did: pray, stay close to God’s people, and be ready.

For worship. The Father promised, the Son sends, and the Spirit clothes: the whole Trinity is at work in the weakest witness. Men who had fled with nothing but their fear would stand up in that same city within weeks and speak with a boldness no council could break, and it was not their own. It was the risen Christ, reigning, pouring out his Spirit on all flesh. Blessed be the God who does not send his people into the world unclothed, but clothes them with power from on high.
verseByVerse.note: The promise of the Father is the Holy Spirit, poured out at Pentecost.

parallels.desc: I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh

verseByVerse.quote: And he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them. While he blessed them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them. While he blessed them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven.

He led them out as far as Bethany. Bethany, of all places, on the slope of the Mount of Olives, about two miles from Jerusalem: the village of Martha and Mary and Lazarus, where he had stayed during the last week, where he had wept at a grave and called a dead man out of it. He goes back there to leave. Acts 1:9–12 gives a fuller account; Luke here compresses the time.

And lifting up his hands he blessed them. That is the posture of the priest. Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them (Leviticus 9:22), and the blessing given to the priests to speak was this: the LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you (Numbers 6:24–26). And Luke, who opened this Gospel with a priest named Zechariah going into the sanctuary while the people waited outside for the blessing, and coming out unable to speak a word (1:22), now closes it with a priest whose hands are raised and whose blessing is not silent. Jesus is the great high priest, blessing his people. The hands lifted over them had holes in them.

While he blessed them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven. He did not finish and then go. He went in the middle of the blessing, which is a way of saying that the blessing never stopped. What those men saw last was his hands raised over them, and he is doing it still: he always lives to make intercession for them (Hebrews 7:25). His last act on earth was blessing. And he was carried up into heaven. Not vanished, as at Emmaus; taken up, the Father receiving the Son. This is not an exit from the story but an enthronement. After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high (Hebrews 1:3), which is exactly what he had told the council would begin from that moment (22:69). And this same Jesus will come again in the same way (Acts 1:11).

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit and was carried up into heaven. Some older editions left out several short phrases in this chapter, because a small group of manuscripts lacks them. Then a very early papyrus copy of Luke, published in the twentieth century, was found to contain them, and opinion moved back; that is why the ESV prints them. Notice the direction of that story. The evidence did not erode the text as it accumulated. It confirmed it.

Did the ascension happen on Easter evening? Luke tells us in Acts that it came forty days later (Acts 1:3, 9). Here he gives the story in brief, without marking the passing of time after v. 49.

Why did Jesus have to leave? He said it was for our good: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you (John 16:7). Ascended, he reigns over all things for his church, intercedes for us as our high priest, and pours out the Spirit, who makes him present to every believer everywhere at once. While he was on earth he could be in only one room; now by his Spirit he is with every one of his people. His ascension also prepares a place for us (John 14:2–3), and guarantees that a human being, in a human body, is already seated in heaven, the pledge that we will follow.

Where is Jesus’ body now? In heaven. The risen and ascended Christ is truly human still, with his glorified body, and that body is in heaven, at the Father’s right hand, until he returns (Acts 3:21). That is why Reformed Christians do not believe his body is physically in the bread at the Lord’s Supper. He is present to his people by his Spirit, really and spiritually, lifting our hearts to him where he is. And one day the heavens will open and we will see him, in the same body, with the same marked hands.

In a sentence. Jesus led them out to Bethany, lifted his hands and blessed them, and while blessing them he left them and was taken up into heaven.

On a Tuesday. Begin and end today under his blessing. Read Numbers 6:24–26 in the morning as words spoken over you by the ascended Christ, and pray them for someone else at night. Then live the day as one whose high priest is praying for him.

For worship. He walked them out to a village he loved, raised the hands that had been nailed down, and went home to his Father in the act of blessing them. Every earthly priest lowered his hands at last and died; this one was lifted up with his hands still raised. He has gone into heaven as a forerunner on our behalf (Hebrews 6:20), a man in our flesh at the Father’s right hand, and the benediction he began on the Mount of Olives will not end until he comes again.
verseByVerse.note: Bethany lay on the Mount of Olives. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit “and was carried up into heaven.”

parallels.desc: Aaron lifted up his hands and blessed them

verseByVerse.quote: And they worshiped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and were continually in the temple blessing God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they worshipped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and were continually in the temple blessing God.

And they worshiped him. Three things in this last sentence, and every one is impossible without the resurrection. The word is proskynēsantes: they fell down before him. It is the first time in Luke that anyone worships Jesus. These are Jewish men who had said every day of their lives, the LORD our God, the LORD is one (Deuteronomy 6:4), and nothing in their religion was more absolute than the ban on worshipping any but God; Jesus himself had said in the wilderness that you shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve (4:8). And they give it, without hesitation and without anyone correcting them, to a man they had eaten fish with. They now know who he is: the Lord, to be worshipped as God. That is not a doctrine developed over centuries by a church drifting from its roots. It is monotheists on a hillside outside Jerusalem, on their faces.

How can Christians worship Jesus if only God is to be worshipped? Because Jesus is God. Christians do not worship a man alongside God; they worship the one God who has made himself known as Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The Son is not a lesser god or a created being. He is the eternal Word who was with God and was God (John 1:1), who took our flesh without ceasing to be divine. So when the disciples fell down before him, they were not breaking the first commandment but keeping it. And the Father wills that all should honour the Son, just as they honour the Father (John 5:23).

And returned to Jerusalem with great joy. The strangest phrase in the sentence, because he had just left. It should have been a bereavement; Luke says great joy. The good news of great joy that the angel announced at his birth (2:10) is now theirs. The reason is that they finally understood where he had gone and what he was doing there. It was not another loss but the coronation of the man they loved: alive, reigning, coming back, and about to send his Spirit. Grief looks at an empty sky. They looked at a throne. That is worth taking home by anyone who half wishes he had been there instead of here. These men had the choice between having him visible in the room and having him seated at the right hand of God with the Spirit about to come, and they were not sorry.

And were continually in the temple blessing God. The Gospel began in that temple: an old priest at the altar of incense, a crowd waiting outside, an angel with a promise, and a man who came out mute and could not give the blessing (1:9–22). It ends in the same building, with a company of ordinary people who cannot stop blessing God. Every promise made at the start has been kept. The horn of salvation raised up in the house of David; the sunrise from on high visiting those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death (1:68–79); the light for revelation to the Gentiles, held once by an old man who was ready to die. All of it has happened, and the temple Zechariah left in silence is now full of people blessing God aloud. Praise is the right response to the gospel.

The end of Luke, the beginning of Acts. Luke’s first volume ends in worship and joy, waiting for the Spirit. His second, Acts, tells what the risen Lord continued to do and teach through his Spirit and his church (Acts 1:1). The story is not over. It continues in every congregation that gathers on the first day of the week to bless God, and it will end only when he comes again.

In a sentence. They worshipped Jesus and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, spending their time in the temple praising God.

On a Tuesday. Is your Christian life marked by great joy, or by a dutiful sigh? Joy comes from looking where they looked: at the throne, not the empty sky. Spend five minutes today simply praising him, without asking for anything: for his death, his rising, his reign, his return. And go to church on Sunday to bless God with his people, as they did.

For worship. The Gospel that began with an angel announcing good news of great joy for all the people ends with that joy spilling out of a temple, and it has never been contained since. The one they worshipped on the hillside is the same Jesus, alive for evermore, seated on the throne of the universe in our flesh, and he will come again. Every Lord’s Day his people gather and do what those first worshippers did, and it is never in vain, for he lives. To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honour and glory and might for ever and ever (Revelation 5:13). Amen.

24.text: <sup>1</sup> But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they went to the tomb, taking the spices they had prepared. <sup>2</sup> And they found the stone rolled away from the tomb, <sup>3</sup> but when they went in they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. <sup>4</sup> While they were perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them in dazzling apparel. <sup>5</sup> And as they were frightened and bowed their faces to the ground, the men said to them, “Why do you seek the living among the dead? <sup>6</sup> He is not here, but has risen. Remember how he told you, while he was still in Galilee, <sup>7</sup> that the Son of Man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men and be crucified and on the third day rise.” <sup>8</sup> And they remembered his words, <sup>9</sup> and returning from the tomb they told all these things to the eleven and to all the rest. <sup>10</sup> Now it was Mary Magdalene and Joanna and Mary the mother of James and the other women with them who told these things to the apostles, <sup>11</sup> but these words seemed to them an idle tale, and they did not believe them. <sup>12</sup> But Peter rose and ran to the tomb; stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths by themselves; and he went home marveling at what had happened. <sup>13</sup> That very day two of them were going to a village named Emmaus, about seven miles from Jerusalem, <sup>14</sup> and they were talking with each other about all these things that had happened. <sup>15</sup> While they were talking and discussing together, Jesus himself drew near and went with them. <sup>16</sup> But their eyes were kept from recognizing him. <sup>17</sup> And he said to them, “What is this conversation that you are holding with each other as you walk?” And they stood still, looking sad. <sup>18</sup> Then one of them, named Cleopas, answered him, “Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in these days?” <sup>19</sup> And he said to them, “What things?” And they said to him, “Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, a man who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people, <sup>20</sup> and how our chief priests and rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him. <sup>21</sup> But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel. Yes, and besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened. <sup>22</sup> Moreover, some women of our company amazed us. They were at the tomb early in the morning, <sup>23</sup> and when they did not find his body, they came back saying that they had even seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive. <sup>24</sup> Some of those who were with us went to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not see.” <sup>25</sup> And he said to them, “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! <sup>26</sup> Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” <sup>27</sup> And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself. <sup>28</sup> So they drew near to the village to which they were going. He acted as if he were going farther, <sup>29</sup> but they urged him strongly, saying, “Stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is now far spent.” So he went in to stay with them. <sup>30</sup> When he was at table with them, he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. <sup>31</sup> And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. And he vanished from their sight. <sup>32</sup> They said to each other, “Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?” <sup>33</sup> And they rose that same hour and returned to Jerusalem. And they found the eleven and those who were with them gathered together, <sup>34</sup> saying, “The Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!” <sup>35</sup> Then they told what had happened on the road, and how he was known to them in the breaking of the bread. <sup>36</sup> As they were talking about these things, Jesus himself stood among them, and said to them, “Peace to you!” <sup>37</sup> But they were startled and frightened and thought they saw a spirit. <sup>38</sup> And he said to them, “Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts? <sup>39</sup> See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.” <sup>40</sup> And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet. <sup>41</sup> And while they still disbelieved for joy and were marveling, he said to them, “Have you anything here to eat?” <sup>42</sup> They gave him a piece of broiled fish, <sup>43</sup> and he took it and ate before them. <sup>44</sup> Then he said to them, “These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.” <sup>45</sup> Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures, <sup>46</sup> and said to them, “Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead, <sup>47</sup> and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. <sup>48</sup> You are witnesses of these things. <sup>49</sup> And behold, I am sending the promise of my Father upon you. But stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.” <sup>50</sup> And he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them. <sup>51</sup> While he blessed them, he parted from them and was carried up into heaven. <sup>52</sup> And they worshiped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, <sup>53</sup> and were continually in the temple blessing God.
